Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.

Abhidhammapiṭake

In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka

Sammohavinodanī nāma

Named the Dispeller of Delusion

Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on the Book of Analysis

1. Khandhavibhaṅgo

1. The Analysis of the Aggregates

1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Suttanta Exposition

Catusaccadaso [P 0.0001][M 0.0001][V 0.0001] nātho, catudhā dhammasaṅgaṇiṃ;

Pakāsayitvā sambuddho, tasseva samanantaraṃ.

The Lord, the seer of the Four Truths, the Fully Awakened One, having expounded the Dhamma collection in four ways, immediately after that,

Upeto buddhadhammehi, aṭṭhārasahi nāyako;

Aṭṭhārasannaṃ khandhādi-vibhaṅgānaṃ vasena yaṃ.

The Leader, endowed with the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, taught the Analysis which proceeds by way of the eighteen analyses of the aggregates and so on.

Vibhaṅgaṃ [V 0.0002] desayī satthā, tassa saṃvaṇṇanākkamo;

Idāni yasmā sampatto, tasmā tassatthavaṇṇanaṃ.

The Teacher taught the Vibhaṅga. Since the turn for its exposition has now arrived, therefore the explanation of its meaning

Karissāmi vigāhetvā, porāṇaṭṭhakathānayaṃ;

Saddhamme gāravaṃ katvā, taṃ suṇātha samāhitāti.

I shall make, having delved into the method of the ancient commentaries. Having paid reverence to the True Dhamma, listen to it attentively.

1. Pañcakkhandhā – rūpakkhandho…pe… viññāṇakkhandhoti idaṃ vibhaṅgappakaraṇassa ādibhūte khandhavibhaṅge suttantabhājanīyaṃ nāma. Tattha pañcāti gaṇanaparicchedo. Tena na tato heṭṭhā na uddhanti dasseti. Khandhāti paricchinnadhammanidassanaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ khandha-saddo sambahulesu ṭhānesu dissati – rāsimhi, guṇe, paṇṇattiyaṃ, ruḷhiyanti. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahāsamudde na sukaraṃ udakassa pamāṇaṃ gahetuṃ – ettakāni udakāḷhakānīti vā ettakāni udakāḷhakasatānīti vā ettakāni udakāḷhakasahassānīti vā ettakāni udakāḷhakasatasahassānīti vā, atha kho asaṅkhyeyyo appameyyo mahāudakakkhandhotveva [M 0.0002] saṅkhyaṃ [P 0.0002] gacchatī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.51; 6.37) hi rāsito khandho nāma. Nahi parittakaṃ udakaṃ udakakkhandhoti vuccati, bahukameva vuccati. Tathā na parittako rajo rajakkhandho, na appamattakā gāvo gavakkhandho, na appamattakaṃ balaṃ balakkhandho, na appamattakaṃ puññaṃ puññakkhandhoti vuccati. Bahukameva hi rajo rajakkhandho, bahukāva gavādayo gavakkhandho, balakkhandho, puññakkhandhoti vuccanti. “Sīlakkhandho samādhikkhandho”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.355) pana guṇato khandho nāma. “Addasā kho bhagavā mahantaṃ dārukkhandhaṃ gaṅgāya nadiyā sotena vuyhamāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.241). Ettha paṇṇattito khandho nāma. “Yaṃ cittaṃ mano mānasaṃ…pe… viññāṇaṃ viññāṇakkhandho”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 63, 65) ruḷhito khandho nāma. Svāyamidha rāsito adhippeto. Ayañhi khandhaṭṭho nāma piṇḍaṭṭho pūgaṭṭho ghaṭaṭṭho rāsaṭṭho. Tasmā ‘rāsilakkhaṇā khandhā’ti veditabbā. Koṭṭhāsaṭṭhotipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati; lokasmiñhi iṇaṃ gahetvā codiyamānā ‘dvīhi khandhehi dassāma, tīhi khandhehi dassāmā’ti vadanti. Iti ‘koṭṭhāsalakkhaṇā khandhā’tipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Evamettha rūpakkhandhoti rūparāsi rūpakoṭṭhāso, vedanākkhandhoti vedanārāsi vedanākoṭṭhāsoti iminā nayena saññākkhandhādīnaṃ attho veditabbo.

1. The Five Aggregates – the aggregate of form… up to… the aggregate of consciousness: this is called the Suttanta Exposition in the Analysis of Aggregates, which is at the beginning of the Vibhaṅga. Herein, 'five' is a numerical delimitation. By this, it is shown that there are neither fewer nor more. 'Aggregates' is an indication of delimited phenomena. Here, the word 'aggregate' is found in many places: in the sense of a mass, a quality, a designation, and by convention. For it is said: "Just as, monks, in the great ocean it is not easy to take the measure of the water, saying: ‘So many measures of water, so many hundreds of measures of water, so many thousands of measures of water, or so many hundreds of thousands of measures of water,’ but rather it is reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of water," (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.51; 6.37). In such instances, 'aggregate' means a mass. For a small amount of water is not called a 'mass of water'; only a large amount is so called. Similarly, a small amount of dust is not called a 'mass of dust'; a few cattle are not called a 'herd of cattle'; a small force is not called a 'mass of force'; and a little merit is not called a 'mass of merit'. Only a large amount of dust is called a 'mass of dust', and only a large number of cattle and so on are called a 'herd of cattle', a 'mass of force', or a 'mass of merit'. But in phrases like "the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration," (Dīgha Nikāya 3.355), 'aggregate' is used in the sense of a quality. "The Blessed One saw a large log being carried along by the current of the Ganges river," (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.241). Here, 'aggregate' is used in the sense of a designation. In passages such as, "Whatever is mind, intellect, consciousness… consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness," (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 63, 65), 'aggregate' is used by convention. Here, however, it is intended in the sense of a mass. For this meaning of 'aggregate' is the meaning of a lump, a multitude, a group, a heap. Therefore, it should be understood that 'aggregates have the characteristic of a mass.' It is also possible to say it has the meaning of a portion; for in the world, when pressed for repayment of a debt, people say, "We will pay in two portions, we will pay in three portions." Thus, it is also possible to say that 'aggregates have the characteristic of a portion.' So here, 'aggregate of form' means a mass of form, a portion of form; 'aggregate of feeling' means a mass of feeling, a portion of feeling. In this way, the meaning of the aggregate of perception and the others should be understood.

Ettāvatā [V 0.0003] sammāsambuddho yvāyaṃ “cattāro ca mahābhūtā catunnañca mahābhūtānaṃ upādāyarūpa”nti atītānāgatapaccuppannādīsu ekādasasu okāsesu vibhatto ‘pañcavīsati rūpakoṭṭhāsā’ti ca ‘channavuti rūpakoṭṭhāsā’ti ca evaṃpabhedo rūparāsi, taṃ sabbaṃ paripiṇḍetvā rūpakkhandho nāmāti dassesi. Yo panāyaṃ “sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā”ti tesuyeva ekādasasu okāsesu vibhatto catubhūmikavedanārāsi, taṃ sabbaṃ paripiṇḍetvā vedanākkhandho nāmāti dassesi. Yo panāyaṃ “cakkhusamphassajā saññā…pe… manosamphassajā saññā”ti tesuyeva ekādasasu okāsesu vibhatto catubhūmikasaññārāsi[P 0.0003], taṃ sabbaṃ paripiṇḍetvā saññākkhandho nāmāti dassesi. Yo panāyaṃ “cakkhusamphassajā cetanā…pe… manosamphassajā cetanā”ti tesuyeva ekādasasu okāsesu vibhatto catubhūmikacetanārāsi, taṃ sabbaṃ paripiṇḍetvā saṅkhārakkhandho nāmāti dassesi. Yo [M 0.0003] panāyaṃ “cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇaṃ, manodhātu, manoviññāṇadhātū”ti tesuyeva ekādasasu okāsesu vibhatto catubhūmikacittarāsi, taṃ sabbaṃ paripiṇḍetvā viññāṇakkhandho nāmāti dassesi.

To this extent, the Fully Enlightened One showed that this mass of form—which is 'the four great elements and form derived from the four great elements,' divided into eleven instances such as past, future, and present, and also of such a kind as 'twenty-five portions of form' and 'ninety-six portions of form'—when all that is grouped together, is called the aggregate of form. And he showed that this mass of feeling—which is 'pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,' divided into those very eleven instances, and which is the four-plane mass of feeling—when all that is grouped together, is called the aggregate of feeling. And he showed that this mass of perception—which is 'perception born of eye-contact…up to…perception born of mind-contact,' divided into those very eleven instances, and which is the four-plane mass of perception—when all that is grouped together, is called the aggregate of perception. And he showed that this mass of formations—which is 'volition born of eye-contact…up to…volition born of mind-contact,' divided into those very eleven instances, and which is the four-plane mass of volitions—when all that is grouped together, is called the aggregate of formations. And he showed that this mass of consciousness—which is 'eye-consciousness, ear-nose-tongue-body consciousness, mind-element, and mind-consciousness-element,' divided into those very eleven instances, and which is the four-plane mass of consciousness—when all that is grouped together, is called the aggregate of consciousness.

Apicettha sabbampi catusamuṭṭhānikaṃ rūpaṃ rūpakkhandho, kāmāvacaraaṭṭhakusalacittādīhi ekūnanavuticittehi sahajātā vedanā vedanākkhandho, saññā saññākkhandho, phassādayo dhammā saṅkhārakkhandho, ekūnanavuti cittāni viññāṇakkhandhoti. Evampi pañcasu khandhesu dhammaparicchedo veditabbo.

Furthermore, here, all form with its four origins is the aggregate of form. Feeling co-arisen with the eighty-nine consciousnesses, beginning with the eight wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses, is the aggregate of feeling. Perception is the aggregate of perception. Mental phenomena beginning with contact are the aggregate of formations. The eighty-nine consciousnesses are the aggregate of consciousness. In this way too, the division of phenomena into the five aggregates should be understood.

1. Rūpakkhandhaniddeso

1. Exposition of the Aggregate of Form

2. Idāni te rūpakkhandhādayo vibhajitvā dassetuṃ tattha katamo rūpakkhandhotiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti tesu pañcasu khandhesu. Katamoti kathetukamyatāpucchā. Rūpakkhandhoti pucchitadhammanidassanaṃ. Idāni taṃ vibhajanto yaṃ kiñci rūpantiādimāha. Tattha yaṃ kiñcīti anavasesapariyādānaṃ. Rūpanti atippasaṅganiyamanaṃ. Evaṃ padadvayenāpi rūpassa anavasesapariggaho kato hoti.

2. Now, to show those aggregates beginning with the aggregate of form by analyzing them, he stated the passage beginning, "Therein, what is the aggregate of form?" Here, "Therein" means among those five aggregates. "What is?" is a question expressing the desire to explain. "The aggregate of form" is the indication of the phenomenon about which the question was asked. Now, analyzing it, he states the passage beginning, "Whatever form…" Therein, "whatever" is an all-inclusive term. "Form" is a restriction to prevent over-extension. Thus, by these two words, a complete inclusion of form is made.

Tattha kenaṭṭhena rūpanti? Ruppanaṭṭhena rūpaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Therein, by what meaning is it 'rūpa'? It is 'rūpa' by the meaning of being afflicted. For this was said by the Blessed One –

“Kiñca[V 0.0004], bhikkhave, rūpaṃ vadetha? Ruppatīti [P 0.0004] kho, bhikkhave, tasmā rūpanti vuccati. Kena ruppati? Sītenapi ruppati, uṇhenapi ruppati, jighacchāyapi ruppati, pipāsāyapi ruppati, ḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarisapasamphassenapi ruppati. Ruppatīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā rūpanti vuccatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.79).

And why, monks, do you call it form? Because it is afflicted, monks, therefore it is called form. By what is it afflicted? It is afflicted by cold, by heat, by hunger, by thirst, by contact with flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things. Because it is afflicted, monks, therefore it is called form.

Tattha kinti kāraṇapucchā; kena kāraṇena rūpaṃ vadetha, kena kāraṇena taṃ rūpaṃ nāmāti attho. Ruppatīti ettha itīti kāraṇuddeso. Yasmā ruppati tasmā rūpanti vuccatīti attho. Ruppatīti kuppati ghaṭṭīyati pīḷiyati bhijjatīti attho. Evaṃ iminā ettakena ṭhānena ruppanaṭṭhena rūpaṃ vuttaṃ. Ruppanalakkhaṇena rūpantipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Ruppanalakkhaṇañhetaṃ.

Herein, 'kiṃ' is a question as to the reason: for what reason do you speak of form, for what reason is that called 'form'?—this is the meaning. Herein, in 'ruppatīti', the particle 'iti' indicates the reason. 'Because it is afflicted, therefore it is called "form"'—this is the meaning. 'It is afflicted' means it is agitated, struck, oppressed, broken—this is the meaning. Thus, by this much, form has been spoken of in the sense of being afflicted. It is also fitting to say that form has the characteristic of being afflicted. For this is indeed the characteristic of being afflicted.

Sītenapi [M 0.0004] ruppatītiādīsu pana sītena tāva ruppanaṃ lokantarikaniraye pākaṭaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇañhi cakkavāḷānaṃ antare ekeko lokantarikanirayo nāma hoti aṭṭhayojanasahassappamāṇo, yassa neva heṭṭhā pathavī atthi, na upari candimasūriyadīpamaṇiāloko, niccandhakāro. Tattha nibbattasattānaṃ tigāvuto attabhāvo hoti. Te vagguliyo viya pabbatapāde dīghaputhulehi nakhehi laggitvā avaṃsirā olambanti. Yadā saṃsappantā aññamaññassa hatthapāsagatā honti atha ‘bhakkho no laddho’ti maññamānā tattha byāvaṭā viparivattitvā lokasandhārake udake patanti, sītavāte paharantepi pakkamadhukaphalāni viya chijjitvā udake patanti. Patitamattāva accantakhārena sītodakena chinnacammanhārumaṃsaaṭṭhīhi bhijjamānehi tattatele patitapiṭṭhapiṇḍi viya paṭapaṭāyamānā vilīyanti. Evaṃ sītena ruppanaṃ lokantarikaniraye pākaṭaṃ. Mahiṃsakaraṭṭhādīsupi himapātasītalesu padesesu etaṃ pākaṭameva. Tattha hi sattā sītena bhinnacchinnasarīrā jīvitakkhayampi pāpuṇanti.

Now, in the phrase 'afflicted by cold' and so on, the affliction by cold, to begin with, is evident in the Lokantarika hells. For between every three world-spheres, there is an inter-world hell called Lokantarika, measuring eight thousand leagues, where there is no earth below, nor any light from the sun, moon, or jeweled lamps above—only perpetual darkness. Beings reborn there have bodies three gāvutas tall. Like bats clinging to a mountain foot with their long, thick claws, they hang upside down. When, crawling, they come within each other's reach, thinking, 'We have found food,' they become active there, turn around, and fall into the inter-world waters. Even when struck by the icy wind, they break apart like ripe madhuka fruits and fall into the water. The moment they fall, their skin, sinews, flesh, and bones being shattered by the intensely caustic cold water, they dissolve with a crackling sound like lumps of dough dropped into boiling oil. Thus, the affliction by cold is evident in the Lokantarika hells. This is also evident in regions like Mahiṃsaka and others, in places cold from snowfall. There, beings, their bodies broken and shattered by the cold, even meet their death.

Uṇhena ruppanaṃ avīcimahāniraye pākaṭaṃ. Tattha hi tattāya lohapathaviyā nipajjāpetvā pañcavidhabandhanādikaraṇakāle sattā mahādukkhaṃ anubhavanti.

The affliction by heat is evident in the Avīci Great Hell. There, beings, having been laid upon the scorching iron ground, experience immense suffering during the fivefold binding and other tortures.

Jighacchāya ruppanaṃ pettivisaye ceva dubbhikkhakāle ca [P 0.0005] pākaṭaṃ. Pettivisayasmiñhi sattā dve tīṇi buddhantarāni kiñcideva āmisaṃ hatthena gahetvā mukhe pakkhipantā nāma na honti[V 0.0005]. Antoudaraṃ ādittasusirarukkho viya hoti. Dubbhikkhe kañjikamattampi alabhitvā maraṇappattānaṃ pamāṇaṃ nāma natthi.

The affliction by hunger is evident in the realm of ghosts and during times of famine. For, in the ghost realm, beings go two or three buddha-intervals without putting even a tiny bit of food into their mouths with their hands. Their insides are like a hollow tree consumed by fire. During famine, there is no measure of those who die without obtaining even a drop of rice-gruel.

Pipāsāya ruppanaṃ kālakañjikādīsu pākaṭaṃ. Tattha hi sattā dve tīṇi buddhantarāni hadayatemanamattaṃ vā jivhātemanamattaṃ vā udakabinduṃ laddhuṃ na sakkonti. ‘Pānīyaṃ pivissāmā’ti nadiṃ gatānampi nadī vālikātalaṃ sampajjati. Mahāsamuddaṃ pakkhantānampi mahāsamuddo piṭṭhipāsāṇo hoti. Te sussantā balavadukkhapīḷitā vicaranti.

The affliction by thirst is evident among the Kālakañjikas and others. There, for two or three buddha-intervals, beings are unable to obtain even a drop of water sufficient to moisten their heart or their tongue. Even when they go to a river thinking, 'We will drink water,' the river becomes a sandy bed. Even when they plunge into the great ocean, the great ocean becomes a slab of rock. Parched and tormented by intense suffering, they wander.

Eko [M 0.0005] kira kālakañjikaasuro pipāsaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto yojanagambhīravitthāraṃ mahāgaṅgaṃ otari. Tassa gatagataṭṭhāne udakaṃ chijjati, dhūmo uggacchati, tatte piṭṭhipāsāṇe caṅkamanakālo viya hoti. Tassa udakasaddaṃ sutvā ito cito ca vicarantasseva ratti vibhāyi. Atha naṃ pātova bhikkhācāraṃ gacchantā tiṃsamattā piṇḍacārikabhikkhū disvā – “ko nāma tvaṃ, sappurisā”ti pucchiṃsu. “Petohamasmi, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ pariyesasī”ti? “Pānīyaṃ, bhante”ti. “Ayaṃ gaṅgā paripuṇṇā, kiṃ tvaṃ na passasī”ti? “Na upakappati, bhante”ti. “Tena hi gaṅgāpiṭṭhe nipajja, mukhe te pānīyaṃ āsiñcissāmā”ti. So vālikāpuḷine uttāno nipajji. Bhikkhū tiṃsamatte patte nīharitvā udakaṃ āharitvā āharitvā tassa mukhe āsiñciṃsu. Tesaṃ tathā karontānaṃyeva velā upakaṭṭhā jātā. Tato “bhikkhācārakālo amhākaṃ, sappurisa; kacci te assādamattā laddhā”ti āhaṃsu. Peto “sace me, bhante, tiṃsamattānaṃ ayyānaṃ tiṃsamattehi pattehi āsittaudakato aḍḍhapasatamattampi paragalagataṃ, petattabhāvato mokkho mā hotū”ti āha. Evaṃ pipāsāya ruppanaṃ pettivisaye pākaṭaṃ.

Once, it is said, a Kālakañjika asura, unable to endure his thirst, descended into the great Ganges, which was a yojana deep and wide. Wherever he went, the water dried up, smoke rose, and it was like walking on a heated stone slab. Hearing the sound of water, he wandered here and there until the night dawned. Then, in the early morning, about thirty alms-round monks saw him while going for alms and asked, 'Who are you, good sir?' 'I am a hungry ghost, venerable sirs.' 'What are you seeking?' 'Water, venerable sirs.' 'This Ganges is full—do you not see it?' 'It is of no use to me, venerable sirs.' 'Then lie down on the bank of the Ganges, and we will pour water into your mouth.' He lay down on a sandbank, face up. The monks took out thirty bowls, fetched water again and again, and poured it into his mouth. As they did so, the time for their alms round drew near. Then they said, 'Good sir, it is time for our alms round. Have you had even a little satisfaction?' The hungry ghost replied, 'Venerable sirs, if even half a handful of the water poured from thirty bowls by thirty venerable ones were to pass my throat, may I not be freed from this state of a hungry ghost.' Thus, the affliction by thirst is evident in the realm of hungry ghosts.

Ḍaṃsādīhi ruppanaṃ ḍaṃsamakkhikādisambabahulesu padesesu pākaṭaṃ. Ettha ca ḍaṃsāti piṅgalamakkhikā, makasāti makasāva vātāti kucchivātapiṭṭhivātādivasena veditabbā. Sarīrasmiñhi [P 0.0006] vātarogo uppajjitvā hatthapādapiṭṭhiādīni bhindati, kāṇaṃ karoti, khujjaṃ karoti, pīṭhasappiṃ karoti. Ātapoti sūriyātapo. Tena ruppanaṃ marukantārādīsu pākaṭaṃ. Ekā kira itthī marukantāre rattiṃ satthato ohīnā divā sūriye uggacchante vālikāya tappamānāya pāde ṭhapetuṃ asakkontī sīsato pacchiṃ otāretvā akkami. Kamena pacchiyā uṇhābhitattāya [V 0.0006] ṭhātuṃ asakkontī tassā upari sāṭakaṃ ṭhapetvā akkami. Tasmimpi santatte aṅkena gahitaṃ puttakaṃ adhomukhaṃ nipajjāpetvā kandantaṃ kandantaṃ akkamitvā saddhiṃ tena tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne uṇhābhitattā kālamakāsi.

The torment by gnats, etc., is evident in places infested with gnats, flies, etc. Herein, `ḍaṃsa` refers to the gadfly, `makasa` to the mosquito, and `vāta` should be understood in terms of abdominal wind, back wind, etc. For when a wind-disease arises in the body, it afflicts the hands, feet, back, etc., makes one one-eyed, hunchbacked, or makes one a cripple who crawls. `Ātapa` refers to the sun’s heat. The torment by this is evident in deserts, etc. It is said that a certain woman, left behind by her caravan in a desert at night, was unable to place her feet on the sand as it was being heated by the rising sun, so she lowered the basket from her head and stepped on it. In time, unable to stand on the basket as it was scorched by the heat, she placed her shawl over it and stepped on that. When that too became hot, she laid the child she was holding in her arms face down and, while he was crying and crying, stepped on him. Together with him, she died in that very place, scorched by the heat.

Sarīsapāti ye keci dīghajātikā sarantā gacchanti. Tesaṃ samphassena ruppanaṃ āsīvisadaṭṭhādīnaṃ vasena veditabbaṃ.

“Creeping creatures” refers to any long-bodied creatures that move by crawling. The torment by their contact should be understood by way of snakebites and the like.

Idāni [M 0.0006] ‘yaṃ kiñci rūpa’nti padena saṃgahitaṃ pañcavīsatikoṭṭhāsachannavutikoṭṭhāsappabhedaṃ sabbampi rūpaṃ atītādikoṭṭhāsesu pakkhipitvā dassetuṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannanti āha. Tato paraṃ tadeva ajjhattadukādīsu catūsu dukesu pakkhipitvā dassetuṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vātiādi vuttaṃ. Tato paraṃ sabbampetaṃ ekādasasu padesesu pariyādiyitvā dassitaṃ rūpaṃ ekato piṇḍaṃ katvā dassetuṃ tadekajjhantiādi vuttaṃ.

Now, by the phrase “whatever form” is encompassed all form, differentiated into the twenty-five or ninety-six kinds. To show this by including it in the categories of past, etc., it is said “past, future, and present.” Then, to show that same form by including it in the four pairs beginning with the internal, it is said “internal or external,” and so on. Then, to show all this form, which has been presented by being encompassed in the eleven aspects, by consolidating it into a single whole, it is said “all together as one,” and so on.

Tattha tadekajjhanti taṃ ekajjhaṃ; abhisaññūhitvāti abhisaṃharitvā; abhisaṅkhipitvāti saṅkhepaṃ katvā; idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sabbampetaṃ vuttappakāraṃ rūpaṃ ruppanalakkhaṇasaṅkhāte ekavidhabhāve paññāya rāsiṃ katvā rūpakkhandho nāmāti vuccatīti. Etena sabbampi rūpaṃ ruppanalakkhaṇe rāsibhāvūpagamanena rūpakkhandhoti dassitaṃ hoti. Na hi rūpato añño rūpakkhandho nāma atthi. Yathā ca rūpaṃ, evaṃ vedanādayopi vedayitalakkhaṇādīsu rāsibhāvūpagamanena. Na hi vedanādīhi aññe vedanākkhandhādayo nāma atthi.

Therein, “all together as one” means “that as one”; “having unified” means “having collected together”; “having condensed” means “having made concise.” This is what is said: When all this form of the kind described is, by means of wisdom, made into a mass in the single state reckoned as the characteristic of affliction, it is called the aggregate of form. By this, it is shown that all form is the aggregate of form by its undergoing the state of a mass in the characteristic of affliction. For there is no aggregate of form apart from form. Just as with form, so also with feeling, etc., by their undergoing the state of a mass in the characteristic of feeling, etc. For there are no aggregates of feeling, etc., apart from feelings, etc.

3. Idāni ekekasmiṃ okāse pakkhittaṃ rūpaṃ visuṃ visuṃ bhājetvā dassento tattha katamaṃ rūpaṃ atītantiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti ekādasasu okāsesu pakkhipitvā ṭhapitamātikāya bhummaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – atītānāgatapaccuppannantiādinā [P 0.0007] nayena ṭhapitāya mātikāya yaṃ atītaṃ rūpanti vuttaṃ, taṃ katamanti? Iminā upāyena sabbapucchāsu attho veditabbo. Atītaṃ niruddhantiādīni padāni nikkhepakaṇḍassa atītattikabhājanīyavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1044) vuttāneva. Cattāro ca mahābhūtāti idaṃ atītanti vuttarūpassa sabhāvadassanaṃ. Yathā cettha evaṃ sabbattha attho veditabbo. Iminā idaṃ dasseti – atītarūpampi bhūtāni ceva bhūtāni upādāya nibbattarūpañca, anāgatampi…pe… dūrasantikampi[V 0.0007]. Na hi bhūtehi ceva bhūtāni upādāya pavattarūpato ca aññaṃ rūpaṃ nāma atthīti.

3. Now, showing the material form placed in each category by analyzing it separately, he says: “Therein, what is past material form?” etc. Therein, “therein” is the locative case referring to the matrix established by inclusion in the eleven categories. This is what is said: Of the matrix established by the method of past, future, and present, etc., that which is called “past material form”—what is that? By this method, the meaning should be understood in all questions. The terms “past,” “ceased,” etc., are just as stated in the commentary on the Exposition of the Past Triad in the Classification Section (Nikkhepakaṇḍa). And “the four great elements”—this is the showing of the intrinsic nature of what is called past form. As here, so everywhere the meaning should be understood. This shows that past form is both the elements themselves and the derived form arisen dependent on the elements, as is future form… far and near. For there is no form apart from the elements themselves and the form arising dependent on them.

Aparo nayo – atītaṃsena saṅgahitanti atītakoṭṭhāseneva saṅgahitaṃ, ettheva gaṇanaṃ gataṃ. Kinti? Cattāro ca mahābhūtā catunnañca mahābhūtānaṃ [M 0.0007] upādāyarūpanti. Evaṃ sabbattha attho veditabbo. Anāgatapaccuppannaniddesapadānipi heṭṭhā vuttatthāneva.

Another method: “Included in the past aspect” means included only in the past division, reckoned therein. How so? “The four great elements and the derived form of the four great elements.” Thus, the meaning should be understood everywhere. The terms indicating future and present are also as previously stated.

Idaṃ pana atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ nāma suttantapariyāyato abhidhammaniddesatoti duvidhaṃ. Taṃ suttantapariyāye bhavena paricchinnaṃ. Paṭisandhito hi paṭṭhāya atītabhavesu nibbattaṃ rūpaṃ, anantarabhave vā nibbattaṃ hotu kappakoṭisatasahassamatthake vā, sabbaṃ atītameva nāma. Cutito paṭṭhāya anāgatabhavesu nibbattanakarūpaṃ, anantarabhave vā nibbattaṃ hotu kappakoṭisatasahassamatthake vā, sabbaṃ anāgatameva nāma. Cutipaṭisandhianantare pavattarūpaṃ paccuppannaṃ nāma. Abhidhammaniddese pana khaṇena paricchinnaṃ. Tayo hi rūpassa khaṇā – uppādo, ṭhiti, bhaṅgoti. Ime tayo khaṇe patvā niruddhaṃ rūpaṃ, samanantaraniruddhaṃ vā hotu atīte kappakoṭisatasahassamatthake vā, sabbaṃ atītameva nāma. Tayo khaṇe asampattaṃ rūpaṃ, ekacittakkhaṇamattena vā asampattaṃ hotu anāgate kappakoṭisatasahassamatthake vā, sabbaṃ anāgatameva nāma. Ime tayo khaṇe sampattaṃ rūpaṃ pana paccuppannaṃ nāma. Tattha kiñcāpi idaṃ suttantabhājanīyaṃ, evaṃ santepi abhidhammaniddeseneva atītānāgatapaccuppannarūpaṃ niddiṭṭhanti [P 0.0008] veditabbaṃ.

This, however, which is called past, future, and present, is twofold: according to the method of the Suttanta and according to the exposition of the Abhidhamma. In the method of the Suttanta, it is defined by existence (bhava). For any material form produced from rebirth-linking onwards in past existences, whether produced in an immediately preceding existence or even at the distance of a hundred thousand crores of aeons—all that is called past. Any material form that will be produced from death onwards in future existences, whether it will be produced in an immediately succeeding existence or even at the distance of a hundred thousand crores of aeons—all that is called future. The material form occurring in the present existence, between rebirth-linking and death, is called present. In the exposition of the Abhidhamma, however, it is defined by a moment (khaṇa). For material form has three moments: arising, presence, and dissolution. Any material form that has undergone these three moments, whether it ceased immediately or ceased even a hundred thousand crores of aeons ago—all that is called past. Any material form that has not yet undergone these three moments, whether it is separated by even a single mind-moment or is to arise even after a hundred thousand crores of aeons—all that is called future. But any material form that has undergone these three moments is called present. Here, although this is an analysis according to the Suttanta, it should nevertheless be understood that past, future, and present material form is explained according to the exposition of the Abhidhamma.

Aparo nayo – idañhi rūpaṃ addhāsantatisamayakhaṇavasena catudhā atītaṃ nāma hoti. Tathā anāgatapaccuppannaṃ. Addhāvasena tāva ekassa ekasmiṃ bhave paṭisandhito pubbe atītaṃ, cutito uddhaṃ anāgataṃ, ubhinnamantare paccuppannaṃ. Santativasena sabhāgaekautusamuṭṭhānaṃ ekāhārasamuṭṭhānañca pubbāpariyavasena pavattamānampi paccuppannaṃ. Tato pubbe visabhāgautuāhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ atītaṃ, pacchā anāgataṃ. Cittajaṃ ekavīthiekajavanaekasamāpattisamuṭṭhānaṃ paccuppannaṃ. Tato pubbe atītaṃ, pacchā anāgataṃ. Kammasamuṭṭhānassa pāṭiyekkaṃ santativasena atītādibhedo natthi. Tesaññeva pana utuāhāracittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ upatthambhakavasena tassa atītādibhedo veditabbo. Samayavasena ekamuhuttapubbaṇhasāyanharattidivādīsu samayesu santānavasena [V 0.0008] pavattamānaṃ taṃ taṃ samayaṃ paccuppannaṃ nāma. Tato pubbe atītaṃ, pacchā anāgataṃ. Khaṇavasena uppādādikkhaṇattayapariyāpannaṃ [M 0.0008] paccuppannaṃ nāma. Tato pubbe atītaṃ, pacchā anāgataṃ.

Another method: This form is called past in four ways: by period (addhā), continuity (santati), occasion (samaya), and moment (khaṇa). Similarly, future and present. By period, to begin with, in one existence, what precedes rebirth-linking is past, what is after death is future, and what is between the two is present. By continuity, homogeneous (sabhāga) materiality arising from a single instance of temperature and a single instance of nutriment, even while occurring in an unbroken series, is present. What precedes it, arising from dissimilar temperature and nutriment, is past; what follows is future. Mind-originated materiality arising from a single cognitive series, a single impulsion, or a single attainment is present. What precedes it is past; what follows is future. For kamma-originated materiality, there is no distinction into past, etc., by its own continuity. However, its distinction into past, etc., should be understood by way of its being supported by that very materiality originated by temperature, nutriment, and mind. By occasion, what occurs in an unbroken series in periods such as a muhutta, forenoon, evening, night, or day, is called present for that occasion. What precedes it is past; what follows is future. By moment, what is included in the three moments of arising, duration, and dissolution is called present. What precedes it is past; what follows is future.

Apica atikkahetupaccayakiccaṃ atītaṃ. Niṭṭhitahetukiccaṃ aniṭṭhitapaccayakiccaṃ paccuppannaṃ. Ubhayakiccamasampattaṃ anāgataṃ. Sakiccakkhaṇe vā paccuppannaṃ. Tato pubbe atītaṃ, pacchā anāgataṃ. Ettha ca khaṇādikathāva nippariyāyā, sesā sapariyāyā. Tāsu nippariyāyakathā idha adhippetā. Ajjhattadukassāpi niddesapadāni heṭṭhā ajjhattattikaniddese (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1050) vuttatthāneva. Oḷārikādīni rūpakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 674) vuttatthāneva.

Moreover, what has passed beyond its function as cause and condition is past. What has fulfilled its causal function but not its conditional function is present. What has not yet attained both functions is future. Or, it is present at the moment of its own function. Before that, it is past; after that, it is future. Here, the discussion of moments and so on is literal, while the rest are figurative. Among these, the literal discussion is intended here. The terms of the internal dyad also have the meaning stated below in the exposition of the internal triad (Dhs-a. 1050). The terms such as "coarse," etc., have the meaning stated in the description of the materiality section (Dhs-a. 674).

6. Hīnadukaniddese tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānanti bahūsu sattesu sāmivacanaṃ. Aparassāpi aparassāpīti hi vuccamāne divasampi kappasatasahassampi vadanto ettakameva vadeyya. Iti satthā dvīheva padehi anavasese satte pariyādiyanto ‘tesaṃ tesaṃ sattāna’nti āha. Ettakena hi sabbampi aparadīpanaṃ [P 0.0009] siddhaṃ hoti. Uññātanti avamataṃ. Avaññātanti vambhetvā ñātaṃ. Rūpantipi na viditaṃ. Hīḷitanti agahetabbaṭṭhena khittaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, jigucchitantipi vadanti. Paribhūtanti kimetenāti vācāya paribhavitaṃ. Acittīkatanti na garukataṃ. Hīnanti lāmakaṃ. Hīnamatanti hīnanti mataṃ, lāmakaṃ katvā ñātaṃ. Hīnasammatanti hīnanti loke sammataṃ, hīnehi vā sammataṃ, gūthabhakkhehi gūtho viya. Aniṭṭhanti appiyaṃ, paṭilābhatthāya vā apariyesitaṃ. Sacepi naṃ koci pariyeseyya, pariyesatu. Etassa pana ārammaṇassa etadeva nāmaṃ. Akantanti akāmitaṃ, nissirikaṃ vā. Amanāpanti manasmiṃ na appitaṃ. Tādisañhi ārammaṇaṃ manasmiṃ na appīyati. Atha vā manaṃ appāyati vaḍḍhetīti manāpaṃ, na manāpaṃ amanāpaṃ.

6. In the explanation of the inferior dyad, `tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ` is a term in the genitive plural, referring to many beings. For even if one were to say `aparassāpi aparassāpi` for an entire day or a hundred thousand eons, one would only be saying that much. Thus, the Teacher, encompassing all beings without omission in just two words, said `tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ`. For by this much, all further elaboration is accomplished. `Uññātaṃ` means despised. `Avaññātaṃ` means known after having been disdained; its very nature is not known. `Hīḷitaṃ` means cast away, rejected as not worth taking; some also say it means 'repulsive' (`jigucchitaṃ`). `Paribhūtaṃ` means scorned with words such as, "What use is this?" `Acittīkataṃ` means not respected. `Hīnaṃ` means base. `Hīnamataṃ` means considered base, known as worthless. `Hīnasammataṃ` means regarded as base in the world, or approved by the base—like feces to those who eat filth. `Aniṭṭhaṃ` means undesirable, unloved, or not sought after for gain. Even if someone were to seek it, let them seek it; however, this is simply the name of this object. `Akantaṃ` means not desired, or devoid of attractiveness. `Amanāpaṃ` means not pleasing to the mind, for such an object is not fixed in the mind. Alternatively, what pleases and increases the mind is `manāpaṃ`; what is not `manāpaṃ` is `amanāpaṃ`.

Aparo nayo – aniṭṭhaṃ sampattivirahato. Taṃ ekantena kammasamuṭṭhānesu akusalakammasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Akantaṃ sukhassa ahetubhāvato. Amanāpaṃ dukkhassa hetubhāvato. Rūpā saddāti idamassa sabhāvadīpanaṃ. Imasmiñhi pade akusalakammajavasena aniṭṭhā pañca kāmaguṇā vibhattā. Kusalakammajaṃ pana aniṭṭhaṃ nāma natthi, sabbaṃ iṭṭhameva.

Another explanation: It is undesirable (`aniṭṭhaṃ`) because it is devoid of attainment. That, among things originated by kamma, is exclusively what is originated by unwholesome kamma. It is undesired (`akantaṃ`) as it is not a cause of happiness. It is not pleasing to the mind (`amanāpaṃ`) as it is a cause of suffering. 'Forms, sounds,' and so on, is a description of its nature. Indeed, in this term, the five strands of sensual pleasure are distinguished as undesirable due to arising from unwholesome kamma. However, there is nothing undesirable arising from wholesome kamma—all of it is entirely desirable.

Paṇītapadaniddeso [V 0.0009] vuttapaṭipakkhanayena veditabbo. Imasmiṃ pana pade kusalakammajavasena iṭṭhā pañca kāmaguṇā vibhattā. Kusalakammajañhi aniṭṭhaṃ nāma [M 0.0009] natthi, sabbaṃ iṭṭhameva. Yathā ca kammajesu evaṃ utusamuṭṭhānādīsupi iṭṭhāniṭṭhatā atthi evāti imasmiṃ duke iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇaṃ paṭivibhattanti veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva ācariyānaṃ samānatthakathā. Vitaṇḍavādī panāha – iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ nāma pāṭiyekkaṃ paṭivibhattaṃ natthi, tesaṃ tesaṃ rucivasena kathitaṃ.

The explanation of the term 'refined' should be understood by the method opposite to what has been stated. In this term, the five strands of sensual pleasure are distinguished as desirable due to arising from wholesome kamma. For there is nothing undesirable that arises from wholesome kamma—all of it is desirable. And just as with kamma-originated things, so too with things originated by temperature and so on, there is desirability and undesirability. Thus, it should be understood that in this dyad, desirable and undesirable objects are distinguished. This, for now, is the common explanation of the teachers. However, the sophist says: "Desirable and undesirable are not separately distinguished as such; rather, they are spoken of according to the preferences of various beings."

Yathāha –

As it is said:

“Manāpapariyantaṃ khvāhaṃ, mahārāja, pañcasu kāmaguṇesu agganti vadāmi. Teva, mahārāja, rūpā ekaccassa manāpā honti, ekaccassa amanāpā honti. Teva, mahārāja, saddā, gandhā, rasā, phoṭṭhabbā ekaccassa manāpā honti, ekaccassa amanāpā hontī”ti [P 0.0010] (saṃ. ni. 1.123).

"I say, great king, that among the five strands of sensual pleasure, that which culminates in the agreeable is supreme. The very same forms, great king, are agreeable to some and disagreeable to others. The very same sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, great king, are agreeable to some and disagreeable to others."

Evaṃ yasmā teyeva rūpādayo eko assādeti abhinandati, tattha lobhaṃ uppādeti. Eko kujjhati paṭihaññati, tattha dosaṃ uppādeti. Ekassa iṭṭhā honti kantā manāpā, ekassa aniṭṭhā akantā amanāpā. Eko cete ‘iṭṭhā kantā manāpā’ti dakkhiṇato gaṇhāti, eko ‘aniṭṭhā akantā amanāpā’ti vāmato. Tasmā iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ nāma pāṭiyekkaṃ paṭivibhattaṃ nāma natthi. Paccantavāsīnañhi gaṇḍuppādāpi iṭṭhā honti kantā manāpā, majjhimadesavāsīnaṃ atijegucchā. Tesañca moramaṃsādīni iṭṭhāni honti, itaresaṃ tāni atijegucchānīti.

Thus, since one person savors and rejoices in these very same forms and so forth, and thereby gives rise to greed, while another becomes angry and repelled, and thereby gives rise to hatred. For one, these are desirable, charming, and agreeable; for another, they are undesirable, uncharming, and disagreeable. And one takes these as 'desirable, charming, and agreeable' from the right, while another takes them as 'undesirable, uncharming, and disagreeable' from the left. Therefore, there is no such thing as desirable and undesirable that is distinguished individually. For indeed, even the arising of boils is desirable, charming, and agreeable to border-dwellers, whereas to those in the middle country, they are utterly repulsive. And for the former, peacock meat and the like are desirable, while for others, those things are utterly repulsive.

So vattabbo – “kiṃ pana tvaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ paṭivibhattaṃ nāma natthīti vadesī”ti? “Āma natthī”ti vadāmi. Puna tatheva yāvatatiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā pañho pucchitabbo – “nibbānaṃ nāma iṭṭhaṃ udāhu aniṭṭha”nti? Jānamāno “iṭṭha”nti vakkhati. Sacepi na vadeyya, mā vadatu. Nibbānaṃ pana ekantaiṭṭhameva. “Nanu eko nibbānassa vaṇṇe kathiyamāne kujjhitvā – ‘tvaṃ nibbānassa vaṇṇaṃ kathesi, kiṃ tattha annapānamālāgandhavilepanasayanacchādanasamiddhā pañca kāmaguṇā atthī’ti vatvā ‘natthī’ti vutte ‘alaṃ tava nibbānenā’ti nibbānassa vaṇṇe kathiyamāne kujjhitvā ubho kaṇṇe thaketīti iṭṭhetaṃ. Etassa pana [V 0.0010] vasena tava vāde nibbānaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ nāma hoti[M 0.0010]. Na panetaṃ evaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Eso hi viparītasaññāya katheti. Saññāvipallāsena ca tadeva ārammaṇaṃ ekassa iṭṭhaṃ hoti, ekassa aniṭṭhaṃ”.

Then it should be said: 'Do you indeed claim that there is no such thing as a desirable and undesirable object individually distinguished?' 'Yes, I say there is none.' Again, having established it thus up to the third time, the question should be asked: 'Is Nibbāna desirable or undesirable?' Knowing, one will say, 'Desirable.' Even if one does not say so, let him not say so. But Nibbāna is exclusively desirable. 'Is it not the case that one, when the praise of Nibbāna is described, becomes angry and says, "You describe the praise of Nibbāna; are the five strands of sensual pleasure—abundant in food, drink, garlands, perfumes, unguents, beds, and coverings—present there?" And when told, "No," retorts, "Enough with your Nibbāna!"—getting angry and covering both ears when the praise of Nibbāna is described? This (Nibbāna) is desirable. But on account of this person, in your view, Nibbāna would be called undesirable. Yet this should not be understood thus. For this person speaks due to a distorted perception. And due to a perversion of perception, the very same object is desirable for one and undesirable for another.'

Iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇaṃ pana pāṭiyekkaṃ vibhattaṃ atthīti. Kassa vasena vibhattanti? Majjhimakasattassa. Idañhi na atiissarānaṃ mahāsammatamahāsudassanadhammāsokādīnaṃ vasena vibhattaṃ. Tesañhi dibbakappampi ārammaṇaṃ amanāpaṃ upaṭṭhāti. Na atiduggatānaṃ dullabhannapānānaṃ vasena vibhattaṃ. Tesañhi kaṇājakabhattasitthānipi pūtimaṃsarasopi atimadhuro amatasadiso ca hoti. Majjhimakānaṃ pana [P 0.0011] gaṇakamahāmattaseṭṭhikuṭumbikavāṇijādīnaṃ kālena iṭṭhaṃ kālena aniṭṭhaṃ labhamānānaṃ vasena vibhattaṃ. Evarūpā hi iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ paricchindituṃ sakkontīti.

But there is indeed such a thing as a desirable and undesirable object, individually distinguished. By whose standard is it distinguished? By the standard of the middling person. Indeed, this is not distinguished based on overly powerful figures such as Mahāsammata, Mahāsudassana, Dhammāsoka, and others. For them indeed, even a divine object appears disagreeable. Nor is it distinguished based on the extremely destitute who lack food and drink. For them indeed, even gruel and rice-leavings, or putrid meat broth, are exceedingly sweet and are like nectar. But it is distinguished based on the middling ones—accountants, high-ranking officials, wealthy merchants, householders, traders, and others—who obtain what is desirable at times and what is undesirable at times. Indeed, such ones are able to distinguish what is desirable and what is undesirable.

Tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero panāha – “iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ nāma vipākavaseneva paricchinnaṃ, na javanavasena. Javanaṃ pana saññāvipallāsavasena iṭṭhasmiṃyeva rajjati, iṭṭhasmiṃyeva dussati; aniṭṭhasmiṃyeva rajjati, aniṭṭhasmiṃyeva dussatī”ti. Vipākavaseneva panetaṃ ekantato paricchijjati. Na hi sakkā vipākacittaṃ vañcetuṃ. Sace ārammaṇaṃ iṭṭhaṃ hoti, kusalavipākaṃ uppajjati. Sace aniṭṭhaṃ, akusalavipākaṃ uppajjati. Kiñcāpi hi micchādiṭṭhikā buddhaṃ vā saṅghaṃ vā mahācetiyādīni vā uḷārāni ārammaṇāni disvā akkhīni pidahanti, domanassaṃ āpajjanti, dhammasaddaṃ sutvā kaṇṇe thakenti, cakkhuviññāṇasotaviññāṇāni pana nesaṃ kusalavipākāneva honti.

The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, however, said: "What is desirable and undesirable is defined solely by way of result (vipāka), not by way of impulsion (javana). The impulsion, however, due to perceptual distortion, is attached to what is desirable or is averse to it; is attached to what is undesirable or is averse to it." But this is definitively determined solely by way of result. For it is not possible to deceive resultant consciousness. If the object is desirable, wholesome resultant consciousness arises. If it is undesirable, unwholesome resultant consciousness arises. Even though those with wrong views may shut their eyes and become distressed upon seeing the Buddha, the Saṅgha, or great stūpas and other such exalted objects, or block their ears upon hearing the sound of the Dhamma, their eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness are nevertheless only wholesome results.

Kiñcāpi gūthasūkarādayo gūthagandhaṃ ghāyitvā ‘khādituṃ labhissāmā’ti somanassajātā honti, gūthadassane pana tesaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tassa gandhaghāyane ghānaviññāṇaṃ, rasasāyane jivhāviññāṇañca akusalavipākameva hoti. Bandhitvā varasayane sayāpitasūkaro ca kiñcāpi viravati, saññāvipallāsena panassa javanasmiṃyeva domanassaṃ uppajjati, kāyaviññāṇaṃ kusalavipākameva. Kasmā? Ārammaṇassa iṭṭhatāya.

Even though pigs and other creatures, upon smelling the stench of feces, become delighted thinking, 'We will get to eat it,' their eye-consciousness upon seeing feces, their nose-consciousness upon smelling its odor, and their tongue-consciousness upon tasting it are all unwholesome results. And though a pig tied up and laid on a luxurious bed may cry out, due to the distortion of perception, displeasure arises only in its impulsion; yet its body-consciousness is only a wholesome result. Why? Because of the object's desirability.

Apica dvāravasenāpi iṭṭhāniṭṭhatā veditabbā. Sukhasamphassañhi gūthakalalaṃ cakkhudvāraghānadvāresu [V 0.0011] aniṭṭhaṃ, kāyadvāre iṭṭhaṃ hoti. Cakkavattino maṇiratanena [M 0.0011] pothiyamānassa, suvaṇṇasūle uttāsitassa ca maṇiratanasuvaṇṇasūlāni cakkhudvāre iṭṭhāni honti, kāyadvāre aniṭṭhāni. Kasmā? Mahādukkhassa uppādanato. Evaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ ekantato vipākeneva paricchijjatīti veditabbaṃ.

Moreover, the desirable and undesirable should be understood by way of the doorways as well. For indeed, a fecal mire pleasant to the touch is undesirable at the eye and nose doorways, but desirable at the body doorway. When a universal monarch is being struck by the jewel treasure or impaled upon a golden stake, the jewel treasure and golden stake are desirable at the eye doorway but undesirable at the body doorway. Why? Because they cause great suffering. Thus, the desirable and undesirable should be understood as being definitively determined solely by way of result.

Taṃ taṃ vā panāti ettha na heṭṭhimanayo oloketabbo. Na hi bhagavā sammutimanāpaṃ bhindati, puggalamanāpaṃ pana bhindati. Tasmā taṃtaṃvāpanavaseneva upādāyupādāya hīnappaṇītatā veditabbā. Nerayikānañhi rūpaṃ [P 0.0012] koṭippattaṃ hīnaṃ nāma; taṃ upādāya tiracchānesu nāgasupaṇṇānaṃ rūpaṃ paṇītaṃ nāma. Tesaṃ rūpaṃ hīnaṃ; taṃ upādāya petānaṃ rūpaṃ paṇītaṃ nāma. Tesampi hīnaṃ; taṃ upādāya jānapadānaṃ rūpaṃ paṇītaṃ nāma. Tesampi hīnaṃ; taṃ upādāya gāmabhojakānaṃ rūpaṃ paṇītaṃ nāma. Tesampi hīnaṃ; taṃ upādāya janapadasāmikānaṃ rūpaṃ paṇītaṃ nāma. Tesampi hīnaṃ; taṃ upādāya padesarājūnaṃ rūpaṃ paṇītaṃ nāma. Tesampi hīnaṃ; taṃ upādāya cakkavattirañño rūpaṃ paṇītaṃ nāma. Tassāpi hīnaṃ; taṃ upādāya bhummadevānaṃ rūpaṃ paṇītaṃ nāma. Tesampi hīnaṃ; taṃ upādāya cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ rūpaṃ paṇītaṃ nāma. Tesampi hīnaṃ; taṃ upādāya tāvatiṃsānaṃ devānaṃ rūpaṃ paṇītaṃ nāma…pe… akaniṭṭhadevānaṃ pana rūpaṃ matthakappattaṃ paṇītaṃ nāma.

Here, in the phrase 'or that and that,' the previous method should not be considered. For the Blessed One does not break what is conventionally agreeable, but he does break what is agreeable to individuals. Therefore, the inferior and superior nature should be understood by taking each case in turn through the phrase 'that and that.' For indeed, the form of hell-beings, even at its peak, is called inferior; taking that as a basis, the form of animals, such as nāgas and garuḍas, is called superior. Their form is inferior; taking that as a basis, the form of hungry ghosts is called superior. Theirs too is inferior; taking that as a basis, the form of rural folk is called superior. Theirs too is inferior; taking that as a basis, the form of village chiefs is called superior. Theirs too is inferior; taking that as a basis, the form of provincial lords is called superior. Theirs too is inferior; taking that as a basis, the form of regional kings is called superior. Theirs too is inferior; taking that as a basis, the form of a wheel-turning monarch is called superior. His too is inferior; taking that as a basis, the form of earth-bound deities is called superior. Theirs too is inferior; taking that as a basis, the form of the devas of the Four Great Kings is called superior. Theirs too is inferior; taking that as a basis, the form of the devas of the Thirty-Three is called superior… and so on… but the form of the Akaniṭṭha devas, having reached the summit, is called superior.

7. Dūradukaniddese itthindriyādīni heṭṭhā vibhattāneva. Imasmiṃ pana duke duppariggahaṭṭhena lakkhaṇaduppaṭivijjhatāya sukhumarūpaṃ dūreti kathitaṃ. Sukhapariggahaṭṭhena lakkhaṇasuppaṭivijjhatāya oḷārikarūpaṃ santiketi. Kabaḷīkārāhārapariyosāne ca niyyātanaṭṭhānepi ‘idaṃ vuccati rūpaṃ dūre’ti na nīyyātitaṃ. Kasmā? Duvidhañhi dūre nāma – lakkhaṇato ca okāsato cāti. Tattha lakkhaṇato dūreti na kathitaṃ, taṃ okāsato kathetabbaṃ. Tasmā dūreti akathitaṃ. Oḷārikarūpaṃ okāsato dūreti dassetuṃ aniyyātetvāva yaṃ vā panaññampītiādimāha. Santikapadaniddesepi eseva nayo. Tattha anāsanneti na āsanne, anupakaṭṭheti nissaṭe, dūreti dūramhi, asantiketi na santike. Idaṃ vuccati rūpaṃ dūreti idaṃ paṇṇarasavidhaṃ sukhumarūpaṃ lakkhaṇato dūre, dasavidhaṃ pana oḷārikarūpaṃ yevāpanakavasena okāsato dūreti vuccati. Santikapadaniddeso uttānatthoyeva.

7. In the exposition of the couplet on the distant, faculties such as the femininity faculty have already been analyzed below. In this couplet, however, subtle materiality is called 'distant' because it is difficult to grasp and its characteristic is difficult to penetrate. Coarse materiality is called 'near' because it is easy to grasp and its characteristic is easy to penetrate. And at the conclusion of the section on edible food, in the place of assignment, the phrase 'this is called materiality that is distant' is not applied. Why? For 'distant' is indeed of two kinds: by characteristic and by location. Therein, it is not stated as 'distant' by characteristic; it is to be stated by location. Therefore, it is not stated as 'distant'. To show that coarse materiality is distant by location, without having applied this, it is said, 'or whatever else...' and so on. This same method applies in the exposition of the term 'near.' Therein, 'not near' means not close; 'not adjacent' means separated; 'distant' means at a distance; 'not near' means not close. 'This is called materiality that is distant' means this fifteenfold subtle materiality is distant by characteristic, while the tenfold coarse materiality is called distant by location by way of generalization. The exposition of the term 'near' is indeed of plain meaning.

Idaṃ [M 0.0012][V 0.0012] vuccati rūpaṃ santiketi idaṃ dasavidhaṃ oḷārikarūpaṃ lakkhaṇato santike, pañcadasavidhaṃ pana sukhumarūpaṃ yevāpanakavasena okāsato santiketi vuccati. Kittakato [P 0.0013] paṭṭhāya pana rūpaṃ okāsavasena santike nāma? Kittakato paṭṭhāya dūre nāmāti? Pakatikathāya kathentānaṃ dvādasahattho savanūpacāro nāma hoti. Tassa orato rūpaṃ santike, parato dūre. Tattha sukhumarūpaṃ dūre hontaṃ lakkhaṇatopi okāsatopi dūre hoti; santike hontaṃ pana okāsatova santike hoti, na lakkhaṇato. Oḷārikarūpaṃ santike hontaṃ lakkhaṇatopi okāsatopi santike hoti; dūre hontaṃ okāsatova dūre hoti, na lakkhaṇato.

'This is called materiality that is near' means this tenfold coarse materiality is near by characteristic, while the fifteenfold subtle materiality is called near by location by way of generalization. From what point, however, is materiality considered near by location? From what point is it considered distant? For those speaking in conventional terms, the range of hearing is twelve cubits. Within that, materiality is near; beyond it, it is distant. Therein, subtle materiality, when it is distant, is distant both by characteristic and by location; but when it is near, it is near only by location, not by characteristic. Coarse materiality, when it is near, is near both by characteristic and by location; when it is distant, it is distant only by location, not by characteristic.

Taṃ taṃ vā panāti ettha na heṭṭhimanayo oloketabbo. Heṭṭhā hi bhindamāno gato. Idha pana na lakkhaṇato dūraṃ bhindati, okāsato dūrameva bhindati. Upādāyupādāya dūrasantikañhi ettha dassitaṃ. Attano hi rūpaṃ santike nāma; antokucchigatassāpi parassa dūre. Antokucchigatassa santike; bahiṭhitassa dūre. Ekamañce sayitassa santike; bahipamukhe ṭhitassa dūre. Antopariveṇe rūpaṃ santike; bahipariveṇe dūre. Antosaṅghārāme rūpaṃ santike; bahisaṅghārāme dūre. Antosīmāya rūpaṃ santike; bahisīmāya dūre. Antogāmakhette rūpaṃ santike; bahigāmakkhette dūre. Antojanapade rūpaṃ santike; bahijanapade dūre. Antorajjasīmāya rūpaṃ santike; bahirajjasīmāya dūre. Antosamudde rūpaṃ santike; bahisamudderūpaṃ dūre. Antocakkavāḷe rūpaṃ santike; bahicakkavāḷe dūreti.

Regarding 'or again, this or that,' here the preceding method should not be considered. For previously, it proceeded by differentiating. Here, however, it does not differentiate 'distant' by characteristic; it differentiates 'distant' only by location. For here, relative distance and nearness are shown. One's own materiality is called near; but the materiality of another, even one inside the womb, is distant. For one inside the womb, it is near; for one outside, it is distant. For one lying on a single bed, it is near; for one standing outside the entrance, it is distant. Materiality within the inner enclosure is near; materiality outside the enclosure is distant. Materiality within the monastery is near; materiality outside the monastery is distant. Materiality within the boundary is near; materiality outside the boundary is distant. Materiality within the village field is near; materiality outside the village field is distant. Materiality within the country is near; materiality outside the country is distant. Materiality within the kingdom's border is near; materiality outside the kingdom's border is distant. Materiality within the ocean is near; materiality outside the ocean is distant. Materiality within the world-system is near; materiality outside the world-system is distant.

Ayaṃ rūpakkhandhaniddeso.

This is the exposition of the aggregate of materiality.

2. Vedanākkhandhaniddeso

2. Exposition of the Aggregate of Feeling

8. Vedanākkhandhaniddesādīsu heṭṭhā vuttasadisaṃ pahāya apubbameva vaṇṇayissāma. Yā kāci vedanāti catubhūmikavedanaṃ pariyādiyati. Sukhā vedanātiādīni atītādivasena niddiṭṭhavedanaṃ sabhāvato dassetuṃ [M 0.0013] vuttāni. Tattha sukhā vedanā atthi kāyikā, atthi cetasikā[V 0.0013]. Tathā dukkhā vedanā. Adukkhamasukhā pana cakkhādayo pasādakāye sandhāya pariyāyena ‘atthi kāyikā, atthi cetasikā’. Tattha sabbāpi kāyikā kāmāvacarā. Tathā cetasikā dukkhā vedanā[P 0.0014]. Cetasikā sukhā pana tebhūmikā. Adukkhamasukhā catubhūmikā. Tassā sabbappakārāyapi santativasena, khaṇādivasena ca atītādibhāvo veditabbo.

8. In the expositions of the aggregate of feeling and so on, having set aside what is similar to what was stated previously, we will now explain only what is new. 'Whatever feeling there is' encompasses feeling pertaining to the four planes. 'Pleasant feeling,' and so forth, are stated to show the intrinsic nature of feeling designated in terms of past, etc. Herein, there is pleasant feeling that is bodily, and there is that which is mental. Likewise for painful feeling. But neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, with reference to the sensitive matter of the eye, etc., is said figuratively to be 'bodily' and 'mental.' Herein, all bodily feeling belongs to the sense-sphere. Likewise, mental painful feeling. Mental pleasant feeling, however, pertains to three planes. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling pertains to four planes. For all its varieties, its state of being past, etc., should be understood by way of continuity and by way of moments.

Tattha santativasena ekavīthiekajavanaekasamāpattipariyāpannā, ekavidhavisayasamāyogappavattā ca paccuppannā. Tato pubbe atītā, pacchā anāgatā. Khaṇādivasena khaṇattayapariyāpannā pubbantāparantamajjhagatā sakiccañca kurumānā vedanā paccuppannā. Tato pubbe atītā, pacchā anāgatā. Tattha khaṇādivasena atītādibhāvaṃ sandhāya ayaṃ niddeso katoti veditabbo.

Herein, by way of continuity, that which is included in a single cognitive series, a single impulsion, a single attainment, and which proceeds in connection with a single kind of object, is present. What is before that is past; what is after is future. By way of moments, feeling that is included in the three moments, that has reached the beginning, end, and middle, and is performing its own function, is present. What is before that is past; what is after is future. It should be understood that this exposition is made with reference to the state of being past, etc., by way of moments.

11. Oḷārikasukhumaniddese akusalā vedanātiādīni jātito oḷārikasukhumabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttāni. Dukkhā vedanā oḷārikātiādīni sabhāvato. Asamāpannassa vedanātiādīni puggalato. Sāsavātiādīni lokiyalokuttarato oḷārikasukhumabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttāni. Tattha akusalā tāva sadarathaṭṭhena dukkhavipākaṭṭhena ca oḷārikā. Kusalā niddarathaṭṭhena sukhavipākaṭṭhena ca sukhumā. Abyākatā nirussāhaṭṭhena avipākaṭṭhena ca sukhumā. Kusalākusalā saussāhaṭṭhena savipākaṭṭhena ca oḷārikā. Abyākatā vuttanayeneva sukhumā.

11. In the exposition of the gross and subtle, 'unwholesome feeling,' and so forth, are stated to show the state of being gross and subtle by way of class. 'Painful feeling is gross,' and so forth, are stated by way of intrinsic nature. 'The feeling of one not in attainment,' and so forth, are stated by way of the individual. 'With taints,' and so forth, are stated to show the state of being gross and subtle by way of the mundane and supramundane. Herein, unwholesome feeling is gross in the sense of being afflictive and having a painful result. Wholesome feeling is subtle in the sense of being unafflictive and having a pleasant result. Indeterminate feeling is subtle in the sense of being without exertion and being without result. Wholesome and unwholesome feeling are gross in the sense of being with exertion and having a result. Indeterminate feeling is subtle by the method already stated.

Dukkhā asātaṭṭhena dukkhaṭṭhena ca oḷārikā. Sukhā sātaṭṭhena sukhaṭṭhena ca sukhumā. Adukkhamasukhā santaṭṭhena paṇītaṭṭhena ca sukhumā. Sukhadukkhā khobhanaṭṭhena pharaṇaṭṭhena ca oḷārikā. Sukhavedanāpi hi khobheti pharati. Tathā dukkhavedanāpi. Sukhañhi uppajjamānaṃ sakalasarīraṃ khobhentaṃ āluḷentaṃ abhisandayamānaṃ maddayamānaṃ chādayamānaṃ sītodakaghaṭena āsiñcayamānaṃ viya uppajjati. Dukkhaṃ uppajjamānaṃ tattaphālaṃ anto pavesantaṃ viya tiṇukkāya bahi jhāpayamānaṃ viya uppajjati. Adukkhamasukhā pana vuttanayeneva sukhumā. Asamāpannassa vedanā nānārammaṇe vikkhittabhāvato oḷārikā[M 0.0014]. Samāpannassa vedanā ekattanimitteyeva caratīti sukhumā. Sāsavā āsavuppattihetuto oḷārikā. Āsavacāro [P 0.0015] nāma ekantaoḷāriko. Anāsavā vuttavipariyāyena sukhumā.

Painful feeling is gross on account of being disagreeable and by its nature as suffering. Pleasant feeling is subtle on account of being agreeable and by its nature as pleasure. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is subtle on account of being peaceful and by its excellent nature. Pleasant and painful feelings are gross on account of being agitating and pervasive. For even pleasant feeling agitates and pervades; likewise painful feeling. When a pleasant feeling arises, it arises as if agitating the entire body, stirring it, suffusing it, saturating it, pressing it, and covering it, like being sprinkled with a jar of cool water. When a painful feeling arises, it is as if a hot iron ball were inserted inside, or as if one were being burned on the outside with a torch. But neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is subtle, in the way stated. The feeling of one who has not attained absorption is gross due to being scattered among various objects. The feeling of one who has attained absorption is subtle because it proceeds only in a single object. Feelings with taints are gross because they are a cause for the arising of taints. The province of the taints is entirely gross. Feelings without taints are subtle, for the opposite reason.

Tattha [V 0.0014] eko neva kusalattike kovido hoti, na vedanāttike. So ‘kusalattikaṃ rakkhāmī’ti vedanāttikaṃ bhindati; ‘vedanāttikaṃ rakkhāmī’ti kusalattikaṃ bhindati. Eko ‘tikaṃ rakkhāmī’ti bhūmantaraṃ bhindati. Eko na bhindati. Kathaṃ? “Sukhadukkhā vedanā oḷārikā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā sukhumā”ti hi vedanāttike vuttaṃ. Taṃ eko paṭikkhipati – na sabbā adukkhamasukhā sukhumā. Sā hi kusalāpi atthi akusalāpi abyākatāpi. Tattha kusalākusalā oḷārikā, abyākatā sukhumā. Kasmā? Kusalattike pāḷiyaṃ āgatattāti. Evaṃ kusalattiko rakkhito hoti, vedanāttiko pana bhinno.

Herein, one person is skilled neither in the wholesome triad nor in the feeling triad. Thinking, 'I will protect the wholesome triad,' he breaks the feeling triad; thinking, 'I will protect the feeling triad,' he breaks the wholesome triad. Another, thinking, 'I will protect a triad,' breaks the distinction between planes. Another does not break it. How so? For it is said in the feeling triad: 'Pleasant and painful feelings are gross; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are subtle.' One person rejects this, saying: 'Not all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are subtle, for they can be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Among these, the wholesome and unwholesome are gross, and the indeterminate are subtle.' Why? 'Because it is so stated in the Pāli of the wholesome triad.' In this way, the wholesome triad is protected, but the feeling triad is broken.

Kusalākusalā vedanā oḷārikā, abyākatā vedanā sukhumā”ti yaṃ pana kusalattike vuttaṃ, taṃ eko paṭikkhipati – na sabbā abyākatā sukhumā. Sā hi sukhāpi atthi dukkhāpi adukkhamasukhāpi. Tattha sukhadukkhā oḷārikā, adukkhamasukhā sukhumā. Kasmā? Vedanāttike pāḷiyaṃ āgatattāti. Evaṃ vedanāttiko rakkhito hoti, kusalattiko pana bhinno. Kusalattikassa pana āgataṭṭhāne vedanāttikaṃ anoloketvā vedanāttikassa āgataṭṭhāne kusalattikaṃ anoloketvā kusalādīnaṃ kusalattikalakkhaṇena, sukhādīnaṃ vedanāttikalakkhaṇena oḷārikasukhumataṃ kathento na bhindati nāma.

As for what was stated in the wholesome triad, 'Wholesome and unwholesome feelings are gross, indeterminate feelings are subtle,' one person rejects this, saying, 'Not all indeterminate feelings are subtle. For they can be pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Among these, pleasant and painful feelings are gross, while neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are subtle.' Why? Because it is so stated in the Pāli of the feeling triad. In this way, the feeling triad is protected, but the wholesome triad is broken. However, one who, in the context where the wholesome triad is stated, does not consider the feeling triad, and in the context where the feeling triad is stated, does not consider the wholesome triad, but speaks of the grossness and subtlety of wholesome states and so forth according to the characteristic of the wholesome triad, and of pleasant feelings and so forth according to the characteristic of the feeling triad—such a one does not break it.

Yampi “kusalākusalā vedanā oḷārikā, abyākatā vedanā sukhumā”ti kusalattike vuttaṃ, tattheko ‘kusalā lokuttaravedanāpi samānā oḷārikā nāma, vipākā antamaso dvipañcaviññāṇasahajātāpi samānā sukhumā nāma hotī’ti vadati. So evarūpaṃ santaṃ paṇītaṃ lokuttaravedanaṃ oḷārikaṃ nāma karonto, dvipañcaviññāṇasampayuttaṃ ahetukaṃ hīnaṃ jaḷaṃ vedanaṃ sukhumaṃ nāma karonto ‘tikaṃ rakkhissāmī’ti bhūmantaraṃ bhindati nāma. Tattha tattha bhūmiyaṃ kusalaṃ pana taṃtaṃbhūmivipākeneva saddhiṃ yojetvā kathento na bhindati nāma. Tatrāyaṃ nayo – kāmāvacarakusalā hi oḷārikā; kāmāvacaravipākā sukhumā[P 0.0016]. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacaralokuttarakusalā [M 0.0015] oḷārikā; rūpāvacarārūpāvacaralokuttaravipākā sukhumāti. Iminā nīhārena kathento na bhindati nāma.

Regarding the statement in the wholesome triad, 'Wholesome and unwholesome feelings are gross, while indeterminate feelings are subtle,' one person says: 'Even a wholesome supramundane feeling is called gross, while a resultant feeling—even one co-arisen with the two sets of fivefold sense consciousness—is called subtle.' By designating such a peaceful and sublime supramundane feeling as gross, and an inferior, rootless, and dull feeling associated with the two sets of fivefold sense consciousness as subtle, such a one, intending to 'protect the triad,' in fact breaks the distinction between planes. However, one who speaks by connecting the wholesome of each respective plane with the resultant of that same plane does not break it. Herein, this is the method: wholesome sense-sphere feelings are gross; sense-sphere resultant feelings are subtle. Wholesome feelings of the form sphere, formless sphere, and the supramundane are gross; resultant feelings of the form sphere, formless sphere, and the supramundane are subtle. One who speaks according to this method does not break it.

Tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero panāha – “akusale oḷārikasukhumatā nāma na uddharitabbā. Tañhi ekantaoḷārikameva. Lokuttarepi oḷārikasukhumatā na uddharitabbā. Tañhi ekantasukhuma”nti[V 0.0015]. Imaṃ kathaṃ āharitvā tipiṭakacūḷābhayattherassa kathayiṃsu – evaṃ therena kathitanti. Tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero āha – “sammāsambuddhena abhidhammaṃ patvā ekapadassāpi dvinnampi padānaṃ āgataṭṭhāne nayaṃ dātuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne nayo adinno nāma natthi, nayaṃ kātuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne nayo akato nāma natthi. Idha panekacco ‘ācariyo asmī’ti vicaranto akusale oḷārikasukhumataṃ uddharamāno kukkuccāyati. Sammāsambuddhena pana lokuttarepi oḷārikasukhumatā uddharitā”ti. Evañca pana vatvā idaṃ suttaṃ āhari – “tatra, bhante, yāyaṃ paṭipadā dukkhā dandhābhiññā, ayaṃ, bhante, paṭipadā ubhayeneva hīnā akkhāyati – dukkhattā dandhattā cā”ti (dī. ni. 3.152). Ettha hi catasso paṭipadā lokiyalokuttaramissakā kathitā.

The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, however, said: 'In the unwholesome, the distinction of gross and subtle should not be drawn, for it is entirely gross. In the supramundane, too, the distinction of gross and subtle should not be drawn, for it is entirely subtle.' Having brought this statement, they told the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya: 'Thus the Elder has spoken.' The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya said: 'When the Perfectly Enlightened One attained the Abhidhamma, there is no instance where a method was not given where it was proper to give a method, even for a single word or for two words that have appeared; there is no instance where a method was not made where it was proper to make a method. But here, a certain person, going about thinking, "I am a teacher," scruples to draw the distinction of gross and subtle in the unwholesome. Yet the Perfectly Enlightened One has drawn the distinction of gross and subtle even in the supramundane.' And having said this, he cited this discourse: 'Therein, venerable sir, that practice which is painful and slow to attain direct knowledge—this practice, venerable sir, is declared to be inferior in both respects: on account of its painfulness and on account of its slowness' (DN 3.252). Herein, four practices, a mixture of mundane and supramundane, are discussed.

Taṃ taṃ vā panāti ettha na heṭṭhimanayo oloketabbo. Taṃtaṃvāpanavaseneva kathetabbaṃ. Duvidhā hi akusalā – lobhasahagatā dosasahagatā ca. Tattha dosasahagatā oḷārikā, lobhasahagatā sukhumā. Dosasahagatāpi duvidhā – niyatā aniyatā ca. Tattha niyatā oḷārikā, aniyatā sukhumā. Niyatāpi kappaṭṭhitikā oḷārikā, nokappaṭṭhitikā sukhumā. Kappaṭṭhitikāpi asaṅkhārikā oḷārikā, sasaṅkhārikā sukhumā. Lobhasahagatāpi dvidhā – diṭṭhisampayuttā diṭṭhivippayuttā ca. Tattha diṭṭhisampayuttā oḷārikā, diṭṭhivippayuttā sukhumā. Diṭṭhisampayuttāpi niyatā oḷārikā, aniyatā sukhumā. Sāpi asaṅkhārikā oḷārikā, sasaṅkhārikā sukhumā.

As for 'taṃ taṃ vā pana,' here the preceding method should not be considered. It should be explained only in the manner of 'taṃ taṃ vā pana.' For unwholesome states are twofold: accompanied by greed and accompanied by hatred. Herein, those accompanied by hatred are gross, and those accompanied by greed are subtle. Those accompanied by hatred are also twofold: fixed and unfixed. Herein, the fixed are gross, and the unfixed are subtle. The fixed are also twofold: those enduring for an aeon are gross, and those not enduring for an aeon are subtle. Those enduring for an aeon are also twofold: the unprompted are gross, and the prompted are subtle. Those accompanied by greed are also twofold: associated with view and dissociated from view. Herein, those associated with view are gross, and those dissociated from view are subtle. Those associated with view are also twofold: the fixed are gross, and the unfixed are subtle. These also are twofold: the unprompted are gross, and the prompted are subtle.

Saṅkhepato akusalaṃ patvā yā vipākaṃ bahuṃ deti sā oḷārikā, yā appaṃ sā sukhumā. Kusalaṃ patvā pana appavipākā oḷārikā, bahuvipākā [M 0.0016] sukhumā. Catubbidhe kusale kāmāvacarakusalā oḷārikā, rūpāvacarakusalā sukhumā. Sāpi oḷārikā, arūpāvacarakusalā sukhumā[P 0.0017]. Sāpi oḷārikā, lokuttarakusalā sukhumā. Ayaṃ tāva bhūmīsu abhedato nayo.

In brief, regarding the unwholesome, that which yields much result is gross, and that which yields little is subtle. But regarding the wholesome, that which yields little result is gross, and that which yields much result is subtle. Among the four kinds of wholesome states, the sensuous-sphere wholesome is gross, and the form-sphere wholesome is subtle. That too is gross, while the formless-sphere wholesome is subtle. That too is gross, while the supramundane wholesome is subtle. This, for now, is the method regarding the planes without differentiation.

Bhedato pana kāmāvacarā dānasīlabhāvanāmayavasena tividhā. Tattha dānamayā oḷārikā, sīlamayā sukhumā. Sāpi oḷārikā, bhāvanāmayā sukhumā. Sāpi duhetukā tihetukāti duvidhā. Tattha duhetukā oḷārikā, tihetukā sukhumā. Tihetukāpi sasaṅkhārikaasaṅkhārikabhedato [V 0.0016] duvidhā. Tattha sasaṅkhārikā oḷārikā, asaṅkhārikā sukhumā. Rūpāvacare paṭhamajjhānakusalavedanā oḷārikā, dutiyajjhānakusalavedanā sukhumā…pe… catutthajjhānakusalavedanā sukhumā. Sāpi oḷārikā, ākāsānañcāyatanakusalavedanā sukhumā ākāsānañcāyatanakusalavedanā oḷārikā…pe…. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakusalavedanā sukhumā. Sāpi oḷārikā, vipassanāsahajātā sukhumā. Sāpi oḷārikā, sotāpattimaggasahajātā sukhumā. Sāpi oḷārikā…pe… arahattamaggasahajātā sukhumā.

By way of differentiation, however, sensuous-sphere states are threefold: constituted by giving, by virtue, and by meditation. Of these, those constituted by giving are gross, and those constituted by virtue are subtle. That too is gross, while those constituted by meditation are subtle. That is also twofold: with two roots and with three roots. Of these, that with two roots is gross, while that with three roots is subtle. The three-rooted is also twofold by way of being prompted and unprompted. Of these, the prompted is gross, and the unprompted is subtle. In the Form Sphere, the wholesome feeling of the first jhāna is gross, while that of the second jhāna is subtle... and so forth... the wholesome feeling of the fourth jhāna is subtle. That too is gross, while the wholesome feeling of the base of the infinity of space is subtle. The wholesome feeling of the base of the infinity of space is gross... and so forth... while the wholesome feeling of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is subtle. That too is gross, while that which arises together with insight is subtle. That too is gross, while that which arises together with the path of stream-entry is subtle. That too is gross... and so forth... while that which arises together with the path of arahantship is subtle.

Catubbidhe vipāke kāmāvacaravipākavedanā oḷārikā, rūpāvacaravipākavedanā sukhumā. Sāpi oḷārikā…pe… lokuttaravipākavedanā sukhumā. Evaṃ tāva abhedato.

In the fourfold resultant, the resultant feeling of the sensuous sphere is gross, and the resultant feeling of the form sphere is subtle. That too is gross... and so forth... while the resultant feeling of the supramundane is subtle. Thus far by way of non-differentiation.

Bhedato pana kāmāvacaravipākā atthi ahetukā, atthi sahetukā. Sahetukāpi atthi duhetukā, atthi tihetukā. Tattha ahetukā oḷārikā, sahetukā sukhumā. Sāpi duhetukā oḷārikā, tihetukā sukhumā. Tatthāpi sasaṅkhārikā oḷārikā, asaṅkhārikā sukhumā. Paṭhamajjhānavipākā oḷārikā, dutiyajjhānavipākā sukhumā…pe… catutthajjhānavipākā sukhumā. Sāpi oḷārikā, ākāsānañcāyatanavipākā sukhumā. Sāpi oḷārikā…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanavipākā sukhumā. Sāpi oḷārikā, sotāpattiphalavedanā sukhumā. Sāpi oḷārikā, sakadāgāmi…pe… arahattaphalavedanā sukhumā.

By way of differentiation, however, some sensuous-sphere resultants are rootless, and some are rooted. Of the rooted, some are two-rooted, and some are three-rooted. Among these, the rootless are gross, and the rooted are subtle. The rooted are also twofold: the two-rooted are gross, and the three-rooted are subtle. Among these too, the prompted are gross, and the unprompted are subtle. The first-jhāna resultants are gross, and the second-jhāna resultants are subtle... and so forth... the fourth-jhāna resultants are subtle. That too is gross, while the resultants of the base of infinite space are subtle. That too is gross... and so forth... while the resultants of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are subtle. That too is gross, while the feeling of stream-entry fruition is subtle. That too is gross, while the feeling of once-returner fruition... and so forth... the feeling of arahant fruition is subtle.

Tīsu [M 0.0017] kiriyāsu kāmāvacarakiriyavedanā oḷārikā, rūpāvacarakiriyavedanā sukhumā. Sāpi oḷārikā, arūpāvacarakiriyavedanā sukhumā. Evaṃ tāva abhedato. Bhedato pana ahetukādivasena bhinnāya kāmāvacarakiriyāya ahetukakiriyavedanā [P 0.0018] oḷārikā, sahetukā sukhumā. Sāpi duhetukā oḷārikā, tihetukā sukhumā. Tatthāpi sasaṅkhārikā oḷārikā, asaṅkhārikā sukhumā. Paṭhamajjhāne kiriyavedanā oḷārikā, dutiyajjhāne sukhumā. Sāpi oḷārikā, tatiye…pe… catutthe sukhumā. Sāpi oḷārikā, ākāsānañcāyatanakiriyavedanā sukhumā. Sāpi oḷārikā, viññāṇañcā…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakiriyavedanā sukhumā. Yā oḷārikā sā hīnā. Yā sukhumā sā paṇītā.

Among the three kinds of functional consciousness, the feeling pertaining to sensuous-sphere functional consciousness is gross, and the feeling pertaining to form-sphere functional consciousness is subtle. That too is gross, while the feeling pertaining to formless-sphere functional consciousness is subtle. Thus far by way of non-differentiation. By way of differentiation, however, in the sensuous-sphere functional consciousness, which is divided by way of being rootless and so forth, the feeling pertaining to rootless functional consciousness is gross, and that pertaining to rooted functional consciousness is subtle. That too is twofold: the two-rooted is gross, and the three-rooted is subtle. Among these too, the prompted is gross, and the unprompted is subtle. In the first jhāna, the feeling pertaining to functional consciousness is gross, and in the second jhāna it is subtle. That too is gross, in the third... and so forth... in the fourth it is subtle. That too is gross, while the feeling pertaining to the functional consciousness of the base of infinite space is subtle. That too is gross, while the feeling pertaining to the functional consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness... and so forth... of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is subtle. What is gross is inferior; what is subtle is superior.

13. Dūradukaniddese [V 0.0017] akusalavedanā visabhāgaṭṭhena visaṃsaṭṭhena ca kusalābyākatāhi dūre. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu dūratā veditabbā. Sacepi hi akusalādivedanāsamaṅgino dukkhādivedanāsamaṅgino ca tayo tayo janā ekamañce nisinnā honti, tesampi tā vedanā visabhāgaṭṭhena visaṃsaṭṭhena ca dūreyeva nāma. Samāpannavedanādisamaṅgīsupi eseva nayo. Akusalā pana akusalāya sabhāgaṭṭhena sarikkhaṭṭhena ca santike nāma. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu santikatā veditabbā. Sacepi hi akusalādivedanāsamaṅgīsu tīsu janesu eko kāmabhave, eko rūpabhave, eko arūpabhave, tesampi tā vedanā sabhāgaṭṭhena sarikkhaṭṭhena ca santikeyeva nāma. Kusalādivedanāsamaṅgīsupi eseva nayo.

13. In the exposition of the dyad of distance, unwholesome feelings are distant from wholesome and indeterminate ones by way of being dissimilar and incompatible. In this way, distance should be understood in all cases. Even if three people possessing unwholesome feelings and so forth, and three people possessing painful feelings and so forth, were sitting on the same couch, those feelings would still be distant by way of being dissimilar and incompatible. The same principle applies to those possessing attained feelings and so on. However, unwholesome feelings are near to other unwholesome feelings by way of being similar and resembling. In this way, nearness should be understood in all cases. Even if among three people possessing unwholesome feelings and so forth, one is in the sense-sphere existence, one in the form-sphere existence, and one in the formless-sphere existence, those feelings would still be near by way of being similar and resembling. The same principle applies to those possessing wholesome feelings and so on.

Taṃ taṃ vā panāti ettha heṭṭhimanayaṃ anoloketvā taṃ taṃ vāpanavaseneva kathetabbaṃ. Kathentena ca na dūrato santikaṃ uddharitabbaṃ, santikato pana dūraṃ uddharitabbaṃ. Duvidhā hi akusalā – lobhasahagatā dosasahagatā ca. Tattha lobhasahagatā lobhasahagatāya santike nāma, dosasahagatāya dūre nāma. Dosasahagatā dosasahagatāya santike nāma, lobhasahagatāya dūre nāma. Dosasahagatāpi niyatā niyatāya santike nāmāti. Evaṃ aniyatā. Kappaṭṭhitikaasaṅkhārikasasaṅkhārikabhedaṃ lobhasahagatādīsu ca diṭṭhisampayuttādibhedaṃ sabbaṃ oḷārikadukaniddese vitthāritavasena anugantvā ekekakoṭṭhāsavedanā [P 0.0019][M 0.0018] taṃtaṃkoṭṭhāsavedanāya eva santike, itarā itarāya dūreti veditabbāti.

As for 'this or that,' here it should be explained on a case-by-case basis, without reference to the preceding analysis. And in explaining, one should not extract the near from the far, but should extract the far from the near. For unwholesome states are of two kinds: accompanied by greed and accompanied by hatred. Therein, those accompanied by greed are called 'near' to those accompanied by greed, and 'distant' from those accompanied by hatred. Those accompanied by hatred are called 'near' to those accompanied by hatred, and 'distant' from those accompanied by greed. Among those accompanied by hatred, the determined are also called 'near' to the determined, and similarly the undetermined. Having followed in detail all the distinctions in the exposition of the coarse dyad—such as those of fixed duration, unprompted, and prompted, and among those accompanied by greed and so forth, the distinctions of being associated with wrong view and so forth—it is to be understood that the feeling of each category is near to a feeling of its own category, while another is distant from another.

Ayaṃ vedanākkhandhaniddeso.

This is the exposition of the aggregate of feeling.

3. Saññākkhandhaniddeso

3. Exposition of the Aggregate of Perception

14. Saññākkhandhaniddese yā kāci saññāti catubhūmikasaññaṃ pariyādiyati. Cakkhusamphassajā saññātiādīni atītādivasena niddiṭṭhasaññaṃ sabhāvato dassetuṃ vuttāni. Tattha cakkhusamphassato cakkhusamphassasmiṃ vā jātā cakkhusamphassajā nāma. Sesāsupi eseva nayo[V 0.0018]. Ettha ca purimā pañca cakkhupasādādivatthukāva. Manosamphassajā hadayavatthukāpi avatthukāpi. Sabbā catubhūmikasaññā.

14. In the exposition of the aggregate of perception, 'whatever perception there is' encompasses perception pertaining to the four planes. The perceptions 'born of eye-contact,' etc., are stated to show the essential nature of perception as designated according to the past, etc. Here, 'born of eye-contact' means born from or in eye-contact. The same principle applies to the others. And here, the first five have eye-sensitivity, etc., as their bases. Perception born of mind-contact may have the heart-basis or be without a basis. All are perception pertaining to the four planes.

17. Oḷārikadukaniddese paṭighasamphassajāti sappaṭighe cakkhupasādādayo vatthuṃ katvā sappaṭighe rūpādayo ārabbha uppanno phasso paṭighasamphasso nāma. Tato tasmiṃ vā jātā paṭighasamphassajā nāma. Cakkhusamphassajā saññā…pe… kāyasamphassajā saññātipi tassāyeva vatthuto nāmaṃ. Rūpasaññā…pe… phoṭṭhabbasaññātipi tassāyeva ārammaṇato nāmaṃ. Idaṃ pana vatthārammaṇato nāmaṃ. Sappaṭighāni hi vatthūni nissāya, sappaṭighāni ca ārammaṇāni ārabbha uppattito esā paṭighasamphassajā saññāti vuttā. Manosamphassajātipi pariyāyena etissā nāmaṃ hotiyeva. Cakkhuviññāṇañhi mano nāma. Tena sahajāto phasso manosamphasso nāma. Tasmiṃ manosamphasse, tasmā vā manosamphassā jātāti manosamphassajā. Tathā sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇaṃ mano nāma. Tena sahajāto phasso manosamphasso nāma. Tasmiṃ manosamphasse, tasmā vā manosamphassā jātāti manosamphassajā.

17. In the exposition of the gross dyad, the contact that arises by taking resistant bases such as eye-sensitivity and resistant objects such as forms as its object is called impact-contact. That which is born from that, or in that, is called perception born of impact-contact. 'Perception born of eye-contact'… up to 'perception born of body-contact' are also names for it by way of the base. 'Perception of forms'… up to 'perception of tangibles' are also names for it by way of the object. This, however, is a name by way of both the base and the object.
