Because it arises by relying on resistant bases and taking resistant objects as its object, this is called 'perception born of impact-contact.' 'Perception born of mind-contact' is also a name for this, in a figurative sense. For eye-consciousness is called 'mind.' The contact that arises together with it is called 'mind-contact.' What is born in that mind-contact, or from that mind-contact, is called 'perception born of mind-contact.' Similarly, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness are called 'mind.' The contact that arises together with them is called 'mind-contact.' What is born in that mind-contact, or from that mind-contact, is called 'perception born of mind-contact.'

Adhivacanasamphassajā saññātipi pariyāyena etissā nāmaṃ hotiyeva. Tayo hi arūpino khandhā sayaṃ piṭṭhivaṭṭakā hutvā attanā sahajātāya saññāya adhivacanasamphassajā saññātipi nāmaṃ karonti. Nippariyāyena pana paṭighasamphassajā saññā nāma pañcadvārikasaññā[P 0.0020], adhivacanasamphassajā saññā nāma manodvārikasaññā. Tattha pañcadvārikasaññā oloketvāpi [M 0.0019] jānituṃ sakkāti oḷārikā. Rajjitvā upanijjhāyantañhi ‘rajjitvā upanijjhāyatī’ti, kujjhitvā upanijjhāyantaṃ ‘kujjhitvā upanijjhāyatī’ti oloketvāva jānanti.

'Perception born of appellative contact' also becomes a name for this in a figurative sense. For the three immaterial aggregates, being themselves like a back-support, cause the perception co-arising with them to be called 'perception born of appellative contact.' In the literal sense, however, perception born of impact-contact is called five-door perception, while perception born of appellative contact is called mind-door perception. Therein, five-door perception is coarse because it can be known even by observing. For when someone is contemplating with lust, one knows by observing, 'He is contemplating with lust'; when someone is contemplating with anger, one knows by observing, 'He is contemplating with anger.'

Tatridaṃ vatthu – dve kira itthiyo nisīditvā suttaṃ kantanti. Dvīsu daharesu gāme carantesu eko purato gacchanto ekaṃ itthiṃ olokesi. Itarā taṃ pucchi ‘kasmā nu kho taṃ eso olokesī’ti? ‘Na eso bhikkhu maṃ visabhāgacittena olokesi, kaniṭṭhabhaginīsaññāya pana olokesī’ti. Tesupi gāme caritvā āsanasālāya nisinnesu itaro bhikkhu taṃ bhikkhuṃ pucchi – ‘tayā sā itthī olokitā’ti? ‘Āma olokitā’. ‘Kimatthāyā’ti? ‘Mayhaṃ bhaginīsarikkhattā taṃ olokesi’nti āha. Evaṃ pañcadvārikasaññā oloketvāpi [V 0.0019] jānituṃ sakkāti veditabbā. Sā panesā pasādavatthukā eva. Keci pana javanappavattāti dīpenti. Manodvārikasaññā pana ekamañce vā ekapīṭhe vā nisīditvāpi aññaṃ cintentaṃ vitakkentañca ‘kiṃ cintesi, kiṃ vitakkesī’ti pucchitvā tassa vacanavaseneva jānitabbato sukhumā. Sesaṃ vedanākkhandhasadisamevāti.

Herein is the story: Two women, it is said, were sitting and spinning thread. While two young monks were walking through the village, one walking ahead glanced at a woman. The other woman asked her, 'Why did he glance at you?' She replied, 'That monk did not glance at me with an inappropriate mind; rather, he glanced at me with the perception of a younger sister.' Later, when they had walked through the village and were seated in the assembly hall, the other monk asked that monk, 'Did you glance at that woman?' He answered, 'Yes, I glanced at her.' 'For what reason?' 'Because she resembled my sister, I glanced at her,' he said. Thus, it should be understood that five-door perception can be known even by observing. This, however, has the sense-faculties as its basis. Some, however, explain that it occurs during the process of apperception (javana). But mind-door perception is subtler, for even if two are sitting on the same bed or the same bench, and one is thinking or reflecting, the other can know it only by asking, 'What were you thinking? What were you reflecting on?' and by means of the other’s words. The rest is similar to the aggregate of feeling.

Ayaṃ saññākkhandhaniddeso.

This is the exposition of the aggregate of perception.

4. Saṅkhārakkhandhaniddeso

4. Exposition of the Aggregate of Volitional Formations

20. Saṅkhārakkhandhaniddese ye keci saṅkhārāti catubhūmikasaṅkhāre pariyādiyati. Cakkhusamphassajā cetanātiādīni atītādivasena niddiṭṭhasaṅkhāre sabhāvato dassetuṃ vuttāni. Cakkhusamphassajātiādīni vuttatthāneva. Cetanāti heṭṭhimakoṭiyā padhānasaṅkhāravasena vuttaṃ. Heṭṭhimakoṭiyā hi antamaso cakkhuviññāṇena saddhiṃ pāḷiyaṃ āgatā cattāro saṅkhārā uppajjanti. Tesu cetanā padhānā āyūhanaṭṭhena pākaṭattā. Tasmā ayameva gahitā. Taṃsampayuttasaṅkhārā pana tāya gahitāya gahitāva honti. Idhāpi purimā pañca cakkhupasādādivatthukāva. Manosamphassajā hadayavatthukāpi avatthukāpi. Sabbā catubhūmikacetanā. Sesaṃ vedanākkhandhasadisamevāti.

20. In the exposition of the aggregate of volitional formations, 'whatever volitional formations there are' encompasses the volitional formations pertaining to the four planes. The volitions 'born of eye-contact' and so forth are stated to show the nature of volitional formations described in terms of past and so forth. 'Born of eye-contact' and so forth are to be understood in the same sense as previously stated. By 'volition' is meant the principal volitional formation at the lowest level. For at the lowest level, at least four volitional formations mentioned in the Pāli arise together with eye-consciousness. Among these, volition is principal because of its prominence in the sense of accumulation. Therefore, this alone is taken. But the volitional formations associated with it are included by its inclusion. Here too, the first five are based on the eye-sensitivity and so forth. The volition born of mind-contact is based on the heart-base or is without a base. All are volitions pertaining to the four planes. The rest is to be understood in the same way as in the exposition of the aggregate of feeling.

Ayaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhaniddeso.

This is the exposition of the aggregate of volitional formations.

5. Viññāṇakkhandhaniddeso

5. Exposition of the Aggregate of Consciousness

26. Viññāṇakkhandhaniddese [P 0.0021][M 0.0020] yaṃ kiñci viññāṇanti catubhūmakaviññāṇaṃ pariyādiyati. Cakkhuviññāṇantiādīni atītādivasena niddiṭṭhaviññāṇaṃ sabhāvato dassetuṃ vuttāni. Tattha cakkhuviññāṇādīni [V 0.0020] pañca cakkhupasādādivatthukāneva, manoviññāṇaṃ hadayavatthukampi avatthukampi. Sabbaṃ catubhūmakaviññāṇaṃ. Sesaṃ vedanākkhandhasadisamevāti.

26. In the exposition of the aggregate of consciousness, 'whatever consciousness' encompasses consciousness pertaining to the four planes. Eye-consciousness and so forth are stated to show the nature of consciousness described in terms of past and so forth. Herein, the five, eye-consciousness and so forth, are based only on the eye-sensitivity and so forth, while mental consciousness is based on the heart-base or is without a base. All is consciousness pertaining to the four planes. The rest is to be understood in the same way as in the exposition of the feeling aggregate.

Ayaṃ viññāṇakkhandhaniddeso.

This is the exposition of the aggregate of consciousness.

Pakiṇṇakakathā

Miscellaneous Discussion

Idāni pañcasupi khandhesu samuggamato, pubbāparato, addhānaparicchedato, ekuppādanānānirodhato, nānuppādaekanirodhato, ekuppādaekanirodhato, nānuppādanānānirodhato, atītānāgatapaccuppannato, ajjhattikabāhirato, oḷārikasukhumato, hīnapaṇītato, dūrasantikato, paccayato, samuṭṭhānato, parinipphannato, saṅkhatatoti soḷasahākārehi pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Now, the five aggregates are to be understood in sixteen miscellaneous ways: by origination, by sequence, by limitation of duration, by single arising and diverse ceasing, by diverse arising and single ceasing, by single arising and single ceasing, by diverse arising and diverse ceasing, by past, future, and present, by internal and external, by coarse and subtle, by inferior and superior, by far and near, by condition, by origin, by consummation, and by the conditioned.

Tattha duvidho samuggamo – gabbhaseyyakasamuggamo, opapātikasamuggamoti. Tattha gabbhaseyyakasamuggamo evaṃ veditabbo – gabbhaseyyakasattānañhi paṭisandhikkhaṇe pañcakkhandhā apacchāapure ekato pātubhavanti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe pātubhūtā kalalasaṅkhātā rūpasantati parittā hoti. Khuddakamakkhikāya ekavāyāmena pātabbamattāti vatvā puna ‘atibahuṃ etaṃ, saṇhasūciyā tele pakkhipitvā ukkhittāya paggharitvā agge ṭhitabindumatta’nti vuttaṃ. Tampi paṭikkhipitvā ‘ekakese telato uddharitvā gahite tassa paggharitvā agge ṭhitabindumatta’nti vuttaṃ. Tampi paṭikkhipitvā ‘imasmiṃ janapade manussānaṃ kese aṭṭhadhā phālite tato ekakoṭṭhāsappamāṇo uttarakurukānaṃ keso; tassa pasannatilatelato uddhaṭassa agge ṭhitabindumatta’nti vuttaṃ. Tampi paṭikkhipitvā ‘etaṃ bahu, jātiuṇṇā nāma sukhumā; tassā ekaaṃsuno pasannatilatele pakkhipitvā uddhaṭassa paggharitvā agge ṭhitabindumatta’nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ [M 0.0021] acchaṃ hoti vippasannaṃ anāvilaṃ parisuddhaṃ pasannatilatelabindusamānavaṇṇaṃ[P 0.0022]. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Herein, origination is twofold: the origination of womb-born beings and the origination of spontaneously born beings. Herein, the origination of womb-born beings should be understood thus: For womb-born beings, at the moment of rebirth-linking, the five aggregates appear simultaneously, without prior or subsequent occurrence. At that moment, the manifested material continuum, called the kalala, is minute. It is said to be of a size that can be blown away by a single breath of a small fly. Then it is said, 'This is too much; it is like a drop remaining on the tip of a fine needle after it has been dipped in oil and lifted up.' That too is rejected, and it is said, 'It is like a drop remaining on the tip of a single hair after it has been drawn out of oil.' That too is rejected, and it is said, 'In this country, when human hair is split eightfold, one portion is the size of a hair of the Uttarakuru people; it is like a drop remaining on the tip of such a hair after it has been drawn out of clear sesame oil.' That too is rejected, and it is said, 'This is too much; jātiuṇṇā is subtle. It is like a drop remaining on the tip of a single strand of it after it has been dipped in clear sesame oil.' But that drop is clear, bright, unclouded, pure, and similar in color to a drop of clear sesame oil. And this too has been said:

Tilatelassa [V 0.0021] yathā bindu, sappimaṇḍo anāvilo;

Evaṃ vaṇṇapaṭibhāgaṃ, kalalanti pavuccatīti.

Just as a drop of sesame oil, a clear globule of ghee, so is the kalala in its color and appearance; thus it is called.

Evaṃ parittāya rūpasantatiyā tīṇi santatisīsāni honti – vatthudasakaṃ, kāyadasakaṃ, itthiyā itthindriyavasena purisassa purisindriyavasena bhāvadasakanti. Tattha vatthurūpaṃ, tassa nissayāni cattāri mahābhūtāni, taṃnissitā vaṇṇagandharasojā, jīvitanti – idaṃ vatthudasakaṃ nāma. Kāyapasādo, tassa nissayāni cattāri mahābhūtāni, tannissitā vaṇṇagandharasojā, jīvitanti – idaṃ kāyadasakaṃ nāma. Itthiyā itthibhāvo, purisassa purisabhāvo, tassa nissayāni cattāri mahābhūtāni, tannissitā vaṇṇagandharasojā, jīvitanti – idaṃ bhāvadasakaṃ nāma.

Thus, in such a limited material continuum, there are three initial continua: the base-decad, the body-decad, and the sex-decad—by way of the female faculty for a female, and by way of the male faculty for a male. Therein, base-materiality, its dependent four great elements, the color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence dependent on them, and life—this is called the base-decad. The body-sensitivity, its dependent four great elements, the color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence dependent on them, and life—this is called the body-decad. The femaleness of a female, the maleness of a male, their dependent four great elements, the color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence dependent on them, and life—this is called the sex-decad.

Evaṃ gabbhaseyyakānaṃ paṭisandhiyaṃ ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena samatiṃsa kammajarūpāni rūpakkhandho nāma hoti. Paṭisandhicittena pana sahajātā vedanā vedanākkhandho, saññā saññākkhandho, saṅkhārā saṅkhārakkhandho, paṭisandhicittaṃ viññāṇakkhandhoti. Evaṃ gabbhaseyyakānaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe pañcakkhandhā paripuṇṇā honti. Sace pana napuṃsakapaṭisandhi hoti, bhāvadasakaṃ hāyati. Dvinnaṃ dasakānaṃ vasena samavīsati kammajarūpāni rūpakkhandho nāma hoti. Vedanākkhandhādayo vuttappakārā evāti. Evampi gabbhaseyyakānaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe pañcakkhandhā paripuṇṇā honti.

Thus, for those lying in the womb, at rebirth-linking, the aggregate of material form, by way of the highest enumeration, consists of thirty kamma-produced material phenomena. But the feeling co-arisen with the rebirth-linking consciousness is the feeling aggregate, the perception is the perception aggregate, the volitional formations are the volitional formations aggregate, and the rebirth-linking consciousness is the consciousness aggregate. Thus, for those lying in the womb, the five aggregates are complete at the moment of rebirth-linking. But if the rebirth-linking is sexless, the sex-decad is lacking. Then the aggregate of material form consists of twenty kamma-produced material phenomena by way of two decads. The feeling aggregate and the others are as previously described. Even so, for those lying in the womb, the five aggregates are complete at the moment of rebirth-linking.

Imasmiṃ ṭhāne tisamuṭṭhānikappaveṇī kathetabbā bhaveyya. Taṃ pana akathetvā ‘opapātikasamuggamo’ nāma dassito. Opapātikānañhi paripuṇṇāyatanānaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe heṭṭhā vuttāni tīṇi, cakkhusotaghānajivhādasakāni cāti satta rūpasantatisīsāni pātubhavanti. Tattha cakkhudasakādīni kāyadasakasadisāneva. Napuṃsakassa pana bhāvadasakaṃ natthi. Evaṃ paripuṇṇāyatanānaṃ opapātikānaṃ samasattati ceva [P 0.0023] samasaṭṭhi ca kammajarūpāni rūpakkhandho nāma. Vedanākkhandhādayo vuttappakārā evāti. Evaṃ opapātikānaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe pañcakkhandhā paripuṇṇā honti. Ayaṃ ‘opapātikasamuggamo’ nāma. Evaṃ tāva pañcakkhandhā ‘samuggamato’ veditabbā.

At this point, the doctrine of threefold simultaneous arising should have been discussed. However, without discussing that, the 'origination of spontaneously born beings' is explained. For beings of spontaneous birth who possess complete sense faculties, at the moment of rebirth-linking, the seven initial continua of materiality appear: the three previously mentioned and the decads of the eye, ear, nose, and tongue. Herein, the eye-decad and so forth are just like the body-decad. But for a neuter being, the sex-decad does not exist. Thus, for beings of spontaneous birth who possess complete sense faculties, there are seventy or sixty kamma-produced material phenomena, which is called the aggregate of material form. The feeling aggregate and the others are as previously described. Thus, for beings of spontaneous birth, the five aggregates are complete at the moment of rebirth-linking. This is called the 'origination of spontaneously born beings.' So far, the five aggregates should be understood in terms of 'origination.'

‘Pubbāparato’ti [M 0.0022] evaṃ pana gabbhaseyyakānaṃ apacchāapure uppannesu pañcasu khandhesu kiṃ rūpaṃ [V 0.0022] paṭhamaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti udāhu arūpanti? Rūpaṃ rūpameva samuṭṭhāpeti, na arūpaṃ. Kasmā? Paṭisandhicittassa na rūpajanakattā. Sabbasattānañhi paṭisandhicittaṃ, khīṇāsavassa cuticittaṃ, dvipañcaviññāṇāni, cattāri arūppavipākānīti soḷasa cittāni rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpenti. Tattha paṭisandhicittaṃ tāva vatthuno dubbalatāya appatiṭṭhitatāya paccayavekallatāya āgantukatāya ca rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpeti. Tattha hi sahajātaṃ vatthu uppādakkhaṇe dubbalaṃ hotīti vatthuno dubbalatāya rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpeti. Yathā ca papāte patanto puriso aññassa nissayo bhavituṃ na sakkoti, evaṃ etampi kammavegakkhittattā papāte patamānaṃ viya appatiṭṭhitaṃ. Iti kammavegakkhittattā, appatiṭṭhitatāyapi rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpeti.

'By sequence'—but for those lying in the womb, when the five aggregates have arisen simultaneously, without prior or subsequent occurrence, does material form first generate material form, or does the immaterial generate it? Material form generates material form itself, not the immaterial. Why? Because rebirth-linking consciousness is not a generator of material form. Indeed, the rebirth-linking consciousness of all beings, the death-consciousness of an arahant, the ten sense-consciousnesses, and the four immaterial-resultant consciousnesses—these sixteen types of consciousness do not generate material form. Herein, rebirth-linking consciousness does not generate material form due to the weakness of the base, its lack of stability, the deficiency of conditions, and its adventitiousness. For here, the co-arisen base is weak at the moment of its arising; thus, due to the weakness of the base, it does not generate material form. Just as a man falling from a precipice cannot be a support for another, so too this consciousness, being propelled by the force of kamma, is unstable, like one falling from a precipice. Thus, being propelled by the force of kamma and lacking stability, it does not generate material form.

Paṭisandhicittañca vatthunā saddhiṃ apacchāapure uppannaṃ. Tassa vatthu purejātaṃ hutvā paccayo bhavituṃ na sakkoti. Sace sakkuṇeyya, rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeyya. Yatrāpi vatthu purejātaṃ hutvā paccayo bhavituṃ sakkoti, paveṇī ghaṭiyati, tatrāpi cittaṃ aṅgato aparihīnaṃyeva rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Yadi hi cittaṃ ṭhānakkhaṇe vā bhaṅgakkhaṇe vā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeyya, paṭisandhicittampi rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeyya. Na pana cittaṃ tasmiṃ khaṇadvaye rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Yathā pana ahicchattakamakulaṃ pathavito uṭṭhahantaṃ paṃsucuṇṇaṃ gahetvāva uṭṭhahati, evaṃ cittaṃ purejātaṃ vatthuṃ nissāya uppādakkhaṇe aṭṭha rūpāni gahetvāva uṭṭhahati. Paṭisandhikkhaṇe ca vatthu purejātaṃ hutvā paccayo bhavituṃ na sakkotīti paccayavekallatāyapi paṭisandhicittaṃ rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpeti.

The rebirth-linking consciousness arises together with its physical base, neither after nor before. Its physical base cannot serve as a pre-arisen condition. If it could, the consciousness would generate material form. Even where the physical base, having pre-arisen, can serve as a condition and a continuity is established, there too the consciousness generates material form only when it is not deficient in its components. If consciousness were to generate material form at the moment of its abiding or dissolution, then the rebirth-linking consciousness too would generate material form. But consciousness does not generate material form at those two moments. Just as a mushroom bud, rising from the earth, takes dust particles with it as it rises, so too consciousness, dependent on a pre-arisen physical base, takes an octad of material qualities with it as it arises. And at the moment of rebirth-linking, because the physical base cannot serve as a pre-arisen condition, the rebirth-linking consciousness also does not generate material form due to this deficiency of a condition.

Yathā ca āgantukapuriso agatapubbaṃ padesaṃ gato aññesaṃ [P 0.0024] – ‘etha bho, antogāme vo annapānagandhamālādīni dassāmī’ti vattuṃ na sakkoti, attano avisayatāya appahutatāya, evameva paṭisandhicittaṃ āgantukanti attano āgantukatāyapi rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpeti. Apica samatiṃsa kammajarūpāni cittasamuṭṭhānarūpānaṃ ṭhānaṃ gahetvā ṭhitānītipi paṭisandhicittaṃ rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpeti.

Just as a stranger, arriving in a place he has never been before, is unable to say to others, 'Come, friends, I will give you food, drink, perfumes, and garlands,' because it is not his domain and he lacks influence, even so, rebirth-linking consciousness, being a newcomer, does not generate material form because of its own state of being a newcomer. Furthermore, because thirty kamma-produced material phenomena stand in the place of mind-produced material phenomena, rebirth-linking consciousness does not generate material form.

Khīṇāsavassa pana cuticittaṃ vaṭṭamūlassa vūpasantattā na samuṭṭhāpeti. Tassa hi sabbabhavesu vaṭṭamūlaṃ vūpasantaṃ abhabbuppattikaṃ punabbhave paveṇī nāma [M 0.0023] natthi. Sotāpannassa pana satta bhave ṭhapetvā aṭṭhameva vaṭṭamūlaṃ vūpasantaṃ. Tasmā tassa cuticittaṃ sattasu bhavesu rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti[V 0.0023], sakadāgāmino dvīsu, anāgāmino ekasmiṃ. Khīṇāsavassa sabbabhavesu vaṭṭamūlassa vūpasantattā neva samuṭṭhāpeti.

For an Arahant, the consciousness at death does not generate material form, for the root of the round of existence has been pacified. For him, the root of the round is pacified in all states of existence, incapable of arising, and there is no continuity in a future existence. For a Stream-enterer, however, leaving aside seven existences, from the eighth the root of the round is pacified. Therefore, his consciousness at death generates material form in seven existences; for a Once-returner, in two; and for a Non-returner, in one. For an Arahant, since the root of the round has been pacified in all states of existence, it does not generate material form at all.

Dvipañcaviññāṇesu pana jhānaṅgaṃ natthi, maggaṅgaṃ natthi, hetu natthīti cittaṅgaṃ dubbalaṃ hotīti cittaṅgadubbalatāya tāni rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpenti. Cattāri arūpavipākāni tasmiṃ bhave rūpassa natthitāya rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpenti. Na kevalañca tāneva, yāni aññānipi tasmiṃ bhave aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalāni, dasa akusalāni, nava kiriyacittāni, cattāri āruppakusalāni, catasso āruppakiriyā, tīṇi maggacittāni, cattāri phalacittānīti dvecattālīsa cittāni uppajjanti, tānipi tattha rūpassa natthitāya eva rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpenti. Evaṃ paṭisandhicittaṃ rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpeti.

In the case of the ten sense-consciousnesses, there are no jhāna factors, no path factors, and no roots. Consequently, their mental factors are weak, and due to this weakness, they do not generate material form. The four immaterial resultant consciousnesses do not generate material form because of the absence of material form in that existence. Not only those, but also the other forty-two types of consciousness that arise in that existence—namely, the eight wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses, the ten unwholesome consciousnesses, the nine functional consciousnesses, the four immaterial wholesome consciousnesses, the four immaterial functional consciousnesses, the three path consciousnesses, and the four fruition consciousnesses—do not generate material form due to the absence of material form there. Thus, the rebirth-linking consciousness does not generate material form.

Utu pana paṭhamaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Ko esa utu nāmāti? Paṭisandhikkhaṇe uppannānaṃ samatiṃsakammajarūpānaṃ abbhantarā tejodhātu. Sā ṭhānaṃ patvā aṭṭha rūpāni samuṭṭhāpeti. Utu nāma cesa dandhanirodho; cittaṃ khippanirodhaṃ. Tasmiṃ dharanteyeva soḷasa cittāni uppajjitvā nirujjhanti. Tesu paṭisandhianantaraṃ paṭhamabhavaṅgacittaṃ uppādakkhaṇeyeva aṭṭha rūpāni samuṭṭhāpeti. Yadā pana saddassa uppattikālo bhavissati, tadā utucittāni saddanavakaṃ nāma samuṭṭhāpessanti. Kabaḷīkārāhāropi ṭhānaṃ patvā [P 0.0025] aṭṭha rūpāni samuṭṭhāpeti. Kuto panassa kabaḷīkārāhāroti? Mātito. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Temperature, however, first generates material form. What is this so-called temperature? It is the internal heat-element among the thirty kamma-born material phenomena that arose at the moment of rebirth-linking. Having reached its static phase, it generates an octad of material qualities. This temperature is of slow cessation; mind is of quick cessation. While it persists, sixteen mind-moments arise and cease. Among these, the first life-continuum consciousness, immediately following the rebirth-linking consciousness, generates an octad of material qualities at its moment of arising. But when the time for the arising of sound comes, then temperature and consciousness will generate the sound-nonad. Edible food, too, having reached its static phase, generates an octad of material qualities. From where does this edible food come? From the mother. And this has been said:

“Yañcassa bhuñjatī mātā, annaṃ pānañca bhojanaṃ;

Tena so tattha yāpeti, mātukucchigato naro”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.235);

“Whatever food, drink, and sustenance the mother consumes,

By that is he sustained there,

The person dwelling in the mother’s womb.”

Evaṃ kucchigato dārako mātarā ajjhohaṭaannapānaojāya yāpeti. Sāva ṭhānappattā aṭṭha rūpāni samuṭṭhāpeti. Nanu ca sā ojā kharā? Vatthu sukhumaṃ? Kathaṃ tattha patiṭṭhātīti? Paṭhamaṃ tāva na patiṭṭhāti; ekassa vā dvinnaṃ vā sattāhānaṃ gatakāle patiṭṭhāti. Tato pana pure vā patiṭṭhātu pacchā vā; yadā mātarā ajjhohaṭaannapānaojā dārakassa sarīre patiṭṭhāti, tadā aṭṭha rūpāni samuṭṭhāpeti.

Thus, the child in the womb is sustained by the nutritive essence of the food and drink consumed by the mother. That very essence, having reached its static phase, generates an octad of material qualities. But is not that nutritive essence coarse and the physical base subtle? How does it become established there? At first, it does not become established; it becomes established only after one or two weeks have passed. But whether it becomes established before or after this, when the nutritive essence of the food and drink consumed by the mother becomes established in the child's body, then it generates an octad of material qualities.

Opapātikassāpi [M 0.0024][V 0.0024] pakatipaṭiyattānaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyānaṃ atthiṭṭhāne nibbattassa tāni gahetvā ajjhoharato ṭhānappattā ojā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Eko annapānarahite araññe nibbattati, mahāchātako hoti, attanova jivhāya kheḷaṃ parivattetvā gilati. Tatrāpissa ṭhānappattā ojā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti.

Even for a spontaneously born being, when prepared staple and non-staple foods are present, and they take and consume them, the nutriment that reaches its proper place generates material form. One is born in a wilderness devoid of food and drink, suffering great hunger, and rolls saliva on their own tongue and swallows it. Even in that case, the nutriment that reaches its proper place generates material form.

Evaṃ pañcavīsatiyā koṭṭhāsesu dveva rūpāni rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpenti – tejodhātu ca kabaḷīkārāhāro ca. Arūpepi dveyeva dhammā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpenti – cittañceva kammacetanā ca. Tattha rūpaṃ uppādakkhaṇe ca bhaṅgakkhaṇe ca dubbalaṃ, ṭhānakkhaṇe balavanti ṭhānakkhaṇe rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Cittaṃ ṭhānakkhaṇe ca bhaṅgakkhaṇe ca dubbalaṃ, uppādakkhaṇeyeva balavanti uppādakkhaṇeyeva rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Kammacetanā niruddhāva paccayo hoti. Atīte kappakoṭisatasahassamatthakepi hi āyūhitaṃ kammaṃ etarahi paccayo hoti. Etarahi āyūhitaṃ anāgate kappakoṭisatasahassapariyosānepi paccayo hotīti. Evaṃ ‘pubbāparato’ veditabbā.

Thus, among the twenty-five kinds of material phenomena, only two produce material form: the fire element and edible food. Even among immaterial phenomena, only two produce material form: mind and kammic volition. Therein, material form is weak at the moments of arising and dissolution, but strong at the moment of abiding—it produces material form at the moment of abiding. The mind is weak at the moments of abiding and dissolution, but strong only at the moment of arising—it produces material form only at the moment of arising. Kammic volition becomes a condition only after it has ceased. For even kamma accumulated a hundred thousand koṭis of aeons ago can be a condition now. And kamma accumulated now can be a condition even at the end of a hundred thousand koṭis of aeons. Thus, it should be understood as 'from before and after.'

‘Addhānaparicchedato’ti rūpaṃ kittakaṃ addhānaṃ tiṭṭhati? Arūpaṃ kittakanti? Rūpaṃ garupariṇāmaṃ dandhanirodhaṃ. Arūpaṃ lahupariṇāmaṃ khippanirodhaṃ. Rūpe dharanteyeva soḷasa cittāni uppajjitvā nirujjhanti. Taṃ [P 0.0026] pana sattarasamena cittena saddhiṃ nirujjhati. Yathā hi puriso ‘phalaṃ pātessāmī’ti muggarena rukkhasākhaṃ pahareyya, phalāni ca pattāni ca ekakkhaṇeyeva vaṇṭato mucceyyuṃ. Tattha phalāni attano bhārikatāya paṭhamataraṃ pathaviyaṃ patanti, pattāni lahukatāya pacchā. Evameva muggarappahārena pattānañca phalānañca ekakkhaṇe vaṇṭato muttakālo viya paṭisandhikkhaṇe rūpārūpadhammānaṃ ekakkhaṇe pātubhāvo; phalānaṃ bhārikatāya paṭhamataraṃ pathaviyaṃ patanaṃ viya rūpe dharanteyeva soḷasannaṃ cittānaṃ uppajjitvā nirujjhanaṃ; pattānaṃ lahukatāya pacchā pathaviyaṃ patanaṃ viya rūpassa sattarasamena cittena saha nirujjhanaṃ.

'In terms of the limitation of duration,' how long does material form endure? How long does the immaterial endure? Material form undergoes a heavy transformation and ceases slowly. The immaterial undergoes a light transformation and ceases quickly. While material form persists, sixteen mind-moments arise and cease. But it ceases together with the seventeenth mind-moment. Just as when a man, intending to knock down fruit, strikes a tree branch with a club, the fruits and leaves are severed from their stems in a single moment. There, due to their weight, the fruits fall to the ground first, while the leaves, being lighter, fall later. Even so, the simultaneous appearance of material and immaterial phenomena at the moment of rebirth-linking is like the moment when fruits and leaves are severed from their stems at the same instant by the blow of a club; the arising and ceasing of sixteen mind-moments while material form persists is like the fruits falling to the ground first due to their weight; and the ceasing of material form together with the seventeenth mind-moment is like the leaves falling to the ground later due to their lightness.

Tattha kiñcāpi rūpaṃ dandhanirodhaṃ garupariṇāmaṃ, cittaṃ khippanirodhaṃ lahupariṇāmaṃ, rūpaṃ pana arūpaṃ arūpaṃ vā rūpaṃ ohāya pavattituṃ na sakkonti. Dvinnampi ekappamāṇāva pavatti. Tatrāyaṃ upamā – eko puriso lakuṇṭakapādo, eko dīghapādo. Tesu ekato maggaṃ gacchantesu yāva dīghapādo [M 0.0025] ekapadavāraṃ akkamati, tāva itaro pade padaṃ akkamitvā soḷasapadavārena gacchati. Dīghapādo lakuṇṭakapādassa soḷasa padavāre attano pādaṃ añchitvā [V 0.0025] ākaḍḍhitvā ekameva padavāraṃ karoti. Iti ekopi ekaṃ atikkamituṃ na sakkoti. Dvinnampi gamanaṃ ekappamāṇameva hoti. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Lakuṇṭakapādapuriso viya arūpaṃ; dīghapādapuriso viya rūpaṃ; dīghapādassa ekaṃ padavāraṃ akkamaṇakāle itarassa soḷasapadavāraakkamanaṃ viya rūpe dharanteyeva arūpadhammesu soḷasannaṃ cittānaṃ uppajjitvā nirujjhanaṃ; dvinnaṃ purisānaṃ lakuṇṭakapādapurisassa soḷasa padavāre itarassa attano pādaṃ añchitvā ākaḍḍhitvā ekapadavārakaraṇaṃ viya rūpassa sattarasamena cittena saddhiṃ nirujjhanaṃ; dvinnaṃ purisānaṃ aññamaññaṃ anohāya ekappamāṇeneva gamanaṃ viya arūpassa rūpaṃ rūpassa arūpaṃ anohāya ekappamāṇeneva pavattananti. Evaṃ ‘addhānaparicchedato’ veditabbā.

Here, although material form is slow to cease and undergoes gross change, while consciousness is quick to cease and undergoes subtle change, material form cannot proceed abandoning immaterial form, nor can immaterial form proceed abandoning material form. Both have their occurrence at the same rate. Herein is this simile: One man has a short leg, another a long leg. As they walk together on a road, for every one step the long-legged man takes, the other takes sixteen steps, placing foot by foot. The long-legged man, drawing in and pulling back his foot at the sixteen steps of the short-legged man, makes only one step. Thus, neither can outpace the other. The walking of both is at the same rate. This should be seen in the same way. The immaterial is like the short-legged man; material form is like the long-legged man. The arising and ceasing of sixteen consciousnesses among the immaterial phenomena while material form endures is like the other taking sixteen steps while the long-legged man takes one step. The ceasing of material form together with the seventeenth consciousness is like the long-legged man making one step by drawing in and pulling back his foot during the sixteen steps of the short-legged man. The proceeding of immaterial form not abandoning material form, and of material form not abandoning immaterial form, both at the same rate, is like the two men walking together without abandoning each other, proceeding at the same rate. Thus, it should be understood as 'in terms of the limitation of duration'.

‘Ekuppādanānānirodhato’ti idaṃ pacchimakammajaṃ ṭhapetvā dīpetabbaṃ. Paṭhamañhi paṭisandhicittaṃ, dutiyaṃ [P 0.0027] bhavaṅgaṃ, tatiyaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ…pe… soḷasamaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ. Tesu ekekassa uppādaṭṭhitibhaṅgavasena tayo tayo khaṇā. Tattha ekekassa cittassa tīsu tīsu khaṇesu samatiṃsa samatiṃsa kammajarūpāni uppajjanti. Tesu paṭisandhicittassa uppādakkhaṇe samuṭṭhitaṃ kammajarūpaṃ sattarasamassa bhavaṅgacittassa uppādakkhaṇeyeva nirujjhati; ṭhitikkhaṇe samuṭṭhitaṃ ṭhitikkhaṇeyeva; bhaṅgakkhaṇe samuṭṭhitaṃ bhaṅgakkhaṇeyeva nirujjhati. Evaṃ dutiyabhavaṅgacittaṃ ādiṃ katvā attano attano sattarasamena cittena saddhiṃ yojetvā nayo netabbo. Iti soḷasa tikā aṭṭhacattālīsa honti. Ayaṃ aṭṭhacattālīsakammajarūpapaveṇī nāma. Sā panesā rattiñca divā ca khādantānampi bhuñjantānampi suttānampi pamattānampi nadīsoto viya ekantaṃ pavattati yevāti. Evaṃ ‘ekuppādanānānirodhato’ veditabbā.

'By way of one arising and many cessations'—this should be explained by excluding the last kamma-born material form. For first is the rebirth-linking consciousness, second the life-continuum consciousness, third the life-continuum consciousness… up to the sixteenth life-continuum consciousness. In these, for each, there are three moments: arising, presence, and dissolution. Therein, for each consciousness, in each of the three moments, thirty kamma-born material forms arise. Among these, the kamma-born material form that arises in the arising moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases in the arising moment of the seventeenth life-continuum consciousness; that which arises in the presence moment ceases in the presence moment; and that which arises in the dissolution moment ceases in the dissolution moment. In this way, beginning with the second life-continuum consciousness, the method should be applied by connecting each with its own seventeenth consciousness. Thus, there are sixteen triads, making forty-eight. This is called the sequence of forty-eight kamma-born material forms. Moreover, this flows continuously like a river, whether by night or day, while eating, drinking, sleeping, or being heedless. Thus, it should be understood as 'by way of one arising and many cessations'.

‘Nānuppādaekanirodhatā’ pacchimakammajena dīpetabbā. Tattha āyusaṃkhārapariyosāne soḷasannaṃ cittānaṃ vāre sati heṭṭhāsoḷasakaṃ uparisoḷasakanti dve ekato yojetabbāni. Heṭṭhāsoḷasakasmiñhi paṭhamacittassa uppādakkhaṇe samuṭṭhitaṃ samatiṃsakammajarūpaṃ uparisoḷasakasmiṃ paṭhamacittassa uppādakkhaṇeyeva nirujjhati; ṭhitikkhaṇe samuṭṭhitaṃ tassa ṭhitikkhaṇeyeva [M 0.0026] bhaṅgakkhaṇe samuṭṭhitaṃ tassa bhaṅgakkhaṇeyeva nirujjhati. Heṭṭhimasoḷasakasmiṃ pana dutiyacittassa…pe… soḷasamacittassa uppādakkhaṇe samuṭṭhitaṃ samatiṃsakammajarūpaṃ cuticittassa uppādakkhaṇeyeva nirujjhati; tassa ṭhitikkhaṇe samuṭṭhitaṃ cuticittassa ṭhitikkhaṇeyeva; bhaṅgakkhaṇe samuṭṭhitaṃ cuticittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇeyeva nirujjhati. Tato paṭṭhāya kammajarūpapaveṇī [V 0.0026] na pavattati. Yadi pavatteyya, sattā akkhayā avayā ajarā amarā nāma bhaveyyuṃ.

'Many arisings, one cessation' should be explained by means of the last kamma-born material form. Here, at the termination of the life-span, when there are sixteen consciousness-moments, the lower sixteen and the upper sixteen should be combined as one. For in the lower sixteen, the thirty kamma-born material forms that arise in the arising moment of the first consciousness cease in the arising moment of the first consciousness in the upper sixteen; that which arises in the presence moment ceases in that presence moment itself; that which arises in the dissolution moment ceases in that dissolution moment itself. But in the lower sixteen, the thirty kamma-born material forms arising in the arising moment of the second consciousness... up to the sixteenth consciousness cease in the arising moment of the death-consciousness; that which arises in its presence moment ceases in the presence moment of the death-consciousness; that which arises in its dissolution moment ceases in the dissolution moment of the death-consciousness. From then on, the sequence of kamma-born material forms does not proceed. If it were to proceed, beings would become undecaying, indestructible, unaging, and immortal.

Ettha pana yadetaṃ ‘sattarasamassa bhavaṅgacittassa uppādakkhaṇeyeva nirujjhatī’tiādinā nayena ‘ekassa cittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppannaṃ rūpaṃ aññassa uppādakkhaṇe nirujjhatī’ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatattā vuttaṃ, taṃ “yassa [P 0.0028] kāyasaṅkhāro nirujjhati, tassa cittasaṅkhāro nirujjhatī”ti? “Āmantā”ti (yama. 2.saṅkhārayamaka.79) imāya pāḷiyā virujjhati. Kathaṃ? Kāyasaṅkhāro hi cittasamuṭṭhāno assāsapassāsavāto. Cittasamuṭṭhānarūpañca cittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppajjitvā yāva aññāni soḷasa cittāni uppajjanti tāva tiṭṭhati. Tesaṃ soḷasannaṃ sabbapacchimena saddhiṃ nirujjhati. Iti yena cittena saddhiṃ uppajjati, tato paṭṭhāya sattarasamena saddhiṃ nirujjhati; na kassaci cittassa uppādakkhaṇe vā ṭhitikkhaṇe vā nirujjhati, nāpi ṭhitikkhaṇe vā bhaṅgakkhaṇe vā uppajjati. Esā cittasamuṭṭhānarūpassa dhammatāti niyamato cittasaṅkhārena saddhiṃ ekakkhaṇe nirujjhanato “āmantā”ti vuttaṃ.

Here, however, what is stated in the commentary, in the manner of 'it ceases precisely at the arising moment of the seventeenth life-continuum consciousness,' and 'the material form arisen at the arising moment of one consciousness ceases at the arising moment of another,' contradicts this Pāli passage: 'When the bodily formation ceases, does the mental formation cease?' 'Yes.' (Yamaka 2, Saṅkhārayamaka, 79). How so? For the bodily formation is the in-and-out breath, which is mind-originated. And mind-originated material form arises at the arising moment of a consciousness and persists until sixteen other consciousnesses have arisen. It ceases together with the very last of those sixteen. Thus, it arises together with a particular consciousness and ceases together with the seventeenth from that starting point. It does not cease at the arising or presence moment of any consciousness, nor does it arise at the presence or dissolution moment. This is the nature of mind-originated material form; because, as a rule, it ceases in a single moment together with the mental formation, 'Yes' is said.

Yo cāyaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānassa khaṇaniyamo vutto kammādisamuṭṭhānassāpi ayameva khaṇaniyamo. Tasmā paṭisandhicittena sahuppannaṃ kammajarūpaṃ tato paṭṭhāya sattarasamena saddhiṃ nirujjhati. Paṭisandhicittassa ṭhitikkhaṇe uppannaṃ aṭṭhārasamassa uppādakkhaṇe nirujjhati. Paṭisandhicittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe uppannaṃ aṭṭhārasamassa ṭhānakkhaṇe nirujjhatīti iminā nayenettha yojanā kātabbā. Tato paraṃ pana utusamuṭṭhānikapaveṇīyeva tiṭṭhati. ‘Nīharitvā jhāpethā’ti vattabbaṃ hoti. Evaṃ ‘nānuppādaekanirodhato’ veditabbā.

The rule of moments stated for mind-originated material form applies equally to material form originating from kamma and other causes. Therefore, the kamma-born material form that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases together with the seventeenth consciousness from that point onward. The material form that arises at the presence moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases at the arising moment of the eighteenth consciousness. The material form that arises at the dissolution moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases at the presence moment of the eighteenth consciousness—this is how the connection should be made here. After that, only the sequence of temperature-originated material form remains. It is said, 'Remove and cremate it.' Thus, 'many arisings, one cessation' should be understood.

‘Ekuppādaekanirodhato’ti rūpaṃ pana rūpena saha ekuppādaṃ ekanirodhaṃ. Arūpaṃ arūpena saha ekuppādaṃ ekanirodhaṃ. Evaṃ ‘ekuppādaekanirodhato’ veditabbā.

'One arising, one cessation': material form arises together and ceases together with other material form. Immaterial form arises together and ceases together with other immaterial form. Thus, 'one arising, one cessation' should be understood.

‘Nānuppādanānānirodhatā’ [M 0.0027] pana catusantatirūpena dīpetabbā. Imassa hi uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā tacapariyantassa sarīrassa tattha tattha catusantatirūpaṃ ghanapuñjabhāvena vattati. Evaṃ vattamānassāpissa na ekuppādāditā sallakkhetabbā. Yathā pana upacikarāji vā kipillikarāji vā olokiyamānā ekābaddhā viya hoti, na pana ekābaddhā. Aññissā hi [V 0.0027] sīsasantike aññissā sīsampi udarampi pādāpi, aññissā udarasantike aññissā sīsampi udarampi pādāpi, aññissā pādasantike aññissā sīsampi udarampi pādāpi honti. Evameva catusantatirūpānampi aññassa uppādakkhaṇe [P 0.0029] aññassa uppādopi hoti ṭhitipi bhaṅgopi, aññassa ṭhitikkhaṇe aññassa uppādopi hoti ṭhitipi bhaṅgopi, aññassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe aññassa uppādopi hoti ṭhitipi bhaṅgopi. Evamettha ‘nānuppādanānānirodhatā’ veditabbā.

'Many arisings, many cessations' should be explained by means of the fourfold continuity of material form. For in this body, from the soles of the feet up to the crown of the head, bounded by the skin, the fourfold continuity of material form occurs here and there as a dense mass. Even while occurring thus, it should not be perceived as having a single arising, and so forth. Just as when observing a line of termites or a line of ants, it appears as if connected as one, but it is not actually connected as one. For near the head of one, there is also the head, belly, and feet of another; near the belly of one, there is also the head, belly, and feet of another; near the feet of one, there is also the head, belly, and feet of another. In the same way, regarding the material forms of the fourfold continuity, at the arising moment of one, there is also the arising, presence, or dissolution of another; at the presence moment of one, there is also the arising, presence, or dissolution of another; at the dissolution moment of one, there is also the arising, presence, or dissolution of another. Thus, in this context, 'many arisings, many cessations' should be understood.

‘Atītādīni’ pana dūradukapariyosānāni pāḷiyaṃ āgatāneva. ‘Paccayasamuṭṭhānāni’pi “kammajaṃ, kammapaccayaṃ, kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhāna”ntiādinā (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 975) nayena heṭṭhā kathitāniyeva. Pañcapi pana khandhā parinipphannāva honti, no aparinipphannā; saṅkhatāva no asaṅkhatā; apica nipphannāpi hontiyeva. Sabhāvadhammesu hi nibbānamevekaṃ aparinipphannaṃ anipphannañca. Nirodhasamāpatti pana nāmapaññatti ca kathanti? Nirodhasamāpatti lokiyalokuttarāti vā saṅkhatāsaṅkhatāti vā parinipphannāparinipphannāti vā na vattabbā. Nipphannā pana hoti samāpajjantena samāpajjitabbato. Tathā nāmapaññatti. Sāpi hi lokiyādibhedaṃ na labhati; nipphannā pana hoti no anipphannā; nāmaggahaṇañhi gaṇhantova gaṇhātīti.

'Past, etc.' are indeed mentioned in the Pāli, ending with the couplet on the distant. 'Arising by conditions' has also been explained above in the manner of "arisen from kamma, conditioned by kamma, arisen from temperature conditioned by kamma, etc." (Dhs-a. 975). Moreover, the five aggregates are only fully perfected, not unperfected; they are conditioned, not unconditioned. Yet, they are indeed produced. Among real phenomena, only Nibbāna is unperfected and unproduced. But what of the attainment of cessation and name-concept? The attainment of cessation cannot be described as mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned, perfected or unperfected. However, it is produced because it is to be attained by one who attains it. The same applies to name-concept. It too does not receive the classification of mundane, etc., but it is produced, not unproduced; for the grasping of a name is grasped by one who is grasping.

Kamādivinicchayakathā

The Discourse on the Determination of Order, etc.

Evaṃ pakiṇṇakato khandhe viditvā puna etesuyeva –

Having thus understood the aggregates miscellaneously, again regarding these very aggregates—

Khandhesu ñāṇabhedatthaṃ, kamatotha visesato;

Anūnādhikato ceva, upamāto tatheva ca.

For the discrimination of knowledge in the aggregates, by order and then specifically; by being neither deficient nor excessive, and likewise by way of simile.

Daṭṭhabbato dvidhā evaṃ, passantassatthasiddhito;

Vinicchayanayo sammā, viññātabbo vibhāvinā.

Thus it is to be seen in two ways, for the accomplishment of purpose by one who sees; the method of discernment should be rightly understood by the discerning.

Tattha [M 0.0028][V 0.0028] ‘kamato’ti idha uppattikkamo, pahānakkamo, paṭipattikkamo, bhūmikkamo, desanākkamoti bahuvidho kamo.

Therein, 'in order' means the order of arising, the order of abandoning, the order of practice, the order of planes, and the order of teaching—thus, the order is of many kinds.

Tattha “paṭhamaṃ kalalaṃ hoti, kalalā hoti abbuda”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.235) evamādi uppattikkamo. “Dassanena pahātabbā dhammā, bhāvanāya pahātabbā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. tikamātikā 8) evamādi pahānakkamo. “Sīlavisuddhi, cittavisuddhī”ti (ma. ni. 1.259; paṭi. ma. 3.41) evamādi paṭipattikkamo. “Kāmāvacarā[P 0.0030], rūpāvacarā”ti evamādi bhūmikkamo. “Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, cattāro sammappadhānā”ti (dī. ni. 3.145) vā “dānakathaṃ sīlakatha”nti (ma. ni. 2.69; dī. ni. 1.298) vā evamādi desanākkamo. Tesu idha uppattikkamo tāva na yujjati, kalalādīnaṃ viya khandhānaṃ pubbāpariyavavatthānena anuppattito; na pahānakkamo kusalābyākatānaṃ appahātabbato; na paṭipattikkamo akusalānaṃ appaṭipajjanīyato; na bhūmikkamo vedanādīnaṃ catubhūmakapariyāpannattā.

Therein, the order of arising is such as: 'First, there is the kalala, from the kalala arises the abbuda' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.235). The order of abandoning is such as: 'States to be abandoned by seeing, states to be abandoned by development' (Dha. Sa. Tikamātikā 8). The order of practice is such as: 'Purification of virtue, purification of mind' (Ma. Ni. 1.259; Paṭi. Ma. 3.41). The order of planes is such as: 'Pertaining to the sense-sphere, pertaining to the form-sphere.' The order of teaching is such as: 'The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts' (Dī. Ni. 3.145) or 'talk on giving, talk on virtue' (Ma. Ni. 2.69; Dī. Ni. 1.298). Among these, in this context, the order of arising is not applicable, since the aggregates do not arise with an established prior and posterior sequence like the kalala and so on. Nor is the order of abandoning, since wholesome and indeterminate states are not to be abandoned. Nor is the order of practice, since unwholesome states are not to be practiced. Nor is the order of planes, since feelings and the like are included within the four planes.

Desanākkamo pana yujjati. Abhedena hi yaṃ pañcasu khandhesu attaggāhapatitaṃ veneyyajanaṃ samūhaghanavinibbhogadassanena attaggāhato mocetukāmo bhagavā hitakāmo tassa janassa sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ cakkhuādīnampi visayabhūtaṃ oḷārikaṃ paṭhamaṃ rūpakkhandhaṃ desesi. Tato iṭṭhāniṭṭharūpasaṃveditaṃ vedanaṃ, yaṃ vedayati taṃ sañjānātīti evaṃ vedanāvisayassa ākāraggāhikaṃ saññaṃ, saññāvasena abhisaṅkhārake saṅkhāre, tesaṃ vedanādīnaṃ nissayaṃ adhipatibhūtañca viññāṇanti evaṃ tāva ‘kamato’ vinicchayanayo viññātabbo.

The order of teaching, however, is applicable. For the Blessed One, desiring their welfare and for the sake of their easy understanding, wished to free those disciples who had fallen into the grasp of self with regard to the five aggregates by showing them the analysis that breaks up the mass of compactness. He first taught the aggregate of form, which is gross and the object of the eye and so on. Then feeling, whereby pleasant and unpleasant objects are experienced; then perception, which grasps the features of the object of feeling in the manner, 'What one feels, that one perceives'; then the formations, which fashion by means of perception; and then consciousness, which is the support and dominant factor for feeling and the others. Thus, for now, the method of discernment is to be understood as 'in order.'

‘Visesato’ti khandhānañca upādānakkhandhānañca visesato. Ko pana tesaṃ viseso? Khandhā tāva avisesato vuttā, upādānakkhandhā sāsavaupādānīyabhāvena visesetvā. Yathāha –

'Specifically' means with distinction as to the aggregates and the aggregates of clinging. What then is their distinction? The aggregates are spoken of without specification, while the aggregates of clinging are specified as being tainted and subject to clinging. As it is said—

“Pañca, bhikkhave, khandhe desessāmi pañcupādānakkhandhe ca, taṃ suṇātha. Katame ca, bhikkhave, pañcakkhandhā? Yaṃ kiñci, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ…pe… santike vā – ayaṃ vuccati, rūpakkhandho. Yā kāci vedanā…pe… yā kāci saññā…pe… ye keci saṅkhārā…pe… yaṃ kiñci viññāṇaṃ [V 0.0029] …pe… santike vā – ayaṃ vuccati, viññāṇakkhandho. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, pañcakkhandhā. Katame ca, bhikkhave, pañcupādānakkhandhā? Yaṃ [M 0.0029] kiñci, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ…pe… santike vā sāsavaṃ upādāniyaṃ – ayaṃ vuccati, rūpūpādānakkhandho. Yā kāci vedanā…pe… yaṃ kiñci viññāṇaṃ…pe… santike vā sāsavaṃ upādāniyaṃ – ayaṃ [P 0.0031] vuccati, bhikkhave, viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, pañcupādānakkhandhā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.48).

“Monks, I will teach the five aggregates and the five aggregates of clinging. Listen to that. And what, monks, are the five aggregates? Whatever form, monks, past, future, or present… far or near—this is called the aggregate of form. Whatever feeling… Whatever perception… Whatever formations… Whatever consciousness… far or near—this is called the aggregate of consciousness. These, monks, are called the five aggregates. And what, monks, are the five aggregates of clinging? Whatever form, monks… far or near, that is tainted and subject to clinging—this is called the aggregate of clinging to form. Whatever feeling… Whatever consciousness… far or near, that is tainted and subject to clinging—this is called, monks, the aggregate of clinging to consciousness. These, monks, are called the five aggregates of clinging.”

Ettha ca yathā vedanādayo anāsavāpi sāsavāpi atthi, na evaṃ rūpaṃ. Yasmā panassa rāsaṭṭhena khandhabhāvo yujjati tasmā khandhesu vuttaṃ. Yasmā rāsaṭṭhena ca sāsavaṭṭhena ca upādānakkhandhabhāvo yujjati tasmā upādānakkhandhesu vuttaṃ. Vedanādayo pana anāsavāva khandhesu vuttā, sāsavā upādānakkhandhesu. ‘Upādānakkhandhā’ti ettha ca upādānagocarā khandhā upādānakkhandhāti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Idha pana sabbepete ekajjhaṃ katvā khandhāti adhippetā.

Here, while feelings and the like can be both taint-free and tainted, this is not so for form. Because it qualifies as an aggregate due to its characteristic of being a mass, it is included among the aggregates. And because it qualifies as an aggregate of clinging due to its characteristic of being a mass and being tainted, it is included among the aggregates of clinging. Feelings and the like, however, are spoken of as aggregates only when they are taint-free; when tainted, they are spoken of as aggregates of clinging. The term ‘aggregates of clinging’ here should be understood to mean 'aggregates that are the object of clinging.' In this context, however, all these are collectively intended by the term ‘aggregates.’

‘Anūnādhikato’ti kasmā pana bhagavatā pañceva khandhā vuttā anūnā anadhikāti? Sabbasaṅkhatasabhāgekasaṅgahato, attattaniyaggāhavatthussa etapparamato, aññesañca tadavarodhato. Anekappabhedesu hi saṅkhatadhammesu sabhāgavasena saṅgayhamānesu rūpaṃ rūpasabhāgasaṅgahavasena eko khandho hoti, vedanā vedanāsabhāgasaṅgahavasena eko khandho hoti. Esa nayo saññādīsupi. Tasmā sabbasaṅkhatasabhāgasaṅgahato pañceva vuttā. Etaparamañcetaṃ attattaniyaggāhavatthu yadidaṃ rūpādayo pañca. Vuttañhetaṃ – “rūpe kho, bhikkhave, sati rūpaṃ upādāya rūpaṃ abhinivissa evaṃ diṭṭhi uppajjati – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti (saṃ. ni. 3.207). Vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu…. Viññāṇe sati viññāṇaṃ upādāya viññāṇaṃ abhinivissa evaṃ diṭṭhi uppajjati – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti. Tasmā attattaniyaggāhavatthussa etaparamatopi pañceva vuttā. Yepi caññe sīlādayo pañca dhammakkhandhā vuttā, tepi saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannattā ettheva avarodhaṃ gacchanti. Tasmā aññesaṃ tadavarodhatopi pañceva vuttāti. Evaṃ ‘anūnādhikato’ vinicchayanayo viññātabbo.

‘Neither less nor more’—why did the Blessed One speak of only five aggregates, neither fewer nor more? Because of the inclusion of all conditioned phenomena of similar nature, because they are the ultimate basis for grasping as self and what belongs to self, and because other classifications are contained within them. For when the manifold conditioned phenomena are grouped by similarity of nature, form becomes one aggregate by being grouped with similar forms, feeling becomes one aggregate by being grouped with similar feelings. The same principle applies to perception and the rest. Thus, because of the inclusion of all conditioned phenomena of similar nature, only five are mentioned. Moreover, these five—form and so on—are the ultimate basis for grasping as self and what belongs to self. As it is said: “When there is form, monks, by clinging to form and being intent upon it, such a view arises: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’… When there is consciousness, by clinging to consciousness and being intent upon it, such a view arises: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’” Therefore, because they are the ultimate basis for grasping as self and what belongs to self, only five are mentioned. And as for other classifications, such as the five groups of Dhamma, they too, being included within the aggregate of formations, are contained herein. Thus, because other classifications are contained within them, only five are mentioned. In this way, the method of discernment should be understood as ‘neither less nor more.’

‘Upamāto’ti ettha hi gilānasālūpamo rūpupādānakkhandho [P 0.0032] gilānūpamassa viññāṇupādānakkhandhassa [V 0.0030] vatthudvārārammaṇavasena nivāsanaṭṭhānato, gelaññūpamo [M 0.0030] vedanupādānakkhandho ābādhakattā, gelaññasamuṭṭhānūpamo saññupādānakkhandho kāmasaññādivasena rāgādisampayuttavedanāsambhavā, asappāyasevanūpamo saṅkhārupādānakkhandho vedanāgelaññassa nidānattā. “Vedanaṃ vedanattāya saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharontī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.79) hi vuttaṃ. Tathā “akusalassa kammassa katattā upacitattā vipākaṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppannaṃ hoti dukkhasahagata”nti (dha. sa. 556). Gilānūpamo viññāṇupādānakkhandho vedanāgelaññena aparimuttattā. Apica cārakakāraṇaaparādhakāraṇakārakaaparādhikūpamā ete bhājanabhojanabyañjanaparivesakabhuñjakūpamā cāti, evaṃ ‘upamāto’ vinicchayanayo viññātabbo.

‘By simile’—here, the aggregate of clinging to form is like a sickroom, serving as the dwelling place for the aggregate of clinging to consciousness, which is like the sick person, by providing the basis, door, and object. The aggregate of clinging to feeling is like the sickness because it is the agent that afflicts. The aggregate of clinging to perception is like the origin of the sickness because perceptions such as sensual perception give rise to feelings associated with lust and the like. The aggregate of clinging to volitional formations is like unsuitable care because it is the cause of the sickness of feeling. As it is said: “They fashion the conditioned as feeling for the sake of feeling” (Saṃ. Ni. 3.79). Similarly: “Due to having done and accumulated unwholesome kamma, painful resultant body-consciousness arises” (Dha. Sa. 556). The aggregate of clinging to consciousness is like the sick person because it is not freed from the sickness of feeling. Furthermore, these can be compared to the attendant, the cause of the offense, the perpetrator of the offense, the offender, as well as the vessel, the food, the seasoning, the server, and the consumer. Thus, the method of analysis should be understood as ‘by simile.’

‘Daṭṭhabbato dvidhā’ti saṅkhepato vitthārato cāti evaṃ dvidhā daṭṭhabbato pettha vinicchayanayo viññātabbo. Saṅkhepato hi pañcupādānakkhandhā āsivisūpame (saṃ. ni. 4.238) vuttanayena ukkhittāsikapaccatthikato, bhārasuttavasena (saṃ. ni. 3.22) bhārato, khajjanīyapariyāyavasena (saṃ. ni. 3.79) khādakato, yamakasuttavasena (saṃ. ni. 3.85) aniccadukkhānattasaṅkhatavadhakato daṭṭhabbā.

'To be seen in two ways' means briefly and in detail. Thus, the method of analysis here should be understood as twofold. Briefly, the five aggregates of clinging should be seen as an enemy with a raised sword (as in SN 4.238), as a burden (as in SN 3.22), as a devourer (as in SN 3.79), and as impermanent, suffering, non-self, conditioned, and a killer (as in SN 3.85).

Vitthārato panettha pheṇapiṇḍo viya rūpaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, udakapubbuḷo viya vedanā, marīcikā viya saññā, kadalikkhandho viya saṅkhārā, māyā viya viññāṇaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

In detail, here form should be seen as like a mass of foam, feeling as like a water bubble, perception as like a mirage, volitional formations as like a plantain trunk, and consciousness as like an illusion. For this has been said:

“Pheṇapiṇḍūpamaṃ rūpaṃ, vedanā pubbuḷūpamā;

Marīcikūpamā saññā, saṅkhārā kadalūpamā;

Māyūpamañca viññāṇaṃ, desitādiccabandhunā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 3.95);

"Form is like a lump of foam, feeling is like a bubble; perception is like a mirage, volitional formations are like a banana trunk; and consciousness is like an illusion, as taught by the Kinsman of the Sun." (SN 3.95)

Tattha rūpādīnaṃ pheṇapiṇḍādīhi evaṃ sadisatā veditabbā – yathā hi pheṇapiṇḍo nissārova evaṃ rūpampi niccasāradhuvasāraattasāravirahena nissārameva. Yathā ca so ‘iminā pattaṃ vā thālakaṃ vā karissāmī’ti gahetuṃ na sakkā, gahitopi tamatthaṃ na sādheti bhijjateva; evaṃ rūpampi [P 0.0033] ‘nicca’nti vā ‘dhuva’nti vā ‘aha’nti vā ‘mama’nti vā gahetuṃ na [V 0.0031] sakkā, gahitampi na tathā tiṭṭhati, aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā asubhaññeva hotīti. Evaṃ ‘pheṇapiṇḍasadisameva’ hoti.

Here, the similarity of form and the rest to a lump of foam and so on should be understood as follows: Just as a lump of foam is without essence, so too form is without essence, being devoid of a permanent essence, a stable essence, or a self-essence. And just as that lump cannot be taken hold of to make a bowl or dish, and even if taken, it does not serve that purpose but simply breaks up, so too form cannot be taken hold of as permanent or stable or as 'I' or 'mine,' and even if taken, it does not remain so but is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and unattractive. Thus, it is 'just like a lump of foam.'

Yathā [M 0.0031] vā pana pheṇapiṇḍo chiddāvachiddo anekasandhighaṭito bahūnnaṃ udakasappādīnaṃ pāṇānaṃ āvāso, evaṃ rūpampi chiddāvachiddaṃ anekasandhighaṭitaṃ. Kulavasena cettha asīti kimikulāni vasanti. Tadeva tesaṃ sūtigharampi vaccakuṭipi gilānasālāpi susānampi. Na te aññattha gantvā gabbhavuṭṭhānādīni karonti. Evampi pheṇapiṇḍasadisaṃ. Yathā ca pheṇapiṇḍo āditova badarapakkamatto hutvā anupubbena pabbatakūṭamattopi hoti, evaṃ rūpampi ādito kalalamattaṃ hutvā anupubbena byāmamattampi gomahiṃsahatthiādīnaṃ vasena pabbatakūṭamattampi hoti, macchakacchapādīnaṃ vasena anekayojanasatappamāṇampi. Evampi pheṇapiṇḍasadisaṃ. Yathā ca pheṇapiṇḍo uṭṭhitamattopi bhijjati, thokaṃ gantvāpi, samuddaṃ patvā pana avassameva bhijjati; evameva rūpampi kalalabhāvepi bhijjati, abbudādibhāve, antarā pana abhejjamānampi vassasatāyukānaṃ vassasataṃ patvā avassameva bhijjati, maraṇamukhe cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ hoti. Evampi pheṇapiṇḍasadisaṃ.

Furthermore, just as a lump of foam is full of holes and fissures, interconnected, and a dwelling place for many water creatures like snakes, so too is form full of holes and fissures, interconnected. In this case, eighty kinds of worms dwell based on their lineage. For them, this same body is a birthing room, a privy, a sickroom, and a cemetery. They do not go elsewhere to perform acts such as emerging from the womb. In this way too, it is like a lump of foam. And just as a lump of foam, initially the size of a jujube berry, gradually becomes as large as a mountain peak, so too form, initially the size of a speck of moisture, gradually grows to the size of a fathom, and in the case of cows, buffaloes, and elephants, even to the size of a mountain peak, or in the case of fish and turtles, extending even hundreds of leagues. In this way too, it is like a lump of foam. And just as a lump of foam breaks up as soon as it arises, or after moving a short distance, or inevitably upon reaching the ocean; so too form breaks up even in the stage of a speck of moisture or an embryonic stage, and though it may not break up in between, upon reaching a hundred years for those with such a lifespan, it inevitably breaks up, crumbling to dust at the moment of death. In this way too, it is like a lump of foam.

Yathā pana pubbuḷo asāro, evaṃ vedanāpi. Yathā ca so abalo, agayhupago, na sakkā taṃ gahetvā phalakaṃ vā āsanaṃ vā kātuṃ, gahitaggahitopi bhijjateva; evaṃ vedanāpi abalā, agayhupagā, na sakkā ‘niccā’ti vā ‘dhuvā’ti vā gahetuṃ, gahitāpi na tathā tiṭṭhati. Evaṃ agayhupagatāyapi vedanā ‘pubbuḷasadisā’. Yathā pana tasmiṃ tasmiṃ udakabindumhi pubbuḷo uppajjati ceva nirujjhati ca, na ciraṭṭhitiko hoti; evaṃ vedanāpi uppajjati ceva nirujjhati ca, na ciraṭṭhitikā hoti, ekaccharakkhaṇe koṭisatasahassasaṅkhyā uppajjitvā nirujjhati. Yathā ca pubbuḷo udakatalaṃ, udakabinduṃ[P 0.0034], udakajallakaṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā puṭaṃ katvā gahaṇavātañcāti cattāri kāraṇāni paṭicca uppajjati; evaṃ vedanāpi vatthuṃ, ārammaṇaṃ, kilesajālaṃ, phassasaṅghaṭṭanañcāti cattāri kāraṇāni paṭicca uppajjati. Evampi vedanā pubbuḷasadisā.

Just as a bubble is insubstantial, so too is feeling. And just as a bubble is weak, not able to be grasped, and cannot be taken to make a plank or a seat—even if grasped, it bursts—so too is feeling weak, not able to be grasped, and cannot be taken as permanent or stable; even when grasped, it does not remain so. Thus, feeling, being unable to be grasped, is 'like a bubble'. Just as a bubble arises and ceases in each drop of water, not lasting long, so too does feeling arise and cease, not lasting long. In the briefest moment, hundreds of thousands of crores arise and cease. And just as a bubble arises dependent on four causes—the surface of the water, a drop of water, the water's surface film, and the gathering wind that forms a hollow—so too does feeling arise due to four causes: the physical basis, the object, the net of defilements, and the impact of contact. Thus, feeling is like a bubble.

Saññāpi asārakaṭṭhena ‘marīcisadisā’. Tathā agayhupagaṭṭhena; na hi sakkā taṃ gahetvā pivituṃ vā nhāyituṃ vā bhājanaṃ vā pūretuṃ. Apica yathā marīci vipphandati, sañjātūmivego [V 0.0032] viya khāyati; evaṃ nīlasaññādibhedā saññāpi nīlādianubhavanatthāya phandati vipphandati. Yathā ca marīci mahājanaṃ vippalambheti[M 0.0032], ‘paripuṇṇavāpī viya paripuṇṇanadī viya dissatī’ti vadāpeti; evaṃ saññāpi vippalambheti, ‘idaṃ nīlakaṃ subhaṃ sukhaṃ nicca’nti vadāpeti. Pītakādīsupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ vippalambhanenāpi marīcisadisā.

Perception is like a mirage in being insubstantial. Similarly, it cannot be grasped; for one cannot take it to drink, bathe, or fill a vessel. Moreover, just as a mirage flickers, appearing as if with the force of a wave, so too does perception, in its varieties such as perception of blue, flicker and quiver for the sake of experiencing blue and so on. And just as a mirage deceives the multitude, making them say, "It appears like a full pond or a full river," so too does perception deceive, making one say, "This blue thing is beautiful, pleasant, and permanent." The same principle applies to yellow and the rest. Thus, in its deceptive nature, perception is like a mirage.

Saṅkhārāpi asārakaṭṭhena ‘kadalikkhandhasadisā’. Tathā agayhupagaṭṭhena. Yatheva hi kadalikkhandhato kiñci gahetvā na sakkā gopānasīādīnamatthāya upanetuṃ, upanītampi na tathā hoti; evaṃ saṅkhārāpi na sakkā niccādivasena gahetuṃ, gahitāpi na tathā honti. Yathā ca kadalikkhandho bahuvaṭṭisamodhāno hoti, evaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhopi bahudhammasamodhāno. Yathā ca kadalikkhandho nānālakkhaṇo, aññoyeva hi bāhirāya pattavaṭṭiyā vaṇṇo, añño tato abbhantarabbhantarānaṃ; evameva saṅkhārakkhandhopi aññadeva phassassa lakkhaṇaṃ, aññaṃ cetanādīnaṃ. Samodhānetvā pana saṅkhārakkhandhotveva vuccatīti. Evampi saṅkhārakkhandho kadalikkhandhasadiso.

Volitional formations are like a plantain trunk in being devoid of essence. Similarly, in being ungraspable. Just as nothing can be taken from a plantain trunk to use for purposes like making a rafter, and even if taken, it does not serve that purpose, so too volitional formations cannot be grasped as permanent, etc., and even if grasped as such, they are not so. And just as a plantain trunk is composed of many layers, so too the aggregate of volitional formations is composed of many phenomena. Moreover, just as a plantain trunk has diverse characteristics—for the outer layer has one color, and the inner layers each have another—so too the aggregate of volitional formations has one characteristic for contact, another for volition, etc. Yet when combined, it is called simply the aggregate of volitional formations. Thus, the aggregate of volitional formations is like a plantain trunk.

Viññāṇampi asārakaṭṭhena ‘māyāsadisaṃ’. Tathā agayhupagaṭṭhena. Yathā ca māyā ittarā lahupaccupaṭṭhānā, evaṃ viññāṇaṃ. Tañhi tatopi ittaratarañceva lahupaccupaṭṭhānatarañca. Teneva hi cittena puriso āgato viya, gato viya, ṭhito viya, nisinno viya hoti. Aññadeva cāgamanakāle cittaṃ, aññaṃ gamanakālādīsu. Evampi viññāṇaṃ māyāsadisaṃ. Māyā ca mahājanaṃ vañceti, yaṃ kiñcideva ‘idaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ rajataṃ muttā’tipi gahāpeti. Viññāṇampi [P 0.0035] mahājanaṃ vañceti, teneva cittena āgacchantaṃ viya, gacchantaṃ viya, ṭhitaṃ viya, nisinnaṃ viya katvā gāhāpeti. Aññadeva ca āgamane cittaṃ, aññaṃ gamanādīsu. Evampi viññāṇaṃ māyāsadisaṃ. Visesato ca subhārammaṇampi oḷārikampi ajjhattikarūpaṃ asubhanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vedanā tīhi dukkhatāhi avinimuttato dukkhāti saññāsaṅkhārā avidheyyato anattāti viññāṇaṃ udayabbayadhammato aniccanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Consciousness is like an illusion because it is insubstantial. Similarly, because it is ungraspable. Just as an illusion is fleeting and swift to arise, so too is consciousness. For it is even more fleeting and swifter to arise than that. Indeed, it is by means of that same mind that a person seems to come, to go, to stand, to sit. The mind at the time of coming is different, and different at the time of going and so forth. In this way, consciousness is like an illusion. An illusion deceives the masses, making them grasp something as 'this is gold, silver, or pearls'. Consciousness too deceives the masses, making them grasp through that same mind as if one is coming, going, standing, or sitting. Different indeed is the mind at the time of coming, and different at the time of going and so forth. In this way, consciousness is like an illusion. In particular, even a beautiful, gross, and internal form should be seen as unlovely. Feeling, because it is inseparable from the three kinds of suffering, should be seen as suffering. Perception and volitional formations, because they are ungovernable, should be seen as non-self. Consciousness, because it is subject to arising and passing away, should be seen as impermanent.

‘Evaṃ passantassatthasiddhito’ti evañca saṅkhepavitthāravasena dvidhā passato yā atthasiddhi hoti, tatopi vinicchayanayo viññātabbo, seyyathidaṃ – saṅkhepato tāva pañcupādānakkhandhesu ukkhittāsikapaccatthikādibhāvena passanto khandhehi na vihaññati. Vitthārato pana rūpādīni pheṇapiṇḍādisadisabhāvena passanto na asāresu sāradassī hoti. Visesato ca ajjhattikarūpaṃ [V 0.0033] asubhato passanto kabaḷīkārāhāraṃ parijānāti[M 0.0033], asubhe subhanti vipallāsaṃ pajahati, kāmoghaṃ uttarati, kāmayogena visaṃyujjati, kāmāsavena anāsavo hoti, abhijjhākāyaganthaṃ bhindati, kāmupādānaṃ na upādiyati. Vedanaṃ dukkhato passanto phassāhāraṃ parijānāti, dukkhe sukhanti vipallāsaṃ pajahati, bhavoghaṃ uttarati, bhavayogena visaṃyujjati, bhavāsavena anāsavo hoti, byāpādakāyaganthaṃ bhindati, sīlabbatupādānaṃ na upādiyati. Saññaṃ saṅkhāre ca anattato passanto manosañcetanāhāraṃ parijānāti, anattani attāti vipallāsaṃ pajahati, diṭṭhoghaṃ uttarati, diṭṭhiyogena visaṃyujjati, diṭṭhāsavena anāsavo hoti, idaṃ saccābhinivesakāyaganthaṃ bhindati, attavādupādānaṃ na upādiyati. Viññāṇaṃ aniccato passanto viññāṇāhāraṃ parijānāti, anicce niccanti vipallāsaṃ pajahati, avijjoghaṃ uttarati, avijjāyogena visaṃyujjati, avijjāsavena anāsavo hoti, sīlabbataparāmāsakāyaganthaṃ bhindati, diṭṭhupādānaṃ na upādiyati.

'Thus, for one who sees, the goal is achieved.' And for one who sees in these two ways—briefly and in detail—the achievement of the goal is to be understood through the method of discernment. That is to say: First, briefly, one who sees the five aggregates of clinging as having the nature of a drawn sword, an enemy, and so on, is not afflicted by the aggregates. In detail, one who sees forms and so on as like a lump of foam, etc., does not perceive substance in what is insubstantial. Specifically, one who sees internal form as unlovely fully understands the nutriment of physical food, abandons the distortion of perceiving beauty in the unlovely, crosses the flood of sensual desire, is freed from the yoke of sensuality, becomes free from the taint of sensual desire, breaks the bodily fetter of covetousness, and does not cling to sensual clinging. One who sees feeling as suffering fully understands the nutriment of contact, abandons the distortion of perceiving pleasure in suffering, crosses the flood of existence, is freed from the yoke of existence, becomes free from the taint of existence, breaks the bodily fetter of ill will, and does not cling to adherence to rules and observances. One who sees perception and volitional formations as non-self fully understands the nutriment of mental volition, abandons the distortion of perceiving self in what is non-self, crosses the flood of views, is freed from the yoke of views, becomes free from the taint of views, breaks the bodily fetter of dogmatic clinging to 'this is the truth', and does not cling to the clinging to the doctrine of self. One who sees consciousness as impermanent fully understands the nutriment of consciousness, abandons the distortion of perceiving permanence in the impermanent, crosses the flood of ignorance, is freed from the yoke of ignorance, becomes free from the taint of ignorance, breaks the bodily fetter of grasping at rules and observances, and does not cling to view-clinging.

Evaṃ mahānisaṃsaṃ, vadhakādivasena dassanaṃ yasmā;

Tasmā khandhe dhīro, vadhakādivasena passeyyāti.

Since seeing them as murderers and so forth brings such great benefit, therefore the wise person should regard the aggregates as murderers and so forth.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Suttanta Division.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. The Exposition of the Abhidhamma Division

32. Idāni [P 0.0036] abhidhammabhājanīyaṃ hoti. Tattha rūpakkhandhaniddeso heṭṭhā rūpakaṇḍe vitthāritanayeneva veditabbo.

32. Now comes the Abhidhamma division. Herein, the exposition of the aggregate of form should be understood in the same detailed manner as in the preceding section on form.

34. Vedanākkhandhaniddese ekavidhenāti ekakoṭṭhāsena. Phassasampayuttoti phassena sampayutto. Sabbāpi catubhūmikavedanā. Sahetukaduke sahetukā catubhūmikavedanā, ahetukā kāmāvacarāva. Iminā upāyena kusalapadādīhi vuttā vedanā jānitabbā. Apicāyaṃ vedanākkhandho ekavidhena phassasampayuttato dassito, duvidhena sahetukāhetukato, tividhena jātito[V 0.0034], catubbidhena bhūmantarato, pañcavidhena indriyato. Tattha sukhindriyadukkhindriyāni kāyappasādavatthukāni kāmāvacarāneva. Somanassindriyaṃ chaṭṭhavatthukaṃ vā avatthukaṃ vā tebhūmakaṃ[M 0.0034]. Domanassindriyaṃ chaṭṭhavatthukaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ. Upekkhindriyaṃ cakkhādicatuppasādavatthukaṃ chaṭṭhavatthukaṃ avatthukañca catubhūmakaṃ. Chabbidhena vatthuto dassito. Tattha purimā pañca vedanā pañcappasādavatthukā kāmāvacarāva chaṭṭhā avatthukā vā savatthukā vā catubhūmikā.

34. In the exposition of the feeling aggregate, 'singlefold' means as one category. “Associated with contact” means associated with contact. All feelings are of the four planes. In the rooted dyad, rooted feelings are of the four planes, while rootless feelings are only of the sensuous sphere. By this method, the feelings mentioned under wholesome terms, etc., should be understood. Furthermore, this feeling aggregate is shown as singlefold by being associated with contact, twofold by being rooted or rootless, threefold by origin, fourfold by the planes of existence, and fivefold by the faculties. Herein, the faculties of pleasure and pain have the sensitive body as their base and are only of the sensuous sphere. The faculty of joy has the sixth base as its base or is without a base and pertains to three planes. The faculty of displeasure has the sixth base as its base and is of the sensuous sphere. The faculty of equanimity has the four sense bases (eye, etc.) as its base, or the sixth base, or is without a base and pertains to the four planes. It is shown as sixfold by base. Herein, the first five feelings have the five sense bases as their base and are only of the sensuous sphere, while the sixth is either without a base or with a base and is of the four planes.

Sattavidhena tattha manosamphassajā bhedato dassitā, aṭṭhavidhena tattha kāyasamphassajā bhedato, navavidhena sattavidhabhede manoviññāṇadhātusamphassajā bhedato, dasavidhena aṭṭhavidhabhede manoviññāṇadhātusamphassajā bhedato. Etesu hi sattavidhabhede manosamphassajā manodhātusamphassajā, manoviññāṇadhātusamphassajāti dvidhā bhinnā. Aṭṭhavidhabhede tāya saddhiṃ kāyasamphassajāpi sukhā dukkhāti dvidhā bhinnā. Navavidhabhede sattavidhe vuttā manoviññāṇadhātusamphassajā kusalādivasena tidhā bhinnā. Dasavidhabhede aṭṭhavidhe vuttā manoviññāṇadhātusamphassajā kusalādivaseneva tidhā bhinnā.

As sevenfold, feelings born of mind-contact are shown by way of division; as eightfold, feelings born of body-contact are shown by way of division; as ninefold, in the sevenfold division, feelings born of contact with the mind-consciousness element are shown by way of division; as tenfold, in the eightfold division, feelings born of contact with the mind-consciousness element are shown by way of division. For in these, in the sevenfold division, the feelings born of mind-contact are divided into two: those born of contact with the mind-element and those born of contact with the mind-consciousness element. In the eightfold division, together with that, the feelings born of body-contact are also divided into two: pleasant and painful. In the ninefold division, the feelings born of contact with the mind-consciousness element, mentioned in the sevenfold division, are divided into three according to wholesome, etc. In the tenfold division, the feelings born of contact with the mind-consciousness element, mentioned in the eightfold division, are divided into three in just the same way according to wholesome, etc.

Kusalattiko cettha kevalaṃ pūraṇatthameva vutto. Sattavidhaaṭṭhavidhanavavidhabhedesu pana nayaṃ dātuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne [P 0.0037] nayo dinno. Abhidhammañhi patvā tathāgatena nayaṃ dātuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne nayo adinno nāma natthi. Ayaṃ tāva dukamūlake eko vāro.

Herein, the wholesome triad is mentioned merely for the sake of completeness. However, in the sevenfold, eightfold, and ninefold divisions, the method is given where it is fitting to give one. For with respect to the Abhidhamma, there is no instance where the Tathāgata did not give a method where it was fitting to give one. This, then, is the first section based on the dyad.

Satthā hi imasmiṃ abhidhammabhājanīye vedanākkhandhaṃ bhājento tike gahetvā dukesu pakkhipi, duke gahetvā tikesu pakkhipi, tike ca duke ca ubhatovaḍḍhananīhārena āhari; sattavidhena, catuvīsatividhena, tiṃsavidhena, bahuvidhenāti sabbathāpi bahuvidhena vedanākkhandhaṃ dassesi. Kasmā? Puggalajjhāsayena ceva desanāvilāsena ca. Dhammaṃ sotuṃ nisinnadevaparisāya hi ye devaputtā tike ādāya dukesu pakkhipitvā kathiyamānaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ sakkonti, tesaṃ sappāyavasena tathā katvā desesi. Ye itarehi ākārehi kathiyamānaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ sakkonti, tesaṃ tehākārehi desesīti. Ayamettha ‘puggalajjhāsayo’. Sammāsambuddho pana attano mahāvisayatāya tike vā dukesu pakkhipitvā, duke vā tikesu ubhatovaḍḍhanena vā, sattavidhādinayena vā, yathā [M 0.0035] yathā icchati tathā tathā desetuṃ sakkoti. Tasmāpi imehākārehi desesīti ayamassa ‘desanāvilāso’.

Indeed, while analyzing the feeling aggregate in this Abhidhamma exposition, the Teacher took triads and placed them in dyads, took dyads and placed them in triads, and brought them forth by the method of mutual augmentation of both triads and dyads; he showed the feeling aggregate in many ways—sevenfold, twenty-fourfold, thirtyfold, and in every possible manner, that is, in many ways. Why? Because of the inclinations of individuals and the elegance of his teaching. For among the assembly of devas seated to hear the Dhamma, there were those devaputtas who could penetrate what was being taught by taking triads and placing them in dyads, so he taught accordingly to suit them. And those who could penetrate what was being taught in other ways, to them he taught in those ways. This herein is the “inclination of individuals.” But the Perfectly Enlightened One, by virtue of his own vast range, is able to teach as he wishes, whether by placing triads in dyads, or dyads in triads, or through mutual augmentation, or by the sevenfold method and so on. Therefore, he taught in these ways; this is his “elegance of teaching.”

Tattha [V 0.0035] tike ādāya dukesu pakkhipitvā desitavāro dukamūlako nāma. Duke ādāya tikesu pakkhipitvā desitavāro tikamūlako nāma. Tike ca duke ca ubhato vaḍḍhetvā desitavāro ubhatovaḍḍhitako nāma. Avasāne sattavidhenātiādivāro bahuvidhavāro nāmāti ime tāva cattāro mahāvārā.

Herein, the section taught by taking triads and placing them in dyads is called the “dyad-rooted section.” The section taught by taking dyads and placing them in triads is called the “triad-rooted section.” The section taught by expanding both triads and dyads is called the “mutually augmented section.” At the end, the section beginning with 'sevenfold', etc., is called the “manifold section.” These, then, are the four great sections.

Tattha dukamūlake dukesu labbhamānena ekekena dukena saddhiṃ tikesu alabbhamāne vedanāttikapītittikasanidassanattike apanetvā, sese labbhamānake ekūnavīsati tike yojetvā, dutiyadukapaṭhamattikayojanavārādīni navavārasatāni paññāsañca vārā honti. Te sabbepi pāḷiyaṃ saṃkhipitvā tattha tattha dassetabbayuttakaṃ dassetvā vuttā. Asammuyhantena pana vitthārato veditabbā.

Herein, in the dyad-rooted section, with each dyad obtainable among the dyads, excluding the triad on feeling, the triad on joy, and the triad on visible manifestation, which are unobtainable among the triads, the remaining nineteen obtainable triads are combined, resulting in nine hundred and fifty sections, such as the section combining the second dyad and the first triad. All these are briefly stated in the Pāli text, showing what is appropriate to be shown here and there. However, one who is not confused should understand them in detail.

Tikamūlakepi tikesu labbhamānena ekekena tikena saddhiṃ dukesu alabbhamāne paṭhamadukādayo duke apanetvā, sese labbhamānake sahetukadukādayo paññāsa duke yojetvā, paṭhamattikadutiyadukayojanavārādīni navavārasatāni paññāsañca [P 0.0038] vārā honti. Tepi sabbe pāḷiyaṃ saṅkhipitvā tattha tattha dassetabbayuttakaṃ dassetvā vuttā. Asammuyhantena pana vitthārato veditabbā.

Similarly, in the triad-rooted section, with each triad obtainable among the triads, excluding the first dyad and others which are unobtainable among the dyads, the remaining fifty obtainable dyads, such as the rooted dyad, are combined, resulting in nine hundred and fifty sections, such as the section combining the first triad and the second dyad. All these are also briefly stated in the Pāli text, showing what is appropriate to be shown here and there. But one who is not confused should understand them in detail.
