Ubhatovaḍḍhitake duvidhabhede dutiyadukaṃ tividhabhede ca paṭhamatikaṃ ādiṃ katvā labbhamānehi ekūnavīsatiyā dukehi labbhamāne ekūnavīsatitike yojetvā dutiyadukapaṭhamatikayojanavārādayo ekūnavīsativārā vuttā. Esa dukatikānaṃ vasena ubhatovaḍḍhitattā ubhatovaḍḍhitako nāma tatiyo mahāvāro.

In the mutually augmented section, taking the second dyad in the twofold division and the first triad in the threefold division as a starting point, and combining the nineteen obtainable dyads with the nineteen obtainable triads, nineteen sections are stated, such as the section combining the second dyad and the first triad. This is called the “mutually augmented section,” the third great section, because it is mutually augmented by way of dyads and triads.

Bahuvidhavārassa sattavidhaniddese ādito paṭṭhāya labbhamānesu ekūnavīsatiyā tikesu ekekena saddhiṃ catasso bhūmiyo yojetvā ekūnavīsati sattavidhavārā vuttā. Catuvīsatividhaniddesepi tesaṃyeva tikānaṃ vasena ekūnavīsativārā vuttā. Tathā bahuvidhavāre cāti[M 0.0036]. Tiṃsavidhavāro ekoyevāti sabbepi aṭṭhapaññāsa vārā honti. Ayaṃ tāvettha vāraparicchedavasena pāḷivaṇṇanā.

In the exposition of the sevenfold method of the manifold section, nineteen sevenfold sections are stated, beginning from the nineteen obtainable triads, each combined with the four planes. In the exposition of the twenty-fourfold method, nineteen sections are stated by way of those same triads. And so too in the manifold section. The thirtyfold section is just one, so all the sections are fifty-eight. This, then, is the commentary on the Pāli text herein by way of the delimitation of sections.

Idāni [V 0.0036] atthavaṇṇanā hoti. Tattha sattavidhaniddeso tāva uttānatthoyeva. Catuvīsatividhaniddese cakkhusamphassapaccayā vedanākkhandho atthi kusaloti kāmāvacaraaṭṭhakusalacittavasena veditabbo. Atthi akusaloti dvādasaakusalacittavasena veditabbo. Atthi abyākatoti tisso manodhātuyo, tisso ahetukamanoviññāṇadhātuyo, aṭṭha mahāvipākāni, dasa kāmāvacarakiriyāti catuvīsatiyā cittānaṃ vasena veditabbo.

Now comes the explanation of the meaning. Herein, the exposition of the sevenfold method is of straightforward meaning. In the exposition of the twenty-fourfold method, the feeling aggregate conditioned by eye-contact, as wholesome, is to be understood by way of the eight wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses. As unwholesome, it is to be understood by way of the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses. As indeterminate, it is to be understood by way of twenty-four types of consciousness: the three mind-elements, the three rootless mind-consciousness elements, the eight great resultants, and the ten sense-sphere functional consciousnesses.

Tattha aṭṭha kusalāni dvādasa akusalāni ca javanavasena labbhanti. Kiriyamanodhātu āvajjanavasena labbhati. Dve vipākamanodhātuyo sampaṭicchanavasena, tisso vipākamanoviññāṇadhātuyo santīraṇatadārammaṇavasena, kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu voṭṭhabbanavasena, aṭṭha mahāvipākacittāni tadārammaṇavasena, nava kiriyacittāni javanavasena labbhanti. Sotaghānajivhākāyadvāresupi eseva nayo.

Herein, the eight wholesome and twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are obtained by way of impulsion. The functional mind-element is obtained by way of adverting. The two resultant mind-elements are obtained by way of receiving. The three resultant mind-consciousness-elements are obtained by way of investigating and registering. The functional rootless mind-consciousness-element is obtained by way of determining. The eight great resultant consciousnesses are obtained by way of registering. The nine functional consciousnesses are obtained by way of impulsion. This same method applies also to the ear, nose, tongue, and body-doors.

Manodvāre pana atthi kusaloti catubhūmakakusalavasena kathitaṃ, atthi akusaloti dvādasaakusalavasena. Atthi abyākatoti ekādasannaṃ kāmāvacaravipākānaṃ, dasannaṃ kiriyānaṃ[P 0.0039], navannaṃ rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakiriyānaṃ, catunnaṃ sāmaññaphalānanti catuttiṃsacittuppādavasena kathitaṃ. Tattha catubhūmakakusalañceva akusalañca javanavasena labbhati. Kiriyato ahetukamanoviññāṇadhātu āvajjanavasena, ekādasa vipākacittāni tadārammaṇavasena, tebhūmakakiriyā ceva sāmaññaphalāni ca javanavaseneva labbhanti. Tāni sattavidhādīsu yattha katthaci ṭhatvā kathetuṃ vaṭṭanti. Tiṃsavidhe pana ṭhatvā dīpiyamānāni sukhadīpanāni hontīti tiṃsavidhasmiṃyeva ṭhatvā dīpayiṃsu.

At the mind-door, 'there is the wholesome' is explained in terms of the wholesome of the four planes; 'there is the unwholesome' is explained in terms of the twelve unwholesome states. 'There is the indeterminate' is explained in terms of thirty-four consciousnesses: the eleven sense-sphere resultant states, the ten functional states, the nine form-sphere and formless-sphere functional states, and the four fruits of recluseship. Among these, the wholesome of the four planes and the unwholesome are obtained by way of impulsion. Of the functional states, the rootless mind-consciousness element is obtained by way of adverting; the eleven resultant consciousnesses by way of registering; and the functional states of the three planes and the fruits of recluseship are obtained by way of impulsion. These can be discussed by being established in any of the sevenfold methods, etc. But when elucidated by being established in the thirtyfold method, they become easy to explain. Thus, they were elucidated by being established in the thirtyfold method alone.

Etāni hi sabbānipi cittāni cakkhudvāre upanissayakoṭiyā, samatikkamavasena, bhāvanāvasenāti tīhākārehi labbhanti. Tathā sotadvāramanodvāresupi. Ghānajivhākāyadvāresu pana samatikkamavasena, bhāvanāvasenāti dvīhevākārehi labbhantīti veditabbāni. Kathaṃ? Idha bhikkhu vihāracārikaṃ caramāno kasiṇamaṇḍalaṃ disvā ‘kiṃ nāmeta’nti pucchitvā [M 0.0037] ‘kasiṇamaṇḍala’nti vutte puna ‘kiṃ iminā karontī’ti pucchati. Athassa ācikkhanti – ‘evaṃ bhāvetvā jhānāni uppādetvā, samāpattipadaṭṭhānaṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā, arahattaṃ pāpuṇantī’ti. Ajjhāsayasampanno kulaputto ‘bhāriyaṃ eta’nti asallakkhetvā ‘mayāpi esa guṇo [V 0.0037] nibbattetuṃ vaṭṭati, na kho pana sakkā esa nipajjitvā niddāyantena nibbattetuṃ, āditova vīriyaṃ kātuṃ sīlaṃ sodhetuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti cintetvā sīlaṃ sodheti. Tato sīle patiṭṭhāya dasa palibodhe upacchinditvā, ticīvaraparamena santosena santuṭṭho, ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ vattapaṭivattaṃ katvā, kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhitvā, kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā, samāpattiyo uppādetvā, samāpattipadaṭṭhānaṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā, arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tattha sabbāpi parikammavedanā kāmāvacarā, aṭṭhasamāpattivedanā rūpāvacarārūpāvacarā, maggaphalavedanā lokuttarāti evaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ catubhūmikavedanānibbattiyā balavapaccayo hotīti catubhūmikavedanā cakkhusamphassapaccayā nāma jātā. Evaṃ tāva ‘upanissayavasena’ labbhanti.

For all these states of mind are obtained in three ways through the eye-door: by way of proximate dependence, by way of transcendence, and by way of development. Similarly, they are obtained through the ear-door and the mind-door. However, through the nose-door, tongue-door, and body-door, they are to be understood as being obtained in only two ways: by way of transcendence and by way of development. How? Here, a bhikkhu, while wandering about, sees a kasiṇa circle and asks, "What is this called?" When told, "It is a kasiṇa circle," he asks further, "What do they do with this?" Then they explain to him: "By developing this, one generates the jhānas, and making the attainment a basis, one develops insight and attains arahantship." A clansman endowed with aspiration, not considering this to be burdensome, reflects: "This quality is worth bringing about by me. But it is surely not possible to bring it about while lying down and sleeping. From the very beginning, one must make an effort and purify one's virtue." Having purified his virtue, he establishes himself in virtue, cuts off the ten impediments, is content with having the three robes at most, fulfills his duties toward his teachers and preceptors, learns the meditation subject, does the preliminary work on the kasiṇa, generates the attainments, develops insight with the attainment as its basis, and reaches arahantship. Herein, all feeling associated with the preliminary work is of the sense-sphere; the feeling of the eight attainments is of the form and formless spheres; and the path and fruition feelings are supramundane. Thus, eye-consciousness becomes a strong condition for the arising of feeling pertaining to the four planes. Therefore, feeling pertaining to the four planes is said to arise conditioned by eye-contact. In this way, they are first obtained 'by way of proximate dependence.'

Cakkhudvāre [P 0.0040] pana rūpe āpāthagate ‘iṭṭhe me ārammaṇe rāgo uppanno, aniṭṭhe paṭigho, asamapekkhanāya moho, vinibandhassa pana me māno uppanno, parāmaṭṭhassa diṭṭhi, vikkhepagatassa uddhaccaṃ, asanniṭṭhāgatassa vicikicchā, thāmagatassa anusayo uppanno’ti pariggahe ṭhito kulaputto attano kilesuppattiṃ ñatvā ‘ime me kilesā vaḍḍhamānā anayabyasanāya saṃvattissanti, handa ne niggaṇhāmī’ti cintetvā ‘na kho pana sakkā nipajjitvā niddāyantena kilese niggaṇhituṃ; āditova vīriyaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati sīlaṃ sodhetu’nti heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tattha sabbāpi parikammavedanā kāmāvacarā, aṭṭhasamāpattivedanā rūpāvacarārūpāvacarā, maggaphalavedanā lokuttarāti evaṃ rūpārammaṇe uppannaṃ kilesaṃ samatikkamitvā gatāti catubhūmikavedanā cakkhusamphassapaccayā nāma jātā. Evaṃ ‘samatikkamavasena’ labbhanti.

When a visible form comes into focus at the eye-door, a clansman, standing firm in comprehension, recognizes the arising of defilements within himself: "Lust has arisen in me toward a pleasing object, aversion toward an unpleasing one, delusion due to inattention, conceit due to attachment, wrong view due to being grasped, restlessness due to distraction, doubt due to lack of resolution, and a latent tendency due to persistence." Knowing the arising of his defilements, he reflects: "These defilements of mine, if allowed to grow, will lead to ruin and disaster. Come, let me restrain them." He then considers: "But it is not possible to restrain defilements while lying down and sleeping; one must exert effort from the very start and purify one's virtue." Proceeding in the manner previously described, he attains arahantship. Herein, all preliminary feeling is of the sense-sphere, the feeling of the eight attainments is of the form and formless spheres, and the path and fruition feelings are supramundane. Thus, because one has gone beyond by transcending the defilement that arose in relation to a visible object, feeling pertaining to the four planes, conditioned by eye-contact, is said to have arisen. In this way, they are obtained 'by way of transcendence.'

Cakkhudvāre pana rūpe āpāthagate eko evaṃ pariggahaṃ paṭṭhapeti – ‘idaṃ rūpaṃ kiṃ nissita’nti? Tato naṃ ‘bhūtanissita’nti ñatvā cattāri mahābhūtāni upādārūpañca rūpanti pariggaṇhāti, tadārammaṇe dhamme arūpanti pariggaṇhāti. Tato sappaccayaṃ nāmarūpaṃ parigaṇhitvā tīṇi lakkhaṇāni āropetvā vipassanāpaṭipāṭiyā saṅkhāre sammasitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tattha sabbāpi [M 0.0038] parikammavedanā kāmāvacarā, aṭṭhasamāpattivedanā rūpāvacarārūpāvacarā, maggaphalavedanā lokuttarāti evaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ sammasitvā nibbattitāti ayaṃ vedanā cakkhusamphassapaccayā nāma jātā. Evaṃ ‘bhāvanāvasena’ labbhanti.

When a visible form comes into range at the eye-door, one establishes comprehension thus: 'On what does this form depend?' Then, knowing that it depends on the elements, he comprehends the four great elements and derived form as form. He comprehends the mental phenomena dependent on that object as immaterial. Having thus comprehended name-and-form with its conditions, he applies the three characteristics and, following the sequence of insight, contemplates formations and attains arahantship. Herein, all preliminary feeling is of the sense-sphere, the feeling of the eight attainments is of the form and formless spheres, and the feeling of the path and fruition is supramundane. Thus, this feeling, produced by contemplating the form-object, is said to be born conditioned by eye-contact. In this way, they are obtained by way of 'development.'

Aparo [V 0.0038] bhikkhu suṇāti – ‘kasiṇaparikammaṃ kira katvā samāpattiyo uppādetvā samāpattipadaṭṭhānaṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇantī’ti. Ajjhāsayasampanno kulaputto ‘bhāriyaṃ eta’nti asallakkhetvā ‘mayāpi esa guṇo nibbattetuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti purimanayeneva paṭipajjitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tattha sabbāpi parikammavedanā kāmāvacarā, aṭṭhasamāpattivedanā rūpāvacarārūpāvacarā, maggaphalavedanā lokuttarāti evaṃ sotaviññāṇaṃ catubhūmikavedanā [P 0.0041] nibbattiyā balavapaccayo hotīti catubhūmikavedanā sotasamphassapaccayā nāma jātā. Evaṃ tāva ‘upanissayavasena’ labbhanti.

Another bhikkhu hears: 'It is said that having performed kasiṇa preparation, produced the attainments, and cultivated insight with the attainments as a basis, they attain arahantship.' A clansman endowed with aspiration, not considering it burdensome, thinks: 'This quality should also be produced by me.' Proceeding in the aforementioned manner, he attains arahantship. Therein, all preliminary feeling is of the sense-sphere, the feeling of the eight attainments is of the form and formless spheres, and the feeling of the path and fruition is supramundane. Thus, ear-consciousness becomes a strong condition for the arising of feeling pertaining to the four planes. Therefore, feeling pertaining to the four planes is said to be born conditioned by ear-contact. In this way, they are obtained by way of 'decisive support.'

Sotadvāre pana sadde āpāthagateti sabbaṃ cakkhudvāre vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ saddārammaṇe uppannaṃ kilesaṃ samatikkamitvā gatāti catubhūmikavedanā sotasamphassapaccayā nāma jātā. Evaṃ ‘samatikkamavasena’ labbhanti.

When a sound, however, comes into range at the ear-door, all should be understood in the same way as described for the eye-door. Thus, having transcended the defilement that has arisen in relation to a sound-object, the feeling pertaining to the four planes is said to be born conditioned by ear-contact. In this way, they are obtained by way of 'transcendence.'

Sotadvāre pana sadde āpāthagate eko evaṃ pariggahaṃ paṭṭhapeti – ayaṃ saddo kiṃ nissitoti sabbaṃ cakkhudvāre vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ saddārammaṇaṃ sammasitvā nibbattitāti ayaṃ vedanā sotasamphassapaccayā nāma jātā. Evaṃ ‘bhāvanāvasena’ labbhanti.

When a sound, however, comes into range at the ear-door, one establishes comprehension thus: 'On what is this sound dependent?' Everything should be understood in the same way as described for the eye-door. Thus, this feeling, produced by contemplating the sound-object, is said to be born conditioned by ear-contact. In this way, they are obtained by way of 'development.'

Ghānajivhākāyadvāresu pana gandhārammaṇādīsu āpāthagatesu ‘iṭṭhe me ārammaṇe rāgo uppanno’ti sabbaṃ cakkhudvāre vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ gandhārammaṇādīsu uppannaṃ kilesaṃ samatikkamitvā gatāti catubhūmikavedanā ghānajivhākāyasamphassapaccayā nāma jātā. Evaṃ tīsu dvāresu ‘samatikkamavasena’ labbhanti.

At the nose-, tongue-, and body-doors, however, when smell-objects and so on come into range, and one reflects, 'Lust has arisen in me for a desirable object,' all should be understood in the same way as described for the eye-door. Thus, having transcended the defilement that has arisen in relation to smell-objects and so on, the feeling pertaining to the four planes is said to be born conditioned by nose-, tongue-, and body-contact. Thus, in these three doors, they are obtained by way of 'transcendence.'

Ghānadvārādīsu pana gandhādīsu āpāthagatesu eko evaṃ pariggahaṃ paṭṭhapeti – ‘ayaṃ gandho, ayaṃ raso, idaṃ phoṭṭhabbaṃ kiṃ nissita’nti sabbaṃ cakkhudvāre vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ gandhārammaṇādīni sammasitvā nibbattitāti [M 0.0039] ayaṃ vedanā ghānajivhākāyasamphassapaccayā nāma jātā. Evaṃ ‘bhāvanāvasena’ labbhanti.

At the nose-door and so on, however, when smells and other objects come into range, one establishes comprehension thus: 'This smell, this taste, this tangible object—on what are they dependent?' All should be understood in the same way as described for the eye-door. Thus, this feeling, produced by contemplating the smell-objects and so on, is said to be born conditioned by nose-, tongue-, and body-contact. In this way, they are obtained by way of 'development.'

Manodvāre pana tīhipi ākārehi labbhanti. Ekacco hi jātiṃ bhayato passati, jaraṃ byādhiṃ maraṇaṃ bhayato passati, bhayato disvā ‘jātijarābyādhimaraṇehi muccituṃ vaṭṭati, na kho [V 0.0039] pana sakkā nipajjitvā niddāyantena jātiādīhi muccituṃ, āditova vīriyaṃ kātuṃ sīlaṃ sodhetuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti cintetvā cakkhudvāre vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tattha sabbāpi parikammavedanā kāmāvacarā, aṭṭhasamāpattivedanā rūpāvacarārūpāvacarā, maggaphalavedanā lokuttarāti evaṃ jātijarābyādhimaraṇaṃ catubhūmikavedanānibbattiyā balavapaccayo hotīti [P 0.0042] catubhūmikavedanā manosamphassapaccayā nāma jātā. Evaṃ tāva ‘upanissayavasena’ labbhanti.

At the mind-door, however, they are obtained in three ways. For a certain one sees birth as fearful, sees aging, sickness, and death as fearful. Seeing them as fearful, he thinks, 'It is proper to be freed from birth, aging, sickness, and death. Yet it is not possible to be freed from birth and so on by lying down and sleeping. It is proper to exert effort from the very beginning and to purify virtue.' Reflecting thus, he practices in the manner described for the eye-door and attains arahantship. Herein, all preliminary feeling is of the sense-sphere, the feeling of the eight attainments is of the form and formless spheres, and the feeling of the path and fruition is supramundane. Thus, birth, aging, sickness, and death become a strong condition for the arising of feeling pertaining to the four planes. Therefore, feeling pertaining to the four planes is said to be born conditioned by mind-contact. Thus far, they are obtained by way of 'decisive support.'

Manodvāre pana dhammārammaṇe āpāthagateti sabbaṃ cakkhudvāre vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ dhammārammaṇe uppannaṃ kilesaṃ samatikkamitvā gatāti catubhūmikavedanā manosamphassapaccayā nāma jātā. Evaṃ ‘samatikkamavasena’ labbhanti.

At the mind-door, however, when a mental object comes into range, all should be understood in the same way as described for the eye-door. Thus, having transcended the defilement that has arisen in relation to a mental object, the feeling pertaining to the four planes is said to be born conditioned by mind-contact. In this way, they are obtained by way of 'transcendence.'

Manodvāre pana dhammārammaṇe āpāthagate eko evaṃ pariggahaṃ paṭṭhapeti – ‘etaṃ dhammārammaṇaṃ kiṃ nissita’nti? ‘Vatthunissita’nti. ‘Vatthu kiṃ nissita’nti? ‘Mahābhūtāni nissita’nti. So cattāri mahābhūtāni upādārūpañca rūpanti pariggaṇhāti, tadārammaṇe dhamme arūpanti pariggaṇhāti. Tato sappaccayaṃ nāmarūpaṃ pariggaṇhitvā tīṇi lakkhaṇāni āropetvā vipassanāpaṭipāṭiyā saṅkhāre sammasitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tattha sabbāpi parikammavedanā kāmāvacarā, aṭṭhasamāpattivedanā rūpāvacarārūpāvacarā, maggaphalavedanā lokuttarāti evaṃ dhammārammaṇaṃ sammasitvā nibbattitāti ayaṃ vedanā manosamphassapaccayā nāma jātā. Evaṃ ‘bhāvanāvasena’ labbhanti. Yā panetā sabbesampi catuvīsatividhādīnaṃ vārānaṃ pariyosānesu cakkhusamphassajā vedanā…pe… manosamphassajā vedanāti cha cha vedanā vuttā, tā sampayuttapaccayavasena vuttāti.

At the mind-door, however, when a mental object comes into range, one establishes comprehension thus: 'On what does this mental object depend?' 'It depends on the physical base.' 'On what does the physical base depend?' 'It depends on the great elements.' So he comprehends the four great elements and derived form as form, and he comprehends the mental phenomena dependent on that object as immaterial. Then, having comprehended name-and-form with its conditions, and having applied the three characteristics, he contemplates the formations in the sequence of insight and attains arahantship. Herein, all preliminary feeling is of the sense-sphere, the feeling of the eight attainments is of the form and formless spheres, and the feeling of the path and fruition is supramundane. Thus, this feeling, produced by contemplating the mental object, is said to be born conditioned by mind-contact. In this way, they are obtained by way of 'development.' Furthermore, at the conclusion of all the twenty-four kinds of sections and so on, the six feelings—the feeling born of eye-contact... up to... the feeling born of mind-contact—are mentioned. They are spoken of by way of the associated condition.

Ayaṃ vedanākkhandhaniddeso.

This is the exposition of the feeling aggregate.

Saññākkhandhādayopi [M 0.0040] iminā upāyena veditabbā. Kevalañhi saññākkhandhaniddese tikesu vedanāttikapītittikāpi labbhanti, dukesu ca sukhasahagatadukādayopi. Saṅkhārakkhandhaniddese phassassāpi saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannattā phassasampayuttoti avatvā cittasampayuttoti vuttaṃ. Dukesu cettha hetudukādayopi labbhanti. Tikā saññākkhandhasadisā eva[V 0.0040]. Viññāṇakkhandhaniddese cakkhusamphassajādibhāvaṃ avatvā cakkhuviññāṇantiādi vuttaṃ. Na hi sakkā viññāṇaṃ manosamphassajanti niddisituṃ. Sesamettha saññākkhandhe vuttasadisameva. Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇampi khandhānaṃ niddeseyeva [P 0.0043] vedanākkhandhaniddesato atirekatikadukā laddhā. Tesaṃ vasena vārappabhedo veditabboti.

The aggregate of perception and the others should also be understood in this way. For, in the exposition of the aggregate of perception, the triads such as the feeling triad and the joy triad are found, and in the dyads, the dyads associated with pleasure and the like are also found. In the exposition of the aggregate of formations, because contact is included in the aggregate of formations, instead of saying "associated with contact," it is said "associated with mind." Here, in the dyads, the dyads such as the root dyad are also found. The triads are just like those of the aggregate of perception. In the exposition of the aggregate of consciousness, instead of saying "arising from eye-contact," it is said "eye-consciousness," and so on. For it is not possible to designate consciousness as "arising from mind-contact." The rest here is just like what was said regarding the aggregate of perception. However, in the exposition of these three aggregates, additional triads and dyads are obtained beyond the exposition of the aggregate of feeling. By means of these, the variations of the rounds should be understood.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Division.

3. Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Questioning Section

150. Idāni pañhāpucchakaṃ hoti. Tattha pañhāpucchane pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ “katikusalā? Katiakusalā? Katiabyākatā”tiādinā nayena yaṃ labbhati, yañca na labbhati, taṃ sabbaṃ pucchitvā vissajjane “rūpakkhandho abyākato”tiādinā nayena yaṃ labbhati tadeva uddhaṭanti veditabbaṃ. Yattha yattha ca ‘eko khandho’ti vā ‘dve khandhā’ti vā paricchedaṃ akatvā “siyā uppannā, siyā anuppannā”tiādinā nayena tanti ṭhapitā, tattha tattha pañcannampi khandhānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Seso tesaṃ tesaṃ khandhānaṃ kusalādivibhāgo heṭṭhā dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 985) vuttoyeva.

150. Now there is the questioning section. Therein, in the questioning regarding the five aggregates by way of “how many are wholesome? how many are unwholesome? how many are indeterminate?” and so on, whatever is obtainable and whatever is not obtainable should all be asked about. In the answering, it should be understood that only what is obtainable is extracted, by way of “the form aggregate is indeterminate,” and so on. And wherever the text is established by way of “they may be arisen, they may be unarisen,” and so on, without making a delimitation such as “one aggregate” or “two aggregates,” there the inclusion of all five aggregates should be understood. The remainder of the classification of those aggregates into wholesome and so on has already been stated below in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Commentary (DhsA. 985).

Ārammaṇattikesu pana cattāro khandhā pañcapaṇṇāsa kāmāvacaradhamme ārabbha rajjantassa dussantassa muyhantassa saṃvarantassa sammasantassa paccavekkhantassa ca parittārammaṇā honti, sattavīsati rūpārūpāvacaradhamme ārabbha rajjantassa dussantassa muyhantassa saṃvarantassa pariggahaṃ paṭṭhapentassa mahaggatārammaṇā, maggaphalanibbānāni paccavekkhantassa appamāṇārammaṇā, paññattiṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle navattabbārammaṇāti.

Regarding the object triads, the four aggregates have limited objects for one who, taking as object the fifty-five sense-sphere phenomena, is lusting, hating, deluded, restraining, comprehending, or reviewing. They have sublime objects for one who, taking as object the twenty-seven fine-material and immaterial phenomena, is lusting, hating, deluded, restraining, or establishing comprehension. They have measureless objects for one reviewing the path, fruition, and Nibbāna. At the time of reviewing a concept, they have an unspecifiable object.

Teyeva [M 0.0041] sekkhāsekkhānaṃ maggapaccavekkhaṇakāle maggārammaṇā honti, maggakāle sahajātahetunā maggahetukā, maggaṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhaṇakāle ārammaṇādhipatinā maggādhipatino[V 0.0041], vīriyajeṭṭhakaṃ vā vīmaṃsajeṭṭhakaṃ vā maggaṃ bhāventassa sahajātādhipatinā maggādhipatino, chandajeṭṭhakaṃ pana cittajeṭṭhakaṃ vā bhāventassa navattabbārammaṇā nāma honti.

For trainees and those beyond training, at the time of reviewing the path, these same aggregates have the path as object. At the time of the path, they are path-rooted by way of co-nascent condition. When reviewing the path, having made the path important, they have the path as their dominant factor by way of object-predominance. For one developing a path with energy as foremost or with investigation as foremost, they have the path as their dominant factor by way of co-nascent predominance. But for one developing a path with desire as foremost or with mind as foremost, they are said to have an unspecifiable object.

Atītāni pana khandhadhātuāyatanāni ārabbha rajjantassa dussantassa muyhantassa saṃvarantassa pariggahaṃ paṭṭhapentassa atītārammaṇā honti, anāgatāni ārabbha anāgatārammaṇā [P 0.0044] honti, paccuppannāni ārabbha paccuppannārammaṇā honti, paññattiṃ vā nibbānaṃ vā paccavekkhantassa navattabbārammaṇā honti.

When, taking past aggregates, elements, and sense bases as object, one is lusting, hating, deluded, restraining, or establishing comprehension, they have past objects. When taking future ones as object, they have future objects. When taking present ones as object, they have present objects. When reviewing a concept or Nibbāna, they have an unspecifiable object.

Tathā attano khandhadhātuāyatanāni ārabbha rajjantassa dussantassa muyhantassa saṃvarantassa pariggahaṃ paṭṭhapentassa ajjhattārammaṇā honti, paresaṃ khandhadhātuāyatanāni ārabbha evaṃ pavattentassa bahiddhārammaṇā, paṇṇattinibbānapaccavekkhaṇakālepi bahiddhārammaṇāyeva, kālena ajjhattaṃ kālena bahiddhā dhammesu evaṃ pavattentassa ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā, ākiñcaññāyatanakāle navattabbārammaṇāti veditabbā.

Similarly, for one who, taking as object one's own aggregates, elements, and sense bases, is lusting, hating, deluded, restraining, or establishing comprehension, the objects are internal. For one acting thus taking as object the aggregates, elements, and sense bases of others, the objects are external. Even at the time of reviewing a concept and Nibbāna, the objects are external. For one acting thus towards phenomena, sometimes internal and sometimes external, the objects are internal-and-external. It should be understood that at the time of the base of nothingness, they have an unspecifiable object.

Iti bhagavā imaṃ khandhavibhaṅgaṃ suttantabhājanīyādivasena tayo parivaṭṭe nīharitvā bhājento dassesi. Tīsupi hi parivaṭṭesu ekova paricchedo. Rūpakkhandho hi sabbattha kāmāvacaroyeva. Cattāro khandhā catubhūmakā lokiyalokuttaramissakā kathitāti.

Thus the Blessed One taught this Analysis of the Aggregates by expounding and analyzing it in three rounds, by way of the Suttanta division and so on. For in all three rounds, there is only one delimitation. The aggregate of form is everywhere only of the sense-sphere. The four aggregates are said to be of four planes, a mixture of the mundane and supramundane.

Sammohavinodaniyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya

From the Sammohavinodanī, the Commentary to the Vibhaṅga

Khandhavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Aggregates is concluded.

2. Āyatanavibhaṅgo

2. The Analysis of the Sense Bases

1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Suttanta Division

154. Idāni [P 0.0045][M 0.0042][V 0.0042] tadanantare āyatanavibhaṅganiddese suttantabhājanīyaṃ tāva dassento dvādasāyatanāni cakkhāyatanaṃ rūpāyatanantiādimāha. Tattha pāḷimuttakena tāva nayena –

154. Now, in the subsequent exposition of the Analysis of the Sense Bases, while first showing the Suttanta division, he said, “The twelve sense bases are the eye base, the form base,” and so on. Therein, first, by the method independent of the Pāli text:

Atthalakkhaṇatāvatva, kamasaṅkhepavitthārā;

Tathā daṭṭhabbato ceva, viññātabbo vinicchayo.

By meaning, characteristic, and extent, by order, brevity, and detail; and also by how it should be regarded, thus the determination should be understood.

Tattha visesato tāva cakkhatīti cakkhu; rūpaṃ assādeti, vibhāveti cāti attho. Rūpayatīti rūpaṃ; vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjamānaṃ hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetīti attho. Suṇātīti sotaṃ. Sappatīti saddo; udāhariyatīti attho. Ghāyatīti ghānaṃ. Gandhayatīti gandho; attano vatthuṃ sūcayatīti attho. Jīvitaṃ avhāyatīti jivhā. Rasanti taṃ sattāti raso; assādentīti attho. Kucchitānaṃ sāsavadhammānaṃ āyoti kāyo. Āyoti uppattideso. Phusīyatīti phoṭṭhabbaṃ. Manatīti mano. Attano lakkhaṇaṃ dhārayantīti dhammā.

Here, specifically: it sees, thus it is the eye; the meaning is that it experiences and makes form clear. It is afflicted, thus it is form; the meaning is that, by undergoing a change of color, it reveals its state of having reached the heart. It hears, thus it is the ear. It travels, thus it is sound; the meaning is that it is uttered. It smells, thus it is the nose. It indicates, thus it is smell; the meaning is that it indicates its own basis. It calls for life, thus it is the tongue. Beings savor it, thus it is taste; the meaning is that they experience it. It is a source of contemptible and cankerous things, thus it is the body. `Āyo` means the place of origin. It is touched, thus it is the tangible. It thinks, thus it is the mind. They bear their own characteristic, thus they are phenomena.

Avisesato pana āyatanato, āyānaṃ tananato, āyatassa ca nayanato āyatananti veditabbaṃ. Cakkhurūpādīsu hi taṃtaṃdvārārammaṇā cittacetasikā dhammā sena sena anubhavanādinā kiccena āyatanti uṭṭhahanti ghaṭṭenti vāyamantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Te ca pana āyabhūte dhamme etāni tanonti vitthārentīti vuttaṃ hoti. Idañca anamatagge saṃsāre pavattaṃ atīva āyataṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ yāva na nivattati tāva nayanteva, pavattayantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Iti [V 0.0043] sabbepi me dhammā āyatanato āyānaṃ tananato āyatassa ca nayanato ‘āyatanaṃ āyatana’nti vuccanti.

But in a general sense, 'āyatana' should be understood from its meaning of striving, from its extending of strivings, and from its leading on of what is extended. For in the case of the eye, forms, and so on, mental and associated mental phenomena, by performing their respective functions such as experiencing through their respective doors and objects, strive (āyanti)—that is, they arise, impinge, and exert themselves; so it is said. And these bases extend (tanonti) and expand (vitthārenti) those phenomena that have become strivings (āyabhūte); so it is said. And this leads on (nayanteva) and propels (pavattaayanti) the suffering of saṃsāra, which is exceedingly extended (āyataṃ) and has occurred in this beginningless saṃsāra, for as long as it does not cease; so it is said. Thus, all these phenomena are called 'āyatana' because of striving, because of extending strivings, and because of leading on what is extended.

Apica nivāsaṭṭhānaṭṭhena, ākaraṭṭhena, samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṭṭhena[P 0.0046], sañjātidesaṭṭhena, kāraṇaṭṭhena ca āyatanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tathā hi loke “issarāyatanaṃ vāsudevāyatana”ntiādīsu nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ āyatananti vuccati[M 0.0043]. “Suvaṇṇāyatanaṃ rajatāyatana”ntiādīsu ākaro. Sāsane pana “manorame āyatane sevanti naṃ vihaṅgamā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.38) samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. “Dakkhiṇāpatho gunnaṃ āyatana”ntiādīsu sañjātideso. “Tatra tatreva sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇāti sati satiāyatane”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.23) kāraṇaṃ.

Furthermore, the term 'āyatana' should be understood in terms of its meaning as a dwelling place, a mine, a gathering place, a place of origin, and a cause. Thus, in the world, in expressions such as 'the abode of the lord (issarāyatana)' or 'the abode of Vāsudeva (vāsudevāyatana),' a dwelling place is called an āyatana. In phrases such as 'a mine of gold (suvaṇṇāyatana)' or 'a mine of silver (rajatāyatana),' it signifies a mine. But in the Teaching, in passages such as 'birds resort to delightful abodes (manorame āyatane sevanti naṃ vihaṅgamā),' it denotes a gathering place. In statements such as 'the southern region is a place of origin for cattle (dakkhiṇāpatho gunnaṃ āyatana),' it means a place of origin. And in passages such as 'in each and every instance, one is capable of realizing it, whenever there is a basis (tatra tatreva sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇāti sati satiāyatane),' it refers to a cause.

Cakkhurūpādīsu cāpi te te cittacetasikā dhammā nivasanti tadāyattavuttitāyāti cakkhādayo nesaṃ nivāsanaṭṭhānaṃ. Cakkhādīsu ca te ākiṇṇā taṃ nissitattā tadārammaṇattā cāti cakkhādayo nesaṃ ākaro. Cakkhādayo ca nesaṃ samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ, tattha tattha vatthudvārārammaṇavasena samosaraṇato. Cakkhādayo ca nesaṃ sañjātideso; taṃ nissayārammaṇabhāvena tattheva uppattito. Cakkhādayo ca nesaṃ kāraṇaṃ, tesaṃ abhāve abhāvatoti. Iti nivāsaṭṭhānaṭṭhena, ākaraṭṭhena, samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṭṭhena, sañjātidesaṭṭhena, kāraṇaṭṭhenāti imehi kāraṇehi ete dhammā ‘āyatanaṃ āyatana’nti vuccanti. Tasmā yathāvuttenatthena cakkhu ca taṃ āyatanañcāti cakkhāyatanaṃ…pe… dhammā ca te āyatanañcāti dhammāyatananti evaṃ tāvettha ‘atthato’ viññātabbo vinicchayo.

And also in the eye, forms, and so on, those respective mental and associated mental phenomena dwell, because their existence is dependent on them—thus, the eye and so on are their dwelling place. And they are abundant in the eye and so on, because they are dependent on them and have them as objects—thus, the eye and so on are their source. The eye and so on are also their gathering place, because they gather there by way of base, door, and object. The eye and so on are also their place of origin, because they arise right there by way of being their support and object. The eye and so on are also their cause, because in their absence, these mental phenomena are absent. Thus, for these reasons—in the sense of a dwelling place, a source, a gathering place, a place of origin, and a cause—these phenomena are called ‘āyatana.’ Therefore, in the sense described, 'the eye and that which is its āyatana' is the eye-āyatana… and so on… 'mental objects and that which is their āyatana' is the mental-object-āyatana. Thus, so far, the analysis should be understood here ‘according to meaning’.

‘Lakkhaṇato’ti cakkhādīnaṃ lakkhaṇatopettha viññātabbo vinicchayo. Tāni ca pana nesaṃ lakkhaṇāni heṭṭhā rūpakaṇḍaniddese vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

'According to characteristic': Here, the analysis should be understood by way of the characteristics of the eye and so on. And those characteristics should be understood in the same way as explained previously in the exposition of the section on form.

‘Tāvatvato’ti tāvabhāvato. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – cakkhādayopi hi dhammā eva. Evaṃ sati dhammāyatanamicceva avatvā kasmā dvādasāyatanāni vuttānīti ce? Cha viññāṇakāyuppattidvārārammaṇavavatthānato. Idha channaṃ viññāṇakāyānaṃ dvārabhāvena ārammaṇabhāvena ca vavatthānato ayameva tesaṃ bhedo hotīti dvādasa vuttāni. Cakkhuviññāṇavīthipariyāpannassa hi viññāṇakāyassa cakkhāyatanameva uppattidvāraṃ, rūpāyatanameva cārammaṇaṃ[P 0.0047][V 0.0044]. Tathā itarāni itaresaṃ. Chaṭṭhassa pana bhavaṅgamanasaṅkhāto manāyatanekadesova uppattidvāraṃ, asādhāraṇañca dhammāyatanaṃ ārammaṇanti[M 0.0044]. Iti channaṃ viññāṇakāyānaṃ uppattidvārārammaṇavavatthānato dvādasa vuttānīti. Evamettha ‘tāvatvato’ viññātabbo vinicchayo.

'According to extent' means according to their specific number. This is what is said: The eye and so on are indeed just phenomena. If this is so, why are the twelve bases mentioned instead of simply saying 'the mental-object-base'? It is for the delimitation of the door of arising and the object for the six classes of consciousness. Here, because the six classes of consciousness are delimited by way of being doors and objects, this very distinction among them arises; thus, twelve are mentioned. For the class of consciousness included in the eye-consciousness process, the eye-base alone is the door of arising, and the form-base alone is the object. Similarly for the others with respect to the others. But for the sixth, a part of the mind-base, reckoned as the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-mana), is the door of arising, and the mental-object-base is its non-common object. Thus, the twelve are mentioned for the delimitation of the door of arising and the object for the six classes of consciousness. This is how the analysis 'according to extent' should be understood here.

‘Kamato’ti idhāpi pubbe vuttesu uppattikkamādīsu desanākkamova yujjati. Ajjhattikesu hi āyatanesu sanidassanasappaṭighavisayattā cakkhāyatanaṃ pākaṭanti paṭhamaṃ desitaṃ. Tato anidassanasappaṭighavisayāni sotāyatanādīni. Atha vā dassanānuttariyasavanānuttariyahetubhāvena bahūpakārattā ajjhattikesu cakkhāyatanasotāyatanāni paṭhamaṃ desitāni. Tato ghānāyatanādīni tīṇi. Pañcannampi gocaravisayattā ante manāyatanaṃ. Cakkhādīnaṃ pana gocarattā tassa tassa anantarāni bāhiresu rūpāyatanādīni. Apica viññāṇuppattikāraṇavavatthānatopi ayameva tesaṃ kamo veditabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ…pe… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇa”nti (ma. ni. 3.421) evaṃ ‘kamato’pettha viññātabbo vinicchayo.

'According to order': Here too, among the orders of arising and so on mentioned previously, only the order of teaching is applicable. Among the internal bases, the eye-base is taught first because it is evident, its domain being visible and resistant. Then come the ear-base and so on, which have an invisible and resistant domain. Alternatively, because of their great benefit as causes for the supreme seeing and supreme hearing, the eye-base and ear-base are taught first among the internal bases. Then the three beginning with the nose-base. The mind-base comes last because its domain is the object-field of all five. But because they are the respective object-fields of the eye and so on, immediately after each of these come the external bases: the form-base, and so on. Moreover, this same order should be understood from the standpoint of establishing the causes for the arising of consciousness. For it has been said: 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises… and so on… dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises.' Thus, the analysis should also be understood here 'according to order'.

‘Saṅkhepavitthārā’ti saṅkhepato hi manāyatanassa ceva dhammāyatanekadesassa ca nāmena, tadavasesānañca āyatanānaṃ rūpena saṅgahitattā dvādasāpi āyatanāni nāmarūpamattameva honti.

'Brevity and Detail': In brief, because the mind-base and a portion of the mental-object-base are included under 'name', while the remaining bases are included under 'form', all twelve bases are merely name-and-form.

Vitthārato pana ajjhattikesu tāva cakkhāyatanaṃ jātivasena cakkhupasādamattameva, paccayagatinikāyapuggalabhedato pana anantappabhedaṃ. Tathā sotāyatanādīni cattāri. Manāyatanaṃ tebhūmakakusalākusalavipākakiriyaviññāṇabhedena ekāsītippabhedaṃ, vatthupaṭipadādibhedato pana anantappabhedaṃ. Rūpagandharasāyatanāni samuṭṭhānabhedato catuppabhedāni, saddāyatanaṃ dvippabhedaṃ. Sabhāgavisabhāgabhedato pana sabbānipi anantappabhedāni. Phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ pathavīdhātutejodhātuvāyodhātuvasena tippabhedaṃ, samuṭṭhānato catuppabhedaṃ, sabhāgavisabhāgato anekappabhedaṃ. Dhammāyatanaṃ tebhūmakadhammārammaṇavasena anekappabhedanti. Evaṃ saṅkhepavitthārā viññātabbo vinicchayo.

In detail, regarding the internal bases, the eye base, as to its intrinsic nature, is merely eye-sensitivity, but it is of endless variety when divided according to conditions, destinations, groups, and individuals. Similarly, the ear base and the other three. The mind base is eighty-onefold, divided according to wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses pertaining to the three planes of existence; but it is of endless variety when divided according to the base, the path of practice, and so on. The form, smell, and taste bases are fourfold according to their origin; the sound base is twofold. But all are of endless variety when divided according to homogeneous and heterogeneous kinds. The tangible base is threefold by way of the earth element, the fire element, and the air element; fourfold according to its origin; and of various kinds according to homogeneous and heterogeneous types. The mental-object base is of various kinds by way of being the mental objects of the three planes of existence. Thus, this analysis should be understood in brief and in detail.

‘Daṭṭhabbato’ti [P 0.0048] ettha pana sabbānevetāni āyatanāni anāgamanato aniggamanato ca daṭṭhabbāni. Na hi tāni pubbe udayā kutoci āgacchanti, nāpi uddhaṃ vayā kuhiñci gacchanti; atha kho pubbe udayā appaṭiladdhasabhāvāni, uddhaṃ [M 0.0045] vayā paribhinnasabhāvāni, pubbantāparantavemajjhe [V 0.0045] paccayāyattavuttitāya avasāni pavattanti. Tasmā anāgamanato aniggamanato ca daṭṭhabbāni. Tathā nirīhato abyāpārato ca. Na hi cakkhurūpādīnaṃ evaṃ hoti – ‘aho vata amhākaṃ sāmaggiyā viññāṇaṃ nāma uppajjeyyā’ti, na ca tāni viññāṇuppādanatthaṃ dvārabhāvena vatthubhāvena ārammaṇabhāvena vā īhanti, na byāpāramāpajjanti; atha kho dhammatāvesā yaṃ cakkhurūpādīnaṃ sāmaggiyaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīni sambhavanti. Tasmā nirīhato abyāpārato ca daṭṭhabbāni. Apica ajjhattikāni suññagāmo viya daṭṭhabbāni dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvavirahitattā, bāhirāni gāmaghātakacorā viya ajjhattikānaṃ abhighātakattā. Vuttañhetaṃ – “cakkhu, bhikkhave, haññati manāpāmanāpehi rūpehīti vitthāro. Apica ajjhattikāni cha pāṇakā viya daṭṭhabbāni, bāhirāni tesaṃ gocarā viyāti. Evampettha ‘daṭṭhabbato’ viññātabbo vinicchayoti.

'By way of how they are to be seen'—here, all these sense bases should be seen as neither coming nor going. For they do not come from anywhere before arising, nor do they go anywhere after passing away; rather, before arising, they have not attained their own nature, and after passing away, their nature has disintegrated. In the middle, between the past and the future, they persist dependent on conditions, without being subject to control. Therefore, they should be seen as neither coming nor going. Similarly, they should be seen as without striving and without activity. For it is not the case that the eye, forms, and so on, think: 'Oh, may consciousness arise from our union!' Nor do they strive or exert themselves to produce consciousness by serving as doors, bases, or objects; rather, it is by the very nature of phenomena that when the eye, forms, and so on, come together, eye-consciousness and so on arise. Therefore, they should be seen as without striving and without activity. Furthermore, the internal sense bases should be seen as like an empty village, being devoid of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self. The external sense bases should be seen as like village-plundering robbers, as they assault the internal ones. As it is said: 'The eye, bhikkhus, is struck by agreeable and disagreeable forms,' and so on in detail. Moreover, the internal sense bases should be seen as like six animals, and the external ones like their feeding grounds. Thus, the analysis 'by way of how they are to be seen' should be understood here.

Idāni tesaṃ vipassitabbākāraṃ dassetuṃ cakkhuṃ aniccantiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha cakkhu tāva hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccanti veditabbaṃ. Aparehipi catūhi kāraṇehi aniccaṃ – uppādavayavantato, vipariṇāmato, tāvakālikato, niccapaṭikkhepatoti.

Now, to show the mode in which they are to be discerned by insight, the passage beginning "the eye is impermanent" is introduced. Herein, the eye should be understood as impermanent in the sense of its non-existence after having come into being. It is also impermanent for four other reasons: because it has an arising and a passing away, because of its transformation, because of its temporariness, and because it is the opposite of permanence.

Tadeva paṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhaṃ. Yasmā vā etaṃ uppannaṃ ṭhitiṃ pāpuṇāti, ṭhitiyaṃ jarāya kilamati, jaraṃ patvā avassaṃ bhijjati; tasmā abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanato, dukkhamato, dukkhavatthuto, sukhapaṭikkhepatoti imehi catūhi kāraṇehi dukkhaṃ.

That same thing is suffering in the sense of oppression. Or, because when it has arisen, it reaches a state of presence; in that state of presence, it is afflicted by aging; and having reached aging, it inevitably disintegrates. Therefore, because of constant oppression, because of its painfulness, because it is a basis for suffering, and because it is the opposite of happiness—for these four reasons, it is suffering.

Avasavattanaṭṭhena pana anattā. Yasmā vā etaṃ uppannaṃ ṭhitiṃ mā pāpuṇātu, ṭhānappattaṃ mā jiratu, jarappataṃ mā bhijjatūti imesu tīsu ṭhānesu kassaci vasavattibhāvo natthi, suññaṃ tena vasavattanākārena; tasmā suññato, assāmikato, akāmakāriyato, attapaṭikkhepatoti imehi catūhi kāraṇehi anattā.

By way of not being subject to control, it is non-self. Or, because with regard to these three states—'May what has arisen not reach a state of presence,' 'May what has reached a state of presence not age,' 'May what has aged not disintegrate'—no one has any control; it is empty of that mode of control. Thus, for these four reasons—because of emptiness, because of ownerlessness, because it is not subject to one's will, and because it is the opposite of self—it is non-self.

Vibhavagatikato[P 0.0049], pubbāparavasena bhavasaṅkantigamanato, pakatibhāvavijahanato ca vipariṇāmadhammaṃ. Idaṃ aniccavevacanameva. Rūpā aniccātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Apicettha ṭhapetvā cakkhuṃ tebhūmakadhammā aniccā, no cakkhu. Cakkhu pana cakkhu ceva aniccañca. Tathā [V 0.0046] sesadhammā dukkhā, no cakkhu. Cakkhu [M 0.0046] pana cakkhu ceva dukkhañca. Sesadhammā anattā, no cakkhu. Cakkhu pana cakkhu ceva anattā cāti. Rūpādīsupi eseva nayo.

By way of its proceeding to destruction, by way of its transition from one state of existence to another in terms of past and future, and by way of its abandoning its natural state, it is a phenomenon subject to change. This is simply a synonym for impermanence. The same method applies to "forms are impermanent," and so on. Moreover, in this context, the phenomena of the three planes of existence other than the eye are impermanent, but they are not the eye. The eye, however, is both the eye and impermanent. Similarly, other phenomena are suffering, but not the eye. The eye, however, is both the eye and suffering. Other phenomena are non-self, but not the eye. The eye, however, is both the eye and non-self. The same method applies to forms and so on.

Imasmiṃ pana suttantabhājanīye tathāgatena kiṃ dassitanti? Dvādasannaṃ āyatanānaṃ anattalakkhaṇaṃ. Sammāsambuddho hi anattalakkhaṇaṃ dassento aniccena vā dasseti, dukkhena vā, aniccadukkhehi vā. Tattha “cakkhu, attāti yo vadeyya, taṃ na upapajjati. Cakkhussa uppādopi vayopi paññāyati. Yassa kho pana uppādopi vayopi paññāyati ‘attā me uppajjati ca veti cā’ti iccassa evamāgataṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ na upapajjati – cakkhu attāti yo vadeyya iti cakkhu anattā”ti (ma. ni. 3.422). Imasmiṃ sutte aniccena anattalakkhaṇaṃ dassesi. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, anattā. Rūpañca hidaṃ, bhikkhave, attā abhavissa, na yidaṃ rūpaṃ ābādhāya saṃvatteyya; labbhetha ca rūpe – evaṃ me rūpaṃ hotu, evaṃ me rūpaṃ mā ahosīti. Yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ anattā tasmā rūpaṃ ābādhāya saṃvattati; na ca labbhati rūpe – evaṃ me rūpaṃ hotu, evaṃ me rūpaṃ mā ahosī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.59; mahāva. 20) imasmiṃ sutte dukkhena anattalakkhaṇaṃ dassesi. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā, yadanattā taṃ netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.15) aniccadukkhehi anattalakkhaṇaṃ dassesi. Kasmā? Aniccadukkhānaṃ pākaṭattā.

In this Suttanta Exposition, what has the Tathāgata shown? The characteristic of non-self in the twelve sense bases. For the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, when showing the characteristic of non-self, does so either through impermanence, through suffering, or through both impermanence and suffering. Herein, 'If one were to say, "The eye is self," that would not be appropriate. The arising and passing away of the eye are evident. But for that which has evident arising and passing away, it would follow that "My self arises and ceases." Therefore, it is not appropriate to say the eye is self. Thus, the eye is non-self.' In this discourse, he has shown the characteristic of non-self through impermanence. 'Bhikkhus, form is non-self. For if, bhikkhus, form were self, this form would not lead to affliction, and one could have it of form: "Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus." But because, bhikkhus, form is non-self, form leads to affliction, and one cannot have it of form: "Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus."' In this discourse, he has shown the characteristic of non-self through suffering. 'Bhikkhus, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is non-self. What is non-self is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' In such passages as these, he has shown the characteristic of non-self through both impermanence and suffering. Why? Because impermanence and suffering are evident.

Hatthato hi taṭṭake vā sarake vā kismiñcideva vā patitvā bhinne ‘aho anicca’nti vadanti. Evaṃ aniccaṃ pākaṭaṃ nāma. Attabhāvasmiṃ pana gaṇḍapiḷakādīsu vā uṭṭhitāsu khāṇukaṇṭakādīhi vā viddhāsu ‘aho dukkha’nti vadanti. Evaṃ dukkhaṃ pākaṭaṃ nāma. Anattalakkhaṇaṃ apākaṭaṃ andhakāraṃ avibhūtaṃ duppaṭivijjhaṃ duddīpanaṃ duppaññāpanaṃ[P 0.0050]. Aniccadukkhalakkhaṇāni uppādā vā tathāgatānaṃ anuppādā vā paññāyanti. Anattalakkhaṇaṃ vinā buddhuppādā na paññāyati, buddhuppādeyeva paññāyati. Mahiddhikā hi mahānubhāvā tāpasaparibbājakā sarabhaṅgasatthārādayopi ‘aniccaṃ dukkha’nti vattuṃ sakkonti, ‘anattā’ti vattuṃ na sakkonti. Sace hi te sampattaparisāya anattāti vattuṃ sakkuṇeyyuṃ, sampattaparisāya maggaphalapaṭivedho bhaveyya. Anattalakkhaṇapaññāpanañhi aññassa kassaci avisayo, sabbaññubuddhānameva visayo. Evametaṃ anattalakkhaṇaṃ apākaṭaṃ. Tasmā satthā [M 0.0047] anattalakkhaṇaṃ dassento [V 0.0047] aniccena vā dassesi, dukkhena vā, aniccadukkhehi vā. Idha pana taṃ aniccadukkhehi dassesīti veditabbaṃ.

For when a plate or a cup or anything else falls from the hand and breaks, they say, 'Alas, impermanent!' Thus, impermanence is indeed evident. But when boils or sores arise on the body, or when one is pierced by stumps or thorns, they say, 'Alas, suffering!' Thus, suffering is indeed evident. The characteristic of non-self, however, is not evident—it is obscure, dark, indistinct, difficult to penetrate, difficult to illuminate, and difficult to make known. The characteristics of impermanence and suffering are discernible whether Tathāgatas arise or not. But the characteristic of non-self is not discernible without the arising of a Buddha—it is discernible only upon a Buddha's arising. For even ascetics and wanderers of great power and great influence, like the Teacher Sarabhaṅga and others, can say, 'Impermanent, suffering,' but they cannot say, 'Non-self.' If they could declare 'Non-self' to an assembled gathering, then for that gathering there would be the penetration of the path and its fruit. But the explanation of the characteristic of non-self is beyond the scope of anyone else—it is the exclusive domain of the Omniscient Buddhas alone. Thus, this characteristic of non-self is not evident. Therefore, the Teacher, when pointing out the characteristic of non-self, did so either through impermanence, through suffering, or through impermanence and suffering. Here, however, it should be understood that he has shown it through impermanence and suffering.

Imāni pana lakkhaṇāni kissa amanasikārā appaṭivedhā, kena paṭicchannattā, na upaṭṭhahanti? Aniccalakkhaṇaṃ tāva udayabbayānaṃ amanasikārā appaṭivedhā, santatiyā paṭicchannattā, na upaṭṭhāti. Dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanassa amanasikārā appaṭivedhā, iriyāpathehi paṭicchannattā, na upaṭṭhāti. Anattalakkhaṇaṃ nānādhātuvinibbhogassa amanasikārā appaṭivedhā, ghanena paṭicchannattā, na upaṭṭhāti. Udayabbayaṃ pana pariggahetvā santatiyā vikopitāya aniccalakkhaṇaṃ yāthāvasarasato upaṭṭhāti. Abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanaṃ manasikatvā iriyāpathe ugghāṭite dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ yāthāvasarasato upaṭṭhāti. Nānādhātuyo vinibbhujitvā ghanavinibbhoge kate anattalakkhaṇaṃ yāthāvasarasato upaṭṭhāti.

But due to not attending to and not penetrating what, and due to being concealed by what, do these characteristics not become manifest? First, the characteristic of impermanence, due to not attending to and not penetrating arising and passing away, and due to being concealed by continuity, does not become manifest. The characteristic of suffering, due to not attending to and not penetrating constant affliction, and due to being concealed by the postures, does not become manifest. The characteristic of non-self, due to not attending to and not penetrating the analysis of the various elements, and due to being concealed by the compact, does not become manifest. However, having comprehended arising and passing away, when continuity is disrupted, the characteristic of impermanence becomes manifest in its true nature. Having attended to constant affliction, when the postures are exposed, the characteristic of suffering becomes manifest in its true nature. Having analyzed the various elements, when the compact is broken down, the characteristic of non-self becomes manifest in its true nature.

Ettha ca aniccaṃ aniccalakkhaṇaṃ, dukkhaṃ dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ, anattā anattalakkhaṇanti ayaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo. Tattha aniccanti khandhapañcakaṃ. Kasmā? Uppādavayaññathattabhāvā, hutvā abhāvato vā; uppādavayaññathattaṃ aniccalakkhaṇaṃ, hutvā abhāvasaṅkhāto ākāravikāro vā. “Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkha”nti vacanato pana tadeva khandhapañcakaṃ dukkhaṃ. Kasmā? Abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanato; abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanākāro dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ. “Yaṃ [P 0.0051] dukkhaṃ taṃ anattā”ti pana vacanato tadeva khandhapañcakaṃ anattā. Kasmā? Avasavattanato; avasavattanākāro anattalakkhaṇaṃ. Iti aññadeva aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā, aññāni aniccadukkhānattalakkhaṇāni. Pañcakkhandhā, dvādasāyatanāni, aṭṭhārasa dhātuyoti idañhi sabbampi aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā nāma. Vuttappakārākāravikārā aniccadukkhānattalakkhaṇānīti.

Herein, this distinction should be understood: what is meant by 'the impermanent' and 'the characteristic of impermanence'; 'suffering' and 'the characteristic of suffering'; 'non-self' and 'the characteristic of non-self.' Therein, 'impermanent' refers to the five aggregates. Why? Because of their nature of arising, passing away, and altering, or because of their non-existence after having been. Arising, passing away, and alteration is the characteristic of impermanence, or it is the change of state described as non-existence after having been. Then, according to the statement, 'What is impermanent is suffering,' those same five aggregates are suffering. Why? Because of constant affliction; the state of constant affliction is the characteristic of suffering. Then, according to the statement, 'What is suffering is non-self,' those same five aggregates are non-self. Why? Because they are not subject to control; the state of not being subject to control is the characteristic of non-self. Thus, the impermanent, suffering, and non-self are one thing, while the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self are another. For all this—the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements—is called impermanent, suffering, and non-self. The changes of state of the kind described are the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self.

Saṅkhepato panettha dasāyatanāni kāmāvacarāni, dve tebhūmakāni. Sabbesupi sammasanacāro kathitoti veditabbo.

In brief, herein ten sense bases are of the sense-sphere, and two are of the three planes. It should be understood that the practice of comprehension is taught in all cases.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Suttanta Exposition.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition

155. Abhidhammabhājanīye [M 0.0048][V 0.0048] yathā heṭṭhā vipassakānaṃ upakāratthāya “cakkhāyatanaṃ rūpāyatana”nti yugalato āyatanāni vuttāni, tathā avatvā ajjhattikabāhirānaṃ sabbākārato sabhāvadassanatthaṃ “cakkhāyatanaṃ sotāyatana”nti evaṃ ajjhattikabāhiravavatthānanayena vuttāni.

155. In the Abhidhamma Exposition, unlike how the sense bases were previously stated in pairs as "the eye base, the form base" for the benefit of insight meditators, here, without stating them in that way, they are stated according to the method of distinguishing between internal and external as "the eye base, the ear base," and so on, for the purpose of showing the intrinsic nature of the internal and external in every aspect.

156. Tesaṃ niddesavāre tattha katamaṃ cakkhāyatanantiādīni heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

156. Regarding their exposition, 'what is the eye-base,' etc., should be understood in the same way as stated earlier.

167. Yaṃ panetaṃ dhammāyatananiddese “tattha katamā asaṅkhatā dhātu? Rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo”ti vuttaṃ, tatrāyamattho – asaṅkhatā dhātūti asaṅkhatasabhāvaṃ nibbānaṃ. Yasmā panetaṃ āgamma rāgādayo khīyanti, tasmā rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayoti vuttaṃ. Ayamettha ācariyānaṃ samānatthakathā.

167. Now, in the exposition of the dhammāyatana, where it is said: "Herein, what is the unconditioned element? The destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion," herein, this is the meaning: the unconditioned element is Nibbāna, which has the nature of being unconditioned. Moreover, since lust and the others are destroyed by relying on it, therefore it is called "the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion." This is the consistent interpretation of the teachers on this matter.

Vitaṇḍavādī panāha – ‘pāṭiyekkaṃ nibbānaṃ nāma natthi, kilesakkhayova nibbāna’nti. ‘Suttaṃ āharā’ti ca vutte “nibbānaṃ nibbānanti kho, āvuso sāriputta, vuccati; katamaṃ nu kho, āvuso, nibbānanti? Yo kho, āvuso, rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo – idaṃ vuccati nibbāna”nti etaṃ jambukhādakasuttaṃ āharitvā ‘iminā suttena veditabbaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ nibbānaṃ nāma natthi, kilesakkhayova nibbāna’nti āha. So vattabbo – ‘kiṃ pana yathā cetaṃ suttaṃ tathā attho’ti? Addhā vakkhati – ‘āma[P 0.0052], natthi suttato muñcitvā attho’ti. Tato vattabbo – ‘idaṃ tāva te suttaṃ ābhataṃ; anantarasuttaṃ āharā’ti. Anantarasuttaṃ nāma – “arahattaṃ arahattanti, āvuso sāriputta, vuccati; katamaṃ nu kho, āvuso, arahattanti? Yo kho, āvuso, rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo – idaṃ vuccati arahatta”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.315) idaṃ tassevānantaraṃ ābhatasuttaṃ.

The debater, however, says: "There is no such thing as a distinct Nibbāna; the destruction of defilements is itself Nibbāna." When told, "Bring a sutta," he cites the Jambukhādaka Sutta: "Friend Sāriputta, it is called Nibbāna, Nibbāna. But what, friend, is Nibbāna? The destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion—this is called Nibbāna." Citing this, he says, "By this sutta, it should be understood that there is no distinct Nibbāna; the destruction of defilements is itself Nibbāna." He should then be asked: "But is the meaning of this sutta just as you say?" Surely, he will reply: "Yes, the meaning cannot be separated from the sutta." Then he should be told: "This is the sutta you have brought; now bring the sutta immediately following it." The immediately following sutta is: "Friend Sāriputta, it is called Arahantship, Arahantship. But what, friend, is Arahantship? The destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion—this is called Arahantship." (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.315) This is the sutta immediately following that one that he has brought.

Imasmiṃ pana naṃ ābhate āhaṃsu – ‘nibbānaṃ nāma dhammāyatanapariyāpanno dhammo, arahattaṃ cattāro khandhā. Nibbānaṃ sacchikatvā viharanto dhammasenāpati [M 0.0049] nibbānaṃ pucchitopi arahattaṃ pucchitopi kilesakkhayameva āha. Kiṃ pana nibbānañca arahattañca ekaṃ udāhu nāna’nti? ‘Ekaṃ [V 0.0049] vā hotu nānaṃ vā. Ko ettha tayā atibahuṃ cuṇṇīkaraṇaṃ karontena attho’? ‘Na tvaṃ ekaṃ nānaṃ jānāsīti. Nanu ñāte sādhu hotī’ti evaṃ punappunaṃ pucchito vañcetuṃ asakkonto āha – ‘rāgādīnaṃ khīṇante uppannattā arahattaṃ rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo’ti vuccatīti. Tato naṃ āhaṃsu – ‘mahākammaṃ te kataṃ. Lañjaṃ datvāpi taṃ vadāpento etadeva vadāpeyya. Yatheva ca te etaṃ vibhajitvā kathitaṃ, evaṃ idampi sallakkhehi – nibbānañhi āgamma rāgādayo khīṇāti nibbānaṃ rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayoti vuttaṃ. Tīṇipi hi etāni nibbānasseva adhivacanānī’ti.

When this was brought up, they said to him: 'Nibbāna is a state included in the mental-object base (dhammāyatana); arahatship consists of the four aggregates. The General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), who lives having realized Nibbāna, when asked about Nibbāna or arahatship, speaks only of the destruction of defilements. But are Nibbāna and arahatship one or different?' 'Whether they are one or different, what is the use of you making too much of a fuss about it?' 'You do not know whether they are one or different. Surely, it is good to know.' Being questioned repeatedly like this and unable to deceive, he said: 'Because it arises when lust, etc., are destroyed, arahatship is called the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion.' Then they said to him: 'You have done a great deed. Even if one were to give you a bribe to make you speak, you would say just this. Just as you have explained this, consider this too: It is relying on Nibbāna that lust, etc., are destroyed; Nibbāna is called the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion. Indeed, these three are just synonyms for Nibbāna.'

Sace evaṃ vutte saññattiṃ gacchati iccetaṃ kusalaṃ; no ce, bahunibbānatāya kāretabbo. Kathaṃ? Evaṃ tāva pucchitabbo – ‘rāgakkhayo nāma rāgasseva khayo udāhu dosamohānampi? Dosakkhayo nāma dosasseva khayo udāhu rāgamohānampi? Mohakkhayo nāma mohasseva khayo udāhu rāgadosānampī’ti? Addhā vakkhati – ‘rāgakkhayo nāma rāgasseva khayo, dosakkhayo nāma dosasseva khayo, mohakkhayo nāma mohasseva khayo’ti.

If, when this is said, he comes to an understanding, that is good. If not, he should be confronted with the 'many Nibbānas' argument. How? He should first be asked thus: 'Is the destruction of lust the destruction of lust alone, or also of hatred and delusion? Is the destruction of hatred the destruction of hatred alone, or also of lust and delusion? Is the destruction of delusion the destruction of delusion alone, or also of lust and hatred?' Surely, he will say: 'The destruction of lust is the destruction of lust alone, the destruction of hatred is the destruction of hatred alone, and the destruction of delusion is the destruction of delusion alone.'

Tato vattabbo – ‘tava vāde rāgakkhayo ekaṃ nibbānaṃ hoti, dosakkhayo ekaṃ, mohakkhayo ekaṃ; tiṇṇaṃ akusalamūlānaṃ khaye tīṇi nibbānāni honti, catunnaṃ upādānānaṃ khaye cattāri, pañcannaṃ nīvaraṇānaṃ khaye pañca, channaṃ taṇhākāyānaṃ khaye cha, sattannaṃ anusayānaṃ khaye satta, aṭṭhannaṃ micchattānaṃ khaye aṭṭha, navannaṃ taṇhāmūlakadhammānaṃ [P 0.0053] khaye nava, dasannaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ khaye dasa, diyaḍḍhakilesasahassassa khaye pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ nibbānanti bahūni nibbānāni honti. Natthi pana te nibbānānaṃ pamāṇanti. Evaṃ pana aggahetvā nibbānaṃ āgamma rāgādayo khīṇāti ekameva nibbānaṃ rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayoti vuccati. Tīṇipi hetāni nibbānasseva adhivacanānīti gaṇha’.

Then it should be said to him: 'According to your view, the destruction of lust is one Nibbāna, the destruction of hatred is one, and the destruction of delusion is one; with the destruction of the three unwholesome roots, there would be three Nibbānas; with the destruction of the four kinds of clinging, four; with the destruction of the five hindrances, five; with the destruction of the six bodies of craving, six; with the destruction of the seven underlying tendencies, seven; with the destruction of the eight wrongnesses, eight; with the destruction of the nine craving-rooted phenomena, nine; with the destruction of the ten fetters, ten; and with the destruction of the one and a half thousand defilements, for each one individually there would be a Nibbāna, and thus many Nibbānas. For you, then, there would be no limit to the number of Nibbānas. But do not take it thus. Understand that it is by relying on Nibbāna that lust and so on are destroyed, and for this reason the one single Nibbāna is called 'the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion.' For these three are indeed but designations for Nibbāna itself.'

Sace [M 0.0050] pana evaṃ vuttepi na sallakkheti, oḷārikatāya kāretabbo. Kathaṃ? ‘Andhabālā hi acchadīpimigamakkaṭādayopi kilesapariyuṭṭhitā vatthuṃ paṭisevanti. Atha nesaṃ paṭisevanapariyante kileso vūpasammati. Tava vāde acchadīpimigamakkaṭādayo nibbānappattā nāma honti. Oḷārikaṃ vata te nibbānaṃ thūlaṃ, kaṇṇehi piḷandhituṃ na sakkāti. Evaṃ pana [V 0.0050] aggahetvā nibbānaṃ āgamma rāgādayo khīṇāti ekameva nibbānaṃ rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayoti vuccati. Tīṇipi hetāni nibbānasseva adhivacanānīti gaṇha’.

But if, even when spoken to thus, he does not comprehend, he should be made to see the point by means of a gross example. How? 'For even blind fools such as bears, leopards, deer, and monkeys, being overcome by defilements, indulge in sensual pleasures. Then, at the conclusion of their indulgence, the defilement subsides. According to your view, bears, leopards, deer, and monkeys would have attained Nibbāna. Truly, your Nibbāna is gross and coarse; it cannot even be worn as an earring! But do not take it thus. Understand that it is by relying on Nibbāna that lust and so on are destroyed, and for this reason the one single Nibbāna is called 'the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion.' For these three are indeed but designations for Nibbāna itself.'

Sace pana evaṃ vuttepi na sallakkheti, gotrabhunāpi kāretabbo. Kathaṃ? Evaṃ tāva pucchitabbo – ‘tvaṃ gotrabhu nāma atthīti vadesī’ti? ‘Āma vadāmī’ti. ‘Gotrabhukkhaṇe kilesā khīṇā, khīyanti, khīyissantī’ti? Na khīṇā, na khīyanti; apica kho khīyissantīti. ‘Gotrabhu pana kiṃ ārammaṇaṃ karotī’ti? ‘Nibbānaṃ’. ‘Tava gotrabhukkhaṇe kilesā na khīṇā, na khīyanti; atha kho khīyissanti. Tvaṃ akhīṇesuyeva kilesesu kilesakkhayaṃ nibbānaṃ paññapesi, appahīnesu anusayesu anusayappahānaṃ nibbānaṃ paññapesi. Taṃ te na sameti. Evaṃ pana aggahetvā nibbānaṃ āgamma rāgādayo khīṇāti ekameva nibbānaṃ rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayoti vuccati. Tīṇipi hetāni nibbānasseva adhivacanānīti gaṇha’.

If, even after being spoken to thus, he does not understand, he should be made to understand by way of the gotrabhū. How? First, he should be asked thus: 'Do you declare that there is something called gotrabhū?' 'Yes, I so declare.' 'In the gotrabhū moment, are the defilements destroyed, being destroyed, or will they be destroyed?' 'They are not destroyed, nor are they being destroyed; but they will be destroyed.' 'And what does the gotrabhū take as its object?' 'Nibbāna.' 'In your gotrabhū moment, defilements are not destroyed, nor are they being destroyed; but they will be destroyed. You designate Nibbāna as the destruction of defilements even when the defilements are not yet destroyed; you designate Nibbāna as the abandoning of underlying tendencies even when the underlying tendencies are not yet abandoned. That is not consistent for you. Rather, not grasping it thus, [understand that] on account of Nibbāna, lust and so forth are destroyed, and thus the one Nibbāna itself is called the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion. Understand that these three are merely designations for Nibbāna itself.'

Sace pana evaṃ vuttepi na sallakkheti, maggena kāretabbo. Kathaṃ? Evaṃ tāva pucchitabbo – ‘tvaṃ maggaṃ nāma vadesī’ti? ‘Āma vademī’ti. ‘Maggakkhaṇe kilesā khīṇā, khīyanti, khiyissantī’ti? Jānamāno vakkhati – ‘khīṇāti vā khīyissantīti vā vattuṃ na vaṭṭati, khīyantīti vattuṃ [P 0.0054] vaṭṭatī’ti. ‘Yadi evaṃ, maggassa kilesakkhayaṃ nibbānaṃ katamaṃ? Maggena khīyanakakilesā katame? Maggo katamaṃ kilesakkhayaṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā katame kilese khepeti? Tasmā mā evaṃ gaṇha. Nibbānaṃ pana āgamma rāgādayo khīṇāti ekameva nibbānaṃ rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayoti vuccati. Tīṇipi hetāni nibbānasseva adhivacanānī’ti.

If, even after being spoken to thus, he does not understand, he should be made to understand by way of the path. How? First, he should be asked: 'Do you speak of something called the path?' 'Yes, I do.' 'At the moment of the path, are defilements destroyed, being destroyed, or will they be destroyed?' Knowing, he will say: 'It is not proper to say that they are destroyed or will be destroyed, but it is proper to say that they are being destroyed.' 'If so, which is the Nibbāna that is the destruction of defilements for the path? Which are the defilements being destroyed by the path? Taking which Nibbāna—the destruction of defilements—as its object, which defilements does the path destroy? Therefore, do not grasp it thus. Rather, on account of Nibbāna, lust and so forth are destroyed, and thus the one Nibbāna itself is called the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion. These three are indeed designations of Nibbāna itself.'

Evaṃ vutte evamāha – ‘tvaṃ āgamma āgammāti vadesī’ti? ‘Āma vademī’ti. ‘Āgamma nāmāti idaṃ te kuto laddha’nti? ‘Suttato laddha’nti[M 0.0051]. ‘Āhara sutta’nti. “Evaṃ avijjā ca taṇhā ca taṃ āgamma, tamhi khīṇā, tamhi bhaggā, na ca kiñci kadācī”ti. Evaṃ vutte paravādī tuṇhībhāvaṃ āpannoti.

When this was said, he said thus: 'Do you say "on account of, on account of"?' 'Yes, I say it.' 'Where did you get this term "on account of" from?' 'I got it from the Sutta.' 'Bring the Sutta.' '"Thus, ignorance and craving, on account of that, are exhausted in that, broken up in that, and nothing whatsoever ever remains."' When this was said, the opponent became silent.

Idhāpi dasāyatanāni kāmāvacarāni, dve pana catubhūmakāni lokiyalokuttaramissakānīti veditabbāni.

Here, too, the ten sense bases are of the sense-sphere, while the two, being of the four planes, are to be understood as mixed, mundane and supramundane.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Division.

3. Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Section of Questions

168. Idhāpi [V 0.0051] pañhāpucchake yaṃ labbhati yañca na labbhati, taṃ sabbaṃ pucchitvā labbhamānavaseneva vissajjanaṃ vuttaṃ; na kevalañca idha, sabbesupi pañhāpucchakesu eseva nayo. Idha pana dasannaṃ āyatanānaṃ rūpabhāvena abyākatatā veditabbā. Dvinnaṃ āyatanānaṃ khandhavibhaṅge catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ viya kusalādibhāvo veditabbo. Kevalañhi cattāro khandhā sappaccayāva saṅkhatāva dhammāyatanaṃ pana “siyā appaccayaṃ, siyā asaṅkhata”nti āgataṃ. Ārammaṇattikesu ca anārammaṇaṃ sukhumarūpasaṅkhātaṃ dhammāyatanaṃ na-vattabbakoṭṭhāsaṃ bhajati. Tañca kho anārammaṇattā na parittādibhāvena navattabbadhammārammaṇattāti ayamettha viseso. Sesaṃ tādisameva. Idhāpi hi cattāro khandhā viya dvāyatanā pañcapaṇṇāsa kāmāvacaradhamme ārabbha rajjantassa dussantassa muyhantassa saṃvarantassa sammasantassa paccavekkhantassa ca parittārammaṇāti sabbaṃ khandhesu vuttasadisamevāti.

168. Here too, in the section on questions, whatever is obtainable and whatever is not obtainable—having asked about all that, the answer is stated in accordance with what is obtainable. Not only here, but in all sections on questions, this is the method. Here, the ten sense bases should be understood as indeterminate by way of their nature as form. The nature of the two sense bases, like that of the four aggregates in the analysis of aggregates, should be understood as wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth. For the four aggregates are always conditioned and formed, but the dhamma-base is said to be 'sometimes unconditioned, sometimes unformed.' And among the triads of objects, the dhamma-base, which is reckoned as subtle matter, being without an object, falls into the category of the unmentionable. However, because it is without an object, it is not to be spoken of as having limited, etc., objects—this is the distinction here. The rest is similar. Here too, just as with the four aggregates, the two sense bases, when one is attached, averse, deluded, restraining, comprehending, and reflecting with regard to the fifty-five sense-sphere phenomena, have limited objects—all this is just as explained in the [section on] aggregates.

Sammohavinodaniyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya

From the Sammohavinodanī, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga.

Āyatanavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Sense Bases is concluded.

3. Dhātuvibhaṅgo

3. The Analysis of Elements

1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Suttanta Division

172. Idāni [P 0.0055][M 0.0052][V 0.0052] tadanantare dhātuvibhaṅge sabbā dhātuyo chahi chahi dhātūhi saṅkhipitvā tīhi chakkehi suttantabhājanīyaṃ dassento cha dhātuyotiādimāha. Tattha chāti gaṇanaparicchedo. Dhātuyoti paricchinnadhammanidassanaṃ. Pathavīdhātūtiādīsu dhātvaṭṭho nāma sabhāvaṭṭho, sabhāvaṭṭho nāma suññataṭṭho, suññataṭṭho nāma nissattaṭṭhoti evaṃ sabhāvasuññatanissattaṭṭhena pathavīyeva dhātu pathavīdhātu. Āpodhātuādīsupi eseva nayo. Evamettha padasamāsaṃ viditvā evamattho veditabbo – pathavīdhātūti patiṭṭhānadhātu. Āpodhātūti ābandhanadhātu. Tejodhātūti paripācanadhātu. Vāyodhātūti vitthambhanadhātu. Ākāsadhātūti asamphuṭṭhadhātu. Viññāṇadhātūti vijānanadhātu.

172. Now, immediately following that, in the Analysis of Elements, showing the Suttanta Division by means of three sets of six after having summarized all elements into six elements each, he said: 'Six elements,' and so forth. Herein, 'six' is a numerical delimitation. 'Elements' is a designation of delimited phenomena. In 'earth element,' and so forth, the meaning of 'element' is intrinsic nature; the meaning of intrinsic nature is emptiness; the meaning of emptiness is being devoid of a self. Thus, by way of the meaning of intrinsic nature, emptiness, and being devoid of a self, earth itself is an element, the earth element. The same method applies to the water element, and so forth. Here, having understood the word combination, the meaning should be understood thus: the earth element is the element of support; the water element is the element of cohesion; the fire element is the element of maturation; the air element is the element of motion; the space element is the element of non-contact; and the consciousness element is the element of cognition.

173. Pathavīdhātudvayanti pathavīdhātu dve ayaṃ. Ayaṃ pathavīdhātu nāma na ekā eva ajjhattikabāhirabhedena pana dve dhātuyo evāti attho. Tenevāha – “atthi ajjhattikā atthi bāhirā”ti. Tattha ajjhattikāti sattasantānapariyāpannā niyakajjhattā. Bāhirāti saṅkhārasantānapariyāpannā anindriyabaddhā. Ajjhattaṃ paccattanti ubhayampetaṃ niyakajjhattādhivacanameva. Idāni taṃ sabhāvākārato dassetuṃ kakkhaḷantiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kakkhaḷanti thaddhaṃ. Kharigatanti pharusaṃ. Kakkhaḷattanti kakkhaḷabhāvo. Kakkhaḷabhāvoti kakkhaḷasabhāvo. Ajjhattaṃ upādinnanti niyakajjhattasaṅkhātaṃ upādinnaṃ. Upādinnaṃ nāma sarīraṭṭhakaṃ. Sarīraṭṭhakañhi kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ vā hotu mā vā, taṃ sandhāya upādinnampi atthi anupādinnampi; ādinnaggahitaparāmaṭṭhavasena [V 0.0053] pana [P 0.0056] sabbampetaṃ upādinnamevāti dassetuṃ “ajjhattaṃ upādinna”nti āha.

173. The phrase 'two earth elements' means 'this earth element is twofold.' The meaning is that this earth element is not just one, but indeed two elements, by way of the internal and external division. Therefore, it is said: 'There is the internal; there is the external.' Herein, 'internal' refers to what is included within the continuum of a being, belonging to one's own self. 'External' refers to what is included in the continuum of formations, not bound to the faculties. 'Internal' and 'personal'—both these are merely synonyms for what belongs to one's own self. Now, to show its nature and characteristics, 'hard,' and so forth, is stated. Herein, 'hard' means rigid. 'Harsh' means rough. 'Hardness' means the state of being hard. 'The nature of hardness' means the intrinsic nature of hardness. 'Internally clung-to' refers to what is designated as one's own self and is clung-to. 'Clung-to' means the bodily octad. For whether the bodily octad is kamma-originated or not, in reference to that, there is both what is clung-to and what is not clung-to. However, to indicate that all of this is indeed clung-to in the sense of being grasped, adhered to, and clung to, it is said: 'internally clung-to.'

Idāni tameva pathavīdhātuṃ vatthuvasena dassetuṃ seyyathidaṃ kesā lomātiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha seyyathidanti nipāto. Tassattho – yā sā ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu sā katamā? Yaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ kakkhaḷaṃ nāma taṃ katamanti? Kesā lomātiādi tassā ajjhattikāya pathavīdhātuyā vatthuvasena pabhedadassanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – kesā nāma ajjhattā upādinnā sarīraṭṭhakā kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇā imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko [M 0.0053] koṭṭhāso. Lomā nāma…pe… karīsaṃ nāma. Idha pana avuttampi paṭisambhidāmagge (paṭi. ma. 1.4) pāḷiāruḷhaṃ matthaluṅgaṃ āharitvā matthaluṅgaṃ nāma ajjhattaṃ upādinnaṃ sarīraṭṭhakaṃ kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇaṃ imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso. Parato āpodhātuādīnaṃ niddese pittādīsupi eseva nayo.

Now, to show that very earth element by way of its substance, 'such as head hairs, body hairs,' and so forth, is stated. Herein, 'such as' is a particle. Its meaning is: 'What is that internal earth element? Or what is that which is internal, personal, called hardness?' 'Head hairs, body hairs,' and so forth—this shows the classification of that internal earth element by way of its substance. This is what is said: Head hairs are a particular part within this body, internally clung-to, belonging to the bodily octad, characterized by hardness. Body hairs are... feces is... Here, however, even though not stated here, by bringing in the brain-pulp, which appears in the Pāli of the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭis. I.4), the brain-pulp is a particular part within this body, internally clung-to, belonging to the bodily octad, characterized by hardness. In the subsequent exposition of the water element, and so forth, the same method applies to bile, and so forth.

Iminā kiṃ dassitaṃ hoti? Dhātumanasikāro. Imasmiṃ pana dhātumanasikāre kammaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā uttamatthaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇitukāmena kiṃ kattabbaṃ? Catupārisuddhisīlaṃ sodhetabbaṃ. Sīlavato hi kammaṭṭhānabhāvanā ijjhati. Tassa sodhanavidhānaṃ visuddhimagge vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Visuddhasīlena pana sīle patiṭṭhāya dasa pubbapalibodhā chinditabbā. Tesampi chindanavidhānaṃ visuddhimagge vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Chinnapalibodhena dhātumanasikārakammaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhitabbaṃ.
