Ācariyenāpi dhātumanasikārakammaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhāpentena sattavidhaṃ uggahakosallaṃ dasavidhañca manasikārakosallaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. Antevāsikenāpi ācariyassa santike bahuvāre sajjhāyaṃ katvā nijjaṭaṃ paguṇaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kātabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ – “ādikammikena bhikkhunā jarāmaraṇā muccitukāmena sattahākārehi uggahakosallaṃ icchitabbaṃ, dasahākārehi manasikārakosallaṃ icchitabba”nti.

What is shown by this? Contemplation of the elements. However, having undertaken the practice in this contemplation of the elements, and having established insight, what should one do who wishes to attain the ultimate goal of arahantship? The fourfold purity of virtue should be purified. For one who is virtuous, the development of the meditation subject succeeds. The method of its purification should be understood in the way stated in the Visuddhimagga. However, by one with purified virtue, having established oneself in virtue, the ten preliminary impediments should be cut off. The method of cutting them off too should be understood in the way stated in the Visuddhimagga. With the impediments cut off, the meditation subject of contemplation of the elements should be learned. And by the teacher, when instructing in the meditation subject of contemplation of the elements, the sevenfold skill in learning and the tenfold skill in attention should be explained. And by the student, having repeatedly recited and studied under the teacher, the meditation subject should be made thoroughly clear and well-practiced. For this is stated in the commentary: 'A monk who is a beginner, wishing to be freed from aging and death, should desire the sevenfold skill in learning and the tenfold skill in attention.'

Tattha vacasā, manasā, vaṇṇato, saṇṭhānato, disato, okāsato, paricchedatoti imehi sattahākārehi imasmiṃ dhātumanasikārakammaṭṭhāne ‘uggahakosallaṃ’ icchitabbaṃ. Anupubbato, nātisīghato, nātisaṇikato, vikkhepapaṭibāhanato[P 0.0057], paṇṇattisamatikkamato, anupubbamuñcanato, lakkhaṇato, tayo ca suttantāti imehi dasahākārehi ‘manasikārakosallaṃ’ icchitabbaṃ. Tadubhayampi parato satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅge āvi bhavissati.

Herein, in this meditation subject of contemplation of the elements, 'skill in learning' should be desired in these seven ways: by speech, by mind, by appearance, by shape, by direction, by location, and by delimitation. And 'skill in attention' should be desired in these ten ways: by gradual progression, not too quickly, not too slowly, by repelling distraction, by transcending designations, by gradual release, by characteristics, and by the three discourses. Both of these will become manifest later in the Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness.

Evaṃ [V 0.0054] uggahitakammaṭṭhānena pana visuddhimagge vutte aṭṭhārasa senāsanadose vajjetvā pañcaṅgasamannāgate senāsane vasantena attanāpi pañcahi padhāniyaṅgehi samannāgatena pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantena vivittokāsagatena kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikātabbaṃ. Manasikarontena ca vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedavasena [M 0.0054] kesādīsu ekekakoṭṭhāsaṃ manasikaritvā avasāne evaṃ manasikāro pavattetabbo – ime kesā nāma sīsakaṭāhapaliveṭhanacamme jātā. Tattha yathā vammikamatthake jātesu kuṇṭhatiṇesu na vammikamatthako jānāti ‘mayi kuṇṭhatiṇāni jātānī’ti, nāpi kuṇṭhatiṇāni jānanti ‘mayaṃ vammikamatthake jātānī’ti, evameva na sīsakaṭāhapaliveṭhanacammaṃ jānāti ‘mayi kesā jātā’ti, nāpi kesā jānanti ‘mayaṃ sīsakaṭāhapaliveṭhanacamme jātā’ti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti kesā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

However, by one who has thus learned the meditation subject, avoiding the eighteen faults of a dwelling as stated in the Visuddhimagga, and residing in a dwelling endowed with five factors, being oneself endowed with the five factors of striving, having returned from the alms round after the meal, and having gone to a secluded place, the meditation subject should be attended to. And while attending to it, having attended to each part—such as head hairs—by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, at the end, attention should be directed thus: 'These so-called hairs have grown on the skin covering the skull.' Just as when kuṇṭha grass grows on the top of an anthill, the anthill does not know, 'Kuṇṭha grass has grown on me,' nor does the kuṇṭha grass know, 'We have grown on the top of the anthill,' so too, the skin covering the skull does not know, 'Hairs have grown on me,' nor do the hairs know, 'We have grown on the skin covering the skull.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual regard and reflection. Thus, the so-called hairs are a separate part within this body—inert, indeterminate, empty, without a living being, rigid—the earth element.

Lomā sarīraveṭhanacamme jātā. Tattha yathā suññagāmaṭṭhāne jātesu dabbatiṇesu na suññagāmaṭṭhānaṃ jānāti ‘mayi dabbatiṇāni jātānī’ti, nāpi dabbatiṇāni jānanti ‘mayaṃ suññagāmaṭṭhāne jātānī’ti, evameva na sarīraveṭhanacammaṃ jānāti ‘mayi lomā jātā’ti, nāpi lomā jānanti ‘mayaṃ sarīraveṭhanacamme jātā’ti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti lomā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

Hairs grow on the skin enveloping the body. There, just as when grass grows in an empty village site, the empty village site does not know, "Grass has grown on me," nor does the grass know, "We have grown in an empty village site," even so, the skin enveloping the body does not know, "Hairs have grown on me," nor do the hairs know, "We have grown on the skin enveloping the body." These things are devoid of mutual awareness and reflection. Thus, hair in this body is a distinct component, inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a being, stiff, the earth element.

Nakhā aṅgulīnaṃ aggesu jātā. Tattha yathā kumārakesu daṇḍakehi madhukaṭṭhike vijjhitvā kīḷantesu na daṇḍakā jānanti ‘amhesu madhukaṭṭhikā ṭhapitā’ti, nāpi madhukaṭṭhikā jānanti ‘mayaṃ daṇḍakesu ṭhapitā’ti, evameva na aṅguliyo jānanti ‘amhākaṃ aggesu nakhā jātā’ti, nāpi nakhā jānanti ‘mayaṃ aṅgulīnaṃ aggesu jātā’ti. Aññamaññaṃ [P 0.0058] ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti nakhā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

Nails grow at the tips of the fingers. There, just as when boys play by piercing honey-sticks with small sticks, the small sticks do not know, "Honey-sticks are placed in us," nor do the honey-sticks know, "We are placed in the small sticks," so too the fingers do not know, "Nails have grown at our tips," nor do the nails know, "We have grown at the tips of the fingers." These things are devoid of mutual awareness and reflection. Thus, nails in this body are a distinct component, inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a being, stiff, the earth element.

Dantā hanukaṭṭhikesu jātā. Tattha yathā vaḍḍhakīhi pāsāṇaudukkhalesu kenacideva silesajātena bandhitvā ṭhapitathambhesu na udukkhalāni jānanti ‘amhesu thambhā ṭhitā’ti, nāpi thambhā [V 0.0055] jānanti ‘mayaṃ udukkhalesu ṭhitā’ti, evameva na hanukaṭṭhikā jānanti ‘amhesu dantā jātā’ti[M 0.0055], nāpi dantā jānanti ‘mayaṃ hanukaṭṭhikesu jātā’ti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti dantā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

Teeth are born in the jawbones. There, just as when carpenters set pillars in stone mortars, having fixed them with some kind of cement, the mortars do not know, "Pillars are established in us," nor do the pillars know, "We are established in the mortars," so too the jawbones do not know, "Teeth are born in us," nor do the teeth know, "We are born in the jawbones." These things are devoid of mutual awareness and reflection. Thus, teeth in this body are a distinct component, inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a being, stiff, the earth element.

Taco sakalasarīraṃ pariyonandhitvā ṭhito. Tattha yathā allagocammapariyonaddhāya mahāvīṇāya na mahāvīṇā jānāti ‘ahaṃ allagocammena pariyonaddhā’ti, nāpi allagocammaṃ jānāti ‘mayā mahāvīṇā pariyoddhā’ti, evameva na sarīraṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ tacena pariyonaddha’nti, nāpi taco jānāti ‘mayā sarīraṃ pariyonaddhanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti taco nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

The skin envelops the entire body. There, just as a great lute covered with wet cowhide does not know, "I am covered with wet cowhide," nor does the wet cowhide know, "By me the great lute is covered," even so the body does not know, "I am covered by skin," nor does the skin know, "By me the body is covered." These things are devoid of mutual awareness and reflection. Thus, skin in this body is a distinct component, inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a being, stiff, the earth element.

Maṃsaṃ aṭṭhisaṅghāṭaṃ anulimpitvā ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā mahāmattikāya littāya bhittiyā na bhitti jānāti ‘ahaṃ mahāmattikāya littā’ti, nāpi mahāmattikā jānāti ‘mayā mahābhitti littā’ti, evameva na aṭṭhisaṅghāṭo jānāti ‘ahaṃ navamaṃsapesisatappabhedena maṃsena litto’ti, nāpi maṃsaṃ jānāti ‘mayā aṭṭhisaṅghāṭo litto’ti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti maṃsaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

Flesh is smeared over the framework of bones. There, just as a wall plastered with much clay does not know, "I am plastered with much clay," nor does the much clay know, "By me a great wall is plastered," so too the framework of bones does not know, "I am smeared with flesh of hundreds of different kinds of fresh muscle," nor does the flesh know, "By me the framework of bones is smeared." These things are devoid of mutual awareness and reflection. Thus, flesh in this body is a distinct component, inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a being, stiff, the earth element.

Nhāru sarīrabbhantare aṭṭhīni ābandhamānā ṭhitā. Tattha yathā vallīhi vinaddhesu kuṭṭadārūsu na kuṭṭadārūni jānanti ‘mayaṃ vallīhi vinaddhānī’ti, nāpi valliyo jānanti ‘amhehi kuṭṭadārūni vinaddhānī’ti, evameva na aṭṭhīni jānanti ‘mayaṃ nhārūhi ābaddhānī’ti, nāpi nhārū jānanti ‘amhehi aṭṭhīni ābaddhānī’ti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā [P 0.0059] ete dhammā. Iti nhāru nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

Sinews bind the bones together within the body. Just as when wall-planks are bound by creepers, the wall-planks do not know, "We are bound by creepers," nor do the creepers know, "By us the wall-planks are bound," so too the bones do not know, "We are bound by sinews," nor do the sinews know, "By us the bones are bound." These things are devoid of mutual awareness and reflection. Thus, sinews in this body are a distinct component, inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a being, stiff, the earth element.

Aṭṭhīsu paṇhikaṭṭhi gopphakaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Gopphakaṭṭhi jaṅghaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Jaṅghaṭṭhi ūruṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Ūruṭṭhi kaṭiṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ[M 0.0056]. Kaṭiṭṭhi piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ [V 0.0056] ukkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Piṭṭhikaṇṭako gīvaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhito. Gīvaṭṭhi sīsaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Sīsaṭṭhi gīvaṭṭhike patiṭṭhitaṃ. Gīvaṭṭhi piṭṭhikaṇṭake patiṭṭhitaṃ. Piṭṭhikaṇṭako kaṭiṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhito. Kaṭiṭṭhi ūruṭṭhike patiṭṭhitaṃ. Ūruṭṭhi jaṅghaṭṭhike patiṭṭhitaṃ. Jaṅghaṭṭhi gopphakaṭṭhike patiṭṭhitaṃ. Gopphakaṭṭhi paṇhikaṭṭhike patiṭṭhitaṃ.

Among the bones, the heel bone supports the ankle bone. The ankle bone supports the shin bone. The shin bone supports the thigh bone. The thigh bone supports the hip bone. The hip bone supports the spinal column. The spinal column supports the neck bone. The neck bone supports the skull bone. The skull bone rests on the neck bone. The neck bone rests on the spinal column. The spinal column rests on the hip bone. The hip bone rests on the thigh bone. The thigh bone rests on the shin bone. The shin bone rests on the ankle bone. The ankle bone rests on the heel bone.

Tattha yathā iṭṭhakadārugomayādisañcayesu na heṭṭhimā heṭṭhimā jānanti ‘mayaṃ uparime uparime ukkhipitvā ṭhitā’ti, nāpi uparimā uparimā jānanti ‘mayaṃ heṭṭhimesu heṭṭhimesu patiṭṭhitā’ti, evameva na paṇhikaṭṭhi jānāti ‘ahaṃ gopphakaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhita’nti, na gopphakaṭṭhi jānāti ‘ahaṃ jaṅghaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhita’nti, na jaṅghaṭṭhi jānāti ‘ahaṃ ūruṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhita’nti, na ūruṭṭhi jānāti ‘ahaṃ kaṭiṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhita’nti, na kaṭiṭṭhi jānāti ‘ahaṃ piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhita’nti, na piṭṭhikaṇṭako jānāti ‘ahaṃ gīvaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhito’ti, na gīvaṭṭhi jānāti ‘ahaṃ sīsaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhita’nti, na sīsaṭṭhi jānāti ‘ahaṃ gīvaṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhita’nti, na gīvaṭṭhi jānāti ‘ahaṃ piṭṭhikaṇṭake patiṭṭhita’nti, na piṭṭhikaṇṭako jānāti ‘ahaṃ kaṭiṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhito’ti, na kaṭiṭṭhi jānāti ‘ahaṃ ūruṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhita’nti, na ūruṭṭhi jānāti ‘ahaṃ jaṅghaṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhita’nti, na jaṅghaṭṭhi jānāti ‘ahaṃ gopphakaṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhita’nti, na gopphakaṭṭhi jānāti ‘ahaṃ paṇhikaṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti aṭṭhi nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

Just as in a pile of bricks, wood, or cow dung, the lower ones do not know, 'We are supporting the upper ones,' nor do the upper ones know, 'We are resting on the lower ones,' so too, the heel bone does not know, 'I am supporting the ankle bone,' nor does the ankle bone know, 'I am supporting the shin bone,' nor does the shin bone know, 'I am supporting the thigh bone,' nor does the thigh bone know, 'I am supporting the hip bone,' nor does the hip bone know, 'I am supporting the spinal column,' nor does the spinal column know, 'I am supporting the neck bone,' nor does the neck bone know, 'I am supporting the skull bone,' nor does the skull bone know, 'I am resting on the neck bone,' nor does the neck bone know, 'I am resting on the spinal column,' nor does the spinal column know, 'I am resting on the hip bone,' nor does the hip bone know, 'I am resting on the thigh bone,' nor does the thigh bone know, 'I am resting on the shin bone,' nor does the shin bone know, 'I am resting on the ankle bone,' nor does the ankle bone know, 'I am resting on the heel bone.' These things are devoid of mutual awareness and reflection. Thus, bone in this body is a distinct component, inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a living being, stiff, the earth element.

Aṭṭhimiñjaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ aṭṭhīnaṃ abbhantare ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā veḷupabbādīnaṃ anto pakkhittesu sinnavettaggādīsu [P 0.0060] na veḷupabbādīni jānanti ‘amhesu vettaggādīni pakkhittānī’ti, nāpi vettaggādīni jānanti ‘mayaṃ veḷupabbādīsu ṭhitānīti, evameva na aṭṭhīni jānanti ‘amhākaṃ anto aṭṭhimiñjaṃ ṭhita’nti, nāpi aṭṭhimiñjaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ aṭṭhīnaṃ anto ṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti aṭṭhimiñjaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

The bone marrow lies within those bones. Just as, when moistened pith of reeds is placed inside bamboo joints, the bamboo joints do not know, 'The pith is placed within us,' nor does the pith know, 'We are placed within the bamboo joints,' in the same way, the bones do not know, 'The bone marrow lies within us,' nor does the bone marrow know, 'I lie within the bones.' These things are devoid of mutual awareness and reflection. Thus, bone marrow in this body is a distinct component, inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a living being, stiff, the earth element.

Vakkaṃ [V 0.0057] galavāṭakato nikkhantena ekamūlena thokaṃ gantvā dvidhā bhinnena thūlanhārunā vinibaddhaṃ hutvā hadayamaṃsaṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā vaṇṭupanibaddhe [M 0.0057] ambaphaladvaye na vaṇṭaṃ jānāti ‘mayā ambaphaladvayaṃ upanibaddha’nti, nāpi ambaphaladvayaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ vaṇṭena upanibaddha’nti, evameva na thūlanhāru jānāti ‘mayā vakkaṃ upanibaddha’nti, nāpi vakkaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ thūlanhārunā upanibaddha’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti vakkaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

The kidneys emerge from the throat cavity with a single root, then split into two and are bound by thick sinews, surrounding the heart muscle. Just as two mango fruits attached to a single stem do not know, 'We are attached to the stem,' nor does the stem know, 'The two mango fruits are attached to me,' in the same way, the thick sinews do not know, 'The kidneys are bound by me,' nor do the kidneys know, 'We are bound by the thick sinews.' These things are devoid of mutual awareness and reflection. Thus, the kidneys in this body are a distinct component, inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a living being, stiff, the earth element.

Hadayaṃ sarīrabbhantare uraṭṭhipañjaramajjhaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā jiṇṇasandamānikapañjarabbhantaraṃ nissāya ṭhapitāya maṃsapesiyā na jiṇṇasandamānikapañjarabbhantaraṃ jānāti ‘maṃ nissāya maṃsapesi ṭhapitā’ti, nāpi maṃsapesi jānāti ‘ahaṃ jiṇṇasandamānikapañjarabbhantaraṃ nissāya ṭhitā’ti, evameva na uraṭṭhipañjarabbhantaraṃ jānāti ‘maṃ nissāya hadayaṃ ṭhita’nti, nāpi hadayaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ uraṭṭhipañjarabbhantaraṃ nissāya ṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti hadayaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

The heart is situated within the body, relying on the middle of the rib cage. Just as an old basket does not know, regarding a piece of meat placed inside it, 'A piece of meat relies on me,' nor does the piece of meat know, 'I rely on an old basket,' just so, the rib cage does not know, 'The heart relies on me,' nor does the heart know, 'I rely on the rib cage.' These things are devoid of mutual awareness and reflection. Thus, the heart in this body is a distinct component, inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a living being, stiff, the earth element.

Yakanaṃ antosarīre dvinnaṃ thanānaṃ abbhantare dakkhiṇapassaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā ukkhalikapālapassamhi lagge yamakamaṃsapiṇḍe na ukkhalikapālapassaṃ jānāti ‘mayi yamakamaṃsapiṇḍo laggo’ti, nāpi yamakamaṃsapiṇḍo [P 0.0061] jānāti ‘ahaṃ ukkhalikapālapasse laggo’ti, evameva na thanānaṃ abbhantare dakkhiṇapassaṃ jānāti ‘maṃ nissāya yakanaṃ ṭhita’nti, nāpi yakanaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ thanānaṃ abbhantare dakkhiṇapassaṃ nissāya ṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti yakanaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

The liver is situated inside the body, supported on the right side between the two breasts. Just as two lumps of meat stuck to the side of a pot-shard do not know, 'We are stuck to the side of the pot-shard,' nor does the pot-shard know, 'Two lumps of meat are stuck to me,' so too the right side between the two breasts does not know, 'The liver is supported by me,' nor does the liver know, 'I am supported on the right side between the two breasts.' These things are devoid of mutual awareness and reflection. Thus, the liver in this body is a distinct component, inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a living being, stiff, the earth element.

Kilomakesu paṭicchannakilomakaṃ hadayañca vakkañca parivāretvā ṭhitaṃ, apaṭicchannakilomakaṃ sakalasarīre cammassa heṭṭhato maṃsaṃ pariyonandhitvā ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā pilotikapaliveṭhite maṃse na maṃsaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ pilotikāya paliveṭhita’nti, nāpi pilotikā jānāti ‘mayā maṃsaṃ paliveṭhita’nti, evameva na vakkahadayāni sakalasarīre maṃsañca [V 0.0058] jānāti ‘ahaṃ kilomakena paṭicchanna’nti, nāpi kilomakaṃ jānāti ‘mayā vakkahadayāni sakalasarīre maṃsañca paṭicchanna’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā [M 0.0058] ete dhammā. Iti kilomakaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

Of the membranes, the concealed membrane is situated surrounding the heart and kidneys; the unconcealed membrane is situated enveloping the flesh beneath the skin throughout the entire body. Just as flesh wrapped in a cloth does not know, 'I am wrapped in a cloth,' nor does the cloth know, 'Flesh is wrapped by me,' so too the kidneys, heart, and flesh throughout the body do not know, 'I am covered by the membrane,' nor does the membrane know, 'The kidneys, heart, and flesh throughout the body are covered by me.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, the membrane is a distinct part in this body—unconscious, indeterminate, empty, without a living principle, rigid, and of the earth element.

Pihakaṃ hadayassa vāmapasse udarapaṭalassa matthakapassaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā koṭṭhakamatthakapassaṃ nissāya ṭhitāya gomayapiṇḍiyā na koṭṭhakamatthakapassaṃ jānāti ‘gomayapiṇḍi maṃ nissāya ṭhitā’ti, nāpi gomayapiṇḍi jānāti ‘ahaṃ koṭṭhakamatthakapassaṃ nissāya ṭhitā’ti, evameva na udarapaṭalassa matthakapassaṃ jānāti ‘pihakaṃ maṃ nissāya ṭhita’nti, nāpi pihakaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ udarapaṭalassa matthakapassaṃ nissāya ṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti pihakaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

The spleen is situated on the left side of the heart, resting against the top of the abdominal lining. Just as a lump of cow dung placed on the top of a storehouse does not know, 'The lump of cow dung is resting on me,' nor does the lump of cow dung know, 'I am resting on the top of the storehouse,' so too the top of the abdominal lining does not know, 'The spleen is resting on me,' nor does the spleen know, 'I am resting on the top of the abdominal lining.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, the spleen is a distinct part in this body—unconscious, indeterminate, empty, without a living principle, rigid, and of the earth element.

Papphāsaṃ sarīrabbhantare dvinnaṃ thanānaṃ abbhantare hadayañca yakanañca uparichādetvā olambantaṃ ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā jiṇṇakoṭṭhabbhantare olambamāne sakuṇakulāvake na jiṇṇakoṭṭhabbhantaraṃ jānāti ‘mayi sakuṇakulāvako olambamāno ṭhito’ti, nāpi sakuṇakulāvako jānāti ‘ahaṃ jiṇṇakoṭṭhabbhantare olambamāno ṭhito’ti[P 0.0062], evameva na sarīrabbhantaraṃ jānāti ‘mayi papphāsaṃ olambamānaṃ ṭhita’nti, nāpi papphāsaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ evarūpe sarīrabbhantare olambamānaṃ ṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti papphāsaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

The lungs are situated hanging inside the body, between the two breasts, covering the heart and liver from above. Just as, when a bird's nest is hanging inside an old storehouse, the old storehouse does not know, 'A bird's nest is hanging inside me,' nor does the bird's nest know, 'I am hanging inside the old storehouse,' so too the inside of the body does not know, 'The lungs are hanging inside me,' nor do the lungs know, 'I am hanging inside such a body.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, the lungs are a distinct part of this body—unconscious, indeterminate, empty, without a living principle, rigid, and of the earth element.

Antaṃ galavāṭakato karīsamaggapariyante sarīrabbhantare ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā lohitadoṇikāya obhujitvā ṭhapite chinnasīsadhamanikaḷevare na lohitadoṇi jānāti ‘mayi dhamanikaḷevaraṃ ṭhita’nti, nāpi dhamanikaḷevaraṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ lohitadoṇikāyaṃ ṭhita’nti, evameva na sarīrabbhantaraṃ jānāti ‘mayi antaṃ ṭhita’nti, nāpi antaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ sarīrabbhantare ṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti antaṃ nāma [M 0.0059] imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

The intestines are situated inside the body, from the gullet down to the end of the path of excrement. Just as when a headless corpse is bent and placed in a trough of blood, the trough of blood does not know, 'A headless corpse is in me,' nor does the headless corpse know, 'I am in a trough of blood,' so too the inside of the body does not know, 'The intestines are in me,' nor do the intestines know, 'I am inside the body.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, the intestines are a distinct part in this body—unconscious, indeterminate, empty, without a living principle, rigid, and of the earth element.

Antaguṇaṃ [V 0.0059] antantare ekavīsati antabhoge bandhitvā ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā pādapuñchanarajjumaṇḍalakaṃ sibbetvā ṭhitesu rajjukesu na pādapuñchanarajjumaṇḍalakaṃ jānāti ‘rajjukā maṃ sibbetvā ṭhitā’ti, nāpi rajjukā jānanti ‘mayaṃ pādapuñchanarajjumaṇḍalakaṃ sibbetvā ṭhitā’ti, evameva na antaṃ jānāti ‘antaguṇaṃ maṃ ābandhitvā ṭhita’nti, nāpi antaguṇaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ antaṃ bandhitvā ṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti antaguṇaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

The mesentery is situated between the intestines, binding the twenty-one intestinal loops. Just as with a foot-wiping mat woven from ropes, the mat does not know, 'The ropes have woven me,' nor do the ropes know, 'We have woven the foot-wiping mat,' so too the intestines do not know, 'The mesentery has bound me,' nor does the mesentery know, 'I have bound the intestines.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, the mesentery is a distinct part in this body—unconscious, indeterminate, empty, without a living principle, rigid, and of the earth element.

Udariyaṃ udare ṭhitaṃ asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ. Tattha yathā suvānadoṇiyaṃ ṭhite suvānavamathumhi na suvānadoṇi jānāti ‘mayi suvānavamathu ṭhito’ti, nāpi suvānavamathu jānāti ‘ahaṃ suvānadoṇiyaṃ ṭhito’ti, evameva na udaraṃ jānāti ‘mayi udariyaṃ ṭhita’nti, nāpi udariyaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ udare ṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti udariyaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

The undigested food—what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and savored—is situated in the stomach. Just as with dog's vomit in a dog's trough, the dog's trough does not know, 'Dog's vomit is in me,' nor does the dog's vomit know, 'I am in the dog's trough,' so too the stomach does not know, 'Undigested food is in me,' nor does the undigested food know, 'I am in the stomach.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, the undigested food is a distinct part of this body—unconscious, indeterminate, empty, without a living principle, rigid, and of the earth element.

Karīsaṃ [P 0.0063] pakkāsayasaṅkhāte aṭṭhaṅgulaveḷupabbasadise antapariyosāne ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā veḷupabbe omadditvā pakkhittāya saṇhapaṇḍumattikāya na veḷupabbaṃ jānāti ‘mayi paṇḍumattikā ṭhitā’ti, nāpi paṇḍumattikā jānāti ‘ahaṃ veḷupabbe ṭhitā’ti, evameva na pakkāsayo jānāti ‘mayi karīsaṃ ṭhita’nti, nāpi karīsaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ pakkāsaye ṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti karīsaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

Feces is situated at the end of the intestines, in what is called the 'receptacle for digested food,' which resembles a bamboo joint eight finger-breadths long. Just as when fine, yellowish clay is pressed and put into a bamboo joint, the bamboo joint does not know, 'Yellowish clay is in me,' nor does the yellowish clay know, 'I am in the bamboo joint,' so too the receptacle for digested food does not know, 'Feces is in me,' nor do the feces know, 'I am in the receptacle for digested food.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, feces is a distinct part in this body—unconscious, indeterminate, empty, without a living principle, rigid, and of the earth element.

Matthaluṅgaṃ sīsakaṭāhabbhantare ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā purāṇalābukaṭāhe pakkhittāya piṭṭhapiṇḍiyā na lābukaṭāhaṃ jānāti ‘mayi piṭṭhapiṇḍi ṭhitā’ti, nāpi piṭṭhapiṇḍi jānāti ‘ahaṃ lābukaṭāhe ṭhitā’ti, evameva na sīsakaṭāhabbhantaraṃ jānāti ‘mayi matthaluṅgaṃ ṭhita’nti, nāpi matthaluṅgaṃ jānāti [M 0.0060] ‘ahaṃ sīsakaṭāhabbhantare ṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti matthaluṅgaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

The brain is situated inside the skull. There, just as when a lump of dough is placed in an old gourd bowl, the gourd bowl does not know, "A lump of dough is situated in me," nor does the lump of dough know, "I am situated in the gourd bowl," so too the inside of the skull does not know, "The brain is situated in me," nor does the brain know, "I am situated inside the skull." These things are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, the brain in this body is a distinct part—unconscious, indeterminate, empty, without a living principle, rigid, and of the earth element.

Yaṃ [V 0.0060] vā panaññampīti iminā āpokoṭṭhāsādīsu tīsu anugataṃ pathavīdhātuṃ lakkhaṇavasena yevāpanakaṃ pathaviṃ katvā dasseti.

By the phrase 'Or whatever else,' the earth element that is included in the three other groups of parts, such as the water element, is shown to be merely earth by way of its characteristic.

Bāhirapathavīdhātuniddese ayoti kāḷalohaṃ. Lohanti jātilohaṃ, vijātilohaṃ, kittimalohaṃ, pisācalohanti catubbidhaṃ. Tattha ayo, sajjhu, suvaṇṇaṃ, tipu, sīsaṃ, tambalohaṃ, vekantakanti imāni satta jātilohāni nāma. Nāganāsikalohaṃ vijātilohaṃ nāma. Kaṃsalohaṃ, vaṭṭalohaṃ, ārakūṭanti tīṇi kittimalohāni nāma. Morakkhakaṃ, puthukaṃ, malinakaṃ, capalakaṃ, selakaṃ, āṭakaṃ, bhallakaṃ, dūsilohanti aṭṭha pisācalohāni nāma. Tesu pañca jātilohāni pāḷiyaṃ visuṃ vuttāneva. Tambalohaṃ, vekantakalohanti imehi pana dvīhi jātilohehi saddhiṃ sesaṃ sabbampi idha lohanti veditabbaṃ.

In the exposition of the external earth element, 'iron' (ayo) means black metal. Metal is of four kinds: natural metal, mixed metal, artificial metal, and demon metal. Among these, iron, silver, gold, tin, lead, copper, and vekanta—these seven are called natural metals. Nāganāsika-metal is called mixed metal. Bell metal, brass, and ārakūṭa—these three are called artificial metals. Morakkha, puthuka, malinaka, capalaka, selaka, āṭaka, bhallaka, and dūsiloha—these eight are called demon metals. Among these, five natural metals are separately mentioned in the Pāli text. But together with these two natural metals, copper and vekanta, all the rest should be understood here as 'metal.'

Tipūti setatipu. Sīsanti kāḷatipu. Sajjhūti [P 0.0064] rajataṃ. Muttāti sāmuddikamuttā. Maṇīti ṭhapetvā pāḷiāgate veḷuriyādayo seso jotirasādibhedo sabbopi maṇi. Veḷuriyoti vaṃsavaṇṇamaṇi. Saṅkhoti sāmuddikasaṅkho. Silāti kāḷasilā, paṇḍusilā, setasilātiādibhedā sabbāpi silā. Pavāḷanti pavāḷameva. Rajatanti kahāpaṇo. Jātarūpanti suvaṇṇaṃ. Lohitaṅkoti rattamaṇi. Masāragallanti kabaramaṇi. Tiṇādīsu bahisārā antamaso nāḷikerādayopi tiṇaṃ nāma. Antosāraṃ antamaso dārukhaṇḍampi kaṭṭhaṃ nāma. Sakkharāti muggamattato yāva muṭṭhippamāṇā marumbā sakkharā nāma. Muggamattato pana heṭṭhā vālikāti vuccati. Kaṭhalanti yaṃ kiñci kapālaṃ. Bhūmīti pathavī. Pāsāṇoti antomuṭṭhiyaṃ asaṇṭhahanato paṭṭhāya hatthippamāṇaṃ asampatto pāsāṇo nāma. Hatthippamāṇato paṭṭhāya pana upari pabbato [M 0.0061] nāma. Yaṃ vā panāti iminā tālaṭṭhi-nāḷikera-phalādibhedaṃ sesapathaviṃ gaṇhāti. Yā ca ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu yā ca bāhirāti iminā dvepi pathavīdhātuyo kakkhaḷaṭṭhena lakkhaṇato ekā pathavīdhātu evāti dasseti.

Tipu means white tin. Sīsa means black tin. Sajjhu means silver. Muttā means ocean pearl. Maṇi: Apart from beryl and others mentioned in the Pāli, all other gems, distinguished by their luster and essence, are maṇi. Veḷuriya means a gem the color of bamboo. Saṅkha means an ocean conch. Silā means all kinds of stone, such as black stone, yellowish stone, white stone, and so forth. Pavāḷa means coral itself. Rajata means a kahāpaṇa coin. Jātarūpa means gold. Lohitaṅka means a red gem. Masāragalla means a variegated gem. Among grasses and so forth, things with outer pith, even down to coconut palms, are called 'grass' (tiṇa). Things with inner pith, even a piece of wood, are called 'wood' (kaṭṭha). Sakkharā means coarse gravel, from the size of a mung bean up to the size of a fist. However, anything smaller than a mung bean is called sand (vālikā). Kaṭhala means any kind of potsherd. Bhūmi means earth (pathavī). Pāsāṇa means a stone, from a size that cannot be held in a closed fist up to one not reaching the size of an elephant, is called pāsāṇa. However, anything from the size of an elephant upwards is called a mountain (pabbata). By the phrase 'Or whatever else,' it includes the remaining earth element, such as palm seeds, coconut fruits, and so forth. And by the phrase 'the internal earth element and the external earth element,' it is shown that both earth elements, by their characteristic of hardness, are essentially one earth element.

174. Āpodhātuniddesādīsu heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Āpo āpogatantiādīsu ābandhanavasena āpo. Tadeva āposabhāvaṃ gatattā āpogataṃ nāma. Snehavasena sneho. Soyeva snehasabhāvaṃ gatattā snehagataṃ nāma. Bandhanattaṃ rūpassāti avinibbhogarūpassa bandhanabhāvo. Pittaṃ semhantiādīnipi [V 0.0061] vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedavasena [P 0.0065] pariggahetvā dhātuvaseneva manasikātabbāni.

174. In the exposition of the water element and so forth, it should be understood in the same way as explained below. In phrases such as 'water, water-property,' 'water' (āpo) is so called because of its binding function. That very thing, having attained the nature of water, is called 'water-property' (āpogata). Because of its cohesive nature, it is 'cohesion' (sneha). That very thing, having attained the nature of cohesion, is called 'cohesion-property' (snehagata). 'The binding function of form' means the binding nature of inseparable form.

Tatrāyaṃ nayo – pittesu hi abaddhapittaṃ jīvitindriyapaṭibaddhaṃ sakalasarīraṃ byāpetvā ṭhitaṃ, baddhapittaṃ pittakosake ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā pūvaṃ byāpetvā ṭhite tele na pūvaṃ jānāti ‘telaṃ maṃ byāpetvā ṭhita’nti, nāpi telaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ pūvaṃ byāpetvā ṭhita’nti, evameva na sarīraṃ jānāti ‘abaddhapittaṃ maṃ byāpetvā ṭhita’nti, nāpi abaddhapittaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ sarīraṃ byāpetvā ṭhita’nti. Yathā ca vassodakena puṇṇe kosātakīkosake na kosātakīkosako jānāti ‘mayi vassodakaṃ ṭhita’nti, nāpi vassodakaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ kosātakīkosake ṭhita’nti, evameva na pittakosako jānāti mayi baddhapittaṃ ṭhitanti, nāpi baddhapittaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ pittakosake ṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti pittaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

Herein is the method: Among biles, unbound bile, connected to the life faculty, remains pervading the entire body, while bound bile remains in the bile sac. Just as, when oil remains pervading a cake, the cake does not know, 'Oil remains pervading me,' nor does the oil know, 'I remain pervading the cake,' even so, the body does not know, 'Unbound bile remains pervading me,' nor does the unbound bile know, 'I remain pervading the body.' And just as, when a gourd is filled with rainwater, the gourd does not know, 'Rainwater remains in me,' nor does the rainwater know, 'I remain in the gourd,' even so, the bile sac does not know, 'Bound bile remains in me,' nor does the bound bile know, 'I remain in the bile sac.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, bile is a distinct constituent in this body—unconscious, indeterminate, empty, without a living principle, like broth, with the characteristic of binding, the water element.

Semhaṃ ekapatthapūrappamāṇaṃ udarapaṭale ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā upari sañjātapheṇapaṭalāya candanikāya na candanikā jānāti ‘mayi pheṇapaṭalaṃ ṭhita’nti, nāpi pheṇapaṭalaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ candanikāya ṭhita’nti, evameva na udarapaṭalaṃ jānāti ‘mayi semhaṃ ṭhita’nti, nāpi semhaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ udarapaṭale ṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti semhaṃ [M 0.0062] nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

Phlegm, to the measure of filling a single bowl, is situated on the membrane of the stomach. There, just as, when a pool of water has a layer of foam formed on its surface, the pool of water does not know, 'A layer of foam is situated upon me,' nor does the layer of foam know, 'I am situated upon the pool of water,' even so, the membrane of the stomach does not know, 'Phlegm is situated upon me,' nor does the phlegm know, 'I am situated upon the membrane of the stomach.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, phlegm is a distinct constituent in this body—unconscious, indeterminate, empty, without a living principle, like broth, with the characteristic of binding, the water element.

Pubbo anibaddhokāso, yattha yattheva khāṇukaṇṭakappaharaṇaaggijālādīhi abhihaṭe sarīrappadese lohitaṃ saṇṭhahitvā paccati, gaṇḍapīḷakādayo vā uppajjanti, tattha tattheva tiṭṭhati. Tattha yathā pharasuppahārādivasena paggharitaniyāse rukkhe na rukkhassa pharasuppahārādippadesā jānanti ‘amhesu niyyāso ṭhito’ti, nāpi niyyāso jānāti ‘ahaṃ rukkhassa pharasuppahārādippadesesu ṭhito’ti, evameva na sarīrassa khāṇukaṇṭakādīhi abhihaṭappadesā jānanti [P 0.0066] ‘amhesu pubbo ṭhito’ti, nāpi pubbo jānāti ‘ahaṃ tesu padesesu ṭhito’ti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti pubbo nāma imasmiṃ [V 0.0062] sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

Pus has no fixed location; it remains wherever the body is struck by splinters, thorns, wounds, fire, and so forth, where blood congeals and festers, or where boils and pustules arise. There, just as, when sap oozes from a tree due to an axe blow and so forth, the parts of the tree struck by the axe blow and so forth do not know, 'Sap remains upon us,' nor does the sap know, 'I remain upon the parts of the tree struck by the axe blow and so forth,' even so, the parts of the body struck by splinters, thorns, and so forth do not know, 'Pus remains upon us,' nor does the pus know, 'I remain upon those parts.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, pus is a distinct constituent in this body—non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, without essence, like broth, with the characteristic of binding, the water element.

Lohitesu saṃsaraṇalohitaṃ abaddhapittaṃ viya sakalasarīraṃ byāpetvā ṭhitaṃ. Sannicitalohitaṃ yakanaṭṭhānassa heṭṭhābhāgaṃ pūretvā ekapattapūraṇappamāṇaṃ vakkahadayayakanapapphāsāni tementaṃ ṭhitaṃ. Tattha saṃsaraṇalohite abaddhapittasadisova vinicchayo. Itaraṃ pana yathā jajjarakapālaṭṭhe udake heṭṭhā leḍḍukhaṇḍāni temayamāne na leḍḍukhaṇḍāni jānanti ‘mayaṃ udakena temiyamānā ṭhitā’ti, nāpi udakaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ leḍḍukhaṇḍāni tememī’ti, evameva na yakanassa heṭṭhābhāgaṭṭhānaṃ vakkādīni vā jānanti ‘mayi lohitaṃ ṭhitaṃ, amhe vā temayamānaṃ ṭhita’nti, nāpi lohitaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ yakanassa heṭṭhābhāgaṃ pūretvā vakkādīni temayamānaṃ ṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti lohitaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

Among the bloods, circulating blood remains pervading the entire body like unbound bile. Accumulated blood remains filling the lower part of the liver's location, measuring about a bowlful, moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs. Regarding circulating blood, the determination is precisely similar to that for unbound bile. However, the other type of blood is like water in a broken pot moistening lumps of clay beneath: the lumps of clay do not know, 'We remain being moistened by water,' nor does the water know, 'I am moistening the lumps of clay.' Even so, neither the lower part of the liver's location nor the kidneys and so forth know, 'Blood remains in us, or remains moistening us,' nor does the blood know, 'I remain filling the lower part of the liver and moistening the kidneys and so forth.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, blood is a distinct constituent in this body—non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, without essence, like broth, with the characteristic of binding, the water element.

Sedo [M 0.0063] aggisantāpādikālesu kesalomakūpavivarāni pūretvā tiṭṭhati ceva paggharati ca. Tattha yathā udakā abbūḷhamattesu bhisamuḷālakumudanāḷakalāpesu na bhisādikalāpavivarāni jānanti ‘amhehi udakaṃ paggharatī’ti, nāpi bhisādikalāpavivarehi paggharantaṃ udakaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ bhisādikalāpavivarehi paggharāmī’ti, evameva na kesalomakūpavivarāni jānanti ‘amhehi sedo paggharatī’ti, nāpi sedo jānāti ‘ahaṃ kesalomakūpavivarehi paggharāmī’ti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti sedo nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

Sweat, during times of intense heat and so forth, fills the openings of the hair pores, where it remains and from which it flows. There, just as with bundles of lotus roots and stalks just drawn out of the water, the openings in the bundles of lotus roots and so forth do not know, 'Water flows out from us,' nor does the water flowing out from the openings in the bundles of lotus roots and so forth know, 'I am flowing out from the openings in the bundles of lotus roots and so forth,' even so, the openings of the hair pores do not know, 'Sweat flows out from us,' nor does the sweat know, 'I am flowing out from the openings of the hair pores.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, sweat is a distinct constituent in this body—non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, without essence, like broth, with the characteristic of binding, the water element.

Medo thūlassa sakalasarīraṃ pharitvā kisassa jaṅghamaṃsādīni [P 0.0067] nissāya ṭhito patthinnasneho. Tattha yathā haliddipilotikapaṭicchanne maṃsapuñje na maṃsapuñjo jānāti ‘maṃ nissāya haliddipilotikā ṭhitā’ti, nāpi haliddipilotikā jānāti ‘ahaṃ maṃsapuñjaṃ nissāya ṭhitā’ti, evameva na sakalasarīre jaṅghādīsu vā maṃsaṃ jānāti ‘maṃ nissāya medo ṭhito’ti, nāpi medo jānāti ‘ahaṃ sakalasarīre jaṅghādīsu vā maṃsaṃ nissāya ṭhito’ti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti medo nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko [V 0.0063] koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto patthinnasneho patthinnayūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

Fat, a spreading oil, pervades the entire body of a stout person, while in a thin person, it is found depending on the flesh of the calves and other parts. There, just as with a lump of meat covered with a turmeric-dyed cloth, the lump of meat does not know, 'The turmeric-dyed cloth is depending on me,' nor does the turmeric-dyed cloth know, 'I am depending on the lump of meat,' even so, the flesh in the entire body or in the calves and so forth does not know, 'Fat is depending on me,' nor does the fat know, 'I am depending on the flesh in the entire body or in the calves and so forth.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, fat is a distinct constituent in this body—non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, without essence, a spreading oil, like spreading broth, with the characteristic of binding, the water element.

Assu yadā sañjāyati tadā akkhikūpake pūretvā tiṭṭhati vā paggharati vā. Tattha yathā udakapuṇṇesu taruṇatālaṭṭhikūpakesu na taruṇatālaṭṭhikūpakā jānanti ‘amhesu udakaṃ ṭhita’nti, nāpi udakaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ taruṇatālaṭṭhikūpakesu ṭhita’nti, evameva na akkhikūpakā jānanti ‘amhesu assu ṭhita’nti, nāpi assu jānāti ‘ahaṃ akkhikūpakesu ṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti assu nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

Tears, when they arise, fill the eye sockets, where they remain or from which they flow. There, just as with the hollows of young palm seeds filled with water, the hollows of the young palm seeds do not know, 'Water is in us,' nor does the water know, 'I am in the hollows of the young palm seeds,' even so, the eye sockets do not know, 'Tears are in us,' nor do the tears know, 'I am in the eye sockets.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, tears are a distinct constituent in this body—non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, without essence, like broth, with the characteristic of binding, the water element.

Vasā aggisantāpādikāle hatthatalahatthapiṭṭhipādatalapādapiṭṭhināsapuṭanalāṭaaṃsakūṭesu ṭhitavilīnasneho. Tattha yathā pakkhittatele ācāme [M 0.0064] na ācāmo jānāti ‘maṃ telaṃ ajjhottharitvā ṭhita’nti, nāpi telaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ ācāmaṃ ajjhottharitvā ṭhita’nti, evameva na hatthatalādippadeso jānāti ‘maṃ vasā ajjhottharitvā ṭhitā’ti, nāpi vasā jānāti ‘ahaṃ hatthatalādippadese ajjhottharitvā ṭhitā’ti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti vasā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

Grease is the melted oiliness that appears on the palms, backs of the hands, soles, backs of the feet, nostrils, forehead, and shoulder blades during times of intense heat and so forth. There, just as with oil poured on rice-scum, the rice-scum does not know, 'Oil has overlaid me,' nor does the oil know, 'I have overlaid the rice-scum,' even so, the areas like the palms do not know, 'Grease has overlaid me,' nor does the grease know, 'I have overlaid the areas like the palms.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, grease is a distinct constituent in this body—non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, without essence, like broth, with the characteristic of binding, the water element.

Kheḷo tathārūpe kheḷuppattipaccaye sati ubhohi kapolapassehi orohitvā jivhāya tiṭṭhati. Tattha yathā abbocchinnaudakanissande nadītīrakūpake na kūpatalaṃ jānāti ‘mayi udakaṃ santiṭṭhatī’ti, nāpi udakaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ kūpatale santiṭṭhāmī’ti[P 0.0068], evameva na jivhātalaṃ jānāti ‘mayi ubhohi kapolapassehi orohitvā kheḷo ṭhito’ti, nāpi kheḷo jānāti ‘ahaṃ ubhohi kapolapassehi orohitvā jivhātale ṭhito’ti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti kheḷo nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

Saliva, when the conditions for its production are present, descends from both sides of the cheeks and rests on the tongue. There, just as in a riverbank well with an uninterrupted flow of water, the bottom of the well does not know, 'Water stands in me,' nor does the water know, 'I stand on the bottom of the well,' so too the surface of the tongue does not know, 'Saliva, having descended from both sides of the cheeks, stands on me,' nor does the saliva know, 'I, having descended from both sides of the cheeks, stand on the surface of the tongue.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual consideration and reflection. Thus, saliva is a specific part in this body—non-sentient, undeclared, empty, without a living being, like broth, of a binding nature, and is the water element.

Siṅghāṇikā yadā sañjāyati tadā nāsāpuṭe pūretvā tiṭṭhati vā paggharati vā. Tattha yathā [V 0.0064] pūtidadhibharitāya sippikāya na sippikā jānāti ‘mayi pūtidadhi ṭhita’nti, nāpi pūtidadhi jānāti ‘ahaṃ sippikāya ṭhita’nti, evameva na nāsāpuṭā jānanti ‘amhesu siṅghāṇikā ṭhitā’ti, nāpi siṅghāṇikā jānāti ‘ahaṃ nāsāpuṭesu ṭhitā’ti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti siṅghāṇikā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

When mucus arises, it fills the nostrils and either stays there or flows out. There, just as in the case of a shell filled with spoiled curds, the shell does not know, 'Spoiled curds are in me,' nor do the spoiled curds know, 'I am in the shell,' so too the nostrils do not know, 'Mucus is in us,' nor does the mucus know, 'I am in the nostrils.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual consideration and reflection. Thus, mucus is a specific part in this body—non-sentient, undeclared, empty, without a living being, like broth, of a binding nature, and is the water element.

Lasikā aṭṭhikasandhīnaṃ abbhañjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā asītisatasandhīsu ṭhitā. Tattha yathā telabbhañjite akkhe na akkho jānāti ‘maṃ telaṃ abbhañjitvā ṭhita’nti, nāpi telaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ akkhaṃ abbhañjitvā ṭhita’nti, evameva na asītisatasandhayo jānanti ‘lasikā amhe abbhañjitvā [M 0.0065] ṭhitā’ti, nāpi lasikā jānāti ‘ahaṃ asītisatasandhayo abbhañjitvā ṭhitā’ti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti lasikā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

Synovial fluid, performing the function of lubricating the bone joints, is situated in the one hundred and eighty joints. There, just as in the case of an axle lubricated with oil, the axle does not know, 'Oil, having lubricated me, remains,' nor does the oil know, 'I, having lubricated the axle, remain,' so too the one hundred and eighty joints do not know, 'Synovial fluid, having lubricated us, remains,' nor does the synovial fluid know, 'I, having lubricated the one hundred and eighty joints, remain.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual consideration and reflection. Thus, synovial fluid is a specific part in this body—non-sentient, undeclared, empty, without a living being, like broth, of a binding nature, and is the water element.

Muttaṃ vatthissa abbhantare ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā candanikāya pakkhitte adhomukhe ravaṇaghaṭe na ravaṇaghaṭo jānāti ‘mayi candanikāraso ṭhito’ti, nāpi candanikāraso jānāti ‘ahaṃ ravaṇaghaṭe ṭhito’ti, evameva na vatthi jānāti ‘mayi muttaṃ ṭhita’nti, nāpi muttaṃ jānāti ‘ahaṃ vatthimhi ṭhita’nti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti muttaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti. Yaṃ vā panāti avasesesu tīsu koṭṭhāsesu āpodhātuṃ sandhāya [P 0.0069] vuttaṃ.

Urine is situated within the bladder. There, just as when cesspool water is poured into a downward-facing earthen pot, the pot does not know, 'Cesspool water is in me,' nor does the cesspool water know, 'I am in the pot,' so too the bladder does not know, 'Urine is in me,' nor does the urine know, 'I am in the bladder.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual consideration and reflection. Thus, urine is a specific part in this body—non-sentient, undeclared, empty, without a living being, like broth, of a binding nature, and is the water element. The phrase 'Or whatever else there may be' is said with reference to the water element in the remaining three parts.

Bāhiraāpodhātuniddese mūlaṃ paṭicca nibbatto raso mūlaraso nāma. Khandharasādīsupi eseva nayo. Khīrādīni pākaṭāneva. Yathā pana bhesajjasikkhāpade evamidha niyamo natthi. Yaṃ kiñci khīraṃ khīrameva. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Bhummānīti āvāṭādīsu ṭhitaudakāni. Antalikkhānīti pathaviṃ appattāni vassodakāni. Yaṃ vā panāti himodakakappavināsakaudakapathavīsandhārakaudakādīni idha yevāpanakaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhāni.

In the exposition of the external water element, the sap produced in dependence on a root is called root-sap. This same method applies to stem-sap and so on. Milk and the like are evident. But there is no rule here as there is in the training rule concerning medicines. Whatever is milk is just milk. This same method applies to the rest. 'Ground waters' means waters situated in pits and so on. 'Aerial waters' means rainwater that has not reached the earth. The phrase 'Or whatever else there may be' includes snow-water, the water that destroys the eon, the water that supports the earth, and so on; these are here included in that category.

175. Tejodhātuniddese [V 0.0065] tejanavasena tejo. Tejova tejobhāvaṃ gatattā tejogataṃ. Usmāti uṇhākāro. Usmāva usmābhāvaṃ gatattā usmāgataṃ. Usumanti caṇḍausumaṃ. Tadeva usumabhāvaṃ gatattā usumagataṃ. Yena cāti yena tejogatena kuppitena. Santappatīti ayaṃ kāyo santappati, ekāhikajarādibhāvena usumajāto hoti. Yena ca jīrīyatīti yena ayaṃ kāyo jīrīyati, indriyavekallataṃ balaparikkhayaṃ valipalitādibhāvañca pāpuṇāti. Yena ca pariḍayhatīti yena kuppitena ayaṃ kāyo ḍayhati, so ca [M 0.0066] puggalo ‘ḍayhāmi ḍayhāmī’ti kandanto satadhotasappigosītacandanādilepanañceva tālavaṇṭavātañca paccāsīsati. Yena ca asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchatīti yenetaṃ asitaṃ vā odanādi, pītaṃ vā pānakādi, khāyitaṃ vā piṭṭhakhajjakādi, sāyitaṃ vā ambapakkamadhuphāṇitādi sammā paripākaṃ gacchati, rasādibhāvena vivekaṃ gacchatīti attho. Ettha ca purimā tayo tejodhātū catusamuṭṭhānā, pacchimo kammasamuṭṭhānova. Ayaṃ tāvettha padasaṃvaṇṇanā.

175. In the exposition of the fire element, 'fire' (tejo) is so called by way of heating. Fire itself, having gone to the state of fire, is 'fiery' (tejogata). 'Heat' (usmā) is the characteristic of warmth. Heat itself, having gone to the state of heat, is 'heated' (usmāgata). 'Feverish heat' (usuma) is intense heat. That itself, having gone to the state of feverish heat, is 'fevered' (usumagata). 'By which' (yena ca) refers to that fiery element by which, when aggravated. 'One is heated' (santappati) means this body becomes heated, becoming feverish through a one-day fever and so on. 'By which one ages' (yena ca jīrīyati) means by which this body ages, reaching impairment of faculties, decline of strength, and the state of wrinkles and grey hair. 'By which one is scorched' (yena ca pariḍayhati) means by which, when aggravated, this body is scorched, and that person, crying 'I am burning, I am burning,' desires anointing with hundred-times-washed ghee and cool sandalwood paste, and the breeze from a palm-leaf fan. 'By which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested' (yena ca asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchati) means by which that which is eaten, such as boiled rice; drunk, such as beverages; chewed, such as cakes and sweets; or tasted, such as ripe mango, honey, or molasses, is properly digested, that is, it is separated into nutritive essence and so on. And here, the first three fire elements are of fourfold origin, while the last is of kamma-origin only. This, for now, is the word-commentary here.

Idaṃ pana manasikāravidhānaṃ – idha bhikkhu ‘yena santappati, ayaṃ imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto paripācanākāro tejodhātū’ti manasi karoti; ‘yena jīrīyati, yena pariḍayhati, yena asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchati, ayaṃ imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko [P 0.0070] koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto paripācanākāro tejodhātū’ti manasi karoti. Yaṃ vā panāti imasmiṃ sarīre pākatiko eko utu atthi, so yevāpanakaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭho.

Now, this is the method of attention: Here, a monk attends thus: 'That by which one is heated—this is a specific part in this body, non-sentient, undeclared, empty, without a living being, of a maturing nature, the fire element.' He attends thus: 'That by which one ages, that by which one is scorched, that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested—this is a specific part in this body, non-sentient, undeclared, empty, without a living being, of a maturing nature, the fire element.' The phrase 'Or whatever else there may be' means that there is in this body a natural physical heat; that itself is included in that category.

Bāhiratejodhātuniddese kaṭṭhaṃ paṭicca pajjalito kaṭṭhupādāno aggi kaṭṭhaggi nāma. Sakalikaggiādīsupi eseva nayo. Saṅkāraggīti kacavaraṃ saṃkaḍḍhitvā jālāpito kacavaraggi. Indaggīti asaniaggi. Aggisantāpoti jālāya vā vītaccikaṅgārānaṃ vā santāpo. Sūriyasantāpoti ātapo. Kaṭṭhasannicayasantāpoti kaṭṭharāsiṭṭhāne santāpo. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Yaṃ vā panāti petaggi kappavināsaggi nirayaggiādayo idha yevāpanakaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhā.

In the exposition of the external fire element, fire kindled dependent on wood, with wood as its fuel, is called wood fire. The same applies to fires from splinters and so forth. ‘Rubbish fire’ is fire kindled by collecting rubbish. ‘Indra’s fire’ is lightning fire. ‘The heat of fire’ is the heat from flames or from embers without flame. ‘The heat of the sun’ is sunlight. ‘The heat of a woodpile’ is the heat in the place of a woodpile. The same applies to the rest. ‘Or whatever’ means that cremation fire, cosmic destruction fire, hell fire, and so forth, are included here under this general heading.

176. Vāyodhātuniddese vāyanavasena vāyo. Vāyova vāyobhāvaṃ gatattā vāyogataṃ. Thambhitattaṃ rūpassāti avinibbhogarūpassa thambhitabhāvo. Uddhaṅgamā vātāti uggārahikkādi pavattakā uddhaṃ ārohanavātā[V 0.0066]. Adhogamā vātāti uccārapassāvādinīharaṇakā adho orohanavātā. Kucchisayā vātāti antānaṃ bahivātā. Koṭṭhāsayā vātāti antānaṃ antovātā. Aṅgamaṅgānusārino vātāti dhamanijālānusārena sakalasarīre aṅgamaṅgāni anusaṭā samiñjanapasāraṇādinibbattakā [M 0.0067] vātā. Satthakavātāti sandhibandhanāni kattariyā chindantā viya pavattavātā. Khurakavātāti khurena viya hadayaṃ phālanavātā. Uppalakavātāti hadayamaṃsameva uppāṭanakavātā. Assāsoti [P 0.0071] antopavisananāsikāvato. Passāsoti bahinikkhamananāsikāvato. Ettha ca purimā sabbe catusamuṭṭhānā, assāsapassāsā cittasamuṭṭhānāva. Ayamettha padavaṇṇanā.

176. In the exposition of the wind element, ‘wind’ is so called because it blows. It is ‘wind-gone’ because it has gone to the state of wind. ‘The solidity of form’ is the state of firmness of inseparable form. ‘Upward-going winds’ are the winds that ascend upwards, causing belching, hiccupping, and so forth. ‘Downward-going winds’ are the winds that descend downwards, carrying out excrement, urine, and so forth. ‘Winds lying in the belly’ are the winds outside the intestines. ‘Winds lying in the bowels’ are the winds inside the intestines. ‘Winds circulating through the limbs’ are the winds that spread throughout the entire body by way of the network of vessels, producing the bending and stretching of limbs, and so forth. ‘Knife-like winds’ are the winds that act as if cutting the joint-bindings with a knife. ‘Razor-like winds’ are the winds that split the heart as if with a razor. ‘Lotus-like winds’ are the winds that uproot the very flesh of the heart. ‘In-breath’ is the wind entering through the nose. ‘Out-breath’ is the wind exiting through the nose. Here, all the former arise from four causes, while in-breath and out-breath arise only from the mind. This is the explanation of the terms here.

Idaṃ pana manasikāravidhānaṃ – idha bhikkhu uddhaṅgamādibhede vāte uddhaṅgamādivasena pariggahetvā ‘uddhaṅgamā vātā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto vitthambhanākāro vāyodhātū’ti manasi karoti. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Yaṃ vā panāti sese vāyokoṭṭhāse anugatā vātā idha yevāpanakaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhā.

Now, this is the method of attention: Here, a bhikkhu, having comprehended the winds according to their distinctions, such as upward-going and so forth, attends thus: ‘Upward-going winds are a particular portion in this body, the wind element, which is inanimate, indeterminate, empty, soulless, and has the characteristic of distension.’ The same applies to the rest. ‘Or whatever’ means that the winds pervading the remaining wind-portions are included here under this general heading.

Bāhiravāyodhātuniddese puratthimā vātāti puratthimadisato āgatā vātā. Pacchimuttaradakkhiṇesupi eseva nayo. Sarajā vātāti saha rajena sarajā. Arajā vātāti rajavirahitā suddhā arajā nāma. Sītāti sītautusamuṭṭhānā sītavalāhakantare samuṭṭhitā. Uṇhāti uṇhautusamuṭṭhānā uṇhavalāhakantare samuṭṭhitā. Parittāti mandā tanukavātā. Adhimattāti balavavātā. Kāḷāti kāḷavalāhakantare samuṭṭhitā, yehi abbhāhato chavivaṇṇo kāḷako hoti. Tesaṃ etaṃ adhivacanantipi eke. Verambhavātāti yojanato upari vāyanavātā. Pakkhavātāti antamaso makkhikāyapi pakkhāyūhanasamuṭṭhitā vātā. Supaṇṇavātāti garuḷavātā. Kāmañca imepi pakkhavātāva ussadavasena pana visuṃ gahitā. Tālavaṇṭavātāti tālapaṇṇehi vā aññena vā kenaci maṇḍalasaṇṭhānena samuṭṭhāpitā vātā. Vidhūpanavātāti bījanapattakena samuṭṭhāpitā vātā. Imāni ca tālavaṇṭavidhūpanāni anuppannampi vātaṃ uppādenti, uppannampi parivattenti. Yaṃ vā panāti idha pāḷiāgate ṭhapetvā sesavātā yevāpanakaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhā.

In the exposition of the external wind element, ‘eastern winds’ are winds coming from the eastern direction. The same applies to the western, northern, and southern winds. ‘Dust-laden winds’ are those with dust. ‘Dustless winds’ are pure, devoid of dust. ‘Cold winds’ arise from the cold season, originating within cold clouds. ‘Hot winds’ arise from the hot season, originating within hot clouds. ‘Slight winds’ are gentle, thin winds. ‘Excessive winds’ are strong winds. ‘Black winds’ arise within dark clouds; when struck by them, the skin’s complexion becomes dark. Some also say this is their designation. ‘Verambha winds’ are winds blowing from above a yojana. ‘Winged winds’ are winds arising even from the flapping of a fly’s wings. ‘Supaṇṇa winds’ are the winds of the garuḷas. Although these too are winged winds, they are mentioned separately due to their prominence. ‘Palm-fan winds’ are winds stirred up by palm leaves or by anything else of a circular shape. ‘Winnowing winds’ are winds stirred up by a winnowing fan. These palm-fans and winnowing fans generate wind even where none existed, and also alter existing wind. ‘Or whatever’ means that other winds, apart from those mentioned in the text, are included here under this general heading.

177. Ākāsadhātuniddese [P 0.0072] appaṭighaṭṭanaṭṭhena na kassatīti ākāso. Ākāsova ākāsabhāvaṃ gatattā ākāsagataṃ. Aghaṭṭanīyatāya [M 0.0068] aghaṃ. Aghameva aghabhāvaṃ gatattā aghagataṃ[V 0.0067]. Vivaroti antaraṃ. Tadeva vivarabhāvaṃ gatattā vivaragataṃ. Asamphuṭṭhaṃ maṃsalohitehīti maṃsalohitehi nissaṭaṃ. Kaṇṇacchiddantiādi pana tasseva pabhedadassanaṃ. Tattha kaṇṇacchiddanti kaṇṇasmiṃ chiddaṃ vivaraṃ maṃsalohitehi asamphuṭṭhokāso. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Yenāti yena vivarena etaṃ asitādibhedaṃ ajjhoharaṇīyaṃ ajjhoharati, anto paveseti. Yatthāti yasmiṃ antoudarapaṭalasaṅkhāte okāse etadeva catubbidhaṃ ajjhoharaṇīyaṃ tiṭṭhati. Yenāti yena vivarena sabbampetaṃ vipakkaṃ kasaṭabhāvaṃ āpannaṃ nikkhamati, taṃ udarapaṭalato yāva karīsamaggā vidatthicaturaṅgulamattaṃ chiddaṃ maṃsalohitehi asamphuṭṭhaṃ nissaṭaṃ ākāsadhātūti veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ vā panāti ettha cammantaraṃ maṃsantaraṃ nhāruntaraṃ aṭṭhintaraṃ lomantaranti idaṃ sabbaṃ yevāpanakaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ.

177. In the exposition of the space element, it is called ‘space’ (ākāsa) because it does not strike against anything, in the sense of non-resistance. It is ‘space-gone’ because it has gone to the state of space. It is called ‘non-striking’ (aghaṃ) because it is not to be struck. It is ‘non-striking-gone’ because it has gone to the state of non-striking. It is called ‘opening’ (vivara) because it is an interval. That very thing is ‘opening-gone’ because it has gone to the state of an opening. It is ‘untouched by flesh and blood’ because it is free from flesh and blood. Terms like ‘ear-hole’ and so forth are given to show the distinctions of that same space. There, the ‘ear-hole’ is the hole, the opening in the ear, the space untouched by flesh and blood. The same applies to the rest. ‘By which’ means by which opening this edible matter, of the kind beginning with what is eaten, is ingested and enters inside. ‘Where’ means in which space, called the inner abdominal membrane, that same fourfold edible matter remains. ‘By which’ means by which opening all this digested matter, which has reached the state of refuse, exits. That opening, from the abdominal membrane up to the passage for excrement, a space of a span and four finger-breadths, which is untouched by flesh and blood and devoid of it, is to be understood as the space element. ‘Or whatever’ here refers to the space within the skin, the space within the flesh, the space within the sinews, the space within the bones, and the space within the hairs—all this is included here under this general heading.

Bāhirakaākāsadhātuniddese asamphuṭṭhaṃ catūhi mahābhūtehīti catūhi mahābhūtehi nissaṭaṃ bhittichiddakavāṭachiddādikaṃ veditabbaṃ. Iminā yasmiṃ ākāse parikammaṃ karontassa catukkapañcakajjhānāni uppajjanti taṃ kathitaṃ.

In the exposition of the external space element, ‘untouched by the four great elements’ means that it should be understood as free from the four great elements, such as holes in walls, gaps in doors, and so forth. By this is described the space wherein a practitioner's preliminary work gives rise to the fourth and fifth jhānas.

178. Viññāṇadhātuniddese cakkhuviññāṇasaṅkhātā dhātu cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Sesāsupi eseva nayo. Iti imāsu chasu dhātūsu pariggahitāsu aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo pariggahitāva honti. Kathaṃ? Pathavītejovāyodhātuggahaṇena tāva phoṭṭhabbadhātu gahitāva hoti, āpodhātuākāsadhātuggahaṇena dhammadhātu, viññāṇadhātuggahaṇena tassā purecārikapacchācārikattā manodhātu gahitāva hoti. Cakkhuviññāṇadhātuādayo sutte āgatā eva. Sesā nava āharitvā dassetabbā[P 0.0073]. Cakkhuviññāṇadhātuggahaṇena hi tassā nissayabhūtā cakkhudhātu, ārammaṇabhūtā rūpadhātu ca gahitāva honti. Evaṃ sotaviññāṇadhātuādiggahaṇena sotadhātuādayoti aṭṭhārasāpi gahitāva honti. Tāsu dasahi dhātūhi rūpapariggaho kathito hoti. Sattahi arūpapariggaho. Dhammadhātuyā siyā rūpapariggaho, siyā arūpapariggaho. Iti aḍḍhekādasahi dhātūhi rūpapariggaho, aḍḍhaṭṭhadhātūhi arūpapariggahoti rūpārūpapariggaho kathito hoti. Rūpārūpaṃ pañcakkhandhā. Taṃ hoti dukkhasaccaṃ. Taṃsamuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ[M 0.0069]. Ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ. Taṃpajānano maggo maggasaccanti idaṃ catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ aṭṭhārasadhātuvasena abhiniviṭṭhassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā matthakaṃ pāpetvā nigamanaṃ kathitanti veditabbaṃ.

178. In the exposition of the consciousness element, the element known as eye-consciousness is the eye-consciousness element. The same method applies to the rest. Thus, when these six elements are comprehended, the eighteen elements are thereby comprehended. How? First, by the comprehension of the earth element, fire element, and wind element, the tangible-object element is thereby comprehended. By the comprehension of the water element and space element, the mind-object element is comprehended. By the comprehension of the consciousness element, the mind-element is thereby comprehended because it precedes and follows it. The eye-consciousness element and others are explicitly mentioned in the Sutta. The remaining nine should be adduced and shown. For by the comprehension of the eye-consciousness element, the eye element, which is its basis, and the visual-form element, which is its object, are thereby comprehended. Similarly, by the comprehension of the ear-consciousness element and others, the ear element and so forth are also comprehended. Thus, all eighteen are thereby comprehended. Among these, the comprehension of form is explained by means of ten elements. The comprehension of the formless is explained by means of seven. The mind-object element may pertain to the comprehension of form or to the comprehension of the formless. Thus, the comprehension of form is explained by means of ten and a half elements, and the comprehension of the formless by means of seven and a half elements. Form and the formless are the five aggregates. That is the Noble Truth of Suffering. The preceding craving that gives rise to it is the Noble Truth of the Origin. The non-occurrence of both is the Noble Truth of Cessation. The path that comprehends it is the Noble Truth of the Path. It should be understood that this meditation on the Four Noble Truths for a bhikkhu who is firmly established in the eighteen elements is thus stated as the conclusion, leading him to the culmination of arahantship.

179. Idāni [V 0.0068] dutiyachakkaṃ dassento aparāpi cha dhātuyotiādimāha. Tattha sukhadhātu dukkhadhātūti kāyappasādavatthukāni sukhadukkhāni sappaṭipakkhavasena yugaḷakato dassitāni. Sukhañhi dukkhassa paṭipakkho, dukkhaṃ sukhassa. Yattakaṃ sukhena pharitaṭṭhānaṃ tattakaṃ dukkhaṃ pharati. Yattakaṃ dukkhena pharitaṭṭhānaṃ tattakaṃ sukhaṃ pharati. Somanassadhātu domanassadhātūti idampi tatheva yugaḷakaṃ kataṃ. Somanassañhi domanassassa paṭipakkho, domanassaṃ somanassassa. Yattakaṃ somanassena pharitaṭṭhānaṃ tattakaṃ domanassaṃ pharati. Yattakaṃ domanassena pharitaṭṭhānaṃ tattakaṃ somanassaṃ pharati.

179. Now, in order to present the second set of six, he says, 'another six elements,' and so forth. Herein, the element of pleasure and the element of pain—bodily pleasure and pain, which have the sensitive body as their basis—are shown as a pair by way of their opposition. For pleasure is the antithesis of pain, and pain is the antithesis of pleasure. Whatever sphere is pervaded by pleasure, that same sphere pain pervades. Whatever sphere is pervaded by pain, that same sphere pleasure pervades. The element of joy and the element of displeasure are likewise made into a pair in the same way. For joy is the antithesis of displeasure, and displeasure is the antithesis of joy. Whatever sphere is pervaded by joy, that same sphere displeasure pervades. Whatever sphere is pervaded by displeasure, that same sphere joy pervades.

Upekkhādhātu avijjādhātūti idaṃ pana dvayaṃ sarikkhakavasena yugaḷakaṃ kataṃ. Ubhayampi hetaṃ avibhūtattā sarikkhakaṃ hoti. Tattha sukhadukkhadhātuggahaṇena taṃ sampayuttā kāyaviññāṇadhātu, vatthubhūtā kāyadhātu, ārammaṇabhūtā phoṭṭhabbadhātu ca gahitāva honti. Somanassadomanassadhātuggahaṇena taṃ sampayuttā manoviññāṇadhātu gahitā hoti. Avijjādhātuggahaṇena dhammadhātu gahitā. Upekkhādhātuggahaṇena cakkhusotaghānajivhāviññāṇadhātumanodhātuyo[P 0.0074], tāsaṃyeva vatthārammaṇabhūtā cakkhudhāturūpadhātuādayo ca gahitāti evaṃ aṭṭhārasapi dhātuyo gahitāva honti. Idāni tāsu dasahi dhātūhi rūpapariggahotiādi sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Evampi ekassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā matthakaṃ pāpetvā nigamanaṃ kathitaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Tattha katamā sukhadhātu yaṃ kāyikaṃ sātanti ādīni heṭṭhā vuttanayāneva.

The element of equanimity and the element of ignorance—these two are, however, made into a pair by way of their similarity. Both are similar because they are not clearly manifest. Here, by the comprehension of the elements of pleasure and pain, the body-consciousness element associated with them, the body element which is their basis, and the tangible-object element which is their object, are thereby comprehended. By the comprehension of the elements of joy and displeasure, the mind-consciousness element associated with them is comprehended. By the comprehension of the element of ignorance, the mind-object element is comprehended. By the comprehension of the element of equanimity, the eye-, ear-, nose-, and tongue-consciousness elements, the mind-element, and their respective bases and objects—the eye element, visual-form element, and so forth—are comprehended. Thus, all eighteen elements are thereby comprehended. Now, 'the comprehension of form by means of ten elements,' and so forth—all this should be understood in the same way as previously explained. In this way, too, it should be understood that the conclusion has been stated for a single bhikkhu, leading to the culmination in arahantship. Herein, 'What is the element of pleasure? That which is bodily pleasant,' and so forth—these are to be understood in the same way as explained earlier.

181. Tatiyachakke kāmoti dve kāmā – vatthukāmo ca kilesakāmo ca. Tattha kilesakāmaṃ sandhāya kāmapaṭisaṃyuttā dhātu kāmadhātu, kāmavitakkassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Vatthukāmaṃ sandhāya kāmoyeva dhātu kāmadhātu, kāmāvacaradhammānametaṃ nāmaṃ. Byāpādapaṭisaṃyuttā dhātu byāpādadhātu, byāpādavitakkassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Byāpādova dhātu byāpādadhātu, dasaāghātavatthukassa [M 0.0070] paṭighassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Vihiṃsā paṭisaṃyuttā dhātu vihiṃsādhātu, vihiṃsāvitakkassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Vihiṃsāyeva dhātu vihiṃsādhātu, parasattavihesanassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Ayaṃ pana heṭṭhā anāgatattā evaṃ atthādivibhāgato veditabbā – vihiṃsanti etāya satte, vihiṃsanaṃ vā etaṃ sattānanti vihiṃsā. Sā viheṭhanalakkhaṇā, karuṇāpaṭipakkhalakkhaṇā vā; parasantāne ubbegajananarasā, sakasantāne karuṇāviddhaṃsanarasā vā; dukkhāyatanapaccupaṭṭhānā; paṭighapadaṭṭhānāti veditabbā. Nekkhammaṃ [V 0.0069] vuccati lobhā nikkhantattā alobho, nīvaraṇehi nikkhantattā paṭhamajjhānaṃ, sabbākusalehi nikkhantattā sabbakusalaṃ. Nekkhammapaṭisaṃyuttā dhātu nekkhammadhātu, nekkhammavitakkassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Nekkhammameva dhātu nekkhammadhātu, sabbassāpi kusalassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Abyāpādapaṭisaṃyuttā dhātu abyāpādadhātu, abyāpādavitakkassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Abyāpādova dhātu abyāpādadhātu, mettāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Avihiṃsāpaṭisaṃyuttā dhātu avihiṃsādhātu, avihiṃsā vitakkassetaṃ [P 0.0075] nāmaṃ. Avihiṃsāva dhātu avihiṃsādhātu, karuṇāyetaṃ nāmaṃ.

181. In the third set of six, 'sensual desire' (kāma) refers to two kinds of sensual desire: sensual objects (vatthukāma) and defilement-sensual desire (kilesakāma). Herein, with reference to defilement-sensual desire, the element associated with sensual desire is the sensual-desire element (kāmadhātu); this is a name for sensual thought (kāmavitakka). With reference to sensual objects, the element that is simply sensual desire is the sensual-desire element; this is a name for phenomena of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacaradhammā). The element associated with ill will is the ill-will element (byāpādadhātu); this is a name for ill-will thought (byāpādavitakka). The element that is simply ill will is the ill-will element; this is a name for aversion (paṭigha) based on the ten grounds for anger (dasa āghātavatthu). The element associated with cruelty is the cruelty element (vihiṃsādhātu); this is a name for cruelty thought (vihiṃsāvitakka). The element that is simply cruelty is the cruelty element; this is a name for the tormenting of other beings (parasattavihesana). This, however, as it has not been mentioned before, should be understood by way of its division into meaning, and so forth: 'vihiṃsā' means that by which beings are harmed, or it is the harming of beings. It has the characteristic of injuring, or the characteristic of being the antithesis of compassion; its function is to generate agitation in the continuity of others, or to destroy compassion in one's own continuity; it manifests as a basis for suffering; and it has aversion (paṭigha) as its proximate cause. 'Renunciation' (nekkhamma) is said to be non-greed because of having departed from greed, the first jhāna because of having departed from the hindrances, and all that is wholesome because of having departed from all that is unwholesome. The element associated with renunciation is the renunciation element (nekkhammadhātu); this is a name for renunciation thought (nekkhammavitakka). The element that is simply renunciation is the renunciation element; this is a name for all that is wholesome (sabbakusala). The element associated with non-ill-will is the non-ill-will element (abyāpādadhātu); this is a name for non-ill-will thought (abyāpādavitakka). The element that is simply non-ill-will is the non-ill-will element; this is a name for loving-kindness (mettā). The element associated with non-cruelty is the non-cruelty element (avihiṃsādhātu); this is a name for non-cruelty thought (avihiṃsāvitakka). The element that is simply non-cruelty is the non-cruelty element; this is a name for compassion (karuṇā).

182. Idāni tamevatthaṃ dassetuṃ tattha katamā kāmadhātūti padabhājanaṃ āraddhaṃ. Tattha paṭisaṃyuttoti saṃpayogavasena paṭisaṃyutto. Takko vitakkotiādīni vuttatthāneva. Viheṭhetīti bādheti, dukkhāpeti. Heṭhanāti pāṇippahārādīhi bādhanā, dukkhuppādanā. Balavaheṭhanā viheṭhanā. Hiṃsanti etāyāti hiṃsanā. Balavahiṃsanā vihiṃsanā. Rosanāti ghaṭṭanā. Virosanāti balavaghaṭṭanā. Sabbattha vā ‘vi’ upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Upahananti etenāti upaghāto, paresaṃ upaghāto parūpaghāto.

182. Now, in order to explain that very meaning, the analysis of the term 'What is the sensual-desire element?' is begun. Herein, 'associated' (paṭisaṃyutta) means associated by way of conjunction (saṃpayoga). 'Thought' (takka), 'discursive thought' (vitakka), and so forth—these have the meanings already explained. 'He harasses' (viheṭheti) means he oppresses (bādheti) or causes suffering (dukkhāpeti). 'Harassment' (heṭhanā) means oppression by blows and so forth, or the production of suffering. Strong harassment is 'viheṭhanā.' 'They harm by this' (hiṃsanti etāya) means 'harming' (hiṃsanā). Strong harming is 'vihiṃsanā.' 'Vexation' (rosanā) means irritation (ghaṭṭanā). 'Strong vexation' (virosanā) means strong irritation. Or, everywhere the word is intensified by the prefix 'vi.' 'They strike by this' (upahananti etena) means 'striking' (upaghāta); striking others is 'striking others' (parūpaghāta).

Mettāyanti etāyāti metti. Mettāyanākāro mettāyanā. Mettāya ayitassa mettāsamaṅgino bhāvo mettāyitattaṃ. Byāpādena vimuttassa cetaso vimutti cetovimutti. Ettha ca purimehi tīhi upacārappattāpi appanāpatāpi mettā kathitā, pacchimena appanāpattāva.

'They love by this' (mettāyanti etāya) means 'loving-kindness' (mettī). The mode of loving-kindness is 'mettāyanā.' The state of one who has entered upon loving-kindness, who is endowed with loving-kindness, is 'mettāyitattaṃ.' The liberation of mind of one freed from ill will is 'liberation of mind' (cetovimutti). Herein, by the first three terms, loving-kindness that has attained either access concentration or absorption is spoken of; by the last, only that which has attained absorption.

Karuṇāyanti [M 0.0071] etāyāti karuṇā. Karuṇāyanākāro karuṇāyanā. Karuṇāya ayitassa karuṇāsamaṅgino bhāvo karuṇāyitattaṃ. Vihiṃsāya vimuttassa cetaso vimutti cetovimutti. Idhāpi purimanayeneva upacārappanābhedo veditabbo. Ubhayatthāpi ca pariyosānapade mettākaruṇāti cetovimuttivisesanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

'They pity by this' (karuṇāyanti etāya) means 'compassion' (karuṇā). The mode of compassion is 'karuṇāyanā.' The state of one who has entered upon compassion, who is endowed with compassion, is 'karuṇāyitattaṃ.' The liberation of mind of one freed from cruelty is 'liberation of mind' (cetovimutti). Herein, too, the distinction between access and absorption should be understood in the same way as before. And in both cases, in the concluding phrase, 'loving-kindness' and 'compassion' are stated for the purpose of specifying the liberation of mind.

Ettha ca kāmavitakko sattesupi uppajjati saṅkhāresupi. Ubhayattha uppannopi kammapathabhedova. Byāpādo pana sattesu uppannoyeva kammapathaṃ bhindati, na itaro. Vihiṃsāyapi eseva nayo. Ettha ca duvidhā kathā – sabbasaṅgāhikā ceva asambhinnā ca. Kāmadhātuggahaṇena hi byāpādavihiṃsādhātuyopi gahitā. Kāmadhātuyāyeva pana nīharitvā nīharitvā dvepi etā dassitāti. Ayaṃ tāvettha sabbasaṅgāhikakathā[P 0.0076]. Ṭhapetvā pana byāpādavihiṃsādhātuyo sesā sabbāpi [V 0.0070] kāmadhātu evāti. Ayaṃ asambhinnakathā nāma. Nekkhammadhātuggahaṇenāpi abyāpādaavihiṃsādhātuyo gahitāyeva. Nekkhammadhātuto pana nīharitvā nīharitvā tadubhayampi dassitanti ayametthāpi sabbasaṅgāhikakathā. Ṭhapetvā abyāpādaavihiṃsādhātuyo avasesā nekkhammadhātūti ayaṃ asambhinnakathā nāma.

Here, sensual thought arises in regard to both beings and formations. Even when arisen in regard to both, it is a breaking of the path of action. Ill will, however, breaks the path of action only when it has arisen in regard to beings, not otherwise. The same principle applies to harmfulness. Here, there are two kinds of discourse: comprehensive and non-mixed. For by the inclusion of the sensual-desire element, the elements of ill will and harmfulness are also included. However, these two are shown by repeatedly extracting them from the sensual-desire element itself. This is the comprehensive discourse here. But setting aside the elements of ill will and harmfulness, all the rest is simply the sensual-desire element. This is called the non-mixed discourse. Similarly, by the inclusion of the renunciation element, the elements of non-ill-will and non-harmfulness are also included. However, those two are shown by repeatedly extracting them from the renunciation element. This, too, is the comprehensive discourse here.
