But setting aside the elements of non-ill-will and non-harmfulness, what remains is the renunciation element. This is called the non-mixed discourse.

Imāhi ca chahi dhātūhi pariggahitā hi aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo pariggahitāva honti. Sabbāpi hi tā kāmadhātutova nīharitvā nīharitvā labhāpetabbā aṭṭhārasa dhātuyova hontīti tiṇṇaṃ chakkānaṃ vasena aṭṭhārasa honti. Evaṃ pana aggahetvā ekekasmiṃ chakke vuttanayena aṭṭhārasa aṭṭhārasa katvā sabbānipi tāni aṭṭhārasakāni ekajjhaṃ abhisaṅkhipitvā aṭṭhāraseva hontīti veditabbā. Iti imasmiṃ suttantabhājanīye soḷasa dhātuyo kāmāvacarā, dve tebhūmikāti evamettha sammasanacārova kathitoti veditabbo.

And by these six elements, the eighteen elements are indeed encompassed. For all of them are obtainable only as eighteen elements by being repeatedly extracted from the sensual-desire element itself; thus, by means of the three sets of six, they become eighteen. However, not taking them in this way, but rather making eighteen in each set of six according to the method explained, when all these groups of eighteen are gathered together and combined, they are still to be understood as just eighteen. Thus, in this Suttanta Exposition, sixteen elements are of the sense-sphere, and two pertain to the three planes. In this way, the course of investigation here is to be understood as explained.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Sutta Exposition.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition.

183. Abhidhammabhājanīye [M 0.0072] sarūpeneva sabbāpi dhātuyo dassento aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo – cakkhudhātu rūpadhātūtiādimāha. Tattha uddesavāre tāva –

183. In the Abhidhamma Exposition, showing all elements in their own nature, he states the eighteen elements, beginning with 'the eye-element, the form-element.' Herein, first in the enumeration section—

Atthato lakkhaṇādito, kamatāvatvasaṅkhato;

Paccayā atha daṭṭhabbā, veditabbo vinicchayo.

By meaning, by characteristic and so forth, by order, by extent, by the unconditioned; by conditions, then, should they be seen; thus the ascertainment should be understood.

Tattha ‘atthato’ti cakkhatīti cakkhu. Rūpayatīti rūpaṃ. Cakkhussa viññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇanti evamādinā tāva nayena cakkhādīnaṃ visesatthato veditabbo vinicchayo. Avisesena pana vidahati, dhīyate, vidhānaṃ, vidhīyate etāya, ettha vā dhīyatīti dhātu. Lokiyā hi dhātuyo kāraṇabhāvena vavatthitā hutvā suvaṇṇarajatādidhātuyo viya suvaṇṇarajatādiṃ [V 0.0071] anekappakāraṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ vidahanti[P 0.0077]; bhārahārehi ca bhāro viya sattehi dhīyante dhārīyanteti attho. Dukkhavidhānamattameva cetā avasavattanato. Etāhi ca karaṇabhūtāhi saṃsāradukkhaṃ sattehi anuvidhīyati; tathāvihitañcetaṃ etāsveva dhīyati ṭhapīyatīti attho. Iti cakkhādīsu ekeko dhammo yathāsambhavaṃ vidahati dhīyatetiādiatthavasena dhātūti vuccati.

Here, 'by meaning'—'it sees' (cakkhati), thus it is the 'eye' (cakkhu). 'It appears' (rūpayati), thus it is 'form' (rūpa). 'The eye's consciousness' is 'eye-consciousness'—in this way, first, the ascertainment should be understood through the distinctive meaning of the eye and so on. Generally, however, 'it fashions' (vidahati), 'it is borne' (dhīyate), it is a 'fashioning' (vidhānaṃ), 'it is fashioned by this' (vidhīyate etāya), or 'here it is borne' (ettha vā dhīyati)—thus it is an 'element' (dhātu). For worldly elements, being established as causes, like the mineral elements of gold, silver, and so on, fashion various kinds of suffering in cyclic existence, such as gold, silver, and so on. And just as a burden is borne by burden-bearers, so they are borne and carried by beings—this is the meaning. And these are merely the fashioning of suffering due to their not being subject to control. And through these elements as instruments, the suffering of cyclic existence is fashioned by beings. Thus fashioned, it is borne and established in these very elements—this is the meaning. Thus, each phenomenon among the eye and so on, according to its occurrence, is called an element in the sense of 'fashioning,' 'bearing,' and so forth.

Apica yathā titthiyānaṃ attā nāma sabhāvato natthi, na evametā. Etā pana attano sabhāvaṃ dhārentīti dhātuyo. Yathā ca loke vicittā haritālamanosilādayo silāvayavā dhātuyoti vuccanti, evametāpi dhātuyo viya dhātuyo. Vicittā hetā ñāṇañeyyāvayavāti. Yathā vā sarīrasaṅkhātassa samudāyassa avayavabhūtesu rasasoṇitādīsu aññamaññaṃ visabhāgalakkhaṇaparicchinnesu dhātusamaññā, evametesupi pañcakkhandhasaṅkhātassa attabhāvassa avayavesu dhātusamaññā veditabbā. Aññamaññavisabhāgalakkhaṇaparicchinnā hete cakkhādayoti. Apica dhātūti nijjīvamattassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tathā hi bhagavā – “cha dhāturo ayaṃ, bhikkhu, puriso”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.343-344) jīvasaññāsamūhanatthaṃ dhātudesanaṃ akāsīti. Tasmā yathāvuttenatthena cakkhu ca taṃ dhātu cāti cakkhudhātu [M 0.0073]…pe… manoviññāṇañca taṃ dhātu cāti manoviññāṇadhātūti evaṃ tāvettha atthato viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Moreover, just as the self of the sectarians does not exist by its own nature, this is not so for these. Rather, they bear their own nature; thus they are called elements. And just as in the world, various colored stones like orpiment, realgar, and so on, which are parts of rock, are called elements, so too these are like elements, and are thus called elements. For these are varied, being constituents of what is to be known by wisdom. Or, just as the designation 'element' applies to chyle, blood, and so on, which are parts of the aggregate called the body and are distinguished by mutually dissimilar characteristics, so too the designation 'element' should be understood to apply to the parts of individual existence comprised of the five aggregates. For these—the eye and so on—are distinguished by their mutually dissimilar characteristics. Furthermore, the term 'element' is a designation for that which is merely devoid of a living being. Indeed, the Blessed One taught the discourse on elements—such as, 'Bhikkhu, this person consists of six elements' (MN 3.343-344)—in order to uproot the perception of a living being. Therefore, the analysis should be understood in terms of meaning in the way stated: the eye and that element are the eye-element … the mind-consciousness and that element are the mind-consciousness-element. Thus far, the analysis should be understood in terms of meaning.

‘Lakkhaṇādito’ti cakkhādīnaṃ lakkhaṇādito pettha veditabbo vinicchayo. Tāni ca pana tesaṃ lakkhaṇādīni heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

'From the characteristics, etc.': Here, the analysis should also be understood from the characteristics and so on of the eye and the others. And those characteristics, etc., of them should be understood in the same way as stated above.

‘Kamato’ti idhāpi pubbe vuttesu uppattikkamādīsu desanākkamova yujjati. So ca panāyaṃ hetuphalānupubbavavatthānavasena vutto. Cakkhudhātu rūpadhātūti idañhi dvayaṃ hetu. Cakkhuviññāṇadhātūti phalaṃ. Evaṃ sabbattha kamato veditabbo vinicchayo.

'In sequence': Here also, among the sequences previously mentioned, such as the sequence of arising, it is the sequence of teaching that is appropriate. And this is stated based on the successive arrangement of cause and effect. For the eye-element and the form-element—these two are the cause. The eye-consciousness-element is the effect. In this way, the analysis should be understood everywhere in sequence.

‘Tāvatvato’ti tāvabhāvato. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tesu tesu hi suttābhidhammapadesesu ābhādhātu, subhadhātu, ākāsānañcāyatanadhātu, viññāṇañcāyatanadhātu, ākiñcaññāyatanadhātu[P 0.0078], nevasaññānāsaññāyatanadhātu, saññāvedayitanirodhadhātu, kāmadhātu, byāpādadhātu, vihiṃsādhātu, nekkhammadhātu, abyāpādadhātu, avihiṃsādhātu, sukhadhātu, dukkhadhātu, somanassadhātu, domanassadhātu, upekkhādhātu[V 0.0072], avijjādhātu, ārambhadhātu, nikkamadhātu, parakkamadhātu, hīnadhātu, majjhimadhātu, paṇītadhātu, pathavīdhātu, āpodhātu, tejodhātu, vāyodhātu, ākāsadhātu, viññāṇadhātu, saṅkhatadhātu, asaṅkhatadhātu, anekadhātunānādhātulokoti evamādayo aññāpi dhātuyo dissanti.

'By extent' means by virtue of being just so many. This is what is meant: in various Sutta and Abhidhamma passages, other elements are also seen, such as the element of light, the element of beauty, the element of the base of infinite space, the element of the base of infinite consciousness, the element of the base of nothingness, the element of the base of neither perception nor non-perception, the element of the cessation of perception and feeling, the element of sensual desire, the element of ill will, the element of cruelty, the element of renunciation, the element of non-ill will, the element of non-cruelty, the element of pleasure, the element of pain, the element of joy, the element of sorrow, the element of equanimity, the element of ignorance, the element of initiative, the element of endeavor, the element of exertion, the inferior element, the middling element, the superior element, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, the consciousness element, the conditioned element, the unconditioned element, the world of many and diverse elements, and so forth.

Evaṃ sati sabbāsaṃ vasena paricchedaṃ akatvā kasmā aṭṭhārasāti ayameva paricchedo katoti ce? Sabhāvato vijjamānānaṃ sabbadhātūnaṃ tadantogadhattā. Rūpadhātuyeva hi ābhādhātu. Subhadhātu pana rūpādippaṭibaddhā. Kasmā? Subhanimittattā. Subhanimittañhi subhadhātu. Tañca rūpādivinimuttaṃ na vijjati, kusalavipākārammaṇā vā rūpādayo eva subhadhātūti rūpādimattamevesā. Ākāsānañcāyatanadhātuādīsu cittaṃ manoviññāṇadhātu. Sesā dhammā dhammadhātu. Saññāvedayitanirodhadhātu pana sabhāvato natthi; dhātudvayanirodhamattameva hi sā. Kāmadhātu dhammadhātumattaṃ vā hoti, yathāha “tattha katamā kāmadhātu? Kāmapaṭisaṃyutto takko …pe… micchāsaṅkappo”ti; aṭṭhārasapi dhātuyo [M 0.0074] vā, yathāha “heṭṭhato avīcinirayaṃ pariyantaṃ katvā uparito paranimmitavasavattideve antokaritvā yaṃ etasmiṃ antare etthāvacarā ettha pariyāpannā khandhadhātuāyatanā, rūpā, vedanā, saññā, saṅkhārā, viññāṇaṃ – ayaṃ vuccati kāmadhātū”ti. Nekkhammadhātu dhammadhātu eva; “sabbepi kusalā dhammā nekkhammadhātū”ti vā vacanato manoviññāṇadhātupi hotiyeva. Byāpādavihiṃsāabyāpādaavihiṃsāsukhadukkhasomanassadomanassupekkhāavijjāārambhanikkamaparakkamadhātuyo dhammadhātuyeva.

If this is so, why is this division made specifically into eighteen, without making a division based on all elements? Because all elements existing by their own nature are included within them. Indeed, the light element is simply the form element. The beautiful element, however, is connected with form and so on. Why? Because it is a beautiful sign. For the beautiful sign is the beautiful element, and it does not exist apart from form and so on. Or, the beautiful element is simply forms and so on that are the object of wholesome resultant consciousness; thus, it is merely form and so on. In the element of the base of infinite space and so on, consciousness is the mind-consciousness element. The remaining phenomena are the phenomena element. The element of the cessation of perception and feeling, however, does not exist by its own nature, for it is merely the cessation of two elements. The sensual-desire element may be merely the phenomena element, as it is said: 'Herein, what is the sensual-desire element? Thought connected with sensuality... wrong intention.' Or it may be all eighteen elements, as it is said: 'Below, having made the Avīci hell the limit, and above, having included the Paranimmitavasavatti devas—whatever aggregates, elements, and sense bases are included within this range, pertaining to this realm, namely form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—this is called the sensual-desire element.' The renunciation element is simply the phenomena element; or, from the statement 'all wholesome phenomena are the renunciation element,' the mind-consciousness element also comes to be. The elements of ill will, cruelty, non-ill will, non-cruelty, pleasure, pain, joy, sorrow, equanimity, ignorance, initiative, endeavor, and exertion are all simply the phenomena element.

Hīnamajjhimapaṇītadhātuyo aṭṭhārasadhātumattameva. Hīnā hi cakkhādayo hīnadhātu. Majjhimapaṇītā cakkhādayo majjhimā ceva paṇītā ca dhātū. Nippariyāyena pana akusalā [P 0.0079] dhammadhātumanoviññāṇadhātuyo hīnadhātu. Lokiyā kusalābyākatā ubhopi cakkhudhātuādayo ca majjhimadhātu. Lokuttarā pana dhammadhātumanoviññāṇadhātuyo paṇītadhātu. Pathavītejovāyodhātuyo phoṭṭhabbadhātuyeva. Āpodhātu ākāsadhātu ca dhammadhātuyeva. Viññāṇadhātu cakkhuviññāṇādisattaviññāṇadhātusaṅkhepoyeva. Sattarasa dhātuyo dhammadhātuekadeso ca saṅkhatadhātu. Asaṅkhatadhātu pana dhammadhātuekadesova. Anekadhātunānādhātuloko pana aṭṭhārasadhātuppabhedamattamevāti. Iti sabhāvato vijjamānānaṃ sabbadhātūnaṃ tadantogadhattā aṭṭhāraseva vuttāti.

The inferior, middling, and superior elements are merely the eighteen elements. Indeed, the eye and so on that are inferior are the inferior element; the eye and so on that are middling and superior are the middling and superior elements respectively. In the direct sense, however, the unwholesome phenomena element and mind-consciousness element are the inferior element. The mundane wholesome and indeterminate elements—both kinds, including the eye-element and so on—are the middling element. The supramundane phenomena element and mind-consciousness element, however, are the superior element. The earth, fire, and wind elements are simply the tangible element. The water element and the space element are simply the phenomena element. The consciousness element is simply a summary of the seven consciousness elements, beginning with eye-consciousness. Seventeen elements and a portion of the phenomena element are the conditioned element. The unconditioned element, however, is only a portion of the phenomena element. The world of many and diverse elements is merely a classification of the eighteen elements. Thus, because all elements existing by their own nature are included within these, only eighteen are stated.

Apica vijānanasabhāve viññāṇe jīvasaññīnaṃ jīvasaññāsamūhanatthampi aṭṭhāraseva vuttā[V 0.0073]. Santi hi sattā vijānanasabhāve viññāṇe jīvasaññino. Tesaṃ cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇamanoviññāṇadhātubhedena tassā anekattaṃ, cakkhurūpādipaccayāyattavuttitāya aniccatañca pakāsetvā dīgharattānusayitaṃ jīvasaññaṃ samūhanitukāmena bhagavatā aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo pakāsitā. Kiñca bhiyyo? Tathā veneyyajjhāsayavasena; ye ca imāya nātisaṅkhepavitthārāya desanāya veneyyā sattā, tadajjhāsayavasena ca aṭṭhāraseva pakāsitā.

Moreover, the eighteen elements are also stated for the purpose of eradicating the perception of a living being in consciousness, which has the nature of cognizing. For there are beings who perceive a living being in consciousness, which has the nature of cognizing. Desiring to eradicate their long-ingrained perception of a living being, the Blessed One revealed the eighteen elements by showing the diversity of consciousness through the distinction into eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness elements, and by demonstrating its impermanence due to its dependence on conditions such as the eye and forms. And what more? Similarly, it is according to the inclinations of those to be trained; and for those beings who are to be trained by this teaching, which is neither too concise nor too elaborate, the eighteen elements were revealed in accordance with their inclinations.

Saṅkhepavitthāranayena [M 0.0075] tathā tathā hi,

Dhammaṃ pakāsayati esa yathā yathāssa;

Saddhammatejavihataṃ vilayaṃ khaṇena,

Veneyyasattahadayesu tamo payātīti.

Indeed, in concise and detailed ways, he expounds the Dhamma in various manners, as it suits them; the darkness in the hearts of beings fit to be taught vanishes in an instant, destroyed by the power of the True Dhamma.

Evamettha ‘tāvatvato’ veditabbo vinicchayo.

Thus, here the determination should be understood as 'to that extent'.

‘Saṅkhato’ti cakkhudhātu tāva jātito eko dhammotveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati cakkhupasādavasena. Tathā sotaghānajivhākāyarūpasaddagandharasadhātuyo sotapasādādivasena. Phoṭṭhabbadhātu pana pathavītejovāyovasena tayo dhammāti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Cakkhuviññāṇadhātu kusalākusalavipākavasena dve dhammāti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Tathā [P 0.0080] sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇadhātuyo. Manodhātu pana pañcadvārāvajjanakusalākusalavipākasampaṭicchanavasena tayo dhammāti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Dhammadhātu tiṇṇaṃ arūpakkhandhānaṃ, soḷasannaṃ sukhumarūpānaṃ, asaṅkhatāya ca dhātuyā vasena vīsatidhammāti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Manoviññāṇadhātu sesakusalākusalābyākataviññāṇavasena chasattatidhammāti saṅkhaṃ gacchatīti evamettha ‘saṅkhato’ veditabbo vinicchayo.

'By way of reckoning'—first, the eye element is reckoned as one phenomenon by way of its nature, through eye-sensitivity. Similarly, the ear, nose, tongue, body, form, sound, smell, and taste elements are reckoned through ear-sensitivity and so on. The tangible element, however, is reckoned as three phenomena by way of the earth, fire, and wind elements. The eye-consciousness element is reckoned as two phenomena by way of wholesome and unwholesome resultants. The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body-consciousness elements. The mind element, however, is reckoned as three phenomena by way of five-door adverting, and wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant receiving. The phenomena element is reckoned as twenty phenomena by way of the three immaterial aggregates, sixteen subtle material qualities, and the unconditioned element. The mind-consciousness element is reckoned as seventy-six phenomena by way of the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate consciousness. Thus, here the determination should be understood as 'by way of reckoning'.

‘Paccayā’ti cakkhudhātuādīnaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātuādīsu paccayato veditabbo vinicchayo. So panetesaṃ paccayabhāvo niddesavāre āvi bhavissati.

'By way of conditions'—the determination should be understood in terms of the conditionality of the eye element and so on in relation to the eye-consciousness element and so on. But this state of being conditions for them will become apparent in the section on exposition.

‘Daṭṭhabbā’ti daṭṭhabbatopettha vinicchayo veditabboti attho. Sabbā eva hi saṅkhatā dhātuyo pubbantāparantavivittato, dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvasuññato, paccayāyattavuttito ca daṭṭhabbā. Visesato panettha bheritalaṃ viya cakkhudhātu daṭṭhabbā, daṇḍo viya rūpadhātu, saddo viya cakkhuviññāṇadhātu[V 0.0074]. Tathā ādāsatalaṃ viya cakkhudhātu, mukhaṃ viya rūpadhātu, mukhanimittaṃ viya cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Atha vā ucchutilāni viya cakkhudhātu, yantacakkayaṭṭhi viya rūpadhātu, ucchurasatelāni viya cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Tathā adharāraṇī viya cakkhudhātu, uttarāraṇī viya rūpadhātu, aggi viya cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Esa nayo sotadhātuādīsupi.

'To be seen'—here, the determination of what is to be seen should be understood. Indeed, all conditioned elements should be seen as devoid of past and future, empty of the nature of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self, and arising dependent on conditions. Here, in particular, the eye element should be seen like a drumhead, the form element like a drum-beater, and the eye-consciousness element like the sound. Similarly, the eye element is like a mirror's surface, the form element like a face, and the eye-consciousness element like the image of a face. Or, the eye element is like sugarcane and sesame seeds, the form element like a mill's wheel-shaft, and the eye-consciousness element like sugarcane juice and sesame oil. Again, the eye element is like the lower fire-drill stick, the form element like the upper fire-drill stick, and the eye-consciousness element like the fire. This same method applies to the ear element and so forth.

Manodhātu pana yathāsambhavato cakkhuviññāṇadhātuādīnaṃ purecarānucarā viya daṭṭhabbā. Dhammadhātuyā vedanākkhandho sallamiva sūlamiva ca daṭṭhabbo[M 0.0076]; saññāsaṅkhārakkhandhā vedanāsallasūlayogā āturā viya; puthujjanānaṃ vā saññā āsādukkhajananato rittamuṭṭhi viya, ayathābhuccanimittaggāhakato vanamigo viya; saṅkhārā paṭisandhiyaṃ pakkhipanato aṅgārakāsuyaṃ khipanakapuriso viya, jātidukkhānubandhanato rājapurisānubandhacorā viya, sabbānatthāvahassa khandhasantānassa hetuto visarukkhabījāni viya; rūpaṃ nānāvidhūpaddavanimittato khuracakkaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The mind element, however, should be seen as like the forerunners and followers of the eye-consciousness element and so forth, as is possible. In the phenomena-element, the feeling aggregate should be seen like a dart or a stake; the perception and formation aggregates, afflicted by the dart and stake of feeling, like sick people. Or, for ordinary people, perception should be seen like an empty fist because it generates suffering from hope, or like a forest deer because it grasps unreal signs. Formations should be seen like a man throwing something into a pit of embers, because they cast one into rebirth-linking; like thieves pursued by royal guards, because they are followed by the suffering of birth; or like the seeds of a poison tree, because they are the cause of the continuum of aggregates that brings all misfortune. Material form should be seen like a razor-wheel because it is a basis for various afflictions.

Asaṅkhatā pana dhātu amatato santato khemato ca daṭṭhabbā. Kasmā? Sabbānatthapaṭipakkhabhūtattā. Manoviññāṇadhātu gahitārammaṇaṃ [P 0.0081] muñcitvāpi aññaṃ gahetvāva pavatanato vanamakkaṭo viya, duddamanato assakhaḷuṅko viya, yatthakāmanipātito vehāsaṃ khittadaṇḍo viya, lobhadosādinānappakārakilesayogato raṅganaṭo viya daṭṭhabboti.

The unconditioned element, however, should be seen as deathless, peaceful, and secure. Why? Because it is the opposite of all misfortune. The mind-consciousness element should be seen like a forest monkey, because it proceeds by grasping another object even after releasing a grasped object; like an untamed horse, because it is difficult to tame; like a stick thrown into the air, falling wherever it wishes; and like a stage actor, because it is connected to various kinds of defilements such as greed and hatred.

184. Niddesavāre cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe cāti idañca dvayaṃ paṭicca aññañca kiriyāmanodhātuñceva sampayuttakhandhattayañcāti attho. Cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā hi cakkhu nissayapaccayo hoti, rūpaṃ ārammaṇapaccayo, kiriyamanodhātu vigatapaccayo, tayo arūpakkhandhā sahajātapaccayo. Tasmā esā cakkhuviññāṇadhātu ime cattāro paṭicca uppajjati nāma. Sotañca paṭiccātiādīsupi eseva nayo.

184. In the exposition section, 'dependent on the eye and forms' means dependent on these two, and also dependent on the functional mind-element and the three associated aggregates. For the eye-consciousness element, the eye is the support condition, form is the object condition, the functional mind-element is the disappearance condition, and the three immaterial aggregates are the conascence condition. Therefore, this eye-consciousness element is said to arise dependent on these four conditions. This same method applies to 'dependent on the ear' and so forth.

Niruddhasamanantarāti niruddhāya samanantarā. Tajjā manodhātūti tasmiṃ ārammaṇe jātā kusalākusalavipākato duvidhā manodhātu sampaṭicchanakiccā. Sabbadhammesu vā pana paṭhamasamannāhāroti etesu cakkhuviññāṇādīsu sabbadhammesu uppajjamānesu paṭhamasamannāhāro; cakkhuviññāṇadhātuādīnaṃ [V 0.0075] vā ārammaṇasaṅkhātesu sabbadhammesu paṭhamasamannāhāroti ayamettha attho veditabbo. Etena pañcadvārāvajjanakiccā kiriyamanodhātu gahitāti veditabbā.

'Immediately upon cessation' means immediately after it has ceased. 'The mind-element born therefrom' means the mind-element, twofold due to wholesome and unwholesome resultant, born in regard to that object, whose function is receiving. 'Or the first adverting to all phenomena' means the first adverting when all these phenomena such as eye-consciousness and so forth arise; or it means the first adverting to all phenomena reckoned as the objects of eye-consciousness and so forth. This is the meaning to be understood here. By this it should be understood that the functional mind-element performing the function of five-door adverting is included.

Manodhātuyāpi uppajjitvā niruddhasamanantarāti ettha pi-kāro sampiṇḍanattho. Tasmā manodhātuyāpi manoviññāṇadhātuyāpīti ayamettha attho veditabbo. Tena yā ca vipākamanodhātuyā uppajjitvā niruddhāya samanantarā uppajjati santīraṇakiccā vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu, yā ca tassā uppajjitvā niruddhāya samanantarā uppajjati voṭṭhabbanakiccā kiriyamanoviññāṇadhātu, yā ca tassā uppajjitvā niruddhāya [M 0.0077] samanantarā uppajjati javanakiccā manoviññāṇadhātu – tā sabbāpi kathitā hotīti veditabbā. Manañca paṭiccāti bhavaṅgamanaṃ. Dhamme cāti catubhūmikadhammārammaṇaṃ. Uppajjati manoviññāṇanti sahāvajjanakaṃ javanaṃ nibbattati.

'Immediately after the mind-element also has arisen and ceased'—here the particle 'pi' (also) has the meaning of combining. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as 'also the mind-element and also the mind-consciousness element.' Thus, whatever resultant mind-consciousness element with the function of investigating arises immediately after the resultant mind-element has arisen and ceased; whatever functional mind-consciousness element with the function of determining arises immediately after that has arisen and ceased; and whatever mind-consciousness element with the function of impulsion arises immediately after that has arisen and ceased—all these are said to be included. 'Dependent on the mind' refers to the life-continuum mind. 'And on phenomena' refers to a mental object belonging to the four planes. 'Mind-consciousness arises' means the impulsion together with adverting is generated.

Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne hatthe gahitapañhaṃ nāma gaṇhiṃsu. Mahādhammarakkhitatthero kira nāma dīghabhāṇakābhayattheraṃ hatthe gahetvā āha – ‘paṭiccāti nāma āgataṭṭhāne [P 0.0082] āvajjanaṃ visuṃ na kātabbaṃ, bhavaṅganissitakameva kātabba’nti. Tasmā idha manoti sahāvajjanakaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ. Manoviññāṇanti javanamanoviññāṇaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana abhidhammabhājanīye soḷasa dhātuyo kāmāvacarā, dve catubhūmikā lokiyalokuttaramissakā kathitāti.

In this context, they took up what is called the 'question grasped in hand.' The Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, it is said, taking the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya by the hand, said: 'Where "dependent" occurs, adverting should not be made separately; it should be made only as dependent on the life-continuum.' Therefore, here, 'mind' refers to the life-continuum together with adverting. 'Mind-consciousness' refers to impulsion mind-consciousness. In this Abhidhamma analysis, sixteen elements are said to be of the sense-sphere, and two are mixed, both mundane and supramundane, belonging to the four planes.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Abhidhamma Analysis.

3. Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Section on Questions

185. Pañhāpucchake aṭṭhārasannaṃ dhātūnaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayānusāreneva kusalādibhāvo veditabbo. Ārammaṇattikesu pana cha dhātuyo parittārammaṇāti idaṃ pana pañcannaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ manodhātuyā ca ekantena pañcasu rūpārammaṇādīsu pavattiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dve dhātuyoti vuttānaṃ pana dhammadhātumanoviññāṇadhātūnaṃ manāyatanadhammāyatanesu vuttanayeneva parittārammaṇāditā [V 0.0076] veditabbā. Iti imasmimpi pañhāpucchake soḷasa dhātuyo kāmāvacarā, dve catubhūmikā lokiyalokuttaramissakā kathitā. Evamayaṃ dhātuvibhaṅgopi teparivaṭṭaṃ nīharitvāva bhājetvā desitoti.

185. In the Section on Questions, the nature of the eighteen elements as wholesome, unwholesome, etc., should be understood according to the method previously stated. Among the object triads, that the six elements are of limited object-range—this is said with reference to the occurrence of the five, eye-consciousness and so on, and the mind-element exclusively in the five, form-objects and so on. As for the two elements mentioned, the nature of the dhamma-element and the mind-consciousness-element as of limited object-range, etc., should be understood in the same way as stated for the mind-base and the dhamma-base. Thus, in this Section on Questions as well, sixteen elements are of the sense-sphere, while two are of the four planes, mixed between mundane and supramundane. In this way, this Analysis of Elements has also been taught by extracting and dividing the three rounds.

Sammohavinodaniyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya

From the Sammohavinodanī, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga.

Dhātuvibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Analysis of Elements is concluded.

4. Saccavibhaṅgo

4. The Analysis of the Truths

1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Suttanta Section

189. Idāni [P 0.0083][M 0.0078][V 0.0077] tadanantare saccavibhaṅge cattārīti gaṇanaparicchedo. Ariyasaccānīti paricchinnadhammanidassanaṃ. Dukkhaṃ ariyasaccantiādimhi pana uddesavāre –

189. Now, immediately following that, in the Analysis of the Truths, 'four' is the numerical determination. 'The Noble Truths'—this is a designation of delimited phenomena. Now, in the summary section, beginning with 'The Noble Truth of Suffering'—

Vibhāgato nibbacana-lakkhaṇādippabhedato;

Atthatthuddhārato ceva, anūnādhikato tathā.

By way of division, by way of derivation, characteristic, and other distinctions; and by way of extraction of the meaning, and likewise by way of neither deficiency nor excess.

Kamato ariyasaccesu, yaṃ ñāṇaṃ tassa kiccato;

Antogadhānaṃ pabhedo, upamāto catukkato.

By way of sequence in the Noble Truths, the knowledge according to its function; the distinction of those included, by way of simile, and by way of the fourfold aspect.

Suññatekavidhādīhi, sabhāgavisabhāgato;

Vinicchayo veditabbo, viññunā sāsanakkame.

By way of emptiness, the onefold method, and so on, by way of similarity and dissimilarity, the ascertainment should be understood by the wise in the order of the Teaching.

Tattha ‘vibhāgato’ti dukkhādīnañhi cattāro cattāro atthā vibhattā tathā avitathā anaññathā, ye dukkhādīni abhisamentehi abhisametabbā. Yathāha, “dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho, saṅkhataṭṭho, santāpaṭṭho, vipariṇāmaṭṭho – ime cattāro dukkhassa dukkhaṭṭhā tathā avitathā anaññathā. Samudayassa āyūhanaṭṭho, nidānaṭṭho, saṃyogaṭṭho, palibodhaṭṭho…pe… nirodhassa nissaraṇaṭṭho, vivekaṭṭho, asaṅkhataṭṭho, amataṭṭho…pe… maggassa niyyānaṭṭho, hetvaṭṭho, dassanaṭṭho, ādhipateyyaṭṭho – ime cattāro maggassa maggaṭṭhā tathā avitathā anaññathā”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.8). Tathā [V 0.0078] “dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho, saṅkhataṭṭho, santāpaṭṭho, viparināmaṭṭho, abhisamayaṭṭho”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.11) evamādi. Iti evaṃ vibhattānaṃ catunnaṃ catunnaṃ atthānaṃ vasena dukkhādīni veditabbānīti. Ayaṃ tāvettha vibhāgato vinicchayo veditabbo.

Here, 'by way of division' means that for suffering and the rest, four meanings each are divided as true, not false, and not otherwise—meanings which are to be fully understood by those who fully understand suffering and the rest. As it is said: 'The meaning of suffering is oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of torment, the meaning of change—these four are the meanings of suffering as suffering, true, not false, and not otherwise. The meaning of the origin is accumulation, the meaning of source, the meaning of conjunction, the meaning of obstruction… The meaning of cessation is release, the meaning of detachment, the meaning of the unconditioned, the meaning of the deathless… The meaning of the path is leading out, the meaning of cause, the meaning of vision, the meaning of dominance—these four are the meanings of the path as path, true, not false, and not otherwise.' (Paṭis. II, 8) Similarly, 'The meaning of suffering is oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of torment, the meaning of change, the meaning of full understanding,' (Paṭis. II, 11) and so on. Thus, suffering and the rest should be understood in terms of these fourfold meanings, thus divided. This, then, is the ascertainment to be understood here by way of division.

‘Nibbacanalakkhaṇādippabhedato’ti [P 0.0084] ettha pana ‘nibbacanato’ tāva idha ‘du’iti ayaṃ saddo kucchite dissati; kucchitañhi puttaṃ duputtoti vadanti. ‘Khaṃ’saddo pana tucche; tucchañhi ākāsaṃ khanti vuccati. Idañca paṭhamasaccaṃ kucchitaṃ anekaupaddavādhiṭṭhānato, tucchaṃ bālajanaparikappitadhuvasubhasukhattabhāvavirahitato. Tasmā kucchitattā tucchattā ca dukkhanti vuccati. ‘Saṃ’iti ca ayaṃ [M 0.0079] saddo “samāgamo sameta”ntiādīsu (vibha. 199; dī. ni. 2.396) saṃyogaṃ dīpeti; ‘u’iti ayaṃ saddo “uppannaṃ udita”ntiādīsu (pārā. 172; cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 141) uppattiṃ. ‘Aya’saddo pana kāraṇaṃ dīpeti. Idañcāpi dutiyasaccaṃ avasesapaccayasamāyoge sati dukkhassuppattikāraṇaṃ. Iti dukkhassa saṃyoge uppattikāraṇattā dukkhasamudayanti vuccati.

'By way of derivation, characteristic, and other distinctions'—here, first of all, 'by way of derivation': the word 'du' is seen in the sense of 'despicable'; for a despicable son is called a 'duputta' (bad son). The word 'khaṃ' signifies 'empty'; for empty space is called 'kha'. And this first truth is despicable because it is the basis of many dangers, and empty because it is devoid of the state of permanence, beauty, and happiness imagined by foolish people. Therefore, because of being despicable and empty, it is called 'dukkha' (suffering). The word 'saṃ' indicates conjunction, as in 'samāgamo sameta' (coming together, assembled). The word 'u' indicates arising, as in 'uppannaṃ udita' (arisen, appeared). The word 'aya' indicates cause. And this second truth is the cause for the arising of suffering when there is a coming together of the remaining conditions. Thus, because it is the cause for the arising of suffering in conjunction with conditions, it is called 'dukkhasamudaya' (the origin of suffering).

Tatiyasaccaṃ pana yasmā ‘ni’saddo abhāvaṃ ‘rodha’saddo ca cārakaṃ dīpeti, tasmā abhāvo ettha saṃsāracārakasaṅkhātassa dukkharodhassa sabbagatisuññattā, samadhigate vā tasmiṃ saṃsāracārakasaṅkhātassa dukkharodhassa abhāvo hoti tappaṭipakkhattātipi dukkhanirodhanti vuccati, dukkhassa vā anuppādanirodhapaccayattā dukkhanirodhanti. Catutthasaccaṃ pana yasmā etaṃ dukkhanirodhaṃ gacchati ārammaṇavasena tadabhimukhībhūtattā, paṭipadā ca hoti dukkhanirodhappattiyā, tasmā dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti vuccati.

As for the third truth, since the word 'ni' indicates absence and the word 'rodha' indicates confinement, therefore, here, there is an absence of the confinement of suffering, which is designated as the prison of saṃsāra, due to its being void of all destinations. Or, when that cessation is attained, there is an absence of the confinement of suffering, which is designated as the prison of saṃsāra, because it is its opposite. Thus, it is called 'dukkhanirodha' (the cessation of suffering). Or, because it is the condition for the non-arising and cessation of suffering, it is called 'dukkhanirodha'. As for the fourth truth, since this path approaches the cessation of suffering by way of object, because it is directed towards it, and it is the path for the attainment of the cessation of suffering, therefore it is called 'the path leading to the cessation of suffering'.

Yasmā panetāni buddhādayo ariyā paṭivijjhanti, tasmā ariyasaccānīti vuccanti. Yathāha – “catārimāni, bhikkhave, ariyasaccāni (saṃ. ni. 5.1097). Katamāni…pe… imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri ariyasaccāni. Ariyā imāni paṭivijjhanti, tasmā ariyasaccānīti vuccantī”ti. Apica ariyassa saccānītipi ariyasaccāni. Yathāha – “sadevake, bhikkhave, loke…pe… sadevamanussāya tathāgato ariyo, tasmā ariyasaccānīti vuccantī”ti. Atha vā etesaṃ abhisambuddhattā ariyabhāvasiddhitopi ariyasaccāni. Yathāha – “imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ [V 0.0079] yathābhūtaṃ abhisambuddhattā tathāgato arahaṃ sammāsambuddho ‘ariyo’ti vuccatī”ti. Apica kho pana ariyāni [P 0.0085] saccānītipi ariyasaccāni; ariyānīti tathāni avitathāni avisaṃvādakānīti attho. Yathāha – “imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri ariyasaccāni tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni, tasmā ariyasaccānīti vuccantī”ti. Evamettha nibbacanato vinicchayo veditabbo.

Since the noble ones, beginning with the Buddhas, penetrate these, they are called the Noble Truths. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, there are these four Noble Truths (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1097). What are they? ... Indeed, bhikkhus, these are the four Noble Truths. The noble ones penetrate these, therefore they are called the Noble Truths.' Moreover, they are also the truths of the Noble One, thus they are the Noble Truths. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, in this world with its gods... with its gods and humans, the Tathāgata is noble, therefore these are called the Noble Truths.' Alternatively, because of having fully awakened to them, the noble state is accomplished, thus they are the Noble Truths. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, it is because he has fully awakened to these four Noble Truths as they truly are that the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is called ‘noble’.' Furthermore, they are noble truths, thus they are the Noble Truths; 'noble' means real, not false, and not deceptive. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, these four Noble Truths are real, not false, not otherwise, therefore they are called the Noble Truths.' Thus, the ascertainment here should be understood by way of derivation.

Kathaṃ ‘lakkhaṇādippabhedato’? Ettha hi bādhanalakkhaṇaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ, santāpanarasaṃ, pavattipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Pabhavalakkhaṇaṃ samudayasaccaṃ, anupacchedakaraṇarasaṃ, palibodhapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Santilakkhaṇaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ, accutirasaṃ, animittapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ[M 0.0080]. Niyyānalakkhaṇaṃ maggasaccaṃ, kilesappahānakaraṇarasaṃ, vuṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Apica pavattipavattakanivattinivattakalakkhaṇāni paṭipāṭiyā. Tathā saṅkhatataṇhāasaṅkhatadassanalakkhaṇāni cāti evamettha ‘lakkhaṇādippabhedato’ vinicchayo veditabbo.

How is it 'by way of characteristic and other distinctions'? Here, the truth of suffering has the characteristic of oppression, the function of tormenting, and manifestation as occurrence. The truth of the origin has the characteristic of origination, the function of causing non-interruption, and manifestation as an impediment. The truth of cessation has the characteristic of peace, the function of immutability, and manifestation as the signless. The truth of the path has the characteristic of leading out, the function of causing the abandoning of defilements, and manifestation as emergence. Moreover, the characteristics of occurrence, causing occurrence, cessation, and causing cessation follow in sequence. Similarly, the characteristics of the conditioned, craving, the unconditioned, and vision are also to be understood. Thus, the ascertainment here should be understood as 'by way of characteristic and other distinctions'.

‘Atthatthuddhārato cevā’ti ettha pana atthato tāva ko saccaṭṭhoti ce? Yo paññācakkhunā upaparikkhamānānaṃ māyāva viparītako, marīcīva visaṃvādako, titthiyānaṃ attāva anupalabbhasabhāvo ca na hoti; atha kho bādhanapabhavasantiniyyānappakārena tacchāviparītabhūtabhāvena ariyañāṇassa gocaro hotiyeva; esa aggilakkhaṇaṃ viya, lokapakati viya ca tacchāviparītabhūtabhāvo saccaṭṭhoti veditabbo. Yathāha – “idaṃ dukkhanti kho, bhikkhave, tathametaṃ avitathametaṃ anaññathameta”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.1090) vitthāro. Apica –

And as to 'by meaning and by extraction of meaning,' first, regarding meaning: what is the meaning of 'truth' here? It is that which, when examined with the eye of wisdom, is not deceptive like an illusion, not misleading like a mirage, nor does it have an unapprehendable nature like the self of sectarians; but rather, by its nature of being true, not reversed, and real in the modes of oppression, origination, peace, and leading out, it becomes the domain of noble knowledge. This nature of being true, not reversed, and real is to be understood as the meaning of 'truth,' like the characteristic of fire or the nature of the world. As it is said: 'This is suffering, bhikkhus—this is true, this is not false, this is not otherwise' (SN 5.1090), and so on in detail. Furthermore:

Nābādhakaṃ yato dukkhaṃ, dukkhā aññaṃ na bādhakaṃ;

Bādhakattaniyāmena, tato saccamidaṃ mataṃ.

Since suffering is oppressive, and nothing other than suffering is oppressive; by the fixed nature of being oppressive, therefore, this is considered truth.

Taṃ vinā nāññato dukkhaṃ, na hoti na ca taṃ tato;

Dukkhahetuniyāmena, iti saccaṃ visattikā.

Without it, suffering does not arise from anything else, nor does that arise from this; by the fixed law of the cause of suffering, thus, craving is the truth.

Nāññā nibbānato santi, santaṃ na ca na taṃ yato;

Santabhāvaniyāmena, tato saccamidaṃ mataṃ.

There is no peace apart from Nibbāna, and since peace is not other than it; by the fixed nature of being peace, therefore, this is considered truth.

Maggā [V 0.0080] aññaṃ na niyyānaṃ, aniyyāno na cāpi so;

Tacchaniyyānabhāvattā, iti so saccasammato.

There is no leading out apart from the path, nor is it not a leading out; because of its nature of truly leading out, thus it is regarded as truth.

Iti tacchāvipallāsa-bhūtabhāvaṃ catūsupi;

Dukkhādīsvavisesena, saccaṭṭhaṃ āhu paṇḍitāti.

Thus, the wise declare the meaning of truth in all four—suffering and so on, without distinction—to be the nature of being true, unperverted, and real.

Evaṃ [P 0.0086] ‘atthato’ vinicchayo veditabbo.

In this way, the ascertainment 'by meaning' should be understood.

Kathaṃ ‘atthuddhārato’? Idhāyaṃ ‘sacca’saddo anekesu atthesu dissati, seyyathidaṃ – “saccaṃ bhaṇe, na kujjheyyā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 224) vācāsacce. “Sacce ṭhitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā cā”tiādīsu (jā. 2.21.433) viratisacce. “Kasmā nu saccāni [M 0.0081] vadanti nānā, pavādiyāse kusalāvadānā”tiādīsu (su. ni. 891) diṭṭhisacce. “Ekañhi saccaṃ na dutiyamatthī”tiādīsu (su. ni. 890) paramatthasacce nibbāne ceva magge ca. “Catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ kati kusalā”tiādīsu (vibha. 216) ariyasacce. Svāyamidhāpi ariyasacce vattatīti evamettha ‘atthuddhārato’pi vinicchayo veditabbo.

How is it 'by extraction of meaning'? Here, the word 'sacca' is seen in many meanings, such as: in 'Speak the truth, do not be angry' (Dhp 224), etc., referring to truth in speech; in 'Ascetics and brahmins established in truth' (Jā 2.21.433), etc., referring to truth as abstinence; in 'Why do the disputants, who call themselves skilled, declare various truths?' (Sn 891), etc., referring to truth of views; in 'For there is only one truth, there is not a second' (Sn 890), etc., referring to the ultimate truth, Nibbāna and the path; in 'Of the four Noble Truths, how many are wholesome?' (Vibh 216), etc., referring to the Noble Truths. Here too, it applies to the Noble Truths. Thus, the ascertainment 'by extraction of meaning' should also be understood here.

‘Anūnādhikato’ti kasmā pana cattāreva ariyasaccāni vuttāni, anūnāni anadhikānīti ce? Aññassāsambhavato, aññatarassa ca anapaneyyabhāvato; na hi etehi aññaṃ adhikaṃ vā etesaṃ vā ekampi apanetabbaṃ sambhoti. Yathāha – “idha, bhikkhave, āgaccheyya samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ‘netaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, aññaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yaṃ samaṇena gotamena desitaṃ. Ahametaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ paññapessāmī’ti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”tiādi. Yathā cāha – “yo hi koci, bhikkhave, samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā evaṃ vadeyya ‘netaṃ dukkhaṃ paṭhamaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, yaṃ samaṇena gotamena desitaṃ. Ahametaṃ dukkhaṃ paṭhamaṃ ariyasaccaṃ paccakkhāya aññaṃ dukkhaṃ paṭhamaṃ ariyasaccaṃ paññapessāmī’ti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.1086).

As to 'neither deficient nor excessive,' why are only four Noble Truths stated, neither deficient nor excessive? Because no other is possible, and none of them can be removed. Indeed, nothing more can arise beyond them, nor can even a single one be taken away from them. As it is said: 'Here, bhikkhus, if any ascetic or brahmin were to come and say, "This is not the Noble Truth of Suffering taught by the ascetic Gotama; setting aside this Noble Truth of Suffering, I will designate another Noble Truth of Suffering," such a thing is impossible,' and so on. And as it is further said: 'Bhikkhus, if any ascetic or brahmin were to say, "This is not the first Noble Truth of Suffering taught by the ascetic Gotama; rejecting this first Noble Truth of Suffering, I will designate another first Noble Truth of Suffering," such a thing is impossible,' and so on (SN 5.1086).

Apica pavattimācikkhanto bhagavā sahetukaṃ ācikkhi, nivattiñca saupāyaṃ. Iti pavattinivattitadubhayahetūnaṃ [V 0.0081] etapparamato cattāreva vuttāni. Tathā pariññeyya pahātabba sacchikātabba bhāvetabbānaṃ, taṇhāvatthutaṇhātaṇhānirodhataṇhānirodhupāyānaṃ, ālayālayarāmatāālayasamugghātaālayasamugghātūpāyānañca vasenāpi cattāreva vuttānīti. Evamettha ‘anūnādhikato’ vinicchayo veditabbo.

Moreover, the Blessed One, while explaining arising, taught it with its cause, and cessation with its means. Thus, because these are the ultimate for the causes of both arising and cessation, only four are stated. Similarly, in terms of what is to be fully understood, abandoned, realized, and developed; in terms of the object of craving, craving, the cessation of craving, and the means to the cessation of craving; and in terms of attachment, delight in attachment, the uprooting of attachment, and the means to the uprooting of attachment—only four are stated. In this way, the discernment 'neither deficient nor excessive' should be understood here.

‘Kamato’ti ayampi desanākkamova. Ettha ca oḷārikattā sabbasattasādhāraṇattā ca suviññeyyanti dukkhasaccaṃ paṭhamaṃ [P 0.0087] vuttaṃ, tasseva hetudassanatthaṃ tadanantaraṃ samudayasaccaṃ, hetunirodhā phalanirodhoti ñāpanatthaṃ tato nirodhasaccaṃ, tadadhigamupāyadassanatthaṃ ante maggasaccaṃ. Bhavasukhassādagadhitānaṃ vā sattānaṃ saṃvegajananatthaṃ paṭhamaṃ dukkhamāha. Taṃ neva akataṃ āgacchati, na issaranimmānādito hoti, ito pana hotīti [M 0.0082] ñāpanatthaṃ tadanantaraṃ samudayaṃ. Tato sahetukena dukkhena abhibhūtattā saṃviggamānasānaṃ dukkhanissaraṇagavesīnaṃ nissaraṇadassanena assāsajananatthaṃ nirodhaṃ. Tato nirodhādhigamatthaṃ nirodhasampāpakaṃ magganti evamettha ‘kamato’ vinicchayo veditabbo.

As for 'in sequence,' this too is simply the order of the teaching. Here, because of its grossness and its commonality to all beings, being easily understood, the Truth of Suffering is stated first. To show its cause, the Truth of Origin immediately after it. To make known that with the cessation of the cause, there is cessation of the result, then the Truth of Cessation. Finally, to show the means of attaining that, the Truth of the Path last. Alternatively, to arouse a sense of urgency in beings addicted to the enjoyment of existence, suffering is stated first. Then, to make known that it does not come uncaused, nor does it arise from the creation of a lord, etc., but rather arises from this, the origin is taught next. Then, for those whose minds are stirred because of being overwhelmed by suffering that has a cause, and who seek an escape from suffering, the cessation is taught to give them reassurance by showing the way out. Then, for the attainment of cessation, the path that leads to cessation. In this way, the discernment 'in sequence' should be understood here.

‘Ariyasaccesu yaṃ ñāṇaṃ tassa kiccato’ti saccañāṇakiccatopi vinicchayo veditabboti attho. Duvidhañhi saccañāṇaṃ – anubodhañāṇañca paṭivedhañāṇañca. Tattha anubodhañāṇaṃ lokiyaṃ anussavādivasena nirodhe magge ca pavattati. Paṭivedhañāṇaṃ lokuttaraṃ nirodhārammaṇaṃ katvā kiccato cattāripi saccāni paṭivijjhati. Yathāha – “yo, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ passati dukkhasamudayampi so passati, dukkhanirodhampi passati, dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadampi passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1100) sabbaṃ vattabbaṃ. Yaṃ panetaṃ lokiyaṃ, tattha dukkhañāṇaṃ pariyuṭṭhānābhibhavanavasena pavattamānaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhiṃ nivatteti, samudayañāṇaṃ ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ, nirodhañāṇaṃ sassatadiṭṭhiṃ, maggañāṇaṃ akiriyadiṭṭhiṃ; dukkhañāṇaṃ vā dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvarahitesu khandhesu dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvasaññāsaṅkhātaṃ phale vippaṭipattiṃ, samudayañāṇaṃ issarappadhānakālasabhāvādīhi loko pavattatīti akāraṇe kāraṇābhimānappavattaṃ hetumhi vippaṭipattiṃ, nirodhañāṇaṃ arūpalokalokathūpikādīsu apavaggaggāhabhūtaṃ nirodhe vippaṭipattiṃ, maggañāṇaṃ kāmasukhallikaattakilamathānuyogappabhede [P 0.0088] avisuddhimagge visuddhimaggaggāhavasena pavattaṃ upāye vippaṭipattiṃ nivatteti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

As to 'from the function of the knowledge regarding the Noble Truths,' this means that the discernment should be understood also from the function of the knowledge of the truths. For the knowledge of the truths is twofold: knowledge through understanding and knowledge through penetration. Here, knowledge through understanding is mundane and operates in dependence on hearsay, etc., regarding cessation and the path. Knowledge through penetration is supramundane; taking cessation as its object, by its function it penetrates all four truths. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, whoever sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering' (SN 5.1100), and so on. As for this mundane knowledge: the knowledge of suffering, operating by way of overcoming obsession, averts the view of self; the knowledge of origin averts the view of annihilation; the knowledge of cessation averts the view of eternalism; the knowledge of the path averts the view of non-action. Alternatively, the knowledge of suffering averts the misconception regarding the fruit, which is the perception of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self in the aggregates devoid of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self; the knowledge of origin averts the misconception regarding the cause, which is the assumption of a cause where there is none, proceeding with the notion that the world arises through a creator, primordial matter, time, or nature, etc.; the knowledge of cessation averts the misconception regarding cessation, which is the grasping of the formless realms, the peak of the world, etc., as liberation; the knowledge of the path averts the misconception regarding the means, which proceeds by grasping an impure path—differentiated as indulgence in sensual pleasures or self-mortification—as the pure path. Therefore, it is said—

Loke [V 0.0082] lokappabhave, lokatthagame sive ca tadupāye;

Sammuyhati tāva naro, na vijānāti yāva saccānīti.

In the world, in the origin of the world, in the cessation of the world, and in the auspicious means to that; so long as a person is confused, he does not know the truths.

Evamettha ‘ñāṇakiccato’pi vinicchayo veditabbo.

In this way, the discernment 'from the function of knowledge' should also be understood here.

‘Antogadhānaṃ pabhedā’ti dukkhasaccasmiñhi, ṭhapetvā taṇhañceva anāsavadhamme ca, sesā sabbadhammā antogadhā; samudayasacce chattiṃsa taṇhāvicaritāni; nirodhasaccaṃ asammissaṃ; maggasacce sammādiṭṭhimukhena vīmaṃsiddhipādapaññindriyapaññābaladhammavicayasambojjhaṅgāni. Sammāsaṅkappāpadesena tayo nekkhammavitakkādayo, sammāvācāpadesena cattāri vacīsucaritāni, sammākammantāpadesena tīṇi kāyasucaritāni, sammāājīvamukhena appicchatā santuṭṭhitā [M 0.0083] ca, sabbesaṃyeva vā etesaṃ sammāvācākammantājīvānaṃ ariyakantasīlattā sīlassa ca saddhāhatthena paṭiggahetabbattā tesaṃ atthitāya ca atthibhāvato saddhindriyasaddhābalachandiddhipādā, sammāvāyāmāpadesena catubbidhasammappadhānavīriyindriyavīriyabalavīriyasambojjhaṅgāni, sammāsatiapadesena catubbidhasatipaṭṭhānasatindriyasatibalasatisambojjhaṅgāni, sammāsamādhiapadesena savitakkasavicārādayo tayo tayo samādhī, cittasamādhisamādhindriyasamādhibalapītipassaddhisamādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgāni antogadhānīti. Evamettha ‘antogadhānaṃ pabhedā’pi vinicchayo veditabbo.

'The classifications of what is included' – In the truth of suffering, except for craving and the taint-free states, all other states are included. In the truth of origin, the thirty-six modes of craving are included. The truth of cessation is unmixed. In the truth of the path, by way of right view, the basis of psychic power of investigation, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, and the enlightenment factor of investigation of states are included. By way of right intention, the three thoughts of renunciation and so on are included. By way of right speech, the four kinds of good verbal conduct are included. By way of right action, the three kinds of good bodily conduct are included. By way of right livelihood, having few wishes and contentment are included. Alternatively, since all these—right speech, right action, and right livelihood—are virtue dear to the noble ones, and since virtue is to be received with the hand of faith, their existence establishes the faculty of faith, the power of faith, and the basis of psychic power of aspiration. By way of right effort, the fourfold right exertions, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, and the enlightenment factor of energy are included. By way of right mindfulness, the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, and the enlightenment factor of mindfulness are included. By way of right concentration, the three kinds of concentration—with applied and sustained thought, and so on—are included, along with concentration of mind, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and the enlightenment factors of joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. Thus, the analysis of 'the classifications of what is included' should also be understood in this way.

‘Upamāto’ti bhāro viya hi dukkhasaccaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, bhārādānamiva samudayasaccaṃ, bhāranikkhepanamiva nirodhasaccaṃ, bhāranikkhepanūpāyo viya maggasaccaṃ; rogo viya ca dukkhasaccaṃ, roganidānamiva samudayasaccaṃ, rogavūpasamo viya nirodhasaccaṃ, bhesajjamiva maggasaccaṃ; dubbhikkhamiva vā dukkhasaccaṃ, dubbuṭṭhi viya samudayasaccaṃ, subhikkhamiva nirodhasaccaṃ[P 0.0089], suvuṭṭhi viya maggasaccaṃ. Apica verīveramūlaverasamugghātaverasamugghātupāyehi, visarukkharukkhamūlamūlupacchedatadupacchedupāyehi, bhayabhayamūlanibbhayatadadhigamupāyehi, orimatīramahoghapārimatīrataṃsampāpakavāyāmehi ca yojetvāpetāni upamāto veditabbānīti. Evamettha ‘upamāto’ vinicchayo veditabbo.

'By analogy': The truth of suffering should be seen as a burden; the truth of origin, as taking up the burden; the truth of cessation, as putting down the burden; and the truth of the path, as the means for putting down the burden. And the truth of suffering is like a disease; the truth of origin, like the cause of the disease; the truth of cessation, like the calming of the disease; and the truth of the path, like the medicine. Or, the truth of suffering is like a famine; the truth of origin, like a drought; the truth of cessation, like a good harvest; and the truth of the path, like good rain. Furthermore, these truths should be understood by analogy, by associating them respectively with: an enemy, the root of the enemy, the uprooting of the enemy, and the means to uproot the enemy; a poisonous tree, its root, the severing of its root, and the means to sever it; fear, the root of fear, fearlessness, and the means to attain it; and the near shore, the great flood, the far shore, and the effort to reach it. Thus, the analysis 'by analogy' should be understood in this way.

‘Catukkato’ti atthi cettha dukkhaṃ na ariyasaccaṃ, atthi ariyasaccaṃ na dukkhaṃ, atthi dukkhañceva [V 0.0083] ariyasaccañca, atthi neva dukkhaṃ na ariyasaccaṃ. Esa nayo samudayādīsu. Tattha maggasampayuttā dhammā sāmaññaphalāni ca “yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkha”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.15) vacanato saṅkhāradukkhatāya dukkhaṃ na ariyasaccaṃ. Nirodho ariyasaccaṃ na dukkhaṃ. Itaraṃ pana ariyasaccadvayaṃ siyā dukkhaṃ aniccato, na pana yassa pariññāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati tathatthena. Sabbākārena pana upādānakkhandhapañcakaṃ dukkhañceva ariyasaccañca aññatra taṇhāya. Maggasampayuttā dhammā sāmaññaphalāni ca yassa pariññatthaṃ bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati tathatthena neva dukkhaṃ na ariyasaccaṃ. Evaṃ samudayādīsupi yathāyogaṃ yojetvā ‘catukkato’pettha vinicchayo veditabbo.

'Fourfold': Here, there is suffering that is not a noble truth; there is a noble truth that is not suffering; there is both suffering and a noble truth; and there is neither suffering nor a noble truth. This method applies to the origin and the rest. In this case, the states associated with the path and the fruits of recluseship are suffering, according to the statement, "Whatever is impermanent is suffering" (SN 22.15), because of the suffering of conditioned things, but they are not a noble truth. Cessation is a noble truth but is not suffering. The other two noble truths may be suffering due to their impermanence, but not in the real sense for the full understanding of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. However, in every way, the five aggregates of clinging, apart from craving, are both suffering and a noble truth. The states associated with the path and the fruits of recluseship, in the real sense for the full understanding of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One, are neither suffering nor a noble truth. In this way, by applying this appropriately to the origin and the rest, the analysis 'fourfold' should also be understood here.

‘Suññatekavidhādīhī’ti [M 0.0084] ettha suññato tāva paramatthena hi sabbāneva saccāni vedakakārakanibbutagamakābhāvato suññānīti veditabbāni. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

'By way of emptiness, singlefold, etc.': Here, firstly, 'by way of emptiness' should be understood thus: in the ultimate sense, all truths are empty due to the absence of an experiencer, a doer, one who is quenched, or one who goes. Hence it is said:

Dukkhameva hi na koci dukkhito, kārako na kiriyāva vijjati;

Atthi nibbuti na nibbuto pumā, maggamatthi gamako na vijjatīti.

There is only suffering, but no one who suffers; No doer is there, though an action is found; Quenching exists, but no person quenched; The path is there, but no goer is found.

Atha vā –

Or:

Dhuvasubhasukhattasuññaṃ, purimadvayamattasuññamamatapadaṃ;

Dhuvasukhaattavirahito, maggo iti suññato tesu.

The first two are empty of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self; the deathless state is empty of self; the path is devoid of permanence, happiness, and self. Thus is the emptiness among them.

Nirodhasuññāni [P 0.0090] vā tīṇi, nirodho ca sesattayasuñño. Phalasuñño vā ettha hetu samudaye dukkhassābhāvato magge ca nirodhassa, na phalena sagabbho pakativādīnaṃ pakati viya. Hetusuññañca phalaṃ dukkhasamudayānaṃ nirodhamaggānañca asamavāyā, na hetusamavetaṃ hetuphalaṃ hetuphalasamavāyavādīnaṃ dviaṇukādīni viya. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Or, the three truths are empty of cessation, and cessation is empty of the remaining three. Or, here the cause is empty of fruit, because suffering is absent in the origin and cessation is absent in the path; it is not pregnant with its fruit like the 'nature' of the naturalists. And the fruit is empty of cause, because suffering and origin, and cessation and path, are not concomitant; it is not a cause-and-fruit where the cause is concomitant with the fruit, like the dyads and so on of those who advocate the concomitance of cause and fruit. Therefore, it is said:

Tayamidha nirodhasuññaṃ, tayena tenāpi nibbuti suññā;

Suñño phalena hetu, phalampi taṃ hetunā suññanti.

Here, the three are empty of cessation; by those three, quenching too is empty. The cause is empty of fruit, and that fruit is empty of cause.

Evaṃ [V 0.0084] tāva ‘suññato’ vinicchayo veditabbo.

Thus far, the analysis 'by way of emptiness' should be understood.

‘Ekavidhādīhī’ti sabbameva cettha dukkhaṃ ekavidhaṃ pavattibhāvato, duvidhaṃ nāmarūpato, tividhaṃ kāmarūpārūpūpapatibhavabhedato, catubbidhaṃ catuāhārabhedato, pañcavidhaṃ pañcupādānakkhandhabhedato. Samudayopi ekavidho pavattakabhāvato, duvidho diṭṭhisampayuttāsampayuttato, tividho kāmabhavavibhavataṇhābhedato, catubbidho catumaggappaheyyato, pañcavidho rūpābhinandanādibhedato, chabbidho chataṇhākāyabhedato. Nirodhopi ekavidho asaṅkhatadhātubhāvato, pariyāyena pana duvidho saupādisesaanupādisesato, tividho bhavattayavūpasamato, catubbidho catumaggādhigamanīyato, pañcavidho pañcābhinandanavūpasamato, chabbidho chataṇhākāyakkhayabhedato. Maggopi ekavidho bhāvetabbato, duvidho samathavipassanābhedato dassanabhāvanābhedato vā[M 0.0085], tividho khandhattayabhedato. Ayañhi sappadesattā nagaraṃ viya rajjena nippadesehi tīhi khandhehi saṅgahito. Yathāha –

‘By way of onefold, etc.’ Here, all suffering is onefold in terms of its nature as an ongoing process, twofold in terms of name-and-form, threefold by the division into the realms of sensual desire, form, and formlessness, fourfold by the division into the four nutriments, and fivefold by the division into the five aggregates subject to clinging. The origin is also onefold in terms of being the cause of that process, twofold as associated with wrong view or not, threefold by the division into craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence, fourfold as to be abandoned by the four paths, fivefold by the division into delight in forms, etc., and sixfold by the division into the six classes of craving. Cessation is also onefold as the unconditioned element, but figuratively twofold as with or without remaining residue, threefold as the pacification of the three kinds of existence, fourfold as to be realized by the four paths, fivefold as the pacification of the five kinds of delight, and sixfold by the division into the destruction of the six classes of craving. The path is also onefold as to be developed, twofold as serenity and insight or as seeing and cultivation, and threefold by the division into the three aggregates. For this path, having its own parts, is encompassed by the three aggregates, which are without parts, just as a city is by a kingdom. As it is said—

“Na kho, āvuso visākha, ariyena aṭṭhaṅgikena maggena tayo khandhā saṅgahitā. Tīhi ca kho, āvuso visākha, khandhehi ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo saṅgahito. Yā cāvuso visākha, sammāvācā, yo ca sammākammanto, yo ca sammāājīvo – ime dhammā sīlakkhandhe saṅgahitā; yo ca sammāvāyāmo, yā ca sammāsati, yo ca sammāsamādhi – ime dhammā samādhikkhandhe saṅgahitā; yā ca sammādiṭṭhi, yo ca sammāsaṅkappo – ime dhammā paññākkhandhe [P 0.0091] saṅgahitā”ti (ma. ni. 1.462).

“Friend Visākha, the three aggregates are not encompassed by the Noble Eightfold Path. Rather, friend Visākha, the Noble Eightfold Path is encompassed by the three aggregates. Friend Visākha, right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these qualities are included in the aggregate of virtue. Right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these qualities are included in the aggregate of concentration. Right view and right intention—these qualities are included in the aggregate of wisdom.”

Ettha hi sammāvācādayo tayo sīlameva. Tasmā te sajātito sīlakkhandhena saṅgahitā. Kiñcāpi hi pāḷiyaṃ sīlakkhandheti bhummena niddeso kato, attho pana karaṇavaseneva veditabbo. Sammāvāyāmādīsu pana tīsu samādhi attano dhammatāya ārammaṇe ekaggabhāvena appetuṃ na sakkoti, vīriye pana paggahakiccaṃ sādhente satiyā ca apilāpanakiccaṃ sādhentiyā laddhūpakāro hutvā sakkoti.

Here, indeed, right speech and the other two are simply virtue. Therefore, they are included in the virtue aggregate by their inherent nature. Although in the Pāli text, the virtue aggregate is designated by way of the ground, its meaning, however, should be understood by way of the instrument. But among right effort and the other two, concentration, by its own nature, cannot apply itself to the object with one-pointedness; however, having received support from effort, which accomplishes the function of upholding, and from mindfulness, which accomplishes the function of non-wavering, it is able to do so.

Tatrāyaṃ upamā – yathā hi nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmāti uyyānaṃ paviṭṭhesu tīsu sahāyesu eko supupphitaṃ campakarukkhaṃ disvā hatthaṃ ukkhipitvāpi gahetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya. Athassa dutiyo [V 0.0085] onamitvā piṭṭhiṃ dadeyya. So tassa piṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhatvāpi kampamāno gahetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya. Athassa itaro aṃsakūṭaṃ upanāmeyya. So ekassa piṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhatvā ekassa aṃsakūṭaṃ olubbha yathāruci pupphāni ocinitvā piḷandhitvā nakkhattaṃ kīḷeyya. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here is the simile: Just as three friends who entered a garden intending to enjoy a festival, one of them, upon seeing a fully blossomed champak tree, might raise his hand but still be unable to grasp the flowers. Then, a second friend might bend down and offer his back. Standing on his back, the first friend, while swaying, might still be unable to grasp them. Then, the third friend might offer his shoulder. Standing on one friend’s back and leaning on the other’s shoulder, he could then pick the flowers as he wishes, adorn himself with them, and enjoy the festival. This example should be understood in this way.

Ekato uyyānaṃ paviṭṭhā tayo sahāyā viya hi ekato jātā sammāvāyāmādayo tayo dhammā, supupphitacampakarukkho viya ārammaṇaṃ, hatthaṃ ukkhipitvāpi gahetuṃ asakkonto viya attano dhammatāya ārammaṇe ekaggabhāvena appetuṃ asakkonto samādhi, piṭṭhiṃ datvā onatasahāyo viya vāyāmo, aṃsakūṭaṃ datvā ṭhitasahāyo [M 0.0086] viya sati. Yathā tesu ekassa piṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhatvā ekassa aṃsakūṭaṃ olubbha itaro yathāruci pupphaṃ gahetuṃ sakkoti, evameva vīriye paggahakiccaṃ sādhente satiyā ca apilāpanakiccaṃ sādhentiyā laddhūpakāro samādhi sakkoti ārammaṇe ekaggabhāvena appetuṃ. Tasmā samādhiyevettha sajātito samādhikkhandhena saṅgahito. Vāyāmasatiyo pana kiriyato saṅgahitā honti.

Like three friends entering a garden together, the three qualities—right effort and so on—are born together. Like a fully blossomed champak tree is the object. Like one who, even raising a hand, cannot grasp it, so concentration, due to its own nature, cannot fix itself upon the object with one-pointedness. Like a friend bending down offering his back, is effort; like a friend standing firm offering his shoulder, is mindfulness. Just as one, standing on another's back and leaning on another’s shoulder, can pluck flowers at will, so too, when effort fulfills its task of exertion and mindfulness fulfills its task of non-forgetfulness, concentration, aided by them, can fix itself upon the object with one-pointedness. Therefore, here, concentration is included in the aggregate of concentration by its inherent nature, while effort and mindfulness are included by way of function.

Sammādiṭṭhisammāsaṅkappesupi paññā attano dhammatāya ‘aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā’ti ārammaṇaṃ nicchetuṃ na sakkoti, vitakke pana ākoṭetvā ākoṭetvā dente sakkoti. Kathaṃ? Yathā hi heraññiko kahāpaṇaṃ hatthe ṭhapetvā sabbabhāgesu [P 0.0092] oloketukāmo samānopi na cakkhutaleneva parivattetuṃ sakkoti, aṅgulipabbehi pana parivattetvā parivattetvā ito cito ca oloketuṃ sakkoti; evameva na paññā attano dhammatāya aniccādivasena ārammaṇaṃ nicchetuṃ sakkoti, abhiniropanalakkhaṇena pana āhananapariyāhananarasena vitakkena ākoṭentena viya parivattentena viya ca ādāya ādāya dinnameva nicchetuṃ sakkoti. Tasmā idhāpi sammādiṭṭhiyeva sajātito paññākkhandhena saṅgahitā, sammāsaṅkappo pana kiriyato saṅgahito hoti. Iti imehi tīhi khandhehi maggo saṅgahaṃ gacchati. Tena vuttaṃ – “tividho khandhattayabhedato”ti. Catubbidho sotāpattimaggādivasena.

As for right view and right intention, wisdom, by its own nature, cannot ascertain the object as ‘impermanent, suffering, and non-self,’ but it can do so by means of thought, which repeatedly strikes and presents it. How? Just as a goldsmith, holding a coin in his hand and wishing to examine it in every aspect, cannot turn it merely with the palm, but by repeatedly turning it with his finger joints, he can examine it here and there—so too, wisdom cannot ascertain the object as impermanent and so forth by its own nature, but by means of thought, which has the characteristic of directing towards and the function of impact and manipulation, as if repeatedly striking and turning it, it can ascertain what is presented by repeatedly taking it up. Therefore, here too, right view is included in the aggregate of wisdom by its inherent nature, while right intention is included by way of function. Thus, the path is gathered under these three aggregates. Hence it is said: ‘threefold by the division into three aggregates.’ It is fourfold by way of the stream-entry path and so on.

Apica sabbāneva saccāni ekavidhāni avitathattā abhiññeyyattā vā, duvidhāni lokiyalokuttarato saṅkhatāsaṅkhatato ca, tividhāni dassanabhāvanāhi pahātabbato appahātabbato nevapahātabbanāpahātabbato [V 0.0086] ca, catubbidhāni pariññeyyādibhedatoti. Evamettha ‘ekavidhādīhi’ vinicchayo veditabbo.

Furthermore, all truths are onefold in that they are unfailing or to be fully understood; twofold as mundane and supramundane, and as conditioned and unconditioned; threefold as to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation, as not to be abandoned, and as neither to be abandoned nor not to be abandoned; and fourfold by way of the divisions of full understanding and so on. Thus, the analysis here should be understood by way of these 'onefold and so on' classifications.

‘Sabhāgavisabhāgato’ti sabbāneva ca saccāni aññamaññaṃ sabhāgāni avitathato attasuññato dukkarapaṭivedhato ca. Yathāha –

‘By way of similarity and dissimilarity’: all the truths are similar to one another by way of being unfailing, by way of being empty of self, and by way of difficult realization. As it is said:

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, ānanda, katamaṃ nu kho dukkarataraṃ vā durabhisambhavataraṃ vā – yo dūratova sukhumena tālacchiggaḷena asanaṃ atipāteyya poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ avirādhitaṃ, yo vā sattadhā [M 0.0087] bhinnassa vālassa koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭivijjheyyā”ti? “Etadeva, bhante, dukkaratarañceva durabhisambhavatarañca – yo sattadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭivijjheyyā”ti. “Tato kho te, ānanda, duppaṭivijjhataraṃ paṭivijjhanti ye idaṃ dukkhanti yathābhūtaṃ paṭivijjhanti…pe… ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti yathābhūtaṃ paṭivijjhantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1115).

“What do you think, Ānanda, which is more difficult and harder to accomplish: to shoot arrows from afar through a tiny keyhole, point after point without missing, or to pierce the tip of a hair split sevenfold with another tip?” “This, venerable sir, is more difficult and harder to accomplish—to pierce the tip of a hair split sevenfold with another tip.” “Ānanda, those who penetrate as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ [...] ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’—they penetrate something even harder to penetrate than that.” (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1115)

Visabhāgāni salakkhaṇavavatthānato. Purimāni ca dve sabhāgāni duravagāhatthena gambhīrattā lokiyattā sāsavattā ca, visabhāgāni phalahetubhedato [P 0.0093] pariññeyyappahātabbato ca. Pacchimānipi dve sabhāgāni gambhīratthena duravagāhattā lokuttarattā anāsavattā ca, visabhāgāni visayavisayībhedato sacchikātabbabhāvetabbato ca. Paṭhamatatiyāni cāpi sabhāgāni phalāpadesato, visabhāgāni saṅkhatāsaṅkhatato. Dutiyacatutthāni cāpi sabhāgāni hetuapadesato, visabhāgāni ekantakusalākusalato. Paṭhamacatutthāni cāpi sabhāgāni saṅkhatato, visabhāgāni lokiyalokuttarato. Dutiyatatiyāni cāpi sabhāgāni nevasekkhānāsekkhabhāvato, visabhāgāni sārammaṇānārammaṇato.

They are dissimilar by way of the defining of individual characteristics. The first two are similar by way of their depth, by way of being difficult to fathom, by way of their mundane nature, and by way of their being with effluents; but they are dissimilar by way of the distinction between fruit and cause, and by way of what is to be fully understood and what is to be abandoned. The latter two are also similar by way of their depth, by way of being difficult to fathom, by way of their supramundane nature, and by way of their being without effluents; but they are dissimilar by way of the distinction between object and subject, and by way of what is to be directly experienced and what is to be developed. The first and third are also similar by way of being designated as fruits, but dissimilar by way of being conditioned and unconditioned. The second and fourth are also similar by way of being designated as causes, but dissimilar by way of being exclusively wholesome and unwholesome. The first and fourth are also similar by way of being conditioned, but dissimilar by way of being mundane and supramundane. The second and third are also similar by way of being neither a trainee nor a non-trainee, but dissimilar by way of having an object and being without an object.

Iti evaṃ pakārehi, nayehi ca vicakkhaṇo;

Vijaññā ariyasaccānaṃ, sabhāgavisabhāgatanti.

Thus, by such kinds and methods, the wise one should discern the similarities and dissimilarities of the Noble Truths.

Suttantabhājanīyauddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the Suttanta analysis is finished.

1. Dukkhasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of Suffering

Jātiniddeso

Exposition on Birth

190. Idāni [V 0.0087] saṅkhepato uddiṭṭhāni dukkhādīni vibhajitvā dassetuṃ ayaṃ tattha katamaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ jātipi dukkhāti niddesavāro āraddho. Tattha jāti veditabbā, jātiyā dukkhaṭṭho veditabbo; jarā, maraṇaṃ, soko[M 0.0088], paridevo, dukkhaṃ, domanassaṃ, upāyāso, appiyasampayogo, piyavippayogo veditabbo; appiyasampayogassa piyavippayogassa dukkhaṭṭho veditabbo; icchā veditabbā, icchāya dukkhaṭṭho veditabbo; khandhā veditabbā, khandhānaṃ dukkhaṭṭho veditabbo.

190. Now, to explain in detail what has been stated concisely—namely, suffering and so on—this section of exposition on “what, therein, is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Birth is suffering” is begun. Herein, birth should be understood, and the nature of suffering in birth should be understood. Aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, despair, association with the disliked, and separation from the liked—these should be understood. The nature of suffering in association with the disliked and separation from the liked should be understood. Desire should be understood, and the nature of suffering in desire should be understood. The aggregates should be understood, and the nature of suffering in the aggregates should be understood.

Tattha dukkhassa ariyasaccassa kathanatthāya ayaṃ mātikā – idañhi dukkhaṃ nāma anekaṃ nānappakāraṃ, seyyathidaṃ – dukkhadukkhaṃ, vipariṇāmadukkhaṃ, saṅkhāradukkhaṃ, paṭicchannadukkhaṃ, appaṭicchannadukkhaṃ, pariyāyadukkhaṃ, nippariyāyadukkhanti.

Here, for the exposition of the Noble Truth of Suffering, this is the outline: Suffering, indeed, is manifold and of various kinds, that is to say: suffering as pain, suffering due to change, suffering due to formations, hidden suffering, unhidden suffering, suffering by way of implication, and suffering without implication.

Tattha kāyikacetasikā dukkhavedanā sabhāvato ca nāmato ca dukkhattā ‘dukkhadukkhaṃ’ nāma. Sukhavedanā vipariṇāmena dukkhuppattihetuto ‘vipariṇāmadukkhaṃ’ nāma. Upekkhāvedanā ceva avasesā ca tebhūmakā saṅkhārā udayabbayapīḷitattā ‘saṅkhāradukkhaṃ’ nāma. Tathā pīḷanaṃ pana maggaphalānampi atthi. Tasmā ete dhammā dukkhasaccapariyāpannattena saṅkhāradukkhaṃ nāmāti veditabbā. Kaṇṇasūladantasūlarāgajapariḷāhadosajapariḷāhādi kāyikacetasiko ābādho pucchitvā jānitabbato [P 0.0094] upakkamassa ca apākaṭabhāvato ‘paṭicchannadukkhaṃ’ nāma, apākaṭadukkhantipi vuccati. Dvattiṃsakammakāraṇādisamuṭṭhāno ābādho apucchitvāva jānitabbato upakkamassa ca pākaṭabhāvato ‘appaṭicchannadukkhaṃ’ nāma, pākaṭadukkhantipi vuccati. Ṭhapetvā dukkhadukkhaṃ sesaṃ dukkhasaccavibhaṅge āgataṃ jātiādi sabbampi tassa tassa dukkhassa vatthubhāvato ‘pariyāyadukkhaṃ’ nāma. Dukkhadukkhaṃ ‘nippariyāyadukkhaṃ’ nāma.

Here, bodily and mental painful feelings are called “suffering as pain” because they are suffering by nature and by name. Pleasant feelings are called “suffering due to change” because they are the cause for the arising of suffering when they change. Neutral feelings and all the remaining formations of the three realms are called “suffering of formations” because they are oppressed by arising and passing away. Such oppression, however, exists even for the path and fruition. Therefore, these phenomena should be understood as “suffering of formations” because they are included in the Truth of Suffering. Bodily and mental ailments, such as earaches, toothaches, the burning of lust, the burning of hatred, etc., are called “concealed suffering” because they must be inquired about to be known and because their commencement is not evident; they are also called “unmanifest suffering.” Ailments arising from the thirty-two kinds of penal actions, etc., are called “unconcealed suffering” because they can be known without inquiry and because their commencement is evident; they are also called “manifest suffering.” Except for suffering as pain, all the rest—such as birth, etc., mentioned in the analysis of the Truth of Suffering—are called “suffering by implication” because they serve as the basis for that particular kind of suffering. Suffering as pain is called “suffering without implication.”

Tattha pariyāyadukkhaṃ nippariyāyadukkhanti imasmiṃ padadvaye ṭhatvā dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ kathetabbaṃ. Ariyasaccañca nāmetaṃ pāḷiyaṃ saṅkhepatopi āgacchati vitthāratopi. Saṅkhepato āgataṭṭhāne saṅkhepenapi vitthārenapi kathetuṃ vaṭṭati[V 0.0088]. Vitthārato āgataṭṭhāne pana vitthāreneva kathetuṃ vaṭṭati, na saṅkhepena. Taṃ idaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne vitthārena āgatanti vitthāreneva kathetabbaṃ. Tasmā yaṃ taṃ niddesavāre “tattha katamaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ? Jātipi dukkhā”tiādīni padāni gahetvā “jāti veditabbā, jātiyā dukkhaṭṭho veditabbo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha jātiādīni tāva “tattha katamā jāti? Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamhi tamhi sattanikāye jāti sañjātī”ti imassa pana padabhājanīyassa vasena veditabbāni.

Here, having established these two terms—suffering by implication and suffering without implication—the Noble Truth of Suffering should be explained. And this Noble Truth occurs in the Pāli texts both in brief and in detail. Where it occurs briefly, it is suitable to explain it both concisely and elaborately. But where it occurs in detail, it is suitable to explain it only in detail, not concisely. Since it occurs in detail in this place, it must be explained in detail. Therefore, in the section of exposition, taking the phrases such as, “Therein, what is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Birth is suffering,” and so on, it is said, “Birth should be understood, the nature of suffering in birth should be understood,” and so forth. There, first, birth and the like should be understood according to the analysis of the phrase: “Therein, what is birth? It is the birth, the coming-to-be, of those various beings in those various classes of beings.”

191. Tatrāyaṃ [M 0.0089] atthavaṇṇanā – tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānanti ayaṃ saṅkhepato anekesaṃ sattānaṃ sādhāraṇaniddeso. Yā devadattassa jāti, yā somadattassa jātīti evañhi divasampi kathiyamāne neva sattā pariyādānaṃ gacchanti, na sabbaṃ aparatthadīpanaṃ sijjhati. Imehi pana dvīhi padehi na koci satto apariyādinno hoti, na kiñci aparatthadīpanaṃ na sijjhati. Tena vuttaṃ – “yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattāna”nti. Tamhi tamhīti ayaṃ jātigativasena anekesaṃ sattanikāyānaṃ sādhāraṇaniddeso. Sattanikāyeti sattānaṃ nikāye, sattaghaṭāyaṃ sattasamūheti attho.

191. Herein, this is the explanation of the meaning: "Of those various beings"—this is a brief common description for many beings. For if one were to say all day, "the birth of Devadatta, the birth of Somadatta," neither would all beings be exhausted, nor would complete clarification be achieved. But with these two terms, no being is left out, and nothing remains unclarified. Therefore, it is said: "Of those various beings." "In those various"—this is a common description for many classes of beings, based on birth and destiny. "Classes of beings" means a collection of beings, a mass of beings, an assembly of beings—this is the meaning.

Jātīti ayaṃ jātisaddo anekattho.
