Tathā hesa “ekampi jātiṃ, dvepi jātiyo”ti (pārā. 12; ma. ni. 2.257) ettha bhave āgato. “Atthi visākhe[P 0.0095], nigaṇṭhā nāma samaṇajātikā”ti (a. ni. 3.71) ettha nikāye. “Tiriyā nāma tiṇajāti nābhiyā uggantvā nabhaṃ āhacca ṭhitā ahosī”ti (a. ni. 5.196) ettha paññattiyaṃ. “Jāti dvīhi khandhehi saṅgahitā”ti (dhātu. 71) ettha saṅkhatalakkhaṇe. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave, mātukucchimhi paṭhamaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ, paṭhamaṃ viññāṇaṃ pātubhūtaṃ, tadupādāya sāvassa jātī”ti (mahāva. 124) ettha paṭisandhiyaṃ. “Sampatijāto, ānanda, bodhisatto”ti (ma. ni. 3.207) ettha pasūtiyaṃ. “Anupakkuṭṭho jātivādenā”ti (dī. ni. 1.331) ettha kule. “Yatohaṃ, bhagini, ariyāya jātiyā jāto”ti (ma. ni. 2.351) ettha ariyasīle. Idha panāyaṃ savikāresu paṭhamābhinibbattakkhandhesu vattati. Tasmā jāyamānakavasena jātīti idamettha sabhāvapaccattaṃ. Sañjāyanavasena sañjātīti upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Okkamanavasena okkanti. Jāyanaṭṭhena vā jāti, sā aparipuṇṇāyatanavasena yuttā. Sañjāyanaṭṭhena sañjāti, sā paripuṇṇāyatanavasena yuttā. Okkamanaṭṭhena okkanti, sā aṇḍajajalābujavasena yuttā. Te hi aṇḍakosañca vatthikosañca [V 0.0089] okkamanti, okkamantāpi pavisantā viya paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhanti. Abhinibbattanaṭṭhena abhinibbatti. Sā saṃsedajaopapātikavasena yuttā. Te hi pākaṭā eva hutvā nibbattanti. Ayaṃ tāva sammutikathā.

The term "jāti" has multiple meanings. For example, in the phrase "one birth, two births," it refers to existence. In the phrase "There are, Visākha, ascetics called Nigaṇṭhas belonging to the samaṇa class," it refers to a sect. In the phrase "A blade of grass named Tiriyā, having sprung from the navel, stood reaching the sky," it denotes a designation. In the phrase "Birth is included in two aggregates," it signifies the characteristic of the conditioned. In the phrase "Monks, the first mind arisen in the mother’s womb, the first consciousness that appeared—that is the birth of a being," it refers to rebirth-linking. In the phrase "The Bodhisatta was just born, Ānanda," it denotes delivery. In the phrase "Not reviled by accusations of birth," it refers to lineage. In the phrase "Sister, since I was born into the noble birth," it signifies noble virtue. Here, however, it refers to the first manifestation of the aggregates subject to change. Therefore, 'jāti' (birth), in the sense of being born, is here its own specific nature. 'Sañjāti' (coming-to-birth), in the sense of coming into being, is the term augmented by a prefix. 'Okkanti' (descent), in the sense of descending. Or, 'jāti' (birth) in the sense of being born, is appropriate for incomplete sense bases. 'Sañjāti' (coming-to-birth) in the sense of coming into being, is appropriate for complete sense bases. 'Okkanti' (descent) in the sense of descending, is appropriate for the egg-born and womb-born. For they descend into the egg-sac and the womb-sac, and even as they descend, they take rebirth-linking as if entering. 'Abhinibbatti' (production) in the sense of being produced. This is appropriate for the moisture-born and spontaneously-born. For they are produced by becoming manifest. This, for now, is the conventional explanation.

Idāni [M 0.0090] paramatthakathā hoti. Khandhā eva hi paramatthato pātubhavanti, na sattā. Tattha ca khandhānanti ekavokārabhave ekassa, catuvokārabhave catunnaṃ, pañcavokārabhave pañcannaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Pātubhāvoti uppatti. Āyatanānanti ettha tatra tatra uppajjamānāyatanavasena saṅgaho veditabbo. Paṭilābhoti santatiyaṃ pātubhāvoyeva; pātubhavantāneva hi tāni paṭiladdhāni nāma honti. Ayaṃ vuccati jātīti ayaṃ jāti nāma kathiyati. Sā panesā tattha tattha bhave paṭhamābhinibbattilakkhaṇā, nīyyātanarasā, atītabhavato idha ummujjanapaccupaṭṭhānā, phalavasena dukkhavicittatāpaccupaṭṭhānā vā.

Now comes the ultimate explanation. Indeed, the aggregates alone manifest in the ultimate sense, not beings. Here, regarding 'aggregates,' in a one-constituent existence, one is taken; in a four-constituent existence, four are taken; in a five-constituent existence, five are to be understood. 'Manifestation' means arising. Regarding 'sense bases,' here, the inclusion should be understood according to the sense bases arising in various places. 'Acquisition' is simply manifestation in continuity; for those that are manifesting are called 'acquired.' This is called birth—this is what is spoken of as birth. Moreover, this birth has the characteristic of initial production in each existence, the function of issuing forth, the manifestation of emerging here from a past existence, or the manifestation of the variegated nature of suffering as its result.

Idāni ‘jātiyā dukkhaṭṭho veditabbo’ti ayañhi jāti sayaṃ na dukkhā, dukkhuppattiyā pana vatthubhāvena dukkhāti [P 0.0096] vuttā. Kataradukkhassa panāyaṃ vatthūti? Yaṃ taṃ bālapaṇḍitasuttādīsu (ma. ni. 3.246 ādayo) bhagavatāpi upamāvasena pakāsitaṃ āpāyikaṃdukkhaṃ, yañca sugatiyaṃ manussaloke gabbhokkantimūlakādibhedaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjati, tassa sabbassāpi esā vatthu. Tatridaṃ gabbhokkantimūlakādibhedaṃ dukkhaṃ – ayañhi satto mātukucchimhi nibbattamāno na uppalapadumapuṇḍarīkādīsu nibbattati. Atha kho heṭṭhā āmāsayassa upari pakkāsayassa udarapaṭalapiṭṭhikaṇḍakānaṃ vemajjhe paramasambādhe tibbandhakāre nānākuṇapagandhaparibhāvite asuciparamaduggandhapavanavicarite adhimattajegucche kucchippadese pūtimacchapūtikummāsacandanikādīsu kimi viya nibbattati. So tattha nibbatto dasa māse mātukucchisambhavena usmanā puṭapākaṃ viya paccamāno piṭṭhapiṇḍi viya sediyamāno samiñjanapasāraṇādirahito adhimattaṃ dukkhaṃ paccanubhotīti. Idaṃ tāva ‘gabbhokkantimūlakaṃ’ dukkhaṃ.

Now, the meaning of suffering in relation to birth should be understood thus: birth itself is not suffering, but it is said to be suffering because it is the basis for the arising of suffering. Of what suffering, then, is it the basis? It is the suffering in the lower realms, which the Blessed One has revealed by way of simile in the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta and other texts, and the suffering that arises in the happy destinations, in the human world, differentiated as rooted in conception in the womb and so on. Of all this, birth is the basis. Here is the suffering differentiated as rooted in conception in the womb and so on: indeed, this being, when being produced in the mother’s womb, is not produced in blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses. Rather, he is produced in the middle of the extremely cramped, pitch-dark space below the stomach and above the intestines, between the abdominal wall and the spinal column, pervaded by the foul stench of various corpses, permeated by the most impure and extremely disgusting air, in an excessively repugnant place, in the uterine region, like a worm in putrid fish, rotten gruel, and cesspools. Having been produced there, for ten months he is cooked by the heat originating from the mother's womb like something in a crucible, steamed like a lump of dough, unable to contract or stretch, and experiences extreme suffering. This, then, is the suffering ‘rooted in conception in the womb’.

Yaṃ pana so mātu sahasā upakkhalanagamananisīdanauṭṭhānaparivattanādīsu surādhuttahatthagato eḷako viya ahiguṇṭhikahatthagato sappapotako viya ca ākaḍḍhanaparikaḍḍhanaodhunananiddhunanādinā upakkamena adhimattaṃ dukkhamanubhavati, yañca mātu sītudakapānakāle sītanarakūpapanno [V 0.0090] viya, uṇhayāgubhattādiajjhoharaṇakāle aṅgāravuṭṭhisamparikiṇṇo viya, loṇambilādiajjhoharaṇakāle khārāpaṭicchakādikammakāraṇappatto viya tibbaṃ dukkhamanubhoti – idaṃ ‘gabbhapariharaṇamūlakaṃ’ dukkhaṃ.

Moreover, when the mother suddenly stumbles, walks, sits, rises, or turns, he experiences extreme suffering through the process of being dragged towards, dragged about, shaken down, and shaken off, like a lamb in the hands of a drunkard or like a young snake in the grasp of a snake charmer. And when the mother drinks cold water, it is as if he has fallen into a cold hell-pit; when she consumes hot gruel, food, and so on, it is as if he is surrounded by a rain of embers; when she consumes salty, sour food, and so on, he suffers intensely as if subjected to the application of caustic substances and other such treatments. This is the suffering ‘rooted in enduring the womb’.

Yaṃ [M 0.0091] panassa mūḷhagabbhāya mātuyā mittāmaccasuhajjādīhipi adassanārahe dukkhuppattiṭṭhāne chedanaphālanādīhi dukkhaṃ uppajjati – idaṃ ‘gabbhavipattimūlakaṃ’ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ vijāyamānāya mātuyā kammajehi vātehi parivattetvā narakapapātaṃ viya atibhayānakaṃ yonimaggaṃ paṭipātiyamānassa [P 0.0097] paramasambādhena yonimukhena tāḷacchiggaḷena viya nikkaḍḍhiyamānassa mahānāgassa narakasattassa viya ca saṅghāṭapabbatehi vicuṇṇiyamānassa dukkhaṃ uppajjati – idaṃ ‘vijāyanamūlakaṃ’ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ pana jātassa taruṇavaṇasadisassa sukumārasarīrassa hatthaggahaṇanhāpanadhovanacoḷaparimajjanādikāle sūcimukhakhuradhāravijjhanaphālanasadisaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjati – idaṃ mātukucchito ‘bahi nikkhamanamūlakaṃ’ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ tato paraṃ pavattiyaṃ attanāva attānaṃ vadhantassa, acelakavatādivasena ātāpanaparitāpanānuyogamanuyuttassa, kodhavasena abhuñjantassa, ubbandhantassa ca dukkhaṃ hoti – idaṃ ‘attūpakkamamūlakaṃ’ dukkhaṃ.

The suffering that arises when the mother has a difficult pregnancy, from cutting, splitting, and so on in a place where suffering arises, unsuitable for being seen even by friends, ministers, and companions—this is the suffering ‘rooted in calamity in the womb’. The suffering that arises when the mother is giving birth, as the fetus is turned by winds born of kamma and made to enter the extremely terrifying birth canal as if falling into a hellish abyss, and is dragged out through the extremely narrow opening of the womb as if through a keyhole, like a great elephant or a being in hell being crushed by the clashing mountains—this is the suffering ‘rooted in giving birth’. The suffering that arises after birth, when the tender body, delicate as a fresh wound, is handled, bathed, washed, and wiped with a cloth, causing pain like being pierced by needle points or cut by razor blades—this is the suffering ‘rooted in emergence from the mother’s womb’. The suffering that arises thereafter, when one harms oneself, engages in the practice of austerity and mortification such as the vow of nakedness, refuses to eat due to anger, or hangs oneself—this is the suffering ‘rooted in self-inflicted action’.

Yaṃ pana parato vadhabandhanādīni anubhavantassa dukkhaṃ uppajjati – idaṃ ‘parūpakkamamūlakaṃ’ dukkhanti. Iti imassa sabbassāpi dukkhassa ayaṃ jāti vatthumeva hotīti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Whatever suffering arises for one experiencing killing, imprisonment, and so on at the hands of others—this is the suffering ‘rooted in external agency’. Thus, for all this suffering, this birth is indeed the foundation. Therefore, it is said:

Jāyetha no ce narakesu satto,

Tatthaggidāhādikamappasayhaṃ;

Labhetha dukkhaṃ nu kuhiṃ patiṭṭhaṃ,

Iccāha dukkhāti munīdha jāti.

If no being were born in hells,

There would be no unbearable burning by fire and so on;

Where then would suffering find a foothold?

Thus the Sage here declares birth itself to be suffering.

Dukkhaṃ tiracchesu kasāpatoda-

Daṇḍābhighātādibhavaṃ anekaṃ;

Yaṃ [V 0.0091] taṃ kathaṃ tattha bhaveyya jātiṃ,

Vinā tahiṃ jāti tatopi dukkhā.

The manifold suffering in the animal realm—from whips, goads, beatings, and so on—

How could that arise there without birth?

Therefore, birth there too is suffering.

Petesu dukkhaṃ pana khuppipāsā-

Vātātapādippabhavaṃ vicittaṃ;

Yasmā ajātassa na tattha atthi,

Tasmāpi dukkhaṃ muni jātimāha.

But the varied suffering among the hungry ghosts—arising from hunger, thirst, wind, heat, and so on—

Since for the unborn, that does not exist there,

Therefore, the Sage declares birth to be suffering.

Tibbandhakāre [M 0.0092] ca asayhasīte,

Lokantare yaṃ asuresu dukkhaṃ;

Na taṃ bhave tattha na cassa jāti,

Yato ayaṃ jāti tatopi dukkhā.

And the suffering among the asuras in the Lokantarika hell,

In the thick darkness and unbearable cold;

That would not exist there, were there no birth;

Therefore, this birth is suffering even there.

Yañcāpi [P 0.0098] gūthanarake viya mātugabbhe,

Satto vasaṃ ciramato bahi nikkhamanañca;

Pappoti dukkhamatighoramidampi natthi,

Jātiṃ vinā itipi jātirayañhi dukkhā.

And also the extremely terrible suffering that a being experiences,

dwelling long in the mother’s womb as if in a cesspool hell, and then emerging from it;

This too would not be obtained without birth.

Therefore, this birth is indeed suffering.

Kiṃ bhāsitena bahunā nanu yaṃ kuhiñci,

Atthīdha kiñcidapi dukkhamidaṃ kadāci;

Nevatthi jātivirahe yadato mahesī,

Dukkhāti sabbapaṭhamaṃ imamāha jātinti.

Why speak so much? Surely, whatever suffering exists here, even a little, at any time,

would never exist without birth.

Therefore, the Great Seer declared this birth to be suffering first of all.

Jarāniddeso

The Exposition of Old Age

192. Jarāniddese jarāti sabhāvapaccattaṃ. Jīraṇatāti ākāraniddeso. Khaṇḍiccantiādayo tayo kālātikkame kiccaniddesā. Pacchimā dve pakatiniddesā. Ayañhi jarāti iminā padena sabhāvato dīpitā, tenassā idaṃ sabhāvapaccattaṃ. Jīraṇatāti iminā ākārato[V 0.0092], tenassāyaṃ ākāraniddeso. Khaṇḍiccanti iminā kālātikkame dantanakhānaṃ khaṇḍitabhāvakaraṇakiccato. Pāliccanti iminā kesalomānaṃ palitabhāvakaraṇakiccato. Valittacatāti iminā maṃsaṃ milāpetvā tace valittabhāvakaraṇakiccato dīpitā. Tenassā ime khaṇḍiccanti ādayo tayo kālātikkame kiccaniddesā. Tehi imesaṃ vikārānaṃ dassanavasena pākaṭībhūtāti pākaṭajarā dassitā. Yatheva hi udakassa vā vātassa vā aggino vā tiṇarukkhādīnaṃ saṃsaggapalibhaggatāya vā jhāmatāya vā gatamaggo pākaṭo hoti, na ca so gatamaggo tāneva udakādīni, evameva jarāya dantādīsu khaṇḍiccādivasena gatamaggo pākaṭo, cakkhuṃ ummīletvāpi gayhati. Na ca khaṇḍiccādīneva jarā; na hi jarā cakkhuviññeyyā hoti.

192. In the exposition of old age, “old age” refers to its intrinsic characteristic. “The state of decay” is a description of its mode. “Brokenness,” and so forth, these three are functional descriptions in terms of the passage of time. The last two are descriptions of its intrinsic nature. For old age is here explained by this term as its intrinsic nature; hence this is its intrinsic characteristic. By “the state of decay” it is explained by its mode; hence this is its description by mode. By “brokenness” it is explained by its function of causing teeth and nails to break with the passage of time. By “graying” it is explained by its function of causing hair to become gray. By “wrinkled skin” it is explained by its function of causing the flesh to shrivel and the skin to become wrinkled. Thus, these three, “brokenness” and so forth, are functional descriptions in terms of the passage of time. Through the observation of these changes, manifest old age is shown. Just as the path taken by water, or wind, or fire—through the dissolution, breaking up, or scorching of grass, trees, and so forth—becomes manifest, yet that path taken is not the water, etc., themselves, in the same way, the path taken by old age—through brokenness, graying, and so forth—becomes manifest in teeth and other features, and is grasped even with eyes open. Yet brokenness and the like are not old age itself; for old age is not perceptible by the eye.

Āyuno [M 0.0093] saṃhāni indriyānaṃ paripākoti imehi pana padehi kālātikkameyeva abhibyattāya āyukkhayacakkhādiindriyaparipākasaṅkhātāya pakatiyā dīpitā. Tenassime pacchimā dve pakatiniddesāti veditabbā. Tattha yasmā jaraṃ pattassa āyu hāyati tasmā jarā “āyuno saṃhānī”ti phalūpacārena vuttā. Yasmā daharakāle suppasannāni sukhumampi [P 0.0099] attano visayaṃ sukheneva gaṇhanasamatthāni cakkhādīni indriyāni jaraṃ pattassa paripakkāni āluḷitāni avisadāni oḷārikampi attano visayaṃ gahetuṃ asamatthāni honti, tasmā “indriyānaṃ paripāko”ti phalūpacāreneva vuttā.

With the words “the decline of life and the ripening of the faculties,” its intrinsic nature—designated as the decline of life and the ripening of the eye and other faculties—is illustrated as being manifested through the passage of time. Therefore, these last two should be understood as descriptions of its intrinsic nature. Here, because the life of one who has reached old age dwindles, old age is called “the decline of life” by way of metaphorical designation based on the result. Because in youth the faculties—namely, the eye and the other faculties—are very clear and capable of easily grasping even subtle objects within their range, but when one reaches old age, they become ripened, disordered, indistinct, and incapable of grasping even coarse objects within their range, it is called “the ripening of the faculties” by way of metaphorical designation based on the result.

Sā panesā evaṃ niddiṭṭhā sabbāpi jarā pākaṭā paṭicchannāti duvidhā hoti. Tattha dantādīsu khaṇḍādibhāvadassanato rūpadhammesu jarā ‘pākaṭajarā’ nāma. Arūpadhammesu pana jarā tādisassa vikārassa adassanato ‘paṭicchannajarā’ nāma. Tattha yvāyaṃ khaṇḍādibhāvo dissati, so tādisānaṃ dantādīnaṃ suviññeyyattā vaṇṇoyeva. Taṃ cakkhunā disvā manodvārena cintetvā “ime dantā jarāya pahaṭā”ti jaraṃ jānāti, udakaṭṭhāne baddhāni gosiṅgādīni oloketvā heṭṭhā udakassa atthibhāvaṃ jānanaṃ viya. Puna avīci savīcīti evampi ayaṃ jarā duvidhā hoti. Tattha maṇikanakarajatapavāḷacandasūriyādīnaṃ mandadasakādīsu pāṇīnaṃ viya ca pupphaphalapallavādīsu apāṇīnaṃ viya ca antarantarā vaṇṇavisesādīnaṃ dubbiññeyyattā jarā ‘avīcijarā’ nāma, nirantarajarāti attho. Tato aññesu pana yathāvuttesu antarantarā vaṇṇavisesādīnaṃ suviññeyyattā jarā ‘savīcijarā’ nāma.

This old age, thus defined, is of two kinds: manifest and concealed. Herein, the old age in material phenomena, seen as the breaking of teeth and so forth, is called ‘manifest old age.’ But the old age in non-material phenomena, because such a change is not observed, is called ‘concealed old age.’ Here, the breaking and so forth that is seen, being easily cognizable in teeth and the like, is merely their appearance. Seeing it with the eye and reflecting through the mind-door, one knows old age: “These teeth are struck by old age,” just as one knows the presence of water below by observing cow horns and such tied at a watering place. Again, this old age is also of two kinds: continuous and intermittent. Herein, the old age in things like gems, gold, silver, coral, the moon, and the sun, as well as in living beings in the subtle decads of their bodies, and in non-living things like flowers, fruits, and leaves—where the subtle changes in color and other features are hard to discern—is called ‘continuous old age,’ meaning uninterrupted old age. But in other cases, as previously mentioned, where the changes in color and other features are easily discerned at intervals, the old age is called ‘intermittent old age.’

Tattha [V 0.0093] savīcijarā upādinnānupādinnakavasena evaṃ dīpetabbā – daharakumārakānañhi paṭhamameva khīradantā nāma uṭṭhahanti, na te thirā. Tesu pana patitesu puna dantā uṭṭhahanti. Te paṭhamameva setā honti, jarāvātena pana pahaṭakāle kāḷakā honti. Kesā pana paṭhamameva tambāpi honti kāḷakāpi setāpi. Chavi pana salohitikā hoti. Vaḍḍhantānaṃ vaḍḍhantānaṃ odātānaṃ odātabhāvo, kāḷakānaṃ kāḷakabhāvo paññāyati, jarāvātena pana pahaṭakāle vaḷiṃ gaṇhāti. Sabbampi sassaṃ vapitakāle setaṃ hoti, pacchā nīlaṃ, jarāvātena pana pahaṭakāle paṇḍukaṃ hoti. Ambaṅkurenāpi dīpetuṃ vaṭṭati eva. Ayaṃ vuccati jarāti ayaṃ [M 0.0094] jarā nāma kathiyati. Sā panesā [P 0.0100] khandhaparipākalakkhaṇā, maraṇūpanayanarasā, yobbanavināsapaccupaṭṭhānā.

Here, intermittent old age should be explained in terms of what is appropriated and unappropriated. In young children, the first teeth, called milk teeth, appear, but they are not firm. When these fall out, new teeth grow in. At first, they are white, but when struck by the wind of old age, they turn black. Hair, too, is initially reddish, black, or white. The skin, however, is ruddy. As they continue to grow, the whiteness of what is white and the blackness of what is black becomes apparent, but when struck by the wind of old age, the skin becomes wrinkled. All crops are white when sown, then turn green, and when struck by the wind of old age, they become yellow. This can also be illustrated with a mango sprout. This is called old age; this is what is designated as old age. It has the characteristic of the ripening of the aggregates, the function of bringing one near to death, and manifests as the destruction of youth.

‘Jarāya dukkhaṭṭho veditabbo’ti ettha pana ayampi sayaṃ na dukkhā, dukkhassa pana vatthubhāvena dukkhāti vuttā. Katarassa dukkhassa? Kāyadukkhassa ceva domanassadukkhassa ca. Jiṇṇassa hi attabhāvo jarasakaṭaṃ viya dubbalo hoti, ṭhātuṃ vā gantuṃ vā nisīdituṃ vā vāyamantassa balavaṃ kāyadukkhaṃ uppajjati; puttadāre yathāpure asallakkhente domanassaṃ uppajjati. Iti imesaṃ dvinnampi dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvena dukkhāti veditabbā. Apica –

Regarding the statement, 'Old age is to be understood in the sense of suffering,' old age itself is not suffering, but it is called suffering because it serves as a basis for suffering. For what suffering? For both bodily suffering and mental suffering. For the body of one who is old becomes weak like an old cart, and when one strives to stand, walk, or sit, intense bodily suffering arises; when their children and wife do not regard them as before, mental suffering arises. Thus, it should be understood as suffering by being the basis for both these kinds of suffering. Moreover—

Aṅgānaṃ sithilabhāvā, indriyānaṃ vikārato;

Yobbanassa vināsena, balassa upaghātato.

Because of the slackening of the limbs and the alteration of the faculties, the destruction of youth and the impairment of strength;

Vippavāsā satādīnaṃ, puttadārehi attano;

Apasādanīyato ceva, bhīyyo bālattapattiyā.

Because of the loss of memory and so forth, and separation from one's own children and wives; and because of being despised and attaining greater foolishness,

Pappoti dukkhaṃ yaṃ macco, kāyikaṃ mānasaṃ tathā;

Sabbametaṃ jarāhetu, yasmā tasmā jarā dukhāti.

The suffering, both physical and mental, that a mortal experiences—all this is due to old age; therefore, old age is suffering.

Maraṇaniddeso

The Exposition of Death

193. Maraṇaniddese cavanakavasena cuti; ekacatupañcakkhandhāya cutiyā sāmaññavacanametaṃ. Cavanatāti bhāvavacanena lakkhaṇanidassanaṃ. Bhedoti cutikhandhānaṃ bhaṅguppattiparidīpanaṃ[V 0.0094]. Antaradhānanti ghaṭassa viya bhinnassa bhinnānaṃ cutikhandhānaṃ yena kenaci pariyāyena ṭhānābhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Maccu maraṇanti maccusaṅkhātaṃ maraṇaṃ. Kālo nāma antako, tassa kiriyā kālakiriyā. Ettāvatā sammutiyā maraṇaṃ dīpitaṃ hoti.

193. In the exposition of death, 'cuti' is passing away in the sense of departure; this is a general term for the passing away of the one, four, or five aggregates. 'Cavanatā,' by way of the abstract noun, is the indication of the characteristic. 'Bheda' is the elucidation of the dissolution of the aggregates of passing away. 'Antaradhāna' is the elucidation of the disappearance of the broken aggregates of passing away, which, by any means, no longer have a place to stand, just like a broken pot. 'Maccu-maraṇa' is death designated as 'maccu.' 'Kāla' is the ender; his action is 'kālakiriyā.' Thus far, death is expounded conventionally.

Idāni paramatthena dīpetuṃ khandhānaṃ bhedotiādimāha. Paramatthena hi khandhāyeva bhijjanti, na satto nāma koci marati. Khandhesu pana bhijjamānesu satto marati bhinnesu matoti vohāro hoti. Ettha ca catupañcavokāravasena khandhānaṃ bhedo, ekavokāravasena kaḷevarassa nikkhepo; catuvokāravasena vā khandhānaṃ bhedo, sesadvayavasena [P 0.0101] kaḷevarassa [M 0.0095] nikkhepo veditabbo. Kasmā? Bhavadvayepi rūpakāyasaṅkhātassa kaḷevarassa sambhavato. Yasmā vā cātumahārājikādīsu khandhā bhijjanteva, na kiñci nikkhipati, tasmā tesaṃ vasena khandhānaṃ bhedo. Manussādīsu kaḷevarassa nikkhepo. Ettha ca kaḷevarassa nikkhepakaraṇato maraṇaṃ “kaḷevarassa nikkhepo”ti vuttaṃ.

Now, to expound it in the ultimate sense, he says, 'the breakup of the aggregates,' and so forth. For in the ultimate sense, only the aggregates disintegrate; no being called a 'person' dies. But when the aggregates are disintegrating, the usage 'a being dies' or 'having disintegrated, is dead' occurs. Here, the breakup of the aggregates is in terms of the four- or five-aggregate existences, and the discarding of the corpse is in terms of a single-aggregate existence. Alternatively, the breakup of the aggregates should be understood in terms of the four-aggregate existence, and the discarding of the corpse in terms of the remaining two. Why? Because in two kinds of existence, there is the occurrence of a corpse, which is designated as a material body. Or, because in the Cātumahārājika realms and so forth, the aggregates simply break up, and nothing is discarded, therefore, in their case, it is the breakup of the aggregates. In the case of humans and so forth, it is the discarding of the corpse. And here, because of the act of discarding the corpse, death is called 'the discarding of the corpse'.

Jīvitindriyassa upacchedoti iminā indriyabaddhasseva maraṇaṃ nāma hoti, anindriyabaddhassa maraṇaṃ nāma natthīti dasseti. ‘Sassaṃ mataṃ, rukkho mato’ti idaṃ pana vohāramattameva. Atthato pana evarūpāni vacanāni sassādīnaṃ khayavayabhāvameva dīpenti. Idaṃ vuccati maraṇanti idaṃ sabbampi maraṇaṃ nāma kathiyati.

By 'the cessation of the life faculty,' it is shown that death exists only for that which is bound by faculties; for that which is not bound by faculties, there is no such thing as death. 'The crop is dead, the tree is dead'—this, however, is merely conventional language. In reality, however, such expressions merely indicate the state of decay and dissolution of crops and so forth. 'This is called death'—all this is called death.

Apicettha khaṇikamaraṇaṃ, sammutimaraṇaṃ, samucchedamaraṇanti ayampi bhedo veditabbo. Tattha ‘khaṇikamaraṇaṃ’ nāma pavatte rūpārūpadhammānaṃ bhedo. ‘Tisso mato, phusso mato’ti idaṃ ‘sammutimaraṇaṃ’ nāma. Khīṇāsavassa appaṭisandhikā kālakiriyā ‘samucchedamaraṇaṃ’ nāma. Imasmiṃ panatthe sammutimaraṇaṃ adhippetaṃ. Jātikkhayamaraṇaṃ, upakkamamaraṇaṃ, sarasamaraṇaṃ, āyukkhayamaraṇaṃ, puññakkhayamaraṇantipi tasseva nāmaṃ. Tayidaṃ cutilakkhaṇaṃ, viyogarasaṃ, vippavāsapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

Moreover, here, momentary death, conventional death, and death by complete cessation—this distinction should also be understood. Among these, 'momentary death' is the dissolution of material and immaterial phenomena in their occurrence. 'Tissa has died, Phussa has died'—this is called 'conventional death.' The passing away of one whose taints are destroyed, without renewed existence, is called 'death by complete cessation.' In this context, however, conventional death is intended. Death by exhaustion of birth, death by an intervening cause, death by loss of vital essence, death by exhaustion of lifespan, and death by exhaustion of merit are also names for it. And this has vanishing as its characteristic, separation as its function, and appearing as estrangement.

‘Maraṇassa dukkhaṭṭho veditabbo’ti ettha pana idampi sayaṃ na dukkhaṃ, dukkhassa pana vatthubhāvena dukkhanti vuttaṃ. Maraṇantikāpi hi sārīrikā vedanā, paṭivāte gahitā ādittatiṇukkā [V 0.0095] viya, sarīraṃ nidahanti. Narakanimittādīnaṃ upaṭṭhānakāle balavadomanassaṃ uppajjati. Iti imesaṃ dvinnampi dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvena dukkhanti veditabbaṃ. Api ca –

Regarding the statement, 'The characteristic of suffering in death should be understood,' here, however, death itself is not suffering, but it is said to be suffering because it is the basis for suffering. For physical feelings at the point of death, like a burning grass torch caught in a strong wind, consume the body. When signs of hell and so forth appear, strong mental distress arises. Thus, it should be understood as suffering because it is the basis for both of these kinds of suffering. Moreover –

Pāpassa pāpakammādi, nimittamanupassato;

Bhaddassāpasahantassa, viyogaṃ piyavatthukaṃ.

For the evil-doer, seeing the sign of evil deeds and so forth; / For the virtuous one, unable to endure separation from beloved things.

Mīyamānassa [P 0.0102] yaṃ dukkhaṃ, mānasaṃ avisesato;

Sabbesañcāpi yaṃ sandhi-bandhanacchedanādikaṃ.

The mental suffering of one who is dying, without exception; / And for all, the severing of connections and bonds and so forth.

Vitujjamānamammānaṃ, hoti dukkhaṃ sarīrajaṃ;

Asayhamappaṭikāraṃ, dukkhassetassidaṃ yato;

Maraṇaṃ vatthu tenetaṃ, dukkhamicceva bhāsitanti.

When the vital parts are being pierced, bodily suffering arises; / Unbearable and without remedy. Since death is the basis of this suffering, / therefore it is declared to be suffering.

Apica [M 0.0096] imāni jātijarāmaraṇāni nāma imesaṃ sattānaṃ vadhakapaccāmittā viya otāraṃ gavesantāni vicaranti. Yathā hi purisassa tīsu paccāmittesu otārāpekkhesu vicarantesu eko vadeyya – “ahaṃ asukaaraññassa nāma vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā etaṃ ādāya tattha gamissāmi, ettha mayhaṃ dukkaraṃ natthī”ti. Dutiyo vadeyya “ahaṃ tava etaṃ gahetvā gatakāle pothetvā dubbalaṃ karissāmi, ettha mayhaṃ dukkaraṃ natthī”ti. Tatiyo vadeyya – “tayā etasmiṃ pothetvā dubbale kate tiṇhena asinā sīsacchedanaṃ nāma mayhaṃ bhāro hotū”ti. Te evaṃ vatvā tathā kareyyuṃ.

Moreover, these birth, aging, and death, like murderous enemies, roam about seeking an opening for these beings. Just as if, when three enemies were roaming about seeking an opening for a man, one might say, 'I will describe the beauty of a certain forest by name and take him there; there is nothing difficult for me in this.' The second might say, 'When you have taken him and gone, I will strike him and make him weak; there is nothing difficult for me in this.' The third might say, 'When he has been struck and made weak by you, let the severing of his head with a sharp sword be my task.' They would speak thus and act accordingly.

Tattha paṭhamapaccāmittassa araññassa vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā taṃ ādāya tattha gatakālo viya suhajjañātimaṇḍalato nikkaḍḍhitvā yattha katthaci nibbattāpanaṃ nāma jātiyā kiccaṃ. Dutiyassa pothetvā dubbalakaraṇaṃ viya nibbattakkhandhesu nipatitvā parādhīnamañcaparāyaṇabhāvakaraṇaṃ jarāya kiccaṃ. Tatiyassa tiṇhena asinā sīsacchedanaṃ viya jīvitakkhayapāpanaṃ maraṇassa kiccanti veditabbaṃ.

Here, the function of birth is to cause rebirth anywhere whatsoever, like the first enemy's act of describing the beauty of the forest and taking him there, dragging him away from the circle of friends and relatives. The function of aging is to cause one to become dependent on others and confined to a bed, like the second's act of striking and weakening, falling upon the arisen aggregates. The function of death is to bring about the destruction of life, like the third's act of severing the head with a sharp sword—this should be understood.

Apicettha jātidukkhaṃ sādīnavamahākantārappaveso viya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Jarādukkhaṃ tattha annapānarahitassa [V 0.0096] dubbalyaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Maraṇadukkhaṃ dubbalassa iriyāpathapavattane vihataparakkamassa vāḷādīhi anayabyasanāpādanaṃ viya daṭṭhabbanti.

Moreover, here, the suffering of birth should be seen as like entering a great, perilous wilderness. The suffering of aging should be seen as like the frailty of one lacking food and drink in that wilderness. The suffering of death should be seen as like the disaster and misfortune caused by wild animals and so forth to a weakened man whose effort is destroyed in the performance of postures—this should be understood.

Sokaniddeso

Exposition of Sorrow

194. Sokaniddese byasatīti byasanaṃ; hitasukhaṃ khipati viddhaṃsetīti attho. Ñātīnaṃ byasanaṃ ñātibyasanaṃ; corarogabhayādīhi ñātikkhayo ñātivināsoti attho. Tena ñātibyasanena phuṭṭhassāti [P 0.0103] ajjhotthaṭassa abhibhūtassa samannāgatassāti attho. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – bhogānaṃ byasanaṃ bhogabyasanaṃ; rājacorādivasena bhogakkhayo bhogavināsoti attho. Rogoyeva byasanaṃ rogabyasanaṃ; rogo hi ārogyaṃ byasati vināsetīti byasanaṃ. Sīlassa byasanaṃ sīlabyasanaṃ; dussīlyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Sammādiṭṭhiṃ vināsayamānā uppannā diṭṭhiyeva byasanaṃ diṭṭhibyasanaṃ. Ettha ca purimāni dve anipphannāni, pacchimāni tīṇi nipphannāni tilakkhaṇabbhāhatāni. Purimāni ca tīṇi neva kusalāni na akusalāni. Sīladiṭṭhibyasanadvayaṃ akusalaṃ.

194. In the exposition on sorrow, ‘byasana’ means ruin, because it ruins; the meaning is that it casts away and destroys well-being and happiness. The ruin of relatives, ñātibyasana, is the destruction or loss of kin due to thieves, disease, fear, and the like. ‘Afflicted by the ruin of relatives’ means overcome, overwhelmed, and possessed by it. The same principle applies to the rest. Here, however, is a distinction: the ruin of wealth, bhogabyasana, is the destruction or loss of wealth due to kings, thieves, and the like. Disease itself is ruin, rogabyasana, for disease ruins, that is, destroys health, hence it is ‘ruin.’ The ruin of virtue, sīlabyasana, is a name for immorality. A view that arises destroying right view is itself the ruin of views, diṭṭhibyasana. Here, the first two are not produced phenomena, while the last three are produced phenomena struck by the three characteristics. The first three are neither wholesome nor unwholesome; the two kinds of ruin, of virtue and of view, are unwholesome.

Aññataraññatarenāti [M 0.0097] gahitesu vā yena kenaci aggahitesu vā mittāmaccabyasanādīsu yena kenaci. Samannāgatassāti samanubandhassa aparimuccamānassa. Aññataraññatarena dukkhadhammenāti yena kenaci sokadukkhassa uppattihetunā. Sokoti socanakavasena soko; idaṃ tehi kāraṇehi upajjanakasokassa sabhāvapaccattaṃ. Socanāti socanākaro. Socitattanti socitabhāvo. Antosokoti abbhantare soko. Dutiyapadaṃ upasaggavasena vaḍḍhitaṃ. So hi abbhantare sukkhāpento viya parisukkhāpento viya uppajjatīti “antosoko antoparisoko”ti vuccati.

‘By any one or another’ means by any one or another of the misfortunes of friends, ministers, and so forth, whether they have been taken to heart or not. ‘Possessed’ means followed closely and not being released from. ‘By any kind of suffering’ refers to any cause for the arising of sorrow and suffering. ‘Sorrow’ (soko) is so called on account of lamenting; this is the inherent individual characteristic of the sorrow that arises from those causes. ‘Lamentation’ (socanā) is the act of lamenting. ‘State of being sorrowful’ (socitattaṃ) is the state of having sorrow. ‘Internal sorrow’ (antosoko) is sorrow within. The second term is intensified by way of a prefix. For it arises within, as if drying one up or completely drying one up, hence it is called ‘internal sorrow, inner despair’ (antosoko antoparisoko).

Cetaso parijjhāyanāti cittassa jhāyanākāro. Soko hi uppajjamāno aggi viya cittaṃ jhāpeti paridahati, “cittaṃ me jhāmaṃ, na me kiñci paṭibhātī”ti vadāpeti. Dukkhito mano dummano, tassa bhāvo domanassaṃ. Anupaviṭṭhaṭṭhena sokova sallanti sokasallaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati sokoti ayaṃ soko nāma kathiyati. So panāyaṃ kiñcāpi atthato domanassavedanāva [V 0.0097] hoti, evaṃ [P 0.0104] santepi antonijjhānalakkhaṇo, cetaso parinijjhāyanaraso, anusocanapaccupaṭṭhāno.

‘The consuming of the mind’ (cetaso parijjhāyana) means the mind’s manner of burning. For sorrow, when it arises, burns and consumes the mind like a fire, making one say, ‘My mind is burnt up, nothing occurs to me.’ A mind afflicted by suffering is a dejected mind; its state is dejection. Sorrow is a dart because it has entered deep within. This is called sorrow; this is how sorrow is designated. Although this is essentially a feeling of dejection, it is characterized by internal burning, its function is the complete burning of the mind, and it manifests as continued grieving.

‘Sokassa dukkhaṭṭho veditabbo’ti ettha pana ayaṃ sabhāvadukkhattā ceva dukkhassa ca vatthubhāvena dukkhoti vutto. Kataradukkhassāti? Kāyikadukkhassa ceva javanakkhaṇe ca domanassadukkhassa. Sokavegena hi hadaye mahāgaṇḍo uṭṭhahitvā paripaccitvā bhijjati, mukhato vā kāḷalohitaṃ nikkhamati, balavaṃ kāyadukkhaṃ uppajjati. “Ettakā me ñātayo khayaṃ gatā, ettakā me bhogā”ti cintentassa ca balavaṃ domanassaṃ uppajjati. Iti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvenapesa dukkhoti veditabbo. Apica –

‘Sorrow should be understood as having the characteristic of suffering.’ Here, it is said to be suffering both because of its inherent painful nature and because it is a basis for suffering. For which suffering? For both bodily suffering and the suffering of mental pain at the moment of impulsion. For by the force of sorrow, a great swelling arises in the heart, matures, and bursts, or black blood is expelled from the mouth, and intense bodily pain arises. And when one thinks, ‘So many of my relatives have perished, so many of my possessions are gone,’ intense mental pain arises. Thus, it should be understood that this is suffering because it is a basis for these two kinds of suffering. Moreover—

Sattānaṃ hadayaṃ soko, sallaṃ viya vitujjati;

Aggitattova nārāco, bhusañca ḍahate puna.

Sorrow, like a dart, pierces the heart of beings; like a fire-heated arrow, it burns intensely again.

Samāvahati ca byādhi-jarāmaraṇabhedanaṃ;

Dukkhampi vividhaṃ yasmā, tasmā dukkhoti vuccatīti.

And it brings about the breaking up by sickness, old age, and death; and because it is also various suffering, therefore it is called suffering.

Paridevaniddeso

The Exposition of Lamentation

195. Paridevaniddese [M 0.0098] ‘mayhaṃ dhītā, mayhaṃ putto’ti evaṃ ādissa ādissa devanti rodanti etenāti ādevo. Taṃ taṃ vaṇṇaṃ parikittetvā parikittetvā devanti etenāti paridevo. Tato parāni dve dve padāni purimadvayasseva ākārabhāvaniddesavasena vuttāni. Vācāti vacanaṃ. Palāpoti tucchaṃ niratthakavacanaṃ. Upaḍḍhabhaṇitaaññabhaṇitādivasena virūpo palāpo vippalāpo. Lālappoti punappunaṃ lapanaṃ. Lālappanākāro lālappanā. Lālappitassa bhāvo lālappitattaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati paridevoti ayaṃ paridevo nāma kathiyati. So lālappanalakkhaṇo, guṇadosaparikittanaraso, sambhamapaccupaṭṭhāno.

195. In the exposition of lamentation, they lament and weep by repeatedly pointing out, ‘My daughter! My son!’—by this is meant lamentation (ādevo). They lament by repeatedly extolling this or that quality—by this is meant lamentation (paridevo). The subsequent pairs of terms are stated by way of explaining the forms of the first two. Speech (vācā) is utterance. Idle talk (palāpo) is empty, meaningless speech. Incoherent babbling (vippalāpo) is distorted idle talk, such as half-spoken words, contradictory words, and so on. Rambling (lālappo) is repetitive speech. The manner of rambling is lālappanā. The state of one who rambles is lālappitattaṃ. This is called lamentation. It has the characteristic of rambling, the function of extolling virtues or faults, and is manifested as agitation.

‘Paridevassa dukkhaṭṭho veditabbo’ti ettha pana ayampi sayaṃ na dukkho, kāyadukkhadomanassadukkhānaṃ pana vatthubhāvena dukkhoti vutto. Paridevanto hi attano khandhaṃ muṭṭhīhi [V 0.0098] potheti, ubhohi hatthehi uraṃ paharati [P 0.0105] piṃsati, sīsena bhittiyā saddhiṃ yujjhati. Tenassa balavaṃ kāyadukkhaṃ uppajjati. ‘Ettakā me ñātayo khayaṃ vayaṃ abbhatthaṃ gatā’tiādīni cinteti. Tenassa balavaṃ domanassaṃ uppajjati. Iti imesaṃ dvinnampi dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvena dukkhoti veditabbo. Apica –

‘The meaning of suffering in lamentation is to be understood.’ Here, however, this itself is not suffering, but it is called suffering because it is the basis for bodily suffering and mental distress. For when lamenting, one strikes one’s own body with fists, beats and crushes one’s chest with both hands, and strikes one’s head against a wall. Thus, strong bodily suffering arises. Thinking, ‘So many of my relatives have gone to destruction, decay, and disappearance,’ strong mental distress arises. Thus, it should be understood as suffering because it is a basis for both these kinds of suffering. Furthermore—

Yaṃ sokasallavihato paridevamāno,

Kaṇṭhoṭṭhatālutalasosajamappasayhaṃ;

Bhiyyodhimattamadhigacchatiyeva dukkhaṃ,

Dukkhoti tena bhagavā paridevamāhāti.

Since one pierced by the dart of sorrow, while lamenting, experiences unbearable suffering from a parched throat, lips, and palate, and attains even more intense suffering, therefore the Blessed One declared lamentation to be suffering.

Dukkhadomanassaniddeso

The Exposition of Suffering and Mental Pain

196-7. Dukkhadomanassaniddesā heṭṭhā dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vaṇṇitattā pākaṭā eva. Lakkhaṇādīni pana tesaṃ tattha vuttāneva.

196-197. The expositions of suffering and mental pain are already clear, as they have been explained below in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī commentary. Their characteristics and so on are also stated there.

‘Dukkhassa dukkhaṭṭho veditabbo, domanassassa dukkhaṭṭho veditabbo’ti ettha pana ubhayampetaṃ sayañca dukkhattā kāyikacetasikadukkhānañca vatthubhāvena dukkhanti vuttaṃ. Hatthapādānañhi kaṇṇanāsikānañca chedanadukkhena dukkhitassa[M 0.0099], anāthasālāyaṃ ucchiṭṭhakapālaṃ purato katvā nipannassa, vaṇamukhehi puḷuvakesu nikkhamantesu balavaṃ kāyadukkhaṃ uppajjati; nānāraṅgarattavatthamanuññālaṅkāraṃ nakkhattaṃ kīḷantaṃ mahājanaṃ disvā balavadomanassaṃ uppajjati. Evaṃ tāva dukkhassa dvinnampi dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvo veditabbo. Apica –

‘The meaning of suffering in suffering is to be understood; the meaning of suffering in mental pain is to be understood.’ Here, both are called suffering because they are themselves suffering and are the basis for bodily and mental sufferings. For one afflicted by the suffering of having hands, feet, ears, or nose cut off; for one lying in a shelter for the destitute with a bowl for scraps before one, with worms emerging from the mouths of wounds, strong bodily suffering arises. Seeing a crowd enjoying a festival, adorned with various colorful clothes and pleasing ornaments, strong mental pain arises. Thus, physical suffering should be understood as the basis for both kinds of suffering. Furthermore—

Pīḷeti kāyikamidaṃ, dukkhaṃ dukkhañca mānasaṃ bhiyyo;

Janayati yasmā tasmā, dukkhanti visesato vuttanti.

Because this bodily suffering afflicts, and furthermore generates mental suffering, it is therefore specifically called suffering.

Cetodukkhasamappitā pana kese pakiriya urāni patipisenti, āvaṭṭanti, vivaṭṭanti, chinnapapātaṃ papatanti, satthaṃ āharanti, visaṃ khādanti, rajjuyā ubbandhanti, aggiṃ pavisanti[V 0.0099]. Taṃ taṃ viparītaṃ vatthuṃ tathā tathā vippaṭisārino pariḍayhamānacittā cintenti. Evaṃ domanassassa ubhinnampi dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvo veditabbo. Apica –

But those overwhelmed by mental suffering, disheveling their hair, beat their breasts, writhe about, collapse as if cut down, take up weapons, consume poison, hang themselves with ropes, or enter a fire. With minds burning with regret, they contemplate various perverse things in various ways. Thus, mental pain should be understood as the basis for both kinds of suffering. Furthermore—

Pīḷeti yato cittaṃ, kāyassa ca pīḷanaṃ samāvahati;

Dukkhanti domanassampi, domanassaṃ tato ahūti.

Because it afflicts the mind and brings affliction to the body, and because mental pain is suffering, it is therefore mental pain.

Upāyāsaniddeso

The Exposition of Distress

198. Upāyāsaniddese [P 0.0106] āyāsanaṭṭhena āyāso; saṃsīdanavisīdanākārappavattassa cittakilamathassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Balavaṃ āyāso upāyāso. Āyāsitabhāvo āyāsitattaṃ. Upāyāsitabhāvo upāyāsitattaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati upāyāsoti ayaṃ upāyāso nāma kathiyati. So panesa byāsattilakkhaṇo, nitthunanaraso, visādapaccupaṭṭhāno.

198. In the exposition of distress, āyāsa is in the sense of being distressed (āyāsanaṭṭhena); it is a name for the mental fatigue that arises in the manner of sinking and collapsing. Strong distress is upāyāsa. The state of being distressed is āyāsitatta. The state of being greatly distressed is upāyāsitatta. This is called upāyāsa; this is said to be upāyāsa. Now, this has entanglement as its characteristic, groaning as its function, and dejection as its manifestation.

‘Upāyāsassa dukkhaṭṭho veditabbo’ti ettha pana ayampi sayaṃ na dukkho, ubhinnampi dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvena dukkhoti vutto. Kupitena hi raññā issariyaṃ acchinditvā hataputtabhātikānaṃ āṇattavadhānaṃ bhayena aṭaviṃ pavisitvā nilīnānaṃ mahāvisādappattānaṃ dukkhaṭṭhānena dukkhaseyyāya dukkhanisajjāya balavaṃ kāyadukkhaṃ uppajjati. ‘Ettakā no ñātakā, ettakā bhogā naṭṭhā’ti cintentānaṃ balavadomanassaṃ uppajjati. Iti imesaṃ dvinnampi dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvena dukkhoti veditabboti. Apica –

‘The meaning of suffering in distress should be understood.’ Here, however, this itself is not suffering, but it is called suffering because it is the basis for both kinds of suffering. For those whose sons and brothers have been killed and whose execution has been ordered by an enraged king who has seized power, who have fled in fear into the forest and are in hiding, and who have fallen into great dejection, intense bodily suffering arises due to their painful condition, painful lying down, and painful sitting. Thinking, ‘So many of our relatives are lost, so much wealth is lost,’ intense mental anguish arises in them. Thus, it should be understood as suffering because it is the basis for both these kinds of suffering. Furthermore—

Cittassa [M 0.0100] paridahanā, kāyassa visādanā ca adhimattaṃ;

Yaṃ dukkhamupāyāso, janeti dukkho tato vutto.

Because distress generates that suffering which is the excessive burning of the mind and dejection of the body, it is therefore called suffering.

Ettha ca mandagginā antobhājaneyeva telādīnaṃ pāko viya soko. Tikkhagginā paccamānassa bhājanato bahinikkhamanaṃ viya paridevo. Bahinikkhantāvasesassa nikkhamitumpi appahontassa antobhājaneyeva yāva parikkhayā pāko viya upāyāso daṭṭhabbo.

Herein, sorrow (soka) is like the cooking of oil and so forth inside a pot with a slow fire. Lamentation (parideva) is like the boiling over from the pot of what is being cooked with a sharp fire. Distress (upāyāsa) should be seen as like the cooking of the remainder inside the pot—which is unable even to escape—until it is completely consumed.

Appiyasampayoganiddeso

Exposition of Association with the Unpleasant

199. Appiyasampayoganiddese [V 0.0100] yassāti ye assa. Aniṭṭhāti apariyesitā. Pariyesitā vā hontu apariyesitā vā, nāmamevetaṃ amanāpārammaṇānaṃ. Manasmiṃ na kamanti, na pavisantīti akantā. Manasmiṃ na appiyanti, na vā manaṃ vaḍḍhentīti amanāpā. Rūpātiādi tesaṃ sabhāvanidassanaṃ. Anatthaṃ kāmenti icchantīti anatthakāmā. Ahitaṃ kāmenti icchantīti ahitakāmā. Aphāsukaṃ dukkhavihāraṃ kāmenti icchantīti aphāsukakāmā. Catūhi [P 0.0107] yogehi khemaṃ nibbhayaṃ vivaṭṭaṃ na icchanti, sabhayaṃ vaṭṭameva nesaṃ kāmenti icchantīti āyogakkhemakāmā.

199. In the exposition on association with the unpleasant, 'yassā' (of whom) means 'ye assa' (whatever belongs to him/her). 'Aniṭṭhā' (undesirable) means 'apariyesitā' (not sought after). Whether sought after or not, this is simply a name for disagreeable objects. They do not please the mind, do not enter it—thus, they are 'akantā' (unpleasing). They do not delight the mind, nor do they increase the mind—thus, they are 'amanāpā' (disagreeable). 'Rūpātiādi' (form and so forth) is an illustration of their intrinsic nature. They desire harm, wish for it—thus, they are 'anatthakāmā' (wishing harm). They desire what is unbeneficial, wish for it—thus, they are 'ahitakāmā' (wishing what is unbeneficial). They desire discomfort, wish for a painful abiding—thus, they are 'aphāsukakāmā' (wishing discomfort). They do not desire security, fearlessness, or liberation from the four yokes; they only wish for the fearful round of existence—thus, they are 'āyogakkhemakāmā' (wishing for what is not security from the yokes).

Apica saddhādīnaṃ vuddhisaṅkhātassa atthassa akāmanato tesaṃyeva hānisaṅkhātassa anatthassa ca kāmanato anatthakāmā. Saddhādīnaṃyeva upāyabhūtassa hitassa akāmanato saddhāhāniādīnaṃ upāyabhūtassa ahitassa ca kāmanato ahitakāmā. Phāsukavihārassa akāmanato aphāsukavihārassa ca kāmanato aphāsukakāmā. Yassa kassaci nibbhayassa akāmanato bhayassa ca kāmanato ayogakkhemakāmāti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Furthermore, because they do not desire the benefit, which is the increase of faith and so forth, but desire the harm, which is the decrease of those very things, they are 'anatthakāmā' (wishing harm). Because they do not desire the beneficial, of which faith and so forth are the means, but desire the unbeneficial, of which the loss of faith and so forth are the means, they are 'ahitakāmā' (wishing what is unbeneficial). Because they do not desire an easeful abiding but desire an un-easeful abiding, they are 'aphāsukakāmā' (wishing discomfort). Because they do not desire fearlessness for anyone whatsoever, but desire fear, they are 'āyogakkhemakāmā' (wishing for what is not security from the yokes). Thus, the meaning here should be understood.

Saṅgatīti gantvā saṃyogo. Samāgamoti āgatehi saṃyogo. Samodhānanti ṭhānanisajjādīsu sahabhāvo. Missībhāvoti sabbakiccānaṃ sahakaraṇaṃ. Ayaṃ sattavasena yojanā. Saṅkhāravasena pana yaṃ labbhati taṃ gahetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ appiyasampayogo nāma kathiyati. So aniṭṭhasamodhānalakkhaṇo, cittavighātakaraṇaraso, anatthabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno.

'Saṅgati' (association) means going and uniting. 'Samāgama' (meeting) means uniting with those who have come. 'Samodhāna' (coexistence) means being together in standing, sitting, and so forth. 'Missībhāva' (mingling) means cooperating in all activities. This is the explanation in terms of beings. But in terms of formations, whatever is applicable should be taken. 'Ayaṃ vuccati' (this is called) means this 'appiyasampayoga' (association with the unpleasant) is so named. Its characteristic is coming together with the undesirable, its function is causing mental distress, and its manifestation is the state of harm.

So [M 0.0101] atthato eko dhammo nāma natthi. Kevalaṃ appiyasampayuttānaṃ duvidhassāpi dukkhassa vatthubhāvato dukkhoti vutto. Aniṭṭhāni hi vatthūni samodhānagatāni vijjhanachedanaphālanādīhi kāyikampi dukkhaṃ uppādenti, ubbegajananato mānasampi. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

In reality, this is not a single phenomenon by name. It is called 'suffering' simply because it is the basis for both kinds of suffering for those who are associated with the unpleasant. For undesirable things, when they come together, generate bodily suffering through piercing, cutting, splitting, and so forth, and also mental suffering by generating agitation. Therefore it is said:

Disvāva appiye dukkhaṃ, paṭhamaṃ hoti cetasi;

Tadupakkamasambhūta-matha kāye yato idha.

Upon seeing the unpleasant, suffering first arises in the mind; then, born from that instigation, it arises here in the body.

Tato [V 0.0101] dukkhadvayassāpi, vatthuto so mahesinā;

Dukkho vuttoti viññeyyo, appiyehi samāgamoti.

Therefore, it should be understood that association with the unpleasant has been declared 'suffering' by the Great Seer, as it is the basis for both kinds of suffering.

Piyavippayoganiddeso

The Exposition of Separation from the Beloved

200. Piyavippayoganiddeso vuttapaṭipakkhanayena veditabbo. Mātā vātiādi panettha atthakāme sarūpena dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha mamāyatīti mātā. Piyāyatīti [P 0.0108] pitā. Bhajatīti bhātā. Tathā bhaginī. Mettāyantīti mittā, minantīti vā mittā; sabbaguyhesu anto pakkhipantīti attho. Kiccakaraṇīyesu sahabhāvaṭṭhena amā hontīti amaccā. Ayaṃ amhākaṃ ajjhattikoti evaṃ jānanti ñāyantīti vā ñātī. Lohitena sambandhāti sālohitā. Evametāni padāni atthato veditabbāni. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ piyehi vippayogo nāma kathiyati. So iṭṭhavatthuviyogalakkhaṇo, sokuppādanaraso, byasanapaccupaṭṭhāno.

200. The exposition of separation from the beloved should be understood by the method of the opposite of what has been stated. Here, 'mother,' and so forth, is stated to show, in their own form, those who desire one's welfare. In this context, 'she regards as 'mine',' thus 'mother.' 'He holds one dear,' thus 'father.' 'He associates with one,' thus 'brother.' Similarly, 'sister.' 'They are friendly,' thus 'friends,' or 'they measure,' thus 'friends'; the meaning is they place one inside all secrets. 'They are together in the performance of duties,' thus 'ministers.' 'This is our own' — thus they know or are known, hence 'relatives.' 'Connected by blood,' thus 'blood relations.' In this way, these terms should be understood according to their meaning. 'This is called' means this is named 'separation from the beloved.' Its characteristic is separation from agreeable objects, its function is to produce sorrow, and its manifestation is misfortune.

So atthato eko dhammo nāma natthi. Kevalaṃ piyavippayuttānaṃ duvidhassāpi dukkhassa vatthubhāvato dukkhoti vutto. Iṭṭhāni hi vatthūni viyujjamānāni sarīrassa sosanamilāpanādibhāvena kāyikampi dukkhaṃ uppādenti, ‘yampi no ahosi, tampi no natthī’ti anusocāpanato mānasampi. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

In reality, this is not a single phenomenon by name. It is simply called 'suffering' because it is the basis for both kinds of suffering for those separated from the beloved. For when agreeable objects are separated, they produce bodily suffering through the body's withering, fading, and so on, and also mental suffering by causing lamentation, 'What we had is now gone.' Therefore, it is said—

Ñātidhanādiviyogā, sokasarasamappitā vitujjanti;

Bālā yato tato yaṃ, dukkhoti mato piyaviyogoti.

Because of separation from relatives, wealth, and so on, fools, plunged into the flood of sorrow, are tormented. For this reason, separation from the beloved is considered suffering.

Icchāniddeso

The Exposition of Desire

201. Icchāniddese jātidhammānanti jātisabhāvānaṃ jātipakatikānaṃ. Icchā uppajjatīti taṇhā uppajjati. Aho vatāti patthanā. Na [M 0.0102] kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbanti yaṃ etaṃ “aho vata mayaṃ na jātidhammā assāma, na ca vata no jāti āgaccheyyā”ti evaṃ pahīnasamudayesu sādhūsu vijjamānaṃ ajātidhammattaṃ, parinibbutesu ca vijjamānaṃ jātiyā anāgamanaṃ icchitaṃ, taṃ icchantassāpi maggabhāvanāya vinā apattabbato anicchantassa ca bhāvanāya pattabbato na icchāya pattabbaṃ nāma hoti. Idampīti etampi; upari sesāni upādāya [V 0.0102] pikāro. Yampicchanti yenapi dhammena alabbhaneyyaṃ vatthuṃ icchanto na labhati, taṃ alabbhaneyyavatthuicchanaṃ dukkhanti veditabbaṃ. Jarādhammānantiādīsupi [P 0.0109] eseva nayo. Evamettha alabbhaneyyavatthūsu icchāva “yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkha”nti vuttā. Sā alabbhaneyyavatthuicchanalakkhaṇā, tappariyesanarasā, tesaṃ appattipaccupaṭṭhānā.

201. In the exposition of desire, 'of those subject to birth' means of those having the intrinsic nature of birth, of those having the condition of birth. 'Desire arises' means craving arises. The expression 'Oh, if only' is a wish. But this is not to be attained by desire. For that which is desired—namely, 'Oh, if only we were not subject to birth, and if only birth would not come to us,' which is the state of not being subject to birth existing in noble ones who have abandoned the origin, and the non-coming of birth existing in those who have attained final Nibbāna—that, even for one desiring it, is not to be attained without the cultivation of the path, while for one not desiring it, it is to be attained by cultivation; therefore, it is not something attainable by desire. 'This too' means 'this also'; the particle 'pi' is used with reference to the remaining cases above. Regarding the phrase 'whatever one desires and does not get': when one desires an unattainable object and does not obtain it by any means, that very desire for an unattainable object should be understood as suffering. The same principle applies also to 'of those subject to aging,' and so on. Thus, here, it is the desire for unattainable objects that is stated as 'whatever one desires and does not obtain, that too is suffering.' Its characteristic is the desire for unattainable objects, its function is the search for them, and its manifestation is their non-attainment.

Dvinnaṃ pana dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvato dukkhāti vuttā. Ekacco hi rājā bhavissatīti sambhāvito hoti. So chinnabhinnagaṇena parivārito pabbatavisamaṃ vā vanagahanaṃ vā pavisati. Atha rājā taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā balakāyaṃ peseti. So rājapurisehi nihataparivāro sayampi laddhappahāro palāyamāno rukkhantaraṃ vā pāsāṇantaraṃ vā pavisati. Tasmiṃ samaye mahāmegho uṭṭhahati, tibbandhakārā kāḷavaddalikā hoti. Atha naṃ samantato kāḷakipillikādayo pāṇā parivāretvā gaṇhanti. Tenassa balavakāyadukkhaṃ uppajjati. ‘Maṃ ekaṃ nissāya ettakā ñātī ca bhogā ca vinaṭṭhā’ti cintentassa balavadomanassaṃ uppajjati. Iti ayaṃ icchā imesaṃ dvinnampi dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvena dukkhāti veditabbā. Apica –

Now, it is called suffering because it is the basis for two kinds of suffering. For example, someone is expected to become a king. Surrounded by a scattered and broken group, he enters a rugged mountain or a dense forest. Then the king, knowing that situation, sends out an army. With his retinue struck down by the king's men, and he himself having received blows, fleeing, he enters among trees or rocks. At that time, a great cloud arises; there is intense darkness and a black downpour. Then creatures like black ants surround him on all sides and seize him. Thus, strong bodily suffering arises for him. Thinking, 'Because of me alone, so many relatives and possessions have been destroyed,' strong mental suffering arises for him. Thus, this desire should be understood as suffering because it is the basis for these two kinds of suffering. Moreover—

Taṃ taṃ patthayamānānaṃ, tassa tassa alābhato;

Yaṃ vighātamayaṃ dukkhaṃ, sattānaṃ idha jāyati.

For those desiring this and that, from the non-obtaining of this and that, whatever suffering of frustration arises here for beings,

Alabbhaneyyavatthūnaṃ, patthanā tassa kāraṇaṃ;

Yasmā tasmā jino dukkhaṃ, icchitālābhamabravīti.

the longing for unattainable objects is its cause; therefore, the Conqueror declared that the non-obtaining of what is desired is suffering.

Upādānakkhandhaniddeso

The Exposition of the Aggregates of Clinging

202. Upādānakkhandhaniddese saṃkhittenāti desanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dukkhañhi ettakāni dukkhasatānīti vā ettakāni dukkhasahassānīti vā ettakāni dukkhasatasahassānīti [M 0.0103] vā saṃkhipituṃ na sakkā, desanā pana sakkā, tasmā “dukkhaṃ nāma aññaṃ kiñci natthi, saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā”ti desanaṃ saṅkhipento evamāha. Seyyathidanti nipāto; tassa te katameti ceti attho. Rūpūpādānakkhandhotiādīnaṃ attho khandhavibhaṅge vaṇṇitoyeva.

202. In the exposition of the aggregates of clinging, it is said concisely, referring to the teaching. For suffering cannot be condensed as being so many hundreds of sufferings, or so many thousands of sufferings, or so many hundreds of thousands of sufferings; but the teaching can be. Therefore, condensing the teaching, he said thus: ‘There is no other suffering; in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.’ ‘Seyyathidaṃ’ is a particle; its meaning is ‘that is to say’ or ‘namely.’ The meaning of ‘the aggregate of clinging to form,’ and so forth, has already been described in the Analysis of the Aggregates.

‘Khandhānaṃ [V 0.0103] dukkhaṭṭho veditabbo’ti ettha pana –

However, here, with regard to ‘The suffering characteristic of the aggregates is to be understood’—

Jātippabhutikaṃ [P 0.0110] dukkhaṃ, yaṃ vuttaṃ idha tādinā;

Avuttaṃ yañca taṃ sabbaṃ, vinā ete na vijjati.

The suffering originating with birth, as stated here by the Such One, and whatever is unstated—all that does not exist apart from these.

Yasmā tasmā upādāna-kkhandhā saṅkhepato ime;

Dukkhāti vuttā dukkhanta-desakena mahesinā.

Therefore, these aggregates of clinging, in brief, were called suffering by the Great Sage, who taught the end of suffering.

Tathā hi indhanamiva pāvako, lakkhamiva paharaṇāni, gorūpamiva ḍaṃsamakasādayo, khettamiva lāvakā, gāmaṃ viya gāmaghātakā, upādānakkhandhapañcakameva jātiādayo nānappakārehi bādhayamānā, tiṇalatādīni viya bhūmiyaṃ, pupphaphalapallavādīni viya rukkhesu, upādānakkhandhesuyeva nibbattanti. Upādānakkhandhānañca ādidukkhaṃ jāti, majjhedukkhaṃ jarā, pariyosānadukkhaṃ maraṇaṃ. Māraṇantikadukkhābhighātena pariḍayhamānadukkhaṃ soko, tadasahanato lālappanadukkhaṃ paridevo. Tato dhātukkhobhasaṅkhātaaniṭṭhaphoṭṭhabbasamāyogato kāyassa ābādhanadukkhaṃ dukkhaṃ. Tena bādhiyamānānaṃ puthujjanānaṃ tattha paṭighuppattito cetobādhanadukkhaṃ domanassaṃ. Sokādivuḍḍhiyā janitavisādānaṃ anutthunanadukkhaṃ upāyāso. Manorathavighātappattānaṃ icchāvighātadukkhaṃ icchitālābhoti evaṃ nānappakārato upaparikkhiyamānā upādānakkhandhāva dukkhāti yadetaṃ ekamekaṃ dassetvā vuccamānaṃ anekehi kappehi na sakkā asesato vattuṃ, taṃ sabbampi dukkhaṃ ekajalabindumhi sakalasamuddajalarasaṃ viya yesu kesuci pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu saṅkhipitvā dassetuṃ “saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā”ti bhagavā avocāti.

For just as fire is fed by fuel, as targets invite blows, as cattle attract flies and mosquitoes, as fields draw reapers, as villages invite raiders—so the five aggregates of clinging are assailed by birth and the rest in various ways. Like grass and creepers upon the earth, like flowers, fruits, and leaves upon the trees, so these sufferings arise within the aggregates of clinging themselves. For the aggregates of clinging, birth is suffering at the start, aging is suffering in the middle, and death is suffering at the end. Sorrow is the suffering of being tormented by the assault of suffering ending in death; lamentation is the suffering of wailing from the inability to bear it. Then, from the conjunction with unpleasant tangible objects, which is a disturbance of the elements, comes the suffering of bodily affliction, which is physical suffering. For ordinary people afflicted by that, distress is the suffering of mental affliction arising from the occurrence of aversion there. Anguish is the suffering of lamenting for those in whom despondency is generated by the increase of sorrow and so forth. The non-obtaining of what is wished for is the suffering of frustrated desire for those whose hopes are crushed. Thus, when examined in various ways, the aggregates of clinging are indeed suffering. Though each aspect is pointed out, not even in many eons could it be fully described. Yet, in order to show all this suffering summarized in the five aggregates of clinging—like the taste of the water of the entire ocean in a single drop—the Blessed One declared: “In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.”

Dukkhasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Truth of Suffering is concluded.

2. Samudayasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Exposition of the Truth of the Origin

203. Samudayasaccaniddese [M 0.0104] yāyaṃ taṇhāti yā ayaṃ taṇhā. Ponobbhavikāti punabbhavakaraṇaṃ [V 0.0104] punobbhavo, punobbhavo sīlamassāti ponobbhavikā. Apica punabbhavaṃ [P 0.0111] deti, punabbhavāya saṃvattati, punappunaṃ bhave nibbattetīti ponobbhavikā. Sā panesā punabbhavassa dāyikāpi atthi adāyikāpi, punabbhavāya saṃvattanikāpi atthi asaṃvattanikāpi, dinnāya paṭisandhiyā upadhivepakkamattāpi. Sā punabbhavaṃ dadamānāpi adadamānāpi, punabbhavāya saṃvattamānāpi asaṃvattamānāpi, dinnāya paṭisandhiyā upadhivepakkamattāpi ponobbhavikā evāti nāmaṃ labhati. Abhinandanasaṅkhātena nandirāgena sahagatāti nandirāgasahagatā, nandirāgena saddhiṃ atthato ekattameva gatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatratatrābhinandinīti yatra yatra attabhāvo tatratatrābhinandinī, rūpādīsu vā ārammaṇesu tatratatrābhinandinī; rūpābhinandinī saddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbadhammābhinandinīti attho. Seyyathidanti nipāto; tassa sā katamāti ceti attho. Kāmataṇhāti kāme taṇhā kāmataṇhā; pañcakāmaguṇikarāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Bhave taṇhā bhavataṇhā; bhavapatthanāvasena uppannassa sassatadiṭṭhisahagatassa rūpārūpabhavarāgassa ca jhānanikantiyā cetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vibhave taṇhā vibhavataṇhā; ucchedadiṭṭhisahagatassa rāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

203. In the exposition of the Truth of the Origin, ‘that craving’ means this very craving. ‘Leading to renewed existence’ (ponobbhavikā): renewed existence is its nature, thus it is ‘leading to renewed existence.’ Furthermore, it gives renewed existence, it leads to renewed existence, it repeatedly generates existence—thus it is ‘leading to renewed existence.’ This craving exists as both giving and not giving renewed existence, as both leading and not leading to renewed existence, and as merely the ripening of the substratum of existence for a rebirth-linking that has been given. Even when giving or not giving renewed existence, leading or not leading to renewed existence, and being merely the ripening of the substratum of existence for a rebirth-linking that has been given, it still receives the name ‘leading to renewed existence.’ ‘Accompanied by delight and lust’ (nandirāgasahagatā) means accompanied by delight and lust, which is characterized as delighting; it is said to have gone to oneness in essence with delight and lust. ‘Seeking delight here and there’ (tatratatrābhinandinī) means delighting wherever there is individual existence, or delighting here and there in objects such as forms; the meaning is delighting in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and mental phenomena. ‘Seyyathidaṃ’ is a particle; its meaning is, ‘Which is that?’ ‘Craving for sensual pleasures’ (kāmataṇhā) is craving for sensual pleasures; this is a designation for passion directed at the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Craving for existence’ (bhavataṇhā) is craving for existence; this is a designation for craving that arises from a longing for existence and is associated with an eternalist view, for passion for the form and formless realms, and for delight in the jhānas. ‘Craving for non-existence’ (vibhavataṇhā) is craving for non-existence; this is a designation for passion associated with an annihilationist view.

Idāni tassā taṇhāya vatthuṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ sā kho panesātiādimāha. Tattha uppajjatīti jāyati. Nivisatīti punappunaṃ pavattivasena patiṭṭhahati. Yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpanti yaṃ lokasmiṃ piyasabhāvañceva madhurasabhāvañca. Cakkhuṃ loketiādīsu lokasmiñhi cakkhādīsu mamattena abhiniviṭṭhā sattā sampattiyaṃ patiṭṭhitā attano cakkhuṃ ādāsādīsu nimittaggahaṇānusārena vippasannapañcapasādaṃ suvaṇṇavimāne ugghāṭitamaṇisīhapañjaraṃ viya maññanti, sotaṃ rajatapanāḷikaṃ viya pāmaṅgasuttakaṃ viya ca [P 0.0112] maññanti, tuṅganāsāti laddhavohāraṃ ghānaṃ vaṭṭetvā ṭhapitaharitālavaṭṭiṃ viya maññanti, jivhaṃ rattakambalapaṭalaṃ viya mudusiniddhamadhurarasadaṃ maññanti, kāyaṃ sālalaṭṭhiṃ viya suvaṇṇatoraṇaṃ viya ca maññanti, manaṃ aññesaṃ manena asadisaṃ uḷāraṃ maññanti, rūpaṃ suvaṇṇakaṇikārapupphādivaṇṇaṃ viya[M 0.0105], saddaṃ mattakaravīkakokilamandadhamitamaṇivaṃsanigghosaṃ viya, attanā paṭiladdhāni catusamuṭṭhānikagandhārammaṇādīni ‘kassa aññassa evarūpāni atthī’ti maññanti. Tesaṃ evaṃ maññamānānaṃ tāni cakkhādīni piyarūpāni ceva honti sātarūpāni ca. Atha nesaṃ tattha anuppannā ceva taṇhā uppajjati, uppannā ca punappunaṃ pavattivasena nivisati. Tasmā bhagavā – “cakkhuṃ loke [V 0.0105] piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ. Etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjatī”tiādimāha. Tattha uppajjamānāti yadā uppajjati tadā ettha uppajjatīti attho. Esa nayo sabbatthāpīti.

Now, to explain in detail the basis of that craving, he said: “Now, that craving…” and so forth. Here, ‘arises’ means it is born. ‘Settles’ means it is established through repeated occurrence. ‘That which is dear and pleasing in the world’ means whatever in the world has a nature that is dear and sweet. Regarding ‘the eye in the world,’ and so forth, beings who are attached to the eye and other senses in the world, rooted in possessiveness, establish themselves in their attainments. They regard their own eye, based on the perception of signs in mirrors and such, as a clear fivefold sensitive faculty—like a golden mansion with an opened jeweled lion-window. They regard the ear like a silver tube or a fine cotton thread. They regard the nose, conventionally called “high-nosed,” as a roll of green orpiment placed there. They regard the tongue like a red blanket-cloth, soft, smooth, and sweet in taste. They regard the body like a sal staff or a golden archway. They regard the mind as incomparable and noble compared to others’ minds. They regard forms like the color of golden kanikara flowers and so forth, sounds like the delightful calls of karavika and cuckoos and the gentle humming notes of jeweled flutes. Having obtained for themselves the four-originated objects of scent and so forth, they think, “Who else has such things?” For those who think thus, these eyes and other senses are both dear and pleasing. Then, in regard to these, craving that had not yet arisen arises, and having arisen, it repeatedly settles through the process of continuity. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “The eye in the world is dear and pleasing. Here, this craving arises when it arises,” and so forth. Here, ‘when it arises’ means that at the time it arises, it arises there—this is the meaning. This method applies everywhere.

Samudayasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the Truth of Origin is concluded.

3. Nirodhasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of Cessation

204. Nirodhasaccaniddese yo tassāyeva taṇhāyāti ettha ‘yo tasseva dukkhassā’ti vattabbe yasmā samudayanirodheneva dukkhaṃ nirujjhati no aññathā, yathāha –

204. In the exposition of the truth of cessation, where the phrase 'of that very craving' occurs, it should be understood as 'of that very suffering.' This is because suffering ceases only through the cessation of its origin, not otherwise, as it was said:

“Yathāpi mūle anupaddave daḷhe,

Chinnopi rukkho punareva rūhati;

Evampi taṇhānusaye anūhate,

Nibbattati dukkhamidaṃ punappuna”nti. (dha. pa. 338);

“Just as a tree, though cut down, sprouts again if its root remains uninjured and firm, so too, if the underlying tendency to craving is not uprooted, this suffering arises again and again.”

Tasmā taṃ dukkhanirodhaṃ dassento samudayanirodhena dassetuṃ evamāha. Sīhasamānavuttino hi tathāgatā. Te dukkhaṃ nirodhentā dukkhanirodhañca dassentā hetumhi paṭipajjanti, na phale. Suvānavuttino pana aññatitthiyā. Te dukkhaṃ nirodhentā dukkhanirodhañca dassentā attakilamathānuyogena [P 0.0113] ceva tasseva ca desanāya phale paṭipajjanti, na hetumhīti. Sīhasamānavuttitāya satthā hetumhi paṭipajjanto yo tassāyevātiādimāha.

Therefore, to show that cessation of suffering, he explains it by showing the cessation of the origin, saying thus. For the Tathāgatas are like lions in their conduct. They, bringing suffering to an end and showing the cessation of suffering, apply themselves to the cause, not to the result. But the followers of other sects are like dogs in their conduct. They, bringing suffering to an end and showing the cessation of suffering, apply themselves to the result by means of self-mortification and by the teaching of that very result, not to the cause. Because the Teacher, being like a lion in his conduct, applies himself to the cause, he says, “of that very…” and so on.

Tattha tassāyevāti yā sā uppatti nivesavasena heṭṭhā pakāsitā tassāyeva. Asesavirāganirodhotiādīni sabbāni nibbānavevacanāneva[M 0.0106]. Nibbānañhi āgamma taṇhā asesā virajjati nirujjhati. Tasmā taṃ “tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodho”ti vuccati. Nibbānañca āgamma taṇhā cajiyati, paṭinissajjiyati, muccati, na alliyati. Tasmā nibbānaṃ “cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayo”ti vuccati. Ekameva hi [V 0.0106] nibbānaṃ. Nāmāni panassa sabbasaṅkhatānaṃ nāmapaṭipakkhavasena anekāni nibbānavevacanāneva honti, seyyathidaṃ – asesavirāganirodho, cāgo, paṭinissaggo, mutti, anālayo, rāgakkhayo, dosakkhayo, mohakkhayo, taṇhākkhayo, anuppādo, appavattaṃ, animittaṃ, appaṇihitaṃ, anāyūhanaṃ, appaṭisandhi, anupapatti, agati, ajātaṃ, ajaraṃ, abyādhi, amataṃ, asokaṃ, aparidevaṃ, anupāyāsaṃ, asaṃkiliṭṭhantiādīni.

Therein, 'of that very' refers to that very craving which was explained previously by way of its arising and settling. 'Complete fading away and cessation,' and so on, are all synonyms for Nibbāna. For it is by reaching Nibbāna that craving completely fades away and ceases. Therefore, it is called 'the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving.' Moreover, by reaching Nibbāna, craving is given up, relinquished, released, and not clung to. Therefore, Nibbāna is called 'giving up, relinquishment, release, and non-attachment.' Indeed, Nibbāna is one. But its names are many, as they are all synonyms for Nibbāna, being the opposite of all conditioned phenomena. For example: complete fading away and cessation, giving up, relinquishment, release, non-attachment, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion, the destruction of craving, non-arising, non-continuance, signlessness, aimlessness, non-accumulation, no-relinking, non-reappearance, no destination, the unborn, the unaging, the unailing, the deathless, the sorrowless, the lamentless, the distressless, the undefiled, and so on.

Idāni maggena chinnāya nibbānaṃ āgamma appavattipattāyapi ca taṇhāya yesu vatthūsu tassā uppatti dassitā, tattheva abhāvaṃ dassetuṃ sā kho panesātiādimāha. Tattha yathā puriso khette jātaṃ tittaalābuvalliṃ disvā aggato paṭṭhāya mūlaṃ pariyesitvā chindeyya, sā anupubbena milāyitvā appavattiṃ gaccheyya. Tato tasmiṃ khette tittaalābu niruddhā pahīnāti vucceyya. Evameva khette tittaalābu viya cakkhādīsu taṇhā. Sā ariyamaggena mūlacchinnā nibbānaṃ āgamma appavattiṃ gacchati. Evaṃ gatā pana tesu vatthūsu khette tittaalābu viya na paññāyati. Yathā ca aṭavito core ānetvā nagarassa dakkhiṇadvāre ghāteyyuṃ, tato aṭaviyaṃ corā matāti vā māritāti vā vucceyyuṃ; evameva aṭaviyaṃ corā viya yā cakkhādīsu taṇhā, sā dakkhiṇadvāre corā viya nibbānaṃ āgamma niruddhattā nibbāne niruddhā. Evaṃ niruddhā pana tesu vatthūsu aṭaviyaṃ [P 0.0114] corā viya na paññāyati. Tenassā tattheva nirodhaṃ dassento “cakkhuṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhatī”tiādimāha. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

Now, to show the absence of craving in those very bases where its arising was shown—even when it has been cut off by the path and has attained non-continuance by reaching Nibbāna—he says, 'But this craving...' and so on. Here, just as a man, seeing a bitter gourd vine grown in a field, might search for its root from the top and cut it, and the vine would gradually wither and cease to be. Then it would be said that in that field, the bitter gourd is destroyed and abandoned. In the same way, craving in the eye and so on is like the bitter gourd in the field. Cut off at the root by the noble path, it reaches non-continuance by attaining Nibbāna. Having thus ceased, it is no longer found in those bases, just as the bitter gourd is no longer found in the field. And just as if bandits were brought from the forest and executed at the southern gate of the city, it would then be said that the bandits in the forest are dead or killed; similarly, the craving in the eye and so on is like the bandits in the forest. Because it is destroyed by reaching Nibbāna—just as the bandits are at the southern gate—it is destroyed in Nibbāna. Having been destroyed thus, it is no longer found in those bases, just as the bandits are no longer found in the forest. Therefore, to show its cessation right there, he says: 'The eye in the world is dear and pleasing. It is here that this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; when ceasing, it ceases,' and so on. The rest here is clear in meaning.

Nirodhasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the Truth of Cessation is concluded.

4. Maggasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of the Path

205. Maggasaccaniddese [M 0.0107] ayamevāti aññamaggapaṭikkhepanatthaṃ niyamanaṃ. Ariyoti taṃtaṃmaggavajjhehi kilesehi ārakattā ariyabhāvakarattā ariyaphalapaṭilābhakarattā ca ariyo. Aṭṭhaṅgāni assāti aṭṭhaṅgiko. Svāyaṃ caturaṅgikā viya senā, pañcaṅgikaṃ viya tūriyaṃ aṅgamattameva [V 0.0107] hoti, aṅgavinimutto natthi. Nibbānatthikehi maggīyati, nibbānaṃ vā maggati, kilese vā mārento gacchatīti maggo. Seyyathidanti so katamoti ceti attho.

205. In the exposition of the Truth of the Path, the phrase 'this very' serves as a restriction for the purpose of excluding other paths. It is 'noble' (ariya) because it is far from the defilements to be abandoned by that respective path, because it produces the noble state, and because it brings about the attainment of the noble fruit. 'Eightfold' (aṭṭhaṅgiko) means having eight factors. Just as an army with four divisions, or a musical ensemble with five parts, consists solely of those factors, there is nothing separate from the factors. It is called a 'path' (maggo) because it is sought by those seeking Nibbāna, or because it seeks Nibbāna, or because it proceeds while destroying the defilements. The phrase 'that is to say' (seyyathidaṃ) has the meaning, 'which is that?'.

Idāni aṅgamattameva maggo hoti, aṅgavinimmutto natthīti dassento sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhīti āha. Tattha sammā dassanalakkhaṇā sammādiṭṭhi. Sammā abhiniropanalakkhaṇo sammāsaṅkappo. Sammā pariggahalakkhaṇā sammāvācā. Sammā samuṭṭhāpanalakkhaṇo sammākammanto. Sammā vodānalakkhaṇo sammāājīvo. Sammā paggahalakkhaṇo sammāvāyāmo. Sammā upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇā sammāsati. Sammā samādhānalakkhaṇo sammāsamādhi.

Now, to show that the path consists only of its factors and that there is nothing separate from its factors, he said: 'right view... up to... right concentration.' Herein, right view has the characteristic of right seeing. Right intention has the characteristic of right directing of the mind. Right speech has the characteristic of right embracing. Right action has the characteristic of right instigating. Right livelihood has the characteristic of right cleansing. Right effort has the characteristic of right striving. Right mindfulness has the characteristic of right attending. Right concentration has the characteristic of right composure.

Tesu ca ekekassa tīṇi tīṇi kiccāni honti, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi tāva aññehipi attano paccanīkakilesehi saddhiṃ micchādiṭṭhiṃ pajahati, nirodhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca passati tappaṭicchādakamohavidhamanavasena asammohato. Sammāsaṅkappādayopi tatheva micchāsaṅkappādīni ca pajahanti, nirodhañca ārammaṇaṃ karonti. Visesato panettha sammāsaṅkappo sahajātadhamme [P 0.0115] abhiniropeti, sammāvācā sammā pariggaṇhāti, sammākammanto sammā samuṭṭhāpeti, sammāājīvo sammā vodāpeti, sammāvāyāmo sammā paggaṇhāti, sammāsati sammā upaṭṭhāti, sammāsamādhi sammā padahati.

And each of these has three functions, namely: Right view, for instance, abandons wrong view along with other defilements that are its adversaries, makes cessation its object, and, through non-delusion, sees the associated states by dispelling the delusion that conceals them. Similarly, right intention and the others also abandon wrong intention and the like, and make cessation their object. Specifically here, right intention rightly directs the co-nascent states, right speech rightly embraces, right action rightly instigates, right livelihood rightly cleanses, right effort rightly exerts, right mindfulness rightly attends, and right concentration rightly composes.

Apicesā sammādiṭṭhi nāma pubbabhāge nānākkhaṇā nānārammaṇā hoti, maggakāle ekakkhaṇā ekārammaṇā, kiccato pana dukkhe ñāṇantiādīni cattāri nāmāni labhati. Sammāsaṅkappādayopi pubbabhāge nānākkhaṇā nānārammaṇā honti, maggakāle ekakkhaṇā ekārammaṇā. Tesu sammāsaṅkappo kiccato nekkhammasaṅkappotiādīni tīṇi [M 0.0108] nāmāni labhati. Sammāvācādayo tayo pubbabhāge nānākkhaṇā nānārammaṇā viratiyopi honti cetanāyopi, maggakkhaṇe pana viratiyova. Sammāvāyāmo sammāsatīti idampi dvayaṃ kiccato sammappadhānasatipaṭṭhānavasena cattāri nāmāni labhati. Sammāsamādhi pana pubbabhāgepi maggakkhaṇepi sammāsamādhiyeva.

Furthermore, this right view, in the preliminary stage, occurs at various moments with various objects, but at the moment of the path, it occurs at a single moment with a single object.
