Functionally, however, it acquires four names, such as 'knowledge of suffering,' and so on. Right intention and the others also occur at various moments with various objects in the preliminary stage, but at the moment of the path, they occur at a single moment with a single object. Among them, right intention functionally acquires three names, such as 'intention of renunciation,' and so on. Right speech, right action, and right livelihood, in the preliminary stage, occur at various moments with various objects, being both abstinences and volitions, but at the moment of the path, they are only abstinences. This pair, right effort and right mindfulness, also functionally acquires four names each by way of the right exertions and the foundations of mindfulness. Right concentration, however, is just right concentration both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path.

Iti imesu aṭṭhasu dhammesu bhagavatā nibbānādhigamāya paṭipannassa yogino bahūpakārattā paṭhamaṃ sammādiṭṭhi desitā. Ayañhi “paññāpajjoto paññāsattha”nti (dha. sa. 16, 20, 29, 34) ca [V 0.0108] vuttā. Tasmā etāya pubbabhāge vipassanāñāṇasaṅkhātāya sammādiṭṭhiyā avijjandhakāraṃ viddhaṃsetvā kilesacore ghātento khemena yogāvacaro nibbānaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tena vuttaṃ “nibbānādhigamāya paṭipannassa yogino bahūpakārattā paṭhamaṃ sammādiṭṭhi desitā”ti.

Thus, among these eight factors, the Blessed One first taught right view because it is of great help to a yogi who is practicing for the attainment of Nibbāna. For this right view is called 'the light of wisdom' and 'the sword of wisdom.' Therefore, by means of this right view in its preliminary stage, which is reckoned as insight-knowledge, the practitioner dispels the darkness of ignorance, slays the thieves that are the defilements, and safely attains Nibbāna. Hence it was said: 'Because it is of great help to a yogi who is practicing for the attainment of Nibbāna, right view was taught first.'

Sammāsaṅkappo pana tassā bahūpakāro, tasmā tadanantaraṃ vutto. Yathā hi heraññiko hatthena parivattetvā parivattetvā cakkhunā kahāpaṇaṃ olokento ‘ayaṃ kūṭo, ayaṃ cheko’ti jānāti, evaṃ yogāvacaropi pubbabhāge vitakkena vitakketvā vipassanāpaññāya olokayamāno ‘ime dhammā kāmāvacarā, ime dhammā rūpāvacarādayo’ti jānāti. Yathā vā pana purisena koṭiyaṃ gahetvā parivattetvā parivattetvā dinnaṃ mahārukkhaṃ tacchako vāsiyā tacchetvā kamme upaneti, evaṃ vitakkena vitakketvā vitakkatvā dinnadhamme yogāvacaro paññāya ‘ime dhammā kāmāvacarā, ime dhammā rūpāvacarā’tiādinā nayena paricchinditvā kamme upaneti. Tena [P 0.0116] vuttaṃ ‘sammāsaṅkappo pana tassā bahūpakāro, tasmā tadanantaraṃ vutto”ti.

Right intention, however, is of great help to that right view; therefore, it is mentioned immediately after. For just as a money-changer, turning a coin over and over in his hand and examining it with his eye, knows, 'This is counterfeit, this is genuine,' so too the practitioner, in the preliminary stage, having repeatedly applied thought, examines with insight-wisdom and knows, 'These phenomena belong to the sense-sphere, these phenomena belong to the form-sphere, and so on.' Or, just as a carpenter, given a large tree which a man holds by the end and turns over and over, shapes it with an adze and prepares it for use, so too the practitioner, with wisdom, defines the phenomena presented by thought—which has thought and re-thought them—according to the method, 'These phenomena belong to the sense-sphere, these phenomena belong to the form-sphere,' and so on, and prepares them for the task. Therefore it is said: 'Right intention, however, is of great help to that; therefore, it is mentioned immediately after.'

Svāyaṃ yathā sammādiṭṭhiyā, evaṃ sammāvācāyapi upakārako. Yathāha – “pubbe kho, gahapati, vitakketvā vicāretvā pacchā vācaṃ bhindatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.463). Tasmā tadanantaraṃ sammāvācā vuttā.

This right intention is helpful to right speech, just as it is to right view. As it is said: 'First, householder, having applied thought and sustained thought, one then breaks into speech.' Therefore, right speech is mentioned immediately after that.

Yasmā pana ‘idañcidañca karissāmā’ti paṭhamaṃ vācāya saṃvidahitvā loke kammante payojenti, tasmā vācā kāyakammassa upakārikāti sammāvācāya anantaraṃ sammākammanto vutto.

And since people in the world first make an arrangement by speech, saying, 'We will do this and that,' and then engage in actions, speech is helpful to bodily action. Therefore, right action is mentioned after right speech.

Catubbidhaṃ [M 0.0109] pana vacīduccaritaṃ, tividhaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ pahāya ubhayaṃ sucaritaṃ pūrentasseva yasmā ājīvaṭṭhamakasīlaṃ pūrati, na itarassa, tasmā tadubhayānantaraṃ sammāājīvo vutto.

Since it is only for one who has abandoned the four kinds of verbal misconduct and the three kinds of bodily misconduct, and is fulfilling both kinds of good conduct, that the virtue with livelihood as the eighth factor is fulfilled, and not for another, therefore right livelihood is mentioned after those two.

Evaṃ suddhājīvena ‘parisuddho me ājīvo’ti ettāvatā paritosaṃ akatvā suttappamattena viharituṃ na yuttaṃ, atha kho sabbairiyāpathesu idaṃ vīriyamārabhitabbanti dassetuṃ tadanantaraṃ sammāvāyāmo vutto.

One with a pure livelihood should not be content with just that, thinking, 'My livelihood is pure,' nor is it proper to live in a drowsy and heedless manner. Rather, to show that this effort should be undertaken in all postures, right effort is mentioned next.

Tato [V 0.0109] āraddhavīriyenāpi kāyādīsu catūsu vatthūsu sati suppatiṭṭhitā kātabbāti dassanatthaṃ tadanantaraṃ sammāsati desitā.

Then, to show that even by one whose energy is aroused, mindfulness should be well established on the four foundations, beginning with the body, right mindfulness is taught next.

Yasmā pana evaṃ suppatiṭṭhitā sati samādhissa upakārānupakārānaṃ dhammānaṃ gatiyo samanvesitvā pahoti ekattārammaṇe cittaṃ samādhātuṃ, tasmā sammāsatianantaraṃ sammāsamādhi desitoti veditabbo.

Because when mindfulness is thus well established, one can investigate the tendencies of phenomena that are helpful or unhelpful to concentration and bring the mind to one-pointedness, therefore it should be understood that right concentration is taught next after right mindfulness.

Sammādiṭṭhiniddese “dukkhe ñāṇa”ntiādinā catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ dassitaṃ. Tattha purimāni dve saccāni vaṭṭaṃ, pacchimāni vivaṭṭaṃ. Tesu bhikkhuno vaṭṭe kammaṭṭhānābhiniveso hoti, vivaṭṭe natthi abhiniveso. Purimāni hi dve saccāni “pañcakkhandhā dukkhaṃ, taṇhā samudayo”ti evaṃ saṅkhepena ca “katame pañcakkhandhā? Rūpakkhandho”tiādinā nayena vitthārena ca ācariyassa santike uggaṇhitvā vācāya punappunaṃ parivattento yogāvacaro kammaṃ karoti; itaresu pana dvīsu saccesu “nirodhasaccaṃ iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpaṃ, maggasaccaṃ iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpa”nti evaṃ savaneneva kammaṃ karoti. So evaṃ kammaṃ karonto cattāri saccāni ekena paṭivedhena paṭivijjhati, ekābhisamayena abhisameti; dukkhaṃ [P 0.0117] pariññāpaṭivedhena paṭivijjhati, samudayaṃ pahānapaṭivedhena, nirodhaṃ sacchikiriyapaṭivedhena, maggaṃ bhāvanāpaṭivedhena paṭivijjhati; dukkhaṃ pariññābhisamayena…pe… maggaṃ bhāvanābhisamayena abhisameti.

In the exposition of right view, the meditation subject of the four truths is shown with phrases like "knowledge of suffering." Therein, the first two truths pertain to the round of existence, while the latter two pertain to the escape from it. For a bhikkhu, the application of the meditation subject is to the round, but there is no application to the escape from it. The first two truths—"the five aggregates are suffering, craving is the origin"—the yogi learns briefly and in detail from the teacher, such as through the explanation, "What are the five aggregates? The aggregate of form," and so on, repeatedly reciting them and engaging in the practice. Regarding the other two truths, the practice is simply hearing: "The truth of cessation is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; the truth of the path is desirable, lovely, and pleasing." By practicing in this way, one penetrates the four truths with a single penetration and comprehends them with a single comprehension; suffering is penetrated through the penetration of full understanding, the origin through the penetration of abandonment, cessation through the penetration of direct realization, and the path through the penetration of cultivation. Suffering is comprehended through the comprehension of full understanding... the path is comprehended through the comprehension of cultivation.

Evamassa pubbabhāge dvīsu saccesu uggahaparipucchāsavanadhāraṇasammasanapaṭivedho hoti, dvīsu savanapaṭivedhoyeva; aparabhāge tīsu kiccato paṭivedho hoti, nirodhe ārammaṇapaṭivedho. Tattha sabbampi paṭivedhañāṇaṃ lokuttaraṃ, savanadhāraṇasammasanañāṇaṃ lokiyaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ, paccavekkhaṇā pana pattasaccassa hoti. Ayañca ādikammiko. Tasmā sā idha na vuttā. Imassa ca bhikkhuno pubbe pariggahato ‘dukkhaṃ parijānāmi[M 0.0110], samudayaṃ pajahāmi, nirodhaṃ sacchikaromi, maggaṃ bhāvemī’ti ābhogasamannāhāramanasikārapaccavekkhaṇā natthi, pariggahato paṭṭhāya hoti; aparabhāge pana dukkhaṃ pariññātameva hoti…pe… maggo bhāvitova hoti.

Thus, in the preliminary stage, for this person, there is penetration of two truths by way of learning, inquiry, listening, retention, and reflection; for the other two truths, there is only penetration by way of listening. In the later stage, there is penetration of three truths in terms of their function, and penetration of cessation as its object. Herein, all knowledge of penetration is supramundane, while the knowledge of listening, retention, and reflection is mundane, belonging to the sense-sphere. Reviewing, however, occurs for the truth that has been attained. And this is for a beginner. Therefore, it is not mentioned here. For this bhikkhu, before grasping, there is no reviewing through initial application, sustained application, or mental advertence with the thought, “I fully understand suffering, I abandon the origin, I realize cessation, I develop the path.” It begins from the point of grasping. But in the later stage, suffering is already fully understood… the path is already developed.

Tattha dve saccāni duddasattā gambhīrāni, dve gambhīrattā duddasāni. Dukkhasaccañhi uppattito pākaṭaṃ; khāṇukaṇṭakappahārādīsu ‘aho dukkha’nti vattabbatampi āpajjati. Samudayampi [V 0.0110] khāditukāmatābhuñjitukāmatādivasena uppattito pākaṭaṃ. Lakkhaṇapaṭivedhato pana ubhayampi gambhīraṃ. Iti tāni duddasattā gambhīrāni. Itaresaṃ pana dvinnaṃ dassanatthāya payogo bhavaggagahaṇatthaṃ hatthappasāraṇaṃ viya, avīciphusanatthaṃ pādappasāraṇaṃ viya, satadhā bhinnavālassa koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭipādanaṃ viya ca hoti. Iti tāni gambhīrattā duddasāni. Evaṃ duddasattā gambhīresu gambhīrattā ca duddasesu catūsu saccesu uggahādivasena pubbabhāgañāṇuppattiṃ sandhāya idaṃ “dukkhe ñāṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Paṭivedhakkhaṇe pana ekameva ñāṇaṃ hoti.

Herein, two truths are profound because they are difficult to see, and two are difficult to see because they are profound. The truth of suffering, indeed, is evident in its arising; even when struck by a stump or thorn, one exclaims, 'Alas, suffering!' The truth of origin, too, is evident in its arising, through desires like wanting to eat or enjoy. However, both are profound in terms of penetration of their characteristics. Thus, they are profound because they are difficult to see. But for the other two, the effort to see them is like stretching out a hand to grasp the peak of existence, like stretching out a foot to touch Avīci, or like joining together the tip of a hair split a hundredfold. Thus, they are difficult to see because they are profound. In this way, regarding the four truths—some profound because they are difficult to see, and others difficult to see because they are profound—the statement 'knowledge of suffering,' etc., is made with reference to the arising of preliminary knowledge through learning and so forth. At the moment of penetration, however, there is only one knowledge.

Sammāsaṅkappaniddese kāmato nissaṭoti nekkhammasaṅkappo. Byāpādato nissaṭoti abyāpādasaṅkappo. Vihiṃsāya nissaṭoti avihiṃsāsaṅkappo. Tattha nekkhammavitakko kāmavitakkassa padaghātaṃ padacchedaṃ karonto [P 0.0118] uppajjati, abyāpādavitakko byāpādavitakkassa, avihiṃsāvitakko vihiṃsāvitakkassa. Nekkhammavitakko ca kāmavitakkassa paccanīko hutvā uppajjati, abyāpādaavihiṃsāvitakkā byāpādavihiṃsāvitakkānaṃ.

In the exposition of right intention: The thought of renunciation is that which has emerged from sensual desire. The thought of non-ill-will is that which has emerged from ill-will. The thought of non-harming is that which has emerged from harm. Herein, the thought of renunciation arises, striking at and cutting off the thought of sensual desire; the thought of non-ill-will arises, striking at and cutting off the thought of ill-will; and the thought of non-harming arises, striking at and cutting off the thought of harm. The thought of renunciation arises as an opponent to the thought of sensual desire, and the thoughts of non-ill-will and non-harming arise as opponents to the thoughts of ill-will and harm.

Tattha yogāvacaro kāmavitakkassa padaghātanatthaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ vā sammasati aññaṃ vā pana kiñci saṅkhāraṃ. Athassa vipassanākkhaṇe vipassanāsampayutto saṅkappo tadaṅgavasena kāmavitakkassa padaghātaṃ padacchedaṃ karonto uppajjati, vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā maggaṃ pāpeti. Athassa maggakkhaṇe maggasampayutto saṅkappo samucchedavasena kāmavitakkassa padaghātaṃ padacchedaṃ karonto uppajjati; byāpādavitakkassāpi padaghātanatthaṃ byāpādavitakkaṃ vā aññaṃ vā saṅkhāraṃ sammasati; vihiṃsāvitakkassa padaghātanatthaṃ vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ vā aññaṃ vā saṅkhāraṃ sammasati. Athassa vipassanākkhaṇeti sabbaṃ purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ.

Herein, the yogi reflects on the thought of sensual desire or any other formation in order to strike at the thought of sensual desire. Then, at the moment of insight, the thought associated with insight arises, striking at and cutting off the thought of sensual desire by way of temporary suppression, and having intensified insight, it leads to the path. Then, at the moment of the path, the thought associated with the path arises, striking at and cutting off the thought of sensual desire by way of complete eradication. Similarly, to strike at the thought of ill-will, one reflects on the thought of ill-will or any other formation; to strike at the thought of harm, one reflects on the thought of harm or any other formation. Then, at the moment of insight, everything should be applied in the same way as before.

Kāmavitakkādīnaṃ [M 0.0111] pana tiṇṇaṃ pāḷiyaṃ vibhattesu aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇesu ekakammaṭṭhānampi apaccanīkaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantato pana kāmavitakkassa tāva asubhesu paṭhamajjhānameva paccanīkaṃ, byāpādavitakkassa mettāya tikacatukkajjhānāni, vihiṃsāvitakkassa karuṇāya tikacatukkajjhānāni. Tasmā asubhe parikammaṃ katvā jhānaṃ samāpannassa samāpattikkhaṇe jhānasampayutto saṅkappo vikkhambhanavasena kāmavitakkassa paccanīko hutvā uppajjati. Jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapentassa vipassanākkhaṇe vipassanāsampayutto saṅkappo tadaṅgavasena kāmavitakkassa paccanīko hutvā uppajjati. Vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā maggaṃ pāpentassa maggakkhaṇe [V 0.0111] maggasampayutto saṅkappo samucchedavasena kāmavitakkassa paccanīko hutvā uppajjati. Evaṃ uppanno nekkhammasaṅkappoti vuccatīti veditabbo.

However, for the three kinds of thoughts, namely, sensual thought, the thought of ill-will, and the thought of harming, there is not a single meditation subject among the thirty-eight objects classified in the texts that is not an opponent. Absolutely speaking, however, for sensual thought, only the first jhāna on the foul is its opponent; for the thought of ill-will, the third and fourth jhānas on loving-kindness are its opponents; and for the thought of harming, the third and fourth jhānas on compassion are its opponents. Therefore, for one who has performed the preliminary work on the foul and attained jhāna, at the moment of attainment, the thought associated with jhāna arises as an opponent to sensual thought by way of suppression. For one who has made jhāna a basis and established insight, at the moment of insight, the thought associated with insight arises as an opponent to sensual thought by way of substitution. For one who has intensified insight and is attaining the path, at the moment of the path, the thought associated with the path arises as an opponent to sensual thought by way of eradication. It should be understood that what has thus arisen is called the thought of renunciation.

Mettāya pana parikammaṃ katvā, karuṇāya parikammaṃ katvā jhānaṃ samāpajjatīti sabbaṃ purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Evaṃ uppanno abyāpādasaṅkappoti vuccati, avihiṃsāsaṅkappoti ca vuccatīti [P 0.0119] veditabbo. Evamete nekkhammasaṅkappādayo vipassanājhānavasena uppattīnaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā; maggakkhaṇe pana imesu tīsu ṭhānesu uppannassa akusalasaṅkappassa padacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamāno ekova kusalasaṅkappo uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāsaṅkappo nāma.

Furthermore, 'having performed the preliminary work on loving-kindness, or having performed the preliminary work on compassion, one attains jhāna'—all this should be applied in the same way as before. It should be understood that what has thus arisen is called the thought of non-ill-will, and is called the thought of non-harming. Thus, these thoughts of renunciation and so on are various in the preliminary stage, owing to the diversity of their arising by way of insight and jhāna. At the moment of the path, however, with respect to these three instances, a single wholesome thought arises, fulfilling the path factor by means of eradicating the arisen unwholesome thought and bringing about its future non-arising. This is called right intention.

Sammāvācāniddesepi yasmā aññeneva cittena musāvādā viramati, aññenaññena pisuṇavācādīhi, tasmā catassopetā veramaṇiyo pubbabhāge nānā; maggakkhaṇe pana micchāvācāsaṅkhātāya catubbidhāya akusaladussīlyacetanāya padacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva sammāvācāsaṅkhātā kusalaveramaṇī uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāvācā nāma.

In the exposition of right speech also, because one refrains from false speech with one mind, and from divisive speech and so forth with other minds, these four abstinences are distinct in the preliminary stage. At the moment of the path, however, a single wholesome abstinence, reckoned as right speech, arises, fulfilling the path factor by eradicating the fourfold unwholesome immoral volition reckoned as wrong speech, and thereby bringing about its future non-arising. This is called right speech.

Sammākammantaniddesepi yasmā aññeneva cittena pāṇātipātā viramati, aññena adinnādānā, aññena kāmesumicchācārā, tasmā tissopetā veramaṇiyo pubbabhāge nānā; maggakkhaṇe pana micchākammantasaṅkhātāya tividhāya akusaladussīlyacetanāya padacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva sammākammantasaṅkhātā akusalaveramaṇī uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammākammanto nāma.

In the exposition of right action also, because one abstains from killing living beings with one mind, from taking what is not given with another, and from sexual misconduct with yet another, these three abstinences are distinct in the preliminary stage. At the moment of the path, however, a single wholesome abstinence, reckoned as right action, arises, fulfilling the path factor by eradicating the threefold unwholesome immoral volition reckoned as wrong action, and thereby bringing about its future non-arising. This is called right action.

Sammāājīvaniddese [M 0.0112] idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Ariyasāvakoti ariyassa buddhassa sāvako. Micchāājīvaṃ pahāyāti pāpakaṃ ājīvaṃ pajahitvā. Sammāājīvenāti buddhapasatthena kusalaājīvena. Jīvikaṃ kappetīti jīvitappavattiṃ pavatteti. Idhāpi yasmā aññeneva cittena kāyadvāravītikkamā viramati; aññena vacīdvāravītikkamā, tasmā pubbabhāge nānākkhaṇesu uppajjati; maggakkhaṇe pana dvīsu dvāresu sattannaṃ kammapathānaṃ vasena uppannāya micchāājīvadussīlyacetanāya padacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva sammāājīvasaṅkhātā kusalaveramaṇī uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāājīvo nāma.

In the exposition of right livelihood: 'Herein' means in this dispensation. 'A noble disciple' means a disciple of the Noble One, the Buddha. 'Having abandoned wrong livelihood' means having given up evil livelihood. 'With right livelihood' means with a wholesome livelihood praised by the Buddha. 'He makes a living' means he carries on the process of life. Herein also, because one abstains from transgression through the bodily door with one mind, and from transgression through the verbal door with another, the abstinence arises at different moments in the preliminary stage. At the moment of the path, however, a single wholesome abstinence, reckoned as right livelihood, arises, fulfilling the path factor by eradicating the immoral volition of wrong livelihood—which arises through the two doors by way of the seven courses of action—and thereby bringing about its future non-arising. This is called right livelihood.

Sammāvāyāmaniddeso [V 0.0112] sammappadhānavibhaṅge anupadavaṇṇanāvasena āvibhavissati. Ayaṃ pana pubbabhāge nānācittesu labhati. Aññeneva hi cittena anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ [P 0.0120] akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya vāyāmaṃ karoti, aññena uppannānaṃ pahānāya; aññeneva ca anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya, aññena uppannānaṃ ṭhitiyā; maggakkhaṇe pana ekacitteyeva labbhati. Ekameva hi maggasampayuttaṃ vīriyaṃ catukiccasādhanaṭṭhena cattāri nāmāni labbhati.

The exposition of right effort will become clear by way of the word-by-word commentary in the Analysis of the Right Strivings. This, however, is obtained in different minds in the preliminary stage. For with one mind, one makes an effort for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; with another, for the abandoning of arisen ones; with yet another, for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; and with another, for the maintenance of arisen ones. At the moment of the path, however, it is obtained in a single mind. For the single energy associated with the path obtains four names on account of accomplishing four functions.

Sammāsatiniddesopi satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅge anupadavaṇṇanāvasena āvibhavissati. Ayampi ca pubbabhāge nānācittesu labbhati. Aññeneva hi cittena kāyaṃ pariggaṇhāti, aññenaññena vedanādīni; maggakkhaṇe pana ekacitteyeva labbhati. Ekāyeva hi maggasampayuttā sati catukiccasādhanaṭṭhena cattāri nāmāni labhati.

The exposition of right mindfulness will also become clear by way of the word-by-word commentary in the Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness. This too is obtained in different minds in the preliminary stage. For with one mind, one comprehends the body; with other minds, feelings and so forth. At the moment of the path, however, it is obtained in a single mind. For the single mindfulness associated with the path obtains four names on account of accomplishing four functions.

Sammāsamādhiniddese cattāri jhānāni pubbabhāgepi nānā, maggakkhaṇepi. Pubbabhāge samāpattivasena nānā, maggakkhaṇe nānāmaggavasena. Ekassa hi paṭhamamaggo paṭhamajjhāniko hoti, dutiyamaggādayopi paṭhamajjhānikā, dutiyādīsu aññatarajjhānikā vā. Ekassa paṭhamamaggo dutiyādīnaṃ aññatarajjhāniko hoti, dutiyādayopi dutiyādīnaṃ aññatarajjhānikā vā paṭhamajjhānikā vā. Evaṃ cattāropi maggā jhānavasena sadisā vā asadisā vā ekaccasadisā vā honti.

In the exposition of right concentration, the four jhānas are distinct both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path. In the preliminary stage, they are distinct by way of attainment; at the moment of the path, by way of the different paths. For one person, the first path is of the first jhāna, and the subsequent paths are also of the first jhāna, or of one of the other jhānas beginning with the second. For another person, the first path is of one of the other jhānas beginning with the second, and the subsequent paths are also of one of the other jhānas beginning with the second, or of the first jhāna. Thus, all four paths, in terms of jhāna, may be similar, dissimilar, or partly similar.

Ayaṃ panassa viseso pādakajjhānaniyāmena hoti. Pādakajjhānaniyāmena tāva paṭhamajjhānalābhino paṭhamajjhānā vuṭṭhāya vipassantassa uppannamaggo [M 0.0113] paṭhamajjhāniko hoti; maggaṅgabojjhaṅgāni panettha paripuṇṇāneva honti. Dutiyajjhānato uṭṭhāya vipassantassa uppanno maggo dutiyajjhāniko hoti; maggaṅgāni panettha satta honti. Tatiyajjhānato uṭṭhāya vipassantassa uppanno maggo tatiyajjhāniko hoti; maggaṅgāni panettha satta, bojjhaṅgāni cha honti. Esa nayo catutthajjhānato paṭṭhāya yāva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanā.

But this distinction occurs by way of the determining base jhāna. According to the determining base jhāna, first, for one who has attained the first jhāna and risen from it to practice insight, the path that arises is associated with the first jhāna; here, the path factors and enlightenment factors are fully complete. For one who rises from the second jhāna to practice insight, the path that arises is associated with the second jhāna; here, there are seven path factors. For one who rises from the third jhāna to practice insight, the path that arises is associated with the third jhāna; here, there are seven path factors and six enlightenment factors. This same principle applies from the fourth jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Āruppe catukkapañcakajjhānaṃ uppajjati. Tañca kho lokuttaraṃ no lokiyanti vuttaṃ. Ettha kathanti? Etthāpi paṭhamajjhānādīsu yato uṭṭhāya sotāpattimaggaṃ paṭilabhitvā āruppasamāpattiṃ bhāvetvā yo āruppe uppanno, taṃjhānikāva tassa tattha tayo maggā uppajjanti[V 0.0113]. Evaṃ [P 0.0121] pādakajjhānameva niyāmeti. Keci pana therā “vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā khandhā niyāmentī”ti vadanti. Keci “puggalajjhāsayo niyāmetī”ti vadanti. Keci “vuṭṭhānagāminīvipassanā niyāmetī”ti vadanti. Tesaṃ vādavinicchayo heṭṭhā cittuppādakaṇḍe lokuttarapadabhājanīyavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 350) vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ayaṃ vuccati sammāsamādhīti yā imesu catūsu jhānesu ekaggatā, ayaṃ pubbabhāge lokiyo, aparabhāge lokuttaro sammāsamādhi nāma vuccatīti. Evaṃ lokiyalokuttaravasena bhagavā maggasaccaṃ desesi.

In the formless realms, the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise. And that is said to be supramundane, not mundane. How is this so? Here too, for one who has risen from the first jhāna and so on, attained the path of stream-entry, and developed the formless attainments, when that person has arisen in a formless realm, the three subsequent paths that arise there for them are associated with that very jhāna. Thus, it is the base jhāna itself that determines it. But some elders say, "The aggregates that are the object of insight determine it." Some say, "The disposition of the person determines it." Some say, "The insight leading to emergence determines it." The resolution of these views should be understood according to the method explained in the commentary on the analysis of the supramundane term in the chapter on the arising of consciousness (DhsA. 350). This is called right concentration: the one-pointedness in these four jhānas. In the preliminary stage it is mundane; in the subsequent stage it is supramundane and is called right concentration. Thus, the Blessed One taught the truth of the path in terms of the mundane and supramundane.

Tattha lokiyamagge sabbāneva maggaṅgāni yathānurūpaṃ chasu ārammaṇesu aññatarārammaṇāni honti. Lokuttaramagge pana catusaccapaṭivedhāya pavattassa ariyassa nibbānārammaṇaṃ avijjānusayasamugghātakaṃ paññācakkhu sammādiṭṭhi. Tathā sampannadiṭṭhissa taṃsampayuttaṃ tividhamicchāsaṅkappasamugghātakaṃ cetaso nibbānapadābhiniropanaṃ sammāsaṅkappo. Tathā passantassa vitakkentassa ca taṃsampayuttāva catubbidhavacīduccaritasamugghātikāya micchāvācāya virati sammāvācā. Tathā viramantassa taṃsampayuttāva micchākammantasamucchedikā tividhakāyaduccaritavirati sammākammanto. Tesaṃyeva sammāvācākammantānaṃ vodānabhūtā taṃsampayuttāva kuhanādisamucchedikā micchāājīvavirati sammāājīvo. Imissā sammāvācākammantājīvasaṃkhātāya sīlabhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhamānassa tadanurūpo taṃsampayuttova kosajjasamucchedako [M 0.0114] anuppannuppannānaṃ akusalakusalānaṃ anuppādapahānuppādaṭṭhitisādhako ca vīriyārambho sammāvāyāmo. Evaṃ vāyamantassa taṃsampayuttova micchāsativiniddhunanako kāyādīsu kāyānupassanādisādhako ca cetaso asammoso sammāsati. Iti anuttarāya satiyā suvihitacittārakkhassa taṃsampayuttāva micchāsamādhisamugghātikā cittekaggatā sammāsamādhīti. Esa [P 0.0122] lokuttaro ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo yo saha lokiyena maggena dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti saṅkhaṃ gato.

Therein, in the mundane path, all the path factors appropriately have one or another of the six sense objects as their object. In the supramundane path, however, for the noble one who proceeds to penetrate the four truths, right view is the wisdom-eye that has Nibbāna as its object and eradicates the latent tendency of ignorance. For one thus endowed with right view, right intention is that which is associated with it, eradicating the threefold wrong intention and directing the mind towards the state of Nibbāna. For one thus seeing and thinking, right speech is the abstinence from wrong speech, which is associated with them, eradicating the fourfold verbal misconduct. For one thus abstaining, right action is the abstinence from the threefold bodily misconduct, which is associated with them, cutting off wrong action. Right livelihood is the abstinence from wrong livelihood, which is associated with them, being the purification of right speech and right action, and cutting off deceit and the like. For one established in this moral foundation—consisting of right speech, right action, and right livelihood—right effort is the commencement of energy, which is associated with it and appropriate to it, eradicating laziness and accomplishing the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, the abandoning of arisen ones, the arising of unarisen wholesome states, and the maintenance of arisen ones. For one thus striving, right mindfulness is the non-forgetfulness of mind, which is associated with it, dispelling wrong mindfulness and accomplishing the contemplation of the body in the body, and so forth. Thus, for one whose mind is well-guarded by supreme mindfulness, right concentration is the one-pointedness of mind, which is associated with it, eradicating wrong concentration. This is the noble eightfold supramundane path, which, together with the mundane path, is designated as the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

So kho panesa maggo sammādiṭṭhisaṅkappānaṃ vijjāya, sesadhammānaṃ caraṇena saṅgahitattā vijjā ceva caraṇañca. Tathā tesaṃ dvinnaṃ vipassanāyānena, itaresaṃ samathayānena saṅgahitattā samatho ceva vipassanā ca. Tesaṃ vā dvinnaṃ paññākkhandhena, tadanantarānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sīlakkhandhena, avasesānaṃ samādhikkhandhena adhipaññāadhisīlaadhicittasikkhāhi ca saṅgahitattā khandhattayañceva sikkhāttayañca hoti; yena samannāgato ariyasāvako dassanasamatthehi cakkhūhi gamanasamatthehi ca [V 0.0114] pādehi samannāgato addhiko viya vijjācaraṇasampanno hutvā vipassanāyānena kāmasukhallikānuyogaṃ, samathayānena attakilamathānuyoganti antadvayaṃ parivajjetvā majjhimapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno paññākkhandhena mohakkhandhaṃ, sīlakkhandhena dosakkhandhaṃ, samādhikkhandhena ca lobhakkhandhaṃ padālento adhipaññāsikkhāya paññāsampadaṃ, adhisīlasikkhāya sīlasampadaṃ, adhicittasikkhāya samādhisampadanti tisso sampattiyo patvā amataṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikaroti, ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇaṃ sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammaratanavicittaṃ sammattaniyāmasaṅkhātaṃ ariyabhūmiñca okkanto hotīti.

This path, indeed, since right view and right intention are included in wisdom, and the remaining factors in conduct, is both wisdom and conduct. Similarly, since those two are included in the vehicle of insight, and the others in the vehicle of tranquility, it is both tranquility and insight. Or, since those two are included in the aggregate of wisdom, the subsequent three in the aggregate of virtue, and the remaining ones in the aggregate of concentration, and are also included in the higher training in wisdom, the higher training in virtue, and the higher training in mind, it is both the three aggregates and the three trainings. Endowed with this path, the noble disciple becomes accomplished in wisdom and conduct, like a traveler endowed with eyes capable of seeing and feet capable of walking. By the vehicle of insight, they avoid the indulgence in sensual pleasures, and by the vehicle of tranquility, they avoid the indulgence in self-mortification. Thus, having avoided both extremes, they enter upon the Middle Path. With the wisdom aggregate, they shatter the mass of delusion; with the virtue aggregate, the mass of hatred; and with the concentration aggregate, the mass of greed. By the higher training in wisdom, they attain the accomplishment of wisdom; by the higher training in virtue, the accomplishment of virtue; and by the higher training in mind, the accomplishment of concentration. Having attained these three accomplishments, they realize the deathless Nibbāna and enter the noble plane, which is beautiful in the beginning, middle, and end, adorned with the jewels of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and designated as the right course of certainty.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Analysis according to the Discourses.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Analysis according to the Abhidhamma.

206-214. Idāni abhidhammabhājanīyaṃ hoti. Tattha “ariyasaccānī”ti avatvā nippadesato paccayasaṅkhātaṃ samudayaṃ dassetuṃ “cattāri saccānī”ti vuttaṃ[M 0.0115]. Ariyasaccānīti hi vutte avasesā ca kilesā, avasesā ca akusalā dhammā, tīṇi ca kusalamūlāni sāsavāni, avasesā ca sāsavā kusalā dhammā na saṅgayhanti. Na ca kevalaṃ taṇhāva dukkhaṃ samudāneti, imepi avasesā ca kilesādayo paccayā samudānentiyeva. Iti imepi paccayā dukkhaṃ samudānentiyevāti nippadesato paccayasaṅkhātaṃ samudayaṃ dassetuṃ “ariyasaccānī”ti avatvā “cattāri saccānī”ti vuttaṃ.

Now comes the Abhidhamma exposition. Here, without stating 'the Noble Truths,' the term 'four truths' is used to show comprehensively the origin, which is reckoned as a condition. For if 'Noble Truths' were said, the remaining defilements, the remaining unwholesome states, the three wholesome roots with taints, and the remaining wholesome states with taints would not be included. And it is not only craving that brings about suffering; these remaining defilements and other conditions also bring it about. Thus, to show comprehensively the origin, which is reckoned as a condition, the term 'four truths' is used without stating 'Noble Truths'.

Niddesavāre [P 0.0123] ca nesaṃ paṭhamaṃ dukkhaṃ aniddisitvā tasseva dukkhassa sukhaniddesatthaṃ dukkhasamudayo niddiṭṭho. Tasmiñhi niddiṭṭhe “avasesā ca kilesā”tiādinā nayena dukkhasaccaṃ sukhaniddesaṃ hoti. Nirodhasaccampettha taṇhāya pahānaṃ “taṇhāya ca avasesānañca kilesānaṃ pahāna”nti evaṃ yathāvuttassa samudayassa pahānavasena pañcahākārehi niddiṭṭhaṃ. Maggasaccaṃ panettha paṭhamajjhānikasotāpattimaggavasena dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ vibhattassa desanānayassa mukhamattameva dassentena niddiṭṭhaṃ. Tattha nayabhedo veditabbo. Taṃ upari pakāsayissāma.

And in the section on exposition, suffering is not initially expounded; instead, the origin of suffering is expounded for the sake of easily expounding suffering itself. For when that is expounded, the truth of suffering becomes easily expounded by the method beginning with 'and the remaining defilements.' Here, the truth of cessation, the abandonment of craving, is expounded in five ways as the abandonment of the previously stated origin, in the manner of 'the abandonment of craving and the remaining defilements.' And here, the truth of the path is expounded by showing merely the introduction to the method of teaching, which is classified in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī according to the stream-entry path of the first jhāna. There, the differences in method should be understood. We will explain that further on.

Yasmā [V 0.0115] pana na kevalaṃ aṭṭhaṅgiko maggova paṭipadā “pubbeva kho panassa kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ ājīvo suparisuddho hotī”ti (ma. ni. 3.433) vacanato pana puggalajjhāsayavasena pañcaṅgikopi maggo paṭipadā evāti desito, tasmā taṃ nayaṃ dassetuṃ pañcaṅgikavāropi niddiṭṭho. Yasmā ca na kevalaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikapañcaṅgikamaggāva paṭipadā, sampayuttakā pana atirekapaññāsadhammāpi paṭipadā eva, tasmā taṃ nayaṃ dassetuṃ tatiyo sabbasaṅgāhikavāropi niddiṭṭho. Tattha “avasesā dhammā dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya sampayuttā”ti idaṃ parihāyati. Sesaṃ sabbattha sadisameva.

Moreover, since the practice is not only the eight-factored path—for it is also taught by the statement 'his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood are already well purified beforehand' (MN 3.433) that, according to an individual's disposition, even a five-factored path is the practice—therefore, to show that method, the five-factored section is also expounded. And since the practice is not only the eight-factored and five-factored paths, but the associated phenomena exceeding fifty are also indeed the practice, therefore, to show that method, the third, all-inclusive section is also expounded. Here, the statement 'the remaining phenomena are associated with the practice leading to the cessation of suffering' is omitted. The rest is similar in all respects.

Tattha aṭṭhaṅgikavārassa “taṇhāya avasesānañca kilesānaṃ pahāna”ntiādīsu pañcasu koṭṭhāsesu paṭhamakoṭṭhāse tāva sotāpattimagge jhānābhinivese suddhikapaṭipadā, suddhikasuññatā, suññatapaṭipadā, suddhikaappaṇihitaṃ, appaṇihitapaṭipadāti imesu pañcasu vāresu dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ catukkapañcakanayānaṃ vasena dasa nayā honti. Evaṃ sesesupīti vīsatiyā abhinivesesu dve nayasatāni. Tāni catūhi adhipatīhi catugguṇitāni aṭṭha[M 0.0116]. Iti suddhikāni dve sādhipatī aṭṭhāti sabbampi nayasahassaṃ hoti. Yathā ca sotāpattimagge, evaṃ sesamaggesupīti cattāri nayasahassāni honti. Yathā ca paṭhamakoṭṭhāse cattāri, evaṃ sesesupīti aṭṭhaṅgikavāre pañcasu koṭṭhāsesu vīsati nayasahassāni honti. Tathā pañcaṅgikavāre sabbasaṅgāhikavāre cāti sabbānipi saṭṭhi [P 0.0124] nayasahassāni satthārā vibhattāni. Pāḷi pana saṅkhepena āgatā. Evamidaṃ tividhamahāvāraṃ pañcadasakoṭṭhāsaṃ saṭṭhinayasahassapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ abhidhammabhājanīyaṃ nāma niddiṭṭhanti veditabbaṃ.

In the eight-factored section, in the first division among the five divisions beginning with 'the abandonment of craving and the remaining defilements,' there are, for the jhāna-absorption in the stream-entry path, ten methods across these five sections: pure practice, pure emptiness, emptiness practice, pure signlessness, and signlessness practice. Thus, in the twenty absorptions, there are two hundred methods. These, multiplied by the four dominants, become eight hundred. Thus, the pure methods are two hundred, and with dominants, eight hundred, making a total of a thousand methods. And just as in the stream-entry path, so too in the remaining paths—thus, there are four thousand methods. And just as in the first division there are four thousand, so too in the remaining divisions—thus, in the eight-factored section across five divisions, there are twenty thousand methods. Similarly, in the five-factored section and in the all-inclusive section—thus, all together, sixty thousand methods have been distinguished by the Teacher. The Pāḷi text, however, is presented concisely. Thus, this threefold great section, with fifteen divisions, adorned with sixty thousand methods, should be understood as the exposition called the Abhidhamma Exposition.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Abhidhamma Exposition.

3. Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Section of Questions.

215. Pañhāpucchake catunnampi saccānaṃ khandhavibhaṅge vuttanayānusāreneva kusalādibhāvo veditabbo. Ārammaṇattikesu pana samudayasaccaṃ kāmāvacaradhamme assādentassa parittārammaṇaṃ hoti, mahaggatadhamme assādentassa mahaggatārammaṇaṃ, paññattiṃ assādentassa navattabbārammaṇaṃ. Dukkhasaccaṃ [V 0.0116] kāmāvacaradhamme ārabbha uppannaṃ parittārammaṇaṃ, rūpārūpāvacaradhamme ārabbha uppattikāle mahaggatārammaṇaṃ, nava lokuttaradhamme paccavekkhaṇakāle appamāṇārammaṇaṃ, paṇṇattiṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle navattabbārammaṇaṃ. Maggasaccaṃ sahajātahetuvasena sabbadāpi maggahetukaṃ vīriyaṃ vā vīmaṃsaṃ vā jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā maggabhāvanākāle maggādhipati, chandacittesu aññatarādhipatikāle navattabbaṃ nāma hoti. Dukkhasaccaṃ ariyānaṃ maggapaccavekkhaṇakāle maggārammaṇaṃ, tesaṃyeva maggaṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhaṇakāle maggādhipati, sesadhammapaccavekkhaṇakāle navattabbaṃ hoti.

215. In the Section of Questions, the nature of the four truths—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—should be understood in accordance with the method explained in the Analysis of the Aggregates. However, in the context of the object triads, the truth of origin has a limited object when one savors sense-sphere phenomena, a sublime object when one savors sublime-sphere phenomena, and a non-designatable object when one savors concepts. The truth of suffering, when arising in dependence on sense-sphere phenomena, has a limited object; when arising at the moment of arising in dependence on fine-material and immaterial-sphere phenomena, it has a sublime object; when reviewing the nine supramundane phenomena, it has an immeasurable object; and when reviewing concepts, it has a non-designatable object. The truth of the path, by way of its co-arisen cause, is always path-rooted. At the time of path development, when energy or investigation has been made chief, it has the path as its dominant condition; when either desire or consciousness is the dominant condition, it is called non-designatable. For noble ones, the truth of suffering has the path as its object during the review of the path; when they review the path, esteeming it, the path is the dominant condition; when reviewing the remaining phenomena, it is called non-designatable.

Dve saccānīti dukkhasamudayasaccāni. Etāni hi atītādibhede dhamme ārabbha uppattikāle atītādiārammaṇāni honti. Samudayasaccaṃ ajjhattādibhede dhamme assādentassa ajjhattādiārammaṇaṃ hoti, dukkhasaccaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanakāle navattabbārammaṇampīti veditabbaṃ. Iti imasmiṃ pañhāpucchake dve saccāni lokiyāni honti, dve lokuttarāni. Yathā [M 0.0117] ca imasmiṃ, evaṃ purimesupi dvīsu. Sammāsambuddhena hi tīsupi suttantabhājanīyādīsu lokiyalokuttarāneva saccāni kathitāni. Evamayaṃ saccavibhaṅgopi teparivaṭṭaṃ nīharitvāva bhājetvā dassitoti.

The two truths are the truth of suffering and the truth of the origin of suffering. These, indeed, arising in dependence upon phenomena distinguished as past and so on, have the past and so on as their object at the time of their arising. The truth of origin, for one who savors phenomena distinguished as internal and so on, has internal and so on as its object; the truth of suffering, at the time of the base of nothingness, is to be understood as also having a non-designatable object. Thus, in this Section of Questions, two truths are mundane, and two are supramundane. And as in this section, so also in the preceding two. For by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, in all three sections—the Suttanta Exposition, the Abhidhamma Exposition, and the Section of Questions—only truths that are mundane and supramundane have been spoken of. Thus, this Analysis of the Truths is also shown by extracting and then analyzing the three rounds.

Sammohavinodanīyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya

In the Sammohavinodanī, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga

Saccavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Analysis of the Truths is completed.

5. Indriyavibhaṅgo

5. The Analysis of the Faculties

1. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Classification

219. Idāni [P 0.0125][M 0.0118][V 0.0117] tadanantare indriyavibhaṅge bāvīsatīti gaṇanaparicchedo. Indriyānīti paricchinnadhammanidassanaṃ. Idāni tāni sarūpato dassento cakkhundriyantiādimāha. Tattha cakkhudvāre indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti cakkhundriyaṃ. Sotaghānajivhākāyadvāre indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti kāyindriyaṃ. Vijānanalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti manindriyaṃ. Itthibhāve indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti itthindriyaṃ. Purisabhāve indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti purisindriyaṃ. Anupālanalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti jīvitindriyaṃ. Sukhalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti sukhindriyaṃ. Dukkhasomanassa domanassa upekkhālakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti upekkhindriyaṃ. Adhimokkhalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti saddhindriyaṃ. Paggahalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti vīriyindriyaṃ. Upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti satindriyaṃ. Avikkhepalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti samādhindriyaṃ. Dassanalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti paññindriyaṃ. Anaññātaññassāmīti pavatte jānanalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ. Ñātānaṃyeva dhammānaṃ puna ājānane indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti aññindriyaṃ. Aññātāvībhāve indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti aññātāvindriyaṃ.

219. Now, immediately following, in the Analysis of the Faculties, 'twenty-two' is the numerical determination. 'Faculties' is the indication of the determined phenomena. Now, showing them according to their own nature, he says, 'the eye faculty,' and so on. Herein, the eye faculty is so called because it exerts control in the eye-door. The ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, and body faculty are so called because they exert control in their respective doors. The mind faculty is so called because it exerts control in the characteristic of cognizing. The femininity faculty is so called because it exerts control in the state of being a woman. The masculinity faculty is so called because it exerts control in the state of being a man. The life faculty is so called because it exerts control in the characteristic of preserving. The pleasure faculty is so called because it exerts control in the characteristic of pleasure. The pain faculty, gladness faculty, sadness faculty, and equanimity faculty are so called because they exert control in their respective characteristics of pain, gladness, sadness, and equanimity. The faith faculty is so called because it exerts control in the characteristic of conviction. The energy faculty is so called because it exerts control in the characteristic of striving. The mindfulness faculty is so called because it exerts control in the characteristic of establishing. The concentration faculty is so called because it exerts control in the characteristic of non-distraction. The wisdom faculty is so called because it exerts control in the characteristic of seeing. The faculty of 'I shall know the unknown' is so called because it exerts control in the characteristic of knowing in the process of 'I shall know the unknown.' The faculty of knowledge is so called because it exerts control in knowing again those very things that are already known. The faculty of one who has known is so called because it exerts control in the state of one who has known.

Idha suttantabhājanīyaṃ nāma na gahitaṃ. Kasmā? Suttante imāya paṭipāṭiyā bāvīsatiyā indriyānaṃ anāgatattā. Suttantasmiñhi katthaci dve indriyāni kathitāni, katthaci tīṇi, katthaci pañca. Evaṃ pana nirantaraṃ dvāvīsati āgatāni nāma natthi. Ayaṃ tāvettha aṭṭhakathānayo. Ayaṃ pana aparo nayo – etesu hi

Here, what is called the Suttanta Classification is not taken up. Why? Because in the Suttas, these twenty-two faculties do not come in this sequence. In the Suttas, sometimes two faculties are taught, sometimes three, sometimes five. But nowhere do all twenty-two appear continuously. This, for now, is the commentarial method here. However, there is another method—for among these,

Atthato [V 0.0118] lakkhaṇādīhi, kamato ca vijāniyā;

Bhedābhedā tathā kiccā, bhūmito ca vinicchayaṃ.

By way of meaning, characteristics, and so on, and by way of order, one should know the determination; likewise by distinctions and non-distinctions, functions, and by way of planes.

Tattha [P 0.0126] cakkhādīnaṃ tāva “cakkhatīti cakkhū”tiādinā nayena attho pakāsito. Pacchimesu pana tīsu paṭhamaṃ ‘pubbabhāge anaññātaṃ amataṃ padaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ vā jānissāmī’ti evaṃ paṭipannassa uppajjanato indriyaṭṭhasambhavato ca anaññātaññassāmītindriyanti vuttaṃ. Dutiyaṃ ājānanato ca indriyaṭṭhasambhavato ca aññindriyaṃ. Tatiyaṃ aññātāvino catūsu saccesu niṭṭhitañāṇakiccassa [M 0.0119] khīṇāsavasseva uppajjanato indriyaṭṭhasambhavato ca aññātāvindriyaṃ.

Herein, first, the meaning of the eye and so on is explained by the method of 'it sees, therefore it is the eye,' and so forth. Regarding the last three, the first, the 'faculty of I shall know the unknown,' is so called because it arises in one who is practicing thus: 'I shall know what was unknown before, the deathless state, or the four truths,' and because the meaning of 'faculty' is established. The second is called the 'faculty of knowledge' because of knowing and because the meaning of 'faculty' is established. The third is called the 'faculty of one who has known' because it arises only in one whose taints are destroyed, who has completed the function of knowledge regarding the four truths, and because the meaning of 'faculty' is established.

Ko panesa indriyaṭṭho nāmāti? Indaliṅgaṭṭho indriyaṭṭho, indadesitaṭṭho indriyaṭṭho, indadiṭṭhaṭṭho indriyaṭṭho, indasiṭṭhaṭṭho indriyaṭṭho, indajuṭṭhaṭṭho indriyaṭṭho. So sabbopi idha yathāyogaṃ yujjati. Bhagavā hi sammāsambuddho paramissariyabhāvato indo. Kusalākusalañca kammaṃ kammesu kassaci issariyābhāvato. Tenevettha kammasañjanitāni indriyāni kusalākusalakammaṃ ulliṅgenti. Tena ca siṭṭhānīti indaliṅgaṭṭhena indasiṭṭhaṭṭhena ca indriyāni. Sabbāneva panetāni bhagavatā yathābhūtato pakāsitāni ca abhisambuddhāni cāti indadesitaṭṭhena indadiṭṭhaṭṭhena ca indriyāni. Teneva bhagavatā munindena kānici gocarāsevanāya, kānici bhāvanāsevanāya sevitānīti indajuṭṭhaṭṭhenapi indriyāni. Apica ādhipaccasaṅkhātena issariyaṭṭhenāpi etāni indriyāni. Cakkhuviññāṇādippavattiyañhi cakkhādīnaṃ siddhamādhipaccaṃ; tasmiṃ tikkhe tikkhattā mande ca mandattāti. Ayaṃ tāvettha ‘atthato’ vinicchayo.

What then is this meaning of 'faculty'? The meaning of 'faculty' is that which bears the mark of a ruler (indaliṅgaṭṭho), that which is declared by a ruler (indadesitaṭṭho), that which is seen by a ruler (indadiṭṭhaṭṭho), that which is ordained by a ruler (indasiṭṭhaṭṭho), and that which is employed by a ruler (indajuṭṭhaṭṭho). All of these meanings apply here as appropriate. For the Blessed One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, is a supreme ruler due to his state of supreme lordship. And wholesome and unwholesome kamma is also a ruler, because there is no lordship of anyone over kamma. Therefore, here, the faculties generated by kamma signify wholesome and unwholesome kamma. And because they are ordained by that kamma, they are faculties by way of bearing the mark of a ruler and by way of being ordained by a ruler. Moreover, all these faculties have been clearly revealed and fully awakened to by the Blessed One as they truly are—hence they are faculties by way of being declared by a ruler and by way of being seen by a ruler. Furthermore, some of these faculties are employed by the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, for cultivating certain ranges, and some for cultivating meditation—thus they are also faculties by way of being employed by a ruler. Additionally, these are faculties because they possess the meaning of lordship, reckoned as dominance. For the eye and others hold established dominance in the arising of eye-consciousness and so forth—because when the faculty is sharp, consciousness is sharp; and when it is dull, consciousness is dull. This, for now, is the determination 'by way of meaning'.

‘Lakkhaṇādīhī’ti lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānehipi cakkhādīnaṃ vinicchayaṃ vijāniyāti attho. Tāni nesaṃ lakkhaṇādīni heṭṭhā vuttanayāneva. Paññindriyādīni hi cattāri atthato amohoyeva. Sesāni tattha sarūpenevāgatāni.

'By means of characteristics, etc.'—this means one should understand the determination of the eye, etc., through characteristics, function, manifestation, and proximate cause. These characteristics, etc., of theirs are as stated below. Indeed, the four faculties beginning with the wisdom faculty are in essence non-delusion. The rest are included there in their own nature.

‘Kamato’ti ayampi desanākkamova. Tattha ajjhattadhammaṃ pariññāya ariyabhūmipaṭilābho hotīti attabhāvapariyāpannāni cakkhundriyādīni paṭhamaṃ desitāni. So panattabhāvo yaṃ dhammaṃ upādāya itthīti vā purisoti [P 0.0127] vā saṅkhaṃ gacchati, ayaṃ soti nidassanatthaṃ tato itthindriyaṃ purisindriyañca[V 0.0119]. So duvidhopi jīvitindriyapaṭibaddhavuttīti ñāpanatthaṃ tato jīvitindriyaṃ. Yāva tassa pavatti tāva etesaṃ vedayitānaṃ anivatti. Yaṃ kiñci vedayitaṃ sabbaṃ taṃ sukhadukkhanti ñāpanatthaṃ tato sukhindriyādīni. Taṃnirodhatthaṃ pana ete dhammā bhāvetabbāti paṭipattidassanatthaṃ tato saddhādīni. Imāya paṭipattiyā esa dhammo paṭhamaṃ attani pātubhavatīti paṭipattiyā amoghabhāvadassanatthaṃ tato anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ. Tasseva phalattā tato anantaraṃ bhāvetabbattā ca tato aññindriyaṃ. Ito paraṃ bhāvanāya imassa adhigamo, adhigate ca panimasmiṃ natthi kiñci uttari [M 0.0120] karaṇīyanti ñāpanatthaṃ ante paramassāsabhūtaṃ aññātāvindriyaṃ desitanti ayamettha kamo.

'In due order'—this too is the order of the teaching. Herein, by fully understanding the internal phenomena, one attains the noble state; thus, the faculties of the eye and so forth, which pertain to individual existence, are first taught. That individual existence, by which one is designated as a woman or a man—to illustrate this, the feminine faculty and masculine faculty are then taught. To make it clear that both are bound to the life faculty, the life faculty is then taught. As long as its continuity exists, so long these feelings persist. To make it clear that whatever is felt is all either pleasure or pain, the pleasure faculty and so forth are then taught. To show the path of practice, namely, that for the cessation of these phenomena these things must be developed, the faculties of faith and so forth are then taught. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the practice, that through this practice this phenomenon first manifests in oneself, the faculty of one who will know the unknown is then taught. Because it is the fruit of that, and must be developed immediately afterward, the faculty of knowledge is then taught. To make it clear that beyond this, the attainment of this is through development, and once this is attained, there is nothing further to be done, the faculty of one who has known is taught last as the ultimate assurance. This is the order here.

‘Bhedābhedā’ti jīvitindriyasseva cettha bhedo. Tañhi rūpajīvitindriyaṃ arūpajīvitindriyanti duvidhaṃ hoti. Sesānaṃ abhedoti evamettha bhedābhedato vinicchayaṃ vijāniyā.

'By way of division and non-division'—here, only the life faculty has a division. For it is twofold: the material life faculty and the immaterial life faculty. The rest are without division. Thus, one should understand the determination by way of division and non-division here.

‘Kiccā’ti kiṃ indriyānaṃ kiccanti ce? Cakkhundriyassa tāva “cakkhāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ indriyapaccayena paccayo”ti vacanato yaṃ taṃ indriyapaccayabhāvena sādhetabbaṃ attano tikkhamandādibhāvena cakkhuviññāṇādidhammānaṃ tikkhamandādisaṅkhātaṃ attākārānuvattāpanaṃ idaṃ ‘kiccaṃ’. Evaṃ sotaghānajivhākāyānaṃ. Manindriyassa pana sahajātadhammānaṃ attano vasavattāpanaṃ, jīvitindriyassa sahajātadhammānupālanaṃ, itthindriyapurisindriyānaṃ itthipurisanimittakuttākappākārānuvidhānaṃ, sukhadukkhasomanassadomanassindriyānaṃ sahajātadhamme abhibhavitvā yathāsakaṃ oḷārikākārānupāpanaṃ, upekkhindriyassa santapaṇītamajjhattākārānupāpanaṃ, saddhādīnaṃ paṭipakkhābhibhavanaṃ sampayuttadhammānañca pasannākārādibhāvasampāpanaṃ, anaññātaññassāmītindriyassa saṃyojanattayappahānañceva sampayuttakānañca [P 0.0128] tappahānābhimukhabhāvakaraṇaṃ, aññindriyassa kāmarāgabyāpādāditanukaraṇapahānañceva sahajātānañca attano vasānuvattāpanaṃ, aññātāvindriyassa sabbakiccesu ussukkappahānañceva amatābhimukhabhāvapaccayatā ca sampayuttānanti evamettha kiccato vinicchayaṃ vijāniyā.

'By way of function'—if it is asked, what is the function of the faculties? First, regarding the eye faculty: as it is said, 'The eye-base is a condition for the eye-consciousness element and its associated states by way of the faculty condition.' Thus, its 'function' is that which is to be accomplished by way of the faculty condition, namely, causing eye-consciousness and other states to conform to its own characteristic of sharpness, dullness, and so forth. Similarly for the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties. For the mind faculty, its function is to bring its co-arisen states under its control. For the life faculty, it is the maintenance of its co-arisen states. For the femininity and masculinity faculties, it is the fashioning of the signs, deportment, conduct, and appearance characteristic of a woman or a man. For the pleasure, pain, joy, and displeasure faculties, it is overpowering their co-arisen states and imparting their respective gross characteristics. For the equanimity faculty, it is imparting a peaceful, refined, and balanced characteristic. For the faith faculty and others, it is overcoming opposing states and imparting the state of clear confidence and other modes to their associated states. For the faculty of one who will know the unknown, it is both the abandoning of the three fetters and directing its associated states toward that abandonment. For the faculty of knowledge, it is both the attenuation and abandoning of sensual desire, ill will, and so forth, and bringing its co-arisen states under its control. For the faculty of one who has known, it is both the abandoning of striving in all activities and being a condition for facing the Deathless, along with its associated states. Thus, one should understand here the determination with respect to function.

‘Bhūmito’ti cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyaitthipurisasukhadukkhadomanassindriyāni cettha kāmāvacarāneva[V 0.0120]. Manindriyajīvitindriyaupekkhindriyāni, saddhāvīriyasatisamādhipaññindriyāni ca catubhūmipariyāpannāni. Somanassindriyaṃ kāmāvacara-rūpāvacara-lokuttaravasena bhūmittayapariyāpannaṃ. Avasāne tīṇi lokuttarānevāti evaṃ bhūmito vinicchayaṃ vijāniyā. Evañhi vijānanto –

'By way of plane'—here, the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, the feminine faculty, the masculine faculty, pleasure, pain, and displeasure belong solely to the sense-sphere. The faculties of mind, life, and equanimity, and the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, are included in all four planes. The faculty of joy is included in three planes: the sense-sphere, the form-sphere, and the supramundane. Finally, the three are exclusively supramundane. Thus, one should understand the determination by way of plane. For one who understands thus—

Saṃvegabahulo bhikkhu, ṭhito indriyasaṃvare;

Indriyāni pariññāya, dukkhassantaṃ nigacchatīti.

The monk abundant in urgency, established in restraint of the faculties; Having fully understood the faculties, he reaches the end of suffering.

220. Niddesavāre [M 0.0121] “yaṃ cakkhu catunnaṃ mahābhūtāna”ntiādi sabbaṃ dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ padabhājane (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 595 ādayo) vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Vīriyindriyasamādhindriyaniddesādīsu ca sammāvāyāmo micchāvāyāmo sammāsamādhi micchāsamādhītiādīni na vuttāni. Kasmā? Sabbasaṅgāhakattā. Sabbasaṅgāhakāni hi idha indriyāni kathitāni. Evaṃ santepettha dasa indriyāni lokiyāni kāmāvacarāneva, tīṇi lokuttarāni, nava lokiyalokuttaramissakānīti.

220. In the section of definitions, 'the eye which is of the four great elements,' and so forth, all should be understood in the same way as stated in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī's word analysis (beginning at Dhs. Aṭṭha. 595 ff.). In the definitions of the faculty of energy and the faculty of concentration, etc., right effort, wrong effort, right concentration, wrong concentration, and so on, are not mentioned. Why? Because of their all-inclusive nature. Indeed, here the faculties are described as all-inclusive. Thus, in this context, ten faculties are mundane, pertaining only to the sense sphere; three are supramundane; and nine are mixed, being both mundane and supramundane.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition.

2. Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Question Section

221. Pañhāpucchake sabbesampi indriyānaṃ kusalādivibhāgo pāḷinayānusāreneva veditabbo.

221. In the Question Section, the classification of all faculties as wholesome and so forth should be understood in accordance with the method of the Pāli text.

223. Ārammaṇattikesu pana sattindriyā anārammaṇāti cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyaitthipurisindriyāni sandhāya vuttaṃ. Jīvitindriyaṃ pana arūpamissakattā idha anābhaṭṭhaṃ. Dvindriyāti dve indriyā; sukhadukkhadvayaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tañhi ekantaparittārammaṇaṃ. Domanassindriyaṃ siyā parittārammaṇaṃ, siyā mahaggatārammaṇanti [P 0.0129] kāmāvacaradhamme ārabbha pavattikāle parittārammaṇaṃ hoti[V 0.0121], rūpāvacarārūpāvacare pana ārabbha pavattikāle mahaggatārammaṇaṃ, paṇṇattiṃ ārabbha pavattikāle navattabbārammaṇaṃ. Navindriyā siyā parittārammaṇāti manindriyajīvitindriyasomanassindriyaupekkhindriyāni ceva saddhādipañcakañca sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ. Jīvitindriyañhi rūpamissakattā anārammaṇesu rūpadhammesu saṅgahitampi arūpakoṭṭhāsena siyāpakkhe saṅgahitaṃ.

223. Now, in the triplets on objects, the statement that seven faculties are without an object is said with reference to the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, femininity, and masculinity. The life faculty, however, is not mentioned here because it is mixed with the immaterial. The term 'two faculties' refers to the pair of pleasure and pain. For these exclusively have a limited object. The displeasure faculty may have a limited object or may have a sublime object; when it arises in relation to sense-sphere phenomena, it has a limited object; when it arises in relation to form-sphere or formless-sphere phenomena, it has a sublime object; when it arises in relation to a concept, its object is inexpressible. The statement that nine faculties may have a limited object is said with reference to the mind faculty, life faculty, joy faculty, equanimity faculty, and the fivefold set of faith and so forth. For the life faculty, although included among the objectless material phenomena due to its association with materiality, is also included in the 'may be' category on account of its immaterial portion.

Cattāri indriyānīti sukhadukkhadomanassaaññātāvindriyāni. Tāni hi maggārammaṇattike na bhajanti. Maggahetukanti sahajātahetuṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Vīriyavīmaṃsājeṭṭhakakāle siyā maggādhipati, chandacittajeṭṭhakakāle siyā navattabbā.

The four faculties are the faculties of pleasure, pain, displeasure, and the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown.' These indeed are not included in the triad with a path-object. 'Path-conditioned' is said with reference to the co-nascent condition. At the time when energy and investigation are foremost, the path may be the dominant condition. At the time when desire and consciousness are foremost, it should not be asserted.

Dasindriyā [M 0.0122] siyā uppannā, siyā uppādinoti satta rūpindriyāni tīṇi ca vipākindriyāni sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Dasindriyāni domanassena saddhiṃ heṭṭhā vuttāneva. Tattha domanassindriyaṃ paṇṇattiṃ ārabbha pavattikāle navattabbārammaṇaṃ, sesāni nibbānapaccavekkhaṇakālepi. Tīṇindriyāni bahiddhārammaṇānīti tīṇi lokuttarindriyāni. Cattārīti sukhadukkhasomanassadomanassāni. Tāni hi ajjhattadhammepi bahiddhādhammepi ārabbha pavattanti. Aṭṭhindriyāti manindriyajīvitindriyaupekkhindriyāni ceva saddhādipañcakañca. Tattha ākiñcaññāyatanakāle navattabbārammaṇatā veditabbā.

The ten faculties 'may be arisen' or 'may be arising'—this is said with reference to the seven material faculties and the three resultant faculties. The ten faculties together with displeasure have been stated previously. Among them, the faculty of displeasure, at the time of its occurrence taking a concept as its object, has an unassertable object; the remaining ones also at the time of reviewing Nibbāna. The three faculties have external objects—these are the three supramundane faculties. The four are pleasure, pain, joy, and displeasure. For they arise taking both internal and external phenomena as their objects. The eight faculties are the mind faculty, life faculty, equanimity faculty, and the fivefold group beginning with faith. Here, the state of having an unassertable object should be understood at the time of the base of nothingness.

Iti imasmimpi pañhāpucchake dasindriyāni kāmāvacarāni, tīṇi lokuttarāni, nava lokiyalokuttaramissakāneva kathitānīti. Ayampi abhidhammabhājanīyena saddhiṃ ekaparicchedova hoti. Ayaṃ pana indriyavibhaṅgo dveparivaṭṭaṃ nīharitvā bhājetvā dassitoti.

Thus, in this section of questions, ten faculties are of the sense-sphere, three are supramundane, and nine are a mixture of mundane and supramundane—so it is said. This too, together with the Abhidhamma division, forms a single chapter. This analysis of the faculties, however, is presented by extracting and dividing it into two rounds.

Sammohavinodaniyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya

In the Sammohavinodanī, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga.

Indriyavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Analysis of the Faculties is concluded.

6. Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅgo

6. The Analysis of Dependent Arising

1. Suttantabhājanīyaṃ uddesavāravaṇṇanā

1. The Exposition of the Summary Section of the Suttanta Division

225. Idāni [P 0.0130][M 0.0123][V 0.0122] tadanantare paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅge yā “ayaṃ avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā nayena tanti nikkhittā, tassā atthasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ karontena vibhajjavādimaṇḍalaṃ otaritvā ācariye anabbhācikkhantena sakasamayaṃ avokkamantena parasamayaṃ anāyūhantena suttaṃ appaṭibāhantena vinayaṃ anulomentena mahāpadese olokentena dhammaṃ dīpentena atthaṃ saṅgahantena tamevatthaṃ puna āvattetvā aparehipi pariyāyehi niddisantena ca yasmā atthasaṃvaṇṇanā kātabbā hoti, pakatiyāpi ca dukkarāva paṭiccasamuppādassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanā, yathāhu porāṇā –

225. Now, immediately following, in the Analysis of Dependent Arising, where the textual thread is laid out in the manner of 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise,' and so on, in explaining its meaning, one must enter the circle of the Vibhajjavādins, without misrepresenting the teachers, without abandoning one's own doctrine, without confounding other doctrines, without rejecting the Suttas, while conforming to the Vinaya, looking to the Great Standards, illuminating the Dhamma, and summarizing the meaning. And having returned to that same meaning, one must also point it out through other methods. Because the explanation of the meaning must be done in this way, and because the explanation of the meaning of Dependent Arising is inherently difficult, as the ancients have said:

“Saccaṃ satto paṭisandhi, paccayākārameva ca;

Duddasā caturo dhammā, desetuñca sudukkarā”ti.

'Truth, a being, rebirth-linking, and the mode of conditionality—these four things are hard to see and very hard to teach.'

Tasmā “aññatra āgamādhigamappattehi na sukarā paṭiccasamuppādassa atthavaṇṇanā”ti paritulayitvā –

Therefore, having considered that 'Except for those who have attained mastery through learning and realization, it is not easy to explain the meaning of Dependent Arising,' –

Vattukāmo ahaṃ ajja, paccayākāravaṇṇanaṃ;

Patiṭṭhaṃ nādhigacchāmi, ajjhogāḷhova sāgaraṃ.

I wish to speak today on the exposition of the mode of conditionality, but I find no foothold, as if plunged into the ocean.

Sāsanaṃ [V 0.0123] panidaṃ nānā-desanānayamaṇḍitaṃ;

Pubbācariyamaggo ca, abbocchinno pavattati.

Yet this Dispensation is adorned with various teachings and methods, and the path of the ancient teachers continues unbroken.

Yasmā tasmā tadubhayaṃ, sannissāyatthavaṇṇanaṃ;

Ārabhissāmi etassa, taṃ suṇātha samāhitā.

Therefore, relying on both, I shall begin the explanation of its meaning. Listen to it with a concentrated mind.

Vuttañhetaṃ pubbācariyehi –

For this was said by the former teachers:

“Yo kocimaṃ aṭṭhiṃ katvā suṇeyya,

Labhetha pubbāpariyaṃ visesaṃ;

Laddhāna pubbāpariyaṃ visesaṃ,

Adassanaṃ maccurājassa gacche”ti.

'Whoever, having made this their core concern, would listen, would gain a special understanding of the sequence. Having gained a special understanding of the sequence, they would go beyond the sight of the King of Death.'

Avijjāpaccayā [P 0.0131][M 0.0124] saṅkhārātiādīsu hi āditoyeva tāva –

Indeed, in the sequence 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations,' and so on, from the very beginning –

Desanābhedato attha-lakkhaṇekavidhādito;

Aṅgānañca vavatthānā, viññātabbo vinicchayo.

The analysis should be understood in terms of the divisions of the teaching, from the meaning, characteristic, and onefoldness, and from the determination of the factors.

Tattha ‘desanābhedato’ti bhagavato hi vallihārakānaṃ catunnaṃ purisānaṃ valliggahaṇaṃ viya ādito vā majjhato vā paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānaṃ, tathā pariyosānato vā majjhato vā paṭṭhāya yāva ādīti catubbidhā paṭiccasamuppādadesanā. Yathā hi vallihārakesu catūsu purisesu eko valliyā mūlameva paṭhamaṃ passati, so taṃ mūle chetvā sabbaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā ādāya kamme upaneti, evaṃ bhagavā “iti kho, bhikkhave, avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā…pe… jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti ādito (ma. ni. 1.402) paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānāpi paṭiccasamuppādaṃ deseti.

Here, 'in terms of the divisions of the teaching': Just as with the grasping of a creeper by four men who are gathering creepers, there are four kinds of teachings on Dependent Arising: from the beginning or from the middle, starting all the way to the end, or likewise from the end or the middle, starting all the way to the beginning. Just as among four men gathering creepers, one man first sees the root of the creeper, he cuts it at the root, pulls the whole thing out, and brings it to use, so too the Blessed One teaches Dependent Arising from the beginning to the end: 'Thus, bhikkhus, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations... with birth as condition, aging-and-death' (MN 1.402).

Yathā pana tesu purisesu eko valliyā majjhaṃ paṭhamaṃ passati, so majjhe chinditvā uparibhāgaṃyeva ākaḍḍhitvā ādāya kamme upaneti, evaṃ bhagavā “tassa taṃ vedanaṃ abhinandato [V 0.0124] abhivadato ajjhosāya tiṭṭhato uppajjati nandī; yā vedanāsu nandī, tadupādānaṃ, tassupādānapaccayā bhavo, bhavapaccayā jātī”ti (ma. ni. 1.409; saṃ. ni. 3.5) majjhato paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānāpi deseti.

And just as among those men, one first sees the middle of the creeper, cuts it in the middle, pulls out only the upper part, and brings it to use, so too the Blessed One teaches from the middle to the end: 'For one who delights in that feeling, welcomes it, and remains holding to it, delight arises; whatever delight there is in feelings, that is clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth...' (MN 1.409; SN 3.5).

Yathā ca tesu purisesu eko valliyā aggaṃ paṭhamaṃ passati, so agge gahetvā aggānusārena yāva mūlā sabbaṃ ādāya kamme upaneti, evaṃ bhagavā “jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, jātipaccayā nu kho, bhikkhave, jarāmaraṇaṃ no vā kathaṃ vā ettha hotī”ti? “Jātipaccayā, bhante, jarāmaraṇaṃ; evaṃ no ettha hoti – jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti. “Bhavapaccayā jāti…pe… avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, avijjāpaccayā nu kho, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā no vā kathaṃ vā ettha hotī”ti? “Avijjāpaccayā, bhante, saṅkhārā; evaṃ no ettha hoti – avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti pariyosānato paṭṭhāya yāva āditopi paṭiccasamuppādaṃ deseti.

And just as among those men, one first sees the tip of the creeper, takes hold of the tip, and following the tip to the root, takes the whole thing and brings it to use, so too the Blessed One teaches Dependent Arising from the end back to the beginning: '“With birth as condition, aging-and-death”—this is what was said. Now, bhikkhus, is it that with birth as condition there is aging-and-death, or not, or how is it in this case?” “With birth as condition, Venerable Sir, there is aging-and-death; this is how it is for us in this case: with birth as condition, aging-and-death.” “With existence as condition, birth... with ignorance as condition, volitional formations”—this is what was said. Now, bhikkhus, is it that with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations, or not, or how is it in this case?” “With ignorance as condition, Venerable Sir, there are volitional formations; this is how it is for us in this case: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations.”'

Yathā pana tesu purisesu eko valliyā majjhameva paṭhamaṃ passati, so majjhe chinditvā heṭṭhā otaranto yāva mūlā [P 0.0132] ādāya kamme upaneti[M 0.0125], evaṃ bhagavā “ime, bhikkhave, cattāro āhārā kiṃ nidānā, kiṃ samudayā, kiṃ jātikā, kiṃ pabhavā? Ime cattāro āhārā taṇhānidānā, taṇhāsamudayā, taṇhājātikā, taṇhāpabhavā. Taṇhā cāyaṃ, bhikkhave, kiṃ nidānā? Vedanā, phasso, saḷāyatanaṃ, nāmarūpaṃ, viññāṇaṃ. Saṅkhārā kiṃ nidānā…pe… saṅkhārā avijjānidānā, avijjāsamudayā, avijjājātikā, avijjāpabhavā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.11) majjhato paṭṭhāya yāva ādito deseti.

Just as among those men, one first sees the middle of a vine, cuts it in the middle, and, descending, takes it down to the root and puts it to use, so the Blessed One teaches from the middle back to the beginning: 'Bhikkhus, these four nutriments—what is their source, what is their origin, from what are they born, from what do they arise? These four nutriments have craving as their source, craving as their origin, are born from craving, and arise from craving. And this craving, bhikkhus—what is its source? Feeling...pe... Volitional formations—what is their source? Volitional formations have ignorance as their source, ignorance as their origin, are born from ignorance, and arise from ignorance' (SN 12.11).

Kasmā panevaṃ desetīti? Paṭiccasamuppādassa samantabhaddakattā, sayañca desanāvilāsappattattā. Samantabhaddako hi paṭiccasamuppādo tato tato ñāyappaṭivedhāya saṃvattatiyeva. Desanāvilāsappatto ca bhagavā catuvesārajjappaṭisambhidāyogena catubbidhagambhīrabhāvappattiyā ca. So desanāvilāsappattattā nānānayeheva dhammaṃ deseti. Visesato panassa yā ādito paṭṭhāya anulomadesanā, sā pavattikāraṇavibhāgasammūḷhaṃ veneyyajanaṃ samanupassato yathāsakehi kāraṇehi pavattisandassanatthaṃ uppattikkamasandassanatthañca pavattitāti ñātabbā.

Why indeed does he teach in this way? Because Dependent Origination is wholly excellent, and because he himself has attained the elegance of teaching. For Dependent Origination is indeed wholly excellent, conducive to the penetration of understanding from every aspect. And the Blessed One has attained the elegance of teaching through the possession of the four fearlessnesses and the analytical knowledges, and through the attainment of the fourfold profundity. Because he has attained the elegance of teaching, he expounds the Dhamma in various ways. Especially, his teaching in forward order from the beginning should be understood as having been set forth for the purpose of showing the process of becoming according to its respective causes to those to be trained who are confused about the divisions of the causes of becoming, and for the purpose of demonstrating the order of arising.

Yā [V 0.0125] pariyosānato paṭṭhāya paṭilomadesanā, sā “kicchaṃ vatāyaṃ loko āpanno jāyati ca jīyati ca mīyati cā”ti (dī. ni. 2.57) ādinā nayena kicchāpannaṃ lokamanuvilokayato pubbabhāgappaṭivedhānusārena tassa tassa jarāmaraṇādikassa dukkhassa attanādhigatakāraṇasandassanatthaṃ. Yā pana majjhato paṭṭhāya yāva ādi, sā āhāranidānavavatthāpanānusārena yāva atītaṃ addhānaṃ atiharitvā puna atītaddhato pabhuti hetuphalapaṭipāṭisandassanatthaṃ. Yā pana majjhato paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānā pavattā, sā paccuppanne addhāne anāgataddhahetusamuṭṭhānato pabhuti anāgataddhasandassanatthaṃ. Tāsu yā sā pavattikāraṇasammūḷhassa veneyyajanassa yathāsakehi kāraṇehi pavattisandassanatthaṃ uppattikkamasandassanatthañca ādito paṭṭhāya anulomadesanā vuttā, sā idha nikkhittāti veditabbā.

The teaching in reverse order, starting from the end, is for one who observes the world fallen into difficulty—in the manner of, 'Alas, this world has fallen into difficulty—it is born, ages, and dies' (DN 2.57)—to show, in accordance with the penetration of the prior part, the cause he himself has realized for each kind of suffering, such as aging-and-death. The teaching that proceeds from the middle back to the beginning is for the purpose of showing the sequence of cause and effect from the past time onwards, having traced it back to the past time in accordance with the establishment of the source of nutriment. The teaching that proceeds from the middle to the end is for the purpose of showing the future time, starting from the arising in the present time of causes for the future time. Among these, that teaching in forward order from the beginning, which was stated for the purpose of showing the process of becoming according to its respective causes to those to be trained who are confused about the causes of becoming, and for the purpose of demonstrating the order of arising—it should be understood that this is the one set forth here.

Kasmā [P 0.0133] panettha avijjā ādito vuttā? Kiṃ pakativādīnaṃ pakati viya avijjāpi akāraṇaṃ mūlakāraṇaṃ lokassāti? Na akāraṇaṃ. “Āsavasamudayā avijjāsamudayo”ti hi avijjāya kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Atthi [M 0.0126] pana pariyāyo yena mūlakāraṇaṃ siyā. Ko pana soti? Vaṭṭakathāya sīsabhāvo. Bhagavā hi vaṭṭakathaṃ kathento dve dhamme sīsaṃ katvā kathesi – avijjaṃ vā bhavataṇhaṃ vā. Yathāha – “purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi na paññāyati avijjāya ‘ito pubbe avijjā nāhosi, atha pacchā samabhavī’ti. Evañcetaṃ, bhikkhave, vuccati, atha ca pana paññāyati ‘idappaccayā avijjā”ti (a. ni. 10.61); bhavataṇhaṃ vā, yathāha – “purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi na paññāyati bhavataṇhāya ‘ito pubbe bhavataṇhā nāhosi, atha pacchā samabhavī’ti. Evañcetaṃ, bhikkhave, vuccati, atha ca pana paññāyati ‘idappaccayā bhavataṇhā”ti (a. ni. 10.62).

Why is ignorance mentioned first here? Is ignorance, like the primordial nature of the naturalists, a root cause of the world that is itself without a cause? No, it is not without a cause. For it is said, 'With the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance'—thus a cause for ignorance is stated. But there is a sense in which it can be a root cause. What is that? Its being the head of the discourse on the round of existence. For when the Blessed One gave a discourse on the round, he made two things the head—either ignorance or craving for existence. As he said: 'Bhikkhus, a first point of ignorance is not discerned, such that one could say: “Before this, ignorance did not exist, and afterwards it came to be.” Yet, bhikkhus, though this is said, it is discerned: “Ignorance is conditioned by this.”' (AN 10.61); or craving for existence, as he said: 'Bhikkhus, a first point of craving for existence is not discerned, such that one could say: “Before this, craving for existence did not exist, and afterwards it came to be.” Yet, bhikkhus, though this is said, it is discerned: “Craving for existence is conditioned by this.”' (AN 10.62).

Kasmā pana bhagavā vaṭṭakathaṃ kathento ime dveva dhamme sīsaṃ katvā kathesīti? Sugatiduggatigāmino kammassa visesahetubhūtattā. Duggatigāmino hi kammassa visesahetu avijjā. Kasmā? Yasmā avijjābhibhūto puthujjano, aggisantāpalaguḷābhighātaparissamābhibhūtā vajjhagāvī tāya parissamāturatāya nirassādampi attano anatthāvahampi ca uṇhodakapānaṃ viya, kilesasantāpato nirassādampi duggativinipātato ca attano anatthāvahampi pāṇātipātādimanekappakāraṃ duggatigāmikammaṃ ārabhati. Sugatigāmino pana kammassa visesahetu bhavataṇhā. Kasmā?
