Yasmā bhavataṇhābhibhūto puthujjano, yathā vuttappakārā gāvī [V 0.0126] sītudakataṇhāya saassādaṃ attano parissamavinodanañca sītudakapānaṃ viya, kilesasantāpavirahato saassādaṃ sugatisampāpanena attano duggatidukkhaparissamavinodanañca pāṇātipātāveramaṇīādimanekappakāraṃ sugatigāmikammaṃ ārabhati.

Why, then, when giving a discourse on the round of existence, did the Blessed One make only these two things the head? Because they are the specific causes for kamma that leads to good and bad destinations. For the specific cause of kamma leading to a bad destination is ignorance. Why? Because an ordinary person, overcome by ignorance—like a cow condemned to slaughter, tormented by the heat of a firebrand and the blows of a club, and overcome by exhaustion, who, afflicted by that exhaustion, drinks hot water even though it is unsatisfying and harmful to itself—similarly, because of the heat of the defilements, undertakes various kinds of kamma leading to a bad destination, such as killing living beings, even though it is unsatisfying and harmful to oneself on account of leading to bad destinations and ruin. On the other hand, the specific cause of kamma leading to a good destination is craving for existence. Why? Because an ordinary person, overcome by craving for existence—like the aforementioned cow who, thirsting for cool water, drinks cool water, which is satisfying and relieves its exhaustion—similarly, because of freedom from the heat of the defilements, undertakes various kinds of kamma leading to a good destination, such as abstaining from killing living beings, which is satisfying and relieves the suffering and exhaustion of a bad destination by leading to the attainment of a good destination.

Etesu pana vaṭṭakathāya sīsabhūtesu dhammesu katthaci bhagavā [P 0.0134] ekadhammamūlikaṃ desanaṃ deseti, seyyathidaṃ – “iti kho, bhikkhave, avijjūpanisā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārūpanisaṃ viññāṇa”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.23). Tathā “upādānīyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati, taṇhāpaccayā upādāna”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.52). Katthaci ubhayamūlikampi, seyyathidaṃ – “avijjānīvaraṇassa, bhikkhave, bālassa taṇhāya sampayuttassa evamayaṃ kāyo samudāgato. Iti ayañceva kāyo bahiddhā ca nāmarūpaṃ itthetaṃ [M 0.0127] dvayaṃ, dvayaṃ paṭicca phasso, saḷevāyatanāni yehi phuṭṭho bālo sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedetī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.19). Tāsu tāsu desanāsu “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti ayamidha avijjāvasena ekadhammamūlikā desanāti veditabbā. Evaṃ tāvettha desanābhedato viññātabbo vinicchayo.

In these phenomena that are the head of the discourse on the round, the Blessed One sometimes gives a discourse rooted in a single principle, such as: “Thus, monks, ignorance is a supporting condition for volitional formations; volitional formations are a supporting condition for consciousness,” and so on (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.23). Similarly, “Monks, when one dwells contemplating the allure in things that are prone to clinging, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging arises,” and so on (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.52). Sometimes, the teaching is rooted in both principles, such as: “Monks, for a fool hindered by ignorance and connected with craving, this body has thus arisen. So there is this body and external name-and-form: thus this duality. Dependent on the duality, contact arises. Through the six sense bases, the fool experiences pleasure and pain” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.19). Among these various discourses, the statement “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise” should be understood here as a discourse rooted in a single principle by way of ignorance. Thus, the analysis here should first be understood in terms of the distinctions among the discourses.

‘Atthato’ti avijjādīnaṃ padānaṃ atthato, seyyathidaṃ – pūretuṃ ayuttaṭṭhena kāyaduccaritādi avindiyaṃ nāma; aladdhabbanti attho. Taṃ avindiyaṃ vindatīti avijjā. Tabbiparītato kāyasucaritādi vindiyaṃ nāma. Taṃ vindiyaṃ na vindatīti avijjā. Khandhānaṃ rāsaṭṭhaṃ, āyatanānaṃ āyatanaṭṭhaṃ, dhātūnaṃ suññaṭṭhaṃ, saccānaṃ tathaṭṭhaṃ, indriyānaṃ ādhipateyyaṭṭhaṃ aviditaṃ karotīti avijjā. Dukkhādīnaṃ pīḷanādivasena vuttaṃ catubbidhaṃ catubbidhaṃ atthaṃ aviditaṃ karotītipi avijjā. Antavirahite saṃsāre sabbayonigatibhavaviññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsesu satte javāpetīti avijjā. Paramatthato avijjamānesu itthipurisādīsu javati, vijjamānesupi khandhādīsu na javatīti avijjā. Apica cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ vatthārammaṇānaṃ paṭiccasamuppādapaṭiccasamuppannānañca dhammānaṃ chādanatopi avijjā.

‘By way of meaning’ refers to the meaning of terms such as ignorance, as follows: because it is unfit to be undertaken, bodily misconduct and so on is called ‘unacquirable’; the meaning is ‘not to be obtained.’ That which makes one acquire what is unacquirable is ignorance. Conversely, because it is fit to be undertaken, bodily good conduct and so on is called ‘acquirable.’ That which makes one not acquire what is acquirable is ignorance. It makes unknown the meaning of the aggregates as a heap, the meaning of the sense bases as a source, the meaning of the elements as void, the meaning of the truths as actual, and the meaning of the faculties as dominant—this is ignorance. It also makes unknown the fourfold meaning of each of the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering, which is explained in terms of oppression and so on—this is ignorance. In the endless round of rebirths, it makes beings run on through all destinations, planes, states of existence, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings—this is ignorance. It makes one run on towards what is non-existent in the ultimate sense, such as a woman or a man, and it makes one not run on towards what is existent in the ultimate sense, such as the aggregates—this is ignorance. Furthermore, it is ignorance because it conceals eye-consciousness and so on, their bases and objects, and the phenomena of dependent origination and those arisen dependently.

Yaṃ paṭicca phalameti so paccayo. Paṭiccāti na vinā tena; taṃ apaccakkhitvāti attho. Etīti uppajjati ceva pavattati cāti attho. Api ca upakārakaṭṭho paccayaṭṭho. Avijjā ca sā paccayo cāti avijjāpaccayo. Tasmā avijjāpaccayā.

That depending on which a result comes to be is a condition. ‘Depending on’ means ‘not without that’; the meaning is ‘not having disregarded that.’ ‘Comes to be’ means both arises and continues. Moreover, the meaning of a condition is that of a support. And that ignorance is a condition, thus ‘ignorance-condition.’ Therefore, ‘with ignorance as condition.’

Saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharontīti [V 0.0127] saṅkhārā. Apica avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārasaddena āgatasaṅkhārā cāti duvidhā saṅkhārā. Tattha puññāpuññāneñjābhisaṅkhārā tayo, kāyavacīcittasaṅkhārā tayoti ime cha avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā[P 0.0135]. Te sabbepi lokiyakusalākusalacetanāmattameva honti.

They construct the conditioned—hence they are formations. Moreover, formations are of two kinds: those that are conditioned by ignorance, and those that are referred to by the word ‘formations.’ Among them, the three—meritorious, demeritorious, and imperturbable formations—and the three—bodily, verbal, and mental formations—these six are formations conditioned by ignorance. All of them are merely worldly wholesome and unwholesome volitions.

Saṅkhatasaṅkhāro, abhisaṅkhatasaṅkhāro, abhisaṅkharaṇasaṅkhāro, payogābhisaṅkhāroti ime pana cattāro saṅkhārasaddena āgatasaṅkhārā. Tattha [M 0.0128] “aniccā vata saṅkhārā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.221, 272; saṃ. ni. 1.186; 2.143) vuttā sabbepi sappaccayā dhammā ‘saṅkhatasaṅkhārā’ nāma. Kammanibbattā tebhūmakā rūpārūpadhammā ‘abhisaṅkhatasaṅkhārā’ti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttā. Tepi “aniccā vata saṅkhārā”ti ettheva saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Visuṃ pana nesaṃ āgataṭṭhānaṃ na paññāyati. Tebhūmakakusalākusalacetanā pana ‘abhisaṅkharaṇakasaṅkhāro’ti vuccati. Tassa “avijjāgatoyaṃ, bhikkhave, purisapuggalo puññañce abhisaṅkharotī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.51) āgataṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati. Kāyikacetasikaṃ pana vīriyaṃ ‘payogābhisaṅkhāro’ti vuccati. So “yāvatikā abhisaṅkhārassa gati, tāvatikaṃ gantvā akkhāhataṃ maññe aṭṭhāsī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.15) āgato.

However, these four—the conditioned formation, the constructed formation, the constructing formation, and the effort-making formation—are formations that are referred to by the word ‘formations.’ Among them, all dependently arisen phenomena mentioned in passages like “Impermanent, alas, are formations” (Dīgha Nikāya 2.221, 272; Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.186; 2.143) are called ‘conditioned formations.’ The material and immaterial phenomena in the three planes of existence produced by kamma are called ‘constructed formations’ in the commentaries. These too are included in the statement ‘Impermanent, alas, are formations.’ However, no specific textual source for them is discernible. But wholesome and unwholesome volitions pertaining to the three planes of existence are called ‘the constructing formation.’ Its textual source is discernible in passages like “This person, monks, overcome by ignorance, constructs a meritorious formation” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.51). Bodily and mental effort, however, is called ‘the effort-making formation.’ It is mentioned in passages like “Having gone as far as the force of the formation extends, he stood there, thinking, ‘I am struck down’” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.15).

Na kevalañca eteyeva, aññepi “saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpajjantassa kho, āvuso visākha, bhikkhuno paṭhamaṃ nirujjhati vacīsaṅkhāro, tato kāyasaṅkhāro, tato cittasaṅkhāro”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.464) nayena saṅkhārasaddena āgatā anekasaṅkhārā. Tesu natthi so saṅkhāro, yo saṅkhatasaṅkhāre saṅgahaṃ na gaccheyya. Ito paraṃ saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇantiādīsu yaṃ vuttaṃ taṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

And not only these, but many other formations are referred to by the word ‘formations’ according to the method in such passages as: “When a monk is attaining the cessation of perception and feeling, friend Visākha, first the verbal formation ceases, then the bodily formation, then the mental formation” (Majjhima Nikāya 1.464). Among those, there is no formation that would not be included in conditioned formations. Hereafter, what is said in passages like ‘with formations as condition, consciousness’ and so on should be understood in the same way as explained.

Avutte pana vijānātīti viññāṇaṃ. Namatīti nāmaṃ. Ruppatīti rūpaṃ. Āye tanoti, āyatañca nayatīti āyatanaṃ. Phusatīti phasso. Vedayatīti vedanā. Paritassatīti taṇhā. Upādiyatīti upādānaṃ. Bhavati bhāvayati cāti bhavo. Jananaṃ jāti. Jīraṇaṃ jarā. Maranti [P 0.0136] etenāti maraṇaṃ. Socanaṃ soko. Paridevanaṃ paridevo. Dukkhayatīti dukkhaṃ; uppādaṭṭhitivasena vā dvedhā khaṇatīti dukkhaṃ. Dummanassa bhāvo domanassaṃ. Bhuso āyāso upāyāso.

‘Consciousness’ (viññāṇa) is so called because it cognizes (vijānāti). ‘Name’ (nāma) is so called because it inclines (namati). ‘Form’ (rūpa) is so called because it is afflicted (ruppati). ‘Sense base’ (āyatana) is so called because it extends (tanoti) an influx (āya) and conducts (nayati) what is extended (āyataṃ). ‘Contact’ (phassa) is so called because it touches (phusati). ‘Feeling’ (vedanā) is so called because it feels (vedayati). ‘Craving’ (taṇhā) is so called because it thirsts (paritassati). ‘Clinging’ (upādāna) is so called because it clings (upādiyati). ‘Becoming’ (bhava) is so called because it becomes (bhavati) and causes to become (bhāvayati). ‘Birth’ (jāti) is generation (jananaṃ). ‘Aging’ (jarā) is growing old (jīraṇaṃ). ‘Death’ (maraṇa) is that by which one dies (maranti etena). ‘Sorrow’ (soka) is sorrowing (socanaṃ). ‘Lamentation’ (parideva) is lamenting (paridevanaṃ). ‘Suffering’ (dukkha) is so called because it afflicts (dukkhayati); or, it wounds (khaṇati) in two ways (dvedhā) by means of arising and persisting. ‘Dejection’ (domanassa) is the state of a sad mind (dummanassa bhāvo). ‘Despair’ (upāyāsa) is intense (bhuso) distress (āyāso).

Sambhavantīti [V 0.0128] nibbattanti. Na kevalañca sokādīheva, atha kho sabbapadehi ‘sambhavantī’ti saddassa yojanā kātabbā. Itarathā hi “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti vutte kiṃ karontīti na paññāyeyyuṃ. “Sambhavantī”ti pana yojanāya sati “avijjā ca sā paccayo cāti avijjāpaccayo; tasmā avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā sambhavantī”ti paccayapaccayuppannavavatthānaṃ kataṃ hoti. Esa nayo sabbattha.

'They arise' means they come into being. And not only with sorrow and the like, but the word 'arise' should be applied to all terms. Otherwise, when it is said, 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations,' it would not be clear what they are doing. But by applying 'arise,' it is established that 'ignorance, and that is a condition, thus “ignorance-as-condition”; therefore, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise'—the distinction between condition and conditioned is made. This method applies everywhere.

Evanti [M 0.0129] niddiṭṭhanayanidassanaṃ. Tena avijjādīheva kāraṇehi, na issaranimmānādīhīti dasseti. Etassāti yathāvuttassa. Kevalassāti asammissassa sakalassa vā. Dukkhakkhandhassāti dukkhasamūhassa, na sattassa, na sukhasubhādīnaṃ. Samudayoti nibbatti. Hotīti sambhavati. Evamettha atthato viññātabbo vinicchayo.

'Thus' is a demonstration of the method as stated. Thereby, it is shown that ignorance and the like are the causes, not a creator or the like. 'Of this' means of what has been stated. 'Entire' means unmixed or whole. 'Mass of suffering' means the aggregate of suffering, not a being, nor pleasure, beauty, and so on. 'Origin' means arising. 'Is' means comes to be. Thus, the determination in this matter should be understood according to its meaning.

‘Lakkhaṇādito’ti avijjādīnaṃ lakkhaṇādito, seyyathidaṃ – aññāṇalakkhaṇā avijjā, sammohanarasā, chādanapaccupaṭṭhānā, āsavapadaṭṭhānā. Abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇā saṅkhārā, āyūhanarasā, cetanāpaccupaṭṭhānā, avijjāpadaṭṭhānā. Vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ viññāṇaṃ, pubbaṅgamarasaṃ, paṭisandhipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, saṅkhārapadaṭṭhānaṃ, vatthārammaṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ vā. Namanalakkhaṇaṃ nāmaṃ, sampayogarasaṃ, avinibbhogapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, viññāṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ, vikiraṇarasaṃ, abyākatapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, viññāṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Āyatanalakkhaṇaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ, dassanādirasaṃ, vatthudvārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ[P 0.0137], nāmarūpapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Phusanalakkhaṇo phasso, saṅghaṭṭanaraso, saṅgatipaccupaṭṭhāno, saḷāyatanapadaṭṭhāno. Anubhavanalakkhaṇā vedanā, visayarasasambhogarasā, sukhadukkhapaccupaṭṭhānā, phassapadaṭṭhānā. Hetulakkhaṇā taṇhā, abhinandanarasā, atittibhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, vedanāpadaṭṭhānā. Gahaṇalakkhaṇaṃ upādānaṃ, amuñcanarasaṃ, taṇhādaḷhattadiṭṭhipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, taṇhāpadaṭṭhānaṃ. Kammakammaphalalakkhaṇo bhavo, bhāvanabhavanaraso, kusalākusalābyākatapaccupaṭṭhāno, upādānapadaṭṭhāno. Jātiādīnaṃ lakkhaṇādīni saccavibhaṅge vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Evamettha lakkhaṇāditopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

'From the standpoint of characteristics, etc.' means from the characteristics, etc., of ignorance and so on, namely: Ignorance has the characteristic of unknowing, its function is delusion, its manifestation is concealment, its proximate cause is the influxes. Volitional formations have the characteristic of forming, their function is accumulation, their manifestation is volition, their proximate cause is ignorance. Consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing, its function is being a forerunner, its manifestation is rebirth-linking, its proximate cause is volitional formations, or the base and object. Name has the characteristic of inclining, its function is association, its manifestation is non-separation, its proximate cause is consciousness. Form has the characteristic of being afflicted, its function is disintegration, its manifestation is the indeterminate, its proximate cause is consciousness. The six sense bases have the characteristic of being sense bases, their function is seeing, etc., their manifestation is the state of being bases and doorways, their proximate cause is name-and-form. Contact has the characteristic of touching, its function is impact, its manifestation is conjunction, its proximate cause is the six sense bases. Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing, its function is enjoying the taste of the object, its manifestation is pleasure and pain, its proximate cause is contact. Craving has the characteristic of being a cause, its function is delighting, its manifestation is insatiability, its proximate cause is feeling. Clinging has the characteristic of grasping, its function is not releasing, its manifestation is strong craving and tenacious view, its proximate cause is craving. Becoming has the characteristic of kamma and kamma-result, its function is generating and being, its manifestation is wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, its proximate cause is clinging. The characteristics, etc., of birth and the rest should be understood in the way stated in the Exposition of the Truths. Thus, in this way, the analysis should also be understood from the standpoint of characteristics, etc.

‘Ekavidhādito’ti ettha avijjā aññāṇādassanamohādibhāvato ekavidhā, appaṭipattimicchāpaṭipattito duvidhā tathā saṅkhārāsaṅkhārato, vedanāttayasampayogato tividhā, catusaccaappaṭivedhato [V 0.0129] catubbidhā, gatipañcakādīnavacchādanato pañcavidhā, dvārārammaṇato pana sabbesupi arūpadhammesu chabbidhatā veditabbā.

'From the single kind onwards' means here ignorance is of one kind due to its nature as non-knowledge, non-seeing, delusion, etc.; of two kinds due to non-practice and wrong practice. Likewise, formations are of two kinds due to being formed and unformed. Ignorance is of three kinds due to association with the three feelings; of four kinds due to non-penetration of the four truths; of five kinds due to concealing the dangers of the five destinations. However, in all immaterial phenomena, a sixfold classification should be understood due to the sense-doors and objects.

Saṅkhārā sāsavavipākadhammadhammādibhāvato ekavidhā, kusalākusalato duvidhā tathā parittamahaggatahīnamajjhimamicchattaniyatāniyatato, tividhā puññābhisaṅkhārādibhāvato, catubbidhā catuyonisaṃvattanato, pañcavidhā pañcagatigāmito.

Formations are of one kind due to their nature as tainted, resultant-natured phenomena, etc.; of two kinds as wholesome and unwholesome, likewise as limited and exalted, inferior and middling, and fixed in wrongness and unfixed; of three kinds due to being meritorious formations, etc.; of four kinds due to leading to the four kinds of birth; of five kinds due to leading to the five destinations.

Viññāṇaṃ [M 0.0130] lokiyavipākādibhāvato ekavidhaṃ, sahetukāhetukādito duvidhaṃ, bhavattayapariyāpannato vedanāttayasampayogato ahetukaduhetukatihetukato ca tividhaṃ, yonigativasena catubbidhaṃ pañcavidhañca.

Consciousness is of one kind due to its nature as mundane, resultant, etc.; of two kinds as rooted and rootless, etc.; of three kinds as comprised within the three planes of existence, associated with the three feelings, and as rootless, with two roots, or with three roots; of four and five kinds by way of birth and destiny.

Nāmarūpaṃ viññāṇasannissayato kammapaccayato ca ekavidhaṃ, sārammaṇānārammaṇato duvidhaṃ, atītādito tividhaṃ, yonigativasena catubbidhaṃ pañcavidhañca.

Name-and-form is of one kind due to dependence on consciousness and due to kamma as condition; of two kinds as with an object and without an object; of three kinds as past, etc.; of four and five kinds by way of birth and destiny.

Saḷāyatanaṃ sañjātisamosaraṇaṭṭhānato ekavidhaṃ, bhūtappasādaviññāṇādito duvidhaṃ, sampattāsampattanobhayagocarato tividhaṃ, yonigatipariyāpannato catubbidhaṃ pañcavidhañcāti iminā nayena phassādīnampi ekavidhādibhāvo veditabboti. Evamettha ekavidhāditopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

The six sense bases are of one kind as the place of arising and convergence; of two kinds from the material elements, sensitivity, consciousness, etc.; of three kinds as having an attainable, unattainable, or both as its range; of four and five kinds as included in the realms of birth and destiny. In this way, the single kind, etc., of contact and the rest should also be understood. Thus, the analysis should be understood here, from the single kind onwards.

‘Aṅgānañca [P 0.0138] vavatthānā’ti sokādayo cettha bhavacakkassa avicchedadassanatthaṃ vuttā. Jarāmaraṇabbhāhatassa hi bālassa te sambhavanti. Yathāha – “assutavā, bhikkhave, puthujjano sārīrikāya dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati sammohamāpajjatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.252). Yāva ca tesaṃ pavatti tāva avijjāyāti punapi avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti sambandhameva hoti bhavacakkaṃ. Tasmā tesampi jarāmaraṇeneva ekasaṅkhepaṃ katvā dvādaseva paṭiccasamuppādaṅgānīti veditabbāni. Evamettha aṅgānaṃ vavatthānatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo. Ayaṃ tāvettha uddesavāravasena saṅkhepakathā.

'And from the determination of the factors': here sorrow, etc., are stated to show the unbroken continuity of the cycle of existence, for these arise in a fool struck by aging and death. As it is said: "When, bhikkhus, an untaught ordinary person is touched by bodily painful feeling, they sorrow, grieve, lament, beat their breast, and become distraught." And as long as these persist, it is because of ignorance. Thus, once again, 'with ignorance as condition, formations,' and so the cycle of existence is indeed connected. Therefore, these too, having been summarized as one with aging-and-death, should be understood as just twelve factors of dependent origination. Thus, the analysis should be understood here from the determination of the factors. This, indeed, is the brief explanation by way of the summary section.

Uddesavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Summary Section is concluded.

Avijjāpadaniddeso

Exposition of the Factor of Ignorance

226. Idāni [V 0.0130] niddesavāravasena vitthārakathā hoti. “Avijjā paccayā saṅkhārā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Tattha avijjāpaccayesu saṅkhāresu dassetabbesu yasmā putte kathetabbe paṭhamaṃ pitā kathīyati. Evañhi sati ‘mittassa [M 0.0131] putto, dattassa putto’ti putto sukathito hoti. Tasmā desanākusalo satthā saṅkhārānaṃ janakatthena pitusadisaṃ avijjaṃ tāva dassetuṃ tattha katamā avijjā? Dukkhe aññāṇantiādimāha.

226. Now, the detailed exposition follows. For it is said: “Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations.” Here, when the volitional formations conditioned by ignorance are to be shown, just as when speaking of a son, the father is spoken of first—for when this is so, the son is well spoken of as ‘the son of Mitta,’ ‘the son of Datta’—so the Teacher, skilled in exposition, first shows ignorance, which is like a father in generating volitional formations. What, then, is ignorance? He says, “Not-knowing concerning suffering,” and so forth.

Tattha yasmā ayaṃ avijjā dukkhasaccassa yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ jānituṃ passituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na deti, chādetvā pariyonandhitvā ganthetvā tiṭṭhati, tasmā “dukkhe aññāṇa”nti vuccati. Tathā yasmā dukkhasamudayassa dukkhanirodhassa dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ jānituṃ passituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na deti, chādetvā pariyonandhitvā ganthetvā tiṭṭhati, tasmā dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya aññāṇanti vuccati. Imesu catūsu ṭhānesu suttantikapariyāyena aññāṇaṃ avijjāti kathitaṃ.

Here, because this ignorance does not allow one to know, see, or penetrate the actual, specific characteristic of the truth of suffering—covering, enveloping, and binding it—it is therefore called ‘not-knowing concerning suffering.’ Similarly, because it does not allow one to know, see, or penetrate the actual, specific characteristic of the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering—covering, enveloping, and binding them—it is therefore called ‘not-knowing concerning the origin of suffering,’ ‘not-knowing concerning the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘not-knowing concerning the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ In these four instances, not-knowing is said to be ignorance (avijjā) according to the Suttanta method.

Nikkhepakaṇḍe (dha. sa. 1067) pana abhidhammapariyāyena “pubbante aññāṇa”nti aparesupi catūsu ṭhānesu aññāṇaṃ gahitaṃ. Tattha [P 0.0139] pubbanteti atīto addhā, atītāni khandhadhātuāyatanāni. Aparanteti anāgato addhā, anāgatāni khandhadhātuāyatanāni. Pubbantāparanteti tadubhayaṃ. Idappaccayatāti saṅkhārādīnaṃ kāraṇāni avijjādīni aṅgāni. Paṭiccasamuppannadhammāti avijjādīhi nibbattā saṅkhārādayo dhammā. Tatrāyaṃ avijjā yasmā atītānaṃ khandhādīnaṃ yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ jānituṃ passituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na deti, chādetvā pariyonandhitvā ganthetvā tiṭṭhati, tasmā “pubbante aññāṇa”nti vuccati. Tathā yasmā anāgatānaṃ khandhādīnaṃ, atītānāgatānaṃ khandhādīnaṃ idappaccayatāya ceva paṭiccasamuppannadhammānañca yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ jānituṃ passituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na deti, chādetvā pariyonandhitvā ganthetvā tiṭṭhati, tasmā idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesu aññāṇanti vuccati. Imesu aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu abhidhammapariyāyena aññāṇaṃ avijjāti kathitaṃ.

In the Nikkhepakaṇḍa (Dhs. 1067), however, according to the Abhidhamma method, ‘not-knowing concerning the past’ is taken, and not-knowing in four other instances as well. There, ‘the past’ means past time, past aggregates, elements, and sense bases. ‘The future’ means future time, future aggregates, elements, and sense bases. ‘Both past and future’ means both of these. ‘This-conditionality’ means the causal factors, the links beginning with ignorance, for formations and so forth. ‘Dependently arisen phenomena’ means the phenomena such as formations produced by ignorance and so forth. Here, because this ignorance does not allow one to know, see, or penetrate the actual, specific characteristic of past aggregates and so forth—covering, enveloping, and binding them—it is therefore called ‘not-knowing concerning the past.’ Similarly, because it does not allow one to know, see, or penetrate the actual, specific characteristic of future aggregates, of past and future aggregates, and of this-conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena—covering, enveloping, and binding them—it is therefore called ‘not-knowing concerning the future,’ ‘not-knowing concerning the past and future,’ and ‘not-knowing concerning this-conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena.’ In these eight instances, not-knowing is said to be ignorance (avijjā) according to the Abhidhamma method.

Evaṃ kiṃ kathitaṃ hoti? Kiccato ceva jātito ca avijjā kathitā nāma hoti. Kathaṃ[V 0.0131]? Ayañhi avijjā imāni aṭṭha ṭhānāni jānituṃ passituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na detīti kiccato kathitā; uppajjamānāpi imesu aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu uppajjatīti jātitopi kathitā. Evaṃ kathetvā puna “yaṃ [M 0.0132] evarūpaṃ aññāṇaṃ adassana”ntiādīni pañcavīsati padāni avijjāya lakkhaṇaṃ dassetuṃ gahitāni.

What, then, has been said in this way? Ignorance is said to be defined both by its function and by its nature. How? This ignorance does not allow one to know, see, or penetrate these eight instances—thus it is defined by its function. Even when arising, it arises in these eight instances—thus it is also defined by its nature. Having spoken thus, further, the twenty-five terms beginning with ‘such not-knowing, non-seeing,’ and so forth, have been taken to show the characteristic of ignorance.

Tattha yasmā ayaṃ avijjā imehi aṭṭhahi padehi kathitāpi puna pañcavīsatiyā padehi lakkhaṇe akathite sukathitā nāma na hoti, lakkhaṇe pana kathiteyeva sukathitā nāma hoti. Yathā puriso naṭṭhaṃ goṇaṃ pariyesamāno manusse puccheyya – “api, ayyā, setaṃ goṇaṃ passatha, rattaṃ goṇaṃ passathā”ti? Te evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – “imasmiṃ raṭṭhe setarattānaṃ goṇānaṃ anto natthi, kiṃ te goṇassa lakkhaṇa”nti? Atha tena ‘saṅghāṭi’ vā ‘naṅgalaṃ’ vāti vutte goṇo sukathito nāma bhaveyya; evameva yasmā ayaṃ avijjā aṭṭhahi padehi kathitāpi puna pañcavīsatiyā padehi lakkhaṇe akathite sukathitā [P 0.0140] nāma na hoti, lakkhaṇe pana kathiteyeva sukathitā nāma hoti. Tasmā yānassā lakkhaṇadassanatthaṃ pañcavīsati padāni kathitāni, tesampi vasena veditabbā.

Here, because although this ignorance has been described with these eight terms, it is not well-described unless its characteristic is described with the twenty-five terms; but only when its characteristic is described is it well-described. Just as a man searching for a lost ox might ask people, “Sirs, have you seen a white ox? Have you seen a red ox?” And they might reply, “In this country, there is no end to white and red oxen. What is the characteristic of your ox?” Then, if he says it is yoke-shouldered or has a plow-shaped mark, the ox would be called well-described. Similarly, although this ignorance has been described with these eight terms, it is not well-described unless its characteristic is explained with the twenty-five terms; but only when its characteristic is explained is it well-described. Therefore, it should be understood also by means of the twenty-five terms that have been explained to show its characteristic.

Seyyathidaṃ – ñāṇaṃ nāma paññā. Sā atthatthaṃ kāraṇakāraṇaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ viditaṃ pākaṭaṃ karoti. Ayaṃ pana avijjā uppajjitvā taṃ viditaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ na detīti ñāṇapaccanīkato aññāṇaṃ. Dassanantipi paññā. Sāpi taṃ ākāraṃ passati. Avijjā pana uppajjitvā taṃ passituṃ na detīti adassanaṃ. Abhisamayotipi paññā. Sā taṃ ākāraṃ abhisameti. Avijjā pana uppajjitvā taṃ abhisametuṃ na detīti anabhisamayo. Anubodho sambodho paṭivedhotipi paññā. Sā taṃ ākāraṃ anubujjhati sambujjhati paṭivijjhati. Avijjā pana uppajjitvā taṃ anubujjhituṃ saṃbujjhituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na detīti ananubodho asambodho appaṭivedho. Saṅgāhanātipi paññā. Sā taṃ ākāraṃ gahetvā ghaṃsitvā gaṇhāti. Avijjā pana uppajjitvā taṃ gahetvā ghaṃsitvā gaṇhituṃ na detīti asaṅgāhanā. Pariyogāhanātipi paññā. Sā taṃ ākāraṃ ogāhitvā anupavisitvā gaṇhāti. Avijjā pana uppajjitvā taṃ ogāhitvā anupavisitvā gaṇhituṃ na detīti apariyogāhanā. Samapekkhanātipi paññā[V 0.0132]. Sā taṃ ākāraṃ samaṃ sammā ca pekkhati. Avijjā pana uppajjitvā taṃ samaṃ sammā ca pekkhituṃ na detīti asamapekkhanā. Paccavekkhaṇātipi paññā. Sā taṃ ākāraṃ paccavekkhati. Avijjā pana uppajjitvā taṃ paccavekkhituṃ na detīti apaccavekkhaṇā. Nāssā [M 0.0133] kiñci kammaṃ paccakkhaṃ atthi, sayañca apaccavekkhitvā kataṃ kammanti apaccakkhakammaṃ. Dummedhabhāvatāya dummejjhaṃ. Bālabhāvatāya bālyaṃ.

That is to say: knowledge is wisdom. It makes the Dhamma of the Four Truths, with its meaning, cause, and reason, known and manifest. But when ignorance arises, it prevents that from being known and made manifest—hence, it is unknowing, being the opposite of knowledge. Seeing is also wisdom. It sees that aspect. But when ignorance arises, it prevents that from being seen—hence, it is non-seeing. Direct realization is also wisdom. It directly realizes that aspect. But when ignorance arises, it prevents that from being directly realized—hence, it is non-direct realization. Comprehension, awakening, and penetration are also wisdom. They comprehend, awaken to, and penetrate that aspect. But when ignorance arises, it prevents that from being comprehended, awakened to, and penetrated—hence, it is non-comprehension, non-awakening, and non-penetration. Grasping is also wisdom. It takes hold of, presses upon, and grasps that aspect. But when ignorance arises, it prevents that from being taken hold of, pressed upon, and grasped—hence, it is non-grasping. Thorough investigation is also wisdom. It plunges into, enters, and grasps that aspect. But when ignorance arises, it prevents that from being plunged into, entered, and grasped—hence, it is non-thorough investigation. Balanced contemplation is also wisdom. It contemplates that aspect evenly and rightly. But when ignorance arises, it prevents that from being contemplated evenly and rightly—hence, it is unbalanced contemplation. Reflection is also wisdom. It reflects on that aspect. But when ignorance arises, it prevents that from being reflected upon—hence, it is non-reflection. No action of it is directly perceived; and an action done without self-reflection is an unperceived action. Due to its nature of being of poor wisdom, it is poor wisdom. Due to its nature of being foolish, it is foolishness.

Sampajaññantipi paññā. Sā atthatthaṃ kāraṇakāraṇaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ sammā pajānāti. Avijjā pana uppajjitvā taṃ ākāraṃ pajānituṃ na detīti asampajaññaṃ. Mohanavasena moho. Pamohanavasena pamoho. Sammohanavasena sammoho. Avindiyaṃ vindatītiādivasena avijjā. Vaṭṭasmiṃ ohanati osīdāpetīti avijjogho. Vaṭṭasmiṃ yojetīti avijjāyogo. Appahīnavasena [P 0.0141] punappunaṃ uppajjanato ca avijjānusayo. Magge pariyuṭṭhitacorā addhike viya kusalacittaṃ pariyuṭṭhāti gaṇhāti vilumpatīti avijjāpariyuṭṭhānaṃ. Yathā nagaradvāre palighasaṅkhātāya laṅgiyā patitāya antonagare manussānaṃ bahinagaragamanampi bahinagare manussānaṃ antonagarapavesanampi pacchijjati, evameva yassa sakkāyanagare ayaṃ patitā tassa nibbānasampāpakaṃ ñāṇagamanaṃ pacchijjatīti avijjālaṅgī nāma hoti. Akusalañca taṃ mūlañca, akusalānaṃ vā mūlanti akusalamūlaṃ. Taṃ pana na aññaṃ, idhādhippeto mohoti moho akusalamūlaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati avijjāti ayaṃ evaṃlakkhaṇā avijjā nāmāti vuccati. Evaṃ pañcavīsatipadavasena avijjāya lakkhaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Clear comprehension is also wisdom. It rightly understands the Dhamma of the Four Truths, with its meaning, cause, and reason. But when ignorance arises, it prevents that aspect from being understood—hence, it is lack of clear comprehension. In the sense of deluding, it is delusion. In the sense of bewildering, it is bewilderment. In the sense of utterly deluding, it is utter delusion. Because it finds what should not be found, and so forth, it is ignorance. It sinks and causes sinking in the round of existence—hence, it is the flood of ignorance. It yokes one to the round of existence—hence, it is the yoke of ignorance. Because it is not abandoned and arises again and again, it is the underlying tendency of ignorance. Like robbers lying in wait on a road for travelers, it surrounds, seizes, and plunders wholesome consciousness—hence, it is the obsession of ignorance. Just as when a crossbar, known as a paligha, has fallen at a city gate, the passage of people inside the city to outside the city and the entry of people outside the city to inside the city is cut off, so too, for one in the city of individuality-view, when this has fallen, the path of knowledge leading to Nibbāna is cut off—hence, it is called the bar of ignorance. It is both unwholesome and a root; or, it is the root of unwholesome things—hence, it is an unwholesome root. But that is none other than delusion; what is intended here is delusion—hence, delusion is an unwholesome root. This is called ignorance; thus, that which has such characteristics is called ignorance. In this way, the characteristic of ignorance should be understood through these twenty-five terms.

Evaṃlakkhaṇā panāyaṃ avijjā dukkhādīsu aññāṇanti vuttāpi dukkhasaccassa ekadeso hoti, sahajātā hoti, taṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, chādeti; samudayasaccassa na ekadeso hoti, sahajātā hoti, taṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, chādeti; nirodhasaccassa neva ekadeso hoti, na sahajātā, na taṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, kevalaṃ chādeti; maggasaccassāpi na ekadeso, na sahajātā, na taṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, kevalaṃ chādeti. Dukkhārammaṇatā avijjā uppajjati, tañca chādeti. Samudayārammaṇatā avijjā uppajjati, tañca chādeti. Nirodhārammaṇatā avijjā nuppajjati, tañca chādeti. Maggārammaṇatā avijjā nūppajjati, tañca chādeti.

Ignorance, thus characterized, though said to be not knowing suffering and so forth, is nevertheless a part of the truth of suffering, arises together with it, takes it as its object, and obscures it. It is not a part of the truth of origin, but arises together with it, takes it as its object, and obscures it. It is neither a part of the truth of cessation, nor does it arise together with it, nor does it take it as its object, but merely obscures it. Similarly, it is neither a part of the truth of the path, nor does it arise together with it, nor does it take it as its object, but merely obscures it. Ignorance arises with suffering as its object, and obscures it. Ignorance arises with origin as its object, and obscures it. Ignorance does not arise with cessation as its object, but it obscures it. Ignorance does not arise with the path as its object, but it obscures it.

Dve saccā duddasattā gambhīrā. Dve saccā gambhīrattā duddasā. Apica kho pana dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ gambhīrañceva duddasañca. Tattha dukkhaṃ nāma pākaṭaṃ, lakkhaṇassa pana duddasattā [V 0.0133] gambhīraṃ nāma jātaṃ. Samudayepi eseva nayo. Yathā pana mahāsamuddaṃ manthetvā ojāya nīharaṇaṃ nāma bhāro, sinerupādato [M 0.0134] vālikāya uddharaṇaṃ nāma bhāro, pabbataṃ pīḷetvā rasassa nīharaṇaṃ nāma bhāro; evameva dve saccāni gambhīratāya eva duddasāni, nirodhasaccaṃ pana atigambhīrañca atiduddasañcāti. Evaṃ duddasattā gambhīrānaṃ gambhīrattā ca duddasānaṃ catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ paṭicchādakaṃ mohandhakāraṃ ayaṃ vuccati avijjāti.

Two truths are profound because they are hard to see. Two truths are hard to see because they are profound. But indeed, the Noble Truth of the cessation of suffering is both profound and hard to see. Here, suffering itself is manifest, but due to its characteristic being hard to see, it is called profound. The same principle applies to the origin. Just as extracting the essence by churning the great ocean is a burden, or removing sand from the foot of Sineru is a burden, or extracting juice by pressing a mountain is a burden; even so, these two truths are hard to see precisely because of their profundity. But the truth of cessation is exceedingly profound and exceedingly hard to see. Thus, this darkness of delusion that obscures the Four Noble Truths—which are profound because they are hard to see, and hard to see because they are profound—is called ignorance.

Avijjāpadaniddeso.

The Exposition of the Term 'Ignorance'.

Saṅkhārapadaniddeso

The Exposition of the Term 'Formations'.

Saṅkhārapade [P 0.0142] heṭṭhā vuttasaṅkhāresu saṅkhārasaddena āgatasaṅkhāre anāmasitvā avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāreyeva dassento tattha katame avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā? Puññābhisaṅkhārotiādimāha. Tattha punāti attano kārakaṃ, pūreti cassa ajjhāsayaṃ, pujjañca bhavaṃ nibbattetīti puñño. Abhisaṅkharoti vipākaṃ kaṭattārūpañcāti abhisaṅkhāro. Puññova abhisaṅkhāro puññābhisaṅkhāro. Puññapaṭipakkhato apuñño. Apuññova abhisaṅkhāro apuññābhisaṅkhāro. Na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Āneñjameva abhisaṅkhāro, āneñjañca bhavaṃ abhisaṅkharotīti āneñjābhisaṅkhāro. Kāyena pavattito, kāyato vā pavatto, kāyassa vā saṅkhāroti kāyasaṅkhāro. Vacīsaṅkhāracittasaṅkhāresupi eseva nayo.

In the exposition of formations, without referring to the formations that come under the term 'formation' among those mentioned below, it shows only the formations conditioned by ignorance, saying: 'Therein, what are the formations conditioned by ignorance? Meritorious formation,' and so forth. Therein, 'puñña' (merit) is so called because it purifies its agent, fulfills one's aspiration, and produces a praiseworthy existence. 'Abhisaṅkharoti' (forms) is so called because it forms the result and the kamma-produced materiality. The formation that is merit is a meritorious formation. Opposite to merit is demerit. The formation that is demerit is a demeritorious formation. That which does not waver is called 'imperturbable.' The formation that is imperturbability is an imperturbable formation, and it forms an imperturbable existence. That which is initiated by the body, or arises from the body, or is a formation of the body, is called a bodily formation. The same principle applies to verbal formation and mental formation.

Tattha paṭhamattiko parivīmaṃsanasuttavasena gahito. Tattha hi “puññañce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti, puññūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ. Apuññañce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti, apuññupagaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ. Āneñjañce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti, āneñjupagaṃ hoti viññāṇa”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.51) vuttaṃ. Dutiyattiko tadanantarassa vibhaṅgasuttassa vasena gahito, sammādiṭṭhisuttapariyāyena (ma. ni. 1.102) gahitotipi vattuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Tattha hi “tayome, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā. Katame tayo? Kāyasaṅkhāro, vacīsaṅkhāro, cittasaṅkhāro”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.2) vuttaṃ. Kasmā panetesaṃ suttānaṃ vasena te gahitāti? Ayaṃ abhidhammo nāma [V 0.0134] na adhunākato, nāpi bāhirakaisīhi vā sāvakehi vā devatāhi [M 0.0135] vā bhāsito. Sabbaññujinabhāsito pana ayaṃ. Abhidhammepi hi suttepi ekasadisāva tanti niddiṭṭhāti imassatthassa dīpanatthaṃ.

Here, the first triad is taken according to the Parivīmaṃsana Sutta. For therein it is said: 'If one fabricates a meritorious formation, consciousness goes to a meritorious state. If one fabricates a demeritorious formation, consciousness goes to a demeritorious state. If one fabricates an imperturbable formation, consciousness goes to an imperturbable state' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.51). The second triad is taken according to the immediately following Vibhaṅga Sutta, and it can also be said to be taken in the way of the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 1.102). For therein it is said: 'Monks, there are these three formations. Which three? Bodily formation, verbal formation, and mental formation' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.2). But why are these taken according to these suttas? This Abhidhamma, indeed, is not newly made, nor spoken by external ascetics, or disciples, or deities. But it is spoken by the All-Knowing Conqueror. For in the Abhidhamma as well as in the Suttas, the same thread is indicated; this is for the purpose of clarifying this meaning.

Idāni te saṅkhāre pabhedato dassetuṃ tattha katamo puññābhisaṅkhārotiādimāha. Tattha kusalā cetanāti aniyamato catubhūmikacetanāpi vuttā. Kāmāvacarā rūpāvacarāti niyamitattā pana aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalacetanā, pañca rūpāvacarakusalacetanāti terasa cetanā puññābhisaṅkhāro [P 0.0143] nāma. Dānamayātiādīhi tāsaṃyeva cetanānaṃ puññakiriyavatthuvasena pavatti dassitā. Tattha aṭṭha kāmāvacarāva dānasīlamayā honti. Bhāvanāmayā pana terasapi. Yathā hi paguṇaṃ dhammaṃ sajjhāyamāno ekaṃ dve anusandhigatepi na jānāti, pacchā āvajjanto jānāti; evameva kasiṇaparikammaṃ karontassa paguṇajjhānaṃ paccavekkhantassa paguṇakammaṭṭhānañca manasikarontassa ñāṇavippayuttāpi bhāvanā hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “bhāvanāmayā pana terasapī”ti.

Now, to show these formations in detail, it says: 'Therein, what is the meritorious formation?' and so forth. Here, 'wholesome volition' is also said to mean volition from all four planes without restriction. However, due to the specification of sense-sphere and form-sphere, eight wholesome volitions of the sense-sphere and five wholesome volitions of the form-sphere—thus thirteen volitions—are called the meritorious formation. By 'born of generosity' and so forth, the occurrence of these very volitions is shown in terms of the grounds for meritorious action. Among them, only the eight sense-sphere volitions are born of generosity and virtue. But all thirteen are born of meditation. For just as one reciting a familiar teaching may not recognize even one or two connected ideas, but later, reflecting, understands; even so, for one performing kasiṇa preliminary work, reviewing a familiar absorption, or attending to a familiar meditation subject, even meditation dissociated from knowledge occurs. Therefore, it is said: 'But all thirteen are born of meditation.'

Tattha dānamayādīsu “dānaṃ ārabbha dānamadhikicca yā uppajjati cetanā sañcetanā cetayitattaṃ – ayaṃ vuccati dānamayo puññābhisaṅkhāroti. Sīlaṃ ārabbha…pe… bhāvanaṃ ārabbha bhāvanamadhikicca yā uppajjati cetanā sañcetanā cetayitattaṃ – ayaṃ vuccati bhāvanāmayo puññābhisaṅkhāro”ti (vibha. 769) ayaṃ saṅkhepadesanā.

Here, regarding 'born of giving' and so forth: 'The volition, intention, and act of intending that arises concerning giving, with giving as its basis—this is called the meritorious formation consisting of giving. The volition, intention, and act of intending that arises concerning virtue... The volition, intention, and act of intending that arises concerning development, with development as its basis—this is called the meritorious formation consisting of development' (Vibh. 769). This is a summary teaching.

Cīvarādīsu pana catūsu paccayesu rūpādīsu vā chasu ārammaṇesu annādīsu vā dasasu dānavatthūsu taṃ taṃ dentassa tesaṃ uppādanato paṭṭhāya pubbabhāge pariccāgakāle pacchā somanassacittena anussaraṇe cāti tīsu kālesu pavattā cetanā dānamayā nāma. Sīlaṃ paripūraṇatthāya pana ‘pabbajissāmī’ti vihāraṃ gacchantassa pabbajantassa manorathaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā ‘pabbajito vatamhi, sādhu suṭṭhū’ti āvajjantassa pātimokkhaṃ saṃvarantassa cīvarādayo paccaye paccavekkhantassa āpāthagatesu rūpādīsu cakkhudvārādīni saṃvarantassa ājīvaṃ sodhentassa ca pavattā cetanā sīlamayā nāma. Paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttena vipassanāmaggena cakkhuṃ aniccato [M 0.0136] dukkhato anattato bhāventassa rūpe…pe… dhamme, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ…pe… manoviññāṇaṃ, cakkhusamphassaṃ…pe… manosamphassaṃ, cakkhusamphassajaṃ vedanaṃ…pe… manosamphassajaṃ vedanaṃ, rūpasaññaṃ [V 0.0135] …pe… dhammasaññaṃ jarāmaraṇaṃ aniccato dukkhato anattato bhāventassa pavattā cetanā bhāvanāmayā nāmāti ayaṃ vitthārakathā.

However, the volition that occurs at three times—from the moment of producing those (gifts) by one who gives them, whether robes and so forth among the four requisites, or forms and so forth among the six objects, or food and so forth among the ten bases of giving; in the preliminary stage, at the time of relinquishment; and afterwards, when recollecting with a joyful mind—is called 'born of giving'. But for the purpose of fulfilling virtue, the volition that occurs when one goes to the monastery thinking 'I will go forth,' when one goes forth, having brought one's aspiration to fruition, reflecting 'Indeed, I have gone forth; excellent, very good!', when restraining oneself by the Pātimokkha, when reviewing the requisites such as robes, when restraining the sense doors such as the eye upon encountering forms and other objects within range, and when purifying one's livelihood—is called 'born of virtue'. As stated in the Paṭisambhidā, the volition that occurs when one develops insight by contemplating the eye as impermanent, suffering, and not-self; forms... and so on... phenomena; eye-consciousness... and so on... mind-consciousness; eye-contact... and so on... mind-contact; the feeling born of eye-contact... and so on... the feeling born of mind-contact; the perception of forms... and so on... the perception of phenomena; and aging-and-death as impermanent, suffering, and not-self—is called 'born of development'. This is the detailed explanation.

Apuññābhisaṅkhāraniddese akusalā cetanāti dvādasaakusalacittasampayuttā cetanā. Kāmāvacarāti kiñcāpi tattha [P 0.0144] ṭhapetvā dve domanassasahagatacetanā sesā rūpārūpabhavepi uppajjanti, tattha pana paṭisandhiṃ na ākaḍḍhanti, kāmāvacareyeva paṭisandhivasena vipākaṃ avacārentīti kāmāvacarātveva vuttā.

In the exposition of demeritorious formations, 'unwholesome volition' refers to the volitions associated with the twelve unwholesome states of consciousness. Although, with the exception of the two volitions accompanied by displeasure, the remaining volitions also arise in the form and formless realms, they do not draw rebirth there. Instead, they produce results only in the sense-sphere by way of rebirth-linking consciousness. Therefore, they are said to be of the sense-sphere.

Āneñjābhisaṅkhāraniddese kusalā cetanā arūpāvacarāti catasso arūpāvacarakusalacetanā. Etā hi catasso aniñjanaṭṭhena aniñjanassa ca abhisaṅkharaṇaṭṭhena āneñjābhisaṅkhāroti vuccanti. Rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānato hi tisso kusalavipākakiriyācetanā dvādasa arūpāvacaracetanāti pañcadasa dhammā aniccalaṭṭhena aphandanaṭṭhena āneñjā nāma. Tattha rūpāvacarā kusalā cetanā aniñjā samānāpi attanā sarikkhakampi asarikkhakampi saiñjanampi aniñjanampi rūpārūpaṃ janetīti āneñjābhisaṅkhāro nāma na hoti. Vipākakiriyacetanā pana avipākattā vipākaṃ na abhisaṅkharonti, tathā arūpāvacarā vipākakiriyacetanāpīti ekādasāpi etā cetanā āneñjāva na abhisaṅkhārā. Catubbidhā pana arūpāvacarakusalacetanā yathā hatthiassādīnaṃ sadisāva chāyā honti, evaṃ attanā sadisaṃ niccalaṃ arūpameva janetīti āneñjābhisaṅkhāroti vuccatīti.

In the exposition of imperturbable volitional formations, 'wholesome volition of the formless sphere' refers to the four wholesome volitions of the formless sphere. For these four are called imperturbable volitional formations because they are imperturbable and because they form the imperturbable. Indeed, the three volitions—wholesome, resultant, and functional—of the fourth form-sphere jhāna, together with the twelve volitions of the formless sphere, are fifteen phenomena called 'imperturbable' by reason of their unmoving and non-trembling nature. Among these, the wholesome volitions of the form sphere, though themselves imperturbable, generate both similar and dissimilar, agitated and imperturbable, form and formless states; hence they are not called imperturbable volitional formations. As for resultant and functional volitions, being non-productive of results, they do not form results, and likewise the resultant and functional volitions of the formless sphere; thus, these eleven volitions are imperturbable but not volitional formations. The fourfold wholesome volitions of the formless sphere, however, just as the shadows of elephants and horses are similar to them, so too do they generate only what is unmoving, formless, and similar to themselves. Thus they are called imperturbable volitional formations.

Evaṃ puñjābhisaṅkhāravasena terasa, apuññābhisaṅkhāravasena dvādasa, āneñjābhisaṅkhāravasena catassoti sabbāpetā paripiṇḍitā ekūnatiṃsa cetanā honti. Iti bhagavā aparimāṇesu cakkavāḷesu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ uppajjanakakusalākusalacetanā mahātulāya dhārayamāno viya, nāḷiyaṃ pakkhipitvā minamāno viya ca sabbaññutañāṇena paricchinditvā ekūnatiṃsameva dassesi.

Thus, by way of meritorious volitional formations, there are thirteen; by way of demeritorious volitional formations, twelve; and by way of imperturbable volitional formations, four—all these, when summed up, amount to twenty-nine volitions. In this way, the Blessed One, as if holding in a great balance the wholesome and unwholesome volitions that arise in countless world-systems among countless beings, and as if measuring them by putting them into a measure, defined them with his omniscient knowledge and showed them to be exactly twenty-nine.

Idāni [M 0.0137] aparimāṇesu cakkavāḷesu aparimāṇā sattā kusalākusalakammaṃ āyūhamānā yehi dvārehi āyūhanti, tāni tīṇi kammadvārāni dassento tattha katamo kāyasaṅkhāro? Kāyasañcetanātiādimāha. Tattha kāyasañcetanāti kāyaviññattiṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā kāyadvārato pavattā [V 0.0136] aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalacetanā dvādasa akusalacetanāti samavīsati cetanā; kāyadvāre ādānaggahaṇacopanaṃ pāpayamānā uppannā vīsati kusalākusalacetanātipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

Now, showing the three doors through which countless beings in countless world-systems accumulate wholesome and unwholesome kamma, he asks: 'What is bodily formation?' He says, 'Bodily volition,' and so forth. Here, 'bodily volition' refers to the twenty volitions that arise through the body-door, giving rise to bodily intimation: eight wholesome volitions of the sense-sphere and twelve unwholesome volitions. It can also be said that these twenty wholesome and unwholesome volitions arise at the body-door, bringing about the movement of taking and grasping.

Vacīsañcetanāti [P 0.0145] vacīviññattiṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā vacīdvārato pavattā tāyeva vīsati cetanā; vacīdvāre hanusañcopanaṃ vākyabhedaṃ pāpayamānā uppannā vīsati cetanātipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Abhiññācetanā panettha parato viññāṇassa paccayo na hotīti na gahitā. Yathā ca abhiññācetanā, evaṃ uddhaccacetanāpi na hoti. Tasmā sāpi viññāṇassa paccayabhāve apanetabbā. Avijjāpaccayā pana sabbāpetā honti.

'Verbal volition' refers to those same twenty volitions that arise through the speech-door, giving rise to verbal intimation. It can also be said that these twenty volitions arise at the speech-door, bringing about the movement of the jaw and the utterance of speech. The volition of supernormal knowledge is not included here, as it does not serve as a condition for consciousness in a subsequent existence. Just as the volition of supernormal knowledge, so too is the volition of restlessness not included. Therefore, it too should be excluded from being a condition for consciousness. But all of these are conditioned by ignorance.

Manosañcetanāti ubhopi viññattiyo asamuṭṭhāpetvā manodvāre uppannā sabbāpi ekūnatiṃsa cetanā. Iti bhagavā aparimāṇesu cakkavāḷesu aparimāṇā sattā kusalākusalakammaṃ āyūhamānā imehi tīhi dvārehi āyūhantīti āyūhanakammadvāraṃ dassesi.

'Mental volition' refers to all twenty-nine volitions that arise at the mind-door without giving rise to either type of intimation. Thus, the Blessed One showed the doors of kamma through which accumulation occurs, explaining that countless beings in countless world-systems accumulate wholesome and unwholesome kamma through these three doors.

Imesaṃ pana dvinnampi tikānaṃ aññamaññaṃ sampayogo veditabbo. Kathaṃ? Puññābhisaṅkhāro hi kāyaduccaritā viramantassa siyā kāyasaṅkhāro, vacīduccaritā viramantassa siyā vacīsaṅkhāro. Evaṃ aṭṭha kusalacetanā kāmāvacarā puññābhisaṅkhāro ca hoti kāyasaṅkhāro ca vacīsaṅkhāro ca. Manodvāre uppannā pana terasa cetanā puññābhisaṅkhāro ca hoti cittasaṅkhāro ca. Apuññābhisaṅkhāropi kāyaduccaritavasena pavattiyaṃ siyā kāyasaṅkhāro, vacīduccaritavasena pavattiyaṃ siyā vacīsaṅkhāro, dve dvārāni muñcitvā manodvāre pavattiyaṃ siyā cittasaṅkhāroti. Evaṃ apuññābhisaṅkhāro kāyasaṅkhāropi hoti vacīsaṅkhāropi cittasaṅkhāropi.

Now, the mutual connection between these two triads should be understood. How? A meritorious volitional formation can be a bodily formation for one who abstains from bodily misconduct, and a verbal formation for one who abstains from verbal misconduct. Thus, the eight wholesome volitions of the sense-sphere are a meritorious volitional formation, and can be a bodily formation and a verbal formation. The thirteen meritorious volitions arising at the mind-door are a meritorious volitional formation and a mental formation. Similarly, a demeritorious volitional formation, when occurring by way of bodily misconduct, can be a bodily formation; when occurring by way of verbal misconduct, it can be a verbal formation; and when occurring at the mind-door, apart from the other two doors, it can be a mental formation. Thus, a demeritorious volitional formation can be a bodily formation, a verbal formation, and a mental formation.

Kāyasaṅkhāro pana siyā puññābhisaṅkhāro, siyā apuññābhisaṅkhāro, na āneñjābhisaṅkhāro. Tathā vacīsaṅkhāro. Cittasaṅkhāro pana siyā puññābhisaṅkhāro[M 0.0138], siyā apuññābhisaṅkhāro, siyā āneñjābhisaṅkhāroti. Ime avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā nāma.

A bodily formation may be a meritorious volitional formation or a demeritorious volitional formation, but not an imperturbable volitional formation. So too a verbal formation. A mental formation, however, may be a meritorious volitional formation, a demeritorious volitional formation, or an imperturbable volitional formation. These are called 'formations conditioned by ignorance.'

Kathaṃ panetaṃ jānitabbaṃ – ime saṅkhārā avijjāpaccayā hontīti? Avijjābhāve bhāvato. Yassa hi dukkhādīsu avijjāsaṅkhātaṃ aññāṇaṃ appahīnaṃ hoti, so dukkhe tāva pubbantādīsu ca aññāṇena saṃsāradukkhaṃ sukhasaññāya gahetvā tassa hetubhūte tividhepi saṅkhāre ārabhati[V 0.0137], samudaye aññāṇena dukkhahetubhūtepi taṇhāparikkhāre saṅkhāre sukhahetuto maññamāno ārabhati, nirodhe pana magge ca aññāṇena dukkhassa anirodhabhūtepi gativisese dukkhanirodhasaññī [P 0.0146] hutvā nirodhassa ca amaggabhūtesupi yaññāmaratapādīsu nirodhamaggasaññī hutvā dukkhanirodhaṃ patthayamāno yaññāmaratapādimukhena tividhepi saṅkhāre ārabhati.

And how is this to be known—that these formations are conditioned by ignorance? By their existence when ignorance is present. For one in whom non-knowledge, which is ignorance regarding suffering and so forth, has not been abandoned, he, through non-knowledge of suffering and of the past and so forth, grasps the suffering of cyclic existence with the perception of happiness, and thus undertakes the threefold formations that are its cause. Through non-knowledge of the origin, he undertakes formations—the accessories of craving that are the cause of suffering—perceiving them as a cause of happiness. Through non-knowledge of cessation and the path, desiring the cessation of suffering, he perceives a particular destination that is not the cessation of suffering as the cessation of suffering, and perceives sacrifices, self-mortification, and so forth, which are not the path to cessation, as the path to cessation; and by way of these, he undertakes the threefold formations.

Apica so tāya catūsu saccesu appahīnāvijjatāya visesato jātijarārogamaraṇādianekādīnavavokiṇṇaṃ puññaphalasaṅkhātaṃ dukkhaṃ dukkhato ajānanto tassa adhigamāya kāyavacīcittasaṅkhārabhedaṃ puññābhisaṅkhāraṃ ārabhati devaccharakāmako viya marupapātaṃ; sukhasammatassāpi ca tassa puññaphalassa ante mahāpariḷāhajanakaṃ vipariṇāmadukkhataṃ appassādatañca apassantopi tappaccayaṃ vuttappakārameva puññābhisaṅkhāraṃ ārabhati salabho viya dīpasikhābhinipātaṃ, madhubindugiddho viya ca madhulittasatthadhārālehanaṃ.

Moreover, not having abandoned ignorance regarding the Four Noble Truths, and especially not knowing as suffering the suffering called the fruit of merit, which is beset with many dangers such as birth, aging, sickness, and death, he undertakes meritorious volitional formations, divided into bodily, verbal, and mental formations, in order to attain that, like one who, desiring celestial nymphs, plunges from a precipice in a desert. And although he regards that fruit of merit as happiness, he does not see that in the end it brings great torment, being the suffering of change, and has little satisfaction. Yet, on account of that, he undertakes meritorious volitional formations of the aforementioned kind, just as a moth plunges into a lamp flame, or as one greedy for a drop of honey licks the blade of a honey-smeared sword.

Kāmūpasevanādīsu ca savipākesu ādīnavaṃ apassanto sukhasaññāya ceva kilesābhibhūtatāya ca dvārattayappavattampi apuññābhisaṅkhāraṃ ārabhati bālo viya gūthakīḷanaṃ, maritukāmo viya ca visakhādanaṃ. Āruppavipākesu cāpi saṅkhāravipariṇāmadukkhataṃ anavabujjhamāno sassatādivipallāsena cittasaṅkhārabhūtaṃ āneñjābhisaṅkhāraṃ ārabhati disāmūḷho viya pisācanagarābhimukhamaggagamanaṃ.

Not seeing the danger in sensual indulgence and so forth, and in their results, the fool, overcome by the perception of happiness and by the defilements, initiates unwholesome volitional formations that operate through the three doors—like a child playing with excrement or one wishing to die consuming poison. And also, not comprehending the suffering of the changing nature of formations in the results of the formless attainments, one initiates the imperturbable volitional formation, which is a mental formation, due to the distortion of eternalism and so forth—like a bewildered person heading toward a city of demons.

Evaṃ yasmā avijjābhāvatova saṅkhārabhāvo, na abhāvato; tasmā jānitabbametaṃ – ime saṅkhārā avijjāpaccayā hontīti. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “avidvā, bhikkhave, avijjāgato puññābhisaṅkhārampi abhisaṅkharoti, apuññābhisaṅkhārampi abhisaṅkharoti, āneñjābhisaṅkhārampi abhisaṅkharoti. Yato [M 0.0139] kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno avijjā pahīnā, vijjā uppannā, so avijjāvirāgā vijjuppādā neva puññābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharotī”ti.

Thus, since formations exist precisely because of the presence of ignorance, not because of its absence, this should be understood: 'These formations arise with ignorance as condition.' And this has also been said: 'Monks, an ignorant person, gone into ignorance, generates meritorious volitional formations, unwholesome volitional formations, and imperturbable volitional formations. But when, monks, a bhikkhu has abandoned ignorance and wisdom has arisen, then, with the fading away of ignorance and the arising of wisdom, he no longer generates a meritorious volitional formation.'

Etthāha – gaṇhāma tāva etaṃ ‘avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo’ti. Idaṃ pana vattabbaṃ – ‘katamesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ kathaṃ paccayo hotī’ti? Tatridaṃ vuccati –

Here it is said: 'Let us first accept this: "Ignorance is a condition for volitional formations." But then this should be stated: 'For which volitional formations and in what way is it a condition?' Herein, it is said:

Paccayo [V 0.0138] hoti puññānaṃ, duvidhānekadhā pana;

Paresaṃ pacchimānaṃ sā, ekadhā paccayo matā.

It is a condition for merits, twofold; and manifold for others. For the last, it is considered a single condition.

Tattha [P 0.0147] ‘puññānaṃ duvidhā’ti ārammaṇapaccayena ca upanissayapaccayena cāti dvedhā paccayo hoti. Sā hi avijjaṃ khayato vayato sammasanakāle kāmāvacarānaṃ puññābhisaṅkhārānaṃ ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo hoti, abhiññācittena samohacittajānanakāle rūpāvacarānaṃ, avijjāsamatikkamanatthāya pana dānādīni ceva kāmāvacarapuññakiriyavatthūni pūrentassa rūpāvacarajjhānāni ca uppādentassa dvinnampi tesaṃ upanissayapaccayena paccayo hoti; tathā avijjāsammūḷhattā kāmabhavarūpabhavasampattiyo patthetvā tāneva puññāni karontassa.

Here, 'for merits, twofold' means that it is a condition in two ways: by way of object condition and decisive support condition. For, when one contemplates ignorance as decaying and vanishing, it is a condition by way of object condition for the meritorious volitional formations of the sense-sphere. And when one knows the deluded mind with the mind of direct knowledge, it is a condition by way of object condition for those of the form-sphere. Moreover, for one who fulfills the bases of meritorious action such as giving and so forth in the sense-sphere, and who generates the jhānas of the form-sphere for the purpose of transcending ignorance, it is a condition for both of these by way of decisive support condition. Similarly, for one who, being utterly deluded by ignorance, performs those very merits, having longed for attainments in the sense-existence and form-existence.

‘Anekadhā pana paresa’nti apuññābhisaṅkhārānaṃ anekadhā paccayo hoti. Kathaṃ? Esā hi avijjaṃ ārabbha rāgādīnaṃ uppajjanakāle ārammaṇapaccayena, garuṃ katvā assādanakāle ārammaṇādhipatiārammaṇūpanissayehi, avijjāsammūḷhassa anādīnavadassāvino pāṇātipātādīni karontassa upanissayapaccayena, dutiyajavanādīnaṃ anantarasamanantarānantarūpanissayāsevananatthivigatapaccayehi, yaṃ kiñci akusalaṃ karontassa hetusahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatapaccayehīti anekadhā paccayo hoti.

'Manifold for others' means that it is a condition for unwholesome volitional formations in many ways. How? For when lust and so forth arise with ignorance as their object, it is a condition by way of object condition. When one delights in it, making it significant, it is a condition by way of object-dominance and object-decisive-support conditions. For one who is utterly deluded by ignorance and does not see the danger, when performing killing and so forth, it is a condition by way of decisive support condition. For the second impulsion and so forth, it is a condition by way of immediacy, contiguity, immediacy-decisive-support, repetition, absence, and disappearance conditions. Whatever unwholesome action one performs, it is a condition by way of root, co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance conditions—thus, it is a condition in many ways.

‘Pacchimānaṃ sā ekadhā paccayo matā’ti āneñjābhisaṅkhārānaṃ upanissayapaccayeneva ekadhā paccayo matā. So panassā upanissayabhāvo puññābhisaṅkhāre vuttanayeneva veditabboti.

'For the last, it is considered a single condition' means that it is considered a single condition for imperturbable volitional formations, precisely by way of decisive support condition. And its state of being a decisive support should be understood in the same way as explained for meritorious volitional formations.

Etthāha – ‘kiṃ panāyamekāva avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo udāhu aññepi paccayā hontī’ti? Kiñcettha yadi tāva ekāva ekakāraṇavādo āpajjati. Atha ‘aññepi santi avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā’ti ekakāraṇaniddeso nupapajjatīti? Na nupapajjati. Kasmā? Yasmā –

Here it is said: 'Is ignorance the only condition for volitional formations, or are there other conditions as well?' And what if, in this case, if it is indeed a single cause, then the doctrine of a single cause would apply? Then, if there are other conditions, does the explanation of a single cause become untenable? No, it does not become untenable. Why? Because—

Ekaṃ [M 0.0140] na ekato idha, nānekamanekatopi no ekaṃ;

Phalamatthi atthi pana eka-hetuphaladīpane attho.

Here, a single [effect] does not arise from a single [cause], nor many from a single [cause], nor a single [effect] from many. But there is a result, and there is also a purpose in illuminating a single cause-and-effect relationship.

Ekato [V 0.0139] hi kāraṇato na idha kiñci ekaṃ phalamatthi, na anekaṃ. Nāpi anekehi kāraṇehi ekaṃ. Anekehi pana kāraṇehi anekameva hoti. Tathā hi anekehi utupathavībījasalilasaṅkhātehi kāraṇehi anekameva rūpagandharasādiaṅkurasaṅkhātaṃ phalamuppajjamānaṃ dissati. Yaṃ panetaṃ “avijjāpaccayā [P 0.0148] saṅkhārā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa”nti ekekahetuphaladīpanaṃ kataṃ, tattha attho atthi, payojanaṃ vijjati.

For here, no single effect arises from a single cause, nor many effects from a single cause. Nor does a single effect arise from many causes. But many effects arise from many causes. Thus, indeed, many effects—such as sprouts characterized by form, scent, taste, and so forth—are seen to arise from many causes like climate, earth, seed, and water. However, regarding that which is stated as an exposition of a single cause and effect—'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises'—therein there is meaning, there is purpose.

Bhagavā hi katthaci padhānattā, katthaci pākaṭattā, katthaci asādhāraṇattā, desanāvilāsassa ca veneyyānañca anurūpato ekamevahetuṃ vā phalaṃ vā dīpeti; “phassapaccayā vedanā”ti (dī. ni. 2.97) hi ekameva hetuṃ phalañcāha. Phasso hi vedanāya padhānahetu yathāphassaṃ vedanāvavatthānato. Vedanā ca phassassa padhānaphalaṃ yathāvedanaṃ phassavavatthānato.

For the Blessed One sometimes explains only a single cause or a single result because of its prominence, or because of its clarity, or because of its uniqueness, and in accordance with the grace of his teaching and the disposition of those to be trained. For example, he says, 'With contact as condition, feeling arises'—here, he mentions only a single cause and a single result. For contact is the primary cause of feeling because feeling is determined according to contact. And feeling is the primary result of contact because contact is determined according to feeling.

“Semhasamuṭṭhānā ābādhā”ti (mahāni. 5) pākaṭattā ekaṃ hetumāha. Pākaṭo hettha semho, na kammādayo. “Ye keci, bhikkhave, akusalā dhammā, sabbete ayonisomanasikāramūlakā”ti asādhāraṇattā ekaṃ hetumāha; asādhāraṇo hi ayonisomanasikāro akusalānaṃ, sādhāraṇāni vatthārammaṇādīnīti.

He states, 'Illnesses arising from phlegm'—because it is evident, he mentions a single cause. Here, phlegm is evident, not karma and so forth. He says, 'Whatever unwholesome states there are, monks, all have unwise attention as their root'—because it is unique, he mentions a single cause; for unwise attention is unique to unwholesome states, whereas the bases, objects, and so forth are common.

Tasmā ayamidha avijjā vijjamānesupi aññesu vatthārammaṇasahajātadhammādīsu saṅkhārakāraṇesu “assādānupassino taṇhā pavaḍḍhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.52) ca “avijjāsamudayā āsavasamudayo”ti (ma. ni. 1.104) ca vacanato aññesampi taṇhādīnaṃ saṅkhārahetūnaṃ hetūti padhānattā, “avidvā, bhikkhave, avijjāgato puññābhisaṅkhārampi abhisaṅkharotī”ti pākaṭattā asādhāraṇattā ca saṅkhārānaṃ hetubhāvena dīpitāti veditabbā. Eteneva ca ekekahetuphaladīpanaparihāravacanena sabbattha ekekahetuphaladīpane payojanaṃ veditabbanti.

Therefore, here, even though other causes of volitional formations exist, such as bases, objects, co-arisen phenomena, and so forth, ignorance should be understood as having been explained as the cause of volitional formations because it is the predominant cause even for other causes of volitional formations, such as craving and so forth, as stated in 'For one who contemplates gratification, craving increases' (SN 2.52) and 'With the arising of ignorance comes the arising of the taints' (MN 1.104); and because it is evident in the statement, 'Monks, an ignorant person, gone into ignorance, generates even a meritorious volitional formation'; and because it is unique. And by this very statement that explains a single cause and effect while omitting others, the purpose in explaining a single cause and effect everywhere should be understood.

Etthāha [M 0.0141] – evaṃ santepi ekantāniṭṭhaphalāya sāvajjāya avijjāya kathaṃ puññāneñjābhisaṅkhārapaccayattaṃ yujjati? Na hi nimbabījato ucchu uppajjatīti. Kathaṃ na yujjissati? Lokasmiñhi –

Here it is said: Even so, how can it be fitting for ignorance, which is faulty and yields an exclusively undesirable result, to be a condition for meritorious and imperturbable volitional formations? For a sugarcane does not arise from a neem seed. How can it not be fitting? For in the world—

Viruddho [V 0.0140] cāviruddho ca, sadisāsadiso tathā;

Dhammānaṃ paccayo siddho, vipākā eva te ca na.

Opposed and unopposed, and likewise similar and dissimilar, are established as conditions for phenomena; but they are not themselves results.

Dhammānañhi ṭhānasabhāvakiccādiviruddho ca aviruddho ca paccayo loke siddho. Purimacittañhi aparacittassa ṭhānaviruddho paccayo, purimasippādisikkhā ca pacchāpavattamānānaṃ sippādikiriyānaṃ. Kammaṃ rūpassa sabhāvaviruddho paccayo, khīrādīni ca dadhiādīnaṃ. Āloko cakkhuviññāṇassa kiccaviruddho, guḷādayo ca āsavādīnaṃ. Cakkhurūpādayo pana cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ ṭhānāviruddhā paccayā[P 0.0149]. Purimajavanādayo pacchimajavanādīnaṃ sabhāvāviruddhā kiccāviruddhā ca.

Indeed, in the world, conditions that are both opposed and unopposed to the state, nature, and function of phenomena are established. For the preceding consciousness is a condition opposed in state to the subsequent consciousness, as is previous training in skills and so forth to the later arising of actions like skills. Kamma is a condition opposed in nature to material form, and milk and so forth are conditions opposed in nature to curd and so forth. Light is a condition opposed in function to eye-consciousness, and sugar and so forth are conditions opposed in function to fermented liquor and so forth. But the eye, visible forms, and so forth are conditions unopposed in state to eye-consciousness and so forth. The preceding impulsions and so forth are conditions unopposed in nature and unopposed in function to the subsequent impulsions and so forth.

Yathā ca viruddhāviruddhā paccayā siddhā, evaṃ sadisāsadisāpi. Sadisameva hi utuāhārasaṅkhātaṃ rūpaṃ rūpassa paccayo hoti, sālibījādīni ca sāliphalādīnaṃ. Asadisampi rūpaṃ arūpassa, arūpañca rūpassa paccayo hoti; golomāvilomavisāṇadadhitilapiṭṭhādīni ca dabbabhūtiṇakādīnaṃ. Yesañca dhammānaṃ ye viruddhāviruddhā sadisāsadisā paccayā, na te dhammā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ vipākāyeva. Iti ayaṃ avijjā vipākavasena ekantāniṭṭhaphalasabhāvavasena ca sāvajjāpi samānā sabbesampi etesaṃ puññābhisaṅkhārādīnaṃ yathānurūpaṃ ṭhānakiccasabhāvaviruddhāviruddhapaccayavasena sadisāsadisapaccayavasena ca paccayo hotīti veditabbā.

Just as opposed and unopposed conditions are established, so too are similar and dissimilar ones. For indeed, a similar material phenomenon, namely that designated as climate and nutriment, is a condition for a material phenomenon, just as rice seeds and so forth are for rice fruits and so forth. A dissimilar material phenomenon is also a condition for an immaterial phenomenon, and an immaterial phenomenon for a material phenomenon; just as cow hair, wool, horns, curd, sesame, and flour are for implements, beings, grass, and so forth. And those phenomena for which there are opposed, unopposed, similar, or dissimilar conditions are not necessarily the results of those phenomena. Thus, this ignorance—although faulty due to its nature of producing an exclusively undesirable result—should be understood to be a condition for all these meritorious formations and the rest, by way of conditions that are, as appropriate, opposed or unopposed in state, function, and nature, and similar or dissimilar.

So cassā paccayabhāvo “yassa hi dukkhādīsu avijjāsaṅkhātaṃ aññāṇaṃ appahīnaṃ hoti, so dukkhe tāva pubbantādīsu ca aññāṇena saṃsāradukkhaṃ sukhasaññāya gahetvā tassa hetubhūte tividhepi saṅkhāre ārabhatī”tiādinā nayena vutto eva.

And its conditionality is stated by the method beginning thus: 'For whomever the unknowing reckoned as ignorance regarding suffering and so forth is unabandoned, that one, through unknowing regarding suffering, regarding the past, and so forth, grasps the suffering of saṃsāra with a perception of pleasure, and undertakes the threefold formations that are its cause,' and so on.

Apica ayaṃ aññopi pariyāyo –

Moreover, there is this other method:

Cutūpapāte saṃsāre, saṅkhārānañca lakkhaṇe;

Yo paṭiccasamuppanna-dhammesu ca vimuyhati.

Whoever is bewildered about passing away and rebirth, in saṃsāra, and in the characteristics of formations, and about dependently arisen phenomena,

Abhisaṅkharoti [V 0.0141] so ete, saṅkhāre tividhe yato;

Avijjā paccayo tesaṃ, tividhānampi yaṃ tatoti.

since he generates these threefold formations, therefore ignorance is the condition for all three of them.

Kathaṃ [M 0.0142] pana yo etesu vimuyhati, so tividhepete saṅkhāre karotīti ce? Cutiyā tāva vimūḷho sabbattha “khandhānaṃ bhedo maraṇa”nti cutiṃ agaṇhanto ‘satto marati, sattassa desantarasaṅkamana’ntiādīni vikappeti. Upapāte vimūḷho sabbattha “khandhānaṃ pātubhāvo jātī”ti upapātaṃ agaṇhanto ‘satto upapajjati, sattassa navasarīrapātubhāvo’tiādīni vikappeti. Saṃsāre vimūḷho yo esa –

If it is asked, 'But how does one who is bewildered about these things generate these threefold formations?': First, bewildered about passing away, not grasping everywhere that 'the breaking up of the aggregates is death,' he speculates thus: 'A being dies, a being transmigrates to another realm,' and so forth. Bewildered about rebirth, not grasping everywhere that 'the manifestation of the aggregates is birth,' he speculates thus: 'A being is reborn, a being acquires a new body,' and so forth. Bewildered about saṃsāra, he who is thus—

“Khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca;

Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā, saṃsāroti pavuccatī”ti.

The continuous sequence of aggregates, and of elements and sense bases, proceeding uninterruptedly, is called saṃsāra.

Evaṃ [P 0.0150] vaṇṇito saṃsāro. Taṃ evaṃ agaṇhanto ‘ayaṃ satto asmā lokā paraṃ lokaṃ gacchati, parasmā lokā imaṃ lokaṃ āgacchatī’tiādīni vikappeti. Saṅkhārānaṃ lakkhaṇe vimūḷho saṅkhārānaṃ sabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇañca agaṇhanto saṅkhāre attato attaniyato dhuvato subhato sukhato ca vikappeti. Paṭiccasamuppannadhammesu vimūḷho avijjādīhi saṅkhārādīnaṃ pavattiṃ agaṇhanto “attā jānāti vā na jānāti vā, so eva karoti ca kāreti ca so paṭisandhiyaṃ upapajjati, tassa aṇuissarādayo kalalādibhāvena sarīraṃ saṇṭhapetvā indriyāni sampādenti, so indriyasampanno phusati vediyati taṇhiyati upādiyati ghaṭiyati, so puna bhavantare bhavatī”ti vā “sabbe sattā niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatā”ti (dī. ni. 1.168) vā vikappeti. So evaṃ avijjāya andhīkato evaṃ vikappento yathā nāma andho pathaviyaṃ vicaranto maggampi amaggampi thalampi ninnampi samampi visamampi paṭipajjati, evaṃ puññampi apuññampi āneñjampi saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharotīti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Thus is saṃsāra described. Not grasping it thus, one speculates: 'This being goes from this world to another world, and from another world comes to this world,' and so forth. Bewildered about the characteristics of formations, not grasping the specific characteristic and the general characteristic of formations, one speculates about formations as self, as belonging to self, as permanent, as beautiful, and as pleasurable. Bewildered about dependently arisen phenomena, not grasping the occurrence of formations from ignorance and so forth, one speculates thus: 'The self knows or does not know; it acts and causes to act; it is reborn at conception; its minute controllers establish the body in the embryonic state and develop the faculties; endowed with faculties, it contacts, feels, craves, clings, and strives; it again becomes in another existence,' or 'All beings are fixed by destiny, connected by chance, and transformed by circumstance' (Dī. Ni. 1.168). Thus, blinded by ignorance and speculating in this way, just as a blind man wandering on the ground proceeds along a path or a non-path, on high ground or in a hollow, on level or uneven ground, so too does one generate meritorious, demeritorious, or imperturbable formations. Therefore it is said—

Yathāpi nāma jaccandho, naro aparināyako;

Ekadā yāti maggena, kummaggenāpi ekadā.

Just as a man born blind, without a guide, sometimes goes by the right path, sometimes by the wrong path.

Saṃsāre [V 0.0142] saṃsaraṃ bālo, tathā aparināyako;

Karoti ekadā puññaṃ, apuññamapi ekadā.

So too the fool, wandering in saṃsāra without a guide, sometimes performs merit, sometimes demerit.

Yadā [M 0.0143] ñatvā ca so dhammaṃ, saccāni abhisamessati;

Tadā avijjūpasamā, upasanto carissatīti.

When, having known the Dhamma, he fully comprehends the Truths, then, with the calming of ignorance, he will fare on at peace.

Ayaṃ avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti padasmiṃ vitthārakathā.

This is the detailed explanation of the phrase 'With ignorance as condition, formations come to be.'

Avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārapadaniddeso.

Exposition of the term 'Formations conditioned by ignorance.'

Viññāṇapadaniddeso

Exposition of the Term 'Consciousness'

227. Saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇapadaniddese cakkhuviññāṇantiādīsu cakkhuviññāṇaṃ kusalavipākaṃ akusalavipākanti duvidhaṃ hoti. Tathā sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇāni. Manoviññāṇaṃ pana kusalākusalavipākā dve manodhātuyo, tisso ahetukamanoviññāṇadhātuyo, aṭṭha sahetukāni kāmāvacaravipākacittāni, pañca rūpāvacarāni, cattāri arūpāvacarānīti bāvīsatividhaṃ [P 0.0151] hoti. Iti imehi chahi viññāṇehi sabbānipi bāttiṃsa lokiyavipākaviññāṇāni saṅgahitāni honti. Lokuttarāni pana vaṭṭakathāyaṃ na yujjantīti na gahitāni.

227. In the exposition of the term 'consciousness conditioned by formations,' in 'eye-consciousness, etc.,' eye-consciousness is of two kinds: wholesome resultant and unwholesome resultant. Likewise are ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness. Mind-consciousness, however, is of twenty-two kinds: the two mind-elements which are wholesome and unwholesome resultants, the three rootless mind-consciousness elements, the eight rooted sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses, the five fine-material-sphere resultants, and the four immaterial-sphere resultants. Thus, by these six consciousnesses, all thirty-two mundane resultant consciousnesses are included. The supramundane, however, are not included, as they are not suitable in the discussion of the round of existence.

Tattha siyā – kathaṃ panetaṃ jānitabbaṃ ‘idaṃ vuttappakāraṃ viññāṇaṃ saṅkhārapaccayā hotī’ti? Upacitakammābhāve vipākābhāvato. Vipākañhetaṃ, vipākañca na upacitakammābhāve uppajjati. Yadi uppajjeyya, sabbesaṃ sabbavipākāni uppajjeyyuṃ; na ca uppajjantīti jānitabbametaṃ – ‘saṅkhārapaccayā idaṃ viññāṇaṃ hotī’ti.

Here, it might be asked: How then is it to be known that 'this consciousness of the aforementioned kind is conditioned by formations'? Because in the absence of accumulated kamma, there is no result. For this is a result, and a result does not arise in the absence of accumulated kamma. If it were to arise, all results would arise for all beings; but they do not arise. Thus, it should be known that 'this consciousness is conditioned by formations.'
