For in the Suttanta, it is said: “And what is name? Feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention.” Here, it is stated: “the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations.” For there, whatever name arises dependent on eye-consciousness is evident because it is not to be grasped without dependence on other phenomena. Showing this, he taught the aggregate of mental formations, having divided it into three parts by way of volition, contact, and attention, together with the two aggregates. Here, however, encompassing all name, both what is stated there and what is unstated, he said: “Three aggregates—the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations.”

Kiṃ pana ime tayo khandhāva nāmaṃ, viññāṇaṃ nāmaṃ nāma na hotīti? No na hoti. Tasmiṃ pana viññāṇe gayhamāne nāmaviññāṇassa ca paccayaviññāṇassa cāti dvinnaṃ viññāṇānaṃ sahabhāvo āpajjati. Tasmā viññāṇaṃ paccayaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā paccayanibbattaṃ nāmaṃ dassetuṃ tayova khandhā vuttāti. Evaṃ tāva ‘desanābhedato’ viññātabbo vinicchayo.

But are these three aggregates alone name, and is consciousness not name? No, it is not so. However, when that consciousness is included, there arises the co-existence of two consciousnesses: name-consciousness and condition-consciousness. Therefore, having placed consciousness in the position of a condition, only three aggregates are stated in order to show the name produced by the condition. Thus, for now, the analysis should be understood ‘by way of distinction in teaching’.

‘Sabbabhavādīsu pavattito’ti ettha pana nāmaṃ ekaṃ sattāvāsaṃ ṭhapetvā sabbabhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisesasattāvāsesu pavattati. Rūpaṃ [M 0.0161] dvīsu bhavesu, catūsu yonīsu, pañcasu gatīsu, purimāsu catūsu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu, pañcasu ca sattāvāsesu pavattati. Evaṃ pavattamāne cetasmiṃ nāmarūpe yasmā abhāvakagabbhaseyyakānaṃ aṇḍajānañca paṭisandhikkhaṇe vatthukāyavasena rūpato dve santatisīsāni tayo ca arūpino khandhā pātubhavanti, tasmā tesaṃ vitthārena [V 0.0161] rūparūpato vīsati dhammā tayo ca arūpino khandhāti [P 0.0170] ete tevīsati dhammā viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpanti veditabbā. Aggahitaggahaṇena pana ekasantatisīsato nava rūpadhamme apanetvā cuddasa, sabhāvakānaṃ bhāvadasakaṃ pakkhipitvā tettiṃsa. Tesampi agahitaggahaṇena santatisīsadvayato aṭṭhārasa rūpadhamme apanetvā pannarasa.

‘By its occurrence in all planes of existence and so on’—Here, mentality occurs in all planes of existence, modes of generation, destinies, stations of consciousness, and the remaining abodes of beings, except for one abode of beings. Form occurs in two planes of existence, four modes of generation, five destinies, the first four stations of consciousness, and five abodes of beings. When this mentality-and-materiality occurs in this way, then, since at the moment of rebirth-linking, for womb-born beings without gender faculty and for egg-born beings, two heads of material continuity arise by way of the heart-base and the body, together with three immaterial aggregates, therefore, for them in detail, twenty material phenomena and three immaterial aggregates—these twenty-three phenomena—should be understood as mentality-and-materiality conditioned by consciousness. But by the method of not taking what has already been taken, after removing nine material phenomena from one head of continuity, fourteen remain; for those with gender faculty, with the gender decad included, there are thirty-three. For these too, by the method of not taking what has already been taken, after removing eighteen material phenomena from the two heads of continuity, fifteen remain.

Yasmā ca opapātikasattesu brahmakāyikādīnaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe cakkhusotavatthudasakānaṃ jīvitindriyanavakassa ca vasena rūparūpato cattāri santatisīsāni tayo ca arūpino khandhā pātubhavanti, tasmā tesaṃ vitthārena rūparūpato ekūnacattālīsa dhammā tayo ca arūpino khandhāti ete dvācattālīsa dhammā viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpanti veditabbā. Agahitaggahaṇena pana santatisīsattayato sattavīsati dhamme apanetvā pannarasa.

And because, at the moment of rebirth-linking for spontaneously born beings such as those of the Brahmā group, four continuities of form by way of the eye-decad, ear-decad, heart-base decad, and the life-faculty ennead, along with three immaterial aggregates, become manifest, therefore, for them, in detail, thirty-nine material phenomena and three immaterial aggregates—these forty-two phenomena—are to be understood as name-and-form conditioned by consciousness. However, by the method of non-inclusion, having removed twenty-seven phenomena from three continuities of form, fifteen remain.

Kāmabhave pana yasmā sesaopapātikānaṃ vā saṃsedajānaṃ vā sabhāvakaparipuṇṇāyatanānaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe rūparūpato satta santatisīsāni tayo ca arūpino khandhā pātubhavanti, tasmā tesaṃ vitthārena rūparūpato sattati dhammā tayo ca arūpino khandhāti ete tesattati dhammā viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpanti veditabbā. Aggahitaggahaṇena pana santatisīsachakkato catupaññāsa dhamme apanetvā ekūnavīsati. Esa ukkaṃsato. Avakaṃsena pana taṃtaṃrūpasantatisīsavikalānaṃ tassa tassa vasena hāpetvā hāpetvā saṅkhepato ca vitthārato ca paṭisandhiviññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpasaṅkhātā veditabbā. Arūpīnaṃ pana tayova arūpino khandhā. Asaññīnaṃ rūpato jīvitindriyanavakamevāti. Esa tāva paṭisandhiyaṃ nayo.

In the sensual existence, however, since at the moment of rebirth-linking for the remaining spontaneously born beings or moisture-born beings whose sense-bases are naturally complete, seven continuities of form and the three immaterial aggregates become manifest, therefore, for them, in detail, seventy phenomena in terms of form and the three immaterial aggregates—these seventy-three phenomena—are to be understood as name-and-form conditioned by consciousness. However, by the method of taking what was not taken, having removed fifty-four phenomena from the six continuities of form, nineteen remain. This is at the highest. At the lowest, however, for those lacking this or that continuity of form, subtracting accordingly, both briefly and in detail, what is designated as name-and-form conditioned by rebirth-linking consciousness is to be understood. For immaterial beings, however, there are only the three immaterial aggregates. For non-percipient beings, in terms of form, there is only the life-faculty nonad. This, indeed, is the method regarding rebirth-linking.

Pavatte pana sabbattha rūpappavattidese paṭisandhicittassa ṭhitikkhaṇe paṭisandhicittena saha pavattaututo utusamuṭṭhānaṃ suddhaṭṭhakaṃ pātubhavati. Paṭisandhicittaṃ pana rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpeti. Tañhi yathā papāte patitapuriso parassa [M 0.0162] paccayo hotuṃ na sakkoti, evaṃ vatthudubbalatāya dubbalattā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetuṃ na sakkoti. Paṭisandhicittato pana uddhaṃ paṭhamabhavaṅgato pabhuti cittasamuṭṭhānakaṃ [P 0.0171] suddhaṭṭhakaṃ. Saddapātubhāvakāle paṭisandhikkhaṇato uddhaṃ pavattaututo ceva cittato ca saddanavakaṃ. Ye pana kabaḷikārāhārūpajīvino gabbhaseyyakasattā tesaṃ –

However, in the course of existence, everywhere in the description of the process of form, at the persistence moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness, the pure octad originating from temperature, which has arisen together with the rebirth-linking consciousness, becomes manifest. But the rebirth-linking consciousness does not generate material form. For just as a man falling from a precipice is unable to be a condition for another, so too, being weak due to the weakness of the base, it is unable to generate material form. But after the rebirth-linking consciousness, starting from the first life-continuum, the pure octad originating from consciousness arises. At the time of the arising of sound, after the moment of rebirth-linking, the sound nonad arises from both the arisen temperature and from consciousness. As for those beings who subsist on edible food and are womb-born—

“Yañcassa [V 0.0162] bhuñjatī mātā, annaṃ pānañca bhojanaṃ;

Tena so tattha yāpeti, mātukucchigato naro”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.235);

“Whatever food, drink, and sustenance his mother enjoys, by that he is sustained there, the person in his mother’s womb.” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.235)

Vacanato mātarā ajjhoharitāhārena anugate sarīre, opapātikānaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ attano mukhagataṃ kheḷaṃ ajjhoharaṇakāle āhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ suddhaṭṭhakanti idaṃ āhārasamuṭṭhānassa suddhaṭṭhakassa utucittasamuṭṭhānānañca ukkaṃsato dvinnaṃ navakānaṃ vasena chabbīsatividhaṃ, pubbe ekekacittakkhaṇe tikkhattuṃ uppajjamānaṃ vuttaṃ kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ sattatividhanti channavutividhaṃ rūpaṃ tayo ca arūpino khandhāti samāsato navanavuti dhammā. Yasmā vāsaddo aniyato kadācideva pātubhāvato, tasmā duvidhampi taṃ apanetvā ime sattanavuti dhammā yathāsambhavaṃ sabbasattānaṃ viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpanti veditabbā. Tesañhi suttānampi pamattānampi carantānampi khādantānampi pivantānampi divā ca rattiñca ete viññāṇapaccayā pavattanti. Tañca tesaṃ viññāṇapaccayabhāvaṃ parato vaṇṇayissāma.

According to this saying, in the body sustained by food ingested by the mother, and for spontaneously born beings, the pure octad originating from food arises when they first ingest their own saliva that has entered their mouth. This pure octad originating from food, along with those originating from temperature and consciousness, are, at their highest, twenty-six kinds by way of two nonads. Previously, it was said that the kamma-originated form arising three times in each moment of consciousness is of seventy kinds. Thus, in summary, there are ninety-six kinds of material phenomena and three immaterial aggregates, totaling ninety-nine phenomena. Since sound is indefinite, appearing only occasionally, therefore, having excluded those two kinds, these ninety-seven phenomena are to be understood as name-and-form conditioned by consciousness for all beings, as is possible. Indeed, for those who are asleep, heedless, walking, eating, or drinking, by day and by night, these phenomena proceed conditioned by consciousness. And we will describe their state of being conditioned by consciousness later.

Yaṃ panetamettha kammajarūpaṃ taṃ bhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsesu sabbapaṭhamaṃ patiṭṭhahantampi tisamuṭṭhānikarūpena anupatthaddhaṃ na sakkoti saṇṭhātuṃ, nāpi tisamuṭṭhānikaṃ tena anupatthaddhaṃ. Atha kho vātabbhāhatāpi catuddisavavatthāpitā naḷakalāpiyo viya, ūmivegabbhāhatāpi mahāsamudde katthaci laddhapatiṭṭhā bhinnavāhanikā viya ca aññamaññūpatthaddhānevetāni apatamānāni saṇṭhahitvā ekampi vassaṃ dvepi vassāni…pe… vassasatampi yāva tesaṃ sattānaṃ āyukkhayo vā puññakkhayo vā tāva pavattantīti. Evaṃ ‘sabbabhavādīsu pavattito’pettha viññātabbo vinicchayo.

And whatever kamma-originated material form is here, even though it first becomes established in the realms of existence, wombs, destinations, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings, it cannot persist without being supported by the form originated from the other three causes, nor can the form from the three causes persist without being supported by it. Rather, just like bundles of reeds set up in the four directions, buffeted by the wind, or like the wreckage of a ship in the great ocean that has found a foothold somewhere, buffeted by the force of the waves—so these, being mutually supported, persist without falling apart. They may last for one year, two years... even up to a hundred years, until the life span of those beings is exhausted or their merit is exhausted, for that long they proceed. Thus, the determination here should be understood as ‘proceeding in all states of existence, etc.’

‘Saṅgahā’ti [P 0.0172][M 0.0163] ettha ca yaṃ āruppe pavattipaṭisandhīsu pañcavokārabhave ca pavattiyā viññāṇapaccayā nāmameva, yañca asaññīsu sabbattha pañcavokārabhave ca pavattiyā viññāṇapaccayā rūpameva, yañca pañcavokārabhave sabbattha viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ nāmañca rūpañca nāmarūpañca nāmarūpanti evaṃ ekadesasarūpekasesanayena saṅgahetvā viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpanti veditabbaṃ. Asaññīsu viññāṇābhāvā ayuttanti ce nāyuttaṃ. Idañhi –

Here, by ‘inclusion’: that which in the formless realm, at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence, is only name conditioned by consciousness; and that which for non-percipient beings everywhere, and in the five-aggregate becoming in the course of existence, is only form conditioned by consciousness; and that which in the five-aggregate becoming everywhere is name-and-form conditioned by consciousness—all this, that is, name, form, and name-and-form, having been collected as ‘name-and-form’ by the method of partial identity and single remainder, should be understood as ‘name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.’ If it is said, “This is incorrect because there is no consciousness in non-percipient beings,” this is not incorrect. For here—

Nāmarūpassa [V 0.0163] yaṃ hetu, viññāṇaṃ taṃ dvidhā mataṃ;

Vipākamavipākañca, yuttameva yato idaṃ.

That consciousness which is the cause of name-and-form is considered twofold: as resultant and non-resultant, since this is indeed fitting.

Yañhi nāmarūpassa hetu viññāṇaṃ taṃ vipākāvipākabhedato dvidhā mataṃ. Idañca asaññasattesu kammasamuṭṭhānattā pañcavokārabhave pavattaabhisaṅkhāraviññāṇapaccayā rūpaṃ, tathā pañcavokāre pavattiyaṃ kusalādicittakkhaṇe kammasamuṭṭhānanti yuttameva idaṃ. Evaṃ ‘saṅgahato’pettha viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Indeed, that consciousness which is the cause of name-and-form is considered twofold by the distinction between resultant and non-resultant. And this is fitting because in non-percipient beings, form is conditioned by the volitional consciousness that occurred in a five-aggregate becoming, due to its being kamma-originated. Similarly, in the five-aggregate becoming, during the course of existence, at the moment of a wholesome consciousness and so on, that form is kamma-originated is indeed fitting. Thus, the determination here should be understood as ‘by way of inclusion.’

‘Paccayanayā’ti ettha hi –

‘By way of conditionality.’ For here—

Nāmassa pākaviññāṇaṃ, navadhā hoti paccayo;

Vatthurūpassa navadhā, sesarūpassa aṭṭhadhā.

Resultant consciousness is a condition for name in nine ways. For the base-form, it is a condition in nine ways, and for the remaining form, in eight ways.

Abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇaṃ, hoti rūpassa ekadhā;

Tadaññaṃ pana viññāṇaṃ, tassa tassa yathārahaṃ.

Volitional consciousness is a condition for form in one way. But other consciousness is a condition for each of them as is appropriate.

Yañhetaṃ paṭisandhiyaṃ pavattiyaṃ vā vipākasaṅkhātaṃ nāmaṃ, tassa rūpamissassa vā rūpaamissassa vā paṭisandhikaṃ vā aññaṃ vā vipākaviññāṇaṃ sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttavipākaāhāraindriyaatthiavigatapaccayehi navadhā paccayo hoti. Vatthurūpassa paṭisandhiyaṃ sahajātaaññamaññanissayavipākaāhāraindriyavippayuttaatthiavigatapaccayehi navadhā paccayo hoti. Ṭhapetvā pana vatthurūpaṃ sesarūpassa imesu navasu aññamaññapaccayaṃ apanetvā sesehi aṭṭhahi paccayehi paccayo hoti. Abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇaṃ pana asaññasattarūpassa vā pañcavokāre vā kammajassa suttantikapariyāyena upanissayavasena [P 0.0173] ekadhāva paccayo hoti. Avasesaṃ paṭhamabhavaṅgato pabhuti sabbampi viññāṇaṃ tassa tassa nāmarūpassa yathārahaṃ [M 0.0164] paccayo hotīti veditabbaṃ. Vitthārato pana tassa paccayanaye dassiyamāne sabbāpi paṭṭhānakathā vitthāretabbā hotīti na taṃ ārabhāma.

That name, designated as resultant, whether at rebirth-linking or in the course of existence, whether mixed with form or unmixed with form—for it, resultant consciousness, whether rebirth-linking or other, is a condition in nine ways: by way of conascence, mutuality, support, association, result, nutriment, faculty, presence, and non-disappearance. For the base-form at rebirth-linking, it is a condition in nine ways: by way of conascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. Excluding the base-form, for the remaining form it is a condition by eight conditions, omitting the mutuality condition from these nine. Formative consciousness, however, is a condition in one way by way of decisive support for the form of non-percipient beings or for that which is kamma-born in the five-aggregate existence, according to the Suttanta method. All remaining consciousness, from the first life-continuum onwards, should be understood as a condition for its respective name-and-form as is appropriate. However, if its mode of conditionality were to be shown in detail, the entire exposition of the Paṭṭhāna would have to be elaborated; therefore, we do not undertake that.

Tattha siyā – kathaṃ panetaṃ jānitabbaṃ “paṭisandhināmarūpaṃ viññāṇapaccayā hotī”ti? Suttato [V 0.0164] yuttito ca. Sutte hi “cittānuparivattino dhammā”tiādinā (dha. sa. dukamātikā 62) nayena bahudhā vedanādīnaṃ viññāṇapaccayatā siddhā. Yuttito pana –

Here it may be asked: How then is it to be understood that ‘rebirth-linking name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness’? By the Suttas and by reasoning. For in the Suttas, through such passages as ‘phenomena that revolve around mind’ (Dhs. Dukamātikā 62), the conditionality of feeling and so on by consciousness is established in many ways. And by reasoning—

Cittajena hi rūpena, idha diṭṭhena sijjhati;

Adiṭṭhassāpi rūpassa, viññāṇaṃ paccayo iti.

For by mind-originated form, seen here, it is established that consciousness is a condition even for unseen form.

Citte hi pasanne appasanne vā tadanurūpāni rūpāni uppajjamānāni diṭṭhāni. Diṭṭhena ca adiṭṭhassa anumānaṃ hotīti iminā idha diṭṭhena cittajarūpena adiṭṭhassāpi paṭisandhirūpassa viññāṇaṃ paccayo hotīti jānitabbametaṃ. Kammasamuṭṭhānassāpi hi tassa cittasamuṭṭhānasseva viññāṇapaccayatā paṭṭhāne (paṭṭhā. 1.1.53, 419) āgatāti. Evaṃ paccayanayato pettha viññātabbo vinicchayo.

For when the mind is serene or agitated, corresponding forms are seen arising. And from what is seen, an inference is made of what is unseen. By this seen mind-originated form here, it should be understood that consciousness is a condition even for the unseen rebirth-linking form. For the fact that consciousness is a condition for kamma-originated form, just as it is for mind-originated form, is stated in the Paṭṭhāna (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.53, 419). Thus, the determination here should be understood in terms of the mode of conditionality.

Ettha ca “viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti bhāsamānena bhagavatā yasmā upaparikkhamānānaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ paramatthato nāmarūpamattameva pavattamānaṃ dissati, na satto, na poso; tasmā appaṭivattiyaṃ samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vā kenaci vā lokasmiṃ anuttaraṃ dhammacakkaṃ pavattitaṃ hotīti.

Here, when the Blessed One says, ‘Name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness,’ because for the wise who examine closely only mere name-and-form is seen occurring in the ultimate sense—not a being, not a person—therefore, an unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma has been set rolling by the Blessed One, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world.

Viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpapadaniddeso.

Exposition of the phrase ‘Name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness.’

Saḷāyatanapadaniddeso

The Exposition of the Six Sense Bases.

229. Nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatananiddese –

229. In the exposition of ‘The six sense bases are conditioned by name-and-form’—

Nāmaṃ khandhattayaṃ rūpaṃ, bhūtavatthādikaṃ mataṃ;

Katekasesaṃ taṃ tassa, tādisasseva paccayo.

Name is the three aggregates; form is considered the elements, bases, and so on. That [name-and-form], treated as a single compound, is a condition for that [six sense bases], which is of the same kind.

Yañhetaṃ [M 0.0165][V 0.0165] saḷāyatanassa paccayabhūtaṃ nāmarūpaṃ, tattha nāmanti vedanādikkhandhattayaṃ, rūpaṃ pana sakasantatipariyāpannaṃ niyamato cattāri bhūtāni cha vatthūni [P 0.0174] jīvitindriyanti evaṃ bhūtavatthādikaṃ matanti veditabbaṃ. Taṃ pana “nāmañca rūpañca nāmarūpañca nāmarūpa”nti evaṃ katekasesaṃ “chaṭṭhāyatanañca saḷāyatanañca saḷāyatana”nti evaṃ katekasesasseva saḷāyatanassa paccayoti veditabbaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā āruppe nāmameva paccayo. Tañca chaṭṭhāyatanasseva, na aññassa. “Nāmapaccayā chaṭṭhāyatana”nti hi abyākatavāre vakkhati. Idha saṅgahitameva hi tattha vibhattanti veditabbaṃ.

Regarding that name-and-form which is the condition for the six sense bases: therein, 'name' is the three aggregates beginning with feeling. 'Form,' however, should be understood as what is included in one's own continuum, specifically the four great elements, the six bases, and the life faculty—thus it is considered the elements, bases, and so on. And that [name-and-form], treated as a single compound (as in 'name and form are name-and-form'), should be understood as a condition for the six sense bases, which are likewise treated as a single compound (as in 'the sixth sense base and the five sense bases are the six sense bases'). Why? Because in the formless realm, name alone is the condition, and that is only for the sixth sense base, not for any other. For in the section on the indeterminate it will be stated: 'The sixth sense base is conditioned by name.' It should be understood that what is here summarized is there analyzed.

Tattha siyā – kathaṃ panetaṃ jānitabbaṃ “nāmarūpaṃ saḷāyatanassa paccayo”ti? Nāmarūpabhāve bhāvato. Tassa tassa hi nāmassa rūpassa ca bhāve taṃ taṃ āyatanaṃ hoti, na aññathā. Sā panassa tabbhāvabhāvībhāvatā paccayanayasmiññeva āvibhavissati. Tasmā –

Here it may be asked: But how is it to be known that 'name-and-form is a condition for the six sense bases'? Because of its existence when name-and-form exists. For when there is the presence of each and every name and form, then each and every sense base exists, not otherwise. And this state of being dependent on that presence will become clear in the section on conditions. Therefore—

Paṭisandhiyaṃ pavatte vā, hoti yaṃ yassa paccayo;

Yathā ca paccayo hoti, tathā neyyaṃ vibhāvinā.

At rebirth-linking or in the course of existence, whatever is a condition for whatever; and how it is a condition, so it should be known by one who discerns.

Tatrāyaṃ atthadīpanā –

Herein is the exposition of the meaning:

Nāmameva hi āruppe, paṭisandhipavattisu;

Paccayo sattadhā chaṭṭhā, hoti taṃ avakaṃsato.

For in the formless realm, at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence, name alone is a condition for the sixth [sense base] in seven ways, at a minimum.

Kathaṃ? ‘Paṭisandhiyaṃ’ tāva avakaṃsato sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttavipākaatthiavigatapaccayehi sattadhā nāmaṃ chaṭṭhāyatanassa paccayo hoti. Kiñci panettha hetupaccayena, kiñci āhārapaccayenāti evaṃ aññathāpi paccayo hoti. Tassa vasena ukkaṃsāvakaṃso veditabbo.

How? First, at rebirth-linking, at a minimum, name is a condition for the sixth sense base in seven ways: by way of conascence, mutuality, support, association, result, presence, and non-disappearance. In some cases it is also a condition by way of root condition, in others by way of nutriment condition, and so on. By means of this, the maximum and minimum modes should be understood.

‘Pavatte’pi vipākaṃ vuttanayeneva paccayo hoti. Itaraṃ pana avakaṃsato vuttappakāresu paccayesu vipākapaccayavajjehi chahi paccayo hoti. Kiñci panettha hetupaccayena, kiñci āhārapaccayenāti evaṃ aññathāpi paccayo hoti. Tassa vasena ukkaṃsāvakaṃso veditabbo.

In the course of existence, too, resultant [name] is a condition in the manner already stated. The other [non-resultant name], however, at a minimum, is a condition in six ways from among the aforementioned types, excluding the resultant condition. In some cases it is also a condition by way of root condition, in others by way of nutriment condition, and so on. By means of this, the maximum and minimum modes should be understood.

Aññasmimpi [V 0.0166] bhave nāmaṃ, tatheva paṭisandhiyaṃ;

Chaṭṭhassa itaresaṃ taṃ, chahākārehi paccayo.

In the other existence, at rebirth-linking, name is a condition in the same way. For the sixth and for the others, it is a condition in six ways.

Āruppato [M 0.0166] hi aññasmimpi pañcavokārabhave taṃ vipākanāmaṃ hadayavatthuno sahāyaṃ hutvā chaṭṭhassa manāyatanassa [P 0.0175] yathā āruppe vuttaṃ tatheva avakaṃsato sattadhā paccayo hoti. Itaresaṃ panetaṃ pañcannaṃ cakkhāyatanādīnaṃ catumahābhūtasahāyaṃ hutvā sahajāta nissayavipākavippayuttaatthiavigatavasena chahākārehi paccayo hoti. Kiñci panettha hetupaccayena, kiñci āhārapaccayenāti evaṃ aññathāpi paccayo hoti. Tassa vasena ukkaṃsāvakaṃso veditabbo.

Indeed, in another five-aggregate existence, that resultant name, being a support for the heart-basis, is a sevenfold condition for the sixth sense base, the mind base, by way of the minimum, just as was stated in the formless realm. And for the remaining five—the eye base and so on—it is a sixfold condition, by being a support for the four great elements, through conascence, dependence, resultant, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. Here, some are by root condition, some by nutriment condition—thus it is also a condition in other ways. By means of this, the maximum and minimum should be understood.

Pavattepi tathā hoti, pākaṃ pākassa paccayo;

Apākaṃ avipākassa, chadhā chaṭṭhassa paccayo.

In the course of existence, too, it is so: resultant [name] is a condition for resultant [name]; non-resultant [name] for non-resultant [name]; and it is a sixfold condition for the sixth [sense base].

Pavattepi hi pañcavokārabhave yathā paṭisandhiyaṃ, tatheva vipākanāmaṃ vipākassa chaṭṭhāyatanassa avakaṃsato sattadhā paccayo hoti. Avipākaṃ pana avipākassa chaṭṭhassa avakaṃsatova tato vipākapaccayaṃ apanetvā chadhāva paccayo hoti. Vuttanayeneva panettha ukkaṃsāvakaṃso veditabbo.

In the course of existence in the five-aggregate existence, too, just as at rebirth-linking, that resultant name is a sevenfold condition for the resultant sixth sense base, by way of the minimum. But the non-resultant [name], by way of the minimum, is a sixfold condition for the non-resultant sixth [sense base], having removed the resultant condition from it. Here, the maximum and minimum should be understood according to the method stated.

Tattheva sesapañcannaṃ, vipākaṃ paccayo bhave;

Catudhā avipākampi, evameva pakāsitaṃ.

Therein, for the remaining five [sense bases], resultant [name] is a condition; and non-resultant [name] is likewise declared to be fourfold.

Tattheva hi pavatte sesānaṃ cakkhāyatanādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ cakkhuppasādādivatthukampi itarampi vipākanāmaṃ pacchājātavippayuttaatthiavigatapaccayehi catudhā paccayo hoti. Yathā ca vipākaṃ, avipākampi evameva pakāsitaṃ. Tasmā kusalādibhedampi tesaṃ catudhā paccayo hotīti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ tāva nāmameva paṭisandhiyaṃ pavatte vā yassa yassa āyatanassa paccayo hoti, yathā ca hoti, tathā veditabbaṃ.

Indeed, in the course of existence therein, for the remaining five—the eye base and so on—the resultant name, both that which has the eye sensitivity and so on as its basis and the other, is a fourfold condition through postnascence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. And just as the resultant, so too the non-resultant is explained in the same way. Therefore, it should be understood that the non-resultant, with its distinctions of wholesome and so on, is also a fourfold condition for them. Thus, so far, it should be understood for which sense base name itself is a condition, at rebirth-linking or in the course of existence, and in what way it is so.

Rūpaṃ panettha āruppa-bhave bhavati paccayo;

Na ekāyatanassāpi, pañcakkhandhabhave pana.

Herein, in the formless existence, form is not a condition for even a single sense base; but in the five-aggregate existence, it is.

Rūpato [V 0.0167] sandhiyaṃ vatthu, chadhā chaṭṭhassa paccayo;

Bhūtāni catudhā honti, pañcannaṃ avisesato.

As for form, at rebirth-linking, the basis is a sixfold condition for the sixth [sense base]. The great elements are a fourfold condition for the five, without distinction.

Rūpato hi paṭisandhiyaṃ vatthurūpaṃ chaṭṭhassa manāyatanassa sahajātaaññamaññanissayavippayuttaatthiavigatapaccayehi chadhā paccayo hoti. Cattāri pana bhūtāni avisesato paṭisandhiyaṃ pavatte ca yaṃ yaṃ āyatanaṃ [M 0.0167] uppajjati, tassa tassa vasena pañcannampi cakkhāyatanādīnaṃ sahajātanissayaatthiavigatapaccayehi [P 0.0176] catudhā paccayā honti.

Indeed, as for form, at rebirth-linking, the material basis is a sixfold condition for the sixth sense base, the mind base, through conascence, mutuality, dependence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. The four great elements, without distinction, are a fourfold condition—through conascence, dependence, presence, and non-disappearance conditions—for each of the five sense bases, the eye base and so on, that arises, both at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence.

Tidhā jīvitametesaṃ, āhāro ca pavattiyaṃ;

Tāneva chadhā chaṭṭhassa, vatthu tasseva pañcadhā.

The life faculty of these is threefold, and nutriment in the course of existence. Those same [five sense bases] are a sixfold condition for the sixth, and the basis is a fivefold condition for that same [sixth sense base].

Etesaṃ pana cakkhādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ paṭisandhiyaṃ pavatte ca atthiavigataindriyavasena rūpajīvitaṃ tidhā paccayo hoti.

But for these five, the eye and so on, at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence, the material life faculty is a threefold condition by way of presence, non-disappearance, and faculty conditions.

‘Āhāro cā’ti āhāro ca atthiavigataāhāravasena tidhā paccayo hoti. So ca kho ye sattā āhārūpajīvino, tesaṃ āhārānugate kāye pavattiyaṃyeva, no paṭisandhiyaṃ. Tāni pana pañca cakkhāyatanādīni chaṭṭhassa cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇasaṅkhātassa manāyatanassa nissayapurejātaindriyavippayuttaatthiavigatavasena chahākārehi paccayā honti pavatte, no paṭisandhiyaṃ. Ṭhapetvā pana pañca viññāṇāni tasseva avasesamanāyatanassa vatthurūpaṃ nissayapurejātavippayuttaatthiavigatavasena pañcadhā paccayo hoti pavatte, no paṭisandhiyaṃ. Evaṃ rūpameva paṭisandhiyaṃ pavatte vā yassa yassa āyatanassa paccayo hoti yathā ca hoti tathā veditabbaṃ.

‘And nutriment’—nutriment also becomes a condition in three ways: by way of presence, non-disappearance, and nutriment conditions. And that, for those beings who subsist on nutriment, is a condition only in the course of existence for the body sustained by nutriment, not at rebirth-linking. Moreover, those five—the eye base and so on—are conditions in six ways for the sixth, the mind base, which is reckoned as eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness: by way of dependence, prenascence, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance—but only in the course of existence, not at rebirth-linking. But excluding the five consciousnesses, the material basis of that same remaining mind base becomes a condition in five ways: by way of dependence, prenascence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance—but only in the course of existence, not at rebirth-linking. Thus, it should be understood for which sense base form itself is a condition, at rebirth-linking or in the course of existence, and in what way it is so.

Nāmarūpaṃ panubhayaṃ, hoti yaṃ yassa paccayo;

Yathā ca tampi sabbattha, viññātabbaṃ vibhāvinā.

For whatever name-and-form, both, are a condition, and in what way, this too should be understood in all cases by the discerning one.

Seyyathidaṃ – paṭisandhiyaṃ tāva pañcavokārabhave khandhattayavatthurūpasaṅkhātaṃ nāmarūpaṃ chaṭṭhāyatanassa sahajātaaññamaññanissayavipākasampayuttavippayuttaatthiavigatapaccayādīhi paccayo [V 0.0168] hotīti idamettha mukhamattaṃ. Vuttanayānusārena pana sakkā sabbaṃ yojetunti na ettha vitthāro dassitoti.

As follows: at rebirth-linking, first, in the five-aggregate existence, name-and-form, reckoned as the three aggregates and the material basis, is a condition for the sixth sense-base by way of conascence, mutuality, dependence, resultant, association, dissociation, presence, non-disappearance, and so on—this is just a brief outline here. Following the method already stated, however, it is possible to apply everything; therefore, no detailed exposition is given here.

Nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanapadaniddeso.

Exposition of the Section ‘With Name-and-Form as Condition, the Six Sense Bases’

Phassapadaniddeso

Exposition of the Section on Contact

230. Saḷāyatanapaccayā [M 0.0168] phassaniddese –

230. In the exposition of ‘With the Six Sense Bases as Condition, Contact’:

Chaḷeva phassā saṅkhepā, cakkhusamphassaādayo;

Viññāṇamiva battiṃsa, vitthārena bhavanti te.

Briefly, there are just six contacts: eye-contact and so on. Like consciousness, these become thirty-two in detail.

‘Saṅkhepato’ [P 0.0177] hi pāḷiyaṃ cakkhusamphassoti ādayo chaḷeva phassā āgatā. Vitthārena pana cakkhusamphassādayo pañca kusalavipākā pañca akusalavipākāti dasa, sesā bāvīsati lokiyavipākaviññāṇasampayuttā ca bāvīsatīti evaṃ sabbepi saṅkhārapaccayā vuttaviññāṇamiva bāttiṃsa honti. Yaṃ panetassa bāttiṃsavidhassāpi phassassa paccayo saḷāyatanaṃ. Tattha –

Indeed, ‘in brief’, in the Pāli text, just six contacts, eye-contact and so on, are given. In detail, however, the five contacts beginning with eye-contact are five wholesome-resultants and five unwholesome-resultants, thus ten; and the remaining twenty-two are associated with the twenty-two mundane resultant consciousnesses. Thus all these contacts conditioned by formations amount to thirty-two, just like the aforementioned consciousnesses. Now, the condition for all these thirty-two kinds of contact is the six sense bases. Herein—

Chaṭṭhena saha ajjhattaṃ, cakkhādiṃ bāhirehipi;

Saḷāyatanamicchanti, chahi saddhiṃ vicakkhaṇā.

The discerning hold that the ‘six sense bases’ refers to the internal bases—the eye and so on, together with the sixth—along with the six external bases.

Tattha ye tāva “upādinnakapavattikathā aya”nti ekasantatipariyāpannameva paccayaṃ paccayuppannañca dīpenti, te chaṭṭhāyatanapaccayā phassoti pāḷianusārato āruppe chaṭṭhāyatanañca aññattha sabbasaṅgahato saḷāyatanañca phassassa paccayoti ekadesasarūpekasesaṃ katvā chaṭṭhena saha ajjhattaṃ cakkhādiṃ saḷāyatananti icchanti. Tañhi chaṭṭhāyatanañca saḷāyatanañca saḷāyatanantveva saṅghaṃ gacchati. Ye pana paccayuppannameva ekasantatipariyāpannaṃ dīpenti, paccayaṃ pana bhinnasantānampi, te yaṃ yaṃ āyatanaṃ phassassa paccayo hoti taṃ sabbaṃ dīpentā [V 0.0169] bāhirampi pariggahetvā tadeva chaṭṭhena saha ajjhattaṃ bāhirehipi rūpāyatanādīhi saddhiṃ saḷāyatananti icchanti. Tampi hi chaṭṭhāyatanañca saḷāyatanañca saḷāyatananti etesaṃ ekasese kate saḷāyatanantveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

Here, those who first explain that 'this is the discourse on the process of what is grasped,' describe only what is included within a single continuity as both condition and conditioned. Following the Pāli passage that 'the sixth sense-base is the condition for contact,' they hold that in the immaterial realm, the sixth sense-base, and elsewhere, all six sense-bases are the condition for contact. By forming a single-remainder compound of a partial form, they consider the internal eye and so on, together with the sixth, to be the six sense-bases. Indeed, both the sixth sense-base and the six sense-bases are counted as the six sense-bases. On the other hand, those who explain only the conditioned as included within a single continuity, but the condition as belonging to separate continuities, describe every sense-base that serves as the condition for contact, even including the external. They consider the sixth sense-base together with the internal and external sense-bases, such as the form-base, etc., to be the six sense-bases. For them too, when the sixth sense-base and the six sense-bases are combined into a single remainder, they are counted simply as the six sense-bases.

Etthāha – na sabbāyatanehi eko phasso sambhoti, nāpi ekamhā āyatanā sabbe phassā, ayañca saḷāyatanapaccayā phassoti ekova vutto, so kasmāti? Tatridaṃ vissajjanaṃ – saccametaṃ. Sabbehi eko ekamhā vā sabbe na sambhonti, sambhoti pana anekehi eko; yathā cakkhusamphasso cakkhāyatanā rūpāyatanā cakkhuviññāṇasaṅkhātā manāyatanā avasesā sampayuttadhammāyatanā cāti evaṃ sabbattha yathānurūpaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tasmā eva hi –

Here it is said: 'A single contact does not arise from all sense-bases, nor do all contacts arise from a single sense-base. Yet it is stated that “contact is conditioned by the six sense-bases,” spoken of as one. Why is this?' The answer is this: It is true. One does not arise from all, nor do all arise from one. However, one does arise from many; for example, eye-contact arises from the eye-base, the form-base, the mind-base reckoned as eye-consciousness, and the remaining associated phenomena-base. In this way, it should be applied appropriately in all cases. Therefore, indeed—

Eko [M 0.0169] panekāyatana-ppabhavo iti dīpito;

Phassoyaṃ ekavacana-niddesenidha tādinā.

One that originates from many bases is thus illuminated; this contact is indicated here in the singular by the Such-a-One.

‘Ekavacananiddesenā’ti [P 0.0178] saḷāyatanapaccayā phassoti iminā hi ekavacananiddesena anekehi āyatanehi eko phasso hotīti tādinā dīpitoti attho. Āyatanesu pana –

'By the singular designation'—by this singular designation, 'contact is conditioned by the six sense-bases,' it is shown by the Such-a-One that one contact arises from many bases; this is the meaning. But regarding the bases—

Chadhā pañca tato ekaṃ, navadhā bāhirāni cha;

Yathāsambhavametassa, paccayatte vibhāvaye.

The five in six ways, then the one in nine ways, and the six external bases—one should discern its conditionality according to what is possible.

Tatrāyaṃ vibhāvanā – cakkhāyatanādīni tāva pañca cakkhusamphassādibhedato pañcavidhassa phassassa nissayapurejātaindriyavippayuttaatthiavigatavasena chadhā paccayā honti. Tato paraṃ ekaṃ vipākamanāyatanaṃ anekabhedassa vipākamanosamphassassa sahajātaaññamaññanissayavipākaāhāraindriyasampayuttaatthiavigatavasena navadhā paccayo hoti. Bāhiresu pana rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhusamphassassa ārammaṇapurejātaatthiavigatavasena catudhā paccayo hoti. Tathā saddāyatanādīni sotasamphassādīnaṃ. Manosamphassassa pana tāni dhammāyatanañca tathā ca ārammaṇapaccayamatteneva cāti evaṃ bāhirāni cha yathāsambhavametassa paccayatte vibhāvayeti.

Here is the analysis: First, the five sense-bases beginning with the eye-base are conditions in six ways for the five kinds of contact beginning with eye-contact, by way of dependence, pre-nascence, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. Then, the single resultant mind-base is a condition in nine ways for the various kinds of resultant mental contact by way of co-nascence, mutuality, dependence, result, nutriment, faculty, association, presence, and non-disappearance. But in regard to external bases, the form-base is a condition in four ways for eye-contact by way of object, pre-nascence, presence, and non-disappearance. Similarly, the sound-base, etc., for ear-contact, etc. But for mental contact, these external bases and the phenomena-base are conditions only by way of the object condition. Thus, one should discern the conditionality of these six external bases according to what is possible.

Saḷāyatanapaccayā phassapadaniddeso.

Exposition of the Term 'Contact Conditioned by the Six Sense-Bases'.

Vedanāpadaniddeso

Exposition of the Term 'Feeling'

231. Phassapaccayā [V 0.0170] vedanāniddese –

231. In the exposition of 'feeling conditioned by contact'—

Dvārato vedanā vuttā, cakkhusamphassajādikā;

Chaḷeva tā pabhedena, ekūnanavutī matā.

Feelings are spoken of by way of the doors, such as those born of eye-contact; they are six, but by division, they are reckoned as eighty-nine.

Cakkhusamphassajāvedanātiādinā hi nayena pāḷiyaṃ imā cakkhusamphassajādikā dvārato chaḷeva vedanā vuttā. Tā pana pabhedena ekūnanavutiyā cittehi sampayuttattā ekūnanavutīti matā.

Indeed, in the Pāli, by the method beginning with 'feeling born of eye-contact' and so forth, these six feelings, such as those born of eye-contact, are spoken of by way of the doors. But by division, they are considered eighty-nine because they are associated with eighty-nine types of consciousness.

Vedanāsu panetāsu, idha bāttiṃsa vedanā;

Vipākacittayuttāva, adhippetāti bhāsitā.

But among these feelings, here thirty-two feelings, those associated only with resultant consciousness, are said to be intended.

Aṭṭhadhā [M 0.0170] tattha pañcannaṃ, pañcadvāramhi paccayo;

Sesānaṃ ekadhā phasso, manodvārepi so tathā.

Therein, for the five in the five-door process, the condition is eightfold. For the remaining, contact is a condition in one way; and so too at the mind-door.

Tattha hi pañcadvāre cakkhupasādādivatthukānaṃ pañcannaṃ vedanānaṃ cakkhusamphassādiko phasso sahajātaaññamaññanissayavipākaāhārasampayuttaatthiavigatavasena [P 0.0179] aṭṭhadhā paccayo hoti. Sesānaṃ pana ekekasmiṃ dvāre sampaṭicchanasantīraṇatadārammaṇavasena pavattānaṃ kāmāvacaravipākavedanānaṃ cakkhusamphassādiko phasso upanissayavasena ekadhāva paccayo hoti.

Indeed, therein, in the five-door process, for the five feelings that have eye-sensitivity and so forth as their physical basis, contact, such as eye-contact, is a condition in eight ways: by way of co-nascence, mutuality, dependence, result, nutriment, association, presence, and non-disappearance. But for the remaining sense-sphere resultant feelings occurring in each door by way of receiving, investigating, and registering, contact, such as eye-contact, is a condition in one way only, by way of decisive support.

‘Manodvārepi so tathā’ti manodvārepi hi tadārammaṇavasena pavattānaṃ kāmāvacaravipākavedanānaṃ so sahajātamanosamphassasaṅkhāto phasso tatheva aṭṭhadhā paccayo hoti, paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutivasena ca pavattānaṃ tebhūmakavipākavedanānampi. Yā panetā manodvāre tadārammaṇavasena pavattā kāmāvacaravedanā, tāsaṃ manodvāre āvajjanasampayutto manosamphasso upanissayavasena ekadhā paccayo hotīti.

By 'and so too at the mind-door'—indeed, at the mind-door, for the sense-sphere resultant feelings occurring by way of registering, that contact, known as co-nascent mind-contact, is a condition in the same eight ways; and also for the three-plane resultant feelings occurring by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death. But as for those sense-sphere feelings occurring by way of registering at the mind-door, for them, mind-contact associated with adverting at the mind-door is a condition in one way, by way of decisive support.

Phassapaccayā vedanāpadaniddeso.

Exposition of the Term 'Feeling Conditioned by Contact'.

Taṇhāpadaniddeso

Exposition of the Term 'Craving'

232. Vedanāpaccayā [V 0.0171] taṇhāniddese –

232. In the exposition of 'craving conditioned by feeling'—

Rūpataṇhādibhedena, cha taṇhā idha dīpitā;

Ekekā tividhā tattha, pavattākārato matā.

Six cravings are here explained, divided into craving for forms and so on. Each of these is considered threefold, based on its mode of occurrence.

Imasmiñhi vedanāpaccayā taṇhāniddese ‘seṭṭhiputto brāhmaṇaputto’ti pitito nāmavasena putto viya imā rūpataṇhā…pe… dhammataṇhāti ārammaṇato nāmavasena cha taṇhā dīpitā pakāsitā kathitāti attho. Tattha rūpe taṇhā rūpataṇhāti iminā nayena padattho veditabbo.

Indeed, in this exposition of 'craving conditioned by feeling,' just as a son is designated by name according to his father as 'the merchant's son' or 'the brahmin's son,' so too, these six cravings—craving for forms... craving for mental phenomena—are shown, revealed, and declared by name according to the object; this is the meaning. Here, the meaning of the term should be understood in this way: 'craving for form' is craving in regard to form.

Tāsu ca pana taṇhāsu ekekā taṇhā pavattiākārato kāmataṇhā, bhavataṇhā, vibhavataṇhāti evaṃ tividhā matā. Rūpataṇhā eva hi yadā cakkhussa āpāthagataṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ kāmassādavasena assādayamānā [M 0.0171] pavattati, tadā kāmataṇhā nāma hoti. Yadā tadevārammaṇaṃ dhuvaṃ sassatanti pavattāya sassatadiṭṭhiyā saddhiṃ pavattati, tadā bhavataṇhā nāma hoti. Sassatadiṭṭhisahagato hi rāgo bhavataṇhāti vuccati. Yadā pana tadevārammaṇaṃ “ucchijjati vinassatī”ti pavattāya ucchedadiṭṭhiyā saddhiṃ pavattati, tadā vibhavataṇhā nāma hoti. Ucchedadiṭṭhisahagato hi [P 0.0180] rāgo vibhavataṇhāti vuccati. Eseva nayo saddataṇhādīsupīti etā aṭṭhārasa taṇhā honti.

But among these cravings, each craving is considered threefold according to its mode of occurrence: as sensual craving, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. Indeed, when craving for forms itself occurs, savoring a visible object that has come into the range of the eye by way of sensual gratification, then it is called sensual craving. When that same object occurs together with the view of eternalism, which holds it to be permanent and eternal, then it is called craving for existence. For desire accompanied by the view of eternalism is called craving for existence. But when that same object occurs together with the view of annihilationism, which holds that 'it is annihilated, it is destroyed,' then it is called craving for non-existence. For desire accompanied by the view of annihilationism is called craving for non-existence. This same method applies to craving for sounds and so forth. Thus, there are eighteen cravings.

Tā ajjhattarūpādīsu aṭṭhārasa, bahiddhā aṭṭhārasāti chattiṃsa. Iti atītā chattiṃsa, anāgatā chattiṃsa, paccuppannā chattiṃsāti aṭṭhasataṃ taṇhā honti. Tā pana saṃṅkhippamānā rūpādiārammaṇavasena cha, kāmataṇhādivasena vā tissova taṇhā hontīti veditabbā. Yasmā panime sattā puttaṃ assādetvā putte mamattena dhātiyā viya rūpādiārammaṇavasena uppajjamānaṃ vedanaṃ assādetvā vedanāya mamattena rūpādiārammaṇadāyakānaṃ cittakāragandhabbagandhikasūdatantavāyarasāyanavidhāyakavejjādīnaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ karonti, tasmā sabbāpesā vedanāpaccayā taṇhā hotīti veditabbā.

These are eighteen with regard to internal forms and so forth, and eighteen with regard to external forms—thus thirty-six. Thus, there are thirty-six in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six in the present—totaling one hundred and eight cravings. However, when condensed, these cravings should be understood as six by way of objects such as forms, or as just three by way of sensual craving and so forth. But because beings, delighting in their children and cherishing them with possessiveness like a wet nurse, delight in feeling that arises by way of objects such as forms, and cherish that feeling with possessiveness, they greatly honor those who provide objects such as forms—such as painters, musicians, perfumers, cooks, weavers, alchemists, physicians, and others. Therefore, it should be understood that all this craving is conditioned by feeling.

Yasmā cettha [V 0.0172] adhippetā, vipākasukhavedanā;

Ekāva ekadhā cesā, tasmā taṇhāya paccayo.

Because here the intended is pleasant resultant feeling; and since this is one and in one way, it is therefore a condition for craving.

‘Ekadhā’ti upanissayapaccayena paccayo hoti. Yasmā vā –

'In one way' means it is a condition by way of decisive support condition. Or because:

Dukkhī sukhaṃ patthayati, sukhī bhiyyopi icchati;

Upekkhā pana santattā, sukhamicceva bhāsitā.

One who suffers longs for happiness, one who is happy desires even more; but equanimity, being tranquil, is spoken of as happiness itself.

Taṇhāya paccayā tasmā, honti tissopi vedanā;

Vedanāpaccayā taṇhā, iti vuttā mahesinā.

Therefore, the three feelings are conditions for craving. 'Craving is conditioned by feeling'—thus it was said by the Great Seer.

Vedanā paccayā cāpi, yasmā nānusayaṃ vinā;

Hoti tasmā na sā hoti, brāhmaṇassa vusīmatoti.

And since feeling does not occur without a latent tendency, it is a condition; therefore, that craving does not arise for the brahmin who has lived the holy life.

Vedanāpaccayā taṇhāpadaniddeso.

The Exposition of the Factor 'Craving Conditioned by Feeling'.

Upādānapadaniddeso

The Exposition of the Factor of Clinging

233. Taṇhāpaccayā [M 0.0172] upādānaniddese –

233. In the exposition of 'Clinging Conditioned by Craving':

Upādānāni cattāri, tāni atthavibhāgato;

Dhammasaṅkhepavitthārā, kamato ca vibhāvaye.

There are four clingings; they should be explained according to their meaning, concisely and extensively in terms of the Dhamma, and in sequence.

Pāḷiyañhi upādānanti kāmupādānaṃ…pe… attavādupādānanti imāni cattāri upādānāni āgatāni. Tesaṃ ayaṃ atthavibhāgo – vatthusaṅkhātaṃ kāmaṃ upādiyatīti kāmupādānaṃ. Kāmo ca so upādānañcātipi kāmupādānaṃ. Upādānanti [P 0.0181] daḷhaggahaṇaṃ. Daḷhattho hettha upasaddo upāyāsa-upakaṭṭhādīsu viya. Tathā diṭṭhi ca sā upādānañcāti diṭṭhupādānaṃ. Diṭṭhiṃ upādiyatīti vā diṭṭhupādānaṃ[V 0.0173]. Sassato attā ca loko cātiādīsu hi purimadiṭṭhiṃ uttaradiṭṭhi upādiyati. Tathā sīlabbataṃ upādiyatīti sīlabbatupādānaṃ. Sīlabbatañca taṃ upādānañcātipi sīlabbatupādānaṃ. Gosīlagovatādīni hi evaṃ suddhīti abhinivesato sayameva upādānānīti. Tathā vadanti etenāti vādo, upādiyanti etenāti upādānaṃ. Kiṃ vadanti upādiyanti vā? Attānaṃ. Attano vādupādānaṃ attavādupādānaṃ. Attavādamattameva vā attāti upādiyanti etenāti attavādupādānaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva tesaṃ atthavibhāgo.

In the Pāli canon, four clingings have been handed down: clinging to sensual pleasures… and so on… up to clinging to the doctrine of self. This is their analysis of meaning: It clings to sensuality, designated as the basis, thus it is 'clinging to sensual pleasures' (kāmupādāna). Or, it is both sensuality and clinging, thus 'clinging to sensual pleasures.' 'Upādāna' means firm grasping. Here, the prefix 'upa-' has the meaning of firmness, as in 'upāyāsa' (tribulation) and 'upakaṭṭha' (nearness). Similarly, it is a view that is also a clinging, thus 'clinging to views' (diṭṭhupādāna). Or, it clings to a view, thus 'clinging to views.' For in views such as 'the self and the world are eternal,' a later view clings to a former view. Similarly, it clings to precepts and practices, thus 'clinging to precepts and practices' (sīlabbatupādāna). Or, it is both precepts and practices and that clinging, thus 'clinging to precepts and practices.' For practices like the cow-asceticism and the dog-asceticism, due to the adherence that 'by this there is purification,' are themselves clingings. Similarly, 'vāda' (doctrine) is that by which they declare; 'upādāna' is that by which they cling. What do they declare or cling to? The self. The clinging to the doctrine of self is 'attavādupādāna.' Or, it is that by which they cling to the mere doctrine of self as 'self,' thus 'clinging to the doctrine of self.' This, for now, is their analysis of meaning.

‘Dhammasaṅkhepavitthāre’ pana kāmupādānaṃ tāva “tattha katamaṃ kāmupādānaṃ? Yo kāmesu kāmacchando kāmarāgo kāmanandī kāmataṇhā kāmasneho kāmapariḷāho kāmamucchā kāmajjhosānaṃ – idaṃ vuccati kāmupādāna”nti āgatattā saṅkhepato taṇhādaḷhattaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṇhādaḷhattaṃ nāma purimataṇhāupanissayapaccayena daḷhasambhūtā uttarataṇhā eva. Keci panāhu – appattavisayapatthanā taṇhā, andhakāre corassa hatthappasāraṇaṃ viya. Sampattavisayaggahaṇaṃ upādānaṃ, tasseva bhaṇḍaggahaṇaṃ viya. Appicchatāsantuṭṭhitāpaṭipakkhā ca te dhammā. Tathā pariyesanārakkhadukkhamūlāti. Sesupādānattayaṃ pana saṅkhepato diṭṭhimattameva.

But in the 'concise and extensive explanation of the Dhamma,' with regard to clinging to sensual pleasures, it is stated: "Herein, what is clinging to sensual pleasures? Whatever desire for sensual pleasures, lust for sensual pleasures, delight in sensual pleasures, craving for sensual pleasures, affection for sensual pleasures, fever for sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures, obsession with sensual pleasures—this is called clinging to sensual pleasures." Because it is stated thus, in brief, the firmness of craving is meant. The firmness of craving is simply the subsequent craving that has arisen strongly with the previous craving as its decisive support condition. Some, however, say: craving is the longing for an unattained object, like a thief stretching out his hand in the dark. Clinging is the grasping of an attained object, like that same thief's seizing of the goods. And these states are the opposite of having few wishes and contentment. Likewise, they are the root of the suffering of seeking and guarding. The remaining three types of clinging, however, are in brief merely view.

Vitthārato pana pubbe rūpādīsu vuttāya aṭṭhasatappabhedāyapi taṇhāya daḷhabhāvo kāmupādānaṃ. Dasavatthukā micchādiṭṭhi diṭṭhupādānaṃ. Yathāha – “tattha katamaṃ diṭṭhupādānaṃ? Natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭhaṃ…pe… sacchikatvā pavedentīti yā [M 0.0173] evarūpā diṭṭhi…pe… vipariyesaggāho – idaṃ vuccati diṭṭhupādāna”nti (dha. sa. 1221; vibha. 938) sīlavatehi suddhiparāmasanaṃ pana sīlabbatupādānaṃ. Yathāha – “tattha [P 0.0182] katamaṃ sīlabbatupādānaṃ? Ito bahiddhā samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sīlena suddhi, vatena suddhi, sīlabbatena suddhīti yā evarūpā diṭṭhi…pe… vipariyesaggāho – idaṃ vuccati sīlabbatupādāna”nti (dha. sa. 1222; vibha. 938). Vīsativatthukā sakkāyadiṭṭhi attavādupādānaṃ. Yathāha – “tattha katamaṃ attavādupādānaṃ? Idha assutavā puthujjano…pe… sappurisadhamme avinīto rūpaṃ attato samanupassati…pe… vipariyesaggāho – idaṃ vuccati attavādupādāna”nti (dha. sa. 1223; vibha. 938). Ayamettha dhammasaṅkhepavitthāro.

In detail, however, the firm state of craving—which has been previously explained as divided into 108 types regarding forms and so on—is clinging to sensual pleasures. Wrong view with its ten bases is clinging to views. As it is said: 'Therein, what is clinging to views? “There is nothing given, nothing offered…” and so on… “which they make known after having realized it for themselves”—whatever such view… and so on… a perverse grasping—this is called clinging to views' (Dhs §1221; Vbh §938). The misapprehension of purification by means of rites and vows, however, is clinging to rites and vows. As it is said: 'Therein, what is clinging to rites and vows? That for ascetics and brahmins outside of this dispensation “purification is through virtue, purification is through vows, purification is through virtue and vows”—whatever such view… and so on… a perverse grasping—this is called clinging to rites and vows' (Dhs §1222; Vbh §938). The twenty-fold personality view is clinging to a doctrine of self. As it is said: 'Therein, what is clinging to a doctrine of self? Here, an uninstructed ordinary person… and so on… untrained in the Dhamma of true men, regards form as self… and so on… a perverse grasping—this is called clinging to a doctrine of self' (Dhs §1223; Vbh §938). This here is the teaching in summary and in detail.

‘Kamato’ti [V 0.0174] ettha pana tividho kamo – uppattikkamo, pahānakkamo, desanākkamo ca. Tattha anamatagge saṃsāre imassa paṭhamaṃ uppattīti abhāvato kilesānaṃ nippariyāyena uppattikkamo na vuccati. Pariyāyena pana yebhuyyena ekasmiṃ bhave attaggāhapubbaṅgamo sassatucchedābhiniveso. Tato “sassato ayaṃ attā”ti gaṇhato attavisuddhatthaṃ sīlabbatupādānaṃ, ucchijjatīti gaṇhato paralokanirapekkhassa kāmupādānanti evaṃ paṭhamaṃ attavādupādānaṃ, tato diṭṭhisīlabbatakāmupādānānīti ayametesaṃ ekasmiṃ bhave uppattikkamo.

As for 'sequentially,' here there are three kinds of sequence: the sequence of arising, the sequence of abandoning, and the sequence of teaching. Among these, since in the beginningless round of rebirths there is no first arising of these defilements, the sequence of arising is not spoken of in an absolute sense. In a relative sense, however, for the most part in a single existence, the adherence to eternalism and annihilationism is preceded by the grasping of a self. Then, for one who holds 'this self is eternal,' there arises clinging to rites and vows for the sake of self-purification; for one who holds 'it is annihilated,' there arises clinging to sensual pleasures, being indifferent to the next world. Thus, first comes clinging to a doctrine of self, then clinging to views, clinging to rites and vows, and clinging to sensual pleasures—this is their sequence of arising in a single existence.

Diṭṭhupādānādīni cettha paṭhamaṃ pahīyanti sotāpattimaggavajjhattā. Kāmupādānaṃ pacchā arahattamaggavajjhattāti. Ayametesaṃ pahānakkamo.

Herein, clinging to views and the others are abandoned first, as they are to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry. Clinging to sensual pleasures is abandoned later, as it is to be abandoned by the path of arahantship. This is their sequence of abandoning.

Mahāvisayattā pana pākaṭattā ca etesu kāmupādānaṃ paṭhamaṃ desitaṃ. Mahāvisayañhi taṃ aṭṭhacittasampayogā. Appavisayāni itarāni catucittasampayogā. Yebhuyyena ca ālayarāmatāya pajāya pākaṭaṃ kāmupādānaṃ, na itarāni. Kāmupādānavā vatthukāmānaṃ samadhigamatthaṃ kotūhalamaṅgalādibahulo hoti, na sassatadiṭṭhīti tadanantaraṃ diṭṭhupādānaṃ. Taṃ pabhijjamānaṃ sīlabbataattavādupādānavasena duvidhaṃ hoti. Tasmiṃ dvaye gokiriyaṃ vā kukkurakiriyaṃ vā disvāpi veditabbato oḷārikanti sīlabbatupādānaṃ paṭhamaṃ desitaṃ, sukhumattā ante attavādupādānanti ayametesaṃ desanākkamo.

However, among these, clinging to sensual pleasures is taught first on account of its vast scope and its obviousness. For it has a vast scope, being associated with eight types of consciousness. The others have a narrow scope, being associated with four types of consciousness. Moreover, for people who delight in attachment, clinging to sensual pleasures is generally obvious, but the others are not. One with clinging to sensual pleasures is much given to curiosities, festivities, and so on, for the sake of obtaining sensual objects, not to eternalist views; therefore, clinging to views is taught immediately after that. When that is broken down, it becomes twofold: clinging to rites and vows, and clinging to a doctrine of self. Between these two, clinging to rites and vows is taught first because it is coarse, being knowable even from seeing the practice of a cow or the practice of a dog. Clinging to a doctrine of self comes last because of its subtlety. This is their sequence of teaching.

Taṇhā [M 0.0174] ca purimassettha, ekadhā hoti paccayo;

Sattadhā aṭṭhadhā vāpi, hoti sesattayassa sā.

Herein, for the first, craving is a condition in one way; for the remaining three, it is a condition sevenfold or even eightfold.

Ettha [P 0.0183] ca evaṃ desite upādānacatukke purimassa kāmupādānassa kāmataṇhā upanissayavasena ekadhāva paccayo hoti taṇhābhinanditesu visayesu uppattito. Sesattayassa pana sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatahetuvasena sattadhā vā upanissayena saha aṭṭhadhā vāpi paccayo hoti. Yadā ca sā upanissayavasena paccayo hoti tadā asahajātāva hotīti.

Herein, in the fourfold clinging thus taught, for the first, which is clinging to sensual pleasures, craving for sensual pleasures is a condition in one way, by way of decisive support, because it arises in objects delighted in through craving. For the remaining three, however, craving is a condition in seven ways—by way of conascence, mutuality, dependence, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root—or even in eight ways together with decisive support. And when it is a condition by way of decisive support, it is non-conascent.

Taṇhāpaccayā upādānapadaniddeso.

The Exposition of the Term 'Clinging' as Conditioned by Craving.

Bhavapadaniddeso

Exposition of the Term 'Becoming'

234. Upādānapaccayā [V 0.0175] bhavaniddese –

234. In the exposition of 'becoming' as conditioned by clinging:

Atthato dhammato ceva, sātthato bhedasaṅgahā;

Yaṃ yassa paccayo ceva, viññātabbo vinicchayo.

The analysis should be understood by way of meaning and by way of the text, with its explanation, by division and summary, and as to what is a condition for what.

Tattha bhavatīti bhavo. Duvidhenāti dvīhi ākārehi pavattitoti attho. Athavā duvidhenāti paccate karaṇavacanaṃ, duvidhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Atthīti saṃvijjati. Kammameva bhavo kammabhavo. Upapattiyeva bhavo upapattibhavo. Ettha ca upapatti bhavatīti bhavo. Kammaṃ pana yathā sukhakāraṇattā “sukho buddhānamuppādo”ti (dha. pa. 194) vutto, evaṃ bhavakāraṇattā phalavohārena bhavoti veditabbaṃ. Tattha katamo kammabhavoti tesu dvīsu bhavesu yo kammabhavoti vutto, so katamoti attho. Puññābhisaṅkhārādayo vuttatthā eva. Sabbanti anavasesaṃ. Bhavaṃ gacchati gameti cāti bhavagāmi. Iminā lokuttaraṃ paṭikkhipati. Ayañhi vaṭṭakathā, tañca vivaṭṭanissitanti. Karīyatīti kammaṃ.

Therein, 'it becomes' (bhavati), thus it is 'becoming' (bhavo). 'In two ways' (duvidhena) means it proceeds in two modes. Alternatively, 'duvidhena' is an instrumental expression, meaning 'it is said to be twofold.' 'There is' (atthi) means it exists. Kamma itself is becoming: kamma-becoming. Rebirth itself is becoming: rebirth-becoming. Herein, rebirth is 'becoming' because it comes to be. But kamma should be understood as 'becoming' by a figurative expression referring to its fruit, because it is a cause of becoming; just as it is said, 'Happy is the arising of the Buddhas' (Dhp 194), because it is a cause of happiness. 'Therein, what is kamma-becoming?': among these two becomings, that which is called kamma-becoming, what is it?—this is the meaning. 'Meritorious formations, etc.' have the meaning already stated. 'All' (sabbaṃ) means without remainder. 'It goes to becoming' (bhavaṃ gacchati) or 'it leads to becoming' (gameti), thus it is 'leading to becoming' (bhavagāmi). By this, the supramundane is rejected, for this is a discourse on the round, whereas that is concerned with the ending of the round. 'It is done' (karīyati), thus it is 'kamma'.

Kāmabhavādīsu kāmasaṅkhāto bhavo kāmabhavo. Esa nayo rūpārūpabhavesu. Saññāvataṃ bhavo, saññā vā ettha bhave atthīti saññābhavo. Vipariyāyena [P 0.0184] asaññābhavo. Oḷārikasaññāya abhāvā [M 0.0175] sukhumāya ca bhāvā neva saññā nāsaññā asmiṃ bhaveti nevasaññānāsaññābhavo. Ekena rūpakkhandhena vokiṇṇo bhavo ekavokārabhavo. Eko vā vokāro assa bhavassāti ekavokārabhavo. Eseva nayo catuvokārapañcavokārabhavesu. Ayaṃ vuccati upapattibhavoti esa navavidhopi upapattibhavo nāma vuccatīti. Evaṃ tāvettha ‘atthato’ viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Among 'sensual becoming, etc.,' the becoming designated as 'sensual' is sensual becoming. The same principle applies to form becoming and formless becoming. The becoming of those with perception, or the becoming wherein perception is present, is perception-becoming. Conversely, there is non-perception-becoming. Because of the absence of coarse perception and the presence of subtle perception, the becoming wherein there is neither perception nor non-perception is neither-perception-nor-non-perception-becoming. The becoming endowed with the single aggregate of form is one-constituent becoming; or, this becoming has one constituent, thus it is one-constituent becoming. The same principle applies to four-constituent and five-constituent becomings. 'This is called rebirth-becoming' means that this ninefold becoming is called rebirth-becoming. Thus, so far, the analysis should be understood 'by way of meaning'.

‘Dhammato’ pana ettha hi puññābhisaṅkhāro dhammato terasa cetanā, apuññābhisaṅkhāro dvādasa, āneñjābhisaṅkhāro catasso. “Sabbampi bhavagāmikamma”nti etena sabbepete dhammā cetanā sampayuttā vā kammasaṅkhātā ācayagāmino dhammā saṅgahitā. Kāmabhavo pañca upādinnakkhandhā, tathā rūpabhavo, arūpabhavo cattāro, saññābhavo catupañca, asaññābhavo eko [V 0.0176] upādinnakkhandho, nevasaññānāsaññābhavo cattāro. Ekavokārabhavādayo ekacatupañcakkhandhā upādinnakkhandhehīti evamettha ‘dhammato’pi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

'By way of the Dhamma,' here, the meritorious formation consists of thirteen volitions, the demeritorious formation of twelve, and the imperturbable formation of four. 'All kamma leading to becoming'—by this, all these phenomena, whether volitions or associated therewith and termed kamma, are included as phenomena that lead to accumulation. Sensual becoming is the five clinging-aggregates; likewise form becoming; formless becoming is four; perceptual becoming four or five; non-perceptual becoming is one clinging-aggregate; and neither-perception-nor-non-perception becoming is four. The one-constituent becomings and others are one, four, or five aggregates, as clinging-aggregates. Thus, the analysis here should also be understood 'by way of the Dhamma'.

‘Sātthato’ti yathā ca bhavaniddese tatheva kāmañca saṅkhāraniddesepi puññābhisaṅkhārādayova vuttā, evaṃ santepi purimā atītakammavasena idha paṭisandhiyā paccayattā vuttā. Ime paccuppannakammavasena āyatiṃ paṭisandhiyā paccayattāti punavacanaṃ sātthakameva. Pubbe vā “tattha katamo puññābhisaṅkhāro? Kusalacetanā kāmāvacarā”ti evamādinā nayena cetanāva saṅkhārāti vuttā. Idha pana “sabbampi bhavagāmikamma”nti vacanato cetanāsampayuttāpi. Pubbe ca viññāṇapaccayameva kammaṃ saṅkhārāti vuttaṃ, idāni asaññābhavanibbattakampi. Kiṃ vā bahunā? “Avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti ettha puññābhisaṅkhārādayova kusalākusaladhammā vuttā. “Upādānapaccayā bhavo”ti idha pana upapattibhavassāpi saṅgahitattā kusalākusalābyākatā dhammā vuttā. Tasmā sabbathāpi [P 0.0185] sātthakamevidaṃ punavacananti. Evamettha ‘sātthato’pi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

'Meaningfully': just as in the exposition of becoming, so too in the exposition of formations, the meritorious formations, etc., are mentioned. Even so, the former formations are spoken of here as conditions for rebirth-linking by way of past kamma. These, by way of present kamma, are conditions for future rebirth-linking—thus, this repetition is indeed meaningful. Previously, it was said, 'Herein, what is the meritorious formation? It is wholesome volition pertaining to the sense sphere,' and so on; thus volition itself was said to be formations. Here, however, by the statement 'All kamma leading to becoming,' even what is associated with volition is included. Previously, only kamma that is a condition for consciousness was called formations, but now even what produces non-perceptual becoming is included. What more is there to say? 'With ignorance as condition, formations'—here, the meritorious formations, etc., are said to be wholesome and unwholesome phenomena. 'With clinging as condition, becoming'—here, because rebirth-becoming is also included, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena are spoken of. Therefore, in every way, this repetition is indeed meaningful. Thus, the analysis here should also be understood 'meaningfully'.

‘Bhedasaṅgahā’ti upādānapaccayā bhavassa bhedato ceva saṅgahato ca. Yañhi kāmupādānapaccayā kāmabhavanibbattakaṃ kammaṃ kariyati, so kammabhavo. Tadabhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo. Esa nayo rūpārūpabhavesu. Evaṃ kāmupādānapaccayā [M 0.0176] dve kāmabhavā, tadantogadhāva saññābhavapañcavokārabhavā; dve rūpabhavā, tadantogadhāva saññābhavaasaññābhavaekavokārabhavapañcavokārabhavā; dve arūpabhavā, tadantogadhāva saññābhavanevasaññānāsaññābhavacatuvokārabhavāti saddhiṃ antogadhehi cha bhavā. Yathā ca kāmupādānapaccayā saddhiṃ antogadhehi cha bhavā tathā sesupādānapaccayāpīti evaṃ upādānapaccayā bhedato saddhiṃ antogadhehi catuvīsati bhavā.

'By way of division and inclusion' means by way of the division and inclusion of becoming conditioned by clinging. For the kamma that produces sensual becoming, conditioned by sensual clinging, is kamma-becoming. The aggregates produced by that are rebirth-becoming. The same method applies to form and formless becomings. Thus, conditioned by sensual clinging, there are two sensual becomings, with perceptual becoming and five-constituent becoming included within them; two form becomings, with perceptual becoming, non-perceptual becoming, one-constituent becoming, and five-constituent becoming included within them; two formless becomings, with perceptual becoming, neither-perception-nor-non-perception becoming, and four-constituent becoming included within them—thus, together with what is included, there are six becomings. Just as conditioned by sensual clinging there are six becomings together with what is included within them, so too for the remaining clingings. Thus, conditioned by clinging, there are twenty-four becomings by way of division, together with what is included within them.

Saṅgahato pana kammabhavaṃ upapattibhavañca ekato katvā kāmupādānapaccayā saddhiṃ antogadhehi eko kāmabhavo, tathā rūpārūpabhavāti tayo bhavā. Tathā sesupādānapaccayāpīti evaṃ upādānapaccayā saṅgahato saddhiṃ antogadhehi dvādasa bhavā. Apica avisesena upādānapaccayā kāmabhavūpagaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo. Tadabhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo. Esa nayo rūpārūpabhavesu. Evaṃ upādānapaccayā saddhiṃ antogadhehi dve kāmabhavā, dve rūpabhavā, dve [V 0.0177] arūpabhavāti aparenapi pariyāyena saṅgahato cha bhavā. Kammabhavaupapattibhavabhedaṃ vā anupagamma saddhiṃ antogadhehi kāmabhavādivasena tayo bhavā honti. Kāmabhavādibhedañcāpi anupagamma kammabhavaupapattibhavavasena dve bhavā honti. Kammupapattibhedañca anupagamma upādānapaccayā bhavoti bhavavasena eko bhavo hotīti. Evamettha upādānapaccayassa bhavassa bhedasaṅgahāpi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

By way of inclusion, grouping kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming together, conditioned by sensual clinging, with what is included within them, there is one sensual becoming; similarly, form and formless becomings—thus, there are three becomings. Likewise, with the remaining clingings. Thus, conditioned by clinging, by way of inclusion, together with what is included within them, there are twelve becomings. Furthermore, generally speaking, the kamma leading to sensual becoming, conditioned by clinging, is kamma-becoming. The aggregates produced by that are rebirth-becoming. The same applies to form and formless becomings. Thus, conditioned by clinging, together with what is included within them, there are two sensual becomings, two form becomings, and two formless becomings—making six becomings by another method of inclusion. Alternatively, without distinguishing between kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming, together with what is included within them, there are three becomings by way of sensual becoming, etc. And without distinguishing between sensual becoming, etc., there are two becomings by way of kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming. And without distinguishing between kamma and rebirth, conditioned by clinging, there is one becoming by way of becoming. Thus, in this context, the analysis of the divisions and inclusions of becoming conditioned by clinging should also be understood.

‘Yaṃ yassa paccayo cevā’ti yañcettha upādānaṃ yassa paccayo hoti, tatopi viññātabbo vinicchayoti attho. Kiṃ panettha kassa paccayo hoti? Yaṃ kiñci yassa kassaci paccayo [P 0.0186] hotiyeva. Ummattako viya hi puthujjano. So ‘idaṃ yuttaṃ, idaṃ ayutta’nti avicāretvā yassa kassaci upādānassa vasena yaṃ kiñci bhavaṃ patthetvā yaṃ kiñci kammaṃ karotiyeva. Tasmā yadekacce “sīlabbatupādānena rūpārūpabhavā na hontī”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Sabbena pana sabbo hotīti gahetabbaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – idhekacco anussavavasena vā diṭṭhānusārena vā “kāmā nāmete manussaloke ceva khattiyamahāsālakulādīsu chakāmāvacaradevaloke ca samiddhā”ti cintetvā tesaṃ adhigamatthaṃ asaddhammasavanādīhi vañcito ‘iminā kammena kāmā sampajjantī’ti maññamāno [M 0.0177] kāmupādānavasena kāyaduccaritādīnipi karoti. So duccaritapāripūriyā apāye uppajjati; sandiṭṭhike vā pana kāme patthayamāno paṭiladdhe vā gopayamāno kāmupādānavasena kāyaduccaritādīnipi karoti. So duccaritapāripūriyā apāye uppajjati. Tatrāssa upapattihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo, kammābhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo saññābhavapañcavokārabhavā pana tadantogadhā eva.

'And what is a condition for what': the meaning is that the analysis should also be understood from the perspective of which clinging is a condition for which becoming. What here is a condition for what? Anything whatsoever is a condition for anything whatsoever. For the ordinary person is indeed like a madman. Without considering, 'This is fitting, this is unfitting,' he longs for any kind of existence and performs any kind of action by means of any kind of clinging. Therefore, what some say, 'Through clinging to rites and rituals, existence in the form and formless realms does not occur,' should not be accepted. Rather, it should be understood that any becoming can arise from any clinging. For example: Here, someone, influenced by hearsay or following a view, thinks, 'Indeed, sensual pleasures are abundant in this human world, among the great warrior clans and so on, and in the six sensual heavens.' Deceived by listening to false teachings and so on, believing, 'Through this action sensual pleasures are attained,' he performs bodily misconduct and so on by means of sensual clinging. Through the full measure of misconduct, he is reborn in the lower realms. Or, desiring visible sensual pleasures, or guarding them once obtained, he performs bodily misconduct and so on by means of sensual clinging. Through the full measure of misconduct, he is reborn in the lower realms. In that case, the kamma that is the cause of his arising is kamma-becoming; the aggregates produced by kamma are rebirth-becoming. Perceptual becoming and five-constituent becoming are, however, included within that.

Aparo pana saddhammasavanādīhi upabrūhitañāṇo “iminā kammena kāmā sampajjantī”ti maññamāno kāmupādānavasena kāyasucaritādīni karoti. So sucaritapāripūriyā devesu vā manussesu vā uppajjati. Tatrāssa upapattihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo, kammābhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo. Saññābhavapañcavokārabhavā pana tadantogadhā eva. Iti kāmupādānaṃ sappabhedassa sāntogadhassa kāmabhavassa paccayo hoti.

Another, whose knowledge is strengthened by listening to the true Dhamma and so on, thinking, 'Through this action sensual pleasures are attained,' performs bodily good conduct and so on by means of sensual clinging. Through the full measure of good conduct, he is reborn among devas or humans. There, the kamma that is the cause of his arising is kamma-becoming; the aggregates produced by kamma are rebirth-becoming. Perception-becoming and five-constituent becoming are, however, included within that. Thus, sensual clinging is a condition for sensual becoming, with its subdivisions and what is included within it.

Aparo “rūpārūpabhavesu tato samiddhatarā kāmā”ti sutvā vā parikappetvā vā kāmupādānavaseneva [V 0.0178] rūpārūpasamāpattiyo nibbattetvā samāpattibalena rūpārūpabrahmaloke uppajjati. Tatrāssa upapattihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo, kammābhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo. Saññāasaññā nevasaññā nāsaññāekavokāracatuvokārapañcavokārabhavā pana tadantogadhā eva. Iti kāmupādānaṃ sappabhedānaṃ sāntogadhānaṃ rūpārūpabhavānampi paccayo hoti[P 0.0187].

Another, having heard or conjectured that 'the pleasures in the form and formless realms are more excellent,' generates the meditative attainments of form and formlessness by means of sensual clinging. By the power of these attainments, he is reborn in the Brahma worlds of form and formlessness. There, the kamma that is the cause of his arising is kamma-becoming; the aggregates produced by kamma are rebirth-becoming. Perception-becoming, non-perception-becoming, neither-perception-nor-non-perception-becoming, one-constituent becoming, four-constituent becoming, and five-constituent becoming are, however, included within that. Thus, sensual clinging is a condition for the form and formless becomings, with their subdivisions and what is included within them.

Aparo “ayaṃ attā nāma kāmāvacarasampattibhave vā rūpārūpabhavānaṃ vā aññatarasmiṃ ucchinno suucchinno hotī”ti ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ upādāya tadupagaṃ kammaṃ karoti. Tassa taṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo, kammābhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo. Saññābhavādayo pana tadantogadhā eva. Iti diṭṭhupādānaṃ sappabhedānaṃ sāntogadhānaṃ tiṇṇampi kāmarūpārūpabhavānaṃ paccayo hoti.

Another, taking up the annihilationist view that 'this self is utterly annihilated in some fortunate existence in the sensual realm or in one of the form or formless realms,' performs kamma leading to that. For him, that kamma is kamma-becoming; the aggregates produced by kamma are rebirth-becoming. Perception-becoming and the others are, however, included within that. Thus, clinging to views is a condition for all three becomings—sensual, form, and formless—with their subdivisions and what is included within them.

Aparo “ayaṃ attā nāma kāmāvacarasampattibhave vā rūpārūpabhavānaṃ vā aññatarasmiṃ sukhī hoti, vigatapariḷāho hotī”ti attavādupādānena tadupagaṃ kammaṃ karoti. Tassa taṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo, tadabhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo. Saññābhavādayo pana tadantogadhā eva[M 0.0178]. Iti attavādupādānaṃ sappabhedānaṃ sāntogadhānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ bhavānaṃ paccayo hoti.

Another, through clinging to the doctrine of self that 'this self is happy and free from distress in some fortunate existence—whether in the sensual realm or in one of the form and formless realms'—performs kamma leading to that. For him, that kamma is kamma-becoming; the aggregates produced by that are rebirth-becoming. Perception-becoming and the others are, however, included within that. Thus, clinging to the doctrine of self is a condition for the three becomings, with their subdivisions and what is included within them.

Aparo “idaṃ sīlabbataṃ nāma kāmāvacarasampattibhave vā rūpārūpabhavānaṃ vā aññatarasmiṃ paripūrentassa sukhaṃ pāripūriṃ gacchatī”ti sīlabbatupādānavasena tadupagaṃ kammaṃ karoti. Tassa taṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo, tadabhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo. Saññābhavādayo pana tadantogadhā eva. Iti sīlabbatupādānampi sappabhedānaṃ sāntogadhānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ bhavānaṃ paccayo hotīti evamettha yaṃ yassa paccayo hoti tatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Another, by means of clinging to rites and rituals, performs kamma leading to that, thinking: 'For one perfecting this morality and these vows in some fortunate existence—whether in the sensual realm or in one of the form and formless realms—happiness reaches fulfillment.' For him, that kamma is kamma-becoming; the aggregates produced by that are rebirth-becoming. Perception-becoming and the others are, however, included within that. Thus, clinging to rites and rituals is also a condition for the three becomings, with their subdivisions and what is included within them. In this way, the analysis of what is a condition for what should also be understood.

Kiṃ panettha kassa bhavassa kathaṃ paccayo hotīti ce?

If it is asked: what here is a condition for what becoming, and how?

Rūpārūpabhavānaṃ, upanissayapaccayo upādānaṃ;

Sahajātādīhipi taṃ, kāmabhavassāti viññeyyaṃ.

For the form and formless becomings, clinging is a decisive support condition. For sensual becoming, it should be understood as a co-nascence condition and so on.

Rūpārūpabhavānañhi kāmabhavapariyāpannassa ca kāmabhave kusalakammasseva upapattibhavassa cetaṃ catubbidhampi upādānaṃ upanissayapaccayena ekadhā paccayo hoti. Kāmabhave attanā sampayuttaakusalakammabhavassa [V 0.0179] sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatahetupaccayappabhedehi sahajātādīhi paccayo hoti. Vippayuttassa pana upanissayapaccayenevāti.

For the form and formless becomings, and for the rebirth-becoming of wholesome kamma included in sensual becoming, all four kinds of clinging are a condition in one way by way of decisive support condition. In sensual becoming, for unwholesome kamma-becoming associated with itself, it is a condition by way of co-nascence and so on, through the distinctions of co-nascence, mutuality, dependence, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root condition. But for the dissociated, it is only by way of decisive support condition.

Upādānapaccayā bhavapadaniddeso.

The exposition of the term 'becoming as conditioned by clinging' is concluded.

Jātijarāmaraṇādipadaniddeso

Exposition of the Terms Beginning with Birth, Aging, and Death

235. Bhavapaccayā [P 0.0188] jātiniddesādīsu jātiādīnaṃ vinicchayo saccavibhaṅge vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Bhavoti panettha kammabhavova adhippeto. So hi jātiyā paccayo, na upapattibhavo. So pana kammapaccayaupanissayapaccayavasena dvidhāva paccayo hotīti.

235. In the exposition of 'birth conditioned by becoming' and so on, the analysis of birth and so on should be understood in the same way as explained in the Analysis of the Truths.
