Here, 'becoming' (bhava) is intended specifically as kamma-becoming. For that is the condition for birth, not rebirth-becoming. That, however, is a condition in two ways: as a kamma-condition and as a decisive-support condition.

Tattha siyā – kathaṃ panetaṃ jānitabbaṃ “bhavo jātiyā paccayo”ti ce? Bāhirapaccayasamattepi hīnapaṇītatādivisesadassanato. Bāhirānañhi janakajanettisukkasoṇitāhārādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ samattepi sattānaṃ yamakānampi sataṃ hīnapaṇītatādiviseso dissati. So ca na ahetuko[M 0.0179], sabbadā ca sabbesañca abhāvato; na kammabhavato aññahetuko, tadabhinibbattakasattānaṃ ajjhattasantāne aññassa kāraṇassa abhāvatoti kammabhavahetukova. Kammañhi sattānaṃ hīnapaṇītādivisesahetu. Tenāha bhagavā – “kammaṃ satte vibhajati yadidaṃ hīnappaṇītatāyā”ti (ma. ni. 3.289). Tasmā jānitabbametaṃ – “bhavo jātiyā paccayo”ti.

Here it might be asked: 'How, then, is it to be known that becoming is a condition for birth?' It is known by observing distinctions such as inferiority and superiority, even when external conditions are the same. For even when external conditions such as procreative parents, semen, blood, and food are the same, a distinction of inferiority and superiority is seen among beings, even among twins. And this is not without a cause, since it does not exist for all beings at all times; nor is it due to any other cause besides kamma-becoming, since there is no other cause in the internal continuum of beings produced by that. Thus, it is caused by kamma-becoming. Indeed, kamma is the cause of distinctions such as inferiority and superiority among beings. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Kamma divides beings, that is, by way of inferiority and superiority' (MN 3.203). Thus, it should be known that 'becoming is a condition for birth.'

Yasmā ca asati jātiyā jarāmaraṇaṃ nāma na hoti, sokādayo ca dhammā na honti, jātiyā pana sati jarāmaraṇañceva jarāmaraṇasaṅkhātadukkhadhammaphuṭṭhassa ca bālassa jarāmaraṇābhisambandhā vā tena tena dukkhadhammena phuṭṭhassa anabhisambandhā vā sokādayo ca dhammā honti, tasmā ayaṃ jātijarāmaraṇassa ceva sokādīnañca paccayo hotīti veditabbā. Sā pana upanissayakoṭiyā ekadhāva paccayo hotīti.

Moreover, because when there is no birth, there is no such thing as aging and death, nor are there states such as sorrow; but when there is birth, there are aging and death, and for a fool touched by the suffering designated as aging and death, sorrow and the like arise—whether through connection with that aging and death or, though not connected with it, through being touched by various kinds of suffering. Therefore, this birth should be understood as the condition for aging and death as well as for sorrow and the like. It is, however, a condition in only one way, in the category of decisive support.

Bhavapaccayā jātiādipadaniddeso.

The exposition of the terms beginning with 'birth as conditioned by becoming' is concluded.

242. Evametassātiādīnaṃ [V 0.0180] attho uddesavāre vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Saṅgatiādīni samudayavevacanāneva.

242. The meaning of phrases like 'thus this' should be understood in the same way as explained in the section on the outline. Terms like 'conjunction' (saṅgati) are merely synonyms for origination (samudaya).

Yasmā panettha sokādayo avasāne vuttā, tasmā yā sā avijjā “avijjāpaccayā [P 0.0189] saṅkhārā”ti evametassa bhavacakkassa ādimhi vuttā, sā –

Since sorrow and the like are mentioned at the end here, therefore that ignorance stated at the beginning of this wheel of becoming—'conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations'—is:

Sokādīhi avijjā, siddhā bhavacakkamaviditādimidaṃ;

Kārakavedakarahitaṃ, dvādasavidhasuññatāsuññaṃ.

Ignorance is established by sorrow and the like; this wheel of becoming, beginning with non-knowing, is devoid of a doer and an experiencer, empty with a twelvefold emptiness.

Satataṃ samitaṃ pavattatīti veditabbaṃ. Kathaṃ panettha sokādīhi avijjā siddhā? Kathamidaṃ bhavacakkaṃ aviditādi? Kathaṃ kārakavedakarahitaṃ? Kathaṃ dvādasavidhasuññatāsuññanti ce? Ettha hi sokadukkhadomanassupāyāsā avijjāya aviyogino, paridevo ca nāma mūḷhassāti tesu tāva siddhesu siddhāva hoti avijjā. Apica “āsavasamudayā avijjāsamudayo”ti hi vuttaṃ. Āsavasamudayā cete sokādayo honti. Kathaṃ? Vatthukāmaviyoge tāva soko kāmāsavasamudayo hoti? Yathāha –

It should be understood as constantly and continuously turning. But how, then, is ignorance established here by sorrow and the like? How is this wheel of becoming characterized by non-knowing? How is it devoid of a doer and an experiencer? How is it empty with a twelvefold emptiness? Here, sorrow, suffering, displeasure, and despair are inseparable from ignorance, and lamentation is indeed of the deluded. Thus, with these being established, ignorance is indeed established. Furthermore, it is said: 'With the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance.' And these, sorrow and the like, arise with the arising of the taints. How? In the separation from desirable objects, sorrow arises from the arising of the taint of sensual desire. As it is said:

“Tassa [M 0.0180] ce kāmayānassa, chandajātassa jantuno;

Te kāmā parihāyanti, sallaviddhova ruppatī”ti. (su. ni. 773);

'When those pleasures of a person who desires, born of longing, diminish, he is afflicted, as if pierced by a dart' (Sn 773).

Yathā cāha – “kāmato jāyatī soko”ti (dha. pa. 215). Sabbepi cete diṭṭhāsavasamudayā honti, yathāha – “tassa ahaṃ rūpaṃ, mama rūpanti pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino taṃ rūpaṃ vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa rūpavipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.1). Yathā ca diṭṭhāsavasamudayā evaṃ bhavāsavasamudayāpi, yathāha – “yepi te devā dīghāyukā vaṇṇavanto sukhabahulā uccesu vimānesu ciraṭṭhitikā tepi tathāgatassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā yebhuyyena bhayaṃ saṃvegaṃ santāsaṃ āpajja”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.78; a. ni. 4.33) pañca pubbanimittāni disvā maraṇabhayena santajjitānaṃ devānaṃ viyāti. Yathā ca bhavāsavasamudayā evaṃ avijjāsavasamudayāpi[V 0.0181], yathāha – “sa kho so, bhikkhave, bālo diṭṭheva dhamme tividhaṃ dukkhadomanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedetī”ti (ma. ni. 3.246).

As it is also said: 'From desire sorrow is born' (Dhp 215). And all these arise from the taint of views, as it is said: 'For one who dwells obsessed with the thought, "I am form, form is mine," that form changes and alters. From the change and alteration of form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise' (SN 3.1). Just as they arise from the taint of views, so too do they arise from the taint of becoming, as it is said: 'Even those gods who are long-lived, beautiful, abounding in happiness, dwelling in lofty palaces, and remaining for a long time, when they hear the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, for the most part they experience fear, trepidation, and terror' (SN 3.78; AN 4.33), like the gods who, seeing the five preliminary signs, are terrified by the fear of death. And just as they arise from the taint of becoming, so too do they arise from the taint of ignorance, as it is said: 'That fool, monks, experiences here and now three kinds of pain and grief' (MN 3.246).

Iti yasmā āsavasamudayā ete honti, tasmā ete sijjhamānā avijjāya hetubhūte āsave sādhenti. Āsavesu ca siddhesu paccayabhāve bhāvato avijjāpi siddhāva hotīti. Evaṃ tāvettha ‘sokādīhi avijjā siddhā’ hotīti veditabbā.

Thus, since these arise from the origin of the taints, therefore, as they are being established, they establish the taints which are the cause of ignorance. And when the taints are established as conditions, ignorance too is thereby established. Thus, it should be understood that here 'ignorance is established by sorrow and the like.'

Yasmā pana evaṃ paccayabhāve bhāvato avijjāya siddhāya puna “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa”nti evaṃ hetuphalaparamparāya [P 0.0190] pariyosānaṃ natthi, tasmā taṃ hetuphalasambandhavasena pavattaṃ dvādasaṅgaṃ ‘bhavacakkaṃ aviditādī’ti siddhaṃ hoti.

Since, in this way, with ignorance established as a condition, and furthermore, 'dependent on ignorance, formations; dependent on formations, consciousness,' and so on, there is no end to this chain of cause and effect. Therefore, that twelve-factored cycle which proceeds through the connection of cause and effect is established as the 'wheel of becoming, beginning with non-knowing.'

Evaṃ sati “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti idaṃ ādimattakathanaṃ virujjhatīti ce? Nayidaṃ ādimattakathanaṃ, padhānadhammakathanaṃ panetaṃ. Tiṇṇañhi vaṭṭānaṃ avijjā padhānā. Avijjāggahaṇena hi avasesaṃ kilesavaṭṭañca kammādīni ca bālaṃ paliveṭhenti, sappasiraggahaṇena sesaṃ sappasarīraṃ viya bāhaṃ. Avijjāsamucchede pana kate tehi vimokkho hoti, sappasiracchede kate paliveṭhitabāhāvimokkho viya. Yathāha – “avijjāyatveva asesavirāganirodhā [M 0.0181] saṅkhāranirodho”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.1; mahāva. 1). Iti yaṃ gaṇhato bandho muñcato ca mokkho hoti, tassa padhānadhammassa kathanamidaṃ, na ādimattakathananti evamidaṃ bhavacakkaṃ aviditādīti veditabbaṃ. Tayidaṃ yasmā avijjādīhi kāraṇehi saṅkhārādīnaṃ pavatti, tasmā tato aññena “brahmā mahābrahmā seṭṭho sajitā”ti evaṃ parikappitena brahmādinā vā saṃsārassa kārakena “so kho pana me ayaṃ attā vado vedeyyo”ti evaṃ parikappitena attanā vā sukhadukkhānaṃ vedakena rahitaṃ. Iti ‘kārakavedakarahita’nti veditabbaṃ.

If it is said, 'Does this statement—"dependent on ignorance, formations"—contradict the idea of a mere beginning?' No, this is not a statement of a mere beginning; rather, it is a statement of the principal factor. For ignorance is the principal factor among the three rounds. Indeed, by grasping ignorance, the remaining round of defilements and actions entangle the fool, just as grasping a snake by the head entangles the arm with the rest of its body. But when ignorance is utterly destroyed, there is liberation from them, just as when a snake's head is cut off, there is liberation for the entangled arm. As it is said: 'With the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations,' and so on (SN 2.1; Mahāva. 1). Thus, this is a statement of that principal factor, by grasping which there is bondage, and by releasing which there is liberation; it is not a statement of a mere beginning. In this way, this wheel of becoming is to be understood as beginning with non-knowing. And because formations and so on proceed due to causes like ignorance, therefore this wheel of becoming is devoid of any other creator of saṃsāra conceived as 'Brahmā, Mahābrahmā, the highest, the victorious,' or of a self conceived as 'This self of mine speaks and feels,' which is an experiencer of pleasure and pain. Thus, it is to be understood as 'devoid of a doer and an experiencer.'

Yasmā panettha avijjā udayabbayadhammakattā dhuvabhāvena, saṃkiliṭṭhattā saṃkilesikattā ca subhabhāvena, udayabbayapaṭipīḷitattā sukhabhāvena, paccayāyattavuttittā vasavattanabhūtena attabhāvena ca suññā, tathā saṅkhārādīnipi aṅgāni; yasmā vā avijjā na attā, na attano[V 0.0182], na attani, na attavatī, tathā saṅkhārādīnipi aṅgāni; tasmā ‘dvādasavidhasuññatāsuññamidaṃ’ bhavacakkanti veditabbaṃ.

Because ignorance here is empty of permanence, due to its nature of arising and passing away; empty of beauty, due to its defiled and defiling nature; empty of happiness, due to being afflicted by arising and passing away; and empty of a self that has control, due to its existence being dependent on conditions—and likewise for the other factors beginning with formations; or because ignorance is not self, not of a self, not in a self, and does not possess a self—and likewise for the other factors beginning with formations; therefore, it should be understood that 'this wheel of becoming is empty with a twelvefold emptiness.'

Evañca viditvā puna –

Having understood thus, again:

Tassa avijjātaṇhā, mūlamatītādayo tayo kālā;

Dve aṭṭha dve eva ca, sarūpato tesu aṅgāni.

Its roots are ignorance and craving; its three periods are the past and so on. The factors in them, in their own nature, are two, eight, and two respectively.

Tassa [P 0.0191] kho panetassa bhavacakkassa avijjā taṇhā cāti dve dhammā mūlanti veditabbā. Tadetaṃ pubbantāharaṇato avijjāmūlaṃ vedanāvasānaṃ, aparantasantānato taṇhāmūlaṃ jarāmaraṇāvasānanti duvidhaṃ hoti. Tattha purimaṃ diṭṭhicaritavasena vuttaṃ, pacchimaṃ taṇhācaritavasena. Diṭṭhicaritānañhi avijjā, taṇhācaritānaṃ taṇhā saṃsāranāyikā. Ucchedadiṭṭhisamugghātāya vā paṭhamaṃ, phaluppattiyā hetūnaṃ anupacchedapakāsanato; sassatadiṭṭhisamugghātāya dutiyaṃ, uppannānaṃ jarāmaraṇapakāsanato; gabbhaseyyakavasena vā purimaṃ, anupubbapavattidīpanato; opapātikavasena pacchimaṃ sahuppattidīpanato.

Of this wheel of becoming, it should be understood that ignorance and craving—these two phenomena—are the roots. This is twofold: when traced back to the past, it has ignorance as its root and ends in feeling; when traced forward in continuity to the future, it has craving as its root and ends in aging and death. Herein, the former is stated by way of the disposition towards views, the latter by way of the disposition towards craving. For those with a disposition towards views, ignorance is the leader in saṃsāra; for those with a disposition towards craving, craving is. Or, the first is for the uprooting of annihilationist views, by revealing the non-interruption of causes for the arising of results; the second is for the uprooting of eternalist views, by revealing the aging and death of what has arisen. Or, the first is by way of those born from the womb, showing the sequential process; the latter is by way of spontaneously born beings, showing simultaneous arising.

Atītapaccuppannānāgatā cassa tayo kālā. Tesu pāḷiyaṃ sarūpato āgatavasena avijjā saṅkhārā cāti dve aṅgāni atītakālāni[M 0.0182], viññāṇādīni bhavāvasānāni aṭṭha paccuppannakālāni, jāti ceva jarāmaraṇañca dve anāgatakālānīti veditabbāni. Puna –

And its three periods are past, present, and future. Among these, as they appear in their own nature in the Pāḷi, ignorance and formations are the two past factors; the eight present factors begin with consciousness and end with becoming; and birth and aging-and-death are the two future factors, so it should be understood. Further:

Hetuphalahetupubbaka-tisandhicatubhedasaṅgahañcetaṃ;

Vīsatiākārāraṃ, tivaṭṭamanavaṭṭhitaṃ bhamati.

This is a compendium of four divisions with three links of cause and effect; with twenty spokes of modes, it revolves through three rounds unceasingly.

Itipi veditabbaṃ. Tattha saṅkhārānañca paṭisandhiviññāṇassa ca antarā eko hetuphalasandhi nāma. Vedanāya ca taṇhāya ca antarā eko phalahetusandhi nāma. Bhavassa ca jātiyā ca antarā eko hetuphalasandhīti. Evamidaṃ hetuphalahetupubbakatisandhīti veditabbaṃ. Sandhīnaṃ ādipariyosānavavatthitā panassa cattāro saṅgahā honti, seyyathidaṃ – avijjāsaṅkhārā eko [V 0.0183] saṅgaho, viññāṇanāmarūpasaḷāyatanaphassavedanā dutiyo, taṇhupādānabhavā tatiyo, jātijarāmaraṇaṃ catutthoti. Evamidaṃ catubhedasaṅgahanti veditabbaṃ.

This too should be understood. Herein, between formations and rebirth-linking consciousness, there is one link called cause-and-effect. Between feeling and craving, there is one link called effect-and-cause. And between becoming and birth, there is one link called cause-and-effect. Thus, this should be understood as the three links of cause and effect. And its four groupings are established by the beginning and end of the links, namely: ignorance and formations are one grouping; consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are the second; craving, clinging, and becoming are the third; and birth, aging, and death are the fourth. Thus, this should be understood as the fourfold grouping.

Atīte hetavo pañca, idāni phalapañcakaṃ;

Idāni hetavo pañca, āyatiṃ phalapañcakanti.

In the past were five causes; now are five results; now are five causes; in the future will be five results.

Etehi pana vīsatiyā ākārehi arehi vīsatiākārāranti veditabbaṃ. Tattha ‘atīte hetavo pañcā’ti avijjā saṅkhārā cāti ime tāva dve vuttā [P 0.0192] eva. Yasmā pana avidvā paritassati, paritasito upādiyati, tassa upādānapaccayā bhavo, tasmā taṇhupādānabhavāpi gahitā honti. Tenāha “purimakammabhavasmiṃ moho avijjā, āyūhanā saṅkhārā, nikanti taṇhā, upagamanaṃ upādānaṃ, cetanā bhavo, ime pañca dhammā purimakammabhavasmiṃ idha paṭisandhiyā paccayā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.47).

And on account of these twenty modes as spokes, it is understood as 'having twenty spokes of modes.' Herein, regarding 'in the past were five causes': ignorance and formations, these two, have already been stated. But since the ignorant one craves, and craving, clings, and with clinging as condition there is becoming, therefore craving, clinging, and becoming are also included. Hence it is said: 'In a previous kamma-existence, delusion is ignorance, accumulation is formations, longing is craving, approach is clinging, and volition is becoming; these five phenomena in a previous kamma-existence are conditions for rebirth-linking here' (Paṭis. I, 52).

Tattha purimakammabhavasminti purime kammabhave, atītajātiyaṃ kammabhave kariyamāneti attho. Moho avijjāti yo tadā dukkhādīsu moho, yena mūḷho kammaṃ karoti, sā avijjā. Āyūhanā saṅkhārāti taṃ kammaṃ karoto purimacetanāyo, yathā ‘dānaṃ dassāmī’ti cittaṃ uppādetvā māsampi saṃvaccharampi dānūpakaraṇāni sajjentassa uppannā purimacetanāyo. Paṭiggāhakānaṃ pana hatthe dakkhiṇaṃ patiṭṭhāpayato cetanā bhavoti vuccati. Ekāvajjanesu vā chasu javanesu cetanā āyūhanasaṅkhārā nāma. Sattamā cetanā bhavo. Yā kāci vā pana cetanā [M 0.0183] bhavo, taṃsampayuttā āyūhanasaṅkhārā nāma. Nikanti taṇhāti yā kammaṃ karontassa tassa phale uppattibhave nikāmanā patthanā sā taṇhā nāma. Upagamanaṃ upādānanti yaṃ kammaṃ bhavassa paccayabhūtaṃ; ‘idaṃ katvā asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne kāme sevissāmi ucchijjissāmī’tiādinā nayena pavattaṃ upagamanaṃ gahaṇaṃ parāmasanaṃ – idaṃ upādānaṃ nāma. Cetanā bhavoti āyūhanāvasāne vuttacetanā bhavoti evamattho veditabbo.

Herein, 'in the previous kamma-existence' means in the former kamma-existence, in the past birth, when kamma-existence was being performed—this is the meaning. Delusion is ignorance: that delusion regarding suffering and so on at that time, by which one, being deluded, performs kamma—that is ignorance. Accumulation is formations: the prior volitions of one performing that kamma, such as the prior volitions that arise when one, having generated the thought 'I will give a gift,' prepares the requisites for giving for even a month or a year. But the volition of one placing the offering into the hands of the recipients is called 'becoming.' Alternatively, in a single cognitive process, the volition in the six impulsions is called 'accumulating formations.' The seventh volition is 'becoming.' Or any volition whatsoever is 'becoming,' and the factors associated with it are called 'accumulating formations.' Longing is craving: that desire and aspiration for the result of that kamma to arise in a future existence, for one performing kamma—that is craving. Approach is clinging: that kamma which is a condition for becoming, and the approaching, grasping, and attachment that occurs in such ways as, 'Having done this, I will enjoy sensual pleasures in such and such a place, or I will be annihilated'—this is called clinging. Volition is becoming: it should be understood that the volition mentioned at the culmination of accumulation is 'becoming'—this is the meaning.

‘Idāni phalapañcaka’nti viññāṇādi vedanāvasānaṃ pāḷiyaṃ āgatameva. Yathāha “idha paṭisandhi viññāṇaṃ, okkanti nāmarūpaṃ, pasādo āyatanaṃ, phuṭṭho phasso, vedayitaṃ vedanā ime pañca dhammā idhūpapattibhavasmiṃ purekatassa kammassa paccayā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.47). Tattha [V 0.0184] paṭisandhi viññāṇanti yaṃ bhavantarapaṭisandhānavasena uppannattā paṭisandhīti vuccati, taṃ viññāṇaṃ. Okkanti nāmarūpanti yā gabbhe rūpārūpadhammānaṃ okkanti, āgantvā pavisanaṃ viya – idaṃ nāmarūpaṃ. Pasādo āyatananti idaṃ cakkhādipañcāyatanavasena [P 0.0193] vuttaṃ. Phuṭṭho phassoti yo ārammaṇaṃ phuṭṭho phusanto uppanno – ayaṃ phasso. Vedayitaṃ vedanāti yaṃ paṭisandhiviññāṇena vā saḷāyatanapaccayena vā phassena sahuppannaṃ vipākavedayitaṃ, sā vedanāti evamattho veditabbo.

'Now are five results' refers to the pentad beginning with consciousness and ending with feeling, as it is given in the Pāḷi. As it is said: 'Here, rebirth-linking is consciousness, descent is name-and-form, sensitivity is the sense base, impingement is contact, and what is felt is feeling—these five phenomena in this arising-existence are conditioned by kamma done previously' (Paṭis. I, 52). Herein, 'rebirth-linking is consciousness' is the consciousness that is called 'rebirth-linking' because it arises by way of linking to another existence. 'Descent is name-and-form' is the descent of material and immaterial phenomena into the womb, as if coming and entering—this is name-and-form. 'Sensitivity is the sense base' refers to what is stated by way of the five sense bases beginning with the eye. 'Impingement is contact' is the contact that arises, impinging upon the object—this is contact. 'What is felt is feeling' is the resultant feeling that arises together with rebirth-linking consciousness, or with contact conditioned by the six sense bases—this is feeling. Thus, the meaning should be understood.

‘Idāni hetavo pañcā’ti taṇhādayo pāḷiyaṃ āgatāva taṇhupādānabhavā. Bhave pana gahite tassa pubbabhāgā taṃsampayuttā vā saṅkhārā gahitāva honti, taṇhupādānaggahaṇena ca taṃsampayuttā, yāya vā mūḷho kammaṃ karoti sā avijjā gahitāva hotīti evaṃ pañca. Tenāha “idha paripakkattā āyatanānaṃ moho avijjā, āyūhanā saṅkhārā, nikanti taṇhā, upagamanaṃ upādānaṃ, cetanā bhavo. Ime pañca dhammā idha kammabhavasmiṃ āyatiṃ paṭisandhiyā paccayā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.47). Tattha idha paripakkattā āyatanānanti paripakkāyatanassa kammakaraṇakāle sammoho dassito. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

'Now are five causes' refers to craving and so on, which are already given in the Pāḷi as craving, clinging, and becoming. But when becoming is included, its preceding parts or associated formations are also included; and by the inclusion of craving and clinging, that ignorance by which a deluded one performs kamma is also included. Thus, there are five. Therefore, it is said: 'Here, due to the maturation of the sense bases, delusion is ignorance, accumulation is formations, longing is craving, approach is clinging, and volition is becoming. These five phenomena in this kamma-existence are conditions for future rebirth-linking' (Paṭis. I, 52). Herein, 'here, due to the maturation of the sense bases' shows the delusion at the time of performing kamma when the sense bases are matured. The rest is evident.

‘Āyatiṃ phalapañcaka’nti viññāṇādīni pañca. Tāni jātiggahaṇena vuttāni. Jarāmaraṇaṃ pana tesaṃyeva jarāmaraṇaṃ. Tenāha “āyatiṃ paṭisandhi [M 0.0184] viññāṇaṃ, okkanti nāmarūpaṃ, pasādo āyatanaṃ, phuṭṭho phasso, vedayitaṃ vedanā. Ime pañca dhammā āyatiṃ upapattibhavasmiṃ idha katassa kammassa paccayā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.47). Evamidaṃ vīsatiākārāraṃ hoti.

'In the future will be five results' refers to the five beginning with consciousness. These are stated by the inclusion of birth. But aging-and-death is the aging-and-death of those very same factors. Hence it is said: 'In the future, rebirth-linking is consciousness, descent is name-and-form, sensitivity is the sense base, impingement is contact, and what is felt is feeling. These five phenomena in a future arising-existence are conditioned by kamma done here' (Paṭis. I, 52). Thus, this comes to have twenty spokes of modes.

Tattha purimabhavasmiṃ pañca kammasambhārā, etarahi pañca vipākasambhārā, etarahi pañca kammasambhārā, anāgate pañca vipākadhammāti dasa dhammā kammaṃ, dasa vipākoti. Dvīsu ṭhānesu kammaṃ kammaṃ nāma, dvīsu ṭhānesu vipāko vipāko nāmāti sabbampetaṃ bhavacakkaṃ paccayākāravaṭṭaṃ kammañceva kammavipāko ca. Tathā dvīsu ṭhānesu kammaṃ kammasaṅkhepo, dvīsu ṭhānesu vipāko vipākasaṅkhepoti sabbampetaṃ kammasaṅkhepo ceva vipākasaṅkhepo ca. Dvīsu ṭhānesu kammaṃ kammavaṭṭaṃ, dvīsu ṭhānesu vipāko vipākavaṭṭanti sabbampetaṃ kammavaṭṭañceva vipākavaṭṭañca. Tathā dvīsu ṭhānesu kammaṃ kammabhavo, dvīsu ṭhānesu vipāko vipākabhavoti sabbampetaṃ [V 0.0185] kammabhavo ceva vipākabhavo ca. Dvīsu ṭhānesu kammaṃ kammapavattaṃ[P 0.0194], dvīsu ṭhānesu vipāko vipākapavattanti sabbampetaṃ kammapavattañceva vipākapavattañca. Tathā dvīsu ṭhānesu kammaṃ kammasantati, dvīsu vipāko vipākasantatīti sabbampetaṃ kammasantati ceva vipākasantati ca. Dvīsu ṭhānesu kammaṃ kiriyā nāma, dvīsu vipāko kiriyāphalaṃ nāmāti sabbampetaṃ kiriyā ceva kiriyāphalañcāti.

Herein, in the past existence, five are the kamma-constituents; presently, five are the resultant constituents; presently, five are the kamma-constituents; in the future, five are resultant states—thus ten states are kamma, and ten are result. In two respects kamma is called kamma, and in two respects result is called result—all this is the wheel of existence, the cycle of conditions, both kamma and kamma-result. Likewise, in two respects kamma is the kamma-compendium; in two respects result is the result-compendium—all this is both the kamma-compendium and the result-compendium. In two respects kamma is the kamma-round; in two respects result is the result-round—all this is both the kamma-round and the result-round. Similarly, in two respects kamma is kamma-becoming; in two respects result is resultant-becoming—all this is both kamma-becoming and resultant-becoming. In two respects kamma is the kamma-process; in two respects result is the resultant-process—all this is both the kamma-process and the resultant-process. Similarly, in two respects kamma is the kamma-continuity; in two respects result is the resultant-continuity—all this is both the kamma-continuity and the resultant-continuity. In two respects kamma is called action; in two respects result is called the fruit of action—all this is both action and the fruit of action.

Evaṃ samuppannamidaṃ sahetukaṃ,

Dukkhaṃ aniccaṃ calamittaraddhuvaṃ;

Dhammehi dhammā pabhavanti hetuso,

Na hettha attāva parova vijjati.

Thus arisen, this suffering is with cause, impermanent, unstable, transient, and not lasting; phenomena arise from phenomena due to causes; herein, neither a self nor another is found.

Dhammā dhamme sañjanenti, hetusambhārapaccayā;

Hetūnañca nirodhāya, dhammo buddhena desito;

Hetūsu uparuddhesu, chinnaṃ vaṭṭaṃ na vaṭṭati.

Phenomena produce phenomena, conditioned by causal constituents; and for the cessation of causes, the Dhamma was taught by the Buddha; when causes are ceased, the cycle is cut off and does not turn.

Evaṃ dukkhantakiriyāya, brahmacariyīdha vijjati;

Satte ca nūpalabbhante, nevucchedo na sassataṃ.

Thus, for the ending of suffering, the holy life is found here; and when beings are not apprehended, there is neither annihilation nor eternalism.

Tivaṭṭamanavaṭṭhitaṃ bhamatīti ettha pana saṅkhārabhavā kammavaṭṭaṃ, avijjātaṇhūpādānāni kilesavaṭṭaṃ, viññāṇanāmarūpasaḷāyatanaphassavedanā vipākavaṭṭanti imehi tīhi vaṭṭehi tivaṭṭamidaṃ bhavacakkaṃ yāva kilesavaṭṭaṃ na upacchijjati [M 0.0185] tāva anupacchinnapaccayattā anavaṭṭhitaṃ punappunaṃ parivaṭṭanato bhamatiyevāti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, regarding 'the triple round revolves without stopping': volitional formations and becoming are the kamma-round; ignorance, craving, and clinging are the defilement-round; consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are the result-round. By these three rounds, this triple-round wheel of existence revolves. As long as the defilement-round is not cut off, because of its unbroken conditionality, it is unsettled and revolves again and again—this should be understood.

Tayidamevaṃ bhamamānaṃ –

This very wheel, thus revolving—

Saccappabhavato kiccā, vāraṇā upamāhi ca;

Gambhīranayabhedā ca, viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

From the arising of the truths, by function, by prevention, by similes, and by distinctions in profound method, it should be understood as is appropriate.

Tattha [V 0.0186] yasmā kusalākusalakammaṃ avisesena samudayasaccanti saccavibhaṅge vuttaṃ, tasmā avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti avijjāya saṅkhārā dutiyasaccappabhavaṃ dutiyasaccaṃ, saṅkhārehi viññāṇaṃ dutiyasaccappabhavaṃ paṭhamasaccaṃ, viññāṇādīhi nāmarūpādīni vipākavedanāpariyosānāni paṭhamasaccappabhavaṃ paṭhamasaccaṃ, vedanāya taṇhā paṭhamasaccappabhavaṃ dutiyasaccaṃ, taṇhāya upādānaṃ dutiyasaccappabhavaṃ dutiyasaccaṃ, upādānato bhavo dutiyasaccappabhavaṃ paṭhamadutiyasaccadvayaṃ, bhavato jāti [P 0.0195] dutiyasaccappabhavaṃ paṭhamasaccaṃ, jātiyā jarāmaraṇaṃ paṭhamasaccappabhavaṃ paṭhamasaccanti. Evaṃ tāvidaṃ ‘saccappabhavato’ viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

Herein, since wholesome and unwholesome kamma are generally stated as the truth of origin in the analysis of the truths, therefore: 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations' means that volitional formations from ignorance are sourced from the second truth, and are the second truth; 'with volitional formations as condition, consciousness' means that consciousness from volitional formations is sourced from the second truth, and is the first truth; 'with consciousness as condition, name-and-form,' up to name-and-form, etc., ending with resultant feeling, are the first truth, sourced from the first truth; 'with feeling as condition, craving' means that craving from feeling is sourced from the first truth, and is the second truth; 'with craving as condition, clinging' means that clinging from craving is sourced from the second truth, and is the second truth; 'with clinging as condition, existence' means that existence from clinging is sourced from the second truth, and is both the first and second truths; 'with existence as condition, birth' means that birth from existence is sourced from the second truth, and is the first truth; 'with birth as condition, aging-and-death' means that aging-and-death from birth is sourced from the first truth, and is the first truth. Thus, this should be understood as 'from the arising of the truths,' as is appropriate.

Yasmā panettha avijjā vatthūsu ca satte sammoheti paccayo ca hoti saṅkhārānaṃ pātubhāvāya, tathā saṅkhārā saṅkhatañca abhisaṅkharonti paccayā ca honti viññāṇassa, viññāṇampi vatthuñca paṭijānāti paccayo ca hoti nāmarūpassa, nāmarūpampi aññamaññañca upatthambheti paccayo ca hoti saḷāyatanassa, saḷāyatanampi savisaye ca vattati paccayo ca hoti phassassa, phassopi ārammaṇañca phusati paccayo ca hoti vedanāya, vedanāpi ārammaṇarasañca anubhavati paccayo ca hoti taṇhāya, taṇhāpi rajjanīye ca dhamme rajjati paccayo ca hoti upādānassa, upādānampi upādānīye ca dhamme upādiyati paccayo ca hoti bhavassa, bhavopi nānāgatīsu ca vikkhipati paccayo ca hoti jātiyā, jātipi khandhe ca janeti tesaṃ abhinibbattibhāvena pavattatā paccayo ca hoti jarāmaraṇassa, jarāmaraṇampi khandhānaṃ pākabhedabhāvañca adhitiṭṭhati paccayo ca hoti bhavantarapātubhāvāya sokādīnaṃ adhiṭṭhānattā, tasmā sabbapadesu dvidhā pavatta‘kiccato’pi idaṃ viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

Furthermore, herein, ignorance both deludes beings concerning objects and is a condition for the manifestation of volitional formations. Similarly, volitional formations both construct the conditioned and are a condition for consciousness. Consciousness both cognizes the object and is a condition for name-and-form. Name-and-form both support each other and are a condition for the six sense bases. The six sense bases both function in their respective spheres and are a condition for contact. Contact both touches the object and is a condition for feeling. Feeling both experiences the taste of the object and is a condition for craving. Craving both delights in desirable things and is a condition for clinging. Clinging both grasps at things to be clung to and is a condition for existence. Existence both scatters beings into various destinies and is a condition for birth. Birth both generates the aggregates, by their mode of renewed production and continuance, and is a condition for aging-and-death. Aging-and-death both presides over the ripening and breaking up of the aggregates and, by being the basis for sorrow and so forth, is a condition for the manifestation of a future existence. Therefore, in all these cases, this should be understood from its twofold function, as is appropriate.

Yasmā [M 0.0186] cettha “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti idaṃ kārakadassananivāraṇaṃ, “saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa”nti attasaṅkantidassananivāraṇaṃ, “viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti attātiparikappitavatthubhedadassanato ghanasaññānivāraṇaṃ, “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”ntiādīsu “attā passati…pe… vijānāti phusati vedayati taṇhiyati upādiyati bhavati jāyati jīyati mīyatī”ti evamādidassananivāraṇaṃ, tasmā micchādassananivāraṇatopetaṃ bhavacakkaṃ ‘nivāraṇato’ viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

Furthermore, herein, the statement 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations' prevents the view of a doer. 'With volitional formations as condition, consciousness' prevents the view of self-transference. 'With consciousness as condition, name-and-form' prevents the perception of solidity by showing the division of the object fantasized as a self. In the statements 'with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases,' etc., it prevents views such as 'the self sees… knows, contacts, feels, craves, clings, becomes, is born, ages, and dies.' Thus, because the wheel of existence prevents wrong views, it should be understood as 'preventive,' as is appropriate.

Yasmā panettha salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇavasena dhammānaṃ adassanato andho viya avijjā[V 0.0187], andhassa upakkhalanaṃ viya avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, upakkhalitassa patanaṃ [P 0.0196] viya saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, patitassa gaṇḍapātubhāvo viya viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ, gaṇḍabhedapīḷakā viya nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ, gaṇḍapīḷakāghaṭṭanaṃ viya saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso, ghaṭṭanadukkhaṃ viya phassapaccayā vedanā, dukkhassa paṭikārābhilāso viya vedanāpaccayā taṇhā, paṭikārābhilāsena asappāyaggahaṇaṃ viya taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ, upādinnaasappāyālepanaṃ viya upādānapaccayā bhavo, asappāyālepanena gaṇḍavikārapātubhāvo viya bhavapaccayā jāti, gaṇḍavikārato gaṇḍabhedo viya jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ.

Furthermore, herein, because of not seeing phenomena in terms of their individual characteristics and common characteristics, ignorance is like a blind man. Just as a blind man stumbles, so volitional formations arise conditioned by ignorance. Just as a stumble leads to a fall, so consciousness arises conditioned by volitional formations. Just as a fall causes a sore to appear, so name-and-form arises conditioned by consciousness. Just as a sore breaks into boils, so the six sense bases arise conditioned by name-and-form. Just as the boils are rubbed, so contact arises conditioned by the six sense bases. Just as rubbing causes suffering, so feeling arises conditioned by contact. Just as suffering creates a desire for a remedy, so craving arises conditioned by feeling. Just as desire leads to seizing unsuitable things, so clinging arises conditioned by craving. Just as unsuitable things are applied, so existence arises conditioned by clinging. Just as the application causes the sore to worsen, so birth arises conditioned by existence. Just as the worsening causes the sore to break open, so aging-and-death arise conditioned by birth.

Yasmā vā panettha avijjā appaṭipattimicchāpaṭipattibhāvena satte abhibhavati paṭalaṃ viya akkhīni, tadabhibhūto ca bālo ponobbhavikehi saṅkhārehi attānaṃ veṭheti kosakārakimi viya kosappadesehi, saṅkhārapariggahitaṃ viññāṇaṃ gatīsu patiṭṭhaṃ labhati pariṇāyakapariggahito viya rājakumāro rajje, upapattinimittaṃ parikappanato viññāṇaṃ paṭisandhiyaṃ anekappakāraṃ nāmarūpaṃ abhinibbatteti māyākāro viya māyaṃ, nāmarūpe patiṭṭhitaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ pāpuṇāti subhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhito vanappagumbo viya, āyatanaghaṭṭanato phasso jāyati araṇīsahitābhimaddanato aggi viya, phassena phuṭṭhassa vedanā pātubhavati agginā phuṭṭhassa ḍāho viya, vedayamānassa taṇhā vaḍḍhati loṇūdakaṃ pivato pipāsā viya, tasito bhavesu abhilāsaṃ karoti pipāsito viya pānīye, tadassupādānaṃ upādānena bhavaṃ upādiyati āmisalobhena maccho baḷisaṃ viya, bhave sati jāti hoti bīje sati aṅkuro viya, jātassa avassaṃ jarāmaraṇaṃ uppannassa [M 0.0187] rukkhassa patanaṃ viya, tasmā evaṃ ‘upamāhi’ petaṃ bhavacakkaṃ viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

Alternatively, here, because ignorance overwhelms beings through non-practice and wrong practice—like a film over the eyes—the deluded person, overwhelmed by it, binds himself with formations productive of renewed existence, like a silkworm wrapping itself in its own threads. Consciousness, seized by formations, finds footing in the realms of existence, like a prince, taken by his guides, in a kingdom. From the conceptualizing of the sign of rebirth, consciousness at the moment of rebirth generates name-and-form in various ways, like a magician creating illusions. Established in name-and-form, the six sense bases attain growth, increase, and fullness, like a forest shrub taking root in fertile soil. From the impacting of the sense bases, contact arises, like fire from the rubbing together of fire-sticks. For one touched by contact, feeling appears, like burning for one touched by fire. For one who feels, craving increases, like thirst for one drinking salt water. Being thirsty, he longs for existences, like a thirsty man for water. That is his clinging; by clinging, he appropriates existence, like a fish by greed for bait. When existence is present, birth occurs, like a sprout when there is a seed. For one who is born, aging and death inevitably follow, like the falling of a tree that has arisen. Therefore, this wheel of existence should be understood through these similes, as is fitting.

Yasmā ca bhagavatā atthatopi dhammatopi desanātopi paṭivedhatopi gambhīrabhāvaṃ sandhāya “gambhīro cāyaṃ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo gambhīrāvabhāso cā”ti (dī. ni. 2.95; saṃ. ni. 2.60) vuttaṃ, tasmā [P 0.0197] ‘gambhīrabhedato’petaṃ bhavacakkaṃ viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

Moreover, because the Blessed One, with reference to its profundity in terms of meaning, phenomena, teaching, and penetration, said: "This dependent origination, Ānanda, is profound and appears profound" (DN 15; SN 12.60), therefore, this wheel of existence should be understood in terms of its profound distinctions, as is fitting.

Tattha yasmā na jātito jarāmaraṇaṃ na hoti, na ca jātiṃ vinā aññato hoti, itthañca jātito samudāgacchatīti evaṃ jātipaccayasamudāgataṭṭhassa duravabodhanīyato jarāmaraṇassa jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho gambhīro, tathā jātiyā bhavapaccaya…pe… saṅkhārānaṃ [V 0.0188] avijjāpaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho gambhīro, tasmā idaṃ bhavacakkaṃ atthagambhīranti. Ayaṃ tāvettha ‘atthagambhīratā’ hetuphalañhi atthoti vuccati, yathāha “hetuphale ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 720).

Herein, because aging-and-death do not arise independently of birth, nor do they arise from anything else apart from birth, but they arise precisely from birth—thus, because the fact of aging-and-death's origination as arisen conditioned by birth is difficult to comprehend, its nature as arisen from birth as its condition is profound. Similarly, the nature of birth's origination as conditioned by existence... and so on... the nature of formations' origination as conditioned by ignorance is profound. Therefore, this wheel of existence is profound in meaning. This, indeed, is the 'profundity of meaning' here, for cause and effect are called 'meaning,' as it is said: "Knowledge of cause and effect is analytical knowledge of meaning" (Vibh 720).

Yasmā pana yenākārena yadavatthā ca avijjā tesaṃ tesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo hoti, tassa duravabodhanīyato avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭho gambhīro, tathā saṅkhārānaṃ…pe… jātiyā jarāmaraṇassa paccayaṭṭho gambhīro, tasmā idaṃ bhavacakkaṃ dhammagambhīranti ayamettha ‘dhammagambhīratā’ hetuno hi dhammoti nāmaṃ, yathāha “hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti.

Because the manner and the state by which ignorance becomes a condition for each of those formations is difficult to understand, the nature of ignorance as a condition for formations is profound. Similarly, the nature of formations as a condition... and so on... the nature of birth as a condition for aging and death is profound. Therefore, this wheel of existence is profound in phenomena. This here is the 'profundity of phenomena,' for a cause is called a phenomenon, as it is said: "Knowledge of the cause is analytical knowledge of phenomena."

Yasmā cassa tena tena kāraṇena tathā tathā pavattetabbattā desanāpi gambhīrā, na tattha sabbaññutañāṇato aññaṃ ñāṇaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ labhati, tathā hetaṃ katthaci sutte anulomato, katthaci paṭilomato; katthaci anulomapaṭilomato, katthaci vemajjhato paṭṭhāya anulomato vā paṭilomato vā, katthaci tisandhicatusaṅkhepaṃ, katthaci dvisandhitisaṅkhepaṃ, katthaci ekasandhidvisaṅkhepaṃ desitaṃ, tasmā idaṃ bhavacakkaṃ desanāgambhīranti ayaṃ desanāgambhīratā.

And because its teaching is also profound, due to its needing to be set forth in this and that way for this and that reason, no other knowledge finds a footing there apart from the knowledge of omniscience. For thus it is taught in some discourses in forward order, in some in reverse order; in some in both forward and reverse order; in some starting from the middle, either in forward or reverse order; in some with three connections and four sections; in some with two connections and three sections; in some with one connection and two sections. Therefore, this wheel of existence is profound in teaching—this is the profundity of teaching.

Yasmā panettha yo avijjādīnaṃ sabhāvo, yena paṭividdhena avijjādayo dhammā salakkhaṇato paṭividdhā honti, so duppariyogāhattā gambhīro, tasmā idaṃ bhavacakkaṃ paṭivedhagambhīraṃ. Tathā hettha avijjāya aññāṇādassanasaccāsampaṭivedhaṭṭho [M 0.0188] gambhīro, saṅkhārānaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇāyūhanasarāgavirāgaṭṭho, viññāṇassa suññataabyāpāraasaṅkantipaṭisandhipātubhāvaṭṭho[P 0.0198], nāmarūpassa ekuppādavinibbhogāvinibbhoganamanaruppanaṭṭho, saḷāyatanassa adhipatilokadvārakhettavisayavisayībhāvaṭṭho, phassassa phusanasaṅghaṭṭanasaṅgatisannipātaṭṭho, vedanāya ārammaṇarasānubhavanasukhadukkhamajjhattabhāvanijjīvavedayitaṭṭho, taṇhāya abhinanditajjhosānasaritālatānadītaṇhāsamuddaduppūraṇaṭṭho, upādānassa ādānaggahaṇābhinivesaparāmāsaduratikkamanaṭṭho, bhavassa āyūhanābhisaṅkharaṇayonigatiṭhitinivāsesu khipanaṭṭho, jātiyā jātisañjātiokkantinibbattipātubhāvaṭṭho, jarāmaraṇassa khayavayabhedavipariṇāmaṭṭho gambhīroti ayamettha paṭivedhagambhīratā.

Moreover, here, the intrinsic nature of ignorance and so forth, by penetrating which the phenomena of ignorance and the rest are penetrated in terms of their own characteristics, is profound due to its being difficult to fathom. Therefore, this wheel of existence is profound in penetration. Likewise, here, the profundity lies in ignorance’s state of non-knowing, non-seeing, and non-penetration of the truths; in the volitional formations’ state of accumulating, striving, with passion and without passion; in consciousness’s state of emptiness, non-activity, non-transference, rebirth-linking, and manifestation; in name-and-form’s state of simultaneous arising, inseparability, bending, and breaking; in the six sense bases’ state of being the dominant condition, the doors of the world, the fields, and the objects and object-experiencer; in contact’s state of touching, collision, meeting, and conjunction; in feeling’s state of experiencing the taste of the object—pleasant, painful, or neutral—and being a lifeless experience; in craving’s state of delighting, clinging, flowing like a stream and a creeper, and being a river and an ocean of craving that is hard to fill; in clinging’s state of taking, grasping, adhering, obsessing, and being hard to overcome; in becoming’s state of casting into striving, volitional formation, womb, destiny, station, and abode; in birth’s state of birth, rebirth, descent, production, and manifestation; and in aging-and-death’s state of decay, dissolution, breaking apart, and change. This is the profundity of penetration here.

Yasmā panettha ekattanayo, nānattanayo, abyāpāranayo, evaṃdhammatānayoti cattāro atthanayā honti[V 0.0189], tasmā ‘nayabhedato’petaṃ bhavacakkaṃ viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ. Tattha “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa”nti evaṃ bījassa aṅkurādibhāvena rukkhabhāvappatti viya santānānupacchedo ‘ekattanayo’ nāma; yaṃ sammā passanto hetuphalasambandhena pavattamānassa santānassa anupacchedāvabodhato ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati, micchā passanto hetuphalasambandhena pavattamānassa santānānupacchedassa ekattaggahaṇato sassatadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyati.

Moreover, in this context, there are four modes of meaning: the unity mode, the diversity mode, the non-agency mode, and the suchness mode. Therefore, this wheel of existence should be understood appropriately according to its distinctions of modes. Here, the statement "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness," illustrates the 'unity mode,' which refers to the unbroken continuity of the stream, like a seed attaining the state of a tree through the state of a sprout and so on. One who sees this rightly abandons the annihilationist view by understanding the unbroken continuity of the stream that proceeds by way of the cause-and-effect connection. On the other hand, one who sees wrongly clings to the eternalist view by grasping the unbroken continuity of the stream that proceeds by way of the cause-and-effect connection as a single entity.

Avijjādīnaṃ pana yathāsakalakkhaṇavavatthānaṃ ‘nānattanayo’ nāma; yaṃ sammā passanto navanavānaṃ uppādadassanato sassatadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati, micchā passanto ekasantānapatitassa bhinnasantānasseva nānattaggahaṇato ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyati.

The determination of the individual characteristics of ignorance and so forth, however, is called the 'diversity mode.' Seeing rightly, one abandons the eternalist view by observing the arising of ever new phenomena; seeing wrongly, one clings to the annihilationist view by grasping the diversity of what falls within a single continuum as if it were a broken continuum.

Avijjāya ‘saṅkhārā mayā uppādetabbā’, saṅkhārānaṃ vā ‘viññāṇaṃ amhehī’ti evamādibyāpārābhāvo ‘abyāpāranayo’ nāma; yaṃ sammā passanto kārakassa abhāvāvabodhato attadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati, micchā passanto yo asatipi byāpāre avijjādīnaṃ sabhāvaniyamasiddho hetubhāvo tassa aggahaṇato akiriyadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyati.

The absence of such activity as 'Formations are to be produced by me' on the part of ignorance, or 'Consciousness by us' on the part of formations, is called the 'non-agency mode.' Seeing rightly, one abandons the view of self by understanding the absence of an agent. Seeing wrongly, one clings to the view of non-action by not grasping the causal nature of ignorance and so forth, which is established by natural law even in the absence of activity.

Avijjādīhi pana kāraṇehi saṅkhārādīnaṃyeva sambhavo khīrādīhi [P 0.0199] dadhiādīnaṃ viya, na aññesanti ayaṃ ‘evaṃdhammatānayo’ nāma; yaṃ sammā passanto [M 0.0189] paccayānurūpato phalāvabodhato ahetukadiṭṭhiñca akiriyadiṭṭhiñca pajahati, micchā passanto paccayānurūpaṃ phalappavattiṃ aggahetvā yato kutoci yassa kassaci asambhavaggahaṇato ahetukadiṭṭhiñceva niyatavādañca upādiyatīti evamidaṃ bhavacakkaṃ –

However, the arising of formations and so on from causes such as ignorance, just like the production of curds and the like from milk and so forth, and not from other things, is called the 'suchness mode.' One who sees this rightly abandons the views of causelessness and non-action by understanding the fruit in accordance with its conditions. But one who sees wrongly, failing to grasp the arising of fruit in accordance with conditions, clings to the view of causelessness and determinism by grasping that anything can arise from any source whatsoever. Thus, this wheel of existence—

Saccappabhavato kiccā, vāraṇā upamāhi ca;

Gambhīranayabhedā ca, viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

From its origin in the truths, by its function, by its prevention, and by similes; by its profound methods and their distinctions, it should be understood as is fitting.

Idañhi gambhīrato agādhaṃ nānānayaggahaṇato durabhiyānaṃ ñāṇāsinā samādhipavarasilāyaṃ sunisitena –

This is indeed profound, unfathomable, difficult to master on account of its various methods, and is to be penetrated with the sword of wisdom, well-sharpened on the excellent whetstone of concentration—

Bhavacakkamapadāletvā[V 0.0190],

Asanivicakkamiva niccanimmathanaṃ;

Saṃsārabhayamatīto,

Na koci supinantarepyatthi.

Without shattering the wheel of existence, which constantly grinds like a thunderbolt-disk, there is no one who has gone beyond the fear of saṃsāra, not even in a dream.

Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā – “gambhīro cāyaṃ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo gambhīrāvabhāso ca. Etassa, ānanda, dhammassa ananubodhā appaṭivedhā evamayaṃ pajā tantākulakajātā kulagaṇṭhikajātā muñjapabbajabhūtā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ saṃsāraṃ nātivattatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.95; saṃ. ni. 2.60). Tasmā attano vā paresaṃ vā hitāya sukhāya paṭipanno avasesakiccāni pahāya –

This too was said by the Blessed One: “Profound, Ānanda, is this dependent origination, and profound it appears. It is through not understanding, not penetrating this Dhamma, Ānanda, that this generation has become entangled like a tangled ball of thread, like a knotted skein of yarn, like matted muñja and babbaja grasses, and cannot pass beyond the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world, saṃsāra” (DN 15; SN 12.60). Therefore, one practicing for the welfare and happiness of oneself or others, having abandoned all remaining duties—

Gambhīre paccayākāra-ppabhede idha paṇḍito;

Yathā gādhaṃ labhetheva-manuyuñje sadā satoti.

The wise one should always mindfully apply themselves here in the profound divisions of the conditional process, so that they might find a firm footing.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition by Way of the Suttas.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Exposition by Way of the Abhidhamma.

243. Evaṃ mahāpathaviṃ pattharanto viya ākāsaṃ vitthārayanto viya ca sabbadhammesu appaṭihatañāṇo satthā suttantabhājanīye niggaṇṭhiṃ nijjaṭaṃ paccayākāraṃ nānācittavasena dassetvā idāni yasmā na kevalaṃ ayaṃ paccayākāro nānācittesuyeva [P 0.0200] hoti, ekacittepi hotiyeva, tasmā abhidhammabhājanīyavasena ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ paccayākāraṃ nānappakārato [M 0.0190] dassetuṃ avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārotiādinā nayena mātikaṃ tāva ṭhapesi. Evaṃ ṭhapitāya pana mātikāya –

243. Thus the Teacher, with knowledge unobstructed in all phenomena, as if spreading out the great earth and extending the sky, having shown in the Exposition by Way of the Suttas the conditional process—unravelled and disentangled—by way of various mind-states, now, because this conditional process occurs not only in various mind-states but also in a single mind-state, he therefore, in order to show in various ways the momentary conditional process in a single mind-moment by means of the Exposition by Way of the Abhidhamma, first laid down the matrix with the method beginning, “With ignorance as condition, formations.” With the matrix thus laid down—

Avijjādīhi [V 0.0191] mūlehi, nava mūlapadā nava;

Nayā tattha catukkāni, vārabhedañca dīpaye.

With roots beginning with ignorance, there are nine root terms and nine methods; therein, the tetrads and the distinctions of rounds should be explained.

Tatrāyaṃ dīpanā – ettha hi avijjāsaṅkhāraviññāṇanāmachaṭṭhāyatanaphassavedanātaṇhāupādānappabhedehi avijjādīhi navahi mūlapadehi avijjādiko, saṅkhārādiko, viññāṇādiko, nāmādiko, chaṭṭhāyatanādiko, phassādiko, vedanādiko, taṇhādiko, upādānādikoti ime nava mūlapadā nava nayā honti.

Here is the explanation: Here, by means of the nine root terms beginning with ignorance—in the divisions of ignorance, formations, consciousness, name, the sixth sense base, contact, feeling, craving, and clinging—there are these nine root terms and nine methods: that beginning with ignorance, that beginning with formations, that beginning with consciousness, that beginning with name, that beginning with the sixth sense base, that beginning with contact, that beginning with feeling, that beginning with craving, and that beginning with clinging.

Tesu yo tāva ayaṃ avijjādiko nayo, tattha paccayacatukkaṃ, hetucatukkaṃ, sampayuttacatukkaṃ, aññamaññacatukkanti cattāri catukkāni honti. Yathā cettha evaṃ sesesupīti ekekasmiṃ naye catunnaṃ catunnaṃ catukkānaṃ vasena chattiṃsa catukkāni. Tattha ekekena catukkena catunnaṃ catunnaṃ vārānaṃ saṅgahitattā catunnampi catukkānaṃ vasena ekekasmiṃ naye soḷasa soḷasa vārāti catucattālīsādhikaṃ vārasataṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Among these, in the method beginning with ignorance, there are four tetrads: the tetrad of conditions, the tetrad of roots, the tetrad of association, and the tetrad of mutuality. As it is here, so too in the remaining cases; thus, in each method there are thirty-six tetrads, by way of four tetrads each. Herein, since each tetrad comprises four variations, and since there are four such tetrads, there are sixteen variations in each method. Thus, it should be understood that there are one hundred and forty-four variations in total.

1. Paccayacatukkaṃ

1. The Tetrad of Conditions

Tattha yadetaṃ sabbapaṭhame avijjāmūlake naye paccayacatukkaṃ, tasmiṃ paṭhamo nāmarūpaṭṭhāne nāmassa, saḷāyatanaṭṭhāne chaṭṭhāyatanassa ca vuttattā aparipuṇṇaaṅgadvayayutto dvādasaṅgikavāro nāma. Dutiyo nāmarūpaṭṭhāne nāmasseva, saḷāyatanaṭṭhāne ca na kassaci vuttattā aparipuṇṇaekaṅgayutto ekādasaṅgikavāro nāma. Tatiyo saḷāyatanaṭṭhāne chaṭṭhāyatanassa vuttattā paripuṇṇaekaṅgayutto dvādasaṅgikavāro nāma. Catuttho pana paripuṇṇadvādasaṅgikoyeva.

Herein, in the tetrad of conditions in the first method rooted in ignorance: the first is called the twelve-factored variation, endowed with two incomplete factors, because in the place of name-and-form, name is mentioned, and in the place of the six sense bases, the sixth sense base is mentioned. The second is called the eleven-factored variation, endowed with one incomplete factor, because in the place of name-and-form, only name is mentioned, and in the place of the six sense bases, nothing is mentioned. The third is called the twelve-factored variation, endowed with one complete factor, because in the place of the six sense bases, the sixth sense base is mentioned. The fourth, however, is simply the complete twelve-factored variation.

Tattha siyā – ayampi chaṭṭhāyatanapaccayā phassoti vuttattā aparipuṇṇekaṅgayuttoyevāti? Na, tassa anaṅgattā. Phassoyeva hettha aṅgaṃ, na chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ. Tasmā tassa anaṅgattā nāyaṃ aparipuṇṇekaṅgayuttoti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vuttaṃ – “paṭhamo sabbasaṅgāhikaṭṭhena[P 0.0201], dutiyo paccayavisesaṭṭhena, tatiyo gabbhaseyyakasattānaṃ vasena, catuttho opapātikasattānaṃ [M 0.0191] vasena gahito. Tathā paṭhamo sabbasaṅgāhikaṭṭhena, dutiyo paccayavisesaṭṭhena, tatiyo aparipuṇṇāyatanavasena, catuttho paripuṇṇāyatanavasena gahito. Tathā paṭhamo sabbasaṅgāhikaṭṭhena, dutiyo [V 0.0192] mahānidānasuttantavasena (dī. ni. 2.95 ādayo), tatiyo rūpabhavavasena, catuttho kāmabhavavasena gahito”ti.

Herein, it might be said: 'Since it is stated that contact is conditioned by the sixth sense base, is this also endowed with one incomplete factor?' No, because that is not a factor. Contact itself is the factor here, not the sixth sense base. Therefore, since that is not a factor, this is not endowed with one incomplete factor. However, in the commentary, it is stated: 'The first is taken in the sense of being all-encompassing, the second in the sense of a specific condition, the third by way of beings born from the womb, and the fourth by way of spontaneously arisen beings. Similarly, the first is taken in the sense of being all-encompassing, the second in the sense of a specific condition, the third by way of incomplete sense bases, and the fourth by way of complete sense bases. Likewise, the first is taken in the sense of being all-encompassing, the second by way of the Mahānidāna Suttanta (Dīgha Nikāya 2.95, etc.), the third by way of the form realm, and the fourth by way of the sensual desire realm.'

Tattha paṭhamo imesu dutiyādīsu tīsu vāresu na katthaci na pavisatīti sabbasaṅgāhikoti vutto. Sesānaṃ viseso parato āvibhavissati. Tassāvibhāvatthaṃ –

Herein, the first is said to be all-encompassing because it does not fail to enter anywhere among these three variations, namely, the second and so on. The distinction of the others will become manifest hereafter. For the purpose of making that manifest—

Yaṃ yattha aññathā vuttaṃ, avuttañcāpi yaṃ yahiṃ;

Yaṃ yathā paccayo yassa, taṃ sabbamupalakkhaye.

Whatever is stated differently in any place, and whatever is unstated anywhere; whatever is a condition for what, and how, all that one should discern.

Tatrāyaṃ nayo – avisesena tāva catūsupi etesu suttantabhājaniye viya saṅkhārāti avatvā saṅkhāroti vuttaṃ, taṃ kasmāti? Ekacittakkhaṇikattā. Tatra hi nānācittakkhaṇiko paccayākāro vibhatto. Idha ekacittakkhaṇiko āraddho. Ekacittakkhaṇe ca bahū cetanā na santīti saṅkhārāti avatvā saṅkhāroti vuttaṃ.

Herein is the method: Generally, in all four of these, unlike in the Suttanta analysis, it is stated as 'formation' (singular) instead of 'formations' (plural). Why is that? Because of its being of a single mind-moment. For there, the structure of conditionality is analyzed as pertaining to various mind-moments. Here, it is undertaken as pertaining to a single mind-moment. And since many volitions do not exist in a single mind-moment, it is stated as 'formation' instead of 'formations.'

Paṭhamavāre panettha ekacittakkhaṇapariyāpannadhammasaṅgahaṇato sabbaṭṭhānasādhāraṇato ca rūpaṃ chaḍḍetvā “viññāṇapaccayā nāma”ntveva vuttaṃ. Tañhi ekacittakkhaṇapariyāpannaṃ sabbaṭṭhānasādhāraṇañca, na katthaci viññāṇappavattiṭṭhāne na pavattati. Yasmā ca ekacittakkhaṇapariyāpanno ekovettha phasso, tasmā tassānurūpaṃ paccayabhūtaṃ āyatanaṃ gaṇhanto saḷāyatanaṭṭhāne “nāmapaccayā chaṭṭhāyatana”nti ekaṃ manāyatanaṃyeva āha. Tañhi ekassa akusalaphassassa anurūpaṃ paccayabhūtaṃ. Kāmañcetaṃ saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇanti etthāpi vuttaṃ, hetuphalavisesadassanatthaṃ pana aṅgapuṇṇatthañca puna idha gahitaṃ. Tatra hi etassa visesena saṅkhāro hetu, avisesena nāmaṃ phalaṃ. Idha panassa avisesena nāmaṃ hetu, visesena phasso phalanti. Sokādayo pana yasmā sabbe ekacittakkhaṇe na sambhavanti, sabbasmiñca cittappavattiṭṭhāne ceva citte ca na pavattanti, tasmā na gahitā. Jātijarāmaraṇāni [P 0.0202] pana acittakkhaṇamattānipi samānāni cittakkhaṇe antogadhattā aṅgaparipūraṇatthaṃ [M 0.0192] gahitāni. Evaṃ tāvettha ‘yaṃ aññathā vuttaṃ. Yañca avuttaṃ’ taṃ veditabbaṃ.

In the first variation here, by including only those phenomena that are encompassed within a single mind-moment and are common to all instances, and by excluding material form, it is simply stated: 'dependent on consciousness, name.' For that is encompassed within a single mind-moment and is common to all instances; it does not fail to arise in any instance where consciousness arises. And because there is only one contact encompassed within a single mind-moment here, therefore, taking the corresponding sense base that serves as a condition, in the place of the six sense bases, it states 'dependent on name, the sixth sense base,' referring only to the mind base. For that is the condition appropriate for a single unwholesome contact. Although it is also stated in 'dependent on formations, consciousness,' it is taken up again here to show the distinction between cause and effect and to complete the factors. For there, formations are the cause for this in a specific sense, while name is the effect in a general sense. Here, however, name is the cause for it in a general sense, while contact is the effect in a specific sense. As for sorrow and the like, since they do not all arise in a single mind-moment, nor do they arise in every instance where consciousness arises, nor in every consciousness, therefore they are not included. Birth, aging, and death, however, although they are not confined to a single mind-moment, are included for the purpose of completing the factors because they are encompassed within the mind-moment. Thus, in this context, 'what has been stated differently and what has not been stated' should be understood.

Yaṃ [V 0.0193] panettha ito paresu vāresu vuttaṃ, tassattho vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Yasmiṃ yasmiṃ pana vāre yo yo viseso āgato, taṃ taṃ tattha tattheva pakāsayissāma.

Whatever is stated here in the subsequent variations, its meaning should be understood according to the method already explained. However, in whichever variation a particular distinction has arisen, we will explain it right there and then.

‘Yaṃ yathā paccayo yassā’ti ettha pana saṅkhārassa avijjā sampayuttadhammasādhāraṇehi sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatapaccayehi chahi hetupaccayena cāti sattadhā paccayo. Tattha yasmā parato hetucatukkādīni tīṇi catukkāni avigatasampayuttaaññamaññapaccayavasena vuttāni, tasmā idha tāni apanetvā avasesānaṃ vasena avijjā saṅkhārassa catudhā paccayoti veditabbo.

Regarding 'Whatever is a condition for what, and how'—herein, however, ignorance is a condition for formation in seven ways: through the root condition, and through the six conditions common to associated phenomena, namely, co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance. Herein, since the three tetrads beginning with the root tetrad are stated hereafter by way of the non-disappearance, association, and mutuality conditions, therefore, excluding those here, it should be understood that by way of the remaining conditions, ignorance is a fourfold condition for formation.

Saṅkhāro viññāṇassa sādhāraṇehi chahi, kammāhārapaccayehi cāti aṭṭhadhā paccayo. Idha pana teyeva tayo apanetvā pañcadhā. Viññāṇaṃ nāmassa sādhāraṇehi chahi, indriyāhārādhipatīhi cāti navadhā. Idha pana tayo apanetvā chadhā. Nāmaṃ chaṭṭhāyatanassa sādhāraṇehi chahi. Kiñci panettha adhipatipaccayena, kiñci āhārapaccayādīhīti anekadhā. Idha pana teyeva tayo apanetvā tidhā catudhā pañcadhā vā. Chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ phassassa yathā viññāṇaṃ nāmassa. Evaṃ phasso vedanāya sādhāraṇehi chahi āhārapaccayena cāti sattadhā. Idha pana teyeva tayo apanetvā catudhā. Vedanā taṇhāya sādhāraṇehi chahi jhānindriyapaccayehi cāti aṭṭhadhā. Idha pana teyeva tayo apanetvā pañcadhā. Taṇhā upādānassa, yathā avijjā saṅkhārassa. Evaṃ upādānaṃ bhavassa sādhāraṇehi chahi maggapaccayena cāti sattadhā. Idha pana teyeva tayo apanetvā catudhā. Bhavo jātiyā, yasmā jātīti idha saṅkhatalakkhaṇaṃ adhippetaṃ, tasmā pariyāyena upanissayapaccayeneva paccayo. Tathā jāti jarāmaraṇassāti.

Formations are a condition for consciousness in eight ways: through the six common conditions, and through the kamma and nutriment conditions. Here, however, excluding those three, it is fivefold. Consciousness is a condition for name in nine ways: through the six common conditions, and through the faculty, nutriment, and dominance conditions. Here, however, excluding those three, it is sixfold. Name is a condition for the sixth sense base through the six common conditions. Some conditions here are through the dominance condition, some through the nutriment condition and others, making it manifold. Here, however, excluding those three, it is threefold, fourfold, or fivefold. The sixth sense base is a condition for contact, just as consciousness is for name. Thus, contact is a condition for feeling in seven ways: through the six common conditions, and through the nutriment condition. Here, however, excluding those three, it is fourfold. Feeling is a condition for craving in eight ways: through the six common conditions, and through the jhāna and faculty conditions. Here, however, excluding those three, it is fivefold. Craving is a condition for clinging, just as ignorance is for formations. Thus, clinging is a condition for becoming in seven ways: through the six common conditions, and through the path condition. Here, however, excluding those three, it is fourfold. Becoming is a condition for birth; since 'birth' here is intended as the characteristic of the conditioned, it is therefore a condition only by way of decisive support condition. Likewise, birth is a condition for aging and death.

Ye pana evaṃ vadanti – “imasmiṃ catukke sabbesampi saṅkhārādīnaṃ avijjādayo sahajātapaccayena paccayā honti. Sahajātapaccayavaseneva hi paṭhamavāro āraddho”ti, te bhavādīnaṃ tathā abhāvaṃ sesapaccayānañca sambhavaṃ [M 0.0193] dassetvā paṭikkhipitabbā. Na hi bhavo jātiyā sahajātapaccayo [P 0.0203] hoti, na jāti jarāmaraṇassa. Ye cetesaṃ saṅkharādīnaṃ avasesā paccayā vuttā, tepi sambhavantiyeva. Tasmā na sakkā chaḍḍetunti. Evaṃ tāva paṭhamavāre yaṃ yattha aññathā vuttaṃ, avuttañcāpi yaṃ yahiṃ, yañca yathā yassa paccayo hoti, taṃ veditabbaṃ. Dutiyavārādīsupi eseva nayo.

Those who speak thus—'In this tetrad, ignorance and the rest are conditions for all formations and so on through the co-nascence condition. For the first round is established by means of the co-nascence condition alone'—should be refuted by showing the absence of such a condition for becoming and so on, and the occurrence of the remaining conditions. For becoming is not a co-nascence condition for birth, nor is birth for aging and death. And the other conditions stated for these formations and so on do indeed occur. Therefore, it is not possible to discard them. Thus, in the first round, whatever is stated differently in a particular place, whatever is unstated anywhere, and in whatever way something is a condition for something else—all that should be understood. The same method applies to the second round and so on.

Ayaṃ [V 0.0194] pana viseso – dutiyavāre “nāmapaccayā phasso”ti vatvā saḷāyatanaṭṭhāne na kiñci vuttaṃ, taṃ kimatthanti? Paccayavisesadassanatthañceva mahānidānadesanāsaṅgahatthañca. Phassassa hi na kevalañca chaṭṭhāyatanameva paccayo, vedanākkhandhādayo pana tayo khandhāpi paccayāyeva. Mahānidānasuttante cassa “atthi idappaccayā phassoti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. Kiṃ paccayā phassoti? Iti ce vadeyya, nāmapaccayā phassoti iccassa vacanīya”nti (dī. ni. 2.96). Evaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ chaḍḍetvā ekādasaṅgiko paṭiccasamuppādo vutto. Tasmā imassa paccayavisesassa dassanatthaṃ imissā ca mahānidānasuttantadesanāya pariggahatthaṃ dutiyavāre “nāmapaccayā phasso”ti vatvā saḷāyatanaṭṭhāne na kiñci vuttanti. Esa tāva dutiyavāre viseso.

This, however, is the distinction: in the second round, after stating ‘contact is conditioned by name,’ nothing was said in the place of the six sense bases. What is the purpose of that? It is for the purpose of showing a specific condition and for including the teaching of the Great Discourse on Causation. For contact, not only is the sixth sense base a condition, but the three aggregates beginning with the feeling aggregate are also conditions. And in the Great Discourse on Causation it is said: 'When asked, “Is there contact with this as condition?” it should be said, “There is, Ānanda.” If one should ask, “With what as condition is there contact?” it should be said, “Contact is conditioned by name”' (DN 2.56). Thus, omitting the six sense bases, dependent origination with eleven factors was taught. Therefore, for the purpose of showing this specific condition and for including this teaching of the Great Discourse on Causation, in the second round, after stating ‘contact is conditioned by name,’ nothing was said in the place of the six sense bases. This, then, is the distinction in the second round.

Tatiyavāre pana “viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti suttantabhājanīye āgatameva catutthamaṅgaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ ekacittakkhaṇikattā paccayākārassa idha ayuttanti ce? Taṃ nāyuttaṃ. Kasmā? Sakakkhaṇe paccayabhāvato. Sacepi hi tattha rūpaṃ cittakkhaṇato uddhaṃ tiṭṭhati, tathāpissa taṃ viññāṇaṃ sakakkhaṇe paccayo hoti. Kathaṃ? Purejātassa tāva cittasamuṭṭhānassa aññassa vā pacchājātapaccayena. Vuttañcetaṃ “pacchājātā cittacetasikā dhammā purejātassa imassa kāyassa pacchājātapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.11). Sahajātassa pana cittasamuṭṭhānassa nissayapaccayena paccayo. Yathāha “cittacetasikā dhammā cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānaṃ nissayapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.8).

In the third round, however, the fourth factor, ‘name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness,’ which is found in the Suttanta analysis, is stated. If it is said that this mode of conditionality is inappropriate here because it is of a single mind-moment, that is not inappropriate. Why? Because it is a condition in its own moment. For even if form persists beyond the mind-moment, still that consciousness is a condition for it in its own moment. How? For pre-nascent form, whether mind-originated or other, it is a condition by way of the post-nascence condition. And this was said: ‘Post-nascent mind and mental factors are a condition for this pre-nascent body by way of the post-nascence condition’ (Paṭṭh 1.1.11). But for co-nascent mind-originated form, it is a condition by way of the dependence condition. As it is said: ‘Mind and mental factors are a condition for mind-originated forms by way of the dependence condition’ (Paṭṭh 1.1.8).

Yadi [M 0.0194] evaṃ, purimavāresu kasmā evaṃ na vuttanti[P 0.0204]? Rūpappavattidesaṃ sandhāya desitattā. Ayañhi paccayākāro rūpappavattidese kāmabhave gabbhaseyyakānañceva aparipuṇṇāyatanaopapātikānañca rūpāvacaradevānañca vasena desito. Tenevettha “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”nti avatvā chaṭṭhāyatananti vuttaṃ. Tattha nāmaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Rūpaṃ pana hadayarūpaṃ veditabbaṃ. Taṃ panetassa chaṭṭhāyatanassa nissayapaccayena ceva purejātapaccayena cāti dvidhā paccayo hotīti esa tatiyavāre viseso.

If so, why was this not stated in the earlier rounds? Because it was taught with reference to the teaching on the occurrence of form. This mode of conditionality, in the teaching on the occurrence of form, is taught with regard to beings in the womb in the sense-sphere existence, spontaneously born beings with incomplete sense bases, and form-sphere devas. Therefore, here, instead of saying 'the six sense bases are conditioned by name-and-form,' it is said 'the sixth sense base...'. Therein, 'name' is in accordance with the method stated before. But 'form' should be understood as heart-base form. That form is a condition for this sixth sense base in two ways: by way of the dependence condition and the pre-nascence condition. This is the distinction in the third round.

Catutthavāro pana yonivasena opapātikānaṃ, āyatanavasena paripuṇṇāyatanānaṃ, bhavavasena kāmāvacarasattānaṃ vasena vutto. Tenevettha “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha nāmaṃ chaṭṭhāyatanassa [V 0.0195] sahajātādīhi, cakkhāyatanādīnaṃ pacchājātapaccayena. Rūpe hadayarūpaṃ chaṭṭhāyatanassa nissayapaccayapurejātapaccayehi, cattāri mahābhūtāni cakkhāyatanādīnaṃ sahajātanissayaatthiavigatehi. Yasmā panesa ekacittakkhaṇiko paccayākāro, tasmā ettha saḷāyatanapaccayāti avatvā “chaṭṭhāyatanapaccayā phasso”ti vuttoti ayaṃ catutthavāre viseso.

The fourth round, however, is stated with reference to spontaneously born beings in terms of generation, with reference to those with complete sense bases in terms of sense bases, and with reference to sense-sphere beings in terms of existence. Therefore, here it is said, 'the six sense bases are conditioned by name-and-form.' Therein, name is a condition for the sixth sense base through co-nascence and other conditions, and for the eye-base and others through the post-nascence condition. In form, the heart-base is a condition for the sixth sense base through the dependence and pre-nascence conditions, while the four great elements are conditions for the eye-base and others through the co-nascence, dependence, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. But since this mode of conditionality is of a single mind-moment, therefore here, without saying 'contact is conditioned by the six sense bases,' it is said 'contact is conditioned by the sixth sense base.' This is the distinction in the fourth round.

Evametesaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ ñatvā puna sabbesveva tesu visesena paṭhamakā dve vārā arūpabhave paccayākāradassanatthaṃ vuttāti veditabbā. Arūpabhavasmiñhi rūpena asammissāni paṭiccasamuppādaṅgāni pavattanti. Tatiyo rūpabhave paccayākāradassanatthaṃ vutto. Rūpabhavasmiñhi satipi rūpasammissatte saḷāyatanaṃ na pavattati. Catuttho kāmabhave paccayākāradassanatthaṃ vutto. Kāmabhavasmiñhi sakalaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ pavattati. Tatiyo vā rūpabhave ceva kāmabhave ca aparipuṇṇāyatanānaṃ akusalappavattikkhaṇaṃ sandhāya vutto. Catuttho vā kāmabhave paripuṇṇāyatanānaṃ. Paṭhamo vā sabbatthagāmitaṃ sandhāya vutto. So hi na katthaci cittappavattidese na pavattati. Dutiyo paccayavisesaṃ sandhāya vutto. Ekādasaṅgikattañhettha phassassa ca nāmapaccayattaṃ paccayaviseso. Tatiyo purimayonidvayaṃ sandhāya vutto. Purimāsu hi dvīsu yonīsu [P 0.0205] so sambhavati, tattha sadā saḷāyatanassa asambhavato. Catuttho pacchimayonidvayaṃ sandhāya vutto. Pacchimāsu hi so dvīsu yonīsu sambhavati, tattha sadā saḷāyatanassa sambhavatoti.

Having thus understood these various distinctions, it should be known that, among all of them, the first two rounds were stated specifically to show the mode of conditions in the formless realm. For in the formless realm, the factors of dependent origination occur unmixed with form. The third was stated to show the mode of conditions in the form realm. For in the form realm, although there is a mixture with form, the sixfold sense base does not occur. The fourth was stated to show the mode of conditions in the desire realm. For in the desire realm, the entire sixfold sense base occurs. Alternatively, the third was stated with reference to the moment of the occurrence of the unwholesome for those with incomplete sense bases in both the form realm and the desire realm. The fourth refers to those with complete sense bases in the desire realm. Or, the first was stated with reference to its universal applicability. For it does not fail to occur in any location of mental activity. The second was stated with reference to a specific condition. Here, the specific condition is its having eleven factors and contact being conditioned by name. The third was stated with reference to the first two modes of generation. For it occurs in those two modes of generation, where the sixfold sense base never occurs. The fourth was stated with reference to the last two modes of generation. For it occurs in those two modes of generation, where the sixfold sense base always occurs.

Ettāvatā [M 0.0195] ca yaṃ vuttaṃ catūsupi vāresu –

Thus, whatever has been said in these four rounds—

Yaṃ yattha aññathā vuttaṃ, avuttañcāpi yaṃ yahiṃ;

Yaṃ yathā paccayo yassa, taṃ sabbamupalakkhayeti.

Whatever is stated differently in one place, and whatever is not stated in another; and how one thing is a condition for another—all that should be carefully noted.

Gāthāya atthadīpanā katā hoti.

The meaning of the verse has been illuminated.

Etenevānusārena, sabbametaṃ nayaṃ ito;

Viseso yo ca taṃ jaññā, catukkesu paresupi.

By this same line of reasoning, one should understand from this all this method, and also whatever distinction there is in the other tetrads.

2. Hetucatukkaṃ

2. The Tetrad of Causes

244. Tattha [V 0.0196] yo tāva idha vutto nayo, so sabbattha pākaṭoyeva. Viseso pana evaṃ veditabbo – hetucatukke tāva avijjā hetu assāti avijjāhetuko. Avijjā assa sahavattanato yāvabhaṅgā pavattikā gamikāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Avijjāpaccayā”ti ca ettāvatā sahajātādipaccayavasena sādhāraṇato saṅkhārassa avijjā paccayoti dassetvā, puna “avijjāhetuko”ti eteneva visesato avigatapaccayatā dassitā. Saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ saṅkhārahetukantiādīsupi eseva nayo.

244. Herein, the method explained so far is evident everywhere. The distinction, however, should be understood as follows: First, in the Tetrad of Causes, 'ignorance is its cause'; thus, it is 'caused by ignorance'. Because ignorance co-exists with it, continuing and leading on until its cessation, it is so called. Further, by the phrase “with ignorance as condition,” it is shown that ignorance is a condition for formations in a general sense, by way of conascent and other conditions. Then, by the phrase “caused by ignorance,” the non-disappearance of the condition is specifically indicated. The same method applies to cases like “with formations as condition, consciousness is caused by formations,” and so forth.

Kasmā pana bhavādīsu hetukaggahaṇaṃ na katanti? Avigatapaccayaniyamābhāvato abhāvato ca avigatapaccayassa. “Tattha katamo upādānapaccayā bhavo? Ṭhapetvā upādānaṃ vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho saṅkhārakkhandho viññāṇakkhandho – ayaṃ vuccati upādānapaccayā bhavo”ti vacanato upādānapaccayā catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ idha bhavoti nāmaṃ. Saṅkhārakkhandhe ca “jāti dvīhi khandhehi saṅgahitā”tiādivacanato (dhātu. 71) jātijarāmaraṇāni antogadhāni.

But why, then, is the term 'caused by' not used in the case of becoming and so forth? Because of the absence of a fixed rule for the non-disappearing condition, and because of the absence of the non-disappearing condition itself. According to the passage: “Herein, what is becoming conditioned by clinging? Setting aside clinging, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness—this is called becoming conditioned by clinging.” Thus, by this statement, the four aggregates are here what is named 'becoming conditioned by clinging.' And in the aggregate of formations, because of statements such as “birth is comprised by two aggregates,” birth, aging, and death are included within.

Tattha yāva upādānaṃ tāva jātijarāmaraṇānaṃ anupalabbhanato upādānaṃ bhavassa na niyamato avigatapaccayo hoti. “Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ jātī”ti ādivacanato saṅkhatalakkhaṇesu jātiyā jarāmaraṇasaṅkhātassa bhavassa jātikkhaṇamatteyeva abhāvato avigatapaccayabhāvo na sambhavati. Tathā jātiyā jarāmaraṇakkhaṇe abhāvato[M 0.0196]. Upanissayapaccayeneva pana bhavo jātiyā. Jāti jarāmaraṇassa paccayoti sabbathāpi avigatapaccayaniyamābhāvato abhāvato ca avigatapaccayassa bhavādīsu hetukaggahaṇaṃ na katanti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, since birth, aging, and death are not found throughout the duration of clinging, clinging is not necessarily a non-disappearing condition for becoming. Because of the statement beginning, “Whatever is the birth of those various phenomena,” and because, among the characteristics of the conditioned, becoming (designated as aging and death) is absent at the very moment of birth, the state of being a non-disappearing condition is not possible for birth. Similarly, because of the absence of birth at the moment of aging and death. However, becoming is a condition for birth only by way of decisive support. Birth is a condition for aging and death. Thus, in all these ways, it should be understood that the term 'caused by' is not used in the case of becoming and so forth, because there is no fixed rule for the non-disappearing condition and because of the absence of the non-disappearing condition itself.

Keci [P 0.0206] panāhu – “bhavo duvidhenā”ti vacanato upapattimissako bhavo, na ca upapattibhavassa upādānaṃ avigatapaccayo hotīti “upādānapaccayā bhavo upādānahetuko”ti avatvā “upādānapaccayā bhavo”ti vutto. Idha pacchinnattā paratopi na vuttanti. Taṃ idha upapattimissakassa bhavassa anadhippetattā ayuttaṃ. Arūpakkhandhā hi idha bhavoti āgatā.

Some, however, say: According to the passage “Becoming is twofold,” becoming is mixed with rebirth-becoming, and for rebirth-becoming, clinging is not a non-disappearing condition. Therefore, instead of saying “Becoming is conditioned by clinging and caused by clinging,” it is simply stated, “Becoming is conditioned by clinging.” Because it is cut off here, it is not stated later either.
