That is inappropriate, because here becoming mixed with rebirth-becoming is not intended. For here, the non-material aggregates are what is meant by ‘becoming.’

Bhavapaccayā [V 0.0197] jātīti ettha ca ṭhapetvā jātijarāmaraṇāni avaseso bhavo jātiyā paccayoti veditabbo. Kasmā? Jātiādīnaṃ jātiyā appaccayattā. Yadi evaṃ, ṭhapetvā jātijarāmaraṇāni bhavo jātiyā paccayoti vattabboti? Āma vattabbo, vattabbapadesābhāvato pana na vutto. Dasamaṅganiddese hi upādānapaccayasambhūto bhavo vattabbo. Ekādasamaṅganiddese jāti vattabbā. Yo pana bhavo jātiyā paccayo, tassa vattabbapadeso natthīti vattabbapadesābhāvato na vutto. Avuttopi pana yuttito gahetabboti. Viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpantiādīsu ca viññāṇādīnaṃ avigatapaccayabhāvasambhavato viññāṇahetukādivacanaṃ katanti esa hetucatukke viseso.

And here, in ‘with becoming as condition, birth,’ it should be understood that the remaining becoming, setting aside birth, aging, and death, is the condition for birth. Why? Because birth and so forth are not conditions for birth. If so, should it be said that, setting aside birth, aging, and death, becoming is the condition for birth? Yes, it should be said, but it was not stated due to the absence of a place to state it. In the exposition of the tenth factor, the becoming that has arisen from clinging should be stated. In the exposition of the eleventh factor, birth should be stated. But as for that becoming which is the condition for birth, there is no place to state it; thus it was not stated due to the absence of a place to state it. Though unstated, it should be understood from reasoning. And in statements like ‘with consciousness as condition, name-and-form’ and so forth, since it is possible for consciousness and the rest to be non-disappearing conditions, the phrase ‘caused by consciousness’ and so forth has been used—this is the distinction in the Tetrad of Causes.

3. Sampayuttacatukkaṃ

3. The Tetrad of Association

245. Sampayuttacatukkepi avijjāpaccayāti ettāvatā sahajātādipaccayavasena saṅkhārassa avijjāpaccayataṃ dassetvā puna “avijjāsampayutto”ti sampayuttapaccayatā dassitā. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Yasmā pana arūpīnaṃ dhammānaṃ rūpadhammehi sampayogo natthi, tasmā viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpantiādīsu tatiyacatutthavārapadesu “viññāṇasampayuttaṃ nāma”ntiādinā nayena yaṃ labbhati, tadeva gahitanti esa sampayuttacatukke viseso.

245. In the Quad of Association, by the phrase 'with ignorance as condition,' the conditionality of formations by ignorance through co-nascence and other conditions is shown; and then by 'associated with ignorance,' the condition of association is shown. The same method applies to the remaining sections. However, since immaterial phenomena are not associated with material phenomena, in phrases such as 'name-and-form conditioned by consciousness,' etc., in the third and fourth sections, only what is obtained by the method of 'name associated with consciousness,' etc., is taken. This is the distinction in the Quad of Association.

4. Aññamaññacatukkaṃ

4. The Mutual Quad

246. Aññamaññacatukkepi [M 0.0197] avijjāpaccayāti sahajātādipaccayavasena saṅkhārassa avijjāpaccayataṃ dassetvā “saṅkhārapaccayāpi avijjā”ti aññamaññapaccayatā dassitā. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Yasmā pana bhavo nippadeso, upādānaṃ sappadesaṃ, sappadesadhammo ca nippadesadhammassa paccayo hoti, na nippadesadhammo sappadesadhammassa, tasmā ettha “bhavapaccayāpi upādāna”nti na vuttaṃ; heṭṭhā vā desanāya pacchinnattā evaṃ na vuttaṃ[P 0.0207]. Yasmā ca nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ atthi, saḷāyatanapaccayā ekacittakkhaṇe nāmarūpaṃ natthi, yassa saḷāyatanaṃ aññamaññapaccayo bhaveyya, tasmā catutthavāre “chaṭṭhāyatanapaccayāpi nāmarūpa”nti yaṃ labbhati tadeva gahitanti esa aññamaññacatukke viseso.

246. In the Mutual Quad, by the phrase 'with ignorance as condition,' the conditionality of formations by ignorance through co-nascence and other conditions is shown; and then by 'ignorance is also conditioned by formations,' mutual conditionality is shown. The same method applies to the remaining sections. However, because becoming is without parts and clinging has parts, and a phenomenon with parts can be a condition for one without parts, but not vice versa, therefore here it is not stated that 'clinging is also conditioned by becoming'; or it is not stated thus because the teaching below is cut off. And since the six sense bases are conditioned by name-and-form, but in a single mind-moment name-and-form is not conditioned by the six sense bases in such a way that the six sense bases could be a mutual condition, therefore in the fourth section, only what is obtained—'name-and-form is also conditioned by the sixth sense base'—is taken. This is the distinction in the Mutual Quad.

Avijjāmūlakanayamātikā.

The Outline of the Mode Rooted in Ignorance.

Saṅkhārādimūlakanayamātikā

The Outline of the Mode Rooted in Formations, and So Forth.

247. Idāni [V 0.0198] saṅkhārapaccayā avijjāti saṅkhāramūlakanayo āraddho. Tatthāpi yathā avijjāmūlake evaṃ cattāri catukkāni soḷasa ca vārā veditabbā. Paṭhamacatukke pana paṭhamavārameva dassetvā desanā saṃkhittā. Yathā cettha evaṃ viññāṇamūlakādīsupi. Tattha sabbesveva tesu saṅkhāramūlakādīsu aṭṭhasu nayesu “saṅkhārapaccayā avijjā”tiādinā nayena sahajātādipaccayavasena avijjāya saṅkhārādipaccayataṃ dassetvā puna “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā nayena ekacittakkhaṇepi paccayākāracakkassa pavatti dassitā.

247. Now, the mode rooted in formations, namely 'ignorance conditioned by formations,' is commenced. Here too, just as in the mode rooted in ignorance, four quads and sixteen sections should be understood. However, in the first quad, only the first section is shown, and the exposition is abbreviated. As it is here, so too in the modes rooted in consciousness, and so forth. In all these eight modes rooted in formations, and so forth, by the method 'ignorance conditioned by formations,' and so forth, the conditionality of ignorance by formations, and so forth, is shown through co-nascence and other conditions; and then by the method 'formations conditioned by ignorance,' and so forth, the occurrence of the wheel of conditional relations even in a single mind-moment is shown.

Kasmā pana bhavamūlakā jātijarāmaraṇamūlakā vā nayā na vuttā? Kiṃ bhavapaccayā avijjā na hotīti? No na hoti. “Saṅkhārapaccayā avijjā”ti evamādīsu pana vuccamānesu na koci bhavapariyāpanno dhammo avijjāya paccayo na vutto. Tasmā apubbassa aññassa avijjāpaccayassa vattabbassa abhāvato bhavamūlako nayo na vutto. Bhavaggahaṇena ca avijjāpi saṅgahaṃ gacchati. Tasmā “bhavapaccayā avijjā”ti vuccamāne “avijjāpaccayā avijjā”tipi vuttaṃ siyā. Na ca ekacittakkhaṇe avijjā avijjāya [M 0.0198] paccayo nāma hoti. Tattha pacchinnattāva jātijarāmaraṇamūlakāpi nayā na gahitā. Apica bhave jātijarāmaraṇānipi antogadhāni. Na cetāni ekacittakkhaṇe avijjāya paccayā hontīti bhavamūlakā jātijarāmaraṇamūlakā vā nayā na vuttāti.

But why were the modes rooted in becoming or rooted in birth, aging, and death not stated? Is it that ignorance is not conditioned by becoming? It is not that it is not. However, when it is said, 'ignorance conditioned by formations,' and so forth, no phenomenon encompassed by becoming is stated as not being a condition for ignorance. Therefore, since there is no other new condition for ignorance to be stated, the mode rooted in becoming was not stated. And by the term 'becoming', ignorance is also included. Thus, if it were said, 'ignorance is conditioned by becoming,' it would also be said, 'ignorance is conditioned by ignorance.' But in a single mind-moment, ignorance is not a condition for ignorance. Because the sequence is cut off at that point, the modes rooted in birth, aging, and death are also not taken. Moreover, birth, aging, and death are included within becoming. And these are not conditions for ignorance in a single mind-moment. Therefore, the modes rooted in becoming or rooted in birth, aging, and death were not stated.

Mātikāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Matrix.

Akusalaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Unwholesome

248-249. Idāni yathā heṭṭhā cittuppādakaṇḍe kusalattikaṃ ādiṃ katvā nikkhittamātikāya paṭipāṭiyā paṭhamaṃ kusalaṃ bhājitaṃ, tathā idha mātikāya anikkhittattā paṭhamaṃ kusalaṃ anāmasitvā “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāro”ti akusaladhammavasena mātikāya nikkhittattā nikkhepapaṭipāṭiyāva avijjādīni paṭiccasamuppādaṅgāni [P 0.0208] bhājetvā dassetuṃ katame dhammā [V 0.0199] akusalātiādimāha. Tassattho heṭṭhā cittuppādakaṇḍe (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 365) vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Yasmā pana ekacittakkhaṇe taṇhāya ca kāmupādānassa ca sambhavo natthi, tasmā yaṃ ettha taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ labbhati, tadeva dassetuṃ diṭṭhi diṭṭhigatantiādi vuttaṃ.

248-249. Now, just as earlier in the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness, beginning with the wholesome triad, the wholesome was first analyzed according to the order of the laid-out matrix, so here, because the matrix has not been laid out, without first addressing the wholesome, and because the matrix is laid out in terms of unwholesome states starting with 'with ignorance as condition, formations,' therefore, in accordance with the order of the laying out, to analyze and show the factors of dependent origination beginning with ignorance, the text begins, 'Which states are unwholesome?' The meaning of this should be understood in the same way as explained earlier in the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness (Dhs. Aṭṭha. 365). However, because craving and clinging to sensual pleasures do not occur in a single mind-moment, to show what clinging is obtained here with craving as condition, 'view, what is held as a view,' etc., is stated.

Bhavaniddese ca yasmā upādānaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchati, tasmā “ṭhapetvā upādānaṃ vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho saṅkhārakkhandho viññāṇakkhandho”ti vuttaṃ. Evañhi vuccamāne upādānassa upādānapaccayattaṃ āpajjeyya. Na ca tadeva tassa paccayo hoti. Jātiādiniddesesu yasmā ete arūpadhammānaṃ jātiādayo, tasmā “khaṇḍiccaṃ, pāliccaṃ, valittacatā, cuti, cavanatā”ti na vuttaṃ.

In the exposition of becoming, because clinging is included within the formations aggregate, therefore it is said, 'except for clinging, the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, the formations aggregate, and the consciousness aggregate.' For if it were expressed in that way, clinging would become a condition for itself. But the very same thing is not a condition for itself. In the expositions of birth and so on, because these are the birth and so on of formless phenomena, therefore 'brokenness of teeth, greyness of hair, wrinkled skin, death, decease' are not mentioned.

250. Evaṃ paṭhamavāraṃ niṭṭhapetvā puna dutiyavāre yasmiṃ samaye paṭhamavārena paccayākāro dassito, tasmiṃyeva samaye aparenapi nayena paccayākāraṃ dassetuṃ visuṃ samayavavatthānavāraṃ avatvā tasmiṃ samaye avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārotiādināva nayena desanā katā. Tattha ṭhapetvā phassanti idaṃ yasmā phassopi nāmapariyāpanno, tasmā phassassa nāmato nīharaṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

250. Having thus completed the first section, then in the second section, in order to show the mode of conditionality by another method at the very same time in which the mode of conditionality was shown in the first section, the teaching is given by the very same method of 'with ignorance as condition, formations,' etc., without stating a separate section establishing the time. There, this phrase 'excluding contact' is stated for the purpose of extracting contact from 'name,' since contact is also included in 'name.'

252. Tatiyavāre [M 0.0199] yassa cittasamuṭṭhānarūpassa viññāṇaṃ paccayo, tasmiṃ pavattamāne yasmā tenupatthaddhānaṃ cakkhāyatanādīnaṃ upacitattaṃ paññāyati, tasmā cakkhāyatanassa upacayotiādi vuttaṃ. Yasmā ca kammajarūpassapi tasmiṃ samaye vattamānassa viññāṇaṃ pacchājātapaccayena paccayo hoti, tasmāpi evaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha kiñcāpi kammajaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānanti dveva santatiyo gahitā, itarāpi pana dve santatiyo gahetabbā. Tāsampi hi viññāṇaṃ paccayo hotiyeva.

252. In the third round, for the consciousness-originated form for which consciousness is a condition, when that consciousness is occurring, because the accumulation of the eye-base, etc., supported by it, is evident, therefore it is said, 'the accumulation of the eye-base,' etc. And also because consciousness is a post-nascence condition for kamma-originated form occurring at that time, thus it is stated. Here, although only two continua—kamma-originated and consciousness-originated—are taken, still the other two continua should also be taken, since consciousness is indeed a condition for those as well.

254. Catutthavāre pana yasmā ekacittakkhaṇepi mahābhūtarūpapaccayā cakkhāyatanādīni, hadayarūpapaccayā chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ, nāmapaccayā ca pacchājātasahajātādivasena yathānurūpaṃ sabbānipi pavattanti, tasmā tattha katamaṃ nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ? Cakkhāyatanantiādi vuttaṃ.

254. In the fourth round, because even in a single mind-moment, the eye-base, etc., arise dependent on the great elements-materiality, the sixth base dependent on the heart-base materiality, and all of them arise appropriately dependent on name by way of post-nascence, co-nascence, etc., therefore it is asked, 'What sixfold base is dependent on name-and-form?' The answer is given as 'the eye-base,' etc.

256. Dutiyacatukke [P 0.0209][V 0.0200] sabbaṃ uttānameva.

256. In the second tetrad, everything is self-evident.

264. Tatiyacatukke yassa sampayuttapaccayabhāvo na hoti, yassa ca hoti, taṃ visuṃ visuṃ dassetuṃ idaṃ vuccati viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ viññāṇasampayuttaṃ nāmantiādi vuttaṃ.

264. In the third tetrad, to show separately that which is not a condition by association and that which is, it is said, 'With consciousness as condition, name-and-form; name associated with consciousness,' etc.

272. Catutthacatukke phassapaccayā nāmaniddese kiñcāpi “ṭhapetvā phassaṃ vedanākkhandho…pe… viññāṇakkhandho – idaṃ vuccati phassapaccayā nāma”nti na vuttaṃ, tathāpi anantarātītapadaniddese “ṭhapetvā phassaṃ vedanākkhandho…pe… viññāṇakkhandho”ti vuttattā avuttampi taṃ vuttameva hoti. Yadeva hi nāmaṃ phassassa paccayo, phassopi tasseva paccayoti.

272. In the fourth tetrad, in the designation of name dependent on contact, although it is not stated, 'excluding contact, the feeling aggregate... the consciousness aggregate – this is called name dependent on contact,' nevertheless, because in the designation of the immediately preceding term it is said, 'excluding contact, the feeling aggregate... the consciousness aggregate,' even what is unsaid is as good as said. For whatever name is a condition for contact, contact is also a condition for that.

Yathā cāyaṃ catucatukko soḷasavārappabhedo avijjāmūlako paṭhamanayo etasmiṃ paṭhamākusalacitte pakāsito, evaṃ saṅkhāramūlakādayo aṭṭha nayāpi veditabbā. Pāḷi pana saṃkhittā. Evameva tasmiṃ paṭhamākusalacitteyeva nava nayā, chattiṃsa catukkāni, catucattālīsādhikañca vārasataṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Just as this fourfold tetrad, divided into sixteen rounds, rooted in ignorance, is the first method explained in this first unwholesome consciousness, so too should the eight methods rooted in formations, etc., be understood. The Pāli, however, is concise. Just so, it should be understood that in that first unwholesome consciousness itself, there are nine methods, thirty-six tetrads, and one hundred and forty-four rounds.

280. Idāni imināva nayena sesākusalacittesupi paccayākāraṃ dassetuṃ katame dhammā akusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha yasmā diṭṭhivippayuttesu taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ natthi, tasmā upādānaṭṭhāne upādānaṃ viya [M 0.0200] daḷhanipātinā adhimokkhena padaṃ pūritaṃ. Domanassasahagatesu ca yasmā vedanāpaccayā taṇhāpi natthi, tasmā taṇhāṭṭhāne taṇhā viya balavakilesena paṭighena padaṃ pūritaṃ. Upādānaṭṭhāne adhimokkheneva. Vicikicchāsampayutte pana yasmā sanniṭṭhānābhāvato adhimokkhopi natthi, tasmā taṇhāṭṭhāne balavakilesabhūtāya vicikicchāya padaṃ pūritaṃ. Upādānaṭṭhānaṃ parihīnameva. Uddhaccasampayutte pana yasmā adhimokkho atthi, tasmā taṇhāṭṭhāne balavakilesena uddhaccena padaṃ pūritaṃ. Upādānaṭṭhāne adhimokkheneva. Sabbattheva ca visesamattaṃ dassetvā pāḷi saṃkhittā. Yo [P 0.0210] cāyaṃ viseso dassito, tattha kevalaṃ adhimokkhaniddesova apubbo. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā āgatameva.

280. Now, to show the mode of conditions in the remaining unwholesome consciousnesses by this very method, the passage beginning, 'Which states are unwholesome?' is commenced. Herein, because in those dissociated from wrong view, craving as a condition for clinging does not exist, therefore, in the place of clinging, the position is filled by resolution, which firmly adheres like clinging. And in those accompanied by displeasure, because feeling as a condition for craving also does not exist, therefore, in the place of craving, the position is filled by aversion, a strong defilement like craving. The position of clinging is filled by resolution. But in that associated with doubt, because there is no settling due to the absence of decision, therefore, in the place of craving, the position is filled by doubt, which is a strong defilement. The position of clinging is omitted. In that associated with restlessness, however, because resolution exists, therefore, in the place of craving, the position is filled by restlessness, a strong defilement. The position of clinging is filled by resolution. And everywhere only a slight distinction is shown, so the Pāli is concise. And of this distinction which is shown, only the specification of resolution is unprecedented. The rest has already come before.

Adhimokkhaniddese pana adhimuccanavasena adhimokkho. Adhimuccati vā tena ārammaṇe cittaṃ [V 0.0201] nibbicikicchatāya sanniṭṭhānaṃ gacchatīti adhimokkho. Adhimuccanākāro adhimuccanā. Tassa cittassa, tasmiṃ vā ārammaṇe adhimuttattāti tadadhimuttatā. Sabbacittesu ca paṭhamacitte vuttanayeneva nayacatukkavārappabhedo veditabbo. Kevalañhi vicikicchāsampayutte upādānamūlakassa nayassa abhāvā aṭṭha nayā, dvattiṃsa catukkāni, aṭṭhavīsādhikañca vārasataṃ hotīti.

In the explanation of resolution, resolution is in the sense of determining. Or, the mind determines, and by that, reaches a decision on the object, free from doubt—this is resolution. The manner of determining is determination. Because that mind is resolved on that object, that is its resolvedness. And in all consciousnesses, the division into methods, tetrads, and rounds should be understood by the method stated in the first consciousness. However, in that associated with doubt, due to the absence of the method rooted in clinging, there are only eight methods, thirty-two tetrads, and one hundred and twenty-eight rounds.

Akusalaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Unwholesome.

Kusalaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Wholesome

292. Idāni imināva nayena kusalacittādīsupi paccayākāraṃ dassetuṃ katame dhammā kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Yathā pana akusale paṭhamaṃ mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā pacchā niddeso kato, na tathā idha. Kasmā? Appanāvāre nānattasambhavato. Lokiyakusalādīsu hi tesaṃ dhammānaṃ dukkhasaccapariyāpannattā “evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassā”ti appanā hoti, lokuttarakusalādīsu “evametesaṃ dhammāna”nti. Tasmā ettha sādhāraṇato mātikaṃ ṭhapetuṃ na sakkāti pāṭiyekkaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ kusalādīnaṃ mātikaṃ uddisitvāva niddeso katoti.

292. Now, by this same method, to show the mode of conditionality even in wholesome consciousnesses and so forth, the section beginning 'Which states are wholesome?' has been commenced. However, unlike in the unwholesome section where first the matrix was laid down and then the exposition was made, it is not so here. Why? Because of the possibility of diversity in the application. For in mundane wholesome states and so forth, since those states are included in the truth of suffering, the application is 'thus of this entire mass of suffering,' while in supramundane wholesome states and so forth, it is 'thus of these states.' Therefore, it is not possible here to establish a common matrix, so the exposition has been made by designating a separate matrix for each of those wholesome states and so forth.

Tattha yasmā ekacittakkhaṇe kusalasaṅkhārena saddhiṃ avijjā natthi, tasmā taṃ avatvā, avijjā viya akusalānaṃ, kusalānaṃ mūlato kusalamūlaṃ, taṇhupādānānañca [M 0.0201] abhāvato taṇhāṭṭhāne taṇhā viya ārammaṇe ajjhogāḷho pasādo, upādānaṭṭhāne upādānaṃ viya daḷhanipātī nāma adhimokkho vutto. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

Herein, since ignorance does not exist together with wholesome formations in a single moment of consciousness, it is not mentioned; rather, just as ignorance is the root for unwholesome states, so the wholesome root is the root for wholesome states. And since craving and clinging are absent, in the place of craving, like craving, there is serenity deeply immersed in the object; and in the place of clinging, like clinging, there is what is called resolution, which is strong and firm. The rest should be understood in the same way as explained before.

Kusalaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Wholesome.

Abyākataniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Indeterminate

306. Abyākataṃ [V 0.0202] heṭṭhā cittuppādakaṇḍe āgatapaṭipāṭiyāva vibhattaṃ. Sabbavāresu ca avijjāmūlakā nayā parihīnā. Kasmā? Avijjāṭṭhāne ṭhapetabbassa abhāvato. Kusalacittesu [P 0.0211] hi avijjāṭṭhāne ṭhapetabbaṃ kusalamūlaṃ atthi, cakkhuviññāṇādīsu natthi. Sahetukesu pana kiñcāpi atthi, evaṃ santepi idha pacchinnattā tattha na gahitaṃ. Pañcaviññāṇasote sotapatitāva hutvā desanā katāti veditabbā.

306. The indeterminate has been classified below in the section on the arising of consciousness according to the sequence that has been presented. And in all sections, the methods rooted in ignorance are omitted. Why? Because there is nothing to be placed in the position of ignorance. For in wholesome consciousnesses there is a wholesome root to be placed in the position of ignorance, but in eye-consciousness and so forth, there is not. However, although in those with roots there is such a factor, even so, because it is cut off here, it is not included there. It should be understood that the exposition has been made as if it has just fallen into the stream of the five consciousnesses.

Visesato panettha cakkhuviññāṇādīsu taṇhāṭṭhānaṃ upādānaṭṭhānañca parihīnaṃ. Kasmā? Taṇhāṭṭhānārahassa balavadhammassa abhāvā adhimokkharahitattā ca. Sesāhetukesu taṇhāṭṭhānameva parihīnaṃ. Sahetukesu pasādasabbhāvato taṇhāṭṭhāne pasādena padaṃ pūritaṃ. Evamettha kusalākusalavipākesu cakkhuviññāṇādīsu saṅkhāraviññāṇanāmachaṭṭhāyatanaphassavedanāmūlakā cha cha, sesāhetukesu adhimokkhamūlakena saddhiṃ satta satta, sahetukesu pasādamūlakena saddhiṃ aṭṭha aṭṭha nayā veditabbā.

Especially here, in eye-consciousness and so forth, the position of craving and the position of clinging are omitted. Why? Because of the absence of a strong factor worthy of the position of craving, and because of the absence of determination. In the remaining rootless states, only the position of craving is omitted. In those with roots, due to the presence of sensitivity, the position of craving is filled by sensitivity. Thus, here, in the case of wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant consciousnesses such as eye-consciousness and so forth, six methods each, rooted in formations, consciousness, name, the sixth sense base, contact, and feeling, are to be understood; in the remaining rootless states, seven methods each, including the one rooted in determination; and in those with roots, eight methods each, including the one rooted in sensitivity.

Tattha cakkhuviññāṇādīsupi catunnampi catukkānaṃ ādivārova vutto. Dutiyavāro paccayavisesaṭṭhena labbhamānopi na vutto. Tatiyacatutthavārā asambhavatoyeva. Rūpamissakā hi te, na ca cakkhuviññāṇādīni rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpenti. Yathā ca paṭhamacatukke dve vārā labbhanti, evaṃ sesacatukkesupi. Tasmā paṭhamacatukke dutiyavāro, sesacatukkesu ca dve dve vārā avuttāpi vuttāva hontīti veditabbā. Sesāhetukābyākate sabbacatukkesu sabbepi vārā labbhanti. Idha pacchinnattā pana parato na gahitā. Sotapatitāva hutvā desanā katāti. Sesasahetukavipākesupi [M 0.0202] eseva nayo aññatra arūpāvacaravipākā. Arūpāvacaravipākasmiñhi vāradvayameva labbhatīti.

Here, even in eye-consciousness and so forth, only the first mode of all four tetrads is stated. The second mode, though obtainable in the sense of a specific condition, is not stated. The third and fourth modes are impossible. For they are mixed with material form, and eye-consciousness and so forth do not generate material form. And just as two modes are obtainable in the first tetrad, so too in the remaining tetrads. Therefore, it should be understood that in the first tetrad the second mode, and in the remaining tetrads two modes each, though unstated, are indeed stated by implication. In the remaining rootless indeterminate states, all modes are obtainable in all tetrads. Here, however, because of being cut off, they are not taken from what follows. The exposition is made as if having just fallen into the stream. The same method applies to the remaining resultant states with roots, except for the formless-sphere resultants. For in the formless-sphere resultants, only two modes are obtainable.

Abyākataniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Indeterminate.

Avijjāmūlakakusalaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Wholesome Rooted in Ignorance.

334. Idāni aparena pariyāyena ekacittakkhaṇe paccayākāraṃ dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā [V 0.0203] kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha avijjāpaccayāti upanissayapaccayataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Teneva niddesavāre “tattha katamā avijjā”ti avibhajitvā “tattha katamo avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāro”ti vibhattaṃ. Kusalacetanāsaṅkhāto [P 0.0212] hi saṅkhāroyeva tasmiṃ samaye cittena sahajāto hoti, na avijjā.

334. Now, by another method, to show the mode of conditions in a single mind-moment, the text beginning 'Which states are wholesome?' is taken up again. Here, 'conditioned by ignorance' is said with reference to the decisive support condition. For this reason, in the exposition section, without analyzing 'Herein, what is ignorance?' it is analyzed as 'Herein, what is the formation conditioned by ignorance?' For the formation, reckoned as wholesome volition, is indeed co-nascent with the consciousness at that time, not ignorance.

Tattha lokiyakusalassa heṭṭhā suttantabhājanīye vuttanayeneva avijjā paccayo hoti. Yasmā pana appahīnāvijjo avijjāya pahānatthaṃ lokuttaraṃ bhāveti, tasmā tassāpi samatikkamavasena paccayo hoti. Avijjāvatoyeva hi kusalāyūhanaṃ hoti, na itarassa. Tattha tebhūmakakusale sammohavasenapi samatikkamabhāvanāvasenapi āyūhanaṃ labbhati; lokuttare samucchedabhāvanāvasenāti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Therein, for the mundane wholesome, ignorance is a condition in the same way as explained below in the Suttanta Analysis. However, since one whose ignorance is not abandoned develops the supramundane for the purpose of abandoning ignorance, it is also a condition for that by way of overcoming. For the accumulation of the wholesome occurs only for one who has ignorance, not for another. Therein, in the wholesome of the three planes, accumulation is obtained both by way of delusion and by way of developing for overcoming; in the supramundane, it is by way of developing for eradication. The rest is as has been explained.

Ayaṃ pana viseso – yathā heṭṭhā ekekakusale catunnaṃ catukkānaṃ vasena nava soḷasakā laddhā, tathā idha na labbhanti. Kasmā? Avijjāya avigatasampayuttaaññamaññapaccayābhāvato. Upanissayavasena panettha paṭhamacatukkameva labbhati. Tampi paṭhamavārameva dassetvā saṃkhittaṃ. Nīharitvā pana dassetabbanti.

However, this is the difference: whereas below, in the case of each single wholesome state, nine sets of sixteen were obtained by way of the four tetrads, here they are not obtained. Why? Because for ignorance there is an absence of non-disappearance, association, and mutuality conditions. Here, only the first tetrad is obtained by way of decisive support. That too is abbreviated, showing only the first mode. However, it should be shown by extracting it in detail.

Avijjāmūlakakusalaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Wholesome Rooted in Ignorance.

Kusalamūlakavipākaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of Resultants Rooted in Wholesome Roots.

343. Idāni abyākatesupi apareneva nayena paccayākāraṃ dassetuṃ katame dhammā abyākatātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha kusalamūlapaccayāti idampi upanissayapaccayataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kusalavipākassa hi kusalamūlaṃ[M 0.0203], akusalavipākassa ca akusalamūlaṃ upanissayapaccayo hoti; nānākkhaṇikakammapaccaye pana vattabbameva natthi. Tasmā esa upanissayapaccayena ceva nānākkhaṇikakammapaccayena ca paccayo hoti. Teneva niddesavāre “tattha [V 0.0204] katamaṃ kusalamūla”nti avibhajitvā “tattha katamo kusalamūlapaccayā saṅkhāro”ti vibhattaṃ. Akusalavipākepi eseva nayo.

343. Now, to show the mode of conditions by another method even in the indeterminate states, the text beginning 'Which states are indeterminate?' is taken up. Herein, 'conditioned by wholesome roots' is also stated with reference to the decisive support condition. For a wholesome root is a decisive support condition for a wholesome resultant, and an unwholesome root for an unwholesome resultant; however, regarding the different-moment kamma condition, there is nothing that needs to be said. Therefore, this is a condition by way of both the decisive support condition and the different-moment kamma condition. For this reason, in the exposition section, without analyzing 'Herein, what is the wholesome root?' it is analyzed as 'Herein, what is the formation conditioned by the wholesome root?' The same method applies to unwholesome resultants as well.

Avijjāmūlakakusalaniddese viya ca imasmimpi vipākaniddese paṭhamaṃ paccayacatukkameva labbhati. Tampi paṭhamavāraṃ dassetvā saṃkhittaṃ. Tasmā ekekasmiṃ vipākacitte ekamekasseva catukkassa vasena kusalamūlamūlake akusalamūlamūlake ca naye vārappabhedo veditabbo. Kiriyādhammānaṃ pana yasmā neva avijjā na kusalākusalamūlāni upanissayapaccayataṃ labhanti, tasmā kiriyavasena paccayākāro na vuttoti.

And just as in the exposition of the wholesome rooted in ignorance, so too in this exposition of resultants, only the first tetrad of conditions is obtained. That too is abbreviated, showing only the first mode. Therefore, in each resultant consciousness, the division of modes in the methods rooted in wholesome roots and rooted in unwholesome roots should be understood by way of each single tetrad. However, since for functional states neither ignorance nor wholesome and unwholesome roots serve as a decisive support condition, the mode of conditions in relation to the functional is not stated.

Evamesa [P 0.0213] –

Thus this—

Akusalakusalābyākata-dhammesu anekabhedato vatvā;

Kusalākusalānaṃ pana, vipāke ca upanissayavasena.

Having spoken of the unwholesome, wholesome, and indeterminate states in many divisions; and then of the wholesome and unwholesome, and of their resultants, by way of decisive support.

Puna ekadhāva vutto, vādippavarena paccayākāro;

Dhammappaccayabhede, ñāṇassa pabhedajananatthaṃ.

Again, the mode of conditions is taught in a single way by the foremost of speakers, for the purpose of generating distinctions of knowledge in the analysis of the conditions for states.

Pariyattisavanacintana-paṭipattikkamavivajjitānañca;

Yasmā ñāṇapabhedo, na kadācipi hoti etasmiṃ.

And since for those devoid of the sequence of learning, listening, reflecting, and practice, a distinction of knowledge never arises in this matter,

Pariyattisavanacintana-paṭipattikkamato sadā dhīro;

Tattha kayirā na haññaṃ, karaṇīyataraṃ tato atthīti.

Therefore, a wise person should always be diligent in the sequence of learning, listening, reflecting, and practice; one should not be negligent in that, thinking, 'There is a more urgent duty than that.'

Ayaṃ pana paccayākāro suttantaabhidhammabhājanīyavasena dveparivaṭṭameva nīharitvā bhājetvā dassito hoti.

This mode of conditions, however, is presented, having been extracted and divided into just two sections according to the Suttanta and Abhidhamma analyses.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Abhidhamma Analysis.

Sammohavinodaniyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya

In the Sammohavinodanī, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga.

Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of Dependent Origination is completed.

7. Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅgo

7. The Exposition of the Foundations of Mindfulness

1. Suttantabhājanīyaṃ uddesavāravaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Summary Section of the Suttanta Division

355. Idāni [P 0.0214][M 0.0204][V 0.0205] tadanantare satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅge cattāroti gaṇanaparicchedo. Tena na tato heṭṭhā na uddhanti satipaṭṭhānaparicchedaṃ dīpeti. Satipaṭṭhānāti tayo satipaṭṭhānā – satigocaropi, tidhā paṭipannesu sāvakesu satthuno paṭidhānunayavītivattatāpi, satipi. “Catunnaṃ, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha…pe… ko ca, bhikkhave, kāyassa samudayo? Āhārasamudayā kāyassa samudayo”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.408) hi satigocaro satipaṭṭhānanti vuccati. Tathā “kāyo upaṭṭhānaṃ, no sati. Sati upaṭṭhānañceva sati cā”tiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 3.35). Tassattho – patiṭṭhāti asminti paṭṭhānaṃ. Kā patiṭṭhāti? Sati. Satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ, padhānaṃ ṭhānanti vā paṭṭhānaṃ; satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ hatthiṭṭhānaassaṭṭhānādīni viya.

355. Now, immediately following that, in the Exposition of the Foundations of Mindfulness, is the section on the enumeration, ‘four.’ By this, it indicates the delimitation of the foundations of mindfulness as neither fewer nor more. As to ‘foundations of mindfulness,’ there are three kinds of ‘foundations of mindfulness’: the domain of mindfulness, the Teacher’s transcending of aversion and attachment in disciples who practice in three ways, and mindfulness itself. For in such passages as, “Monks, I will teach the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness. Listen to that… What, monks, is the arising of the body? With the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of the body,” the domain of mindfulness is called a ‘foundation of mindfulness.’ Similarly, in such passages as, “The body is an establishment, not mindfulness. Mindfulness is both an establishment and mindfulness.” The meaning of that is: that in which one stands firm is a foundation (paṭṭhāna). What stands firm? Mindfulness. The foundation of mindfulness is satipaṭṭhāna. Or, a foundation is a principal standing place; the foundation of mindfulness is satipaṭṭhāna, like the standing place of an elephant, the standing place of a horse, and so on.

“Tayo satipaṭṭhānā yadariyo sevati, yadariyo sevamāno satthā gaṇaṃ anusāsitumarahatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.304, 311) ettha tidhā paṭipannesu sāvakesu satthuno paṭighānunayavītivattatā satipaṭṭhānanti vuttā. Tassattho – paṭṭhapetabbato paṭṭhānaṃ, pavattayitabbatoti attho. Kena paṭṭhapetabbatoti? Satiyā; satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. “Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā satta bojjhaṅge paripūrentī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.147) pana satiyeva satipaṭṭhānanti vuccati. Tassattho – patiṭṭhātīti paṭṭhānaṃ, upaṭṭhāti okkanditvā pakkhanditvā pavattatīti attho; satiyeva paṭṭhānaṭṭhena satipaṭṭhānaṃ; athavā saraṇaṭṭhena sati, upaṭṭhānaṭṭhena [P 0.0215] paṭṭhānaṃ. Iti sati ca sā paṭṭhānañcātipi satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Idamidha [V 0.0206] adhippetaṃ. Yadi evaṃ, kasmā satipaṭṭhānāti bahuvacanaṃ katanti? Satiyā bahuttā; ārammaṇabhedena hi bahukā tā satiyoti.

In the passage, “There are three foundations of mindfulness that the noble one cultivates, and cultivating these, the Teacher is worthy to instruct the assembly,” the Teacher’s transcending of aversion and attachment in disciples who practice in three ways is called a ‘foundation of mindfulness.’ The meaning is this: it is a ‘foundation’ because it is to be established; that is, it is to be set in motion. By what is it to be established? By mindfulness. The establishing by mindfulness is satipaṭṭhāna. But in passages like, “When the four foundations of mindfulness are developed and cultivated, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment,” mindfulness itself is called the ‘foundation of mindfulness.’ The meaning here is: it stands firm, thus it is a foundation; it is present, proceeding by leaping upon and springing upon its object. Mindfulness itself, in the sense of being a foundation, is the foundation of mindfulness. Alternatively, ‘sati’ has the sense of remembering, and ‘paṭṭhāna’ has the sense of establishing. Thus, it is both mindfulness and a foundation, hence satipaṭṭhāna. This is what is intended here. If so, why is ‘foundations of mindfulness’ spoken of in the plural? Because of the multiplicity of mindfulness; for mindfulnesses are many due to the diversity of their objects.

Kasmā [M 0.0205] pana bhagavatā cattārova satipaṭṭhānā vuttā, anūnā anadhikāti? Veneyyahitattā. Taṇhācaritadiṭṭhicaritasamathayānikavipassanāyānikesu hi mandatikkhavasena dvidhā pavattesu mandassa taṇhācaritassa oḷārikaṃ kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ visuddhimaggo, tikkhassa sukhumaṃ vedanānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ. Diṭṭhicaritassapi mandassa nātippabhedagataṃ cittānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ visuddhimaggo, tikkhassa atippabhedagataṃ dhammānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ. Samathayānikassa ca mandassa akicchena adhigantabbanimittaṃ paṭhamaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ visuddhimaggo, tikkhassa oḷārikārammaṇe asaṇṭhahanato dutiyaṃ. Vipassanāyānikassāpi mandassa nātippabhedagatārammaṇaṃ tatiyaṃ, tikkhassa atippabhedagatārammaṇaṃ catutthaṃ. Iti cattārova vuttā, anūnā anadhikāti.

Why then did the Blessed One teach exactly four foundations of mindfulness, neither fewer nor more? For the benefit of those to be trained. For among those with craving-tendencies and view-tendencies, and those who are serenity-practitioners and insight-practitioners—who proceed in two ways, as dull or sharp—for the dull one with a craving-tendency, the gross contemplation of the body as a foundation of mindfulness is the path to purification; for the sharp one, the subtle contemplation of feelings. For the dull one with a view-tendency, the contemplation of mind as a foundation of mindfulness, which is not excessively differentiated, is the path to purification; for the sharp one, the contemplation of phenomena, which is excessively differentiated. For the dull serenity-practitioner, the first foundation of mindfulness, with its sign attainable without difficulty, is the path to purification; for the sharp one, the second is the path, due to their inability to become established on a gross object. For the dull insight-practitioner, the third, with an object that is not excessively differentiated, is the path; for the sharp one, the fourth, with an object that is excessively differentiated. Thus, exactly four were taught, neither fewer nor more.

Subhasukhaniccaattabhāvavipallāsappahānatthaṃ vā. Kāyo hi asubho. Tattha subhavipallāsavipallatthā sattā. Tesaṃ tattha asubhabhāvadassanena tassa vipallāsassa pahānatthaṃ paṭhamaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Sukhaṃ, niccaṃ, attāti gahitesupi ca vedanādīsu vedanā dukkhā, cittaṃ aniccaṃ, dhammā anattā. Etesu ca sukhaniccaattabhāvavipallāsavipallatthā sattā. Tesaṃ tattha dukkhādibhāvadassanena tesaṃ vipallāsānaṃ pahānatthaṃ sesāni tīṇi vuttānīti. Evaṃ subhasukhaniccaattabhāvavipallāsappahānatthaṃ vā cattārova vuttā anūnā anadhikāti veditabbā. Na kevalañca vipallāsapahānatthameva, atha kho caturoghayogāsavaganthaupādānaagatippahānatthampi catubbidhāhārapariññatthañca cattārova vuttāti veditabbā. Ayaṃ tāva pakaraṇanayo.

Or, it is for the sake of abandoning the distortions regarding beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self. The body is indeed unattractive. Beings are distorted by the perception of beauty in it. To abandon this distortion by seeing the state of unattractiveness in the body, the first foundation of mindfulness was taught. And although feelings and so on are grasped as pleasant, permanent, and self, feelings are suffering, the mind is impermanent, and phenomena are non-self. Beings are distorted by the perceptions of pleasure, permanence, and self in these. To abandon these distortions by seeing their nature as suffering and so on, the remaining three were taught. Thus, it should be understood that the four are taught, neither fewer nor more, for the sake of abandoning the distortions regarding beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self. And it should be understood that the four were taught not only for abandoning the distortions, but also for abandoning the four floods, yokes, taints, bonds, clingings, and wrong courses, and for the full understanding of the four kinds of nutriment. This, for now, is the method of the treatise.

Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “saraṇavasena ceva ekattasamosaraṇavasena ca ekameva satipaṭṭhānaṃ ārammaṇavasena cattāroti etadeva vuttaṃ. Yathā [P 0.0216] hi catudvāre nagare pācīnato āgacchantā pācīnadisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā pācīnadvārena nagarameva pavisanti, dakkhiṇato, pacchimato, uttarato āgacchantā uttaradisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā uttaradvārena nagarameva pavisanti, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Nagaraṃ viya hi nibbānamahānagaraṃ, dvāraṃ viya aṭṭhaṅgiko lokuttaramaggo. Pācīnadisādayo viya kāyādayo.

In the commentary, however, it is said: “By way of recollection and by way of converging into one, there is only one foundation of mindfulness; but by way of object, there are four.” Just as in a city with four gates, those coming from the east take goods originating in the eastern region and enter the city through the eastern gate, while those coming from the south, west, and north take goods originating in the northern region and enter the city through the northern gate—in the same way, this matter should be understood. For the great city of Nibbāna is like the city, the Noble Eightfold Path is like the gate, and the body and so on are like the eastern direction and so on.

Yathā [V 0.0207] pācīnato āgacchantā pācīnadisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā pācīnadvārena nagarameva pavisanti, evaṃ kāyānupassanāmukhena āgacchantā [M 0.0206] cuddasavidhena kāyānupassanaṃ bhāvetvā kāyānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena ariyamaggena ekaṃ nibbānameva osaranti. Yathā dakkhiṇato āgacchantā dakkhiṇadisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇadvārena nagarameva pavisanti, evaṃ vedanānupassanāmukhena āgacchantā navavidhena vedanānupassanaṃ bhāvetvā vedanānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena ariyamaggena ekaṃ nibbānameva osaranti. Yathā pacchimato āgacchantā pacchimadisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā pacchimadvārena nagarameva pavisanti, evaṃ cittānupassanāmukhena āgacchantā soḷasavidhena cittānupassanaṃ bhāvetvā cittānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena ariyamaggena ekaṃ nibbānameva osaranti. Yathā uttarato āgacchantā uttaradisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā uttaradvārena nagarameva pavisanti, evaṃ dhammānupassanāmukhena āgacchantā pañcavidhena dhammānupassanaṃ bhāvetvā dhammānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena ariyamaggena ekaṃ nibbānameva osarantīti. Evaṃ saraṇavasena ceva ekattasamosaraṇavasena ca ekameva satipaṭṭhānaṃ ārammaṇavasena cattāroti vuttāti veditabbā.

Just as those coming from the east, taking goods originating from the eastern quarter, enter the city through the eastern gate, so too, those approaching by way of the contemplation of the body, having developed the fourteenfold contemplation of the body, converge upon the one Nibbāna by means of the Noble Path produced through the power of developing the contemplation of the body. Just as those coming from the south, taking goods originating from the southern quarter, enter the city through the southern gate, so too, those approaching by way of the contemplation of feelings, having developed the ninefold contemplation of feelings, converge upon the one Nibbāna by means of the Noble Path produced through the power of developing the contemplation of feelings. Just as those coming from the west, taking goods originating from the western quarter, enter the city through the western gate, so too, those approaching by way of the contemplation of the mind, having developed the sixteenfold contemplation of the mind, converge upon the one Nibbāna by means of the Noble Path produced through the power of developing the contemplation of the mind. Just as those coming from the north, taking goods originating from the northern quarter, enter the city through the northern gate, so too, those approaching by way of the contemplation of phenomena, having developed the fivefold contemplation of phenomena, converge upon the one Nibbāna by means of the Noble Path produced through the power of developing the contemplation of phenomena. Thus, it should be understood that by way of its destination and by way of converging into one, there is only one foundation of mindfulness, but by way of its objects, it is said to be four.

Idha bhikkhūti ettha kiñcāpi bhagavatā devaloke nisīditvā ayaṃ satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅgo kathito, ekabhikkhupi tattha bhagavato santike nisinnako nāma natthi. Evaṃ santepi yasmā ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhikkhū bhāventi, bhikkhugocarā hi ete, tasmā idha bhikkhūti ālapati. Kiṃ panete satipaṭṭhāne bhikkhūyeva bhāventi, na bhikkhunīādayoti? Bhikkhunīādayopi [P 0.0217] bhāventi. Bhikkhū pana aggaparisā. Iti aggaparisattā idha bhikkhūti ālapati. Paṭipattiyā vā bhikkhubhāvadassanato evamāha. Yo hi imaṃ paṭipattiṃ paṭipajjati, so bhikkhu nāma hoti. Paṭipannako hi devo vā hotu manusso vā, bhikkhūti saṅkhaṃ gacchatiyeva. Yathāha –

Here, regarding the phrase 'a bhikkhu,' although the Blessed One delivered this analysis of the foundations of mindfulness while seated in the world of the devas, there was not a single bhikkhu seated there in the presence of the Blessed One. Even so, since bhikkhus develop these four foundations of mindfulness, and these are the domain of bhikkhus, he therefore addresses 'a bhikkhu.' But do only bhikkhus develop these foundations of mindfulness, and not bhikkhunīs and others? Bhikkhunīs and others also develop them. However, bhikkhus are the foremost assembly. Thus, because they are the foremost assembly, he addresses 'a bhikkhu.' Or, he speaks thus because the state of a bhikkhu is shown through the practice. For whoever undertakes this practice is called a bhikkhu. Indeed, whether a deva or a human, one who is practicing is reckoned as a bhikkhu. As it is said:

“Alaṅkato cepi samañcareyya,

Santo danto niyato brahmacārī;

Sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṃ,

So brāhmaṇo so samaṇo sa bhikkhū”ti. (dha. pa. 142);

“Though he be adorned, if he should live in peace,

calm, tamed, established in the holy life,

having laid down the rod toward all beings—

he is a brahmin, he is a recluse, he is a bhikkhu.”

Kāyānupassanāuddesavaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Summary of the Contemplation of the Body

Ajjhattanti [M 0.0207][V 0.0208] niyakajjhattaṃ adhippetaṃ. Tasmā ajjhattaṃ kāyeti attano kāyeti attho. Tattha kāyeti rūpakāye. Rūpakāyo hi idha aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ kesādīnañca dhammānaṃ samūhaṭṭhena, hatthikāyaassakāyarathakāyādayo viya, kāyoti adhippeto. Yathā ca samūhaṭṭhena evaṃ kucchitānaṃ āyaṭṭhena. Kucchitānañhi paramajegucchānaṃ so āyotipi kāyo. Āyoti uppattideso. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – āyanti tatoti āyo. Ke āyanti? Kucchitā kesādayo. Iti kucchitānaṃ kesādīnaṃ āyoti kāyo.

'Internally' (ajjhattaṃ) refers to one's own internality. Therefore, 'internally in the body' means 'in one's own body.' Here, 'body' (kāya) refers to the physical body. For here the physical body is intended as a 'body' in the sense of a collection of things such as limbs, parts, hair, and so on, just like an elephant's body, a horse's body, a chariot's body, and so on. And just as it is understood in the sense of a collection, so too in the sense of being a source of repulsive things. For it is also called 'body' (kāya) because it is the source (āya) of the most repulsive and disgusting things. 'Āya' means the place of origin. The meaning of the word here is this: 'They come there' (āyanti tato), therefore it is a 'source' (āyo). What comes? Repulsive things like hair and so on. Thus, the body (kāya) is the source (āya) of repulsive things like hair and the like.

Kāyānupassīti kāyaṃ anupassanasīlo, kāyaṃ vā anupassamāno kāyeti ca vatvāpi puna kāyānupassīti dutiyaṃ kāyaggahaṇaṃ asammissato vavatthānaghanavinibbhogādidassanatthaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ. Tena na kāye vedanānupassī cittadhammānupassī vā; atha kho kāye kāyānupassī yevāti kāyasaṅkhāte vatthusmiṃ kāyānupassanākārasseva dassanena asammissato vavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Tathā na kāye aṅgapaccaṅgavinimuttaekadhammānupassī, nāpi kesalomādivinimuttaitthipurisānupassī. Yopi cettha kesalomādiko bhūtupādāyasamūhasaṅkhāto kāyo, tatthāpi na bhūtupādāyavinimuttaekadhammānupassī; atha kho rathasambhārānupassako viya aṅgapaccaṅgasamūhānupassī, nagarāvayavānupassako viya kesalomādisamūhānupassī, kadalikkhandhapattavaṭṭivinibhuñjako viya rittamuṭṭhiviniveṭhako [P 0.0218] viya ca bhūtupādāyasamūhānupassīyevāti nānappakārato samūhavasena kāyasaṅkhātassa vatthuno dassanena ghanavinibbhogo dassito hoti. Na hettha yathāvuttasamūhavinimutto kāyo vā itthī vā puriso vā añño vā koci dhammo dissati. Yathāvuttadhammasamūhamatteyeva pana tathā tathā sattā micchābhinivesaṃ karonti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

'Contemplating the body' (kāyānupassī) means one is by nature a contemplator of the body, or one who is contemplating the body. And having said 'in the body' (kāye), the second mention of 'body' in 'contemplating the body' (kāyānupassī) should be understood as being for the purpose of showing its unmixed demarcation, the analysis of its compactness, and so on. By this, one is not a contemplator of feeling in the body, nor a contemplator of mind or phenomena; rather, one is solely a contemplator of the body in the body. Thus, by showing only the mode of contemplating the body in the object designated as 'body,' the unmixed demarcation is shown. Likewise, one is not a contemplator of a single phenomenon in the body apart from its limbs and parts, nor a contemplator of a woman or a man apart from hair, body hair, and so on. Even in this body, which is designated as a collection of primary elements and derived matter, one is not a contemplator of a single phenomenon apart from the primary elements and derived matter. Instead, just as one observing the components of a chariot contemplates the collection of its components, or as one observing the parts of a city contemplates the collection of its parts, or as one who separates the sheaths of a banana trunk or one who unwraps an empty fist, one contemplates the collection of the primary elements and derived matter. Thus, by showing the object designated as 'body' as a collection in various ways, the analysis of its compactness is shown. Here, no body, woman, man, or any other phenomenon is seen apart from the aforementioned collection. Yet, it is just regarding this collection of phenomena that beings in various ways form wrong adherence. Therefore, the ancients have said:

“Yaṃ passati na taṃ diṭṭhaṃ, yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ taṃ na passati;

Apassaṃ bajjhate mūḷho, bajjhamāno na muccatī”ti.

“What one sees is not the seen;

what is seen, that one does not see.

Not seeing, the fool is bound;

being bound, one is not freed.”

Ghanavinibbhogādidassanatthanti [M 0.0208] vuttaṃ. Ādisaddena cettha ayampi attho veditabbo – ayañhi etasmiṃ kāye kāyānupassīyeva, na aññadhammānupassī. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathā anudakabhūtāyapi marīciyā udakānupassino honti, na evaṃ aniccadukkhānattaasubhabhūteyeva imasmiṃ [V 0.0209] kāye niccasukhaattasubhabhāvānupassī; atha kho kāyānupassī aniccadukkhānattaasubhākārasamūhānupassīyevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā yvāyaṃ mahāsatipaṭṭhāne “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā…pe… so satova assasatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.374; ma. ni. 1.107) nayena assāsapassāsādicuṇṇakajātaaṭṭhikapariyosāno kāyo vutto, yo ca “idhekacco pathavīkāyaṃ aniccato anupassati, tathā āpokāyaṃ, tejokāyaṃ, vāyokāyaṃ, kesakāyaṃ, lomakāyaṃ, chavikāyaṃ, cammakāyaṃ, maṃsakāyaṃ, rudhirakāyaṃ, nhārukāyaṃ, aṭṭhikāyaṃ, aṭṭhimiñjakāya”nti paṭisambhidāyaṃ kāyo vutto, tassa sabbassa imasmiṃyeva kāye anupassanato kāye kāyānupassīti evampi attho daṭṭhabbo.

It was said for the purpose of showing the breaking down of compactness, and so forth. Here, by the word 'and so forth,' this meaning should also be understood: for in this body, one is a contemplator of the body, not a contemplator of other phenomena. What is meant by this? Just as in a waterless mirage there are those who contemplate water, it is not so that one contemplates the state of permanence, pleasure, self, or beauty in this body—which is in fact impermanent, suffering, not-self, and foul. Rather, it is said that one is a contemplator of the body, that is, a contemplator of the aggregate of aspects that are impermanent, suffering, not-self, and foul. Alternatively, the meaning 'a contemplator of the body in the body' should also be understood in this way: because the body described in the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness, by the method beginning with 'Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has gone to the forest... mindfully breathes in,' (D. ni. 2.374; M. ni. 1.107) and ending with the bones reduced to powder, and the body described in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, 'Here, someone contemplates the earth-body as impermanent, and similarly the water-body, fire-body, air-body, hair-body, body-hair-body, skin-body, hide-body, flesh-body, blood-body, sinew-body, bone-body, bone-marrow-body,' are all contemplated in this very body.

Atha vā kāye ahanti vā mamanti vā evaṃ gahetabbassa kassaci ananupassanato, tassa tasseva pana kesalomādikassa nānādhammasamūhassa anupassanato kāye kesādidhammasamūhasaṅkhāte kāyānupassīti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Apica “imasmiṃ kāye aniccato anupassati, no niccato”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 3.35) anukkamena paṭisambhidāyaṃ āgatanayassa sabbasseva aniccalakkhaṇādino ākārasamūhasaṅkhātassa kāyassa [P 0.0219] anupassanatopi kāye kāyānupassīti evampi attho daṭṭhabbo.

Alternatively, the meaning should be understood thus: one is a contemplator of the body in the body—which is designated as an aggregate of phenomena such as hair—because one does not contemplate anything in the body that could be grasped as 'I' or 'mine,' but rather contemplates that very aggregate of various phenomena such as hair, body hair, and so on. Furthermore, the meaning 'a contemplator of the body in the body' should also be understood as arising from the contemplation of the body designated as the entire aggregate of aspects beginning with the characteristic of impermanence, according to the method that comes sequentially in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. ma. 3.35), beginning with, 'In this body, one contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent.'

Tathā hi ayaṃ kāye kāyānupassanāpaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno bhikkhu imaṃ kāyaṃ aniccānupassanādīnaṃ sattannaṃ anupassanānaṃ vasena aniccato anupassati no niccato, dukkhato anupassati no sukhato, anattato anupassati no attato, nibbindati no nandati, virajjati no rajjati, nirodheti no samudeti, paṭinissajjati no ādiyati. So taṃ aniccato anupassanto niccasaññaṃ pajahati, dukkhato anupassanto sukhasaññaṃ pajahati, anattato anupassanto attasaññaṃ pajahati[M 0.0209], nibbindanto nandiṃ pajahati, virajjanto rāgaṃ pajahati, nirodhento samudayaṃ pajahati, paṭinissajjanto ādānaṃ pajahatīti (paṭi. ma. 3.35) veditabbo.

For indeed, this bhikkhu, practicing the path of contemplating the body in the body, contemplates this body by way of the seven contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence: he contemplates it as impermanent, not as permanent; as suffering, not as pleasure; as not-self, not as self; he becomes disenchanted, he does not delight; he becomes dispassionate, he is not impassioned; he brings it to cessation, he does not cause it to originate; he relinquishes, he does not grasp. Contemplating it as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence. Contemplating it as suffering, he abandons the perception of pleasure. Contemplating it as not-self, he abandons the perception of self. Becoming disenchanted, he abandons delight. Becoming dispassionate, he abandons passion. Bringing it to cessation, he abandons origination. Relinquishing, he abandons grasping. This should be understood (Paṭi. ma. 3.35).

Viharatīti catūsu iriyāpathavihāresu aññataravihārasamāyogaparidīpanametaṃ, ekaṃ iriyāpathabādhanaṃ aparena iriyāpathena vicchinditvā apatamānaṃ attabhāvaṃ harati pavattetīti attho.

'He dwells' (viharati) here elucidates the connection with one of the four postures. The meaning is that having cut off the affliction of one posture by means of another, one maintains and continues one's individual existence without collapsing.

Bahiddhā [V 0.0210] kāyeti parassa kāye. Ajjhattabahiddhā kāyeti kālena attano kāye, kālena parassa kāye. Paṭhamanayena hi attano kāye kāyapariggaho vutto, dutiyanayena parassa kāye, tatiyanayena kālena attano kālena parassa kāye. Ajjhattabahiddhā pana ghaṭitārammaṇaṃ nāma natthi. Paguṇakammaṭṭhānassa pana aparāparaṃ sañcaraṇakālo ettha kathito. Ātāpīti kāyapariggāhakavīriyasamāyogaparidīpanametaṃ. So hi yasmā tasmiṃ samaye yaṃ taṃ vīriyaṃ tīsu bhavesu kilesānaṃ ātāpanato ātāpoti vuccati, tena samannāgato hoti, tasmā ātāpīti vuccati.

'External body' means the body of another. 'Internal and external body' means at one time one's own body, at another time the body of another. For by the first method, the comprehension of the body with regard to one's own body is stated; by the second method, with regard to the body of another; by the third method, at one time with regard to one's own body, at another time with regard to the body of another. But there is no object called 'internal and external' that is a composite focus. However, for one proficient in the meditation subject, the time for moving from one to the other is discussed here. 'Ardent' (ātāpī) is an elucidation of the conjunction with energy for comprehending the body. For since at that time one is endowed with that energy which is called 'ardor' because it burns up the defilements in the three realms of existence, one is therefore called 'ardent.'

Sampajānoti kāyapariggāhakena sampajaññasaṅkhātena ñāṇena samannāgato. Satimāti kāyapariggāhikāya satiyā samannāgato. Ayaṃ pana yasmā satiyā ārammaṇaṃ pariggahetvā paññāya anupassati, na hi sativirahitassa anupassanā nāma atthi, tenevāha – “satiñca khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbatthikaṃ vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234), tasmā ettha “kāye kāyānupassī viharatī”ti ettāvatā kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānakammaṭṭhānaṃ [P 0.0220] vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā yasmā anātāpino antosaṅkhepo antarāyakaro hoti, asampajāno upāyapariggahe anupāyaparivajjane ca sammuyhati, muṭṭhassatī upāyāpariccāge anupāyāpariggahe ca asamatthova hoti, tenassa taṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ na sampajjati; tasmā yesaṃ dhammānaṃ ānubhāvena taṃ sampajjati tesaṃ dassanatthaṃ “ātāpī sampajāno satimā”ti idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

'Clearly comprehending' (sampajāno) means endowed with the knowledge designated as clear comprehension, which comprehends the body. 'Mindful' (satimā) means endowed with mindfulness that comprehends the body. Since one, having grasped the object with mindfulness, contemplates it with wisdom—for there is indeed no contemplation for one devoid of mindfulness, for which reason he said: 'Bhikkhus, I declare mindfulness to be beneficial in all situations' (Saṃ. ni. 5.234)—therefore, by the phrase 'dwells contemplating the body in the body,' the meditation subject of the establishment of mindfulness in body contemplation is stated. Alternatively, because for one who is not ardent, inner constriction is an obstacle; one who is not clearly comprehending becomes bewildered in adopting skillful means and avoiding unskillful means; and one with lapsed mindfulness is incapable of abandoning unskillful means and adopting skillful means, that meditation subject does not succeed for him. Therefore, to show the qualities by whose power it does succeed, the words 'ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful' were spoken. This should be understood.

Iti [M 0.0210] kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ sampayogaṅgañca dassetvā idāni pahānaṅgaṃ dassetuṃ vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassanti vuttaṃ. Tattha vineyyāti tadaṅgavinayena vā vikkhambhanavinayena vā vinayitvā. Loketi ettha yvāyaṃ ajjhattādibhedo kāyo pariggahito sveva idha loko nāma. Tasmiṃ loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ vinayitvāti attho. Yasmā panettha abhijjhāgahaṇena kāmacchando, domanassaggahaṇena byāpādo saṅgahaṃ gacchati, tasmā nīvaraṇapariyāpannabalavadhammadvayadassanena nīvaraṇappahānaṃ vuttaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Thus, having shown the establishment of mindfulness of body contemplation and its factor of conjunction, now, to show the factor of abandoning, it is said: 'having subdued covetousness and grief in the world.' Herein, 'having subdued' (vineyya) means having subdued either by removal for the time being (tadaṅgavinayena) or by suppression (vikkhambhanavinayena). 'In the world' (loke): here, this very body, which is comprehended as divided into internal and so on, is itself what is meant by 'world.' The meaning is: having subdued covetousness and grief in that world. Since, herein, by the term 'covetousness' sensual desire is included, and by the term 'grief' ill will is included, it should be understood that the abandonment of the hindrances is stated by showing this pair of powerful states that are comprised within the hindrances.

Visesena cettha abhijjhāvinayena kāyasampattimūlakassa anurodhassa, domanassavinayena kāyavipattimūlakassa virodhassa, abhijjhāvinayena ca kāye abhiratiyā, domanassavinayena kāyabhāvanāya anabhiratiyā, abhijjhāvinayena kāye abhūtānaṃ subhasukhabhāvādīnaṃ pakkhepassa, domanassavinayena [V 0.0211] kāye bhūtānaṃ asubhāsukhabhāvādīnaṃ apanayanassa ca pahānaṃ vuttaṃ. Tena yogāvacarassa yogānubhāvo yogasamatthatā ca dīpitā hoti. Yogānubhāvo hi esa yadidaṃ anurodhavirodhavippamutto, aratiratisaho, abhūtapakkhepabhūtāpanayanavirahito ca hoti. Anurodhavirodhavippamutto cesa aratiratisaho abhūtaṃ apakkhipanto bhūtañca anapanento yogasamattho hotīti.

Here, in particular, the following abandonings are stated: through the removal of covetousness, of attachment rooted in physical good fortune; through the removal of displeasure, of aversion rooted in physical misfortune; through the removal of covetousness, of delight in the body; through the removal of displeasure, of non-delight in the development of the body; through the removal of covetousness, of projecting unreal qualities such as beauty and pleasure onto the body; and through the removal of displeasure, of removing real qualities such as ugliness and displeasure from the body. Thus, the meditator’s meditative power and capacity for the practice are demonstrated. For this is meditative power: that one is free from attachment and aversion, endures discontent and delight, and is without projecting the unreal and removing the real. Being free from attachment and aversion, enduring discontent and delight, neither projecting the unreal nor removing the real—one is capable in the practice.

Aparo nayo – “kāye kāyānupassī”ti ettha anupassanāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Viharatīti ettha vuttavihārena kammaṭṭhānikassa kāyapariharaṇaṃ. Ātāpītiādīsu ātāpena sammappadhānaṃ, satisampajaññena sabbatthikakammaṭṭhānaṃ, kammaṭṭhānapariharaṇūpāyo vā; satiyā vā kāyānupassanāvasena paṭiladdhasamatho, sampajaññena vipassanā[P 0.0221], abhijjhādomanassavinayena bhāvanāphalaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānuddesassa atthavaṇṇanā.

Another method: Here, by 'contemplating the body in the body,' the meditation subject, namely contemplation, is stated. By 'He dwells' (viharati), the meditator's maintenance of the body in accordance with the stated manner of dwelling is indicated. In 'ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful,' and so forth: by ardor, right effort is indicated; by mindfulness and clear comprehension, the all-pervasive meditation subject, or alternatively, the means of maintaining the meditation subject; or alternatively, it should be understood that serenity is attained through mindfulness by way of contemplating the body, insight through clear comprehension, and the fruit of development through the removal of covetousness and displeasure. This, for now, is the explanation of the meaning of the summary on the establishment of mindfulness of the contemplation of the body.

Vedanānupassanādiuddesavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Summary Section on the Contemplation of Feelings and So Forth

Vedanānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānuddesādīsupi ajjhattādīni vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Etesupi hi attano vedanādīsu, parassa vedanādīsu, kālena attano kālena parassa vedanādīsūti tividho pariggaho [M 0.0211] vutto. Vedanāsu vedanānupassītiādīsu ca vedanādīnaṃ punavacane payojanaṃ kāyānupassanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Vedanāsu vedanānupassī, citte cittānupassī, dhammesu dhammānupassīti ettha pana vedanāti tisso vedanā. Tā ca lokiyā eva; cittampi lokiyaṃ, tathā dhammā. Tesaṃ vibhāgo niddesavāre pākaṭo bhavissati. Kevalaṃ panidha yathā vedanā anupassitabbā tathā anupassanto “vedanāsu vedanānupassī”ti veditabbo. Esa nayo cittadhammesu. Kathañca vedanā anupassitabbāti? Sukhā tāva vedanā dukkhato, dukkhā sallato, adukkhamasukhā aniccato. Yathāha –

Also in the summary sections on the establishments of mindfulness beginning with the contemplation of feelings, 'internal' and so forth should be understood in the manner already stated. For in these too, the threefold comprehension is stated: regarding one's own feelings and so on, another's feelings and so on, and at one time one's own, at another time another's feelings and so on. The purpose of repeating 'feelings' and so on in phrases like 'contemplating feelings in feelings' should be understood in the same way as explained in the contemplation of the body. In 'contemplating feelings in feelings, contemplating the mind in the mind, contemplating phenomena in phenomena,' 'feelings' here refers to the three kinds of feelings. And these are only mundane; similarly, the mind is mundane, and so are phenomena. Their detailed explanation will become clear in the exposition section. Here, however, one who contemplates feelings in the way they should be contemplated is to be understood as 'one contemplating feelings in feelings.' This method also applies to the mind and phenomena. And how are feelings to be contemplated? Pleasant feeling as suffering, painful feeling as a dart, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent. As it is said—

“Yo sukhaṃ dukkhato adda, dukkhamaddakkhi sallato;

Adukkhamasukhaṃ santaṃ, addakkhi naṃ aniccato;

Sa ve sammadaso bhikkhu, upasanto carissatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 4.253);

"He who sees pleasure as suffering, and suffering as a dart, who sees the peaceful, neither-painful-nor-pleasant state as impermanent—such a monk, seeing rightly, will fare on calmed."

Sabbā [V 0.0212] eva cetā dukkhātipi anupassitabbā. Vuttañcetaṃ – “yaṃ kiñci vedayitaṃ taṃ dukkhasminti vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.259). Sukhadukkhatopi ca anupassitabbā, yathāha – “sukhā kho, āvuso visākha, vedanā ṭhitisukhā, vipariṇāmadukkhā”ti (ma. ni. 1.465) sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Apica aniccādisattānupassanāvasenapi (paṭi. ma. 3.35) anupassitabbā. Sesaṃ niddesavāreyeva pākaṭaṃ bhavissati.

All these should indeed be contemplated as suffering. For it was said: 'Whatever is felt, that I say is suffering' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.259). And they should also be contemplated from the perspective of pleasure and pain, as he said: 'Pleasant feeling, friend Visākha, is pleasant while it lasts, but painful when it changes' (Ma. Ni. 1.465), which should be elaborated in full. Furthermore, they should be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence (cf. Paṭi. Ma. 3.35). The rest will become clear in the exposition section.

Cittadhammesupi cittaṃ tāva ārammaṇādhipatisahajātabhūmikammavipākakiriyādinānattabhedānaṃ aniccādinupassanānaṃ niddesavāre āgatasarāgādibhedānañca vasena [P 0.0222] anupassitabbaṃ. Dhammā salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇānaṃ suññatādhammassa aniccādisattānupassanānaṃ niddesavāre āgatasantāsantādibhedānañca vasena anupassitabbā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Kāmañcettha yassa kāyasaṅkhāte loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ pahīnaṃ, tassa vedanādilokesupi taṃ pahīnameva. Nānāpuggalavasena pana nānācittakkhaṇikasatipaṭṭhānabhāvanāvasena ca sabbattha vuttaṃ. Yato vā ekattha pahīnaṃ, sesesupi pahīnaṃ hoti. Tenevassa tattha pahānadassanatthampi evaṃ vuttanti veditabbanti.

Regarding the mind and phenomena: the mind should be contemplated by way of the diversity of its distinctions, such as object, predominance, co-arising, plane, kamma, result, and functional action; by way of the contemplations beginning with impermanence; and by way of the distinctions such as 'with lust,' etc., that appear in the exposition section. Phenomena should be contemplated by way of their individual and general characteristics, and the nature of emptiness; by way of the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence, etc.; and by way of the distinctions of presence and absence, etc., that appear in the exposition section. The rest is as already stated. Granted, for one who has abandoned covetousness and displeasure regarding the world designated as the body, they are also abandoned regarding the worlds of feelings, etc. However, it is stated for all cases with reference to different individuals and with reference to the cultivation of the establishments of mindfulness for various mind-moments. Alternatively, since when it is abandoned in one, it is abandoned in the others, it should be understood that this is said in order to show its abandonment in each of those cases as well.

Uddesavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Summary Section is concluded.

Kāyānupassanāniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition on the Contemplation of the Body

356. Idāni [M 0.0212] seyyathāpi nāma cheko vilīvakārako thūlakilañjasaṇhakilañjacaṅkoṭakapeḷāpuṭādīni upakaraṇāni kattukāmo ekaṃ mahāveḷuṃ labhitvā catudhā chinditvā tato ekekaṃ veḷukhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā phāletvā taṃ taṃ upakaraṇaṃ kareyya, yathā vā pana cheko suvaṇṇakāro nānāvihitaṃ piḷandhanavikatiṃ kattukāmo suparisuddhaṃ suvaṇṇaghaṭikaṃ labhitvā catudhā bhinditvā tato ekekaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ gahetvā taṃ taṃ piḷandhanaṃ kareyya, evameva bhagavā satipaṭṭhānadesanāya sattānaṃ anekappakāraṃ visesādhigamaṃ kattukāmo ekameva sammāsatiṃ “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā – idha bhikkhu ajjhattaṃ kāye kāyānupassī viharatī”tiādinā nayena ārammaṇavasena [V 0.0213] catudhā bhinditvā tato ekekaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā vibhajanto kathañca bhikkhu ajjhattaṃ kāyetiādinā nayena niddesavāraṃ vattumāraddho.

356. Now, just as a skilled wicker-worker, wishing to make various implements such as large baskets, small baskets, receptacles, and cases, would obtain a large bamboo, split it into four parts, and then take each piece of bamboo, splitting it, to craft those various implements; or as a skilled goldsmith, wishing to create various kinds of ornamental work, would obtain a very pure ingot of gold, divide it into four parts, and then take each portion to fashion that various ornamental work—in the same way, the Blessed One, wishing to bring about the attainment of various kinds of distinction for beings through the teaching of the establishments of mindfulness, took the single right mindfulness and, based on the object, divided it into four parts in the way beginning, 'Here, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body internally.' Then, taking each establishment of mindfulness and analyzing it, he began to state the exposition section in the way beginning, 'And how does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body internally?'

Tattha kathañcātiādi vitthāretuṃ kathetukamyatāpucchā. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – kena ca ākārena kena pakārena bhikkhu ajjhattaṃ kāye kāyānupassī viharatīti? Sesapucchāvāresupi eseva nayo. Idha bhikkhūti imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhu. Ayañhettha idha-saddo ajjhattādivasena sabbappakārakāyānupassanānibbattakassa puggalassa sannissayabhūtasāsanaparidīpano aññasāsanassa tathābhāvapaṭisedhano ca. Vuttañhetaṃ – “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo…pe… suññā parappavādā samaṇebhi [P 0.0223] aññehī”ti (ma. ni. 1.139; a. ni. 4.241). Tena vuttaṃ “imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhū”ti.

Here, the phrase "And how?" and so on is a question expressing the desire to elaborate in detail. The concise meaning here is: "By what means, in what way, does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body internally?" The same method applies to the remaining sets of questions. "Here, a monk" refers to a monk in this dispensation. The word "here" in this context reveals the dispensation as the support for a person who develops all kinds of contemplation of the body, such as internal contemplation, and it negates the existence of such a state in other dispensations. For it is said: "Here alone, monks, is there a true ascetic... empty are the doctrines of other ascetics" (MN 1.139; AN 4.241). Therefore, it is said: "a monk in this dispensation."

Ajjhattaṃ kāyanti attano kāyaṃ. Uddhaṃ pādatalāti pādatalato upari. Adho kesamatthakāti kesaggato heṭṭhā. Tacapariyantanti tiriyaṃ tacaparicchinnaṃ. Pūraṃ nānappakārassa asucino paccavekkhatīti nānappakārakesādiasucibharito ayaṃ kāyoti passati. Kathaṃ? Atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā…pe… muttanti. Tattha atthīti saṃvijjanti. Imasminti yvāyaṃ uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā tiriyaṃ tacapariyanto pūro nānappakārassa asucinoti vuccati tasmiṃ. Kāyeti sarīre. Sarīrañhi [M 0.0213] asucisañcayato kucchitānaṃ kesādīnañceva cakkhurogādīnañca rogasatānaṃ āyabhūtato kāyoti vuccati.

"Internally, the body" means one's own body. "From the soles of the feet upward" means upward from the soles of the feet. "From the top of the head downward" means downward from the tip of the hair. "Bounded by the skin" means horizontally delimited by the skin. ‘Full of various kinds of impurities’ means one sees that this body is filled with various kinds of impurities such as head-hairs and so on. How? "There are in this body: head-hairs..." and so on up to "urine." Here, "there are" means they exist. "In this" refers to that which is called "upward from the soles of the feet, downward from the tip of the hair, horizontally delimited by the skin, full of various kinds of impurities." "Body" means the physical form. For the physical form is called "body" (kāya) because it is a collection of impurities, a receptacle for foul things like hair, and the abode of hundreds of diseases like eye diseases.

Kesā lomāti ete kesādayo dvattiṃsākārā. Tattha atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā, atthi imasmiṃ kāye lomāti evaṃ sambandho veditabbo. Imasmiñhi pādatalato paṭṭhāya upari, kesamatthakā paṭṭhāya heṭṭhā, tacato paṭṭhāya tiriyantatoti ettake byāmamatte kaḷevare sabbākārenapi vicinanto na koci kiñci muttaṃ vā maṇiṃ vā veḷuriyaṃ vā agaruṃ vā kuṅkumaṃ vā kappūraṃ vā vāsacuṇṇādiṃ vā aṇumattampi sucibhāvaṃ passati, atha kho paramaduggandhajegucchaṃ assirīkadassanaṃ nānappakāraṃ kesalomādibhedaṃ asuciṃyeva passati. Tena vuttaṃ – atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā lomā…pe… muttanti. Ayamettha padasambandhato vaṇṇanā.

"Head-hairs, body-hairs"—these are the thirty-two constituents beginning with head-hairs. Here, the connection should be understood thus: "There are in this body head-hairs; there are in this body body-hairs," and so on. For when one examines this very body—from the soles of the feet upwards, from the crown of the head downwards, and bounded by the skin on all sides—in this fathom-long frame, searching in every possible way, one does not see even the slightest bit of purity, whether it be a pearl, a gem, lapis lazuli, agarwood, saffron, camphor, scented powder, or any other such thing. Instead, one sees only what is utterly foul-smelling, disgusting, unlovely in appearance, consisting of various kinds of impurities distinguished as head-hairs, body-hairs, and so on. Therefore, it is said: "There are in this body head-hairs, body-hairs..." up to "urine." This is the explanation of the word connections here.

Imaṃ pana kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇitukāmena kulaputtena āditova catubbidhaṃ sīlaṃ [V 0.0214] sodhetvā suparisuddhasīle patiṭṭhitena, yvāyaṃ dasasu palibodhesu palibodho atthi taṃ upacchinditvā, paṭikkūlamanasikārakammaṭṭhānabhāvanāya paṭhamajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā, jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā, arahattaṃ anāgāmiphalādīsu vā aññataraṃ pattassa sabbantimena paricchedena sāṭṭhakathāya pāḷiyā kataparicayassa tantiācariyassāpi kalyāṇamittassa santike uggahetabbaṃ. Visuddhaṃ tathārūpaṃ [P 0.0224] kalyāṇamittaṃ ekavihāre alabhantena tassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā uggahetabbaṃ. Tattha catubbidhasīlavisodhanañceva (visuddhi. 1.19) palibodho (visuddhi. 1.41) ca palibodhupacchedo ca ācariyassa santikaṃ upasaṅkamanavidhānañca sabbampi visuddhimagge vitthārato kathitaṃ. Tasmā taṃ tattha kathitanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Now, a noble son who wishes to attain arahantship by developing this meditation subject should first purify the fourfold virtue. Being established in perfectly purified virtue, having cut off any impediment among the ten impediments, having generated the first jhāna through the meditation on repulsiveness, and having established insight with that jhāna as a basis, he should learn this meditation subject from a good friend. This good friend should be a teacher of the texts who has attained arahantship or one of the other fruits, such as non-returning, and who has thoroughly mastered the Pāli texts and commentaries down to the last detail. If such a pure and suitable spiritual friend cannot be found in one’s own monastery, one should go to the place where he resides and learn from him. The purification of the fourfold virtue, the impediments, the removal of impediments, and the method of approaching a teacher—all are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. Therefore, they should be understood in the way described there.

Ācariyena pana kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathentena tividhena kathetabbaṃ. Eko bhikkhu pakatiyā uggahitakammaṭṭhāno hoti. Tassa ekaṃ dve nisajjavāre sajjhāyaṃ kāretvā kathetabbaṃ. Eko santike vasitvā uggaṇhitukāmo hoti. Tassa āgatāgatavelāya kathetabbaṃ. Eko uggaṇhitvā aññattha gantukāmo hoti. Tassa nātipapañcaṃ nātisaṅkhepaṃ katvā [M 0.0214] nijjaṭaṃ niggaṇṭhikaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetabbaṃ. Kathentena kiṃ ācikkhitabbanti? Sattadhā uggahakosallaṃ dasadhā ca manasikārakosallaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ.

When the teacher explains the meditation subject, it should be explained in three ways. One monk has naturally grasped the meditation subject. For him, after having him recite once or twice during a sitting, it should be explained. Another monk, wishing to learn by staying nearby, should be told whenever he comes. Another monk, having learned, wishes to go elsewhere. For him, the meditation subject should be explained neither too elaborately nor too concisely, making it clear and straightforward. What should be pointed out when explaining? The sevenfold skill in learning and the tenfold skill in attention should be pointed out.

Tattha vacasā manasā vaṇṇato saṇṭhānato disato okāsato paricchedatoti evaṃ sattadhā uggahakosallaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. Imasmiñhi paṭikkūlamanasikārakammaṭṭhāne yopi tipiṭako hoti, tenapi manasikārakāle paṭhamaṃ vācāya sajjhāyo kātabbo. Ekaccassa hi sajjhāyaṃ karontasseva kammaṭṭhānaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, malayavāsīmahādevattherassa santike uggahitakammaṭṭhānānaṃ dvinnaṃ therānaṃ viya. Thero kira tehi kammaṭṭhānaṃ yācito ‘cattāro māse imaṃ evaṃ sajjhāyaṃ karothā’ti dvattisākārapāḷiṃ adāsi. Te, kiñcāpi tesaṃ dve tayo nikāyā paguṇā, padakkhiṇaggāhitāya pana cattāro māse dvattiṃsākāraṃ sajjhāyantāva sotāpannā ahesuṃ.

Here, skill in learning should be explained in seven ways: by speech, by mind, by color, by shape, by direction, by location, and by delimitation. For in this meditation subject on repulsiveness, even one who knows the Tipiṭaka must first recite verbally when applying the mind.
