Indeed, for some, the meditation subject becomes clear simply by reciting, as was the case with two elders who learned the meditation subject in the presence of the great elder Malayavāsī Mahādeva. It is said that when those elders requested the meditation subject from him, the elder gave them the thirty-two-part Pāli text, saying, “Recite this in this way for four months.” Although they were already proficient in two or three Nikāyas, by reciting the thirty-two parts for four months with proper grasping, they became stream-enterers.

Tasmā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathentena ācariyena antevāsiko vattabbo – ‘paṭhamaṃ tāva vācāya sajjhāyaṃ karohī’ti. Karontena ca tacapañcakādīni paricchinditvā anulomapaṭilomavasena sajjhāyo kātabbo. “Kesā lomā nakhā dantā taco”ti hi vatvā puna paṭilomato “taco dantā nakhā lomā kesā”ti vattabbaṃ. Tadanantaraṃ vakkapañcake “maṃsaṃ nhāru aṭṭhi aṭṭhimiñjaṃ [V 0.0215] vakka”nti vatvā puna paṭilomato “vakkaṃ [P 0.0225] aṭṭhimiñjaṃ aṭṭhi nhāru maṃsaṃ taco dantā nakhā lomā kesā”ti vattabbaṃ. Tato papphāsapañcake “hadayaṃ yakanaṃ kilomakaṃ pihakaṃ papphāsa”nti vatvā puna paṭilomato “papphāsaṃ pihakaṃ kilomakaṃ yakanaṃ hadayaṃ vakkaṃ aṭṭhimiñjaṃ aṭṭhi nhāru maṃsaṃ taco dantā nakhā lomā kesā”ti vattabbaṃ.

Therefore, when teaching the meditation subject, the teacher should instruct the student: ‘First, you should recite verbally.’ While reciting, one should delimit the pentads, beginning with the skin-pentad, and recite them in forward and reverse order. For having said, ‘Head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin,’ one should then say in reverse order: ‘Skin, teeth, nails, body-hairs, head-hairs.’ Next, in the kidney-pentad, having said, ‘Flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys,’ one should then say in reverse order: ‘Kidneys, bone marrow, bones, sinews, flesh, skin, teeth, nails, body-hairs, head-hairs.’ After that, in the lung-pentad, having said, ‘Heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs,’ one should then say in reverse order: ‘Lungs, spleen, membranes, liver, heart, kidneys, bone marrow, bones, sinews, flesh, skin, teeth, nails, body-hairs, head-hairs.’

Tato imaṃ tantiṃ anāruḷhampi paṭisambhidāmagge (paṭi. ma. 1.4) āgataṃ matthaluṅgaṃ karīsāvasāne tantiṃ āropetvā imasmiṃ matthaluṅgapañcake “antaṃ antaguṇaṃ udariyaṃ karīsaṃ matthaluṅga”nti vatvā puna paṭilomato “matthaluṅgaṃ karīsaṃ udariyaṃ antaguṇaṃ antaṃ papphāsaṃ pihakaṃ kilomakaṃ yakanaṃ hadayaṃ vakkaṃ aṭṭhimiñjaṃ aṭṭhi nhāru maṃsaṃ taco dantā nakhā lomā kesā”ti vattabbaṃ.

Then, the brain (matthaluṅga), which is mentioned in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 1.4) though not included in this sequence, should be placed in the sequence at the end of the feces. In this brain-pentad, having said, ‘Intestines, mesentery, stomach contents, feces, brain,’ one should then say in reverse order: ‘Brain, feces, stomach contents, mesentery, intestines, lungs, spleen, membranes, liver, heart, kidneys, bone marrow, bones, sinews, flesh, skin, teeth, nails, body-hairs, head-hairs.’

Tato [M 0.0215] medachakke “pittaṃ semhaṃ pubbo lohitaṃ sedo medo”ti vatvā puna paṭilomato “medo sedo lohitaṃ pubbo semhaṃ pittaṃ matthaluṅgaṃ karīsaṃ udariyaṃ antaguṇaṃ antaṃ papphāsaṃ pihakaṃ kilomakaṃ yakanaṃ hadayaṃ vakkaṃ aṭṭhimiñjaṃ aṭṭhi nhāru maṃsaṃ taco dantā nakhā lomā kesā”ti vattabbaṃ.

Then, in the fat-hexad, having said, ‘Bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat,’ one should then say in reverse order: ‘Fat, sweat, blood, pus, phlegm, bile, brain, feces, stomach contents, mesentery, intestines, lungs, spleen, membranes, liver, heart, kidneys, bone marrow, bones, sinews, flesh, skin, teeth, nails, body-hairs, head-hairs.’

Tato muttachakke “assu vasā kheḷo siṅghāṇikā lasikā mutta”nti vatvā puna paṭilomato “muttaṃ lasikā siṅghāṇikā kheḷo vasā assu medo sedo lohitaṃ pubbo semhaṃ pittaṃ matthaluṅgaṃ karīsaṃ udariyaṃ antaguṇaṃ antaṃ papphāsaṃ pihakaṃ kilomakaṃ yakanaṃ hadayaṃ vakkaṃ aṭṭhimiñjaṃ aṭṭhi nhāru maṃsaṃ taco dantā nakhā lomā kesā”ti evaṃ kālasatampi kālasahassampi kālasatasahassampi vācāya sajjhāyo kātabbo. Vacasā sajjhāyena hi kammaṭṭhānatanti paguṇā hoti; na ito cito ca cittaṃ vidhāvati; koṭṭhāsā pākaṭā honti, hatthasaṅkhalikā viya khāyanti, vatipādapanti viya ca khāyanti. Yathā ca pana vacasā, tatheva manasāpi sajjhāyo kātabbo. Vacasā sajjhāyo hi manasā sajjhāyassa paccayo hoti. Manasā sajjhāyo lakkhaṇapaṭivedhassa paccayo hoti. Lakkhaṇapaṭivedho maggaphalapaṭivedhassa paccayo hoti.

Then, in the urine-hexad, having said, ‘Tears, grease, saliva, mucus, lymph, urine,’ one should then say in reverse order: ‘Urine, lymph, mucus, saliva, grease, tears, fat, sweat, blood, pus, phlegm, bile, brain, feces, stomach contents, mesentery, intestines, lungs, spleen, membranes, liver, heart, kidneys, bone marrow, bones, sinews, flesh, skin, teeth, nails, body-hairs, head-hairs.’ In this way, verbal recitation should be done a hundred times, a thousand times, or a hundred thousand times. For through verbal recitation, the sequence of the meditation subject becomes familiar; the mind does not wander here and there; the parts become clear, appearing like a chain of bones and like a row of stepping stones. And just as one recites verbally, so too should one recite mentally. For verbal recitation is a condition for mental recitation. Mental recitation is a condition for the penetration of characteristics. The penetration of characteristics is a condition for the penetration of the path and its fruit.

‘Vaṇṇato’ti kesādīnaṃ vaṇṇo vavatthapetabbo. ‘Saṇṭhānato’ti tesaṃyeva saṇṭhānaṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ[V 0.0216]. ‘Disato’ti [P 0.0226] imasmiṃ sarīre nābhito uddhaṃ uparimā disā, adho heṭṭhimā disā. Tasmā “ayaṃ koṭṭhāso imissā nāma disāyā”ti disā vavatthapetabbā. ‘Okāsato’ti “ayaṃ koṭṭhāso imasmiṃ nāma okāse patiṭṭhito”ti evaṃ tassa tassa okāso vavatthapetabbo. ‘Paricchedato’ti sabhāgaparicchedo visabhāgaparicchedoti dve paricchedā. Tattha “ayaṃ koṭṭhāso heṭṭhā ca upari ca tiriyañca iminā nāma paricchinno”ti evaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo veditabbo. “Kesā na lomā, lomāpi na kesā”ti evaṃ amissīkatavasena visabhāgaparicchedo veditabbo.

“By color” means the color of the hair and so on should be determined. “By shape” means the shape of those same things should be determined. “By direction” means that in this body, above the navel is the upper direction, and below is the lower direction. Therefore, the direction should be determined as, “This part belongs to such-and-such a direction.” “By location” means, “This part is situated in such-and-such a location,” thus its specific location should be determined. “By delimitation” means there are two kinds of delimitation: delimitation by what is similar and delimitation by what is dissimilar. Herein, delimitation by what is similar should be understood as, “This part is bounded below, above, and across by such-and-such.” Delimitation by what is dissimilar should be understood as, “Head-hairs are not body-hairs, and body-hairs are not head-hairs,” thus by way of non-mixing.

Evaṃ [M 0.0216] sattadhā uggahakosallaṃ ācikkhantena pana “idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ asukasmiṃ sutte paṭikkūlavasena kathitaṃ, asukasmiṃ dhātuvasenā”ti ñatvā ācikkhitabbaṃ. Idañhi mahāsatipaṭṭhāne (dī. ni. 2.372; ma. ni. 1.105 ādayo) paṭikkūlavaseneva kathitaṃ, mahāhatthipadopama (ma. ni. 1.300 ādayo) -mahārāhulovāda (ma. ni. 2.113 ādayo) -dhātuvibhaṅgesu (ma. ni. 3.342 ādayo) dhātuvasena kathitaṃ. Kāyagatāsatisutte (ma. ni. 3.153 ādayo) pana yassa vaṇṇato upaṭṭhāti, taṃ sandhāya cattāri jhānāni vibhattāni. Tattha dhātuvasena kathitaṃ vipassanākammaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, paṭikkūlavasena kathitaṃ samathakammaṭṭhānaṃ. Tadetaṃ idha samathakammaṭṭhānaṃ avisesato sabbasādhāraṇavasena kathitanti vadantiyevāti.

Furthermore, when explaining the sevenfold skill in learning, one should teach having known that: ‘This meditation subject is taught by way of repulsiveness in such-and-such a discourse, and by way of elements in such-and-such a discourse.’ For this is taught by way of repulsiveness in the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness (Dīgha Nikāya 2.372; Majjhima Nikāya 1.105ff.), and by way of elements in the Great Elephant Footprint Simile (Majjhima Nikāya 1.300ff.), the Greater Discourse of Advice to Rāhula (Majjhima Nikāya 2.113ff.), and the Discourse on the Analysis of the Elements (Majjhima Nikāya 3.342ff.). In the Discourse on Mindfulness Directed to the Body (Majjhima Nikāya 3.153ff.), however, the four jhānas are distinguished with reference to one to whom it appears by way of color. Herein, what is taught by way of elements is a meditation subject for insight, while what is taught by way of repulsiveness is a meditation subject for serenity. They say that this serenity meditation subject is taught here without distinction, as being common to all.

Evaṃ sattadhā uggahakosallaṃ ācikkhitvā “anupubbato, nātisīghato, nātisaṇikato, vikkhepapaṭibāhanato, paṇṇattisamatikkamanato, anupubbamuñcanato, appanāto, tayo ca suttantā”ti evaṃ dasadhā manasikārakosallaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. Tattha ‘anupubbato’ti idañhi sajjhāyakaraṇato paṭṭhāya anupaṭipāṭiyā manasikātabbaṃ, na ekantarikāya. Ekantarikāya hi manasikaronto yathā nāma akusalo puriso dvattiṃsapadaṃ nisseṇiṃ ekantarikāya ārohanto kilantakāyo patati, na ārohanaṃ sampādeti; evameva bhāvanāsampattivasena adhigantabbassa assādassa anadhigamā kilantacitto patati, na bhāvanaṃ sampādeti.

Having explained the sevenfold skill in learning thus, one should then teach the tenfold skill in attention: “gradually, not too quickly, not too slowly, preventing distraction, transcending designations, releasing gradually, absorption, and the three discourses.” Herein, “gradually” means one should attend to it in due sequence from the beginning of recitation, not skipping any. For if one attends by skipping, it is like an unskillful person climbing a ladder with thirty-two rungs by skipping steps—his body grows tired, he falls, and fails to complete the climb. Similarly, with a mind exhausted from not attaining the satisfaction to be gained through meditative accomplishment, one collapses and fails to complete the meditation.

Anupubbato manasikarontenāpi ca ‘nātisīghato’ manasikātabbaṃ. Atisīghato manasikaroto hi [P 0.0227] yathā nāma tiyojanaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjitvā okkamanavissajjanaṃ asallakkhetvā [V 0.0217] sīghena javena sattakkhattumpi gamanāgamanaṃ karoto purisassa kiñcāpi addhānaṃ parikkhayaṃ gacchati, atha kho pucchitvāva gantabbaṃ hoti; evameva kevalaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariyosānaṃ pāpuṇāti, avibhūtaṃ pana hoti, na visesaṃ āvahati. Tasmā nātisīghato manasikātabbaṃ.

Even when attending gradually, one should attend “not too quickly.” For if one attends too quickly, it is like a man traveling a three-league road without noticing the ascents and descents—though he may complete the journey quickly by running back and forth seven times, yet he has to ask the way to go. Likewise, one may reach the end of the meditation subject, but it remains unclear and does not bring distinction. Therefore, one should attend not too quickly.

Yathā ca nātisīghato evaṃ ‘nātisaṇikato’pi. Atisaṇikato manasikaroto hi yathā nāma tadaheva tiyojanaṃ maggaṃ gantukāmassa purisassa [M 0.0217] antarāmagge rukkhapabbatagahanādīsu vilambamānassa maggo parikkhayaṃ na gacchati, dvīhatīhena pariyosāpetabbo hoti; evameva kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariyosānaṃ na gacchati, visesādhigamassa paccayo na hoti.

Just as one should not be too quick, so too one should attend “not too slowly.” For if one attends too slowly, it is like a man who wishes to travel three leagues on that very day: if he lingers along the way among trees, mountains, and thickets, the journey does not come to an end; it has to be completed in two or three days. Similarly, the meditation subject does not reach completion, and it is not a condition for the attainment of distinction.

‘Vikkhepapaṭibāhanato’ti kammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇe cetaso vikkhepo paṭibāhitabbo. Appaṭibāhato hi yathā nāma ekapadikaṃ papātamaggaṃ paṭipannassa purisassa akkamanapadaṃ asallakkhetvā ito cito ca vilokayato padavāro virajjhati, tato sataporise papāte patitabbaṃ hoti; evameva bahiddhā vikkhepe sati kammaṭṭhānaṃ parihāyati, paridhaṃsati. Tasmā vikkhepapaṭibāhanato manasikātabbaṃ.

“By preventing distraction” means that the mind’s distraction towards external, diverse objects should be prevented by abandoning the meditation subject. For if it is not prevented, it is just as if a man walking along a single-file cliff path, without noting where he steps, looks this way and that, his footing fails, and he must fall into a hundred-man-high chasm. Just so, when there is external distraction, the meditation subject declines and vanishes. Therefore, one must attend by preventing distraction.

‘Paṇṇattisamatikkamanato’ti yā ayaṃ “kesā lomā”ti ādikā paṇṇatti taṃ atikkamitvā paṭikkūlanti cittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ. Yathā hi udakadullabhakāle manussā araññe udapānaṃ disvā tattha tālapaṇṇādikaṃ kiñcideva saññāṇaṃ bandhitvā tena saññāṇena āgantvā nhāyanti ceva pivanti ca, yadā pana tesaṃ abhiṇhasañcārena āgatāgatapadaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, tadā saññāṇena kiccaṃ na hoti, icchiticchitakkhaṇe gantvā nhāyanti ceva pivanti ca; evameva pubbabhāge ‘kesā lomā’ti paṇṇattivasena manasikaroto paṭikkūlabhāvo pākaṭo hoti. Atha ‘kesā lomā’ti paṇṇattiṃ samatikkamitvā paṭikkūlabhāveyeva cittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ.

“By transcending designations” means that one must go beyond the designation, such as “hair, body hair,” and so on, and establish the mind on the repulsive. Just as, in a time when water is scarce, people who see a well in the forest tie a palm leaf or some other marker there and return with that marker to bathe and drink—but when, through frequent travel, the path becomes clear, the marker is no longer needed, and they can go whenever they wish to bathe and drink—so too, in the preparatory stage, the repulsive aspect becomes clear through attending in terms of the designation of “hair, body hair.” Then, having transcended the designation of “hair, body hair,” one must establish the mind solely on the repulsive aspect.

‘Anupubbamuñcanato’ti yo yo koṭṭhāso na upaṭṭhāti, taṃ taṃ muñcantena anupubbamuñcanato manasikātabbaṃ. Ādikammikassa hi ‘kesā’ti manasikaroto manasikāro gantvā ‘mutta’nti [P 0.0228] imaṃ pariyosānakoṭṭhāsameva āhacca tiṭṭhati. ‘Mutta’nti ca manasikaroto manasikāro gantvā ‘kesā’ti imaṃ ādikoṭṭhāsameva āhacca tiṭṭhati. Athassa manasikaroto keci [V 0.0218] koṭṭhāsā upaṭṭhahanti, keci na upaṭṭhahanti. Tena ye ye upaṭṭhahanti tesu tesu tāva kammaṃ kātabbaṃ, yāva dvīsu upaṭṭhitesu tesampi eko suṭṭhutaraṃ upaṭṭhahati. Evaṃ upaṭṭhitaṃ pana tameva punappunaṃ manasikarontena appanā uppādetabbā.

“By gradually releasing” means that one should attend by releasing whatever section does not present itself. For a beginner, when attending to “hair,” the attention goes and strikes only the final section, “urine.” And when attending to “urine,” the attention goes and strikes only the initial section, “hair.” Then, as one attends, some sections present themselves, and some do not. Therefore, on whichever ones present themselves, on those one should work first, until when two have presented themselves, even of those, one presents itself much better. Having thus established a presenting section, one should repeatedly attend to just that to generate absorption.

Tatrāyaṃ upamā – yathā hi dvattiṃsatālake tālavane vasantaṃ makkaṭaṃ gahetukāmo luddo ādimhi ṭhitatālassa paṇṇaṃ sarena vijjhitvā ukkuṭṭhiṃ kareyya; atha so makkaṭo paṭipāṭiyā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ tāle [M 0.0218] patitvā pariyantatālameva gaccheyya; tatthapi gantvā luddena tatheva kate puna teneva nayena āditālaṃ āgaccheyya; so evaṃ punappunaṃ paṭipāṭiyā gacchanto ukkuṭṭhukkuṭṭhiṭṭhāneyeva uṭṭhahitvā puna anukkamena ekasmiṃ tāle nipatitvā tassa vemajjhe makuḷatālapaṇṇasūciṃ daḷhaṃ gahetvā vijjhiyamānopi na uṭṭhaheyya, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Herein is this simile: Suppose a hunter, desiring to catch a monkey dwelling in a palm grove of thirty-two palm trees, were to pierce the leaf of the first standing palm tree with an arrow and make a shout. Then that monkey, moving from tree to tree in sequence, would reach the very last palm tree. Even having gone there, if the hunter were to do the same, it would return to the first palm tree by that very method. Thus, repeatedly going back and forth in sequence, rising up at the very places of the shouts, and then gradually falling on one palm tree, it would firmly grasp the needle-like shoot of a young palm leaf in its very middle, and even when being shot, it would not rise up. This accomplishment is to be understood in this way.

Tatridaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – yathā hi tālavane dvattiṃsatālā, evaṃ imasmiṃ kāye dvattiṃsa koṭṭhāsā; makkaṭo viya cittaṃ; luddo viya yogāvacaro; makkaṭassa dvattiṃsatālake tālavane nivāso viya yogino cittassa dvattiṃsakoṭṭhāsake kāye ārammaṇavasena anusaṃcaraṇaṃ; luddena ādimhi ṭhitatālassa paṇṇaṃ sarena vijjhitvā ukkuṭṭhiyā katāya makkaṭassa tasmiṃ tasmiṃ tāle patitvā pariyantatālagamanaṃ viya yogino ‘kesā’ti manasikāre āraddhe paṭipāṭiyā gantvā pariyosānakoṭṭhāse eva cittassa saṇṭhānaṃ; puna paccāgamanepi eseva nayo; punappunaṃ paṭipāṭiyā gacchamānassa makkaṭassa ukkuṭṭhukkuṭṭhiṭṭhāne uṭṭhānaṃ viya punappunaṃ manasikaroto kesuci kesuci upaṭṭhitesu anupaṭṭhahante vissajjetvā upaṭṭhitesu parikammakaraṇaṃ; anukkamena ekasmiṃ tāle nipatitvā tassa vemajjhe makuḷatālapaṇṇasūciṃ daḷhaṃ gahetvā vijjhiyamānassāpi [P 0.0229] anuṭṭhānaṃ viya avasāne dvīsu upaṭṭhitesu yo suṭṭhutaraṃ upaṭṭhāti tameva punappunaṃ manasikaritvā appanāya uppādanaṃ.

Herein is the comparison: Just as there are thirty-two palm trees in a palm grove, so too there are thirty-two constituents in this body; the mind is like the monkey; the yogi is like the hunter. The monkey's dwelling in the palm grove of thirty-two palm trees is like the yogi's mind wandering among the thirty-two constituents of the body by way of its object. Just as, when the hunter pierces the leaf of the first standing palm tree with an arrow and makes a shout, the monkey's falling on this and that palm tree and reaching the last palm tree is like, when the yogi begins with the attention 'head hairs,' the mind's going in sequence and settling on the very last constituent; and the same method applies to its return. Just as the monkey, repeatedly going in sequence, rises up at the places of the shouts, so too, when the yogi repeatedly attends, dismissing those that do not appear among those that appear here and there, he performs the preliminary work on those that do appear. Just as, in due course, the monkey, falling on one palm tree, firmly grasps the needle-like shoot of a young palm leaf in its very middle, and does not rise up even when being shot, so too, at the end, when two constituents appear, repeatedly attending to the one that appears more clearly, one generates absorption.

Aparāpi upamā – yathā nāma piṇḍapātiko bhikkhu dvattiṃsakulaṃ gāmaṃ upanissāya vasanto paṭhamagehe eva dve bhikkhā labhitvā parato ekaṃ vissajjeyya; punadivase tisso labhitvā parato dve vissajjeyya; tatiyadivase ādimhiyeva pattapūraṃ labhitvā āsanasālaṃ gantvā paribhuñjeyya, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dvattiṃsakulagāmo viya hi dvattiṃsākāro; piṇḍapātiko viya yogāvacaro; tassa taṃ gāmaṃ upanissāya vāso viya yogino dvattiṃsākāre parikammakaraṇaṃ; paṭhamagehe [V 0.0219] dve bhikkhā labhitvā parato ekissā vissajjanaṃ viya dutiyadivase tisso labhitvā parato dvinnaṃ vissajjanaṃ viya ca manasikaroto manasikaroto anupaṭṭhahante anupaṭṭhahante vissajjetvā upaṭṭhitesu upaṭṭhitesu [M 0.0219] yāva koṭṭhāsadvaye parikammakaraṇaṃ; tatiyadivase ādimhiyeva pattapūraṃ labhitvā āsanasālāyaṃ nisīditvā paribhogo viya dvīsu yo suṭṭhutaraṃ upaṭṭhahati tameva punappunaṃ manasikaritvā appanāya uppādanaṃ.

Herein is another simile: Just as a monk on almsround, dwelling dependent on a village of thirty-two families, might receive two alms-portions at the very first house and pass by one house beyond that; on the next day, receiving three, he might pass by two houses beyond that; and on the third day, receiving a full bowl right at the beginning, he might go to the assembly hall and eat—this is to be understood as a similar success. For the village of thirty-two families is like the thirty-two constituents; the yogi is like the monk on almsround; his performing preliminary work on the thirty-two constituents is like that monk's dwelling dependent on that village. Just as receiving two alms-portions at the first house and passing by one beyond that, and like receiving three on the second day and passing by two beyond that, so too, while repeatedly attending, one dismisses those that do not appear and performs preliminary work on those that do appear, until it is down to two constituents. Just as on the third day, receiving a full bowl right at the beginning and sitting in the assembly hall to eat, so too, repeatedly attending to whichever of the two appears more clearly, one generates absorption.

‘Appanāto’ti appanākoṭṭhāsato. Kesādīsu ekekasmiṃ koṭṭhāse appanā hotīti veditabbāti ayamettha adhippāyo.

'From absorption' means from the constituent of absorption. It should be understood that absorption occurs in each constituent, beginning with the head hairs. This is the intended meaning here.

‘Tayo ca suttantā’ti adhicittaṃ, sītibhāvo, bojjhaṅgakosallanti ime tayo suttantā vīriyasamādhiyojanatthaṃ veditabbāti ayamettha adhippāyo. Tattha –

'And three discourses' refers to the higher mind, coolness, and skill in the factors of enlightenment—these three discourses should be understood as for the purpose of yoking energy and concentration. This is the intended meaning here. Therein:

“Adhicittamanuyuttena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā tīṇi nimittāni kālena kālaṃ manasikātabbāni…kālena kālaṃ samādhinimittaṃ manasikātabbaṃ, kālena kālaṃ paggahanimittaṃ manasikātabbaṃ, kālena kālaṃ upekkhānimittaṃ manasikātabbaṃ. Sace, bhikkhave, adhicittamanuyutto bhikkhu ekantaṃ samādhinimittaṃyeva manasikareyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ cittaṃ kosajjāya saṃvatteyya. Sace, bhikkhave, adhicittamanuyutto bhikkhu ekantaṃ paggahanimittaṃyeva manasikareyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ cittaṃ uddhaccāya saṃvatteyya. Sace, bhikkhave, adhicittamanuyutto bhikkhu ekantaṃ upekkhānimittaṃyeva manasikareyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ cittaṃ na sammāsamādhiyeyya [P 0.0230] āsavānaṃ khayāya. Yato ca kho, bhikkhave, adhicittamanuyutto bhikkhu kālena kālaṃ samādhinimittaṃ, paggahanimittaṃ, upekkhānimittaṃ manasikaroti, taṃ hoti cittaṃ mudu ca kammaniyañca pabhassarañca, na ca pabhaṅgu, sammā samādhiyati āsavānaṃ khayāya.

"Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind should from time to time attend to three signs... from time to time the sign of concentration should be attended to, from time to time the sign of exertion should be attended to, from time to time the sign of equanimity should be attended to. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend exclusively to the sign of concentration, it is possible that that mind would conduce to laziness. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend exclusively to the sign of exertion, it is possible that that mind would conduce to agitation. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend exclusively to the sign of equanimity, it is possible that that mind would not be rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. But when, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind from time to time attends to the sign of concentration, the sign of exertion, and the sign of equanimity, that mind becomes pliable, workable, and radiant, and not brittle, and is rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints."

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, suvaṇṇakāro vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā ukkaṃ bandhati, ukkaṃ bandhitvā ukkāmukhaṃ ālimpeti, ukkāmukhaṃ ālimpetvā saṇḍāsena jātarūpaṃ gahetvā ukkāmukhe pakkhipeyya, ukkāmukhe pakkhipitvā kālena kālaṃ abhidhamati, kālena kālaṃ udakena paripphoseti, kālena kālaṃ ajjhupekkhati[M 0.0220]. Sace, bhikkhave, suvaṇṇakāro [V 0.0220] vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā taṃ jātarūpaṃ ekantaṃ abhidhameyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ jātarūpaṃ ḍaheyya. Sace, bhikkhave, suvaṇṇakāro vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā taṃ jātarūpaṃ ekantaṃ udakena paripphoseyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ jātarūpaṃ nibbāyeyya. Sace, bhikkhave, suvaṇṇakāro vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā taṃ jātarūpaṃ ekantaṃ ajjhupekkheyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ jātarūpaṃ na sammā paripākaṃ gaccheyya.

"Just as, bhikkhus, a goldsmith or a goldsmith's apprentice sets up a furnace; having set up the furnace, he smears the mouth of the crucible; having smeared the mouth of the crucible, he takes gold with tongs and places it in the mouth of the crucible; having placed it in the mouth of the crucible, from time to time he blows on it, from time to time he sprinkles it with water, and from time to time he just observes it. If, bhikkhus, a goldsmith or a goldsmith's apprentice were to blow exclusively on that gold, it is possible that that gold would burn. If, bhikkhus, a goldsmith or a goldsmith's apprentice were to sprinkle that gold exclusively with water, it is possible that that gold would cool down. If, bhikkhus, a goldsmith or a goldsmith's apprentice were to observe that gold exclusively, it is possible that that gold would not reach proper refinement."

“Yato ca kho, bhikkhave, suvaṇṇakāro vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā taṃ jātarūpaṃ kālena kālaṃ abhidhamati, kālena kālaṃ udakena paripphoseti, kālena kālaṃ ajjhupekkhati, taṃ hoti jātarūpaṃ mudu ca kammaniyañca pabhassarañca, na ca pabhaṅgu, sammā upeti kammāya; yassā yassā ca piḷandhanavikatiyā ākaṅkhati – yadi paṭṭikāya yadi kuṇḍalāya yadi gīveyyakāya yadi suvaṇṇamālāya, tañcassa atthaṃ anubhoti.

But when, bhikkhus, a goldsmith or a goldsmith's apprentice from time to time blows on that gold, from time to time sprinkles it with water, and from time to time observes it, that gold becomes pliable, workable, and radiant, and not brittle, and is rightly fit for work. Whatever kind of ornament he wishes to make—whether a belt, an earring, a necklace, or a golden garland—it serves his purpose.

“Evameva kho, bhikkhave, adhicittamanuyuttena…pe… sammā samādhiyati āsavānaṃ khayāya; yassa yassa ca abhiññāsacchikaraṇīyassa dhammassa cittaṃ abhininnāmeti abhiññā sacchikiriyāya, tatra tatreva sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇāti sati satiāyatane”ti (a. ni. 3.103) idaṃ suttaṃ adhicittanti veditabbaṃ.

So too, bhikkhus, for one devoted to the higher mind... is rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints; and to whatever state realizable by direct knowledge he inclines his mind for realizing it by direct knowledge, in each and every case he attains the capacity to be a direct witness, whenever there is a basis for it.” (AN 3.103). This discourse is to be understood as the one on the higher mind.

“Chahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu bhabbo anuttaraṃ sītibhāvaṃ sacchikātuṃ. Katamehi chahi? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ niggahetabbaṃ tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ niggaṇhāti, yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paggahetabbaṃ tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paggaṇhāti, yasmiṃ samaye [P 0.0231] cittaṃ sampahaṃsitabbaṃ tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ sampahaṃseti, yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ ajjhupekkhitabbaṃ tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati, paṇītādhimuttiko ca hoti nibbānābhirato ca. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, chahi dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu bhabbo anuttaraṃ sītibhāvaṃ sacchikātu”nti (a. ni. 6.85) idaṃ suttaṃ sītibhāvoti veditabbaṃ.

Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with six qualities is capable of realizing the unsurpassed cool state. With what six? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu restrains the mind when it should be restrained, exerts the mind when it should be exerted, gladdens the mind when it should be gladdened, and observes the mind with equanimity when it should be observed with equanimity; and he is one whose resolve is for the sublime and who delights in Nibbāna. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these six qualities is capable of realizing the unsurpassed cool state.” (AN 6.85) This discourse is to be understood as the one on the cool state.

Bojjhaṅgakosallaṃ [M 0.0221] pana “evameva kho, bhikkhave, yasmiṃ samaye līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, akālo [V 0.0221] tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234) saṃyuttamahāvagge bojjhaṅgasaṃyutte āgatameva.

But skill in the factors of enlightenment is found in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, Great Chapter, in the Connected Discourses on the Factors of Enlightenment, as follows: “So too, bhikkhus, when the mind is sluggish, that is not the time to develop the enlightenment factor of tranquility.” (SN 5.112)

Iti idaṃ sattavidhaṃ uggahakosallaṃ suggahitaṃ katvā imañca dasavidhaṃ manasikārakosallaṃ suṭṭhu vavatthapetvā tena yoginā ubhayakosallavasena kammaṭṭhānaṃ sādhukaṃ uggahetabbaṃ. Sace panassa ācariyena saddhiṃ ekavihāreyeva phāsu hoti, evaṃ vitthārena akathāpetvā kammaṭṭhānamanuyuñjantena visesaṃ labhitvā uparūpari kathāpetabbaṃ. Aññattha vasitukāmena yathāvuttena vidhinā vitthārato kathāpetvā punappunaṃ parivattetvā sabbaṃ gaṇṭhiṭṭhānaṃ chinditvā kammaṭṭhānabhāvanāya ananurūpaṃ senāsanaṃ pahāya mahāvāsatādiaṭṭhārasadosavajjite anurūpe vihāre viharantena khuddakapalibodhupacchedaṃ katvā yo tāva rāgacarito hoti, tena yasmā rāgo pahātabbo, tasmā paṭikkūlamanasikāre parikammaṃ kātabbaṃ.

Thus, having well mastered this sevenfold skill in learning and thoroughly established this tenfold skill in attention, that yogi should properly take up a meditation subject with both skills. If, however, he finds it comfortable to dwell in the same monastery as his teacher, then without requesting detailed instruction, he should apply himself to the meditation subject and, having attained a special state, seek further clarification from time to time. If he wishes to dwell elsewhere, he should first request detailed instruction as described, repeatedly reviewing it and cutting through all knotty points. Then, abandoning any lodging unsuitable for meditation practice, he should dwell in a suitable monastery—one free from the eighteen faults, such as that of a large residence. Having cut off minor hindrances, if he is of a lustful temperament, because lust must be abandoned, he should undertake the preparatory work of attention to repulsiveness.

Karontena pana kesesu tāva nimittaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Ekaṃ vā dve vā kese luñcitvā hatthatale ṭhapetvā vaṇṇo tāva vavatthapetabbo. Chinnaṭṭhānepi kese oloketuṃ vaṭṭati; udakapatte vā yāgupatte vā oloketumpi vaṭṭatiyeva. Kāḷakakāle disvā kāḷakāti manasikātabbā; setakāle setāti. Missakakāle pana ussadavasena manasikātabbā honti. Yathā ca kesesu, evaṃ sakalepi tacapañcake disvāva nimittaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Evaṃ nimittaṃ gahetvā sabbakoṭṭhāsesu vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedavasena vavatthapetvā vaṇṇasaṇṭhānagandhaāsayokāsavasena pañcadhā paṭikkūlato vavatthapetabbā.

When undertaking this, one should first take up the sign in the hair. How? Pluck one or two hairs and place them in the palm of the hand, then the color should be determined. It is also suitable to observe the hair at the cut end, or to look at it in a water bowl or a rice-gruel bowl. If seen as black, it should be attended to as “black.” If white, as “white.” If mixed, it should be attended to according to the predominant aspect. Just as with the hair, so too the sign should be taken by observing it in the entire pentad ending in skin. Having thus taken up the sign, it should be defined in all parts by way of color, shape, direction, location, and boundary. Then, it should be defined as repulsive in five ways: by color, shape, smell, origin, and location.

Tatrāyaṃ [P 0.0232] sabbakoṭṭhāsesu anupubbakathā – kesā tāva pakativaṇṇena kāḷakā addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇā, saṇṭhānato dīghavaṭṭalikā tulādaṇḍasaṇṭhānā, disato uparimadisāya jātā, okāsato ubhosu passesu kaṇṇacūḷikāhi, purato nalāṭantena, pacchato galavāṭakena [M 0.0222] paricchinnā. Sīsakaṭāhaveṭhanaṃ allacammaṃ kesānaṃ okāso. Paricchedato kesā sīsaveṭhanacamme vīhaggamattaṃ pavisitvā patiṭṭhitena heṭṭhā attano mūlatalena, upari ākāsena, tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnā. Dve kesā ekato natthīti ayaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo.

Here is the detailed description of all the parts, step by step: First, the hair: by nature it is black, the color of collyrium. In shape, it is long and round like a balance-rod. In direction, it grows upwards. In location, it is bounded on both sides by the tops of the ears, in front by the edge of the forehead, and in back by the hollow of the neck. The moist skin covering the skull is the location of the hairs. Regarding boundaries: the hairs, having penetrated the skin covering the head to the extent of a grain of rice, are bounded below by their own root-surface, above by space, and horizontally by each other. That no two hairs are together is the demarcation from their own kind.

‘Kesā na lomā, lomā na kesā’ti evaṃ avasesehi ekatiṃsakoṭṭhāsehi amissīkatā [V 0.0222] kesā nāma pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāsoti ayaṃ visabhāgaparicchedo. Idaṃ kesānaṃ vaṇṇādito vavatthāpanaṃ.

“Head hair is not body hair, body hair is not head hair.” Thus, unmixed with the remaining thirty-one parts, head hair is a distinct part. This is the demarcation from what is dissimilar. This is the determination of head hair with respect to color and so on.

Idaṃ pana tesaṃ vaṇṇādivasena pañcadhā paṭikkūlato vavatthāpanaṃ – kesā ca nāmete vaṇṇatopi paṭikkūlā, saṇṭhānatopi gandhatopi āsayatopi okāsatopi paṭikkūlā. Manuññepi hi yāgupatte vā bhattapatte vā kesavaṇṇaṃ kiñci disvā ‘kesamissakamidaṃ, haratha na’nti jigucchanti. Evaṃ kesā vaṇṇato paṭikkūlā. Rattiṃ bhuñjantāpi kesasaṇṭhānaṃ akkavākaṃ vā makacivākaṃ vā chupitvāpi tatheva jigucchanti. Evaṃ saṇṭhānato paṭikkūlā.

Furthermore, this is the fivefold determination of their repulsiveness based on color and so on: Hair is repulsive in color, shape, smell, origin, and location. For even when people see something the color of hair in a pleasing gruel bowl or rice bowl, they feel disgust, thinking, “This is mixed with hair; take it away!” Thus, hair is repulsive in color. Even those eating at night, if they touch something with the shape of a hair, they feel the same disgust. Thus, hair is repulsive in shape.

Telamakkhanapupphadhūmādisaṅkhāravirahitānañca kesānaṃ gandho paramajeguccho hoti, tato jegucchataro aggimhi pakkhittānaṃ. Kesā hi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānato appaṭikkūlāpi siyuṃ, gandhena pana paṭikkūlāyeva. Yathā hi daharassa kumārassa vaccaṃ vaṇṇato haḷiddivaṇṇaṃ, saṇṭhānatopi haliddipiṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ; saṅkhāraṭṭhāne chaḍḍitañca uddhumātakakāḷasunakhasarīraṃ vaṇṇato tālapakkavaṇṇaṃ, saṇṭhānato vaṭṭetvā vissaṭṭhamudiṅgasaṇṭhānaṃ, dāṭhāpissa sumanamakuḷasadisāti [P 0.0233] ubhayampi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānato siyā appaṭikkūlaṃ, gandhena pana paṭikkūlameva; evaṃ kesāpi siyuṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānato appaṭikkūlā, gandhena pana paṭikkūlā evāti.

The smell of hair, devoid of preparations such as oil, flowers, or incense, is utterly loathsome—even more so when thrown into a fire. For though hair might not be repulsive in color or form, its smell is indeed repulsive. Just as a young child's excrement may be the color of turmeric and have the shape of a turmeric lump; and a bloated, black dog carcass cast aside in a refuse heap may be the color of a ripe palm fruit and have the shape of a mudiṅga drum that has been squashed and cast aside, its fangs like unopened jasmine buds—both may appear unrepulsive in color and form, yet their smell is undeniably repulsive. In the same way, hair too might seem unrepulsive in color and form, but its smell is truly repulsive.

Yathā pana asuciṭṭhāne gāmanissandena jātāni sūpeyyapaṇṇāni nāgarikamanussānaṃ jegucchāni honti aparibhogāni, evaṃ kesāpi pubbalohitamuttakarīsapittasemhādinissandena jātattā atijegucchāti idaṃ nesaṃ ‘āsayato’ pāṭikulyaṃ. Ime ca kesā nāma gūtharāsimhi uṭṭhitakaṇṇikaṃ [M 0.0223] viya ekattiṃsakoṭṭhāsarāsimhi jātā. Te susānasaṅkāraṭṭhānādīsu jātasākaṃ viya, parikhādīsu jātakamalakuvalayādipupphaṃ viya ca asuciṭṭhāne jātattā paramajegucchāti idaṃ tesaṃ ‘okāsato’ pāṭikkūlyaṃ.

Just as pot-herbs that grow in a filthy place from village drainage are loathsome and unfit for consumption by city dwellers, so too are these hairs, being born from the discharge of pus, blood, urine, feces, bile, phlegm, and the like, utterly loathsome—this is their repulsiveness 'by way of source'. And these hairs, like a mushroom that has sprung up on a heap of dung, are born within the mass of the thirty-one bodily parts. Like vegetables growing in a charnel ground or a rubbish heap, or like a lotus or water lily growing in a ditch, they are born in an impure place and thus are extremely loathsome—this is their repulsiveness 'by way of location'.

Yathā ca kesānaṃ, evaṃ sabbakoṭṭhāsānaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānagandhāsayokāsavasena pañcadhā paṭikkūlatā vavatthapetabbā. Vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedavasena pana sabbepi visuṃ visuṃ vavatthapetabbā.

Just as with the hair, so too for all bodily parts should repulsiveness be determined in five ways: by way of color, shape, smell, source, and location. Moreover, all parts should be determined individually by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation.

Tattha [V 0.0223] lomā tāva pakativaṇṇato na kesā viya asambhinnakāḷakā, kāḷapiṅgalā pana honti; saṇṭhānato onataggatālamūlasaṇṭhānā; disato dvīsu disāsu jātā; okāsato ṭhapetvā kesānaṃ patiṭṭhitokāsañca hatthapādatalāni ca yebhuyyena avasesasarīraveṭhanacamme jātā; paricchedato sarīraveṭhanacamme likkhāmattaṃ pavisitvā patiṭṭhitena heṭṭhā attano mūlatalena, upari ākāsena, tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnā. Dve lomā ekato natthi. Ayaṃ tesaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

Herein, first regarding body hair: by their natural color, they are not uniformly black like head hair, but are rather blackish-brown. In shape, they are shaped like the root of a palm leaf with a bent tip. By direction, they grow in two directions. By location, excepting the place where head hair is established and the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, they grow for the most part on the remaining body-enveloping skin. By delimitation, having entered the body-enveloping skin by the measure of a louse's egg, they are delimited below by their own root-base, above by space, and sideways by one another. No two hairs arise from the same place. This is their delimitation by what is similar. Their delimitation by what is dissimilar is like that of head hair.

Nakhāti vīsatiyā nakhapaṭṭānaṃ nāmaṃ. Te sabbepi vaṇṇato setā; saṇṭhānato macchasakalikasaṇṭhānā; disato pādanakhā heṭṭhimadisāya jātā, hatthanakhā uparimadisāyāti dvīsu disāsu jātā; okāsato aṅgulīnaṃ aggapiṭṭhesu patiṭṭhitā; paricchedato dvīsu disāsu aṅgulikoṭimaṃsehi, anto aṅgulipiṭṭhimaṃsena, bahi ceva agge ca ākāsena, tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnā. Dve nakhā ekato natthi. Ayaṃ [P 0.0234] nesaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

'Nails' is the name for the twenty nail plates. In color, they are all white. In shape, they resemble fish scales. By direction, toenails grow in the lower direction and fingernails in the upper direction—thus they grow in two directions. By location, they are established on the backs of the tips of the fingers and toes. By delimitation, they are bounded on two sides by the flesh of the finger and toe tips, inside by the flesh of the back of the fingers and toes, outside and at the tip by space, and sideways by each other. No two nails arise from the same place. This is their delimitation by what is similar. Their delimitation by what is dissimilar is like that of head hair.

Dantāti paripuṇṇadantassa dvattiṃsa dantaṭṭhikāni. Tepi vaṇṇato setā; saṇṭhānato anekasaṇṭhānā. Tesañhi heṭṭhimāya tāva dantapāḷiyā majjhe cattāro dantā mattikāpiṇḍe paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitaalābubījasaṇṭhānā. Tesaṃ ubhosu passesu ekeko ekamūlako ekakoṭiko mallikamakuḷasaṇṭhāno. Tato ekeko dvimūlako dvikoṭiko yānakaupatthambhanikasaṇṭhāno. Tato dve dve timūlā tikoṭikā. Tato dve dve catumūlā catukoṭikāti. Uparimapāḷiyāpi eseva nayo[M 0.0224]. Disato uparimadisāya jātā. Okāsato dvīsu hanukaṭṭhikesu patiṭṭhitā. Paricchedato heṭṭhā hanukaṭṭhike patiṭṭhitena attano mūlatalena, upari ākāsena, tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnā. Dve dantā ekato natthi. Ayaṃ nesaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

'Teeth' refers to the thirty-two tooth-bones of one with a full set. In color, they are white. In shape, they are of various shapes. In the lower row of teeth, the four middle teeth are shaped like gourd seeds placed in a row on a lump of clay. On both sides of these, there is one each that is single-rooted and single-pointed, resembling a jasmine bud. Next to these, one each that is double-rooted and double-pointed, shaped like a vehicle's prop. Then two each that are triple-rooted and triple-pointed. Then two each that are quadruple-rooted and quadruple-pointed. The upper row follows the same method. By direction, they grow in the upper direction. By location, they are established in the two jawbones. By delimitation, they are bounded below by their own root-base established in the jawbone, above by space, and sideways by each other. No two teeth arise from the same place. This is their delimitation by what is similar. Their delimitation by what is dissimilar is like that of head hair.

Tacoti sakalasarīraṃ veṭhetvā ṭhitacammaṃ. Tassa upari kāḷasāmapītādivaṇṇā chavi nāma, yā sakalasarīratopi saṅkaḍḍhiyamānā badaraṭṭhimattā hoti. Taco pana vaṇṇato setoyeva. So cassa setabhāvo aggijālābhighātapaharaṇapahārādīhi viddhaṃsitāya chaviyā pākaṭo hoti. Saṇṭhānato sarīrasaṇṭhānova hoti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo.

'Skin' is the hide that envelops the entire body. Upon it is the epidermis, which is of black, dark, yellow, or other colors; if it were stripped from the entire body and gathered, it would be about the size of a jujube stone. The skin itself, however, is white in color. And its whiteness becomes apparent when the epidermis is destroyed by the impact of a flame, by a weapon, or by a blow. In shape, it has the shape of the body. This is the summary here.

Vitthārato [V 0.0224] pana pādaṅgulittaco kosakārakakosasaṇṭhāno. Piṭṭhipādattaco puṭabandhaupāhanasaṇṭhāno. Jaṅghattaco bhattapuṭakatālapaṇṇasaṇṭhāno. Ūruttaco taṇḍulabharitadīghatthavikasaṇṭhāno. Ānisadattaco udakapūritapaṭaparissāvanasaṇṭhāno. Piṭṭhittaco phalakonaddhacammasaṇṭhāno. Kucchittaco vīṇādoṇikonaddhacammasaṇṭhāno. Urattaco yebhuyyena caturassasaṇṭhāno. Ubhayabāhuttaco tūṇīronaddhacammasaṇṭhāno. Piṭṭhihatthattaco khurakosakasaṇṭhāno, phaṇakatthavikasaṇṭhāno vā. Hatthaṅgulittaco kuñcikākosakasaṇṭhāno. Gīvattaco galakañcukasaṇṭhāno. Mukhattaco chiddāvacchiddo kīṭakulāvakasaṇṭhāno. Sīsattaco pattatthavikasaṇṭhānoti.

In detail, the skin of the toes has the shape of a silkworm's cocoon. The skin of the top of the foot has the shape of a wrapped shoe. The skin of the shins has the shape of a palm-leaf rice-packet. The skin of the thighs has the shape of a long sack filled with rice. The skin of the buttocks has the shape of a cloth water-strainer filled with water. The skin of the back has the shape of a hide stretched on a board. The skin of the belly has the shape of a hide stretched over the sound-box of a lute. The skin of the chest is for the most part square-shaped. The skin of both arms has the shape of a hide stretched over a quiver. The skin of the back of the hands has the shape of a razor-case, or a comb-pouch. The skin of the fingers has the shape of a key-case. The skin of the neck has the shape of a throat-guard. The skin of the face, with its holes and openings, has the shape of an insect's nest. The skin of the head has the shape of a bowl-bag.

Tacapariggaṇhakena ca yogāvacarena uttaroṭṭhato paṭṭhāya [P 0.0235] upari mukhaṃ ñāṇaṃ pesetvā paṭhamaṃ tāva mukhaṃ pariyonandhitvā ṭhitacammaṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ. Tato nalāṭaṭṭhicammaṃ. Tato thavikāya pakkhittapattassa ca thavikāya ca antarena hatthamiva sīsaṭṭhikassa ca sīsacammassa ca antarena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā aṭṭhikena saddhiṃ cammassa ekābaddhabhāvaṃ viyojentena sīsacammaṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ. Tato khandhacammaṃ. Tato anulomena paṭilomena ca dakkhiṇahatthacammaṃ. Atha teneva nayena vāmahatthacammaṃ. Tato piṭṭhicammaṃ. Taṃ taṃ vavatthapetvā anulomena ca paṭilomena ca dakkhiṇapādacammaṃ. Atha teneva [M 0.0225] nayena vāmapādacammaṃ. Tato anukkameneva vatthiudarahadayagīvacammāni vavatthapetabbāni. Atha gīvācammānantaraṃ heṭṭhimahanucammaṃ vavatthapetvā adharoṭṭhapariyosānaṃ pāpetvā niṭṭhapetabbaṃ. Evaṃ oḷārikoḷārikaṃ pariggaṇhantassa sukhumampi pākaṭaṃ hoti.

The meditator, grasping the skin, should first direct awareness upward from the upper lip to the face and discern the skin covering it. Then, the skin of the forehead bone. Next, directing awareness between the skull bone and the scalp—like a hand between a bowl placed in a bag and the bag itself—and separating the skin's attachment to the bone, one should discern the scalp. Then, the skin of the shoulders. Then, in forward and reverse order, the skin of the right hand. Then, in the same way, the skin of the left hand. Then, the skin of the back. Having discerned that, one should discern, in forward and reverse order, the skin of the right foot. Then, in the same way, the skin of the left foot. Next, in sequence, the skins of the groin, abdomen, chest, and neck should be discerned. Then, after the skin of the neck, one should discern the skin of the lower jaw, bringing it to a conclusion at the lower lip to complete the process. For one who grasps in this gross-by-gross manner, even the subtle becomes manifest.

Disato dvīsu disāsu jāto. Okāsato sakalasarīraṃ pariyonandhitvā ṭhito. Paricchedato heṭṭhā patiṭṭhitatalena, upari ākāsena paricchinno. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

From the perspective of direction, it arises in two directions. From the perspective of location, it pervades the entire body. From the perspective of delimitation, it is bounded below by the surface on which it rests and above by space. This is its homogeneous limitation. Its heterogeneous limitation, however, is just like that of the head hair.

Maṃsanti nava maṃsapesisatāni. Taṃ sabbampi vaṇṇato rattaṃ kiṃsukapupphasadisaṃ; saṇṭhānato jaṅghapiṇḍikamaṃsaṃ tālapaṇṇapuṭabhattasaṇṭhānaṃ, ūrumaṃsaṃ nisadapotakasaṇṭhānaṃ, ānisadamaṃsaṃ uddhanakoṭisaṇṭhānaṃ, piṭṭhimaṃsaṃ tālaguḷapaṭalasaṇṭhānaṃ, phāsukadvayamaṃsaṃ potthalikāya kucchiyaṃ tanumattikālepanasaṇṭhānaṃ, thanamaṃsaṃ vaṭṭetvā avakkhittamattikāpiṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ, bāhudvayamaṃsaṃ [V 0.0225] diguṇaṃ katvā ṭhapitaniccammamahāmūsikasaṇṭhānaṃ. Evaṃ oḷārikoḷārikaṃ maṃsaṃ pariggaṇhantassa sukhumampi pākaṭaṃ hoti. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātaṃ. Okāsato sādhikāni tīṇi aṭṭhisatāni anulimpetvā ṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato heṭṭhā aṭṭhisaṅghāte patiṭṭhitatalena, upari tacena, tiriyaṃ aññamaññena [P 0.0236] paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

As for flesh, there are nine hundred pieces of flesh. All of it is red in color, like the kiṃsuka flower. In shape, the flesh of the calves resembles a rice-bundle in a palm-leaf container; the thigh flesh resembles a small grinding stone; the buttock flesh resembles the rim of a stove; the back flesh resembles layers of palm sugar; the flesh of the two sides resembles a thin plaster of clay on the belly of a doll; the breast flesh resembles a ball of clay rolled and thrown down; the flesh of both arms resembles large, skinned mice, doubled over and placed. By discerning the flesh in this gross-by-gross manner, even the subtle becomes clear. From the perspective of direction, it arises in two directions. From the perspective of space, it overlays more than three hundred bones. From the perspective of limitation, it is bounded below by the surface resting on the collection of bones, above by the skin, and laterally by each other. This is its homogeneous limitation. Its heterogeneous limitation, however, is just like that of the head hair.

‘Nhārū’ti nava nhārusatāni. Vaṇṇato sabbepi nhārū setā; saṇṭhānato nānāsaṇṭhānā. Etesu hi gīvāya uparibhāgato paṭṭhāya pañca mahānhārū sarīraṃ vinaddhamānā hadayassa purimapassena otiṇṇā, pañca pacchimapassena, pañca dakkhiṇapassena, pañca vāmapassena, dakkhiṇahatthaṃ vinaddhamānāpi hatthassa purimapassena pañca, pacchimapassena pañca, tathā vāmahatthaṃ vinaddhamānāpi. Dakkhiṇapādaṃ vinaddhamānāpi pādassa purimapassena pañca, pacchimapassena pañca, tathā vāmapādaṃ vinaddhamānāpīti. Evaṃ sarīradhārakā nāma saṭṭhi mahānhārū kāyaṃ vinaddhamānā otiṇṇā, ye kaṇḍarātipi vuccanti. Te sabbepi kandalamakuḷasaṇṭhānā.

‘Sinews’ refers to nine hundred sinews. In color, all the sinews are white; in shape, they are of various shapes. Among these, starting from the upper part of the neck, five great sinews bind the body, descending along the front side of the heart region, five along the back side, five along the right side, and five along the left side; also binding the right hand, five descend along the front side of the hand, and five along the back side; likewise binding the left hand. Also binding the right foot, five descend along the front side of the foot, and five along the back side; likewise binding the left foot. Thus, sixty great sinews that support the body, which are also called tendons, descend binding the body, all shaped like kandala buds.

Aññe [M 0.0226] pana taṃ taṃ padesaṃ ajjhottharitvā ṭhitā tato sukhumatarā suttarajjukasaṇṭhānā. Aññe tato sukhumatarā pūtilatāsaṇṭhānā. Aññe tato sukhumatarā mahāvīṇātantisaṇṭhānā. Aññe thūlasuttakasaṇṭhānā. Hatthapādapiṭṭhiyaṃ nhārū sakuṇapādasaṇṭhānā. Sīsanhārū dārakānaṃ sīsajālakasaṇṭhānā. Piṭṭhinhārū ātape pasāritaallajālasaṇṭhānā. Avasesā taṃtaṃaṅgapaccaṅgānugatā nhārū sarīre paṭimukkajālakañcukasaṇṭhānā. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātā. Okāsato sakalasarīre aṭṭhīni ābandhitvā ṭhitā. Paricchedato heṭṭhā tiṇṇaṃ aṭṭhisatānaṃ upari patiṭṭhitatalehi, upari maṃsacammāni āhacca ṭhitapadesehi, tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnā. Ayaṃ nesaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

Others, having spread over various regions, are finer, shaped like thin threads. Some are even finer, resembling pūtika creepers. Others are finer still, like the strings of a great lute. Some resemble thick cords. The sinews on the back of the hands and feet are shaped like a bird's foot. The head sinews resemble a child’s hairnet. The back sinews are like a wet net spread out in the sun. The remaining sinews, following each major and minor limb, resemble a net-coat put upon the body. From the perspective of direction, they arise in two directions. From the perspective of space, they are positioned throughout the entire body, binding the bones. From the perspective of limitation, they are bounded below by the surfaces resting on the three hundred bones, above by the places where they abut the flesh and skin, and laterally by one another. This is their homogeneous limitation. Their heterogeneous limitation, however, is just like that of the head hair.

Aṭṭhīti ṭhapetvā dvattiṃsa dantaṭṭhīni avasesāni catusaṭṭhi hatthaṭṭhīni, catusaṭṭhi pādaṭṭhīni, catusaṭṭhi maṃsanissitāni muduaṭṭhīni, dve paṇhikaṭṭhīni, ekekasmiṃ pāde dve gopphakaṭṭhīni, dve jaṅghaṭṭhīni, dve jaṇṇukaṭṭhīni, dve [P 0.0237] ūruṭṭhīni, dve kaṭiṭṭhīni, aṭṭhārasa piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṭṭhīni, catuvīsati [V 0.0226] phāsukaṭṭhīni, cuddasa uraṭṭhīni, ekaṃ hadayaṭṭhi, dve akkhakaṭṭhīni, dve koṭṭhaṭṭhīni, dve bāhaṭṭhīni, dve dve aggabāhaṭṭhīni, satta gīvaṭṭhīni, dve hanukaṭṭhīni, ekaṃ nāsikaṭṭhi, dve akkhiṭṭhīni, dve kaṇṇaṭṭhīni, ekaṃ nalāṭaṭṭhi, ekaṃ muddhaṭṭhi, nava sīsakapālaṭṭhīnīti evaṃ timattāni aṭṭhisatāni.

‘Bones’—excluding the thirty-two teeth-bones—are the remaining: sixty-four hand bones, sixty-four foot bones, sixty-four soft bones dependent on flesh, two heel bones, two ankle bones in each foot, two shin bones, two knee bones, two thigh bones, two hip bones, eighteen spinal vertebrae, twenty-four ribs, fourteen chest bones, one heart-bone, two collarbones, two shoulder blades, two upper arm bones, two forearm bones in each arm, seven neck bones, two jawbones, one nose bone, two eye-socket bones, two ear bones, one forehead bone, one crown bone, and nine skull-cap bones—thus amounting to approximately three hundred bones.

Tāni sabbānipi vaṇṇato setāni, saṇṭhānato nānāsaṇṭhānāni. Tattha hi aggapādaṅguliṭṭhīni katakabījasaṇṭhānāni. Tadanantarāni majjhapabbaṭṭhīni panasaṭṭhisaṇṭhānāni. Mūlapabbaṭṭhīni paṇavasaṇṭhānāni. Piṭṭhipādaṭṭhīni koṭṭhitakandalakandarāsisaṇṭhānāni. Paṇhikaṭṭhi ekaṭṭhitālaphalabījasaṇṭhānaṃ. Gopphakaṭṭhīni bandhakīḷāgoḷakasaṇṭhānāni. Jaṅghaṭṭhīnaṃ gopphakaṭṭhīsu patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ anapanītatacasindikaḷīrasaṇṭhānaṃ. Khuddakajaṅghaṭṭhikaṃ dhanukadaṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ, mahantaṃ milātasappapiṭṭhisaṇṭhānaṃ. Jaṇṇukaṭṭhi ekato parikkhīṇapheṇakasaṇṭhānaṃ.

All these bones are white in color and various in shape. Among them, the bones of the tips of the toes resemble kataka seeds. The bones of the middle joints thereafter resemble jackfruit seeds. The bones of the base joints resemble paṇava drums. The bones of the back of the foot resemble a heap of pounded kandala root-bulbs. The heel bone resembles a single palmyra fruit seed. The ankle bones resemble tied play-balls. The place where the shin bones are established on the ankle bones resembles an unpeeled sindikaḷīra bamboo shoot. The smaller shin bone is shaped like a bow-staff, while the larger one resembles the back of a withered snake. The kneecap resembles a lump of foam worn away on one side.

Tattha jaṅghaṭṭhikassa patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ atikhiṇaggagosiṅgasaṇṭhānaṃ. Ūruṭṭhi duttacchitavāsipharasudaṇḍakasaṇṭhānaṃ. Tassa kaṭiṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ kīḷāgoḷakasaṇṭhānaṃ. Tena kaṭiṭṭhino patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ aggacchinnamahāpunnāgaphalasaṇṭhānaṃ. Kaṭiṭṭhīni dvepi ekābaddhāni hutvā kumbhakārakauddhanasaṇṭhānāni, pāṭiyekkaṃ kammārakūṭayottakasaṇṭhānāni. Koṭiyaṃ ṭhitaānisadaṭṭhi [M 0.0227] adhomukhaṃ katvā gahitasappaphaṇasaṇṭhānaṃ sattasu ṭhānesu chiddāvachiddaṃ. Piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṭṭhīni [P 0.0238] abbhantarato uparūpari ṭhapitasīsakapaṭṭaveṭhakasaṇṭhānāni, bāhirato vaṭṭanāvaḷisaṇṭhānāni. Tesaṃ antarantarā kakacadantasadisā dve tayo kaṇṭakā honti. Catuvīsatiyā phāsukaṭṭhīsu aparipuṇṇāni aparipuṇṇāsitasaṇṭhānāni, paripuṇṇāni paripuṇṇāsitasaṇṭhānāni. Sabbānipi odātakukkuṭassa pasāritapakkhasaṇṭhānāni.

There, the place where the shinbone is established resembles the very sharp tip of a cow's horn. The thighbone is like the badly hewn handle of an adze. The place where it is established in the hip bone is shaped like a play ball. The place of establishment in the hip bone resembles a large punnaga fruit with its top cut off. The two hipbones, joined together, are like a potter's furnace; individually, they resemble a blacksmith's anvil-block. The tailbone at the end is like a snake's hood held upside down, perforated in seven places. The vertebrae, on the inside, are like head-cloth wrappings placed one on top of another; on the outside, they resemble a series of coils. Between them are two or three thorn-like projections, similar to saw teeth. Among the twenty-four ribs, the incomplete ones resemble incomplete sickles, and the complete ones resemble complete sickles. All are like the outstretched wings of a white rooster.

Cuddasa uraṭṭhīni jiṇṇasandamānikapañjarasaṇṭhānāni. Hadayaṭṭhi dabbiphaṇasaṇṭhānaṃ. Akkhakaṭṭhīni khuddakalohavāsidaṇḍasaṇṭhānāni. Koṭṭhaṭṭhīni ekato parikkhīṇasīhaḷakudālasaṇṭhānāni. Bāhuṭṭhīni ādāsadaṇḍakasaṇṭhānāni. Aggabāhuṭṭhīni yamakatālakandasaṇṭhānāni. Maṇibandhaṭṭhīni ekato allīyāpetvā ṭhapitasīsakapaṭṭaveṭhakasaṇṭhānāni. Piṭṭhihatthaṭṭhīni koṭṭitakandalakandarāsisaṇṭhānāni. Hatthaṅgulīsu mūlapabbaṭṭhīni paṇavasaṇṭhānāni; majjhapabbaṭṭhīni aparipuṇṇapanasaṭṭhisaṇṭhānāni; aggapabbaṭṭhīni katakabījasaṇṭhānāni. Satta gīvaṭṭhīni [V 0.0227] daṇḍena vijjhitvā paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitavaṃsakaḷīracakkalikasaṇṭhānāni. Heṭṭhimahanukaṭṭhi kammārānaṃ ayokūṭayottakasaṇṭhānaṃ, uparimaṃ avalekhanasatthakasaṇṭhānaṃ.

The fourteen chest bones resemble the frame of an old carriage. The breastbone is shaped like the hood of a spoon. The collarbones are like the handles of small iron adzes. The shoulder blades resemble Sinhalese hoes worn away on one side. The upper arm bones are like mirror handles. The forearm bones resemble paired palm shoots. The wrist bones are like head-cloth wrappings pressed together. The bones of the back of the hand are like a heap of pounded kandala root-bulbs. In the fingers, the bones of the base joints are like small drums; the bones of the middle joints resemble unripe jackfruit seeds; the bones of the tip joints are like kataka seeds. The seven neck bones are like discs of bamboo shoots pierced with a rod and placed in order. The lower jawbone is like a blacksmith's iron anvil-block; the upper one resembles a scraping knife.

Akkhikūpanāsākūpaṭṭhīni apanītamiñjataruṇatālaṭṭhisaṇṭhānāni. Nalāṭaṭṭhi adhomukhaṭhapitasaṅkhathālakakapālasaṇṭhānaṃ. Kaṇṇacūḷikaṭṭhīni nhāpitakhurakosakasaṇṭhānāni. Nalāṭakaṇṇacūḷikānaṃ upari paṭṭabandhanokāse aṭṭhi saṅkuṭitaghaṭapuṇṇapaṭalakhaṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ. Muddhaṭṭhi mukhacchinnavaṅkanāḷikerasaṇṭhānaṃ. Sīsaṭṭhīni sibbetvā ṭhapitajajjaralābukaṭāhasaṇṭhānāni.

The bones of the eye sockets and nasal cavity are like the stones of young palm fruits with the pith removed. The forehead bone is like the shell of a conch-bowl placed face down. The temporal bones resemble a barber's razor case. Above the forehead and temporal bones, in the place for tying a headband, the bone is like a shrunken piece from the crust of a full pot. The crown bone resembles a curved coconut shell cut at the opening. The skull bones are like an old gourd-vessel sewn together.

Disato dvīsu disāsu jātāni. Okāsato avisesena sakalasarīre [P 0.0239] ṭhitāni. Visesena panettha sīsaṭṭhīni gīvaṭṭhīsu patiṭṭhitāni, gīvaṭṭhīni piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṭṭhīsu, piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṭṭhīni kaṭiṭṭhīsu, kaṭiṭṭhīni ūruṭṭhīsu, ūruṭṭhīni jaṇṇukaṭṭhīsu, jaṇṇukaṭṭhīni jaṅghaṭṭhīsu, jaṅghaṭṭhīni gopphakaṭṭhīsu, gopphakaṭṭhīni piṭṭhipādaṭṭhīsu patiṭṭhitāni. Paricchedato anto aṭṭhimiñjena, upari maṃsena, agge mūle ca aññamaññena paricchinnāni. Ayaṃ nesaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

As to direction, they arise from two directions. As to location, they are situated without distinction throughout the entire body. Specifically, the head bones are established on the neck bones, the neck bones on the spinal column bones, the spinal column bones on the hip bones, the hip bones on the thigh bones, the thigh bones on the knee bones, the knee bones on the shin bones, the shin bones on the ankle bones, and the ankle bones on the bones of the back of the foot. As to delimitation, they are bounded inside by bone marrow, above by flesh, and at the tips and roots by each other. This is their delimitation by similar parts. But their delimitation by dissimilar parts is just like that of the hair.

Aṭṭhimiñjanti [M 0.0228] tesaṃ tesaṃ aṭṭhīnaṃ abbhantaragataṃ miñjaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato setaṃ. Saṇṭhānato mahantamahantānaṃ aṭṭhīnaṃ abbhantaragataṃ veḷunāḷiyaṃ pakkhittaseditamahāvettaggasaṇṭhānaṃ, khuddānukhuddakānaṃ abbhantaragataṃ veḷuyaṭṭhipabbesu pakkhittaseditatanuvettaggasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātaṃ. Okāsato aṭṭhīnaṃ abbhantare patiṭṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato aṭṭhīnaṃ abbhantaratalehi paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

Bone marrow is the marrow that has gone inside those various bones. As to color, it is white. As to shape, in the very large bones, what is inside resembles a large rattan tip that has been steamed and placed inside a bamboo tube; in the very small bones, what is inside resembles a thin rattan tip that has been steamed and placed between the joints of a bamboo stick. As to direction, it arises from two directions. As to location, it is established inside the bones. As to delimitation, it is bounded by the inner surfaces of the bones. This is its delimitation by similar parts. But its delimitation by dissimilar parts is just like that of the hair.

Vakkanti ekabandhanā dve maṃsapiṇḍā. Taṃ vaṇṇato mandarattaṃ pāḷibhaddakaṭṭhivaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato dārakānaṃ yamakakīḷāgoḷakasaṇṭhānaṃ, ekavaṇṭapaṭibaddhaambaphaladvayasaṇṭhānaṃ vā. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato galavāṭakā nikkhantena ekamūlena thokaṃ gantvā dvidhā bhinnena thūlanhārunā vinibaddhaṃ hutvā hadayamaṃsaṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato vakkaṃ vakkabhāgena paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

The kidneys are two lumps of flesh with a single binding. As to color, they are slightly reddish, the color of Pālibhaddaka wood. As to shape, they resemble a pair of children's play-balls, or a pair of mango fruits attached to a single stalk. As to direction, they arise from the upper direction. As to location, having emerged from the throat passage with a single root and gone a short distance, they split in two and, bound by a thick sinew, are situated surrounding the heart-flesh. As to delimitation, the kidney is delimited by the kidney-part. This is its delimitation by similar parts. But its delimitation by dissimilar parts is just like that of the hair.

Hadayanti hadayamaṃsaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato rattaṃ padumapattapiṭṭhivaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato bāhirapattāni apanetvā [V 0.0228] adhomukhaṭhapitapadumamakuḷasaṇṭhānaṃ. Bahi maṭṭhaṃ; anto kosātakīphalassa abbhantarasadisaṃ. Paññavantānaṃ thokaṃ vikasitaṃ, mandapaññānaṃ makuḷitameva. Anto cassa punnāgaṭṭhipatiṭṭhānamatto āvāṭako hoti, yattha aḍḍhapasatamattaṃ lohitaṃ saṇṭhāti; yaṃ nissāya manodhātu manoviññāṇadhātu ca vattanti. Taṃ panetaṃ rāgacaritassa [P 0.0240] rattaṃ hoti, dosacaritassa kāḷakaṃ, mohacaritassa maṃsadhovanudakasadisaṃ, vitakkacaritassa kulatthayūsavaṇṇaṃ, saddhācaritassa kaṇikārapupphavaṇṇaṃ, paññācaritassa acchaṃ vippasannaṃ anāvilaṃ paṇḍaraṃ parisuddhaṃ niddhotajātimaṇi viya jutimantaṃ khāyati. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato sarīrabbhantare dvinnaṃ thanānaṃ majjhe patiṭṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato hadayaṃ hadayabhāgena paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

The heart is the heart-flesh. In color, it is red, like the back of a lotus petal. In shape, it resembles a lotus bud with its outer petals removed, placed upside down. The outside is smooth; the inside resembles the interior of a kosātakī fruit. For the wise, it is slightly open; for the dull-witted, it remains merely a bud. Inside it, there is a cavity the size of a punnāga seed's pit, where about half a pasata of blood is contained; upon which the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element depend. Now, for one of lustful character, this is red; for one of hateful character, it is dark; for one of deluded character, it is like water used to wash meat; for one of speculative character, it is the color of horse-gram broth; for one of faithful character, it is the color of a kaṇikāra flower; for one of wise character, it appears clear, very clear, untroubled, white, pure, and radiant like a polished, high-quality gem. In direction, it originates from the upper direction. In location, it is situated within the body, in the middle of the two breasts. In delimitation, the heart is delimited by the heart-part. This is its delimitation by way of its own kind. But its delimitation by way of what is different is just like that of the hair.

Yakananti yamakamaṃsapaṭalaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato rattapaṇḍukadhātukaṃ, nātirattakumudassa pattapiṭṭhivaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato mūle ekaṃ, agge yamakaṃ koviḷārapattasaṇṭhānaṃ[M 0.0229]. Tañca dandhānaṃ ekameva hoti mahantaṃ, paññavantānaṃ dve vā tīṇi vā khuddakāni. Disato uparimadisāya jātaṃ. Okāsato dvinnaṃ thanānaṃ abbhantare dakkhiṇapassaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato yakanaṃ yakanabhāgena paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

The liver is a double layer of flesh. In color, it is reddish-pale, like the back of a not-too-red water lily leaf. In shape, it is single at the base and double at the tip, resembling a koviḷāra leaf. For the dull-witted, it is just one large one; for the wise, there are two or three small ones. In direction, it originates from the upper direction. In location, it is situated inside, between the two breasts, adhering to the right side. In delimitation, the liver is delimited by the liver-part. This is its delimitation by way of its own kind. But its delimitation by way of what is different is just like that of the hair.

Kilomakanti paṭicchannāpaṭicchannabhedato duvidhaṃ pariyonahanamaṃsaṃ. Taṃ duvidhampi vaṇṇato setaṃ, dukūlapilotikavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato attano okāsasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato paṭicchannakilomakaṃ uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Itaraṃ dvīsu disāsu jātaṃ. Okāsato paṭicchannakilomakaṃ hadayañca vakkañca paṭicchādetvā ṭhitaṃ. Apaṭicchannakilomakaṃ sakalasarīre cammassa heṭṭhato maṃsaṃ pariyonaddhitvā ṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato heṭṭhā maṃsena, upari cammena, tiriyaṃ kilomakabhāgena paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

The kilomaka is enveloping flesh of two kinds: concealed and unconcealed. Both are white in color, like a piece of fine cloth. In shape, it conforms to the shape of its own location. In direction, the concealed kilomaka arises in the upper direction, while the other arises in two directions. In location, the concealed kilomaka is situated covering the heart and kidneys; the unconcealed kilomaka is situated enveloping the flesh beneath the skin throughout the entire body. In delimitation, it is bounded below by flesh, above by skin, and across by the kilomaka-part. This is its delimitation by way of its own kind. But its delimitation by way of what is different is just like that of the hair.

Pihakanti udarajivhāmaṃsaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato nīlaṃ nigguṇḍikapupphavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato sattaṅgulappamāṇaṃ abandhanaṃ kāḷavacchakajivhāsaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato hadayassa vāmapasse udarapaṭalassa matthakapassaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ, yasmiṃ paharaṇappahārena bahi nikkhante sattānaṃ jīvitakkhayo hoti. Paricchedato [P 0.0241] pihakabhāgena paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

The spleen is the flesh of the belly-tongue. In color, it is blue, like the color of the nigguṇḍika flower. In shape, it is about seven fingers in length, unattached, and shaped like the tongue of a black calf. In direction, it originates from the upper direction. In location, it is situated on the left side of the heart, adhering to the upper part of the abdominal membrane; if it is forced outward by a blow, the destruction of a being's life occurs. In delimitation, the spleen is delimited by the spleen-part. This is its delimitation by way of its own kind. But its delimitation by way of what is different is just like that of the hair.

Papphāsanti [V 0.0229] dvattiṃsamaṃsakhaṇḍappabhedaṃ papphāsamaṃsaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato rattaṃ nātipakkaudumbaraphalavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato visamacchinnabahalapūvakhaṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ. Abbhantare asitapītānaṃ abhāve uggatena kammajatejusmanā abbhāhatattā saṅkhāditapalālapiṇḍamiva nirasaṃ nirojaṃ. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato sarīrabbhantare dvinnaṃ thanānamantare hadayañca yakanañca paṭicchādetvā olambantaṃ ṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato phapphāsabhāgena paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

The lungs are lung-flesh, divided into thirty-two pieces of flesh. They are red in color, like a not-too-ripe udumbara fruit. In shape, they resemble an unevenly cut thick piece of cake. Inside, in the absence of food and drink, because they are afflicted by the rising heat born of kamma, they are tasteless and without nutritive essence, like a chewed lump of straw. In direction, they originate from the upper direction. In location, they are situated hanging inside the body between the two breasts, covering the heart and liver. In delimitation, they are delimited by the lung-part. This is their delimitation by way of their own kind. But their delimitation by way of what is different is just like that of the hair.

Antanti purisassa dvattiṃsa hatthā, itthiyā aṭṭhavīsatihatthā ekavīsatiyā ṭhānesu obhaggā antavaṭṭi. Tadetaṃ vaṇṇato setaṃ sakkharasudhāvaṇṇaṃ[M 0.0230]. Saṇṭhānato lohitadoṇiyaṃ ābhujitvā ṭhapitasīsacchinnasappasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātaṃ. Okāsato upari galavāṭake heṭṭhā ca karīsamagge vinibandhattā galavāṭakakarīsamaggapariyante sarīrabbhantare ṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato antabhāgena paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

The intestines are an intestinal coil, thirty-two cubits long for a man and twenty-eight for a woman, folded in twenty-one places. In color, they are white, like sugar or chalk. In shape, they resemble a snake with its head cut off, coiled and placed in a trough of blood. In direction, they originate in two directions. In location, being fastened above at the throat-pit and below at the passage for excrement, they are situated within the body between the limits of the throat-pit and the passage for excrement. In delimitation, they are delimited by the intestinal-part. This is their delimitation by way of their own kind. But their delimitation by way of what is different is just like that of the hair.

Antaguṇanti antabhogaṭṭhānesu bandhanaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato setaṃ dakasītalikamūlavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato dakasītalikamūlasaṇṭhānameva. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātaṃ. Okāsato kudāḷapharasukammādīni karontānaṃ yantākaḍḍhanakāle yantasuttamiva, yantaphalakāni antabhoge ekato agaḷante ābandhitvā pādapuñchanarajjumaṇḍalakassa antarā taṃ sibbetvā ṭhitarajjukā viya ekavīsatiyā ṭhānesu antabhogānaṃ antarā ṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato antaguṇabhāgena paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

The mesentery is the binding at the intestinal coils. In color, it is white, like the color of a dakasītalika root. In shape, it is just like the shape of a dakasītalika root. In direction, it originates in two directions. In location, it is situated between the intestinal coils in twenty-one places, binding them together so they do not come apart, just as a machine-cord functions when those doing work with hoes, axes, and so on, are pulling the machine, and like a rope fixed by being stitched inside a coiled foot-wiping rope. In delimitation, it is delimited by the mesentery-part. This is its delimitation by way of its own kind. But its delimitation by way of what is different is just like that of the hair.

Udariyanti udare bhavaṃ asitapitakhāyitasāyitaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato ajjhohaṭāhāravaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato parissāvane sithilabandhataṇḍulasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato udare ṭhitaṃ. Udaraṃ nāma ubhato nippīḷiyamānassa [P 0.0242] allasāṭakassa majjhe sañjātaphoṭakasadisaṃ antapaṭalaṃ; bahi maṭṭhaṃ, anto maṃsakasambukapaliveṭhanakiliṭṭhapāvārakapupphakasadisaṃ, kuthitapanasatacassa abbhantarasadisantipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati; yattha takkoṭakā, gaṇḍuppādakā, tālahīrakā, sūcimukhakā, paṭatantasuttakā iccevamādidvattiṃsakulappabhedā kimayo ākulabyākulā saṇḍasaṇḍacārino hutvā nivasanti; ye pānabhojanādimhi avijjamāne ullaṅghitvā viravantā hadayamaṃsaṃ abhihananti, pānabhojanādiajjhoharaṇavelāya ca uddhaṃmukhā hutvā paṭhamajjhohaṭe dve tayo [V 0.0230] ālope turitaturitā vilumpanti; yaṃ tesaṃ kimīnaṃ sūtigharaṃ, vaccakuṭi, gilānasālā, susānañca hoti.

The stomach contents are what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, existing in the stomach. In color, they resemble the color of ingested food. In shape, they are like loosely bound rice grains in a strainer. In direction, they originate from the upper region. In location, they reside in the stomach. The stomach is an inner membrane like a blister formed in the middle of a wet cloth being pressed from both sides. Outside, it is smooth, but inside, it resembles a dirty cloak wrapped around a fleshy mollusc. One could also say its interior is like the inside of a rotting jackfruit. There, creatures such as takkoṭakā, gaṇḍuppādakā, tālahīrakā, sūcimukhakā, paṭatantasuttakā, and so on, with thirty-two classes in total, live in tangled masses, moving around in groups, dwelling there. When food and drink are lacking, they rise up, crying out and striking at the heart's flesh; and when food and drink are being swallowed, they turn upward and quickly devour two or three mouthfuls of the first ingested food. For these worms, it is a maternity ward, a toilet, a hospital, and a cemetery.

Yattha seyyathāpi nāma caṇḍālagāmadvāre candanikāya nidāghasamaye thūlaphusitake deve vassante udakena vuyhamānaṃ muttakarīsacammaaṭṭhinhārukhaṇḍakheḷasiṅghāṇikalohitappabhuti nānākuṇapajātaṃ nipatitvā kaddamodakāluḷitaṃ [M 0.0231] dvīhatīhaccayena sañjātakimikulaṃ sūriyātapavegasantāpakuthitaṃ upari pheṇapubbulake muñcantaṃ abhinīlavaṇṇaṃ paramaduggandhajegucchaṃ neva upagantuṃ na daṭṭhuṃ araharūpataṃ āpajjitvā tiṭṭhati, pageva ghāyituṃ vā sāyituṃ vā; evameva nānappakārapānabhojanādidantamusalasañcuṇṇitaṃ jivhāhatthaparivattitakheḷalālāpalibuddhaṃ taṅkhaṇavigatavaṇṇagandharasādisampadaṃ tantavāyakhalisuvānavamathusadisaṃ nipatitvā pittasemhavātapaliveṭhitaṃ hutvā udaraggisantāpavegakuthitaṃ kimikulākulaṃ uparūpari pheṇapubbulakāni muñcantaṃ paramakasambuduggandhajegucchabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā tiṭṭhati; yaṃ sutvāpi pānabhojanādīsu amanuññatā saṇṭhāti, pageva paññācakkhunā avaloketvā, yattha ca patitaṃ pānabhojanādi pañcadhā vibhāgaṃ gacchati – ekaṃ bhāgaṃ pāṇakā khādanti, ekaṃ bhāgaṃ udaraggi jhāpeti, eko bhāgo muttaṃ hoti, eko karīsaṃ, eko rasabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā soṇitamaṃsādīni upabrūhayati. Paricchedato udarapaṭalena [P 0.0243] ceva udariyabhāgena ca paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

Just as, for example, at the entrance of an outcaste village, in a cesspit, during the hot season, when a heavy rain falls, various kinds of foul things—such as urine, feces, skin, bones, sinews, fragments, spittle, mucus, and blood—are carried along by the water and fall, mixed with muddy water. After two or three days, it becomes infested with worms, agitated by the scorching sun’s heat, putrid, releasing foam and bubbles on the surface, turning a deep blue color, extremely foul-smelling and repulsive, so much so that it becomes something not fit to approach or look at, let alone smell or taste it. In the same way, various kinds of food and drink, crushed by the tooth-mortar, turned over by the tongue, and smeared with spittle and saliva, lose their qualities of color, aroma, and taste the moment they are swallowed. They fall and become like weaver's paste and dog's vomit, enveloped in bile, phlegm, and wind. Agitated by the heat of the stomach’s fire, putrid, teeming with worms, releasing bubbles and foam on the surface, they become utterly foul-smelling, repulsive, and extremely impure. Even hearing about this, distaste for food and drink arises, let alone seeing it with the eye of wisdom. And when food and drink have fallen therein, they divide into five parts: one part is consumed by living beings, one part is burned by the stomach fire, one part becomes urine, one part becomes feces, and one part transforms into a nutrient essence that sustains blood, flesh, and so on. In delimitation, it is delimited by the stomach membrane and the stomach contents. This is its homogeneous delimitation. But the heterogeneous delimitation is like that of hair.

Karīsanti vaccaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato yebhuyyena ajjhohaṭāhāravaṇṇameva hoti. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato heṭṭhimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato pakkāsaye ṭhitaṃ. Pakkāsayo nāma heṭṭhā nābhipiṭṭhikaṇṭakamūlānamantare antāvasāne ubbedhena aṭṭhaṅgulamatto veḷunāḷikasadiso, yattha seyyathāpi nāma uparūpari bhūmibhāge patitaṃ vassodakaṃ ogaḷitvā heṭṭhā bhūmibhāgaṃ pūretvā tiṭṭhati; evameva yaṃ kiñci āmāsaye patitaṃ pānabhojanādikaṃ udaragginā pheṇuddehakaṃ pakkaṃ pakkaṃ nisadāya pisitamiva saṇhabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā antabilena ogaḷitvā ogaḷitvā madditvā veḷupabbe pakkhipamānapaṇḍumattikā viya sannicitaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati. Paricchedato pakkāsayapaṭalena ceva karīsabhāgena ca paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

Feces is excrement. In color, it is mostly the color of ingested food. In shape, its shape conforms to the space it occupies. In direction, it originates in the lower direction. In location, it is situated in the alvine receptacle. The alvine receptacle is about eight fingerbreadths in height, like a bamboo tube, situated between the navel and the roots of the backbone, at the end of the intestines. Just as rainwater falling on higher ground flows down and fills the lower ground, so too any food or drink that falls into the stomach is cooked by the internal fire, becomes frothy, thoroughly ripened, and, like flour crushed by a grindstone, becomes soft. It then flows down repeatedly through the intestinal opening, being pressed and squeezed, accumulating and remaining there like pale mud being stuffed into a bamboo joint. In delimitation, it is delimited by the membrane of the alvine receptacle and the feces portion. This is its homogeneous delimitation. But the heterogeneous delimitation is like that of hair.

Matthaluṅganti [V 0.0231] sīsakaṭāhabbhantare ṭhitamiñjarāsi. Taṃ vaṇṇato setaṃ ahicchattakapiṇḍikavaṇṇaṃ, dadhibhāvaṃ asampattaduṭṭhakhīravaṇṇantipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato [M 0.0232] sīsakaṭāhabbhantare cattāro sibbinimagge nissāya samodhānetvā ṭhapitā cattāro piṭṭhapiṇḍā viya samohitaṃ tiṭṭhati. Paricchedato sīsakaṭāhassa abbhantaratalehi ceva matthaluṅgabhāgena ca paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

The brain is the marrow mass located inside the skull. In color, it is white, resembling the color of a lump of a toadstool, or spoiled milk that has not fully curdled. In shape, it conforms to the space it occupies. In direction, it originates in the upper region. In location, it is placed inside the skull, relying on the four suture paths and being held together, like four lumps of dough placed together. In delimitation, it is delimited by the inner surfaces of the skull and the brain portion. This is its homogeneous delimitation. But the heterogeneous delimitation is like that of hair.

Pittanti dve pittāni – baddhapittañca abaddhapittañca. Tattha baddhapittaṃ vaṇṇato bahalamadhukatelavaṇṇaṃ, abaddhapittaṃ milātaākulitapupphavaṇṇaṃ. Taṃ saṇṭhānato ubhayampi okāsasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato baddhapittaṃ uparimāya disāya jātaṃ, itaraṃ dvīsu disāsu jātaṃ. Okāsato abaddhapittaṃ ṭhapetvā kesalomadantanakhānaṃ maṃsavinimuttaṭṭhānañceva thaddhasukkhacammañca udakamiva telabinduṃ avasesasarīraṃ byāpetvā ṭhitaṃ, yamhi kupite akkhīni pītakāni honti bhamanti, gattaṃ kampati kaṇḍuyati. Baddhapittaṃ hadayapapphāsānamantare yakanamaṃsaṃ [P 0.0244] nissāya patiṭṭhite mahākosātakīkosakasadise pittakosake ṭhitaṃ, yamhi kupite sattā ummattakā honti, vipallatthacittā hirottappaṃ chaḍḍetvā akattabbaṃ karonti, abhāsitabbaṃ bhāsanti, acintetabbaṃ cintenti. Paricchedato pittabhāgena paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

Bile is of two kinds: bound bile and unbound bile. Among these, bound bile is in color like thick honey-oil, while unbound bile is the color of faded or withered flowers. In shape, both conform to the space they occupy. In direction, bound bile originates in the upper region, while the other originates in two directions. In location, unbound bile, except for the hair, body hair, teeth, and nails, and places devoid of flesh, as well as hard, dry skin, is situated spreading throughout the remaining body like an oil drop in water. When it is aggravated, the eyes become yellow and roll, the body trembles and itches. Bound bile resides in the bile sac, which is like a large bitter gourd pod, established between the heart and lungs, relying on the liver flesh. When it is aggravated, beings become insane, their minds deranged; they abandon shame and conscience, do what should not be done, say what should not be said, and think what should not be thought. In delimitation, it is delimited by the bile portion. This is its homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is like that of hair.
