Semhanti sarīrabbhantare ekapattapūrappamāṇaṃ semhaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato setaṃ nāgabalapaṇṇarasavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato udarapaṭale ṭhitaṃ, yaṃ pānabhojanādīni ajjhoharaṇakāle seyyathāpi nāma udake sevālapaṇakaṃ kaṭṭhe vā kapāle vā patante chijjitvā dvidhā hutvā puna ajjhottharitvā tiṭṭhati, evameva pānabhojanādimhi nipatante chijjitvā dvidhā hutvā puna ajjhottharitvā tiṭṭhati; yamhi ca mandībhūte pakkagaṇḍo viya pūtikukkuṭaṇḍamiva ca udaraṃ paramajegucchaṃ kuṇapagandhaṃ hoti; tato uggatena ca gandhena uddekopi mukhampi duggandhaṃ pūtikuṇapasadisaṃ hoti; so ca puriso ‘apehi, duggandhaṃ vāyasī’ti vattabbataṃ āpajjati; yañca vaḍḍhitvā bahalattamāpannaṃ pidhānaphalakamiva vaccakuṭiyā udarapaṭalassa abbhantareyeva kuṇapagandhaṃ sannirujjhitvā tiṭṭhati. Paricchedato [V 0.0232] semhabhāgena paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

There is phlegm inside the body, about the measure of a full bowl. In color, it is white, the color of the sap of a nāgabalā leaf. In shape, it conforms to its location. It originates from the upper direction. It is situated on the surface of the stomach; when food and drink are being swallowed, just as when a piece of wood or a potsherd falls upon algae or moss in water, it splits in two and then covers over again, so too, when food and drink fall upon it, it splits in two and then covers over again. And when this phlegm becomes sluggish, the abdomen becomes extremely disgusting and corpse-smelling, like a ripe boil or a putrid hen's egg. From the stench rising from it, both the belch and the mouth become foul-smelling, like a putrid corpse. And that person becomes one to whom it is said, 'Go away, you stinking crow!' And when it increases and becomes thick, it remains, obstructing the corpse-smell right inside the abdominal lining, like the lid-plank of a latrine. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by the phlegm portion. This is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is like that of hair.

Pubboti [M 0.0233] pūtilohitavasena pavattapubbo. So vaṇṇato paṇḍupalāsavaṇṇo, matakasarīre pana pūtibahalācāmavaṇṇo hoti. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhāno. Disato dvīsu disāsu jāto. Okāsato pana pubbassa okāso nāma nibaddho natthi yattha so sannicito tiṭṭheyya; yatra yatra pana khāṇukaṇṭakappaharaṇaggijālādīhi abhihate sarīrappadese lohitaṃ saṇṭhahitvā paccati, gaṇḍapiḷakādayo vā uppajjanti, tatra tatreva tiṭṭhati. Paricchedato pubbabhāgena paricchinno[P 0.0245]. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

Pus is that which has arisen by way of putrid blood. In color, it is like a withered palāsa leaf, but in a dead body it is the color of thick, putrid discharge. In shape, it conforms to its location. It originates in two directions. As for location, pus has no fixed place where it might collect and remain; but wherever in the body a part is struck by stakes, thorns, blows, flames of fire, and so on, or where blood collects and festers, or where boils and sores arise, there it remains. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by the pus portion. This is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is like that of hair.

Lohitanti dve lohitāni – sannicitalohitañca saṃsaraṇalohitañca. Tattha sannicitalohitaṃ vaṇṇato nipakkabahalalākhārasavaṇṇaṃ, saṃsaraṇalohitaṃ acchalākhārasavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato ubhayampi okāsasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato sannicitalohitaṃ uparimāya disāya jātaṃ, itaraṃ dvīsu disāsu jātaṃ. Okāsato saṃsaraṇalohitaṃ, ṭhapetvā kesalomadantanakhānaṃ maṃsavinimmuttaṭṭhānañceva thaddhasukkhacammañca, dhamanijālānusārena sabbaṃ upādinnakasarīraṃ pharitvā ṭhitaṃ; sannicitalohitaṃ yakanaṭṭhānassa heṭṭhābhāgaṃ pūretvā ekapattapūramattaṃ hadayavakkapapphāsānaṃ upari thokaṃ thokaṃ paggharantaṃ vakkahadayayakanapapphāse temayamānaṃ ṭhitaṃ. Tasmiñhi vakkahadayādīni atemente sattā pipāsitā honti. Paricchedato lohitabhāgena paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

Blood is of two kinds: pooled blood and circulating blood. Of these, pooled blood is the color of thick, ripe lac-juice, while circulating blood is the color of clear lac-juice. In shape, both conform to their locations. In terms of direction, pooled blood originates from the upper direction, while the other arises in two directions. As for location, circulating blood, except for hair, body hair, teeth, nails, fleshless areas, and tough, dry skin, remains spread throughout the entire appropriated body along the network of veins. Pooled blood fills the lower part of the liver's location, about the measure of a full bowl, dripping little by little onto the heart, kidneys, and lungs, remaining there moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs. For when it does not moisten the kidneys, heart, and so on, beings become thirsty. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by the blood portion. This is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is like that of hair.

Sedoti lomakūpādīhi paggharaṇakaāpodhātu. So vaṇṇato vippasannatilatelavaṇṇo. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhāno. Disato dvīsu disāsu jāto. Okāsato sedassokāso nāma nibaddho natthi, yattha so lohitaṃ viya sadā tiṭṭheyya; yadā pana aggisantāpasūriyasantāpautuvikārādīhi sarīraṃ santappati tadā udakato abbuḷhamattavisamacchinnabhisamūḷālakumudanāḷakalāpo viya sabbakesalomakūpavivarehi paggharati. Tasmā tassa saṇṭhānampi kesalomakūpavivarānaṃyeva vasena veditabbaṃ. Sedapariggaṇhakena ca yoginā kesalomakūpavivare pūretvā ṭhitavaseneva sedo manasikātabbo. Paricchedato sedabhāgena paricchinno. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

Sweat is the water element that oozes from the pores and so on. In color, it is the color of very clear sesame oil. In shape, it conforms to its location. It originates in two directions. As for location, there is no fixed location for sweat where it might always remain like blood; but when the body is heated by fire, the sun, seasonal changes, and so on, then it streams out from all the pores and hair follicles like a bundle of lotus roots, water-lily roots, and stalks, just pulled from the water and unevenly cut. Therefore, its shape should also be understood in accordance with the pores and hair follicles. And a yogi comprehending sweat should attend to it as simply filling and remaining in the pores and hair follicles. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by the sweat portion. This is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is like that of hair.

Medoti [M 0.0234][V 0.0233] thinasineho. So vaṇṇato phālitahaliddivaṇṇo. Saṇṭhānato thūlasarīrassa tāva cammamaṃsantare ṭhapitahaliddivaṇṇadukūlapilotikasaṇṭhāno hoti, kisasarīrassa jaṅghamaṃsaṃ ūrumaṃsaṃ piṭṭhikaṇṭakanissitaṃ piṭṭhamaṃsaṃ udaravaṭṭimaṃsanti etāni nissāya diguṇaṃ tiguṇaṃ katvā ṭhapitahaliddivaṇṇadukūlapilotikasaṇṭhāno. Disato dvīsu [P 0.0246] disāsu jāto. Okāsato thūlassa sakalasarīraṃ pharitvā, kisassa jaṅghamaṃsādīni nissāya ṭhito, yaṃ sinehasaṅkhaṃ gatampi paramajegucchattā neva muddhani telatthāya, na nāsātelādīnaṃ atthāya gaṇhanti. Paricchedato heṭṭhā maṃsena, upari cammena, tiriyaṃ medabhāgena paricchinno. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

Fat means thick grease. In color, it is the color of split turmeric. In shape, for a stout-bodied person, it is like the shape of a turmeric-colored cloth fragment placed between the skin and flesh; for a thin-bodied person, it is like the shape of a turmeric-colored cloth fragment placed doubled or tripled, relying on the flesh of the calves, the flesh of the thighs, the back flesh relying on the spine, and the abdominal wall flesh. It originates in two directions. As for location, in a stout person, it pervades the entire body, while in a thin person, it remains relying on the flesh of the calves, etc. And though it counts as grease, due to extreme disgust, people do not take it for head oil or nose oil, etc. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited below by flesh, above by skin, and laterally by the fat portion. This is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is like that of hair.

Assūti akkhīhi pagdharaṇakaāpodhātu. Taṃ vaṇṇato vippasannatilatelavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato akkhikūpakesu ṭhitaṃ. Na cetaṃ pittakosake pittamiva akkhikūpakesu sadā sannicitaṃ tiṭṭhati; yadā pana sattā somanassajātā mahāhasitaṃ hasanti, domanassajātā rodanti paridevanti tathārūpaṃ visabhāgāhāraṃ āharanti, yadā ca nesaṃ akkhīni dhūmarajapaṃsukādīhi abhihaññanti, tadā etehi somanassadomanassavisabhāgāhārautūhi samuṭṭhahitvā akkhikūpake pūretvā tiṭṭhati vā paggharati vā. Assupariggaṇhakena pana yoginā akkhikūpake pūretvā ṭhitavaseneva pariggaṇhitabbaṃ. Paricchedato assubhāgena paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

Tears means the water element that flows from the eyes. In color, they are the color of very clear sesame oil. In shape, they conform to their location. They originate from the upper direction. As for location, they remain in the eye sockets. But they do not always remain accumulated in the eye sockets like bile in the bile sac; but when beings experience joy and laugh heartily, or when they experience sorrow and weep and lament, or when they consume incompatible food, or when their eyes are affected by smoke, dust, or the like, then, arising from these—joy, sorrow, incompatible food, or seasonal conditions—they fill the eye sockets and either remain there or flow out. A yogi attending to tears, however, should mentally note them as simply filling and remaining in the eye sockets. In terms of delimitation, they are delimited by the tear portion. This is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is like that of hair.

Vasāti vilīnasneho. Sā vaṇṇato nāḷikeratelavaṇṇā, ācāme āsittatelavaṇṇātipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Saṇṭhānato nhānakāle pasannaudakassa upari paribbhamantasinehabinduvisaṭasaṇṭhānā. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātā. Okāsato yebhuyyena hatthatalahatthapiṭṭhipādatalapādapiṭṭhināsāpuṭanalāṭaaṃsakūṭesu ṭhitā. Na cesā etesu okāsesu sadā vilīnāva hutvā tiṭṭhati; yadā pana aggisantāpasūriyasantāpautuvisabhāgadhātuvisabhāgehi te padesā usmā jātā honti, tadā tattha nhānakāle pasannaudakūpari sinehabinduvisaṭo viya ito cito ca saṃsarati. Paricchedato vasābhāgena paricchinnā[M 0.0235]. Ayamassā sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

Grease means dissolved oiliness. In color, it is the color of coconut oil, or it is also proper to say the color of oil poured into gruel. In shape, at the time of bathing, it is like the shape of scattered oil drops moving on the surface of clear water. It originates in two directions. As for location, it is mostly found on the palms of the hands, the backs of the hands, the soles of the feet, the backs of the feet, the nostrils, the forehead, and the shoulder blades. But it does not always remain dissolved in these locations; but when those areas become heated due to fire, sun, seasonal imbalances, or elemental imbalances, then it moves here and there, like oil drops scattered on the surface of clear water during bathing. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by the grease portion. This is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is like that of hair.

Kheḷoti [V 0.0234] antomukhe pheṇamissā āpodhātu. So vaṇṇato seto pheṇavaṇṇo. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhāno, pheṇasaṇṭhānatotipi [P 0.0247] vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Disato uparimāya disāya jāto. Okāsato ubhohi kapolapassehi oruyha jivhāya ṭhito. Na cesa ettha sadā sannicito hutvā tiṭṭhati. Yadā pana sattā tathārūpaṃ āhāraṃ passanti vā saranti vā uṇhatittakaṭukaloṇambilānaṃ vā kiñci mukhe ṭhapenti, yadā vā nesaṃ hadayaṃ ākilāyati, kismiñcideva vā jigucchā uppajjati, tadā kheḷo uppajjitvā ubhohi kapolapassehi oruyha jivhāya saṇṭhāti. Aggajivhāya cesa tanuko hoti, mūlajivhāya bahalo; mukhe pakkhittañca puthukaṃ vā taṇḍulaṃ vā aññaṃ vā kiñci khādanīyaṃ, nadīpuḷine khatakūpakasalilaṃ viya, parikkhayaṃ agacchantova temetuṃ samattho hoti. Paricchedato kheḷabhāgena paricchinno. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

Saliva means the water element mixed with foam inside the mouth. In color, it is white, the color of foam. In shape, it conforms to its location, or it is also proper to say it resembles foam. It originates from the upper direction. As for location, it remains on the tongue, descending from both sides of the cheeks. But it does not always remain collected there. However, when beings see or remember such food, or place something hot, bitter, pungent, salty, or sour in their mouths, or when their heart is agitated, or when any disgust arises, then saliva arises, descends from both sides of the cheeks, and settles on the tongue. At the tip of the tongue it is thin, but at the base of the tongue it is thick. And any chewable item, such as flattened rice or rice grains, placed in the mouth, it is able to moisten without diminishing, like water in a dug well on a riverbank. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by the saliva portion. This is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is like that of hair.

Siṅghāṇikāti matthaluṅgato paggharaṇakaasuci. Sā vaṇṇato taruṇatālaṭṭhimiñjavaṇṇā. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhānā. Disato uparimāya disāya jātā. Okāsato nāsāpuṭe pūretvā ṭhitā. Na cesā ettha sadā sannicitā hutvā tiṭṭhati; atha kho yathā nāma puriso paduminīpattena dadhiṃ bandhitvā heṭṭhā kaṇṭakena vijjheyya, atha tena chiddena dadhimatthu gaḷitvā bahi pateyya, evameva yadā sattā rodanti vā visabhāgāhārautuvasena vā sañjātadhātukkhobhā honti, tadā antosīsato pūtisemhabhāvaṃ āpannaṃ matthaluṅgaṃ gaḷitvā tālumatthakavivarena otaritvā nāsāpuṭe pūretvā tiṭṭhati vā paggharati vā. Siṅghāṇikā pariggaṇhakena pana yoginā nāsāpuṭe pūretvā ṭhitavaseneva pariggaṇhitabbā. Paricchedato siṅghāṇikābhāgena paricchinnā. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

Mucus is the impure substance that flows from the brain. In color, it resembles the color of the pith of a young palmyra fruit. In shape, its shape is that of the space it occupies. It originates from the upper direction. It remains filling the nostrils. But it does not always remain accumulated there; rather, just as if a man were to wrap curd in a lotus leaf and pierce it from below with a thorn, and then whey would drip out and fall through that hole, just so, when beings cry or when disharmony of the elements arises due to unsuitable food or the seasons, the fluid from the brain, having become putrid phlegm inside the head, flows down through the opening at the top of the palate and remains filling the nostrils or drips out. However, a yogi should apprehend mucus only when it remains filling the nostrils. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by the mucus portion. This is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is like that of hair.

Lasikāti sarīrasandhīnaṃ abbhantare picchilakuṇapaṃ. Sā vaṇṇato kaṇikāraniyyāsavaṇṇā. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhānā. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātā. Okāsato aṭṭhisandhīnaṃ abbhañjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā asītisatasandhīnaṃ abbhantare ṭhitā. Yassa cesā mandā hoti, tassa uṭṭhahantassa [M 0.0236] nisīdantassa abhikkamantassa paṭikkamantassa sammiñjantassa pasārentassa aṭṭhikāni kaṭakaṭāyanti, accharāsaddaṃ karonto viya vicarati, ekayojanadviyojanamattampi addhānaṃ gatassa [P 0.0248] vāyodhātu kuppati, gattāni dukkhanti. Yassa pana bahukā hoti tassa uṭṭhānanisajjādīsu na aṭṭhīni kaṭakaṭāyanti, dīghampi addhānaṃ gatassa [V 0.0235] na vāyodhātu kuppati, na gattāni dukkhanti. Paricchedato lasikābhāgena paricchinnā. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

The synovial fluid is the viscous decay inside the body joints. In color, it resembles the sap of the kanikāra tree. In shape, its shape is that of the space it occupies. It arises in two locations. Located inside the joints, it serves the function of lubrication for the one hundred and eighty joints. For one whose synovial fluid is deficient, when standing, sitting, walking forward or backward, bending or stretching, the bones creak, and he moves about as if making a cracking sound. Even after traveling a distance of one or two yojanas, the wind element becomes disturbed, and the limbs ache. But for one whose synovial fluid is abundant, the bones do not creak when standing, sitting, etc., nor does the wind element become disturbed even after traveling a long distance, and the limbs do not ache. It is delimited by the synovial fluid portion—this is its similar delimitation. The dissimilar delimitation is like that of the hair.

Muttanti vaṇṇato māsakhārodakavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato adhomukhaṭhapitaudakakumbhantaragataudakasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato heṭṭhimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato vatthissa abbhantare ṭhitaṃ. Vatthi nāma vatthipuṭo vuccati, yattha seyyathāpi nāma candanikāya pakkhitte amukhe ravaṇaghaṭe candanikaraso pavisati, na cassa pavisanamaggo paññāyati; evameva sarīrato muttaṃ pavisati, na cassa pavisanamaggo paññāyati, nikkhamanamaggo pana pākaṭo hoti; yamhi ca muttassa bharite ‘passāvaṃ karomā’ti sattānaṃ āyūhanaṃ hoti. Paricchedato vatthiabbhantarena ceva muttabhāgena ca paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

The urine is yellowish in color, like water mixed with lye. In shape, it resembles water contained within an upside-down water pot. In direction, it originates from the downward direction. In location, it is situated within the bladder. The bladder is called the urinary bag; just as the sap of the candanikā plant enters a covered water pot, and the way it enters is not apparent, so too urine enters from the body, and its entry path is not apparent, but the exit path is evident; and when the bladder is full, beings have the impulse, 'I must urinate.' It is delimited internally by the bladder and by the portion of urine—this is its similar delimitation. But the dissimilar delimitation is like that of hair.

Evañhi kesādike koṭṭhāse vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedavasena vavatthapetvā anupubbato nātisīghato nātisaṇikatotiādinā nayena vaṇṇasaṇṭhānagandhāsayokāsavasena pañcadhā ‘paṭikkūlā paṭikkūlā’ti manasikaroto paṇṇattisamatikkamavasena, seyyathāpi cakkhumato purisassa dvattiṃsavaṇṇānaṃ kusumānaṃ ekasuttagaṇṭhitaṃ mālaṃ olokentassa sabbapupphāni apubbāpariyamiva pākaṭāni honti, evameva “atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā”ti imaṃ kāyaṃ olokentassa sabbe te dhammā apubbāpariyamiva pākaṭā honti. Tena vuttaṃ manasikārakosallakathāyaṃ “ādikammikassa hi ‘kesā’ti manasikaroto manasikāro gantvā ‘mutta’nti imaṃ pariyosānakoṭṭhāsameva āhacca tiṭṭhatī”ti.

Thus, having distinguished the sections like hair, etc., by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, and by attending to them gradually, neither too quickly nor too slowly, one contemplates them in five ways—by way of color, shape, smell, support, and location—repeating 'repulsive, repulsive,' thus transcending conventional perception. Just as a man with good eyesight, looking at a garland of thirty-two kinds of flowers strung on a single thread, sees all the flowers distinctly in their order, so too, while contemplating the body with the thought, 'In this body, there is hair,' all these phenomena become distinctly apparent in their order. Therefore, it is said in the discussion of skillful attention: 'For a beginner, when attention is directed to 'hair,' it goes and strikes only the final section, ‘urine,’ and remains there.'

Sace pana bahiddhāpi manasikāraṃ upasaṃharati, athassa evaṃ sabbakoṭṭhāsesu pākaṭībhūtesu āhiṇḍantā manussatiracchānādayo sattākāraṃ vijahitvā koṭṭhāsarāsivaseneva upaṭṭhahanti; tehi ca ajjhohariyamānaṃ pānabhojanādi koṭṭhāsarāsimhi pakkhipiyamānamiva upaṭṭhāti. Athassa anupubbamuñcanādivasena [P 0.0249][M 0.0237] ‘paṭikūlā paṭikūlā’ti punappunaṃ manasikaroto anukkamena appanā uppajjati.

If, however, one applies attention even externally, then when all the parts have become clearly visible, beings such as humans and animals, wandering around, appear not in their usual forms but merely as heaps of constituents. And the food and drink being consumed by them appear as if being thrown into that heap of constituents. Then, as one repeatedly attends to 'repulsive, repulsive' by way of gradual release, etc., absorption arises in due course.

Tattha kesādīnaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedavasena upaṭṭhānaṃ uggahanimittaṃ, sabbākārato paṭikūlavasena upaṭṭhānaṃ paṭibhāganimittaṃ. Taṃ punappunaṃ āvajjentassa manasikarontassa [V 0.0236] takkāhataṃ vitakkāhataṃ karontassa cattāro khandhā paṭikūlārammaṇā honti, paṭhamajjhānavasena appanā pavattati. Pubbabhāge parikammaupacāracittāni savitakkasavicārāni sappītikāni somanassasahagatāni paṭikūlanimittārammaṇāni; appanāpi savitakkasavicārā sappītikā somanassasahagatāva. Bhūmantarena pana mahaggatā rūpāvacarā honti. Paṭikkūlepi ca etasmiṃ ārammaṇe ānisaṃsadassāvitāya somanassaṃ uppajjati, ekattārammaṇabaleneva vā taṃ uppajjati. Dutiyajjhānādīni panettha na nibbattanti. Kasmā? Oḷārikattā. Idañhi ārammaṇaṃ oḷārikaṃ. Vitakkabalenevettha cittekaggatā jāyati, na vitakkasamatikkamenāti. Ayaṃ tāva samathavasena kammaṭṭhānakathā.

Here, attending to hair and so on in terms of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation is the learning sign. Attending to the same in all aspects as repulsive is the counterpart sign. For one who repeatedly turns the mind towards it, attends to it, and makes it struck by initial and sustained thought, the four aggregates have a repulsive object, and absorption arises in the manner of the first jhāna. In the preliminary stage, the preliminary and access consciousnesses are with initial and sustained thought, with rapture, accompanied by joy, and have the repulsive sign as their object; the absorption, too, is with initial and sustained thought, with rapture, and accompanied by joy. But by way of another plane, these become exalted and pertain to the form sphere. And even in this repulsive object, joy arises from seeing the advantages, or it arises by the power of the object's unity. But the second jhāna and so on do not occur in this case. Why? Because of coarseness. For this object is coarse. Unification of mind arises here through the power of initial thought alone, not through the transcendence of initial thought. This, so far, is the discourse on the meditation subject in terms of serenity.

Avisesato pana sādhāraṇavasena evaṃ veditabbaṃ – idañhi kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetukāmena kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetvā sajjhāyakāle eva kesādīnaṃ vaṇṇanimittasaṇṭhānanimittadisānimittaokāsanimittaparicchedanimittāni vācāya pothetvā pothetvā ekekakoṭṭhāse ‘ayaṃ etaṃsarikkhako’ti tividhena sajjhāyo kātabbo. Kathaṃ? Tacapañcake tāva heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva anulomato pañcāhaṃ, paṭilomato pañcāhaṃ, anulomapaṭilomato pañcāhanti addhamāsaṃ sajjhāyo kātabbo. Tato ācariyassa santikaṃ gantvā vakkapañcakaṃ uggaṇhitvā tatheva addhamāsaṃ sajjhāyo kātabbo. Tato te dasapi koṭṭhāse ekato katvā addhamāsaṃ. Puna papphāsapañcakādīsupi ekekaṃ uggaṇhitvā addhamāsaṃ. Tato te pañcadasapi koṭṭhāse addhamāsaṃ. Matthaluṅgapañcakaṃ addhamāsaṃ. Tato tevīsati koṭṭhāse addhamāsaṃ. Medachakkaṃ addhamāsaṃ. Tato te chabbīsatipi koṭṭhāse ekato katvā addhamāsaṃ. Muttachakkaṃ addhamāsaṃ. Tato sabbepi [P 0.0250] dvattiṃsa koṭṭhāse ekato katvā addhamāsanti evaṃ cha māse sajjhāyo kātabbo.

However, in a general sense, it should be understood thus: one who wishes to develop this meditation subject, having taken up the meditation subject, should during the time of recitation repeatedly strike with speech the signs of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation of the hair of the head, etc. Then, for each part, the recitation should be done in three ways, with the thought, 'This is similar to that.' How? First, regarding the skin pentad, recitation should be done for half a month: for five days in forward order, five days in reverse order, and for five days in both forward and reverse order. Then, having gone to the teacher, one should learn the kidney pentad and similarly recite for half a month. After that, combining those ten parts, recite for half a month. Again, for the lung pentad and so forth, having learned each one, recite for half a month. Then, combining those fifteen parts, recite for half a month. For the brain pentad, half a month. Then, for the twenty-three parts, half a month. For the fat hexad, half a month. Then, combining those twenty-six parts, half a month. For the urine hexad, half a month. Finally, combining all thirty-two parts, half a month. In this way, recitation should be done for six months.

Tattha – upanissayasampannassa sappaññassa bhikkhuno kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhantasseva koṭṭhāsā upaṭṭhahanti, ekaccassa na upaṭṭhahanti. Tena ‘na upaṭṭhahantī’ti vīriyaṃ [M 0.0238] na vissajjetabbaṃ. Yattakā koṭṭhāsā upaṭṭhahanti tattake gahetvā sajjhāyo kātabbo. Evaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathentena pana neva paññavato na mandapaññassa vasena kathetabbaṃ, majjhimapaññassa vasena kathetabbaṃ. Majjhimapaññassa hi vasena ācariyā chahi māsehi paricchinditvā tantiṃ ṭhapayiṃsu. Yassa pana ettāvatāpi koṭṭhāsā pākaṭā na honti, tena tato parampi sajjhāyo kātabbo eva; no ca kho aparicchinditvā, cha cha māse paricchinditvāva kātabbo.

In this regard, for a wise monk endowed with supportive conditions, the parts become manifest even as he is learning the meditation subject; for another, they do not. Therefore, one should not abandon effort, thinking, 'They do not become manifest.' Whatever parts do become manifest, those should be taken up and recited. When teaching the meditation subject, however, one should not teach according to the capacity of one with great wisdom or one with little wisdom, but according to the capacity of one with middling wisdom. For it was for those of middling wisdom that the teachers established the tradition, delimiting it at six months. If, however, the parts do not become clear for someone even after this much time, they should continue to recite further; yet not without delimitation, but only after delimiting it in six-month periods.

Sajjhāyaṃ [V 0.0237] karontena vaṇṇo na paccavekkhitabbo, na lakkhaṇaṃ manasikātabbaṃ, koṭṭhāsavaseneva sajjhāyo kātabbo. Ācariyenāpi ‘vaṇṇavasena sajjhāyaṃ karohī’ti niyametvā na kathetabbaṃ. Niyametvā kathite ko dosoti? Sampattiyampi vipattisaññāāpajjanaṃ. Sace hi ācariyena ‘vaṇṇavasena sajjhāyaṃ karohī’ti vutte imassa bhikkhuno tathā karontassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ vaṇṇato na upaṭṭhāti, paṭikūlavasena vā dhātuvasena vā upaṭṭhāti, athesa ‘na idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ vilakkhaṇa’nti saññī hoti, ācariyena kathitameva kappetvā gaṇhāti. ‘Paṭikūlavasena sajjhāyaṃ karohī’ti vuttepi sace tassa tathā karontassa paṭikkūlato na upaṭṭhāti, vaṇṇavasena vā dhātuvasena vā upaṭṭhāti, athesa ‘nayidaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ vilakkhaṇa’nti saññī hoti, ācariyena kathitameva kappetvā gaṇhāti. ‘Dhātuvasena taṃ sajjhāyaṃ karohī’ti vuttepi sace tassa tathā karontassa dhātuto na upaṭṭhāti, vaṇṇavasena vā paṭikūlavasena vā upaṭṭhāti, athesa ‘nayidaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ vilakkhaṇa’nti saññī hoti, ācariyena kathitameva kappetvā gaṇhāti. Ayaṃ ācariyena niyametvā kathite doso.

When reciting, one should not examine the color, nor pay attention to the characteristics; recitation should be done only by way of the sections. Even the teacher should not prescribe, 'Recite by way of color.' What is the fault if a rule is prescribed? It is the arising of the perception of failure even in success. For if the teacher says, 'Recite by way of color,' and while that monk is doing so, the meditation object does not appear to him in terms of color, but appears as repulsive or by way of elements, then he thinks, 'This meditation object is not as it should be,' and he assumes only what the teacher has said. Similarly, if told, 'Recite by way of repulsiveness,' and while doing so, repulsiveness does not appear to him, but color or elements do, he thinks, 'This meditation object is not as it should be,' and assumes only what the teacher has said. Likewise, if told, 'Recite by way of elements,' and while doing so, the elements do not appear to him, but color or repulsiveness does, he thinks, 'This meditation object is not as it should be,' and assumes only what the teacher has said. This is the fault when the teacher prescribes a rule.

Kinti pana vattabbo hotīti? ‘Koṭṭhāsavasena sajjhāyaṃ karohī’ti vattabbo. Kathaṃ? ‘Kesakoṭṭhāso lomakoṭṭhāsoti sajjhāyaṃ karohī’ti vattabbo. Sace panassa evaṃ koṭṭhāsavasena sajjhāyaṃ karontassa vaṇṇato [P 0.0251] upaṭṭhāti, athānena ovādācariyassa ācikkhitabbaṃ – ‘ahaṃ dvattiṃsākāraṃ koṭṭhāsavasena sajjhāyaṃ karomi; mayhaṃ pana vaṇṇato upaṭṭhātī’ti. Ācariyena ‘kammaṭṭhānaṃ viya akammaṭṭhānaṃ, vilakkhaṇaṃ eta’nti na visaṃvādetabbaṃ. ‘Sādhu, sappurisa, pubbe tayā vaṇṇakasiṇe parikammaṃ katapubbaṃ bhavissati. Etadeva kammaṭṭhānaṃ tuyhaṃ sappāyaṃ. Vaṇṇavaseneva [M 0.0239] sajjhāyaṃ karohī’ti vattabbo. Tenapi vaṇṇavaseneva sajjhāyo kātabbo.

How then should one be told? One should be told, 'Recite by way of sections.' How? One should be told, 'Recite as the hair section, the body hair section.' But if, while reciting in this way by sections, the color appears to him, then he should inform his advising teacher: 'I recite the thirty-two aspects by way of sections, but the color appears to me.' The teacher should not gainsay him, saying, 'This is a meditation subject as if it were not a meditation subject; this is abnormal.' Instead, he should say, 'Good, worthy one, you must have previously performed the preliminary work on the color kasiṇa. This very meditation subject is suitable for you. Recite just by way of color.' Then, he should recite just by way of color.

So evaṃ karonto ajjhattaṃ nīlakaṃ pītakaṃ lohitakaṃ odātakanti cattāri vaṇṇakasiṇāni labhati. Kathaṃ? Tassa hi kesalomapittesu ceva akkhīnañca kāḷakaṭṭhāne vaṇṇaṃ ‘nīlaṃ nīla’nti manasikarontassa catukkapañcakajjhānāni uppajjanti; jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Medasmiṃ pana akkhīnañca pītakaṭṭhāne vaṇṇaṃ ‘pītakaṃ pītaka’nti manasikarontassa catukkapañcakajjhānāni uppajjanti; jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Maṃsalohitesu pana akkhīnañca rattaṭṭhāne vaṇṇaṃ ‘lohitakaṃ lohitaka’nti manasikarontassa catukkapañcakajjhānāni uppajjanti; jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā [V 0.0238] vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Nakhadantacammaaṭṭhīsu pana akkhīnañca paṇḍaraṭṭhāne vaṇṇaṃ ‘odātaṃ odāta’nti manasikarontassa catukkapañcakajjhānāni uppajjanti, jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Idaṃ vaṇṇavasena abhiniviṭṭhassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā nigamanaṃ.

Doing so, he internally attains the four color kasiṇas: blue, yellow, red, and white. How? For one who attends to the color in the hair of the head, hair of the body, bile, and the black parts of the eyes as 'blue, blue,' the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise. Having made jhāna the basis and established insight, he attains arahantship. And for one who attends to the color in the fat and the yellow parts of the eyes as 'yellow, yellow,' the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise. Having made jhāna the basis and established insight, he attains arahantship. And for one who attends to the color in the flesh, blood, and the red parts of the eyes as 'red, red,' the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise. Having made jhāna the basis and established insight, he attains arahantship. And for one who attends to the color in the nails, teeth, skin, bones, and the white parts of the eyes as 'white, white,' the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise. Having made jhāna the basis and established insight, he attains arahantship. This is the conclusion, up to arahantship, for a bhikkhu who has applied himself by way of color.

Aparassa koṭṭhāsavasena sajjhāyaṃ karontassa paṭikūlato upaṭṭhāti. Athānena ovādācariyassa ācikkhitabbaṃ. Ācariyena ‘kammaṭṭhānaṃ viya akammaṭṭhānaṃ, vilakkhaṇaṃ eta’nti na visaṃvādetabbaṃ. ‘Sādhu, sappurisa, pubbe tayā paṭikūlamanasikāre yogo kato bhavissati. Etadeva kammaṭṭhānaṃ tuyhaṃ sappāyaṃ. Paṭikūlavaseneva sajjhāyaṃ karohī’ti vattabbo. Tenapi paṭikūlavasena sajjhāyo kātabbo. Tassa kesā nāma ‘ajaññā duggandhā jegucchā paṭikūlā’ti evaṃ paṭikūlavasena sajjhāyaṃ karontassa paṭikūlārammaṇe paṭhamajjhānaṃ nibbattati. So jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Idaṃ [P 0.0252] paṭikūlavasena abhiniviṭṭhassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā nigamanaṃ.

For another, while reciting by way of the parts, it appears from the aspect of repulsiveness. Then this should be told to his advising teacher. The teacher should not contradict him, saying, 'This is a meditation subject that is like a non-meditation subject; this is unusual.' He should be told: 'Good, worthy man, you must have previously applied yourself to attention on the repulsive. This very meditation subject is suitable for you. Recite by way of repulsiveness.' He, too, should recite by way of repulsiveness. For him, while reciting by way of repulsiveness regarding the hairs of the head as 'impure, foul-smelling, disgusting, repulsive,' the first jhāna arises with a repulsive object. Having made that jhāna the basis and established insight, he attains arahantship. This is the conclusion, up to arahantship, for a bhikkhu who has applied himself by way of repulsiveness.

Aparassa koṭṭhāsavasena sajjhāyaṃ karontassa dhātuto upaṭṭhāti. Dhātuto upaṭṭhahantaṃ kīdisaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhātīti? Kesā tāva vammikamatthake jātakunthatiṇakāni viya hutvā upaṭṭhahanti. Lomā purāṇagāmaṭṭhāne jātadabbatiṇakāni viya. Nakhā daṇḍakesu ṭhapitamadhukaphalaṭṭhikosakā viya. Dantā mattikāpiṇḍe pavesetvā ṭhapitaalābubījāni viya. Taco vīṇāpabbake pariyonaddhaallagocammaṃ viya, maṃsaṃ bhittiyaṃ anulittamattikā [M 0.0240] viya. Nhāru dabbasambhārabaddhavallī viya. Aṭṭhi ussāpetvā ṭhapitabhittidabbasambhāro viya. Aṭṭhimiñjaṃ mahāveḷumhi pakkhittaseditavettaggaṃ viya. Vakkaṃ, hadayaṃ, yakanaṃ, kilomakaṃ, pihakaṃ, papphāsanti ime cha koṭṭhāsā sūnakāragharaṃ viya hutvā upaṭṭhahanti. Dvattiṃsahatthaṃ antaṃ lohitadoṇiyaṃ saṃvellitvā ṭhapitagharasappo viya. Antaguṇaṃ pādapuñchanake sibbitarajjukā viya. Udariyaṃ parissāvane sithilabandhataṇḍulaṃ viya. Karīsaṃ veṇupabbe pakkhittapaṇḍumattikā viya. Matthaluṅgaṃ omadditvā ṭhapitā cattāro taṇḍulapiṭṭhapiṇḍā viya. Dvādasavidhā āpodhātu paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitesu dvādasasu udakasarāvakesu pūritaudakaṃ viya hutvā upaṭṭhāti.

For another, while reciting by way of the parts, it appears from the aspect of the elements. When it appears from the aspect of the elements, what is it like? The hairs of the head appear like kuntha grass growing on an anthill. The hairs of the body are like dabba grass growing in an old village site. The nails are like the kernels of madhuka fruit placed on sticks. The teeth are like gourd seeds set into a lump of clay. The skin is like a wet cowhide stretched over the body of a lute. The flesh is like clay plastered on a wall. The sinews are like vines binding a bundle of materials. The bones are like a framework of wood set up for a wall. The bone marrow is like a steamed rattan shoot placed inside a large bamboo. The kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, and lungs—these six parts appear like a butcher's shop. The intestines, thirty-two hands long, are like a house snake coiled up in a trough of blood. The mesentery is like a cord sewn into a foot-wiping cloth. The contents of the stomach are like loosely tied rice in a strainer. The feces are like pale yellow clay put into a section of bamboo. The brain is like four balls of rice-flour dough kneaded and set down. The twelvefold water element appears like water filling twelve small water bowls placed in a row.

Athānena ovādācariyassa ācikkhitabbaṃ. Ācariyena ‘kammaṭṭhānaṃ viya akammaṭṭhānaṃ, vilakkhaṇaṃ [V 0.0239] eta’nti na visaṃvādetabbaṃ. ‘Sādhu, sappurisa, pubbe tayā dhātumanasikāre yogo kato bhavissati. Etadeva kammaṭṭhānaṃ tuyhaṃ sappāyaṃ. Dhātuvaseneva sajjhāyaṃ karohī’ti vattabbo. Tenapi dhātuvasena sajjhāyo kātabbo.

Then this should be told to his advising teacher. The teacher should not contradict him, saying, 'This is a meditation subject that is like a non-meditation subject; this is unusual.' He should be told: 'Good, worthy man, you must have previously applied yourself to attention on the elements. This very meditation subject is suitable for you. Recite by way of the elements.' He, too, should recite by way of the elements.

Tatridaṃ manasikāramukheneva sajjhāyavidhānaṃ – idha bhikkhu ‘kesā sīsaṃ pariyonaddhitvā ṭhitacamme jātā. Te na jānanti ‘mayaṃ sīsaṃ pariyonaddhitvā ṭhitacamme jātā’ti; sīsaṃ pariyonaddhitvā ṭhitacammampi na jānāti ‘kesā mayi jātā’ti; acetanā ete abyākatā suññā thaddhā patthinnā pathavīdhātu esā’ti manasikaroti. ‘Lomā sarīraṃ pariyonahanacamme jātā. Te na jānanti ‘mayaṃ sarīraṃ pariyonahanacamme [P 0.0253] jātā’ti. Sarīraṃ pariyonahanacammampi na jānāti ‘lomā mayi jātā’ti etepi acetanā. Nakhā aṅgulīnaṃ aggesu jātā. Te na jānanti ‘mayaṃ aṅgulīnaṃ aggesu jātā’ti. Aṅgulīnaṃ aggānipi na jānanti ‘nakhā amhesu jātā’ti. Etepi acetanā. Dantā hanukaṭṭhike jātā. Te na jānanti ‘mayaṃ hanukaṭṭhike jātā’ti. Hanukaṭṭhikampi na jānāti ‘dantā mayi jātā’ti. Etepi acetanā. Taco na jānāti ‘sarīraṃ mayā pariyonaddha’nti. Sarīrampi na jānāti ‘ahaṃ tacena pariyonaddha’nti. Ayampi acetano. Maṃsaṃ na jānāti ‘mayā sarīraṃ anulitta’nti. Sarīrampi na jānāti ‘ahaṃ maṃsena anulitta’nti. Idampi acetanaṃ. Nhāru na jānāti ‘ahaṃ [M 0.0241] aṭṭhipuñjaṃ ābandhitvā ṭhita’nti. Aṭṭhipuñjopi na jānāti ‘nhārujālenāhaṃ ābaddho’ti. Idampi acetanaṃ.

Herein is the method of recitation by way of the gateway of attention: Here, a bhikkhu reflects thus: 'Hairs have grown in the skin that covers the head. They do not know, "We have grown in the skin that covers the head." The skin that covers the head also does not know, "Hairs have grown on me." These are non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, rigid, solidified—this is the earth element.' 'Body hairs have grown in the skin that covers the body. They do not know, "We have grown in the skin that covers the body." The skin that covers the body also does not know, "Body hairs have grown on me." These too are non-sentient.' 'Nails have grown at the tips of the fingers. They do not know, "We have grown at the tips of the fingers." The tips of the fingers also do not know, "Nails have grown on us." These too are non-sentient.' 'Teeth have grown in the jawbone. They do not know, "We have grown in the jawbone." The jawbone also does not know, "Teeth have grown in me." These too are non-sentient.' 'The skin does not know, "The body is covered by me." The body also does not know, "I am covered by the skin." This too is non-sentient.' 'Flesh does not know, "The body is smeared by me." The body also does not know, "I am smeared with flesh." This too is non-sentient.' 'Sinews do not know, "I stand having bound the pile of bones." The pile of bones also does not know, "I am bound by a network of sinews." This too is non-sentient.'

Sīsaṭṭhi na jānāti ‘ahaṃ gīvaṭṭhike patiṭṭhita’nti. Gīvaṭṭhikampi na jānāti ‘mayi sīsaṭṭhikaṃ patiṭṭhita’nti. Gīvaṭṭhi na jānāti ‘ahaṃ piṭṭhikaṇṭake ṭhita’nti. Piṭṭhikaṇṭaṭṭhikopi kaṭiṭṭhikaṃ ūruṭṭhikaṃ jaṅghaṭṭhikaṃ gopphakaṭṭhikaṃ na jānāti ‘ahaṃ paṇhikaṭṭhike patiṭṭhita’nti. Paṇhikaṭṭhikampi na jānāti ‘ahaṃ gopphakaṭṭhikaṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitanti…pe… gīvaṭṭhikaṃ na jānāti ‘ahaṃ sīsaṭṭhikaṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhita’nti.

The skull-bone does not know, 'I am established on the neck-bone.' The neck-bone also does not know, 'The skull-bone is established on me.' The neck-bone does not know, 'I am situated on the spinal column.' The spinal column bone also does not know the hip-bone, the thigh-bone, the shin-bone, or the ankle-bone; nor does the ankle-bone know, 'I am established on the heel-bone.' The heel-bone also does not know, 'I stand supporting the ankle-bone,' and so on, until the neck-bone does not know, 'I stand supporting the skull-bone.'

Paṭipāṭiyā aṭṭhīni ṭhitāni koṭiyā,

Anekasandhiyamito na kehici;

Baddho [V 0.0240] nahārūhi jarāya codito,

Acetano kaṭṭhakaliṅgarūpamo.

The bones stand in sequence, end to end, restrained by many joints, not by anyone; bound by sinews, urged on by old age, it is insentient, like a wooden puppet.

‘Idampi acetanaṃ. Aṭṭhimiñjaṃ; vakkaṃ…pe… matthaluṅgaṃ acetanaṃ abyākataṃ suññaṃ thaddhaṃ patthinnaṃ pathavīdhātū’ti manasikaroti. ‘Pittaṃ semhaṃ…pe… muttaṃ acetanaṃ abyākataṃ suññaṃ yūsagataṃ āpodhātū’ti manasikaroti.

He reflects: 'This too is non-sentient. Bone marrow, kidneys...brain—these are non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, stiff, solidified, the earth element.' Thus he reflects: 'Bile, phlegm...urine—these are non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, fluid-like, the water element.'

Ime dve mahābhūte pariggaṇhantassa udare ussadā tejodhātu pākaṭā hoti, nāsāya ussadā vāyodhātu pākaṭā hoti. Ime cattāro mahābhūte pariggaṇhantassa upādārūpaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Mahābhūtaṃ nāma upādārūpena paricchinnaṃ, upādārūpaṃ mahābhūtena. Yathā ātapo nāma chāyāya paricchinno, chāyā ātapena; evameva mahābhūtaṃ upādārūpena paricchinnaṃ[P 0.0254], upādārūpaṃ mahābhūtena. Athassa evaṃ “cattāri mahābhūtāni tevīsati upādārūpāni rūpakkhandho”ti rūpakkhandhaṃ pariggaṇhantassa āyatanadvāravasena arūpino khandhā pākaṭā honti. Iti rūpārūpapariggaho pañcakkhandhā honti, pañcakkhandhā dvādasāyatanāni honti, dvādasāyatanāni aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo hontīti khandhāyatanadhātuvasena yamakatālakandhaṃ phālento viya dve koṭṭhāse katvā nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapeti.

For one who comprehends these two great elements, the fire element becomes evident as heat in the belly, and the wind element becomes evident as breath at the nose. For one who comprehends these four great elements, derived form becomes evident. A great element is delimited by derived form, and derived form by a great element. Just as sunlight is delimited by shadow, and shadow by sunlight, even so, a great element is delimited by derived form, and derived form by a great element. Then, to him, it occurs thus: 'The four great elements and the twenty-three derived forms are the form aggregate.' When one comprehends the form aggregate, the formless aggregates become evident through the sense-base doors. Thus, the comprehension of form and formless becomes the five aggregates. The five aggregates become the twelve sense bases, and the twelve sense bases become the eighteen elements. In this way, in terms of aggregates, sense bases, and elements, like splitting a twin palm-stump into two parts, he determines name-and-form.

So “idaṃ nāmarūpaṃ na ahetu na appaccayā nibbattaṃ, sahetu sappaccayā nibbattaṃ. Ko panassa hetu? Ko pana paccayo”ti upaparikkhanto “avijjāpaccayā [M 0.0242] taṇhāpaccayā kammapaccayā āhārapaccayā cā”ti tassa paccayaṃ vavatthapetvā “atītepi paccayā ceva paccayasamuppannadhammā ca anāgatepi etarahipi paccayā ceva paccayasamuppannadhammā ca, tato uddhaṃ satto vā puggalo vā natthi, suddhasaṅkhārapuñjo evā”ti – evaṃ tīsu addhāsu kaṅkhaṃ vitarati. Ayaṃ pana vipassanāsaṅkhārasallakkhaṇā ñātapariññā nāma.

He investigates: 'This name-and-form has not arisen without a cause, without a condition; it has arisen with a cause, with a condition. What is its cause? What is its condition?' Investigating, he determines its condition thus: 'With ignorance as condition, craving as condition, kamma as condition, and nutriment as condition.' Having determined its condition, he reflects: 'In the past also, there were conditions and conditionally arisen phenomena; in the future also, and at present also, there are conditions and conditionally arisen phenomena. Beyond these, there is no being or person, only a mere heap of formations.' Thus, he overcomes doubt regarding the three periods of time. This discernment of formations by insight is called understanding by comprehension.

Evaṃ saṅkhāre sallakkhetvā ṭhitassa pana bhikkhussa dasabalassa sāsane mūlaṃ otiṇṇaṃ nāma hoti, patiṭṭhā laddhā nāma, cūḷasotāpanno nāma hoti niyatagatiko. Tathārūpaṃ pana utusappāyaṃ, puggalasappāyaṃ, bhojanasappāyaṃ, dhammasavaṇasappāyaṃ labhitvā ekāsane ekapallaṅkavaragato [V 0.0241] tīṇi lakkhaṇāni āropetvā vipassanāpaṭipāṭiyā saṅkhāre sammasanto arahattaṃ gaṇhātīti idaṃ dhātuvasena abhiniviṭṭhassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā nigamanaṃ.

For a bhikkhu who abides thus, having discerned the formations, it is said that his root has descended into the Dispensation of the Ten-Powered One, that a footing has been obtained, and he is called a 'lesser stream-enterer,' one of fixed destiny. When such a one obtains a suitable season, suitable person, suitable food, and suitable hearing of the Dhamma, and, having gone to a choice seat in a single cross-legged posture, applying the three characteristics and rightly considering the formations in the sequence of insight, he attains Arahantship. This is the conclusion, up to Arahantship, for a bhikkhu who is intent on the elements.

Yassa pana neva vaṇṇato upaṭṭhāti na paṭikūlato na suññato tena ‘na me upaṭṭhātī’ti na kammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā nisīditabbaṃ, koṭṭhāsamanasikāreyeva pana yogo kātabbo. Porāṇakattherā kira ‘koṭṭhāsamanasikārova pamāṇa’nti āhaṃsu. Iccassa punappunaṃ koṭṭhāsavasena sajjhāyaṃ karontassa koṭṭhāsā paguṇā honti. Kadā pana paguṇā nāma hontīti? Yadā ‘kesā’ti āvajjitamatte manasikāro gantvā ‘matthaluṅga’nti antimakoṭṭhāse patiṭṭhāti, ‘matthaluṅga’nti āvajjitamatte manasikāro āgantvā ‘kesā’ti ādikoṭṭhāse patiṭṭhāti.

For one to whom it appears neither by its color, nor as repulsive, nor as empty, one should not, thinking, 'It does not appear to me,' dismiss the meditation subject and sit down, but should persist in applying effort to the attention on the parts. The ancient elders, it is said, declared, 'Attention to the parts alone is the measure.' Thus, for one who repeatedly rehearses in terms of the parts, the parts become familiar. But when are they called familiar? When, upon merely adverting to 'head hairs,' the attention goes and settles on the last part, 'brain,' and upon merely adverting to 'brain,' the attention comes back and settles on the first part, 'head hairs.'

Athassa yathā nāma cakkhumato purisassa dvattiṃsavaṇṇānaṃ [P 0.0255] pupphānaṃ ekasuttaganthitaṃ mālaṃ olokentassa paṭipāṭiyā vā pana nikhāte dvattiṃsavatipāde paṭikkamitvā olokentassa paṭipāṭiyāva dvattiṃsavaṇṇāni pupphāni vatipādā vā pākaṭā honti, evameva dvattiṃsa koṭṭhāsā upaṭṭhahanti, vicarantā tiracchānagatāpi manussāpi sattāti na upaṭṭhahanti, koṭṭhāsāti upaṭṭhahanti, khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ koṭṭhāsantare pakkhippamānaṃ viya hoti.

Then, just as for a man with good sight, when looking at a garland of flowers of thirty-two colors strung on a single thread, or when looking back while walking along a row of thirty-two planted posts, the thirty-two colored flowers or the posts become clearly visible in order—in the same way, the thirty-two parts of the body become evident to him. As he wanders, neither animals nor humans appear as beings; only the parts appear. Food, hard and soft, seems like something being placed into the spaces between the parts.

Koṭṭhāsānaṃ paguṇakālato paṭṭhāya tīsu mukhesu ekena mukhena vimuccissati. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ vaṇṇato vā paṭikūlato vā suññato vā upaṭṭhāti[M 0.0243]. Yathā nāma pūve pacitukāmā itthī madditvā ṭhapitapiṭṭhato yaṃ yaṃ icchati taṃ taṃ pacati, yathā vā pana same bhūmippadese ṭhapitaṃ udakapūraṃ kumbhaṃ yato yato āvijjhanti tato tatova udakaṃ nikkhamati; evameva koṭṭhāsānaṃ paguṇakālato paṭṭhāya tīsu mukhesu ekena mukhena vimuccissati. Ākaṅkhamānassa vaṇṇato, ākaṅkhamānassa paṭikūlato, ākaṅkhamānassa suññato kammaṭṭhānaṃ upaṭṭhahissatiyeva. Ayaṃ ettako uggahasandhi nāma. Imasmiṃ uggahasandhismiṃ ṭhatvā arahattaṃ pattā bhikkhu gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattā.

From the time the parts become familiar, one will be liberated through one of three openings. The meditation subject will appear either by its color, as repulsive, or as empty. Just as a woman wishing to bake cakes can bake whatever she desires from the kneaded dough set aside, or just as water pours out from wherever a pot filled with water placed on level ground is pierced, so too, from the time the parts become familiar, one will be liberated through one of three openings. For one who wishes, the meditation subject will appear by its color; for one who wishes, it will appear as repulsive; for one who wishes, it will appear as empty. This much is called the stage of grasping. Standing in this stage of grasping, the monks who have attained arahantship are beyond counting.

Yassa pana uggahasandhismiṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ na upaṭṭhāti, tena kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetvā, sace yattha ācariyo vasati, so āvāso sappāyo hoti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ; no ce, sappāyaṭṭhāne vasitabbaṃ. Vasantena aṭṭhārasa vihāradose (visuddhi. 1.52) vajjetvā pañcaṅgasamannāgate senāsane [V 0.0242] vasitabbaṃ, sayampi pañcaṅgasamannāgatena bhavitabbaṃ. Tato pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantena rattiṭṭhānaṃ vā divāṭṭhānaṃ vā pavisitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikātabbaṃ.

But for one to whom the meditation subject does not appear at the stage of grasping, he should grasp the meditation subject. If the monastery where the teacher resides is suitable, that is good; if not, one should live in a suitable place. While living there, one should avoid the eighteen faults of a monastery (Visuddhimagga I, 52) and live in a dwelling endowed with five factors, and oneself should also be endowed with five factors. Then, after returning from the alms round after the meal, one should enter the night quarters or day quarters and attend to the meditation subject.

Kathaṃ? Ādito tāva heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva anupubbato manasikātabbaṃ, na ekantarikā. Anupubbato manasikaronto hi dvattiṃsapadaṃ nisseṇiṃ padapaṭipāṭiyā akkamanto pāsādaṃ āruyha pāsādānisaṃsaṃ anubhavanakapuriso viya ‘kesā lomā’ti paṭipāṭiyā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaronto kammaṭṭhānato ca na parihāyati, pāsādānisaṃsasadise ca nava lokuttaradhamme anubhavati. Anupubbato manasikarontenāpi ca nātisīghato nātisaṇikato [P 0.0256] manasikātabbaṃ. Atisīghato manasikarontassa hi kiñcāpi kammaṭṭhānaṃ paguṇaṃ hoti, avibhūtaṃ pana hoti. Tattha opammaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

How? First, one should attend to it sequentially in the way stated previously, not skipping any. For by attending to it sequentially, like a person who, climbing a staircase of thirty-two steps in due order, ascends to a palace and experiences the benefits of the palace, so one who attends to the meditation subject in the order of 'head hairs, body hairs,' and so on, does not fall away from the meditation subject and experiences the nine supramundane states, which are like the benefits of a palace. And even when attending to it sequentially, one should not attend to it too quickly or too slowly. For if one attends to it too quickly, although the meditation subject becomes familiar, it remains unclear. The simile for that has been stated previously.

Atisaṇikato manasikarontassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariyosānaṃ na gacchati, antarāva osakkitabbaṃ hoti. Yathā hi puriso tiyojanaṃ maggaṃ sāyaṃ kacchaṃ bandhitvā paṭipanno nikkhantaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya sītalacchāyaṃ disvā vissamati, ramaṇīyaṃ vālikatalaṃ disvā piṭṭhiṃ pasāreti, vanapokkharaṇiṃ disvā pānīyaṃ pivati nhāyati, pabbataṃ disvā āruyha pabbatarāmaṇeyyakaṃ passati, taṃ antarāyeva sīho vā byaggho vā dīpi vā hanati, corā vā pana [M 0.0244] viluppanti ceva hananti ca; evameva atisaṇikaṃ manasikarontassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariyosānaṃ na gacchati, antarāva osakkitabbaṃ hoti.

When one attends too slowly, the meditation subject does not reach completion; it has to be abandoned midway. Just as a man who sets out in the evening, having girded himself for a journey of three leagues, sees a cool shade right from the starting point and rests, or sees a delightful sandy stretch and stretches out his back, or sees a forest pond and drinks and bathes, or sees a mountain and climbs it to behold its beauty—but in the meantime a lion or a tiger or a leopard kills him, or robbers plunder and kill him—so too, when one attends too slowly, the meditation subject does not reach completion; it has to be abandoned midway.

Tasmā nātisīghaṃ nātisaṇikaṃ ekadivasaṃ tiṃsavāre manasikātabbaṃ; pātova dasa vāre, majjhanhike dasavāre, sāyanhe dasa vāre sajjhāyo kātabbo, no kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yathā hi pātova uṭṭhāya mukhaṃ no dhovituṃ na vaṭṭati, khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ no khādituṃ no bhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati; etaṃ pana vaṭṭeyya; idameva ekantena no kātuṃ na vaṭṭati; karonto mahantaṃ atthaṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhati. Yathā hi ekassa purisassa tīṇi khettāni; ekaṃ khettaṃ aṭṭhakumbhaṃ deti, ekaṃ soḷasa, ekaṃ dvattiṃsa; tena tīṇipi khettāni paṭijaggituṃ asakkontena dve chaḍḍetvā ekaṃ dvattiṃsakumbhadāyakameva paṭijaggitabbaṃ; tattheva kasanavapananiddānādīni kātabbāni; tadevassa itaresu dvīsu uṭṭhānakadāyaṃ dassati; evameva sesaṃ mukhadhovanādikammaṃ chaḍḍetvāpi ettheva [V 0.0243] kammaṃ kātabbaṃ, no kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Karonto mahantaṃ atthaṃ gaṇhitvā tiṭṭhatīti ettāvatā majjhimā paṭipadā nāma kathitā.

Therefore, it should be attended to thirty times a day—not too quickly and not too slowly. In the morning, ten times; at midday, ten times; in the evening, ten times—the recitation should be done; it is not right not to do it. Just as upon rising in the morning, it is not right not to wash one's face, and it is not right not to eat hard and soft food; but to omit those things might be permissible, whereas this alone is absolutely not to be omitted. By doing so, one secures a great benefit. For example, a man has three fields. One field yields eight bushels, another sixteen, and another thirty-two. If he cannot tend to all three fields, he should abandon two and tend only to the one that yields thirty-two bushels. There, he should perform tasks like plowing, sowing, and weeding. That very field will give him the yield of the effort put into the other two. Similarly, even if one must abandon other tasks like washing the face, this work must still be done; it is not right not to do it. By doing so, one secures a great benefit. Thus far, the Middle Path has been explained.

Evaṃ paṭipannenāpi vikkhepo paṭibāhitabbo. Kammaṭṭhānañhi vissajjetvā citte bahiddhā vikkhepaṃ gacchante kammaṭṭhānato parihāyati, vaṭṭabhayaṃ samatikkamituṃ na sakkoti. Yathā hi eko puriso sahassuddhāraṃ sādhetvā vaḍḍhiṃ labhitvā addhānaṃ paṭipanno antarāmagge kumbhīlamakaragāharakkhasasamuṭṭhitāya [P 0.0257] gambhīragirikandarāya upari atthataṃ ekapadikaṃ daṇḍakasetuṃ āruyha gacchanto akkamanapadaṃ vissajjetvā ito cito ca olokento paripatitvā kumbhīlādibhattaṃ hoti, evameva ayampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā sacitte bahiddhā vikkhepaṃ gacchante kammaṭṭhānato parihāyati, vaṭṭabhayaṃ samatikkamituṃ na sakkoti.

Even when practicing in this way, distraction must be warded off. For when one relinquishes the meditation subject and the mind wanders externally, one falls away from the meditation subject and cannot overcome the danger of the round of existence. Just as a man who has acquired a thousand [coins as] capital and obtained interest, setting out on a journey, climbs a single-plank bridge of poles erected over a deep mountain gorge infested with crocodiles, makaras, and ogres, but then, relinquishing his footing and looking around here and there, falls and becomes food for crocodiles and the like—so too, this meditator, relinquishing the meditation subject and allowing his mind to wander externally, falls away from the meditation subject and cannot overcome the danger of the round of existence.

Tatridaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – purisassa sahassuddhāraṃ sādhetvā vaḍḍhiṃ laddhakālo viya hi imassa bhikkhuno ācariyasantike kammaṭṭhānassa uggahitakālo; antarā gambhīragirikandarā viya saṃsāro; tassa kumbhīlādīhi daṭṭhakālo viya vaṭṭamūlakāni mahādukkhāni; ekapadikadaṇḍakasetu viya imassa bhikkhuno sajjhāyavīthi; tassa purisassa ekapadikaṃ [M 0.0245] daṇḍakasetuṃ āruyha akkamanapadaṃ vissajjetvā ito cito ca olokentassa paripatitvā kumbhīlādīnaṃ bhattabhāvaṃ āpannakālo viya imassa bhikkhuno kammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā bahiddhā vikkhittacittassa kammaṭṭhānato parihāyitvā vaṭṭabhayaṃ samatikkamituṃ asamatthabhāvo veditabbo.

Here is the application of the simile: The time when the man acquired a thousand [coins as] capital and obtained interest is like the time when this monk learned the meditation subject from his teacher. The deep mountain gorge along the way is like saṃsāra. The time when he is bitten by crocodiles and the like is like the great sufferings rooted in the round of existence. The single-plank bridge of poles is like this monk’s path of recitation. The time when that man, having climbed the single-plank bridge of poles, relinquished his footing, looked here and there, fell, and became food for crocodiles and the like, is to be understood as this monk's state of being unable to overcome the danger of the round of existence, having relinquished the meditation subject with his mind scattered externally and having fallen away from the meditation subject.

Tasmā kesā manasikātabbā. Kese manasikaritvā cittuppādassa bahiddhā vikkhepaṃ paṭibāhitvā suddhacitteneva ‘lomā nakhā dantā taco’ti manasikātabbaṃ. Evaṃ manasikaronto kammaṭṭhānato na parihāyati, vaṭṭabhayaṃ samatikkamati. Opammaṃ panettha tadeva parivattetvā veditabbaṃ. Sahassuddhāraṃ sādhetvā vaḍḍhiṃ labhitvā chekassa purisassa daṇḍakasetuṃ āruyha nivāsanapārupanaṃ saṃvidhāya dhātupatthaddhakāyaṃ katvā sotthinā paratīragamanaṃ viya chekassa bhikkhuno kese manasikaritvā cittuppādassa bahiddhā vikkhepaṃ paṭibāhitvā suddhacitteneva ‘lomā nakhā dantā taco’ti manasikarontassa kammaṭṭhānato aparihāyitvā vaṭṭabhayaṃ samatikkamanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Therefore, the hair should be attended to. Having attended to the hair, warding off external distraction of the mind, with a purified mind, one should attend to 'body hair, nails, teeth, skin.' Attending in this way, one does not fall away from the meditation subject and overcomes the danger of the round of existence. Here, the same simile should be understood, having been adapted. Just as a skilled man, having acquired a thousand [coins as] capital and obtained interest, climbs onto a bridge of poles, arranges his lower and upper garments, makes his body firm with supports, and safely crosses to the other shore, so too, it should be understood that a skilled monk, having attended to the hair, warding off external distraction of the mind, and with a purified mind attending to 'body hair, nails, teeth, skin,' by not falling away from the meditation subject, overcomes the danger of the round of existence.

Evaṃ [V 0.0244] bahiddhā vikkhepaṃ paṭibāhantenāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva paṇṇattiṃ samatikkamanato manasikātabbaṃ. ‘Kesā lomā’ti paṇṇattiṃ vissajjetvā ‘paṭikūlaṃ paṭikūla’nti sati ṭhapetabbā. Paṭhamaṃyeva pana paṭikūlato na upaṭṭhāti[P 0.0258]. Yāva na upaṭṭhāti tāva paṇṇatti na vissajjetabbā. Yadā upaṭṭhāti tadā paṇṇattiṃ vissajjetvā ‘paṭikūla’nti manasikātabbaṃ. Karontena ca heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva pañcahākārehi paṭikūlato manasikātabbā. Tacapañcakasmiñhi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānagandhāsayokāsavaseneva pañcavidhampi pāṭikūlyaṃ labbhati. Sesesupi yaṃ yaṃ labbhati, tassa tassa vasena manasikāro pavattetabbo.

Having thus warded off external distraction, one should attend as previously explained, so as to transcend concepts. Having relinquished the concept 'hair, body hair,' mindfulness should be established on 'repulsive, repulsive.' At first, however, repulsiveness does not present itself. Until it presents itself, the concept should not be relinquished. When it does present itself, one should relinquish the concept and attend to 'repulsive.' In practicing, one should attend to repulsiveness in the five ways as previously explained. For in the pentad ending with skin, repulsiveness is obtained in five ways: through color, shape, smell, abode, and location. For the remaining parts, attention should be directed based on whatever is obtained for each.

Tattha kesādayo pañca koṭṭhāsā subhanimittaṃ rāgaṭṭhāniyaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇanti saṅkhaṃ gatā. Ye keci rajjanakasattā nāma, sabbe te imesu pañcasu koṭṭhāsesu rajjanti. Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu mahājanassa rajjanaṭṭhāne ‘paṭikūla’nti appanaṃ pāpeti. Tattha appanāppattito paṭṭhāya parato akilamantova appanaṃ pāpuṇāti.

Here, the five parts beginning with the hair are considered an attractive sign, a basis for lust, and a desirable object. Whatever beings are of a lustful nature, all of them lust after these five parts. But this monk brings about absorption on 'repulsive' in the place where the multitude lusts. From the attainment of absorption onwards, he subsequently attains absorption without exertion.

Tatridaṃ opammaṃ – yathā hi cheko dhanuggaho rājānaṃ ārādhetvā satasahassuṭṭhānakaṃ gāmavaraṃ labhitvā sannaddhapañcāvudho tattha gacchanto antarāmagge [M 0.0246] dvattiṃsa core disvā tesu pañcacorajeṭṭhake ghāteyya; tesaṃ ghātitakālato paṭṭhāya tesu dve ekamaggaṃ paṭipajjamānā nāma na honti; evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dhanuggahassa rājānaṃ ārādhetvā gāmavaraṃ laddhakālo viya hi imassa bhikkhuno ācariyasantike kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetvā ṭhitakālo; dvattiṃsa corā viya dvattiṃsa koṭṭhāsā; pañca corajeṭṭhakā viya kesādayo pañca; corajeṭṭhakānaṃ ghātitakālo viya imassa bhikkhuno sabbasattānaṃ rajjanaṭṭhāne tacapañcake ‘paṭikūla’nti appanāya pāpitakālo; sesacorānaṃ pāṇippahāreneva palāyitakālo viya sesakoṭṭhāsesu akilamantasseva appanāppatti veditabbā.

Here is the simile: Just as a skilled archer, having pleased the king, obtained a choice village worth a hundred thousand, and armed with five weapons, set out for it. On the way, he encountered thirty-two bandits and killed the five chief bandits among them. From the moment they were slain, not even two of them traveled the same path. This should be regarded as analogous: The time when the archer pleased the king and obtained the choice village is like the time when this monk learned the meditation subject from his teacher and became established in it; the thirty-two bandits are like the thirty-two parts of the body; the five chief bandits are like the five parts beginning with the hair; the time when the chief bandits were killed is like the time when this monk brought about absorption on 'repulsive' to the skin-pentad, the place of attachment for all beings; the time when the remaining bandits fled merely at a wave of the hand is to be understood as the attainment of absorption regarding the remaining parts without any effort.

Evaṃ paṇṇattiṃ samatikkamantena ca anupubbamuñcanato manasikāro pavattetabbo – kese manasikarontena manasikaronteneva kesesu sāpekkhena hutvā lomesu sati pesetabbā. Yāva lomā na upaṭṭhahanti tāva ‘kesā kesā’ti manasikātabbā. Yadā pana lomā upaṭṭhahanti tadā kese vissajjetvā lomesu sati upaṭṭhapetabbā. Evaṃ nakhādīsupi manasikāro pavattetabbo.

When transcending this concept, attention should be directed by gradually releasing—while attending to the hair, one should direct mindfulness to the body hairs while still having regard for the hair. As long as the body hairs do not present themselves, one should attend, thinking, 'Hair, hair.' But when the body hairs do present themselves, then, abandoning the hair, mindfulness should be established on the body hairs. In the same way, attention should be directed to the nails and so on.

Tatridaṃ [V 0.0245] opammaṃ – yathā hi jalūkā gacchamānā yāva purato [P 0.0259] patiṭṭhaṃ na labhati tāva pacchato naṅguṭṭhena gahitaṭṭhānaṃ na muñcati; yadā pana purato patiṭṭhaṃ labhati tadā naṅguṭṭhaṃ ukkhipitvā mukhena gahitaṭṭhāne ṭhapeti; evameva kese manasikarontena manasikaronteneva kesesu sāpekkhena hutvā lomesu sati pesetabbā. Yāva lomā na upaṭṭhahanti tāva ‘kesā kesā’ti manasikātabbā. Yadā lomā upaṭṭhahanti tadā kese vissajjetvā lomesu sati upaṭṭhapetabbā. Evaṃ nakhādīsupi manasikāro pavattetabbo.

Here is the simile: Just as a leech, while moving, does not release the spot held by its tail until it finds a foothold ahead; but when it does find a foothold ahead, it lifts its tail and places it at the spot held by its mouth. So too, while attending to the hair, one should direct mindfulness to the body hairs while still having regard for the hair. Until the body hairs present themselves, one should attend, thinking, 'Hair, hair.' When the body hairs present themselves, one should relinquish the hair and establish mindfulness on the body hairs. In the same way, attention should be directed to the nails and so on.

Evaṃ pavattentena appanā hotīti vuttamanasikārakosallaṃ sampādetabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Idañhi appanākammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontassa appanaṃ pāpuṇāti; paṭhamaṃyeva tāva na upaṭṭhāti; anamataggasmiñhi saṃsāravaṭṭe ca nānārammaṇesu vaḍḍhitaṃ cittaṃ ‘kesā’ti āvajjitamatte sajjhāyasotānusārena gantvā matthaluṅge patiṭṭhāti. ‘Matthaluṅga’nti āvajjitamatte sajjhāyasotānusārena āgantvā kesesu patiṭṭhāti. Manasikarontassa manasikarontassa pana so so koṭṭhāso upaṭṭhāti. Sati [M 0.0247] samādhināpi tiṭṭhamānā pavattati. Tena yo yo koṭṭhāso adhikataraṃ upaṭṭhāti tattha tattha dviguṇena yogaṃ katvā appanā pāpetabbā. Evaṃ appanāya pāpitakālato paṭṭhāya sesakoṭṭhāsesu akilamanto appanaṃ pāpeti. Tattha tālavanamakkaṭova opammaṃ.

Thus, when it is said that absorption occurs by proceeding in this way, skill in the aforesaid mental attention must be developed. How? For one who attends to this meditation subject for absorption, absorption is attained; at first, however, it does not become manifest. For in the beginningless round of existence, the mind has grown accustomed to various objects, and when one merely turns the mind to 'hairs,' following the current of recitation, it goes and settles on the brain. When one merely turns the mind to 'brain,' following the current of recitation, it comes and settles on the hairs. But as one attends again and again, that particular part becomes manifest. Mindfulness, being established, proceeds also by means of concentration. Therefore, whichever part becomes more manifest, one must make double the effort there and attain absorption. From the time absorption is attained in this way, one attains absorption in the remaining parts without weariness. Here, the simile of the monkey in the palmyra forest applies.

Apicettha evampi yojanā veditabbā – dvattiṃsatālakasmiñhi tālavane makkaṭo paṭivasati. Taṃ gahetukāmo luddo koṭiyaṃ ṭhitatālamūle ṭhatvā ukkuṭṭhimakāsi. Mānajātiko makkaṭo taṃ taṃ tālaṃ laṅghitvā pariyantatāle aṭṭhāsi. Luddo tatthapi gantvā ukkuṭṭhimakāsi. Makkaṭo puna tatheva purimatāle patiṭṭhāsi. So aparāparaṃ anubandhiyamāno kilamanto tassa tasseva tālassa mūle ṭhatvā ukkuṭṭhukkuṭṭhikāle uṭṭhahitvā gacchanto gacchanto atikilamanto ekassa tālassa makuḷapaṇṇasūciṃ daḷhaṃ gahetvā dhanukoṭiyā vijjhitvā gaṇhantopi na palāyati.

Here too, this application should be understood: In a palmyra forest of thirty-two palm trees, a monkey dwells. A hunter, wishing to catch it, stood at the base of a palm tree at one edge and made a threatening call. The proud monkey, leaping from one palm tree to another, stood at the palm tree at the opposite edge. The hunter went there too and made a threatening call. The monkey then settled again on the first palm tree. Being pursued again and again, it grew weary. Going back and forth, it became utterly exhausted and tightly grasped the needle-like tip of a palm sprout leaf. Even when pierced with the tip of the bow and seized, it did not flee.

Tattha dvattiṃsa tālā viya dvattiṃsa koṭṭhāsā; makkaṭo viya cittaṃ; luddo viya yogāvacaro; luddena tālamūle ṭhatvā [P 0.0260] ukkuṭṭhikāle mānajātikassa makkaṭassa palāyitvā pariyantakoṭiyaṃ ṭhitakālo viya anamatagge saṃsāravaṭṭe ca nānārammaṇesu vaḍḍhitacittassa ‘kesā’ti āvajjitamatte sajjhāyasotānusārena gantvā matthaluṅge patiṭṭhānaṃ; pariyantakoṭiyaṃ ṭhatvā [V 0.0246] ukkuṭṭhe orimakoṭiṃ āgamanakālo viya ‘matthaluṅga’nti āvajjitamatte sajjhāyasotānusārena gantvā kesesu patiṭṭhānaṃ; aparāparaṃ anubandhiyamānassa kilamantassa ukkuṭṭhukkuṭṭhiṭṭhāne uṭṭhānakālo viya manasikarontassa manasikarontassa tasmiṃ tasmiṃ koṭṭhāse upaṭṭhahante satiyā patiṭṭhāya patiṭṭhāya gamanaṃ; dhanukoṭiyā vijjhitvā gaṇhantassāpi apalāyanakālo viya yo koṭṭhāso adhikataraṃ upaṭṭhāti, tasmiṃ dviguṇaṃ manasikāraṃ katvā appanāya pāpanaṃ.

There, the thirty-two parts are like the thirty-two palm trees; the mind is like the monkey; the yogī is like the hunter. Just as when the hunter, standing at the base of a palm tree, makes a threatening call, the proud monkey flees and stands at the palm tree at the far edge—so too, when one merely turns the mind, which has grown accustomed to various objects in the beginningless round of existence, to 'hairs,' it follows the current of recitation and settles on the brain. Just as when the threatening call is made, the monkey, standing at the palm tree at the far edge, returns to the near edge—so too, when one merely turns the mind to 'brain,' it follows the current of recitation and settles on the hairs. Just as the monkey, growing weary from being pursued again and again, rises up in the place where the threatening call is made—so too, as one directs attention repeatedly, the mind goes to each part as it becomes manifest, with mindfulness being established again and again. Just as the monkey does not flee even when pierced with the tip of the bow and seized—so too, one attains absorption by applying double the attention to whichever part becomes more manifest.

Tattha appanāya pāpitakālato paṭṭhāya sesakoṭṭhāsesu akilamantova appanaṃ pāpessati. Tasmā ‘paṭikūlaṃ paṭikūla’nti punappunaṃ āvajjitabbaṃ samannāharitabbaṃ, takkāhataṃ vitakkāhataṃ kātabbaṃ. Evaṃ karontassa cattāro khandhā paṭikūlārammaṇā honti, appanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Pubbabhāgacittāni parikammaupacārasaṅkhātāni savitakkasavicārānīti sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttasadisameva. Ekaṃ pana koṭṭhāsaṃ manasikarontassa ekameva [M 0.0248] paṭhamajjhānaṃ nibbattati. Pāṭiyekkaṃ manasikarontassa dvattiṃsa paṭhamajjhānāni nibbattanti. Hatthe gahitapañhāvatthu pākatikameva.

There, from the time absorption is attained, one will attain absorption in the remaining parts without weariness. Therefore, one should repeatedly turn the mind to and attend to 'repulsive, repulsive,' and it should be struck by reasoning and struck by initial thought. By doing so, the four aggregates become a repulsive object, and one attains absorption. The preliminary states of mind, known as preparatory and access, are accompanied by initial and sustained thought—all this is just as previously described. However, when attending to one part, only one first jhāna is produced. When attending to each part individually, thirty-two first jhānas are produced. The question-object grasped in the hand is simply the natural one.

So taṃ nimittanti so bhikkhu taṃ kammaṭṭhānanimittaṃ. Āsevatīti sevati bhajati. Bhāvetīti vaḍḍheti. Bahulīkarotīti punappunaṃ karoti. Svāvatthitaṃ vavatthapetīti suvavatthitaṃ karoti. Bahiddhā kāye cittaṃ upasaṃharatīti evaṃ katvā bahiddhā parassa kāye attano cittaṃ upasaṃharati ṭhapeti peseti.

`So taṃ nimittaṃ` ('He... that sign'): `so` refers to that monk; `taṃ nimittaṃ` refers to that meditation sign. `Āsevati` ('He cultivates it'): he resorts to it, frequents it. `Bhāveti` ('He develops it'): he makes it grow. `Bahulīkaroti` ('He makes it much'): he does it repeatedly. `Svāvatthitaṃ vavatthapeti` ('He establishes it as well-established'): he makes it well-defined. `Bahiddhā kāye cittaṃ upasaṃharati` ('He directs his mind externally towards the body'): having done so, he directs, places, and sends his own mind externally to another's body.

Atthissa kāyeti atthi assa kāye. Ajjhattabahiddhākāye cittaṃ upasaṃharatīti kālena attano kālena paresaṃ kāye cittaṃ upanāmeti. Atthi [P 0.0261] kāyeti idaṃ yasmā na ekantena attano kāyo nāpi parasseva kāyo adhippeto, tasmā vuttaṃ. Ettha pana attano jīvamānakasarīre ‘paṭikūla’nti parikammaṃ karontassa appanāpi upacārampi jāyati. Parassa jīvamānakasarīre ‘paṭikūla’nti manasikarontassa neva appanā jāyati, na upacāraṃ. Nanu ca dasasu asubhesu ubhayampetaṃ jāyatīti? Āma, jāyati. Tāni hi anupādinnakapakkhe ṭhitāni. Tasmā tattha appanāpi upacārampi jāyati. Idaṃ pana upādinnakapakkhe ṭhitaṃ. Tenevettha ubhayampetaṃ na jāyati. Asubhānupassanāsaṅkhātā pana vipassanābhāvanā hotīti veditabbā. Imasmiṃ pabbe kiṃ kathitanti? Samathavipassanā kathitā.

There is a body: that is, there is a body in this person. He directs his mind internally and externally towards the body: at times he applies his mind to his own body, and at times to the bodies of others. 'There is a body'—this is said because neither one's own body alone nor another's body alone is intended. Here, when one practices the preliminary work of 'repulsiveness' on one's own living body, both absorption and access concentration arise. But when one attends to 'repulsiveness' on the living body of another, neither absorption nor access concentration arises. But do not both arise in the ten foulness meditation subjects? Yes, they do. For those are established in the unappropriated class. Therefore, both absorption and access concentration arise there. This, however, is established in the appropriated class. Hence, in this case, neither of these arises. It should be understood that insight development, known as the contemplation of foulness, occurs. What has been discussed in this section? Serenity and insight have been discussed.

Idānettha [V 0.0247] evaṃ sabbaṃ manasikārasādhāraṇaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ. Etesañhi –

Now here, all these miscellaneous points should be understood as common to all acts of mental attention. For of these—

Nimittato lakkhaṇato, dhātuto atha suññato;

Khandhādito ca viññeyyo, kesādīnaṃ vinicchayo.

By sign, by characteristic, by element, and also by emptiness; and by aggregates and so on, the analysis of hair and the like should be understood.

Tattha ‘nimittato’ti dvattiṃsākāre saṭṭhisataṃ nimittāni, yesaṃ vasena yogāvacaro dvattiṃsākāraṃ koṭṭhāsato pariggaṇhāti, seyyathidaṃ – kesassa vaṇṇanimittaṃ, saṇṭhānanimittaṃ, disānimittaṃ, okāsanimittaṃ, paricchedanimittanti pañca nimittāni honti. Lomādīsupi eseva nayo.

Here, 'by sign' refers to one hundred and sixty signs in the thirty-two aspects, by means of which the yogī comprehends the thirty-two aspects as parts. Namely: the sign of the hair's color, the sign of its shape, the sign of its direction, the sign of its location, and the sign of its demarcation—these are the five signs. The same method applies to body hair and so on.

‘Lakkhaṇato’ti dvattiṃsākāre aṭṭhavīsatisataṃ lakkhaṇāni honti, yesaṃ vasena yogāvacaro dvattiṃsākāraṃ lakkhaṇato manasikaroti, seyyathidaṃ [M 0.0249] – kese thaddhattalakkhaṇaṃ, ābandhattalakkhaṇaṃ, uṇhattalakkhaṇaṃ, vitthambhanalakkhaṇanti cattāri lakkhaṇāni honti. Lomādīsupi eseva nayo.

Regarding 'by characteristic,' there are one hundred and twenty-eight characteristics in the thirty-two aspects. Through these, the yogī attends to the thirty-two aspects by their characteristics, as follows: In hair, there is the characteristic of stiffness, the characteristic of binding, the characteristic of heat, and the characteristic of distending—these are the four characteristics. The same method applies to body hair and so on.

‘Dhātuto’ti dvattiṃsākāre “catudhāturo ayaṃ, bhikkhu, puriso”ti vuttāsu dhātūsu aṭṭhavīsatisataṃ dhātuyo honti, yāsaṃ vasena yogāvacaro dvattiṃsākāraṃ dhātuto pariggaṇhāti, seyyathidaṃ – kese kakkhaḷatā pathavīdhātu, ābandhanatā āpodhātu, uṇhatā tejodhātu, vitthambhanatā vāyodhātūti catasso dhātuyo honti. Lomādīsupi eseva nayo.

Regarding 'by elements': In the thirty-two aspects, among the elements spoken of in the phrase, 'This person, O monk, is composed of four elements,' there are one hundred and twenty-eight elements. By means of these, the yogī comprehends the thirty-two aspects by way of elements. That is: in hair, hardness is the earth element, binding is the water element, heat is the fire element, and distending is the air element—these are the four elements. The same method applies to body hair and so on.

‘Suññato’ti dvattiṃsākāre channavuti suññatā honti, yāsaṃ vasena [P 0.0262] yogāvacaro dvattiṃsākāraṃ suññato vipassati, seyyathidaṃ – kesā suññā attena vā attaniyena vā niccena vā dhuvena vā sassatena vā avipariṇāmadhammena vāti. Kese tāva attasuññatā, attaniyasuññatā, niccabhāvasuññatāti tisso suññatā honti. Lomādīsupi eseva nayo.

Regarding 'by emptiness,' in the thirty-two aspects there are ninety-six emptinesses, through which the yogī contemplates the thirty-two aspects as empty, that is: hairs are empty of self or of what belongs to self, of permanence or of stability or of lastingness or of a nature not subject to change. In hair, there are three emptinesses: emptiness of self, emptiness of what belongs to self, and emptiness of a permanent state. The same method applies to body hair and so on.

‘Khandhādito’ti dvattiṃsākāre kesādīsu khandhādivasena pariggayhamānesu kesā kati khandhā honti, kati āyatanāni, kati dhātuyo, kati saccāni, kati satipaṭṭhānānītiādinā nayena pettha vinicchayo viññātabbo.

Regarding 'by aggregates and so on': When the hairs and so on among the thirty-two aspects are comprehended by way of aggregates, etc., the analysis here should be understood by the method of inquiring: 'Of how many aggregates do the hairs consist? How many sense bases, how many elements, how many truths, how many foundations of mindfulness?' and so on.

357. Evaṃ [V 0.0248] ajjhattādibhedato tividhena kāyānupassanaṃ vitthārato dassetvā idāni “kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno”tiādīni padāni bhājetvā dassetuṃ anupassītiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha yāya anupassanāya kāyānupassī nāma hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ tattha katamā anupassanā? Yā paññā pajānanātiādi vuttaṃ. Ātāpītiādīsupi eseva nayo.

357. Having thus explained in detail the threefold contemplation of the body according to its divisions of internal, external, and so on, the analysis of the phrases 'contemplating the body, ardent, fully aware,' etc., is now begun, starting with 'contemplating,' in order to explain them. Here, in order to show by what contemplation one is called a 'contemplator of the body,' it is said: 'What is that contemplation? It is the wisdom that is discerning,' etc. The same method applies to 'ardent,' etc., as well.

Tattha paññā pajānanātiādīni heṭṭhā cittuppādakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 16) vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Upetotiādīni sabbāni aññamaññavevacanāni. Apica āsevanavasena upeto, bhāvanāvasena suṭṭhu upetoti samupeto[M 0.0250]. Upāgato samupāgato, upapanno sampannoti imesupi dvīsu dukesu ayameva nayo. Bahulīkāravasena pana samannāgatoti evamettha yojanā veditabbā. Iminā ātāpena upetoti ādīsupi eseva nayo.

Here, the phrases 'wisdom is discerning,' etc., should be understood in the same way as explained earlier in the commentary on the section on the arising of consciousness. The terms 'endowed,' etc., are all synonyms of one another. Moreover, 'endowed' (upeta) is by way of frequenting; 'well endowed' (suṭṭhu upeta) is by way of development—thus 'fully endowed' (samupeta). 'Approached' (upāgata), 'fully approached' (samupāgata); 'possessed' (upapanna), 'well-possessed' (sampanna)—in these two pairs too, the same method applies. But in terms of repeated practice, one is 'fully endowed' (samannāgata)—this is how the connection should be understood here. The same method applies to 'endowed with this ardour' (iminā ātāpena upeto), etc., as well.

Viharatīti pade ‘tattha katamo vihāro’ti pucchaṃ akatvā puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya desento iriyatītiādimāha. Tassattho – catunnaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ aññatarasamaṅgībhāvato iriyati. Tehi iriyāpathacatukkehi kāyasakaṭavattanena vattati. Ekaṃ iriyāpathadukkhaṃ aparena iriyāpathena bādhitvā ciraṭṭhitikabhāvena sarīrakkhanato pāleti. Ekasmiṃ iriyāpathe asaṇṭhahitvā sabbiriyāpathavatanato yapeti. Tena tena iriyāpathena tathā tathā kāyassa yāpanato yāpeti. Cirakālavattāpanato carati. Iriyāpathena iriyāpathaṃ vicchinditvā jīvitaharaṇato viharati.
