Regarding the word 'abides' (viharati), without raising the question 'What is abiding here?', the teaching is given from the standpoint of the person, saying 'moves' (iriyati), etc. Its meaning is: one moves (iriyati) by being endowed with one of the four postures. One acts (vattati) by the turning of the body-cart through these four postures. One protects (pāleti) the body by counteracting the discomfort of one posture with another, thereby maintaining a long-lasting state. One maintains oneself (yapeti) by not remaining fixed in one posture but functioning through all postures. One maintains (yāpeti) the body in that way by means of that posture. One continues (carati) by causing it to be maintained for a long time. One dwells (viharati) by interrupting one posture with another, thereby carrying on life.

362. Sveva kāyo lokoti yasmiṃ kāye kāyānupassī viharati, sveva kāyo lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena loko. Yasmā panassa kāye pahīyamānaṃ abhijjhādomanassaṃ vedanādīsupi pahīyati eva, tasmā pañcapi upādānakkhandhā lokoti vuttaṃ.

362. That very body is the world: the body in which one dwells contemplating the body is the 'world' in the sense of breaking apart and crumbling. But since the covetousness and displeasure that are abandoned in relation to the body are also abandoned in relation to feelings, etc., therefore the five aggregates of clinging are also called the world.

Santātiādīsupi [P 0.0263] nirodhavasena santatāya santā. Bhāvanāya samitattā samitā. Vatthupariññāya appavattivūpasamavasena vūpasantā. Nirodhasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ gatāti atthaṅgatā. Punappunaṃ nibbattiyā paṭibāhitattā ativiya atthaṃ gatāti abbhatthaṅgatā. Appitāti vināsitā, appavattiyaṃ ṭhapitātipi attho. Byappitāti suvināsitā, ativiya appavattiyaṃ ṭhapitātipi attho. Yathā puna na anvassavanti evaṃ sositattā sositā. Suṭṭhu sositāti visositā[V 0.0249], sukkhāpitāti attho. Vigatantā katāti byantī katā. Ettha ca anupassanāya kammaṭṭhānavihārena kammaṭṭhānikassa kāyapariharaṇaṃ, ātāpena sammappadhānaṃ, satisampajaññena kammaṭṭhānapariharaṇūpāyo; satiyā vā kāyānupassanāvasena paṭiladdho samatho, sampajaññena vipassanā, abhijjhādomanassavinayena bhāvanāphalaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

In the case of `santā` and so on, it is `santā` because it is appeased by way of cessation. It is `samitā` because it is calmed through cultivation. It is `vūpasantā` by way of the pacification of non-arising through the full understanding of the basis. It is `atthaṅgatā` because it has gone to the state called cessation. It is `abbhatthaṅgatā` because it has gone to an utter cessation, being repeatedly prevented from arising. `Appitā` means destroyed, or the meaning is 'placed in non-arising.' `Byappitā` means thoroughly destroyed, or the meaning is 'placed in utter non-arising.' It is `sositā` because it is dried up in such a way that the taints do not flow out again. It is `visositā` because it is thoroughly dried up, meaning 'made completely dry.' It is `byantīkatā` because it is made to have its ends removed. And here, it should be understood that for the meditator, the maintenance of the body is by means of the meditative abiding of contemplation; right exertion is by means of ardour; the means of maintaining the meditation subject is by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension; or, that tranquility is attained by means of mindfulness in the sense of contemplation of the body, insight is by means of clear comprehension, and the fruit of cultivation is said to be the removal of covetousness and displeasure.

Kāyānupassanāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the contemplation of the body is concluded.

Vedanānupassanāniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Contemplation of Feelings

363. Vedanānupassanāniddesepi [M 0.0251] heṭṭhā vuttasadisaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamānotiādīsu pana sukhaṃ vedananti kāyikaṃ vā cetasikaṃ vā sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘ahaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānātīti attho. Tattha kāmaṃ uttānaseyyakāpi dārakā thaññapivanādikāle sukhaṃ vedayamānā ‘sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmā’ti pajānanti, na panetaṃ evarūpaṃ jānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Evarūpañhi jānanaṃ sattūpaladdhiṃ nappajahati, sattasaññaṃ na ugghāṭeti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā vā na hoti. Imassa pana bhikkhuno jānanaṃ sattūpaladdhiṃ pajahati, sattasaññaṃ ugghāṭeti, kammaṭṭhānañceva satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā ca hoti. ‘Idañhi ko vedayati, kassa vedanā, kiṃ kāraṇā vedanā’ti evaṃ sampajānavediyanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

363. In the exposition on the contemplation of feelings, too, it should be understood in the same way as stated previously. When it is said, "Feeling a pleasant feeling," and so forth, the meaning is that one understands, "I am feeling a pleasant feeling," whether one is feeling a bodily or mental pleasant feeling. Here, it is true that even infants lying on their backs, when feeling pleasure while drinking mother's milk and so on, understand, "We are feeling a pleasant feeling." But this is not the kind of knowing being referred to. For such knowing does not abandon the perception of a being, does not uproot the notion of a being, and is neither a meditation subject nor the development of mindfulness. However, this monk’s knowing abandons the perception of a being, uproots the notion of a being, and is both a meditation subject and the development of mindfulness. It is said with reference to feeling with clear comprehension: "Who feels this? Whose feeling is this? What is the cause of this feeling?"

Tattha ko vedayatīti? Na koci satto vā puggalo vā vedayati. Kassa vedanāti? Na kassaci sattassa vā puggalassa vā vedanā. Kiṃ kāraṇā vedanāti? Vatthuārammaṇā ca panesā vedanā. Tasmā esa evaṃ pajānāti – ‘taṃ taṃ sukhādīnaṃ vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva vedayati; taṃ pana vedanāpavattiṃ [P 0.0264] upādāya ‘ahaṃ vedayāmī’ti vohāramattaṃ hotī’ti. Evaṃ vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva vedayatīti sallakkhento ‘esa sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānātīti veditabbo, cittalapabbate aññataro thero viya.

Here, 'Who feels?' means no being or person feels. 'Whose feeling?' means the feeling belongs to no being or person. 'What is the cause of feeling?' This feeling, moreover, has a basis and an object. Therefore, one understands thus: 'It is feeling itself that feels, having taken as its object this or that basis of pleasant feelings and so on; but the notion "I feel" is merely a convention based on the occurrence of that feeling.' Reflecting thus that only feeling feels by taking a basis as its object, one is to be understood as understanding, 'I feel a pleasant feeling,' like a certain elder on Mount Cittalapabbata.

Thero kira aphāsukakāle balavavedanāya nitthunanto aparāparaṃ parivattati. Tameko daharo āha [V 0.0250] – “kataraṃ vo, bhante, ṭhānaṃ rujatī”ti? “Āvuso, pāṭiyekkaṃ rujanaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthi; vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva vedayatī”ti. “Evaṃ jānanakālato paṭṭhāya adhivāsetuṃ vaṭṭati no, bhante”ti. “Adhivāsemi, āvuso”ti. “Adhivāsanā, bhante, seyyo”ti. Thero adhivāsesi. Vāto yāva hadayā phālesi. Mañcake antāni rāsīkatāni ahesuṃ. Thero daharassa dassesi – “vaṭṭatāvuso, ettakā adhivāsanā”ti? Daharo tuṇhī ahosi. Thero vīriyasamādhiṃ yojetvā sahapaṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇitvā samasīsī hutvā parinibbāyi.

The elder, it seems, during a time of discomfort, groaned and tossed about due to severe pain. A young monk asked him, "Venerable sir, which part of you is in pain?" "Friend, there is no particular place of pain; it is feeling itself that feels, taking a basis as its object," replied the elder. "Since you know this, venerable sir, is it not right for you to endure it?" said the young monk. "I do endure it, friend," said the elder. "Endurance, venerable sir, is better," replied the young monk. The elder endured. The wind element tore through him, up to his heart. His intestines became heaped up on the bed. The elder showed the young monk, "Friend, is this much endurance sufficient?" The young monk remained silent. The elder, applying effort and concentration, attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges, and then, lying perfectly still, passed into final Nibbāna.

Yathā [M 0.0252] ca sukhaṃ, evaṃ dukkhaṃ…pe… nirāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘nirāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī”ti pajānāti. Iti bhagavā rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathento vedanāvasena kathesi. Duvidhañhi kammaṭṭhānaṃ – rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ arūpakammaṭṭhānañca; rūpapariggaho arūpapariggahotipi etadeva vuccati. Tattha bhagavā rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathento saṅkhepamanasikāravasena vā vitthāramanasikāravasena vā catudhātuvavatthānaṃ kathesi. Tadubhayampi visuddhimagge sabbākārato dassitameva.

Just as with pleasant feeling, so too with painful feeling... and so on... experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that is unworldly, he understands: 'I am experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that is unworldly.' Thus, the Blessed One, having taught the meditation subject of form, taught the meditation subject of the formless by way of feeling. For the meditation subject is twofold: the meditation subject of form and the meditation subject of the formless; this is also called the comprehension of form and the comprehension of the formless. Therein, the Blessed One, when teaching the meditation subject of form, taught the analysis of the four elements either by way of brief attention or by way of detailed attention. Both of these are shown in all aspects in the Visuddhimagga.

Arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ pana kathento yebhuyyena vedanāvasena kathesi. Tividho hi arūpakammaṭṭhāne abhiniveso – phassavasena, vedanāvasena, cittavasenāti. Kathaṃ? Ekaccassa hi saṃkhittena vā vitthārena vā pariggahite rūpakammaṭṭhāne tasmiṃ ārammaṇe cittacetasikānaṃ paṭhamābhinipāto taṃ ārammaṇaṃ phusanto uppajjamāno phasso pākaṭo hoti. Ekaccassa taṃ ārammaṇaṃ anubhavantī uppajjamānā vedanā pākaṭā hoti. Ekaccassa taṃ ārammaṇaṃ pariggahetvā vijānantaṃ uppajjamānaṃ viññāṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti.

Now, when teaching the formless meditation subject, he mostly taught it by way of feeling. For there are three kinds of engagement with the formless meditation subject—by way of contact, by way of feeling, and by way of consciousness. How so? For one person, when the form meditation subject has been grasped briefly or in detail, the contact that arises touching that object—being the first impact of mind and mental factors upon that object—becomes manifest. For another, the feeling that arises experiencing that object becomes manifest. For yet another, the consciousness that arises cognizing that object, having apprehended it, becomes manifest.

Tattha [P 0.0265] yassa phasso pākaṭo hoti, sopi ‘na kevalaṃ phassova uppajjati; tena saddhiṃ tadevārammaṇaṃ anubhavamānā vedanāpi uppajjati, sañjānamānā saññāpi, cetayamānā cetanāpi, vijānanamānaṃ viññāṇampi uppajjatī’ti phassapañcamakeyeva pariggaṇhāti. Yassa vedanā pākaṭā hoti, sopi ‘na kevalaṃ vedanāva uppajjati; tāya saddhiṃ tadevārammaṇaṃ phusamāno phassopi uppajjati, sañjānanamānā saññāpi, cetayamānā cetanāpi, vijānanamānaṃ viññāṇampi uppajjatī’ti phassapañcamakeyeva pariggaṇhāti. Yassa viññāṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, sopi ‘na kevalaṃ viññāṇameva uppajjati; tena saddhiṃ tadevārammaṇaṃ phusamāno phassopi [V 0.0251] uppajjati, anubhavamānā vedanāpi, sañjānanamānā saññāpi, cetayamānā cetanāpi uppajjatī’ti phassapañcamakeyeva pariggaṇhāti.

Here, for one to whom contact is evident, they also comprehend: 'Not only does contact itself arise; along with it, experiencing that same object, feeling also arises; perceiving, perception also arises; intending, volition also arises; cognizing, consciousness also arises.' Thus, they comprehend it as simply the pentad beginning with contact. For one to whom feeling is evident, they also comprehend: 'Not only does feeling itself arise; along with it, contacting that same object, contact also arises; perceiving, perception also arises; intending, volition also arises; cognizing, consciousness also arises.' Thus, they comprehend it as simply the pentad beginning with contact. For one to whom consciousness is evident, they also comprehend: 'Not only does consciousness itself arise; along with it, contacting that same object, contact also arises; experiencing, feeling also arises; perceiving, perception also arises; intending, volition also arises.' Thus, they comprehend it as simply the pentad beginning with contact.

So ‘ime phassapañcamakā dhammā kiṃnissitā’ti upadhārento ‘vatthunissitā’ti pajānāti. Vatthu nāma karajakāyo; yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “idañca pana me viññāṇaṃ etthasitaṃ, etthapaṭibaddha”nti (dī. ni. 1.235). So atthato bhūtāni [M 0.0253] ceva upādārūpāni ca. Evamettha vatthu rūpaṃ, phassapañcamakā nāmanti nāmarūpameva passati. Rūpañcettha rūpakkhandho, nāmaṃ cattāro arūpino khandhāti pañcakkhandhamattaṃ hoti. Nāmarūpavinimuttā hi pañcakkhandhā pañcakkhandhavinimuttaṃ vā nāmarūpaṃ natthi.

So, when considering, 'On what do these phenomena, with contact as the fifth, depend?', one understands that they depend on a base. The base is the kamma-born body; referring to this, it is said: 'And this consciousness of mine is based here, bound here' (DN I 235). So, in essence, it includes both the primary elements and derived form. Thus, here the base is form, and the phenomena with contact as the fifth are name—thus one sees only name-and-form. Here, form is the form aggregate, and name is the four immaterial aggregates—thus there is merely the five aggregates. For there are no five aggregates apart from name-and-form, nor name-and-form apart from the five aggregates.

So ‘ime pañcakkhandhā kiṃhetukā’ti upaparikkhanto ‘avijjādihetukā’ti passati; tato paccayo ceva paccayuppannañca idaṃ; añño satto vā puggalo vā natthi; suddhasaṅkhārapuñjamattamevāti sappaccayanāmarūpavasenava tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā vipassanāpaṭipāṭiyā ‘aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā’ti sammasanto vicarati. So ‘ajja ajjā’ti paṭivedhaṃ ākaṅkhamāno tathārūpe divase utusappāyaṃ, puggalasappāyaṃ, bhojanasappāyaṃ, dhammasavanasappāyaṃ vā labhitvā ekapallaṅkena nisinnova vipassanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā arahatte patiṭṭhāti. Evaṃ imesaṃ tiṇṇampi janānaṃ yāva arahattā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathitaṃ hoti.

When examining, 'What is the cause of these five aggregates?' one sees that they are caused by ignorance and so forth; then this is the condition and the conditionally arisen; there is no other being or person; it is merely a heap of bare formations. By attributing the three characteristics to name-and-form dependent on conditions, one proceeds through the sequence of insight, contemplating 'impermanent, suffering, not-self.' Desiring breakthrough 'today, today,' on such a day, having obtained suitable weather, suitable person, suitable food, or suitable hearing of the Dhamma, sitting in one cross-legged posture, and bringing insight to its peak, one is established in arahantship. Thus, the meditation subject for these three types of individuals is taught up to arahantship.

Idha pana bhagavā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathento vedanāvasena [P 0.0266] kathesi. Phassavasena vā hi viññāṇavasena vā kathiyamānaṃ na pākaṭaṃ hoti, andhakāraṃ viya khāyati. Vedanāvasena pana pākaṭaṃ hoti. Kasmā? Vedanānaṃ uppattipākaṭatāya. Sukhadukkhavedanānañhi uppatti pākaṭā. Yadā sukhaṃ uppajjati, sakalasarīraṃ khobhentaṃ maddantaṃ pharamānaṃ abhisandayamānaṃ satadhotasappiṃ khādāpayantaṃ viya, satapākatelaṃ makkhāpayamānaṃ viya, udakaghaṭasahassena pariḷāhaṃ nibbāpayamānaṃ viya, ‘aho sukhaṃ! Aho sukhanti’! Vācaṃ nicchārayamānameva uppajjati. Yadā dukkhaṃ uppajjati, sakalasarīraṃ khobhentaṃ maddantaṃ pharamānaṃ abhisandayamānaṃ tattaphālaṃ pavesentaṃ viya, vilīnatambalohena āsiñcantaṃ viya, sukkhatiṇavanappatimhi araññe dāruukkākalāpaṃ pakkhipamānaṃ viya ‘aho dukkhaṃ! Aho dukkhanti!’ Vippalāpayamānameva uppajjati. Iti sukhadukkhavedanānaṃ uppatti pākaṭā hoti.

Here, however, the Blessed One, when teaching the formless meditation subject, taught it by way of feeling. For when taught by way of contact or by way of consciousness, it is not clear—it appears like darkness. But when taught by way of feeling, it is clear. Why? Because the arising of feelings is evident. For the arising of pleasant and painful feelings is evident. When pleasant feeling arises, it arises agitating, crushing, pervading, and saturating the entire body, as if making one eat ghee washed a hundred times, as if anointing with oil boiled a hundred times, as if extinguishing a burning fever with a thousand pots of water, and as if making one utter, 'Ah, happiness! Ah, happiness!' When painful feeling arises, it arises agitating, crushing, pervading, and saturating the entire body, as if inserting a hot iron plate, as if pouring molten copper, as if throwing a bundle of firebrands into a forest of dry grass, and as if making one cry out, 'Ah, pain! Ah, pain!' Thus, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings is evident.

Adukkhamasukhā [V 0.0252] pana duddīpanā andhakārā avibhūtā. Sā sukhadukkhānaṃ apagame sātāsātapaṭikkhepavasena majjhattākārabhūtā adukkhamasukhā vedanāti nayato gaṇhantassa pākaṭā hoti. Yathā kiṃ? Antarā piṭṭhipāsāṇaṃ āruhitvā palāyantassa migassa anupathaṃ gacchanto migaluddako piṭṭhipāsāṇassa orabhāge aparabhāgepi padaṃ disvā majjhe apassantopi [M 0.0254] ‘ito āruḷho, ito oruḷho, majjhe piṭṭhipāsāṇe iminā padesena gato bhavissatī’ti nayato jānāti. Evaṃ āruḷhaṭṭhāne padaṃ viya hi sukhāya vedanāya uppatti pākaṭā hoti; oruḷhaṭṭhāne padaṃ viya dukkhāya vedanāya uppatti pākaṭā hoti. ‘Ito āruḷho, ito oruḷho, majjhe evaṃ gato’ti nayato gahaṇaṃ viya sukhadukkhānaṃ apagame sātāsātapaṭikkhepavasena majjhattākārabhūtā adukkhamasukhā vedanāti nayato gaṇhantassa pākaṭā hoti.

The neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, however, is difficult to discern, obscure, and unclear. It becomes evident to one who grasps it by inference as the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, which is of a neutral nature in the absence of pleasure and pain and by way of rejecting the agreeable and disagreeable. How so? Just as when a deer hunter, following the trail of a deer that has fled after climbing a rocky ridge, sees footprints on the lower and upper parts of the ridge but not in the middle, he infers: 'It climbed up here, descended here, and must have passed through this part of the rocky ridge in the middle.' Similarly, the arising of pleasant feeling is evident like a footprint at the place of ascent; the arising of painful feeling is evident like a footprint at the place of descent. The inference 'It climbed here, descended here, and passed through the middle like this' is akin to how the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, which is of a neutral nature in the absence of pleasure and pain and by way of rejecting the agreeable and disagreeable, becomes evident to one who grasps it by inference.

Evaṃ bhagavā paṭhamaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā pacchā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathento vedanāvasena vinivattetvā dassesi; na kevalañca idheva evaṃ dasseti, dīghanikāyamhi mahānidāne, sakkapañhe, mahāsatipaṭṭhāne[P 0.0267], majjhimanikāyamhi satipaṭṭhāne ca cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaye, mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaye, cūḷavedalle, mahāvedalle, raṭṭhapālasutte, māgaṇḍiyasutte, dhātuvibhaṅge, āneñjasappāye, saṃyuttanikāyamhi cūḷanidānasutte, rukkhopame, parivīmaṃsanasutte, sakale vedanāsaṃyutteti evaṃ anekesu suttesu paṭhamaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā pacchā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ vedanāvasena vinivattetvā dassesi. Yathā ca tesu tesu, evaṃ imasmimpi satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅge paṭhamaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā pacchā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ vedanāvasena vinivattetvā dassesi.

Thus, the Blessed One, having first taught the meditation subject of form, later, when teaching the meditation subject of the formless, showed how to turn away by means of feeling. And not only here did he show it thus, but also in the Dīghanikāya in the Mahānidāna Sutta, the Sakkapañha Sutta, and the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta; in the Majjhimanikāya in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, the Cūḷavedalla Sutta, the Mahāvedalla Sutta, the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, and the Āneñjasappāya Sutta; in the Saṃyuttanikāya in the Cūḷanidāna Sutta, the Rukkhopama Sutta, the Parivīmaṃsana Sutta, and in the entirety of the Vedanāsaṃyutta—in these many discourses, he first taught the meditation subject of form and later showed how to turn away to the formless by means of feeling. Just as in those discourses, so too in this Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness, he first taught the meditation subject of form and later showed how to turn away to the formless by means of feeling.

Tattha sukhaṃ vedanantiādīsu ayaṃ aparopi pajānanapariyāyo – sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmīti pajānātīti sukhavedanākkhaṇe dukkhāya vedanāya abhāvato sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Tena yā pubbe bhūtapubbā dukkhā vedanā, tassā idāni abhāvato imissā ca sukhāya ito paṭhamaṃ abhāvato vedanā nāma aniccā addhuvā vipariṇāmadhammāti itiha tattha sampajāno hoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā –

Here, in the passage beginning 'feeling a pleasant feeling,' there is this further way of understanding: 'Feeling a pleasant feeling, one understands: “I feel a pleasant feeling.”' At the moment of a pleasant feeling, because of the absence of a painful feeling, while feeling a pleasant feeling one understands, 'I feel a pleasant feeling.' Through this, because the painful feeling that was present before is now absent, and because this pleasant feeling was absent before this, one is clearly aware that 'feeling is impermanent, not lasting, and subject to change.' This too was stated by the Blessed One:

“Yasmiṃ, aggivessana, samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, sukhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Yasmiṃ[V 0.0253], aggivessana, samaye dukkhaṃ…pe… adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, adukkhamasukhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Sukhāpi kho, aggivessana[M 0.0255], vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā. Dukkhāpi kho…pe… adukkhamasukhāpi kho, aggivessana, vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā…pe… nirodhadhammā. Evaṃ passaṃ, aggivessana, sutavā ariyasāvako sukhāyapi vedanāya nibbindati, dukkhāyapi vedanāya nibbindati, adukkhamasukhāyapi vedanāya nibbindati, nibbindaṃ virajjati, virāgā vimuccati, vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti; ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti (ma. ni. 2.205).

“At the time, Aggivessana, when one feels a pleasant feeling, one does not at that time feel a painful feeling, nor a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; one feels only a pleasant feeling at that time. At the time, Aggivessana, when one feels a painful… and so on… a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one does not at that time feel a pleasant feeling, nor a painful feeling; one feels only a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling at that time. Pleasant feeling, Aggivessana, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Painful feeling too… and so on… neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling too, Aggivessana, is impermanent, conditioned… and so on… subject to cessation. Seeing thus, Aggivessana, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with pleasant feeling, becomes disenchanted with painful feeling, and becomes disenchanted with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. In the liberated one, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”

Sāmisaṃ [P 0.0268] vā sukhantiādīsu sāmisā sukhā nāma pañcakāmaguṇāmisanissitā cha gehassitasomanassavedanā; nirāmisā sukhā nāma cha nekkhammassitasomanassavedanā; sāmisā dukkhā nāma cha gehassitadomanassavedanā; nirāmisā dukkhā nāma cha nekkhammassitadomanassavedanā; sāmisā adukkhamasukhā nāma cha gehasitaupekkhāvedanā; nirāmisā adukkhamasukhā nāma cha nekkhammassitaupekkhāvedanā. Tāsaṃ vibhāgo uparipaṇṇāse pāḷiyaṃ (ma. ni. 3.304 ādayo) āgatoyeva. So taṃ nimittanti so taṃ vedanānimittaṃ. Bahiddhā vedanāsūti parapuggalassa vedanāsu. Sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamānanti parapuggalaṃ sukhavedanaṃ vedayamānaṃ. Ajjhattabahiddhāti kālena attano kālena parassa vedanāsu cittaṃ upasaṃharati. Imasmiṃ vāre yasmā neva attā, na paro niyamito; tasmā vedanāpariggahamattameva dassetuṃ “idha bhikkhu sukhaṃ vedanaṃ sukhā vedanā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Imasmiṃ pana pabbe suddhavipassanāva kathitāti.

In the passage beginning 'a worldly pleasant feeling,' worldly pleasant feelings are the six kinds of pleasant mental feeling based on the bait of the five strands of sensual pleasure, associated with the household life. Unworldly pleasant feelings are the six kinds of pleasant mental feeling based on renunciation. Worldly painful feelings are the six kinds of painful mental feeling associated with the household life. Unworldly painful feelings are the six kinds of painful mental feeling based on renunciation. Worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are the six kinds of feeling of equanimity associated with the household life. Unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are the six kinds of feeling of equanimity based on renunciation. Their analysis is found in the Pāli text of the Uparipaṇṇāsa (e.g., MN 3.304 ff.). 'That sign' means the sign of that feeling. 'In feelings externally' means in the feelings of another person. 'Feeling a pleasant feeling' means another person feeling a pleasant feeling. 'Internally and externally' means that one directs the mind at times to one's own feelings and at times to another's feelings. In this section, since neither self nor other is specified, in order to show merely the comprehension of feeling, it is said, 'Here, a bhikkhu, a pleasant feeling, a pleasant feeling,' and so on. The rest here is self-evident. In this section, however, only pure insight is discussed.

Vedanānupassanāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Exposition on the Contemplation of Feeling is finished.

Cittānupassanāniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition on the Contemplation of Mind

365. Cittānupassanāniddesepi [V 0.0254] heṭṭhā vuttasadisaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Sarāgaṃ vā cittantiādīsu pana sarāganti aṭṭhavidhaṃ lobhasahagataṃ. Vītarāganti lokiyakusalābyākataṃ. Idaṃ pana yasmā sammasanaṃ na [M 0.0256] dhammasamodhānaṃ, tasmā idha ekapadepi lokuttaraṃ na labbhati. Yasmā pahānekaṭṭhavasena rāgādīhi saha vattanti pahīyanti, tasmā dvīsu padesu nippariyāyena na labbhantīti na gahitāni. Sesāni cattāri akusalacittāni neva purimapadaṃ, na pacchimapadaṃ bhajanti. Sadosanti duvidhaṃ domanassasahagataṃ. Vītadosanti lokiyakusalābyākataṃ. Sesāni dasa akusalacittāni neva purimapadaṃ, na pacchimapadaṃ bhajanti. Samohanti vicikicchāsahagatañceva uddhaccasahagatañcāti duvidhaṃ. Yasmā pana moho sabbākusalesu uppajjati, tasmā [P 0.0269] sesānipi idha vaṭṭanti eva. Imasmiṃ yeva hi duke dvādasākusalacittāni pariyādiṇṇānīti. Vītamohanti lokiyakusalābyākataṃ. Saṃkhittanti thinamiddhānupatitaṃ. Etañhi saṅkuṭitacittaṃ nāma. Vikkhittanti uddhaccasahagataṃ. Etañhi pasaṭacittaṃ nāma.

365. In the Exposition on the Contemplation of Mind too, it should be understood in the same way as stated above, according to the method described. However, in the passage beginning 'a mind with lust,' 'with lust' refers to the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed. 'Without lust' refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate consciousness. But since this is an analysis and not a synthesis of phenomena, the supramundane is not found here even in a single term. Because, in the sense of being something to be abandoned, defilements such as lust are either present or are being abandoned, they are not included as being unconditionally found in these two terms. The remaining four unwholesome types of consciousness do not belong to either the first term or the second term. 'With hate' refers to the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure. 'Without hate' refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate consciousness. The remaining ten unwholesome types of consciousness do not belong to either the first term or the second term. 'With delusion' refers to the two types, that accompanied by doubt and that accompanied by restlessness. However, since delusion arises in all unwholesome states, the remaining ones are also applicable here. Indeed, in this very pair, the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness are encompassed. 'Without delusion' refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate consciousness. 'Contracted' refers to that which is overcome by sloth and torpor. This is called a 'shrunken mind.' 'Distracted' refers to that which is accompanied by restlessness. This is called a 'scattered mind.'

Mahaggatanti rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacarañca. Amahaggatanti kāmāvacaraṃ. Sauttaranti kāmāvacaraṃ. Anuttaranti rūpāvacarañca arūpāvacarañca. Tatrāpi sauttaraṃ rūpāvacaraṃ, anuttaraṃ arūpāvacarameva. Samāhitanti yassa appanāsamādhi upacārasamādhi vā atthi. Asamāhitanti ubhayasamādhivirahitaṃ. Vimuttanti tadaṅgavikkhambhanavimuttīhi vinimuttaṃ. Avimuttanti ubhayavimuttirahitaṃ; samucchedapaṭippassaddhinissaraṇavimuttīnaṃ pana idha okāsova natthi. Sarāgamassa cittanti sarāgaṃ assa cittaṃ. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthameva. Imasmimpi pabbe suddhavipassanāva kathitāti.

“Expanded” refers to the form sphere and the formless sphere. “Unexpanded” refers to the sense sphere. “Surpassable” refers to the sense sphere. “Unsurpassable” refers to the form sphere and the formless sphere. Among these, the form sphere is surpassable, while the formless sphere is unsurpassable. “Concentrated” refers to one who has either absorption concentration or access concentration. “Unconcentrated” refers to one devoid of both concentrations. “Liberated” refers to one liberated by liberation by substitution of opposites and liberation by suppression. “Unliberated” refers to one devoid of both kinds of liberation; but here there is no place for liberation by cutting off, liberation by tranquillization, or liberation by escape. “His mind is with lust,” means his mind is lustful. The rest, being stated according to the method previously stated, is obvious in meaning. In this section too, only pure insight is discussed.

Cittānupassanāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the exposition on the contemplation of mind is completed.

Dhammānupassanāniddesavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Exposition on the Contemplation of Dhammas

Nīvaraṇapabbavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on the Hindrances

367. Ettāvatā [V 0.0255] yasmā kāyānupassanāya rūpakkhandhapariggahova kathito, vedanānupassanāya vedanākkhandhapariggahova cittānupassanāya viññāṇakkhandhapariggahova tasmā idāni sampayuttadhammasīsena saññāsaṅkhārakkhandhapariggahampi kathetuṃ dhammānupassanaṃ dassento kathañca bhikkhūtiādimāha. Tattha santanti abhiṇhasamudācāravasena saṃvijjamānaṃ. Asantanti asamudācāravasena [M 0.0257] vā pahīnattā vā avijjamānaṃ. Yathā cāti yena kāraṇena kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti. Tañca pajānātīti tañca kāraṇaṃ pajānāti. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo.

367. Up to this point, since the comprehension of the form aggregate has been explained by way of the contemplation of the body, the comprehension of the feeling aggregate by way of the contemplation of feeling, and the comprehension of the consciousness aggregate by way of the contemplation of mind, therefore now, in order to explain the comprehension of the perception and formation aggregates under the heading of associated phenomena, he, showing the contemplation of dhammas, says, “And how, bhikkhus?” and so on. Therein, “present” means existing by way of frequent occurrence. “Absent” means not existing by way of non-occurrence or because of having been abandoned. “And how” (yathā ca) means by what cause the arising of sensual desire occurs. “And he understands that” means he understands that cause. The meaning should be understood in this way in all passages.

Tattha subhanimitte ayonisomanasikārena [P 0.0270] kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti. Subhanimittaṃ nāma subhampi subhanimittaṃ, subhārammaṇampi subhanimittaṃ. Ayonisomanasikāro nāma anupāyamanasikāro uppathamanasikāro, anicce niccanti vā dukkhe sukhanti vā anattani attāti vā asubhe subhanti vā manasikāro. Taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato kāmacchando uppajjati. Tenāha bhagavā –

Here, through unwise attention to an attractive sign, the arising of sensual desire occurs. An attractive sign means both what is attractive and what has an attractive object. Unwise attention means inappropriate attention, wrong-path attention—such as attention to the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, the non-self as self, or the unattractive as attractive. When one frequently engages in this, sensual desire arises. Therefore, the Blessed One has said:

“Atthi, bhikkhave, subhanimittaṃ. Tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro – ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā kāmacchandassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā kāmacchandassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

“Bhikkhus, there is an attractive sign. Frequent unwise attention to it is food for the arising of unarisen sensual desire and for the growth and abundance of arisen sensual desire.”

Asubhanimitte pana yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Asubhanimittaṃ nāma asubhampi asubhanimittaṃ, asubhārammaṇampi asubhanimittaṃ. Yonisomanasikāro nāma upāyamanasikāro pathamanasikāro, anicce aniccanti vā dukkhe dukkhanti vā anattani anattāti vā asubhe asubhanti vā manasikāro. Taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato kāmacchando pahīyati. Tenāha bhagavā –

However, through wise attention to an unattractive sign, its abandonment occurs. An unattractive sign means both what is unattractive and what has an unattractive object. Wise attention means appropriate attention, right-path attention—such as attention to the impermanent as impermanent, the painful as painful, the non-self as non-self, or the unattractive as unattractive. When one frequently cultivates this, sensual desire is abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Atthi, bhikkhave, asubhanimittaṃ. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro ayamanāhāro [V 0.0256] anuppannassa vā kāmacchandassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā kāmacchandassa bhiyyobhāvāya, vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

“Bhikkhus, there is an unattractive sign. Frequent wise attention to it is non-food for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, or for the growth and abundance of arisen sensual desire.”

Apica cha dhammā kāmacchandassa pahānāya saṃvattanti – asubhanimittassa uggaho, asubhabhāvanānuyogo, indriyesu guttadvāratā, bhojane mattaññutā, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti. Dasavidhañhi asubhanimittaṃ uggaṇhantassāpi kāmacchando pahīyati, bhāventassāpi; indriyesu pihitadvārassāpi[M 0.0258]; catunnaṃ pañcannaṃ ālopānaṃ okāse sati udakaṃ pivitvā yāpanasīlatāya bhojane mattaññunopi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire: the grasping of an unattractive sign, engaging in the development of unattractiveness, guarding the sense doors, moderation in food, good friendship, and suitable talk. Indeed, for one who grasps the ten kinds of unattractive signs, sensual desire is abandoned; for one who develops them, it is abandoned; for one who has guarded sense doors, it is abandoned; for one who is moderate in food—by the habit of sustaining oneself by drinking water after four or five mouthfuls—it is abandoned. Thus it is said:

“Cattāro pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive;

Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno”ti. (theragā. 983);

“Leaving four or five mouthfuls uneaten, one should drink water; this is sufficient for the easeful abiding of a resolute bhikkhu.” (Theragā. 983)

Asubhakammikatissattherasadise asubhabhāvanārate kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi kāmacchando pahīyati; ṭhānanisajjādīsu dasaasubhanissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena [P 0.0271] vuttaṃ “cha dhammā kāmacchandassa pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnassa kāmacchandassa arahattamaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

For one who associates with good friends, such as the Elder Tissa the practitioner of unattractiveness, who was devoted to the development of unattractiveness, sensual desire is abandoned. Even through suitable talk grounded in the ten unattractive things, in situations like standing, sitting, and so on, it is abandoned. Therefore, it is said, “Six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire.” He understands that the sensual desire abandoned by these six things does not arise again in the future, through the path of arahantship.

Paṭighanimitte ayonisomanasikārena pana byāpādassa uppādo hoti. Tattha paṭighampi paṭighanimittaṃ nāma; paṭighārammaṇampi paṭighanimittaṃ. Ayonisomanasikāro sabbattha ekalakkhaṇova. Taṃ tasmiṃ nimitte bahulaṃ pavattayato byāpādo uppajjati. Tenāha bhagavā –

But through unwise attention to a sign of irritation, the arising of ill will occurs. Here, irritation itself is called a sign of irritation; an object that provokes irritation is also a sign of irritation. Unwise attention has the same characteristic everywhere. When one frequently engages in such a sign, ill will arises. Therefore, the Blessed One has said:

“Atthi, bhikkhave, paṭighanimittaṃ. Tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro – ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā byāpādassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā byāpādassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

“Bhikkhus, there is a sign of irritation. Frequent unwise attention to it is food for the arising of unarisen ill will and for the growth and abundance of arisen ill will.”

Mettāya pana cetovimuttiyā yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Tattha mettāti vutte appanāpi upacāropi vaṭṭati; cetovimuttīti appanāva. Yonisomanasikāro vuttalakkhaṇova. Taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato byāpādo pahīyati. Tenāha bhagavā –

However, through wise attention to the liberation of mind by loving-kindness, its abandonment occurs. Here, when loving-kindness is mentioned, both absorption and access are applicable; but “liberation of mind” refers only to absorption. Wise attention has the characteristics as previously described. For one who frequently cultivates this, ill will is abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said—

“Atthi[V 0.0257], bhikkhave, mettācetovimutti. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro – ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā byāpādassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā byāpādassa bhiyyobhāvāya, vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232 thokaṃ visadisaṃ).

“Bhikkhus, there is the liberation of mind by loving-kindness. Frequent wise attention to it is not the nutriment for the arising of unarisen ill will, nor for the increase and abundance of arisen ill will.” (SN 5.232, slightly different)

Apica cha dhammā byāpādassa pahānāya saṃvattanti – mettānimittassa uggaho, mettābhāvanānuyogo, kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇā, paṭisaṅkhānabahulīkatā[M 0.0259], kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti. Odissakānodissakadisāpharaṇānañhi aññataravasena mettaṃ uggaṇhantassāpi byāpādo pahīyati. Odhiso anodhiso disāpharaṇavasena mettaṃ bhāventassāpi. ‘Tvaṃ etassa kuddho kiṃ karissasi, kimassa sīlādīni vināsetuṃ sakkhissasi? Nanu tvaṃ attano kammena āgantvā attano kammeneva gamissasi? Parassa kujjhanaṃ nāma vītaccitaṅgāratattaayosalākagūthādīni gahetvā parassa paharitukāmatāsadisaṃ hoti. Esopi tava kuddho kiṃ karissati? Kiṃ te sīlādīni vināsetuṃ sakkhissati? Esa attano kammenāgantvā attano kammeneva gamissati; appaṭicchitapaheṇakaṃ viya paṭivātakhittarajomuṭṭhi viya [P 0.0272] ca etassevesa kodho matthake patissatī’ti. Evaṃ attano ca parassa ca kammassakataṃ paccavekkhatopi, ubhayakammassakataṃ paccavekkhitvā paṭisaṅkhāne ṭhitassāpi, assaguttattherasadise mettābhāvanārate kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi byāpādo pahīyati; ṭhānanisajjādīsu mettānissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ “cha dhammā byāpādassa pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnassa byāpādassa anāgāmimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Furthermore, six things conduce to the abandoning of ill will: the apprehension of the sign of loving-kindness, the application to the development of loving-kindness, reflection on the ownership of actions, the frequent cultivation of contemplation, good friendship, and suitable conversation. Indeed, for one who apprehends loving-kindness in any way, whether by directing it specifically or by pervading the directions non-specifically, ill will is abandoned. Also for one who develops loving-kindness by pervading the directions specifically and non-specifically. 'Why are you angry with that person? What can you do to destroy his virtue and so forth? Surely, you have come by your own kamma and will depart by your own kamma? Being angry with another is like picking up burning embers, hot iron rods, or excrement with the intention to strike another. And what can he, being angry at you, do? Can he destroy your virtue and so forth? He has come by his own kamma and will depart by his own kamma; like an unaccepted gift or a fistful of dust thrown against the wind, this anger will fall back on his own head.' Thus, for one who reflects on the ownership of actions for oneself and for others, for one who stands firm in contemplation after reflecting on the ownership of actions for both, and for one who associates with good friends like the Elder Assagutta who delighted in the development of loving-kindness, ill will is abandoned. It is also abandoned through suitable conversation grounded in loving-kindness in standing, sitting, and so on. Therefore, it is said: 'Six things conduce to the abandoning of ill will.' Moreover, one understands that for ill will abandoned by these six things, its non-arising in the future is by way of the path of the non-returner.

Aratītiādīsu ayonisomanasikārena thinamiddhassa uppādo hoti. Arati nāma ukkaṇṭhitatā. Tandī nāma kāyālasiyatā. Vijambhikā nāma kāyavināmanā. Bhattasammado nāma bhattamucchā bhattapariḷāho. Cetaso līnattaṃ nāma cittassa līnākāro. Imesu aratiādīsu ayonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato thinamiddhaṃ uppajjati. Tenāha bhagavā –

In the case of discontent and so forth, sloth and torpor arise due to unwise attention. Discontent is dissatisfaction. Lethargy is bodily sluggishness. Yawning is the stretching of the body. Drowsiness after a meal is the stupor or feverishness from food. Sinking of mind is the mind's shrunken state. When one frequently applies unwise attention to these states of discontent and so forth, sloth and torpor arise. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Atthi, bhikkhave, arati tandī vijambhikā bhattasammado cetaso ca līnattaṃ. Tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro – ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā thinamiddhassa uppādāya[V 0.0258], uppannassa vā thinamiddhassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

"Bhikkhus, there is discontent, lethargy, yawning, drowsiness after a meal, and sinking of mind. Therein, frequent unwise attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, and for the increase and abundance of arisen sloth and torpor." (SN 5.232)

Ārambhadhātuādīsu pana yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Ārambhadhātu nāma paṭhamārambhavīriyaṃ. Nikkamadhātu nāma kosajjato [M 0.0260] nikkhantattā tato balavataraṃ. Parakkamadhātu nāma paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanato tatopi balavataraṃ. Imasmiṃ tippabhede vīriye yonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato thinamiddhaṃ pahīyati. Tenāha bhagavā –

But in the elements of initiative, etc., their abandonment occurs through wise attention. The element of initiative is the initial effort of energy. The element of exertion is so called because it is an emergence from idleness, and is therefore stronger than that. The element of striving is even stronger than that because it advances from one stage to the next. For one who frequently applies wise attention to this threefold energy, sloth and torpor are abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Atthi, bhikkhave, ārambhadhātu, nikkamadhātu, parakkamadhātu. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro – ayamanāhāro anuppannassa vā thinamiddhassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā thinamiddhassa bhiyyobhāvāya, vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

"Bhikkhus, there is the element of initiative, the element of exertion, and the element of striving. Therein, frequent wise attention is the non-nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, and for the abandoning of arisen sloth and torpor." (SN 5.232)

Apica cha dhammā thinamiddhassa pahānāya saṃvattanti – atibhojane [P 0.0273] nimittaggāho, iriyāpathasamparivattanatā, ālokasaññāmanasikāro, abbhokāsavāso, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti. Āharahatthaka bhuttavamitaka tatravaṭṭaka alaṃsāṭaka kākamāsakabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhāne nisinnassa hi samaṇadhammaṃ karoto thinamiddhaṃ mahāhatthī viya ottharantaṃ āgacchati. Catupañcaālopaokāsaṃ pana ṭhapetvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā yāpanasīlassa bhikkhuno taṃ na hotīti atibhojane nimittaṃ gaṇhantassāpi thinamiddhaṃ pahīyati. Yasmiṃ iriyāpathe thinamiddhaṃ okkamati tato aññaṃ parivattentassāpi, rattiṃ candālokadīpālokaukkāloke divā sūriyālokaṃ manasikarontassāpi, abbhokāse vasantassāpi, mahākassapattherasadise pahīnathinamiddhe kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi thinamiddhaṃ pahīyati; ṭhānanisajjādīsu dhutaṅganissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ “cha dhammā thinamiddhassa pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnassa thinamiddhassa arahattamaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Furthermore, six things conduce to the abandoning of sloth and torpor: the apprehension of the sign of moderation in eating, the changing of bodily postures, the application of the perception of light, dwelling in the open, good friendship, and suitable conversation. Indeed, for one who eats a meal like one who fills himself with his hand, or like one who has vomited and then fills the void, or like a tatravaṭṭaka bird, or eating until satisfied, or a crow's portion, and then sits in his night-quarters or day-quarters undertaking the duties of a contemplative, sloth and torpor come overwhelming him like a great elephant. But for a bhikkhu who is accustomed to sustaining himself by drinking water after leaving aside four or five mouthfuls, that does not happen. Even for one who apprehends the sign of moderation in eating, sloth and torpor are abandoned. Also for one who changes to another posture when sloth and torpor overcome him in a certain posture, also for one who applies his mind to the light of the moon, lamps, or torches at night, and to the light of the sun by day, also for one who dwells in the open, also for one who associates with good friends like the Elder Mahākassapa, who have abandoned sloth and torpor, sloth and torpor are abandoned. It is also abandoned through suitable conversation grounded in the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) in standing, sitting, and so on. Therefore, it is said: "Six things conduce to the abandoning of sloth and torpor." Moreover, one understands that for sloth and torpor abandoned by these six things, its non-arising in the future is by way of the Arahant's path.

Cetaso avūpasame ayonisomanasikārena uddhaccakukkuccassa uppādo hoti. Avūpasamo nāma avūpasantākāro; uddhaccakukkuccamevetaṃ atthato. Tattha ayonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato uddhaccakukkuccaṃ uppajjati. Tenāha bhagavā –

When the mind is uncalmed, restlessness and remorse arise through unwise attention. Uncalmness means a state of being uncalmed; this is, in essence, restlessness and remorse. For one who frequently applies unwise attention to that, restlessness and remorse arise. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Atthi[V 0.0259], bhikkhave, cetaso avūpasamo. Tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro – ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā uddhaccakukkuccassa [M 0.0261] uppādāya, uppannassa vā uddhaccakukkuccassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

"Bhikkhus, there is uncalmness of mind. Therein, frequent unwise attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, and for the increase and abundance of arisen restlessness and remorse." (Saṃ. Ni. 5.232)

Samādhisaṅkhāte pana cetaso vūpasame yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Tenāha bhagavā –

But in the calming of the mind, which is designated as concentration, its abandonment occurs through wise attention. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Atthi, bhikkhave, cetaso vūpasamo. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro – ayamanāhāro anuppannassa vā uddhaccakukkuccassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā uddhaccakukkuccassa bhiyyobhāvāya, vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

“Monks, there is calmness of mind. Therein, the frequent practice of wise attention is the non-nutriment for the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, and for the increase and expansion of arisen restlessness and remorse.” (SN 5.232)

Apica cha dhammā uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānāya saṃvattanti – bahussutatā, paripucchakatā, vinaye pakataññutā, vuḍḍhasevitā[P 0.0274], kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti. Bāhusaccenapi hi ekaṃ vā dve vā tayo vā cattāro vā pañca vā nikāye pāḷivasena ca atthavasena ca uggaṇhantassāpi uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyati. Kappiyākappiyaparipucchābahulassāpi, vinayapaññattiyaṃ ciṇṇavasībhāvatāya pakataññunopi, vuḍḍhe mahallakatthere upasaṅkamantassāpi, upālittherasadise vinayadhare kalyāṇamitte sevantassapi uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyati; ṭhānanisajjādīsu kappiyākappiyanissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ “cha dhammā uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīne uddhaccakukkucce uddhaccassa arahattamaggena kukkuccassa anāgāmimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Furthermore, six things conduce to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse: erudition, inquisitiveness, proficiency in the Vinaya, association with elders, good friendship, and suitable conversation. Indeed, for one who, through erudition, learns one, two, three, four, or five Nikāyas by way of the text and by way of the meaning, restlessness and remorse are abandoned. Also for one who frequently asks about what is allowable and what is not; for one who is proficient in the Vinaya regulations due to having practiced and achieved mastery; for one who approaches the senior elders; and for one who associates with good friends who are masters of the Vinaya, like the Elder Upāli, restlessness and remorse are abandoned. It is also abandoned through suitable conversation grounded in what is allowable and what is not regarding standing, sitting, and so on. Therefore, it is said: 'Six things conduce to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse.' One understands that, for restlessness and remorse abandoned by these six things, the future non-arising of restlessness is by means of the path of arahantship, and of remorse by means of the path of the non-returner.

Vicikicchāṭhānīyesu dhammesu ayonisomanasikārena vicikicchāya uppādo hoti. Vicikicchāṭhānīyā dhammā nāma punappunaṃ vicikicchāya kāraṇattā vicikicchāva. Tattha ayonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato vicikicchā uppajjati. Tenāha bhagavā –

Doubt arises through unwise attention to things that are grounds for doubt. Things that are grounds for doubt are so named because, being repeatedly a cause for doubt, they are doubt itself. For one who frequently applies unwise attention to them, doubt arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Atthi, bhikkhave, vicikicchāṭhānīyā dhammā. Tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro [V 0.0260] – ayamāhāro anuppannāya vā vicikicchāya uppādāya, uppannāya vā vicikicchāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

“Monks, there are grounds for doubt. Therein, the frequent practice of unwise attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen doubt, and for the increase and expansion of arisen doubt.” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.232)

Kusalādidhammesu [M 0.0262] yonisomanasikārena panassā pahānaṃ hoti. Tenāha bhagavā –

But its abandonment occurs through wise attention to wholesome and other such states. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Atthi, bhikkhave, kusalākusalā dhammā, sāvajjānavajjā dhammā, hīnappaṇītā dhammā, kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā dhammā. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro – ayamanāhāro anuppannāya vā vicikicchāya uppādāya, uppannāya vā vicikicchāya bhiyyobhāvāya, vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

“Monks, there are wholesome and unwholesome states, blameworthy and blameless states, inferior and superior states, dark and bright states with their counterparts. Therein, frequent wise attention is a non-nutriment for the arising of unarisen doubt, and for the increase and expansion of arisen doubt.”

Apica cha dhammā vicikicchāya pahānāya saṃvattanti – bahussutatā, paripucchakatā, vinaye pakataññutā, adhimokkhabahulatā, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti. Bāhusaccenapi hi ekaṃ vā…pe… pañca vā nikāye pāḷivasena ca atthavasena ca uggaṇhantassāpi vicikicchā pahīyati. Tīṇi ratanāni ārabbha paripucchābahulassāpi, vinaye ciṇṇavasībhāvassāpi, tīsu ratanesu okappaniyasaddhāsaṅkhātaadhimokkhabahulassāpi[P 0.0275], saddhādhimutte vakkalittherasadise kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi vicikicchā pahīyati. Ṭhānanissajjādīsu tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇanissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ “cha dhammā vicikicchāya pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnāya vicikicchāya sotāpattimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Furthermore, six states conduce to the abandonment of doubt: erudition, inquisitiveness, proficiency in the Vinaya, strong resolve, good friendship, and beneficial discourse. For even for one who learns one, up to five Nikāyas by text and meaning through extensive learning, doubt is abandoned. For one who frequently asks about the Three Jewels, who has attained mastery in the Vinaya, who has strong resolve consisting of unwavering faith in the Three Jewels, and who associates with good friends resolved in faith, like the Elder Vakkali, doubt is abandoned. Doubt is also abandoned through suitable talk, such as in standing and sitting, grounded in the qualities of the Three Jewels. Therefore, it is said: 'Six states conduce to the abandonment of doubt.' When doubt is abandoned by these six states, one understands that, by the path of stream-entry, it will not arise again in the future.

Nīvaraṇapabbavaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Chapter on the Hindrances.

Bojjhaṅgapabbavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment.

Bojjhaṅgapabbe santanti paṭilābhavasena vijjamānaṃ. Asantanti appaṭilābhavasena avijjamānaṃ. Yathā ca anuppannassātiādīsu pana satisambojjhaṅgassa tāva –

In the chapter on the factors of enlightenment, 'present' means existing by way of acquisition, and 'absent' means non-existent by way of non-acquisition. Furthermore, concerning the phrases such as 'of the unarisen,' first, regarding the enlightenment factor of mindfulness—

“Atthi[V 0.0261], bhikkhave, satisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro – ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā satisambojjhaṅgassa [M 0.0263] bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.183) – evaṃ uppādo hoti. Tattha satiyeva satisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā. Yonisomanasikāro vuttalakkhaṇoyeva. Taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato satisambojjhaṅgo uppajjati.

“Monks, there are states that are a basis for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. Therein, the frequent practice of wise attention is the nutriment that conduces to the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness, and to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness.” (SN 5.183) – In this way, its arising occurs. Herein, mindfulness itself constitutes the states that are a basis for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. Wise attention has the characteristic already described. When one frequently directs it there, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness arises.

Apica cattāro dhammā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – satisampajaññaṃ, muṭṭhassatipuggalaparivajjanatā, upaṭṭhitassatipuggalasevanatā, tadadhimuttatāti. Abhikkantādīsu hi sattasu ṭhānesu satisampajaññena, bhattanikkhittakākasadise muṭṭhassatipuggale parivajjanena, tissadattattheraabhayattherasadise upaṭṭhitassatipuggale sevanena, ṭhānanisajjādīsu satisamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatāya ca satisambojjhaṅgo uppajjati. Evaṃ catūhi kāraṇehi uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Furthermore, four states conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness: mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding persons of lapsed mindfulness, associating with persons of established mindfulness, and an inclination towards that. For the enlightenment factor of mindfulness arises through mindfulness and clear comprehension in the seven instances such as going forward; by avoiding persons of lapsed mindfulness, who are like a crow that has dropped its food; by associating with persons of established mindfulness, like the Elders Tissadatta and Abhaya; and through a mind inclined, sloping, and tending towards arousing mindfulness in postures such as standing and sitting. One understands that for this factor, arisen through these four causes, the fulfillment of its development occurs by means of the path of arahantship.

Dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa pana –

As for the enlightenment factor of the investigation of phenomena—

“Atthi, bhikkhave, kusalākusalā dhammā…pe… kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā dhammā. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro – ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232) –

Monks, there are wholesome and unwholesome states... dark and bright states with their counterparts. Therein, frequent wise attention is a nutriment for the arising of the unarisen investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor, and for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor." (SN 5.232) –

Evaṃ uppādo hoti.

Thus it arises.

Apica [P 0.0276] satta dhammā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – paripucchakatā, vatthuvisadakiriyā, indriyasamattapaṭipādanā, duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā, paññavantapuggalasevanā, gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇā, tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha paripucchakatāti khandhadhātuāyatanaindriyabalabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgajhānasamathavipassanānaṃ atthasannissitaparipucchābahulatā. Vatthuvisadakiriyāti ajjhattikabāhirānaṃ vatthūnaṃ visadabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Yadā hissa kesanakhalomāni dīghāni honti, sarīraṃ [V 0.0262] vā ussannadosañceva sedamalamakkhitañca, tadā ajjhattikaṃ vatthu avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ. Yadā [M 0.0264] pana cīvaraṃ jiṇṇaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ duggandhaṃ hoti, senāsanaṃ vā uklāpaṃ, tadā bāhiraṃ vatthu avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ. Tasmā kesādichedanena uddhaṃvirecanaadhovirecanādīhi sarīrasallahukabhāvakaraṇena, ucchādananhāpanena ca ajjhattikavatthu visadaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sūcikammadhovanarajanaparibhaṇḍakaraṇādīhi bāhiravatthu visadaṃ kātabbaṃ. Etasmiñhi ajjhattikabāhiravatthumhi avisade uppannesu cittacetasikesu ñāṇampi avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ; aparisuddhāni dīpakapallakavaṭṭitelāni nissāya uppannadīpasikhāya obhāso viya. Visade pana ajjhattikabāhiravatthumhi uppannesu cittacetasikesu ñāṇampi visadaṃ hoti parisuddhāni dīpakapallakavaṭṭitelāni nissāya uppannadīpasikhāya obhāso viya. Tena vuttaṃ “vatthuvisadakiriyā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattatī”ti.

Furthermore, seven states lead to the arising of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor: inquisitiveness, clarifying the object, balancing the faculties, avoiding foolish persons, associating with wise persons, reviewing profound knowledge, and inclination towards it. Here, inquisitiveness means frequently inquiring about the meaning related to aggregates, elements, sense bases, faculties, powers, enlightenment factors, path factors, jhāna, serenity, and insight. Clarifying the object means making internal and external objects clear. When one's head hair, body hair, and nails are long, or when the body is afflicted with excessive impurities, sweat, and dirt, then the internal object is unclear and impure. When robes are old, stained, and foul-smelling, or when the dwelling is untidy, then the external object is unclear and impure. Therefore, the internal object should be clarified by cutting head hair, etc., lightening the body through upper and lower purgatives, and by anointing and bathing. The external object should be clarified by needlework, washing, dyeing, and attending to the requisites. For when internal and external objects are unclear, the knowledge arising in the mind and mental factors is also unclear and impure—like the light of a lamp flame dependent on impure wicks, oil, and vessel. But when internal and external objects are clear, the knowledge arising in the mind and mental factors is also clear—like the light of a lamp flame dependent on pure wicks, oil, and vessel. Therefore, it is said: "Clarifying the object leads to the arising of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor."

Indriyasamattapaṭipādanā nāma saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ samabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Sace hissa saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti, itarāni mandāni, tato vīriyindriyaṃ paggahakiccaṃ, satindriyaṃ upaṭṭhānakiccaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ avikkhepakiccaṃ, paññindriyaṃ dassanakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Tasmā taṃ dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena vā yathā vā manasikaroto balavaṃ jātaṃ, tathā amanasikārena hāpetabbaṃ. Vakkalittheravatthu cettha nidassanaṃ. Sace pana vīriyindriyaṃ [P 0.0277] balavaṃ hoti, atha neva saddhindriyaṃ adhimokkhakiccaṃ kātuṃ sakkoti, na itarāni itarakiccabhedaṃ. Tasmā taṃ passaddhādibhāvanāya hāpetabbaṃ. Tatrāpi soṇattheravatthu dassetabbaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi ekassa balavabhāve sati itaresaṃ attano kiccesu asamatthatā veditabbā.

The balanced cultivation of faculties means making the faculties of faith and others equal. If his faculty of faith is strong, while the others are weak, then the faculty of energy cannot perform its function of striving, the faculty of mindfulness cannot perform its function of establishing, the faculty of concentration cannot perform its function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom cannot perform its function of seeing. Therefore, that strong faculty should be diminished by reflecting on the nature of the Dhamma or by not attending to it in the way it became strong. The story of Vakkali Thera is an example here. But if the faculty of energy is strong, then the faculty of faith cannot perform its function of conviction, nor can the others perform their respective functions. Therefore, that strong faculty should be diminished by developing tranquility and so forth. In this case, the story of Soṇa Thera should be cited. Similarly, in the remaining cases, when one faculty is strong, the inability of the others to perform their own functions should be understood.

Visesato panettha saddhāpaññānaṃ samādhivīriyānañca samataṃ pasaṃsanti. Balavasaddho hi mandapañño muddhappasanno hoti, avatthusmiṃ pasīdati. Balavapañño mandasaddho kerāṭikapakkhaṃ bhajati, bhesajjasamuṭṭhito viya rogo atekiccho hoti ‘cittuppādamatteneva kusalaṃ hotī’ti atidhāvitvā dānādīni puññāni akaronto niraye uppajjati. Ubhinnaṃ pana samatāya vatthusmiṃyeva pasīdati. Balavasamādhiṃ pana mandavīriyaṃ, samādhissa kosajjapakkhattā, kosajjaṃ adhibhavati. Balavavīriyaṃ mandasamādhiṃ, vīriyassa uddhaccapakkhattā, uddhaccaṃ adhibhavati. Samādhi pana vīriyena saṃyojito kosajje patituṃ na labhati. Vīriyaṃ samādhinā saṃyojitaṃ uddhacce patituṃ na labhati. Tasmā tadubhayampi samaṃ kātabbaṃ. Ubhayasamatāya hi appanā hoti[M 0.0265][V 0.0263]. Apica samādhikammikassa balavatīpi saddhā vaṭṭati. Evaṃ so saddahanto okappento appanaṃ pāpuṇissati.

Here, particularly, they praise the balance of faith and wisdom, and of concentration and energy. For one with strong faith but weak wisdom is naively credulous, trusting without proper grounds. One with strong wisdom but weak faith becomes cunning, incurable like a disease caused by medicine. Overestimating that "merit arises merely from a thought," and rushing ahead, they neglect acts of generosity and other merits, and thus are reborn in hell. But when both are balanced, one trusts only in what is truly trustworthy. One with strong concentration but weak energy is overwhelmed by sloth, because concentration is on the side of sloth. One with strong energy but weak concentration is overwhelmed by restlessness, because energy is on the side of restlessness. Concentration, when yoked with energy, cannot fall into sloth. Energy, when yoked with concentration, cannot fall into restlessness. Therefore, both should be balanced. For through the balance of both, full absorption is attained. Moreover, for one engaged in concentration practice, strong faith is fitting. Thus, by trusting and resolving, one will attain absorption.

Samādhipaññāsu pana samādhikammikassa ekaggatā balavatī vaṭṭati. Evañhi so appanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Vipassanākammikassa paññā balavatī vaṭṭati. Evañhi so lakkhaṇapaṭivedhaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ubhinnaṃ pana samatāya appanā hotiyeva. Sati pana sabbattha balavatī vaṭṭati. Sati hi cittaṃ uddhaccapakkhikānaṃ saddhāvīriyapaññānaṃ vasena uddhaccapātato, kosajjapakkhikena ca samādhinā kosajjapātato rakkhati. Tasmā sā, loṇadhūpanaṃ viya sabbabyañjanesu, sabbakammikaamacco viya ca sabbarājakiccesu, sabbattha icchitabbā. Tenāha “sati ca pana sabbatthikā vuttā bhagavatā. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Cittañhi satipaṭisaraṇaṃ, ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā [P 0.0278] ca sati; na vinā satiyā cittassa paggahaniggaho hotī”ti.

In the case of concentration and wisdom, for one engaged in concentration, one-pointedness of mind should be strong. Thus he attains absorption. For one engaged in insight, wisdom should be strong. Thus he attains penetration of characteristics. But when both are balanced, absorption certainly takes place. Mindfulness, however, should be strong everywhere. For mindfulness protects the mind from falling into agitation, which is the pitfall of faith, energy, and wisdom, and from falling into sluggishness, which is the pitfall of concentration. Therefore, like salt that flavors all dishes, or like a prime minister in all royal duties, it should be desired in all things. Thus it is said, "The Blessed One has declared mindfulness to be useful in all things. Why? Because the mind has mindfulness as its support, and mindfulness has the characteristic of protection; without mindfulness, there is no upholding or restraining of the mind."

Duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā nāma khandhādibhede anogāḷhapaññānaṃ dummedhapuggalānaṃ ārakā parivajjanaṃ. Paññavantapuggalasevanā nāma samapaññāsalakkhaṇapariggāhikāya udayabbayapaññāya samannāgatapuggalasevanā. Gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇā nāma gambhīresu khandhādīsu pavattāya gambhīrapaññāya pabhedapaccavekkhaṇā. Tadadhimuttatā nāma ṭhānanisajjādīsu dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatā. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Avoiding a person of little wisdom means keeping at a distance from unwise individuals whose wisdom has not penetrated the divisions of the aggregates and so on. Associating with a wise person means associating with those endowed with the wisdom of arising and passing away that comprehends the fifty characteristics of equanimity. Reflecting on profound knowledge and conduct means examining in detail with profound wisdom that operates within the profound aggregates and other aspects. Devotion to that means the mind's inclination, bending, and tendency for the purpose of arousing the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor in postures such as standing and sitting. He understands that when this arises, the perfection of development is achieved through the path of arahantship.

Vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa –

Of the enlightenment factor of energy:

“Atthi, bhikkhave, ārambhadhātu nikkamadhātu parakkamadhātu. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro – ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232) –

"Bhikkhus, there is the element of initiative, the element of exertion, the element of striving. Frequent cultivation of wise attention to that is nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of energy, and for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of energy."

Evaṃ uppādo hoti.

Thus is its arising.

Apica [V 0.0264] ekādasa dhammā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – apāyabhayapaccavekkhaṇatā, ānisaṃsadassāvitā, gamanavīthipaccavekkhaṇatā, piṇḍapātāpacāyanatā[M 0.0266], dāyajjamahattapaccavekkhaṇatā, satthumahattapaccavekkhaṇatā, jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇatā, sabrahmacārimahattapaccavekkhaṇatā, kusītapuggalaparivajjanatā, āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanatā, tadadhimuttatāti.

Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of energy: reflecting on the fear of the planes of misery, seeing the benefit, reflecting on the path to be trodden, reflecting on the honor due to almsfood, reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance, reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, reflecting on the greatness of one's heritage, reflecting on the greatness of one's companions in the holy life, avoiding lazy people, associating with energetic people, and devotion to that.

Tattha nirayesu pañcavidhabandhanakammakāraṇato paṭṭhāya mahādukkhaṃ anubhavanakālepi, tiracchānayoniyaṃ jālakkhipakumīnādīhi gahitakālepi, pācanakaṇṭakādippahārāvitunnassa pana sakaṭavahanādikālepi, pettivisaye anekānipi vassasahassāni ekaṃ buddhantarampi khuppipāsāhi āturībhūtakālepi, kālakañjikaasuresu saṭṭhihatthaasītihatthappamāṇena [P 0.0279] aṭṭhicammamatteneva attabhāvena vātātapādidukkhānubhavanakālepi na sakkā vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṃ uppādetuṃ. ‘Ayameva te, bhikkhu, kālo vīriyakaraṇāyā’ti evaṃ apāyabhayaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi vīriyasambojjhaṅgo uppajjati. ‘Na sakkā kusītena nava lokuttaradhammā laddhuṃ; āraddhavīriyeneva sakkā; ayamānisaṃso vīriyassā’ti evaṃ ānisaṃsadassāvinopi uppajjati. ‘Sabbabuddhapaccekabuddhamahāsāvakeheva te gatamaggo gantabbo; so ca na sakkā kusītena gantu’nti evaṃ gamanavīthiṃ paccavekkhantassāpi uppajjati. ‘Ye taṃ piṇḍapātādīhi upaṭṭhahanti, ime te manussā neva ñātakā, na dāsakammakarā, nāpi taṃ nissāya ‘jīvissāmā’ti te paṇītāni piṇḍapātādīni denti; atha kho attano kārānaṃ mahapphalataṃ paccāsiṃsamānā denti. Satthārāpi ‘ayaṃ ime paccaye paribhuñjitvā kāyadaḷhībahulo sukhaṃ viharissatī’ti na evañca sampassatā tuyhaṃ paccayā anuññatā; atha kho ‘ayaṃ ime paribhuñjamāno samaṇadhammaṃ katvā vaṭṭadukkhato muccissatī’ti te paccayā anuññātā. So dāni tvaṃ kusīto viharanto na taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ apacāyissasi. Āraddhavīriyasseva hi piṇḍapātāpacāyanaṃ nāma hotī’ti evaṃ piṇḍapātāpacāyanaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi uppajjati, mahāmittattherassa viya.

Therein, in the hells, while experiencing great suffering, beginning with the fivefold binding and torture; or in the animal realm, when seized by nets, traps, fish-hooks, and so on; or when tormented by blows from goads, thorns, and so on, while pulling carts and the like; or in the realm of ghosts, while afflicted by hunger and thirst for many thousands of years, even for an entire Buddha-interval; or among the Kālakañjika asuras, with bodies consisting of only bones and skin, measuring sixty or eighty cubits, experiencing suffering from wind, heat, and so on—in such states, it is not possible to arouse the enlightenment factor of energy. But for one who reflects on the fear of the planes of misery, thinking, 'This, bhikkhu, is the time for you to make an effort,' the enlightenment factor of energy arises. For one who sees the benefit, thinking, 'It is not possible for a lazy person to attain the nine supramundane states; it is possible only for one who has aroused energy—this is the benefit of energy,' it arises. For one who reflects on the path to be trodden, thinking, 'The path trodden by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and great disciples must be trodden by you; and that cannot be trodden by a lazy person,' it arises. For one who reflects on the honor due to almsfood, thinking, 'Those who attend on you with almsfood and so on are neither your relatives nor your slaves or servants, nor do they give you fine almsfood and so on thinking, "We shall live by depending on him." Rather, they give, hoping for great fruit from their own actions. The Teacher, too, did not allow you these requisites thinking, "Having used these, he will live happily with a strong body." Rather, he allowed you these requisites thinking, "Having used these, he will fulfill the duties of a recluse and be freed from the suffering of the cycle of rebirths." Now, if you live lazily, you will not be honoring that almsfood. For honoring almsfood is only for one whose energy is aroused,' it arises—as it did for the Elder Mahāmitta.

Thero kira kassakaleṇe nāma paṭivasati. Tassa ca gocaragāme ekā mahāupāsikā theraṃ puttaṃ katvā paṭijaggati. Sā ekadivasaṃ araññaṃ gacchantī dhītaraṃ āha – “amma, asukasmiṃ ṭhāne purāṇataṇḍulā, asukasmiṃ khīraṃ, asukasmiṃ sappi, asukasmiṃ phāṇitaṃ. Tava [V 0.0265] bhātikassa ayyamittassa āgatakāle bhattaṃ pacitvā khīrasappiphāṇitehi saddhiṃ dehi[M 0.0267], tvañca bhuñjeyyāsī”ti. “Tvaṃ pana kiṃ bhuñjissasi, ammā”ti? “Ahaṃ pana hiyyo pakkaṃ pārivāsikabhattaṃ kañjiyena bhuttamhī”ti. “Divā kiṃ bhuñjissasi, ammā”ti? “Sākapaṇṇaṃ pakkhipitvā kaṇataṇḍulehi ambilayāguṃ pacitvā ṭhapehi, ammā”ti.

The elder, it is said, resided in a place called Kassaka Cave. In his alms-resort village, a great female lay disciple looked after the elder, having adopted him as her son. One day, as she was going to the forest, she said to her daughter: "Dear, in such and such a place there is old rice, in such and such a place milk, in such and such a place ghee, and in such and such a place molasses. When your brother, the venerable Mitta, comes, cook rice and give it to him with the milk, ghee, and molasses, and you eat as well." "But what will you eat, mother?" "I ate yesterday's leftover rice with sour gruel." "What will you eat during the day, mother?" "Cook some sour gruel with leafy greens and broken rice, and set it aside, dear."

Thero cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ nīharantova taṃ saddaṃ sutvā attānaṃ ovadi – ‘mahāupāsikā kira kañjiyena [P 0.0280] pārivāsikabhattaṃ bhuñji; divāpi kaṇapaṇṇambilayāguṃ bhuñjissati; tuyhaṃ atthāya pana purāṇataṇḍulādīni ācikkhati. Taṃ nissāya kho panesā neva khettaṃ, na vatthuṃ, na bhattaṃ, na vatthaṃ paccāsīsati; tisso pana sampattiyo patthayamānā deti. Tvaṃ etissā tā sampattiyo dātuṃ sakkhissasi, na sakkhissasīti? Ayaṃ kho pana piṇḍapāto tayā sarāgena sadosena samohena na sakkā bhuñjitu’nti pattaṃ thavikāya pakkhipitvā gaṇṭhikaṃ muñcitvā nivattitvā kassakaleṇameva gantvā pattaṃ heṭṭhāmañce cīvaraṃ cīvaravaṃse ṭhapetvā ‘arahattaṃ apāpuṇitvā na nikkhamissāmī’ti vīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā nisīdi. Dīgharattaṃ appamatto hutvā nivutthabhikkhu vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā purebhattameva arahattaṃ patvā vikasamānamiva padumaṃ mahākhīṇāsavo sitaṃ karontova nisīdi. Leṇadvāre rukkhamhi adhivatthā devatā –

The elder, having put on his robe and just as he was taking out his alms bowl, heard that sound and admonished himself: 'The great laywoman, it seems, ate yesterday's leftover cooked rice with sour rice-gruel; during the day she will eat sour gruel with broken rice and greens; yet for your sake she points out old rice and so forth. Relying on this, she does not long for fields, nor property, nor food, nor cloth; but aspiring to the three attainments, she gives. Will you be able to give her those attainments, or not? Moreover, this almsfood cannot be eaten by you with greed, hatred, or delusion.' Placing the bowl in its bag, untying the knot, he turned back and went to the Farmer's Cave itself. Setting the bowl under the bed and the robe on the robe-pole, he resolved with determination: 'I will not leave until I attain arahantship,' and sat down. For a long time, he remained diligent, and as a monk who had dwelled in seclusion, having developed insight, he attained arahantship before the meal. Like a blossoming lotus, the great one whose taints were destroyed sat smiling. The deity dwelling in the tree at the entrance to the cave—

“Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Yassa te āsavā khīṇā, dakkhiṇeyyosi mārisā”ti.

Homage to you, O thoroughbred among men, homage to you, O highest of men; whose taints are destroyed, you are worthy of offerings, O venerable sir.

Udānaṃ udānetvā – ‘bhante, piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ tumhādisānaṃ arahantānaṃ bhikkhaṃ datvā mahallakitthiyo dukkhā muccissantī’ti āha.

Having uttered this solemn utterance, she said: 'Venerable sir, by giving alms to arahants like you who have entered for alms, elderly women will be freed from suffering.'

Thero uṭṭhahitvā dvāraṃ vivaritvā kālaṃ olokento ‘pātoyevā’ti ñatvā pattacīvaramādāya gāmaṃ pāvisi. Dārikāpi bhattaṃ sampādetvā ‘idāni me bhātā āgamissati, idāni me bhātā āgamissatīti dvāraṃ vivaritvā olokayamānā nisīdi. Sā, there gharadvāraṃ sampatte, pattaṃ gahetvā sappiphāṇitayojitassa khīrapiṇḍapātassa pūretvā hatthe ṭhapesi. Thero ‘sukhaṃ hotū’ti anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Sāpi taṃ olokayamānā aṭṭhāsi.

The elder rose, opened the door, and observing the time, knowing it was early morning, took his bowl and robe and entered the village. The young girl, having prepared the meal, sat opening the door and looking out, thinking, 'Now my brother will come, now my brother will come.' When the elder reached the house door, she took the bowl, filled it with milk-rice mixed with ghee and molasses, and placed it in his hands. The elder said, 'May you be happy,' gave his blessing, and departed. She stood watching him.

Therassa [M 0.0268][V 0.0266] hi tadā ativiya parisuddho chavivaṇṇo ahosi, vippasannāni indriyāni, mukhaṃ bandhanā muttatālapakkaṃ viya ativiya virocittha. Mahāupāsikā araññā āgantvā – “kiṃ, amma, bhātiko te āgato”ti pucchi. Sā sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Upāsikā ‘ajja me puttassa pabbajitakiccaṃ matthakaṃ patta’nti ñatvā “abhiramati te, amma, bhātā buddhasāsane, na ukkaṇṭhatī”ti āha.

Indeed, at that time the elder's complexion was exceedingly pure, his faculties serene, and his face shone brilliantly like a ripe palm fruit freed from its stalk. The great laywoman, returning from the forest, asked, 'Well, my dear, has your brother come?' She related all that had happened. The laywoman, realizing, 'Today my son's purpose for going forth has reached its culmination,' said, 'Your brother delights in the Buddha's Dispensation, my dear; he is not discontented.'

Mahantaṃ kho panetaṃ satthu dāyajjaṃ yadidaṃ satta ariyadhanāni nāma. Taṃ na sakkā kusītena gahetuṃ. Yathā hi [P 0.0281] vippaṭipannaṃ puttaṃ mātāpitaro ‘ayaṃ amhākaṃ aputto’ti paribāhiraṃ karonti; so tesaṃ accayena dāyajjaṃ na labhati; evaṃ kusītopi idaṃ ariyadhanadāyajjaṃ na labhati, āraddhavīriyova labhatīti dāyajjamahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati. ‘Mahā kho pana te satthā. Satthuno hi te mātukucchismiṃ paṭisandhigaṇhanakālepi abhinikkhamanepi abhisambodhiyampi dhammacakkapavattanayamakapāṭihāriyadevorohanaāyusaṅkhāravossajjanesupi parinibbānakālepi dasasahassilokadhātu kampittha. Yuttaṃ nu te evarūpassa satthuno sāsane pabbajitvā kusītena bhavitu’nti evaṃ satthumahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati.

Moreover, this is the great inheritance of the Teacher, namely, the seven noble treasures. That cannot be obtained by the lazy. Just as parents disown a wayward child, saying, 'This is not our child,' and exclude him, so he does not receive their inheritance after their death; in the same way, the lazy do not obtain this noble inheritance of treasures—only the energetic do. Thus, reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance also gives rise to energy. 'Great indeed is your Teacher!
