For at the time of your Teacher’s conception in his mother’s womb, his renunciation, his supreme enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of Dhamma, the twin miracle, the descent from the deva realm, the relinquishing of the life-span, and his final passing away—the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. Is it fitting for you, having gone forth in the Dispensation of such a Teacher, to be lazy?' Thus, reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher also gives rise to energy.

‘Jātiyāpi tvaṃ idāni na lāmakajātikosi; asambhinnāya mahāsammatapaveṇiyā āgate okkākarājavaṃse jāto; sirisuddhodanamahārājassa ca mahāmāyādeviyā ca nattā; rāhulabhaddassa kaniṭṭho. Tayā nāma evarūpena jinaputtena hutvā na yuttaṃ kusītena viharitu’nti evaṃ jātimahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati. ‘Sāriputtamoggallānā ceva asītimahāsāvakā ca vīriyeneva lokuttaradhammaṃ paṭivijjhiṃsu. Tvaṃ etesaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjasi, nappaṭipajjasī’ti evaṃ sabrahmacārimahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati.

'Even by birth, you are not of ignoble birth now; you have been born into the unbroken lineage of the Okkāka royal family, descended from Mahā Sammata; you are the grandson of the great King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā; and the younger brother of the venerable Rāhula. It is not fitting for you, a son of the Conqueror, to live lazily.' Thus, energy arises when reflecting on the greatness of birth. 'Sāriputta and Moggallāna, along with the eighty great disciples, realized the supramundane Dhamma through effort. Are you following the path of these spiritual companions, or are you not?' Thus, energy arises when reflecting on the greatness of one's spiritual companions.

Kucchiṃ pūretvā ṭhitaajagarasadise vissaṭṭhakāyikacetasikavīriye kusītapuggale parivajjentassāpi āraddhavīriye pahitatte puggale sevantassāpi ṭhānanisajjādīsu viriyuppādanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Energy also arises for one who avoids the lazy person—who, having filled his belly, is like a motionless python, having abandoned bodily and mental effort—for one who associates with an energetic and resolute person, and for one whose mind is inclined towards arousing energy in standing, sitting, and other postures. When it has thus arisen, one understands that its development reaches fulfillment through the path of arahantship.

Pītisambojjhaṅgassa [M 0.0269] –

For the enlightenment factor of rapture—

“Atthi[V 0.0267], bhikkhave, pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro – ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232) –

'Monks, there are things that are a basis for the enlightenment factor of rapture. Frequent wise attention to them is the nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of rapture, and for the increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of rapture.'

Evaṃ uppādo hoti. Tattha pītiyeva pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā nāma. Tassā uppādakamanasikāro [P 0.0282] yonisomanasikāro nāma.

Thus there is an arising. Herein, the things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of rapture are simply rapture itself. The attention that produces it is called wise attention.

Apica ekādasa dhammā pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – buddhānussati, dhammasaṅghasīlacāgadevatānussati, upasamānussati, lūkhapuggalaparivajjanatā, siniddhapuggalasevanatā, pasādanīyasuttantapaccavekkhaṇatā, tadadhimuttatāti.

Furthermore, eleven things conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of joy: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Sangha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of deities, recollection of peace, avoiding coarse individuals, associating with refined individuals, reflecting on inspiring discourses, and being inclined toward that.

Buddhaguṇe anussarantassāpi hi yāva upacārā sakalasarīraṃ pharamāno pītisambojjhaṅgo uppajjati; dhammasaṅghaguṇe anussarantassāpi, dīgharattaṃ akkhaṇḍaṃ katvā rakkhitaṃ catupārisuddhisīlaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, gihino dasasīlaṃ pañcasīlaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, dubbhikkhabhayādīsu paṇītaṃ bhojanaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ datvā ‘evaṃ nāma adamhā’ti cāgaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, gihinopi evarūpe kāle sīlavantānaṃ dinnadānaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, yehi guṇehi samannāgatā devatā devattaṃ pattā tathārūpānaṃ guṇānaṃ attani atthitaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, samāpattiyā vikkhambhite kilese saṭṭhipi sattatipi vassāni na samudācarantīti paccavekkhantassāpi, cetiyadassanabodhidassanatheradassanesu asakkaccakiriyāya saṃsūcitalūkhabhāve buddhādīsu pasādasinehābhāvena gadrabhapiṭṭhe rajasadise lūkhapuggale parivajjentassāpi, buddhādīsu pasādabahule muducitte siniddhapuggale sevantassāpi, ratanattayaguṇaparidīpake pasādanīyasuttante paccavekkhantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu pītiuppādanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Indeed, for one recollecting the virtues of the Buddha, the enlightenment factor of joy arises, suffusing the entire body up to access concentration; similarly, for one recollecting the virtues of the Dhamma and the Sangha; for one reviewing the fourfold purity of morality, unbroken and long-preserved; for laypeople reflecting on their observance of the ten or five precepts; for one reflecting on generosity after giving excellent food to fellow practitioners in times of famine and fear, thinking, 'Indeed, we have given thus'; for laypeople too reflecting on gifts given to virtuous ones on such occasions; for one reflecting on the presence in oneself of similar virtues that deities possess to attain their divine state; for one reflecting that defilements suppressed by meditative attainment do not arise even for sixty or seventy years; for one avoiding coarse individuals who, like dust on a donkey's back, show disrespect and carelessness toward shrines, Bodhi trees, and elder monks, and lack devotion and affection for the Buddha and others; for one associating with gentle, devoted, and affectionate people who have strong faith in the Buddha and others; for one reflecting on inspiring discourses that illuminate the virtues of the Triple Gem; and even for one whose mind is inclined, sloping, and bent for the sake of arousing joy in standing, sitting, and so forth, joy arises. Thus, when it has arisen, one understands that its development reaches fulfillment through the path of arahantship.

Passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa [M 0.0270] –

For the enlightenment factor of tranquility—

“Atthi[V 0.0268], bhikkhave, kāyapassaddhi cittapassaddhi. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro – ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232) –

'Monks, there is bodily tranquility and mental tranquility. Frequent systematic attention to that is food for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of tranquility, and for the increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of tranquility.' (SN 5.232)

Evaṃ uppādo hoti. Apica satta dhammā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – paṇītabhojanasevanatā, utusukhasevanatā[P 0.0283], iriyāpathasukhasevanatā, majjhattapayogatā, sāraddhakāyapuggalaparivajjanatā, passaddhikāyapuggalasevanatā, tadadhimuttatāti. Paṇītañhi siniddhaṃ sappāyabhojanaṃ bhuñjantassāpi, sītuṇhesu utūsu ṭhānādīsu ca iriyāpathesu sappāyaṃ utuñca iriyāpathañca sevantassāpi passaddhi uppajjati. Yo pana mahāpurisajātiko sabbautuiriyāpathakkhamova hoti, na taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yassa sabhāgavisabhāgatā atthi, tasseva visabhāge utuiriyāpathe vajjetvā sabhāge sevantassāpi uppajjati. Majjhattapayogo vuccati attano ca parassa ca kammassakatapaccavekkhaṇā; iminā majjhattapayogena uppajjati. Yo leḍḍudaṇḍādīhi paraṃ viheṭhayamānova vicarati, evarūpaṃ sāraddhakāyaṃ puggalaṃ parivajjentassāpi, saṃyatapādapāṇiṃ passaddhakāyaṃ puggalaṃ sevantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu passaddhiuppādanatthāya ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Thus there is an arising. Moreover, seven things conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of tranquility: enjoying refined food, enjoying agreeable weather, enjoying comfortable postures, application of balance, avoiding agitated individuals, associating with serene individuals, and being inclined toward it. Indeed, tranquility arises even in one who consumes refined, smooth, and wholesome food, and even in one who enjoys wholesome weather and postures in hot and cold seasons and places. However, this is not said with reference to one of a great man's nature who is capable in all weathers and postures. It arises even in one who has harmonious and disharmonious tendencies, by avoiding unsuitable weather and postures and cultivating suitable ones. Application of balance means reflecting on one’s own and others’ ownership of kamma; tranquility arises through this application of balance. Even when avoiding people who wander about harming others with clods of earth, sticks, and so forth, who are agitated in body; and even when associating with restrained and serene individuals; and even for one whose mind is inclined, sloping, and bent for the sake of producing tranquility in postures like standing and sitting, tranquility arises. Thus, when it has arisen, one understands that its development reaches fulfillment through the path of arahantship.

Samādhisambojjhaṅgassa –

For the enlightenment factor of concentration—

“Atthi, bhikkhave, samathanimittaṃ abyagganimittaṃ. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro – ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232) –

'Monks, there is the sign of serenity and the sign of non-distraction. Frequent systematic attention to that is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, and for the increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration.'

Evaṃ uppādo hoti. Tattha samathova samathanimittaṃ, avikkhepaṭṭhena ca abyagganimittanti.

Thus there is an arising. Herein, serenity itself is the sign of serenity; and non-distraction is the sign of non-distraction by way of non-dispersion.

Apica [M 0.0271] ekādasa dhammā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – vatthuvisadakiriyatā[V 0.0269], indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā, nimittakusalatā, samaye cittassa paggaṇhanatā, samaye cittassa niggahaṇanatā, samaye sampahaṃsanatā, samaye ajjhupekkhaṇatā, asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanatā, samāhitapuggalasevanatā, jhānavimokkhapaccavekkhaṇatā, tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha vatthuvisadakiriyatā ca indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā ca vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

Furthermore, eleven things conduce to the arising of the concentration enlightenment factor: clarifying the basis, bringing the faculties to evenness, skill in the sign, uplifting the mind at the proper time, restraining the mind at the proper time, gladdening the mind at the proper time, observing with equanimity at the proper time, avoiding individuals whose minds are unconcentrated, associating with individuals whose minds are concentrated, reviewing the jhānas and liberations, and inclination toward that. Herein, clarifying the basis and bringing the faculties to evenness should be understood in the way already stated.

Nimittakusalatā nāma kasiṇanimittassa uggahaṇakusalatā. Samaye cittassa paggahaṇanatāti yasmiṃ samaye atisithilavīriyatādīhi [P 0.0284] līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye dhammavicayavīriyapītisambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanena tassa paggaṇhanaṃ. Samaye cittassa niggahaṇanatāti yasmiṃ samaye accāraddhavīriyatādīhi uddhaṭaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisamādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanena tassa niggaṇhanaṃ. Samaye sampahaṃsanatāti yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paññāpayogamandatāya vā upasamasukhānadhigamena vā nirassādaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye aṭṭhasaṃvegavatthupaccavekkhaṇena saṃvejeti. Aṭṭha saṃvegavatthūni nāma jātijarābyādhimaraṇāni cattāri, apāyadukkhaṃ pañcamaṃ, atīte vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, anāgate vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, paccuppanne āhārapariyeṭṭhimūlakaṃ dukkhanti. Ratanattayaguṇānussaraṇena ca pasādaṃ janeti. Ayaṃ vuccati samaye sampahaṃsanatāti.

Skill in the sign means skill in grasping the kasiṇa sign. Uplifting the mind at the proper time means that when the mind is sluggish due to excessive slackness of energy, etc., at that time one uplifts it by arousing the investigation-of-states, energy, and rapture enlightenment factors. Restraining the mind at the proper time means that when the mind is agitated due to excessive energy, etc., at that time one restrains it by arousing the tranquility, concentration, and equanimity enlightenment factors. Gladdening the mind at the proper time means that when the mind is lacking zest due to sluggishness in the application of wisdom or non-attainment of the bliss of peace, at that time one stirs it to urgency by reflecting on the eight grounds for urgency. The eight grounds for urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, and death—these four; the suffering of the lower realms as the fifth; suffering rooted in the past round of existence; suffering rooted in the future round of existence; and suffering rooted in the present, in the search for food. And one generates confidence by recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem. This is called gladdening the mind at the proper time.

Samaye ajjhupekkhanatā nāma yasmiṃ samaye sammāpaṭipattiṃ āgamma alīnaṃ anuddhaṭaṃ anirassādaṃ ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ samathavīthipaṭipannaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tadāyaṃ paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu na byāpāraṃ āpajjati sārathī viya samappavattesu assesu. Ayaṃ vuccati samaye ajjhupekkhanatāti. Asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanatā nāma upacāraṃ vā appanaṃ vā appattānaṃ vikkhittacittānaṃ puggalānaṃ ārakā parivajjanaṃ. Samāhitapuggalasevanatā nāma upacārena vā appanāya vā samāhitacittānaṃ sevanā bhajanā payirupāsanā. Tadadhimuttatā nāma ṭhānanisajjādīsu samādhiuppādanatthaṃyeva ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatā. Evañhi paṭipajjato esa uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Equanimity at the proper time means that when the mind, having undertaken right practice, is neither sluggish nor agitated nor lacking zest, but proceeds evenly on the object, following the path of serenity, then one does not engage in uplifting, restraining, or gladdening, like a charioteer with horses moving evenly. This is called equanimity at the proper time. Avoiding individuals whose minds are unconcentrated means avoiding from afar individuals whose minds are scattered and who have not attained either access or absorption. Associating with individuals whose minds are concentrated means associating with, frequenting, and attending upon individuals whose minds are concentrated in access or absorption. Inclination towards that means having a mind bent and inclined solely towards arousing concentration in postures such as standing and sitting. For one who practices thus, this arises. And having arisen for him, he understands that its perfection of development is through the path to arahantship.

Upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa –

For the equanimity enlightenment factor:

“Atthi, bhikkhave, upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro [V 0.0270] – ayamāhāro anuppannassa [M 0.0272] vā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa [P 0.0285] uppādāya, uppannassa vā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232) –

“Bhikkhus, there are states that are the basis for the equanimity enlightenment factor. Therein, the frequent practice of wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen equanimity enlightenment factor and for the increase, growth, development, and perfection of the arisen equanimity enlightenment factor.” (SN 46.53)

Evaṃ uppādo hoti. Tattha upekkhāva upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā nāma. Apica pañca dhammā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – sattamajjhattatā, saṅkhāramajjhattatā, sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatā, sattasaṅkhāramajjhattapuggalasevanatā, tadadhimuttatāti.

Thus it arises. Here, the states that are the basis for the equanimity enlightenment factor are equanimity itself. Furthermore, five things conduce to the arising of the equanimity enlightenment factor: equanimity towards beings, equanimity towards formations, avoiding individuals who are attached to beings and formations, associating with individuals who are equanimous towards beings and formations, and inclination towards that.

Tattha dvīhākārehi sattamajjhattataṃ samuṭṭhāpeti – ‘tvaṃ attano kammena āgantvā attanova kammena gamissasi. Esopi attano kammena āgantvā attanova kammena gamissati. Tvaṃ kaṃ kelāyasī’ti evaṃ kammassakatapaccavekkhaṇena ca ‘paramatthato sattoyeva natthi. So tvaṃ kaṃ kelāyasī’ti evaṃ nissattapaccavekkhaṇena ca. Dvīhevākārehi saṅkhāramajjhattataṃ samuṭṭhāpeti – ‘idaṃ cīvaraṃ anupubbena vaṇṇavikārañceva jiṇṇabhāvañca upagantvā pādapuñchanacoḷakaṃ hutvā yaṭṭhikoṭiyā chaḍḍanīyaṃ bhavissati. Sace panassa sāmiko bhaveyya, nāssa evaṃ vinassituṃ dadeyyā’ti evaṃ assāmikabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena ca. ‘Anaddhaniyaṃ idaṃ tāvakālika’nti evaṃ tāvakālikabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena ca. Yathā ca cīvare, evaṃ pattādīsupi yojanā kātabbā.

Here, one arouses equanimity towards beings in two ways: by reflecting on kamma as one's own property, thus: ‘You have come by your own kamma, and by your own kamma you will go. This one too has come by his own kamma, and by his own kamma he will go. To whom are you attached?’; and by reflecting on the absence of a self, thus: ‘In the ultimate sense, no being exists. To whom are you attached?’. One arouses equanimity towards formations in two ways: by reflecting on the state of ownerlessness, thus: ‘This robe, undergoing gradual changes in color and aging, will eventually become a foot-wiping rag and be discarded at the end of a stick. If it had an owner, he would not allow it to be destroyed in this way’; and by reflecting on its temporary nature, thus: ‘This is not long-lasting, it is temporary.’ And as with the robe, so the application should be made with the bowl and other requisites.

Sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatāti ettha yo puggalo gihī vā attano puttadhītādike, pabbajito vā attano antevāsikasamānupajjhāyakādike mamāyati, sahattheneva nesaṃ kesacchedanasūcikammacīvaradhovanarajanapattapacanādīni karoti, muhuttampi apassanto ‘asuko sāmaṇero kuhiṃ? Asuko daharo kuhi’nti? Bhantamigo viya ito cito ca āloketi; aññena kesacchedanādīnaṃ atthāya ‘muhuttaṃ tāva asukaṃ pesethā’ti yāciyamānopi ‘amhepi taṃ attano kammaṃ na kārema, tumhe naṃ gahetvā kilamessathā’ti na deti – ayaṃ sattakelāyano nāma.

Regarding this, a person—whether a householder who considers their own sons, daughters, and the like as ‘mine,’ or a monastic who considers their own pupils, co-residents, preceptors, and the like as ‘mine’—personally performs for them tasks such as cutting their hair, sewing, washing robes, dyeing robes, preparing the bowl, and so on. If for a moment they do not see them, they wonder, ‘Where is that novice? Where is that young one?’ Like a startled deer, they look here and there. Even when asked by another for the purpose of cutting hair and the like, saying, ‘Please send that one for just a moment,’ they refuse, saying, ‘We do not even make him do our own work; you will only weary him by taking him.’ This is called one who is attached to beings.

Yo [M 0.0273] pana cīvarapattathālakakattarayaṭṭhiādīni [P 0.0286] mamāyati, aññassa hatthena parāmasitumpi na deti, tāvakālikaṃ yācitopi ‘mayampi imaṃ mamāyantā na paribhuñjāma, tumhākaṃ kiṃ dassāmā’ti vadati – ayaṃ saṅkhārakelāyano nāma. Yo pana tesu dvīsupi vatthūsu majjhatto udāsīno – ayaṃ sattasaṅkhāramajjhatto nāma. Iti ayaṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo evarūpe sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggale [V 0.0271] ārakā parivajjentassāpi, sattasaṅkhāramajjhattapuggale sevantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu taduppādanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

One who considers robes, alms bowls, plates, staffs, and so on as ‘mine,’ who does not allow others to even touch them with their hands, and who, when asked for them temporarily, says, ‘We ourselves, being attached to this, do not use it; what could we give to you?’—this is called one who is attached to formations. But one who is balanced and indifferent regarding these two matters—this is called one who is equanimous towards beings and formations. Thus, this equanimity enlightenment factor arises in one who avoids from afar such a person who is attached to beings and formations, who associates with those who are equanimous towards beings and formations, and whose mind is inclined, leaning, and directed towards arousing it in postures such as standing and sitting. When it has thus arisen, one understands that its perfection of development is through the path to arahantship. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.

Bojjhaṅgapabbavaṇṇanā.

The Description of the Section on the Enlightenment Factors.

Imesupi dvīsu pabbesu suddhavipassanāva kathitā. Iti ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā pubbabhāge nānācittesu labbhanti. Aññeneva hi cittena kāyaṃ pariggaṇhāti, aññena vedanaṃ, aññena cittaṃ, aññena dhamme pariggaṇhāti; lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe pana ekacitteyeva labbhanti. Ādito hi kāyaṃ pariggaṇhitvā āgatassa vipassanāsampayuttā sati kāyānupassanā nāma. Tāya satiyā samannāgato puggalo kāyānupassī nāma. Vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā ariyamaggaṃ pattassa maggakkhaṇe maggasampayuttā sati kāyanupassanā nāma. Tāya satiyā samannāgato puggalo kāyānupassī nāma. Vedanaṃ pariggaṇhitvā…. Cittaṃ pariggaṇhitvā…. Dhamme pariggaṇhitvā āgatassa vipassanāsampayuttā sati dhammānupassanā nāma. Tāya satiyā samannāgato puggalo dhammānupassī nāma. Vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā ariyamaggaṃ pattassa maggakkhaṇe maggasampayuttā sati dhammānupassanā nāma. Tāya satiyā samannāgato puggalo dhammānupassī nāma. Evaṃ tāva desanā puggale tiṭṭhati. Kāye pana ‘subha’nti vipallāsappahānā kāyapariggāhikā sati maggena samijjhatīti kāyānupassanā nāma. Vedanāya ‘sukha’nti vipallāsappahānā vedanāpariggāhikā sati maggena samijjhatīti vedanānupassanā nāma. Citte ‘nicca’nti vipallāsappahānā cittapariggāhikā sati maggena samijjhatīti cittānupassanā nāma. Dhammesu ‘attā’ti vipallāsappahānā dhammapariggāhikā [P 0.0287] sati maggena samijjhatīti dhammānupassanā nāma. Iti ekāva maggasampayuttā sati catukiccasādhanaṭṭhena cattāri [M 0.0274] nāmāni labhati. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe pana ekacitteyeva labbhantī’ti.

In these two sections, only pure insight is taught. Thus, these four foundations of mindfulness are obtained with different minds in the preliminary stage. For with one mind one comprehends the body, with another feelings, with another the mind, and with another phenomena; but at the moment of the supramundane path, they are obtained with a single mind. Initially, for one who has come having comprehended the body, the mindfulness associated with insight is called contemplation of the body. A person endowed with that mindfulness is called a contemplator of the body. For one who has aroused insight and attained the noble path, the mindfulness associated with the path at the moment of the path is called contemplation of the body. A person endowed with that mindfulness is called a contemplator of the body. Having comprehended feelings… Having comprehended the mind… For one who has come having comprehended phenomena, the mindfulness associated with insight is called contemplation of phenomena. A person endowed with that mindfulness is called a contemplator of phenomena. For one who has aroused insight and attained the noble path, the mindfulness associated with the path at the moment of the path is called contemplation of phenomena. A person endowed with that mindfulness is called a contemplator of phenomena. Thus far, the teaching stands in relation to the person. But regarding the body, the mindfulness that comprehends the body, through abandoning the perversion of 'beautiful', succeeds through the path and is called contemplation of the body. Regarding feelings, the mindfulness that comprehends feelings, through abandoning the perversion of 'pleasant', succeeds through the path and is called contemplation of feelings. Regarding the mind, the mindfulness that comprehends the mind, through abandoning the perversion of 'permanent', succeeds through the path and is called contemplation of the mind. Regarding phenomena, the mindfulness that comprehends phenomena, through abandoning the perversion of 'self', succeeds through the path and is called contemplation of phenomena. Thus, the single mindfulness associated with the path obtains four names by way of accomplishing four functions. Therefore, it is said: ‘But at the moment of the supramundane path, they are obtained with a single mind.’

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Sutta Exposition.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition

374. Abhidhammabhājanīye [V 0.0272] lokuttarasatipaṭṭhānavasena desanāya āraddhattā yathā kāyādiārammaṇesu lokiyasatipaṭṭhānesu tanti ṭhapitā, evaṃ aṭṭhapetvā sabbānipi kāyānupassādīni satipaṭṭhānāni dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ (dha. sa. 355 ādayo) vibhattassa desanānayassa mukhamattameva dassentena niddiṭṭhāni.

374. In the Abhidhamma Exposition, because the teaching is commenced by way of the supramundane foundations of mindfulness, all the foundations of mindfulness, such as contemplation of the body, are indicated merely by showing the beginning of the method of exposition that is delineated in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī (beginning with Dhs. 355), without establishing them in the same way as the framework is established for the worldly foundations of mindfulness with objects such as the body.

Tattha nayabhedo veditabbo. Kathaṃ? Kāyānupassanāya tāva sotāpattimagge jhānābhinivese suddhikapaṭipadā, suddhikasuññatā, suññatapaṭipadā, suddhikaappaṇihitaṃ, appaṇihitapaṭipadāti imesu pañcasu ṭhānesu dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ catukkapañcakanayānaṃ vasena dasa nayā honti. Evaṃ sesesupīti vīsatiyā abhinivesesu dve nayasatāni. Tāni catūhi adhipatīhi catuguṇitāni aṭṭha. Iti suddhikāni dve sādhipatīni aṭṭhāti sabbampi nayasahassaṃ hoti. Tathā vedanānupassanādīsu suddhikasatipaṭṭhāne cāti sotāpattimagge pañca nayasahassāni. Yathā ca sotāpattimagge, evaṃ sesamaggesupīti kusale vīsati nayasahassāni; suññatāpaṇihitānimittādibhedesu pana tato tiguṇe vipāke saṭṭhi nayasahassānīti. Evameva sakiccasādhakānañceva saṃsiddhikakiccānañca kusalavipākasatipaṭṭhānānaṃ niddesavasena duvidho kāyānupassanādivasena ca suddhikavasena ca kusale pañcannaṃ vipāke pañcannanti dasannaṃ niddesavārānaṃ vasena dasappabhedo asītinayasahassapatimaṇḍito abhidhammabhājanīyaniddeso.

Here, the distinctions in methods should be understood. How? First, in contemplation of the body on the path of stream-entry, in regard to jhāna-absorption, in these five aspects—the path of purification, pure emptiness, the path of emptiness, pure desirelessness, and the path of desirelessness—by way of two each of the methods of four and five, there are ten methods. Thus, in the remaining cases as well, in the twenty absorptions, there are two hundred methods. These, multiplied fourfold by the four dominant conditions, become eight hundred. Thus, the two hundred pure methods, together with the eight hundred with dominant conditions, make a total of a thousand methods. Similarly, for contemplation of feelings, etc., and for the pure foundation of mindfulness, there are five thousand methods on the path of stream-entry. And just as on the path of stream-entry, so too on the remaining paths—thus, in the wholesome, there are twenty thousand methods. Moreover, in the distinctions of emptiness, desirelessness, and signlessness, in the result that is threefold that, there are sixty thousand methods. In this very way, the exposition of the Abhidhamma division is adorned with eighty thousand methods, of ten kinds through ten explanatory sections (five for the wholesome and five for the resultant), explained in two ways (by way of contemplation of the body, etc., and by way of purity), concerning the wholesome and resultant foundations of mindfulness for both those who accomplish their own task and those whose tasks are naturally accomplished.

3. Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Question Section

386. Pañhāpucchake pāḷianusāreneva satipaṭṭhānānaṃ kusalādibhāvo veditabbo. Ārammaṇattikesu pana sabbānipi etāni appamāṇaṃ nibbānaṃ [M 0.0275] ārabbha pavattanato appamāṇārammaṇāneva, na maggārammaṇāni; sahajātahetuvasena pana maggahetukāni; vīriyaṃ vā vīmaṃsaṃ vā jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā maggabhāvanākāle maggādhipatīni; chandacittajeṭṭhakāya [P 0.0288] maggabhāvanāya navattabbāni maggādhipatīnīti phalakālepi navattabbāneva; atītādīsu ekārammaṇabhāvenapi navattabbāni; nibbānassa pana bahiddhādhammattā bahiddhārammaṇāni nāma hontīti. Evametasmiṃ pañhāpucchake nibbattitalokuttarāneva satipaṭṭhānāni kathitāni. Sammāsambuddhena hi suttantabhājanīyasmiṃyeva [V 0.0273] lokiyalokuttaramissakā satipaṭṭhānā kathitā; abhidhammabhājanīyapañhāpucchakesu pana lokuttarāyevāti. Evamayaṃ satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅgopi teparivaṭṭaṃ nīharitvā bhājetvā dassitoti.

386. In the Question Section, the wholesome and other states of the foundations of mindfulness should be understood precisely according to the Pāli text. Among the object triads, all of these, because they occur having the immeasurable Nibbāna as their object, are immeasurable-object states, not path-object states. However, through the condition of being co-nascent causes, they are path-causal states. When energy or investigation is made predominant during the cultivation of the path, they are path-dominance states. They should not be designated as path-dominance states due to the cultivation of the path where desire or consciousness are predominant, and likewise they should not be designated as such even at the fruition stage. They also should not be designated as such due to having a single object in the past, etc. But since Nibbāna is an external phenomenon, they are called external-object states. Thus, in this Question Section, only the arisen supramundane foundations of mindfulness are taught. For by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, in the Sutta division, foundations of mindfulness that are a mixture of mundane and supramundane were taught; but in the Abhidhamma division and the Question Section, only the supramundane ones were taught. In this way, this Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness too, after extracting the threefold revolution, is divided and shown.

Sammohavinodaniyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya

In the Sammohavinodanī, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga,

Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness is completed.

8. Sammappadhānavibhaṅgo

8. The Analysis of Right Exertion

1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Sutta Division

390. Idāni [P 0.0289][M 0.0276][V 0.0274] tadanantare sammappadhānavibhaṅge cattāroti gaṇanaparicchedo. Tena na tato heṭṭhā na uddhanti sammappadhānaparicchedaṃ dīpeti. Sammappadhānāti kāraṇappadhānā upāyappadhānā yonisopadhānā. Idha bhikkhūti imasmiṃ sāsane paṭipannako bhikkhu. Anuppannānanti anibbattānaṃ. Pāpakānanti lāmakānaṃ. Akusalānaṃ dhammānanti akosallasambhūtānaṃ dhammānaṃ. Anuppādāyāti na uppādanatthāya. Chandaṃ janetīti kattukamyatāsaṅkhātaṃ kusalacchandaṃ janeti uppādeti. Vāyamatīti payogaṃ parakkamaṃ karoti. Vīriyaṃ ārabhatīti kāyikacetasikaṃ vīriyaṃ karoti. Cittaṃ paggaṇhātīti teneva sahajātavīriyena cittaṃ ukkhipati. Padahatīti padhānavīriyaṃ karoti. Paṭipāṭiyā panetāni cattāripi padāni āsevanābhāvanābahulīkammasātaccakiriyāhi yojetabbāni.

390. Now, immediately following that, in the Analysis of the Right Efforts, 'four' is a numerical determination. By this, it indicates the delimitation of the right efforts, that they are neither fewer nor more than that. Right efforts are the effort of the cause, the effort of the means, and the effort of wise application. 'Here, a bhikkhu' means a bhikkhu practicing in this dispensation. 'Unarisen' means not yet arisen. 'Unwholesome' means inferior. 'Unskillful states' means states originating from unskillfulness. 'For non-arising' means for the purpose of not arising. 'He generates desire' means he generates, produces, wholesome desire characterized by the wish to act. 'He exerts' means he makes an application of effort, an exertion. 'He arouses energy' means he makes bodily and mental energy. 'He uplifts his mind' means he raises up the mind with that co-nascent energy. 'He strives' means he makes the effort of striving. In sequence, these four terms should be connected with cultivation, development, making abundant, and perseverance.

Uppannānaṃ pāpakānanti anuppannanti avattabbataṃ āpannānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ. Pahānāyāti pajahanatthāya. Anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānanti anibbattānaṃ kosallasambhūtānaṃ dhammānaṃ. Uppādāyāti uppādanatthāya. Uppannānanti nibbattānaṃ. Ṭhitiyāti ṭhitatthāya. Asammosāyāti anassanatthaṃ. Bhiyyobhāvāyāti punappunaṃ bhāvāya. Vepullāyāti [P 0.0290] vipulabhāvāya. Bhāvanāyāti vaḍḍhiyā. Pāripūriyāti paripūraṇatthāya. Ayaṃ tāva catunnaṃ sammappadhānānaṃ uddesavāravasena ekapadiko atthuddhāro.

'Of arisen unwholesome states' refers to unwholesome states that have reached a state where they cannot be called 'unarisen'. 'For abandonment' means for the purpose of abandoning. 'Of unarisen wholesome states' refers to unproduced states born of skillfulness. 'For arising' means for the purpose of production. 'Of arisen' refers to those that have arisen. 'For maintenance' means for the purpose of continuance. 'For non-confusion' means for the purpose of not being forgotten. 'For increase' means for repeated cultivation. 'For abundance' means for the state of abundance. 'For development' means for growth. 'For fulfillment' means for the purpose of completion. This, for now, is the explanation of each term of the four right efforts according to the summary section.

391. Idāni paṭipāṭiyā tāni padāni bhājetvā dassetuṃ kathañca bhikkhu anuppannānantiādinā [V 0.0275] nayena niddesavāro āraddho. Tattha yaṃ heṭṭhā dhammasaṅgahe āgatasadisaṃ, taṃ tassa vaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana tasmiṃ anāgataṃ, tattha chandaniddese tāva yo chandoti yo chandaniyavasena chando. Chandikatāti chandikabhāvo, chandakaraṇākāro vā. Kattukamyatāti kattukāmatā. Kusaloti cheko. Dhammacchandoti sabhāvacchando. Ayañhi chando nāma taṇhāchando, diṭṭhichando, vīriyachando, dhammacchandoti bahuvidho nānappakārako. Tesu [M 0.0277] dhammacchandoti imasmiṃ ṭhāne kattukamyatākusaladhammacchando adhippeto.

391. Now, to explain by analyzing those terms in sequence, the detailed explanation section begins with the method, 'And how does a bhikkhu... for the non-arising...'. Herein, what is similar to what has come in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī should be understood in the way stated in its commentary. But as for what is not found there, in the explanation of desire, firstly, 'what is desire' refers to desire in the sense of inclination. 'The state of desiring' means the state of having desire, or the manner of causing desire. 'The wish to act' means the desire to act. 'Skillful' means expert. 'Desire for the Dhamma' means desire for the true nature. For this desire is indeed of many kinds and various types: desire as craving, desire as views, desire as energy, and desire for the Dhamma. Among these, in this context, 'desire for the Dhamma' is intended as the skillful desire which is the wish to act.

Imaṃ chandaṃ janetīti chandaṃ kurumānova chandaṃ janeti nāma. Sañjanetīti upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Uṭṭhapetīti chandaṃ kurumānova taṃ uṭṭhapeti nāma. Samuṭṭhapetīti upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Nibbattetīti chandaṃ kurumānova taṃ nibbatteti nāma. Abhinibbattetīti upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Apica chandaṃ karontova chandaṃ janeti nāma. Tameva satataṃ karonto sañjaneti nāma. Kenacideva antarāyena patitaṃ puna ukkhipanto uṭṭhapeti nāma. Pabandhaṭṭhitiṃ pāpento samuṭṭhapeti nāma. Taṃ pākaṭaṃ karonto nibbatteti nāma. Anosakkanatāya alīnavuttitāya anolīnavuttitāya abhimukhabhāvena nibbattento abhinibbatteti nāma.

The phrase 'he generates desire' means he generates desire by making desire. 'He produces' is the word augmented by a prefix. 'He arouses' means he arouses it by making desire. 'He thoroughly arouses' is the word augmented by a prefix. 'He brings forth' means he brings it forth by making desire. 'He thoroughly brings forth' is the word augmented by a prefix. Moreover, by making desire, one is said to 'generate desire'. By making it continuously, one is said to 'produce'. By lifting up again that which has fallen due to some obstacle, one is said to 'arouse'. By bringing it to a state of unbroken continuity, one is said to 'thoroughly arouse'. By making it manifest, one is said to 'bring forth'. By bringing it forth through not retreating, through conduct that is not sluggish, through conduct that is not fainthearted, and through facing it directly, one is said to 'thoroughly bring forth'.

394. Vīriyaniddese vīriyaṃ karontova vīriyaṃ ārabhati nāma. Dutiyapadaṃ upasaggena vaḍḍhitaṃ. Vīriyaṃ [P 0.0291] karontoyeva ca āsevati bhāveti nāma. Punappunaṃ karonto vahulīkaroti. Āditova karonto ārabhati. Punappunaṃ karonto samārabhati. Bhāvanāvasena bhajanto āsevati. Vaḍḍhento bhāveti. Sabbakiccesu tadeva bahulīkaronto bahulīkarotīti veditabbo.

394. In the exposition of energy, one is said to initiate energy by making energy. The second term is augmented by a prefix. And by making energy, one is said to cultivate and develop it. By doing it again and again, one makes it abundant. By making it from the outset, one initiates. By making it repeatedly, one fully undertakes. By engaging with it by way of development, one cultivates. By increasing it, one develops. It should be understood that by making that very energy abundant in all activities, one makes it abundant.

395. Cittapaggahaniddese vīriyapaggahena yojento cittaṃ paggaṇhāti, ukkhipatīti attho. Punappunaṃ paggaṇhanto sampaggaṇhāti. Evaṃ sampaggahitaṃ yathā na patati tathā naṃ vīriyupatthambhena upatthambhento upatthambheti. Upatthambhitampi thirabhāvatthāya punappunaṃ upatthambhento paccupatthambheti nāma.

395. In the exposition of uplifting the mind, by applying it with the uplifting of energy, one uplifts the mind; the meaning is that one raises it up. By repeatedly uplifting it, one thoroughly uplifts it. Thus, when the mind is thoroughly uplifted, one supports it with the support of energy so that it does not fall away. Even when supported, to make it stable, one repeatedly supports it; this is called re-supporting.

406. Ṭhitiyātipadassa niddese sabbesampi asammosādīnaṃ ṭhitivevacanabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ yā ṭhiti so asammosotiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha hi heṭṭhimaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ padaṃ uparimassa uparimassa padassa [V 0.0276] attho, uparimaṃ uparimaṃ padaṃ heṭṭhimassa heṭṭhimassa atthotipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti. Ayaṃ tāva pāḷivaṇṇanā.

406. In the exposition of the term 'for stability,' to show that all terms such as 'for non-confusion' are synonyms for stability, it is said: 'That which is stability is non-confusion,' and so on. Here, indeed, each preceding term is the meaning of each succeeding term, and it can also be said that each succeeding term is the meaning of each preceding term. The rest is clear in meaning everywhere. This, for now, is the explanation of the Pāli.

Ayaṃ panettha vinicchayakathā. Ayañhi sammappadhānakathā nāma duvidhā – lokiyā lokuttarā ca. Tattha lokiyā sabbapubbabhāge hoti. Sā [M 0.0278] kassapasaṃyuttapariyāyena lokiyamaggakkhaṇe veditabbā. Vuttañhi tattha –

Here is the definitive explanation of this matter. This discourse on right effort is of two kinds—mundane and supramundane. Among these, the mundane occurs in all preliminary stages. It should be understood as occurring at the moment of the mundane path, by way of the discourse in the Kassapa Saṃyutta. For it is said there—

“Cattāro me, āvuso, sammappadhānā. Katame cattāro?

'Friend, for me there are four right efforts. Which four?'

Idhāvuso, bhikkhu ‘anuppannā me pāpakā akusalā dhammā uppajjamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyu’nti ātappaṃ karoti; ‘uppannā me pāpakā akusalā dhammā appahīyamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyu’nti ātappaṃ karoti; ‘anuppannā me kusalā dhammā anuppajjamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyu’nti ātappaṃ karoti. ‘Uppannā me kusalā dhammā nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyu’nti ātappaṃ karotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.145).

Here, friend, a bhikkhu generates ardour lest unarisen evil unwholesome states should arise and conduce to harm. He generates ardour lest arisen evil unwholesome states, not being abandoned, should conduce to harm. He generates ardour lest unarisen wholesome states, not arising, should conduce to harm. He generates ardour lest arisen wholesome states, ceasing, should conduce to harm.

Ettha ca ‘anuppannā me kusalā dhammā’ti samathavipassanā ceva maggo ca. Uppannā [P 0.0292] kusalā nāma samathavipassanāva. Maggo pana sakiṃ uppajjitvā nirujjhamāno anatthāya saṃvattanako nāma natthi. So hi phalassa paccayaṃ datvāva nirujjhati. Purimasmiṃ vā samathavipassanāva gahetabbāti vuttaṃ, taṃ pana na yuttaṃ.

Here, the phrase 'unarisen wholesome states' refers to both serenity and insight, and also the path. The arisen wholesome states are indeed serenity and insight. However, the path, having arisen once and then ceasing, is not something that conduces to harm. For it ceases only after giving rise to the fruit. Or, it was said that in the former case, only serenity and insight should be taken, but that is not correct.

Tattha “uppannā samathavipassanā nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvattantī”ti atthassa āvibhāvatthaṃ idaṃ vatthu – eko kira khīṇāsavatthero ‘mahācetiyañca mahābodhiñca vandissāmī’ti samāpattilābhinā bhaṇḍagāhakasāmaṇerena saddhiṃ janapadato mahāvihāraṃ āgantvā vihārapariveṇaṃ pāvisi; sāyanhasamaye mahābhikkhusaṅghe cetiyaṃ vandamāne cetiyaṃ vandanatthāya na nikkhami. Kasmā? Khīṇāsavānañhi tīsu ratanesu mahantaṃ gāravaṃ hoti. Tasmā bhikkhusaṅghe vanditvā paṭikkante manussānaṃ sāyamāsabhuttavelāya sāmaṇerampi ajānāpetvā ‘cetiyaṃ vandissāmī’ti ekakova nikkhami. Sāmaṇero ‘kiṃ nu kho thero avelāya ekakova gacchati, jānissāmī’ti upajjhāyassa padānupadikova nikkhami. Thero anāvajjanena tassa āgamanaṃ [V 0.0277] ajānanto dakkhiṇadvārena mahācetiyaṅgaṇaṃ āruḷho. Sāmaṇeropi anupadaṃyeva āruḷho.

There, to clarify the meaning of "arisen serenity and insight, ceasing, conduce to harm," this story is told: A certain elder, a Khīnāsava, intending to pay homage to the Great Cetiya and the Great Bodhi Tree, arrived at the Great Monastery from the countryside together with a novice, his baggage-bearer, who was skilled in attaining meditative absorptions. He entered the monastery enclosure. In the evening, when the great community of monks was paying homage to the Cetiya, he did not go out to pay homage to the Cetiya. Why? Because Khīnāsavas have great reverence for the Three Jewels. Therefore, after the community of monks had paid homage and departed, and at the time when people were having their evening meal, without informing the novice, he went out alone, thinking, "I will pay homage to the Cetiya." The novice wondered, "Why is the elder going out alone at an unseemly time? I will find out," and followed closely behind his teacher's footsteps. The elder, unaware of his arrival due to lack of attention, ascended to the courtyard of the Great Cetiya through the southern gate. The novice also ascended immediately behind him.

Mahāthero [M 0.0279] mahācetiyaṃ ulloketvā buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ gahetvā sabbaṃ cetaso samannāharitvā haṭṭhapahaṭṭho mahācetiyaṃ vandati. Sāmaṇero therassa vandanākāraṃ disvā ‘upajjhāyo me ativiya pasannacitto vandati; kiṃ nu kho pupphāni labhitvā pūjaṃ kareyyā’ti cintesi. There vanditvā uṭṭhāya sirasi añjaliṃ ṭhapetvā mahācetiyaṃ ulloketvā ṭhite sāmaṇero ukkāsitvā attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpesi. Thero parivattetvā olokento “kadā āgatosī”ti pucchi. “Tumhākaṃ cetiyaṃ vandanakāle, bhante; ativiya pasannā cetiyaṃ vandittha; kinnu kho pupphāni labhitvā pūjeyyāthā”ti? “Āma, sāmaṇera, imasmiṃ cetiye viya aññatra ettakaṃ dhātunidhānaṃ nāma natthi. Evarūpaṃ asadisaṃ mahāthūpaṃ pupphāni labhitvā ko na pūjeyyā”ti? “Tena hi, bhante, adhivāsetha, āharissāmī”ti tāvadeva jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā iddhiyā himavantaṃ gantvā vaṇṇagandhasampannāni pupphāni gahetvā parissāvanaṃ pūretvā mahāthere [P 0.0293] dakkhiṇamukhato pacchimamukhe asampatteyeva āgantvā pupphaparissāvanaṃ hatthe ṭhapetvā “pūjetha bhante”ti āha. Thero “atimandāni no, sāmaṇera, pupphānī”ti āha. “Gacchatha, bhante, bhagavato guṇe āvajjetvā pūjethā”ti.

The great elder, gazing upon the Great Cetiya, took delight with the Buddha as his object, gathered his whole mind, and with great joy paid homage to the Great Cetiya. The novice, seeing the elder’s manner of paying homage, thought, “My preceptor is paying homage with an exceedingly joyful mind; perhaps he has obtained flowers to make an offering.” Having paid homage, the elder rose, placed his hands in reverence on his head, gazed at the Great Cetiya, and stood there. The novice cleared his throat to announce his presence. The elder turned around, looked, and asked, “When did you arrive?” “At the time you were paying homage to the Cetiya, venerable sir. You paid homage with great joy; perhaps you have obtained flowers to offer?” “Yes, novice, nowhere else is there such a great relic repository as in this Cetiya. Who would not offer flowers upon obtaining them for such an incomparable great stupa?” “Then, venerable sir, please consent—I will bring them.” Right then, he entered into meditative absorption, traveled by psychic power to the Himalayas, gathered flowers of excellent color and fragrance, filled a basket with them, and returned before the great elder had even turned his face to the west from the south. Placing the basket of flowers in the elder’s hands, he said, “Please offer them, venerable sir.” The elder said, “Novice, these flowers are too plain for us.” “Go, venerable sir, reflect on the virtues of the Blessed One, and then offer them.”

Thero pacchimamukhanissitena sopānena āruyha kucchivedikābhūmiyaṃ pupphapūjaṃ kātuṃ āraddho. Vedikābhūmi paripuṇṇā; pupphāni patitvā dutiyabhūmiyaṃ jaṇṇuppamāṇena odhinā pūrayiṃsu. Tato otaritvā pādapiṭṭhikapantiṃ pūjesi; sāpi paripūri; paripuṇṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā heṭṭhimatale vikiranto agamāsi; sabbaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ paripūri; tasmiṃ paripuṇṇe “sāmaṇera, pupphāni na khīyantī”ti āha. “Parissāvanaṃ, bhante, adhomukhaṃ karothā”ti. Adhomukhaṃ katvā cālesi. Tadā pupphāni khīṇāni. Thero parissāvanaṃ sāmaṇerassa datvā saddhiṃ hatthipākārena cetiyaṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā catūsu ṭhānesu vanditvā pariveṇaṃ gacchanto cintesi – ‘yāva mahiddhiko vatāyaṃ sāmaṇero; sakkhissati nu kho imaṃ iddhānubhāvaṃ rakkhitunti? Tato ‘na sakkhissatī’ti disvā sāmaṇeraṃ āha – “sāmaṇera, tvaṃ idāni mahiddhiko; evarūpaṃ pana iddhiṃ nāsetvā pacchimakāle [M 0.0280] kāṇapesakāriyā hatthena madditaṃkañjiyaṃ pivissasī”ti. Daharakabhāvassa nāmesa doso yaṃ so upajjhāyassa kathāya saṃvejetvā ‘kammaṭṭhānaṃ [V 0.0278] me, bhante, ācikkhathā’ti na yāci; ‘amhākaṃ upajjhāyo kiṃ vadatī’ti taṃ pana asuṇanto viya agamāsi.

The elder, having ascended the staircase facing west, began to offer flowers on the platform of the relic chamber. The platform was full; the flowers fell and filled the second level up to the knee. Then descending, he offered flowers on the row of footrest stones; that too was filled. Knowing it was full, he scattered flowers on the lower ground and went on; the entire courtyard of the Cetiya was filled. When it was full, he said, “Novice, the flowers are not exhausted.” “Venerable sir, turn the bowl upside down,” he replied. Turning it upside down, he shook it. Then the flowers were exhausted. The elder gave the bowl to the novice and together with the elephant enclosure, circumambulated the Cetiya three times, paid homage at the four places, and while returning to his dwelling, he thought, 'This novice is indeed of great psychic power; but will he be able to protect this psychic ability?' Then, seeing that he would not, he said to the novice, “Novice, you now possess great psychic power; but having lost such psychic ability, in your last days, you will drink rice gruel kneaded by the hand of a blind serving-woman.” Such is the fault of youth that, moved by his preceptor's words, he did not request, “Venerable sir, teach me a meditation subject,” but as if not hearing what his preceptor said, he went on.

Thero mahācetiyañca mahābodhiñca vanditvā sāmaṇeraṃ pattacīvaraṃ gāhāpetvā anupubbena kuṭeḷitissamahāvihāraṃ agamāsi. Sāmaṇero upajjhāyassa padānupadiko hutvā bhikkhācāraṃ na gacchati. “Kataraṃ gāmaṃ pavisatha, bhante”ti pucchitvā pana ‘idāni me upajjhāyo gāmadvāraṃ sampatto bhavissatī’ti ñatvā attano ca upajjhāyassa ca pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā ākāsenāgantvā therassa pattacīvaraṃ datvā [P 0.0294] piṇḍāya pavisati. Thero sabbakālaṃ ovadati – “sāmaṇera, mā evamakāsi; puthujjaniddhi nāma calā anibaddhā; asappāyaṃ rūpādiārammaṇaṃ labhitvā appamattakeneva bhijjati; santāya samāpattiyā parihīnā brahmacariyavāse santhambhituṃ na sakkontī”ti. Sāmaṇero ‘kiṃ katheti mayhaṃ upajjhāyo’ti sotuṃ na icchati, tatheva karoti. Thero anupubbena cetiyavandanaṃ karonto kammupendavihāraṃ nāma gato. Tattha vasantepi there sāmaṇero tatheva karoti.

The elder, having paid homage to the Great Cetiya and the Great Bodhi Tree, had the novice take his bowl and robe, and gradually went to the Kuṭelitissa Great Monastery. The novice, following closely behind his preceptor, did not go for alms. However, after asking, “Which village do you enter, venerable sir?” and knowing, “Now my preceptor will have reached the village gate,” he took his own and his preceptor's bowl and robe, came through the air, gave the elder his bowl and robe, and entered for alms. The elder constantly advised: “Novice, do not act thus. The psychic power of ordinary beings is fickle and unstable; encountering unsuitable objects such as forms, it is destroyed by even a slight cause; those who have fallen away from the attainment of peace are unable to stand firm in the holy life.” The novice, not wishing to hear, “What is my preceptor saying?”, continued to act in the same way. The elder, gradually paying homage at the cetiyas, went to a monastery named Kammupenda. Even while the elder was staying there, the novice acted in the same way.

Athekadivasaṃ ekā pesakāradhītā abhirūpā paṭhamavaye ṭhitā kammupendagāmato nikkhamitvā padumassaraṃ oruyha gāyamānā pupphāni bhañjati. Tasmiṃ samaye sāmaṇero padumassaramatthakena gacchati gacchanto pana, sakkaralasikāya kāṇamakkhikā viya, tassā gītasadde bajjhi; tāvadeva iddhi antarahitā, chinnapakkho kāko viya ahosi. Santasamāpattibalena pana tattheva udakapiṭṭhe apatitvā simbalitūlaṃ viya patamānaṃ anupubbena padumassaratīre aṭṭhāsi. So vegena gantvā upajjhāyassa pattacīvaraṃ datvā nivatti. Mahāthero ‘pagevetaṃ mayā diṭṭhaṃ, nivāriyamānopi na nivattissatī’ti kiñci avatvā piṇḍāya pāvisi.

Then one day, a beautiful weaver's daughter, in the prime of her youth, emerging from Kammupenda village, descended to the Paduma lotus pond and, while singing, plucked flowers. At that time, the novice was passing over the Paduma lotus pond. As he was going, however, like a blind fly to molasses, he was captivated by the sound of her song; in that very moment, his psychic power vanished, and he became like a crow with broken wings. Yet, by the power of his peaceful attainment, he did not fall right there onto the water's surface, but descending like a tuft of silk-cotton, he gradually came to stand on the bank of the lotus pond. He quickly went, gave his preceptor his bowl and robe, and returned. The great elder, thinking, “This I have already foreseen; even if warned, he will not turn back,” said nothing and entered for alms.

Sāmaṇero gantvā padumassaratīre aṭṭhāsi tassā paccuttaraṇaṃ āgamayamāno. Sāpi sāmaṇeraṃ ākāsena gacchantañca punāgantvā ṭhitañca disvā ‘addhā [M 0.0281] esa maṃ nissāya ukkaṇṭhito’ti ñatvā ‘paṭikkama sāmaṇerā’ti āha. Sopi paṭipakkami. Itarā paccuttaritvā sāṭakaṃ nivāsetvā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā ‘kiṃ, bhante’ti pucchi. So tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Sā bahūhi kāraṇehi gharāvāse ādīnavaṃ brahmacariyavāse ānisaṃsañca dassetvā ovadamānāpi [V 0.0279] tassa ukkaṇṭhaṃ vinodetuṃ asakkontī ‘ayaṃ mama kāraṇā evarūpāya iddhiyā parihīno; na dāni yuttaṃ pariccajitu’nti. ‘Idheva tiṭṭhā’ti vatvā gharaṃ gantvā mātāpitūnaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Tepi āgantvā nānappakāraṃ ovadamānā vacanaṃ aggaṇhantaṃ āhaṃsu – “tvaṃ amhe uccākulāti mā sallakkhesi. Mayaṃ pesakārā. Sakkhissasi pesakārakammaṃ kātu”nti? Sāmaṇero āha – “upāsaka, gihībhūto nāma pesakārakammaṃ vā kareyya naḷakārakammaṃ vā, kiṃ iminā, mā sāṭakamatte lobhaṃ karothā”ti[P 0.0295]. Pesakārako udare baddhasāṭakaṃ datvā gharaṃ netvā dhītaraṃ adāsi.

The novice went and stood on the bank of the Paduma lotus pond, waiting for her to come up from the water. She, seeing the novice both going through the air and then returning to stand there, knew, “Surely he is distressed on account of me,” and said, “Go back, novice.” And so he went back. The other, having come up from the water and put on her garment, approached him and asked, “What is it, venerable sir?” He explained the matter to her. Though she admonished him, showing in many ways the drawbacks of household life and the benefits of the holy life, she was unable to dispel his distress. She thought, “Because of me, he has lost such psychic power; it is not right for me to abandon him now.” Saying, “Wait right here,” she went home and informed her parents of the situation. They also came and admonished him in various ways, but seeing that he would not accept their words, they said, “Do not consider us to be of high birth. We are weavers. Will you be able to do the work of a weaver?” The novice replied, “Layman, one who has become a householder might do the work of a weaver or the work of a reed-worker. What of this? Do not be avaricious over a mere garment.” The weaver gave him a garment to tie around his waist, took him home, and gave him his daughter.

So pesakārakammaṃ uggaṇhitvā pesakārehi saddhiṃ sālāya kammaṃ karoti. Aññesaṃ itthiyo pātova bhattaṃ sampādetvā āhariṃsu. Tassa bhariyā na tāva āgacchati. So itaresu kammaṃ vissajjetvā bhuñjamānesu tasaraṃ vaṭṭento nisīdi. Sā pacchā āgamāsi. Atha naṃ so ‘aticirena āgatāsī’ti tajjesi. Mātugāmo ca nāma api cakkavattirājānaṃ attani paṭibaddhacittaṃ ñatvā dāsaṃ viya sallakkheti. Tasmā sā evamāha – “aññesaṃ ghare dārupaṇṇaloṇādīni sannihitāni; bāhirato āharitvā dāyakā pesakārakāpi atthi. Ahaṃ pana ekikā; tvampi ‘mayhaṃ ghare idaṃ atthi, idaṃ natthī’ti na jānāsi. Sace icchasi bhuñja, no ce icchasi mā bhuñjā”ti. So ‘na kevalaṃ ussūre bhattaṃ āharasi, vācāyapi maṃ ghaṭṭesī’ti kujjhitvā aññaṃ paharaṇaṃ apassanto tameva tasaradaṇḍakaṃ tasarato luñcitvā khipi. Sā taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā īsakaṃ parivatti. Tasaradaṇḍakassa ca koṭi nāma tikhiṇā hoti. Sā tassā parivattamānāya akkhikoṭiyaṃ pavisitvā aṭṭhāsi. Sā ubhohi hatthehi vegena akkhiṃ aggahesi. Bhinnaṭṭhānato lohitaṃ paggharati.

He learned the work of a weaver and worked in the hall with the other weavers. The wives of the others prepared the morning meal early and brought it. His wife, however, had not yet come. While the others, having set aside their work, were eating, he sat winding a shuttle. She came later. Then he scolded her, saying, “You have come very late.” Now, it is the nature of a woman that even if she knows a wheel-turning monarch's heart is bound to her, she regards him as a slave. Therefore, she said, “In others' homes, firewood, greens, salt, and so on are at hand; there are also donors and weavers who bring things from outside. But I am alone; and you do not even know what is in my home and what is not. If you wish to eat, eat; if you do not wish to eat, do not eat.” Angered, he thought, “Not only do you bring the meal late, but you also strike me with your words!” Not seeing anything else to strike her with, he pulled the shuttle-stick from the shuttle and threw it. Seeing it coming, she turned slightly. The tip of a shuttle-stick is sharp. As she was turning, it entered the corner of her eye and lodged there. She quickly grabbed her eye with both hands. Blood flowed from the pierced spot.

So [M 0.0282] tasmiṃ kāle upajjhāyassa vacanaṃ anussari ‘idaṃ sandhāya maṃ upajjhāyo “anāgate kāle kāṇapesakāriyā hatthena madditaṃ kañjiyaṃ pivissasī”ti āha. Idaṃ therena diṭṭhaṃ bhavissati. Aho dīghadassī ayyo’ti mahāsaddena rodituṃ ārabhi. Tamenaṃ aññe “alaṃ, āvuso, mā rodi; akkhi nāma bhinnaṃ na sakkā rodanena paṭipākatikaṃ kātu”nti āhaṃsu. So “nāhaṃ etamatthaṃ rodāmi; apica kho idaṃ sandhāya rodāmī”ti sabbaṃ pavattiṃ paṭipāṭiyā kathesi. Evaṃ uppannā samathavipassanā nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvattanti.

At that moment, he recalled the words of his preceptor: “It was with reference to this that my preceptor told me, ‘In the future, you will drink rice-gruel squeezed by the hand of a one-eyed weaver woman.’” He thought, “This must have been foreseen by the elder. Oh, how far-seeing is the noble one!” and he began to weep loudly. The others said to him, “Enough, friend, do not weep. A pierced eye cannot be restored to its original state by weeping.” He replied, “I am not weeping for that reason; rather, I am weeping with reference to this,” and he recounted the whole affair in due order. Thus, serenity and insight, once arisen, lead to ruin when they are obstructed.

Aparampi [V 0.0280] vatthu – tiṃsamattā bhikkhū kalyāṇiyaṃ mahācetiyaṃ vanditvā aṭavimaggena mahāmaggaṃ otaramānā antarāmagge jhāmakkhette kammaṃ katvā āgacchantaṃ ekaṃ manussaṃ addasaṃsu. Tassa sarīraṃ masimakkhitaṃ hoti, masimakkhitameva ca ekaṃ kāsāvaṃ kacchaṃ pīḷetvā nivatthaṃ. Olokiyamāno jhāmakhāṇuko viya khāyati. So divasabhāge [P 0.0296] kammaṃ katvā upaḍḍhajhāyamānānaṃ dārūnaṃ kalāpaṃ ukkhipitvā piṭṭhiyaṃ vippakiṇṇehi kesehi kummaggena āgantvā bhikkhūnaṃ sammukhe aṭṭhāsi. Sāmaṇerā disvā aññamaññaṃ olokayamānā “āvuso, tuyhaṃ pitā, tuyhaṃ mahāpitā, tuyhaṃ mātulo”ti hasamānā gantvā “ko nāmosi tvaṃ, upāsakā”ti nāmaṃ pucchiṃsu. So nāmaṃ pucchito vippaṭisārī hutvā dārukalāpaṃ chaḍḍetvā vatthaṃ saṃvidhāya nivāsetvā mahāthere vanditvā “tiṭṭhatha tāva, bhante”ti āha. Mahātherā aṭṭhaṃsu.

Another story: About thirty monks, having paid homage at the Great Shrine of Kalyāṇī, were descending from the forest path onto the main road when, on the way, they saw a man coming from having worked in a burnt field. His body was smeared with soot, and he wore a single ochre-colored garment, also smeared with soot, tucked tightly as a loincloth. When looked at, he appeared like a burnt stump. Having worked during the day, he lifted a bundle of half-burnt firewood onto his back, his hair disheveled, and came along a crooked path to stand before the monks. The novice monks, seeing him, looked at each other and, laughing, said, 'Friend, is this your father? Your grandfather? Your uncle?' Then they went up to him and asked, 'What is your name, lay follower?' When asked his name, he became remorseful, threw down the bundle of firewood, adjusted his garment, and put it on properly. He then paid homage to the elder monks and said, 'Please wait a moment, venerable sirs.' The elder monks waited.

Daharasāmaṇerā āgantvā mahātherānaṃ sammukhāpi parihāsaṃ karonti. Upāsako āha – “bhante, tumhe maṃ passitvā parihasatha; ettakeneva matthakaṃ pattamhāti sallakkhetha. Ahampi pubbe tumhādisova samaṇo ahosiṃ. Tumhākaṃ pana cittekaggatāmattampi natthi. Ahaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo ahosiṃ; ākāsaṃ gahetvā pathaviṃ karomi, pathaviṃ ākāsaṃ; dūraṃ gaṇhitvā santikaṃ karomi, santikaṃ dūraṃ; cakkavāḷasahassaṃ khaṇena vinivijjhāmi. Hatthe me passatha; idāni pana makkaṭahatthasadisā. Ahaṃ imeheva hatthehi idha nisinnova candimasūriye parāmasiṃ. Imesaṃyeva pādānaṃ candimasūriye pādakathalikaṃ katvā nisīdiṃ. Evarūpā me iddhi pamādena antarahitā. Tumhe mā pamajjittha. Pamādena hi evarūpaṃ [M 0.0283] byasanaṃ pāpuṇanti. Appamattā viharantā jātijarāmaraṇassa antaṃ karonti. Tasmā tumhe maññeva ārammaṇaṃ karitvā appamattā hotha, bhante”ti tajjetvā ovādamadāsi. Te tassa kathentasseva saṃvegaṃ āpajjitvā vipassamānā tiṃsa janā tattheva arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti. Evampi uppannā samathavipassanā nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvattantīti veditabbā. Ayaṃ tāva lokiyasammappadhānakathāya vinicchayo.

The young novices came and joked even in the presence of the elder monks. The lay follower said: 'Venerable sirs, you see me and joke; do you consider that you have reached the pinnacle with just this? I too was once a monk like you. But you do not even have a trace of one-pointedness of mind. In this dispensation, I was one of great psychic power and great might; I took the sky and made it earth, and the earth sky; I took what was distant and made it near, and what was near distant; in an instant, I could pierce through a thousand world-systems. Look at my hands; now they are like a monkey’s. With these very hands, while sitting right here, I touched the sun and moon. For these very feet, I made the sun and moon a footstool and sat down. Such psychic power of mine has vanished through negligence. Do not be negligent. For through negligence, one reaches such ruin. Those who dwell heedfully make an end of birth, aging, and death. Therefore, taking me as your object of attention, be heedful, venerable sirs,' he admonished and gave advice. While he was speaking, they were stirred with a sense of urgency and, developing insight, the thirty of them attained arahantship right there. Thus, it should be understood that even serenity and insight, having arisen, conduce to misfortune when they cease. This, then, is the analysis of the discourse on mundane right effort.

Lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe panetaṃ ekameva vīriyaṃ catukiccasādhanavasena cattāri nāmāni labhati. Tattha anuppannānanti asamudācāravasena vā ananubhūtārammaṇavasena vā anuppannānaṃ; aññathā hi anamatagge saṃsāre anuppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā nāma natthi. Anuppannā pana uppajjamānāpi eteyeva uppajjanti[P 0.0297], pahīyamānāpi eteyeva pahīyanti.

At the moment of the supramundane path, however, this single effort obtains four names by way of accomplishing four functions. Here, 'unarisen' refers to states that are unarisen either by way of non-manifestation or by way of their objects not being experienced; for otherwise, in beginningless saṃsāra, there are no evil, unwholesome states that have not arisen. However, unarisen states, when arising, arise in this very way, and when being abandoned, are abandoned in this very way.

Tattha [V 0.0281] ekaccassa vattavasena kilesā na samudācaranti. Ekaccassa ganthadhutaṅgasamādhivipassanā navakammikānaṃ aññataravasena. Kathaṃ? Ekacco hi vattasampanno hoti. Tassa dvāsītikhuddakavattāni (cūḷava. 243 ādayo), cuddasa mahāvattāni (cūḷava. 356 ādayo), cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇapānīyamāḷauposathāgāraāgantukagamikavattāni ca karontasseva kilesā okāsaṃ na labhanti; aparabhāge panassa vattaṃ vissajjetvā bhinnavattassa vicarato ayonisomanasikārañceva sativossaggañca āgamma uppajjanti. Evaṃ asamudācāravasena anuppannā uppajjanti nāma.

Here, for a certain person, the defilements do not manifest due to his duties. For another, it is due to one of the following: study, ascetic practices, concentration, insight, or new construction work. How so? One person is accomplished in his duties. For him, while performing the eighty-two minor duties (Cūḷavagga 243ff.), the fourteen major duties (Cūḷavagga 356ff.), and the duties concerning the shrine courtyard, the Bodhi tree courtyard, the water pavilion, the Uposatha hall, and for incoming and outgoing monks, the defilements find no opportunity. But later, when he has abandoned the duties and wanders about with his duties broken, they arise on account of unwise attention and a lapse of mindfulness. Thus, what was unarisen by way of non-manifestation is said to arise.

Ekacco ganthayutto hoti; ekampi nikāyaṃ gaṇhāti, dvepi, tayopi, cattāropi, pañcapi. Tasseva tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ atthavasena pāḷivasena anusandhivasena pubbāparavasena gaṇhantassa sajjhāyantassa cintentassa vācentassa desentassa pakāsentassa kilesā okāsaṃ na labhanti; aparabhāge panassa ganthakammaṃ pahāya kusītassa vicarato ayonisomanasikārasativossagge āgamma uppajjanti. Evampi asamudācāravasena anuppannā uppajjanti nāma.

One is devoted to study; he masters one collection, or two, or three, or four, or five. For him, while mastering the Tipiṭaka, the Buddha's word, by way of its meaning, its text, its connections, and its sequence—reciting it, pondering it, repeating it, teaching it, and explaining it—the defilements find no opportunity. But later, having abandoned the work of study, while he wanders about lazily, they arise on account of unwise attention and a lapse of mindfulness. In this way too, what was unarisen by way of non-manifestation is said to arise.

Ekacco pana dhutaṅgadharo hoti, terasa dhutaṅgaguṇe samādāya vattati. Tassa dhutaṅgaguṇe pariharantassa kilesā okāsaṃ na labhanti; aparabhāge [M 0.0284] panassa dhutaṅgāni vissajjetvā bāhullāya āvaṭṭassa vicarato ayonisomanasikārasativossagge āgamma uppajjanti. Evampi asamudācāravasena anuppannā uppajjanti nāma.

Another person is an upholder of the ascetic practices; he lives having undertaken the thirteen ascetic qualities. For him, while he maintains these ascetic qualities, the defilements find no opportunity. Later, however, having abandoned the ascetic practices and reverted to a life of abundance, while he wanders about, they arise on account of unwise attention and a lapse of mindfulness. In this way too, what was unarisen by way of non-manifestation is said to arise.

Ekacco pana aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu ciṇṇavasī hoti. Tassa paṭhamajjhānādīsu āvajjanavasīādīnaṃ vasena viharantassa kilesā okāsaṃ na labhanti; aparabhāge panassa parihīnajjhānassa vā vissaṭṭhajjhānassa vā bhassādīsu anuyuttassa viharato ayonisomanasikārasativossagge āgamma uppajjanti. Evampi asamudācāravasena anuppannā kilesā uppajjanti nāma.

Another person has practiced and gained mastery in the eight attainments. For him, while dwelling by way of the masteries of adverting and so on in the first jhāna and the others, the defilements find no opportunity. But later, when he dwells engaged in idle talk and so on, having declined from jhāna or abandoned jhāna, they arise on account of unwise attention and a lapse of mindfulness. In this way too, defilements that were unarisen by way of non-manifestation are said to arise.

Ekacco pana vipassako hoti; sattasu vā vipassanāsu aṭṭhārasasu [P 0.0298] vā mahāvipassanāsu kammaṃ karonto viharati. Tassevaṃ viharato kilesā okāsaṃ na labhanti; aparabhāge panassa vipassanākammaṃ pahāya kāyadaḷhībahulassa viharato ayonisomanasikārasativossagge [V 0.0282] āgamma uppajjanti. Evampi asamudācāravasena anuppannā kilesā uppajjanti nāma.

Some, however, are insight meditators; they dwell engaged in the practice of insight among the seven kinds of insight or the eighteen great insights. While dwelling thus, their defilements find no opportunity. But later, when they abandon the practice of insight and dwell much in bodily rigidity, defilements arise on the occasion of inappropriate attention and the lapse of mindfulness. In this way, too, defilements unarisen due to non-engagement are said to arise.

Ekacco pana navakammiko hoti, uposathāgārabhojanasālādīni karoti. Tassa tesaṃ upakaraṇāni cintentassa kilesā okāsaṃ na labhanti; aparabhāge panassa navakamme niṭṭhite vā vissaṭṭhe vā ayonisomanasikārasativossagge āgamma uppajjanti. Evampi asamudācāravasena anuppannā kilesā uppajjanti nāma.

Some, however, are engaged in new construction, building Uposatha halls, dining halls, and so forth. While they are considering the requisites for these, defilements find no opportunity. But later, when the new construction is finished or relinquished, defilements arise on the occasion of inappropriate attention and the lapse of mindfulness. In this way, too, defilements unarisen due to non-engagement are said to arise.

Ekacco pana brahmalokā āgato suddhasatto hoti. Tassa anāsevanāya kilesā okāsaṃ na labhanti; aparabhāge panassa laddhāsevanassa ayonisomanasikārasativossagge āgamma uppajjanti. Evampi asamudācāravasena anuppannā kilesā uppajjanti nāma. Evaṃ tāva asamucāravasena anuppannatā veditabbā.

Some, however, are pure beings who have come from the Brahma world. For them, defilements find no opportunity due to non-indulgence. But later, having indulged, defilements arise on the occasion of inappropriate attention and the lapse of mindfulness. In this way, too, defilements unarisen due to non-engagement are said to arise. In this way, the non-arising of defilements due to non-engagement should be understood.

Kathaṃ ananubhūtārammaṇavasena? Idhekacco ananubhūtapubbaṃ manāpiyādibhedaṃ ārammaṇaṃ labhati. Tassa tattha ayonisomanasikārasativossagge āgamma rāgādayo kilesā uppajjanti. Evaṃ ananubhūtārammaṇavasena [M 0.0285] anuppannā uppajjanti nāma. Lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe pana ekameva vīriyaṃ.

How do defilements arise through the condition of an unexperienced object? Here, someone obtains an object, classified as pleasant and so on, that was never before experienced. In regard to that, defilements such as lust arise on the occasion of inappropriate attention and the lapse of mindfulness. Thus, defilements unarisen through the condition of an unexperienced object are said to arise. But at the moment of the supramundane path, there is only a single energy.

Ye ca evaṃ anuppannā uppajjeyyuṃ, te yathā neva uppajjanti, evaṃ nesaṃ anuppādakiccaṃ uppannānañca pahānakiccaṃ sādheti. Tasmā uppannānaṃ pāpakānanti ettha pana catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ – vattamānuppannaṃ, bhutvā vigatuppannaṃ, okāsakatuppannaṃ, bhūmiladdhuppannanti. Tattha ye kilesā vijjamānā uppādādisamaṅgino – idaṃ vattamānuppannaṃ nāma. Kamme pana javite ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavitvā niruddhavipāko bhutvā vigataṃ nāma. Kammaṃ uppajjitvā niruddhaṃ bhutvā vigataṃ nāma. Tadubhayampi bhutvā vigatuppannanti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Kusalākusalakammaṃ aññassa kammassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassa okāsaṃ karoti. Evaṃ [P 0.0299] kate okāse vipāko uppajjamāno okāsakaraṇato paṭṭhāya uppannoti vuccati. Idaṃ okāsakatuppannaṃ nāma.

The task of preventing the arising of those defilements that might arise in this way, and of abandoning those that have already arisen, is accomplished. Therefore, regarding 'arisen unwholesome things,' here the 'arisen' is of four kinds: presently arisen, arisen and passed, arisen due to opportunity, and arisen by obtaining a basis. Among these, defilements that exist and are connected with arising, etc., are called 'presently arisen.' As for kamma, when it has run its course, and its result, having experienced the savor of the object, has ceased, this is called 'having been and gone.' Kamma that has arisen and ceased is also called 'having been and gone.' Both of these are classified as 'arisen and passed.' Wholesome or unwholesome kamma prevents the result of another kamma and creates an opportunity for its own result. When an opportunity has been so made, the result, as it arises, is said to have 'arisen' from the making of the opportunity. This is called 'arisen due to opportunity.'

Pañcakkhandhā [V 0.0283] pana vipassanāya bhūmi nāma. Te atītādibhedā honti. Tesu anusayitakilesā pana atītā vā anāgatā vā paccuppannā vāti na vattabbā. Atītakkhandhesu anusayitāpi hi appahīnāva honti. Anāgatakkhandhesu, paccuppannakkhandhesu anusayitāpi appahīnāva honti. Idaṃ bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ nāma. Tenāhu porāṇā – “tāsu tāsu bhūmīsu asamugghātitā kilesā bhūmiladdhuppannāti saṅkhaṃ gacchantī”ti.

The five aggregates, however, are called the basis for insight. They are of kinds such as past, etc. As for these, it cannot be said that the latent defilements are past, future, or present. For the latent defilements, even in past aggregates, are unabandoned. The latent defilements in future aggregates and present aggregates are also unabandoned. This is called 'arisen by obtaining a basis.' Therefore, the ancients said: 'The defilements not uprooted in their respective bases are reckoned as 'arisen by obtaining a basis.''

Aparampi catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ – samudācāruppannaṃ, ārammaṇādhigahituppannaṃ, avikkhambhituppannaṃ, asamugdhātituppannanti. Tattha sampati vattamānaṃyeva ‘samudācāruppannaṃ’ nāma. Sakiṃ cakkhūni ummīletvā ārammaṇe nimitte gahite anussaritānussaritakkhaṇe kilesā nuppajjissantīti na vattabbā. Kasmā? Ārammaṇassa adhigahitattā. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā khīrarukkhassa kuṭhāriyā āhatāhataṭṭhāne khīraṃ na nikkhamissatīti na vattabbaṃ, evaṃ. Idaṃ ‘ārammaṇādhigahituppannaṃ’ nāma. Samāpattiyā avikkhambhitakilesā pana imasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne nuppajjissantīti na vattabbā. Kasmā? Avikkhambhitattā. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā sace khīrarukkhaṃ kuṭhāriyā āhaneyyuṃ, ‘imasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne khīraṃ na nikkhameyyā’ti [M 0.0286] na vattabbaṃ, evaṃ. Idaṃ ‘avikkhambhituppannaṃ’ nāma. Maggena asamugghātitakilesā pana bhavagge nibbattassāpi nuppajjissantīti purimanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ. Idaṃ ‘asamugghātituppannaṃ’ nāma.

Furthermore, the 'arisen' is fourfold: arisen by way of active manifestation, arisen by apprehension of the object, arisen by non-suppression, and arisen by non-eradication. Herein, what is presently occurring is called 'arisen by way of active manifestation.' One cannot say that defilements will not arise at the moment of repeatedly recollecting after opening the eyes once and grasping the sign of an object. Why? Because the object has been apprehended. To what is this comparable? Just as one cannot say that sap will not exude from a milk-tree at the very place where it was struck by an axe, so it is. This is called 'arisen by apprehension of the object.' Moreover, one cannot say that defilements not suppressed by an attainment will not arise in such and such a place. Why? Because they are not suppressed. To what is this comparable? Just as if one were to strike a milk-tree with an axe, one cannot say, 'Sap will not exude from this particular place,' so it is. This is called 'arisen by non-suppression.' As for defilements not eradicated by the path, that they will not fail to arise even for one reborn in the peak of existence should be explained in detail according to the previous method. This is called 'arisen by non-eradication.'

Imesu uppannesu vattamānuppannaṃ, bhutvāvigatuppannaṃ, okāsakatuppannaṃ, samudācāruppannanti catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ na maggavajjhaṃ; bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ, ārammaṇādhiggahituppannaṃ, avikkhambhituppannaṃ, asamugghātituppannanti catubbidhaṃ maggavajjhaṃ. Maggo hi uppajjamāno ete kilese pajahati. So ye kilese pajahati, te atītā vā anāgatā vā paccuppannā vāti na vattabbā. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Among these kinds of 'arisen' defilements, four kinds are not to be abandoned by the path: the presently arisen, the arisen and passed, the arisen due to opportunity, and the arisen by way of active manifestation. Four kinds are to be abandoned by the path: the arisen by obtaining a basis, the arisen by apprehension of the object, the arisen by non-suppression, and the arisen by non-eradication. For the path, when arising, abandons these defilements. The defilements that it abandons should not be said to be past, future, or present. And this has been stated:

“Hañci atīte kilese pajahati, tena hi khīṇaṃ khepeti, niruddhaṃ [P 0.0300] nirodheti, vigataṃ vigameti, atthaṅgataṃ atthaṃ gameti, atītaṃ yaṃ natthi taṃ pajahati. Hañci anāgate kilese pajahati, tena hi ajātaṃ pajahati, anibbattaṃ anuppannaṃ apātubhūtaṃ pajahati, anāgataṃ yaṃ natthi taṃ pajahati. Hañci paccuppanne kilese pajahati, tena hi ratto rāgaṃ pajahati, duṭṭho dosaṃ, mūḷho mohaṃ, vinibaddho mānaṃ, parāmaṭṭho diṭṭhiṃ, vikkhepagato [V 0.0284] uddhaccaṃ, aniṭṭhaṅgato vicikicchaṃ, thāmagato anusayaṃ pajahati; kaṇhasukkadhammā yuganaddhā samameva vattanti; saṃkilesikā maggabhāvanā hoti…pe… tena hi natthi maggabhāvanā, natthi phalasacchikiriyā, natthi kilesappahānaṃ, natthi dhammābhisamayo’ti. ‘Atthi maggabhāvanā…pe… atthi dhammābhisamayo’ti. Yathā kathaṃ viya? Seyyathāpi taruṇo rukkho…pe… apātubhūtāneva na pātubhavanti”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.21).

“If one abandons defilements in the past, then one destroys what is already destroyed, brings to cessation what has already ceased, makes depart what has already departed, makes vanish what has already vanished—one abandons what is past, which no longer exists. If one abandons defilements in the future, then one abandons what is unborn, unproduced, unarisen, unmanifested—one abandons what is future, which does not exist. If one abandons defilements in the present, then one who is lustful abandons lust, one who is hateful abandons hate, one who is deluded abandons delusion, one who is bound abandons conceit, one who grasps abandons views, one who is distracted abandons restlessness, one who is undecided abandons doubt, one who is entrenched abandons latent tendencies; dark and bright qualities proceed yoked together simultaneously; the development of the path becomes defiling… Therefore, there is no development of the path, no realization of the fruit, no abandoning of defilements, no penetration of the Dhamma. But there is development of the path… there is penetration of the Dhamma. How so? Just as with a young tree… what has not yet manifested does not manifest.”

Iti pāḷiyaṃ ajātaphalarukkho āgato; jātaphalarukkhena pana dīpetabbaṃ. Yathā hi saphalo taruṇaambarukkho. Tassa phalāni manussā paribhuñjeyyuṃ, sesāni pātetvā pacchiyo pūreyyuṃ. Athañño puriso taṃ pharasunā chindeyya. Tenassa neva atītāni phalāni nāsitāni honti, na anāgatapaccuppannāni ca nāsitāni; atītāni hi manussehi paribhuttāni, anāgatāni anibbattāni na sakkā nāsetuṃ[M 0.0287]. Yasmiṃ pana samaye so chinno tadā phalāniyeva natthīti paccuppannānipi anāsitāni. Sace pana rukkho acchinno assa, athassa pathavīrasañca āporasañca āgamma yāni phalāni nibbatteyyuṃ, tāni nāsitāni honti. Tāni hi ajātāneva na jāyanti, anibbattāneva na nibbattanti, apātubhūtāneva na pātubhavanti. Evameva maggo nāpi atītādibhede kilese pajahati, nāpi na pajahati. Yesañhi kilesānaṃ maggena khandhesu apariññātesu uppatti siyā, maggena uppajjitvā khandhānaṃ pariññātattā te kilesā ajātāva na jāyanti, anibbattāva na nibbattanti, apātubhūtāva na pātubhavanti. Taruṇaputtāya itthiyā puna avijāyanatthaṃ byādhitānaṃ [P 0.0301] rogavūpasamatthaṃ pītabhesajjehi cāpi ayamattho vibhāvetabbo. Evaṃ maggo ye kilese pajahati, te atītā vā anāgatā vā paccuppannā vāti na vattabbā. Na ca maggo kilese na pajahati. Ye pana maggo kilese pajahati, te sandhāya ‘uppannānaṃ pāpakāna’ntiādi vuttaṃ.

Thus in the Pāli text, a tree with unborn fruit is mentioned; but this should be illustrated by a tree with born fruit. It is like a young mango tree bearing fruit. People might enjoy its fruits, and shake down the remaining ones to fill their baskets. Then another person might cut it down with an axe. By this act, its past fruits are not destroyed, nor are its future and present fruits destroyed. For the past fruits were already enjoyed by people, and the future ones, being unproduced, cannot be destroyed. And at the time it is cut down, there are no fruits at all, so the present ones are also not destroyed. If, however, the tree were not cut down, then the fruits that would have been produced by drawing nourishment from the earth and water are destroyed. For they, being unborn, do not come to be born; being unproduced, do not come to be produced; being unmanifested, do not become manifest.
