Tasmā pañcaṅgikova lokuttaramaggo”ti. “Cetanābahuttā ca pamuccissāma; aṭṭhaṅgikova lokuttaramaggoti ca vakkhāma”. “Tvaṃ tāva mahācattārīsakabhāṇako hosi, na hosī”ti pucchitabbo. Sace “na homī”ti vadati, “tvaṃ abhāṇakattā na jānāsī”ti vattabbo. Sace “bhāṇakosmī”ti vadati, “suttaṃ āharā”ti vattabbo. Sace suttaṃ āharati iccetaṃ kusalaṃ, no ce āharati sayaṃ uparipaṇṇāsato āharitabbaṃ –

“If you say it is eight-factored by including right speech and the others, then there are four volitions of right speech, three volitions of right action, and seven volitions of right livelihood—how will you escape this multiplicity of volitions? Therefore, the supramundane path is only five-factored.” “We will escape the multiplicity of volitions and also maintain that the supramundane path is eight-factored.” He should be asked: “Are you a reciter of the Mahācattārīsaka Sutta, or are you not?” If he says, “I am not,” one should say, “Because you are not a reciter, you do not know.” If he says, “I am a reciter,” one should say, “Bring forth the discourse.” If he brings forth the discourse, that is good. If he does not bring it forth, one should bring it forth oneself from the Uparipaṇṇāsa:

“Katamā [V 0.0304] ca, bhikkhave, sammāvācā? Sammāvācaṃpahaṃ, bhikkhave, dvāyaṃ vadāmi – atthi, bhikkhave, sammāvācā sāsavā puññabhāgiyā upadhivepakkā; atthi, bhikkhave, sammāvācā ariyā anāsavā lokuttarā maggaṅgā.

“And what, bhikkhus, is right speech? Bhikkhus, I say that right speech is twofold: there is, bhikkhus, right speech that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions; and there is, bhikkhus, right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.”

“Katamā ca, bhikkhave, sammāvācā sāsavā [P 0.0321] puññabhāgiyā upadhivepakkā? Musāvādā veramaṇī, pisuṇāya vācāya veramaṇī, pharusāya [M 0.0307] vācāya veramaṇī, samphappalāpā veramaṇī – ayaṃ, bhikkhave, sammāvācā sāsavā puññabhāgiyā upadhivepakkā.

“And what, bhikkhus, is right speech that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from malicious speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter—this, bhikkhus, is right speech that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions.”

“Katamā ca, bhikkhave, sammāvācā ariyā anāsavā lokuttarā maggaṅgā? Yā kho, bhikkhave, ariyacittassa anāsavacittassa ariyamaggasamaṅgino ariyamaggaṃ bhāvayato catūhi vacīduccaritehi ārati virati paṭivirati veramaṇī – ayaṃ, bhikkhave, sammāvācā ariyā anāsavā lokuttarā maggaṅgā…pe….

“And what, bhikkhus, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? It is, bhikkhus, the abstaining, refraining, abstinence, desisting from the four kinds of verbal misconduct in one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path and is developing the noble path—this, bhikkhus, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path…”

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sammākammanto? Sammākammantaṃpahaṃ, bhikkhave, dvayaṃ vadāmi…pe… upadhivepakko.

“And what, bhikkhus, is right action? Right action, bhikkhus, I say, is twofold… ripening in acquisitions.”

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sammākammanto ariyo anāsavo lokuttaro…pe….

“And what, bhikkhus, is right action that is noble, taintless, supramundane…?”

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sammāājīvo? Sammāājīvaṃpahaṃ, bhikkhave, dvāyaṃ vadāmi…pe… upadhivepakko.

“And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood? Right livelihood, bhikkhus, I say, is twofold… ripening in acquisitions.”

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sammāājīvo ariyo anāsavo lokuttaro maggaṅgo? Yā kho, bhikkhave, ariyacittassa anāsavacittassa ariyamaggasamaṅgino ariyamaggaṃ bhāvayato micchāājīvā ārati virati paṭivirati veramaṇī – ayaṃ, bhikkhave, sammāājīvo ariyo anāsavo lokuttaro maggaṅgo”ti (ma. ni. 3.138 ādayo).

“And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? It is, bhikkhus, the abstaining, refraining, abstinence, desisting from wrong livelihood in one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path, and who is developing the noble path. This, bhikkhus, is right livelihood that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.”

Evamettha [V 0.0305] catūhi vacīduccaritehi, tīhi kāyaduccaritehi, micchājīvato cāti ekekāva virati ariyā anāsavā lokuttarā maggaṅgāti vuttā. “Kuto ettha cetanābahuttaṃ? Kuto pañcaṅgiko maggo? Idaṃ te suttaṃ akāmakassa lokuttaramaggo aṭṭhaṅgikoti dīpeti”. Sace ettakena sallakkheti iccetaṃ kusalaṃ, no ce sallakkheti aññānipi kāraṇāni āharitvā saññāpetabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Thus, in this context, each single abstention from the four kinds of verbal misconduct, the three kinds of bodily misconduct, and wrong livelihood is described as noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path. “Whence here the multiplicity of volitions? Whence the five-factored path? This discourse shows that for one who is unwilling, the supramundane path is eight-factored.” If with this much he understands, that is good; if he does not understand, he should be made to understand by adducing other reasons. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Yasmiṃ kho, subhadda, dhammavinaye ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo na upalabbhati, samaṇopi tattha na upalabbhati…pe… imasmiṃ kho, subhadda, dhammavinaye ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo upalabbhati; idheva[M 0.0308], subhadda, samaṇo…pe… suññā parappavādā samaṇehi aññehīti (dī. ni. 2.214).

“Subhadda, in whatever Dhamma and Discipline the Noble Eight-factored Path is not found, no ascetic is found there… But in this Dhamma and Discipline, Subhadda, the Noble Eight-factored Path is found; here, Subhadda, an ascetic is found… The teachings of others are void of ascetics.”

Aññesupi anekesu suttasatesu aṭṭhaṅgikova maggo āgato. Kathāvatthuppakaraṇepi vuttaṃ –

In many hundreds of other suttas, the eight-factored path is also mentioned. And in the Kathāvatthu it is said:

“Maggānaṃ aṭṭhaṅgiko seṭṭho, saccānaṃ caturo padā;

Virāgo seṭṭho dhammānaṃ, dvipadānañca cakkhumā”ti (kathā. 872) –

“Of paths, the eight-factored is the best; of truths, the four statements; dispassion is the best of states; and of two-footed beings, the One with Vision.”

“Attheva [P 0.0322] suttantoti”? “Āmantā”“tena hi aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti. Sace pana ettakenāpi saññattiṃ na gacchati, “gaccha, vihāraṃ pavisitvā yāguṃ pivāhī”ti uyyojetabbo. Uttarimpana kāraṇaṃ vakkhatīti aṭṭhānametaṃ. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

“Is this indeed in the Suttanta?” “Yes.” “Then the path is eight-factored.” But if even with this he does not attain understanding, he should be dismissed with the words, “Go, enter the monastery and drink rice gruel.” Furthermore, it is not the occasion to state further reasons. The rest here is of clear meaning.

Nayā panettha gaṇetabbā. Aṭṭhaṅgikamaggasmiñhi ekato pucchitvā ekato vissajjane catūsu maggesu cattāri nayasahassāni vibhattāni. Pañcaṅgikamagge ekato pucchitvā ekato vissajjane cattāri; pāṭiyekkaṃ pucchitvā pāṭiyekkaṃ vissajjane cattāri cattārīti pañcasu aṅgesu vīsati. Iti purimāni aṭṭha imāni ca vīsatīti sabbānipi maggavibhaṅge aṭṭhavīsati nayasahassāni vibhattāni. Tāni ca kho nibbattitalokuttarāni kusalāneva. Vipāke pana kusalato tiguṇā nayā kātabbāti.

Herein, the methods should be reckoned. For in the eight-factored path, when questioned together and answered together, four thousand methods are distinguished in the four paths. For the five-factored path, when questioned together and answered together, four thousand; when questioned individually and answered individually, four thousand each—thus twenty thousand in the five factors. Thus, the former eight thousand and these twenty thousand make a total of twenty-eight thousand methods distinguished in the Analysis of the Path. And these, indeed, are only wholesome states that have arisen as supramundane. But in terms of the resultant, the methods should be made threefold those of the wholesome.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Division.

3. Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā

3. The Exposition of the Question Section

504. Pañhāpucchake [V 0.0306] pāḷianusāreneva maggaṅgānaṃ kusalādibhāvo veditabbo. Ārammaṇattikesu pana sabbānipetāni appamāṇaṃ nibbānaṃ ārabbha pavattito appamāṇārammaṇāneva, na maggārammaṇāni. Neva hi maggo na phalaṃ maggaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti. Sahajātahetuvasena panettha kusalāni maggahetukāni; vīriyaṃ vā vīmaṃsaṃ vā jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā maggabhāvanākāle maggādhipatīni; chandacittajeṭṭhikāya maggabhāvanāya na vattabbāni maggādhipatīnīti; phalakālepi na vattabbāneva.

504. In the Question Section, the wholesome and other natures of the path factors should be understood according to the Pāḷi itself. However, in the triads concerning objects, all these, having arisen with the immeasurable Nibbāna as their object, have only an immeasurable object, not a path-object. For neither the path nor the fruit makes the path its object. Here, by way of the co-nascent condition, the wholesome factors have the path as their root condition; when energy or investigation is made foremost during the development of the path, they are path-dominant; in the development of the path with desire or consciousness as foremost, they cannot be said to be path-dominant; even at the time of fruition, they cannot be said to be so.

Atītādīsu [M 0.0309] ekārammaṇabhāvenapi na vattabbāni; nibbānassa pana bahiddhādhammattā bahiddhārammaṇāni nāma hontīti evametasmiṃ pañhāpucchakepi nibbattitalokuttarāneva maggaṅgāni kathitāni. Sammāsambuddhena hi suttantabhājanīyasmiṃyeva lokiyalokuttarāni maggaṅgāni kathitāni; abhidhammabhājanīye pana pañhāpucchake ca lokuttarānevāti evamayaṃ maggavibhaṅgopi teparivaṭṭaṃ nīharitvāva bhājetvā dassitoti.

They cannot be said to have a past, etc., object; but since Nibbāna is an external phenomenon, they are called 'having an external object.' Thus, even in this Question Section, only the supramundane path factors that have arisen are spoken of. For the Perfectly Enlightened One has spoken of both mundane and supramundane path factors only in the Suttanta Division; but in the Abhidhamma Division and in the Question Section, only the supramundane ones. Thus, this Analysis of the Path, too, is shown as divided only after being extracted from the three rounds.

Sammohavinodaniyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya

In the Sammohavinodanī, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga.

Maggaṅgavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Analysis of the Path Factors is concluded.

12. Jhānavibhaṅgo

12. The Analysis of Jhāna

1. Suttantabhājanīyaṃ

1. The Suttanta Division

Mātikāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Matrix

508. Idāni [P 0.0323][M 0.0310][V 0.0307] tadanantare jhānavibhaṅge yā tāva ayaṃ sakalassāpi suttantabhājanīyassa paṭhamaṃ mātikā ṭhapitā, tattha idhāti vacanaṃ pubbabhāgakaraṇīyasampadāya sampannassa sabbappakārajjhānanibbattakassa puggalassa sannissayabhūtasāsanaparidīpanaṃ, aññasāsanassa ca tathābhāvapaṭisedhanaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo…pe… suññā parappavādā samaṇehi aññehī”ti (a. ni. 4.241). Bhikkhūti tesaṃ jhānānaṃ nibbattakapuggalaparidīpanaṃ. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutoti idamassa pātimokkhasaṃvare patiṭṭhitabhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Viharatīti idamassa tadanurūpavihārasamaṅgībhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Ācāragocarasampannoti idamassa heṭṭhā pātimokkhasaṃvarassa upari jhānānuyogassa ca upakāradhammaparidīpanaṃ. Aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvīti idamassa pātimokkhato acavanadhammatāparidīpanaṃ. Samādāyāti idamassa sikkhāpadānaṃ anavasesato ādānaparidīpanaṃ. Sikkhatīti idamassa sikkhāya samaṅgībhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Sikkhāpadesūti idamassa sikkhitabbadhammaparidīpanaṃ.

508. Now, in the Jhāna Division which immediately follows, as to the matrix that has been first established for the entire Suttanta Division: therein, the word “here” illuminates the teaching that serves as the foundation for an individual endowed with the accomplishment of preliminary duties, capable of producing all types of jhāna, and it refutes the existence of such a state in other teachings. For it has been said: “Here, bhikkhus, is a recluse… and so on… empty are the doctrines of other recluses” (AN 4.241). “Bhikkhu” illuminates the individual who produces these jhānas. “Restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha” illuminates his state of being established in the Pātimokkha restraint. “Dwells” illuminates his possession of a suitable mode of life. “Endowed with conduct and resort” illuminates the qualities that support the Pātimokkha restraint below and the pursuit of jhāna above. “Seeing danger in the slightest faults” illuminates his quality of not deviating from the Pātimokkha. “Undertakes” illuminates his complete adoption of the training rules. “Trains” illuminates his possession of the training. “In the training rules” illuminates the things to be trained in.

Indriyesūti idamassa guttadvāratāya bhūmiparidīpanaṃ; rakkhitabbokāsaparidīpanantipi vadanti eva. Guttadvāroti idamassa chasu dvāresu saṃvihitārakkhabhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Bhojane mattaññūti idamassa santosādiguṇaparidīpanaṃ. Pubbarattāpararattaṃ jāgariyānuyogamanuyuttoti idamassa kāraṇabhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Sātaccaṃ [P 0.0324] nepakkanti idamassa paññāpariggahitena vīriyena sātaccakāritāparidīpanaṃ[V 0.0308]. Bodhipakkhikānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhāvanānuyogamanuyuttoti idamassa paṭipattiyā nibbedhabhāgiyattaparidīpanaṃ.

“In the sense faculties” illuminates the ground for his guardedness of the doors; some also say it illuminates the occasion for guarding. “Guarded in the doors” illuminates his well-protected state at the six doors. “Moderate in eating” illuminates his qualities such as contentment. “Devoted to wakefulness in the first and last watches of the night” illuminates his diligence. “Perseverance and clear comprehension” illuminates his constant activity with energy encompassed by wisdom. “Devoted to the practice of the qualities conducive to enlightenment” illuminates his practice as being of the nature of penetration.

So abhikkante…pe… tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī hotīti idamassa sabbattha satisampajaññasamannāgatattaparidīpanaṃ. So vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajatīti idamassa anurūpasenāsanapariggahaparidīpanaṃ. Araññaṃ…pe… paṭisallānasāruppanti idamassa senāsanappabhedanirādīnavatānisaṃsaparidīpanaṃ. So [M 0.0311] araññagato vāti idamassa vuttappakārena senāsanena yuttabhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Nisīdatīti idamassa yogānurūpairiyāpathaparidīpanaṃ. Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti idamassa yogārambhaparidīpanaṃ. So abhijjhaṃ loke pahāyātiādi panassa kammaṭṭhānānuyogena nīvaraṇappahānaparidīpanaṃ. Tasseva pahīnanīvaraṇassa vivicceva kāmehītiādi paṭipāṭiyā jhānuppattiparidīpanaṃ.

“When going forth… and so on… and being silent, he acts with clear comprehension”—this illuminates his being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension in all situations. “He resorts to a secluded dwelling”—this illuminates his choosing of a suitable dwelling. “The wilderness… and so on… suitable for seclusion”—this illuminates the classification, freedom from disadvantage, and advantages of dwellings. “Having gone to the wilderness, etc.”—this illuminates his being associated with a dwelling of the type described. “He sits down”—this illuminates his posture suitable for meditation. “Establishing mindfulness in front of him”—this illuminates the beginning of meditation. “Having abandoned covetousness for the world, etc.”—this illuminates his abandoning of the hindrances by application to the meditation subject. For one who has abandoned the hindrances, “secluded from sensual pleasures, etc.”—this illuminates the progressive arising of jhāna.

Api ca idha bhikkhūti imasmiṃ sāsane jhānuppādako bhikkhu. Idāni yasmā jhānuppādakena bhikkhunā cattāri sīlāni sodhetabbāni, tasmāssa pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutoti iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlavisuddhiṃ upadisati. Ācāragocarasampannotiādinā ājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ. Samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesūti iminā tesaṃ dvinnaṃ sīlānaṃ anavasesato ādānaṃ. Indriyesu guttadvāroti iminā indriyasaṃvarasīlaṃ. Bhojane mattaññūti iminā paccayasannissitasīlaṃ. Pubbarattāpararattantiādinā sīle patiṭṭhitassa jhānabhāvanāya upakārake dhamme. So abhikkantetiādinā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ aparihānāya kammaṭṭhānassa ca asammosāya satisampajaññasamāyogaṃ. So vivittantiādinā bhāvanānurūpasenāsanapariggahaṃ. So [P 0.0325] araññagato vātiādinā taṃ senāsanaṃ upagatassa jhānānurūpairiyāpathañceva jhānabhāvanārambhañca. So abhijjhantiādinā jhānabhāvanārambhena jhānapaccanīkadhammappahānaṃ. So ime pañca nīvaraṇe pahāyātiādinā evaṃ pahīnajjhānapaccanīkadhammassa sabbajjhānānaṃ uppattikkamaṃ upadisatīti.

Furthermore, here, 'a bhikkhu' refers to a bhikkhu who develops jhāna in this Dispensation. Now, because a bhikkhu who develops jhāna must purify the fourfold virtue, therefore, 'restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint' indicates the purification of virtue through the Pātimokkha restraint. 'Accomplished in conduct and resort' indicates the purification of livelihood. 'Undertakes and trains in the training rules' signifies the complete undertaking of these two virtues. 'Guarded in the sense-doors' indicates the virtue of sense restraint. 'Knowing moderation in food' indicates the virtue dependent on the requisites. 'The first watch of the night and the last watch of the night,' and so on, refers to the qualities supportive of jhāna development for one established in virtue. 'In going forward,' and so on, refers to the application of mindfulness and clear comprehension to prevent the decline of these qualities and confusion regarding the meditation subject. 'He frequents a secluded dwelling,' and so on, refers to the selection of a dwelling suitable for meditation. 'Having gone to the forest,' and so on, refers to the posture suitable for jhāna and the commencement of jhāna development for one who has approached that dwelling. 'Having given up covetousness,' and so on, refers to the abandonment of factors opposed to jhāna through the commencement of jhāna development. 'Having abandoned these five hindrances,' and so on, indicates the progressive order of attainment of all the jhānas for one who has thus abandoned the factors opposed to jhāna.

Mātikāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Matrix.

Niddesavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Niddesa.

509. Idāni [V 0.0309] yathānikkhittaṃ mātikaṃ paṭipāṭiyā bhājetvā dassetuṃ idhāti imissā diṭṭhiyātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha imissā diṭṭhiyātiādīhi dasahi padehi sikkhattayasaṅkhātaṃ sabbaññubuddhasāsanameva kathitaṃ. Tañhi buddhena bhagavatā diṭṭhattā diṭṭhīti vuccati. Tasseva khamanavasena khanti, ruccanavasena ruci, gahaṇavasena ādāyo, sabhāvaṭṭhena dhammo, sikkhitabbaṭṭhena [M 0.0312] vinayo, tadubhayenāpi dhammavinayo, pavuttavasena pāvacanaṃ, seṭṭhacariyaṭṭhena brahmacariyaṃ, anusiṭṭhidānavasena satthusāsananti vuccati. Tasmā imissā diṭṭhiyātiādīsu imissā buddhadiṭṭhiyā, imissā buddhakhantiyā, imissā buddharuciyā, imasmiṃ buddhaādāye, imasmiṃ buddhadhamme, imasmiṃ buddhavinaye.

509. Now, to explain the matrix laid out in sequence, the section beginning 'here, in this view' is introduced. Herein, by these ten terms—such as 'this view'—the entire teaching of the Omniscient Buddha, known as the threefold training, is described. For it is called 'view' because it is seen by the Blessed One. By way of forbearance, it is called 'patience'; by way of inclination, 'preference'; by way of taking up, 'adoption'; by its intrinsic nature, the 'Dhamma'; by its training aspect, the 'Vinaya'; by both, the 'Dhamma-Vinaya'; by its pronouncement, the 'teaching'; by its superior conduct, the 'holy life'; by its giving of instruction, the 'Teacher’s dispensation.' Therefore, in terms like 'this view,' it means this Buddha-view, this Buddha-patience, this Buddha-preference, this Buddha-adoption, this Buddha-Dhamma, this Buddha-Vinaya.

“Ye ca kho tvaṃ, gotami, dhamme jāneyyāsi – ‘ime dhammā sarāgāya saṃvattanti no virāgāya, saṃyogāya saṃvattanti no visaṃyogāya, ācayāya saṃvattanti no apacayāya, upādāya saṃvattanti no paṭinissaggiyā, mahicchatāya saṃvattanti no appicchatāya, asantuṭṭhiyā saṃvattanti no santuṭṭhiyā, saṅgaṇikāya saṃvattanti no pavivekāya, kosajjāya saṃvattanti no vīriyārambhāya, dubbharatāya saṃvattanti no subharatāyā’ti ekaṃsena hi, gotami, dhāreyyāsi – ‘neso dhammo, neso vinayo, netaṃ satthusāsana’nti. Ye ca kho tvaṃ, gotami, dhamme jāneyyāsi – ‘ime dhammā virāgāya saṃvattanti no sarāgāya…pe… subharatāya saṃvattanti no dubbharatāyā’ti. Ekaṃsena hi, gotami, dhāreyyāsi – ‘eso dhammo, eso vinayo, etaṃ satthusāsana”nti (a. ni. 8.53; cūḷava. 406).

“Gotami, of those things of which you know: ‘These things lead to passion, not to dispassion; they lead to bondage, not to freedom from bondage; they lead to accumulation, not to dispersal; they lead to grasping, not to relinquishment; they lead to great ambition, not to modest desires; they lead to discontent, not to contentment; they lead to gregariousness, not to solitude; they lead to laziness, not to the arousing of energy; they lead to being hard to support, not to being easy to support,’ you may hold it for certain, Gotami: ‘This is not the Dhamma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher’s instruction.’ But of those things of which you know: ‘These things lead to dispassion, not to passion… they lead to being easy to support, not to being hard to support,’ you may hold it for certain, Gotami: ‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.’”

Evaṃ vutte imasmiṃ buddhadhammavinaye[P 0.0326], imasmiṃ buddhapāvacane, imasmiṃ buddhabrahmacariye, imasmiṃ buddhasatthusāsaneti evamattho veditabbo.

When this is said, the meaning should be understood as: in this Buddha-Dhamma-Vinaya, in this Buddha's teaching, in this Buddha's holy life, in this Buddha's dispensation of the Teacher.

Apicetaṃ sikkhāttayasaṅkhātaṃ sakalaṃ sāsanaṃ bhagavatā diṭṭhattā sammādiṭṭhipaccayattā sammādiṭṭhipubbaṅgamattā ca diṭṭhi, bhagavato khamanavasena khanti, ruccanavasena ruci, gahaṇavasena ādāyo. Attano kārakaṃ apāyesu apatamānaṃ dhāretīti dhammo. Sova saṃkilesapakkhaṃ vinatīti [V 0.0310] vinayo. Dhammo ca so vinayo cāti dhammavinayo. Kusaladhammehi vā akusaladhammānaṃ esa vinayoti dhammavinayo. Teneva vuttaṃ – “ye ca kho tvaṃ, gotami, dhamme jāneyyāsi – ‘ime dhammā virāgāya saṃvattanti no sarāgāya…pe… ekaṃsena, gotami, dhāreyyāsi ‘eso dhammo, eso vinayo, etaṃ satthusāsana’nti.

Furthermore, this entire teaching, known as the threefold training, is 'view' because it was seen by the Blessed One, because it has right view as its condition, and because it has right view as its forerunner. It is 'patience' (khanti) due to the Blessed One's forbearance, 'preference' (ruci) due to His approval, and 'adoption' (ādāyo) due to His taking it up. It holds its practitioner from falling into the states of woe; therefore, it is 'Dhamma.' It removes the side of defilement; hence, it is 'Vinaya.' Both that Dhamma and that Vinaya together are 'Dhamma-Vinaya.' Or, it is the removal of unwholesome states by means of wholesome states; therefore, it is 'Dhamma-Vinaya.' For this reason it has been said: “Gotami, of those things of which you know—‘These things lead to dispassion, not to passion…’—you may hold it for certain, Gotami: ‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.’”

Dhammena [M 0.0313] vā vinayo, na daṇḍādīhīti dhammavinayo, vuttampi cetaṃ –

Or, the discipline is by the Dhamma, not by punishments and so forth; hence, the Dhamma-Vinaya. And this was also said:

“Daṇḍeneke damayanti, aṅkusehi kasāhi ca;

Adaṇḍena asatthena, nāgo danto mahesinā”ti. (cūḷava. 342; ma. ni. 2.352);

“Some tame with sticks, with hooks, and with whips; but the great sage tamed the great being without stick or weapon.”

Tathā –

Likewise:

“Dhammena nīyamānānaṃ, kā usūyā vijānata”nti; (Mahāva. 63);

“For those guided by the Dhamma, what envy is there among the discerning?”

Dhammāya vā vinayo dhammavinayo. Anavajjadhammatthañhesa vinayo, na bhavabhogāmisatthaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā – “nayidaṃ, bhikkhave, brahmacariyaṃ vussati janakuhanattha”nti (a. ni. 4.25) vitthāro. Puṇṇattheropi āha – “anupādāparinibbānatthaṃ kho, āvuso, bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.259). Visiṭṭhaṃ vā nayatīti vinayo. Dhammato vinayo dhammavinayo. Saṃsāradhammato hi sokādidhammato vā esa visiṭṭhaṃ nibbānaṃ nayati. Dhammassa vā vinayo, na titthakarānanti dhammavinayo; dhammabhūto hi bhagavā, tasseva vinayo. Yasmā vā dhammāyeva abhiññeyyā pariññeyyā pahātabbā bhāvetabbā sacchikātabbā ca, tasmā esa dhammesu vinayo, na sattesu, na jīvesu cāti dhammavinayo. Sātthasabyañjanatādīhi aññesaṃ vacanato padhānaṃ vacananti pavacanaṃ; pavacanameva pāvacanaṃ. Sabbacariyāhi visiṭṭhacariyābhāvena brahmacariyaṃ. Devamanussānaṃ [P 0.0327] satthubhūtassa bhagavato sāsananti satthusāsanaṃ; satthubhūtaṃ vā sāsanantipi satthusāsanaṃ. “So vo mamaccayena satthā”ti (dī. ni. 2.216) hi dhammavinayova satthāti vuttoti evametesaṃ padānaṃ attho veditabbo.

Or, the Vinaya is for the sake of the Dhamma, hence Dhamma-Vinaya. This Discipline is for the sake of blameless states; it is not for the sake of existence, enjoyment, and material gain. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, this holy life is not lived for the sake of deceiving people" (A. Ni. 4.25), and so on in detail. The Elder Puṇṇa also said: "Friend, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging" (M. Ni. 1.259). Or, because it leads to what is distinguished, it is the Vinaya. The Vinaya from the Dhamma is the Dhamma-Vinaya. For from the phenomena of saṃsāra or from the phenomena of sorrow and so on, it leads to the distinguished Nibbāna. Or, the Discipline of the Dhamma, not of the sectarians, is the Dhamma-Vinaya; for the Blessed One is Dhamma-become, and this is His Discipline. Or, because only phenomena are to be directly known, fully understood, abandoned, developed, and realized, this is a Discipline in phenomena, not in beings or souls—thus it is the Dhamma-Vinaya. Because it is the foremost teaching among others due to its meaningfulness and excellent phrasing, it is the 'pavacana'; 'pavacana' itself is 'pāvacana'. Because it is the distinguished conduct among all conducts, it is the 'brahmacariya'. The teaching of the Blessed One, who is the teacher of gods and humans, is the 'satthusāsana'; or, the teaching that has become the teacher is also the 'satthusāsana'. For it is said: "After my passing, it will be your teacher" (Dī. Ni. 2.216), where the Dhamma-Vinaya itself is called the teacher. Thus, the meaning of these terms should be understood.

Yasmā [V 0.0311] pana imasmiṃyeva sāsane sabbapakārajjhānanibbattako bhikkhu dissati, na aññatra, tasmā tattha tattha ‘imissā’ti ca ‘imasmi’nti ca ayaṃ niyamo katoti veditabboti. Ayaṃ ‘idhā’ti mātikāpadaniddesassa attho.

Since it is only in this dispensation that a monk who brings forth all kinds of jhāna is seen, and not elsewhere, it should be understood that in each and every case the specification is made with 'of this' and 'in this.' This is the meaning of 'here' in the explanation of the matrix heading.

510. Bhikkhuniddese samaññāyāti paññattiyā, vohārenāti attho. Samaññāya eva hi ekacco bhikkhūti paññāyati. Tathā hi nimantanādimhi bhikkhūsu gaṇīyamānesu sāmaṇerepi gahetvā ‘sataṃ bhikkhū, sahassaṃ bhikkhū’ti vadanti. Paṭiññāyāti attano paṭijānanena. Paṭiññāyapi [M 0.0314] hi ekacco bhikkhūti paññāyati. Tassa “ko ettha āvuso”ti? “Ahaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhū”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 10.96) sambhavo daṭṭhabbo. Ayaṃ pana ānandattherena vuttattā dhammikā paṭiññā. Rattibhāge pana dussīlāpi paṭipathaṃ āgacchantā “ko etthā”ti vutte adhammikāya paṭiññāya abhūtatthāya “mayaṃ bhikkhū”ti vadanti.

510. In the exposition of 'bhikkhu,' 'by designation' means by convention; this is the meaning. For it is by designation alone that someone is known as a bhikkhu. Thus, when counting bhikkhus for an invitation and so on, they include even novices and say, "a hundred bhikkhus, a thousand bhikkhus." 'By acknowledgement' means by one's own declaration. For it is also by acknowledgement that someone is known as a bhikkhu. Its occurrence should be seen in such cases as when one is asked, "Who is here, friend?" and replies, "I, friend, am a bhikkhu" (cf. A. Ni. 10.96). This, however, is a lawful acknowledgement, as it was spoken by the Elder Ānanda. But at night, when immoral persons are coming along a path and are asked, "Who is there?" they make an unlawful and false acknowledgement, saying, "We are bhikkhus."

Bhikkhatīti yācati. Yo hi koci bhikkhati, bhikkhaṃ esati gavesati, so taṃ labhatu vā mā vā, atha kho bhikkhatīti bhikkhu. Bhikkhakoti byañjanena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ; bhikkhanadhammatāya bhikkhūti attho. Bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti buddhādīhi ajjhupagataṃ bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatattā bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagato nāma. Yo hi koci appaṃ vā mahantaṃ vā bhogakkhandhaṃ pahāya agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito, kasigorakkhādīhi jīvitakappanaṃ hitvā liṅgasampaṭicchaneneva bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti bhikkhu. Parappaṭibaddhajīvikattā vā vihāramajjhe kājabhattaṃ bhuñjamānopi bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti bhikkhu. Piṇḍiyālopabhojanaṃ nissāya pabbajjāya ussāhajātattā vā bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti bhikkhu.

'He begs' means he asks. Whoever begs, seeks, and searches for alms, whether he obtains it or not, he is a bhikkhu because he begs. 'Bhikkhaka' is a word extended by a syllable; the meaning is 'bhikkhu' due to the nature of begging. 'He has undertaken the life of alms-gathering' means he is so-called because he has undertaken the life of alms-gathering that was undertaken by the Buddha and others. Whoever, having abandoned a small or great mass of wealth, has gone forth from home to homelessness, and having given up making a living by agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so on, has undertaken the life of alms-gathering merely by accepting the emblem, is a bhikkhu. Or, because his livelihood is dependent on others, even while eating community food in the middle of the monastery, he has undertaken the life of alms-gathering and is thus a bhikkhu. Or, because enthusiasm for the going forth has arisen in him through reliance on eating morsel-food, he has undertaken the life of alms-gathering and is thus a bhikkhu.

Agghaphassavaṇṇabhedena bhinnaṃ paṭaṃ dhāretīti bhinnapaṭadharo. Tattha satthakacchedanena agghabhedo veditabbo. Sahassagghanakopi hi paṭo satthakena khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ [P 0.0328] chinno bhinnaggho hoti, purimagghato upaḍḍhampi na agghati. Suttasaṃsibbanena phassabhedo veditabbo. Sukhasamphassopi hi paṭo suttehi saṃsibbito bhinnaphasso hoti, kharasamphassataṃ pāpuṇāti. Sūcimalādīhi vaṇṇabhedo veditabbo. Suparisuddhopi hi paṭo sūcikammato paṭṭhāya sūcimalena, hatthasedamalajallikādīhi[V 0.0312], avasāne rajanakappakaraṇehi ca bhinnavaṇṇo hoti, pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahati. Evaṃ tīhākārehi bhinnapaṭadhāraṇato bhinnapaṭadharoti bhikkhu. Gihīvatthavisabhāgānaṃ vā kāsāvānaṃ dhāraṇamatteneva bhinnapaṭadharoti bhikkhu.

He wears a robe that is 'broken' in terms of value, touch, and color; therefore, he is a 'bhinnapaṭadharo' (wearer of a broken robe). Therein, the breaking of value should be understood as by cutting with a knife. For even a robe worth a thousand, when cut into pieces with a knife, becomes of broken value; it is not worth even half its former value. The breaking of touch should be understood as by sewing with thread. For even a robe of pleasant touch, when sewn with threads, becomes of broken touch and attains a rough texture. The breaking of color should be understood as by needle-filth and so on. For even a perfectly pure robe, from the start of the needlework, becomes of broken color from needle-filth, from hand-sweat, dirt, grime, and so on, and finally from the processes of dyeing and finishing, thereby abandoning its natural color. Thus, because of wearing a robe broken in these three ways, he is a bhikkhu, a 'wearer of a broken robe.' Or, simply by wearing saffron robes that are dissimilar to the clothes of householders, he is a bhikkhu, a 'wearer of a broken robe.'

Bhindati pāpake akusale dhammeti bhikkhu. Sotāpattimaggena pañca kilese bhindatīti bhikkhu. Sakadāgāmimaggena cattāro, anāgāmimaggena cattāro, arahattamaggena aṭṭha kilese bhindatīti bhikkhu. Ettāvatā [M 0.0315] cattāro maggaṭṭhā dassitā. Bhinnattāti iminā pana cattāro phalaṭṭhā. Sotāpanno hi sotāpattimaggena pañca kilese bhinditvā ṭhito. Sakadāgāmī sakadāgāmimaggena cattāro, anāgāmī anāgāmimaggena cattāro, arahā arahattamaggena aṭṭha kilese bhinditvā ṭhito. Evamayaṃ catubbidho phalaṭṭho bhinnattā pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhikkhu nāma.

He is a bhikkhu because he breaks down evil, unwholesome states. He is a bhikkhu because by the path of stream-entry he breaks down five defilements. By the path of once-returning, four; by the path of non-returning, four; by the path of arahantship, he breaks down eight defilements—thus he is a bhikkhu. Thus far, the four who stand on the path have been shown. By the fact that the defilements have been broken, however, the four who stand in the fruit are shown. For a stream-enterer stands having broken five defilements by the path of stream-entry. A once-returner stands having broken four defilements by the path of once-returning. A non-returner stands having broken four defilements by the path of non-returning. An arahant stands having broken eight defilements by the path of arahantship. Thus, this fourfold one who stands in the fruit is called a bhikkhu because of the breaking of evil, unwholesome states.

Odhiso kilesānaṃ pahānāti ettha dve odhī – maggodhi ca kilesodhi ca. Odhi nāma sīmā, mariyādā. Tattha sotāpanno maggodhinā odhiso kilesānaṃ pahānā bhikkhu. Tassa hi catūsu maggesu ekeneva odhinā kilesā pahīnā, na sakalena maggacatukkena. Sakadāgāmīanāgāmīsupi eseva nayo. Sotāpanno ca kilesodhināpi odhiso kilesānaṃ pahānā bhikkhu. Tassa hi pahātabbakilesesu odhināva kilesā pahīnā, na sabbena sabbaṃ. Arahā pana anodhisova kilesānaṃ pahānā bhikkhu. Tassa hi maggacatukkena anodhināva kilesā pahīnā, na ekāya maggasīmāya. Pahātabbakilesesu ca anodhisova kilesā pahīnā. Ekāpi hi kilesasīmā ṭhitā nāma natthi. Evaṃ so ubhayathāpi anodhiso kilesānaṃ pahānā bhikkhu.

Here, in the phrase 'abandonment of defilements with a limit,' there are two kinds of limits: the limit of the path and the limit of the defilements. 'Odhi' means a boundary, a limit. In this regard, a Stream-enterer is a bhikkhu on account of the abandonment of defilements with a limit, by way of the limit of the path. For him, defilements are abandoned by only one limit among the four paths, not by the entire fourfold path. The same principle applies to Once-returners and Non-returners. Moreover, a Stream-enterer is also a bhikkhu on account of the abandonment of defilements with a limit, by way of the limit of the defilements. For him, among the defilements to be abandoned, defilements are abandoned only with a limit, not entirely. An Arahant, however, is a bhikkhu on account of the abandonment of defilements without a limit. For him, defilements are abandoned by the fourfold path without a limit, not by a single boundary of the path. And among the defilements to be abandoned, defilements are abandoned without a limit. Not even a single boundary of defilements remains. Thus, in both ways, he is a bhikkhu on account of the abandonment of defilements without a limit.

Sekkhoti puthujjanakalyāṇakena saddhiṃ satta ariyā. Tisso sikkhā sikkhantīti sekkhā. Tesu yo koci sekkho bhikkhuti veditabbo. Na [P 0.0329] sikkhatīti asekkho. Sekkhadhamme atikkamma aggaphale ṭhito tato uttari sikkhitabbābhāvato khīṇāsavo asekkhoti vuccati. Avaseso puthujjanabhikkhu tisso sikkhā neva sikkhati, na sikkhitvā ṭhitoti nevasekkhanāsekkhoti veditabbo.

A 'learner' (sekha) refers to the seven noble individuals together with the virtuous worldling. They are called 'learners' because they train in the three trainings. Any among them who is a learner should be understood as a bhikkhu. One who does not train is a 'non-learner' (asekha). Having transcended the qualities of a learner and being established in the highest fruition, because there is nothing further to be trained in, the one whose taints are destroyed is called a 'non-learner'. The remaining worldling bhikkhu neither trains in the three trainings nor stands having trained; thus he should be understood as 'neither-a-learner-nor-a-non-learner' (nevasekkhanāsekha).

Sīlaggaṃ [V 0.0313] samādhiggaṃ paññaggaṃ vimuttagganti idaṃ aggaṃ patvā ṭhitattā aggo bhikkhu nāma. Bhadroti apāpako. Kalyāṇaputhujjanādayo hi yāva arahā tāva bhadrena sīlena samādhinā paññāya vimuttiyā vimuttiñāṇadassanena ca samannāgatattā bhadro bhikkhūti saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti. Maṇḍo bhikkhūti pasanno bhikkhu; sappimaṇḍo viya anāvilo vippasannoti attho. Sāroti tehiyeva sīlasārādīhi samannāgatattā, nīlasamannāgamena nīlo paṭo viya, sāro bhikkhūti veditabbo. Vigatakilesapheggubhāvato vā khīṇāsavova sāroti veditabbo.

He is called a 'foremost' (agga) bhikkhu because he has reached and is established in what is foremost: foremost virtue, foremost concentration, foremost wisdom, and foremost liberation. He is called 'virtuous' (bhadra) because he is without evil. Indeed, from virtuous worldlings up to Arahants, they are reckoned as 'virtuous bhikkhus' because they are endowed with virtuous conduct, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. A 'maṇḍa' bhikkhu means a clear bhikkhu; the meaning is that he is untroubled and perfectly clear, like the cream of ghee. He is called 'the core' (sāra) because he is endowed with those very core qualities of virtue and so forth; just as a cloth is called blue from being imbued with blue, so should he be understood as a 'core bhikkhu'. Alternatively, the one whose taints are destroyed should be understood as 'the core' because the hollowness of defilements has departed.

Tattha [M 0.0316] ca “bhindati pāpake akusale dhammeti bhikkhu, odhiso kilesānaṃ pahānā bhikkhu, sekkho bhikkhū”ti imesu tīsu ṭhānesu satta sekkhā kathitā. “Bhinnattā pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānanti bhikkhu, anodhiso kilesānaṃ pahānā bhikkhu, asekkho bhikkhu, aggo bhikkhu, maṇḍo bhikkhū”ti imesu pañcasu ṭhānesu khīṇāsavova kathito. “Nevasekkhanāsekkho”ti ettha puthujjanova kathito. Sesaṭṭhānesu puthujjanakalyāṇako, satta sekkhā, khīṇāsavoti ime sabbepi kathitā.

And herein, in these three instances—'a bhikkhu because he breaks down evil, unwholesome states,' 'a bhikkhu on account of the abandonment of defilements with a limit,' and 'a bhikkhu who is a learner'—the seven learners are spoken of. In these five instances—'a bhikkhu because evil, unwholesome states have been broken down,' 'a bhikkhu on account of the abandonment of defilements without a limit,' 'a bhikkhu who is a non-learner,' 'a foremost bhikkhu,' and 'a maṇḍa bhikkhu'—only the one whose taints are destroyed is spoken of. In the case of 'neither-a-learner-nor-a-non-learner,' only a worldling is spoken of. In the remaining instances, the virtuous worldling, the seven learners, and the one whose taints are destroyed—all these are spoken of.

Evaṃ samaññādīhi bhikkhuṃ dassetvā idāni upasampadāvasena dassetuṃ samaggena saṅghenātiādimāha. Tattha samaggena saṅghenāti sabbantimena paricchedena pañcavaggakaraṇīye kamme yāvatikā bhikkhū kammappattā, tesaṃ āgatattā chandārahānaṃ chandassa āhaṭattā sammukhībhūtānañca appaṭikkosanato ekasmiṃ kamme samaggabhāvaṃ upagatena. Ñatticatutthenāti tīhi anussāvanāhi ekāya ca ñattiyā kātabbena. Kammenāti dhammikena vinayakammena. Akuppenāti [P 0.0330] vatthuñattianussāvanasīmāparisasampattisampannattā akopetabbataṃ appaṭikkositabbataṃ upagatena. Ṭhānārahenāti kāraṇārahena satthusāsanārahena.

Having thus shown the bhikkhu by means of designations and so forth, now, in order to show him by way of higher ordination, it is said, 'by the united Sangha,' and so on. Herein, 'by the united Sangha' means: by a Sangha that has attained unity in a single act—in an act to be done by a chapter of five with the ultimate demarcation—because as many bhikkhus as are eligible for the act are present, because the consent of those worthy of giving consent has been brought, and because there is no protest from those who are present. 'By a motion-and-four' means to be done with one motion and three announcements. 'By an act' means by a lawful Vinaya act. 'By an unshakeable' act means having attained the state of being unshakeable and unopposable, due to being endowed with the completeness of the object, the motion, the announcements, the boundary, and the assembly. 'Worthy of the position' means worthy of the cause, worthy of the Teacher’s dispensation.

Upasampanno nāma uparibhāvaṃ samāpanno, pattoti attho. Bhikkhubhāvo hi uparibhāvo. Tañcesa yathāvuttena kammena samāpannattā upasampannoti vuccati. Etena yā imā ehibhikkhūpasampadā, saraṇāgamanūpasampadā, ovādapaṭiggahaṇūpasampadā, pañhabyākaraṇūpasampadā, garudhammapaṭiggahaṇūpasampadā, dūtenūpasampadā, aṭṭhavācikūpasampadā, ñatticatutthakammūpasampadāti aṭṭha upasampadā vuttā, tāsaṃ ñatticatutthakammūpasampadā, dūtenūpasampadā, aṭṭhavācikūpasampadāti imā [V 0.0314] tissova thāvarā. Sesā buddhe dharamāneyeva ahesuṃ. Tāsu upasampadāsu imasmiṃ ṭhāne ayaṃ ñatticatutthakammūpasampadāva adhippetā.

One who is 'highly ordained' (upasampanna) means one who has attained a higher state; that is, one who has reached it. For the state of a bhikkhu is indeed a higher state. And because one has attained it through the aforesaid act, one is called 'highly ordained.' By this, the eight kinds of higher ordination that have been spoken of are: the 'Come, bhikkhu' ordination, the refuge-taking ordination, the acceptance-of-admonition ordination, the answering-questions ordination, the acceptance-of-weighty-rules ordination, the messenger ordination, the eight-word ordination, and the motion-and-four act ordination. Among these, these three alone are enduring: the motion-and-four act ordination, the messenger ordination, and the eight-word ordination. The rest existed only while the Buddha was living. Among these ordinations, in this context, it is this motion-and-four act ordination that is intended.

511. Pātimokkhasaṃvaraniddese pātimokkhanti sikkhāpadasīlaṃ. Tañhi, yo naṃ pāti rakkhati, taṃ mokkheti mocayati āpāyikādīhi dukkhehi, tasmā pātimokkhanti vuttaṃ. Sīlaṃ patiṭṭhātiādīni tasseva vevacanāni. Tattha sīlanti kāmañcetaṃ saha kammavācāpariyosānena ijjhanakassa [M 0.0317] pātimokkhassa vevacanaṃ, evaṃ santepi dhammato etaṃ sīlaṃ nāma pāṇātipātādīhi vā viramantassa vattappaṭipattiṃ vā pūrentassa cetanādayo dhammā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ “kiṃ sīla”nti? Cetanā sīlaṃ, cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ, saṃvaro sīlaṃ, avītikkamo sīla”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.39).

511. In the exposition of Pātimokkha restraint, 'Pātimokkha' means the virtue of the training rules. For it protects (pāti) one who guards it, and it liberates (mokkheti) him from sufferings such as those of the woeful states; therefore, it is called 'Pātimokkha.' 'Virtue,' 'foundation,' and so forth, are its synonyms. Herein, 'virtue,' although it is a synonym for the Pātimokkha which is accomplished at the conclusion of the formal act, even so, in terms of its nature, this 'virtue' should be understood as the mental states, such as volition, of one who refrains from killing living beings and so forth, or of one who fulfills the duties and observances. For it is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'What is virtue? Volition is virtue, mental factors are virtue, restraint is virtue, non-transgression is virtue' (Paṭi. Ma. 1.39).

Tattha cetanā sīlaṃ nāma pāṇātipātādīhi vā viramantassa vattapaṭipattiṃ vā pūrentassa cetanā. Cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ nāma pāṇātipātādīhi viramantassa virati. Apica cetanā sīlaṃ nāma pāṇātipātādīni pajahantassa satta kammapathacetanā. Cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ nāma “abhijjhaṃ pahāya vigatābhijjhena cetasā viharatī”tiādinā nayena saṃyuttamahāvagge vuttā anabhijjhāabyāpādasammādiṭṭhidhammā. Saṃvaro sīlanti ettha pañcavidhena saṃvaro veditabbo – pātimokkhasaṃvaro, satisaṃvaro, ñāṇasaṃvaro[P 0.0331], khantisaṃvaro, vīriyasaṃvaroti. Tassa nānākaraṇaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.6) vuttaṃ. Avītikkamo sīlanti samādiṇṇasīlassa kāyikavācasiko avītikkamo. Ettha ca saṃvarasīlaṃ avītikkamasīlanti idameva nippariyāyato sīlaṃ; cetanā sīlaṃ cetasikaṃ sīlanti pariyāyato sīlanti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, 'virtue as volition' is the volition of one who refrains from killing living beings and so forth, or who fulfills the obligatory practices. 'Virtue as mental concomitants' is the abstinence of one who refrains from killing living beings and so forth. Furthermore, 'virtue as volition' refers to the seven volitions of the paths of action in one who abandons killing and so forth. 'Virtue as mental concomitants' refers to the states of non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view, as stated in the Mahāvagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, in the passage beginning 'Having abandoned covetousness, he dwells with a heart free from covetousness.' 'Virtue as restraint' here should be understood as fivefold: Pātimokkha restraint, mindfulness restraint, knowledge restraint, patience restraint, and energy restraint. Their distinctions are explained in the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhimagga 1.6). 'Virtue as non-transgression' is the bodily and verbal non-transgression of one who has undertaken the moral discipline. Herein, restraint-virtue and non-transgression-virtue are virtue in the ultimate sense (nippariyāyato); virtue as volition and virtue as mental concomitants are virtue in a conventional sense (pariyāyato), it should be understood.

Yasmā pana pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlena bhikkhu sāsane patiṭṭhāti nāma, tasmā taṃ ‘patiṭṭhā’ti vuttaṃ; patiṭṭhahati vā ettha bhikkhu, kusaladhammā eva vā ettha patiṭṭhahantīti patiṭṭhā. Ayamattho –

Since a monk is established in the Dispensation by the moral discipline of Pātimokkha restraint, therefore it is called 'foundation' (patiṭṭhā); for here a monk becomes established, or wholesome states become established here; thus it is 'foundation.' This is the meaning:

“Sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño, cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayaṃ;

Ātāpī nipako bhikkhu, so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭa”nti ca. (saṃ. ni. 1.23);

'Established in virtue, a wise person develops mind and wisdom; an ardent, sagacious monk disentangles this tangle.' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.23);

“Patiṭṭhā[V 0.0315], mahārāja, sīlaṃ sabbesaṃ kusaladhammāna”nti ca “sīle patiṭṭhitassa kho, mahārāja, sabbe kusalā dhammā na parihāyantī”ti (mi. pa. 2.1.9) ca ādisuttavasena veditabbo.

'Virtue, great king, is the foundation for all wholesome states,' and 'For one established in virtue, great king, all wholesome states do not decline.' (Milindapañha 2.1.9). This should be understood by way of suttas such as these.

Tadetaṃ pubbuppattiatthena ādi. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

This is the beginning (ādi) in the sense of prior origination. And this has also been said:

“Tasmātiha tvaṃ, uttiya, ādimeva visodhehi kusalesu dhammesu. Ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ? Sīlañca suvisuddhaṃ diṭṭhi ca ujukā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.382).

'Therefore, here, Uttiya, you should first purify the very beginning of wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? Well-purified virtue and an upright view.' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.382).

Yathā [M 0.0318] hi nagaravaḍḍhakī nagaraṃ māpetukāmo paṭhamaṃ nagaraṭṭhānaṃ sodheti, tato aparabhāge vīthicatukkasiṅghāṭakādiparicchedena vibhajitvā nagaraṃ māpeti; evameva yogāvacaro āditova sīlaṃ visodheti, tato aparabhāge samathavipassanāmaggaphalanibbānāni sacchikaroti. Yathā vā pana rajako paṭhamaṃ tīhi khārehi vatthaṃ dhovitvā parisuddhe vatthe yadicchakaṃ raṅgajātaṃ upaneti; yathā vā pana cheko cittakāro rūpaṃ likhitukāmo āditova bhittiparikammaṃ karoti, tato aparabhāge rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti; evameva yogāvacaro āditova sīlaṃ visodhetvā aparabhāge samathavipassanādayo dhamme sacchikaroti. Tasmā sīlaṃ “ādī”ti vuttaṃ.

Just as a city architect, wishing to build a city, first clears the site for the city and then later divides it into streets, squares, crossroads, and so forth, before constructing the city, so too does a yogi first purify his moral discipline and later realize tranquility, insight, the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna. Or, just as a washerman first cleans a cloth with three kinds of alkali and then applies any desired dye to the purified cloth, or just as a skilled painter, wishing to paint a picture, first prepares the wall and later creates the image, so too does a yogi first purify his moral discipline and later realize the states of tranquility, insight, and so on. Therefore, moral discipline is called 'the beginning' (ādi).

Tadetaṃ caraṇasarikkhatāya caraṇaṃ. Caraṇāti hi pādā vuccanti. Yathā hi chinnacaraṇassa purisassa disaṃgamanābhisaṅkhāro na jāyati, paripuṇṇapādasseva jāyati; evameva yassa sīlaṃ bhinnaṃ hoti khaṇḍaṃ aparipuṇṇaṃ, tassa nibbānagamanāya [P 0.0332] ñāṇagamanaṃ na sampajjati. Yassa pana taṃ abhinnaṃ hoti akkhaṇḍaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ tassa nibbānagamanāya ñāṇagamanaṃ sampajjati. Tasmā sīlaṃ “caraṇa”nti vuttaṃ.

This is called 'conduct' (caraṇa) because it is similar to feet. For 'caraṇa' refers to the feet. Just as a man whose feet are cut off cannot generate the volition to go in any direction, but one with intact feet can, in the same way, for one whose moral discipline is broken, fragmented, and incomplete, the going by knowledge to Nibbāna does not succeed. But for one whose moral discipline is unbroken, unfragmented, and complete, the going by knowledge to Nibbāna succeeds. Therefore, moral discipline is called 'conduct' (caraṇa).

Tadetaṃ saṃyamanavasena saṃyamo, saṃvaraṇavasena saṃvaro. Ubhayenāpi sīlasaṃyamo ceva sīlasaṃvaro ca kathito. Vacanattho panettha saṃyameti vītikkamavipphandanaṃ, puggalaṃ vā saṃyameti, vītikkamavasena tassa vipphandituṃ na detīti saṃyamo. Vītikkamassa pavesanadvāraṃ saṃvarati pidahatītipi saṃvaro. Mokkhanti uttamaṃ mukhabhūtaṃ vā. Yathā hi sattānaṃ catubbidho āhāro mukhena [V 0.0316] pavisitvā aṅgamaṅgāni pharati, evaṃ yoginopi catubhūmakakusalaṃ sīlamukhena pavisitvā atthasiddhiṃ sampādeti. Tena vuttaṃ “mokkha”nti. Pamukhe sādhūti pāmokkhaṃ; pubbaṅgamaṃ seṭṭhaṃ padhānanti attho. Kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ samāpattiyāti catubhūmakakusalānaṃ paṭilābhatthāya pāmokkhaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ seṭṭhaṃ padhānanti veditabbaṃ.

This is restraint (saṃyama) in the sense of controlling, and restraint (saṃvara) in the sense of covering. By both, moral restraint as controlling (sīlasaṃyama) and moral restraint as covering (sīlasaṃvara) are spoken of. Herein, the verbal meaning of 'restraint' (saṃyama) is that it restrains the agitation of transgression, or it restrains the person, meaning it does not allow one to be agitated by way of transgression. 'Restraint' (saṃvara) also means that it shuts or closes the door of entry to transgression. 'Release' (mokkha) means the highest, or that which is the foremost entrance. Just as the four kinds of nutriment for beings enter through the mouth and pervade the limbs, so too, for the yogi, the wholesome states of the four planes enter through the entrance of moral discipline and accomplish the attainment of the goal. Therefore, it is called 'release' (mokkha). That which is good in the forefront is 'pre-eminent' (pāmokkha); the meaning is foremost, leading, excellent, and principal. It should be understood that it is 'pre-eminent' (pāmokkha)—foremost, leading, excellent, and principal—for the attainment of the wholesome states of the four planes.

Kāyiko avītikkamoti tividhaṃ kāyasucaritaṃ. Vācasikoti catubbidhaṃ vacīsucaritaṃ. Kāyikavācasikoti tadubhayaṃ. Iminā ājīvaṭṭhamakasīlaṃ pariyādāya dasseti. Saṃvutoti pihito; saṃvutindriyo pihitindriyoti [M 0.0319] attho. Yathā hi saṃvutadvāraṃ gehaṃ “saṃvutagehaṃ pihitageha”nti vuccati, evamidha saṃvutindriyo “saṃvuto”ti vutto. Pātimokkhasaṃvarenāti pātimokkhena ca saṃvarena ca, pātimokkhasaṅkhātena vā saṃvarena. Upetotiādīni vuttatthāneva.

Bodily non-transgression (kāyiko avītikkamo) is the threefold good bodily conduct. Verbal (vācasiko) is the fourfold good verbal conduct. Bodily-verbal (kāyikavācasiko) is both of these. By this, he shows the eightfold moral discipline connected with livelihood to be included. Restrained (saṃvuto) means covered; 'restrained faculties' means 'covered faculties.' Just as a house with closed doors is called 'a closed house, a covered house,' so here one with restrained faculties is called 'restrained.' By Pātimokkha restraint (pātimokkhasaṃvarena) means by the Pātimokkha and by restraint, or by restraint designated as the Pātimokkha. 'Endowed with' (upeto) and so forth have the same meaning as previously stated.

512. Iriyatītiādīhi sattahipi padehi pātimokkhasaṃvarasīle ṭhitassa bhikkhuno iriyāpathavihāro kathito.

512. With the words beginning with 'He comports himself,' by all seven terms, the postures and modes of conduct of a monk established in the moral discipline of Pātimokkha restraint are described.

513. Ācāragocaraniddese kiñcāpi bhagavā samaṇācaraṃ samaṇagocaraṃ kathetukāmo “ācāragocarasampannoti atthi ācāro, atthi anācāro”ti padaṃ uddhari. Yathā pana maggakusalo puriso maggaṃ acikkhanto ‘vāmaṃ muñca dakkhiṇaṃ gaṇhā’ti paṭhamaṃ muñcitabbaṃ sabhayamaggaṃ uppathamaggaṃ ācikkhati[P 0.0333], pacchā gahetabbaṃ khemamaggaṃ ujumaggaṃ; evameva maggakusalapurisasadiso dhammarājā paṭhamaṃ pahātabbaṃ buddhappaṭikuṭṭhaṃ anācāraṃ ācikkhitvā pacchā ācāraṃ ācikkhitukāmo “tattha katamo anācāro”tiādimāha. Purisena hi ācikkhitamaggo sampajjeyya vā na vā, tathāgatena ācikkhitamaggo apaṇṇako, indena vissaṭṭhaṃ vajiraṃ viya, avirajjhanako nibbānanagaraṃyeva samosarati. Tena vuttaṃ – “puriso maggakusaloti kho, tissa, tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.84).

513. In the exposition of conduct and resort, although the Blessed One wished to speak of the conduct and resort of an ascetic, he took up the term 'one accomplished in conduct and resort,' saying 'there is conduct, there is misconduct.' Just as a person skilled in the path, when showing the way, first points out the path to be abandoned—the fearful path, the wrong path—saying, 'Let go of the left, take the right,' and later indicates the safe path, the straight path; in the same way, the King of Dhamma, like a person skilled in the path, first points out the misconduct condemned by the Buddha, which is to be abandoned, and then, wishing to explain proper conduct, begins with, 'And what, therein, is misconduct?' For a path shown by an ordinary person may or may not succeed, but the path shown by the Tathāgata is unerring, like a thunderbolt hurled by Indra; it unfailingly leads straight to the city of Nibbāna. Therefore, it is said: 'Indeed, Tissa, 'a skilled pathfinder' is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.84).

Yasmā vā sasīsaṃ nahānena pahīnasedamalajallikassa purisassa mālāgandhavilepanādivibhūsanavidhānaṃ viya pahīnapāpadhammassa kalyāṇadhammasamāyogo sampannarūpo hoti, tasmā sedamalajallikkaṃ viya pahātabbaṃ paṭhamaṃ anācāraṃ ācikkhitvā, pahīnasedamalajallikassa mālāgandhavilepanādivibhūsanavidhānaṃ [V 0.0317] viya pacchā ācāraṃ ācikkhitukāmopi tattha katamo anācārotiādimāha. Tattha kāyiko vītikkamoti tividhaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ; vācasiko vītikkamoti catubbidhaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ; kāyikavācasiko vītikkamoti tadubhayaṃ. Evaṃ ājīvaṭṭhamakasīlasseva vītikkamaṃ dassesi.

Just as for a man who has bathed his head and removed sweat, dirt, and grime, the act of adorning himself with garlands, perfumes, and ointments is fitting, so too for one who has abandoned evil qualities, the association with wholesome qualities is perfected. Therefore, having first described the misconduct that should be abandoned like sweat, dirt, and grime, and afterwards, wishing to describe good conduct like the act of adorning for one who has removed sweat, dirt, and grime, he says, 'And what, therein, is misconduct?' and so on. Herein, 'bodily transgression' is the threefold bodily misconduct; 'verbal transgression' is the fourfold verbal misconduct; 'bodily and verbal transgression' is both. Thus, he showed the transgression of the virtue that has livelihood as the eighth precept.

Yasmā pana na kevalaṃ kāyavācāhi eva anācāraṃ ācarati, manasāpi ācarati eva, tasmā taṃ dassetuṃ “sabbampi dussīlyaṃ anācāro”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha [M 0.0320] ekacciyaṃ anācāraṃ vibhajitvā dassento idhekacco veḷudānenātiādimāha. Tattha veḷudānenāti paccayahetukena veḷudānena. Vihāre uṭṭhitañhi araññato vā āharitvā rakkhitagopitaṃ veḷuṃ ‘evaṃ me paccayaṃ dassantī’ti upaṭṭhākānaṃ dātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Evañhi jīvitaṃ kappento anesanāya micchājīvena jīvati. So diṭṭheva dhamme garahaṃ pāpuṇāti, samparāye ca apāyaparipūrako hoti. Attano puggalikaveḷuṃ kulasaṅgahatthāya dadanto kuladūsakadukkaṭamāpajjati; parapuggalikaṃ theyyacittena dadamāno bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo. Saṅghikepi eseva nayo. Sace pana taṃ issaravatāya deti garubhaṇḍavissajjanamāpajjati[P 0.0334].

But since one commits misconduct not only through body and speech, but also through the mind, therefore, to show this, it is said: 'All immorality is misconduct.' Here, explaining some misconduct in detail, he says, 'Here, someone by the giving of bamboo,' and so on. In this context, 'by the giving of bamboo' means by giving bamboo for the sake of requisites. For it is not proper to give bamboo that has grown in the monastery or has been brought from the forest and is kept safe, to supporters, thinking, 'In this way they will provide me with requisites.' Indeed, one who makes a living in this way lives by wrong livelihood through improper search. Such a person incurs blame in this very life, and in the next life becomes one who fills the woeful states. If one gives personal bamboo for the sake of gaining favor with families, one incurs a dukkaṭa offense for corrupting families; if one gives another person's bamboo with a thieving mind, one should be made to pay its value. The same principle applies to property belonging to the Saṅgha. But if one gives it as if he were the owner, one incurs the offense of disposing of heavy goods.

Kataro pana veḷu garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti, kataro na hotīti? Yo tāva aropimo sayaṃjātako, so saṅghena paricchinnaṭṭhāneyeva garubhaṇḍaṃ, tato paraṃ na garubhaṇḍaṃ; ropitaṭṭhāne sabbena sabbaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ. So pana pamāṇena paricchinno telanāḷippamāṇopi garubhaṇḍaṃ, na tato heṭṭhā. Yassa pana bhikkhuno telanāḷiyā vā kattaradaṇḍena vā attho, tena phātikammaṃ katvā gahetabbo. Phātikammaṃ tadagghanakaṃ vā atirekaṃ vā vaṭṭati, ūnakaṃ na vaṭṭati. Hatthakammampi udakāharaṇamattaṃ vā appaharitakaraṇamattaṃ vā na vaṭṭati, taṃ thāvaraṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tasmā pokkharaṇito vā paṃsuṃ uddharitvā sopānaṃ vā attharāpetvā visamaṭṭhānaṃ vā samaṃ katvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Phātikammaṃ akatvā gahito tattha vasanteneva paribhuñjitabbo; pakkamantena saṅghikaṃ katvā ṭhapetvā gantabbaṃ. Asatiyā gahetvā gatena yattha gato sarati, tato paccāharitabbo. Sace antarā bhayaṃ hoti, sampattavihare ṭhapetvā gantabbaṃ.

Which bamboo, then, is heavy goods, and which is not? That which is not planted and self-grown is heavy goods only within the area designated by the Saṅgha; beyond that, it is not heavy goods. In a planted area, all of it is heavy goods. Moreover, if it is defined by measure, even a piece the size of an oil-tube is heavy goods, but not if it is smaller than that. If a bhikkhu needs an oil-tube or a walking stick, he should perform a transaction (phātikamma) before taking it. The transaction is allowable if it is of equivalent or greater value, but not of lesser value. As for manual labor, merely carrying water or clearing a little greenery is not allowable; it is allowable to do work that is lasting. Therefore, it is allowable to take it after removing mud from a pond, having steps laid, or leveling uneven ground. If taken without a transaction, it should be used only by one dwelling there; upon departing, one must make it Saṅgha property and leave it behind. If one takes it unmindfully and leaves, it must be returned from wherever he is when he remembers. If there is danger on the way, it should be left at a monastery one has reached before proceeding.

Manussā vihāraṃ gantvā veḷuṃ yācanti. Bhikkhū ‘saṅghiko’ti dātuṃ na visahanti. Manussā punappunaṃ yācanti vā tajjenti vā. Tadā bhikkhūhi ‘daṇḍakammaṃ katvā gaṇhathā’ti vattuṃ [V 0.0318] vaṭṭati; veḷudānaṃ nāma na hoti. Sace te daṇḍakammatthāya vāsipharasuādīni vā khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ vā denti, gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “daḍḍhagehā manussā gaṇhitvā gacchantā na vāretabbā”ti vuttaṃ.

People go to the monastery and ask for bamboo. The bhikkhus are unable to give it, saying, 'It is Saṅgha property.' The people ask repeatedly or threaten. Then, it is proper for the bhikkhus to say, 'Do some work as a penalty and take it'; this is not called a giving of bamboo. If, for the purpose of this work, they give adzes, axes, and so on, or hard and soft food, it is not proper to accept it. However, in the Vinaya commentary, it is said: 'People whose houses have burned down, when taking things and leaving, should not be stopped.'

Sace [M 0.0321] saṅghassa veḷugumbe veḷudūsikā uppajjanti, taṃ akoṭṭāpentānaṃ veḷu nassati, kiṃ kātabbanti? Bhikkhācāre manussānaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. Sace koṭṭetuṃ na icchanti ‘samabhāgaṃ labhissathā’ti vattabbā; na icchantiyeva ‘dve koṭṭhāse labhissathā’ti vattabbā. Evampi anicchantesu ‘naṭṭhena attho natthi, tumhākaṃ khaṇe sati daṇḍakammaṃ karissatha, koṭṭetvā gaṇhathā’ti vattabbā; veḷudānaṃ nāma na hoti. Veḷugumbe aggimhi uṭṭhitepi, udakena vuyhamānaveḷūsupi eseva nayo. Rukkhesupi ayameva kathāmaggo. Rukkho pana sūcidaṇḍakappamāṇo garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti. Saṅghike rukkhe koṭṭāpetvā saṅghaṃ anāpucchitvāpi saṅghikaṃ āvāsaṃ kātuṃ [P 0.0335] labbhati. Vacanapathacchedanatthaṃ pana āpucchitvāva kātabbo.

If, in a bamboo grove belonging to the Saṅgha, bamboo blight appears, and if, by not having it cut down, the bamboo is destroyed, what is to be done? It should be announced to the people on the alms-round. If they do not wish to cut them down, they should be told, 'You will receive an equal share.' If they still do not wish to, they should be told, 'You will receive two shares.' Even if they still do not wish to, they should be told, 'There is no use in them being destroyed; when you have time, you may do work with the poles; cut them down and take them.' This is not considered a gift of bamboo. The same method applies when a fire arises in the bamboo grove or when the bamboos are being carried away by water. This same line of reasoning applies to trees as well. A tree, however, of a size suitable for a needle-case or a staff is considered heavy goods. In the case of a tree belonging to the Saṅgha, having had it cut down, it is permissible to build a residence for the Saṅgha even without asking the Saṅgha. But to forestall criticism, it should be done only after having asked.

Puggalikaṃ kātuṃ labbhati, na labbhatīti? Na labbhati. Hatthakammasīsena pana ekasmiṃ gehe mañcaṭṭhānamattaṃ labbhati, tīsu gehesu ekaṃ gehaṃ labhati. Sace dabbhasambhārā puggalikā honti, bhūmi saṅghikā, ekaṃ gehaṃ katvā samabhāgaṃ labhati, dvīsu gehesu ekaṃ gehaṃ labhati. Saṅghikarukkhe saṅghikaṃ āvāsaṃ bādhente saṅghaṃ anāpucchā hāretuṃ vaṭṭati, na vaṭṭatīti? Vaṭṭati. Vacanapathacchedanatthaṃ pana āpucchitvāva hāretabbo. Sace rukkhaṃ nissāya saṅghassa mahanto lābho hoti, na hāretabbo. Puggalikarukkhe saṅghikaṃ āvāsaṃ bādhente rukkhasāmikassa ācikkhitabbaṃ. Sace harituṃ na icchati, chedāpetvā hāretabbo. ‘Rukkhaṃ me dethā’ti codentassa rukkhaṃ agghāpetvā mūlaṃ dātabbaṃ. Saṅghike rukkhe puggalikāvāsaṃ, puggalike ca puggalikāvāsaṃ bādhentepi eseva nayo. Valliyampi ayameva kathāmaggo. Valli pana yattha vikkāyati, dullabhā hoti, tattha garubhaṇḍaṃ. Sā ca kho upaḍḍhabāhuppamāṇato paṭṭhāya; tato heṭṭhā vallikhaṇḍaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ na hoti.

Is it permissible to make it personal property? It is not permissible. However, as payment for manual labor, one may receive a space the size of a bed in one house, or one house out of three houses. If the building materials are personal but the land belongs to the Saṅgha, having built one house, one receives an equal share; or out of two houses, one receives one house. If a Saṅgha tree obstructs a Saṅgha dwelling, is it permissible to remove it without asking the Saṅgha? It is permissible. But to forestall criticism, it should be removed only after having asked. If the Saṅgha derives great benefit from the tree, it should not be removed. If a personal tree obstructs a Saṅgha dwelling, the tree's owner should be informed. If he does not wish to remove it, it should be caused to be cut down and removed. To one who demands, 'Give me the tree,' the tree should be appraised and its value given. The same method applies when a Saṅgha tree obstructs a personal dwelling, and when a personal tree obstructs a personal dwelling. This same line of reasoning applies to vines as well. A vine, however, is considered heavy goods where it is sold and is scarce. And this is so from the measure of half an arm upwards; below that, a piece of vine is not considered heavy goods.

Pattadānādīsupi pattadānenāti paccayahetukena pattadānenātiādi sabbaṃ veḷudāne vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Garubhaṇḍatāya panettha ayaṃ vinicchayo. Pattampi hi yattha vikkāyati, gandhikādayo [V 0.0319] gandhapaliveṭhanādīnaṃ atthāya gaṇhanti, tādise dullabhaṭṭhāneyeva garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti. Esa tāva kiṃsukapattakaṇṇapiḷandhanatālapattādīsu vinicchayo.

In matters such as the giving of leaves, and so on, all should be understood according to the method explained for the giving of bamboo—that is, 'the giving of leaves' means 'for the sake of requisites,' and so on. Regarding its being heavy goods, this is the ruling: A leaf, for instance, is considered heavy goods only in a place where it is sold and is scarce, such as where perfumers and others acquire it for the purpose of wrapping perfumes and so on. This is the ruling for items like kimsuka leaves, ear-ornaments, palm leaves, and so on.

Tālapaṇṇampi [M 0.0322] imasmiṃyeva ṭhāne kathetabbaṃ. Tālapaṇṇampi hi sayaṃjāte tālavane saṅghena paricchinnaṭṭhāneyeva garubhaṇḍaṃ, na tato paraṃ. Ropimatālesu sabbampi garubhaṇḍaṃ. Tassa pamāṇaṃ heṭṭhimakoṭiyā aṭṭhaṅgulappamāṇopi rittapotthako. Tiṇampi ettheva pakkhipitvā kathetabbaṃ. Yattha pana tiṇaṃ natthi tattha muñjapalālanāḷikerapaṇṇādīhipi chādenti. Tasmā tānipi tiṇeneva saṅgahitāni. Iti muñjapalālādīsu yaṃkiñci muṭṭhippamāṇaṃ tiṇaṃ, nāḷikerapaṇṇādīsu ca ekapaṇṇampi [P 0.0336] saṅghassa dinnaṃ vā tatthajātakaṃ vā bahiārāme saṅghassa tiṇavatthumhi jātatiṇaṃ vā rakkhitagopitaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti. Taṃ pana saṅghakamme ca cetiyakamme ca kate atirekaṃ puggalikakamme dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Heṭṭhā vuttaveḷumhipi eseva nayo.

The palm leaf should also be discussed in this same context. For the palm leaf, when naturally grown in a palm grove designated by the Saṅgha, is heavy goods only within that area, not beyond it. In cultivated palm groves, all of it is heavy goods. Its measure is even an empty manuscript of eight fingers in length at its lower edge. Grass should also be included and discussed here. Where there is no grass, they thatch with muñja grass, straw, coconut leaves, and the like. Therefore, these too are included under the category of grass. Thus, in the case of muñja grass, straw, and so on, any amount of grass about a handful, and in the case of coconut leaves and so on, even a single leaf—if given to the Saṅgha, or naturally grown there, or grown in the Saṅgha’s grass plot in an outer monastery, or that which has been protected and guarded—is heavy goods. However, after work for the Saṅgha and for a cetiya has been done, it is permissible to give the excess for personal work. This same method applies to the bamboo mentioned above.

Pupphadāne “ettakesu rukkhesu pupphāni vissajjetvā yāgubhattavatthe upanentu, ettakesu senāsanapaṭisaṅkharaṇe upanentū”ti evaṃ niyamitaṭṭhāne eva pupphāni garubhaṇḍāni honti. Paratīre sāmaṇerā pupphāni ocinitvā rāsiṃ karonti, pañcaṅgasamannāgato pupphabhājako bhikkhusaṅghaṃ gaṇetvā koṭṭhāse karoti, so sampattaparisāya saṅghaṃ anāpucchitvāva dātuṃ labhati; asammatena pana āpucchitvāva dātabbaṃ. Bhikkhu pana kassa pupphāni dātuṃ labhati, kassa na labhatīti? Mātāpitūnaṃ gehaṃ haritvāpi gehato pakkosāpetvāpi ‘vatthupūjaṃ karothā’ti dātuṃ labhati, piḷandhanatthāya dātuṃ na labhati; sesañātīnaṃ pana haritvā na dātabbaṃ, pakkosāpetvā ‘pūjaṃ karothā’ti dātabbaṃ; sesajanassa pūjanaṭṭhānaṃ sampattassa apaccāsīsantena dātabbaṃ; pupphadānaṃ nāma na hoti. Vihāre bahūni pupphāni pupphanti. Bhikkhunā piṇḍāya carantena manusse disvā ‘vihāre bahūni pupphāni, pūjethā’ti vattabbaṃ. Vacanamatte doso natthi. ‘Manussā khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ ādāya āgamissantī’ti cittena pana na vattabbaṃ. Sace vadati, khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ na paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Manussā attano dhammatāya ‘vihāre pupphāni atthī’ti pucchitvā ‘asukadivase vihāraṃ āgamissāma, sāmaṇerānaṃ pupphāni ocinituṃ mā dethā’ti vadanti. Bhikkhū sāmaṇerānaṃ kathetuṃ pamuṭṭhā. Sāmaṇerehi pupphāni ocinitvā ṭhapitāni. Manussā bhikkhū upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, mayaṃ tumhākaṃ asukadivaseyeva ārocayimha [M 0.0323] – ‘sāmaṇerānaṃ pupphāni ocinituṃ mā dethā’ti. Kasmā na vārayitthā”ti? “Sati [V 0.0320] me pamuṭṭhā, pupphāni ocinitamattāneva, tāva na pūjā katā”ti vattabbaṃ. “Gaṇhatha pūjethā”ti na vattabbaṃ. Sace vadati, āmisaṃ na paribhuñjitabbaṃ.

Regarding the giving of flowers: 'Having offered flowers from this many trees, let them bring gruel, rice, and robes; from this many, let them bring items for the repair of lodgings.' In such designated places, flowers are considered heavy items. Elsewhere, novices pick flowers and make a pile. A flower-distributor endowed with five qualities counts the Saṅgha and makes portions. He may distribute to the assembled community without asking the Saṅgha. But one who is unappointed must ask before distributing. To whom may a monk give flowers, and to whom may he not? He may take them to his parents' house, or have them summoned from their house, saying, 'Make an offering to a sacred object.' But he may not give them for adornment. To other relatives, he should not take them, but he may have them summoned, saying, 'Make an offering.' To other people who have arrived at the place of worship, he may give, not expecting anything in return. This is not called a 'giving of flowers.' Many flowers bloom in the monastery. A monk, while on his alms round, upon seeing people, may say, 'There are many flowers in the monastery; you may make an offering.' There is no fault in merely speaking. But he should not say this with the thought, 'People will bring food and drink.' If he says this, he should not consume the food and drink. People, according to their custom, ask, 'Are there flowers in the monastery?' and say, 'We will come to the monastery on such-and-such a day; do not let the novices pick the flowers.' The monks forget to tell the novices. The novices pick the flowers and set them aside. The people approach the monks and say, 'Venerable sirs, we informed you on such-and-such a day: “Do not let the novices pick the flowers.” Why did you not prevent them?' He should reply, 'I was forgetful; the flowers have merely been picked, an offering has not yet been made.' He should not say, 'Take them and make an offering.' If he says this, he should not consume the material gain.

Aparo bhikkhu sāmaṇerānaṃ ācikkhati “asukagāmavāsino pupphāni mā ocinitthā”ti āhaṃsūti. Manussāpi [P 0.0337] āmisaṃ āharitvā dānaṃ datvā vadanti – “amhākaṃ manussā na bahukā, sāmaṇere amhehi saha pupphāni ocinituṃ āṇāpethā”ti. “Sāmaṇerehi bhikkhā laddhā; ye bhikkhācāraṃ na gacchanti, te sayameva jānissanti, upāsakā”ti vattabbaṃ. Ettakaṃ nayaṃ labhitvā sāmaṇere putte vā bhātike vā katvā pupphāni ocināpetuṃ doso natthi; pupphadānaṃ nāma na hoti.

Another monk informs the novices, 'The inhabitants of such-and-such a village said, “Do not pick the flowers.”' People also, having brought material offerings and given a gift, say, 'There are not many of us; please command the novices to pick flowers with us.' It should be said, 'The novices have received alms; those who do not go on the alms round will know for themselves, lay devotees.' Having obtained this guideline, there is no fault in having the novices pick flowers, treating them as sons or brothers; this is not called a 'giving of flowers'.

Phaladāne phalampi pupphaṃ viya niyamitameva garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti. Vihāre bahukamhi phalāphale sati aphāsukamanussā āgantvā yācanti. Bhikkhū ‘saṅghika’nti dātuṃ na ussahanti. Manussā vippaṭisārino akkosanti paribhāsanti. Tattha kiṃ kātabbanti? Phalehi vā rukkhehi vā paricchinditvā katikā kātabbā – ‘asukesu ca rukkhesu ettakāni phalāni gaṇhantā, ettakesu vā rukkhesu phalāni gaṇhantā na vāretabbā’ti. Corā pana issarā vā balakkārena gaṇhantā na vāretabbā; kuddhā te sakalavihārampi nāseyyuṃ. Ādīnavo pana kathetabboti.

Regarding the giving of fruit, fruit, like flowers, is a heavy item only when designated. When there is abundant fruit and produce in the monastery, needy people come and ask. The monks are not willing to give, thinking, 'It is the Saṅgha's property.' The people, being disappointed, scold and revile. What is to be done in this case? An agreement should be made, having demarcated either by fruits or by trees: 'Those taking this many fruits from such-and-such trees, or taking fruits from this many trees, should not be prevented.' However, thieves or powerful people taking by force should not be prevented; for, if angered, they might destroy the entire monastery. But the dangers should be explained.

Sinānadāne sinānacuṇṇāni koṭṭitāni na garubhaṇḍāni. Akoṭṭito rukkhattacova garubhaṇḍaṃ. Cuṇṇaṃ pana agilānassa rajananipakkaṃ vaṭṭati. Gilānassa yaṃkiñci cuṇṇaṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Mattikāpi ettheva pakkhipitvā kathetabbā. Mattikāpi yattha dullabhā hoti, tattheva garubhaṇḍaṃ. Sāpi heṭṭhimakoṭiyā tiṃsapalaguḷapiṇḍappamāṇāva tato heṭṭhā na garubhaṇḍanti.

Regarding the giving of bathing materials, pounded bathing powders are not heavy items. Unpounded tree bark, however, is a heavy item. For one who is not sick, colored and prepared powder is allowable. For a sick person, any kind of powder is allowable. Clay should also be included and discussed here. Where clay is scarce, it is a heavy item. Even that, of the lowest grade, up to the size of a thirty-pala lump of molasses, is a heavy item; below that, it is not.

Dantakaṭṭhadāne dantakaṭṭhaṃ acchinnakameva garubhaṇḍaṃ. Yesaṃ sāmaṇerānaṃ saṅghato dantakaṭṭhavāro pāpuṇāti, te attano ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ dātuṃ na labhanti. Yehi pana ‘ettakāni dantakaṭṭhāni āharitabbānī’ti paricchinditvā vāraṃ gahitāni, te atirekāni ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ dātuṃ labhanti. Ekena bhikkhunā dantakaṭṭhamāḷakato bahūni dantakaṭṭhāni [M 0.0324] na gahetabbāni, devasikaṃ ekekameva gahetabbaṃ. Pāṭiyekkaṃ vasantenāpi bhikkhusaṅghaṃ gaṇayitvā yattakāni [V 0.0321] attano pāpuṇanti tattakāneva gahetvā gantabbaṃ; antarā āgantukesu vā āgatesu [P 0.0338] disaṃ vā pakkamantena āharitvā gahitaṭṭhāneyeva ṭhapetabbāni.

Regarding the giving of tooth-sticks, an uncut tooth-stick is a heavy item. Those novices whose turn it is to receive tooth-sticks from the Saṅgha are not allowed to give them individually to their own teachers or preceptors. However, those who have taken their turn after specifying, 'This many tooth-sticks should be brought,' are allowed to give the excess to their teachers or preceptors. A single monk should not take many tooth-sticks from the tooth-stick rack; only one each day should be taken. Even when living separately, after counting the community of monks, one should take only as many as one is entitled to and then leave. If visitors arrive in the meantime, or if one is leaving for another region, they should be brought back and placed in the very spot from where they were taken.

Cāṭukamyatāyātiādīsu cāṭukamyatā vuccati attānaṃ dāsaṃ viya nīcaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā parassa khalitavacanampi saṇṭhapetvā piyakāmatāya paggayhavacanaṃ. Muggasūpyatāyāti muggasūpasamānāya saccālikena jīvitakappanatāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yathā hi muggasūpe paccante bahū muggā pākaṃ gacchanti, thokā na gacchanti; evameva saccālikena jīvitakappake puggale bahu alikaṃ hoti, appakaṃ saccaṃ. Yathā vā muggasūpassa appavisanaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthi, evameva saccālikavuttino puggalassa appaviṭṭhavācā nāma natthi; siṅghāṭakaṃ viya icchiticchitadhārāya patiṭṭhāti. Tenassa sā musāvāditā muggasūpyatāti vuttā. Pāribhaṭayatāti paribhaṭakammabhāvo. Paribhaṭassa hi kammaṃ pāribhaṭayaṃ, tassa bhāvo pāribhaṭayatā; alaṅkārakaraṇādīhi dārakakīḷāpanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

In the context of 'cāṭukamyatā,' etc., cāṭukamyatā is said to be placing oneself in a lowly position as if one were a servant, even setting right another's faulty speech, and speaking words of praise out of a desire to be dear. 'Muggasūpyatā' is a designation for making a living by a mixture of truth and falsehood, comparable to mung bean soup. For just as in mung bean soup, while cooking, many mung beans become cooked, but a few do not; even so, in a person who makes a living by a mixture of truth and falsehood, there is much falsehood and little truth. Or, just as there is no place that mung bean soup does not enter, so too for a person whose livelihood is false speech, there is no speech that has not been uttered; it is established like a crossroads in whatever direction is desired. Therefore, that lying of his is called 'muggasūpyatā.' 'Pāribhaṭayatā' means the state of a courtier's action. The action of a courtier is 'pāribhaṭayaṃ,' and the state of that is 'pāribhaṭayatā'; this is a designation for amusing children by doing things such as decorating themselves.

Jaṅghapesanikanti gāmantaradesantarādīsu tesaṃ tesaṃ gihīnaṃ sāsanapaṭisāsanaharaṇaṃ. Idañhi jaṅghapesanikaṃ nāma attano mātāpitūnaṃ, ye cassa mātāpitaro upaṭṭhahanti, tesaṃ sāsanaṃ gahetvā katthaci gamanavasena vaṭṭati. Cetiyassa vā saṅghassa vā attano vā kammaṃ karontānaṃ vaḍḍhakīnampi sāsanaṃ harituṃ vaṭṭati. Manussā “dānaṃ dassāma, pūjaṃ karissāma, bhikkhusaṅghassa ācikkhathā”ti vadanti; “asukattherassa nāma dethā”ti piṇḍapātaṃ vā bhesajjaṃ vā cīvaraṃ vā denti; “vihāre pūjaṃ karothā”ti mālāgandhavilepanādīni vā dhajapatākādīni vā nīyyādenti, sabbaṃ harituṃ vaṭṭati; jaṅghapesanikaṃ nāma na hoti. Sesānaṃ sāsanaṃ gahetvā gacchantassa padavāre padavāre doso.

Going on foot as a messenger means carrying messages or errands for laypeople in various villages or regions. However, it is permissible to go somewhere with a message from one's own parents or from those who care for one's parents. It is also permissible to carry messages for a shrine, the Saṅgha, or for carpenters doing work for oneself. If people say, 'We will give alms, we will make offerings—inform the community of monks,' or if they give almsfood, medicine, or robes saying, 'Give this to such-and-such elder,' or if they send garlands, perfumes, ointments, banners, flags, etc., saying, 'Make an offering at the monastery,' it is permissible to carry all these things; this is not considered going on foot as a messenger. For carrying other messages, if one goes, there is an offense at every step.

Aññataraññatarenāti etesaṃ vā veḷudānādīnaṃ aññataraññatarena vejjakammabhaṇḍāgārikakammaṃ piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍakammaṃ [P 0.0339] saṅghuppādacetiyuppādaupaṭṭhāpanakammanti evarūpānaṃ vā micchājīvena jīvitakappanakakammānaṃ yena kenaci. Buddhapaṭikuṭṭhenāti buddhehi garahitena paṭisiddhena. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ sabbopi anācāro nāma kathīyati. Ācāraniddeso vuttapaṭipakkhanayeneva veditabbo.

'By any means whatsoever' refers to any of these actions of making a living by wrong livelihood, such as one or another of giving bamboo, performing medical services, managing storerooms, giving alms in return for alms, or arranging for gains for the Saṅgha or a shrine—any such improper means of sustaining life, condemned and censured by the Buddhas. 'This is called' means all such misconduct is declared. The explanation of proper conduct should be understood in the manner opposite to what has been described.
