514. Gocaraniddesepi [M 0.0325][V 0.0322] paṭhamaṃ agocarassa vacane kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Tattha ca gocaroti piṇḍapātādīnaṃ atthāya upasaṅkamituṃ yuttaṭṭhānaṃ gocaro, ayuttaṭṭhānaṃ agocaro. Vesiyā gocaro assāti vesiyagocaro; mittasanthavavasena upasaṅkamitaṭṭhānanti attho. Tattha vesiyā nāma rūpūpajīviniyo yena kenacideva sulabhajjhācāratāmittasatthavasinehavasena upasaṅkamanto vesiyāgocaro nāma hoti. Tasmā evaṃ upasaṅkamituṃ na vaṭṭati. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Ārakkhavipattito. Evaṃ upasaṅkamantassa hi ciraṃ rakkhitagopitopi samaṇadhammo katipāheneva nassati; sacepi na nassati garahaṃ labhati. Dakkhiṇāvasena pana upasaṅkamantena satiṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā upasaṅkamitabbaṃ. Vidhavā vuccanti matapatikā vā pavutthapatikā vā. Thullakumāriyoti mahallikā aniviṭṭhakumāriyo. Paṇḍakāti lokāmisanissitakathābahulā ussannakilesā avūpasantapariḷāhā napuṃsakā. Tesaṃ sabbesampi upasaṅkamane ādīnavo vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Bhikkhunīsupi eseva nayo. Apica bhikkhū nāma ussannabrahmacariyā honti, tathā bhikkhuniyo. Te aññamaññaṃ santhavavasena katipāheneva rakkhitagopitasamaṇadhammaṃ nāsenti. Gilānapucchakena pana gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Bhikkhunā pupphāni labhitvā pūjanatthāyapi ovādadānatthāyapi gantuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva.

514. Regarding the explanation of the resort, first, the reason for stating what is not a resort should be understood in the way stated below. Herein, a resort (gocara) is a suitable place to approach for almsfood and other requisites, while a non-resort (agocara) is an unsuitable place. 'A courtesan's resort' (vesiyāgocaro) means a place approached by way of friendship and intimacy. Herein, 'courtesans' (vesiyā) are women who live by their beauty; one who approaches them because they are easily accessible for intimacy, through friendship, flattery, or affection, is said to have a courtesan-resort. Therefore, it is not proper to approach in this way. For what reason? Because of the failure in guarding oneself. For one who approaches them, his monastic conduct, though long guarded and protected, is destroyed in just a few days; and even if it is not destroyed, he incurs blame. However, when approaching for the sake of a donation, one should do so having established mindfulness. 'Widows' (vidhavā) refers to women whose husbands have died or have gone away. 'Mature maidens' (thullakumāriyo) are older, unmarried women. 'Eunuchs' (paṇḍakā) are impotent men who are full of talk connected with worldly bait, have abundant defilements, and unallayed passions. The danger in approaching all these should be understood in the way already stated. The same principle applies to bhikkhunīs. Moreover, bhikkhus are devoted to the holy life, and so too are bhikkhunīs. Through mutual intimacy, in just a few days they destroy their guarded monastic conduct. However, it is proper to go to inquire after one who is ill. And it is certainly proper for a bhikkhu who has received flowers to go for the purpose of making an offering or for the purpose of giving an exhortation.

Pānāgāranti surāpānagharaṃ. Taṃ brahmacariyantarāyakarehi surāsoṇḍehi avivittaṃ hoti. Tattha tehi saddhiṃ saha soṇḍavasena [P 0.0340] upasaṅkamituṃ na vaṭṭati; brahmacariyantarāyo hoti. Saṃsaṭṭho viharati rājūhītiādīsu rājānoti abhisittā vā hontu anabhisittā vā ye rajjaṃ anusāsanti. Rājamahāmattāti rājūnaṃ issariyasadisāya mahatiyā issariyamattāya samannāgatā. Titthiyāti viparītadassanā bāhiraparibbājakā. Titthiyasāvakāti bhattivasena tesaṃ paccayadāyakā. Etehi saddhiṃ saṃsaggajāto hotīti attho.

A tavern is a house for drinking liquor. It is not secluded from drunkards, who are obstacles to the holy life. Therefore, it is not proper to approach there together with them in the manner of a drunkard; it becomes an obstacle to the holy life. In the passage 'He lives associated with kings, etc.,' 'kings' means those who rule a kingdom, whether they are consecrated or not. Royal high officials are those endowed with great authority similar to the authority of kings. Sectarians are outside wanderers with wrong view. Disciples of sectarians are donors of requisites to them out of devotion. The meaning is that one becomes associated with these.

Ananulomikena saṃsaggenāti ananulomikasaṃsaggo nāma tissannaṃ sikkhānaṃ ananulomo paccanīkasaṃsaggo, yena brahmacariyantarāyaṃ paññattivītikkamaṃ sallekhaparihāniñca pāpuṇāti, seyyathidaṃ – rājarājamahāmattehi saddhiṃ sahasokitā, sahananditā, samasukhadukkhatā, uppannesu [M 0.0326] kiccakaraṇīyesu attanāva yogaṃ āpajjanatā, titthiyatitthiyasāvakehi saddhiṃ ekacchandarucisamācāratā ekacchandarucisamācārabhāvāvaho vā sinehabahumānasanthavo. Tattha rājarājamahāmattehi [V 0.0323] saddhiṃ saṃsaggo brahmacariyantarāyaṃ karoti. Itarehi titthiyasāvakehi tesaṃ laddhigahaṇaṃ. Tesaṃ pana vādaṃ bhinditvā attano laddhiṃ gaṇhāpetuṃ samatthena upasaṅkamituṃ vaṭṭati.

By unsuitable association: unsuitable association is an association that is uncongenial and contrary to the three trainings, through which one incurs an obstacle to the holy life, transgression of a rule, and a decline in the practice of effacement. This is as follows: sharing sorrow, sharing joy, and having the same happiness and sorrow with kings and high officials; personally undertaking the application when duties and tasks arise; having the same wish, inclination, and conduct as sectarians and their disciples, or intimacy, great esteem, and affection that brings about a state of having the same wish, inclination, and conduct. Therein, association with kings and high officials creates an obstacle to the holy life. Association with the others—the disciples of sectarians—leads to adopting their doctrine. However, it is proper for one who is capable to approach them in order to refute their doctrine and make them accept one's own doctrine.

Idāni aparenapi pariyāyena agocaraṃ dassetuṃ yāni vā pana tāni kulānītiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha assaddhānīti buddhādīsu saddhāvirahitāni; buddho sabbaññū, dhammo niyyāniko, saṅgho suppaṭipannoti na saddahanti. Appasannānīti cittaṃ pasannaṃ anāvilaṃ kātuṃ na sakkonti. Akkosakaparibhāsakānīti akkosakāni ceva paribhāsakāni ca; ‘corosi, bālosi, mūḷhosi, oṭṭhosi, goṇosi, gadrabhosi, āpāyikosi, nerayikosi, tiracchānagatosi, natthi tuyhaṃ sugati, duggatiyeva pāṭikaṅkhā’ti evaṃ dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosanti; ‘hotu, idāni taṃ paharissāma, bandhissāma[P 0.0341], vadhissāmā’ti evaṃ bhayadassanena paribhāsanti cāti attho. Anatthakāmānīti atthaṃ na icchanti, anatthameva icchanti. Ahitakāmānīti ahitameva icchanti, hitaṃ na icchanti. Aphāsukakāmānīti phāsukaṃ na icchanti, aphāsukameva icchanti. Ayogakkhemakāmānīti catūhi yogehi khemaṃ nibbhayaṃ na icchanti, sabhayameva icchanti. Bhikkhūnanti ettha sāmaṇerāpi saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Bhikkhunīnanti ettha sikkhamānasāmaṇeriyopi. Sabbesampi hi bhagavantaṃ uddissa pabbajitānañceva saraṇagatānañca catunnampi parisānaṃ tāni anatthakāmāniyeva. Tathārūpāni kulānīti evarūpāni khattiyakulādīni kulāni. Sevatīti nissāya jīvati. Bhajatīti upasaṅkamati. Payirupāsatīti punappunaṃ upasaṅkamati. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ vesiyādigocarassa vesiyādiko, rājādisaṃsaṭṭhassa rājādiko, assaddhakulādisevakassa assaddhakulādiko cāti tippakāropi ayuttagocaro agocaroti veditabbo.

Now, to explain the non-resort in another way, the passage beginning 'Or whatever families...' is introduced. Here, 'faithless' means families devoid of faith in the Buddha, etc.; they do not have faith that 'The Buddha is all-knowing, the Dhamma leads to deliverance, the Sangha is of good conduct.' 'Lacking confidence' means they are unable to make their minds confident and untroubled. 'Abusive and reviling' means those who abuse and revile; they abuse with the ten grounds for abuse, saying: 'You are a thief, a fool, a deluded one, a camel, an ox, a donkey; you are bound for the plane of misery, for hell, for the animal realm; for you there is no good destination, only a bad destination is to be expected.' And they revile by showing a threat, thus: 'Just you wait, now we will strike you, bind you, kill you'—this is the meaning. 'Those who wish one harm' do not desire one's benefit, they only desire one's harm. 'Those who wish one ill' desire only one's misfortune, not one's welfare. 'Those who wish one discomfort' do not desire one's comfort, but only one's discomfort. 'Those who wish one insecurity' do not desire security from the four yokes, but only fear. Here, 'of bhikkhus' includes novices. 'Of bhikkhunīs' includes female probationers and female novices. For all who have gone forth for the sake of the Blessed One and for those who have gone for refuge—for all four assemblies—such families wish only their harm. 'Such families' refers to families of this kind, such as khattiya families. 'He resorts to' means he lives in dependence on them. 'He associates with' means he approaches them. 'He attends upon' means he repeatedly approaches them. 'This is called...': this threefold unsuitable resort—namely, that of one who has a courtesan-resort, etc.; that of one who is associated with kings, etc.; and that of one who resorts to faithless families, etc.—should be understood as a non-resort.

Tassa iminā pariyāyena agocaratā veditabbā. Vesiyādiko tāva pañcakāmaguṇanissayato agocaroti veditabbo, yathāha – “ko ca, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno agocaro paravisayo? Yadidaṃ pañca kāmaguṇā”ti [M 0.0327] (saṃ. ni. 5.372) rājādiko jhānānuyogassa anupanissayato lābhasakkārāsanicakkanipphādanato diṭṭhivipattihetuto ca, assaddhakulādiko saddhāhānicittasantāsāvahanato agocaroti.

Its nature as a non-resort should be understood in this way. First, association with courtesans and the like is a non-resort because it is based on the five cords of sensual pleasure, as it is said: 'And what, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu's non-resort and alien domain? It is these five cords of sensual pleasure.' Association with kings and the like is a non-resort because it does not provide a basis for the practice of jhāna, leads to the production of gain, honor, and praise, and is a cause for the corruption of view. Association with faithless families and the like is a non-resort because it leads to the decline of faith and brings about mental agitation.

Gocaraniddese na vesiyagocarotiādīni vuttapaṭipakkhavasena veditabbāni. Opānabhūtānītiādīsu [V 0.0324] pana opānabhūtānīti udapānabhūtāni; bhikkhusaṅghassa, cātumahāpathe khatapokkharaṇī viya, yathāsukhaṃ ogāhanakkhamāni cittamahāmattassa gehasadisāni. Tassa kira gehe kālatthambho yuttoyeva[P 0.0342]. Gharadvāraṃ sampattānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paccayavekallaṃ nāma natthi. Ekadivasaṃ bhesajjavattameva saṭṭhi kahāpaṇāni nikkhamanti. Kāsāvapajjotānīti bhikkhubhikkhunīhi nivatthapārutānaṃ kāsāvānaṃyeva pabhāya ekobhāsāni bhūtapālaseṭṭhikulasadisāni. Isivātapaṭivātānīti gehaṃ pavisantānaṃ nikkhamantānañca bhikkhubhikkhunīsaṅkhātānaṃ isīnaṃ cīvaravātena ceva samiñjanapasāraṇādijanitasarīravātena ca paṭivātāni pavāyitāni viniddhutakibbisāni vā.

In the explanation of the suitable resort, 'not the courtesan’s resort' and so on should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated. In the passage beginning with 'like watering places,' 'like watering places' means like wells; they are like the house of the householder Citta, fit to be entered at will by the Sangha of bhikkhus, like a lotus pond dug at a crossroads. In his house, it seems, a 'time-post' is always set up. For bhikkhus arriving at his door, there is never any lack of requisites. On a single day, sixty kahāpaṇas are spent on medicines alone. 'Illuminated by saffron robes' means made into a single radiance by the glow of the saffron robes worn and draped by bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs, like the family of the treasurer Bhūtapāla. 'Fanned by the winds of sages' means fanned by the wind from the robes and the wind from the bodies generated by the bending and stretching of the sages—that is, the bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs—entering and leaving the house; or it means their stains have been blown away.

515. Aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvitāniddese aṇumattānīti aṇuppamāṇā. Vajjāti dosā. Yāni tāni vajjānīti yāni tāni garahitabbaṭṭhena vajjāni. Appamattakānīti parittamattakāni khuddakappamāṇāni. Oramattakānīti parittatopi orimappamāṇattā oramattakāni. Lahusānīti lahukāni. Lahusammatānīti lahūti sammatāni. Saṃyamakaraṇīyānīti saṃyamena kattabbapaṭikammāni. Saṃvarakaraṇīyānīti saṃvarena kātabbāni saṃvarena kattabbapaṭikammāni. Cittuppādakaraṇīyānīti cittuppādamattena kattabbapaṭikammāni. Manasikārapaṭibaddhānīti manasā āvajjitamatteneva kattabbapaṭikammāni. Kāni pana tānīti? Divāvihāravāsī sumatthero tāva āha – “anāpattigamanīyāni cittuppādamattakāni yāni ‘na puna evarūpaṃ karissāmī’ti manasā āvajjitamatteneva sujjhanti. Adhiṭṭhānāvikammaṃ nāmetaṃ kathita”nti. Antevāsiko panassa tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero panāha – “idaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlasseva bhājanīyaṃ. Tasmā sabbalahukaṃ dukkaṭadubbhāsitaṃ idha vajjanti veditabbaṃ. Vuṭṭhānāvikammaṃ nāmetaṃ kathita”nti. Itiimesūti [M 0.0328] evaṃpakāresu imesu. Vajjadassāvīti vajjato dosato dassanasīlo. Bhayadassāvīti [P 0.0343] catubbidhassa bhayassa kāraṇattā bhayato dassanasīlo. Ādīnavadassāvīti idha nindāvahanato, āyatiṃ dukkhavipākato, upariguṇānaṃ antarāyakaraṇato, vippaṭisārajananato ca etena nānappakārena ādīnavato dassanasīlo.

515. In the exposition of 'one who sees danger in minor faults': 'Minor' (aṇumattāni) means of minute measure (aṇuppamāṇā). 'Faults' (vajjā) are defects (dosā). Those things that are faults (vajjāni) are those that are faults in the sense of being blameworthy (garahitabbaṭṭhena). 'Trifling' (appamattakāni) means of small measure (parittamattakāni), of minor quantity (khuddakappamāṇāni). 'Slight' (oramattakāni) means of a lower measure even than trifling (parittatopi orimappamāṇattā). 'Light' (lahusāni) means trivial (lahukāni). 'Considered light' (lahusammatāni) means regarded as trivial (lahūti sammatāni). 'Requiring restraint' (saṃyamakaraṇīyāni) refers to corrective actions (paṭikammāni) that must be done through restraint (saṃyamena). 'Requiring guarding' (saṃvarakaraṇīyāni) means actions that must be done through guarding (saṃvarena kātabbāni), corrective actions that must be done through guarding (saṃvarena kattabbapaṭikammāni). 'Requiring mental effort' (cittuppādakaraṇīyāni) refers to corrective actions that must be done merely by a moment of mental arising (cittuppādamattena). 'Connected with attention' (manasikārapaṭibaddhāni) means corrective actions that can be done merely by a moment of mental advertence (manasā āvajjitamatteneva). But what are these? The elder Sumana, a dweller in day-residences, said: 'Those that do not lead to an offense, requiring only a moment of mental arising—those that are purified simply by adverting with the mind, "I will not do such a thing again." This is called "remedy through determination" (adhiṭṭhānāvikamma).' But his pupil, the elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, said: 'This pertains to the morality of Pātimokkha restraint itself. Therefore, the very lightest wrongdoing or wrong speech should be understood as a fault here. This is called "remedy through rising" (vuṭṭhānāvikamma).' 'Thus, in these' (itiimesu) means 'in these of such kinds' (evaṃpakāresu imesu). 'A seer of faults' (vajjadassāvī) means one whose habit is to see a fault as a defect (vajjato dosato dassanasīlo). 'A seer of danger' (bhayadassāvī) means one whose habit is to see a fault as danger, because it is a cause of the fourfold fear (catubbidhassa bhayassa kāraṇattā). 'A seer of drawbacks' (ādīnavadassāvī) means one whose habit is to see drawbacks in various ways: from incurring blame here, from painful results in the future, from obstructing higher qualities, and from generating remorse.

Nissaraṇadassāvīti yaṃ tattha nissaraṇaṃ tassa dassanasīlo. Kiṃ panettha nissaraṇanti? Ācariyattheravāde [V 0.0325] tāva “anāpattigamanīyatāya sati adhiṭṭhānāvikammaṃ nissaraṇa”nti kathitaṃ. Antevāsikattheravāde tāva “āpattigamanīyatāya sati vuṭṭhānāvikammaṃ nissaraṇa”nti kathitaṃ.

'One who sees the escape' (nissaraṇadassāvī) means one whose habit is to see the escape (nissaraṇaṃ) there. But what is the escape here? In the tradition of the teacher-elders, it is said: 'When there is no possibility of incurring an offense (anāpattigamanīyatāya sati), the remedy through determination (adhiṭṭhānāvikammaṃ) is the escape (nissaraṇaṃ).' In the tradition of the pupil-elders, it is said: 'When there is a possibility of incurring an offense (āpattigamanīyatāya sati), the remedy through rising (vuṭṭhānāvikammaṃ) is the escape (nissaraṇaṃ).'

Tattha tathārūpo bhikkhu aṇumattāni vajjāni vajjato bhayato passati nāma. Taṃ dassetuṃ ayaṃ nayo kathito – paramāṇu nāma, aṇu nāma, tajjārī nāma, rathareṇu nāma, likkhā nāma, ūkā nāma, dhaññamāso nāma, aṅgulaṃ nāma, vidatthi nāma, ratanaṃ nāma, yaṭṭhi nāma, usabhaṃ nāma, gāvutaṃ nāma, yojanaṃ nāma. Tattha ‘paramāṇu’ nāma ākāsakoṭṭhāsiko maṃsacakkhussa āpāthaṃ nāgacchati, dibbacakkhusseva āgacchati. ‘Aṇu’ nāma bhitticchiddatālacchiddehi paviṭṭhasūriyarasmīsu vaṭṭi vaṭṭi hutvā paribbhamanto paññāyati. ‘Tajjārī’ nāma gopathamanussapathacakkapathesu chijjitvā ubhosu passesu uggantvā tiṭṭhati. ‘Rathareṇu’ nāma tattha tattheva allīyati. Likkhādayo pākaṭā eva. Etesu pana chattiṃsa paramāṇavo ekassa aṇuno pamāṇaṃ. Chattiṃsa aṇū ekāya tajjāriyā pamāṇaṃ. Chattiṃsa tajjāriyo eko rathareṇu. Chattiṃsa rathareṇū ekā likkhā. Satta likkhā ekā ūkā. Satta ūkā eko dhaññamāso. Sattadhaññamāsappamāṇaṃ ekaṃ aṅgulaṃ. Tenaṅgulena dvādasaṅgulāni vidatthi. Dve vidatthiyo ratanaṃ. Satta ratanāni yaṭṭhi. Tāya yaṭṭhiyā vīsati yaṭṭhiyo usabhaṃ. Asīti usabhāni gāvutaṃ. Cattāri gāvutāni yojanaṃ. Tena yojanena aṭṭhasaṭṭhiyojanasatasahassubbedho sinerupabbatarājā. Yo bhikkhu aṇumattaṃ vajjaṃ aṭṭhasaṭṭhiyojanasatasahassubbedhasinerupabbatasadisaṃ katvā daṭṭhuṃ sakkoti – ayaṃ bhikkhu aṇumattāni [M 0.0329] vajjāni bhayato passati nāma. Yopi bhikkhu sabbalahukaṃ [P 0.0344] dukkaṭadubbhāsitamattaṃ paṭhamapārājikasadisaṃ katvā daṭṭhuṃ sakkoti – ayaṃ aṇumattāni vajjāni vajjato bhayato passati nāmāti veditabbo.

Therein, such a monk is one who sees minor faults as a fault and as danger. To show this, the following method is explained: there is what is called a paramāṇu (ultimate atom), an aṇu (atom), a tajjārī, a rathareṇu (chariot’s dust), a likkhā (a nit), an ūkā (a louse), a dhaññamāso (a grain of rice), an aṅgula (a finger-breadth), a vidatthi (a span), a ratana (a cubit), a yaṭṭhi (a staff), an usabha, a gāvuta (a league), and a yojana. Among these, a 'paramāṇu' is a fraction of space so minute that it does not enter the range of the fleshly eye, but comes only into the range of the divine eye. An 'aṇu' is seen as tiny particles swirling in sunbeams that enter through cracks in walls or gaps in lattices. A 'tajjārī' is what, on the paths of cattle, humans, and wheels, having been broken up, rises and stands on both sides. 'Rathareṇu' is the dust that clings here and there. The rest, from likkhā onwards, are well-known. Among these measurements: thirty-six paramāṇus make one aṇu. Thirty-six aṇus make one tajjārī. Thirty-six tajjārīs make one rathareṇu. Thirty-six rathareṇus make one likkhā. Seven likkhās make one ūkā. Seven ūkās make one dhaññamāso. Seven dhaññamāsas make one aṅgula. By that aṅgula, twelve aṅgulas are a vidatthi. Two vidatthis are a ratana. Seven ratanas are a yaṭṭhi. By that yaṭṭhi, twenty yaṭṭhis are an usabha. Eighty usabhas are a gāvuta. Four gāvutas are a yojana. By this yojana, Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, is sixty-eight hundred-thousand yojanas high. A monk who is able to see a minor fault as being like Mount Sineru, which is sixty-eight hundred-thousand yojanas high—this monk is called one who sees minor faults as danger. And a monk who is able to see even the most trivial wrongdoing or wrong speech as being like the first pārājika offense—such a one is to be understood as one who sees minor faults as a fault and as danger.

516. Samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesūtipadaniddese bhikkhusikkhāti bhikkhūhi sikkhitabbasikkhā. Sā bhikkhunīhi sādhāraṇāpi asādhāraṇāpi bhikkhusikkhā eva nāma. Bhikkhunīsikkhāti bhikkhunīhi sikkhitabbasikkhā. Sāpi bhikkhūhi sādhāraṇāpi asādhāraṇāpi bhikkhunīsikkhā eva nāma. Sāmaṇerasikkhamānasāmaṇerīnaṃ sikkhāpi ettheva paviṭṭhā. Upāsakasikkhāti upāsakehi sikkhitabbasikkhā. Sā pañcasīladasasīlavasena vaṭṭati. Upāsikāsikkhāti upāsikāhi sikkhitabbasikkhā. Sāpi pañcasīladasasīlavasena vaṭṭati. Tattha bhikkhubhikkhunīnaṃ sikkhā yāva arahattamaggā vaṭṭati. Upāsakaupāsikānaṃ sikkhā [V 0.0326] yāva anāgāmimaggā. Tatrāyaṃ bhikkhu attanā sikkhitabbasikkhāpadesu eva sikkhati. Sesasikkhā pana atthuddhāravasena sikkhāpadassa atthadassa dassanatthaṃ vuttā. Iti imāsu sikkhāsūti evaṃpakārāsu etāsu sikkhāsu. Sabbena sabbanti sabbena sikkhāsamādānena sabbaṃ sikkhaṃ. Sabbathā sabbanti sabbena sikkhitabbākārena sabbaṃ sikkhaṃ. Asesaṃ nissesanti sesābhāvato asesaṃ; satisammosena bhinnassāpi sikkhāpadassa puna pākatikakaraṇato nissesaṃ. Samādāya vattatīti samādiyitvā gahetvā vattati. Tena vuccatīti yena kāraṇena etaṃ sabbaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ sabbena sikkhitabbākārena samādiyitvā sikkhati pūreti, tena vuccati “samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesū”ti.

516. In the exposition of the phrase 'undertaking, one trains in the training rules': 'The bhikkhu's training' refers to the training that should be undertaken by bhikkhus. That training, whether shared with bhikkhunīs or not, is indeed called the bhikkhu's training. 'The bhikkhunī's training' refers to the training that should be undertaken by bhikkhunīs. That, too, whether shared with bhikkhus or not, is indeed called the bhikkhunī's training. The training of male novices, female probationers, and female novices is also included here. 'The male lay follower's training' refers to the training that should be undertaken by male lay followers. It proceeds by way of the five precepts and the ten precepts. 'The female lay follower's training' refers to the training that should be undertaken by female lay followers. That, too, proceeds by way of the five precepts and the ten precepts. Therein, the training for bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs proceeds up to the path of arahantship. The training for male and female lay followers proceeds up to the path of non-returning. In this context, this bhikkhu trains only in the training rules that he himself should undertake. The remaining trainings, however, are stated for the purpose of showing the meaning of the training rule by way of extracting its meaning. 'Thus, in these trainings' means 'in these trainings of such a kind'. 'Completely and entirely' means all the training through the complete undertaking of the training. 'In every way' means all the training in every manner in which it should be trained. 'Without remainder' is so called due to the absence of a remainder; 'without exception' is so called because even a training rule that has been broken due to a lapse of mindfulness is restored to its original state. 'One lives undertaking it' means one lives having undertaken and grasped it. Therefore, it is said—for the reason that, having undertaken this entire training rule in every manner in which it should be trained, one trains in it and fulfills it, for that reason it is said: 'Undertaking, one trains in the training rules.'

517-8. Indriyesu guttadvāro bhojane mattaññūtipadadvayassa niddese kaṇhapakkhassa paṭhamavacane payojanaṃ ācāraniddese vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Tattha katamā indriyesu aguttadvāratātiādīsu pana yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ nikkhepakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttameva.

517-8. In the exposition of the two terms, 'guarded as to the doors of the senses' and 'knowing moderation in food,' the purpose in the first statement of the dark fortnight should be understood in the same way as explained in the exposition on conduct. As to this, whatever should be said concerning such questions as, 'What is unguardedness as to the doors of the senses?' and so on, all that has already been stated in the commentary on the Section on Summary.

519. Jāgariyānuyoganiddese [P 0.0345] pubbarattāpararattanti ettha aḍḍharattasaṅkhātāya rattiyā pubbe pubbarattaṃ; iminā paṭhamayāmañceva pacchābhattañca gaṇhāti[M 0.0330]. Rattiyā pacchā apararattaṃ; iminā pacchimayāmañceva purebhattañca gaṇhāti. Majjhimayāmo panassa bhikkhuno niddākilamathavinodanokāsoti na gahito. Jāgariyānuyoganti jāgariyassa asupanabhāvassa anuyogaṃ. Anuyutto hotīti taṃ anuyogasaṅkhātaṃ āsevanaṃ bhāvanaṃ anuyutto hoti sampayutto. Niddese panassa idha bhikkhu divasanti pubbaṇho, majjhanho, sāyanhoti tayopi divasakoṭṭhāsā gahitā. Caṅkamena nisajjāyāti sakalampi divasaṃ iminā iriyāpathadvayeneva viharanto. Cittassa āvaraṇato āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi pañcahipi nīvaraṇehi sabbākusaladhammehi vā cittaṃ parisodheti. Tehi dhammehi visodheti parimoceti. Ṭhānaṃ panettha kiñcāpi na gahitaṃ, caṅkamanisajjāsannissitaṃ pana katvā gahetabbameva. Paṭhamayāmanti sakalasmimpi paṭhamayāme. Majjhimayāmanti rattindivassa chaṭṭhakoṭṭhāsasaṅkhāte majjhimayāme.

519. In the exposition of the practice of wakefulness: Here, 'the first part of the night' refers to the time before the middle of the night; by this, one includes both the first watch and the time after the meal. The 'latter part of the night' is the time after the midpoint of the night; by this, one includes both the last watch and the time before the meal. The middle watch, however, is not included for this bhikkhu, as it is an occasion for dispelling sleepiness and fatigue. 'The practice of wakefulness' means the commitment to wakefulness, the state of not sleeping. 'He is devoted' means he is engaged in, develops, and is connected to that practice designated as devotion. In the exposition, 'during the day' here means that all three parts of the day—morning, midday, and evening—are included. 'By walking and sitting' means dwelling throughout the entire day in just these two postures. He purifies the mind from obstructive states—from the five hindrances or from all unwholesome states that obstruct the mind. He cleanses and liberates it from those states. Although 'place' is not mentioned here, it should be understood as being connected with walking and sitting. 'The first watch' means throughout the entire first watch. 'The middle watch' means the middle watch, which is counted as the sixth part of a day and night.

Sīhaseyyanti ettha kāmabhogīseyyā, petaseyyā, sīhaseyyā, tathāgataseyyāti catasso seyyā. Tattha “yebhuyyena, bhikkhave, kāmabhogī vāmena passena sentī”ti ayaṃ kāmabhogīseyyā. Tesu hi yebhuyyena dakkhiṇapassena sayāno nāma natthi. “Yebhuyyena, bhikkhave[V 0.0327], petā uttānā sentī”ti ayaṃ petaseyyā; appamaṃsalohitattā hi aṭṭhisaṅghāṭajaṭitā ekena passena sayituṃ na sakkonti, uttānāva senti. Sīho, bhikkhave, migarājā dakkhiṇena passena seyyaṃ kappeti…pe… attamano hotī”ti (a. ni. 4.246) ayaṃ sīhaseyyā; tejussadattā hi sīho migarājā dve purimapāde ekasmiṃ ṭhāne dve pacchimapāde ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapetvā naṅguṭṭhaṃ antarasatthimhi pakkhipitvā [P 0.0346] purimapādapacchimapādanaṅguṭṭhānaṃ ṭhitokāsaṃ sallakkhetvā dvinnaṃ purimapādānaṃ matthake sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā sayati; divasampi sayitvā pabujjhamāno na uttasanto pabujjhati, sīsaṃ pana ukkhipitvā purimapādādīnaṃ ṭhitokāsaṃ sallakkheti; sace kiñci ṭhānaṃ vijahitvā ṭhitaṃ hoti ‘nayidaṃ tuyhaṃ jātiyā na sūrabhāvassa anurūpa’nti anattamano hutvā tattheva sayati, na gocarāya pakkamati; avijahitvā ṭhite pana ‘tuyhaṃ jātiyā ca sūrabhāvassa ca anurūpamida’nti haṭṭhatuṭṭho uṭṭhāya sīhavijambhitaṃ vijambhitvā kesarabhāraṃ [M 0.0331] vidhunitvā tikkhattuṃ sīhanādaṃ naditvā gocarāya pakkamati. Catutthajjhānaseyyā pana tathāgataseyyāti vuccati. Tāsu idha sīhaseyyā āgatā. Ayañhi tejussadairiyāpathattā uttamaseyyā nāma.

Regarding the lion's posture, here there are four postures: the posture of sensualists, the posture of ghosts, the lion's posture, and the posture of the Tathāgata. Among these, 'For the most part, bhikkhus, sensualists sleep on their left side'—this is the posture of sensualists. For among them, for the most part, there is no one who sleeps on their right side. 'For the most part, bhikkhus, ghosts sleep on their backs'—this is the posture of ghosts; for being scant of flesh and blood, and bound together by a framework of bones, they cannot sleep on one side, but lie on their backs. 'The lion, bhikkhus, the king of beasts, settles himself to sleep on his right side... and is content'—this is the lion's posture. For due to his majesty, the lion, the king of beasts, places his two front paws together in one spot and his two hind paws together in one spot, tucks his tail between his thighs, marks the position of his front paws, hind paws, and tail, rests his head on his two front paws, and sleeps. Even after sleeping all day, when he awakens, he does so without alarm. He lifts his head and observes the position of his front paws and the rest. If any part has shifted from its place, thinking, 'This is not fitting for your birth and courageous nature,' he becomes displeased and lies down right there, not going out to roam for food. But if they have not shifted, thinking, 'This is fitting for your birth and courageous nature,' he rises, happy and delighted, gives a lion's stretch, shakes his mane, roars a lion's roar three times, and then goes out to roam for food. The posture of the fourth jhāna, however, is called the posture of the Tathāgata. Here, the lion's posture is meant. For this, due to its being a majestic posture, is called the supreme posture.

Pāde pādanti dakkhiṇapāde vāmapādaṃ. Accādhāyāti atiādhāya īsakaṃ atikkamma ṭhapetvā gopphakena hi gopphake jāṇunā vā jāṇumhi saṅghaṭṭiyamāne abhiṇhaṃ vedanā uppajjati, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ na hoti, seyyā aphāsukā hoti; yathā pana na saṅghaṭṭeti, evaṃ atikkamma ṭhapite vedanā nuppajjati, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, seyyā phāsukā hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “pāde pādaṃ accādhāyā”ti. Sato sampajānoti satiyā ceva sampajānapaññāya ca samannāgato hutvā. Iminā supariggāhakaṃ satisampajaññaṃ kathitaṃ. Uṭṭhānasaññaṃ manasikaritvāti asukavelāya nāma uṭṭhahissāmī’ti evaṃ uṭṭhānavelāparicchedakaṃ uṭṭhānasaññaṃ citte upetvā. Evaṃ katvā nipanno hi yathāparicchinnakāleyeva uṭṭhātuṃ yutto.

‘One foot on the other’ means the right foot on the left foot. ‘Accādhāya’ means placing it slightly beyond, slightly overlapping. For when the ankle presses against the ankle or the knee against the knee, frequent pain arises, the mind is not unified, and the posture is uncomfortable. But when they are placed so as not to press, no pain arises, the mind is unified, and the posture is comfortable. Therefore it is said, ‘placing one foot on the other, slightly overlapping.’ ‘Mindful and fully aware’ means being endowed with mindfulness and the wisdom of clear comprehension. By this, well-grasped mindfulness and clear comprehension are explained. ‘Having attended to the perception of rising’ means bringing to mind the perception of rising, which determines the time of rising, thus: ‘At such and such a time, I will rise.’ For one who lies down having done so is fit to rise at the predetermined time.

520-521. Sātaccaṃ nepakkanti satataṃ pavattayitabbato sātaccasaṅkhātaṃ vīriyañceva paripākagatattā nepakkasaṅkhātaṃ paññañca yutto anuyutto pavattayamānoyeva jāgariyānuyogaṃ anuyutto viharatīti attho. Ettha ca vīriyaṃ lokiyalokuttaramissakaṃ kathitaṃ, paññāpi vīriyagatikā eva; vīriye lokiyamhi lokiyā, lokuttare lokuttarāti attho.

520-521. ‘Persistence’ (sātacca) is energy, so designated because it should be continuously maintained; and ‘discernment’ (nepakka) is wisdom, so designated because it has reached maturity. The meaning is that one who, endowed with and devoted to both, maintains them, lives engaged in the practice of wakefulness. Here, energy is said to be a mixture of mundane and supramundane; wisdom, too, follows the course of energy, being mundane when the energy is mundane, and supramundane when it is supramundane. Such is the meaning.

522. Bodhipakkhiyānaṃ [V 0.0328] dhammānanti catusaccabodhisaṅkhātassa [P 0.0347] maggañāṇassa pakkhe bhavānaṃ dhammānaṃ. Ettāvatā sabbepi sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhamme samūhato gahetvā lokiyāyapi bhāvanāya ekārammaṇe ekato pavattanasamatthe bojjhaṅgeyeva dassento satta bojjhaṅgātiādimāha. Te lokiyalokuttaramissakāva kathitāti veditabbā. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthameva.

522. ‘The factors that pertain to enlightenment’ are the states that are on the side of the path-knowledge, which is designated as the enlightenment of the Four Truths. Thus far, having collectively taken all thirty-seven factors pertaining to enlightenment, and showing that even in mundane cultivation they are capable of occurring together on a single object, he speaks of the seven factors of enlightenment and so forth. It should be understood that these are described as a mixture of the mundane and supramundane. The rest here has a plain meaning, due to the method explained previously.

523. Abhikkantetiādiniddese abhikkante paṭikkanteti ettha tāva abhikkantaṃ vuccati purato gamanaṃ. Paṭikkantanti nivattanaṃ. Tadubhayampi catūsu iriyāpathesu [M 0.0332] labbhati. Gamane tāva purato kāyaṃ abhiharanto abhikkamati nāma, paṭinivattanto paṭikkamati nāma. Ṭhānepi ṭhitakova kāyaṃ purato onāmento abhikkamati nāma, pacchato apanāmento paṭikkamati nāma. Nisajjāyapi nisinnakova āsannassa purimaaṅgābhimukho saṃsaranto abhikkamati nāma, pacchimaaṅgappadesaṃ paccāsaṃsaranto paṭikkamati nāma. Nipajjāyapi eseva nayo.

523. In the explanation of terms like ‘going forward’ and so on, first, ‘going forward’ means moving forward. ‘Turning back’ means returning. Both of these are found in the four postures. Regarding walking, when one directs the body forward, it is called ‘going forward’; when one turns back, it is called ‘turning back.’ Even while standing, if one, while standing, inclines the body forward, it is called ‘going forward’; if one moves it backward, it is called ‘turning back.’ In sitting, if one, while seated, moves towards the front part of what is nearby, it is called ‘going forward’; if one moves back towards the back part, it is called ‘turning back.’ The same method applies to lying down.

Sampajānakārī hotīti sampajaññena sabbakiccakārī, sampajaññasseva vā kārī. So hi abhikkantādīsu sampajaññaṃ karoteva, na katthaci sampajaññavirahito hoti. Taṃ pana sampajaññaṃ yasmā satisampayuttameva hoti, tenassa niddese “sato sampajāno abhikkamati, sato sampajāno paṭikkamatī”ti vuttaṃ.

‘He acts with clear comprehension’ means he performs all activities with clear comprehension, or he is a doer of clear comprehension itself. For he indeed practices clear comprehension in going forward and so on, and is nowhere without clear comprehension. But since that clear comprehension is always associated with mindfulness, therefore in its explanation it is said: ‘Mindful and clearly comprehending, he goes forward; mindful and clearly comprehending, he returns.’

Ayañhi abhikkamanto vā paṭikkamanto vā na muṭṭhassatī asampajāno hoti; satiyā pana samannāgato paññāya ca sampajānoyeva abhikkamati ceva paṭikkamati ca; sabbesu abhikkamādīsu catubbidhaṃ sampajaññaṃ otāreti. Catubbidhañhi sampajaññaṃ – sātthakasampajaññaṃ, sappāyasampajaññaṃ, gocarasampajaññaṃ, asammohasampajaññanti. Tattha abhikkamanacitte uppanne cittavaseneva agantvā ‘kinnu me ettha gatena attho atthi, natthī’ti atthānatthaṃ pariggahetvā atthapariggaṇhanaṃ ‘sātthakasampajaññaṃ’. Tattha ca ‘attho’ti cetiyadassanabodhidassanasaṅghadassanatheradassanaasubhadassanādivasena dhammato vaḍḍhi. Cetiyaṃ vā bodhiṃ vā disvāpi hi buddhārammaṇaṃ [P 0.0348] pītiṃ, saṅghadassanena saṅghārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ uppādetvā tadeva khayavayato sammasanto arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. There disvā tesaṃ ovāde patiṭṭhāya, asubhaṃ disvā tattha paṭhamajjhānaṃ uppādetvā tadeva khayavayato sammasanto arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tasmā etesaṃ dassanaṃ [V 0.0329] sātthaṃ. Keci pana “āmisatopi vaḍḍhi atthoyeva; taṃ nissāya brahmacariyānuggahāya paṭipannattā”ti vadanti.

For when going forward or turning back, one is not unmindful and without clear comprehension; but endowed with mindfulness and wisdom, one goes forward and turns back with clear comprehension. In all activities of going forward and so on, one applies the fourfold clear comprehension. The fourfold clear comprehension is: clear comprehension of purpose, clear comprehension of suitability, clear comprehension of domain, and clear comprehension of non-delusion. Here, when the thought of going forward arises, without going merely by the impulse of the mind, one considers: ‘Is there any purpose for me in going there, or not?’ Having discerned the purpose or lack thereof, the ascertainment of purpose is called ‘clear comprehension of purpose.’ In this regard, ‘purpose’ refers to growth in the Dhamma through seeing stupas, seeing the Bodhi tree, seeing the Saṅgha, seeing elders, seeing the unattractive, and so on. For having seen a stupa or the Bodhi tree, one arouses joy with the Buddha as its object; having seen the Saṅgha, one arouses joy with the Saṅgha as its object; and by contemplating that very joy as subject to destruction and vanishing, one attains arahantship. Having seen elders and established oneself in their advice, or having seen the unattractive and aroused the first jhāna there, and by contemplating that very jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing, one attains arahantship. Therefore, seeing these things is purposeful. Some, however, say: ‘Even growth related to material things is a purpose, because one has undertaken the practice for the support of the holy life, relying on it.’

Tasmiṃ pana gamane sappāyāsappāyaṃ pariggahetvā sappāyapariggaṇhanaṃ ‘sappāyasampajaññaṃ’, seyyathidaṃ – cetiyadassanaṃ tāva sātthaṃ. Sace pana cetiyassa mahatiyā pūjāya dasadvādasayojanantare parisā sannipatanti[M 0.0333], attano vibhavānurūpaṃ itthiyopi purisāpi alaṅkatapaṭiyattā cittakammarūpakāni viya sañcaranti, tatra cassa iṭṭhe ārammaṇe lobho, aniṭṭhe paṭigho, asamapekkhane moho uppajjati, kāyasaṃsaggāpattiṃ vā āpajjati, jīvitabrahmacariyānaṃ vā antarāyo hoti. Evaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ asappāyaṃ hoti. Vuttappakāraantarāyābhāve sappāyaṃ. Bodhidassanepi eseva nayo. Saṅghadassanampi sātthaṃ. Sace pana antogāme mahāmaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā sabbarattiṃ dhammassavanaṃ karontesu manussesu vuttappakāreneva janasannipāto ceva antarāyo ca hoti. Evaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ asappāyaṃ hoti; antarāyābhāve sappāyaṃ hoti. Mahāparisaparivārānaṃ therānaṃ dassanepi eseva nayo.

In that journey, discerning what is suitable and unsuitable, the ascertainment of suitability is called ‘clear comprehension of suitability’; for example, seeing a stupa is purposeful. However, if a large gathering assembles within ten or twelve yojanas for a grand offering at the stupa, and men and women, adorned and prepared according to their means, move about like painted figures, then desire may arise toward a pleasing object, aversion toward a displeasing one, and delusion in the case of indifference. One may commit an offense involving bodily contact or face a threat to one’s life and the holy life. Thus, that place becomes unsuitable. In the absence of obstacles of the type mentioned, it is suitable. The same principle applies to seeing the Bodhi tree. Seeing the Saṅgha is also purposeful. However, if a great pavilion is built within a village, and people listen to the Dhamma all night, a gathering of people and an obstacle of the type mentioned may occur. Thus, that place becomes unsuitable; in the absence of obstacles, it is suitable. The same principle applies when seeing elders surrounded by a large assembly.

Asubhadassanampi sātthaṃ. Tadatthadīpanatthañca idaṃ vatthu – eko kira daharabhikkhu sāmaṇeraṃ gahetvā dantakaṭṭhatthāya gato. Sāmaṇero maggā okkamitvā purato gacchanto asubhaṃ disvā paṭhamajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā tadeva pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāre sammasanto tīṇi phalāni sacchikatvā uparimaggatthāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariggahetvā aṭṭhāsi. Daharo taṃ apassanto “sāmaṇerā”ti pakkosi. So ‘mayā pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya bhikkhunā saddhiṃ dve kathā nāma na kathitapubbā, aññasmiṃ divase uparivisesaṃ nibbattessāmī’ti cintetvā “kiṃ, bhante”ti paṭivacanaṃ adāsi. “Ehī”ti ca vutto ekavacaneneva āgantvā “bhante, iminā tāva maggena gantvā mayā ṭhitokāse muhuttaṃ puratthābhimukho [P 0.0349] ṭhatvā olokethā”ti āha. So tathā katvā tena pattavisesameva pāpuṇi. Evaṃ ekaṃ asubhaṃ dvinnaṃ janānaṃ atthāya jātaṃ. Evaṃ sātthampi panetaṃ purisassa mātugāmāsubhaṃ asappāyaṃ, mātugāmassa ca purisāsubhaṃ, sabhāgameva sappāyanti. Evaṃ sappāyapariggaṇhanaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ nāma.

The contemplation of the foul is also beneficial. To illustrate this point, here is a story: A certain young monk once took a novice with him to fetch a toothstick. The novice, stepping off the path and walking ahead, saw a foul object and generated the first jhāna. Making that the basis, he contemplated the formations and realized three fruits. Then, he stood, having taken up a meditation subject for the higher path. Not seeing him, the young monk called out, "Novice!" He thought, "Since the day I went forth, I have never spoken two words with a monk. On another day, I will generate a higher distinction." So he replied, "Yes, venerable sir?" And when told, "Come here," he came and said, "Venerable sir, please go along this path and stand for a moment facing east where I was standing and look." The monk did so and attained the very same special attainment. Thus, one foul object became beneficial for two people. However, though beneficial, for a man the foulness of a woman is unsuitable, and for a woman the foulness of a man is unsuitable; only the foulness of one's own kind is suitable. Thus, discerning what is suitable is called 'suitable clear comprehension.'

Evaṃ pariggahitasātthasappāyassa pana aṭṭhatiṃsāya kammaṭṭhānesu attano cittaruciyaṃ kammaṭṭhānasaṅkhātaṃ [V 0.0330] gocaraṃ uggahetvā bhikkhācāragocare taṃ gahetvāva gamanaṃ ‘gocarasampajaññaṃ’ nāma. Tassāvibhāvanatthaṃ idaṃ catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ –

Now, for one who has thus discerned what is beneficial and suitable, having taken up a meditation subject, which is his resort, from among the thirty-eight meditation subjects, according to his own inclination, his going with that meditation subject as his resort for alms is called 'clear comprehension of resort.' To clarify this, this tetrad should be understood:

Idhekacco bhikkhu harati na paccāharati, ekacco na harati paccāharati, ekacco pana neva harati na paccāharati, ekacco harati ca paccāharati [M 0.0334] ca. Tattha yo bhikkhu divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhetvā, tathā rattiyā paṭhamayāme majjhimayāme seyyaṃ kappetvā pacchimayāmepi nisajjācaṅkamehi vītināmetvā pageva cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇavattaṃ katvā bodhirukkhe udakaṃ āsiñcitvā pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā ācariyupajjhāyavattādīni sabbāni khandhakavattāni samādāya vattati, so sarīraparikammaṃ katvā senāsanaṃ pavisitvā dve tayo pallaṅke usumaṃ gāhāpento kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjitvā, bhikkhācāravelāya uṭṭhahitvā kammaṭṭhānasīseneva pattacīvaramādāya senāsanato nikkhamitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontova cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā, sace buddhānussatikammaṭṭhānaṃ hoti taṃ avissajjetvāva cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ pavisati, aññaṃ ce kammaṭṭhānaṃ hoti sopānamūle ṭhatvā hatthena gahitabhaṇḍaṃ viya taṃ ṭhapetvā buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ gahetvā cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ āruyha mahantaṃ cetiyaṃ ce, tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā catūsu ṭhānesu vanditabbaṃ, khuddakaṃ ce, tatheva padakkhiṇaṃ katvā aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu vanditabbaṃ. Cetiyaṃ vanditvā bodhiyaṅgaṇaṃ pattenāpi buddhassa bhagavato sammukhā viya nipaccākāraṃ dassetvā bodhi vanditabbā.

Here, one monk takes but does not bring back; another does not take but brings back; another neither takes nor brings back; and another both takes and brings back. Among these, the monk who purifies his mind during the day by walking and sitting, freeing it from obstructive states, and similarly, having spent the first and middle watches of the night in sleep, passes the last watch also with sitting and walking meditation—having performed the duties at the shrine courtyard and the Bodhi tree courtyard early in the morning, having sprinkled water on the Bodhi tree, having prepared drinking and washing water, and having undertaken all the duties of the Vinaya, such as those towards his teachers and preceptors, he conducts himself thus. Having attended to his bodily needs, he enters his dwelling, warms up his body by sitting for two or three sessions, and diligently applies himself to his meditation subject. At the time for the alms round, he rises, takes his bowl and robe with his meditation subject foremost in mind, and leaves his dwelling. Keeping his meditation subject in mind, he goes to the shrine courtyard. If his meditation subject is the recollection of the Buddha, he enters the shrine courtyard without abandoning it. If it is another meditation subject, he stands at the foot of the stairs, sets it aside as if placing down an object held in his hand, takes up joy with the Buddha as the object, and ascends to the shrine courtyard. If it is a large shrine, he is to circumambulate it three times and pay respects at the four designated spots. If it is a small one, he is to similarly circumambulate it and pay respects at the eight designated spots. Having paid respects at the shrine, he proceeds to the Bodhi tree courtyard. Even with his bowl, he should show reverence as if face-to-face with the Blessed One, the Buddha, and then pay respects to the Bodhi tree.

So evaṃ cetiyañca bodhiñca vanditvā paṭisāmitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā, paṭisāmitaṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ hatthena gaṇhanto [P 0.0350] viya, nikkhittakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā gāmasamīpe kammaṭṭhānasīseneva cīvaraṃ pārupitvā gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisati. Atha naṃ manussā disvā ‘ayyo no āgato’ti paccuggantvā pattaṃ gahetvā āsanasālāya vā gehe vā nisīdāpetvā yāguṃ datvā yāva bhattaṃ na niṭṭhāti tāva pāde dhovitvā telena makkhetvā purato nisīditvā pañhaṃ vā pucchanti dhammaṃ vā sotukāmā honti. Sacepi na kathāpenti “janasaṅgahatthaṃ dhammakathā nāma kātabbāyevā”ti aṭṭhakathācariyā vadanti. Dhammakathā hi kammaṭṭhānavinimuttā nāma natthi. Tasmā kammaṭṭhānasīseneva āhāraṃ paribhuñjitvā anumodanaṃ vatvā nivattiyamānehipi manussehi anugatova gāmato nikkhamitvā tattha te nivattetvā maggaṃ paṭipajjati.

Having thus paid homage to the shrine and the Bodhi tree, he goes to the place where he had put his things. As if taking up a stored item with his hand, he takes up the meditation subject he had set aside and, with the meditation subject foremost in his mind, he puts on his robe near the village and enters the village for alms. Then, seeing him, people say, "Our venerable one has come," and they go forth to meet him, take his bowl, seat him in the hall or in a house, offer him rice gruel, and while the meal is not yet finished, they wash his feet, anoint them with oil, and sit down in front of him. They either ask questions or wish to hear the Dhamma. Even if they do not initiate conversation, the commentary teachers say, "A Dhamma talk should indeed be given for the sake of benefiting the people." For there is no Dhamma talk that is entirely separate from a meditation subject. Therefore, with the meditation subject still foremost in mind, he consumes the food, gives a blessing, and, accompanied by the people as they see him off, he leaves the village. Having sent them back, he proceeds on his way.

Atha [V 0.0331] naṃ puretaraṃ nikkhamitvā bahigāme katabhattakiccā sāmaṇeradaharabhikkhū disvā paccuggantvā pattacīvaramassa gaṇhanti. Porāṇakabhikkhū kira ‘amhākaṃ upajjhāyo, amhākaṃ ācariyo’ti na mukhaṃ oloketvā vattaṃ karonti, sampattaparicchedeneva karonti. Te taṃ pucchanti “bhante, ete manussā [M 0.0335] tumhākaṃ kiṃ honti? Mātipakkhato sambandhā pitipakkhato”ti? “Kiṃ disvā pucchathā”ti? “Tumhesu etesaṃ pemaṃ bahumāna”nti. “Āvuso, yaṃ mātāpitūhipi dukkaraṃ taṃ ete manussā amhākaṃ karonti. Pattacīvarampi no etesaṃ santakameva, etesaṃ ānubhāvena neva bhaye bhayaṃ, na chātake chātakaṃ jānāma. Edisā nāma amhākaṃ upakārino natthī”ti tesaṃ guṇe kathento gacchati. Ayaṃ vuccati ‘harati na paccāharatī’ti.

Then, the novices and junior monks, who had gone out earlier and completed their meal outside the village, saw him and went forth to receive his bowl and robe. It seems the monks of old did not perform their duties by showing favoritism, saying, 'Our preceptor, our teacher,' but performed them simply for any senior monk who arrived. They asked him, 'Venerable sir, what are these people to you? Are they relatives from your mother's side or your father's side?' 'What did you see that makes you ask?' 'Their great affection and respect for you.' 'Friends, what is difficult even for parents to do, these people do for us. Even our bowl and robe belong to them. By their influence, we know neither fear in times of danger nor hunger in times of famine. We have no such benefactors as these.' Speaking thus of their virtues, he went on his way. This is called 'one who takes but does not bring back.'

Yassa pana pageva vuttappakāraṃ vattapaṭipattiṃ karontassa kammajatejo pajjalati, anupādinnakaṃ muñcitvā upādinnakaṃ gaṇhāti, sarīrato sedā muccanti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vīthiṃ nārohati, so pageva pattacīvaramādāya vegasāva cetiyaṃ vanditvā gorūpānaṃ nikkhamanavelāyameva gāmaṃ yāgubhikkhāya pavisitvā yāguṃ labhitvā āsanasālaṃ gantvā pivati. Athassa dvattikkhattuṃ ajjhoharaṇamatteneva kammajatejodhātu upādinnakaṃ muñcitvā anupādinnakaṃ [P 0.0351] gaṇhāti, ghaṭasatena nhāto viya tejodhātupariḷāhanibbānaṃ patvā kammaṭṭhānasīsena yāguṃ paribhuñjitvā pattañca mukhañca dhovitvā antarābhatte kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikatvā avasesaṭṭhāne piṇḍāya caritvā kammaṭṭhānasīsena āhāraṃ paribhuñjitvā tato paṭṭhāya poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ upaṭṭhahamānaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvāva āgacchati. Ayaṃ vuccati ‘na harati paccāharatī’ti. Edisā ca bhikkhū yāguṃ pivitvā vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā buddhasāsane arahattaṃ pattā nāma gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattā. Sīhaḷadīpeyeva tesu tesu gāmesu āsanasālāya na taṃ āsanaṃ atthi, yattha yāguṃ pivitvā arahattaṃ pattā bhikkhū natthīti.

But for one who, while performing the duties as described earlier, has the kamma-born heat element blazing up, who lets go of the ungrasped and grasps the grasped, from whose body sweat pours, and whose meditation subject does not ascend to the path—such a one, taking his bowl and robe, quickly pays homage at the shrine early in the morning and, just at the time the cows are let out, enters the village for rice gruel. Having obtained the gruel, he goes to the assembly hall and drinks it. Then, after swallowing just two or three mouthfuls, the kamma-born heat element releases the grasped and grasps the ungrasped. Like one bathed with a hundred pots of water, he attains the quenching of the burning from the heat element. He consumes the gruel with his meditation subject as the foremost thing, washes his bowl and mouth, and during the time before the meal, he applies his mind to the meditation subject. Then he goes for alms in the remaining places, consumes his food with his meditation subject as the foremost thing, and from then on, taking up the meditation subject as it arises in succession, he returns. This is called 'one who does not carry it away, but brings it back.' Such monks, having drunk the gruel and begun insight meditation, who have attained arahantship in the Buddha’s Dispensation are beyond counting. Indeed, in the island of Sri Lanka, in village after village, there is no seat in an assembly hall where a monk who drank gruel and attained arahantship has not sat.

Yo pamādavihārī hoti nikkhittadhuro sabbavattāni bhinditvā pañcavidhacetokhīlavinibandhabaddhacitto viharanto ‘kammaṭṭhānaṃ nāma atthī’tipi saññaṃ akatvā gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā ananulomikena gihīsaṃsaggena saṃsaṭṭho caritvā ca bhuñjitvā ca tuccho nikkhamati – ayaṃ vuccati ‘neva harati na paccāharatī’ti.

One who lives heedlessly, having cast off the burden, breaking all observances, dwelling with a mind bound by the five kinds of mental barrenness and bondage—not even forming the perception that 'there is such a thing as a meditation subject'—enters a village for alms, associates with householders in an unsuitable manner, and after wandering and eating, he departs empty. This is called 'one who neither carries it away nor brings it back.'

Yo [V 0.0332] panāyaṃ “harati ca paccāharati cā”ti vutto, so gatapaccāgatikavattavasena veditabbo – atthakāmā hi kulaputtā sāsane pabbajitvā [M 0.0336] dasampi vīsampi tiṃsampi cattārīsampi paññāsampi satampi ekato vasantā katikavattaṃ katvā viharanti – “āvuso, tumhe na iṇaṭṭā, na bhayaṭṭā, na ājīvikāpakatā pabbajitā; dukkhā muñcitukāmā panettha pabbajitā. Tasmā gamane uppannakilesaṃ gamaneyeva niggaṇhatha. Ṭhāne, nisajjāya, sayane uppannakilesaṃ sayaneyeva niggaṇhathā”ti.

But the one described as 'one who both carries it away and brings it back' should be understood in terms of the observance of going and returning. For clansmen, wishing for their own welfare, having gone forth in the Dispensation and dwelling together in groups of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or a hundred, live having made an agreement: 'Friends, you have not gone forth because of debt, nor out of fear, nor because of a ruined livelihood; you have gone forth here wishing to be freed from suffering. Therefore, when a defilement arises while walking, suppress it right there while walking. When a defilement arises while standing, sitting, or lying down, suppress it right there while standing, sitting, or lying down.'

Te evaṃ katikavattaṃ katvā bhikkhācāraṃ gacchantā, aḍḍhausabhausabhaaḍḍhagāvutagāvutantaresu pāsāṇā honti, tāya saññāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontāva gacchanti. Sace kassaci gamane kileso uppajjati, tattheva naṃ niggaṇhāti. Tathā asakkonto tiṭṭhati. Athassa pacchato āgacchantopi tiṭṭhati. So ‘ayaṃ bhikkhu tuyhaṃ uppannaṃ vitakkaṃ jānāti, ananucchavikaṃ te eta’nti attānaṃ paṭicodetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā ariyabhūmiṃ okkamati. Tathā asakkonto nisīdati. Athassa pacchato āgacchantopi nisīdatīti so eva nayo. Ariyabhūmiṃ [P 0.0352] okkamituṃ asakkontopi taṃ kilesaṃ vikkhambhetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontova gacchati, na kammaṭṭhānavippayuttena cittena pādaṃ uddharati, uddharati ce paṭinivattitvā purimapadesaññeva eti, ālindakavāsī mahāphussadevatthero viya. So kira ekūnavīsati vassāni gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūrento eva vihāsi. Manussāpi antarāmagge kasantā ca vapantā ca maddantā ca kammāni ca karontā theraṃ tathāgacchantaṃ disvā “ayaṃ thero punappunaṃ nivattitvā gacchati, kiṃ nu kho maggamūḷho udāhu kiñci pamuṭṭho”ti samullapanti. So taṃ anādiyitvā kammaṭṭhānayuttacitteneva samaṇadhammaṃ karonto vīsativassabbhantare arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Arahattapattadivase cassa caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ adhivatthā devatā aṅgulīhi dīpaṃ ujjāletvā aṭṭhāsi. Cattāropi mahārājāno sakko ca devānamindo brahmā ca sahampati upaṭṭhānaṃ āgamiṃsu. Tañca obhāsaṃ disvā vanavāsī mahātissatthero taṃ dutiyadivase pucchi – “rattibhāge āyasmato santike obhāso ahosi. Kiṃ so obhāso”ti? Thero vikkhepaṃ karonto “obhāso nāma dīpobhāsopi hoti, maṇiobhāsopī”ti evamādimāha. Tato “paṭicchādetha tumhe”ti nibaddho “āmā”ti paṭijānitvā ārocesi.

Having made this agreement, as they go on their alms round, there are stones at intervals of half an usabha, an usabha, half a gāvuta, or a gāvuta. By means of that sign, they go along applying their minds to their meditation subject. If a defilement arises in someone while walking, he suppresses it right there. If he is unable to do so, he stands still. Then the one coming behind him also stands still. Reflecting, 'This monk knows the thought that has arisen in you; this is unbecoming of you,' he reproaches himself, develops insight, and enters the noble plane. If he is unable to do so, he sits down. Then the one coming behind him also sits down—the same principle applies. Even if unable to enter the noble plane, he suppresses that defilement and goes on applying his mind to his meditation subject. He does not lift a foot with a mind disconnected from his meditation subject. If he does lift it, he turns back and returns to the very same spot—just like the Elder Mahāphussadeva, a resident of the verandah. It is said that he lived for nineteen years fulfilling the observance of going and returning. People along the way—plowing, sowing, threshing, and doing other work—seeing the elder walking in this way, would remark to one another, 'This elder keeps turning back as he walks. Is he lost, or has he forgotten something?' Paying them no heed, he continued to practice the ascetic's duties with a mind yoked to his meditation subject and attained arahantship within twenty years. On the day he attained arahantship, the deity dwelling at the end of his walking path stood there, illuminating it with a light from her fingers. The Four Great Kings, Sakka, lord of the devas, and Brahmā Sahampati came to attend upon him. Seeing that radiance, the Elder Mahātissa, a forest-dweller, asked him the next day, 'Venerable sir, there was a radiance in your presence during the night. What was that radiance?' The elder, attempting a diversion, said things like, 'Radiance can be the light of a lamp, or the light of a gem.' Then, when pressed with, 'You must not conceal it,' he admitted, 'Yes,' and related what had happened.

Kāḷavallimaṇḍapavāsī [M 0.0337] mahānāgatthero viya ca. Sopi kira gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūrento ‘paṭhamaṃ [V 0.0333] tāva bhagavato mahāpadhānaṃ pūjessāmī’ti satta vassāni ṭhānacaṅkamameva adhiṭṭhāsi; puna soḷasa vassāni gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūretvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. So kammaṭṭhānayutteneva cittena pādaṃ uddharanto vippayuttena cittena uddhate pāde paṭinivattento gāmasīmaṃ gantvā ‘gāvī nu kho, pabbajito nu kho’ti āsaṅkanīyappadese ṭhatvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvā kacchakantarato udakena pattaṃ dhovitvā udakagaṇḍūsaṃ karoti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? ‘Mā me bhikkhaṃ dātuṃ vā vandituṃ vā āgate manusse ‘dīghāyukā hothā’ti vacanamattenāpi kammaṭṭhānavikkhepo ahosī’ti. ‘Ajja, bhante, katimī’ti divasaṃ vā bhikkhugaṇanaṃ vā pañhaṃ vā pucchito pana udakaṃ gilitvā āroceti; sace divasādipucchakā na honti, nikkhamanavelāyaṃ gāmadvāre niṭṭhubhitvāva [P 0.0353] yāti.

Like the great elder Mahānāga, who dwelt in the Kāḷavalli pavilion. It is said that he, fulfilling the practice of going and returning, resolved for seven years to maintain only standing and walking meditation, thinking, ‘First, I will honor the Blessed One’s great striving.’ Then, after completing sixteen years of the practice of going and returning, he attained arahantship. He would lift his foot with a mind indeed joined with his meditation subject, and if a foot was lifted with a mind disjoined, he would turn back. Upon reaching the village boundary, he would stand in a place where it might be wondered, ‘Is this a cow or a monk?’ Then, he would put on his robe, wash his alms bowl with water from his waistband, and take a mouthful of water. Why? ‘Lest any disturbance to my meditation arise even from the mere words of people who come to offer alms or pay respects, saying, “May you live long.”’ If asked, ‘Venerable sir, what day is it today?’ or a question about the day or the number of monks, he would swallow the water and then reply. If no one asked about the day or such matters, he would spit it out at the village gate when leaving and then go on his way.

Kalambatitthavihāre vassūpagatā paññāsa bhikkhū viya ca. Te kira āsāḷhipuṇṇimāyaṃ katikavattaṃ akaṃsu – “arahattaṃ appatvā aññamaññaṃ nālapissāmā”ti. Gāmañca piṇḍāya pavisantā udakagaṇḍūsaṃ katvā pavisiṃsu, divasādīsu pucchitesu vuttanayena paṭipajjiṃsu. Tattha manussā niṭṭhubhanaṭṭhānaṃ disvā jāniṃsu – ‘ajja eko āgato, ajja dve’ti; evañca cintesuṃ – ‘kinnu kho ete amheheva saddhiṃ na sallapanti udāhu aññamaññampi? Yadi aññamaññampi na sallapanti, addhā vivādajātā bhavissanti; etha ne aññamaññaṃ khamāpessāmā’ti sabbe vihāraṃ gantvā paññāsāya bhikkhūsu dvepi bhikkhū ekokāse nāddasaṃsu. Tato yo tesu cakkhumā puriso so āha – “na, bho, kalahakārakānaṃ vasanokāso īdiso hoti. Susammaṭṭhaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇaṃ, sunikkhittā sammajjaniyo, sūpaṭṭhitaṃ pānīyaparibhojanīya”nti. Te tatova nivattā. Tepi bhikkhū antotemāseyeva arahattaṃ patvā mahāpavāraṇāya visuddhipavāraṇaṃ pavāresuṃ.

Like the fifty monks who had entered the rains retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery. It is said that on the full moon day of Āsāḷhī, they made an agreement: "Until we attain arahantship, we will not speak to one another." When they entered the village for alms, they would take a mouthful of water before entering. When questioned about the day and so on, they responded in the manner previously stated. The people, seeing the spitting place, realized: "Today one has come, today two have come." And they thought: "Why don’t these monks speak with us, or even with each other? If they don’t speak even among themselves, surely they must have a dispute. Come, let us reconcile them." All went to the monastery, but among the fifty monks, they did not see even two monks in one place. Then, a discerning man among them said: "Friends, the dwelling place of quarrelers is not like this. The courtyard around the shrine and the Bodhi tree is well-swept, the brooms are neatly placed, and drinking water and water for use is well-prepared." They turned back from there. Those monks all attained arahantship within those three months and, on the great Pavāraṇā day, they performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony of purification.

Evaṃ kāḷavallimaṇḍapavāsī mahānāgatthero viya, kalambutitthavihāre vassūpagatabhikkhū viya ca kammaṭṭhānayutteneva cittena pādaṃ uddharanto gāmasamīpaṃ [M 0.0338] gantvā udakagaṇḍūsaṃ katvā vīthiyo sallakkhetvā yattha surāsoṇḍadhuttādayo kalahakārakā caṇḍahatthiassādayo vā natthi, taṃ vīthiṃ paṭipajjati. Tattha piṇḍāya caramāno na turitaturito viya javena gacchati, na hi javanapiṇḍapātikadhutaṅgaṃ nāma kiñci atthi, visamabhūmibhāgappattaṃ pana udakasakaṭaṃ viya niccalo hutvā gacchati, anugharaṃ paviṭṭho ca dātukāmaṃ vā adātukāmaṃ vā sallakkhetuṃ tadanurūpaṃ kālaṃ āgamento bhikkhaṃ gahetvā antogāme vā bahigāme vā vihārameva vā āgantvā[V 0.0334], yathāphāsuke patirūpe okāse nisīditvā, kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaronto āhāre paṭikūlasaññaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā, akkhabbhañjanavaṇālepanaputtamaṃsūpamavasena paccavekkhanto aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ āhāraṃ āhāreti neva davāya, na madāya, na maṇḍanāya, na vibhūsanāya…pe… phāsuvihāro cāti. Bhuttāvī ca udakakiccaṃ katvā muhuttaṃ [P 0.0354] bhattakilamathaṃ paṭippassambhetvā yathā purebhattaṃ, evaṃ pacchābhattaṃ purimayāmaṃ pacchimayāmañca kammaṭṭhānameva manasikaroti. Ayaṃ vuccati ‘harati ca paccāharati cā’ti.

Just as the great elder Mahānāga, who dwelt in the Kāḷavalli pavilion, and the monks who spent the rains retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery, with a mind devoted to the meditation subject, he lifts his foot and goes near the village. Having taken a mouthful of water, he observes the streets and proceeds along a path where there are no drunkards, gamblers, troublemakers, or violent elephants and horses. While walking for alms there, he does not hurry or rush with speed, for there is no such thing as a swift alms-gatherer's ascetic practice. Instead, like a water cart reaching uneven ground, he moves steadily and calmly. Upon entering a house, whether the people wish to give or not, he observes accordingly and, after waiting a suitable time, receives alms. Then, whether inside the village, outside, or back at the monastery, he sits in a comfortable and suitable spot, focuses on his meditation subject, establishes the perception of the repulsiveness of food, and reflects on it as if it were eye-salve, ointment for a wound, or a child’s flesh. He consumes the food endowed with eight factors—neither for amusement, nor intoxication, nor adornment, nor embellishment… but merely for the sake of sustaining this body and for a comfortable living. Having eaten, he completes his water duties, rests a while to relieve the fatigue of the meal, and then, just as before the meal, so after the meal—during the first watch of the night and the last watch—he continues to focus on his meditation subject. This is called ‘taking and bringing back.’

Imaṃ pana haraṇapaccāharaṇasaṅkhātaṃ gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūrento, yadi upanissayasampanno hoti, paṭhamavaye eva arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, no ce paṭhamavaye pāpuṇāti atha majjhimavaye, no ce majjhimavaye pāpuṇāti atha pacchimavaye, no ce pacchimavaye pāpuṇāti atha maraṇasamaye, no ce maraṇasamaye pāpuṇāti atha devaputto hutvā, no ce devaputto hutvā pāpuṇāti anuppanne buddhe nibbatto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikaroti, no ce paccekabodhiṃ sacchikaroti atha buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāve khippābhiñño vā hoti – seyyathāpi thero bāhiyo dārucīriyo, mahāpañño vā – seyyathāpi thero sāriputto, mahiddhiko vā – seyyathāpi thero mahāmoggallāno, dhutaṅgadharo vā – seyyathāpi thero mahākassapo, dibbacakkhuko vā – seyyathāpi thero anuruddho, vinayadharo vā – seyyathāpi thero upāli, dhammakathiko vā – seyyathāpi thero puṇṇo mantāṇiputto, āraññiko vā – seyyathāpi thero revato, bahussuto vā – seyyathāpi thero ānando, sikkhākāmo vā – seyyathāpi thero rāhulo buddhaputtoti. Iti imasmiṃ catukke yvāyaṃ harati ca paccāharati ca, tassa gocarasampajaññaṃ sikhāppattaṃ hoti.

Now, fulfilling this practice of going and returning, known as ‘taking and bringing back,’ if one is endowed with supporting conditions, one attains arahantship in the first period of life. If not in the first period, then in the middle period. If not in the middle period, then in the final period. If not in the final period, then at the moment of death. If not at the moment of death, then after becoming a deva. If not after becoming a deva, then one realizes paccekabodhi when a Buddha has not arisen. If one does not realize paccekabodhi, then in the presence of Buddhas, one becomes either swift in direct knowledge—like the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya, or greatly wise—like the Elder Sāriputta, or of great psychic power—like the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, or a bearer of ascetic practices—like the Elder Mahākassapa, or possessing the divine eye—like the Elder Anuruddha, or a master of the Discipline—like the Elder Upāli, or a preacher of the Dhamma—like the Elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, or a forest-dweller—like the Elder Revata, or very learned—like the Elder Ānanda, or eager to train—like the Elder Rāhula, the Buddha's son. Thus, in this tetrad, for one who takes and brings back, the clear comprehension of the proper range is fully attained.

Abhikkamādīsu [M 0.0339] pana asammuyhanaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ. Taṃ evaṃ veditabbaṃ – idha bhikkhu abhikkamanto vā paṭikkamanto vā yathā andhabālaputhujjanā abhikkamādīsu ‘attā abhikkamati, attanā abhikkamo nibbattito’ti vā ‘ahaṃ abhikkamāmi, mayā abhikkamo nibbattito’ti vā sammuyhanti, tathā asammuyhanto ‘abhikkamāmī’ti citte uppajjamāne teneva cittena saddhiṃ cittasamuṭṭhānavāyodhātu viññattiṃ janayamānā uppajjati. Iti cittakiriyāvāyodhātuvipphāravasena ayaṃ kāyasammato aṭṭhisaṅghāto abhikkamati. Tassevaṃ abhikkamato ekekapāduddharaṇe pathavīdhātu āpodhātūti dve dhātuyo omattā honti mandā, itarā dve adhimattā [P 0.0355] honti balavatiyo; tathā atiharaṇavītiharaṇesu. Vossajjane tejodhātu vāyodhātūti [V 0.0335] dve dhātuyo omattā honti mandā, itarā dve adhimattā honti balavatiyo; tathā sannikkhepanasannirujjhanesu tattha uddharaṇe pavattā rūpārūpadhammā atiharaṇaṃ na pāpuṇanti; tathā atiharaṇe pavattā vītiharaṇaṃ, vītiharaṇe pavattā vossajjanaṃ, vossajjane pavattā sannikkhepanaṃ, sannikkhepane pavattā sannirujjhanaṃ na pāpuṇanti; tattha tattheva pabbaṃ pabbaṃ sandhi sandhi odhi odhi hutvā tattakapāle pakkhittatilaṃ viya paṭapaṭāyantā bhijjanti. Tattha ko eko abhikkamati? Kassa vā ekassa abhikkamanaṃ? Paramatthato hi dhātūnaṃyeva gamanaṃ, dhātūnaṃ ṭhānaṃ, dhātūnaṃ nisajjā, dhātūnaṃ sayanaṃ, tasmiṃ tasmiñhi koṭṭhāse saddhiṃ rūpehi –

Regarding going forward and other activities, non-confusion is the clear comprehension of non-delusion. This should be understood as follows: Here, when a bhikkhu goes forward or backward, unlike blind, foolish ordinary people who are confused regarding going forward and other activities, thinking, 'The self goes forward; going forward is produced by the self,' or 'I go forward; going forward is produced by me,' he, being unconfused, knows that when the thought 'I am going forward' arises in the mind, along with that thought, the wind element, produced by the mind, arises, generating bodily intimation. Thus, this body—a collection of bones conventionally called such—goes forward due to the activity of the mind and the expansion of the wind element. As he goes forward thus, with each lifting of a foot, two elements—the earth element and the water element—become weak and diminished, while the other two become strong and dominant; the same applies to extending and retracting. When putting the foot down, two elements—the fire element and the wind element—become weak and diminished, while the other two become strong and dominant; the same applies to placing and settling the foot. There, the material and immaterial phenomena occurring during lifting do not reach extending; similarly, those occurring during extending do not reach retracting, those during retracting do not reach putting down, those during putting down do not reach placing, those during placing do not reach settling; in each case, at each joint, each juncture, each section, they break apart crackling like sesame seeds thrown into a hot potsherd. Here, who is it that goes forward? Or whose going forward is it? In reality, it is merely the elements' going, the elements' standing, the elements' sitting, the elements' lying down, in each respective part, together with form—

Aññaṃ uppajjate cittaṃ, aññaṃ cittaṃ nirujjhati;

Avīcimanusambandho, nadīsotova vattatīti.

One mind arises, another mind ceases; like a river's flow, it continues without interruption.

Evaṃ abhikkamādīsu asammuyhanaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ nāmāti.

Thus, in going forward and so on, non-confusion is called the clear comprehension of non-delusion.

Niṭṭhito abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hotītipadassa attho.

The meaning of the phrase 'one acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning' is concluded.

Ālokite vilokiteti ettha pana ālokitaṃ nāma purato pekkhanaṃ, vilokitaṃ nāma anudisāpekkhanaṃ. Aññānipi heṭṭhā upari pacchato pekkhanavasena olokitaullokitāpalokitāni nāma [M 0.0340] honti. Tāni idha na gahitāni. Sāruppavasena pana imāneva dve gahitāni. Iminā vā mukhena sabbānipi tāni gahitānevāti.

Regarding 'looking forward and looking around,' here 'looking forward' means looking straight ahead, and 'looking around' means looking in the intermediate directions. Other terms like 'looking down,' 'looking up,' and 'looking away' are also used for observing below, above, and behind. These are not included here. However, for the sake of suitability, only these two are taken. Or, by means of this approach, all of them are indeed included.

Tattha ‘ālokessāmī’ti citte uppanne cittavaseneva anoloketvā atthapariggaṇhanaṃ ‘sātthakasampajaññaṃ’. Taṃ āyasmantaṃ nandaṃ kāyasakkhiṃ katvā veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Here, when the thought 'I will look' arises, not looking merely by the power of thought, but grasping the purpose, is 'clear comprehension of purpose.' This should be understood by making Venerable Nanda a bodily witness. For it was said by the Blessed One:

“Sace, bhikkhave, nandassa puratthimā disā āloketabbā hoti, sabbaṃ cetasā samannāharitvā nando puratthimaṃ disaṃ āloketi – ‘evaṃ me puratthimaṃ disaṃ ālokayato na abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssavissantī’ti. Itiha sātthakasampajāno [P 0.0356] hoti. “Sace, bhikkhave, nandassa pacchimā disā, uttarā disā, dakkhiṇā disā, uddhaṃ, adho, anudisā anuviloketabbā hoti, sabbaṃ cetasā samannāharitvā [V 0.0336] nando anudisaṃ anuviloketi – evaṃ me anudisaṃ anuvilokayato…pe… sampajāno hotī”ti (a. ni. 8.9).

“Monks, if Nanda needs to look to the eastern direction, he focuses his entire mind and attends to it, and Nanda looks to the eastern direction, thinking, ‘As I look to the eastern direction in this way, no covetousness or displeasure, evil unwholesome qualities, will flow in after me.’ Thus, he acts with clear comprehension of purpose. If, monks, Nanda needs to look to the western direction, the northern direction, the southern direction, upwards, downwards, or the intermediate directions, he focuses his entire mind and attends to it, and Nanda looks to the intermediate directions, thinking, ‘As I look to the intermediate directions in this way... he acts with clear comprehension of purpose.’” (AN 8.9).

Apica idhāpi pubbe vuttacetiyadassanādivaseneva sātthakatā ca sappāyatā ca veditabbā.

Furthermore, here too, purposefulness and suitability should be understood in the same way as previously explained regarding things like seeing a shrine.

Kammaṭṭhānassa pana avijahanameva ‘gocarasampajaññaṃ’. Tasmā khandhadhātuāyatanakammaṭṭhānikehi attano kammaṭṭhānavaseneva, kasiṇādikammaṭṭhānikehi vā pana kammaṭṭhānasīseneva ālokanavilokanaṃ kātabbaṃ.

Not abandoning the meditation subject is indeed 'clear comprehension of the domain.' Therefore, those who have aggregates, elements, or sense bases as their meditation subject should look forward or around within the confines of their meditation subject, and those who have kasiṇas and so on as their meditation subject should do so focusing on their meditation topic.

Abbhantare attā nāma āloketā vā viloketā vā natthi. ‘Ālokessāmī’ti pana citte uppajjamāne teneva cittena saddhiṃ cittasamuṭṭhānā vāyodhātu viññattiṃ janayamānā uppajjati. Iti cittakiriyāvāyodhātuvipphāravasena heṭṭhimaṃ akkhidalaṃ adho sīdati, uparimaṃ uddhaṃ laṅgheti. Koci yantakena vivaranto nāma natthi. Tato cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dassanakiccaṃ sādhentaṃ uppajjatī’ti evaṃ pajānanaṃ panettha ‘asammohasampajaññaṃ’ nāma.

Inside, there is no self that looks forward or looks around. However, when the thought 'I will look' arises, the wind element produced by the mind arises together with that thought, generating bodily intimation. Thus, through the activity of the mind and the expansion of the wind element, the lower eyelid sinks down, and the upper one rises up. There is no one opening them with a mechanism. Then, eye-consciousness arises, accomplishing the function of seeing. Understanding this is here called 'clear comprehension of non-delusion.'

Apica [M 0.0341] mūlapariññāāgantukatāvakālikabhāvavasena panettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ. Mūlapariññāvasena tāva –

Moreover, here, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood in terms of root-comprehension, the nature of a visitor, and the momentary nature. First, regarding root-comprehension:

Bhavaṅgāvajjanañceva, dassanaṃ sampaṭicchanaṃ;

Santīraṇaṃ voṭṭhabbanaṃ, javanaṃ bhavati sattamaṃ.

Life-continuum and advertence, seeing, receiving, investigating, determining; impulsion is the seventh.

Tattha bhavaṅgaṃ upapattibhavassa aṅgakiccaṃ sādhayamānaṃ pavattati; taṃ āvattetvā kiriyamanodhātu āvajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā; tannirodhā cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dassanakiccaṃ sādhayamānaṃ; tannirodhā vipākamanodhātu sampaṭicchanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā; tannirodhā vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu santīraṇakiccaṃ sādhayamānā; tannirodhā kiriyamanoviññāṇadhātu voṭṭhabbanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā; tannirodhā sattakkhattuṃ javanaṃ javati. Tattha paṭhamajavanepi ‘ayaṃ itthī, ayaṃ puriso’ti rajjanadussanamuyhanavasena ālokitavilokitaṃ na hoti; dutiyajavanepi…pe… sattamajavanepi. Etesu pana, yuddhamaṇḍale [P 0.0357] yodhesu viya, heṭṭhupariyavasena [V 0.0337] bhijjitvā patitesu ‘ayaṃ itthī, ayaṃ puriso’ti rajjanādivasena ālokitavilokitaṃ hoti. Evaṃ tāvettha ‘mūlapariññāvasena’ asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

There, the life-continuum, fulfilling the function of being a factor of the rebirth-existence, flows on. Turning from that, the functional mind-element, fulfilling the function of adverting, arises. Upon its cessation, eye-consciousness, fulfilling the function of seeing, arises. Upon its cessation, the resultant mind-element, fulfilling the function of receiving, arises. Upon its cessation, the resultant mind-consciousness-element, fulfilling the function of investigating, arises. Upon its cessation, the functional mind-consciousness-element, fulfilling the function of determining, arises. Upon its cessation, impulsion occurs seven times. Here, even in the first impulsion, there is no looking forward or looking around with attraction, aversion, or delusion, thinking 'this is a woman, this is a man.' Similarly in the second impulsion... up to the seventh impulsion. But in these, as with warriors on a battlefield, it is only after they have been broken and have fallen in disarray that the looking forward and looking around with attraction and so forth occurs, as 'this is a woman, this is a man.' Thus, in this way, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood by way of root-comprehension.

Cakkhudvāre pana rūpe āpāthagate bhavaṅgacalanato uddhaṃ sakasakakiccanipphādanavasena āvajjanādīsu uppajjitvā niruddhesu avasāne javanaṃ uppajjati. Taṃ pubbe uppannānaṃ āvajjanādīnaṃ gehabhūte cakkhudvāre āgantukapuriso viya hoti. Tassa yathā paragehe kiñci yācituṃ paviṭṭhassa āgantukapurisassa gehasāmikesupi tuṇhīmāsinesu āṇākaraṇaṃ na yuttaṃ, evaṃ āvajjanādīnaṃ gehabhūte cakkhudvāre āvajjanādīsupi arajjantesu adussantesu amuyhantesu ca rajjanadussanamuyhanaṃ ayuttanti. Evaṃ ‘āgantukabhāvavasena’ asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

When a visible form comes into the range of the eye-door, after the vibration of the life-continuum, and after advertence and the other states have arisen and ceased while accomplishing their respective functions, at the end, impulsion arises. In the eye-door, which is the house of the previously arisen advertence and other states, that impulsion is like a visitor. Just as it is not proper for a visitor who has entered another’s house to ask for something to give orders when the householders are sitting in silence, so too, in the eye-door, the house of advertence and the other states, when those states themselves are not experiencing attraction, aversion, or delusion, it is improper for impulsion to have attraction, aversion, or delusion. Thus, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood by way of its nature as a visitor.

Yāni panetāni cakkhudvāre voṭṭhabbanapariyosānāni cittāni uppajjanti, tāni saddhiṃ sampayuttadhammehi tattha tattheva bhijjanti, aññamaññaṃ na passantīti ittarāni tāvakālikāni honti. Tattha yathā ekasmiṃ ghare sabbesu mānusakesu matesu avasesassa ekakassa taṅkhaṇaṃyeva maraṇadhammassa na yuttā naccagītādīsu abhirati nāma, evameva ekadvāre sasampayuttesu āvajjanādīsu [M 0.0342] tattha tattheva matesu avasesassa taṅkhaṇaṃññeva maraṇadhammassa javanassāpi rajjanadussanamuyhanavasena abhirati nāma na yuttāti. Evaṃ ‘tāvakālikabhāvavasena’ asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, those consciousnesses that arise at the eye-door, ending with determining, disintegrate right there and then together with their associated states. They do not perceive one another; thus, they are trifling and temporary. Here, just as in a house where all the people have died, it is not fitting for the one remaining person, who is himself subject to death at that very moment, to delight in dancing, singing, and the like; so too, at a single door, when advertence and the other states with their concomitants have ceased right there and then, it is not fitting for the remaining impulsion, which is itself subject to death at that very moment, to delight by way of attraction, aversion, or delusion. Thus, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood by way of its temporary nature.

Apica khandhāyatanadhātupaccayapaccavekkhaṇavasenapetaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ettha hi cakkhu ceva rūpāni ca rūpakkhandho, dassanaṃ viññāṇakkhandho, taṃsampayuttā vedanā vedanākkhandho, saññā saññākkhandho, phassādikā saṅkhārakkhandho. Evametesaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ samavāye ālokanavilokanaṃ paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi? Ko viloketi?

Furthermore, this should be understood by way of reviewing the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and conditions.
