Here, the eye and forms are the aggregate of form; seeing is the aggregate of consciousness; feeling associated with that is the aggregate of feeling; perception is the aggregate of perception; and contact and so on are the aggregate of formations. Thus, looking forward and looking around are discerned in the combination of these five aggregates. Here, who is it that looks forward? Who looks around?

Tathā cakkhu cakkhāyatanaṃ, rūpaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ, dassanaṃ manāyatanaṃ, vedanādayo taṃsampayuttā dhammā dhammāyatanaṃ. Evametesaṃ catunnaṃ āyatanānaṃ samavāye [P 0.0358] ālokanavilokanaṃ paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi? Ko viloketi?

Likewise, the eye is the eye-base, form is the form-base, seeing is the mind-base, and feeling and other associated states are the dhamma-base. Thus, with the concurrence of these four bases, looking forward and looking around are discerned. Here, who is it that looks forward? Who looks around?

Tathā cakkhu cakkhudhātu, rūpaṃ rūpadhātu, dassanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātu, taṃsampayuttā vedanādayo [V 0.0338] dhammā dhammadhātu. Evametāsaṃ catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ samavāye ālokanavilokanaṃ paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi? Ko viloketi?

Similarly, the eye is the eye-element, form is the form-element, seeing is the eye-consciousness-element, and the associated feelings and other states are the dhamma-element. Thus, with the combination of these four elements, looking forward and looking around are discerned. Here, who is it that looks forward? Who looks around?

Tathā cakkhu nissayapaccayo, rūpaṃ ārammaṇapaccayo, āvajjanaṃ anantarasamanantaraanantarūpanissayanatthivigatapaccayo, āloko upanissayapaccayo, vedanādayo sahajātādipaccayā. Evametesaṃ paccayānaṃ samavāye ālokanavilokanaṃ paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi? Ko viloketīti? Evamettha khandhāyatanadhātupaccayapaccavekkhaṇavasenāpi asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Similarly, the eye is the dependence condition; form is the object condition; adverting is the contiguity, immediate contiguity, decisive support by contiguity, absence, and disappearance condition; light is the decisive support condition; and feeling and the other states are the conascence and other conditions. Thus, through the combination of these conditions, looking forward and looking around are discerned. Here, who is it that looks forward? Who looks around? In this way, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should also be understood by way of reviewing the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and conditions.

Samiñjite pasāriteti pabbānaṃ samiñjanapasāraṇe. Tattha cittavaseneva samiñjanapasāraṇaṃ akatvā hatthapādānaṃ samiñjanapasāraṇapaccayā atthānatthaṃ pariggahetvā tattha atthapariggaṇhanaṃ ‘sātthakasampajaññaṃ’. Tattha hatthapāde aticiraṃ samiñjitvā vā pasāretvā eva vā ṭhitassa khaṇe khaṇe vedanā uppajjanti, cittaṃ ekaggataṃ na labhati, kammaṭṭhānaṃ paripatati, visesaṃ nādhigacchati; kāle samiñjantassa kāle pasārentassa pana tā vedanā nuppajjanti, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ phātiṃ gacchati, visesamadhigacchatīti. Evaṃ ‘atthānatthapariggaṇhanaṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

'Bending and stretching' refers to the bending and stretching of the limbs. Here, without performing the bending and stretching merely according to the mind's inclination, one discerns the benefit and harm on account of the bending and stretching of the hands and feet. The discernment of benefit in this is 'clear comprehension of purpose.' If one keeps the hands and feet bent or stretched for too long, moment by moment feelings arise, the mind does not attain one-pointedness, the meditation subject declines, and one does not achieve a special attainment. But for one who bends and stretches at the right time, those feelings do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject prospers, and one achieves a special attainment. Thus, the 'discernment of benefit and harm' should be understood.

Atthe [M 0.0343] pana satipi sappāyāsappāyaṃ pariggahetvā sappāyapariggaṇhanaṃ ‘sappāyasampajaññaṃ’.

But even when there is a purpose, by discerning what is suitable and unsuitable, the discernment of what is suitable is 'clear comprehension of suitability.'

Tatrāyaṃ nayo – mahācetiyaṅgaṇe kira daharabhikkhū sajjhāyaṃ gaṇhanti. Tesaṃ piṭṭhipasse daharabhikkhuniyo dhammaṃ suṇanti. Tatreko daharo hatthaṃ pasārento kāyasaṃsaggaṃ patvā teneva kāraṇena gihī jāto. Aparo bhikkhu pādaṃ pasārento aggimhi pasāresi. Aṭṭhiṃ āhacca pādo jhāyi. Aparo bhikkhu vammike pasāresi. So āsīvisena daṭṭho. Aparo bhikkhu cīvarakuṭidaṇḍake pasāresi. Taṃ maṇisappo ḍaṃsi. Tasmā evarūpe [P 0.0359] asappāye apasāretvā sappāye pasāretabbaṃ. Idamettha sappāyasampajaññaṃ.

Herein is the method: In the great cetiya courtyard, it is said that young monks were reciting. Behind them, young nuns were listening to the Dhamma. There, one young monk, stretching out his hand, made physical contact, and for that very reason, became a layman. Another monk stretched out his foot into a fire. His foot was burned, having reached the bone. Another monk stretched out his foot into an anthill. He was bitten by a venomous snake. Another monk stretched out his foot toward a pole of a robe-hut. A jeweled snake bit him. Therefore, one should not stretch out in such unsuitable places, but should stretch out in suitable ones. This, here, is comprehension of suitability.

‘Gocarasampajaññaṃ’ pana mahātheravatthunā dīpetabbaṃ – mahāthero kira divāṭṭhāne nisinno antevāsikehi saddhiṃ kathayamāno sahasā hatthaṃ samiñjitvā puna yathāṭhāne [V 0.0339] ṭhapetvā saṇikaṃ samiñjesi. Taṃ antevāsikā pucchiṃsu – “kasmā, bhante, sahasā hatthaṃ samiñjitvā puna yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā saṇikaṃ samiñjitthā”ti? “Yato paṭṭhāya mayā, āvuso, kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikātuṃ āraddho, na me kammaṭṭhānaṃ muñcitvā hattho samiñjitapubbo. Idāni pana me tumhehi saddhiṃ kathayamānena kammaṭṭhānaṃ muñcitvā samiñjito. Tasmā puna yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā samiñjesi”nti. “Sādhu, bhante, bhikkhunā nāma evarūpena bhavitabba”nti. Evametthāpi kammaṭṭhānāvijahanameva ‘gocarasampajañña’nti veditabbaṃ.

Comprehension of range, however, should be illustrated by the story of the great elder. It is said that the great elder, while sitting in his daytime dwelling and conversing with his resident pupils, suddenly contracted his hand, then placed it back in its original position and contracted it slowly. His resident pupils asked him, "Venerable sir, why did you contract your hand suddenly, then place it back and contract it slowly?" He replied, "Friends, from the time I began to apply my mind to the meditation subject, my hand has never before been contracted after having abandoned the meditation subject. But just now, while conversing with you, it was contracted after abandoning the meditation subject. That is why I placed it back and contracted it again." They said, "Excellent, venerable sir! A monk should indeed be of such a kind." Thus, here too, not abandoning the meditation subject is itself to be understood as 'comprehension of range.'

‘Abbhantare attā nāma koci samiñjento vā pasārento vā natthi. Vuttappakāracittakiriyāvāyodhātuvipphārena pana, suttākaḍḍhanavasena dāruyantassa hatthapādacalanaṃ viya, samiñjanapasāraṇaṃ hotī’ti parijānanaṃ panettha ‘asammohasampajañña’nti veditabbaṃ.

Inside, there is no self whatsoever that contracts or stretches out. Rather, contraction and stretching out occur due to the impulse of the air element generated by the activity of the mind of the aforesaid kind, just as the movement of the hands and feet of a wooden puppet occurs due to the pulling of strings. Knowing this is to be understood here as 'comprehension as non-delusion.'

Saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇeti ettha saṅghāṭicīvarānaṃ nivāsanapārupanavasena pattassa bhikkhāpaṭiggahaṇādivasena paribhogo ‘dhāraṇaṃ’ nāma. Tattha saṅghāṭicīvaradhāraṇe tāva nivāsetvā pārupitvā ca piṇḍāya carato “āmisalābho sītassa paṭighātāyā”tiādinā nayena bhagavatā vuttappakāroyeva ca attho ‘attho’ nāma. Tassa vasena ‘sātthakasampajaññaṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

Regarding 'wearing the outer robe, bowl, and robes,' here 'wearing' refers to the use of the outer robe and other robes for dressing and covering, and of the bowl for receiving alms, and so on. In the case of wearing the robes, for one who goes for alms after having dressed, the purpose is just as stated by the Blessed One: 'The gain of requisites is for warding off the cold,' and so on. Based on this, 'comprehension of purpose' should be understood.

Uṇhapakatikassa [M 0.0344] pana dubbalassa ca cīvaraṃ sukhumaṃ sappāyaṃ, sītālukassa ghanaṃ dupaṭṭaṃ; viparītaṃ asappāyaṃ. Yassa kassaci jiṇṇaṃ asappāyameva. Aggaḷādidānena hissa taṃ palibodhakaraṃ hoti. Tathā paṭṭuṇṇadukūlādibhedaṃ corānaṃ lobhanīyacīvaraṃ. Tādisañhi araññe ekakassa nivāsantarāyakaraṃ jīvitantarāyakarañcāpi hoti. Nippariyāyena pana yaṃ nimittakammādimicchājīvavasena uppannaṃ, yañcassa sevamānassa akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti, taṃ asappāyaṃ[P 0.0360]; viparītaṃ sappāyaṃ. Tassa vasenettha ‘sappāyasampajaññaṃ’ kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva ca ‘gocarasampajaññaṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

For one who is of a hot constitution and weak, a fine robe is suitable, while for one who is susceptible to cold, a thick double-robe is appropriate. The opposite is unsuitable. For anyone, a worn-out robe is unsuitable. For by giving it in exchange for a door-bolt or the like, it becomes a hindrance to him. Similarly, robes of the kind of silk, wool, fine linen, etc., that are coveted by thieves are unsuitable. For one who is alone in the wilderness, such a robe can become an obstacle to one's dwelling and even endanger one's life. Unconditionally, any robe acquired through wrong livelihood, such as making signs, or which, when used, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline, is unsuitable; the opposite is suitable. Based on this, 'comprehension of suitability' should be understood here, and by way of not abandoning the meditation subject, 'comprehension of range' should be understood.

Abbhantare attā nāma koci cīvaraṃ pārupanto natthi. Vuttappakāracittakiriyāvāyodhātuvipphāreneva pana cīvarapārupanaṃ hoti. Tattha cīvarampi acetanaṃ, kāyopi acetano. Cīvaraṃ na jānāti – ‘mayā kāyo pārupito’ti, kāyopi na jānāti – ‘ahaṃ cīvarena pārupito’ti. Dhātuyova dhātusamūhaṃ paṭicchādenti, paṭapilotikāya potthakarūpapaṭicchādane viya. Tasmā neva sundaraṃ cīvaraṃ labhitvā somanassaṃ kātabbaṃ[V 0.0340], na asundaraṃ labhitvā domanassaṃ. Nāgavammikacetiyarukkhādīsu hi keci mālāgandhadhūpavatthādīhi sakkāraṃ karonti, keci gūthamuttakaddamadaṇḍasatthappahārādīhi asakkāraṃ. Na tehi nāgavammikarukkhādayo somanassaṃ vā domanassaṃ vā karonti. Evameva neva sundaraṃ cīvaraṃ labhitvā somanassaṃ kātabbaṃ, na asundaraṃ labhitvā domanassanti. Evaṃ pavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasenettha ‘asammohasampajaññaṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

Inside, there is no self whatsoever that puts on a robe. The act of putting on a robe occurs merely through the impulse of the air element generated by the activity of the mind, as described above. Here, the robe is insentient, and the body is also insentient. The robe does not know, 'The body is covered by me,' nor does the body know, 'I am covered by the robe.' Elements merely cover a group of elements, like a piece of cloth covering a manuscript. Therefore, one should not feel joy upon obtaining a beautiful robe nor sorrow upon obtaining an unattractive one. For some honor nāgas, anthills, shrines, and trees with flowers, perfumes, incense, cloths, and so on, while others dishonor them with excrement, urine, mud, sticks, blows with weapons, and so on—yet those nāgas, anthills, and trees feel neither joy nor sorrow. So too should one not feel joy upon obtaining a beautiful robe nor sorrow upon obtaining an unattractive one. In this way, by means of such ongoing reflection, 'comprehension as non-delusion' is to be understood here.

Pattadhāraṇepi pattaṃ sahasāva aggahetvā ‘imaṃ gahetvā piṇḍāya caramāno bhikkhaṃ labhissāmī’ti evaṃ pattaggahaṇapaccayā paṭilabhitabbaatthavasena ‘sātthakasampajaññaṃ’ veditabbaṃ. Kisadubbalasarīrassa pana garupatto asappāyo; yassa kassaci catupañcagaṇṭhikāhato dubbisodhanīyo asappāyova. Duddhotapatto hi na vaṭṭati; taṃ dhovantasseva cassa palibodho hoti. Maṇivaṇṇapatto pana lobhanīyova cīvare vuttanayeneva asappāyo. Nimittakammādivasena pana laddho, yañcassa sevamānassa akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti, ayaṃ ekantāsappāyova viparīto sappāyo. Tassa vasenettha ‘sappāyasampajaññaṃ’ kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva ‘gocarasampajaññaṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

In holding the bowl also, one should not grasp it hastily, but should reflect, 'By taking this and going for alms, I will obtain food.' Thus, by way of the purpose to be gained from the act of taking the bowl, 'comprehension of purpose' should be understood. But for one with a lean and weak body, a heavy bowl is unsuitable; for anyone, a bowl with four or five dents that is hard to clean is unsuitable. A poorly washed bowl is not proper, and it becomes a hindrance to the one washing it. A bowl the color of jewels, being alluring, is unsuitable—in the way previously stated for robes. A bowl obtained through wrong livelihood, such as making signs, or one which, when used, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline, is entirely unsuitable; the opposite is suitable. Based on that, 'comprehension of suitability' should be understood here, and by way of not abandoning the meditation subject, 'comprehension of range' should be understood.

Abbhantare [M 0.0345] attā nāma koci pattaṃ gaṇhanto natthi. Vuttappakāracittakiriyāvāyodhātuvipphāravaseneva pana pattaggahaṇaṃ nāma hoti. Tattha pattopi acetano, hatthāpi acetanā. Patto na jānāti – ‘ahaṃ hatthehi gahito’ti. Hatthāpi na jānanti – ‘patto amhehi [P 0.0361] gahito’ti. Dhātuyova dhātusamūhaṃ gaṇhanti, saṇḍāsena aggivaṇṇapattagahaṇe viyāti. Evaṃ pavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasenettha ‘asammohasampajaññaṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

Inside, there is no one called 'self' who takes the bowl. Rather, the taking of the bowl occurs merely by the power of the diffusion of the mind's activity and the wind element, as described. Here, the bowl is insentient, and the hands are insentient. The bowl does not know, 'I am taken by the hands.' The hands also do not know, 'The bowl is taken by us.' Elements merely grasp a collection of elements, like grasping a fiery-colored bowl with tongs. Thus, clear comprehension as non-delusion should be understood here through reflection on the ongoing process.

Apica yathā chinnahatthapāde vaṇamukhehi paggharitapubbalohitakimikule nīlamakkhikasamparikiṇṇe anāthasālāyaṃ anāthamanusse disvā dayālukā purisā tesaṃ vaṇabandhapaṭṭacoḷakāni ceva kapālādīhi ca bhesajjāni upanāmenti. Tattha coḷakānipi kesañci saṇhāni kesañci thūlāni pāpuṇanti. Bhesajjakapālakānipi kesañci susaṇṭhānāni kesañci dussaṇṭhānāni pāpuṇanti. Na te tattha sumanā vā honti dummanā vā. Vaṇapaṭicchādanamatteneva hi coḷakena, bhesajjapariggahaṇamatteneva ca kapālakena tesaṃ attho. Evameva yo bhikkhu vaṇacoḷakaṃ viya cīvaraṃ, bhesajjakapālakaṃ viya ca pattaṃ, kapāle bhesajjamiva [V 0.0341] ca patte laddhabhikkhaṃ sallakkheti – ayaṃ saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe asammohasampajaññena uttamasampajānakārīti veditabbo.

Moreover, just as when compassionate people, seeing helpless people in a shelter for the helpless—with severed hands and feet, from whose wound openings pus, blood, and swarms of worms oozed, and who were swarming with blue flies—bring them bandages, dressings, and cloths for their wounds, as well as medicines in bowls and such. There, some receive soft cloths, others coarse cloths. Some receive well-shaped medicine bowls, others poorly shaped ones. Yet they are neither pleased nor displeased. For their purpose is merely the covering of the wound with the cloth, and the receiving of medicine with the bowl. Just so, a monk who considers his robe like a wound-covering cloth, his bowl like a medicine bowl, and the almsfood received in the bowl like medicine in a bowl—this monk is to be understood as one who acts with the highest clear comprehension, by means of clear comprehension as non-delusion, in wearing the robes and carrying the bowl.

Asitādīsu asiteti piṇḍapātādibhojane. Pīteti yāguādipāne. Khāyiteti piṭṭhakhajjakādikhādane. Sāyiteti madhuphāṇitādisāyane. Tattha “neva davāyā”tiādinā nayena vutto aṭṭhavidhopi attho ‘attho’ nāma. Tassa vasena ‘sātthakasampajaññaṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

Regarding 'eaten,' etc.: 'eaten' (asita) refers to the eating of food such as alms-food. 'Drunk' (pīta) refers to the drinking of beverages such as gruel. 'Chewed' (khāyita) refers to the chewing of edibles such as flour-based cakes and snacks. 'Tasted' (sāyita) refers to the tasting of savories such as honey and molasses. Here, the eightfold purpose spoken of in the manner of the passage beginning 'not for sport,' and so on, is called 'purpose.' By means of this, 'clear comprehension of purpose' should be understood.

Lūkhapaṇītatittamadhurādīsu pana yena bhojanena yassa aphāsu hoti, taṃ tassa asappāyaṃ. Yaṃ pana nimittakammādivasena paṭiladdhaṃ, yañcassa bhuñjato akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti, taṃ ekantaṃ asappāyameva; viparītaṃ sappāyaṃ. Tassa vasenettha ‘sappāyasampajaññaṃ’ kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva ca ‘gocarasampajaññaṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

Regarding coarse, refined, bitter, sweet, and so on, whatever food causes discomfort to someone is unsuitable for them. Moreover, whatever is obtained by means of signs, acts, and so on, and whatever, when eaten, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline, is altogether unsuitable; the opposite is suitable. By means of this, 'clear comprehension of suitability' should be understood here, and by means of not abandoning the meditation subject, 'clear comprehension of the resort' should also be understood.

Abbhantare attā nāma koci bhuñjako natthi. Vuttappakāracittakiriyāvāyodhātuvipphāreneva pana pattapaṭiggahaṇaṃ nāma hoti. Cittakiriyāvāyodhātuvipphāreneva hatthassa patte otāraṇaṃ nāma hoti. Cittakiriyāvāyodhātuvipphāreneva ālopakaraṇaṃ, ālopauddharaṇaṃ, mukhavivaraṇañca [M 0.0346] hoti. Na koci kuñcikāya, na yantakena hanukaṭṭhiṃ vivarati. Cittakiriyāvāyodhātuvipphāreneva [P 0.0362] ālopassa mukhe ṭhapanaṃ, uparidantānaṃ musalakiccasādhanaṃ, heṭṭhādantānaṃ udukkhalakiccasādhanaṃ, jivhāya hatthakiccasādhanañca hoti. Iti naṃ tattha aggajivhāya tanukakheḷo mūlajivhāya bahalakheḷo makkheti. Taṃ heṭṭhādantaudukkhale jivhāhatthaparivattitaṃ kheḷaudakatemitaṃ uparidantamusalasañcuṇṇitaṃ koci kaṭacchunā vā dabbiyā vā anto pavesento nāma natthi; vāyodhātuyāva pavisati. Paviṭṭhaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ koci palālasanthāraṃ katvā dhārento nāma natthi; vāyodhātuvaseneva tiṭṭhati. Ṭhitaṃ ṭhitaṃ koci uddhanaṃ katvā aggiṃ jāletvā pacanto nāma natthi; tejodhātuyāva paccati. Pakkaṃ pakkaṃ koci daṇḍakena vā yaṭṭhiyā vā bahi nīhārako nāma natthi; vāyodhātuyeva nīharati. Iti vāyodhātu atiharati ca vītiharati ca dhāreti ca parivatteti ca sañcuṇṇeti ca visoseti ca nīharati ca. Pathavīdhātu dhāreti ca parivatteti ca sañcuṇṇeti ca visoseti ca nīharati ca. Āpodhātu sineheti ca allattañca anupāleti. Tejodhātu antopaviṭṭhaṃ paripāceti. Ākāsadhātu [V 0.0342] añjaso hoti. Viññāṇadhātu tattha tattha sammāpayogamanvāya ābhujatīti. Evaṃ pavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasenettha ‘asammohasampajaññaṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

Within, there is no self, no eater to be found. However, the receiving of the bowl occurs simply through the diffusion of the mind's activity and the wind element. It is simply through the diffusion of the mind's activity and the wind element that the hand is lowered into the bowl. It is simply through the diffusion of the mind's activity and the wind element that the morsel is made, the morsel is lifted, and the mouth is opened. No one opens the jawbone with a key or a mechanism. It is simply through the diffusion of the mind's activity and the wind element that the morsel is placed in the mouth, the upper teeth perform the function of a pestle, the lower teeth perform the function of a mortar, and the tongue performs the function of a hand. Thus, the thin saliva at the tip of the tongue and the thick saliva at the root moisten it there. That food, turned by the tongue-hand in the lower-teeth-mortar, moistened with saliva-water, and crushed by the upper-teeth-pestle—no one inserts it inside with a spoon or ladle; it enters by the wind element alone. Once inside, no one spreads it like a straw mat to hold it; it remains by the power of the wind element. As it stays, no one sets up a fireplace, lights a fire, and cooks it; it is cooked by the fire element alone. When cooked, no one takes it out with a stick or rod; the wind element itself removes it. Thus, the wind element carries forward, distributes, holds, turns, grinds, dries, and removes. The earth element holds, turns, grinds, dries, and removes. The water element moistens and maintains wetness. The fire element digests what has entered inside. The space element provides a path. The consciousness element inclines towards each appropriate application. In this way, through reflection on this process, clear comprehension as non-delusion should be understood here.

Apica gamanato, pariyesanato, paribhogato, āsayato, nidhānato, aparipakkato, paripakkato, phalato, nissandanato, sammakkhanatoti evaṃ dasavidhapaṭikūlabhāvapaccavekkhaṇatopettha ‘asammohasampajaññaṃ’ veditabbaṃ. Vitthārakathā panettha visuddhimagge āhārapaṭikūlasaññāniddesato gahetabbā.

Furthermore, clear comprehension as non-delusion should be understood here by reflecting on the ten aspects of repulsiveness: with respect to going, seeking, consuming, the receptacle, the repository, the undigested, the digested, the result, the discharge, and the smearing. A detailed explanation of this should be taken from the exposition on the perception of repulsiveness in food in the Visuddhimagga.

Uccārapassāvakammeti uccārassa ca passāvassa ca karaṇe. Tattha pakkakāle uccārapassāvaṃ akarontassa sakalasarīrato sedā muccanti, akkhīni bhamanti, cittaṃ na ekaggaṃ hoti, aññe ca rogā uppajjanti; karontassa pana sabbaṃ taṃ na hotīti ayamettha attho. Tassa vasena ‘sātthakasampajaññaṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

In 'the act of defecation and urination,' this means in the doing of defecation and urination. Here, for one who does not defecate or urinate at the proper time, sweat exudes from the entire body, the eyes become dizzy, the mind is not concentrated, and other diseases arise; but for one who does so, all that does not happen—this is the purpose here. Based on this, 'clear comprehension of purpose' should be understood.

Aṭṭhāne uccārapassāvaṃ karontassa pana āpatti hoti, ayaso vaḍḍhati, jīvitantarāyo hoti; patirūpe ṭhāne karontassa sabbaṃ taṃ [M 0.0347] na hotīti idamettha sappāyaṃ. Tassa vasena ‘sappāyasampajaññaṃ’ kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva [P 0.0363] ca ‘gocarasampajaññaṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

For one who defecates or urinates in an improper place, an offense is incurred, disrepute increases, and life is endangered; for one who does so in a proper place, all that does not happen—this is what is suitable here. By means of this, 'clear comprehension of suitability' should be understood, and by means of not abandoning the meditation subject, 'clear comprehension of the resort' should also be understood.

Abbhantare attā nāma koci uccārapassāvakammaṃ karonto natthi. Cittakiriyāvāyodhātuvipphāreneva pana uccārapassāvakammaṃ hoti. Yathā pana pakke gaṇḍe gaṇḍabhedena pubbalohitaṃ akāmatāya nikkhamati, yathā ca atibharitā udakabhājanā udakaṃ akāmatāya nikkhamati, evaṃ pakkāsayamuttavatthīsu sannicitā uccārapassāvā vāyuvegasamuppīḷitā akāmatāyapi nikkhamanti. So panāyaṃ evaṃ nikkhamanto uccārapassāvo neva tassa bhikkhuno attano hoti na parassa; kevalaṃ pana sarīranissandova hoti. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā udakatumbhato purāṇaudakaṃ chaḍḍentassa neva taṃ attano hoti na paresaṃ, kevalaṃ paṭijagganamattameva hoti, evanti. Evaṃ pavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasenettha ‘asammohasampajaññaṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

Within, there is no being called a self that performs the act of defecation and urination. Rather, the act of defecation and urination occurs simply through the diffusion of the mind-activity and the wind element. Just as pus and blood involuntarily ooze out from a ripe abscess when it bursts, or as water involuntarily spills from an overfilled water vessel, so too the accumulated excrement and urine, pressed by the force of wind in the stomach and bladder, exit even involuntarily. When this excrement and urine exit in this way, they belong neither to that monk himself nor to others; they are merely a bodily discharge. What is that like? It is just like when one throws away old water from a water gourd, it belongs neither to oneself nor to others; it is merely a matter of upkeep. Thus, through reflection on this process, 'non-deluded clear comprehension' should be understood here.

Gatādīsu [V 0.0343] gateti gamane. Ṭhiteti ṭhāne. Nisinneti nisajjāya. Sutteti sayane. Tattha abhikkantādīsu vuttanayeneva sampajānakāritā veditabbā.

Among going and so on: 'going' means movement; 'standing' means being in a standing posture; 'sitting' means sitting; 'lying down' means reclining. Here, the way of acting with clear comprehension should be understood in the same manner as stated regarding going forth and so on.

Ayaṃ panettha aparopi nayo – eko hi bhikkhu gacchanto aññaṃ cintento aññaṃ vitakkento gacchati. Eko kammaṭṭhānaṃ avissajjetvāva gacchati. Tathā eko bhikkhu tiṭṭhanto, nisīdanto, sayanto aññaṃ cintento aññaṃ vitakkento sayati. Eko kammaṭṭhānaṃ avissajjetvāva sayati.

Herein there is another method: One monk walks thinking one thing and pondering another. Another walks without relinquishing his meditation subject. Similarly, one monk stands, sits, or lies down thinking one thing and pondering another. Another lies down without relinquishing his meditation subject.

Ettakena pana na pākaṭaṃ hotīti caṅkamena dīpayiṃsu. Yo hi bhikkhu caṅkamanaṃ otaritvā caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ ṭhito pariggaṇhāti; ‘pācīnacaṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ pavattā rūpārūpadhammā pacchimacaṅkamanakoṭiṃ appatvā ettheva niruddhā, pacchimacaṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ pavattāpi pācīnacaṅkamanakoṭiṃ appatvā ettheva niruddhā, caṅkamanavemajjhe pavattā ubho koṭiyo appatvā ettheva niruddhā, caṅkamane pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ṭhānaṃ appatvā ettheva niruddhā, ṭhāne pavattā nisajjaṃ, nisajjāya pavattā sayanaṃ appatvā ettheva niruddhā’ti evaṃ pariggaṇhanto pariggaṇhantoyeva bhavaṅgaṃ otāreti; uṭṭhahanto [P 0.0364] kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvāva uṭṭhāti – ayaṃ bhikkhu gatādīsu sampajānakārī nāma hotīti.

However, since this alone was not clear, they explained it by means of walking meditation. For when a monk has entered upon walking meditation and, standing at the end of the walking path, discerns thus: ‘The material and immaterial phenomena that arise at the eastern end of the walking path cease right there without reaching the western end; those that arise at the western end also cease right there without reaching the eastern end; those that arise in the middle of the path cease right there without reaching either end; the material and immaterial phenomena that arise in walking cease right there without reaching standing; those that arise in standing cease right there without reaching sitting; those that arise in sitting cease right there without reaching lying down’—thus discerning, he lets the life-continuum lapse; when rising, he rises only after taking up the meditation subject—this monk is called one who acts with clear comprehension in going, etc.

Evaṃ [M 0.0348] pana sutte kammaṭṭhānaṃ avibhūtaṃ hoti. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ avibhūtaṃ na kātabbaṃ. Tasmā yo bhikkhu yāva sakkoti tāva caṅkamitvā ṭhatvā nisīditvā sayamāno evaṃ pariggahetvā sayati – ‘kāyo acetano, mañco acetano. Kāyo na jānāti – ahaṃ mañce sayitoti. Mañcopi na jānāti – mayi kāyo sayitoti. Acetano kāyo acetane mañce sayito’ti. Evaṃ pariggaṇhanto pariggaṇhantoyeva cittaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ otāreti, pabujjhamāno kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvāva pabujjhati. Ayaṃ sutte sampajānakārī nāma hotīti.

Yet, in sleep, the meditation subject is not distinct. The meditation subject should not be indistinct. Therefore, a monk, as much as he is able, having walked, stood, and sat, when lying down, discerns thus: ‘The body is non-conscious, the bed is non-conscious. The body does not know, “I lie on the bed.” The bed also does not know, “The body lies on me.” The non-conscious body lies on the non-conscious bed.’ Discerning thus, he lets his mind sink into the life-continuum. Awakening, he awakens only after taking up the meditation subject. This is called one who acts with clear comprehension in sleep.

Jāgariteti jāgaraṇe. Tattha ‘kiriyāmayapavattassa appavattiyā sati jāgaritaṃ nāma na hoti; kiriyāmayapavattavaḷañje pavattante jāgaritaṃ nāma hotī’ti pariggaṇhanto bhikkhu jāgarite sampajānakārī nāma hoti. Apica rattindivaṃ cha koṭṭhāse katvā pañca koṭṭhāse jaggantopi jāgarite sampajānakārī nāma hoti.

“Being awake” refers to wakefulness. Here, a monk who comprehends that “there is no wakefulness when the process of activity is inactive; wakefulness exists when the process of activity is active,” is called one who acts with clear comprehension in wakefulness. Furthermore, even if one divides the day and night into six parts and remains awake for five of them, one is still called one who acts with clear comprehension in wakefulness.

Bhāsiteti [V 0.0344] kathane. Tattha ‘upādārūpassa saddāyatanassa appavatte sati bhāsitaṃ nāma na hoti; tasmiṃ pavattante hotī’ti pariggāhako bhikkhu bhāsite sampajānakārī nāma hoti. Vimuttāyatanasīsena dhammaṃ desentopi bāttiṃsa tiracchānakathā pahāya dasakathāvatthunissitaṃ kathaṃ kathentopi bhāsite sampajānakārī nāma hoti.

“Speaking” refers to utterance. Here, a monk who comprehends that “when the sound sense-base, which is derived form, is inactive, there is no utterance; utterance exists when it is active,” is called one who acts with clear comprehension in speaking. Even when teaching the Dhamma focusing on liberation, abandoning the thirty-two kinds of worldly talk and speaking on topics based on the ten grounds for discussion, one is still called one who acts with clear comprehension in speaking.

Tuṇhībhāveti akathane. Tattha ‘upādārūpassa saddāyatanassa pavattiyaṃ sati tuṇhībhāvo nāma natthi; appavattiyaṃ hotī’ti pariggāhako bhikkhu tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī nāma hoti. Aṭṭhatiṃsāya ārammaṇesu cittaruciyaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā nisinnopi dutiyajjhānaṃ samāpannopi tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārīyeva nāma hoti.

“Being silent” refers to not speaking. Here, a monk who comprehends that “there is no silence when the sound sense-base, which is derived form, is active; silence exists when it is inactive,” is called one who acts with clear comprehension in silence. Even when seated, having taken up a meditation subject among the thirty-eight objects according to one’s mental preference, or even when attaining the second jhāna, one is still called one who acts with clear comprehension in silence.

Ettha ca eko iriyāpatho dvīsu ṭhānesu āgato. So heṭṭhā abhikkante paṭikkanteti ettha bhikkhācāragāmaṃ gacchato ca āgacchato ca addhānagamanavasena kathito. Gate ṭhite nisinneti ettha vihāre cuṇṇikapāduddhārairiyāpathavasena kathitoti veditabbo.

Here, one posture is mentioned in two places. Previously, in 'going forward and returning,' it was spoken of in the sense of a journey, with reference to a monk going to and returning from the alms-gathering village. In 'walking, standing, sitting,' it is to be understood as spoken of in the sense of minor postures within the monastery, such as lifting the feet.

524. Tattha katamā satītiādi sabbaṃ uttānatthameva.

524. Here, “What is mindfulness?” and so forth—all of this is straightforward in meaning.

526. So [P 0.0365][M 0.0349] vivittanti iminā kiṃ dasseti? Etassa bhikkhuno upāsanaṭṭhānaṃ yogapathaṃ sappāyasenāsanaṃ dasseti. Yassa hi abbhantare ettakā guṇā atthi, tassa anucchaviko araññavāso. Yassa panete natthi, tassa ananucchaviko. Evarūpassa hi araññavāso kāḷamakkaṭaacchataracchadīpimigādīnaṃ aṭavīvāsasadiso hoti. Kasmā? Icchāya ṭhatvā paviṭṭhattā. Tassa hi araññavāsamūlako koci attho natthi; araññavāsañceva āraññake ca dūseti; sāsane appasādaṃ uppādeti. Yassa pana abbhantare ettakā guṇā atthi, tasseva so anucchaviko. So hi araññavāsaṃ nissāya vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhitvā parinibbāti, sakalaaraññavāsaṃ upasobheti, āraññikānaṃ sīsaṃ dhovati, sakalasāsanaṃ pasāreti. Tasmā satthā evarūpassa bhikkhuno upāsanaṭṭhānaṃ yogapathaṃ sappāyasenāsanaṃ dassento so vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajatītiādimāha. Tattha vivittanti suññaṃ appasaddaṃ appanigghosaṃ. Etameva hi atthaṃ dassetuṃ tañca anākiṇṇantiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha anākiṇṇanti asaṅkiṇṇaṃ asambādhaṃ. Tattha yassa senāsanassa sāmantā gāvutampi aḍḍhayojanampi [V 0.0345] pabbatagahanaṃ vanagahanaṃ nadīgahanaṃ hoti, na koci avelāya upasaṅkamituṃ sakkoti – idaṃ santikepi anākiṇṇaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana aḍḍhayojanikaṃ vā yojanikaṃ vā hoti – idaṃ dūratāya eva anākiṇṇaṃ nāma hoti.

526. “He resorts to a secluded dwelling”—what does this indicate? It indicates the suitable place of resort, the path of practice, and the suitable lodging for this monk. For one who possesses such qualities internally, wilderness dwelling is appropriate. But for one who lacks these, it is inappropriate. For such a person, wilderness dwelling is like that of black monkeys, bears, hyenas, leopards, and deer living in the jungle. Why? Because they have entered it based on desire. For such a person, there is no benefit based on wilderness dwelling; they defile both the wilderness dwelling and the wilderness-dwellers, and they give rise to a lack of faith in the Dispensation. But for one who possesses such qualities internally, it is appropriate. Relying on wilderness dwelling, such a one establishes insight, attains arahantship, and attains final Nibbāna, thus beautifying the entire wilderness dwelling, clearing the name of wilderness-dwellers, and propagating the entire Dispensation. Therefore, the Teacher, showing the suitable place of resort, the path of practice, and the suitable lodging for such a monk, said, “He resorts to a secluded dwelling,” and so forth. Here, “secluded” means empty, with little sound, and with little noise. To convey this very meaning, it is also said, “unfrequented,” and so on. Here, “unfrequented” means uncrowded and unconfined. In this regard, if a dwelling’s surroundings—for a gāvuta or half a yojana—are a thicket of mountains, a thicket of forest, or a thicket of rivers, so that no one can approach at an improper time, this is called “unfrequented” even when it is near. But if it is half a yojana or a yojana away, this is called “unfrequented” due to distance.

527. Seti ceva āsati ca etthāti senāsanaṃ. Tassa pabhedaṃ dassetuṃ mañco pīṭhantiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha mañcoti cattāro mañcā – masārako, bundikābaddho, kuḷīrapādako, āhaccapādakoti. Tathā pīṭhaṃ. Bhisīti pañca bhisiyo – uṇṇābhisi, coḷabhisi, vākabhisi, tiṇabhisi, paṇṇabhisīti. Bimbohananti sīsupadhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ vitthārato vidatthicaturaṅgulaṃ vaṭṭati, dīghato mañcavitthārappamāṇaṃ. Vihāroti samantā parihārapathaṃ antoyeva rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānāni dassetvā katasenāsanaṃ. Aḍḍhayogoti [P 0.0366] supaṇṇavaṅkagehaṃ. Pāsādoti dve kaṇṇikāni gahetvā kato dīghapāsādo. Aṭṭoti paṭirājādipaṭibāhanatthaṃ iṭṭhakāhi kato bahalabhittiko catupañcabhūmiko patissayaviseso. Māḷoti bhojanasālasadiso maṇḍalamāḷo; vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana ekakūṭasaṅgahito [M 0.0350] caturassapāsādoti vuttaṃ. Leṇanti pabbataṃ khaṇitvā vā pabbhārassa appahonakaṭṭhāne kuṭṭaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā vā katasenāsanaṃ. Guhāti bhūmidari vā yattha rattindivaṃ dīpaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, pabbataguhā vā bhūmiguhā vā. Rukkhamūlanti rukkhassa heṭṭhā parikkhittaṃ vā aparikkhittaṃ vā. Veḷugumboti veḷugaccho. Yattha vā pana bhikkhū paṭikkamantīti ṭhapetvā vā etāni mañcādīni yattha bhikkhū sannipatanti, yaṃ tesaṃ sannipātārahaṭṭhānaṃ, sabbametaṃ senāsanaṃ.

527. A `senāsana` is so called because one lies down (`seti`) and sits (`āsati`) there. To show its different kinds, “bed, chair,” and so forth are mentioned. Herein, “bed” refers to four kinds of beds: masāraka, bundikābaddha, kuḷīrapādaka, and āhaccapādaka. Likewise for “chair.” “Mattress” refers to five kinds of mattresses: a wool mattress, a cloth mattress, a bark-fibre mattress, a grass mattress, and a leaf mattress. “Head cushion” (bimbohana) is said to be a pillow for the head. In width, it may be a span and four fingers; in length, it should be the measure of the bed's width. “Monastery” is a dwelling made with designated places for the night and for the day within it, and with a surrounding path. “Aḍḍhayoga” is a house with a curved roof like a garuḍa’s wing. “Mansion” is a long mansion built with two pinnacles. “Tower” is a special kind of residence, with thick walls made of bricks, having four or five stories, for defense against hostile kings and others. “Hall” is a circular hall similar to a dining hall; but in the Vinaya commentary, it is described as a square mansion with a single peak. “Shelter” is a dwelling made by excavating a mountain or by erecting a wall in a place where a mountain overhang is insufficient. “Cave” is a fissure in the earth where it is suitable to have a lamp day and night, or a mountain cave, or an underground cave. “Root of a tree” is the area beneath a tree, whether enclosed or not. “Bamboo grove” is a clump of bamboo. Or, setting aside these beds and so forth, any place where monks go into retreat, where they assemble, any place suitable for their assembly—all this is a dwelling.

528. Bhajatīti upeti. Sambhajatīti tattha abhirativasena anukkaṇṭhito suṭṭhu upeti. Sevatīti nivāsanavasena sevati nisevatīti anukkaṇṭhamāno sannisito hutvā sevati. Saṃsevatīti senāsanavattaṃ sampādento sammā sevati.

528. “Resorts to” means to approach. “Frequents” means to approach well, delighting in it and without discontent. “Serves” means to serve by way of dwelling there. “Closely serves” means to serve without discontent, having become settled. “Properly serves” means to serve rightly, fulfilling the duties of the dwelling.

529. Idāni yaṃ taṃ vivittanti vuttaṃ, tassa pabhedaṃ dassetuṃ araññaṃ rukkhamūlantiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha araññanti vinayapariyāyena tāva “ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañca avasesaṃ arañña”nti (pārā. 12) āgataṃ. Suttantapariyāyena āraññikaṃ bhikkhuṃ sandhāya “āraññakaṃ nāma senāsanaṃ pañcadhanusatikapacchima”nti (pāci. 573) āgataṃ. Vinayasuttantā pana ubhopi pariyāyadesanā nāma. Abhidhammo nippariyāyadesanāti abhidhammapariyāyena [V 0.0346] araññaṃ dassetuṃ nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlāti vuttaṃ; indakhīlato bahi nikkhamitvāti attho.

529. Now, to show the different kinds of what was called 'secluded,' the passage beginning 'forest, root of a tree...' is introduced. Here, “forest,” according to the Vinaya, is stated as: “Setting aside the village and the village environs, the remainder is forest.” According to the Suttanta, with reference to a forest-dwelling monk, it is stated: “A forest dwelling is a lodging at least five hundred bow-lengths away.” Both the Vinaya and the Suttanta, however, are teachings of conventional meaning. The Abhidhamma is the teaching of ultimate meaning; thus, to explain “forest” according to the Abhidhamma, it is said, “having gone outside the city’s gate-pillar”; the meaning is, having gone outside of the gate-pillar.

530. Rukkhamūlādīnaṃ pakatiyā ca suviññeyyabhāvato rukkhamūlaṃyeva rukkhamūlantiādi vuttaṃ. Apicettha rukkhamūlanti yaṃkiñci sītacchāyaṃ vivittaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ. Pabbatanti selaṃ. Tattha hi udakasoṇḍīsu udakakiccaṃ katvā [P 0.0367] sītāya rukkhacchāyāya nisinnassa nānādisāsu khāyamānāsu sītena vātena bījiyamānassa cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti. Kandaranti kaṃ vuccati udakaṃ, tena daritaṃ udakena bhinnaṃ pabbatappadesaṃ; yaṃ nitumbantipi nadīkuñjantipi vadanti. Tattha hi rajatapaṭṭasadisā vālikā honti, matthake maṇivitānaṃ viya vanagahanaṃ, maṇikkhandhasadisaṃ udakaṃ sandati. Evarūpaṃ kandaraṃ oruyha pānīyaṃ pivitvā gattāni sītaṃ katvā vālikaṃ ussāpetvā paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ paññapetvā [M 0.0351] nisinnassa samaṇadhammaṃ karoto cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti. Giriguhanti dvinnaṃ pabbatānaṃ antaraṃ, ekasmiṃyeva vā umaṅgasadisaṃ mahāvivaraṃ. Susānalakkhaṇaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.34) vuttaṃ.

530. Because “root of a tree” and so forth are naturally easy to understand, it is said, “a root of a tree is simply a root of a tree,” and so on. Moreover, herein, “root of a tree” is any cool, shaded, and secluded root of a tree. “Mountain” is a rock. There, having performed one’s duties with water at a water cistern, for one sitting in the cool shade of a tree, with the various directions appearing clearly, being fanned by a cool wind, the mind becomes concentrated. “Ravine” (kandara): `kaṃ` means water; `darita` means split by that—a mountainous region split by water, which is also called a river-glen or river-bend. There, the sand is like a silver sheet, the forest thicket overhead is like a jeweled canopy, and the water flows like a mass of gems. For one who descends into such a ravine, drinks the water, cools their limbs, smooths out the sand, lays out their rag-robe, and sits practicing the ascetic’s duties, the mind becomes concentrated. “Mountain cleft” is the space between two mountains, or a large tunnel-like opening in a single mountain. The characteristics of a charnel ground are stated in the Visuddhimagga.

531. Vanapatthanti gāmantaṃ atikkamitvā manussānaṃ anupacāraṭṭhānaṃ, yattha na kasanti na vapanti. Tenevassa niddese “vanapatthanti dūrānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ adhivacana”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Yasmā vā rukkhamūlādīsu idamevekaṃ bhājetvā dassitaṃ, tasmāssa nikkhepapaṭipāṭiyā niddesaṃ akatvā sabbapariyante niddeso katoti veditabbo. Abbhokāsanti acchannaṃ. Ākaṅkhamāno panettha cīvarakuṭiṃ katvā vasati. Palālapuñjanti palālarāsi. Mahāpalālapuñjato hi palālaṃ nikkaḍḍhitvā pabbhāraleṇasadise ālaye karonti, gacchagumbādīnampi upari palālaṃ pakkhipitvā heṭṭhā nisinnā samaṇadhammaṃ karonti; taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Vanapatthaniddese salomahaṃsānanti yattha paviṭṭhassa lomahaṃso uppajjati; evarūpānaṃ bhīsanakasenāsanānaṃ. Pariyantānanti dūrabhāvena pariyante ṭhitānaṃ. Na manussūpacārānanti kasanavapanavasena manussehi upacaritabbaṃ vanantaṃ atikkamitvā ṭhitānaṃ. Durabhisambhavānanti aladdhavivekassādehi abhibhuyya vasituṃ nasakkuṇeyyānaṃ.

531. "Vanapattha" (a forest wilderness) refers to a place beyond village boundaries, having passed beyond an area not frequented by humans, where they do not plough or sow. Hence, in its explanation, it is said: "'Vanapattha' is a designation for remote dwellings," and so forth. And since this alone is singled out for explanation among places like the root of a tree, etc., its explanation should be understood as having been given at the very end, without following the usual order of enumeration. "Abbhokāsa" (the open air) means uncovered. Here, if one wishes, one may make a robe-hut and dwell there. "Palālapuñja" (a heap of straw) refers to a pile of straw. For from a large heap of straw, they pull out straw to make shelters resembling overhanging caves; or they place straw over shrubs and thickets, and sit beneath to practice the ascetic's duties—this is what is meant. In the explanation of a forest wilderness, "salomahaṃsāni" refers to terrifying dwellings where, upon entering, one's hair stands on end. "Pariyantāni" refers to those situated at the periphery, being remote. "Na manussūpacārāni" means places that have passed beyond the forest area frequented by humans for ploughing and sowing. "Durabhisambhavāni" means places that are difficult to master and dwell in for those who have not attained the taste of seclusion.

532. Appasaddādiniddese appasaddanti vacanasaddena appasaddaṃ.

532. In the explanation of 'appasadda' and so forth, 'appasadda' means having little sound with respect to the sound of speech.

533. Appanigghosanti [V 0.0347] nagaranigghosasaddena appanigghosaṃ. Yasmā [P 0.0368] pana ubhayampetaṃ saddaṭṭhena ekaṃ, tasmāssa niddese “yadeva taṃ appasaddaṃ tadeva taṃ appanigghosa”nti vuttaṃ. Vijanavātanti anusañcaraṇajanassa sarīravātena virahitaṃ. Vijanavādantipi pāṭho; antojanavādena virahitanti attho. Yasmā pana yaṃ appanigghosaṃ, tadeva janasañcaraṇena ca janavādena ca virahitaṃ hoti, tasmāssa niddese “yadeva taṃ appanigghosaṃ tadeva taṃ vijanavāta”nti vuttaṃ. Manussarāhaseyyakanti manussānaṃ rahassakiriyaṭṭhāniyaṃ. Yasmā pana taṃ janasañcaraṇarahitaṃ hoti, tenassa niddese “yadeva taṃ vijanavātaṃ tadeva taṃ manussarāhaseyyaka”nti vuttaṃ. Paṭisallānasāruppanti vivekānurūpaṃ. Yasmā pana taṃ niyameneva [M 0.0352] manussarāhaseyyakaṃ hoti, tasmāssa niddese “yadeva taṃ manussarāhaseyyakaṃ tadeva taṃ paṭisallānasāruppa”nti vuttaṃ.

533. "Appanigghosa" means having little noise with respect to the sounds of a city. However, since both of these are one in the sense of sound, therefore in its explanation it is said, "Whatever is of little sound, that is also 'appanigghosa'." "Vijanavāta" means devoid of the bodily wind of people who wander about. There is also the reading "vijanavāda," meaning devoid of the chatter of people within. However, since whatever is 'appanigghosa' is also devoid of the movement of people and the chatter of people, therefore in its explanation it is said, "Whatever is 'appanigghosa' is also 'vijanavāta'." "Manussarāhaseyyaka" refers to a place suitable for the secret activities of humans. However, since that is devoid of human movement, therefore in its explanation it is said, "Whatever is 'vijanavāta' is also 'manussarāhaseyyaka'." "Paṭisallānasāruppa" means suitable for seclusion. However, since that is by definition a secluded resting place for humans, therefore in its explanation it is said, "Whatever is 'manussarāhaseyyaka' is also 'paṭisallānasāruppa'."

534. Araññagatādiniddese araññaṃ vuttameva. Tathā rukkhamūlaṃ. Avasesaṃ pana sabbampi senāsanaṃ suññāgārena saṅgahitaṃ.

534. In the explanation of "gone to the wilderness" and so forth, "arañña" has already been explained. Likewise, "rukkhamūla" (the root of a tree). All the remaining dwelling places, however, are included under "suññāgāra" (an empty place).

535. Pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvāti samantato ūrubaddhāsanaṃ bandhitvā. Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyāti uparimaṃ sarīraṃ ujuṃ ṭhapetvā aṭṭhārasa piṭṭhikaṇṭake koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭipādetvā. Evañhi nisinnassa cammamaṃsanhārūni na paṇamanti. Athassa yā tesaṃ paṇamanapaccayā khaṇe khaṇe vedanā uppajjeyyuṃ, tā nuppajjanti. Tāsu na uppajjamānāsu cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ na paripatati, vuḍḍhiṃ phātiṃ upagacchati.

535. "Pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā" means having bound the cross-legged posture, with the thighs locked all around. "Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya" means having kept the upper body straight, setting the eighteen vertebrae tip to tip. For one sitting thus, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend. Then those feelings that would arise moment by moment on account of their bending do not arise. When they do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject does not fall away, and it grows and expands.

536. Ujuko hoti kāyo ṭhito paṇihitoti idampi hi imamevatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

536. "The body is erect, established, and set upright"—this too is said with reference to this very meaning.

537. Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti kammaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ satiṃ ṭhapayitvā, mukhasamīpe vā katvāti attho. Teneva vuttaṃ “ayaṃ sati upaṭṭhitā hoti sūpaṭṭhitā nāsikagge vā mukhanimitte vā”ti. Mukhanimittanti cettha uttaroṭṭhassa vemajjhappadeso daṭṭhabbo, yattha nāsikavāto paṭihaññati; atha vā [P 0.0369] parīti pariggahaṭṭho, mukhanti niyyānaṭṭho, satīti upaṭṭhānaṭṭho; tena vuccati “parimukhaṃ sati”nti evaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.164) vuttanayenapettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepo “pariggahitaniyyānaṃ satiṃ katvā”ti.

537. "Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā" means having established mindfulness facing the meditation subject, or having placed it near the mouth—this is the meaning. Hence, it is said: "This mindfulness is present, well-established, either at the tip of the nose or at the sign of the mouth." Here, 'the sign of the mouth' should be understood as the middle part of the upper lip where the breath from the nose strikes. Alternatively, 'pari' is in the sense of grasping, 'mukha' is in the sense of emergence, and 'sati' is in the sense of establishing; therefore it is said 'parimukhaṃ sati.' In this way, the meaning here should be understood according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. In brief, this means 'having made mindfulness grasp the point of emergence.'

538. Abhijjhāniddeso [V 0.0348] uttānatthoyeva. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepavaṇṇanā – abhijjhaṃ loke pahāyāti lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena pañcupādānakkhandhā loko. Tasmā pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu rāgaṃ pahāya kāmacchandaṃ vikkhambhetvāti ayamettha attho.

538. The explanation of "abhijjhā" is of straightforward meaning. Here is a brief clarification: "Abhijjhāṃ loke pahāya" (having abandoned covetousness in the world) means that the five aggregates subject to clinging are 'the world' in the sense of breaking up and dissolving. Thus, the meaning here is: having abandoned lust for the five aggregates of clinging and suppressed sensual desire.

539. Vigatābhijjhenāti vikkhambhanavasena pahīnattā vigatābhijjhena, na cakkhuviññāṇasadisenāti attho.

539. "Vigatābhijjhena" means with covetousness departed, because it has been abandoned by way of suppression, not in the manner of eye-consciousness—this is the meaning.

541. Abhijjhāya [M 0.0353] cittaṃ parisodhetīti abhijjhāto cittaṃ parisodheti; yathā naṃ sā muñcati ceva, muñcitvā ca na puna gaṇhāti, evaṃ karotīti attho. Niddesapadesu panassa āsevanto sodheti, bhāvento visodheti, bahulīkaronto parisodhetīti evamattho veditabbo. Mocetītiādīsupi eseva nayo.

541. "Abhijjhāya cittaṃ parisodheti" means one purifies the mind from covetousness; that is, one acts in such a way that covetousness releases the mind and, having released it, does not grasp it again—this is the meaning. However, in the sections of the explanation, the meaning should be understood thus: by practicing, one purifies; by developing, one thoroughly purifies; by making it abundant, one completely purifies. The same method applies to terms like 'moceti' (releases) and so forth.

542-543. Byāpādadosaṃ pahāyātiādīnampi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Byāpajjati iminā cittaṃ pūtikummāsādayo viya pakatiṃ jahatīti byāpādo. Vikārappattiyā padussati, paraṃ vā padūseti vināsetīti padoso. Ubhayametaṃ kodhassevādhivacanaṃ. Teneva vuttaṃ “yo byāpādo so padoso; yo padoso so byāpādo”ti. Yasmā cesa sabbasaṅgāhikavasena niddiṭṭho, tasmā “sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī”ti avatvā “abyāpannacitto”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ.

542-543. The meaning of 'having abandoned ill-will and malice' and so forth should also be understood in this same way. 'Byāpāda' (ill-will) is so called because by it the mind is afflicted and, like rotten gruel and so forth, abandons its natural state. 'Padosa' (malice) is so called because, having reached a state of distortion, it becomes corrupted, or it corrupts and destroys another. Both of these are designations for anger. Therefore it was said, "What is ill-will is malice; what is malice is ill-will." And since this was indicated in an all-encompassing way, instead of saying, 'compassionate for the welfare of all living beings,' only 'with a mind free from ill-will' was said.

546. Thinaṃ cittagelaññaṃ, middhaṃ cetasikagelaññaṃ; thinañca middhañca thinamiddhaṃ. Santā hontīti ime dvepi dhammā nirodhasantatāya santā hontīti. Idaṃ sandhāyettha vacanabhedo kato.

546. Sloth is a sickness of the mind; torpor is a sickness of the mental concomitants. Sloth and torpor together are sloth-and-torpor. "They are calmed" means these two states are calmed by the cessation of their continuity. Here, the variation in wording is made with this in mind.

549. Ālokasaññīti rattimpi divāpi diṭṭhālokasañjānanasamatthāya vigatanīvaraṇāya parisuddhāya saññāya samannāgato.

549. "Perceiving light" means being endowed with a perception that is capable of discerning light both by night and by day, free from the hindrances, and purified.

550. Sato sampajānoti satiyā ca ñāṇena ca samannāgato. Idaṃ ubhayaṃ ālokasaññāya upakārakattā vuttaṃ.

550. "Mindful and clearly comprehending" means endowed with mindfulness and knowledge. This pair is stated because they are helpful to the perception of light.

553. Vigatathinamiddhatāya [P 0.0370] pana ālokasaññāya niddesapadesu cattattātiādīni aññamaññavevacanāneva[V 0.0349]. Tattha cattattāti cattakāraṇā. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Cattattāti idaṃ panettha sakabhāvapariccajanavasena vuttaṃ. Vantattāti idaṃ puna anādiyanabhāvadassanavasena. Muttattāti idaṃ santatito vinimocanavasena. Pahīnattāti idaṃ muttassāpi katthaci ṭhānābhāvavasena. Paṭinissaṭṭhattāti idaṃ pubbe ādinnapubbassa nissaggadassanavasena. Paṭimuñcato vā nissaṭṭhattā bhāvanābalena abhibhuyya [M 0.0354] nissaṭṭhattāti attho. Pahīnapaṭinissaṭṭhattāti yathāvikkhambhanavaseneva pahānaṃ hoti, punappunaṃ santatiṃ na ajjhāruhati, tathā paṭinissaṭṭhattāti. Ālokā hotīti sappabhā hoti. Nirāvaraṇaṭṭhena vivaṭā. Nirupakkilesaṭṭhena parisuddhā. Pabhassaraṭṭhena pariyodātā.

553. However, in the descriptive passages concerning the absence of sloth-and-torpor and the perception of light, terms like "cattattā" and so on are simply synonyms for each other. Here, "cattattā" means the act of casting off. The same method applies to the remaining terms. "Cattattā" here is stated in the sense of abandoning one's own nature. "Vantattā" (vomited out) is stated in the sense of showing the state of not taking up again. "Muttattā" (freed) is stated in the sense of complete release from continuity. "Pahīnattā" (abandoned) is stated in the sense of the absence of a place to stand, even for what is freed. "Paṭinissaṭṭhattā" (relinquished) is stated in the sense of showing the discarding of what was previously taken up. Or, it means it is relinquished by one who lets go, having been overcome by the power of development. "Pahīnapaṭinissaṭṭhattā" (abandoned and relinquished) means that abandonment occurs by way of suppression, and it does not repeatedly rise into continuity; thus, it is relinquished. "There is light" means it is luminous. It is open in the sense of being unobstructed, pure in the sense of being free from defilements, and radiant in the sense of being very pure.

556. Uddhaccakukkuccanti ettha uddhatākāro uddhaccaṃ, ārammaṇe anicchayatāya vatthujjhācāro kukkuccaṃ. Idhāpi “santā hontī”ti purimanayeneva vacanabhedo veditabbo.

556. "Restlessness and remorse": here, "restlessness" is the state of agitation, and "remorse" is worrying about a matter due to uncertainty regarding the object. Here too, the variation in wording, "they are calmed," should be understood according to the previous method.

558. Tiṇṇavicikicchoti vicikicchaṃ taritvā atikkamitvā ṭhito. Niddesepissa tiṇṇoti idaṃ vicikicchāya animuggabhāvadassanavasena vuttaṃ. Uttiṇṇoti idaṃ tassā atikkamadassanavasena. Nittiṇṇoti idaṃ bhāvanābalena abhibhuyya upaddave tiṇṇabhāvadassanavasena. Pāraṅgatoti nibbicikicchābhāvasaṅkhātaṃ vicikicchāpāraṃ gato. Pāramanuppattoti tadeva pāraṃ bhāvanānuyogena pattoti. Evamassa paṭipattiyā saphalataṃ dasseti.

558. "Having crossed beyond doubt" means one who stands firm, having overcome and transcended doubt. In the explanation, "tiṇṇo" (crossed) is stated in the sense of showing the state of not being submerged by doubt. "Uttiṇṇo" (fully crossed) is stated in the sense of showing its transcendence. "Nittiṇṇo" (completely crossed over) is stated in the sense of showing the state of having crossed over troubles by overcoming them through the power of development. "Pāraṅgato" (gone to the far shore) means having gone to the far shore of doubt, which is the state of being free from doubt. "Pāramanuppatto" (attained the far shore) means having attained that very far shore through application to development. Thus, the fruitfulness of his practice is shown.

559. Akathaṃkathīti ‘kathamidaṃ kathamida’nti evaṃ pavattāya kathaṃkathāya virahito. Kusalesu dhammesūti anavajjadhammesu. Na kaṅkhatīti ‘ime nu kho kusalā’ti kaṅkhaṃ na uppādeti. Na vicikicchatīti te dhamme sabhāvato vinicchetuṃ na kicchati, na kilamati. Akathaṃkathī hotīti ‘kathaṃ nu kho ime kusalā’ti [P 0.0371] kathaṃkathāya rahito hoti. Nikkathaṃkathī vigatakathaṃkathoti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Vacanattho panettha kathaṃkathāto nikkhantoti nikkathaṃkatho. Vigatā kathaṃkathā assāti vigatakathaṃkatho.

559. "Free from uncertainty" means devoid of the uncertainty that proceeds as, 'How is this? How is that?' "In wholesome qualities" means in blameless states. "He does not doubt" means he does not generate doubt, thinking, 'Are these indeed wholesome?' "He is not perplexed" means he does not struggle or become weary in determining those states according to their intrinsic nature. "He is free from uncertainty" means he is devoid of the uncertainty, 'How indeed are these wholesome?' "Without uncertainty, one who has overcome uncertainty" are synonyms for that. Here the meaning of the word is: 'one who has gone out from uncertainty' is 'without uncertainty'; 'one from whom uncertainty has departed' is 'one who has overcome uncertainty.'

562. Upakkileseti upakkilesabhūte. Te hi cittaṃ upagantvā kilissanti. Tasmā upakkilesāti vuccanti.

562. "Defilements" means states that are defiling. For they approach the mind and defile it. Therefore they are called "defilements."

563. Paññāya [V 0.0350] dubbalīkaraṇeti yasmā ime nīvaraṇā uppajjamānā anuppannāya lokiyalokuttarāya paññāya uppajjituṃ na denti, uppannā api aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañca vā abhiññāyo upacchinditvā pātenti, tasmā ‘paññāya dubbalīkaraṇā’ti vuccanti. ‘Anuppannā ceva paññā na uppajjati, uppannā [M 0.0355] ca paññā nirujjhatī’ti idampi hi imamevatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sesamettha sabbaṃ heṭṭhā tattha tattha pakāsitattā uttānatthameva.

563. "Weakening of wisdom": because these hindrances, when arising, do not allow unarisen mundane and supramundane wisdom to arise, and they cut off and bring down the eight attainments or the five direct knowledges even after they have arisen; therefore they are called "weakening of wisdom." The statement, "Unarisen wisdom does not arise, and arisen wisdom ceases," was also said with reference to this very meaning. The rest here is all of plain meaning, since it has been explained in various places below.

564. Vivicceva kāmehītiādīsupi niddesesu yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ heṭṭhā cittuppādakaṇḍe (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 160) rūpāvacaraniddese idheva ca tattha tattha vuttameva. Kevalañhi dutiyatatiyacatutthajjhānaniddesesupi yathā tāni jhānāni heṭṭhā ‘tivaṅgikaṃ jhānaṃ hoti, duvaṅgikaṃ jhānaṃ hotī’ti vuttāni, evaṃ avatvā “ajjhattaṃ sampasādana”ntiādivacanato pariyāyena sampasādādīhi saddhiṃ tāni aṅgāni gahetvā “jhānanti sampasādo pītisukhaṃ cittassekaggatā”tiādinā nayena taṃ taṃ jhānaṃ niddiṭṭhanti ayamettha viseso.

564. In the expositions of "quite secluded from sensual pleasures," etc., whatever needed to be said has already been stated below in the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness (Dhs-A 160) in the exposition of the form sphere, and here and there in this text. However, in the expositions of the second, third, and fourth jhānas, instead of stating that those jhānas are a "three-factored jhāna," a "two-factored jhāna," etc., as was said below, here, based on the statement "internal confidence," etc., those factors are taken together with confidence and so on by an alternative method, and the respective jhānas are explained by the method beginning, "Jhāna is confidence, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind." This is the distinction here.

588. Yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhantītipadaniddese pana kiñcāpi ‘ācikkhanti desentī’tiādīni sabbāneva aññamaññavevacanāni, evaṃ santepi ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’tiādiuddesavasena ācikkhanti, niddesavasena desenti, paṭiniddesavasena paññāpenti, tena tena pakārena atthaṃ ṭhapetvā paṭṭhapenti, tassa tassatthassa kāraṇaṃ dassentā vivaranti, byañjanavibhāgaṃ dassentā vibhajanti, nikkujjitabhāvaṃ gambhīrabhāvañca nīharitvā vā sotūnaṃ ñāṇassa patiṭṭhaṃ janayantā uttāniṃ karonti, sabbehipi imehi ākārehi sotūnaṃ aññāṇandhakāraṃ vidhamentā pakāsentīti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

588. In the explanation of the phrase "what the noble ones declare," although all the terms such as "declare," "teach," etc., are synonyms for one another, still, they "declare" by way of summaries such as "equanimous, mindful, dwelling happily"; they "teach" by way of expositions; they "make known" by way of detailed explanations; they "set forth" by establishing the meaning in various ways; they "reveal" by showing the reasons for each point; they "analyze" by showing the division of the expression; and they "make plain" by removing the state of being overturned and profundity, thereby generating a foundation for the listeners' knowledge. Thus, they "illuminate" by dispelling the darkness of ignorance in the listeners through all these modes. This is how the meaning should be understood.

Samatikkamaniddesepi tattha tattha tehi tehi dhammehi vuṭṭhitattā atikkamanto, uparibhūmippattiyā [P 0.0372] vītikkanto, tato aparihānibhāvena samatikkantoti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

In the exposition of transcendence, it should be understood that one transcends by emerging from those respective states, surpasses by attaining a higher plane, and fully transcends by way of non-decline from that.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Suttanta Division.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Division.

623. Abhidhammabhājanīye [V 0.0351] heṭṭhā cittuppādakaṇḍe āgatanayeneva tanti ṭhapitā. Tasmā tattha sabbesampi kusalavipākakiriyavasena niddiṭṭhānaṃ jhānānaṃ [M 0.0356] tattha vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Suddhikanavakādibhedopi sabbo tattha vuttasadisoyevāti.

623. In the Abhidhamma Division, the textual thread is established by the same method that was given below in the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness. Therefore, the meaning of all the jhānas explained there by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional should be understood according to the method stated there. The division into the plain ninefold set and so on is all just the same as what was stated there.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Division.

3. Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Interrogation Section.

638. Pañhāpucchake pāḷianusāreneva jhānānaṃ kusalādibhāvo veditabbo. Ārammaṇattikesu pana tiṇṇaṃ jhānānaṃ nimittārammaṇattā parittārammaṇādibhāvena navattabbatā veditabbā. Lokuttarā panettha maggakāle phalakāle vā siyā appamāṇārammaṇā. Catutthaṃ jhānaṃ siyā parittārammaṇanti ettha kusalato terasa catutthajjhānāni sabbatthapādakacatutthaṃ, iddhividhacatutthaṃ, dibbasotañāṇacatutthaṃ, cetopariyañāṇacatutthaṃ, pubbenivāsañāṇacatutthaṃ, dibbacakkhuñāṇacatutthaṃ, yathākammūpagañāṇacatutthaṃ, anāgataṃsañāṇacatutthaṃ, ākāsānañcāyatanādicatutthaṃ, lokuttaracatutthanti.

638. In the Interrogation Section, the nature of the jhānas as wholesome and so on should be understood in accordance with the Pāḷi text itself. But in the triads concerning the object, the unstatability of the three jhānas should be understood in terms of having a limited object, etc., because they have a sign as their object. Here, the supramundane jhānas may have an immeasurable object at the time of the path or at the time of fruition. As to 'The fourth jhāna may have a limited object,' here, from the wholesome side, there are thirteen fourth jhānas: the fourth jhāna that is the basis for all, the fourth jhāna of the kinds of supernormal power, the fourth jhāna of the divine ear knowledge, the fourth jhāna of the knowledge of others' minds, the fourth jhāna of the knowledge of recollection of past lives, the fourth jhāna of the divine eye knowledge, the fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma, the fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the future, the fourth jhāna of the base of the infinity of space and so on, and the supramundane fourth jhāna.

Tattha sabbatthapādakacatutthaṃ navattabbārammaṇameva hoti.

Among these, the fourth jhāna that is the basis for all has only an unstatable object.

Iddhividhacatutthaṃ cittavasena kāyaṃ pariṇāmentassa adissamānena kāyena pāṭihāriyakaraṇe kāyārammaṇattā parittārammaṇaṃ, kāyavasena cittaṃ pariṇāmentassa dissamānena kāyena pāṭihāriyaṃ katvā brahmalokaṃ gacchantassa samāpatticittārammaṇattā mahaggatārammaṇaṃ.

The fourth jhāna of the kinds of supernormal power has a limited object when one transforms the body by means of the mind and performs a miracle with an invisible body, because it has the body as its object. It has an exalted object when one transforms the mind by means of the body, performs a miracle with a visible body, and goes to the Brahmā world, because it has the mind of attainment as its object.

Dibbasotañāṇacatutthaṃ saddārammaṇattā parittārammaṇaṃ.

The fourth jhāna of the divine ear knowledge has a limited object because it has sound as its object.

Cetopariyañāṇacatutthaṃ [V 0.0352] kāmāvacaracittajānanakāle parittārammaṇaṃ, rūpāvacarārūpāvacaracittajānanakāle mahaggatārammaṇaṃ, lokuttaracittajānanakāle appamāṇārammaṇaṃ. Cetopariyañāṇalābhī pana puthujjano puthujjanānaṃyeva cittaṃ jānāti, na ariyānaṃ. Sotāpanno sotāpannassa ceva puthujjanassa ca; sakadāgāmī sakadāgāmino ceva heṭṭhimānañca [P 0.0373] dvinnaṃ; anāgāmī anāgāmino ceva heṭṭhimānañca tiṇṇaṃ; khīṇāsavo sabbesampi jānāti.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of others' minds has a limited object at the time of knowing sense-sphere consciousness, an exalted object at the time of knowing form-sphere and formless-sphere consciousness, and an immeasurable object at the time of knowing supramundane consciousness. However, an ordinary person who has obtained the knowledge of others' minds knows only the minds of other ordinary people, not those of noble ones. A stream-enterer knows the minds of a stream-enterer and an ordinary person; a once-returner, the minds of a once-returner and the two lower ones; a non-returner, the minds of a non-returner and the three lower ones; a taint-destroyed one knows the minds of all.

Pubbenivāsañāṇacatutthaṃ [M 0.0357] kāmāvacarakkhandhānussaraṇakāle parittārammaṇaṃ, rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakkhandhānussaraṇakāle mahaggatārammaṇaṃ, “atīte buddhapaccekabuddhakhīṇāsavā maggaṃ bhāvayiṃsu, phalaṃ sacchikariṃsū”ti anussaraṇakāle appamāṇārammaṇaṃ, nāmagottānussaraṇakāle navattabbārammaṇaṃ.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of recollection of past lives has a limited object at the time of recollecting sense-sphere aggregates; an exalted object at the time of recollecting form-sphere and formless-sphere aggregates; an immeasurable object at the time of recollecting, 'In the past, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and taint-destroyed ones developed the path and realized the fruit'; and an unstatable object at the time of recollecting names and clans.

Dibbacakkhuñāṇacatutthaṃ vaṇṇārammaṇattā parittārammaṇaṃ.

The fourth jhāna of the divine eye knowledge has a limited object because it has color as its object.

Yathākammūpagañāṇacatutthaṃ kāmāvacarakammānussaraṇakāle parittārammaṇaṃ, rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakammānussaraṇakāle mahaggatārammaṇaṃ.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma has a limited object at the time of recollecting kamma pertaining to the sense sphere, and an exalted object at the time of recollecting kamma pertaining to the form sphere and formless sphere.

Anāgataṃsañāṇacatutthaṃ anāgate kāmadhātuyā nibbattijānanakāle parittārammaṇaṃ, rūpārūpabhavesu nibbattijānanakāle mahaggatārammaṇaṃ, “anāgate buddhapaccekabuddhakhīṇāsavā maggaṃ bhāvessanti, phalaṃ sacchikarissantī”ti jānanakāle appamāṇārammaṇaṃ, “anāgate saṅkho nāma rājā bhavissatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 3.108) nayena nāmagottānussaraṇakāle navattabbārammaṇaṃ.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the future has a limited object at the time of knowing future rebirth in the sense-sphere realm; an exalted object at the time of knowing rebirth in the form and formless existences; an immeasurable object at the time of knowing, 'In the future, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and taint-destroyed ones will develop the path and will realize the fruit'; and an unstatable object at the time of recollecting names and clans by the method of 'In the future there will be a king named Saṅkha' (Dī. Ni. 3.108).

Ākāsānañcāyatanaākiñcaññāyatanacatutthaṃ navattabbārammaṇaṃ. Viññāṇañcāyatananevasaññānāsaññāyatanacatutthaṃ mahaggatārammaṇaṃ.

The fourth jhāna of the base of the infinity of space and the base of nothingness has an unstatable object. The fourth jhāna of the base of the infinity of consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception has an exalted object.

Lokuttaracatutthaṃ appamāṇārammaṇaṃ.

The supramundane fourth jhāna has an immeasurable object.

Kiriyatopi tesaṃ dvādasannaṃ jhānānaṃ idameva ārammaṇavidhānaṃ. Tīṇi jhānāni namaggārammaṇāti [V 0.0353] paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ vā cetopariyādiñāṇaṃ vā maggaṃ ārammaṇaṃ kareyya, tīṇi jhānāni tathā appavattito namaggārammaṇā, sahajātahetuvasena pana siyā maggahetukā; vīriyajeṭṭhikāya vā vīmaṃsājeṭṭhikāya vā maggabhāvanāya maggādhipatino; chandacittajeṭṭhakakāle phalakāle ca navattabbā.

From the functional side, too, this same classification of objects applies to those twelve jhānas. As to 'The three jhānas do not have the path as object': if reviewing knowledge or the knowledge of others' minds, etc., were to take the path as object, the three jhānas, since they do not occur in that way, do not have the path as object. However, they may be path-rooted by way of co-nascent condition; or path-dominated for one whose path-development is led by energy or by investigation. But at a time when it is led by desire or consciousness, and at the time of fruition, they are unstatable.

Catutthaṃ jhānanti idhāpi kusalato terasasu catutthajjhānesu sabbatthapādakaiddhividhadibbasotadibbacakkhuyathākammūpagañāṇacatutthañceva catubbidhañca āruppacatutthaṃ maggārammaṇādibhāvena na vattabbaṃ. Cetopariyapubbenivāsaanāgataṃsañāṇacatutthaṃ pana maggārammaṇaṃ [P 0.0374] hoti. Na vattabbaṃ maggahetukaṃ maggādhipatīti vā; lokuttaracatutthaṃ maggārammaṇaṃ na hoti; maggakāle pana [M 0.0358] sahajātahetuvasena maggahetukaṃ; vīriyavīmaṃsājeṭṭhikāya maggabhāvanāya maggādhipati; chandacittajeṭṭhikāya ceva maggabhāvanāya phalakāle ca na vattabbaṃ. Kiriyatopi dvādasasu jhānesu ayameva nayo.

As to 'The fourth jhāna': here too, among the thirteen wholesome fourth jhānas, the fourth jhāna that is the basis for all, of the kinds of supernormal power, of the divine ear, of the divine eye, of the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma, and the fourfold fourth jhāna of the immaterial sphere—these cannot be said to have the path as object, etc. However, the fourth jhānas of the knowledge of others' minds, of the recollection of past lives, and of the knowledge of the future do have the path as object. But it cannot be said that they are path-rooted or path-dominated. The supramundane fourth jhāna does not have the path as object; but at the time of the path it is path-rooted by way of co-nascent condition; it is path-dominated for one whose path-development is led by energy or investigation; but it is unstatable for one whose path-development is led by desire or consciousness, and at the time of fruition. This same method applies to the twelve jhānas from the functional side too.

Tīṇi jhānāni na vattabbāti atītādīsu ekadhammampi ārabbha appavattito navattabbāti veditabbā.

As to 'The three jhānas are unstatable': they should be understood as 'unstatable' because they do not proceed in relation to any single state among the past, etc.

Catutthaṃ jhānanti kusalato terasasu catutthajjhānesu sabbatthapādakacatutthaṃ navattabbārammaṇameva. Iddhividhacatutthaṃ kāyavasena cittapariṇāmane samāpatticittārammaṇattā atītārammaṇaṃ; “anāgate imāni pupphāni mā milāyiṃsu, dīpā mā nibbāyiṃsu, eko aggikkhandho samuṭṭhātu, pabbato samuṭṭhātū”ti adhiṭṭhānakāle anāgatārammaṇaṃ; cittavasena kāyapariṇāmanakāle kāyārammaṇattā paccuppannārammaṇaṃ. Dibbasotañāṇacatutthaṃ saddārammaṇattā paccuppanārammaṇaṃ. Cetopariyañāṇacatutthaṃ atīte sattadivasabbhantare uppajjitvā niruddhacittajānanakāle atītārammaṇaṃ; anāgate sattadivasabbhantare uppajjanakacittajānanakāle anāgatārammaṇaṃ. “Yathā imassa bhoto manosaṅkhārā paṇihitā imassa cittassa anantarā amuṃ nāma vitakkaṃ vitakkessatīti. So bahuñcepi ādisati, tatheva taṃ hoti no aññathā”ti iminā hi suttena (a. ni. 3.61) cetopariyañāṇasseva pavatti pakāsitā. Addhānapaccuppannasantatipaccuppannavaseneva paccuppannaṃ ārabbha pavattikāle paccuppannārammaṇaṃ. Vitthārakathā panettha heṭṭhāaṭṭhakathākaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

The fourth jhāna: in terms of the wholesome, among the thirteen fourth jhānas, the universally foundational fourth jhāna has only an unassertable object. The fourth jhāna of the power of psychic feats, when transforming the mind by means of the body, has a past object because its object is the attainment-consciousness; at the time of resolving, such as, 'In the future, may these flowers not wither, may these lamps not be extinguished, may a mass of fire arise, may a mountain arise,' it has a future object; at the time of transforming the body by means of the mind, it has a present object because its object is the body. The fourth jhāna of the divine ear knowledge has a present object because its object is sound. The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of others' minds has a past object when it knows a mind that arose and ceased within the past seven days; it has a future object when it knows a mind that will arise within the next seven days. For by this sutta (AN 3.61) the functioning of the knowledge of others' minds is explained: 'In whatever way the mental formations of this venerable one are directed, he will think such and such a thought immediately after this consciousness. Even if he declares much, it is just so and not otherwise.' When it occurs in relation to a present object by way of the temporal present and the continuity present, it has a present object. The detailed account here should be understood in the way stated in the commentary section below.

Pubbenivāsañāṇacatutthaṃ [V 0.0354] atītakkhandhānussaraṇakāle atītārammaṇaṃ, nāmagottānussaraṇakāle navattabbārammaṇaṃ. Dibbacakkhuñāṇacatutthaṃ vaṇṇārammaṇattā paccuppannārammaṇaṃ. Yathākammūpagañāṇacatutthaṃ atītakammameva ārammaṇaṃ karotīti atītārammaṇaṃ. Anāgataṃsañāṇacatutthaṃ anāgatakkhandhānussaraṇakāle anāgatārammaṇaṃ, nāmagottānussaraṇakāle [P 0.0375] navattabbārammaṇaṃ. Ākāsānañcāyatanaākiñcaññāyatanacatutthaṃ navattabbārammaṇameva. Viññāṇañcāyatananevasaññānāsaññāyatanacatutthaṃ atītārammaṇameva. Lokuttaracatutthaṃ navattabbārammaṇameva. Kiriyatopi dvādasasu catutthajjhānesu eseva nayo.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of recollection of past lives has a past object when recollecting past aggregates; it has an unassertable object when recollecting name and clan. The fourth jhāna of the divine eye knowledge has a present object because its object is color. The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma has a past object, as it takes only past kamma as its object. The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the future has a future object when recollecting future aggregates; it has an unassertable object when recollecting name and clan. The fourth jhānas of the base of infinite space and the base of nothingness have only an unassertable object. The fourth jhānas of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception have only a past object. The supramundane fourth jhāna has only an unassertable object. This same method applies also to the twelve fourth jhānas that are functional.

Tīṇi [M 0.0359] jhānāni bahiddhārammaṇāti ajjhattato bahiddhābhūtaṃ nimittaṃ ārabbha pavattito bahiddhārammaṇā.

The three jhānas have an external object: they have an external object because they occur in relation to a sign that has become external to what is internal.

Catutthaṃ jhānanti idhāpi kusalato terasasu catutthajjhānesu sabbatthapādakacatutthaṃ bahiddhārammaṇameva.

The fourth jhāna: here too, in terms of the wholesome, among the thirteen fourth jhānas, the universally foundational fourth jhāna has only an external object.

Iddhividhacatutthaṃ kāyavasena cittapariṇāmanepi cittavasena kāyapariṇāmanepi attanova kāyacittārammaṇattā ajjhattārammaṇaṃ; “bahiddhā hatthimpi dassetī”tiādinā nayena pavattakāle bahiddhārammaṇaṃ.

The fourth jhāna of the power of psychic feats, both when transforming the mind by means of the body and when transforming the body by means of the mind, has an internal object because its object is one's own body and mind. When it occurs in the way of such displays as 'he displays an elephant externally,' it has an external object.

Dibbasotañāṇacatutthaṃ attano kucchigatasaddārammaṇakāle ajjhattārammaṇaṃ, parassa saddārammaṇakāle bahiddhārammaṇaṃ, ubhayavasenāpi ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇaṃ.

The fourth jhāna of the divine ear knowledge has an internal object when its object is a sound within one's own belly; it has an external object when its object is another's sound; and by way of both, it has an internal-and-external object.

Cetopariyañāṇacatutthaṃ bahiddhārammaṇameva.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of others' minds has only an external object.

Pubbenivāsañāṇacatutthaṃ attano khandhānussaraṇakāle ajjhattārammaṇaṃ, parassa khandhānañceva nāmagottassa ca anussaraṇakāle bahiddhārammaṇaṃ.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of recollection of past lives has an internal object when recollecting one's own aggregates, and an external object when recollecting another's aggregates as well as their name and clan.

Dibbacakkhuñāṇacatutthaṃ attano rūpārammaṇakāle ajjhattārammaṇaṃ, parassa rūpārammaṇakāle bahiddhārammaṇaṃ, ubhayavasenāpi ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇaṃ.

The fourth jhāna of the divine eye knowledge has an internal object when its object is one's own form; it has an external object when its object is another's form; and by way of both, it has an internal-and-external object.

Yathākammūpagañāṇacatutthaṃ [V 0.0355] attano kammajānanakāle ajjhattārammaṇaṃ, parassa kammajānanakāle bahiddhārammaṇaṃ, ubhayavasenāpi ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇaṃ.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma has an internal object when knowing one's own kamma; it has an external object when knowing another's kamma; and by way of both, it has an internal-and-external object.

Anāgataṃsañāṇacatutthaṃ attano anāgate nibbattijānanakāle ajjhattārammaṇaṃ, parassa khandhānussaraṇakāle ceva nāmagottānussaraṇakāle ca bahiddhārammaṇaṃ, ubhayavasenāpi ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇaṃ.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the future has an internal object when knowing one's own future rebirth; it has an external object when recollecting another's aggregates and their name and clan; and by way of both, it has an internal-and-external object.

Ākāsānañcāyatanacatutthaṃ bahiddhārammaṇaṃ. Ākiñcaññāyatanacatutthaṃ navattabbārammaṇaṃ. Viññāṇañcāyatananevasaññānāsaññāyatanacatutthaṃ ajjhattārammaṇaṃ.

The fourth jhāna of the base of infinite space has an external object. The fourth jhāna of the base of nothingness has an unassertable object. The fourth jhānas of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception have an internal object.

Lokuttaracatutthaṃ bahiddhārammaṇameva. Kiriyatopi dvādasasu jhānesu ayameva nayoti.

The supramundane fourth jhāna has only an external object. This same method applies also to the twelve functional jhānas.

Imasmiṃ [P 0.0376][M 0.0360] pana jhānavibhaṅge sammāsambuddhena suttantabhājanīyepi lokiyalokuttaramissakāneva jhānāni kathitāni; abhidhammabhājanīyepi pañhāpucchakepi.
