Tayopi hi ete nayā tebhūmakadhammamissakattā ekaparicchedā eva. Evamayaṃ jhānavibhaṅgopi teparivaṭṭaṃ nīharitvāva bhājetvā dassitoti.

Now, in this Analysis of Jhāna, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One has taught jhānas that are a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane in the Suttanta Exposition, in the Abhidhamma Exposition, and in the Interrogation. For these three methods, because they are a mixture of phenomena belonging to the three planes, constitute a single section. Thus this Analysis of Jhāna is presented by dividing it after having set forth the three rounds.

Sammohavinodaniyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya

In the Sammohavinodanī, the Commentary to the Vibhaṅga

Jhānavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Analysis of Jhāna is concluded.

13. Appamaññāvibhaṅgo

13. The Analysis of the Immeasurables

1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sutta-Analysis

642. Idāni [P 0.0377][M 0.0361][V 0.0356] tadanantare appamaññāvibhaṅge catassoti gaṇanaparicchedo. Appamaññāyoti pharaṇaappamāṇavasena appamaññāyo. Etā hi ārammaṇavasena appamāṇe vā satte pharanti, ekasattampi vā anavasesapharaṇavasena pharantīti pharaṇaappamāṇavasena appamaññāyoti vuccanti. Idha bhikkhūti imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhu. Mettāsahagatenāti mettāya samannāgatena. Cetasāti cittena. Ekaṃ disanti ekissā disāya. Paṭhamapariggahitaṃ sattaṃ upādāya ekadisāpariyāpannasattapharaṇavasena vuttaṃ. Pharitvāti phusitvā ārammaṇaṃ katvā. Viharatīti brahmavihārādhiṭṭhitaṃ iriyāpathavihāraṃ pavatteti. Tathā dutiyanti yathā puratthimādīsu disāsu yaṃ kiñci ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tatheva tadanantaraṃ dutiyaṃ tatiyaṃ catutthañcāti attho.

642. Now, immediately after that, in the Analysis of the Immeasurables, the word ‘four’ is a numerical determination. ‘Immeasurables’ (appamaññāyo) are so called on account of their immeasurable pervasion. For these states pervade immeasurable beings by way of their object, or they pervade even a single being by way of complete pervasion; thus they are called ‘immeasurables’ on account of their immeasurable pervasion. ‘Here, a bhikkhu’ (idha bhikkhu) means a bhikkhu in this Dispensation. ‘With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness’ (mettāsahagatena cetasā) means with a mind endowed with loving-kindness. ‘With a mind’ (cetasā) means with a citta. ‘One direction’ (ekaṃ disaṃ) means in one direction. This is stated with reference to the pervasion of beings included in one direction, taking as basis a being first encompassed. ‘Having pervaded’ (pharitvā) means having touched, having made it the object. ‘He dwells’ (viharati) means he maintains the mode of posture established in a divine abiding. ‘Similarly the second’ (tathā dutiyaṃ) means: just as he dwells having pervaded any one direction such as the eastern, so too, immediately after that, the second, the third, and the fourth. This is the meaning.

Iti uddhanti teneva ca nayena uparimaṃ disanti vuttaṃ hoti. Adho tiriyanti adhodisampi tiriyaṃdisampi evameva. Ettha ca adhoti heṭṭhā, tiriyanti anudisā. Evaṃ sabbadisāsu assamaṇḍale assamiva mettāsahagataṃ cittaṃ sāretipi paccāsāretipīti ettāvatā ekamekaṃ disaṃ pariggahetvā odhiso mettāpharaṇaṃ dassitaṃ. Sabbadhītiādi pana anodhiso dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha sabbadhīti sabbattha. Sabbattatāyāti sabbesu hīnamajjhimukkaṭṭhamittasapattamajjhattādippabhedesu attatāya ‘ayaṃ parasatto’ti vibhāgaṃ akatvā attasamatāyāti vuttaṃ hoti; atha vā sabbattatāyāti sabbena cittabhāvena īsakampi [P 0.0378] bahi avikkhipamānoti [V 0.0357] vuttaṃ hoti. Sabbāvantanti sabbasattavantaṃ, sabbasattayuttanti attho. Lokanti sattalokaṃ.

‘Thus above’ means that the upper direction is spoken of in the very same way. ‘Below, across’ means the lower direction and the transverse directions are likewise. And here, ‘below’ means beneath; ‘across’ means the intermediate directions. Thus, in all directions, as if training a horse in a ring, he makes the mind accompanied by loving-kindness go forth and come back. Thus far, having encompassed each single direction, the specified pervasion of loving-kindness has been shown. But the words beginning with ‘everywhere’ are stated to show the unspecified pervasion. Therein, ‘everywhere’ (sabbadhi) means in every place. ‘Identifying with all’ (sabbattatāya) means identifying with all beings—without making the distinction, ‘This is another being,’ among the various kinds such as inferior, middling, and superior beings, or friends, enemies, and neutral ones—that is, with equality with oneself. Or else, ‘identifying with all’ means without scattering even a little of the whole state of mind outwards. ‘All-encompassing’ (sabbāvantaṃ) means encompassing all beings, connected with all beings; this is the meaning. ‘The world’ (lokaṃ) means the world of beings.

Vipulenātievamādipariyāyadassanato panettha puna “mettāsahagatenā”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā vā ettha odhiso pharaṇe viya puna ‘tathā’saddo ‘iti’saddo vā na vutto, tasmā puna “mettāsahagatena cetasā”ti vuttaṃ; nigamanavasena vā etaṃ vuttaṃ. Vipulenāti ettha ca pharaṇavasena vipulatā daṭṭhabbā. Bhūmivasena pana taṃ mahaggataṃ, paguṇavasena appamāṇaṃ[M 0.0362], sattārammaṇavasena ca appamāṇaṃ, byāpādapaccatthikappahānena averaṃ, domanassappahānato abyāpajjhaṃ, niddukkhanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayaṃ tāva “mettāsahagatena cetasā”tiādinā nayena ṭhapitāya mātikāya attho.

Because of the exposition by way of the passage beginning ‘extensive,’ etc., it is here said again, ‘with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness.’ Or, because here, unlike in the specified pervasion, the word ‘similarly’ or ‘thus’ is not stated again, therefore it is said again, ‘with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness’; or this is said by way of conclusion. And here, by ‘extensive,’ extensiveness should be seen by way of pervasion. But by way of plane, it is sublime; by way of proficiency, it is immeasurable; and by way of beings as its object, it is immeasurable. Through the abandoning of ill will, its adversary, it is without enmity; from the abandoning of grief, it is unafflicted; it is said to be without suffering. This, then, is the meaning of the matrix established by the passage beginning with ‘with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness.’

643. Idāni yadetaṃ “kathañca, bhikkhave, mettāsahagatena cetasā”tiādinā nayena vuttaṃ padabhājanīyaṃ, tattha yasmā idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ dosacaritassa sappāyaṃ, tasmā yathārūpe puggale ayaṃ mettā appanaṃ pāpuṇāti, taṃ mettāya vatthubhūtaṃ puggalaṃ tāva dassetuṃ seyyathāpi nāma ekaṃ puggalantiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha seyyathāpi nāmāti opammatthe nipāto, yathā ekaṃ puggalanti attho. Piyanti pemanīyaṃ. Manāpanti hadayavuḍḍhikaraṃ. Tattha pubbeva sannivāsena paccuppannahitena vā piyo nāma hoti, sīlādiguṇasamāyogena manāpo nāma; dānasamānattatāhi vā piyatā, piyavacanaatthacariyatāhi manāpatā veditabbā. Yasmā cettha piyatāya imassa byāpādassa pahānaṃ hoti, tato mettā sukhaṃ pharati, manāpatāya udāsīnatā na saṇṭhāti, hirottappañca paccupaṭṭhāti, tato hirottappānupālitā mettā na parihāyati, tasmā taṃ upamaṃ katvā idaṃ vuttaṃ – piyaṃ manāpanti. Mettāyeyyāti mettāya phareyya; tasmiṃ puggale mettaṃ kareyya pavatteyyāti attho. Evameva [P 0.0379] sabbe satteti yathā piyaṃ puggalaṃ mettāyeyya, evaṃ tasmiṃ puggale appanāppattāya vasībhāvaṃ upagatāya mettāya majjhattaverisaṅkhātepi sabbe satte anukkamena pharatīti attho. Metti mettāyanātiādīni vuttatthāneva.

643. Now, in the word-by-word analysis of the passage beginning, ‘And how, bhikkhus, with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness…,’ since this meditation subject is suitable for one of a hateful temperament, in order to show first the kind of person in whom this loving-kindness reaches absorption—the person who is the basis for loving-kindness—the passage beginning ‘Just as one person…’ is stated. Herein, ‘just as’ is a particle in the sense of a simile; the meaning is ‘just as one person.’ ‘Dear’ means lovable. ‘Agreeable’ means gladdening the heart. Herein, one is called ‘dear’ either through having lived together previously or through a present benefit, and ‘agreeable’ through connection with qualities such as virtuous conduct. Or dearness should be understood from generosity and equal treatment, and agreeableness from kind speech and beneficial conduct. Because here, through dearness, the abandoning of ill will occurs, and then loving-kindness pervades happily; through agreeableness, indifference does not become established, and moral shame and moral dread are present. Then, loving-kindness guarded by moral shame and moral dread does not decline. Therefore, having made that a simile, this is said: ‘dear and agreeable.’ ‘One should treat with loving-kindness’ means one should pervade with loving-kindness; the meaning is that one should produce and sustain loving-kindness towards that person. ‘Just so all beings’ means that just as one would treat a dear person with loving-kindness, so too, when loving-kindness has attained absorption and reached a state of mastery with regard to that person, one pervades in sequence all beings, including those reckoned as neutral or as enemies. The terms ‘loving-kindness,’ ‘the state of loving-kindness,’ etc., have the meaning already stated.

644. Vidisaṃ vāti padaṃ tiriyaṃ vāti etassa atthavibhāvanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

644. The phrase ‘or the intermediate directions’ is stated to clarify the meaning of ‘or across’.

645. Pharitvāti [V 0.0358] ārammaṇakaraṇavasena phusitvā. Adhimuñcitvāti adhikabhāvena muñcitvā, yathā muttaṃ sumuttaṃ hoti suppasāritaṃ suvitthataṃ tathā muñcitvāti attho.

645. ‘Having pervaded’ means having touched by way of making it an object. ‘Having resolved upon’ means having released with intensity; just as what is released is well-released, well-spread out, well-extended, so ‘having released’ is the meaning.

648. Sabbadhiādiniddese yasmā tīṇipi etāni padāni sabbasaṅgāhikāni, tasmā nesaṃ ekatova atthaṃ dassetuṃ sabbena sabbantiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

648. In the exposition of the terms beginning with ‘everywhere,’ since all three of these terms are all-inclusive, the phrase beginning ‘with all, in every way’ is stated to show their meaning as one. Its meaning has already been stated above.

650. Vipulādiniddese [M 0.0363] yasmā yaṃ appanāppattaṃ hutvā anantasattapharaṇavasena vipulaṃ, taṃ niyamato bhūmivasena mahaggataṃ hoti. Yañca mahaggataṃ taṃ appamāṇagocaravasena appamāṇaṃ. Yaṃ appamāṇaṃ taṃ paccatthikavighātavasena averaṃ. Yañca averaṃ taṃ vihatabyāpajjatāya abyāpajjaṃ. Tasmā “yaṃ vipulaṃ taṃ mahaggata”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Avero abyāpajjoti cettha liṅgavipariyāyena vuttaṃ. Manena vā saddhiṃ yojanā kātabbā – yaṃ appamāṇaṃ cittaṃ, so avero mano; yo avero so abyāpajjoti. Apicettha heṭṭhimaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ padaṃ uparimassa uparimassa, uparimaṃ vā uparimaṃ heṭṭhimassa heṭṭhimassa atthotipi veditabbo.

650. In the exposition of the terms beginning with ‘vast,’ because that which, having attained absorption, is vast by way of pervading infinite beings, that, as a rule, becomes sublime by way of plane. And that which is sublime is immeasurable by way of an immeasurable range. That which is immeasurable is without enmity by way of destroying adversaries. And that which is without enmity is unafflicted because affliction has been destroyed. Therefore it is said, ‘What is vast is sublime,’ etc. Here, ‘without enmity’ and ‘unafflicted’ are stated with a change of gender. Or a connection should be made with the mind: the mind that is immeasurable is a mind without enmity; the mind that is without enmity is unafflicted. Moreover, here it should be understood that each lower term is the meaning of each term above it, or each higher term is the meaning of each term below it.

653. Seyyathāpi nāma ekaṃ puggalaṃ duggataṃ durupetanti idampi karuṇāya vatthubhūtaṃ puggalaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Evarūpasmiñhi puggale balavakāruññaṃ uppajjati. Tattha duggatanti dukkhena samaṅgībhāvaṃ gataṃ. Durupetanti kāyaduccaritādīhi upetaṃ. Gatikulabhogādivasena vā tamabhāve ṭhito puggalo duggato, kāyaduccaritādīhi upetattā tamaparāyaṇabhāve ṭhito durupetoti evamettha attho veditabbo.

653. ‘Just as a person is wretched and unfortunate’—this too is said to show a person who is a basis for compassion. For in such a person, strong compassion arises. Here, ‘wretched’ means one who has come to be endowed with suffering. ‘Unfortunate’ means endowed with bodily misconduct and so on. Alternatively, a person is ‘wretched’ when established in the absence of such things as a good destination, family, and wealth; and one is ‘unfortunate’ because, being endowed with bodily misconduct and so on, one is established in a state where that is one’s future destination. Thus the meaning should be understood here.

663. Ekaṃ puggalaṃ piyaṃ manāpanti idampi muditāya vatthubhūtaṃ puggalaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha [P 0.0380] gatikulabhogādivasena jotibhāve ṭhito piyo, kāyasucaritādīhi upetattā jotiparāyaṇabhāve ṭhito manāpoti veditabbo.

663. ‘A person who is dear and agreeable’—this too is said to show a person who is a basis for altruistic joy. Here, one is ‘dear’ when established in a state of radiance by way of destination, family, wealth, etc.; and one should be understood as ‘agreeable’ because, being endowed with good bodily conduct and so on, one is established in a state of having a radiant future destination.

673. Neva manāpaṃ na amanāpanti idampi upekkhāya vatthubhūtaṃ puggalaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha mittabhāvaṃ asampattatāya neva manāpo, amittabhāvaṃ asampattatāya na amanāpoti veditabbo. Sesamettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā cittuppādakaṇḍe vuttameva. Bhāvanāvidhānampi etesaṃ kammaṭṭhānānaṃ visuddhimagge vitthārato kathitamevāti.

673. ‘Neither agreeable nor disagreeable’—this too is said to show a person who is a basis for equanimity. Here, one is ‘not agreeable’ because a state of friendship has not been reached, and one should be understood as ‘not disagreeable’ because a state of enmity has not been reached. Whatever else might need to be said here has all been said above in the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness. The method for developing these meditation subjects has also been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Sutta-Analysis.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition.

Abhidhammabhājanīyaṃ [M 0.0364][V 0.0359] kusalatopi vipākatopi kiriyatopi heṭṭhā cittuppādakaṇḍe bhājitanayeneva bhājitaṃ. Atthopissa tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

The Abhidhamma Exposition is analyzed in terms of the wholesome, resultant, and functional, just as it was analyzed above in the chapter on the arising of consciousness. Its meaning, too, should be understood in the way stated there.

3. Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Interrogation.

Pañhāpucchake pāḷianusāreneva mettādīnaṃ kusalādibhāvo veditabbo. Ārammaṇattikesu pana sabbāpi tīsu tikesu navatabbārammaṇā eva. Ajjhattārammaṇattike bahiddhārammaṇāti. Imasmiṃ pana appamaññāvibhaṅge sammāsambuddhena suttantabhājanīyepi lokiyā eva appamaññāyo kathitā, abhidhammabhājanīyepi pañhāpucchakepi. Tayopi hi ete nayā lokiyattā ekaparicchedā eva. Evamayaṃ appamaññāvibhaṅgopi teparivaṭṭaṃ nīharitvāva bhājetvā dassitoti.

In the Interrogation, the nature of loving-kindness and other states as wholesome, etc., should be understood in accordance with the Pāḷi text. In the triads concerning the object, however, in all three triads they have only objects that are not to be classified. In the triad of internal objects, they are external objects. In this Analysis of the Immeasurables, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One has taught that the immeasurables are only worldly, both in the Suttanta Exposition and in the Abhidhamma Exposition, as well as in the Interrogation. For all three of these methods, being worldly, belong to a single section. Thus this Analysis of the Immeasurables is analyzed and shown after extracting the three rounds.

Sammohavinodaniyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya

In the Sammohavinodanī, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga.

Appamaññāvibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Immeasurables is finished.

14. Sikkhāpadavibhaṅgo

14. Analysis of the Training Rules.

1. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition.

703. Idāni [P 0.0381][M 0.0365][V 0.0360] tadanantare sikkhāpadavibhaṅge pañcāti gaṇanaparicchedo. Sikkhāpadānīti sikkhitabbapadāni; sikkhākoṭṭhāsāti attho. Apica upari āgatā sabbepi kusalā dhammā sikkhitabbato sikkhā. Pañcasu pana sīlaṅgesu yaṃkiñci aṅgaṃ tāsaṃ sikkhānaṃ patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena padanti sikkhānaṃ padattā sikkhāpadāni. Pāṇātipātāti pāṇassa atipātā ghātanā māraṇāti attho. Veramaṇīti virati. Adinnādānāti adinnassa ādānā; parapariggahitassa haraṇāti attho. Kāmesūti vatthukāmesu. Micchācārāti kilesakāmavasena lāmakācārā. Musāvādāti abhūtavādato. Surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānāti ettha surāti piṭṭhasurā, pūvasurā, odanasurā, kiṇṇapakkhittā, sambhārasaṃyuttāti pañca surā. Merayanti pupphāsavo, phalāsavo, guḷāsavo, madhvāsavo, sambhārasaṃyuttoti pañca āsavā. Tadubhayampi madanīyaṭṭhena majjaṃ. Yāya cetanāya taṃ pivanti, sā pamādakāraṇattā pamādaṭṭhānaṃ; tasmā surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā. Ayaṃ tāvettha mātikānikkhepassa attho.

703. Now, in the immediately following Analysis of the Training Rules, the word 'five' is a numerical determination. 'Training rules' (sikkhāpadāni) means items to be trained in; the meaning is 'portions of training.' Moreover, all the wholesome states that come up for discussion are 'training' (sikkhā) because they are to be trained in. Among the five factors of virtue, however, any one factor is a 'basis' (pada) in the sense of being a foundation for those trainings; hence they are 'training rules' (sikkhāpadāni) because they are the basis of the trainings. 'Destruction of life' (pāṇātipāta) means the falling upon, slaying, killing of a living being. 'Abstinence' (veramaṇī) means abstaining (virati). 'Taking what is not given' (adinnādāna) means the taking of what is not given; the meaning is the theft of what is possessed by another. 'In sensual pleasures' (kāmesu) means in objective sensual pleasures. 'Wrong conduct' (micchācāra) means base conduct due to defilement-based desire. 'From false speech' (musāvādā) means from speaking what is not real. As to 'an occasion for heedlessness due to liquor, wine, and intoxicants' (surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāna): here, 'liquor' (surā) is of five kinds: liquor from flour, liquor from cakes, liquor from rice, liquor to which a fermenting agent has been added, and liquor compounded with ingredients. 'Wine' (meraya) is of five kinds: fermented drink from flowers, from fruits, from molasses, from honey, and fermented drink compounded with ingredients. Both of these are 'intoxicants' (majja) because they are intoxicating. The volition with which one drinks them is an 'occasion for heedlessness' (pamādaṭṭhāna) because it is a cause of heedlessness; therefore, it is 'an occasion for heedlessness due to liquor, wine, and intoxicants.' This, for now, is the meaning of the exposition of the mātikā.

704. Padabhājanīye pana yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacarantiādi sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthameva. Yasmā pana na kevalaṃ viratiyeva sikkhāpadaṃ, cetanāpi sikkhāpadameva, tasmā taṃ dassetuṃ dutiyanayo dassito. Yasmā ca na kevalaṃ eteyeva dve dhammā sikkhāpadaṃ, cetanāsampayuttā pana paropaṇṇāsadhammāpi sikkhitabbakoṭṭhāsato sikkhāpadameva, tasmā tatiyanayopi dassito.

704. In the Analysis of Terms, however, the entire passage beginning 'at a time when a sense-sphere...' has a plain meaning because of the method stated above. But since not only abstinence (virati) is a training rule (sikkhāpada), but volition (cetanā) too is a training rule, the second method is shown to demonstrate this. And since not only these two states are a training rule, but the fifty-odd states associated with volition are also a training rule by way of being a portion of what is to be trained in, the third method is also shown.

Tattha [V 0.0361] duvidhaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ pariyāyasikkhāpadaṃ nippariyāyasikkhāpadañca. Tattha virati nippariyāyasikkhāpadaṃ. Sā hi “pāṇātipātā veramaṇī”ti [P 0.0382] pāḷiyaṃ āgatā, no cetanā. Viramanto ca tāya eva tato tato viramati, na cetanāya. Cetanaṃ pana āharitvā dassesi. Tathā sesacetanāsampayuttadhamme. Vītikkamakāle hi veracetanā dussīlyaṃ nāma. Tasmā sā viratikālepi susīlyavasena vuttā. Phassādayo taṃsampayuttattā gahitāti.

Herein, the training rule is twofold: the training rule in a figurative sense (pariyāya-sikkhāpada) and the training rule in a literal sense (nippariyāya-sikkhāpada). Of these, abstinence (virati) is the training rule in the literal sense. For it is what comes in the Pāḷi text as 'abstinence from the destruction of life,' not volition (cetanā). And one who abstains, abstains from this or that by means of that abstinence itself, not by volition. But volition is brought in and shown. Likewise for the other states associated with volition. For at the time of transgression, the volition of enmity is called 'immorality.' Therefore, at the time of abstinence, it (volition) is spoken of in terms of 'good morality.' Contact and the other factors are included because they are associated with it.

Idāni [M 0.0366] etesu sikkhāpadesu ñāṇasamuttejanatthaṃ imesaṃ pāṇātipātādīnaṃ dhammato, koṭṭhāsato, ārammaṇato, vedanāto, mūlato, kammato, sāvajjato, payogato ca vinicchayo veditabbo.

Now, in order to stimulate knowledge concerning these training rules, the analysis of the destruction of life and other such actions should be understood in terms of their nature, portion, object, feeling, root, action, blameworthiness, and means.

Tattha ‘dhammato’ti pañcapete pāṇātipātādayo cetanādhammāva honti. ‘Koṭṭhāsato’ pañcapi kammapathā eva.

Herein, 'in terms of nature': all five—destruction of life and so on—are states of volition. 'In terms of portion': all five are courses of action.

‘Ārammaṇato’ pāṇātipāto jīvitindriyārammaṇo. Adinnādānaṃ sattārammaṇaṃ vā saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ vā. Micchācāro itthipurisārammaṇo. Musāvādo sattārammaṇo vā saṅkhārārammaṇo vā. Surāpānaṃ saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ.

'In terms of object': destruction of life has the life faculty as its object. Taking what is not given has either a being or a formation as its object. Sexual misconduct has a woman or a man as its object. False speech has either a being or a formation as its object. The consumption of intoxicants has a formation as its object.

‘Vedanāto’ pāṇātipāto dukkhavedano. Adinnādānaṃ tivedanaṃ. Tañhi haṭṭhatuṭṭhassa adinnaṃ ādiyato sukhavedanaṃ hoti, bhītakāle dukkhavedanaṃ, majjhattassa hutvā gaṇhato adukkhamasukhavedanaṃ. Micchācāro sukhavedano vā adukkhamasukhavedano vā. Musāvādo adinnādānaṃ viya tivedano. Surāpānaṃ sukhamajjhattavedanaṃ.

'In terms of feeling': destruction of life is accompanied by painful feeling. Taking what is not given is threefold in feeling. For when one who is joyful and delighted takes what is not given, it is accompanied by pleasant feeling; at a time of fear, by painful feeling; when one takes it while being neutral, by neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Sexual misconduct is accompanied by either pleasant feeling or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. False speech, like taking what is not given, is threefold in feeling. The consumption of intoxicants is accompanied by pleasant or neutral feeling.

‘Mūlato’ pāṇātipāto dosamohamūlo. Adinnādānaṃ kiñcikāle lobhamohamūlaṃ, kiñcikāle dosamohamūlaṃ. Micchācāro lobhamohamūlo. Musāvādo kiñcikāle lobhamohamūlo, kiñcikāle dosamohamūlo. Surāpānaṃ lobhamohamūlaṃ.

'In terms of root': destruction of life is rooted in hatred and delusion. Taking what is not given is sometimes rooted in greed and delusion, and sometimes in hatred and delusion. Sexual misconduct is rooted in greed and delusion. False speech is sometimes rooted in greed and delusion, and sometimes in hatred and delusion. The consumption of intoxicants is rooted in greed and delusion.

‘Kammato’ musāvādo cettha vacīkammaṃ. Sesā kāyakammameva.

'In terms of action': herein, false speech is verbal action. The rest are only bodily action.

‘Sāvajjato’ [V 0.0362] pāṇātipāto atthi appasāvajjo, atthi mahāsāvajjo. Tathā adinnādānādīni. Tesaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ heṭṭhā dassitameva.

'In terms of blameworthiness': destruction of life is sometimes slightly blameworthy, sometimes very blameworthy. So too with taking what is not given and the others. The distinctions among them have already been shown below.

Ayaṃ pana aparo nayo – kunthakipillikassa hi vadho appasāvajjo, tato mahantatarassa mahāsāvajjo; sopi appasāvajjo, tato mahantatarāya sakuṇikāya mahāsāvajjo; tato godhāya, tato sasakassa, tato migassa, tato gavayassa, tato assassa, tato hatthissa vadho mahāsāvajjo, tatopi dussīlamanussassa[P 0.0383], tato gorūpasīlakamanussassa, tato saraṇagatassa, tato pañcasikkhāpadikassa, tato sāmaṇerassa, tato puthujjanabhikkhuno[M 0.0367], tato sotāpannassa, tato sakadāgāmissa, tato anāgāmissa, tato khīṇāsavassa vadho atimahāsāvajjoyeva.

But this is another method: killing a small insect like an ant is slightly blameworthy; killing a larger one is more blameworthy. Killing a small bird is also slightly blameworthy; killing a larger one is more blameworthy; then killing a lizard, a hare, a deer, a gayal, a horse, or an elephant is very blameworthy. More blameworthy than that is killing an immoral human being; then a virtuous human being; then one who has gone for refuge; then one who observes the five training rules; then a novice; then an ordinary monk; then a stream-enterer; then a once-returner; then a non-returner; the killing of a perfected one, whose taints are destroyed, is extremely blameworthy indeed.

Adinnādānaṃ dussīlassa santake appasāvajjaṃ, tato gorūpasīlakassa santake mahāsāvajjaṃ; tato saraṇagatassa, tato pañcasikkhāpadikassa, tato sāmaṇerassa, tato puthujjanabhikkhuno, tato sotāpannassa, tato sakadāgāmissa, tato anāgāmissa santake mahāsāvajjaṃ, tato khīṇāsavassa santake atimahāsāvajjaṃyeva.

Taking what is not given from the possession of an immoral person is slightly blameworthy; from the possession of a virtuous person is very blameworthy; then from one who has gone for refuge; then from one who observes the five training rules; then from a novice; then from an ordinary monk; then from a stream-enterer; then from a once-returner; then from a non-returner is very blameworthy; taking from the possession of a perfected one, whose taints are destroyed, is extremely blameworthy indeed.

Micchācāro dussīlāya itthiyā vītikkame appasāvajjo, tato gorūpasīlakāya mahāsāvajjo; tato saraṇagatāya, pañcasikkhāpadikāya, sāmaṇeriyā, puthujjanabhikkhuniyā, sotāpannāya, sakadāgāminiyā, tato anāgāminiyā vītikkame mahāsāvajjo, khīṇāsavāya pana bhikkhuniyā ekantamahāsāvajjova.

Transgression in sexual misconduct with an immoral woman is slightly blameworthy; with a virtuous woman, it is very blameworthy; then with one who has gone for refuge; one who observes the five training rules; a female novice; an ordinary nun; a female stream-enterer; a female once-returner; then with a female non-returner, it is very blameworthy; but with a nun who is a perfected one, it is exclusively very blameworthy.

Musāvādo kākaṇikamattassa atthāya musākathane appasāvajjo, tato aḍḍhamāsakassa, māsakassa, pañcamāsakassa, aḍḍhakahāpaṇassa, kahāpaṇassa, tato anagghaniyabhaṇḍassa atthāya musākathane mahāsāvajjo, musā kathetvā pana saṅghaṃ bhindantassa ekantamahāsāvajjova.

Speaking falsely for the sake of a mere kākaṇikā is slightly blameworthy; then for half a māsaka, a māsaka, five māsakas, half a kahāpaṇa, a kahāpaṇa; then speaking falsely for the sake of priceless goods is very blameworthy; but for one who splits the Saṅgha by speaking falsely, it is exclusively very blameworthy.

Surāpānaṃ pasatamattassa pāne appasāvajjaṃ, añjalimattassa pāne mahāsāvajjaṃ; kāyacālanasamatthaṃ pana bahuṃ pivitvā gāmaghātanigamaghātakammaṃ karontassa ekantamahāsāvajjameva.

The consumption of intoxicants, in the case of drinking a mere spoonful, is slightly blameworthy; in the case of drinking a cupped handful, it is very blameworthy. But for one who, having drunk a large amount sufficient to agitate the body, commits the act of destroying a village or town, it is exclusively very blameworthy indeed.

Pāṇātipātañhi [V 0.0363] patvā khīṇāsavassa vadho mahāsāvajjo; adinnādānaṃ patvā khīṇāsavasantakassa haraṇaṃ, micchācāraṃ patvā khīṇāsavāya bhikkhuniyā vītikkamanaṃ, musāvādaṃ patvā musāvādena saṅghabhedo, surāpānaṃ patvā kāyacālanasamatthaṃ bahuṃ pivitvā gāmanigamaghātanaṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ. Sabbehipi panetehi musāvādena saṅghabhedanameva mahāsāvajjaṃ. Tañhi kappaṃ niraye pācanasamatthaṃ mahākibbisaṃ.

With respect to destruction of life, the killing of a perfected one is very blameworthy. With respect to taking what is not given, the theft of a perfected one's property; with respect to sexual misconduct, transgression with a nun who is a perfected one; with respect to false speech, splitting the Saṅgha by false speech; with respect to the consumption of intoxicants, drinking a large amount sufficient to agitate the body and destroying a village or town, is very blameworthy. But of all these, splitting the Saṅgha by false speech is the most blameworthy. For that is a great crime capable of making one boil in hell for an aeon.

‘Payogato’ti [M 0.0368] pāṇātipāto sāhatthikopi hoti āṇattikopi. Tathā adinnādānaṃ. Micchācāramusāvādasurāpānāni sāhatthikānevāti.

'In terms of means': destruction of life can be by one's own hand or by command. So too taking what is not given. Sexual misconduct, false speech, and the consumption of intoxicants are only by one's own hand.

Evamettha [P 0.0384] pāṇātipātādīnaṃ dhammādivasena vinicchayaṃ ñatvā pāṇātipātā veramaṇītiādīnampi dhammato, koṭṭhāsato, ārammaṇato, vedanāto, mūlato, kammato, khaṇḍato, samādānato, payogato ca vinicchayo veditabbo.

Thus, having understood the analysis of the destruction of life and other such actions by way of their nature and so on, the analysis of abstinence from the destruction of life and other such precepts should also be understood in terms of nature, portion, object, feeling, root, action, breach, undertaking, and means.

Tattha ‘dhammato’ti pariyāyasīlavasena paṭipāṭiyā pañca cetanādhammāva. ‘Koṭṭhāsato’ti pañcapi kammapathā eva. ‘Ārammaṇato’ti pāṇātipātā veramaṇī parassa jīvitindriyaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā attano veracetanāya viramati. Itarāsupi eseva nayo. Sabbāpi hi etā vītikkamitabbavatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā veracetanāhiyeva viramanti. ‘Vedanāto’ti sabbāpi sukhavedanā vā honti majjhattavedanā vā. ‘Mūlato’ti ñāṇasampayuttacittena viramantassa alobhaadosaamohamūlā honti, ñāṇavippayuttacittena viramantassa alobhaadosamūlā honti. ‘Kammato’ti musāvādā veramaṇīyevettha vacīkammaṃ; sesā kāyakammaṃ. ‘Khaṇḍato’ti gahaṭṭhā yaṃ yaṃ vītikkamanti, taṃ tadeva khaṇḍaṃ hoti bhijjati, avasesaṃ na bhijjati. Kasmā? Gahaṭṭhā hi anibaddhasīlā honti, yaṃ yaṃ sakkonti taṃ tadeva gopenti. Sāmaṇerānaṃ pana ekasmiṃ vītikkamante sabbāni bhijjanti. Na kevalañca etāni, sesasīlānipi bhijjantiyeva. Tesaṃ pana vītikkamo daṇḍakammavatthuko. ‘Puna evarūpaṃ na karissāmī’ti daṇḍakamme kate sīlaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hoti. ‘Samādānato’ti sayameva ‘pañca sīlāni adhiṭṭhahāmī’ti adhiṭṭhahantenapi, pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ samādiyantenapi samādiṇṇāni honti. Aññassa santike nisīditvā ‘pañca sīlāni samādiyāmī’ti samādiyantenapi, pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ samādiyantenapi [V 0.0364] samādinnāneva honti. ‘Payogato’ sabbānipi sāhatthikapayogānevāti veditabbāni.

Here, 'in terms of nature' refers to the five volitional states themselves, in sequence, by way of the virtue of the course. 'In terms of divisions' refers to just the five paths of action. 'In terms of object'—abstinence from killing takes the life faculty of another as its object and refrains through the volition of abstinence. The same method applies to the others. For all these, taking the object to be transgressed as the object, they refrain through the volition of abstinence. 'In terms of feeling'—all are accompanied by either pleasant or neutral feeling. 'In terms of roots'—for one who refrains with a mind associated with wisdom, the roots are non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; for one who refrains with a mind dissociated from wisdom, the roots are non-greed and non-hatred. 'In terms of kamma'—here, abstinence from false speech is verbal kamma; the rest are bodily kamma. 'In terms of breach'—when laypeople violate any precept, only that specific precept is broken; the rest are not broken. Why? Because laypeople have an unbound virtue; they guard only what they are able. But for novices, when one is violated, all are broken. And not only these, but the other precepts are also broken. Their violation, however, is a basis for a disciplinary action. When the disciplinary action has been performed with the resolve, 'I will not do such a thing again,' the virtue becomes complete. 'In terms of undertaking'—they are undertaken whether by one who resolves by oneself, 'I resolve upon the five precepts,' or by one who undertakes them one by one. They are also undertaken whether by one who undertakes them in the presence of another, saying, 'I undertake the five precepts,' or by one who undertakes them one by one. 'In terms of application'—all are to be understood as applications involving one's own hand.

712. Idāni yāsaṃ sikkhānaṃ koṭṭhāsabhāvena imāni pañca sikkhāpadāni vuttāni, tāni dassetuṃ katame dhammā sikkhāti ayaṃ sikkhāvāro āraddho. Tattha [P 0.0385] yasmā sabbepi catubhūmakakusalā dhammā sikkhitabbabhāvato [M 0.0369] sikkhā, tasmā te dassetuṃ yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacarantiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha heṭṭhā cittuppādakaṇḍe (dha. sa. 1) vuttanayeneva pāḷiṃ vitthāretvā attho veditabbo. Idha pana mukhamattameva dassitanti.

712. Now, to show the trainings of which these five training rules have been stated as a portion, the section on the trainings is begun with the question: 'What things are trainings?' Here, since all wholesome states pertaining to the four planes are trainings because they are to be trained in, to show them the passage beginning 'At what time... pertaining to the sense sphere,' etc., is stated. There, the meaning should be understood by elaborating the Pāli text in the way stated previously in the chapter on the arising of consciousness (Dhs §1). Here, however, only a brief indication is given.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition.

3. Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Question-and-Answer Section

714. Pañhāpucchake pāḷianusāreneva sikkhāpadānaṃ kusalādibhāvo veditabbo. Ārammaṇattikesu pana yāni sikkhāpadāni ettha sattārammaṇānīti vuttāni, tāni yasmā sattoti saṅkhaṃ gate saṅkhāreyeva ārammaṇaṃ karonti, yasmā ca sabbānipi etāni sampattavirativaseneva niddiṭṭhāni, tasmā “parittārammaṇā”ti ca “paccuppannārammaṇā”ti ca vuttaṃ. Yato pana viramati tassa vatthuno accantabahiddhattā sabbesampi bahiddhārammaṇatā veditabbāti.

714. In the Question-and-Answer Section, the status of the training rules as wholesome, etc., should be understood in accordance with the Pāli text itself. Regarding the triads concerning the object, those training rules that are here said to have beings as their object—since they take as their object only formations that have come to be reckoned as 'a being,' and since all of them are specified only by way of abstinence on the occasion—are therefore said to be 'with a limited object' and 'with a present object.' However, because the object from which one refrains is entirely external, all of them should be understood as having an external object.

Imasmiṃ pana sikkhāpadavibhaṅge sammāsambuddhena abhidhammabhājanīyepi pañhāpucchakepi lokiyāneva sikkhāpadāni kathitāni. Ubhopi hi ete nayā lokiyattā ekaparicchedā eva. Evamayaṃ sikkhāpadavibhaṅgo dveparivaṭṭaṃ nīharitvāva bhājetvā dassitoti.

In this Analysis of the Training Rules, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One has taught only the mundane training rules, both in the Abhidhamma Exposition and in the Question-and-Answer Section. For both these methods, being mundane, are a single section. Thus this Analysis of the Training Rules has been shown by extracting and dividing two cycles.

Sammohavinodaniyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya

In the Dispeller of Delusion, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga,

Sikkhāpadavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Training Rules is finished.

15. Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅgo

15. The Analysis of the Discriminations

1. Suttantabhājanīyaṃ

1. The Exposition According to the Suttas

1. Saṅgahavāravaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Summary Section

718. Idāni [P 0.0386][M 0.0370][V 0.0365] tadanantare paṭisambhidāvibhaṅge catassoti gaṇanaparicchedo. Paṭisambhidāti pabhedā. Yasmā pana parato atthe ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidātiādimāha, tasmā na aññassa kassaci pabhedā, ñāṇasseva pabhedāti veditabbā. Iti “catasso paṭisambhidā”ti padena cattāro ñāṇappabhedāti ayamattho saṅgahito. Atthapaṭisambhidāti atthe paṭisambhidā; atthappabhedassa sallakkhaṇavibhāvanāvavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ atthe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇanti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Dhammappabhedassa hi sallakkhaṇavibhāvanāvavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ dhamme pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā nāma. Niruttippabhedassa sallakkhaṇavibhāvanāvavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ niruttābhilāpe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā nāma. Paṭibhānappabhedassa sallakkhaṇavibhāvanāvavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ paṭibhāne pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā nāma.

718. Now, immediately following, in the Analysis of the Discriminations, 'four' is a delimitation by counting. 'Discriminations' means distinctions. And since further on the text says, beginning with 'knowledge in meaning is the discrimination of meaning,' it should be understood that these are not distinctions of anything else, but distinctions of knowledge itself. Thus, by the phrase 'four discriminations,' the meaning 'four kinds of distinctions of knowledge' is encompassed. 'Discrimination of meaning' is discrimination in meaning; the meaning is: it is knowledge that has penetrated the distinctions of meaning and is capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining their characteristics. The same method applies to the remaining terms. For the knowledge that has penetrated the distinctions of the Dhamma and is capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining their characteristics is called the 'discrimination of the Dhamma.' The knowledge that has penetrated the distinctions of linguistic expression and is capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining their characteristics is called the 'discrimination of language.' The knowledge that has penetrated the distinctions of ready wit and is capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining their characteristics is called the 'discrimination of ready wit.'

Idāni yathānikkhittā paṭisambhidā bhājetvā dassento atthe ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidātiādimāha. Tattha atthoti saṅkhepato hetuphalaṃ. Tañhi hetuvasena araṇīyaṃ gantabbaṃ pattabbaṃ, tasmā atthoti vuccati. Pabhedato pana yaṃkiñci paccayasamuppannaṃ, nibbānaṃ, bhāsitattho, vipāko, kiriyāti ime pañca dhammā atthoti veditabbā. Taṃ atthaṃ paccavekkhantassa tasmiṃ atthe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā.

Now, showing the analysis of the discriminations as they have been laid down, he says, beginning with, 'Knowledge in meaning is the discrimination of meaning.' Herein, 'meaning' (attha), in brief, is cause and effect. For that is to be striven for, gone to, and attained by means of a cause; therefore it is called 'meaning.' In detail, however, these five things should be understood as 'meaning': whatever is dependently arisen, Nibbāna, the meaning of what is spoken, resultant, and functional. For one who reviews that meaning, the knowledge that has penetrated the distinctions in that meaning is the discrimination of meaning.

Dhammoti [V 0.0366] saṅkhepato paccayo. So hi yasmā taṃ taṃ vidahati pavatteti ceva pāpeti ca, tasmā dhammoti vuccati. Pabhedato pana yo koci phalanibbattako hetu, ariyamaggo, bhāsitaṃ[P 0.0387], kusalaṃ, akusalanti ime pañca dhammā dhammoti veditabbā. Taṃ dhammaṃ paccavekkhantassa tasmiṃ dhamme pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā.

'Dhamma,' in brief, is condition. Since it arranges, sets going, and brings to attainment this and that, it is called 'Dhamma.' In detail, however, these five things should be understood as 'Dhamma': any cause that produces a result, the noble path, what is spoken, the wholesome, and the unwholesome. For one who reviews that Dhamma, the knowledge that has penetrated the distinctions in that Dhamma is the discrimination of Dhamma.

Tatra dhammaniruttābhilāpe ñāṇanti tasmiṃ atthe ca dhamme ca yā sabhāvanirutti, tassā abhilāpe taṃ sabhāvaniruttiṃ saddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ [M 0.0371] katvā paccavekkhantassa tasmiṃ sabhāvaniruttābhilāpe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā. Evamayaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā saddārammaṇā nāma jātā, na paññattiārammaṇā. Kasmā? Yasmā saddaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ sabhāvanirutti, ayaṃ na sabhāvaniruttī”ti jānanti. Paṭisambhidāppatto hi “phasso”ti vutte “ayaṃ sabhāvaniruttī”ti jānāti, “phassā”ti vā “phassa”nti vā vutte pana “ayaṃ na sabhāvaniruttī”ti jānāti. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo. Aññaṃ panesa nāmaākhyātaupasaggabyañjanasaddaṃ jānāti na jānātīti? Yadaggena saddaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ sabhāvanirutti, ayaṃ na sabhāvaniruttī”ti jānāti, tadaggena tampi jānissatīti. Taṃ pana nayidaṃ paṭisambhidākiccanti paṭikkhipitvā idaṃ vatthu kathitaṃ –

The phrase 'knowledge in the linguistic expression of the Dhamma' means this: with regard to that meaning and Dhamma, there is a natural expression. For one who reviews the expression of this, taking that natural expression—the sound—as object, the knowledge that has penetrated the distinctions in that expression of the natural language is the discrimination of language. Thus this discrimination of language has come to have sound as its object, not concept. Why? Because on hearing a sound, one knows, 'This is the natural expression; this is not the natural expression.' For one who has attained the discriminations, when 'phasso' (contact) is said, one knows, 'This is the natural expression'; but when 'phassā' or 'phassaṃ' is said, one knows, 'This is not the natural expression.' The same method applies to feeling and so on. But does this person know or not know other sounds such as nouns, verbs, prepositions, and consonants? Insofar as on hearing a sound one knows, 'This is the natural expression; this is not the natural expression,' to that extent one will also know these. But having rejected this with the thought, 'This is not the function of the discriminations,' this story is told:

Tissadattatthero kira bodhimaṇḍe suvaṇṇasalākaṃ gahetvā aṭṭhārasasu bhāsāsu ‘katarabhāsāya kathemī’ti pavāresi. Taṃ pana tena attano uggahe ṭhatvā pavāritaṃ, na paṭisambhidāya ṭhitena. So hi mahāpaññatāya taṃ taṃ bhāsaṃ kathāpetvā kathāpetvā uggaṇhi; tato uggahe ṭhatvā evaṃ pavāresi.

The Elder Tissadatta, it is said, holding a golden stylus at the Bodhi-terrace, invited the assembly in eighteen languages, saying, 'In which language shall I speak?' But this invitation was made by him standing on his own learning, not standing on the discriminations. For, being of great wisdom, he learned each language by having it spoken to him again and again; then, standing on his learning, he made this invitation.

Bhāsaṃ nāma sattā uggaṇhantīti vatvā ca panettha idaṃ kathitaṃ. Mātāpitaro hi daharakāle kumārake mañce vā pīṭhe vā nipajjāpetvā taṃ taṃ kathayamānā tāni tāni kiccāni karonti. Dārakā tesaṃ taṃ taṃ bhāsaṃ vavatthāpenti – iminā idaṃ vuttaṃ, iminā idaṃ vuttanti. Gacchante gacchante kāle sabbampi bhāsaṃ jānanti. Mātā damiḷī, pitā andhako. Tesaṃ jāto dārako sace mātukathaṃ paṭhamaṃ suṇāti, damiḷabhāsaṃ bhāsissati; sace pitukathaṃ paṭhamaṃ suṇāti, andhakabhāsaṃ bhāsissati. Ubhinnampi pana kathaṃ assuṇanto māgadhabhāsaṃ bhāsissati.

And having said, 'Beings learn language,' this is stated here. For parents, in the children's early youth, lay them down on a bed or a chair and do various tasks while speaking this and that. The children determine their various words, thinking: 'By this, this was said; by this, that was said.' As time goes on, they come to know the whole language. Suppose the mother is a Tamil and the father an Andhaka. If their child hears the mother's speech first, it will speak the Tamil language; if it hears the father's speech first, it will speak the Andhaka language. But if it does not hear the speech of either, it will speak the Māgadhī language.

Yopi [V 0.0367] agāmake mahāraññe nibbatto, tattha añño kathento nāma natthi, sopi attano dhammatāya vacanaṃ samuṭṭhāpento māgadhabhāsameva [P 0.0388] bhāsissati. Niraye, tiracchānayoniyaṃ, pettivisaye, manussaloke, devaloketi sabbattha māgadhabhāsāva ussannā. Tattha sesā oṭṭakirātaandhakayonakadamiḷabhāsādikā aṭṭhārasa bhāsā parivattanti[M 0.0372]. Ayamevekā yathābhuccabrahmavohāraariyavohārasaṅkhātā māgadhabhāsā na parivattati. Sammāsabuddhopi tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ tantiṃ āropento māgadhabhāsāya eva āropesi. Kasmā? Evañhi atthaṃ āharituṃ sukhaṃ hoti. Māgadhabhāsāya hi tantiṃ āruḷhassa buddhavacanassa paṭisambhidāppattānaṃ sotapathāgamanameva papañco; sote pana saṅghaṭṭitamatteyeva nayasatena nayasahassena attho upaṭṭhāti. Aññāya pana bhāsāya tantiṃ āruḷhaṃ pothetvā pothetvā uggahetabbaṃ hoti. Bahumpi uggahetvā pana puthujjanassa paṭisambhidāppatti nāma natthi. Ariyasāvako no paṭisambhidāppato nāma natthi.

Even if one is born in a great forest without a village where there is no one else to speak to, that person, by their own nature, will speak only the Māgadhī language when they begin to speak. In hell, the animal realm, the sphere of spirits, the human world, and the deva world—everywhere the Māgadhī language is pre-eminent. There, the other eighteen languages—such as those of the Oṭṭas, Kirātas, Andhakas, Yonakas, and Damiḷas—undergo change. This one language alone, the Māgadhī language, which is known as the true speech, the speech of Brahmā, and the speech of the noble ones, does not change. Even the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, when he established the Tipiṭaka, the Buddha's word, in the textual canon, established it in the Māgadhī language. Why? Because in this way it is easy to convey the meaning. For those who have attained the analytical knowledges, regarding the Buddha's word established in the canon in the Māgadhī language, its mere arrival at the ear is a proliferation; but as soon as it strikes the ear, the meaning presents itself in a hundred, in a thousand ways. But if it is established in the canon in another language, it must be learned by beating it again and again. Even after learning much, a worldling does not attain the analytical knowledges. There is no noble disciple who has not attained the analytical knowledges.

Ñāṇesu ñāṇanti sabbatthakañāṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā ñāṇaṃ paccavekkhantassa pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭibhānapaṭisambhidāti. Imā pana catassopi paṭisambhidā dvīsu ṭhānesu pabhedaṃ gacchanti, pañcahi kāraṇehi visadā hontīti veditabbā. Katamesu dvīsu? Sekkhabhūmiyañca asekkhabhūmiyañca. Tattha sāriputtattherassa mahāmoggallānattherassa mahākassapattherassa mahākaccāyanattherassa mahākoṭṭhitattherassāti asītiyāpi mahātherānaṃ paṭisambhidā asekkhabhūmiyaṃ pabhedaṃ gatā. Ānandattherassa cittassa gahapatino dhammikassa upāsakassa upālissa gahapatino khujjuttarāya upāsikāyāti evamādīnaṃ paṭisambhidā sekkhabhūmiyaṃ pabhedaṃ gatāti imāsu dvīsu bhūmīsu pabhedaṃ gacchanti.

‘Knowledge in knowledges’: this is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity, which is the differentiated knowledge that arises when one reviews knowledge, taking the all-embracing knowledge as object. These four analytical knowledges are differentiated in two planes, and it should be understood that they become clear for five reasons. In which two? In the learner's plane and the non-learner's plane. Therein, the analytical knowledges of the eighty great elders—such as the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita—were differentiated in the non-learner's plane. The analytical knowledges of such persons as the Venerable Ānanda, the householder Citta, the lay follower Dhammika, the householder Upāli, and the lay female follower Khujjuttarā were differentiated in the learner's plane. Thus they are differentiated in these two planes.

Katamehi pañcahi kāraṇehi paṭisambhidā visadā hontīti? Adhigamena, pariyattiyā, savanena, paripucchāya, pubbayogenāti. Tattha ‘adhigamo’ nāma arahattaṃ. Tañhi pattassa paṭisambhidā visadā honti. ‘Pariyatti’ nāma buddhavacanaṃ. Tañhi uggaṇhantassa paṭisambhidā visadā honti. ‘Savanaṃ’ nāma dhammassavanaṃ. Sakkaccañhi dhammaṃ suṇantassa paṭisambhidā [P 0.0389] visadā honti. ‘Paripucchā’ nāma aṭṭhakathā. Uggahitapāḷiyā atthaṃ kathentassa hi paṭisambhidā visadā honti. ‘Pubbayogo’ nāma pubbayogāvacaratā, atītabhave haraṇapaccāharaṇanayena pariggahitakammaṭṭhānatā; pubbayogāvacarassa hi paṭisambhidā visadā honti[V 0.0368]. Tattha arahattappattiyā punabbasukuṭumbikaputtassa tissattherassa paṭisambhidā visadā ahesuṃ. So kira tambapaṇṇidīpe buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā paratīraṃ gantvā yonakadhammarakkhitattherassa santike buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā āgacchanto [M 0.0373] nāvaṃ abhiruhanatitthe ekasmiṃ pade uppannakaṅkho yojanasatamaggaṃ nivattitvā ācariyassa santikaṃ gacchanto antarāmagge ekassa kuṭumbikassa pañhaṃ kathesi. So pasīditvā satasahassagghanikaṃ kambalaṃ adāsi. Sopi taṃ āharitvā ācariyassa adāsi. Thero vāsiyā koṭṭetvā nisīdanaṭṭhāne paribhaṇḍaṃ kāresi. Kimatthāyāti? Pacchimāya janatāya anuggahatthāyāti. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “amhākaṃ gatamaggaṃ āvajjetvā anāgate sabrahmacārino paṭipattiṃ pūretabbaṃ maññissantī”ti. Tissattheropi ācariyassa santike kaṅkhaṃ chinditvā jambukolapaṭṭane oruyha cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ sammajjanavelāya vālikavihāraṃ patvā sammajji. Tassa sammajjitaṭṭhānaṃ disvā ‘idaṃ vītarāgassa bhikkhuno sammaṭṭhaṭṭhāna’nti therassa vīmaṃsanatthāya pañhaṃ pucchiṃsu. Thero paṭisambhidāppattatāya pucchitapucchite pañhe kathesīti.

By what five reasons do the analytical knowledges become clear? By attainment, by learning, by hearing, by questioning, and by previous practice. Herein, 'attainment' means arahantship; for one who has attained it, the analytical knowledges become clear. 'Learning' means the Buddha's word; for one who learns it, the analytical knowledges become clear. 'Hearing' means listening to the Dhamma; for one who listens to the Dhamma attentively, the analytical knowledges become clear. 'Questioning' means explaining the meaning; for one who explains the meaning of the learned Pāli, the analytical knowledges become clear. 'Previous practice' means being accustomed to previous practice, having mastered a meditation subject in a past life by the method of taking it up and reviewing it; for one accustomed to previous practice, the analytical knowledges become clear. Herein, the analytical knowledges of the Elder Tissa, son of a householder from Punabbasu, became clear upon his attainment of arahantship. It is said that after learning the Buddha's word on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, he went to the further shore and learned the Buddha's word in the presence of the Elder Yonaka Dhammarakkhita. While returning, as he was boarding a ship at the landing place, a doubt arose in him about a single word. He turned back along the hundred-yojana path to go to his teacher, and on the way he answered a question for a certain householder. Pleased, the householder gave him a woolen blanket worth a hundred thousand. He took it and gave it to his teacher. The Elder had it cut up with an adze and made into furnishings for the sitting place. For what purpose? For the benefit of future generations. It is said that he thought: 'Reflecting on the path we have taken, our future companions in the holy life will think to fulfill the practice.' The Elder Tissa, having resolved his doubt in the presence of his teacher, disembarked at the port of Jambukola and, arriving at the Sand Monastery at the time for sweeping the cetiya-courtyard, he swept it. Seeing the place he had swept, others thought, 'This is a place swept by a passionless bhikkhu,' and to test the elder, they asked him a question. As he had attained the analytical knowledges, the elder answered every question that was asked.

Pariyattiyā pana tissadattattherassa ceva nāgasenattherassa ca paṭisambhidā visadā ahesuṃ. Sakkaccadhammasavanena sudhammasāmaṇerassa paṭisambhidā visadā ahesuṃ. So kira talaṅgaravāsī dhammadinnattherassa bhāgineyyo khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ patto mātulattherassa dhammavinicchayaṭṭhāne nisīditvā suṇantoyeva tīṇi piṭakāni paguṇāni akāsi. Uggahitapāḷiyā atthaṃ kathentassa pana tissadattattherassa eva paṭisambhidā visadā ahesuṃ. Gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pana pūretvā yāva anulomaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ [P 0.0390] ussukkāpetvā āgatānaṃ visadabhāvappattapaṭisambhidānaṃ pubbayogāvacarānaṃ anto natthi.

Through learning, the analytical knowledges of both the Elder Tissadatta and the Elder Nāgasena became clear. Through attentive listening to the Dhamma, the analytical knowledges of the novice Sudhamma became clear. It is said that he, a resident of Talaṅgara and nephew of the Elder Dhammadinna, attained arahantship as if on a razor's edge. While sitting and just listening in the place where his maternal uncle, the elder, gave decisions on the Dhamma, he mastered the three Piṭakas. For the Elder Tissadatta, too, his analytical knowledges became clear when explaining the meaning of the learned Pāli. As for the previous practitioners who had fulfilled the duty of going and returning and had striven at their meditation subject up to conformity knowledge, there is no limit to those whose analytical knowledges attained a state of clarity.

Etesu pana kāraṇesu pariyatti, savanaṃ, paripucchāti imāni tīṇi pabhedasseva balavakāraṇāni. Pubbayogo adhigamassa balavapaccayo, pabhedassa hoti na hotīti? Hoti, na pana tathā. Pariyattisavanaparipucchā hi pubbe hontu vā mā vā, pubbayogena pubbe ceva etarahi ca saṅkhārasammasanaṃ vinā paṭisambhidā nāma natthi. Ime pana dvepi ekato hutvā paṭisambhidā upatthambhetvā visadā karontīti.

Among these reasons, learning, hearing, and questioning—these three are strong reasons for the analysis. Previous practice is a strong condition for attainment. Is it also a reason for the analysis or not? It is, but not in the same way. For whether learning, hearing, and questioning were present in the past or not, without previous practice and without contemplation of formations both in the past and now, there are no analytical knowledges. But these two—previous practice and attainment—having come together, support the analytical knowledges and make them clear.

Saṅgahavāravaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Summary Chapter.

2. Saccavārādivaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Section on Truth, etc.

719. Idāni [M 0.0374][V 0.0369] ye saṅgahavāre pañca atthā ca dhammā ca saṅgahitā, tesaṃ pabhedadassananayena paṭisambhidā vibhajituṃ puna catassotiādinā nayena pabhedavāro āraddho. So saccavārahetuvāradhammavārapaccayākāravārapariyattivāravasena pañcavidho. Tattha paccayasamuppannassa dukkhasaccassa paccayena pattabbassa nibbānassa ca atthabhāvaṃ, phalanibbattakassa samudayassa nibbānasampāpakassa ariyamaggassa ca dhammabhāvañca dassetuṃ ‘saccavāro’ vutto. Yassa kassaci pana hetuphalanibbattakassa hetuno dhammabhāvaṃ, hetuphalassa ca atthabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ ‘hetuvāro’ vutto. Tattha ca hetuphalakkamavasena uppaṭipāṭiyā paṭhamaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā niddiṭṭhā. Ye pana dhammā tamhā tamhā rūpārūpappabhedā hetuto jātā, tesaṃ atthabhāvaṃ, tassa tassa ca rūpārūpadhammappabhedassa hetuno dhammabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ ‘dhammavāro’ vutto. Jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ pana atthabhāvaṃ, jarāmaraṇādisamudayasaṅkhātānaṃ jātiādīnañca dhammabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ ‘paccayākāravāro’ vutto. Tato pariyattisaṅkhātassa tassa tassa bhāsitassa dhammabhāvaṃ, bhāsitasaṅkhātena paccayena pattabbassa bhāsitatthassa ca atthabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ ‘pariyattivāro’ vutto.

719. Now, concerning the five topics of meaning and phenomena summarized in the Summary Chapter, the Chapter on Analysis has been undertaken in order to analyze the analytical knowledges by the method of showing their distinctions, again by the method beginning 'fourfold.' This chapter is fivefold: the sections on truth, cause, phenomena, the mode of conditions, and textual study. Herein, the 'Section on Truth' is so called to show that the truth of suffering, which is conditionally arisen, and Nibbāna, which is attainable by a condition, have the status of a meaning (or result), and that the origin that produces the fruit and the Noble Path that leads to Nibbāna have the status of a phenomenon (or cause). The 'Section on Cause' is so called to show that any cause that produces a fruit has the status of a phenomenon, and that the fruit of the cause has the status of a meaning. And there, the analytical knowledge of phenomena is explained first, in reverse order, not in the sequence of cause and effect. The 'Section on Phenomena' is so called to show that the various phenomena of form and formlessness born from a cause have the status of a meaning, and that the cause for each of those varieties of phenomena of form and formlessness has the status of a phenomenon. The 'Section on the Mode of Conditions' is so called to show that aging and death, etc., have the status of a meaning, and that birth, etc., which are designated as the origin of aging and death, have the status of a phenomenon. The 'Section on Textual Study' is so called to show that the spoken word designated as the scriptures has the status of a phenomenon, and that the meaning of what is spoken, attainable by the condition of what is spoken, has the status of a meaning.

Tattha ca yasmā bhāsitaṃ ñatvā tassattho ñāyati, tasmā bhāsitabhāsitatthakkamena uppaṭipāṭiyā paṭhamaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā niddiṭṭhā. Pariyattidhammassa ca pabhedadassanatthaṃ “tattha katamā dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti pucchāpubbaṅgamo [P 0.0391] paṭiniddesavāro vutto. Tattha suttantiādīhi navahi aṅgehi nippadesato tanti gahitā. Ayaṃ imassa bhāsitassa attho, ayaṃ imassa bhāsitassa atthoti imasmimpi ṭhāne bhāsitavasena nippadesato tanti eva gahitāti.

And there, because the meaning is known after knowing what is spoken, the analytical knowledge of phenomena is therefore explained first, in reverse order to the sequence of the spoken word and its meaning. To show the distinctions of the Dhamma of the scriptures, the section of detailed explanation is stated, preceded by the question, “Therein, what is the analytical knowledge of phenomena?” Here, the canon is grasped without remainder by the nine limbs beginning with the discourses. In the case of “This is the meaning of this spoken word, this is the meaning of that spoken word,” too, the canon is grasped without remainder by way of what is spoken.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Suttanta Exposition.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Abhidhamma Exposition.

725. Tattha tisso paṭisambhidā lokiyā. Atthapaṭisambhidā lokiyalokuttaramissakā[V 0.0370]. Sā hi nibbānārammaṇānaṃ maggaphalañāṇānaṃ vasena [M 0.0375] lokuttarāpi hoti. Abhidhammabhājanīye kusalākusalavipākakiriyānaṃ vasena catūhi vārehi vibhattaṃ. Tattha yattakāni heṭṭhā cittuppādakaṇḍe (dha. sa. 1 ādayo) kusalacittāni vibhattāni, tesaṃ sabbesampi vasena ekekasmiṃ cittaniddese catasso catasso paṭisambhidā vibhattāti veditabbā. Akusalacittesupi eseva nayo. Vipākakiriyavāresu vipākakiriyānaṃ atthena saṅgahitattā, dhammapaṭisambhidaṃ chaḍḍetvā, ekekasmiṃ vipākacitte ca kiriyacitte ca tisso tissova paṭisambhidā vibhattā. Pāḷi pana mukhamattameva dassetvā saṃkhittā. Sā heṭṭhā āgatavitthāravaseneva veditabbā.

725. Therein, three analytical knowledges are mundane. The analytical knowledge of meaning is mixed, being both mundane and supramundane, for it becomes supramundane by way of the path and fruition knowledges that have Nibbāna as their object. In the Abhidhamma Exposition, the analysis is divided into four sections by way of wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional states. Herein, it should be understood that for as many wholesome consciousnesses as have been analyzed previously in the chapter on the arising of consciousness (Dhammasaṅgaṇī §1ff.), for all of them, four analytical knowledges are analyzed in each explanation of a consciousness. The same method applies to unwholesome consciousnesses. In the sections on resultant and functional states, because they are included by the meaning of resultant and functional, having omitted the analytical knowledge of phenomena, only three analytical knowledges are analyzed in each resultant consciousness and functional consciousness. The Pāli text, however, is abbreviated, showing only an outline. It should be understood by way of the detailed explanation given previously.

Kasmā pana yathā kusalākusalavāresu “tesaṃ vipāke ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti vuttaṃ, evamidha “yesaṃ dhammānaṃ ime vipākā, tesu ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti evaṃ na vuttanti? Heṭṭhā vuttattā. Yadi evaṃ, “tesaṃ vipāke ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti heṭṭhā vuttattā ayaṃ atthapaṭisambhidāpi idha na vattabbā siyāti? No na vattabbā. Kasmā? Heṭṭhā vipākakiriyacittuppādavasena avuttattā. Kiriyavāre ca “yesaṃ dhammānaṃ ime kiriyā”ti vacanameva na yujjatīti dvīsupi imesu vāresu tisso tissova paṭisambhidā vibhattā.

But why, just as in the sections on wholesome and unwholesome states it is said, “Knowledge of their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning,” is it not said here, “Knowledge of those phenomena of which these are the results is the analytical knowledge of phenomena”? Because it was stated previously. If so, since “Knowledge of their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning” was stated previously, should this analytical knowledge of meaning also not be stated here? No, it should be stated. Why? Because it was not stated previously in connection with the arising of resultant and functional consciousnesses. And in the section on functional states, the very statement “those phenomena of which these are the functions” is not appropriate. Thus, in both these sections, only three analytical knowledges are distinguished.

Tattha yāya niruttiyā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ paññatti hotīti yāya niruttiyā tesaṃ phasso hotītiādinā nayena vuttānaṃ dhammānaṃ “ayaṃ phasso, ayaṃ vedanā”ti evaṃ paññatti hoti. Tattha dhammaniruttābhilāpe ñāṇanti tasmiṃ atthe dhamme ca pavattamānāya tassā dhammaniruttiyā sabhāvapaññattiyā abhilāpe ñāṇaṃ. Abhilāpasaddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppannañāṇameva idhāpi kathitaṃ. Yena ñāṇenāti yena paṭibhānapaṭisambhidāñāṇena. Tāni [P 0.0392] ñāṇāni jānātīti itarāni tīṇi paṭisambhidāñāṇāni jānāti.

Herein, regarding the phrase ‘by whatever expression the designation of those phenomena occurs,’ this means that by the method beginning ‘by whatever expression contact occurs,’ the designation of the phenomena spoken of is made thus: ‘This is contact, this is feeling.’ Herein, ‘knowledge in the verbal expression of the language of phenomena’ means knowledge in the verbal expression of that language of phenomena—which is a natural designation—that occurs in regard to that meaning and phenomenon. Here too, what is spoken of is the knowledge that arises having taken the sound of the verbal expression as its object. ‘By which knowledge?’ means by the knowledge that is the analytical knowledge of inspired speech. ‘It knows those knowledges’ means it knows the other three analytical knowledges.

Idāni yathā yaṃ ñāṇaṃ tāni ñāṇāni jānāti, tathā tassa tesu pavattiṃ dassetuṃ imāni ñāṇāni idamatthajotakānīti vuttaṃ. Tattha idamatthajotakānīti imassa atthassa jotakāni pakāsakāni; imaṃ nāma atthaṃ jotenti pakāsenti paricchindantīti attho. Iti ñāṇesu ñāṇanti iminā ākārena pavattaṃ tīsu ñāṇesu ñāṇaṃ paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā nāma.

Now, to show how that knowledge knows those knowledges and thus how it operates in regard to them, it is said: “These knowledges are illuminators of this meaning.” Herein, “illuminators of this meaning” means they are illuminators and revealers of this meaning; the meaning is that they illuminate, reveal, and define this meaning. Thus, “knowledge in knowledges”: the knowledge that operates in this way in regard to the three knowledges is called the analytical knowledge of inspired speech.

Tattha [M 0.0376][V 0.0371] kiñcāpi ayaṃ paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā ‘imissā idaṃ kiccaṃ, imissā idaṃ kicca’nti itarāsaṃ paṭisambhidānaṃ kiccaṃ jānāti, sayaṃ pana tāsaṃ kiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, bahussutadhammakathiko viya appassutadhammakathikassa. Dve kira bhikkhū. Eko bahussuto, eko appassuto. Te ekatova ekaṃ dhammakathāmaggaṃ uggaṇhiṃsu. Tattha appassuto sarasampanno ahosi, itaro mandassaro. Tesu appassuto gatagataṭṭhāne attano sarasampattiyā sakalaparisaṃ khobhetvā dhammaṃ kathesi. Dhammaṃ suṇamānā haṭṭhatuṭṭhamānasā hutvā – ‘yathā esa dhammaṃ kathesi, eko tipiṭakadharo maññe bhavissatī’ti vadanti. Bahussutabhikkhu pana – ‘dhammasavane jānissatha ayaṃ tipiṭakadharo vā no vā’ti āha. So kiñcāpi evamāha, yathā pana sakalaparisaṃ khobhetvā dhammaṃ kathetuṃ sakkoti, evamassa kathanasamatthatā natthi. Tattha kiñcāpi paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā, bahussuto viya appassutassa, itarāsaṃ kiccaṃ jānāti, sayaṃ pana taṃ kiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkotīti veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

Herein, although this analytical knowledge of inspired speech knows the function of the other analytical knowledges, saying, “This is the function of this one, this is the function of that one,” it cannot itself perform their functions—like a learned Dhamma speaker in relation to one who is not learned. There were, it is said, two bhikkhus: one very learned, the other not very learned. They both learned the same method of teaching the Dhamma together. The one who was not very learned was endowed with an eloquent voice, while the other had a poor voice. The one who was not very learned, relying on his eloquence, stirred up the entire assembly and taught the Dhamma wherever he went. Those listening to the Dhamma became delighted and joyful, saying, “From the way he teaches the Dhamma, one would think he is a master of the Tipiṭaka!” But the learned bhikkhu said, “You will know whether or not he is a master of the Tipiṭaka when you listen to the Dhamma.” Although he spoke thus, he did not have the ability to stir up the whole assembly and teach the Dhamma as the other did. Therefore, it should be understood that although the analytical knowledge of inspired speech, like the learned one in relation to the unlearned one, knows the functions of the others, it cannot itself perform those functions. The rest is clear in meaning.

746. Evaṃ kusalacittuppādādivasena paṭisambhidā vibhajitvā idāni tāsaṃ uppattiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ khettaṃ dassetuṃ puna catasso paṭisambhidātiādimāha. Tattha tisso paṭisambhidā kāmāvacarakusalato catūsu ñāṇasampayuttesu cittuppādesūti idaṃ sekkhānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Tesañhipi dhammapaccavekkhaṇakāle heṭṭhā vuttaṃ pañcappakāraṃ dhammaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā catūsu ñāṇasampayuttakusalacittesu dhammapaṭisambhidā uppajjati. Tathā niruttipaccavekkhaṇakāle saddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā niruttipaṭisambhidā; ñāṇaṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle [P 0.0393] sabbatthakañāṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā paṭibhānapaṭisambhidāti.

746. Having thus analyzed the analytical knowledges by way of the arising of wholesome consciousness, etc., now to show the field that is the ground for their arising, the text again says, “Four analytical knowledges,” and so on. Herein, that three analytical knowledges arise from sense-sphere wholesome consciousness in the four consciousnesses associated with knowledge—this is said with reference to trainees. For in their case too, at the time of reviewing the Dhamma, having taken as object the fivefold Dhamma mentioned previously, the analytical knowledge of phenomena arises in the four wholesome consciousnesses associated with knowledge. Similarly, at the time of reviewing language, having taken sound as object, the analytical knowledge of language arises; and at the time of reviewing knowledge, having taken the all-embracing knowledge as object, the analytical knowledge of inspired speech arises.

Kiriyato catūsūti idaṃ pana asekkhānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Tesañhi dhammaṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle heṭṭhā vuttaṃ pañcappakāraṃ dhammaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā catūsu ñāṇasampayuttakiriyacittesu dhammapaṭisambhidā uppajjati. Tathā niruttipaccavekkhaṇakāle saddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā niruttipaṭisambhidā; ñāṇaṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle sabbatthakañāṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā paṭibhānapaṭisambhidāti.

The statement ‘from functional, in the four,’ however, is said with reference to non-trainees. For in their case, at the time of reviewing the Dhamma, having taken as object the fivefold Dhamma mentioned previously, the analytical knowledge of phenomena arises in the four functional consciousnesses associated with knowledge. Similarly, at the time of reviewing language, having taken sound as object, the analytical knowledge of language arises; and at the time of reviewing knowledge, having taken the all-embracing knowledge as object, the analytical knowledge of perspicuity arises.

Atthapaṭisambhidā etesu ceva uppajjatīti idaṃ pana sekkhāsekkhānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Tathā hi sekkhānaṃ atthapaccavekkhaṇakāle heṭṭhā vuttappabhedaṃ atthaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā catūsu ñāṇasampayuttakusalacittesu ayaṃ [M 0.0377] uppajjati, maggaphalakāle ca maggaphalesu. Asekkhassa pana atthaṃ [V 0.0372] paccavekkhaṇakāle heṭṭhā vuttappabhedameva atthaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā catūsu ñāṇasampayuttakiriyacittesu uppajjati, phalakāle ca uparime sāmaññaphaleti. Evametā sekkhāsekkhānaṃ uppajjamānā imāsu bhūmīsu uppajjantīti bhūmidassanatthaṃ ayaṃ nayo dassitoti.

The statement ‘The analytical knowledge of meaning arises in these as well’ is said with reference to trainees and non-trainees. For in the case of trainees, at the time of reviewing the meaning, having taken as object the meaning with its divisions as spoken of previously, this arises in the four wholesome consciousnesses associated with knowledge, and at the time of path and fruition, in the path and fruition states. For a non-trainee, at the time of reviewing the meaning, having taken as object the very same meaning with its divisions as spoken of previously, it arises in the four functional consciousnesses associated with knowledge, and at the time of fruition, in the higher fruit of asceticism. Thus, this method is shown to illustrate the planes, indicating that when these analytical knowledges arise for trainees and non-trainees, they arise in these planes.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Abhidhamma Section.

3. Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Question Section.

747. Pañhāpucchake pāḷianusāreneva catunnaṃ paṭisambhidānaṃ kusalādibhāvo veditabbo. Ārammaṇattikesu pana niruttipaṭisambhidā saddameva ārammaṇaṃ karotīti parittārammaṇā. Atthapaṭisambhidā kāmāvacaravipākakiriyasaṅkhātañceva paccayasamuppannañca atthaṃ paccavekkhantassa parittārammaṇā; vuttappabhedameva rūpāvacarārūpāvacaraṃ atthaṃ paccavekkhantassa mahaggatārammaṇā; lokuttaravipākatthañceva paramatthañca nibbānaṃ paccavekkhantassa appamāṇārammaṇā. Dhammapaṭisambhidā kāmāvacaraṃ kusaladhammaṃ akusaladhammaṃ paccayadhammañca paccavekkhantassa parittārammaṇā; rūpāvacarārūpāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paccayadhammañca paccavekkhantassa mahaggatārammaṇā[P 0.0394]; lokuttaraṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paccayadhammañca paccavekkhantassa appamāṇārammaṇā. Paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā kāmāvacarakusalavipākakiriyañāṇāni paccavekkhantassa parittārammaṇā; rūpāvacarārūpāvacarāni kusalavipākakiriyañāṇāni paccavekkhantassa tesaṃ ārammaṇāni vijānantassa mahaggatārammaṇā; lokuttarāni kusalavipākañāṇāni paccavekkhantassa appamāṇārammaṇā.

747. In the Question Section, the nature of the four analytical knowledges as skillful, etc., should be understood in accordance with the Pāḷi text. Now, in the triads concerning the object, the analytical knowledge of language takes only sound as its object; thus, it has a limited object. The analytical knowledge of meaning, for one reviewing the meaning designated as sense-sphere resultant and functional and the dependently arisen, has a limited object; for one reviewing the meaning of the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere of the kind already mentioned, it has a sublime object; for one reviewing the supramundane resultant meaning and the ultimate meaning, Nibbāna, it has an immeasurable object. The analytical knowledge of phenomena, for one reviewing sense-sphere skillful phenomena, unskillful phenomena, and conditional phenomena, has a limited object; for one reviewing fine-material-sphere and immaterial-sphere skillful phenomena and conditional phenomena, it has a sublime object; for one reviewing supramundane skillful phenomena and conditional phenomena, it has an immeasurable object. The analytical knowledge of perspicuity, for one reviewing the knowledges of sense-sphere skillful, resultant, and functional states, has a limited object; for one reviewing the knowledges of fine-material-sphere and immaterial-sphere skillful, resultant, and functional states, while understanding their objects, it has a sublime object; for one reviewing supramundane skillful and resultant knowledges, it has an immeasurable object.

Atthapaṭisambhidā sahajātahetuvasena siyā maggahetukā, vīriyajeṭṭhikāya maggabhāvanāya siyā maggādhipati, chandacittajeṭṭhikāya navattabbā, phalakālepi navattabbā eva. Dhammapaṭisambhidā maggaṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle maggārammaṇā, maggaṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa ārammaṇādhipativasena maggādhipati. Paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā maggañāṇaṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle maggārammaṇā, maggaṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa maggādhipati, sesañāṇaṃ pañcavekkhaṇakāle navattabbārammaṇā[M 0.0378][V 0.0373]. Niruttipaṭisambhidā paccuppannameva saddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karotīti paccuppannārammaṇā.

The analytical knowledge of meaning may have the path as its root-condition by way of the conascence condition; in the development of the path with energy as predominant, it may have the path as its dominant condition; with desire or consciousness as predominant, it is unstatable; and at the time of fruition, too, it is unstatable. The analytical knowledge of phenomena, when reviewing the path, has the path as its object; for one who reviews it giving prominence to the path, it has the path as its dominant condition by way of object-predominance. The analytical knowledge of perspicuity, when reviewing path-knowledge, has the path as its object; for one who reviews it giving prominence to the path, it has the path as its dominant condition; when reviewing the remaining knowledges, it has an unstatable object. The analytical knowledge of language takes only a present sound as its object, thus it has a present object.

Atthapaṭisambhidā atītaṃ vipākatthaṃ kiriyatthaṃ paccayasamuppannañca paccavekkhantassa atītārammaṇā, anāgataṃ paccavekkhantassa anāgatārammaṇā, paccuppannaṃ paccavekkhantassa paccuppannārammaṇā, lokuttaraṃ paramatthaṃ paccavekkhantassa navattabbārammaṇā. Dhammapaṭisambhidā atītaṃ kusalaṃ akusalaṃ paccayadhammañca paccavekkhantassa atītārammaṇā, anāgataṃ paccavekkhantassa anāgatārammaṇā, paccuppannaṃ paccavekkhantassa paccuppannārammaṇā. Paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā atītaṃ kusalañāṇaṃ vipākañāṇaṃ kiriyañāṇañca paccavekkhantassa atītārammaṇā, anāgataṃ paccavekkhantassa anāgatārammaṇā, paccuppannaṃ paccavekkhantassa paccuppannārammaṇā.

The analytical knowledge of meaning, for one reviewing past resultant meaning, functional meaning, and the dependently arisen, has a past object; for one reviewing the future, it has a future object; for one reviewing the present, it has a present object; for one reviewing the supramundane ultimate meaning, it has an unstatable object. The analytical knowledge of phenomena, for one reviewing past skillful, unskillful, and conditional phenomena, has a past object; for one reviewing the future, it has a future object; for one reviewing the present, it has a present object. The analytical knowledge of perspicuity, for one reviewing past skillful knowledge, resultant knowledge, and functional knowledge, has a past object; for one reviewing the future, it has a future object; for one reviewing the present, it has a present object.

Niruttipaṭisambhidā saddārammaṇattā bahiddhārammaṇā. Itarāsu tīsu atthapaṭisambhidā ajjhattaṃ vipākatthaṃ kiriyatthaṃ paccayasamuppannañca paccavekkhantassa ajjhattārammaṇā, bahiddhā paccavekkhantassa bahiddhārammaṇā, ajjhattabahiddhā paccavekkhantassa ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā[P 0.0395], paramatthaṃ paccavekkhantassa bahiddhārammaṇā eva. Dhammapaṭisambhidā ajjhattaṃ kusalākusalaṃ paccayadhammaṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle ajjhattārammaṇā, bahiddhā kusalākusalaṃ paccayadhammaṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle bahiddhārammaṇā, ajjhattabahiddhā kusalākusalaṃ paccayadhammaṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā. Paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā ajjhattaṃ kusalavipākakiriyañāṇaṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle ajjhattārammaṇā, bahiddhā…pe… ajjhattabahiddhā kusalavipākakiriyañāṇaṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇāti.

The analytical knowledge of language, since it has sound as its object, has an external object. Among the other three, the analytical knowledge of meaning, for one reviewing internally the resultant meaning, the functional meaning, and the dependently arisen, has an internal object; for one reviewing externally, it has an external object; for one reviewing internally and externally, it has an internal-and-external object; for one reviewing the ultimate meaning, it has only an external object. The analytical knowledge of phenomena, when reviewing internally skillful and unskillful phenomena and conditional phenomena, has an internal object; when reviewing them externally, it has an external object; when reviewing them internally and externally, it has an internal-and-external object. The analytical knowledge of perspicuity, when reviewing internally the knowledges of skillful, resultant, and functional states, has an internal object; when reviewing them externally ... and when reviewing them internally and externally, it has an internal-and-external object.

Idhāpi tisso paṭisambhidā lokiyā; atthapaṭisambhidā lokiyalokuttarā. Imasmiñhi paṭisambhidāvibhaṅge sammāsambuddhena tayopi nayā lokiyalokuttaramissakattā ekaparicchedāva kathitā. Tīsupi hi etāsu tisso paṭisambhidā lokiyā, atthapaṭisambhidā lokiyalokuttarāti. Evamayaṃ paṭisambhidāvibhaṅgopi teparivaṭṭaṃ nīharitvāva bhājetvā dassitoti.

Here too, three analyses are mundane; the analysis of meaning is mundane and supramundane. For in this Analysis of the Analyses, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One has explained all three methods as a single section because they are a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane. For in all three of these methods, three analyses are mundane, while the analysis of meaning is mundane and supramundane. Thus this Analysis of the Analyses, too, is explained by dividing it after bringing out the three rounds.

Sammohavinodaniyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya

In the Sammohavinodanī, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga.

Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Analysis of the Analyses is concluded.

16. Ñāṇavibhaṅgo

16. The Analysis of Knowledge

1. Ekakamātikādivaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Matrix of Single Items and Others

751. Idāni [P 0.0396][M 0.0379][V 0.0374] tadanantare ñāṇavibhaṅge ekavidhena ñāṇavatthūtiādinā nayena paṭhamaṃ ekavidhādīhi dasavidhapariyosānehi dasahi paricchedehi mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā nikkhittapadānukkamena niddeso kato.

751. Now, immediately following that, in the Analysis of Knowledge, the exposition has been made according to the sequence of the terms set down in the matrix, which is first established by ten sections—beginning with the onefold and culminating in the tenfold classification—in accordance with the method that starts, “the basis of knowledge in one way.”

Tattha ekavidhenāti ekappakārena, ekakoṭṭhāsena vā. Ñāṇavatthūti ettha pana ñāṇañca taṃ vatthu ca nānappakārānaṃ sampattīnanti ñāṇavatthu; okāsaṭṭhena ñāṇassa vatthūtipi ñāṇavatthu.
