Idha pana purimenevatthena ñāṇavatthu veditabbaṃ. Teneva ekavidhaparicchedāvasāne “yāthāvakavatthuvibhāvanā paññā – evaṃ ekavidhena ñāṇavatthū”ti vuttaṃ. Pañca viññāṇāti cakkhuviññāṇādīni pañca. Na hetūtiādīni heṭṭhā dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1.6) vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Saṅkhepato panettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ taṃ niddesavāre āvi bhavissati. Yathā cettha, evaṃ dukamātikādipadesupi yaṃ vattabbaṃ taṃ tattheva āvi bhavissati. Nikkhepaparicchedamattaṃ panettha evaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ettha hi “na hetu ahetukā”tiādīhi tāva dhammasaṅgahamātikāvasena, “aniccā jarābhibhūtā”tiādīhi amātikāvasenāti saṅkhepato duvidhehi pabhedato aṭṭhasattatiyā padehi ekakamātikā nikkhittā.

Herein, 'in one way' means in a single manner, or as one portion. As to 'basis of knowledge': here, that knowledge is the basis for various kinds of attainments, thus it is a 'basis of knowledge.' Or, it is the basis for knowledge in the sense of being an occasion, thus it is a 'basis of knowledge.' Here, however, 'basis of knowledge' should be understood in the former sense. For that reason, at the end of the section on the onefold classification, it is said: 'Wisdom that makes clear the basis as it really is—thus, the basis of knowledge in one way.' 'The five consciousnesses' are the five beginning with eye-consciousness. The terms beginning with 'not a root' should be understood in the way stated in the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī (Dhs-A 1.6). What needs to be said here in brief will become clear in the exposition section. Just as here, so too in the passages on the matrix of dyads, etc., whatever needs to be said will become clear right there. Here, only the extent of the classification should be understood thus. For here, the matrix of single items is set down with seventy-eight terms, classified briefly in two ways: by way of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī matrix with terms like 'not a root, rootless,' and by way of what is not in the matrix with terms like 'impermanent, overcome by aging.'

Dukānurūpehi pana pañcatiṃsāya dukehi dukamātikā nikkhittā.

The matrix of dyads, however, is set down with thirty-five corresponding dyads.

Tikānurūpehi “cintāmayā paññā”tiādīhi catūhi bāhirattikehi, “vipākā paññā”tiādīhi [V 0.0375] aniyamitapaññāvasena vuttehi cuddasahi mātikātikehi, vitakkattike paṭhamapadena niyamitapaññāvasena vuttehi terasahi, dutiyapadena niyamitapaññāvasena vuttehi sattahi, tatiyapadena niyamitapaññāvasena vuttehi dvādasahi, pītittike ca paṭhamapadena niyamitapaññāvasena vuttehi terasahi, tathā dutiyapadena, tatiyapadena niyamitapaññāvasena vuttehi dvādasahīti aṭṭhāsītiyā tikehi tikamātikā nikkhittā.

The matrix of triplets is set down with eighty-eight corresponding triplets: with four external triplets such as “wisdom born of reflection”; with fourteen matrix triplets such as “resultant wisdom,” stated in terms of indeterminate wisdom; with thirteen triplets stated in terms of determinate wisdom by the first term of the triplet on thought-conception, seven by its second term, and twelve by its third term; and in the triplet on rapture, with thirteen triplets stated in terms of determinate wisdom by its first term, and similarly twelve each by its second and third terms.

Catukkamātikā [P 0.0397][M 0.0380] pana ‘kammassakatañāṇa’ntiādīhi ekavīsatiyā catukkehi, pañcakamātikā dvīhi pañcakehi, chakkamātikā ekena chakkena, sattakamātikā “sattasattati ñāṇavatthūnī”ti evaṃ saṅkhepato vuttehi ekādasahi sattakehi, aṭṭhakamātikā ekena aṭṭhakena, navakamātikā ekena navakena.

The matrix of tetrads, however, is set down with twenty-one tetrads beginning with 'knowledge of ownership of kamma'; the matrix of pentads with two pentads; the matrix of hexads with one hexad; the matrix of heptads with eleven heptads, stated concisely as 'seventy-seven bases of knowledge'; the matrix of octads with one octad; and the matrix of nonads with one nonad.

10. Dasakamātikāvaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Matrix of Decads

760. Dasakamātikā “dasa tathāgatassa tathāgatabalānī”tiādinā ekeneva dasakena nikkhittā. Tattha dasāti gaṇanaparicchedo. Tathāgatassāti yathā vipassīādayo pubbakā isayo āgatā tathā āgatassa; yathā ca te gatā tathā gatassa. Tathāgatabalānīti aññehi asādhāraṇāni tathāgatasseva balāni; yathā vā pubbabuddhānaṃ balāni puññussayasampattiyā āgatāni tathā āgatabalānītipi attho. Tattha duvidhaṃ tathāgatassa balaṃ – kāyabalañca ñāṇabalañca. Tesu kāyabalaṃ hatthikulānusāreneva veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ porāṇehi –

760. The matrix of decads is set down with a single decad beginning with “the ten Tathāgata-powers of the Tathāgata.” Herein, “ten” is a numerical determination. “Of the Tathāgata” means: he has come (āgata) in the same way (tathā) as the former seers such as Vipassī came; and he has gone (gata) in the same way (tathā) as they went. “The Tathāgata-powers” are powers belonging only to the Tathāgata, not shared with others. Or the meaning is “powers that have come about” (āgatabalāni), just as the powers of previous Buddhas came about through the accomplishment of an abundance of merit. The Tathāgata’s power is twofold: bodily power and knowledge-power. Of these, bodily power should be understood in accordance with the elephant clans. For this was stated by the ancients:

Kāḷāvakañca gaṅgeyyaṃ, paṇḍaraṃ tambapiṅgalaṃ;

Gandhamaṅgalahemañca, uposathachaddantime dasāti. –

Kāḷāvaka and Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tamba, Piṅgala; Gandha, Maṅgala, and Hema, Uposatha, Chaddanta—these ten.

Imāni hi dasa hatthikulāni.

For these are the ten elephant clans.

Tattha ‘kāḷāvaka’nti pakatihatthikulaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yaṃ dasannaṃ purisānaṃ kāyabalaṃ taṃ ekassa kāḷāvakahatthino. Yaṃ dasannaṃ kāḷāvakānaṃ balaṃ taṃ ekassa gaṅgeyassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ gaṅgeyyānaṃ taṃ ekassa paṇḍarassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ paṇḍarānaṃ taṃ ekassa tambassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ tambānaṃ taṃ ekassa [V 0.0376] piṅgalassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ piṅgalānaṃ taṃ ekassa gandhahatthino. Yaṃ dasannaṃ gandhahatthīnaṃ taṃ ekassa maṅgalassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ maṅgalānaṃ taṃ ekassa hemavatassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ hemavatānaṃ taṃ ekassa uposathassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ uposathānaṃ taṃ ekassa chaddantassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ chaddantānaṃ taṃ ekassa tathāgatassa. Nārāyanasaṅkhātabalantipi idameva vuccati. Tadetaṃ pakatihatthīnaṃ [M 0.0381] gaṇanāya hatthikoṭisahassānaṃ, purisagaṇanāya dasannaṃ purisakoṭisahassānaṃ balaṃ hoti. Idaṃ tāva tathāgatassa kāyabalaṃ.

Herein, ‘Kāḷāvaka’ should be seen as the ordinary elephant clan. The bodily strength of ten men is that of one Kāḷāvaka elephant. The strength of ten Kāḷāvaka elephants is that of one Gaṅgeyya. The strength of ten Gaṅgeyyas is that of one Paṇḍara. The strength of ten Paṇḍaras is that of one Tamba. The strength of ten Tambas is that of one Piṅgala. The strength of ten Piṅgalas is that of one Gandha elephant. The strength of ten Gandha elephants is that of one Maṅgala. The strength of ten Maṅgalas is that of one Hemavata. The strength of ten Hemavatas is that of one Uposatha. The strength of ten Uposathas is that of one Chaddanta. The strength of ten Chaddantas is that of one Tathāgata. This is also called the strength reckoned as Nārāyaṇa’s. By the count of ordinary elephants, this is the strength of a thousand koṭis of elephants; by the count of men, it is the strength of ten thousand koṭis of men. This, for a start, is the Tathāgata’s bodily power.

Ñāṇabalaṃ [P 0.0398] pana idha tāva pāḷiyaṃ āgatameva dasabalañāṇaṃ. Mahāsīhanāde (ma. ni. 1.146 ādayo) dasabalañāṇaṃ, catuvesārajjañāṇaṃ, aṭṭhasu parisāsu akampanañāṇaṃ, catuyoniparicchedakañāṇaṃ, pañcagatiparicchedakañāṇaṃ, saṃyuttake (saṃ. ni. 2.33-34) āgatāni tesattati ñāṇāni, sattasattati ñāṇānīti evaṃ aññānipi anekāni ñāṇasahassāni – etaṃ ñāṇabalaṃ nāma. Idhāpi ñāṇabalameva adhippetaṃ ñāṇañhi akampiyaṭṭhena upatthambhakaṭṭhena ca balanti vuttaṃ.

The power of knowledge, however, is here, to begin with, the knowledge of the ten powers that has come down in the Pāli. In the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, there is the knowledge of the ten powers, the knowledge of the four kinds of confidence, the knowledge of being unshaken in the eight assemblies, the knowledge that distinguishes the four kinds of birth, and the knowledge that distinguishes the five destinations; in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, there are the seventy-three knowledges and the seventy-seven knowledges—and thus many other thousands of knowledges. This is what is called the power of knowledge. Here too, it is the power of knowledge that is intended, for knowledge is called 'power' because of its quality of being unshakable and its quality of being a support.

Yehi balehi samannāgatoti yehi dasahi ñāṇabalehi upeto samupeto. Āsabhaṃ ṭhānanti seṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ uttamaṭṭhānaṃ; āsabhā vā pubbabuddhā, tesaṃ ṭhānanti attho. Api ca gavasatajeṭṭhako usabho, gavasahassajeṭṭhako vasabho; vajasatajeṭṭhako vā usabho, vajasahassajeṭṭhako vasabho; sabbagavaseṭṭho sabbaparissayasaho seto pāsādiko mahābhāravaho asanisatasaddehipi akampanīyo nisabho. So idha usabhoti adhippeto. Idampi hi tassa pariyāyavacanaṃ. Usabhassa idanti āsabhaṃ. Ṭhānanti catūhi pādehi pathaviṃ uppīḷetvā acalaṭṭhānaṃ. Idaṃ pana āsabhaṃ viyāti āsabhaṃ. Yatheva hi nisabhasaṅkhāto usabho usabhabalena samannāgato catūhi pādehi pathaviṃ uppīḷetvā acalaṭṭhānena tiṭṭhati, evaṃ tathāgatopi dasahi tathāgatabalehi samannāgato catūhi vesārajjapādehi aṭṭhaparisapathaviṃ uppīḷetvā sadevake loke kenaci paccatthikena paccāmittena akampiyo acalaṭṭhānena tiṭṭhati. Evaṃ tiṭṭhamāno ca taṃ āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, upagacchati, na paccakkhāti, attani āropeti. Tena vuttaṃ “āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānātī”ti.

‘Endowed with which powers’ means endowed, fully endowed with those ten powers of knowledge. ‘The bull’s position’ means the best position, the supreme position; or, the former Buddhas were bulls (āsabhā), so the meaning is their position. Moreover, the chief of a hundred cows is an usabha; the chief of a thousand cows is a vasabha. Or, the chief of a hundred herds is an usabha; the chief of a thousand herds is a vasabha. The supreme bull of all cattle—who endures all adversities, is white, majestic, a great bearer of burdens, and unshakable even by the sound of a hundred thunderbolts—is a nisabha. It is this one that is intended here by usabha, for this is a synonym for it. Āsabhaṃ means ‘belonging to the bull (usabha).’ ‘Position’ means an unshakable standing, pressing down on the earth with four feet. But this is āsabhaṃ because it is ‘like a bull’ (āsabhaṃ viya). For just as the bull called nisabha, endowed with a bull’s strength, stands in an unshakable position, pressing down on the earth with its four feet, so the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten Tathāgata-powers, stands in an unshakable position, unshaken by any adversary or foe in this world with its gods, pressing down on the earth of the eight assemblies with his four feet of the confidences. And standing thus, he claims that bull’s position, resorts to it, does not repudiate it, and applies it to himself. Therefore it is said, ‘he claims the bull’s position.’

Parisāsūti aṭṭhasu parisāsu. Sīhanādaṃ nadatīti seṭṭhanādaṃ abhītanādaṃ nadati, sīhanādasadisaṃ [V 0.0377] vā nādaṃ nadati. Ayamattho sīhanādasuttena dīpetabbo. Yathā vā sīho sahanato ca hananato ca sīhoti vuccati, evaṃ tathāgato lokadhammānaṃ sahanato [M 0.0382] parappavādānañca hananato sīhoti vuccati. Evaṃ vuttassa sīhassa nādaṃ sīhanādaṃ. Tattha [P 0.0399] yathā sīho sīhabalena samannāgato sabbattha visārado vigatalomahaṃso sīhanādaṃ nadati, evaṃ tathāgatasīhopi tathāgatabalehi samannāgato aṭṭhasu parisāsu visārado vigatalomahaṃso “iti rūpa”ntiādinā nayena nānāvidhadesanāvilāsasampannaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadati. Tena vuttaṃ “parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadatī”ti.

‘In the assemblies’ means in the eight assemblies. ‘He roars a lion’s roar’ means he utters the supreme roar, the fearless roar, or he utters a roar like a lion’s. This meaning should be illustrated by way of the Sīhanāda Sutta. Just as a lion (sīha) is so called because it endures (sahanato) and because it strikes (hananato), so the Tathāgata is called a lion (sīha) because he endures worldly states and because he strikes down the doctrines of others. The roar of a lion so called is a lion’s roar. Herein, just as a lion, endowed with a lion’s strength, roars its lion’s roar everywhere with confidence and without bristling fur, so the Tathāgata-lion, endowed with the Tathāgata-powers, roars his lion’s roar in the eight assemblies with confidence and without bristling fur, a roar endowed with the grace of manifold teachings, in the manner of ‘Such is form….’ Therefore it is said, ‘he roars a lion’s roar in the assemblies.’

Brahmacakkaṃ pavattetīti ettha brahmanti seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ visuddhaṃ. Cakkasaddo ca panāyaṃ –

‘He sets the Brahma-wheel in motion’: Herein, ‘brahma’ means best, supreme, pure. And this word ‘wheel’ (cakka)—

Sampattiyaṃ lakkhaṇe ca, rathaṅge iriyāpathe;

Dāne ratanadhammūra, cakkādīsu ca dissati;

Dhammacakke idha mato, tañca dvedhā vibhāvaye.

It is seen in the sense of accomplishment and characteristic, chariot-wheel and posture; giving, the jewel, the Dhamma, the thigh, and the discus weapon, etc. Here it is intended as the Dhamma-wheel, and that should be explained in two ways.

“Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, cakkāni yehi samannāgatānaṃ devamanussāna”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 4.31) hi ayaṃ sampattiyaṃ dissati. “Heṭṭhā pādatalesu cakkāni jātānī”ti (dī. ni. 2.35) ettha lakkhaṇe. “Cakkaṃva vahato pada”nti (dha. pa. 1) ettha rathaṅge. “Catucakkaṃ navadvāra”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.29) ettha iriyāpathe. “Dadaṃ bhuñja mā ca pamādo, cakkaṃ pavattaya sabbapāṇina”nti (jā. 1.7.149) ettha dāne. “Dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pāturahosī”ti ettha ratanacakke. “Mayā pavattitaṃ cakka”nti (su. ni. 562) ettha dhammacakke. “Icchāhatassa posassa cakkaṃ bhamati matthake”ti (jā. 1.1.104; 1.5.103) ettha uracakke. “Khurapariyantena cepi cakkenā”ti (dī. ni. 1.166) ettha paharaṇacakke. “Asanivicakka”nti (dī. ni. 3.61; saṃ. ni. 2.162) ettha asanimaṇḍale. Idha panāyaṃ dhammacakke mato.

In such passages as, “These four wheels, bhikkhus, are possessed by gods and humans…” (AN 4.31), it is seen in the sense of an accomplishment. In, “Wheels are born on the soles of the feet” (DN 30), it refers to a mark. In, “Like the wheel following the foot of the ox” (Dhp 1), it refers to a chariot's wheel. In, “Four-wheeled and nine-gated” (SN 1.29), it refers to the postures. In, “Give, enjoy, and be not heedless; turn the wheel for all living beings” (Ja 1.7.149), it refers to giving. In, “The divine wheel-treasure appeared,” it refers to the jewel-wheel. In, “The wheel set in motion by me” (Snp 3.12), it refers to the Dhamma-wheel. In, “The wheel spins on the head of a man overcome by desire” (Ja 1.1.104; 1.5.103), it refers to a torture-wheel. In, “Even if with a razor-edged wheel” (DN 1.166), it refers to a weapon-wheel. In, “The thunderbolt-wheel” (DN 3.61; SN 2.162), it refers to a circle of lightning. Here, however, it is intended as the Dhamma-wheel.

Taṃ pana dhammacakkaṃ duvidhaṃ hoti – paṭivedhañāṇañca desanāñāṇañca. Tattha paññāpabhāvitaṃ attano ariyaphalāvahaṃ paṭivedhañāṇaṃ; karuṇāpabhāvitaṃ sāvakānaṃ ariyaphalāvahaṃ desanāñāṇaṃ. Tattha paṭivedhañāṇaṃ uppajjamānaṃ uppannanti duvidhaṃ. Tañhi abhinikkhamanato [V 0.0378] yāva arahattamaggā uppajjamānaṃ[M 0.0383], phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāma; tusitabhavanato vā yāva mahābodhipallaṅke arahattamaggā uppajjamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāma; dīpaṅkarabyākaraṇato paṭṭhāya vā yāva arahattamaggā uppajjamānaṃ[P 0.0400], phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāma. Desanāñāṇampi pavattamānaṃ pavattanti duvidhaṃ. Tañhi yāva aññākoṇḍaññassa sotāpattimaggā pavattamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe pavattaṃ nāma. Tesu paṭivedhañāṇaṃ lokuttaraṃ, desanāñāṇaṃ lokiyaṃ. Ubhayampi panetaṃ aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ buddhānaṃyeva orasañāṇaṃ.

That Dhamma-wheel is twofold: the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching. Herein, the knowledge of penetration, produced by wisdom, brings the noble fruit to oneself; the knowledge of teaching, produced by compassion, brings the noble fruit to the disciples. Herein, the knowledge of penetration is twofold: arising and arisen. For it is arising from the great renunciation up to the path of arahantship, and at the moment of fruition, it is called arisen. Or it is arising from the Tusita heaven up to the path of arahantship at the seat of great awakening, and at the moment of fruition, it is called arisen. Or starting from the prophecy of Dīpaṅkara up to the path of arahantship, it is arising, and at the moment of fruition, it is called arisen. The knowledge of teaching is also twofold: occurring and occurred. For it is occurring up to the path of stream-entry for Aññākoṇḍañña, and at the moment of fruition, it is called occurred. Of these, the knowledge of penetration is supramundane, while the knowledge of teaching is mundane. Yet both of these are unique to the Buddhas alone, their own special knowledge.

Idāni yehi dasahi balehi samannāgato tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, yāni āditova “dasa tathāgatassa tathāgatabalānī”ti nikkhittāni, tāni vitthārato dassetuṃ katamāni dasa? Idha tathāgato ṭhānañca ṭhānatotiādimāha. Tattha ṭhānañca ṭhānatoti kāraṇañca kāraṇato. Kāraṇañhi yasmā tattha phalaṃ tiṭṭhati tadāyattavuttitāya uppajjati ceva pavattati ca, tasmā ṭhānanti vuccati. Taṃ bhagavā “ye ye dhammā yesaṃ yesaṃ dhammānaṃ hetū paccayā uppādāya taṃ taṃ ṭhāna”nti ca ‘ye ye dhammā yesaṃ yesaṃ dhammānaṃ na hetū na paccayā uppādāya taṃ taṃ aṭṭhāna’nti ca pajānanto ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Yampīti yena ñāṇena. Idampi tathāgatassāti idampi ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇaṃ tathāgatassa tathāgatabalaṃ nāma hotīti attho. Evaṃ sabbapadesu yojanā veditabbā.

Now, to explain in detail the ten powers with which the Tathāgata is endowed when he claims the leader's place—those that were stated at the outset as “the ten powers of a Tathāgata”—what are the ten? Herein, the Tathāgata speaks of “the possible as possible,” and so on. Therein, “the possible as possible” means “cause as cause.” For since the fruit stands therein, its existence being dependent on it, it both arises and continues; therefore, the cause is called “the possible.” The Blessed One, knowing, “Whatever things are the cause and condition for the arising of whatever other things, that is the possible,” and “Whatever things are not the cause or condition for the arising of whatever other things, that is the impossible,” understands as it actually is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible. The phrase `yampi` means 'by which knowledge.' The phrase 'this too is the Tathāgata’s' means that this knowledge of the possible and impossible is called a power of the Tathāgata. The application should be understood in all instances in this way.

Kammasamādānānanti samādiyitvā katānaṃ kusalākusalakammānaṃ; kammameva vā kammasamādānaṃ. Ṭhānaso hetusoti paccayato ceva hetuto ca. Tattha gatiupadhikālapayogā vipākassa ṭhānaṃ, kammaṃ hetu.

“Of undertakings of kamma” means of the wholesome and unwholesome kammas done after having undertaken them; or kamma itself is the undertaking of kamma. “As to ground and cause” means as to condition and as to cause. Herein, the destination, basis, time, and means are the ground for the result; kamma is the cause.

Sabbattha gāmininti sabbagatigāminiñca agatigāminiñca. Paṭipadanti maggaṃ. Yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti bahūsupi manussesu ekameva pāṇaṃ ghātentesu ‘imassa cetanā nirayagāminī bhavissati, imassa tiracchānayonigāminī’ti iminā nayena ekavatthusmimpi kusalākusalacetanāsaṅkhātānaṃ paṭipattīnaṃ aviparītato sabhāvaṃ pajānāti.

“Leading everywhere” means leading to all destinations and to that which is not a destination. “The path” means the way. “He understands as it actually is” means that even when many people kill a single living being, he knows: “This one’s intention will lead to hell, this one’s will lead to the animal realm.” In this way, even in a single case, he understands without distortion the true nature of the paths, which are designated as wholesome and unwholesome intentions.

Anekadhātunti [P 0.0401][M 0.0384] cakkhudhātuādīhi kāmadhātuādīhi vā dhātūhi bahudhātuṃ. Nānādhātunti tāsaṃyeva [V 0.0379] dhātūnaṃ vilakkhaṇatāya nānappakāradhātuṃ. Lokanti khandhāyatanadhātulokaṃ. Yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti tāsaṃ tāsaṃ dhātūnaṃ aviparītato sabhāvaṃ paṭivijjhati.

“The world of many elements” means having many elements, due to the elements such as the eye element and so on, or the desire-realm element and so on. “The world of various elements” means having various kinds of elements, due to the distinct characteristics of those same elements. “The world” means the world of aggregates, sense bases, and elements. “He understands as it really is” means he penetrates without distortion the true nature of those various elements.

Nānādhimuttikatanti hīnādīhi adhimuttīhi nānādhimuttikabhāvaṃ.

“The diversity of inclinations” means the state of having diverse inclinations due to inclinations that are inferior, and so on.

Parasattānanti padhānasattānaṃ. Parapuggalānanti tato paresaṃ hīnasattānaṃ; ekatthameva vā etaṃ padadvayaṃ veneyyavasena pana dvedhā vuttaṃ. Indriyaparopariyattanti saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ parabhāvañca aparabhāvañca vuḍḍhiñca hāniñcāti attho.

“Of other beings” means of principal beings. “Of other individuals” means of inferior beings other than those; or these two terms have the same meaning, but are stated in two ways on account of the trainees. “The superiority and inferiority of the faculties” means the superiority and inferiority, the increase and decrease, of the faculties such as faith and so on.

Jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnanti paṭhamādīnaṃ catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ, “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādīnaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ vimokkhānaṃ, savitakkasavicārādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ samādhīnaṃ, paṭhamajjhānasamāpattiādīnañca navannaṃ anupubbasamāpattīnaṃ. Saṃkilesanti hānabhāgiyadhammaṃ. Vodānanti visesabhāgiyadhammaṃ. Vuṭṭhānanti yena kāraṇena jhānādīhi vuṭṭhahanti, taṃ kāraṇaṃ.

“Of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments” refers to the four jhānas beginning with the first; the eight liberations beginning with “Possessed of form, he sees forms”; the three concentrations beginning with that accompanied by initial application and sustained application; and the nine successive attainments beginning with the first jhāna attainment. “Defilement” refers to states partaking of decline. “Purification” refers to states partaking of distinction. “Emergence” refers to the cause by which one emerges from the jhānas and so on.

Pubbenivāsānussatinti pubbe nivutthakkhandhānussaraṇaṃ.

“The recollection of past abodes” is the recollection of the aggregates in which one has dwelled in the past.

Cutūpapātanti cutiñca upapātañca.

“The passing away and reappearance” means passing away and arising.

Āsavānaṃ khayanti kāmāsavādīnaṃ khayasaṅkhātaṃ āsavanirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ.

“The destruction of the taints” means Nibbāna, the cessation of the taints, which is the destruction of the taints of sensual desire and so on.

Imānīti yāni heṭṭhā “dasa tathāgatassa tathāgatabalānī”ti avoca, imāni tānīti appanaṃ karotīti. Evamettha anupubbapadavaṇṇanaṃ ñatvā idāni yasmā tathāgato paṭhamaṃyeva ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇena veneyyasattānaṃ āsavakkhayādhigamassa ceva anadhigamassa ca ṭhānāṭṭhānabhūtaṃ kilesāvaraṇābhāvaṃ passati, lokiyasammādiṭṭhiṭhānadassanato niyatamicchādiṭṭhiṭhānābhāvadassanato ca. Atha nesaṃ kammavipākañāṇena vipākāvaraṇābhāvaṃ passati[P 0.0402], tihetukapaṭisandhidassanato. Sabbatthagāminīpaṭipadāñāṇena kammāvaraṇābhāvaṃ passati, ānantariyakammābhāvadassanato. Evaṃ anāvaraṇānaṃ anekadhātunānādhātuñāṇena anukūladhammadesanatthaṃ cariyāvisesaṃ passati, dhātuvemattadassanato. Atha nesaṃ [M 0.0385] nānādhimuttikatāñāṇena adhimuttiṃ passati, payogaṃ anādiyitvāpi [V 0.0380] adhimuttivasena dhammadesanatthaṃ. Athevaṃ diṭṭhādhimuttīnaṃ yathāsatti yathābalaṃ dhammaṃ desetuṃ indriyaparopariyattañāṇena indriyaparopariyattaṃ passati, saddhādīnaṃ tikkhamudubhāvadassanato. Evaṃ pariññātindriyaparopariyattāpi panete sace dūre honti, atha jhānādipariññāṇena jhānādīsu vasībhūtattā iddhivisesena khippaṃ upagacchati. Upagantvā ca nesaṃ pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇena pubbajātibhāvanaṃ, dibbacakkhānubhāvato pattabbena cetopariyañāṇena sampatticittavisesaṃ passanto āsavakkhayañāṇānubhāvena āsavakkhayagāminiyā paṭipadāya vigatasammohattā āsavakkhayāya dhammaṃ deseti. Tasmā iminā anukkamena imāni dasabalāni vuttānīti veditabbāni. Ayaṃ tāva mātikāya atthavaṇṇanā.

“These”—he makes an application, meaning “these are those which were stated below as ‘the ten powers of a Tathāgata.’” Having understood the sequential explanation of the terms here, now, because the Tathāgata first discerns through the knowledge of the possible and impossible the absence of the obstruction of defilements for trainees—which is the ground for whether they attain or fail to attain the destruction of the taints—by seeing the ground for mundane right view and the absence of the ground for fixed wrong view. Then, through the knowledge of kamma and its results, he perceives the absence of the obstruction of result, seeing their three-rooted rebirth-linking. Through the knowledge of the path leading everywhere, he perceives the absence of the obstruction of kamma, seeing the absence of immediately resultant kamma. Thus, for those free from obstructions, through the knowledge of the many and various elements, he discerns their special conduct for the purpose of teaching the suitable Dhamma, seeing the diversity in their elements. Then, through the knowledge of the diversity of inclinations, he perceives their inclinations, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma according to their inclination, even if they have not undertaken the practice. Moreover, for those with such seen inclinations, in order to teach the Dhamma according to their capacity and strength, he perceives the superiority and inferiority of their faculties with the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of others’ faculties, seeing the sharpness or dullness of their faith and other faculties. Having fully understood the superiority and inferiority of their faculties, if they are far away, he swiftly approaches them by means of special psychic power, due to his mastery over the jhānas and so on. Upon reaching them, with the knowledge of the recollection of past abodes he sees the state of their past births. Seeing the special state of their present mind with the knowledge of others’ minds, which is attainable through the power of the divine eye, and being without delusion regarding the path leading to the destruction of the taints through the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, he teaches the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints. Therefore, it should be understood that these ten powers are explained in this sequence. This, then, is the explanation of the meaning of the matrix.

(1.) Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Exposition of the Singles

761. Idāni yathānikkhittāya mātikāya “pañcaviññāṇā na hetumevā”tiādinā nayena āraddhe niddesavāre na hetumevāti sādhāraṇahetupaṭikkhepaniddeso. Tattha “hetuhetu, paccayahetu, uttamahetu, sādhāraṇahetūti catubbidho hetū”tiādinā nayena yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ rūpakaṇḍe “sabbaṃ rūpaṃ na hetumevā”tiādīnaṃ atthavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 594) vuttameva. Ahetukamevātiādīsu byañjanasandhivasena makāro veditabbo; ahetukā evāti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Apica “hetū dhammā nahetū dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. dukamātikā 1) dhammakoṭṭhāsesu pañcaviññāṇāni hetū dhammāti vā sahetukā dhammāti [P 0.0403] vā na honti. Ekantena pana na hetūyeva, ahetukā yevāti imānipi nayenettha sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Abyākatamevāti padaṃ vipākābyākatavasena vuttaṃ. Sārammaṇamevāti olubbhārammaṇavasena. Paccayārammaṇaṃ olubbhārammaṇanti hi duvidhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne olubbhārammaṇameva dhuraṃ, paccayārammaṇampi labbhatiyeva. Acetasikamevāti padaṃ cittaṃ, rūpaṃ, nibbānanti tīsu acetasikesu cittameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. No apariyāpannamevāti gatipariyāpannacutipariyāpannasaṃsāravaṭṭabhavapariyāpannabhāvato pariyāpannā eva, no apariyāpannā. Lokato vaṭṭato na niyyantīti aniyyānikā[M 0.0386]. Uppannaṃ manoviññāṇaviññeyyamevāti rūpakaṇḍe cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ paccuppannāneva rūpādīni ārabbha pavattito atītādivisayaṃ manoviññāṇampi pañcaviññāṇasotapatitameva katvā “upapannaṃ chahi viññāṇehi viññeyya”nti (dha. sa. 584) vuttaṃ. Pañcaviññāṇā pana yasmā paccuppannāpi cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ [V 0.0381] ārammaṇā na honti, manoviññāṇasseva honti, tasmā “manoviññāṇaviññeyyamevā”ti vuttaṃ. Aniccamevāti hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccāyeva. Jarābhibhūtamevāti jarāya abhibhūtattā jarābhibhūtā eva.

761. Now, in accordance with the matrix as laid down, in the section of the exposition that begins with 'the five consciousnesses are by no means roots,' there is an exposition refuting the common root. Here, whatever needs to be said—such as 'the root is fourfold: root as cause, root as condition, root as supreme, and root as common'—has already been stated in the explanation of the meaning of 'all material form is by no means a root,' etc., in the section on material form (Dhs. A. 594). In such phrases as 'are rootless indeed,' the letter 'm' should be understood as a euphonic conjunction; the meaning is 'are indeed rootless.' The same method applies to the remaining phrases. Furthermore, in the divisions of phenomena such as 'phenomena that are roots, phenomena that are not roots' (Dhs. Duka Mātikā 1), the five consciousnesses are not 'phenomena that are roots' or 'phenomena with roots.' But they are absolutely not roots, they are indeed rootless; this meaning should be understood for all phrases here. The phrase 'are indeterminate indeed' is stated in the sense of being indeterminate as resultant. The phrase 'have an object indeed' is stated in the sense of having a clinging object. For an object is of two kinds: condition-object and clinging-object. In this instance, however, the clinging-object is primary, though the condition-object is also obtained. The phrase 'are not mental factors indeed' is stated with reference to consciousness among the three things that are not mental factors—consciousness, material form, and Nibbāna. The phrase 'are not unencompassed indeed' means they are encompassed, not unencompassed, because they are encompassed by destination, by decease, and by the round of saṃsāra. 'They are not leading out' means they do not lead out from the world, from the round. Regarding the phrase 'when arisen, cognizable only by mind-consciousness': In the section on material form, it was said, 'what has arisen is cognizable by the six consciousnesses' (Dhs. 584). This was said by considering mind-consciousness, which takes past and other objects, to be included in the stream of the five consciousnesses, since eye-consciousness and so on arise in dependence on present visible forms, etc. However, since the five consciousnesses themselves, even when present, are not objects for eye-consciousness and so on, but only for mind-consciousness, it is therefore said, 'cognizable only by mind-consciousness.' 'They are impermanent indeed' means they are indeed impermanent in the sense of ceasing to be after having been. 'They are overcome by decay indeed' means they are indeed overcome by decay because they are overwhelmed by decay.

762. Uppannavatthukā uppannārammaṇāti anāgatapaṭikkhepo. Na hi te anāgatesu vatthārammaṇesu uppajjanti.

762. 'Having an arisen basis and an arisen object' is a rejection of the future. For they do not arise in relation to future bases and objects.

Purejātavatthukā purejātārammaṇāti sahuppattipaṭikkhepo. Na hi te sahuppannaṃ vatthuṃ vā ārammaṇaṃ vā paṭicca uppajjanti, sayaṃ pana pacchājātā hutvā purejātesu vatthārammaṇesu uppajjanti.

'Having a pre-arisen basis and a pre-arisen object' is a rejection of simultaneous arising. For they do not arise dependent on a simultaneously arisen base or object, but rather, having arisen later, they arise in dependence on pre-arisen bases and objects.

Ajjhattikavatthukāti ajjhattajjhattavasena vuttaṃ. Tāni hi ajjhattike pañca pasāde vatthuṃ katvā uppajjanti. Bāhirārammaṇāti bāhirarūpādiārammaṇā. Tattha catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ – pañcaviññāṇā hi pasādavatthukattā ajjhattikā ajjhattikavatthukā, manoviññāṇaṃ hadayarūpaṃ vatthuṃ katvā uppajjanakāle ajjhattikaṃ bāhiravatthukaṃ, pañcaviññāṇasampayuttā tayo khandhā bāhirā ajjhattikavatthukā[P 0.0404], manoviññāṇasampayuttā tayo khandhā hadayarūpaṃ vatthuṃ katvā uppajjanakāle bāhirā bāhiravatthukā.

'Having an internal basis' is stated in the sense of being internal and having an internal basis. For they arise having the five internal sensitive faculties as their basis. 'Having an external object' means having external objects, such as external visible forms, etc., as objects. Here, a tetrad should be understood: (1) the five consciousnesses, having the sensitive faculties as their basis, are internal and have an internal basis; (2) mind-consciousness, when arising having the heart-base as its basis, is internal and has an external basis; (3) the three aggregates associated with the five consciousnesses are external and have an internal basis; and (4) the three aggregates associated with mind-consciousness, when arising having the heart-base as its basis, are external and have an external basis.

Asambhinnavatthukāti aniruddhavatthukā. Na hi te niruddhaṃ atītaṃ vatthuṃ paṭicca uppajjanti. Asambhinnārammaṇatāyapi eseva nayo.

'Having an unbroken basis' means having a basis that has not ceased. For these consciousnesses do not arise in dependence on a ceased, past basis. The same method applies to having an unbroken object.

Aññaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa vatthu ca ārammaṇañcātiādīsu cakkhuviññāṇassa hi aññaṃ vatthu, aññaṃ ārammaṇaṃ. Aññaṃ sotaviññāṇādīnaṃ. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ sotapasādādīsu aññataraṃ vatthuṃ, saddādīsu vā aññataraṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā kappato kappaṃ gantvāpi na uppajjati; cakkhupasādameva pana vatthuṃ katvā rūpañca ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjati. Evamassa vatthupi dvārampi ārammaṇampi nibaddhaṃ, aññaṃ vatthuṃ vā dvāraṃ vā ārammaṇaṃ vā na saṅkamati, nibaddhavatthu [M 0.0387] nibaddhadvāraṃ nibaddhārammaṇameva hutvā uppajjati. Sotaviññāṇādīsupi eseva nayo.

In phrases such as 'the basis and object for eye-consciousness are distinct': For eye-consciousness, the basis is one thing and the object is another. For ear-consciousness and so on, their respective bases and objects are also distinct. Eye-consciousness does not arise even if it were to take as its basis one of the other sensitive faculties, such as the ear, or as its object one of the other objects, such as a sound, even if it were to continue for an aeon. Rather, it arises only when it takes the eye-sensitivity as its basis and a visible form as its object. Thus, its basis, its door, and its object are fixed; it does not pass over to another basis, door, or object. It arises only with a fixed basis, a fixed door, and a fixed object. The same method applies to ear-consciousness and so on.

763. Na [V 0.0382] aññamaññassa gocaravisayaṃ paccanubhontīti ettha aññamaññassa cakkhu sotassa, sotaṃ vā cakkhussāti evaṃ ekaṃ ekassa gocaravisayaṃ na paccanubhotīti attho. Sace hi nīlādibhedaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ samodhānetvā sotindriyassa upaneyya ‘iṅgha tāva naṃ vavatthāpehi vibhāvehi – kiṃ nāmetaṃ ārammaṇa’nti, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ vināpi mukhena attano dhammatāya evaṃ vadeyya – ‘are andhabāla, vassasatampi vassasahassampi paridhāvamāno aññatra mayā kuhiṃ etassa jānanakaṃ labhissasi; āhara naṃ cakkhupasāde upanehi; ahametaṃ ārammaṇaṃ jānissāmi – yadi vā nīlaṃ yadi vā pītakaṃ. Na hi eso aññassa visayo; mayhameveso visayo’ti. Sesaviññāṇesupi eseva nayo. Evamete aññamaññassa gocaravisayaṃ na paccanubhonti nāma.

763. 'They do not experience each other’s domain and sphere': Here, the meaning is that one does not experience the domain and sphere of another—for example, the eye that of the ear, or the ear that of the eye. For if, having taken a visible object such as blue, one were to present it to the ear faculty and say, “Come now, determine and analyze this object—what is this object called?”—the eye-consciousness, even without a mouth, would speak thus by its own nature: “You blind fool! Even if you run around for a hundred or a thousand years, where apart from me will you find one who can know this? Bring it, present it to the eye-sensitivity; I will know this object—whether it is blue or yellow. This is not the sphere of another; it is my sphere alone.” The same method applies to the other consciousnesses. Thus, indeed, these do not experience each other’s domain and sphere.

764. Samannāharantassāti āvajjaneneva samannāharantassa.

764. 'For one who adverts': This means for one who adverts simply by means of adverting.

Manasikarontassāti āvajjaneneva manasikarontassa. Etāni hi cittāni āvajjanena samannāhaṭakāle manasikatakāleyeva ca uppajjanti.

'For one who attends': This means for one who attends simply by means of adverting. For these consciousnesses arise only at the time of being adverted to by adverting and at the time of being attended to.

Na abbokiṇṇāti aññena viññāṇena abbokiṇṇā nirantarāva nuppajjanti. Etena tesaṃ anantaratā paṭikkhittā.

"Not mixed": They do not arise uninterruptedly, intermingled with another consciousness. By this, their immediacy is refuted.

765. Na apubbaṃ acarimanti etena sabbesampi sahuppatti paṭikkhittā. Na [P 0.0405] aññamaññassa samanantarāti etena samanantaratā paṭikkhittā.

765. "Not without a preceding and a succeeding one": By this, the simultaneous arising of all of them is refuted. "Not immediate to one another": By this, immediacy is refuted.

766. Āvaṭṭanā vātiādīni cattāripi āvajjanasseva nāmāni. Tañhi bhavaṅgassa āvaṭṭanato āvaṭṭanā, tasseva ābhujanato ābhogo, rūpādīnaṃ samannāharaṇato samannāhāro, tesaṃyeva manasikaraṇato manasikāroti vuccati. Evamettha saṅkhepato pañcannaṃ viññāṇānaṃ āvajjanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā āvajjanādikiccaṃ kātuṃ samatthabhāvo paṭikkhitto.

766. "Or turning," etc.—these four are all names for adverting. For it is called “turning” (āvaṭṭanā) because it turns from the life-continuum; “application” (ābhoga) because it bends towards the object; “adverting” (samannāhāra) because it brings visible forms, etc., to mind; and “attention” (manasikāra) because it attends to them. Thus, in brief, the capacity of the five consciousnesses to perform the function of adverting, etc., by standing in the place of adverting is refuted.

Na kañci dhammaṃ paṭivijānātīti “manopubbaṅgamā dhammā”ti (dha. pa. 1-2) evaṃ vuttaṃ ekampi kusalaṃ vā akusalaṃ vā na paṭivijānāti.

"It does not discern any phenomenon": As stated, "Mind precedes all phenomena" (Dhp. 1–2), it does not discern even a single wholesome or unwholesome phenomenon.

Aññatra [M 0.0388][V 0.0383] abhinipātamattāti ṭhapetvā rūpādīnaṃ abhinipātamattaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – supaṇḍitopi puriso, ṭhapetvā āpāthagatāni rūpādīni, aññaṃ kusalākusalesu ekadhammampi pañcahi viññāṇehi na paṭivijānāti. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ panettha dassanamattameva hoti. Sotaviññāṇādīni savanaghāyanasāyanaphusanamattāneva. Dassanādimattato pana muttā aññā etesaṃ kusalādipaṭiviññatti nāma natthi.

"Except for mere impingement": This means setting aside the mere impingement of visible forms and so on. This is what is meant: even a very wise person, setting aside visible forms and so on that have come into range, does not discern with the five consciousnesses a single other phenomenon among wholesome and unwholesome ones. Here, eye-consciousness is merely seeing. Ear-consciousness and the others are merely hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching. But apart from mere seeing and so on, there is for them no such thing as the discerning of wholesome and unwholesome states.

Manodhātuyāpīti sampaṭicchanamanodhātuyāpi. Sampiṇḍanattho cettha pikāro. Tasmā manodhātuyāpi tato parāhi manoviññāṇadhātūhipīti sabbehipi pañcadvārikaviññāṇehi na kañci kusalākusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭivijānātīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

"And also by the mind-element": This refers to the receiving mind-element also. The particle 'pi' here has a cumulative sense. Therefore, the meaning should be understood thus: that by the mind-element also, and by the mind-consciousness-elements that follow it—that is, by all the consciousnesses of the five-door process—no wholesome or unwholesome phenomenon is discerned.

Na kañci iriyāpathaṃ kappetītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Na hi pañcadvārikaviññāṇehi gamanādīsu kañci iriyāpathaṃ kappeti, na kāyakammaṃ na vacīkammaṃ paṭṭhapeti, na kusalākusalaṃ dhammaṃ samādiyati, na samādhiṃ samāpajjati lokiyaṃ vā lokuttaraṃ vā, na samādhito vuṭṭhāti lokiyā vā lokuttarā vā, na bhavato cavati, na bhavantare upapajjati. Sabbampi hetaṃ kusalākusaladhammapaṭivijānanādivacanapariyosānaṃ kiccaṃ manodvārikacitteneva hoti, na pañcadvārikenāti sabbassāpetassa kiccassa karaṇe sahajavanakāni vīthicittāni paṭikkhittāni. Yathā cetesaṃ [P 0.0406] etāni kiccāni natthi, evaṃ niyāmokkamanādīnipi. Na hi pañcadvārikajavanena micchattaniyāmaṃ okkamati, na sammattaniyāmaṃ; na cetaṃ javanaṃ nāmagottamārabbha javati, na kasiṇādipaṇṇattiṃ; na lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāvasena pavattati, na vuṭṭhānagāminībalavavipassanāvasena; na rūpārūpadhamme ārabbha javati, na nibbānaṃ; na cetena saddhiṃ paṭisambhidāñāṇaṃ uppajjati, na abhiññāñāṇaṃ, na sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ, na paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ, na sabbaññutañāṇaṃ. Sabbopi panesa pabhedo manodvārikajavaneyeva labbhati.

The same principle applies also to such statements as: 'It does not determine any posture.' Indeed, by means of the five-door consciousnesses one does not determine any posture in walking and so on; one does not initiate bodily or verbal action; one does not undertake wholesome or unwholesome states; one does not attain any concentration, mundane or supramundane; one does not emerge from concentration, mundane or supramundane; one does not pass away from an existence; and one does not reappear in another existence. All this activity, which culminates in the discerning of wholesome and unwholesome states, is performed only by mind-door consciousness, not by the five-door consciousnesses. Thus, for the performance of all this activity, the process-consciousnesses together with their javanas are rejected. Just as these functions do not belong to them, so too such functions as entering the fixed courses. Indeed, with a five-door javana one does not enter the fixed course of wrongness, nor the fixed course of rightness; this javana does not run on taking as its object name and lineage, or concepts like kasiṇas; it does not proceed by way of insight that takes characteristics as its object, nor by way of the powerful insight leading to emergence; it does not run on taking as its object material or immaterial phenomena, or Nibbāna; nor do the analytical knowledges arise together with it, nor the higher knowledges, nor the knowledge of a disciple's perfections, nor the knowledge of a Solitary Buddha, nor omniscient knowledge. But all this variety is found only in mind-door javana.

Na supati na paṭibujjhati na supinaṃ passatīti sabbenāpi ca pañcadvārikacittena neva niddaṃ okkamati, na niddāyati, na paṭibujjhati, na kiñca supinaṃ passatīti imesu tīsu ṭhānesu saha javanena vīthicittaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ.

One does not sleep, wake up, or dream—indeed, with any five-door consciousness, one neither enters sleep, nor sleeps, nor wakes up, nor sees any dream. In these three instances, the process-consciousness together with the javana is rejected.

Niddāyantassa hi mahāvaṭṭiṃ jāletvā dīpe cakkhusamīpe upanīte paṭhamaṃ cakkhudvārikaṃ āvajjanaṃ [V 0.0384] bhavaṅgaṃ na āvaṭṭeti, manodvārikameva āvaṭṭeti. Atha [M 0.0389] javanaṃ javitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otarati. Dutiyavāre cakkhudvārikaṃ āvajjanaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭeti. Tato cakkhuviññāṇādīni javanapariyosānāni pavattanti. Tadanantaraṃ bhavaṅgaṃ pavattati. Tatiyavāre manodvārikaāvajjanena bhavaṅge āvaṭṭite manodvārikajavanaṃ javati. Tena cittena ñatvā ‘kiṃ ayaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne āloko’ti jānāti.

For one who is sleeping, indeed, after lighting a large wick and placing the lamp near the eye, at first the eye-door adverting does not interrupt the life-continuum; only the mind-door adverting interrupts it. Then, after the impulsion has run its course, consciousness descends into the life-continuum. On the second occasion, the eye-door adverting interrupts the life-continuum. After that, eye-consciousness and so on proceed up to the termination of the impulsion. Immediately after that, the life-continuum flows on. On the third occasion, when the life-continuum has been interrupted by mind-door adverting, mind-door impulsion runs. Through that consciousness, one recognizes, 'What is this light in this place?'

Tathā niddāyantassa kaṇṇasamīpe tūriyesu paggahitesu, ghānasamīpe sugandhesu vā duggandhesu vā pupphesu upanītesu, mukhe sappimhi vā phāṇite vā pakkhitte, piṭṭhiyaṃ pāṇinā pahāre dinne paṭhamaṃ sotadvārikādīni āvajjanāni bhavaṅgaṃ na āvaṭṭenti, manodvārikameva āvaṭṭeti. Atha javanaṃ javitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otarati. Dutiyavāre sotadvārikādīni āvajjanāni bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭenti. Tato sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇādīni javanapariyosānāni pavattanti. Tadanantaraṃ bhavaṅgaṃ pavattati. Tatiyavāre manodvārikaāvajjanena bhavaṅge āvaṭṭite manodvārikajavanaṃ javati. Tena cittena ñatvā ‘kiṃ ayaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne saddo – saṅkhasaddo, bherisaddo’ti vā ‘kiṃ ayaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne gandho – mūlagandho, sāragandho’ti vā ‘kiṃ [P 0.0407] idaṃ mayhaṃ mukhe pakkhittarasaṃ – sappīti vā phāṇita’nti vā ‘kenamhi piṭṭhiyaṃ pahato, atithaddho me pahāro’ti vā vattāro honti. Evaṃ manodvārikajavaneneva paṭibujjhati, na pañcadvārikena. Supinampi teneva passati, na pañcadvārikena.

Similarly, when musical instruments are played near the ears of one who is asleep, or when fragrant or foul-smelling flowers are brought near the nose, or when ghee or molasses is placed in the mouth, or when a blow is struck on the back with the hand, at first, the adverting of the ear-door and so on does not interrupt the life-continuum; only the mind-door adverting interrupts it. Then, after the impulsion has run its course, consciousness descends into the life-continuum. On the second occasion, the adverting of the ear-door and so on interrupts the life-continuum. After that, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and so on, proceed up to the end of the impulsion. Immediately after that, the life-continuum flows on. On the third occasion, when the life-continuum is interrupted by mind-door adverting, mind-door impulsion runs. By means of that consciousness, one is able to say: 'What is this sound in this place—a conch sound, a drum sound?' or 'What is this smell in this place—a root-scent, a heartwood-scent?' or 'What is this taste placed in my mouth—ghee or molasses?' or 'By whom was I struck on the back? The blow is very hard!' Thus, one awakens only through mind-door impulsion, not through a five-door process. Dreams, too, are seen only through that, not through a five-door process.

Tañca panetaṃ supinaṃ passanto catūhi kāraṇehi passati – dhātukkhobhato vā anubhūtapubbato vā devatopasaṃhārato vā pubbanimittato vāti. Tattha pittādīnaṃ khobhakaraṇapaccayayogena khubhitadhātuko ‘dhātukkhobhato’ supinaṃ passati. Passanto ca nānāvidhaṃ supinaṃ passati – pabbatā patanto viya, ākāsena gacchanto viya, vāḷamigahatthicorādīhi anubaddho viya ca hoti. ‘Anubhūtapubbato’ passanto pubbe anubhūtapubbaṃ ārammaṇaṃ passati. ‘Devatopasaṃhārato’ passantassa devatā atthakāmatāya vā anatthakāmatāya vā atthāya vā anatthāya vā nānāvidhāni ārammaṇāni upasaṃharanti. So tāsaṃ devatānaṃ ānubhāvena tāni ārammaṇāni passati. Pubbanimittato passanto puññāpuññavasena uppajjitukāmassa atthassa vā anatthassa vā pubbanimittabhūtaṃ supinaṃ passati [V 0.0385] bodhisattamātā viya puttapaṭilābhanimittaṃ, bodhisatto [M 0.0390] viya pañca mahāsupine (a. ni. 5.196), kosalarājā viya ca soḷasa supineti (jā. 1.1.41).

And one sees that dream for four reasons: due to a disturbance of the elements, due to past experience, due to the influence of deities, or as a portent. Herein, one whose elements are disturbed by the conjunction of causes that agitate bile and so on sees a dream 'due to a disturbance of the elements.' And while seeing, one sees various kinds of dreams—as if falling from a mountain, as if traveling through the sky, or as if being pursued by wild beasts, elephants, thieves, and so on. One who sees 'due to past experience' sees an object previously experienced. For one who sees 'due to the influence of deities,' deities present various objects, whether out of a desire for one's welfare or a desire for one's harm, for one's benefit or for one's detriment. By the power of those deities, one sees those objects. One who sees 'as a portent' sees a dream that is a preliminary sign of a benefit or harm about to arise, in accordance with one's merit or demerit—like the Bodhisatta's mother seeing the sign of obtaining a son, like the Bodhisatta seeing the five great dreams (AN 5.196), or like the king of Kosala seeing the sixteen dreams (Ja 77).

Tattha yaṃ dhātukkhobhato anubhūtapubbato ca supinaṃ passati, na taṃ saccaṃ hoti. Yaṃ devatopasaṃhārato passati, taṃ saccaṃ vā hoti alikaṃ vā. Kuddhā hi devatā upāyena vināsetukāmā viparītampi katvā dassenti. Tatridaṃ vatthu – rohaṇe kira nāgamahāvihāre mahāthero bhikkhusaṅghaṃ anapaloketvāva ekaṃ nāgarukkhaṃ chindāpesi. Rukkhe adhivatthā devatā therassa kuddhā paṭhamameva naṃ palobhetvā pacchā ‘ito te sattadivasamatthake upaṭṭhāko rājā marissatī’ti supine ārocesi. Thero naṃ kathaṃ āharitvā rājorodhānaṃ ācikkhi. Tā ekappahāreneva mahāviravaṃ viraviṃsu. Rājā ‘kiṃ eta’nti pucchi. Tā ‘evaṃ therena vutta’nti ārocayiṃsu. Rājā divase gaṇāpetvā sattāhe vītivatte kujjhitvā therassa hatthapāde chindāpesi.

Therein, a dream one sees due to a disturbance of the elements or from past experience is not true. A dream one sees due to the influence of deities may be true or false. For angry deities, wishing to destroy by some means, may also show things in a distorted way. Herein is the story: At Rohaṇa, it is said, in the Nāgamahāvihāra, a great elder, without informing the community of monks, had a nāga tree cut down. The deity dwelling in the tree, angry with the elder, first enticed him and then later announced in a dream, 'Seven days from now, your patron king will die.' The elder, taking this message, told it to the royal women. They at once raised a great cry. The king asked, 'What is this?' They replied, 'Thus has the elder spoken.' The king had the days counted, and when seven days had passed, he became furious and had the elder’s hands and feet cut off.

Yaṃ pana pubbanimittato passati taṃ ekantasaccameva hoti. Etesañca catunnaṃ [P 0.0408] mūlakāraṇānaṃ saṃsaggabhedatopi supinabhedo hotiyeva. Tañca panetaṃ catubbidhaṃ supinaṃ sekkhaputhujjanāva passanti appahīnavipallāsattā; asekkhā na passanti pahīnavipallāsattā.

But what one sees as a portent is invariably true. Moreover, due to the combination and separation of these four root causes, there is indeed a variety of dreams. And these four kinds of dreams are seen only by trainees and worldlings because their perversions have not been abandoned; those beyond training do not see them because their perversions have been abandoned.

Kiṃ pana taṃ passanto sutto passati, paṭibuddho? Udāhu neva sutto passati na paṭibuddhoti? Kiñcettha yadi tāva sutto passati, abhidhammavirodho āpajjati. Bhavaṅgacittena hi supati. Tañca rūpanimittādiārammaṇaṃ rāgādisampayuttaṃ vā na hoti. Supinaṃ passantassa ca īdisāni cittāni uppajjanti. Atha paṭibuddho passati, vinayavirodho āpajjati. Yañhi paṭibuddho passati, taṃ sabbohārikacittena passati. Sabbohārikacittena ca kate vītikkame anāpatti nāma natthi. Supinaṃ passantena pana kate vītikkame ekantaṃ anāpatti eva. Atha neva sutto na paṭibuddho passati, na supinaṃ nāma passati. Evañhi sati supinassa abhāvova āpajjati? Na abhāvo[M 0.0391]. Kasmā? Yasmā kapimiddhapareto passati. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ – “kapimiddhapareto kho, mahārāja, supinaṃ passatī”ti (mi. pa. 5.3.5). ‘Kapimiddhapareto’ti makkaṭaniddāya yutto. Yathā hi makkaṭassa niddā lahuparivattā hoti, evaṃ yā niddā punappunaṃ kusalādicittavokiṇṇattā lahuparivattā; yassā pavattiyaṃ punappunaṃ bhavaṅgato uttaraṇaṃ hoti, tāya yutto supinaṃ passati. Tenāyaṃ supino kusalopi hoti akusalopi abyākatopi 386. Tattha supinante cetiyavandanadhammassavanadhammadesanādīni karontassa kusalo, pāṇātipātādīni karontassa akusalo, dvīhi antehi mutto āvajjanatadārammaṇakkhaṇe abyākatoti veditabbo. Supineneva ‘diṭṭhaṃ viya me, sutaṃ viya me’ti kathanakālepi abyākatoyeva.

Now, does one who sees a dream see it while asleep or while awake? Or does one see it neither asleep nor awake? Herein, if one sees it while asleep, a contradiction with the Abhidhamma arises. For one sleeps with the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta), and that does not take a form-sign, etc., as its object, nor is it associated with lust, etc. But for one who sees a dream, such states of consciousness arise. If one sees it while awake, a contradiction with the Vinaya arises. For what one sees while awake, one sees with a consciousness of ordinary discourse, and when a transgression is committed with a consciousness of ordinary discourse, there is no such thing as non-offense. But when a transgression is committed by one seeing a dream, it is invariably a non-offense. If one sees it neither asleep nor awake, then one does not see a dream at all. This being so, would it not lead to the non-existence of dreams? No, it does not lead to non-existence. Why? Because one sees it when overcome by 'monkey-sleep' (kapimiddha). For it was said: 'Overcome by monkey-sleep, O great king, one sees a dream' (Miln 299). 'Overcome by monkey-sleep' means endowed with monkey-sleep. For just as a monkey’s sleep is easily disturbed, so too is that sleep which is easily disturbed due to being repeatedly interspersed with wholesome and other states of consciousness; endowed with that sleep, during the occurrence of which there is repeated emergence from the life-continuum, one sees a dream. Therefore, this dream can be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Herein, for one who in a dream performs such acts as venerating a shrine, listening to the Dhamma, or teaching the Dhamma, it is wholesome; for one who commits such acts as killing living beings, it is unwholesome; at the moments of adverting and registration, being free from both extremes, it should be understood as indeterminate. Even at the time of relating what was seen in the dream, saying 'it was as if I saw, it was as if I heard,' it is still indeterminate.

Kiṃ pana supine kataṃ kusalākusalaṃ kammaṃ savipākaṃ avipākanti? Savipākaṃ; dubbalattā pana paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhituṃ na sakkoti, dinnāya aññakammena paṭisandhiyā pavatte vedanīyaṃ hoti.

Now, is wholesome or unwholesome kamma done in a dream with result or without result? It is with result; but due to its weakness, it is not able to bring about rebirth-linking. When rebirth-linking has been given by another kamma, it becomes experienceable in the course of existence.

Evaṃ yāthāvakavatthuvibhāvanā paññāti pañcannaṃ viññāṇānaṃ na hetvaṭṭho yāthāvaṭṭho. Taṃ [P 0.0409] yāthāvaṭṭhaṃ vatthuṃ vibhāvetīti yāthāvakavatthuvibhāvanā. Tathā pañcannaṃ viññāṇānaṃ ahetukaṭṭho, jarābhibhūtaṭṭho, na supinaṃ passanaṭṭho, yāthāvaṭṭho. Taṃ yāthāvaṭṭhaṃ vatthuṃ vibhāvetīti yāthāvakavatthuvibhāvanā. Iti yā heṭṭhā “yāthāvakavatthuvibhāvanā paññā”ti mātikāya nikkhittā, sā evaṃ yāthāvakavatthuvibhāvanā paññāti veditabbā. Tassā eva ca vasena evaṃ ekavidhena ñāṇavatthūti evaṃ ekekakoṭṭhāsena ñāṇagaṇanā ekena vā ākārena ñāṇaparicchedo hoti.

Thus, regarding 'wisdom that clarifies the object as it really is': for the five consciousnesses, their actual state is not that of being a cause. Because it clarifies that object in its actual state, it is 'wisdom that clarifies the object as it really is.' Similarly, for the five consciousnesses, their actual state is being without a cause, being overcome by old age, and not seeing dreams. Because it clarifies that object in its actual state, it is 'wisdom that clarifies the object as it really is.' Thus, that which was laid down in the matrix above as 'wisdom that clarifies the object as it really is,' should be understood in this way as 'wisdom that clarifies the object as it really is.' And by virtue of this very wisdom, the basis for knowledge is thus of one kind; thus the enumeration of knowledge is by a single section, or the delimitation of knowledge is by a single mode.

Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Ones.

(2.) Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā

(2.) The Commentary on the Exposition of the Twos.

767. Duvidhena ñāṇavatthuniddese catūsu bhūmīsu kusaleti sekkhaputhujjanānaṃ catubhūmakakusalapaññā. Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅge vuttesu pañcasu atthesu [M 0.0392] attano attano bhūmipariyāpannaṃ vipākasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ jāpeti janeti pavattetīti atthajāpikā. Arahato abhiññaṃ uppādentassa samāpattiṃ uppādentassa kiriyābyākateti abhiññāya ceva samāpattiyā ca parikammasamaye kāmāvacarakiriyapaññā. Sā hi abhiññāsamāpattipabhedaṃ kiriyasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ jāpeti janeti pavattetīti atthajāpikā paññāti vuttā. Ayaṃ pana aparopi pāḷimuttako [V 0.0387] aṭṭhakathānayo – yāpi hi purimā kāmāvacarakiriyā pacchimāya kāmāvacarakiriyāya anantarādivasena paccayo hoti, sāpi taṃ kiriyatthaṃ jāpetīti atthajāpikā paññā nāma. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacaresupi eseva nayo.

767. In the twofold exposition of the bases of knowledge, 'wholesome in the four planes' refers to the wholesome wisdom of the four planes belonging to trainees and worldlings. In the Analysis of Discriminations, concerning the five meanings mentioned, it is called 'meaning-producing' because it produces, generates, and sets in motion the meaning designated as 'result' that is included in its own plane. For an arahant who is producing a direct knowledge or an attainment, there is functional-indeterminate consciousness. At the time of preparation for both direct knowledge and attainment, there is sense-sphere functional wisdom. For that wisdom is called 'meaning-producing wisdom' because it produces, generates, and sets in motion the meaning designated as 'functional,' which is a division of direct knowledge and attainment. This, however, is another commentarial method not found in the Pāli text: when a preceding sense-sphere functional consciousness is a condition for a subsequent sense-sphere functional consciousness by way of proximity, etc., that too is called 'meaning-producing wisdom' because it produces the meaning of that functional state. The same method applies also to the fine-material and immaterial spheres.

Dutiyapadaniddese catūsu bhūmīsu vipāketi kāmāvacaravipāke paññā sahajātādipaccayavasena kāmāvacaravipākatthaṃ jāpetvā ṭhitāti jāpitatthā. Rūpāvacarādivipākapaññāsupi eseva nayo. Sabbāpi vā esā attano attano kāraṇehi jāpitā janitā pavattitā sayampi atthabhūtātipi jāpitatthā. Arahato uppannāya abhiññāya uppannāya samāpattiyāti vuttakiriyapaññāyapi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana aparopi pāḷimuttako aṭṭhakathānayo – kāmāvacarakiriyapaññāpi hi sahajātādivasena kāmāvacarakiriyasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ jāpetvā ṭhitāti jāpitatthā. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakiriyapaññāsupi [P 0.0410] eseva nayo. Sabbāpi vā esā attano attano kāraṇehi jāpitā janitā pavattitā sayañca atthabhūtātipi jāpitatthā. Sesamettha sabbaṃ dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayattā pākaṭamevāti.

In the exposition of the second term, 'resultant in the four planes' means that the wisdom in the sense-sphere resultant is established, having produced the meaning of the sense-sphere resultant by way of the conascence condition and so on; thus it is 'of produced meaning.' The same method applies also to the wisdom in the resultants of the fine-material sphere, etc. Or, all this wisdom, having been produced, generated, and set in motion by its own respective causes, is itself an actual phenomenon; thus it is 'of produced meaning.' The same method also applies to the aforesaid functional wisdom that has arisen for an arahant in direct knowledge and in attainment. This, however, is another commentarial method not found in the Pāli text: the sense-sphere functional wisdom, too, is established, having produced the meaning designated as 'sense-sphere functional' by way of the conascence condition and so on; thus it is 'of produced meaning.' The same method applies also to the functional wisdom of the fine-material and immaterial spheres. Or, all this wisdom, having been produced, generated, and set in motion by its own respective causes, is itself an actual phenomenon; thus it is 'of produced meaning.' The rest here is all evident, since the method has been explained in the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī.

Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Exposition of the Twos.

(3.) Tikaniddesavaṇṇanā

(3.) Commentary on the Exposition of the Threes

768. Tividhena ñāṇavatthuniddese yogavihitesūti yogo vuccati paññā; paññāvihitesu paññāpariṇāmitesūti attho. Kammāyatanesūti ettha kammameva kammāyatanaṃ; atha vā kammañca taṃ āyatanañca ājīvādīnantipi [M 0.0393] kammāyatanaṃ. Sippāyatanesupi eseva nayo. Tattha duvidhaṃ kammaṃ – hīnañca ukkaṭṭhañca. Tattha hīnaṃ nāma vaḍḍhakīkammaṃ, pupphachaḍḍakakammanti evamādi. Ukkaṭṭhaṃ nāma kasi, vaṇijjā, gorakkhanti evamādi. Sippampi duvidhaṃ hīnañca ukkaṭṭhañca. Tattha hīnaṃ sippaṃ nāma naḷakārasippaṃ, pesakārasippaṃ, kumbhakārasippaṃ, cammakārasippaṃ, nhāpitasippanti evamādi. Ukkaṭṭhaṃ nāma sippaṃ muddā, gaṇanā, lekhañcāti evamādi vijjāva vijjāṭṭhānaṃ. Taṃ dhammikameva gahitaṃ. Nāgamaṇḍalaparittasadisaṃ, phudhamanakamantasadisaṃ, sālākiyaṃ[V 0.0388], sallakattiyantiādīni pana vejjasatthāni “icchāmahaṃ, ācariya, sippaṃ sikkhitu”nti (mahāva. 329) sippāyatane paviṭṭhattā na gahitāni.

768. In the threefold exposition of the bases of knowledge, 'established by application' means: 'application' (yoga) is a term for wisdom; the meaning is 'established in wisdom, transformed by wisdom.' Here, in 'in the spheres of action,' action itself is the sphere of action; or, both action and that sphere, including livelihood and so on, constitute the sphere of action. The same method applies to 'in the spheres of crafts.' Here, action is twofold: inferior and superior. Inferior action includes such things as carpentry and flower-sweeping. Superior action includes such things as agriculture, trade, and cattle-herding. Crafts are also twofold: inferior and superior. Inferior crafts include such things as basketry, weaving, pottery, leatherwork, and barbering. Superior crafts include such things as seal-making, calculation, and writing; this is a field of knowledge. Only what is righteous is included. However, medical sciences such as the Nāga-circle protective charm, the Phudhamana spell, ophthalmology, and surgery are not included here, although they are considered crafts, as when one says, 'Teacher, I wish to learn a craft' (Mahāvagga 1.75).

Tattha eko paṇḍito manussānaṃ phāsuvihāratthāya attano ca dhammatāya gehapāsādayānanāvādīni uppādeti. So hi ‘ime manussā vasanaṭṭhānena vinā dukkhitā’ti hitakiriyāya ṭhatvā dīghacaturassādibhedaṃ gehaṃ uppādeti, sītuṇhapaṭighātatthāya ekabhūmikadvibhūmikādibhede pāsāde karoti, ‘yāne asati anusañcaraṇaṃ nāma dukkha’nti jaṅghākilamathapaṭivinodanatthāya vayhasakaṭasandamānikādīni uppādeti, ‘nāvāya asati samuddādīsu sañcāro nāma natthī’ti nānappakāraṃ nāvaṃ uppādeti. So sabbampetaṃ neva aññehi kayiramānaṃ passati, na kataṃ uggaṇhāti, na [P 0.0411] kathentānaṃ suṇāti, attano pana dhammatāya cintāya karoti. Paññavatā hi attano dhammatāya katampi aññehi uggaṇhitvā karontehi katasadisameva hoti. Ayaṃ tāva hīnakamme nayo.

Therein, a wise person, for the comfortable living of human beings and from his own nature, creates such things as houses, mansions, vehicles, and boats. Indeed, thinking, 'Without a dwelling place, these people suffer,' and undertaking a beneficial action, he creates houses of various kinds, such as long and square ones. To ward off cold and heat, he makes mansions of one, two, or more stories. Thinking, 'Without vehicles, travel is difficult,' he creates litters, carts, palanquins, and the like to relieve the weariness of the legs. Thinking, 'Without boats, there is no travel on the sea and so on,' he creates various kinds of boats. He does not see all this being done by others, nor does he learn what has been done, nor does he hear it from those who describe it; rather, he does it from his own nature, through his own thought. For what is done by a wise person from his own nature becomes the very model for what is done by others who learn and do it. This, for a start, is the method regarding inferior action.

Ukkaṭṭhakammepi ‘kasikamme asati manussānaṃ jīvitaṃ na pavattatī’ti eko paṇḍito manussānaṃ phāsuvihāratthāya yuganaṅgalādīni kasibhaṇḍāni uppādeti; tathā nānappakāraṃ vāṇijakammaṃ gorakkhañca uppādeti. So sabbampetaṃ neva aññehi kariyamānaṃ passati…pe… katasadisameva hoti. Ayaṃ ukkaṭṭhakamme nayo.

Also in superior action, thinking, 'Without agriculture, the life of human beings cannot be sustained,' a wise person, for their comfortable living, creates agricultural implements such as yokes and ploughs; likewise, he originates various kinds of trade and cattle-herding. He does not see all this being done by others, nor does he learn what has been done, nor does he hear it from those who describe it; rather, he does it from his own nature, through his own thought. For what is done by a wise person from his own nature becomes the very model for what is done by others who learn and do it. This is the method regarding superior action.

Duvidhepi pana sippāyatane eko paṇḍito manussānaṃ phāsuvihāratthāya naḷakārasippādīni hīnasippāni, hatthamuddāya gaṇanasaṅkhātaṃ muddaṃ, acchinnakasaṅkhātaṃ gaṇanaṃ, mātikāppabhedakādibhedañca lekhaṃ uppādeti. So sabbampetaṃ neva aññehi kariyamānaṃ passati…pe… katasadisameva hoti. Ayaṃ sippāyatane nayo.

Furthermore, in the twofold sphere of crafts, a wise person, for the comfortable living of human beings, originates inferior crafts such as basketry, and superior crafts such as the seal-making known as counting by hand-signs, the calculation known as 'unbroken,' and writing with its divisions such as the different kinds of matrices. He does not see all this being done by others, nor does he learn what has been done, nor does he hear it from those who describe it; rather, he does it from his own nature, through his own thought. For what is done by a wise person from his own nature becomes the very model for what is done by others who learn and do it. This is the method regarding the sphere of crafts.

Ekacco [M 0.0394] pana paṇḍito amanussasarīsapādīhi upaddutānaṃ manussānaṃ tikicchanatthāya dhammikāni nāgamaṇḍalamantādīni vijjāṭṭhānāni uppādeti, tāni neva aññehi kariyamānāni passati, na katāni uggaṇhāti, na kathentānaṃ suṇāti, attano pana dhammatāya cintāya karoti. Paññavatā hi attano dhammatāya katampi aññehi uggaṇhitvā karontehi katasadisameva hoti.

However, a certain wise person, for the purpose of treating human beings afflicted by non-human beings, reptiles, and the like, originates righteous fields of knowledge such as the Nāga-circle spells. He neither sees these being performed by others, nor learns them when performed, nor hears of them from those who describe them, but creates them from his own nature, through his own thought. For what is done by a wise person from his own nature becomes the very model for what is done by others who learn and do it.

Kammassakataṃ [V 0.0389] vāti “idaṃ kammaṃ sattānaṃ sakaṃ, idaṃ no saka”nti evaṃ jānanañāṇaṃ. Saccānulomikaṃ vāti vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Tañhi catunnaṃ saccānaṃ anulomanato saccānulomikanti vuccati. Idānissa pavattanākāraṃ dassetuṃ rūpaṃ aniccanti vātiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha ca aniccalakkhaṇameva āgataṃ, na dukkhalakkhaṇaanattalakkhaṇāni, atthavasena pana āgatānevāti daṭṭhabbāni – yañhi aniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattāti.

‘Or ownership of kamma’ is the knowledge of knowing thus: ‘This kamma is beings’ own; this is not their own.’ ‘Or knowledge in conformity with the truths’ is insight knowledge. For because it conforms to the four truths, it is called ‘conformity with the truths.’ Now, to show its mode of occurrence, ‘form is impermanent,’ and so on, is stated. Here, only the characteristic of impermanence is given, not the characteristics of suffering and non-self; however, they should be understood as included by way of the meaning, for what is impermanent is suffering, and what is suffering is non-self.

Yaṃ evarūpinti yaṃ evaṃ heṭṭhā niddiṭṭhasabhāvaṃ anulomikaṃ. Khantintiādīni sabbāni paññāvevacanāneva. Sā hi heṭṭhā vuttānaṃ kammāyatanādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ kāraṇānaṃ apaccanīkadassanena anulometīti anulomikā. Tathā [P 0.0412] sattānaṃ hitacariyāya anulometi, maggasaccassa anulometi, paramatthasaccassa nibbānassa anulomanato anulometītipi anulomikā. Sabbānipi etāni kāraṇāni khamati sahati daṭṭhuṃ sakkotīti khanti, passatīti diṭṭhi, rocetīti ruci, mudatīti mudi, pekkhatīti pekkhā. Sabbepissā te kammāyatanādayo dhammā nijjhānaṃ khamanti, visesato ca pañcakkhandhasaṅkhātā dhammā punappunaṃ aniccadukkhānattavasena nijjhāyamānā taṃ nijjhānaṃ khamantīti dhammanijjhānakhantī.

‘That which is of such a nature’ means that which is conforming, having the nature described above. ‘Patience,’ and so on, are all synonyms for wisdom. For this wisdom conforms by seeing the non-opposition to the five causes mentioned above, such as the spheres of action; thus it is ‘conforming.’ Likewise, it conforms to the welfare of beings and to the truth of the path; and because it conforms to the ultimate truth, Nibbāna, it is also ‘conforming.’ Because it accepts, endures, and is able to see all these causes, it is ‘patience’ (khanti); because it sees, ‘view’ (diṭṭhi); because it approves, ‘approval’ (ruci); because it is pleased, ‘pleasure’ (mudi); because it considers, ‘consideration’ (pekkhā). All those phenomena—the spheres of action and so on—endure its investigation; and especially the phenomena comprised in the five aggregates, being repeatedly investigated by way of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, endure that investigation. Thus it is ‘patience in the investigation of phenomena’.

Parato assutvā paṭilabhatīti aññassa upadesavacanaṃ assutvā sayameva cintento paṭilabhati. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ cintāmayā paññā nāma vuccati. Sā panesā na yesaṃ kesañci uppajjati, abhiññātānaṃ pana mahāsattānameva uppajjati. Tatthāpi saccānulomikañāṇaṃ dvinnaṃyeva bodhisattānaṃ uppajjati. Sesapaññā sabbesampi pūritapāramīnaṃ mahāpaññānaṃ uppajjatīti veditabbā.

He attains it without hearing from others: without hearing the instruction of another, he attains it by reflecting for himself. This is called wisdom born of reflection. But this does not arise for just anyone; it arises only for renowned great beings. Even then, knowledge in conformity with the truths arises only for two Bodhisattas. The remaining wisdom, it should be understood, arises for all greatly wise ones who have fulfilled the perfections.

Parato [M 0.0395] sutvā paṭilabhatīti ettha kammāyatanādīni parena kariyamānāni vā katāni vā disvāpi yassa kassaci kathayamānassa vacanaṃ sutvāpi ācariyassa santike uggahetvāpi paṭiladdhā sabbā parato sutvāyeva paṭiladdhā nāmāti veditabbā.

He attains it after hearing from another: here, all that is attained—whether by seeing crafts and so on being done or having been done by another, or by hearing the speech of someone explaining, or by learning from a teacher—should be understood as ‘attained after hearing from another.’

Samāpannassāti samāpattisamaṅgissa; antosamāpattiyaṃ pavattā paññā bhāvanāmayā nāmāti attho.

‘For one who has attained’ means for one endowed with attainment. The wisdom that occurs within an attainment is called wisdom born of development; this is the meaning.

769. Dānaṃ [V 0.0390] ārabbhāti dānaṃ paṭicca; dānacetanāpaccayāti attho. Dānādhigacchāti dānaṃ adhigacchantassa; pāpuṇantassāti attho. Yā uppajjatīti yā evaṃ dānacetanāsampayuttā paññā uppajjati, ayaṃ dānamayā paññā nāma. Sā panesā ‘dānaṃ dassāmī’ti cintentassa, dānaṃ dentassa, dānaṃ datvā taṃ paccavekkhantassa [P 0.0413] pubbacetanā, muñcacetanā, aparacetanāti tividhena uppajjati.

769. ‘Concerning giving’ means with reference to giving; the meaning is ‘conditioned by the volition for giving.’ ‘One who obtains giving’ means for one who is obtaining giving; the meaning is ‘for one who attains it.’ ‘That which arises’: the wisdom that thus arises associated with the volition for giving is called wisdom consisting of giving. This arises in three ways—as prior volition, volition at the time of giving, and subsequent volition—for one who thinks, ‘I will give a gift,’ for one who is giving a gift, and for one who reflects on it after having given.

Sīlaṃ ārabbha sīlādhigacchāti idhāpi sīlacetanāsampayuttāva sīlamayā paññāti adhippetā. Ayampi ‘sīlaṃ pūressāmī’ti cintentassa, sīlaṃ pūrentassa, sīlaṃ pūretvā taṃ paccavekkhantassa pubbacetanā, muñcacetanā, aparacetanāti tividheneva uppajjati. Bhāvanāmayā heṭṭhā vuttāyeva.

‘Regarding virtue, one attains virtue’: here too, what is intended by ‘wisdom consisting of virtue’ is the wisdom associated with the volition for virtue. This also arises in three ways—as prior volition, volition at the time of observance, and subsequent volition—for one who thinks, ‘I will fulfill my virtue,’ for one who is fulfilling virtue, and for one who reviews it after having fulfilled it. Wisdom consisting of development is as stated above.

770. Adhisīlapaññādīsu sīlādīni duvidhena veditabbāni – sīlaṃ, adhisīlaṃ; cittaṃ, adhicittaṃ; paññā, adhipaññāti. Tattha “uppādā vā tathāgatānaṃ anuppādā vā tathāgatānaṃ ṭhitāva sā dhātu dhammaṭṭhitatā dhammaniyāmatā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.20; a. ni. 3.137) imāya tantiyā saṅgahitavasena pañcapi sīlāni dasapi sīlāni sīlaṃ nāma. Tañhi tathāgate uppannepi anuppannepi hoti. Anuppanne ke paññāpentīti? Tāpasaparibbājakā, sabbaññubodhisattā, cakkavattirājāno ca paññāpenti. Uppanne sammāsambuddhe bhikkhusaṅgho, bhikkhunīsaṅgho, upāsakā, upāsikāyo ca paññāpenti. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ pana sabbasīlehi adhikaṃ uppanneyeva tathāgate uppajjati, no anuppanne. Sabbaññubuddhāyeva ca naṃ paññāpenti. “Imasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ vītikkame idaṃ nāma hotī”ti paññāpanañhi aññesaṃ avisayo, buddhānaṃyeva esa visayo, buddhānaṃ balaṃ. Iti yasmā pātimokkhasaṃvaro adhisīlaṃ, tasmā taṃ adhisīlapaññaṃ dassetuṃ pātimokkhasaṃvaraṃ saṃvarantassātiādi vuttaṃ.

770. In regard to higher virtue, wisdom, and so on, virtue and the rest should be understood in two ways: virtue and higher virtue; mind and higher mind; wisdom and higher wisdom. Herein, in accordance with the textual passage, ‘Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, that element remains—the stableness of the Dhamma, the fixed course of the Dhamma’ (SN 12.20; AN 3.137), the five precepts and the ten precepts are called ‘virtue.’ For this exists whether Tathāgatas have arisen or not. When they have not arisen, who promulgates them? Ascetics and wanderers, bodhisattas aspiring to omniscience, and wheel-turning monarchs. When a Perfectly Enlightened One has arisen, the communities of bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs, and male and female lay followers promulgate them. However, the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint, which is superior to all virtues, arises only when a Tathāgata has arisen, not otherwise. Only Omniscient Buddhas promulgate it. For to declare, ‘In this case, a transgression is called thus,’ is beyond the scope of others; it is the domain of the Buddhas alone, a Buddha’s power. Thus, because Pātimokkha restraint is higher virtue, to indicate the wisdom concerning higher virtue, it is said, ‘for one restraining oneself with the Pātimokkha restraint,’ and so on.

Heṭṭhā [M 0.0396] vuttāya eva pana tantiyā saṅgahitavasena vaṭṭapādikā aṭṭha samāpattiyo cittaṃ nāma. Tañhi tathāgate uppannepi hoti anuppannepi. Anuppanne ke nibbattentīti? Tāpasaparibbājakā ceva sabbaññubodhisattā ca cakkavattirājāno ca. Uppanne bhagavati visesatthikā bhikkhuādayopi nibbattentiyeva. Vipassanāpādikā pana aṭṭha samāpattiyo sabbacittehi [V 0.0391] adhikā, uppanneyeva tathāgate uppajjanti, no anuppanne. Sabbaññubuddhā eva ca etā paññāpenti[P 0.0414]. Iti yasmā aṭṭha samāpattiyo adhicittaṃ, tasmā adhicittapaññaṃ dassetuṃ rūpāvacarārūpāvacarasamāpattiṃ samāpajjantassātiādi vuttaṃ.

Again, in accordance with the same textual passage stated above, the eight mundane attainments are called 'mind.' For these exist whether Tathāgatas have arisen or not. When they have not arisen, who brings them into being? Ascetics and wanderers, bodhisattas aspiring to omniscience, and wheel-turning monarchs. When the Blessed One has arisen, bhikkhus and others who seek distinction also bring them into being. However, the eight attainments that are a basis for insight, which are superior to all other states of mind, arise only when a Tathāgata has arisen, not otherwise. And only Omniscient Buddhas promulgate them. Thus, because the eight attainments are higher mind, to indicate the wisdom concerning higher mind, the passage beginning 'for one attaining the fine-material and immaterial-sphere attainments' was stated.

Heṭṭhā vuttāya eva pana tantiyā saṅgahitavasena kammassakatañāṇaṃ paññā nāma. Tañhi tathāgate uppannepi hoti anuppannepi. Anuppanne velāmadānavessantaradānādivasena uppajjati; uppanne tena ñāṇena mahādānaṃ pavattentānaṃ pamāṇaṃ natthi. Maggaphalapaññā pana sabbapaññāhi adhikā, uppanneyeva tathāgate vitthārikā hutvā pavattati, no anuppanne. Iti yasmā maggaphalapaññā adhipaññā, tasmā atirekapaññāya paññaṃ dassetuṃ catūsu maggesūtiādi vuttaṃ.

Again, in accordance with the same textual passage stated above, the knowledge of kamma as one's own possession is called 'wisdom.' For this exists whether Tathāgatas have arisen or not. When they have not arisen, it arises by way of generosity such as the gifts of Velāma and Vessantara; when a Tathāgata has arisen, there is no limit to those who, possessing this knowledge, give great gifts. However, the wisdom of the path and fruition is superior to all wisdoms and unfolds extensively only when a Tathāgata has arisen, not otherwise. Thus, because the wisdom of the path and fruition is higher wisdom, to indicate this surpassing wisdom, the passage beginning 'in the four paths' was stated.

Tattha siyā – sīlaṃ, adhisīlaṃ; cittaṃ, adhicittaṃ; paññā, adhipaññāti imesu chasu koṭṭhāsesu vipassanā paññā katarasannissitāti? Adhipaññāsannissitā. Tasmā yathā omakatarappamāṇaṃ chattaṃ vā dhajaṃ vā upādāya atirekappamāṇaṃ atichattaṃ atidhajoti vuccati, evamidampi pañcasīlaṃ dasasīlaṃ upādāya pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ ‘adhisīlaṃ’ nāma; vaṭṭapādikā aṭṭha samāpattiyo upādāya vipassanāpādikā aṭṭha samāpattiyo ‘adhicittaṃ’ nāma, kammassakatapaññaṃ upādāya vipassanāpaññā ca maggapaññā ca phalapaññā ca ‘adhipaññā’ nāmāti veditabbā.

Here, it might be asked: Among these six divisions—virtue, higher virtue; mind, higher mind; wisdom, higher wisdom—on which is insight wisdom dependent? It is dependent on higher wisdom. Therefore, just as with reference to an umbrella or a flag of a lesser measure, one of a superior measure is called a 'surpassing umbrella' or a 'surpassing flag,' so too here: with reference to the five precepts and the ten precepts, the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint is called 'higher virtue'; with reference to the eight mundane attainments, the eight attainments that serve as a basis for insight are called 'higher mind'; and with reference to the wisdom of kamma as one's own possession, insight wisdom, path wisdom, and fruition wisdom are called 'higher wisdom.' This should be understood.

771. Āyakosallādiniddese yasmā āyoti vuḍḍhi, sā anatthahānito atthuppattito ca duvidhā; apāyoti avuḍḍhi, sāpi atthahānito anatthuppattito ca duvidhā; tasmā taṃ dassetuṃ ime dhamme manasikarototiādi vuttaṃ. Idaṃ vuccatīti yā imesaṃ akusaladhammānaṃ anuppattippahānesu kusaladhammānañca uppattiṭṭhitīsu paññā – idaṃ āyakosallaṃ [M 0.0397] nāma vuccati.
