Yā panesā kusaladhammānaṃ anuppajjananirujjhanesu akusaladhammānañca uppattiṭṭhitīsu paññā – idaṃ apāyakosallaṃ nāmāti attho. Āyakosallaṃ tāva paññā hotu; apāyakosallaṃ kathaṃ paññā nāma jātāti? Paññavāyeva hi ‘mayhaṃ evaṃ manasikaroto anuppannā kusalā dhammā nuppajjanti uppannā ca nirujjhanti; anuppannā akusalā dhammā uppajjanti, uppannā pavaḍḍhantī’ti [P 0.0415] pajānāti. So evaṃ ñatvā anuppannānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppajjituṃ na deti, uppanne pajahati; anuppanne kusale uppādeti, uppanne bhāvanāpāripūriṃ [V 0.0392] pāpeti. Evaṃ apāyakosallampi paññā evāti veditabbaṃ. Sabbāpi tatrūpāyā paññā upāyakosallanti idaṃ pana accāyikakicce vā bhaye vā uppanne tassa tikicchanatthaṃ ṭhānuppattiyakāraṇajānanavaseneva veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

771. In the exposition of skill in growth and so on: since 'growth' (āya) means increase, it is twofold, consisting in the removal of what is detrimental and the arising of what is beneficial. 'Decline' (apāya) means non-increase, and it too is twofold, consisting in the removal of what is beneficial and the arising of what is detrimental. Therefore, to show this, the passage beginning 'by giving attention to these states' was stated. This is said: the wisdom concerning the non-arising and abandoning of unwholesome states and the arising and establishment of wholesome states—this is called skill in growth. Conversely, the wisdom concerning the non-arising and cessation of wholesome states and the arising and establishment of unwholesome states—this is called skill in decline. Now, let skill in growth be wisdom; but how can skill in decline be called wisdom? Because it is a wise person who understands: 'When I give attention in such a way, unarisen wholesome states do not arise and arisen ones cease; unarisen unwholesome states arise and arisen ones increase.' Knowing this, one does not allow unarisen unwholesome states to arise and abandons arisen ones; one arouses unarisen wholesome states and brings arisen ones to fulfillment by development. Thus, skill in decline should also be understood to be wisdom. All wisdom that is a means in that connection is 'skill in means.' This, however, should be understood as the knowledge of the appropriate response that arises for the purpose of remedying an urgent matter or a danger that has arisen. The meaning of the rest is clear everywhere.

Tikaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Triads.

(4.) Catukkaniddesavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Tetrads

793. Catubbidhena ñāṇavatthuniddese atthi dinnantiādīsu dinnapaccayā phalaṃ atthīti iminā upāyena attho veditabbo. Idaṃ vuccatīti yaṃ ñāṇaṃ ‘idaṃ kammaṃ sakaṃ, idaṃ no saka’nti jānāti – idaṃ kammassakatañāṇaṃ nāma vuccatīti attho. Tattha tividhaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ, catubbidhaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ, tividhaṃ manoduccaritanti idaṃ na sakakammaṃ nāma. Tīsu dvāresu dasavidhampi sucaritaṃ sakakammaṃ nāma. Attano vāpi hotu parassa vā sabbampi akusalaṃ na sakakammaṃ nāma. Kasmā? Atthabhañjanato anatthajananato ca. Attano vā hotu parassa vā sabbampi kusalaṃ sakakammaṃ nāma. Kasmā? Anatthabhañjanato atthajananato ca. Evaṃ jānanasamatthe imasmiṃ kammassakatañāṇe ṭhatvā bahuṃ dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ pūretvā uposathaṃ samādiyitvā sukhena sukhaṃ sampattiyā sampattiṃ anubhavitvā nibbānaṃ pattānaṃ gaṇanaparicchedo natthi. Yathā hi sadhano puriso pañcasu sakaṭasatesu sappimadhuphāṇitādīni ceva loṇatilataṇḍulādīni ca āropetvā kantāramaggaṃ paṭipanno kenacideva karaṇīyena atthe uppanne sabbesaṃ upakaraṇānaṃ gahitattā na cinteti, na paritassati, sukheneva khemantaṃ [M 0.0398] pāpuṇāti; evameva imasmimpi kammassakatañāṇe ṭhatvā bahuṃ dānaṃ datvā…pe… nibbānaṃ pattānaṃ gaṇanapatho natthi. Ṭhapetvā saccānulomikaṃ ñāṇanti maggasaccassa paramatthasaccassa ca anulomanato saccānulomikanti laddhanāmaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesā sabbāpi sāsavā kusalā paññā kammassakatañāṇamevāti attho.

793. In the exposition of the fourfold basis of knowledge, the meaning should be understood by this method: “From a gift given, there is a fruit,” and so on. This is said: the knowledge that knows, “This is my own kamma, this is not my own kamma”—this is called the knowledge of kamma as one’s own property. Herein, the threefold bodily misconduct, the fourfold verbal misconduct, and the threefold mental misconduct—this is not called one’s own kamma. The tenfold good conduct at the three doors is called one’s own kamma. Whether it is one’s own or another’s, all that is unwholesome is not called one’s own kamma. Why? Because it destroys the beneficial and generates the harmful. Whether it is one’s own or another’s, all that is wholesome is called one’s own kamma. Why? Because it destroys the harmful and generates the beneficial. Having become established in this knowledge of kamma as one’s own property, being capable of knowing thus, having given many gifts, fulfilled the moral precepts, undertaken the uposatha observance, and experienced happiness upon happiness and prosperity upon prosperity, there is no counting or limit of those who attain Nibbāna. For just as a wealthy man, having loaded five hundred carts with such things as ghee, honey, and molasses, and with salt, sesame seeds, and rice, and set out on a wilderness track, when some need arises, does not worry or become anxious because all necessities have been taken, and he reaches a place of safety with ease; in the same way, for those who have become established in this knowledge of kamma as one’s own property, having given many gifts… and attained Nibbāna, there is no way of counting them. Excluding the knowledge in conformity with the truths—that is, setting aside the insight knowledge that has obtained the name “in conformity with the truths” because it conforms to the truth of the path and the ultimate truth—all other tainted wholesome wisdom is simply the knowledge of kamma as one’s own property. This is the meaning.

794. Maggasamaṅgissa [V 0.0393] ñāṇaṃ dukkhepetaṃ ñāṇanti ettha ekameva [P 0.0416] maggañāṇaṃ catūsu saccesu ekapaṭivedhavasena catūsu ṭhānesu saṅgahitaṃ.

794. Herein, regarding 'the knowledge of one endowed with the path is this knowledge in suffering,' it is the one and the same path-knowledge that is included in four instances because it penetrates the four truths in a single act.

796. Dhamme ñāṇanti ettha maggapaññā tāva catunnaṃ saccānaṃ ekapaṭivedhavasena dhamme ñāṇaṃ nāma hotu; phalapaññā kathaṃ dhamme ñāṇaṃ nāmāti? Nirodhasaccavasena. Duvidhāpi hesā paññā aparappaccaye atthapaccakkhe ariyasaccadhamme kiccato ca ārammaṇato ca pavattattā dhamme ñāṇanti veditabbā. So iminā dhammenāti ettha maggañāṇaṃ dhammagocarattā gocaravohārena dhammoti vuttaṃ, upayogatthe vā karaṇavacanaṃ; imaṃ dhammaṃ ñātenāti attho; catusaccadhammaṃ jānitvā ṭhitena maggañāṇenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Diṭṭhenāti dassanena; dhammaṃ passitvā ṭhitenāti attho. Pattenāti cattāri ariyasaccāni patvā ṭhitattā dhammaṃ pattena. Viditenāti maggañāṇena cattāri ariyasaccāni viditāni pākaṭāni katāni. Tasmā taṃ dhammaṃ viditaṃ nāma hoti. Tena viditadhammena. Pariyogāḷhenāti catusaccadhammaṃ pariyogāhetvā ṭhitena. Nayaṃ netīti atīte ca anāgate ca nayaṃ neti harati peseti. Idaṃ pana na maggañāṇassa kiccaṃ, paccavekkhaṇañāṇassa kiccaṃ. Satthārā pana maggañāṇaṃ atītānāgate nayaṃ nayanasadisaṃ kataṃ. Kasmā? Maggamūlakattā. Bhāvitamaggassa hi paccavekkhaṇā nāma hoti. Tasmā satthā maggañāṇameva nayaṃ nayanasadisaṃ akāsi. Apica evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo – yadetaṃ iminā catusaccagocaraṃ maggañāṇaṃ adhigataṃ, tena ñāṇena kāraṇabhūtena atītānāgate paccavekkhaṇañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ nayaṃ neti.

796. Regarding 'knowledge in the Dhamma': first, let it be that path wisdom is called 'knowledge in the Dhamma' by way of its single penetration of the four truths. But how is fruition wisdom called 'knowledge in the Dhamma'? By way of the truth of cessation. For both these kinds of wisdom should be understood as 'knowledge in the Dhamma' because they proceed by way of function and object with regard to the noble truths, which are the Dhamma that is not reliant on another and is directly visible. Regarding 'by this Dhamma': here path knowledge is called 'Dhamma' by way of usage based on its domain, since its domain is the Dhamma; or it is an instrumental expression in the sense of means. The meaning is: 'by one who has known this Dhamma'; that is to say, by the path knowledge of one who stands having known the Dhamma of the four truths. 'Seen' means by seeing; the meaning is: by one who stands having seen the Dhamma. 'Attained' means by one who has attained the Dhamma, because of having stood having attained the four noble truths. 'Known' means that the four noble truths have been known, made manifest, by path knowledge. Therefore that Dhamma is called 'known.' 'By that known Dhamma.' 'Thoroughly penetrated' means by one who stands having thoroughly penetrated the Dhamma of the four truths. 'Leads the way' means it leads, carries, and sends forth a method into the past and the future. This, however, is not the function of path knowledge but the function of reviewing knowledge. But the Teacher has made path knowledge similar to leading the way. Why? Because reviewing knowledge has the path as its root. For one who has developed the path, there is reviewing. Therefore the Teacher made path knowledge itself similar to leading the way. Moreover, the meaning here should be seen thus: whatever path knowledge having the four truths as its domain has been attained, by means of that knowledge, which has become the cause, one leads the way—designated as reviewing knowledge—into the past and future.

Idāni yathā tena nayaṃ neti, taṃ ākāraṃ dassetuṃ ye hi keci atītamaddhānantiādimāha. Tattha abbhaññaṃsūti jāniṃsu paṭivijjhiṃsu. Imaññevāti yaṃ dukkhaṃ atīte abbhaññaṃsu, yañca anāgate abhijānissanti, na taññeva imaṃ; sarikkhaṭṭhena pana evaṃ vuttaṃ. Atītepi hi ṭhapetvā taṇhaṃ tebhūmakakkhandheyeva [M 0.0399] dukkhasaccanti paṭivijjhiṃsu, taṇhaṃyeva [P 0.0417] samudayasaccanti nibbānameva nirodhasaccanti ariyamaggameva maggasaccanti paṭivijjhiṃsu, anāgatepi evameva paṭivijjhissanti, etarahipi evameva paṭivijjhantīti sarikkhaṭṭhena “imaññevā”ti vuttaṃ. Idaṃ vuccati anvaye ñāṇanti idaṃ anugamanañāṇaṃ nayanañāṇaṃ kāraṇañāṇanti vuccati.

Now, to show the manner in which one leads the way by that, he says, 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins in past time…,' and so on. Herein, 'they fully knew' means they knew, they penetrated. Regarding 'this very': the suffering that they fully knew in the past, and that they will fully know in the future, is not this very same suffering; but it is said thus in the sense of similarity. For in the past, too, setting aside craving, they penetrated the aggregates belonging to the three planes themselves as the truth of suffering, craving itself as the truth of origination, Nibbāna itself as the truth of cessation, and the noble path itself as the truth of the path. In the future, too, they will penetrate in the same way, and even now they are penetrating in the same way. Thus it is said, 'this very,' in the sense of similarity. This is called knowledge of consequence. This is called knowledge of inference, knowledge of guidance, and knowledge of causality.

Pariye [V 0.0394] ñāṇanti cittaparicchedañāṇaṃ. Parasattānanti ṭhapetvā attānaṃ sesasattānaṃ. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Cetasā ceto paricca pajānātīti attano cittena tesaṃ cittaṃ sarāgādivasena paricchinditvā nānappakārato jānāti. Sarāgaṃ vātiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅge vuttameva. Ayaṃ pana viseso – idha anuttaraṃ vā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ vā cittanti ettha lokuttarampi labbhati. Avipassanūpagampi hi paracittañāṇassa visayo hotiyeva.

'Knowledge of encompassing' is the knowledge that penetrates the mind. 'Of other beings' means of the remaining beings, setting aside oneself. 'Of other individuals' is a synonym for that. 'Having encompassed their mind with his own mind, he understands' means that with his own mind he penetrates their mind in various ways, understanding it as a mind with lust, and so on. Whatever should be said regarding 'a mind with lust,' etc., has already been said below in the Exposition of the Foundations of Mindfulness. This, however, is the difference: here, in the passage 'an unsurpassed mind' or 'a liberated mind,' the supramundane is also included. For even one who has not attained insight is indeed an object for the knowledge of others' minds.

Avasesā paññāti dhamme ñāṇādikā tisso paññā ṭhapetvā sesā sabbāpi paññā ñāṇanti sammatattā sammutiñāṇaṃ nāma hoti. Vacanattho panettha sammutimhi ñāṇanti sammutiñāṇaṃ.

The remaining wisdom: Setting aside the three kinds of wisdom beginning with knowledge in the Dhamma, all the remaining wisdom is designated as 'knowledge.' Because it is so designated (sammata), it is called 'conventional knowledge' (sammutiñāṇa). The verbal meaning here is 'knowledge in convention,' hence 'conventional knowledge'.

797. Kāmāvacarakusale paññāti ayañhi ekantena vaṭṭasmiṃ cutipaṭisandhiṃ ācinateva, tasmā “ācayāya no apacayāyā”ti vuttā. Lokuttaramaggapaññā pana yasmā cutipaṭisandhiṃ apacinateva, tasmā “apacayāya no ācayāyā”ti vuttā. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacarapaññā cutipaṭisandhimpi ācinati, vikkhambhanavasena kilese ceva kilesamūlake ca dhamme apacinati, tasmā “ācayāya ceva apacayāya cā”ti vuttā. Sesā neva cutipaṭisandhiṃ ācinati na apacinati, tasmā “neva ācayāya no apacayāyā”ti vuttā.

797. The wisdom in sense-sphere wholesome consciousness exclusively accumulates death and rebirth-linking in the round of existence; therefore, it is said to be 'for accumulation, not for diminution.' The wisdom of the supramundane path, however, only diminishes death and rebirth-linking; hence, it is said to be 'for diminution, not for accumulation.' The wisdom of the form sphere and the formless sphere both accumulates death and rebirth-linking and diminishes defilements and phenomena rooted in defilements by way of suppression; therefore, it is said to be 'both for accumulation and for diminution.' The remaining wisdom neither accumulates nor diminishes death and rebirth-linking; hence, it is said to be 'neither for accumulation nor for diminution.'

798. Na ca abhiññāyo paṭivijjhatīti idaṃ paṭhamajjhānapaññaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sā hissa kāmavivekena pattabbattā kilesanibbidāya saṃvattati. Tāya cesa kāmesu vītarāgo hoti, abhiññāpādakabhāvaṃ pana appattatāya neva pañca abhiññāyo paṭivijjhati, nimittārammaṇattā na saccāni paṭivijjhati. Evamayaṃ paññā nibbidāya hoti no paṭivedhāya. Svevāti [P 0.0418] paṭhamajjhānaṃ patvā ṭhito. Kāmesu vītarāgo samānoti tathā vikkhambhitānaṃyeva kāmānaṃ vasena vītarāgo. Abhiññāyo paṭivijjhatīti [M 0.0400] pañca abhiññāyo paṭivijjhati. Idaṃ catutthajjhānapaññaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Catutthajjhānapaññā hi abhiññāpādakabhāvenāpi pañca abhiññāyo paṭivijjhati, abhiññābhāvappattiyāpi paṭivijjhati eva. Tasmā sā paṭivedhāya hoti. Paṭhamajjhānapaññāya eva pana kilesesupi nibbindattā no nibbidāya. Yā panāyaṃ dutiyatatiyajjhānapaññā, sā katarakoṭṭhāsaṃ bhajatīti? Somanassavasena paṭhamajjhānampi bhajati, avitakkavasena catutthajjhānampi. Evamesā paṭhamajjhānasannissitā vā catutthajjhānasannissitā vā kātabbā. Nibbidāya [V 0.0395] ceva paṭivedhāya cāti maggapaññā sabbasmimpi vaṭṭe nibbindanato nibbidāya, chaṭṭhaṃ abhiññaṃ paṭivijjhanato paṭivedhāya ca hoti.

798. 'And it does not penetrate the direct knowledges'—this is said with reference to the wisdom of the first jhāna. For since it is to be attained through seclusion from sensual pleasures, it leads to disenchantment with the defilements. Through it one becomes dispassionate toward sensual pleasures, but because it has not attained the state of being a basis for the direct knowledges, it does not penetrate the five direct knowledges. Because its object is a sign, it does not penetrate the truths. Thus this wisdom is for disenchantment, not for penetration. 'That very person' means one who stands having attained the first jhāna. 'Being dispassionate toward sensual pleasures' means being dispassionate by way of those sensual pleasures that have been suppressed. 'Penetrates the direct knowledges' means it penetrates the five direct knowledges. This is said with reference to the wisdom of the fourth jhāna. For the wisdom of the fourth jhāna penetrates the five direct knowledges both by being a basis for the direct knowledges and by having attained the state of direct knowledge. Therefore it is for penetration. But it is not for disenchantment, because one is already disenchanted with the defilements by means of the first jhāna wisdom itself. As for the wisdom of the second and third jhānas, to which category does it belong? By way of gladness, it partakes of the first jhāna; by way of the absence of applied thought, it partakes of the fourth jhāna. Thus it should be treated as being dependent on either the first jhāna or the fourth jhāna. 'For both disenchantment and penetration'—the wisdom of the path is for disenchantment because it leads to disenchantment with the entire round of existence, and it is for penetration because it penetrates the sixth direct knowledge.

799. Paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhītiādīsu yvāyaṃ appaguṇassa paṭhamajjhānassa lābhī. Taṃ tato vuṭṭhitaṃ ārammaṇavasena kāmasahagatā hutvā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti tudanti codenti. Tassa kāmānupakkhandānaṃ saññāmanasikārānaṃ vasena sā paṭhamajjhānapaññā hāyati parihāyati; tasmā hānabhāginīti vuttā. Tadanudhammatāti tadanurūpasabhāvā. Sati santiṭṭhatīti idaṃ micchāsatiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na sammāsatiṃ. Yassa hi paṭhamajjhānānurūpasabhāvā paṭhamajjhānaṃ santato paṇītato disvā assādayamānā abhinandamānā nikanti uppajjati, tassa nikantivasena sā paṭhamajjhānapaññā neva hāyati, na vaḍḍhati, ṭhitikoṭṭhāsikā hoti. Tena vuttaṃ ṭhitibhāginī paññāti. Avitakkasahagatāti avitakkaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ santato paṇītato manasikaroto ārammaṇavasena avitakkasahagatā. Samudācarantīti paguṇato paṭhamajjhānato vuṭṭhitaṃ dutiyajjhānādhigamatthāya tudanti codenti. Tassa upari dutiyajjhānānupakkhandānaṃ saññāmanasikārānaṃ vasena sā paṭhamajjhānapaññā visesabhūtassa dutiyajjhānassa uppattiṭṭhānatāya visesabhāginīti vuttā. Nibbidāsahagatāti tameva [P 0.0419] paṭhamajjhānato vuṭṭhitaṃ nibbidāsaṅkhātena vipassanāñāṇena sahagatā. Vipassanāñāṇañhi jhānaṅgabhede vattante nibbindati ukkaṇṭhati, tasmā nibbidāti vuccati. Samudācarantīti nibbānasacchikiriyatthāya tudanti codenti. Virāgūpasañhitāti virāgasaṅkhātena nibbānena upasaṃhitā. Vipassanāñāṇamhi sakkā iminā maggena virāgaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikātunti pavattito “virāgūpasañhita”nti vuccati. Taṃsampayuttā saññāmanasikārāpi virāgūpasañhitā eva nāma. Tassa tesaṃ saññāmanasikārānaṃ vasena sā paṭhamajjhānapaññā ariyamaggapaṭivedhassa [M 0.0401] padaṭṭhānatāya nibbedhabhāginīti vuttā. Evaṃ catūsu ṭhānesu paṭhamajjhānapaññāva kathitā. Dutiyajjhānapaññādīsupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo.

799. In the case of 'one who attains the first jhāna,' etc., this refers to one who attains the first jhāna, which is of lesser quality. Having emerged from it, perceptions and instances of attention connected with sensual pleasures arise, assailing and provoking him. By the power of these perceptions and instances of attention that are conducive to sensual pleasures, the wisdom of the first jhāna declines and deteriorates; thus, it is called 'liable to decline.' 'Conforming to it' means having a nature in accordance with it. 'Mindfulness is established': this is said with reference to wrong mindfulness, not right mindfulness. For one in whom, having a nature in accordance with the first jhāna, craving arises as he sees the first jhāna as peaceful and sublime, delighting in it and enjoying it, by the power of that craving the wisdom of the first jhāna neither declines nor grows but becomes stagnant. Therefore, it is said that 'wisdom is liable to stagnation.' 'Accompanied by what is without applied thought' refers to one attending to the second jhāna, which is without applied thought, as peaceful and sublime. 'They arise' means that having emerged from the proficient first jhāna, they assail and provoke him for the sake of attaining the second jhāna. By the power of perceptions and instances of attention that are conducive to the higher second jhāna, the wisdom of the first jhāna is called 'liable to distinction' because it serves as the basis for the arising of the superior second jhāna. 'Accompanied by disenchantment' refers to that same one who has emerged from the first jhāna and is accompanied by insight knowledge, which is designated as disenchantment. For insight knowledge, when it occurs in relation to the breaking up of the jhāna factors, becomes disenchanted and dissatisfied; thus, it is called 'disenchantment.' 'They arise' means they assail and provoke him for the sake of realizing Nibbāna. 'Connected with dispassion' means connected with Nibbāna, which is designated as dispassion. Because insight knowledge proceeds with the thought, 'It is possible by this path to realize dispassion, Nibbāna,' it is called 'connected with dispassion.' The perceptions and instances of attention associated with it are also called 'connected with dispassion.' By the power of these perceptions and instances of attention, the wisdom of the first jhāna is called 'liable to penetration' because it serves as the basis for the penetration of the noble path. Thus, the wisdom of the first jhāna is discussed in these four instances. The meaning regarding the wisdom of the second jhāna and so on should be understood in the same way.

801. Kicchena kasirena samādhiṃ uppādentassāti lokuttarasamādhiṃ uppādentassa pubbabhāge āgamanakāle kicchena kasirena dukkhena sasaṅkhārena sappayogena kilamantassa kilese vikkhambhetvā āgatassa. Dandhaṃ taṇṭhānaṃ abhijānantassāti vikkhambhitesu kilesesu vipassanāparivāse ciraṃ vasitvā taṃ lokuttarasamādhisaṅkhātaṃ ṭhānaṃ dandhaṃ saṇikaṃ abhijānantassa paṭivijjhantassa[V 0.0396], pāpuṇantassāti attho. Ayaṃ vuccatīti yā esā evaṃ uppajjati, ayaṃ kilesavikkhambhanapaṭipadāya dukkhattā, vipassanāparivāsapaññāya ca dandhattā maggakāle ekacittakkhaṇe uppannāpi paññā āgamanavasena dukkhapaṭipadā dandhābhiññā nāmāti vuccati. Upari tīsu padesupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo.

801. 'One who arouses concentration with difficulty and trouble': this refers to one who, in the preliminary part, at the time of approach to arousing supramundane concentration, struggles with difficulty, trouble, pain, with exertion, and with effort, and who has arrived having suppressed the defilements. 'Slowly understanding that state': this means that after the defilements have been suppressed, having dwelt for a long time in the preparatory stage of insight, one slowly, gradually understands, penetrates, and attains that state designated as supramundane concentration. 'This is called': this wisdom, which arises in such a way in a single mind-moment at the time of the path, is called 'painful practice with slow direct knowledge' on account of its approach, because of the painfulness of the practice of suppressing the defilements and the slowness of the wisdom in the preparatory stage of insight. In the three cases that follow, the meaning should be understood in the same way.

802. Samādhissa na nikāmalābhissāti yo samādhissa na nikāmalābhī hoti, so tassa na nikāmalābhī nāma. Yassa samādhi uparūpari samāpajjanatthāya ussakkituṃ paccayo na hoti, tassa appaguṇajjhānalābhissāti attho. Ārammaṇaṃ thokaṃ pharantassāti paritte suppamatte vā sarāvamatte vā ārammaṇe parikammaṃ katvā tattheva appanaṃ patvā taṃ avaḍḍhitaṃ thokameva ārammaṇaṃ pharantassāti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Nanikāmalābhīpaṭipakkhato hi paguṇajjhānalābhī ettha nikāmalābhīti vutto. Avaḍḍhitārammaṇapaṭipakkhato ca vaḍḍhitārammaṇaṃ vipulanti vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisameva.

802. Not an obtainer of concentration at will: one who is not an obtainer of concentration at will is called 'not an obtainer at will.' For one whose concentration is not a condition for striving to attain successively higher states of concentration, the meaning is 'an obtainer of a jhāna of inferior quality.' Pervading a small object: this means having done the preliminary work on a small, well-measured, or bowl-sized object, and having reached absorption right there, one pervades just that small, undeveloped object. The same method applies to the remaining terms. For here, in contrast to one who is not an obtainer at will, an obtainer of a proficient jhāna is called 'an obtainer at will.' And in contrast to an undeveloped object, a developed object is called 'vast.' The rest is similar.

Jarāmaraṇepetaṃ [P 0.0420] ñāṇanti nibbānameva ārammaṇaṃ katvā catunnaṃ saccānaṃ ekapaṭivedhavasena etaṃ vuttaṃ.

This is knowledge in aging and death: this is said by way of a single penetration of the four truths, having made Nibbāna itself the object.

Jarāmaraṇaṃ ārabbhātiādīni pana ekekaṃ vatthuṃ ārabbha pavattikāle pubbabhāge saccavavatthāpanavasena vuttāni. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

But the phrases beginning with 'with reference to aging and death' are spoken by way of establishing the truths in the preliminary stage, at the time of occurrence, with reference to each individual item. The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Catukkaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Fours.

(5.) Pañcakaniddesavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Fives

804. Pañcavidhena [M 0.0402] ñāṇavatthuniddese pītipharaṇatādīsu pītiṃ pharamānā uppajjatīti dvīsu jhānesu paññā pītipharaṇatā nāma. Sukhaṃ pharamānā uppajjatīti tīsu jhānesu paññā sukhapharaṇatā nāma. Paresaṃ cetopharamānā uppajjatīti cetopariyapaññā cetopharaṇatā nāma. Ālokaṃ [V 0.0397] pharamānā uppajjatīti dibbacakkhupaññā ālokapharaṇatā nāma. Paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ paccavekkhaṇānimittaṃ nāma. Teneva vuttaṃ “dvīsu jhānesu paññā pītipharaṇatā”tiādi. Tattha ca pītipharaṇatā sukhapharaṇatā dve pādā viya, cetopharaṇatā ālokapharaṇatā dve hatthā viya, abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ majjhimakāyo viya, paccavekkhaṇānimittaṃ sīsaṃ viya. Iti bhagavā pañcaṅgikaṃ sammāsamādhiṃ aṅgapaccaṅgasampannaṃ purisaṃ viya katvā dassesi. Ayaṃ pañcaṅgiko sammāsamādhīti ayaṃ hatthapādasīsasadisehi pañcahi aṅgehi yutto sammāsamādhīti pādakajjhānasamādhiṃ kathesi.

804. In the exposition of the fivefold basis of knowledge, concerning joy-pervasion and so on: the wisdom that arises in the two jhānas while one pervades with joy is called joy-pervasion. The wisdom that arises in the three jhānas while one pervades with happiness is called happiness-pervasion. The wisdom that arises while one pervades the minds of others—the wisdom of knowing the minds of others—is called mind-pervasion. The wisdom that arises while one pervades with light—the wisdom of the divine eye—is called light-pervasion. The knowledge of reviewing is called the sign of reviewing. Hence it is said: 'In the two jhānas, wisdom is joy-pervasion,' and so on. Herein, joy-pervasion and happiness-pervasion are like two feet; mind-pervasion and light-pervasion are like two hands; the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge is like the torso; and the sign of reviewing is like the head. Thus the Blessed One showed the five-factored right concentration to be like a person endowed with major and minor limbs. 'This is the five-factored right concentration'—thus he described the concentration of the basic jhāna, endowed with these five factors comparable to hands, feet, and head.

Ayaṃ samādhi paccuppannasukho cevātiādīsu arahattaphalasamādhi adhippeto. So hi appitappitakkhaṇe sukhattā paccuppannasukho. Purimo purimo pacchimassa pacchimassa samādhisukhassa paccayattā āyatiṃ sukhavipāko. Santaṃ sukhumaṃ phalacittaṃ paṇītaṃ madhurarūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Phalasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhitassa hi sabbakāyānugataṃ sukhasamphassaṃ phoṭṭhabbaṃ paṭicca sukhasahagataṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppajjati. Imināpi pariyāyena āyatiṃ sukhavipāko. Kilesehi [P 0.0421] ārakattā ariyo. Kāmāmisavaṭṭāmisalokāmisānaṃ abhāvā nirāmiso. Buddhādīhi mahāpurisehi sevitattā akāpurisasevito. Aṅgasantatāya ārammaṇasantatāya sabbakilesadarathasantatāya ca santo. Atappanīyaṭṭhena paṇīto. Kilesapaṭippassaddhiyā laddhattā kilesapaṭippassaddhibhāvassa vā laddhattā paṭippassaddhiladdho. Paṭippassaddhaṃ paṭippassaddhīti hi idaṃ atthato ekaṃ. Paṭippassaddhakilesena vā arahatā laddhattāpi paṭippassaddhiladdho. Ekodibhāvena adhigatattā ekodibhāvameva vā adhigatattā ekodibhāvādhigato. Appaguṇasāsavasamādhi viya sasaṅkhārena sappayogena cittena paccanīkadhamme niggayha kilese vāretvā anadhigatattā na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagato. Tañca samādhiṃ samāpajjanto tato vā [M 0.0403] vuṭṭhahanto sativepullappattattā satova samāpajjati satova vuṭṭhahati. Yathāparicchinnakālavasena vā sato samāpajjati sato vuṭṭhahati. Tasmā yadettha “ayaṃ samādhi paccuppannasukho ceva āyatiñca sukhavipāko”ti evaṃ paccavekkhamānassa paccattaṃyeva aparappaccayaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjati – taṃ ekamaṅgaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Evamimehi pañcahi paccavekkhaṇañāṇehi ayaṃ samādhi pañcañāṇiko sammāsamādhi nāma vuttoti.

In such phrases as 'this concentration has present happiness and a happy result in the future,' the concentration of the fruit of arahantship is intended. For it is present happiness because it is happiness at every moment of absorption. It has a happy result in the future because each preceding moment is a condition for the happiness of concentration of each succeeding moment. It produces the peaceful, subtle, sublime, and sweet fruition-consciousness. For when one has emerged from the attainment of fruition, body-consciousness accompanied by happiness arises dependent on the tangible object that is the pleasant contact pervading the entire body. In this way too, it has a happy result in the future. It is noble because it is far from the defilements. It is unworldly because of the absence of sensual allurements, the allurements of the round, and worldly allurements. It is not frequented by inferior persons because it is frequented by great persons such as the Buddha. It is peaceful because its factors are pacified, its object is pacified, and all its defilements and anxieties are pacified. It is sublime in the sense of being incapable of causing torment. It is attained through the tranquillization of defilements, or because the state of tranquillization of defilements has been attained. For 'tranquil' and 'tranquillity' are one in meaning. Or, it is 'attained through tranquillization' because it is attained by an arahant whose defilements have been tranquillized. It is attained through one-pointedness because it is attained by means of one-pointedness, or because one-pointedness itself is attained. Because it is not attained by restraining opposing states and warding off defilements with a mind that requires effort and exertion—as is the case with an inferior concentration tainted by taints—it is not a state arrived at by effortful suppression and restraint. One who enters or emerges from that concentration does so mindfully, having reached an abundance of mindfulness; one enters mindfully and emerges mindfully. Or one enters mindfully and emerges mindfully in accordance with a pre-determined period of time. Therefore, when one reviews this concentration thus, 'This concentration has present happiness and a happy result in the future,' knowledge arises in oneself without dependence on another—this is one factor. The same method applies to the rest. Thus, on account of these five kinds of reviewing knowledge, this concentration is called 'right concentration endowed with five knowledges.'

Pañcakaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Fives.

(6.) Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixes

805. Chabbidhena [V 0.0398] ñāṇavatthuniddese iddhividhe ñāṇanti “ekopi hutvā bahudhā hotī”tiādinayappavatte (dī. ni. 1.484; paṭi. ma. 1.102) iddhividhe ñāṇaṃ. Iminā avitakkāvicārā upekkhāsahagatā rūpāvacarā bahudhābhāvādisādhikā ekacittakkhaṇikā appanāpaññāva kathitā. Sotadhātuvisuddhiyā ñāṇanti dūrasantikādibhedasaddārammaṇāya dibbasotadhātuyā ñāṇaṃ. Imināpi avitakkāvicārā upekkhāsahagatā rūpāvacarā pakatisotavisayātītasaddārammaṇā ekacittakkhaṇikā appanāpaññāva kathitā. Paracitte [P 0.0422] ñāṇanti parasattānaṃ cittaparicchede ñāṇaṃ. Imināpi yathāvuttappakārā paresaṃ sarāgādicittārammaṇā ekacittakkhaṇikā appanāpaññāva kathitā. Pubbenivāsānussatiyā ñāṇanti pubbenivāsānussatisampayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Imināpi yathāvuttappakārā pubbe nivutthakkhandhānussaraṇasatisampayuttā ekacittakkhaṇikā appanāpaññāva kathitā. Sattānaṃ cutūpapāte ñāṇanti sattānaṃ cutiyañca upapāte ca ñāṇaṃ. Imināpi yathāvuttappakārā cavanakaupapajjanakānaṃ sattānaṃ vaṇṇadhātuārammaṇā ekacittakkhaṇikā appanāpaññāva kathitā. Āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇanti saccaparicchedajānanañāṇaṃ. Idaṃ lokuttarameva. Sesāni lokiyānīti.

805. In the exposition of the sixfold basis of knowledge: The knowledge of the kinds of psychic power is the knowledge of psychic power as described in the method beginning with 'having been one, he becomes many' (Dī. Ni. 1.484; Paṭi. Ma. 1.102). By this is described the absorption-wisdom of a single mind-moment—which accomplishes the state of becoming many and so on, is without initial and sustained thought, is accompanied by equanimity, and belongs to the form sphere. The knowledge of the purification of the ear-element is the knowledge pertaining to the divine ear element, which has as its object sounds of different kinds, whether distant or near. By this too is described the absorption-wisdom of a single mind-moment—which takes as its object sounds beyond the range of the ordinary ear, is without initial and sustained thought, is accompanied by equanimity, and belongs to the form sphere. The knowledge of others' minds is the knowledge that discerns the minds of other beings. By this too is described the absorption-wisdom of a single mind-moment of the kind described above, which takes as its object the minds of others, whether with lust or otherwise. The knowledge of recollecting past lives is the knowledge associated with the recollection of past lives. By this too is described the absorption-wisdom of a single mind-moment of the kind described above, which is associated with mindfulness recollecting the aggregates previously dwelt in. The knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings is the knowledge of the passing away and arising of beings. By this too is described the absorption-wisdom of a single mind-moment of the kind described above, which takes as its object the color-element of beings who are passing away or being reborn. The knowledge of the destruction of the taints is the knowledge of discerning the truths. This alone is supramundane; the rest are mundane.

Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixes.

(7.) Sattakaniddesādivaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Exposition Beginning with the Sevens

806. Sattavidhena [M 0.0404] ñāṇavatthuniddese jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇantiādinā nayena pavattinivattivasena ekādasasu paṭiccasamuppādaṅgesu ekekasmiṃ kālattayabhedato paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ vatvā puna “yampissa taṃ dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa”nti evaṃ tadeva ñāṇaṃ saṅkhepato khayadhammatādīhi pakārehi vuttaṃ. Tattha jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ, asati jātiyā natthi jarāmaraṇanti ñāṇadvayaṃ paccuppannaddhānavasena vuttaṃ. Atītampi addhānaṃ, anāgatampi addhānanti evaṃ atīte ñāṇadvayaṃ, anāgate ñāṇadvayanti cha. Tāni dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇena saddhiṃ satta. Tattha dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇanti [V 0.0399] paccayākārañāṇaṃ. Paccayākāro hi dhammānaṃ pavattiṭṭhitikāraṇattā dhammaṭṭhitīti vuccati; tattha ñāṇaṃ dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ. Etasseva chabbidhassa ñāṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Evaṃ ekekasmiṃ aṅge imāni satta satta katvā ekādasasu aṅgesu sattasattati honti. Tattha khayadhammanti khayagamanasabhāvaṃ. Vayadhammanti vayagamanasabhāvaṃ. Virāgadhammanti [P 0.0423] virajjanasabhāvaṃ. Nirodhadhammanti nirujjhanasabhāvaṃ. Iminā kiṃ kathitaṃ? Aparavipassanāya purimavipassanāsammasanaṃ kathitaṃ. Tena kiṃ kathitaṃ hoti? Sattakkhattuṃ vipassanāpaṭivipassanā kathitā. Paṭhamañāṇena hi sabbasaṅkhāre aniccā dukkhā anattāti disvā taṃ ñāṇaṃ dutiyena daṭṭhuṃ vaṭṭati, dutiyaṃ tatiyena, tatiyaṃ catutthena, catutthaṃ pañcamena, pañcamaṃ chaṭṭhena, chaṭṭhaṃ sattamena. Evaṃ satta vipassanāpaṭivipassanā kathitā hontīti.

806. In the exposition of the sevenfold basis of knowledge, having explained the knowledge of reviewing in relation to the eleven links of dependent origination—such as "with birth as condition, aging and death"—by way of their occurrence and cessation, divided into the three periods of time, that same knowledge is then further stated concisely through aspects such as being subject to destruction with the phrase, "and that is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena." Herein, the two knowledges—"with birth as condition, aging and death" and "when there is no birth, there is no aging and death"—are stated with reference to the present time. Considering also the past period and the future period, there are thus six: two knowledges for the past and two for the future. These, together with the knowledge of the stability of phenomena, make seven. Herein, "the knowledge of the stability of phenomena" refers to the knowledge of the conditional structure. The conditional structure is called the stability of phenomena because it is the cause for the occurrence and persistence of phenomena; the knowledge of that is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena. This is just another term for that sixfold knowledge. Thus, applying these seven to each of the eleven links makes seventy-seven in total. Herein, "subject to destruction" means having the nature of going to destruction. "Subject to decay" means having the nature of going to decay. "Subject to fading away" means having the nature of fading away. "Subject to cessation" means having the nature of ceasing. What is said by this? The reviewing and comprehending of earlier insight by subsequent insight is explained. What is meant by this? Sevenfold insight and counter-insight are explained. For by the first knowledge, having seen all formations as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, that knowledge should be seen by the second, the second by the third, the third by the fourth, the fourth by the fifth, the fifth by the sixth, and the sixth by the seventh. Thus, sevenfold insight and counter-insight are explained.

Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Sevens.

807. Aṭṭhavidhena ñāṇavatthuniddese sotāpattimagge paññāti sotāpattimaggamhi paññā. Iminā sampayuttapaññāva kathitā. Sesapadesupi eseva nayoti.

807. In the exposition of the eightfold basis of knowledge, "wisdom in the path of stream-entry" is wisdom in the stream-entry path. By this, only associated wisdom is spoken of. This same method applies in the remaining sections.

Aṭṭhakaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Eights.

808. Navavidhena ñāṇavatthuniddese anupubbavihārasamāpattīsūti anupubbavihārasaṅkhātāsu samāpattīsu. Tāsaṃ anupubbena anupaṭipāṭiyā vihāritabbaṭṭhena anupubbavihāratā, samāpajjitabbaṭṭhena samāpattitā daṭṭhabbā. Tattha paṭhamajjhānasamāpattiyā paññātiādayo aṭṭha sampayuttapaññā veditabbā[M 0.0405]. Navamā paccavekkhaṇapaññā. Sā hi nirodhasamāpattiṃ santato paṇītato paccavekkhamānassa pavattati. Tena vuttaṃ – “saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhitassa paccavekkhaṇañāṇa”nti.

808. In the exposition of the ninefold basis of knowledge, "in the successive meditative abidings and attainments" means in the attainments designated as successive abidings. Their nature as "successive abidings" should be understood from the fact that they are to be abided in successively, in sequence, and their nature as "attainments" from the fact that they are to be attained. Herein, the eight associated wisdoms beginning with the wisdom in the attainment of the first jhāna should be understood. The ninth is the wisdom of reviewing. This arises for one who is reviewing the attainment of cessation as peaceful and sublime. Hence it is said: "the knowledge of reviewing of one who has arisen from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling."

Navakaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Nines.

(10.) Dasakaniddesavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Tens

Paṭhamabalaniddeso

Exposition of the First Power

809. Dasavidhena [V 0.0400] ñāṇavatthuniddese aṭṭhānanti hetupaṭikkhepo. Anavakāsoti paccayapaṭikkhepo. Ubhayenāpi kāraṇameva paṭikkhipati. Kāraṇañhi tadāyattavuttitāya attano phalassa ṭhānanti ca avakāsoti ca vuccati. Yanti yena kāraṇena. Diṭṭhisampannoti maggadiṭṭhiyā sampanno sotāpanno ariyasāvako. Kañci [P 0.0424] saṅkhāranti catubhūmakesu saṅkhatasaṅkhāresu kañci ekaṃ saṅkhārampi. Niccato upagaccheyyāti niccoti gaṇheyya. Netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti etaṃ kāraṇaṃ natthi, na upalabbhati. Yaṃ puthujjanoti yena kāraṇena puthujjano. Ṭhānametaṃ vijjatīti etaṃ kāraṇaṃ atthi; sassatadiṭṭhiyā hi so tebhūmakesu saṅkhāresu kañci saṅkhāraṃ niccato gaṇheyyāti attho. Catutthabhūmakasaṅkhāro pana tejussadattā divasaṃ santatto ayoguḷo viya makkhikānaṃ diṭṭhiyā vā aññesaṃ vā akusalānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ na hoti. Iminā nayena kañci saṅkhāraṃ sukhatotiādīsupi attho veditabbo. Sukhato upagaccheyyāti “ekantasukhī attā hoti arogo parammaraṇā”ti (ma. ni. 3.21) evaṃ attadiṭṭhivasena sukhato gāhaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhivippayuttacittena pana ariyasāvako pariḷāhābhibhūto pariḷāhavūpasamatthaṃ, mattahatthīparitāsito viya, sucikāmo pokkhabrāhmaṇo gūthaṃ kañci saṅkhāraṃ sukhato upagacchati. Attavāde kasiṇādipaṇṇattisaṅgahatthaṃ saṅkhāranti avatvā kañci dhammanti vuttaṃ. Idhāpi ariyasāvakassa catubhūmakavasena paricchedo veditabbo, puthujjanassa tebhūmakavasena; sabbavāresu vā ariyasāvakassāpi tebhūmakavaseneva paricchedo vaṭṭati. Yaṃ yañhi puthujjano [M 0.0406] gaṇhāti, tato tato ariyasāvako gāhaṃ viniveṭheti. Puthujjano hi yaṃ yaṃ niccaṃ sukhaṃ attāti gaṇhāti, taṃ taṃ ariyasāvako aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti gaṇhanto gāhaṃ viniveṭheti.

809. In the exposition of the tenfold basis of knowledge, 'impossibility' refers to the rejection of a cause. 'No opportunity' refers to the rejection of a condition. Both reject the reason itself. For a reason, because its fruit is dependent on it, is called both a 'basis' and an 'opportunity.' 'By which' means by that reason. 'Endowed with view' refers to a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, accomplished in the view of the path. 'Any formation' refers to any one conditioned formation among the four planes. 'Would regard as permanent' means would grasp it as permanent. 'This is not a possible basis' means this reason does not exist; it is not found. 'That an ordinary person...' means 'for the reason that an ordinary person...' 'This is a possible basis' means this reason exists; for an ordinary person, due to the view of eternalism, would grasp any formation among the three planes as permanent, is the meaning. The fourth-plane formation, however, due to its brilliant nature, is not an object for views or for other unwholesome states, just as a red-hot iron ball is not for flies. By this method, the meaning should be understood similarly for 'regard as pleasant,' etc. 'Would regard as pleasant' refers to grasping it as pleasant through the view of self, as in the statement: 'The self is entirely happy and free from illness after death' (MN 102). However, a noble disciple with a mind dissociated from wrong view, when overcome by affliction, regards a certain formation as pleasant for the purpose of pacifying the affliction, just as one terrified by a mad elephant, or as the brahmin Pokkha, desiring purity, would regard filth. In the case of the self-doctrine, in order to include concepts such as kasiṇas, it says 'any phenomenon' instead of 'any formation.' Here too, the noble disciple should be understood as limited in terms of the four planes, while the ordinary person is limited in terms of the three planes. Alternatively, in all cases, even the noble disciple may be limited in terms of the three planes. For whatever an ordinary person grasps, the noble disciple disentangles that grasping. Whatever the ordinary person grasps as permanent, pleasant, or self, the noble disciple, by grasping that as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, disentangles the grasping.

Mātarantiādīsu janikāva mātā. Manussabhūtova khīṇāsavo arahāti adhippeto. Kiṃ pana ariyasāvako aññaṃ jīvitā voropeyyāti? Etampi aṭṭhānaṃ. Sacepi bhavantaragataṃ ariyasāvakaṃ attano ariyasāvakabhāvaṃ ajānantampi koci evaṃ vadeyya – ‘imaṃ kunthakipillikaṃ jīvitā voropetvā sakalacakkavāḷagabbhe cakkavattirajjaṃ paṭipajjāhī’ti, neva so taṃ jīvitā voropeyya. Atha vāpi [P 0.0425] naṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘sace imaṃ na ghātessasi, sīsaṃ [V 0.0401] te chindissāmā’ti, sīsamevassa chindeyyuṃ, neva so taṃ ghāteyya. Puthujjanabhāvassa pana mahāsāvajjabhāvadassanatthaṃ ariyasāvakassa ca baladīpanatthametaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – sāvajjo puthujjanabhāvo, yatra hi nāma puthujjano mātughātādīnipi ānantariyāni karissati. Mahābalo ariyasāvako; so etāni kammāni na karotīti.

In the case of 'mother,' etc., the one who gives birth is the mother. An arahant who has destroyed the taints is meant as a human being. But would a noble disciple deprive another of life? This too is impossible. Even if someone were to say to a noble disciple who has passed into another existence—even one unaware of his own status as a noble disciple—"Kill this tiny ant and gain universal sovereignty over the entire world-sphere," he would not kill it. Or if they were to say to him, "If you do not kill this, we will cut off your head," they might indeed cut off his head, but he would not kill it. This is stated to show the grave faultiness of the ordinary person’s state and to highlight the strength of a noble disciple. The meaning here is this: the state of an ordinary person is blameworthy, for an ordinary person might even commit the deeds with immediate result, such as matricide and the like. But a noble disciple is immensely powerful; he does not commit such deeds.

Paduṭṭhena cittenāti dosasampayuttena vadhakacittena. Lohitaṃ uppādeyyāti jīvamānakasarīre khuddakamakkhikāya pivanamattampi lohitaṃ uppādeyya. Saṅghaṃ bhindeyyāti samānasaṃvāsakaṃ samānasīmāyaṃ ṭhitaṃ pañcahi kāraṇehi saṅghaṃ bhindeyya, vuttañhetaṃ – “pañcahupāli, ākārehi saṅgho bhijjati – kammena, uddesena, voharanto, anussāvanena, salākaggāhenā”ti (pari. 458).

"With a malevolent mind" means with a mind associated with aversion, a murderous mind. "Would draw blood" means would cause even a drop of blood the size of that which a small fly could drink to flow from a living body. "Would split the Sangha" means would split a Sangha dwelling in communion within the same boundary by five means. As it is said: "Upāli, the Sangha is split in five ways: by an act, by a recitation, by a declaration, by a proclamation, or by the taking of a ballot" (Pvr 458).

Tattha ‘kammenā’ti apalokanādīsu catūsu kammesu aññatarena kammena. ‘Uddesenā’ti pañcasu pātimokkhuddesesu aññatarena uddesena. ‘Voharanto’ti kathayanto, tāhi tāhi uppattīhi ‘adhammaṃ dhammo’tiādīni aṭṭhārasa bhedakaravatthūni dīpento. ‘Anussāvanenā’ti ‘nanu tumhe jānātha mayhaṃ uccākulā pabbajitabhāvaṃ bahussutabhāvañca! Mādiso nāma uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ satthusāsanaṃ gāheyyāti cittampi uppādetuṃ tumhākaṃ na yuttaṃ. Kiṃ mayhaṃ avīci nīluppalavanaṃ viya sītalo? Kimahaṃ apāyato na bhāyāmī’tiādinā nayena kaṇṇamūle vacībhedaṃ katvā anussāvanena[M 0.0407]. ‘Salākaggāhenā’ti evaṃ anussāvetvā tesaṃ cittaṃ upatthambhetvā anivattanadhamme katvā “gaṇhatha imaṃ salāka”nti salākaggāhena. Ettha ca kammameva uddeso vā pamāṇaṃ vohārānussāvanasalākaggāhā pana pubbabhāgā. Aṭṭhārasavatthudīpanavasena hi voharantena tattha rucijananatthaṃ anussāvetvā salākāya gāhitāyapi abhinnova hoti saṅgho. Yadā pana evaṃ cattāro vā atirekā vā salākaṃ gāhetvā āveṇikaṃ kammaṃ vā uddesaṃ vā karonti, tadā saṅgho [P 0.0426] bhinno nāma hoti.

Here, 'by an act' means by any of the four formal acts, such as the act of declaration. 'By a recitation' means by any of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha. 'By a declaration' means speaking, explaining the eighteen grounds for schism, such as 'the Dhamma is not-Dhamma.' 'By a proclamation' means creating a verbal split by proclaiming in their ear in this way: 'Don’t you know that I have gone forth from a high family and am very learned? It is not fitting for you to even think that someone like me would take up a counterfeit Dhamma and a counterfeit Vinaya as the Teacher's teaching. Is Avīci cool for me like a grove of blue lotuses? Do I not fear the plane of misery?' 'By the taking of a ballot' means, after proclaiming thus, having bolstered their minds and made them irreversible, by the taking of a ballot, saying, 'Take this ballot.' Here, the act or the recitation is the standard, while the declaration, proclamation, and taking of a ballot are the preliminary stages. For the Sangha is not yet split even when one who is declaring the eighteen grounds, after making a proclamation to generate interest in them, has the ballots taken. But when four or more, having taken the ballots, perform a separate formal act or recitation, then the Sangha is said to be split.

Evaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo saṅghaṃ bhindeyyāti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Ettāvatā mātughātādīni pañca ānantariyakammāni dassitāni honti, yāni puthujjano karoti, na ariyasāvako. Tesaṃ āvibhāvatthaṃ –

Thus, it is not a possible basis that a person endowed with view would split the Sangha. By this much, the five deeds with immediate result—matricide and so on—are shown, which an ordinary person commits, but a noble disciple does not. To make them manifest:

Kammato [V 0.0402] dvārato ceva, kappaṭṭhitiyato tathā;

Pākasādhāraṇādīhi, viññātabbo vinicchayo.

The determination should be understood by way of the action, the door, and likewise the aeon-duration; by way of ripening, commonality, and so on.

Tattha ‘kammato’ tāva – ettha hi manussabhūtasseva manussabhūtaṃ mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ vā api parivattaliṅgaṃ jīvitā voropentassa kammaṃ ānantariyaṃ hoti. Tassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhissāmī’ti sakalacakkavāḷaṃ mahācetiyappamāṇehi kañcanathūpehi pūretvāpi, sakalacakkavāḷaṃ pūretvā nisinnabhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvāpi, buddhassa bhagavato saṅghāṭikaṇṇaṃ amuñcitvāva vicaritvāpi, kāyassa bhedā nirayameva upapajjati. Yo pana sayaṃ manussabhūto tiracchānabhūtaṃ mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ vā, sayaṃ vā tiracchānabhūto manussabhūtaṃ, tiracchānabhūtoyeva vā tiracchānabhūtaṃ jīvitā voropeti, tassa kammaṃ ānantariyaṃ na hoti, kammaṃ pana bhāriyaṃ hoti, ānantariyaṃ āhacceva tiṭṭhati. Manussajātikānaṃ pana vasena ayaṃ pañho kathito.

Here, first, regarding 'by action': in this case, it is only when a human being deprives of life their mother or father who is also a human being, even one who has changed gender, that the action is one with immediate result. Even if, thinking, 'I will ward off its ripening,' one were to fill the entire world-system with golden stūpas the size of great shrines, or give a great offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus seated filling the entire world-system, or wander about without ever letting go of the corner of the Blessed One's outer robe, with the breakup of the body, one is reborn right in hell. However, if a human being kills a mother or father who is an animal, or an animal kills a human parent, or an animal kills an animal parent, for such a one the action is not one with immediate result, but the action is weighty; it stands bordering on an action with immediate result. This question, however, has been stated with reference to those of human birth.

Ettha eḷakacatukkaṃ, saṅgāmacatukkaṃ, coracatukkañca kathetabbaṃ. ‘Eḷakaṃ māremī’ti abhisandhināpi hi eḷakaṭṭhāne ṭhitaṃ manusso manussabhūtaṃ mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ vā mārento ānantariyaṃ phusati. Eḷakābhisandhinā pana mātāpitiabhisandhinā vā eḷakaṃ mārento ānantariyaṃ na phusati. Mātāpitiabhisandhinā mātāpitaro mārento phusateva. Esa nayo itarasmimpi [M 0.0408] catukkadvaye. Yathā ca mātāpitūsu, evaṃ arahantepi etāni catukkāni veditabbāni. Manussaarahantameva ca māretvā ānantariyaṃ phusati, na yakkhabhūtaṃ; kammaṃ pana bhāriyaṃ ānantariyasadisameva. Manussaarahantassa ca puthujjanakāleyeva satthappahāre vā vise vā dinnepi yadi so arahattaṃ patvā teneva marati, arahantaghāto hotiyeva. Yaṃ pana puthujjanakāle dinnaṃ dānaṃ arahattaṃ [P 0.0427] patvā paribhuñjati, puthujjanasseva taṃ dinnaṃ hoti. Sesaariyapuggale mārentassa ānantariyaṃ natthi, kammaṃ pana bhāriyaṃ ānantariyasadisameva.

Here, the tetrad concerning a goat, the tetrad concerning battle, and the tetrad concerning a thief should be discussed. For even with the intention of killing a goat, a person who kills their human mother or father standing in the place of the goat incurs an action with immediate result. But one who kills a goat, whether with the intention of killing a goat or with the intention of killing one's parents, does not incur an action with immediate result. One who kills one's parents with the intention of killing one's parents does indeed incur it. This same method applies to the other two tetrads. And just as with parents, so too these tetrads should be understood regarding arahants. One incurs an action with immediate result only by killing a human arahant, not one who is a yakkha; however, the kamma is weighty, just like an action with immediate result. And even if a blow with a weapon or poison is given to a human while they are still a worldling, if they attain arahantship and then die from that very cause, it still constitutes the killing of an arahant. But a gift given when one was a worldling, which one enjoys after attaining arahantship, is considered as given to a worldling. For one who kills other noble individuals, there is no action with immediate result; however, the kamma is weighty, just like an action with immediate result.

Lohituppāde tathāgatassa abhejjakāyatāya parūpakkamena cammacchedaṃ katvā lohitapaggharaṇaṃ nāma natthi. Sarīrassa pana antoyeva ekasmiṃ ṭhāne lohitaṃ samosarati. Devadattena paṭividdhasilāto bhijjitvā gatā sakalikāpi tathāgatassa pādantaṃ pahari. Pharasunā pahaṭo viya pādo antolohitoyeva ahosi. Tathā karontassa ānantariyaṃ hoti. Jīvako [V 0.0403] pana tathāgatassa ruciyā satthakena cammaṃ chinditvā tamhā ṭhānā duṭṭhalohitaṃ nīharitvā phāsukamakāsi. Tathā karontassa puññakammameva hoti.

Regarding the malicious shedding of blood: because the Tathāgata’s body is impenetrable, there is no such thing as another person's assault cutting the skin and causing blood to flow. But blood does collect internally in one place in the body. A splinter that broke off from the rock hurled by Devadatta struck the Tathāgata’s foot. The foot was only bruised internally, as if struck by an axe. For one who does such a thing, there is an action with immediate result. But when Jīvaka, with the Tathāgata’s consent, cut the skin with a lancet, removed the bad blood from that spot, and made him comfortable, for one who does so there is only a meritorious action.

Atha ye ca parinibbute tathāgate cetiyaṃ bhindanti, bodhiṃ chindanti, dhātumhi upakkamanti, tesaṃ kiṃ hotīti? Bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ hoti ānantariyasadisaṃ. Sadhātukaṃ pana thūpaṃ vā paṭimaṃ vā bādhayamānaṃ bodhisākhañca chindituṃ vaṭṭati. Sacepi tattha nilīnā sakuṇā cetiye vaccaṃ pātenti, chindituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Paribhogacetiyato hi sarīracetiyaṃ mahantataraṃ. Cetiyavatthuṃ bhinditvā gacchantaṃ bodhimūlampi chinditvā harituṃ vaṭṭati. Yā pana bodhisākhā bodhigharaṃ bādhati, taṃ geharakkhaṇatthaṃ chindituṃ na labbhati. Bodhiatthañhi gehaṃ, na gehatthāya bodhi. Āsanagharepi eseva nayo. Yasmiṃ pana āsanaghare dhātu nihitā hoti, tassa rakkhaṇatthāya bodhisākhaṃ chindituṃ vaṭṭati. Bodhijagganatthaṃ ojoharaṇasākhaṃ vā pūtiṭṭhānaṃ vā chindituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva; sarīrapaṭijaggane viya puññampi hoti.

Then what is the result for those who, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, destroy a shrine, cut down the Bodhi tree, or make an attempt on a relic? It is a weighty kamma, similar to an action with immediate result. However, it is permissible to cut a branch of the Bodhi tree that is damaging a stūpa or an image containing relics. Even if birds perched on it drop their excrement on the shrine, it is still permissible to cut it. For a shrine of bodily relics is more important than a shrine of use. It is permissible to cut and remove even the root of a Bodhi tree that is growing through and breaking the foundation of a shrine. But a branch of the Bodhi tree that damages the Bodhi-house should not be cut to protect the house, for the house exists for the sake of the Bodhi tree, not the Bodhi tree for the sake of the house. This same principle applies to a seat-house. However, if relics are enshrined in a seat-house, it is permissible to cut a branch of the Bodhi tree to protect it. For the maintenance of the Bodhi tree, it is permissible to cut a sap-drawing branch or a rotten part; as in caring for one's own body, there is merit in this.

Saṅghabhede sīmaṭṭhakasaṅghe asannipatite visuṃ parisaṃ gahetvā katavohārānussāvanasalākaggāhassa kammaṃ vā karontassa uddesaṃ vā uddisantassa [M 0.0409] bhedo ca hoti ānantariyakammañca. Samaggasaññāya pana vaṭṭati. Samaggasaññāya hi karontassa neva bhedo hoti na ānantariyakammaṃ. Tathā navato ūnaparisāyaṃ. Sabbantimena pana paricchedena navannaṃ janānaṃ yo saṅghaṃ bhindati, tassa ānantariyakammaṃ [P 0.0428] hoti. Anuvattakānaṃ adhammavādīnaṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ kammaṃ; dhammavādino anavajjā. Tattha navannameva saṅghabhede idaṃ suttaṃ – “ekato, upāli, cattāro honti, ekato cattāro, navamo anussāveti salākaṃ gāheti – ‘ayaṃ dhammo, ayaṃ vinayo, idaṃ satthusāsanaṃ, idaṃ gaṇhatha, idaṃ rocethā’ti. Evaṃ kho, upāli, saṅgharāji ceva hoti saṅghabhedo ca. Navannaṃ vā, upāli, atirekanavannaṃ vā saṅgharāji ceva hoti saṅghabhedo cā”ti (cūḷava. 351).

Regarding schism of the Saṅgha: when the Saṅgha within a single boundary has not assembled, for one who forms a separate faction and performs a formal act, recites the Pātimokkha, or announces a motion and takes voting tickets, there is both schism and an action with immediate result. But it is permissible if done with the perception of unity. For one acting with the perception of unity, there is neither schism nor an action with immediate result. The same applies to a faction of less than nine. But as the final determination, for one who splits a Saṅgha of nine persons, there is an action with immediate result. For the followers who hold the unrighteous view, the kamma is greatly blameworthy; those who hold the righteous view are blameless. Regarding the schism of nine, this sutta applies: 'Upāli, when four are on one side and four on another, and a ninth announces and takes the voting slips, saying: “This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s teaching. Take this, approve of this!”—in this way, Upāli, there is both a crack in the Saṅgha and a schism of the Saṅgha. A crack in the Saṅgha and a schism of the Saṅgha, Upāli, occur with nine or more than nine.' (Cv VII.5.1)

Etesu ca pana pañcasu saṅghabhedo vacīkammaṃ, sesāni kāyakammānīti. Evaṃ kammatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Now, among these five, schism of the Saṅgha is verbal action, while the rest are bodily actions. Thus the determination should be understood also by way of action.

‘Dvārato’ti sabbāneva cetāni kāyadvāratopi vacīdvāratopi samuṭṭhahanti. Purimāni panettha [V 0.0404] cattāri āṇattikavijjāmayapayogavasena vacīdvārato samuṭṭhahitvāpi kāyadvārameva pūrenti. Saṅghabhedo hatthamuddāya bhedaṃ karontassa kāyadvārato samuṭṭhahitvāpi vacīdvārameva pūretīti. Evamettha dvāratopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

'By way of the door': All these actions arise from both the body-door and the speech-door. Here, the first four, though arising from the speech-door by way of an application of command or magical power, are fulfilled only through the body-door. Schism of the Sangha, when one causes the split by a hand gesture, though arising from the body-door, is fulfilled only through the speech-door. Thus here the determination should be understood also by way of the door.

‘Kappaṭṭhitiyato’ti saṅghabhedoyeva cettha kappaṭṭhitiyo. Saṇṭhahante hi kappe kappavemajjhe vā saṅghabhedaṃ katvā kappavināseyeva muccati. Sacepi hi ‘sve kappo vinassissatī’ti ajja saṅghabhedaṃ karoti, sveyeva muccati, ekadivasameva niraye paccati. Evaṃ karaṇaṃ pana natthi. Sesāni cattāri kammāni ānantariyāneva honti, na kappaṭṭhitiyānīti. Evamettha kappaṭṭhitiyatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

'By way of aeon-duration': Here, only schism of the Sangha is aeon-lasting. For if one causes a schism while the aeon stands, or in the middle of an aeon, one is released only at the destruction of the aeon. Even if one causes a schism today thinking, 'The aeon will be destroyed tomorrow,' one is released on the morrow, being tormented in hell for only one day. But such an action does not occur. The other four actions are only ones with immediate result, not aeon-lasting ones. Thus here the determination should be understood also by way of aeon-duration.

‘Pākato’ti yena ca pañcapetāni kammāni katāni honti, tassa saṅghabhedoyeva paṭisandhivasena vipaccati. Sesāni “ahosi kammaṃ nāhosi kammavipāko”ti evamādīsu saṅkhaṃ gacchanti. Saṅghabhedābhāve lohituppādo, tadabhāve arahantaghāto, tadabhāve sace pitā [M 0.0410] sīlavā hoti, mātā dussīlā no vā tathā sīlavatī, pitughāto paṭisandhivasena vipaccati. Sace mātā mātughāto. Dvīsupi sīlena vā dussīlena vā samānesu mātughātova paṭisandhivasena vipaccati; mātā hi dukkarakāriṇī bahūpakārā ca puttānanti. Evamettha pākatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

'By way of ripening': For one by whom all five of these actions have been committed, only schism of the Sangha ripens by way of rebirth-linking. The others are reckoned among such categories as 'there was an action, there was no result of the action.' In the absence of schism of the Sangha, the malicious shedding of the Buddha's blood ripens. In its absence, the killing of an arahant. In its absence, if the father is virtuous and the mother is unvirtuous or not as virtuous, parricide ripens by way of rebirth-linking. If the mother is, matricide does. When both are equal in virtue or lack of virtue, matricide itself ripens by way of rebirth-linking, for a mother is one who performs difficult tasks and is of great help to her children. Thus here the determination should be understood also by way of ripening.

‘Sādhāraṇādīhī’ti [P 0.0429] purimāni cattāri sabbesampi gahaṭṭhapabbajitānaṃ sādhāraṇāni. Saṅghabhedo pana “na kho, upāli, bhikkhunī saṅghaṃ bhindati, na sikkhamānā, na sāmaṇero, na sāmaṇerī, na upāsako, na upāsikā saṅghaṃ bhindati. Bhikkhu kho, upāli, pakatatto samānasaṃvāsako samānasīmāyaṃ ṭhito saṅghaṃ bhindatī”ti (cūḷava. 351) vacanato vuttappakārassa bhikkhunova hoti, na aññassa; tasmā asādhāraṇo. Ādisaddena sabbepete dukkhavedanāsahagatā dosamohasampayuttā cāti evamettha sādhāraṇādīhipi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

'By way of commonality, etc.': The first four actions are common to all, both householders and the ordained. But schism of the Sangha, according to the passage: 'A bhikkhunī, Upāli, does not split the Sangha, nor a probationer, nor a male novice, nor a female novice, nor a male lay follower, nor a female lay follower. It is a bhikkhu, Upāli, in good standing, in communion, and standing within the same boundary, who splits the Sangha' (Cv VII.5.1), belongs only to a bhikkhu of the kind described, not to another; therefore it is not common. By the word 'etc.' it is meant that all these actions are accompanied by painful feeling and are associated with hatred and delusion. Thus here the determination should be understood also by way of commonality, etc.

Aññaṃ satthāranti ‘ayaṃ me satthā satthukiccaṃ kātuṃ samattho’ti bhavantarepi aññaṃ titthakaraṃ ‘ayaṃ me satthā’ti evaṃ gaṇheyya – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti attho. Aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ nibbatteyyāti sabbamandapaññopi sattamaṃ bhavaṃ atikkamitvā aṭṭhamaṃ nibbatteyya – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati[V 0.0405]. Uttamakoṭiyā hi sattamaṃ bhavaṃ sandhāyevesa “niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo”ti vutto. Kiṃ pana taṃ niyāmeti? Kiṃ pubbahetu niyāmeti udāhu paṭiladdhamaggo udāhu upari tayo maggāti? Sammāsambuddhena gahitaṃ nāmamattametaṃ. Puggalo pana niyato nāma natthi. “Pubbahetu niyāmetī”ti vutte hi upari tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ upanissayo vutto hoti, paṭhamamaggassa upanissayābhāvo āpajjati. Iccassa ahetu appaccayā nibbattiṃ pāpuṇāti. “Paṭiladdhamaggo niyāmetī”ti vutte upari tayo maggā akiccakā honti, paṭhamamaggova sakiccako, paṭhamamaggeneva kilese khepetvā parinibbāyitabbaṃ hoti. “Upari tayo maggā niyāmentī”ti vutte paṭhamamaggo akiccako hoti, upari tayo maggāva sakiccakā, paṭhamamaggaṃ anibbattetvā upari tayo maggā nibbattetabbā honti, paṭhamamaggena ca anuppajjitvāva kilesā khepetabbā honti. Tasmā na añño koci niyāmeti, upari tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanāva niyāmeti. Sace hi tesaṃ vipassanā [M 0.0411] tikkhā sūrā hutvā vahati, ekaṃyeva bhavaṃ nibbattetvā arahattaṃ patvā [P 0.0430] parinibbāti. Tato mandatarapañño dutiye vā tatiye vā catutthe vā pañcame vā chaṭṭhe vā bhave arahattaṃ patvā parinibbāti. Sabbamandapañño sattamaṃ bhavaṃ nibbattetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, aṭṭhame bhave paṭisandhi na hoti. Iti sammāsambuddhena gahitaṃ nāmamattametaṃ. Satthā hi buddhatulāya tuletvā sabbaññutañāṇena paricchinditvā ‘ayaṃ puggalo sabbamahāpañño tikkhavipassako ekameva bhavaṃ nibbattetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhissatī’ti ‘ekabījī’ti nāmaṃ akāsi; ‘ayaṃ puggalo dutiyaṃ, tatiyaṃ, catutthaṃ, pañcamaṃ, chaṭṭhaṃ bhavaṃ nibbattetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhissatī’ti ‘kolaṃkolo’ti nāmaṃ akāsi; ‘ayaṃ puggalo sattamaṃ bhavaṃ nibbattetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhissatī’ti ‘sattakkhattuparamo’ti nāmaṃ akāsi.

Another teacher—thinking, 'This is my teacher, capable of performing a teacher's duties'—might in another existence take another teacher as his teacher, thinking, 'This is my teacher.' But such a situation does not exist. That one would be reborn in an eighth existence—that even one of dullest wisdom, having surpassed the seventh existence, would be reborn in the eighth—such a situation does not exist. For it is with reference to the seventh existence at most that one is called 'fixed, destined for enlightenment.' But what determines this? Is it determined by a prior cause, or by the attained path, or by the three higher paths? This is merely a designation made by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. In truth, there is no fixed individual. If it were said that 'a prior cause determines it,' then the supportive condition for the three higher paths would be stated, but it would follow that there is no supportive condition for the first path. Thus, its arising would be without cause or condition. If it were said that 'the attained path determines it,' then the three higher paths would be rendered functionless, and only the first path would have a function; one would have to eradicate defilements solely by the first path and attain final Nibbāna. If it were said that 'the three higher paths determine it,' then the first path would be rendered functionless, and only the three higher paths would have a function; one would have to generate the three higher paths without having generated the first path, and eradicate defilements without the first path having even arisen. Therefore, nothing else determines it—only the insight pertaining to the three higher paths determines it. For if their insight is sharp and keen, one is reborn in just one more existence, attains arahantship, and attains final Nibbāna. One of duller wisdom attains arahantship and final Nibbāna in the second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth existence. The one of dullest wisdom is reborn in the seventh existence and attains arahantship; there is no rebirth-linking in an eighth existence. Thus, this is merely a designation made by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. For the Teacher, having weighed them on the Buddha's scale and having comprehended them with his omniscient knowledge, gave names accordingly: 'This person, of great wisdom and sharp insight, will be reborn in one existence and attain arahantship'—thus he named him 'the one-seeder.' 'This person will be reborn in a second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth existence and will attain arahantship'—thus he named him 'the family-to-family goer.' 'This person will be reborn in the seventh existence and will attain arahantship'—thus he named him 'the seven-times-at-most.'

Koci pana puggalo sattannaṃ bhavānaṃ niyato nāma natthi. Ariyasāvako pana yena kenacipi ākārena mandapañño samāno aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ appatvā antarāva parinibbāti. Sakkasadisopi vaṭṭābhirato sattamaṃyeva bhavaṃ gacchati. Sattame bhave sabbakārena pamādavihārinopi vipassanāñāṇaṃ paripākaṃ gacchati. Appamattakepi ārammaṇe nibbinditvā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇāti. Sacepi hissa sattame bhave niddaṃ vā okkamantassa, parammukhaṃ vā gacchantassa, pacchato ṭhatvā tikhiṇena asinā kocideva sīsaṃ pāteyya, udake vā osādetvā māreyya, asani vā panassa sīse pateyya, evarūpepi kāle sappaṭisandhikā kālaṃkiriyā [V 0.0406] nāma na hoti, arahattaṃ patvāva parinibbāti. Tena vuttaṃ – “aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ nibbatteyya – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti.

But there is no person at all who is fixed for seven existences. A noble disciple, however, even if of dull wisdom in some way, attains final Nibbāna without reaching an eighth existence. Even one like Sakka, who delights in the round of existence, goes only to a seventh existence. In the seventh existence, even for one who dwells heedlessly in every way, the knowledge of insight matures. Becoming disenchanted with even a trifling object, they attain Nibbāna. Even if, in their seventh existence, while they are falling asleep or have turned their back, someone should stand behind them and cut off their head with a sharp sword, or drown them in water, or a thunderbolt should fall on their head—even at such a time, a death with rebirth-linking does not occur. They attain final Nibbāna only after having attained arahantship. Therefore it was said: 'That they would generate an eighth existence—this is not a possible case.'

Ekissā lokadhātuyāti dasasahassilokadhātuyā. Tīṇi hi khettāni – jātikhettaṃ, āṇākhettaṃ, visayakkhettanti. Tattha ‘jātikkhettaṃ’ nāma dasasahassilokadhātu. Sā hi tathāgatassa mātukucchiokkamanakāle, nikkhamanakāle, sambodhikāle, dhammacakkapavattane, āyusaṅkhāravossajjane, parinibbāne ca kampati. Koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷaṃ pana ‘āṇākhettaṃ’ nāma. Āṭānāṭiyamoraparittadhajaggaparittaratanaparittādīnañhi [P 0.0431] ettha āṇā vattati. ‘Visayakhettassa’ pana parimāṇaṃ natthi. Buddhānañhi “yāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ tāvatakaṃ ñeyyaṃ, yāvatakaṃ ñeyyaṃ tāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ[M 0.0412], ñāṇapariyantikaṃ ñeyyaṃ, ñeyyapariyantikaṃ ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 3.5) vacanato avisayo nāma natthi.

'In one world-system' means in the ten-thousand-world-system. There are three fields: the birth-field, the authority-field, and the range-field. Here, the 'birth-field' is the name for the ten-thousand-world-system. For it trembles at the time of the Tathāgata's descent into his mother’s womb, at his emergence from the womb, at his enlightenment, at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, at his relinquishing of the life-formation, and at his final Nibbāna. A hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems, however, are called the 'authority-field.' For here the authority of the Āṭānāṭiya, Mora, Dhajagga, Ratana, and other protective chants holds sway. But the 'range-field' has no limit. For of the Buddhas, in accordance with the saying, 'As far as knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable; as far as the knowable extends, so far extends knowledge. The knowable is the boundary of knowledge; knowledge is the boundary of the knowable,' there is nothing that is not their range.

Imesu pana tīsu khettesu, ṭhapetvā imaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ, aññasmiṃ cakkavāḷe buddhā uppajjantīti suttaṃ natthi, na uppajjantīti pana atthi. Tīṇi piṭakāni – vinayapiṭakaṃ, suttantapiṭakaṃ, abhidhammapiṭakanti. Tisso saṅgītiyo – mahākassapattherassa saṅgīti, yasattherassa saṅgīti, moggaliputtatissattherassa saṅgītīti. Imā tisso saṅgītiyo āruḷhe tepiṭake buddhavacane imaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ muñcitvā aññattha buddhā uppajjantīti suttaṃ natthi, nuppajjantīti pana atthi.

But in these three fields, apart from this world-system, there is no sutta stating that Buddhas arise in another world-system, but there is one stating that they do not. There are three Piṭakas: the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Suttanta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. There are three Councils: the Council of the Elder Mahākassapa, the Council of the Elder Yasa, and the Council of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa. In the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, as established at these three Councils, there is no sutta stating that Buddhas arise elsewhere apart from this world-system, but there is one stating that they do not.

Apubbaṃ acarimanti apure apacchā; ekato nuppajjanti, pure vā pacchā vā uppajjantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha bodhipallaṅke “bodhiṃ appatvā na uṭṭhahissāmī”ti nisinnakālato paṭṭhāya yāva mātukucchismiṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇaṃ tāva pubbenti na veditabbaṃ. Bodhisattassa hi paṭisandhiggahaṇe dasasahassacakkavāḷakampaneneva jātikkhettapariggaho kato, aññassa buddhassa uppatti nivāritā hoti. Parinibbānato paṭṭhāya ca yāva sāsapamattāpi dhātuyo tiṭṭhanti tāva pacchāti na veditabbaṃ. Dhātūsu hi ṭhitāsu buddhā ṭhitāva honti. Tasmā etthantare aññassa buddhassa uppatti nivāritāva hoti, dhātuparinibbāne pana jāte aññassa buddhassa uppatti na nivāritā.

'Neither before nor after' means not simultaneously; they do not arise together, but it is said that they arise either before or after. Here, 'before' should not be understood as the period from the time of sitting on the seat of enlightenment, resolving, 'I will not rise until I attain enlightenment,' up to the taking of rebirth-linking in the mother's womb. For at the Bodhisatta’s taking of rebirth-linking, the occupation of the birth-field is made by the very trembling of the ten-thousand-world-system, and the arising of another Buddha is prevented. And the period starting from the final Nibbāna, for as long as even a mustard-seed-sized relic remains, should not be understood as 'after'. For as long as the relics remain, the Buddha is considered to remain. Therefore, during this interval, the arising of another Buddha is prevented. But when the final passing away of the relics has occurred, the arising of another Buddha is not prevented.

Tīṇi [V 0.0407] hi antaradhānāni nāma – pariyattiantaradhānaṃ, paṭivedhaantaradhānaṃ, paṭipattiantaradhānanti. Tattha ‘pariyattī’ti tīṇi piṭakāni; ‘paṭivedho’ti saccapaṭivedho; ‘paṭipattī’ti paṭipadā. Tattha paṭivedho ca paṭipatti ca hotipi na hotipi. Ekasmiñhi kāle paṭivedhakarā bhikkhū bahū honti; ‘esa bhikkhu puthujjano’ti aṅguliṃ pasāretvā dassetabbo hoti. Imasmiṃyeva dīpe ekavāraṃ kira puthujjanabhikkhu [P 0.0432] nāma nāhosi. Paṭipattipūrakāpi kadāci bahū honti, kadāci appā. Iti paṭivedho ca paṭipatti ca hotipi na hotipi.

There are three kinds of disappearances: the disappearance of learning, the disappearance of realization, and the disappearance of practice. Here, ‘learning’ refers to the three Piṭakas; ‘realization’ means the realization of the truths; ‘practice’ refers to the path. Here, realization and practice may sometimes exist and sometimes not exist. For at one time there are many bhikkhus who are realizers; one has to point with an outstretched finger and say, ‘This bhikkhu is an ordinary person.’ It is said that on this very island there was a time when there was no bhikkhu who was an ordinary person. Those who fulfill the practice are also sometimes many, sometimes few. Thus, realization and practice may sometimes exist and sometimes not exist.

Sāsanaṭṭhitiyā pana pariyattiyeva pamāṇaṃ. Paṇḍito hi tepiṭakaṃ sutvā dvepi pūreti. Yathā amhākaṃ bodhisatto āḷārassa santike pañcābhiññā satta ca samāpattiyo nibbattetvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiyā parikammaṃ pucchi, so ‘na jānāmī’ti āha; tato udakassa [M 0.0413] santikaṃ gantvā adhigatavisesaṃ saṃsandetvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanassa parikammaṃ pucchi; so ācikkhi; tassa vacanasamanantarameva mahāsatto taṃ sampādesi; evameva paññavā bhikkhu pariyattiṃ sutvā dvepi pūreti. Tasmā pariyattiyā ṭhitāya sāsanaṃ ṭhitaṃ hoti. Yadā pana sā antaradhāyati tadā paṭhamaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ nassati. Tattha paṭṭhānaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ antaradhāyati. Anukkamena pacchā dhammasaṅgaho. Tasmiṃ antarahite itaresu dvīsu piṭakesu ṭhitesu sāsanaṃ ṭhitameva hoti.

For the stability of the Dispensation, learning is the standard. For a wise person, having heard the Tipiṭaka, fulfills both practice and realization. Just as our Bodhisatta, having generated the five supernormal knowledges and the seven attainments in the presence of Āḷāra, asked about the preliminary practice for the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and Āḷāra said, ‘I do not know.’ Then, going to Uddaka and comparing it with the special attainment he had already gained, he asked about the preliminary practice for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Uddaka explained it, and immediately after his words, the Great Being accomplished it. In the same way, a wise bhikkhu, having heard the learning, fulfills both. Therefore, as long as learning stands, the Dispensation stands. But when it disappears, first the Abhidhamma Piṭaka perishes. Within that, the Paṭṭhāna disappears first of all. In sequence, afterwards, the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. When that has disappeared, as long as the other two Piṭakas remain, the Dispensation is still considered to stand.

Tattha suttantapiṭake antaradhāyamāne paṭhamaṃ aṅguttaranikāyo ekādasakato paṭṭhāya yāva ekakā antaradhāyati. Tadanantaraṃ saṃyuttanikāyo cakkapeyyālato paṭṭhāya yāva oghataraṇā antaradhāyati. Tadanantaraṃ majjhimanikāyo indriyabhāvanato paṭṭhāya yāva mūlapariyāyā antaradhāyati. Tadanantaraṃ dīghanikāyo dasuttarato paṭṭhāya yāva brahmajālā antaradhāyati. Ekissāpi dvinnampi gāthānaṃ pucchā addhānaṃ gacchati; sāsanaṃ dhāretuṃ na sakkoti sabhiyapucchā (su. ni. 515 ādayo) viya āḷavakapucchā (su. ni. 183 ādayo; saṃ. ni. 1.246) viya ca. Etā kira kassapabuddhakālikā antarā sāsanaṃ dhāretuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu.

Therein, when the Suttanta Piṭaka is disappearing, first the Aṅguttara Nikāya, from the Book of the Elevens down to the Book of the Ones, disappears. After that, the Saṃyutta Nikāya, from the Wheel Repetition down to the Crossing the Flood, disappears. After that, the Majjhima Nikāya, from the Development of the Faculties down to the Root Exposition, disappears. After that, the Dīgha Nikāya, from the Dasuttara down to the Brahmajāla, disappears. The questioning about even a single verse or two verses is lost to time; it is not able to maintain the Dispensation, like Sabhiya's question (Sn. 515 ff.) or Āḷavaka's question (Sn. 183 ff.; SN 1.246). It is said that these, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, were unable to maintain the Dispensation in the interim.

Dvīsu pana piṭakesu antarahitesupi vinayapiṭake ṭhite sāsanaṃ tiṭṭhati. Parivārakhandhakesu antarahitesu ubhatovibhaṅge ṭhite ṭhitameva hoti. Ubhatovibhaṅge antarahite mātikāya [V 0.0408] ṭhitāyapi ṭhitameva hoti. Mātikāya antarahitāya pātimokkhapabbajjāupasampadāsu ṭhitāsu sāsanaṃ tiṭṭhati. Liṅgaṃ addhānaṃ gacchati. Setavatthasamaṇavaṃso pana kassapabuddhakālato paṭṭhāya sāsanaṃ dhāretuṃ nāsakkhi. Pacchimakassa pana saccapaṭivedhato pacchimakassa sīlabhedato ca paṭṭhāya sāsanaṃ osakkitaṃ nāma hoti. Tato paṭṭhāya aññassa buddhassa uppatti na vāritā.

But even when two Piṭakas have disappeared, as long as the Vinaya Piṭaka remains, the Dispensation lasts. When the Parivāra and Khandhaka sections have disappeared, as long as the Ubhato-vibhaṅga remains, it still lasts. When the Ubhato-vibhaṅga has disappeared, as long as the Mātikā remains, it still lasts. When the Mātikā has disappeared, as long as the Pātimokkha, going forth, and higher ordination remain, the Dispensation lasts. The outward form is lost to time. But the white-robed lineage of ascetics, from the time of Kassapa Buddha onwards, was unable to uphold the Dispensation. However, from the time of the last penetration of the truth and the last breaking of morality, the Dispensation is said to have declined.
