From that time onwards, the arising of another Buddha is not obstructed.

Tīṇi [P 0.0433] parinibbānāni nāma – kilesaparinibbānaṃ, khandhaparinibbānaṃ, dhātuparinibbānanti. Tattha ‘kilesaparinibbānaṃ’ bodhipallaṅke ahosi, ‘khandhaparinibbānaṃ’ kusinārāyaṃ, ‘dhātuparinibbānaṃ’ anāgate bhavissati. Sāsanassa kira osakkanakāle [M 0.0414] imasmiṃ tambapaṇṇidīpe dhātuyo sannipatitvā mahācetiyaṃ gamissanti, mahācetiyato nāgadīpe rājāyatanacetiyaṃ, tato mahābodhipallaṅkaṃ gamissanti. Nāgabhavanatopi devalokatopi brahmalokatopi dhātuyo mahābodhipallaṅkameva gamissanti. Sāsapamattāpi dhātu na antarā nassissati. Sabbā dhātuyo mahābodhipallaṅke rāsibhūtā suvaṇṇakkhandho viya ekaghanā hutvā chabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo vissajjessanti. Tā dasasahassilokadhātuṃ pharissanti. Tato dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatā sannipatitvā “ajja satthā parinibbāti, ajja sāsanaṃ osakkati, pacchimadassanaṃ dāni idaṃ amhāka”nti dasabalassa parinibbutadivasato mahantataraṃ kāruññaṃ karissanti. Ṭhapetvā anāgāmikhīṇāsave avasesā sakabhāvena sandhāretuṃ na sakkhissanti. Dhātūsu tejodhātu uṭṭhahitvā yāva brahmalokā uggacchissati. Sāsapamattāyapi dhātuyā sati ekajālāva bhavissati; dhātūsu pariyādānaṃ gatāsu pacchijjissati. Evaṃ mahantaṃ ānubhāvaṃ dassetvā dhātūsu antarahitāsu sāsanaṃ antarahitaṃ nāma hoti. Yāva evaṃ na antaradhāyati tāva acarimaṃ nāma hoti. Evaṃ apubbaṃ acarimaṃ uppajjeyyuṃ – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

There are three kinds of final liberation: the final liberation from defilements, the final liberation of the aggregates, and the final liberation of the relics. Among these, the 'final liberation from defilements' occurred at the seat of enlightenment, the 'final liberation of the aggregates' took place in Kusinārā, and the 'final liberation of the relics' will occur in the future. At the time of the decline of the Dispensation, it is said that the relics will gather in this island of Tambapaṇṇi and proceed to the Great Stupa. From the Great Stupa, they will go to the Rājāyatana Shrine in Nāgadīpa, and from there to the great seat of enlightenment. Even from the abodes of the nāgas, the world of devas, and the world of brahmās, the relics will proceed only to the great seat of enlightenment. Not even a mustard-seed-sized relic will be lost along the way. All the relics, gathered in a heap at the great seat of enlightenment, will become solid like a mass of gold and emit six-colored rays. These rays will pervade the ten-thousandfold world-system. Then, the deities from the ten-thousandfold universe will assemble and, thinking, 'Today the Teacher attains final liberation, today the Dispensation declines—this is our last sight of him,' will express even greater sorrow than on the day of the Ten-Powered One’s final liberation. Except for the non-returners and those whose taints are destroyed, the rest will be unable to maintain their composure. The fire element within the relics will arise and ascend as far as the brahmā world. Even if only a mustard-seed-sized relic remains, it will become a single flame; when the relics are entirely consumed, the flame will be extinguished. Having displayed such great power, when the relics vanish, the Dispensation is said to have disappeared. As long as it does not disappear in this way, it is not yet the final end. That they should arise thus, without prior and without successor—this is not possible.

Kasmā pana apubbaṃ acarimaṃ na uppajjantīti? Anacchariyattā. Buddhā hi acchariyamanussā, yathāha – “ekapuggalo, bhikkhave, loke upajjamāno uppajjati acchariyamanusso. Katamo ekapuggalo? Tathāgato, bhikkhave, arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti (a. ni. 1.172). Yadi ca dve vā cattāro vā aṭṭha vā soḷasa vā ekato uppajjeyyuṃ, na acchariyā bhaveyyuṃ. Ekasmiñhi vihāre dvinnaṃ cetiyānampi lābhasakkāro uḷāro na hoti, bhikkhūpi bahutāya na acchariyā jātā, evaṃ buddhāpi bhaveyyuṃ; tasmā nuppajjanti. Desanāya [P 0.0434][V 0.0409] ca visesābhāvato. Yañhi satipaṭṭhānādibhedaṃ dhammaṃ eko deseti, aññena uppajjitvāpi sova desetabbo siyā. Tato anacchariyo siyā. Ekasmiṃ pana dhammaṃ desente desanāpi acchariyā hoti. Vivādabhāvato ca. Bahūsu ca buddhesu uppannesu bahūnaṃ ācariyānaṃ antevāsikā viya ‘amhākaṃ buddho pāsādiko, amhākaṃ buddho madhurassaro lābhī puññavā’ti vivadeyyuṃ; tasmāpi evaṃ nuppajjanti.

But why do they not arise simultaneously? Because it would not be extraordinary. For Buddhas are extraordinary beings, as it is said: 'Monks, one person arising in the world is an extraordinary person. Who is that one person? The Tathāgata, monks, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One' (A. Ni. 1.172). If two or four or eight or sixteen were to arise at once, they would not be extraordinary. For in a single monastery, the gain and honor for even two shrines would not be great, and monks are not considered extraordinary if they are numerous—so too would it be with Buddhas. Therefore, they do not arise simultaneously. And because there would be no distinction in their teachings. For if one teaches the Dhamma divided into the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, another who arises would have to teach the very same. Thus, it would not be extraordinary. But when one teaches the Dhamma, the teaching itself is extraordinary. And because of the potential for disputes. If many Buddhas were to arise, their disciples, like the disciples of many teachers, might argue, saying, 'Our Buddha is pleasing, our Buddha has a sweet voice, he is gainful and meritorious.' Therefore, they do not arise in this way.

Apicetaṃ [M 0.0415] kāraṇaṃ milindaraññā puṭṭhena nāgasenattherena vitthāritameva. Vuttañhi tattha (mi. pa. 5.1.1) –

Moreover, this reason was explained in detail by the Elder Nāgasena when questioned by King Milinda. For it is said there (Milindapañha 5.1.1):

“Bhante nāgasena, bhāsitampetaṃ bhagavatā – “aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā dve arahanto sammāsambuddhā apubbaṃ acarimaṃ uppajjeyyuṃ – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti (a. ni. 1.277; ma. ni. 3.129). Desentā ca, bhante nāgasena, sabbepi tathāgatā sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhamme desenti, kathayamānā ca cattāri ariyasaccāni kathenti, sikkhāpentā ca tīsu sikkhāsu sikkhāpenti, anusāsamānā ca appamādapaṭipattiyaṃ anusāsanti. Yadi, bhante nāgasena, sabbesampi tathāgatānaṃ ekā desanā ekā kathā ekā sikkhā ekānusiṭṭhi, kena kāraṇena dve tathāgatā ekakkhaṇe nuppajjanti? Ekenapi tāva buddhuppādena ayaṃ loko obhāsajāto. Yadi dutiyo buddho bhaveyya, dvinnaṃ pabhāya ayaṃ loko bhiyyoso mattāya obhāsajāto bhaveyya. Ovadantā ca dve tathāgatā sukhaṃ ovadeyyuṃ, anusāsamānā ca sukhaṃ anusāseyyuṃ. Tattha me kāraṇaṃ dassehi yathāhaṃ nissaṃsayo bhaveyya”nti.

“Venerable Nāgasena, this has been said by the Blessed One: ‘Monks, this is impossible, there is no possibility that in one world-system two Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas, should arise neither one before nor one after—such a thing cannot occur.’ (A. Ni. 1.277; Ma. Ni. 3.129). But, Venerable Nāgasena, all Tathāgatas teach the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and when teaching, they speak of the four noble truths, and when training, they train in the three trainings, and when instructing, they instruct in the practice of diligence. If, Venerable Nāgasena, all Tathāgatas have the same teaching, the same discourse, the same training, and the same instruction, then for what reason do two Tathāgatas not arise at the same time? Even with the arising of one Buddha, this world becomes filled with light. If a second Buddha were to arise, this world would become even more intensely filled with light by the radiance of two. Two Tathāgatas advising would advise easily, and two instructing would instruct easily. Show me the reason in this matter, so that I may be free from doubt.”

“Ayaṃ, mahārāja, dasasahassī lokadhātu ekabuddhadhāraṇī, ekasseva tathāgatassa guṇaṃ dhāreti. Yadi dutiyo buddho uppajjeyya, nāyaṃ dasasahassī lokadhātu dhāreyya, caleyya kampeyya nameyya onameyya vinameyya vikireyya vidhameyya viddhaṃseyya, na ṭhānamupagaccheyya.

“This ten-thousandfold world-system, great king, can bear only one Buddha; it can sustain the qualities of only one Tathāgata. If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world-system would not be able to sustain it. It would move, shake, bend, stoop, collapse, scatter, disintegrate, and be utterly destroyed; it would find no standing place.”

“Yathā, mahārāja, nāvā ekapurisasandhāraṇī bhaveyya, ekasmiṃ purise abhirūḷhe sā [V 0.0410] nāvā samupādikā bhaveyya. Atha dutiyo puriso āgaccheyya [P 0.0435] tādiso āyunā vaṇṇena vayena pamāṇena kisathūlena sabbaṅgapaccaṅgena. So taṃ nāvaṃ abhirūheyya. Apinu sā, mahārāja, nāvā dvinnampi dhāreyyā”ti? “Na hi, bhante, caleyya kampeyya nameyya onameyya vinameyya vikireyya vidhameyya viddhaṃseyya, na ṭhānamupagaccheyya, osīdeyya udake”ti[M 0.0416]. “Evameva kho, mahārāja, ayaṃ dasasahassī lokadhātu ekabuddhadhāraṇī ekasseva tathāgatassa guṇaṃ dhāreti. Yadi dutiyo buddho uppajjeyya, nāyaṃ dasasahassī lokadhātu dhāreyya, caleyya…pe… na ṭhānamupagaccheyya.

“Just as, great king, a boat might be designed to carry only one person. With one man aboard, the boat would be properly balanced. But if a second man were to come—equal in age, complexion, stature, size, and build—and he too were to board the boat, could the boat, great king, carry both?” “No, venerable sir. It would shake, tremble, bend, sag, collapse, scatter, crumble, and be destroyed; it would not remain in place; it would sink in the water.” “In the same way, great king, this ten-thousandfold world-system can bear only one Buddha; it can sustain the qualities of only one Tathāgata. If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world-system would not be able to bear it. It would shake... and not remain in place.”

“Yathā vā pana, mahārāja, puriso yāvadatthaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjeyya chādentaṃ yāvakaṇṭhamabhipūrayitvā. So tato pīṇito paripuṇṇo nirantaro tandīgato anonamitadaṇḍajāto punadeva tattakaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjeyya. Apinu kho so, mahārāja, puriso sukhito bhaveyyā”ti? “Na hi, bhante, sakiṃ bhuttova mareyyā”ti. Evameva kho, mahārāja, ayaṃ dasasahassī lokadhātu ekabuddhadhāraṇī…pe… na ṭhānamupagaccheyyā”ti.

“Or again, great king, suppose a man were to eat food to his satisfaction, filling himself right up to his throat. Then, having become replete, full, continuously sated, overcome with drowsiness, unable to bend over, he were to eat that same amount of food again. Would that man, great king, be comfortable?” “No, venerable sir, he might die from that one meal alone.” “Just so, great king, this ten-thousandfold world-system can bear only one Buddha... it would find no standing place.”

“Kiṃ nu kho, bhante nāgasena, atidhammabhārena pathavī calatī”ti? “Idha, mahārāja, dve sakaṭā ratanaparipūritā bhaveyyuṃ yāvasmā mukhasamā. Eka sakaṭato ratanaṃ gahetvā ekamhi sakaṭe ākireyyuṃ. Apinu taṃ, mahārāja, sakaṭaṃ dvinnampi sakaṭānaṃ ratanaṃ dhāreyyā”ti? “Na hi, bhante, nābhipi tassa caleyya, arāpi tassa bhijjeyyuṃ, nemipi tassa opateyya, akkhopi tassa bhijjeyyā”ti. “Kinnu kho, mahārāja, atiratanabhārena sakaṭaṃ bhijjatī”ti? “Āma, bhante”ti. “Evameva kho, mahārāja, atidhammabhārena pathavī calatīti.

“Venerable Nāgasena, is it because of the excessive burden of the Dhamma that the earth trembles?” “Here, great king, suppose there were two carts filled to the brim with jewels. If one were to take the jewels from one cart and pour them into the other, could that single cart bear the jewels of both?” “No, venerable sir. Its hub would not hold, its spokes would break, its rim would collapse, and its axle would snap.” “Is it then, great king, because of the excessive burden of the jewels that the cart breaks?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Just so, great king, the earth trembles under the excessive burden of the Dhamma.”

“Apica, mahārāja, imaṃ kāraṇaṃ buddhabalaparidīpanāya osāritaṃ. Aññampi tattha patirūpaṃ kāraṇaṃ suṇohi yena kāraṇena dve sammāsambuddhā ekakkhaṇe nuppajjanti. Yadi, mahārāja, dve sammāsambuddhā ekakkhaṇe uppajjeyyuṃ, parisāya vivādo uppajjeyya – ‘tumhākaṃ buddho, amhākaṃ buddho’ti ubhatopakkhajātā bhaveyyuṃ. Yathā, mahārāja, dvinnaṃ balavāmaccānaṃ parisāya vivādo uppajjeyya – ‘tumhākaṃ amacco, amhākaṃ [V 0.0411] amacco’ti ubhatopakkhajātā honti; evameva kho, mahārāja, yadi dve sammāsambuddhā ekakkhaṇe [P 0.0436] uppajjeyyuṃ, tesaṃ parisāya vivādo uppajjeyya [M 0.0417] – ‘tumhākaṃ buddho, amhākaṃ buddho’ti ubhatopakkhajātā bhaveyyuṃ. Idaṃ tāva mahārāja ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ yena kāraṇena dve sammāsambuddhā ekakkhaṇe nuppajjanti.

“Moreover, great king, this reason has been adduced to illuminate the power of the Buddha. Now listen to another suitable reason why two Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas do not arise at the same time. If, great king, two Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas were to arise at the same time, a dispute would arise in the assembly—‘Your Buddha, our Buddha’—and they would split into two factions. Just as, great king, if there were two powerful ministers, a dispute would arise among their retinues—‘Your minister, our minister’—and they would split into two factions; so too, great king, if two Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas were to arise at the same time, a dispute would arise in their assembly—‘Your Buddha, our Buddha’—and they would split into two factions. This, great king, is one reason why two Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas do not arise at the same time.”

“Aparampi uttariṃ kāraṇaṃ suṇohi yena kāraṇena dve sammāsambuddhā ekakkhaṇe nuppajjanti. Yadi, mahārāja, dve sammāsambuddhā ekakkhaṇe uppajjeyyuṃ ‘aggo buddho’ti yaṃ vacanaṃ taṃ micchā bhaveyya, ‘jeṭṭho buddho’ti ‘seṭṭho buddho’ti ‘visiṭṭho buddho’ti ‘uttamo buddho’ti ‘pavaro buddho’ti ‘asamo buddho’ti ‘asamasamo buddho’ti ‘appaṭisamo buddho’ti ‘appaṭibhāgī buddho’ti ‘appaṭipuggalo buddho’ti yaṃ vacanaṃ taṃ micchā bhaveyya. Idampi kho tvaṃ, mahārāja, kāraṇaṃ tathato sampaṭiccha yena kāraṇena dve sammāsambuddhā ekakkhaṇe nuppajjanti.

“Listen to a further, superior reason why two Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas do not arise at the same time. If, great king, two Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas were to arise at the same time, the statement ‘the Buddha is foremost’ would be false. The statements ‘the Buddha is eldest,’ ‘the Buddha is best,’ ‘the Buddha is most distinguished,’ ‘the Buddha is highest,’ ‘the Buddha is supreme,’ ‘the Buddha is incomparable,’ ‘the Buddha is equal to the incomparable,’ ‘the Buddha is unequaled,’ ‘the Buddha is without a rival,’ and ‘the Buddha is without a peer’ would be false. You should accept this reason, great king, as it really is, why two Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas do not arise at the same time.”

“Apica, mahārāja, buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ sabhāvapakati esā yaṃ ekoyeva buddho loke uppajjati. Kasmā kāraṇā? Mahantattā sabbaññubuddhaguṇānaṃ. Aññampi, mahārāja, yaṃ loke mahantaṃ taṃ ekaṃyeva hoti. Pathavī, mahārāja, mahantā, sā ekāyeva; sāgaro mahanto, so ekoyeva; sineru girirājā mahanto, so ekoyeva; ākāso mahanto, so ekoyeva; sakko mahanto, so ekoyeva; mahābrahmā mahanto, so ekoyeva; tathāgato arahaṃ sammāsambuddho mahanto, so ekoyeva lokasmiṃ. Yattha te uppajjanti tattha aññesaṃ okāso na hoti. Tasmā, mahārāja, tathāgato arahaṃ sammāsambuddho ekoyeva loke uppajjatī”ti.

“Furthermore, great king, it is the inherent nature of the Blessed Buddhas that only one Buddha arises in the world. For what reason? Because of the greatness of the qualities of an omniscient Buddha. Furthermore, great king, whatever is great in the world is one alone. The earth, great king, is great, and it is one alone; the ocean is great, and it is one alone; Sineru, king of mountains, is great, and it is one alone; space is great, and it is one alone; Sakka is great, and he is one alone; Mahābrahmā is great, and he is one alone; the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is great, and he is one alone in the world. Where such a one arises, there is no room for another. Therefore, great king, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One arises alone in the world.”

“Sukathito, bhante nāgasena, pañho opammehi kāraṇehī”ti (mi. pa. 5.1.1).

“Venerable Nāgasena, the question has been well explained with similes and reasons.”

Ekissā [M 0.0418] lokadhātuyāti ekasmiṃ cakkavāḷe. Heṭṭhā imināva padena dasa cakkavāḷasahassāni gahitāni. Tānipi ekacakkavāḷeneva paricchindituṃ vaṭṭanti. Buddhā hi uppajjamānā imasmiṃyeva cakkavāḷe uppajjanti; uppajjanaṭṭhāne pana vārite ito aññesu cakkavāḷesu [V 0.0412] na uppajjantīti vāritameva hoti. Apubbaṃ acarimanti ettha cakkaratanapātubhāvato pubbe pubbaṃ, tasseva antaradhānato pacchā carimaṃ. Tattha dvidhā cakkaratanassa antaradhānaṃ hoti – cakkavattino kālakiriyāya vā pabbajjāya vā. Antaradhāyamānañca pana taṃ kālakiriyato vā pabbajjato vā sattame [P 0.0437] divase antaradhāyati. Tato paraṃ cakkavattino pātubhāvo avārito. Kasmā pana ekacakkavāḷe dve cakkavattino nuppajjantīti? Vivādupacchedato anacchariyabhāvato cakkaratanassa mahānubhāvato ca. Dvīsu hi uppajjantesu ‘amhākaṃ rājā mahanto, amhākaṃ rājā mahanto’ti vivādo uppajjeyya. ‘Ekasmiṃ dīpe cakkavattī, ekasmiṃ dīpe cakkavattī’ti ca anacchariyo bhaveyya. Yo cāyaṃ cakkaratanassa dvisahassadīpaparivāresu catūsu mahādīpesu issariyānuppadānasamattho mahānubhāvo, so parihāyeyya. Iti vivādupacchedato anacchariyabhāvato cakkaratanassa mahānubhāvato ca na ekacakkavāḷe dve uppajjanti.

“In a single world-system means in a single world-sphere. Herein, by this very term, ten thousand world-spheres are included. Even these can be defined as a single world-sphere. For Buddhas, when they arise, arise only in this world-sphere; since the place of arising is limited, it follows that they are prevented from arising in other world-spheres. Not before, not after: here, ‘before’ is before the appearance of the wheel-treasure, and ‘after’ is after its disappearance. The disappearance of the wheel-treasure occurs in two ways: through the wheel-turning monarch’s death or his going forth. When it disappears, it does so on the seventh day after his death or going forth. After that, the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch is not prevented. But why do two wheel-turning monarchs not arise in a single world-sphere? To avoid disputes, to prevent it from being unmarvelous, and because of the great power of the wheel-treasure. For if two were to arise, a dispute would arise: ‘Our king is great! Our king is great!’ And it would be no marvel to have ‘one wheel-turning monarch on one continent, another on another.’ Moreover, that great power of the wheel-treasure, which is capable of bestowing sovereignty over the four great continents with their two thousand surrounding islands, would be diminished. Thus, to avoid disputes, to prevent it from being unmarvelous, and because of the great power of the wheel-treasure, two do not arise in a single world-sphere.”

Yaṃ ittho arahaṃ assa sammāsambuddhoti ettha tiṭṭhatu tāva sabbaññuguṇe nibbattetvā lokattāraṇasamattho buddhabhāvo, paṇidhānamattampi itthiyā na sampajjati.

“Regarding the statement, ‘that a woman might be an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha’: let alone the state of Buddhahood, capable of saving the world after having developed the qualities of omniscience, even the mere aspiration is not fulfilled for a woman.”

“Manussattaṃ liṅgasampatti, hetu satthāradassanaṃ;

Pabbajjā guṇasampatti, adhikāro ca chandatā;

Aṭṭhadhammasamodhānā, abhinīhāro samijjhatī”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.59);

“Human status, attainment of the male sex, the cause, the sight of a Teacher; the going forth, the perfection of qualities, a decisive act, and strong desire: from the combination of these eight things, the resolve succeeds.”

Imāni hi paṇidhānasampattikāraṇāni. Iti paṇidhānampi sampādetuṃ asamatthāya itthiyā kuto buddhabhāvoti “aṭṭhānametaṃ, anavakāso yaṃ itthī arahaṃ assa sammāsambuddho”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbākāraparipūro vā puññussayo sabbākāraparipūrameva attabhāvaṃ nibbattetīti purisova arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho.

“These are the causes for the fulfillment of the aspiration. Thus, for a woman who is incapable of even fulfilling the aspiration, how could there be Buddhahood? Therefore it was said: ‘This is impossible, it cannot happen that a woman could be an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha.’ Or, a store of merit that is complete in all aspects produces an existence that is complete in all aspects; therefore only a man becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha.”

Yaṃ [M 0.0419] itthī rājā assa cakkavattītiādīsupi yasmā itthiyā kosohitavatthaguyhādīnaṃ abhāvena lakkhaṇāni na paripūrenti, itthiratanabhāvena sattaratanasamaṅgitā na sampajjati, sabbamanussehi ca adhiko attabhāvo na hoti, tasmā “aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ itthī rājā assa cakkavattī”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā ca sakkattādīnipi tīṇi ṭhānāni uttamāni, itthiliṅgañca hīnaṃ[V 0.0413], tasmā tassā sakkattādīnipi paṭisiddhāni. Nanu ca yathā itthiliṅgaṃ evaṃ purisaliṅgampi brahmaloke natthi, tasmā “yaṃ puriso brahmattaṃ kāreyya – ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī”tipi na vattabbaṃ siyāti? No na vattabbaṃ. Kasmā? Idha purisassa tattha nibbattanato. Brahmattanti hi mahābrahmattaṃ adhippetaṃ. Itthī ca idha jhānaṃ bhāvetvā [P 0.0438] kālaṃ katvā brahmapārisajjānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjati, na mahābrahmānaṃ. Puriso pana tattha na uppajjatīti na vattabbo. Samānepi cettha ubhayaliṅgābhāve purisasaṇṭhānāva brahmāno, na itthisaṇṭhānā. Tasmā suvuttamevetaṃ.

“In cases such as ‘that a woman might be a wheel-turning monarch’: because a woman, through the absence of a sheath-enclosed male organ, does not fulfill the marks; because, being of the nature of the woman-treasure, she is not endowed with the seven treasures; and because her physical form is not superior to all other humans, it is therefore said: ‘This is impossible, it cannot happen that a woman could be a wheel-turning monarch.’ And since the three positions—of Sakka, Māra, and Brahmā—are supreme, and the female sex is inferior, these positions are also denied to her. But might one not object: ‘Just as the female sex does not exist in the Brahmā world, so too the male sex is absent there. Therefore, should it not be said that the statement, “That a man might attain the state of a Brahmā—this is possible,” is untenable?’ No, that should not be said. Why? Because a man from here is reborn there. For by ‘the state of a Brahmā,’ the state of a Mahābrahmā is intended. A woman, having developed jhāna here and died, is reborn in the company of Brahmā’s retinue, not as a Mahābrahmā. But it cannot be said that a man is not reborn there. Although both sexes are absent there, the Brahmās have a male form, not a female form. Therefore, this is well said.”

Kāyaduccaritassātiādīsu yathā nimbabījakosātakībījādīni madhuraṃ phalaṃ na nibbattenti, asātaṃ amadhurameva nibbattenti, evaṃ kāyaduccaritādīni madhuraṃ vipākaṃ na nibbattenti, amadhurameva nibbattenti. Yathā ca ucchubījasālibījādīni madhuraṃ sādhurasameva phalaṃ nibbattenti, na asātaṃ kaṭukaṃ, evaṃ kāyasucaritādīni madhurameva vipākaṃ nibbattenti, na amadhuraṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

“Regarding bodily misconduct and so on: just as seeds of neem, sponge gourd, and the like do not produce sweet fruit but produce only disagreeable, unsweet fruit, so bodily misconduct and the like do not produce a sweet result but produce only an unsweet one. And just as seeds of sugarcane, rice, and the like produce sweet, delicious fruit, not disagreeable, bitter fruit, so bodily good conduct and the like produce only a sweet result, not an unsweet one. And this has been said:”

“Yādisaṃ vapate bījaṃ, tādisaṃ harate phalaṃ;

Kalyāṇakārī kalyāṇaṃ, pāpakārī ca pāpakanti. (saṃ. ni. 1.256);

“As is the seed that one sows, so is the fruit that one reaps. The doer of good reaps good, and the doer of evil reaps evil.”

Tasmā “aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso, yaṃ kāyaduccaritassā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

“Therefore it was said: ‘This is impossible, it cannot happen that for one of bodily misconduct…,’ and so on.”

Kāyaduccaritasamaṅgītiādīsu samaṅgīti pañcavidhā samaṅgitā – āyūhanasamaṅgitā, cetanāsamaṅgitā, kammasamaṅgitā, vipākasamaṅgitā, upaṭṭhānasamaṅgitāti. Tattha kusalākusalakammāyūhanakkhaṇe ‘āyūhanasamaṅgitā’ vuccati. Tathā ‘cetanāsamaṅgitā’. Yāva pana arahattaṃ na pāpuṇanti tāva sabbepi sattā pubbe upacitaṃ vipākārahaṃ kammaṃ sandhāya kammasamaṅginoti vuccanti – esā ‘kammasamaṅgitā’. ‘Vipākasamaṅgitā’ pana vipākakkhaṇeyeva veditabbā. Yāva pana sattā arahattaṃ na pāpuṇanti tāva tesaṃ [M 0.0420] tato tato cavitvā niraye tāva uppajjamānānaṃ aggijālalohakumbhīādīhi upaṭṭhānākārehi nirayo, gabbhaseyyakattaṃ āpajjamānānaṃ mātukucchi, devesu uppajjamānānaṃ kapparukkhavimānādīhi upaṭṭhānākārehi devalokoti [V 0.0414] evaṃ upapattinimittaṃ upaṭṭhāti. Iti nesaṃ iminā uppattinimittūpaṭṭhānena aparimuttattā ‘upaṭṭhānasamaṅgitā’ nāma. Sāva calati, sesā niccalā. Niraye hi upaṭṭhitepi devaloko upaṭṭhāti; devaloke upaṭṭhitepi nirayo upaṭṭhāti; manussaloke upaṭṭhitepi tiracchānayoni upaṭṭhāti; tiracchānayoniyā ca upaṭṭhitāyapi manussaloko upaṭṭhātiyeva.

In such contexts as 'endowed with bodily misconduct,' the endowment (samaṅgitā) is fivefold: the endowment of undertaking, the endowment of volition, the endowment of kamma, the endowment of result, and the endowment of manifestation. Herein, at the moment of undertaking wholesome or unwholesome kamma, it is called 'the endowment of undertaking.' Similarly, 'the endowment of volition.' As long as they have not attained arahantship, all beings are said to be 'endowed with kamma' in reference to previously accumulated kamma that is ready to yield its result—this is 'the endowment of kamma.' 'The endowment of result,' however, is to be understood only at the moment of the result. As long as beings have not attained arahantship, when they pass away from one state and are reborn in hell, hell manifests to them with such appearances as blazing flames and cauldrons of molten metal. For those entering a womb, the mother’s womb appears. For those reborn among the devas, the deva world appears with such manifestations as wish-fulfilling trees and celestial mansions. Thus, because they are not free from this manifestation of the sign of rebirth, it is called 'the endowment of manifestation.' This one is changeable; the others are unchangeable. For even when hell has manifested, the deva world may manifest; and when the deva world has manifested, hell may manifest; when the human world has manifested, the animal realm may manifest; and when the animal realm has manifested, the human world may still manifest.

Tatridaṃ [P 0.0439] vatthu – soṇagiripāde kira acelavihāre soṇatthero nāma eko dhammakathiko. Tassa pitā sunakhavājiko nāma luddako ahosi. Thero taṃ paṭibāhantopi saṃvare ṭhapetuṃ asakkonto ‘mā nassi varāko’ti mahallakakāle akāmakaṃ pabbājesi. Tassa gilānaseyyāya nipannassa nirayo upaṭṭhāsi. Soṇagiripādato mahantā mahantā sunakhā āgantvā khāditukāmā viya samparivāresuṃ. So mahābhayabhīto “vārehi, tāta soṇa! Vārehi, tāta soṇā”ti āha. “Kiṃ mahātherā”ti? “Na passasi, tātā”ti taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhi. Soṇatthero ‘kathañhi nāma mādisassa pitā niraye nibbattissati, patiṭṭhāhamassa bhavissāmī’ti sāmaṇerehi nānāpupphāni āharāpetvā cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇesu mālāsanthārapūjañca āsanapūjañca kāretvā pitaraṃ mañcena cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ haritvā mañce nipajjāpetvā “ayaṃ me, mahāthera, pūjā tumhākaṃ atthāya katā; ‘ayaṃ me, bhagavā, duggatapaṇṇākāro’ti vatvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā cittaṃ pasādehī”ti āha. So mahāthero pūjaṃ disvā tathākaronto cittaṃ pasādesi. Tāvadevassa devaloko upaṭṭhāsi, nandavanacittalatāvanamissakavanaphārusakavanavimānāni ceva devanāṭakāni ca parivāretvā ṭhitāni viya ahesuṃ. So “apetha, soṇa! Apetha, soṇā”ti āha. “Kimidaṃ, mahātherā”ti? “Etā te, tāta, mātaro āgacchantī”ti. ‘Thero saggo upaṭṭhito mahātherassā’ti cintesi[M 0.0421]. Evaṃ upaṭṭhānasamaṅgitā calatīti veditabbā. Etāsu samaṅgitāsu idha āyūhanacetanākammasamaṅgitāvasena “kāyaduccaritasamaṅgī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

Here is the story. At the foot of Soṇagiri, it is said, in a monastery of naked ascetics, there was an elder named Soṇa, a preacher of the Dhamma. His father was a hunter named Sunakhavājika. Although the elder tried to restrain him, he was unable to establish him in self-control. Thinking, 'Let this poor man not be lost,' he ordained him in his old age, though the father was unwilling. When the father was lying on his sickbed, hell manifested to him. From the foot of Soṇagiri, huge dogs came and surrounded him as if wanting to devour him. Terrified by this great fear, he cried out, 'Ward them off, dear Soṇa! Ward them off, dear Soṇa!' 'What is it, great elder?' 'Don’t you see, dear one?' he said, and described what was happening. The Elder Soṇa thought, 'How could the father of one like me be reborn in hell? I will be his support.' He had the novices bring various flowers and had offerings of strewn garlands and seats made in the stūpa courtyard and the Bodhi-tree courtyard. Then he had his father carried on a bed to the stūpa courtyard, laid him down on the bed, and said: 'Great elder, this offering has been made for your sake. Say, “This, Blessed One, is a poor person’s gift,” pay homage to the Blessed One, and gladden your mind.' Seeing the offering, the great elder did so and gladdened his mind. Instantly, the deva world manifested to him. The Nandana Grove, the Cittalatā Grove, the Missaka Grove, the Phārusaka Grove, celestial mansions, and celestial dancers seemed to be standing surrounding him. He said, 'Go away, Soṇa! Go away, Soṇa!' 'What is this, great elder?' 'These, dear one, are your mothers coming.' The elder thought, 'Heaven has manifested to the great elder.' Thus it should be understood that the endowment of manifestation is changeable. Among these endowments, here the statement 'endowed with bodily misconduct,' etc., is said by way of the endowment of undertaking, the endowment of volition, and the endowment of kamma. The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Paṭhamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the First Power.

Dutiyabalaniddeso

Exposition of the Second Power

810. Dutiyabalaniddese [V 0.0415] gatisampattipaṭibāḷhānīti gatisampattiyā paṭibāhitāni nivāritāni paṭisedhitāni. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca gatisampattīti sampannā gati devaloko ca manussaloko ca. Gativipattīti vipannā gati cattāro apāyā. Upadhisampattīti attabhāvasamiddhi. Upadhivipattīti hīnaattabhāvatā. Kālasampattīti surājasumanussakālasaṅkhāto [P 0.0440] sampannakālo. Kālavipattīti durājadumanussakālasaṅkhāto vipannakālo. Payogasampattīti sammāpayogo. Payogavipattīti micchāpayogo.

810. In the Exposition of the Second Power, the words gatisampattipaṭibāḷhāni mean obstructed, warded off, and prevented by accomplishment in destination. The same method applies to the other terms. Herein, accomplishment in destination (gatisampatti) is a fortunate destination, that is, the deva world and the human world. Failure in destination (gativipatti) is an unfortunate destination, that is, the four planes of misery. Accomplishment in the basis of existence (upadhisampatti) is excellence of personal existence. Failure in the basis of existence (upadhivipatti) is deficiency of personal existence. Accomplishment of time (kālasampatti) is a fortunate time, defined as a time of good rulers and good people. Failure of time (kālavipatti) is an unfortunate time, defined as a time of bad rulers and bad people. Accomplishment of endeavor (payogasampatti) is right endeavor. Failure of endeavor (payogavipatti) is wrong endeavor.

Tattha ekaccassa bahūni pāpakammāni honti. Tāni gativipattiyaṃ ṭhitassa vipacceyyuṃ. So pana ekena kalyāṇakammena gatisampattiyaṃ devesu vā manussesu vā nibbatto. Tādise ca ṭhāne akusalassa vāro natthi, ekantaṃ kusalasseva vāroti. Evamassa tāni kammāni gatisampattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccantīti pajānāti.

Herein, someone has much evil kamma. That kamma would ripen if one were in an unfortunate destination. But by a single wholesome kamma, one is reborn in a fortunate destination, among devas or humans. In such a place, there is no opportunity for the unwholesome to ripen; it is exclusively the opportunity for the wholesome. Thus one understands that that kamma, being obstructed by accomplishment in destination, does not ripen.

Aparassāpi bahūni pāpakammāni honti. Tāni upadhivipattiyaṃ ṭhitassa vipacceyyuṃ. So pana ekena kalyāṇakammena upadhisampattiyaṃ ṭhito susaṇṭhitaṅgapaccaṅgo abhirūpo dassanīyo brahmavacchasadiso. Sacepi dāsiyā kucchismiṃ dāsajāto hoti ‘evarūpo attabhāvo kiliṭṭhakammassa nānucchaviko’ti hatthimeṇḍaassabandhakagopālakakammādīni taṃ na kārenti; sukhumavatthāni nivāsāpetvā bhaṇḍāgārikaṭṭhānādīsu ṭhapenti. Sace itthī hoti, hatthibhattapacanādīni na kārenti; vatthālaṅkāraṃ datvā sayanapālikaṃ vā naṃ karonti, somadevi viya vallabhaṭṭhāne vā ṭhapenti. Bhātikarājakāle kira gomaṃsakhādake bahujane gahetvā rañño [M 0.0422] dassesuṃ. Te ‘daṇḍaṃ dātuṃ sakkothā’ti puṭṭhā ‘na sakkomā’ti vadiṃsu. Atha ne rājaṅgaṇe sodhake akaṃsu. Tesaṃ ekā dhītā abhirūpā dassanīyā pāsādikā. Taṃ disvā rājā antepuraṃ abhinetvā vallabhaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sesañātakāpi tassā ānubhāvena sukhaṃ jīviṃsu. Tādisasmiñhi attabhāve pāpakammānipi vipākaṃ dātuṃ na sakkonti. Evaṃ upadhisampattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccantīti pajānāti.

Another person has many evil kammas. Those kammas would ripen if one had a failure in the basis of existence. But by a single wholesome kamma, one is established in an accomplishment in the basis of existence, with well-proportioned major and minor limbs, handsome, comely, and like a son of Brahmā. Even if one is born as a slave from the womb of a female slave, people think, 'Such a personal existence is not suitable for defiled work,' and they do not make him do the work of an elephant keeper, ram keeper, horse groom, or cowherd. They have him dress in fine clothes and establish him in positions such as treasurer. If it is a woman, they do not make her do work such as cooking elephant-feed; they give her clothes and ornaments and make her a guardian of the bedchamber, or they establish her in a favored position like Somādevī. It is said that in the time of King Bhātikarāja, many people who ate beef were seized and shown to the king. When asked, 'Can you pay the fine?' they said, 'We cannot.' Then the king made them cleaners in the royal courtyard. One of their daughters was beautiful, comely, and inspiring. Seeing her, the king led her into the inner palace and established her in a favored position. Her other relatives also lived happily because of her power. In such a personal existence, even evil kammas cannot give their result. Thus one understands that, being obstructed by an accomplishment in the basis of existence, they do not ripen.

Ekassa bahūni pāpakammāni honti. Tāni kālavipattiyaṃ ṭhitassa vipacceyyuṃ. So pana [V 0.0416] ekena kalyāṇakammena paṭhamakappikānaṃ vā cakkavattirañño vā buddhānaṃ vā uppattisamaye surājasumanussakāle nibbatto. Tādise ca kāle nibbattassa akusalassa vipākaṃ dātuṃ okāso natthi, ekantaṃ kusalasseva okāsoti. Evaṃ kālasampattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccantīti pajānāti.

Someone has many evil kammas. Those kammas would ripen if one were in a time of failure. But by a single wholesome kamma, one is reborn during an accomplishment of time: the time of the people of the first aeon, or of a wheel-turning monarch, or at the time of the arising of Buddhas, in a time of good rulers and good people. For one reborn at such a time, there is no opportunity for the unwholesome to give its result; it is exclusively the opportunity for the wholesome. Thus one understands that, being obstructed by an accomplishment of time, they do not ripen.

Aparassāpi bahūni pāpakammāni honti. Tāni payogavipattiyaṃ [P 0.0441] ṭhitassa vipacceyyuṃ. So pana ekena kalyāṇakammena payogasampattiyaṃ ṭhito pāṇātipātādīhi virato kāyavacīmanosucaritāni pūreti. Tādise ṭhāne akusalassa vipaccanokāso natthi, ekantaṃ kusalasseva okāsoti. Evaṃ payogasampattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccantīti pajānāti.

Another person has many evil kammas. Those kammas would ripen if one were established in a failure of endeavor. But by a single wholesome kamma, one is established in an accomplishment of endeavor, abstaining from the destruction of life and so on, and fulfilling good conduct of body, speech, and mind. In such a case, there is no opportunity for the unwholesome to ripen; it is exclusively the opportunity for the wholesome. Thus one understands that, being obstructed by an accomplishment of endeavor, they do not ripen.

Aparassāpi bahūni pāpakammāni honti. Tāni gatisampattiyaṃ ṭhitassa na vipacceyyuṃ. So panekena pāpakammena gativipattiyaṃyeva nibbatto. Tatthassa tāni kammāni upagantvā vārena vārena vipākaṃ denti – kālena niraye nibbattāpenti, kālena tiracchānayoniyaṃ, kālena pettivisaye, kālena asurakāye, dīghenāpi addhunā apāyato sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ na denti. Evaṃ gatisampattipaṭibāhitattā vipākaṃ dātuṃ asakkontāni gativipattiṃ āgamma vipaccantīti pajānāti.

Another person has many evil kammas. Those kammas would not ripen if one were established in an accomplishment in destination. But by a single evil kamma, one is reborn in a failure in destination. There, those kammas, approaching in turn, give their results: at times they cause rebirth in hell, at times in the animal womb, at times in the sphere of afflicted spirits, at times in the host of asuras; for a long time they do not allow one to lift one’s head from the planes of misery. Thus one understands that kammas which were unable to give their result because they were obstructed by an accomplishment in destination ripen upon arriving at a failure in destination.

Aparassāpi bahūni pāpakammāni honti. Tāni upadhisampattiyaṃ ṭhitassa na vipacceyyuṃ[V 0.0417]. So pana ekena pāpakammena upadhivipattiyaṃyeva patiṭṭhito dubbaṇṇo durūpo dussaṇṭhito bībhaccho pisācasadiso. So sace dāsiyā kucchiyaṃ dāsajāto ‘imāni etassa anucchavikānī’ti sabbāni naṃ kiliṭṭhakammāni [M 0.0423] kārenti antamaso pupphachaḍḍakakammaṃ upādāya. Sace itthī hoti ‘imāni etissā anucchavikānī’ti sabbāni naṃ hatthibhattapacanādīni kiliṭṭhakammāni kārenti. Kulagehe jātampi baliṃ sādhayamānā rājapurisā ‘gehadāsī’ti saññaṃ katvā bandhitvā gacchanti, kotalavāpīgāme mahākuṭumbikassa gharaṇī viya. Evaṃ upadhisampattipaṭibāhitattā vipākaṃ dātuṃ asakkontāni upadhivipattiṃ āgamma vipaccantīti pajānāti.

Another person also has many evil kammas. These would not ripen while one is established in an accomplishment in the basis of existence. But by a single evil kamma, one is established in a failure in the basis of existence, becoming ugly, deformed, misshapen, repulsive, and like a goblin. If such a person is born as a slave in a slave woman’s womb, they make him perform all the degrading tasks—even up to the task of throwing away flowers—thinking, 'These are fitting for him.' If it is a woman, they make her perform all the degrading tasks, such as cooking elephant fodder. Even if born in a good family, royal officials collecting taxes might seize and bind her, perceiving her as a 'household slave,' just like the wife of a wealthy householder in the village of Kotalavāpī. Thus one understands that evil kammas, being unable to give their result because they were obstructed by an accomplishment in the basis of existence, ripen upon encountering a failure in the basis of existence.

Aparassāpi bahūni pāpakammāni honti. Tāni kālasampattiyaṃ nibbātassa na vipacceyyuṃ. So pana ekena pāpakammena kālavipattiyaṃ durājadumanussakāle kasaṭe niroje dasavassāyukakāle nibbatto, yadā pañca gorasā pacchijjanti, kudrūsakaṃ aggabhojanaṃ hoti. Kiñcāpi manussaloke nibbatto, migapasusarikkhajīviko pana hoti. Evarūpe kāle kusalassa vipaccanokāso natthi, ekantaṃ akusalasseva hoti. Evaṃ kālasampattipaṭibāhitattā vipākaṃ [P 0.0442] dātuṃ asakkontāni kālavipattiṃ āgamma vipaccantīti pajānāti.

Another person also has many evil kammas. These would not ripen for one born during an accomplishment of time. But by a single evil kamma, one is born during a failure of time—in a time of wicked rulers and evil people, a wretched, diseased time when the lifespan is ten years, when the five products of the cow disappear, and coarse grain becomes the chief food. Although born in the human world, one's livelihood is like that of beasts and wild animals. In such a time, there is no opportunity for the wholesome to ripen; it is exclusively for the unwholesome. Thus one understands that kammas which were unable to give their result because they were obstructed by an accomplishment of time ripen upon encountering a failure of time.

Aparassāpi bahūni pāpakammāni honti. Tāni payogasampattiyaṃ ṭhitassa na vipacceyyuṃ. So pana payogavipattiyaṃ ṭhito pāṇātipātādīni dasa akusalakammāni karoti. Tamenaṃ sahoḍḍhaṃ gahetvā rañño dassenti. Rājā bahūkammakāraṇāni kāretvā ghātāpeti. Evaṃ payogasampattipaṭibāhitattā vipākaṃ dātuṃ asakkontāni payogavipattiṃ āgamma vipaccantīti pajānāti. Evaṃ catūhi sampattīhi paṭibāhitaṃ pāpakammaṃ vipākaṃ adatvā catasso vipattiyo āgamma deti.

Another person also has many evil kammas. These would not ripen when one is established in an accomplishment of endeavor. But when established in a failure of endeavor, one commits the ten unwholesome kammas, such as killing living beings. They seize him red-handed and bring him before the king. The king, having inflicted many punishments, has him executed. Thus one understands that kammas which were unable to give their result because they were obstructed by an accomplishment of endeavor ripen upon encountering a failure of endeavor. In this way, one understands that evil kamma, having been obstructed by the four accomplishments and thus not giving its result, gives it upon encountering the four failures.

Yathā hi kocideva puriso kenacideva kammena rājānaṃ ārādheyya. Athassa rājā ṭhānantaraṃ datvā janapadaṃ dadeyya. So taṃ sammā paribhuñjituṃ asakkonto makkaṭena gahitabhattapuṭaṃ viya bhindeyya; yassa yaṃ yānaṃ vā vāhanaṃ vā dāsaṃ vā dāsiṃ vā ārāmaṃ vā vatthuṃ vā sampannarūpaṃ passati, sabbaṃ balakkārena gaṇheyya. Manussā ‘rājavallabho’ti kiñci vattuṃ na sakkuṇeyyuṃ. So aññassa vallabhatarassa rājamahāmattassa virujjheyya. So taṃ gahetvā supothitaṃ pothāpetvā bhūmiṃ piṭṭhiyā ghaṃsāpento nikkaḍḍhāpetvā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ‘asuko nāma te[M 0.0424], deva, janapadaṃ bhindatī’ti gaṇhāpeyya. Rājā bandhanāgāre bandhāpetvā ‘asukena nāma kassa kiṃ avahaṭa’nti nagare bheriṃ carāpeyya. Manussā āgantvā ‘mayhaṃ idaṃ gahitaṃ, mayhaṃ idaṃ gahita’nti viravasahassaṃ uṭṭhāpeyyuṃ. Rājā bhiyyoso mattāya kuddho nānappakārena taṃ bandhanāgāre kilametvā ghātāpetvā ‘gacchatha naṃ susāne chaḍḍetvā saṅkhalikā āharathā’ti vadeyya. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Just as a certain man might please the king by some deed. Then the king, granting him a position, might give him a district. Unable to govern it properly, he might ruin it, like a food-packet seized by a monkey. Whatever vehicle, conveyance, male slave, female slave, park, or property he sees that is well-appointed, he would seize by force. People, thinking, "He is the king's favorite," would not be able to say anything. He might then offend another, more favored royal minister. That minister, having seized him, would have him thoroughly beaten, have him dragged out with his back scraping the ground, and then, approaching the king, would have him arrested, saying, "Sire, so-and-so is ruining your district." The king would have him imprisoned and order a drum to be beaten in the city, proclaiming, "What has been taken from whom by so-and-so?" People would come forward, raising a thousand cries, shouting, "He took this from me, he took that from me!" The king, becoming even more furious, would have him tormented in prison in various ways and then executed, saying, "Go, discard him in the charnel ground and bring back the chains." This should be understood as a comparable case.

Tassa hi purisassa hi kenacideva kammena rājānaṃ ārādhetvā ṭhānantaraṃ laddhakālo viya puthujjanassāpi kenacideva puññakammena sagge nibbattakālo. Tasmiṃ janapadaṃ bhinditvā manussānaṃ santakaṃ gaṇhante kassaci kiñci vattuṃ avisahanakālo viya imasmimpi sagge nibbatte [V 0.0418] akusalassa vipaccanokāsaṃ alabhanakālo. Tassa ekadivasaṃ ekasmiṃ rājavallabhatare [P 0.0443] virajjhitvā tena kuddhena naṃ pothāpetvā rañño ārocetvā bandhanāgāre bandhāpitakālo viya imassa saggato cavitvā niraye nibbattakālo. Manussānaṃ ‘mayhaṃ idaṃ gahitaṃ, mayhaṃ idaṃ gahita’nti viravakālo viya tasmiṃ niraye nibbatte sabbākusalakammānaṃ sannipatitvā gahaṇakālo. Susāne chaḍḍetvā saṅkhalikānaṃ āharaṇakālo viya ekekasmiṃ kamme khīṇe itarassa itarassa vipākena nirayato sīsaṃ anukkhipitvā sakalakappaṃ nirayamhi paccanakālo. Kappaṭṭhitikakammañhi katvā ekakappaṃ nirayamhi paccanakasattā neva eko, na dve, na sataṃ, na sahassaṃ. Evaṃ paccanakasattā kira gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattā.

For the time when that man, having pleased the king by some deed, obtains a higher position is like the time when an ordinary person is reborn in heaven due to some meritorious deed. The time when no one is able to say anything to him as he ruins the district and seizes people’s possessions is like the time when, having been reborn in this heaven, there is no opportunity for unwholesome kamma to ripen. The time when, having one day offended a more favored royal minister, he is beaten by that angry minister, reported to the king, and imprisoned, is like the time when this person, having fallen from heaven, is reborn in hell. The time of the people crying, "He took this from me, he took that from me," is like the time when, having been reborn in that hell, all his unwholesome kammas converge and seize him. The time of his body being discarded in the charnel ground and the chains being brought back is like the time of his suffering in hell for an entire aeon; for when one kamma is exhausted, by the result of another and yet another, he suffers without ever raising his head from hell. Indeed, those beings who have committed kamma that endures for an aeon and suffer in hell for that entire aeon are not just one, or two, or a hundred, or a thousand—it is said that the beings who suffer in that way surpass any reckoning.

Atthekaccāni kalyāṇāni kammasamādānāni gativipattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccantītiādīsupi evaṃ yojanā veditabbā. Idhekaccassa bahūni kalyāṇakammāni honti. Tāni gatisampattiyaṃ ṭhitassa vipacceyuṃ. So pana ekena pāpakammena gativipattiyaṃ niraye vā asurakāye vā nibbatto. Tādise ca ṭhāne kusalaṃ vipākaṃ dātuṃ na sakkoti, ekantaṃ akusalameva sakkotīti. Evamassa tāni kammāni gativipattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccantīti pajānāti.

In such statements as, "Some wholesome undertakings of kamma do not ripen because they are obstructed by an unfavorable rebirth," the application should be understood in this way: Here, a certain person may have many wholesome deeds. Those deeds would ripen if he were established in a favorable rebirth. But due to one evil deed, he is reborn in an unfavorable rebirth—in hell or the realm of asuras. In such a place, the wholesome is unable to give its result; only the unwholesome is able. Thus, one understands that those deeds, being obstructed by an unfavorable rebirth, do not ripen.

Aparassāpi bahūni kalyāṇakammāni honti. Tāni upadhisampattiyaṃ ṭhitassa vipacceyyuṃ. So pana ekena pāpakammena upadhivipattiyaṃ patiṭṭhito dubbaṇṇo hoti pisācasadiso. So sacepi rājakule nibbatto pituaccayena [M 0.0425] ‘kiṃ imassa nissirīkassa rajjenā’ti rajjaṃ na labhati. Senāpatigehādīsu nibbattopi senāpatiṭṭhānādīni na labhati.

Another person also has many wholesome deeds. These would ripen were he established in favorable conditions of existence. But due to a single evil deed, he is established in unfavorable conditions of existence and becomes ugly, like a goblin. Even if born into a royal family, he does not inherit the kingdom at his father's death, as people think, "What use is kingship to this inglorious one?" Even if born in the household of a general or the like, he does not attain positions such as generalship.

Imassa panatthassāvibhāvatthaṃ dīparājavatthu kathetabbaṃ – rājā kira putte jāte deviyā pasīditvā varaṃ adāsi. Sā varaṃ gahetvā ṭhapesi. Kumāro sattaṭṭhavassakāleva rājaṅgaṇe kukkuṭe yujjhāpesi. Eko kukkuṭo uppatitvā kumārassa akkhīni bhindi. Kumāramātā devī puttassa pannarasasoḷasavassakāle ‘rajjaṃ vāressāmī’ti rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āha – “deva, tumhehi kumārassa jātakāle varo dinno. Mayā so gahetvā ṭhapito; idāni naṃ gaṇhāmī”ti. “Sādhu, devi, gaṇhāhī”ti. “Mayā, deva, tumhākaṃ santikā kiñci aladdhaṃ nāma natthi[P 0.0444]. Idāni pana mama puttassa rajjaṃ vāremī”ti. “Devi, tava putto aṅgavikalo. Na sakkā tassa rajjaṃ dātu”nti[V 0.0419]. “Tumhe mayhaṃ ruccanakavaraṃ adātuṃ asakkontā kasmā varaṃ adatthā”ti? Rājā ativiya nippīḷiyamāno “na sakkā tuyhaṃ puttassa sakalalaṅkādīpe rajjaṃ dātuṃ; nāgadīpe pana chattaṃ assāpetvā vasatū”ti nāgadīpaṃ pesesi. So dīparājā nāma ahosi. Sace cakkhuvikalo nābhavissā tiyojanasatike sakalatambapaṇṇidīpe sabbasampattiparivāraṃ rajjaṃ alabhissā. Evaṃ upadhivipattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccantīti pajānāti.

To clarify this matter, the story of the island king should be told. It is said that a king, pleased with the queen upon the birth of their son, granted her a boon. She accepted the boon and set it aside. When the prince was seven or eight years old, he arranged cockfights in the royal courtyard. One cock flew up and destroyed the prince’s eyes. When the prince was fifteen or sixteen, his mother, the queen, approached the king to say, "Sire, you granted a boon at the prince's birth. I accepted it and set it aside; now I claim it." The king replied, "Very well, queen, take it." She said, "Sire, there is nothing I have not received from you. But now, I request the kingdom for my son." The king replied, "Queen, your son is disabled. It is not possible to give him the kingdom." She retorted, "If you were unable to grant me a desirable boon, why did you offer one?" The king, being greatly pressed, said, "It is not possible to give your son the kingdom over the entire island of Laṅkā; but let him dwell in Nāgadīpa, having raised the umbrella of sovereignty." So he was sent to Nāgadīpa. He became known as the island king. Had he not been blind, he would have obtained the kingdom over the entire island of Tambapaṇṇi, three hundred leagues in extent, with all its wealth and retinue. Thus, one understands that those deeds, being obstructed by unfavorable conditions of existence, do not ripen.

Aparassāpi bahūni kalyāṇakammāni honti. Tāni kālasampattiyaṃ ṭhitassa vipacceyyuṃ. So pana ekena pāpakammena kālavipattiyaṃ durājadumanussakāle kasaṭe niroje appāyuke gatikoṭike nibbatto. Tādise ca kāle kalyāṇakammaṃ vipākaṃ dātuṃ na sakkotīti. Evaṃ kālavipattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccantīti pajānāti.

Another person also has many wholesome deeds. These would ripen were he established in a favorable time. But through a single evil deed, he is reborn in an unfavorable time—a time of wicked rulers and evil people, a time that is wretched, barren, short-lived, and degenerate. And in such a time, wholesome kamma is not able to give its result. Thus, one understands that those deeds, being obstructed by an unfavorable time, do not ripen.

Aparassāpi bahūni kalyāṇakammāni honti. Tāni payogasampattiyaṃ ṭhitassa vipacceyyuṃ. Ayaṃ pana payogavipattiyaṃ ṭhito pāṇaṃ hanti…pe… sabbaṃ dussīlyaṃ pūreti. Tathā tena saddhiṃ samajātikānipi kulāni āvāhavivāhaṃ na karonti; ‘itthidhutto surādhutto akkhadhutto ayaṃ pāpapuriso’ti ārakā parivajjenti. Kalyāṇakammāni vipaccituṃ na sakkonti. Evaṃ payogavipattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccantīti pajānāti. Evaṃ catasso sampattiyo [M 0.0426] āgamma vipākadāyakaṃ kalyāṇakammaṃ catūhi vipattīhi paṭibāhitattā na vipaccati.

For another, there are also many good deeds. These might ripen for one established in success of effort. But this one, established in failure of effort, kills living beings… and so on… he fulfills all immoral conduct. Likewise, families of similar status do not enter into marriage alliances with him; they avoid him from afar, saying, ‘This wicked man is a womanizer, a drunkard, and a gambler.’ His good deeds are not able to ripen. Thus, one understands that they do not ripen, being obstructed by failure of effort. In this way, a good deed capable of yielding a result, though founded on the four successes, does not ripen because it is hindered by the four failures.

Aparassāpi bahūni kalyāṇakammāni honti. Tāni gativipattiyaṃ ṭhitassa na vipacceyyuṃ. So pana ekena kalyāṇakammena gatisampattiyaṃyeva nibbatto. Tatthassa tāni kammāni upagantvā vārena vārena vipākaṃ denti – kālena manussaloke nibbattāpenti, kālena devaloke. Evaṃ gativipattipaṭibāhitattā vipākaṃ dātuṃ asakkontāni gatimampattiṃ āgamma vipaccantīti pajānāti.

For another, there are also many good deeds. These would not ripen for one established in failure of destiny. But he, by a single good deed, is reborn in a successful destiny. There, those deeds approach him and give their results in turn—at times causing rebirth in the human world, at times in the deva world. Thus, one understands that those deeds, being unable to give a result because they are obstructed by a failed destiny, ripen by being founded on a successful destiny.

Aparassāpi bahūni kalyāṇakammāni honti. Tāni upadhivipattiyaṃ ṭhitassa na vipacceyyuṃ. So pana ekena kalyāṇakammena [P 0.0445] upadhisampattiyaṃyeva patiṭṭhito abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko brahmavacchasadiso. Tassa upadhisampattiyaṃ ṭhitattā kalyāṇakammāni vipākaṃ denti. Sace rājakule nibbattati aññesu jeṭṭhakabhātikesu santesupi ‘etassa attabhāvo [V 0.0420] samiddho, etassa chatte ussāpite lokassa phāsu bhavissatī’ti tameva rajje abhisiñcanti. Uparājagehādīsu nibbatto pituaccayena oparajjaṃ, senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ, bhaṇḍāgārikaṭṭhānaṃ, seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ labhati. Evaṃ upadhivipattipaṭibāhitattā vipākaṃ dātuṃ asakkontāni upadhisampattiṃ āgamma vipaccantīti pajānāti.

For another, there are also many good deeds. These would not ripen for one established in failure of basis. But he, by a single good deed, is established in success of basis—handsome, beautiful, pleasing, like a son of Brahmā. Because he is established in success of basis, his good deeds give their results. If he is reborn in a royal family, even if there are other, elder brothers, they anoint him alone as king, thinking, ‘This one’s existence is prosperous; when his parasol is raised, there will be ease for the world.’ If reborn in the household of a viceroy or the like, upon his father’s demise, he obtains the position of viceroy, commander-in-chief, treasurer, or wealthy merchant. Thus, one understands that those deeds, being unable to give a result because they are obstructed by a failed basis, ripen by being founded on a successful basis.

Aparassāpi bahūni kalyāṇakammāni honti. Tāni kālavipattiyaṃ ṭhitassa na vipacceyyuṃ. So pana ekena kalyāṇakammena kālasampattiyaṃ nibbatto surājasumanussakāle. Tādisāya kālasamiddhiyā nibbattassa kalyāṇakammaṃ vipākaṃ deti.

For another, there are also many good deeds. These would not ripen for one established in failure of time. But he, by a single good deed, is reborn in a successful time—during the era of a virtuous king and good people. For one reborn in such a prosperous time, a good deed gives its result.

Tatridaṃ mahāsoṇattherassa vatthu kathetabbaṃ – brāhmaṇatissabhaye kira cittalapabbate dvādasa bhikkhusahassāniṃ paṭivasanti. Tathā tissamahāvihāre. Dvīsupi mahāvihāresu tiṇṇaṃ vassānaṃ vaṭṭaṃ ekarattameva mahāmūsikāyo khāditvā thusamattameva ṭhapesuṃ. Cittalapabbate bhikkhusaṅgho ‘tissamahāvihāre vaṭṭaṃ vattissati, tattha gantvā vasissāmā’ti vihārato nikkhami. Tissamahāvihārepi bhikkhusaṅgho ‘cittalapabbate vaṭṭaṃ vattissati, tattha gantvā vasissāmā’ti vihārato nikkhami. Ubhatopi [M 0.0427] ekissā gambhīrakandarāya tīre samāgatā pucchitvā vaṭṭassa khīṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā ‘tattha gantvā kiṃ karissāmā’ti catuvīsati bhikkhusahassāni gambhīrakandaravanaṃ pavisitvā nisīditvā nisinnanīhāreneva anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyiṃsu. Pacchā bhaye vūpasante bhikkhusaṅgho sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ gahetvā dhātuyo saṃharitvā cetiyaṃ akāsi.

Here, the story of the Elder Mahāsoṇa should be told. It is said that during the terror of Brāhmaṇa-Tissa, twelve thousand monks were dwelling on Cittalapabbata. Likewise at Tissamahāvihāra. In both great monasteries, the provisions for three years were devoured by large rats in a single night, leaving only husks. The community of monks at Cittalapabbata left the monastery, thinking, ‘The provisions will be available at Tissamahāvihāra; let us go and dwell there.’ The community of monks at Tissamahāvihāra also left the monastery, thinking, ‘The provisions will be available at Cittalapabbata; let us go and dwell there.’ Both groups met on the bank of a deep ravine, and having inquired and learned that the provisions were depleted, they thought, ‘What shall we do by going there?’ Then, twenty-four thousand monks entered the forest of the deep ravine, sat down, and in that very seated posture, they attained final Nibbāna with no residue remaining. Later, when the terror had subsided, the community of monks, with the help of Sakka, king of the devas, collected the relics and built a cetiya.

Brāhmaṇatissacoropi janapadaṃ viddhaṃsesi. Saṅgho sannipatitvā mantetvā “coraṃ paṭibāhatū”ti sakkasantikaṃ aṭṭha there pesesi. Sakko devarājā “mayā, bhante, uppanno coro na [P 0.0446] sakkā paṭibāhituṃ. Saṅgho parasamuddaṃ gacchatu. Ahaṃ samuddārakkhaṃ karissāmī”ti. Saṅgho sabbadisāhi nāgadīpaṃ gantvā jambukolapaṭṭane tibhūmikaṃ mahāuḷumpaṃ bandhāpesi. Ekā bhūmikā udake osīdi. Ekissā bhikkhusaṅgho nisinno. Ekissā pattacīvarāni ṭhapayiṃsu. Saṃyuttabhāṇakacūḷasīvatthero, isidattatthero, mahāsoṇattheroti tayo therā tāsaṃ parisānaṃ pāmokkhā. Tesu dve therā mahāsoṇattheraṃ āhaṃsu – “āvuso mahāsoṇa, abhiruha mahāuḷumpa”nti. “Tumhe pana, bhante”ti? “Āvuso, udake maraṇampi thale maraṇampi ekameva[V 0.0421]. Na mayaṃ gamissāma. Taṃ nissāya pana anāgate sāsanassa paveṇī ṭhassati. Gaccha tvaṃ, āvuso”ti. “Nāhaṃ, bhante, tumhesu agacchantesu gamissāmī”ti yāvatatiyaṃ kathetvāpi theraṃ āropetuṃ asakkontā nivattiṃsu.

The robber Brāhmaṇa-Tissa also devastated the countryside. The Saṅgha assembled, deliberated, and sent eight elders to Sakka, saying, ‘May he repel the robber!’ Sakka, king of the devas, replied, ‘Venerable sirs, the robber who has arisen cannot be repelled by me. Let the Saṅgha go to the other side of the ocean. I will provide protection on the ocean.’ The Saṅgha went from all directions to Nāgadīpa and had a large three-tiered raft built at the port of Jambukola. One tier sank into the water. On one, the community of monks sat. On another, they placed their bowls and robes. Three elders—Saṃyuttabhāṇaka Cūḷasīva, Isidatta, and Mahāsoṇa—were the leaders of those assemblies. Two of the elders said to the Elder Mahāsoṇa, ‘Friend Mahāsoṇa, board the great raft.’ ‘But what about you, venerable sirs?’ ‘Friend, death in the water and death on land are one and the same. We will not go. But through reliance on you, the lineage of the teaching will be established in the future. You go, friend.’ ‘Venerable sirs, I will not go if you do not go.’ Though they spoke to him a third time, being unable to make the elder board, they turned back.

Atha cūḷasīvatthero isidattattheraṃ āha – “āvuso isidatta, anāgate mahāsoṇattheraṃ nissāya sāsanapaveṇī ṭhassati; mā kho taṃ hatthato vissajjehī”ti. “Tumhe pana, bhante”ti? “Ahaṃ mahācetiyaṃ vandissāmī”ti dve there anusāsitvā anupubbena cārikaṃ caranto mahāvihāraṃ sampāpuṇi. Tasmiṃ samaye mahāvihāro suñño. Cetiyaṅgaṇe eraṇḍā jātā. Cetiyaṃ gacchehi parivāritaṃ, sevālena pariyonaddhaṃ. Thero dharamānakabuddhassa nipaccākāraṃ dassento viya mahācetiyaṃ vanditvā pacchimadisāya sālaṃ pavisitvā olokento ‘evarūpassa nāma lābhaggayasaggappattassa sarīradhātucetiyaṭṭhānaṃ anāthaṃ jāta’nti cintayamāno nisīdi.

Then, the elder Cūḷasīva said to the elder Isidatta, 'Friend Isidatta, in the future, the lineage of the Teaching will be established depending on the elder Mahāsoṇa; do not let him slip from your hands.' 'But what about you, venerable sir?' 'I will pay homage to the Great Stupa.' Having thus instructed the two elders, he journeyed by stages and reached the Great Monastery. At that time, the Great Monastery was deserted. In the stupa courtyard, castor-oil plants had grown. The stupa was surrounded by thickets and overgrown with moss. The elder, as if showing reverence to the living Buddha, paid homage to the Great Stupa, entered a hall on the western side, and looking around, sat down, thinking, 'Alas, the site of the bodily relic stupa of such a one who attained the pinnacle of gain and fame has become unprotected!'

Atha [M 0.0428] avidūre rukkhe adhivatthā devatā addhikamanussarūpena taṇḍulanāḷiñca guḷapiṇḍañca ādāya therassa santikaṃ gantvā “kattha gacchatha, bhante”ti? “Ahaṃ dakkhiṇadisaṃ, upāsakā”ti. “Ahampi tattheva gantukāmo, saha gacchāma, bhante”ti. “Ahaṃ dubbalo; tava gatiyā gantuṃ na sakkhissāmi; tvaṃ purato gaccha, upāsakā”ti. “Ahampi tumhākaṃ gatiyā gamissāmī”ti therassa pattacīvaraṃ aggahesi. Tissavāpipāḷiṃ āruḷhakāle ca pattaṃ āharāpetvā pānakaṃ katvā adāsi. Therassa pītamatteyeva balamattā saṇṭhāti. Devatā pathaviṃ saṅkhipitvā veṇunadīsantike ekaṃ chaḍḍitavihāraṃ patvā therassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ paṭijaggitvā adāsi.

Then a deity dwelling in a nearby tree, taking the form of a traveler, came to the elder with a nāḷi of rice and a lump of jaggery and asked, 'Where are you going, venerable sir?' 'I am going to the southern direction, lay follower.' 'I also wish to go there; let us go together, venerable sir.' 'I am weak; I cannot keep up with your pace. You go ahead, lay follower.' 'I will go at your pace,' said the deity, and took the elder's bowl and robe. When they had ascended the embankment of the Tissavāpi reservoir, the deity had the elder bring out his bowl, prepared a drink, and gave it to him. As soon as the elder drank it, a measure of strength was established in him. The deity, having contracted the earth, arrived at an abandoned monastery near the Veṇu River, prepared a dwelling place for the elder, and gave it to him.

Punadivase [P 0.0447] therena mukhe dhovitamatte yāguṃ pacitvā adāsi; yāguṃ pītassa bhattaṃ pacitvā upanāmesi. Thero “tuyhaṃ ṭhapehi, upāsakā”ti pattaṃ hatthena pidahi. “Ahaṃ na dūraṃ gamissāmī”ti devatā therasseva patte bhattaṃ pakkhipitvā katabhattakiccassa therassa pattacīvaramādāya maggaṃ paṭipannā pathaviṃ saṅkhipitvā jajjaranadīsantikaṃ netvā “bhante, etaṃ paṇṇakhādakamanussānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ, dhūmo paññāyati. Ahaṃ purato gamissāmī”ti theraṃ vanditvā attano bhavanaṃ agamāsi. Thero sabbampi bhayakālaṃ paṇṇakhādakamanusse nissāya vasi.

The next day, as soon as the elder had washed his face, the deity cooked rice gruel and gave it to him. After he had drunk the gruel, the deity cooked a meal and brought it to him. The elder covered his bowl with his hand, saying, 'Keep it for yourself, lay follower.' 'I will not be going far,' said the deity, and having placed the meal in the elder's own bowl, took the bowl and robe of the elder who had completed his meal duties. Setting out on the path, the deity contracted the earth and led him to the vicinity of the Jajjara River. 'Venerable sir, this is the dwelling place of the leaf-eating people; smoke can be seen. I will go on ahead.' Having paid homage to the elder, the deity departed to its own abode. The elder dwelt there, relying on the leaf-eating people throughout the entire time of danger.

Isidattattheropi anupubbena cārikaṃ caranto aḷajanapadaṃ sampāpuṇi. Tattha manussā nātipakkāni [V 0.0422] madhukaphalāni bhinditvā aṭṭhiṃ ādāya tacaṃ chaḍḍetvā agamaṃsu. Thero “āvuso mahāsoṇa, bhikkhāhāro paññāyatī”ti vatvā pattacīvaraṃ āharāpetvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ nīharitvā aṭṭhāsi. Taruṇadārakā theraṃ ṭhitaṃ disvā ‘iminā koci attho bhavissatī’ti vālukaṃ puñchitvā madhukaphalattacaṃ patte pakkhipitvā adaṃsu; therā paribhuñjiṃsu. Sattāhamattaṃ soyeva āhāro ahosi.

The elder Isidatta, also journeying by stages, reached the country of Aḷaja. There, people were breaking open half-ripe madhuka fruits, taking the kernels, and discarding the skins as they went. The elder said, 'Friend Mahāsoṇa, alms-food is apparent,' and having had his bowl and robe brought, he donned his robe, took out his bowl, and stood. Young boys, seeing the elder standing there, thought, 'He must have some need,' and after sweeping away the sand, they placed the skins of the madhuka fruits in the bowl and gave them. The elders partook of them. For about a week, that was their only food.

Anupubbena coriyassaraṃ sampāpuṇiṃsu. Manussā kumudāni gahetvā kumudanāle chaḍḍetvā agamaṃsu. Thero “āvuso mahāsoṇa, bhikkhāhāro paññāyatī”ti vatvā pattacīvaraṃ āharāpetvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ nīharitvā aṭṭhāsi. Gāmadārakā kumudanāle sodhetvā patte pakkhipitvā adaṃsu; therā paribhuñjiṃsu. Sattāhamattaṃ sova āhāro ahosi.

Journeying by stages, they reached Coriyassara. People were taking the water lilies, discarding the stalks, and going on their way. The elder said, 'Friend Mahāsoṇa, alms-food is apparent,' and having had his bowl and robe brought, he donned his robe, took out his bowl, and stood. Village boys cleaned the water lily stalks, placed them in the bowl, and gave them. The elders partook of them. For about a week, that was their only food.

Anupubbena [M 0.0429] carantā paṇṇakhādakamanussānaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne ekaṃ gāmadvāraṃ sampāpuṇiṃsu. Tattha ekissā dārikāya mātāpitaro araññaṃ gacchantā “sace koci ayyo āgacchati, katthaci gantuṃ mā adāsi; ayyassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkheyyāsi, ammā”ti āhaṃsu. Sā there disvā pattaṃ gahetvā nisīdāpesi. Gehe dhaññajāti nāma natthi. Vāsiṃ pana gahetvā guñjacocarukkhattacaṃ guñjalatāpattehi saddhiṃ ekato koṭṭetvā tayo piṇḍe katvā ekaṃ isidattattherassa ekaṃ mahāsoṇattherassa patte ṭhapetvā ‘atirekapiṇḍaṃ isidattattherassa patte ṭhapessāmī’ti hatthaṃ pasāresi. Hattho parivattitvā mahāsoṇattherassa patte [P 0.0448] patiṭṭhāpesi. Isidattatthero ‘brāhmaṇatissabhaye guñjacocapiṇḍe vipākadāyakakammaṃ desakālasampadāya kīvapamāṇaṃ vipākaṃ dassatī’ti āha. Te taṃ paribhuñjitvā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ agamaṃsu. Sāpi araññato āgatānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ ācikkhi “dve therā āgatā. Tesaṃ me vasanaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhita”nti. Te ubhopi therānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā “bhante, yaṃ mayaṃ labhāma, tena tumhe paṭijaggissāma; idheva vasathā”ti paṭiññaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Therāpi sabbabhayakālaṃ te upanissāya vasiṃsu.

Journeying by stages, they arrived at a village gate in the dwelling place of the leaf-eating people. There, the parents of a certain girl, as they were going to the forest, had told her, 'My dear, if any noble one comes, do not let him go anywhere; you must show him the dwelling place.' Seeing the elders, she took their bowls and had them sit down. There was no kind of grain in the house. Taking an adze, she pounded together the bark of the guñja-coca tree with the leaves of the guñja creeper, made three balls of it, and placed one in the elder Isidatta's bowl and one in the elder Mahāsoṇa's bowl. Then, thinking, 'I will place the extra ball in the elder Isidatta's bowl,' she stretched out her hand. But her hand turned and placed it in the elder Mahāsoṇa's bowl. The elder Isidatta exclaimed, 'In this time of the Brahmin Tissa terror, what a great result the kamma of giving this ball of guñja-coca will yield, due to the perfection of the time and place!' Having eaten it, they went to their dwelling place. She too, when her parents returned from the forest, told them, 'Two elders have come. I have shown them the dwelling place.' Both parents went to the elders, paid homage, and took a vow, saying, 'Venerable sirs, we will look after you with whatever we get. Please dwell right here.' The elders also dwelt there, relying on them throughout the entire time of danger.

Brāhmaṇatissacore mate pitumahārājā chattaṃ ussāpesi. ‘Bhayaṃ vūpasantaṃ, janapado sampuṇṇo’ti sutvā parasamuddato bhikkhusaṅgho nāvāya mahātitthapaṭṭane oruyha ‘mahāsoṇatthero kahaṃ vasatī’ti pucchitvā therassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Thero pañcasatabhikkhuparivāro kālakagāme [V 0.0423] maṇḍalārāmavihāraṃ sampāpuṇi. Tasmiṃ samaye kālakagāme sattamattāni kulasatāni paṭivasanti. Rattibhāge devatā āhiṇḍitvā “mahāsoṇatthero pañcabhikkhusataparivāro maṇḍalārāmavihāraṃ patto. Ekeko navahatthasāṭakena saddhiṃ ekekakahāpaṇagghanakaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ detū”ti manusse avocuṃ. Punadivase ca therā kālakagāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu. Manussā nisīdāpetvā yāguṃ adaṃsu. Maṇḍalārāmavāsī tissabhūtitthero saṅghatthero hutvā nisīdi. Eko mahāupāsako taṃ vanditvā “bhante, mahāsoṇatthero nāma kataro”ti pucchi. Tena samayena thero navako hoti pariyante nisinno. Thero hatthaṃ pasāretvā “mahāsoṇo nāma [M 0.0430] esa, upāsakā”ti āha. Upāsako taṃ vanditvā pattaṃ gaṇhāti. Thero na deti. Tissabhūtitthero “āvuso soṇa, yathā tvaṃ na jānāsi, mayampi evameva na jānāma; puññavantānaṃ devatā paripācenti; pattaṃ dehi, sabrahmacārīnaṃ saṅgahaṃ karohī”ti āha. Thero pattaṃ adāsi. Mahāupāsako pattaṃ ādāya gantvā kahāpaṇagghanakassa piṇḍapātassa pūretvā navahatthasāṭakaṃ ādhārakaṃ katvā āharitvā therassa hatthe ṭhapesi; aparopi upāsako therassāti satta sāṭakasatāni satta ca piṇḍapātasatāni therasseva adaṃsu.

When the bandit Brāhmaṇa Tissa died, his father, the great king, raised the parasol. Hearing that 'fear has subsided, the country is prosperous,' a community of monks from across the sea disembarked by ship at the port of Mahātittha. They asked, 'Where does the Elder Mahāsoṇa reside?' and went to the Elder's presence. The Elder, with a retinue of five hundred monks, arrived at the Maṇḍalārāma Monastery in Kālakagāma. At that time, about seven hundred families resided in Kālakagāma. During the night, deities wandered about and addressed the people, saying, 'The Elder Mahāsoṇa, with a retinue of five hundred monks, has arrived at the Maṇḍalārāma Monastery. Let each one give alms-food worth one kahāpaṇa, together with a nine-cubit cloth.' The next day, the elders entered Kālakagāma for alms. The people had them seated and offered rice gruel. The Elder Tissabhūti, a resident of Maṇḍalārāma and the elder of the Sangha, sat down. A great lay follower paid him respects and asked, 'Venerable sir, which one is the Elder Mahāsoṇa?' At that time, Mahāsoṇa was a junior monk and was seated at the edge. The Elder Tissabhūti stretched out his hand and said, 'This is Mahāsoṇa, O lay follower.' The lay follower paid respects to him and reached for his bowl, but the elder did not give it. The Elder Tissabhūti said, 'Friend Soṇa, just as you do not know, we also do not know; deities provide for the meritorious. Give the bowl and support your fellow monks.' The Elder gave the bowl. The great lay follower took the bowl, filled it with alms-food worth a kahāpaṇa, made the nine-cubit cloth a support, brought it back, and placed it in the Elder's hands. Other lay followers also gave seven hundred cloths and seven hundred portions of alms-food to that Elder alone.

Thero bhikkhusaṅghassa [P 0.0449] saṃvibhāgaṃ katvā anupubbena mahāvihāraṃ pāpuṇitvā mukhaṃ dhovitvā mahābodhiṃ vanditvā mahācetiyaṃ vanditvā thūpārāme ṭhito cīvaraṃ pārupitvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivāro dakkhiṇadvārena nagaraṃ pavisitvā dvārato yāva vaḷañjanakasālā etasmiṃ antare saṭṭhikahāpaṇagghanakaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ labhi. Tato paṭṭhāya pana sakkārassa pamāṇaṃ natthi. Evaṃ kālavipattiyaṃ madhukaphalattacopi kumudanāḷipi dullabhā jātā. Kālasampattiyaṃ evarūpo mahālābho udapādi.

The elder, having made a distribution to the community of monks, gradually reached the Mahāvihāra. After washing his face, he venerated the Great Bodhi Tree and the Great Cetiya. Standing at the Thūpārāma, having put on his robe and accompanied by a retinue of monks, he entered the city through the southern gate. From the gate up to the Vaḷañjanaka Hall, within that distance, he received alms-food worth sixty kahāpaṇas. From that time onward, there was no limit to the honor shown to him. Thus, in a time of misfortune, even the bark of madhuka fruits and lotus stalks became rare. In a time of prosperity, such great gain arose.

Vattabbakanigrodhattherassāpi sāmaṇerakāle brāhmaṇatissabhayaṃ udapādi. Sāmaṇero ca upajjhāyo cassa parasamuddaṃ nāgamiṃsu; ‘paṇṇakhādakamanusse upanissāya vasissāmā’ti paccantābhimukhā ahesuṃ. Sāmaṇero sattāhamattaṃ anāhāro hutvā ekasmiṃ gāmaṭṭhāne tālarukkhe tālapakkaṃ disvā upajjhāyaṃ āha – “bhante, thokaṃ āgametha; tālapakkaṃ pātessāmī”ti. “Dubbalosi tvaṃ, sāmaṇera, mā abhiruhī”ti. “Abhiruhissāmi, bhante”ti khuddakavāsiṃ gahetvā tālaṃ āruyha tālapiṇḍaṃ chindituṃ ārabhi. Vāsiphalaṃ nikkhamitvā bhūmiyaṃ pati.

For the Elder Vattabbaka Nigrodha also, fear of Brāhmaṇa Tissa arose during his time as a novice. The novice and his preceptor did not go across the ocean; they headed towards the border region, thinking, 'We will live depending on leaf-eating people.' After being without food for about a week, the novice saw a ripe palm fruit on a palm tree in a village settlement and said to his preceptor, 'Venerable sir, wait a moment; I will knock down a palm fruit.' 'You are weak, novice, do not climb up.' 'I will climb, venerable sir.' Taking a small adze, he climbed the palm tree and began to cut a cluster of palm fruits. The blade of the adze came loose and fell to the ground.

Thero [V 0.0424] cintesi “ayaṃ kilantova rukkhaṃ āruḷho; kiṃ nu kho idāni karissatī”ti sāmaṇero tālapaṇṇaṃ phāletvā phāletvā vāsidaṇḍake bandhitvā ghaṭṭento ghaṭṭento bhūmiyaṃ pātetvā “bhante, sādhu vatassa sace vāsiphalaṃ ettha paveseyyāthā”ti āha. Thero ‘upāyasampanno sāmaṇero’ti vāsiphalaṃ pavesetvā adāsi. So vāsiṃ ukkhipitvā tālaphalāni pātesi. Thero vāsiṃ pātāpetvā pavaṭṭitvā [M 0.0431] gataṃ tālaphalaṃ bhinditvā sāmaṇeraṃ otiṇṇakāle āha “sāmaṇera, tvaṃ dubbalo, idaṃ tāva khādāhī”ti. “Nāhaṃ, bhante, tumhehi akhādite khādissāmī”ti vāsiṃ gahetvā tālaphalāni bhinditvā pattaṃ nīharitvā tālamiñjaṃ pakkhipitvā therassa datvā sayaṃ khādi. Yāva tālaphalāni ahesuṃ, tāva tattheva vasitvā phalesu khīṇesu anupubbena paṇṇakhādakamanussānaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne ekaṃ chaḍḍitavihāraṃ pavisiṃsu. Sāmaṇero therassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ paṭijaggi. Thero sāmaṇerassa ovādaṃ datvā vihāraṃ pāvisi. Sāmaṇero ‘anāyatane naṭṭhānaṃ attabhāvānaṃ pamāṇaṃ natthi, buddhānaṃ [P 0.0450] upaṭṭhānaṃ karissāmī’ti cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā appaharitaṃ karoti; sattāhamattaṃ nirāhāratāya pavedhamāno patitvā nipannakova tiṇāni uddharati. Ekacce ca manussā araññe carantā madhuṃ labhitvā dārūni ceva sākapaṇṇañca gahetvā tiṇacalanasaññāya ‘migo nu kho eso’ti sāmaṇerassa santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ karosi, sāmaṇerā”ti āhaṃsu. “Tiṇagaṇṭhiṃ gaṇhāmi, upāsakā”ti. “Aññopi koci atthi, bhante”ti? “Āma, upāsakā, upajjhāyo me antogabbhe”ti. “Mahātherassa datvā khādeyyāsi, bhante”ti sāmaṇerassa madhuṃ datvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhitvā “mayaṃ sākhābhaṅgaṃ karontā gamissāma. Etāya saññāya theraṃ gahetvā āgaccheyyāsi, ayyā”ti vatvā agamaṃsu.

The elder thought, 'This one has climbed the tree while exhausted; what will he do now?' The novice, repeatedly splitting palm leaves, tied them to the handle of the adze and, by shaking them, lowered it to the ground, saying, 'Venerable sir, it would be good if you could insert the adze-blade here.' The elder, thinking, 'The novice is resourceful,' inserted the adze-blade and gave it to him. He pulled up the adze and knocked down the palm fruits. The elder, having had the adze dropped down, split a palm fruit that had rolled away, and when the novice had descended, said, 'Novice, you are weak; eat this for now.' 'No, venerable sir, I will not eat before you have eaten.' Taking the adze, he split the palm fruits, took out the bowl, placed the palm pith inside, gave it to the elder, and then ate himself. As long as there were palm fruits, they stayed right there. When the fruits were exhausted, they gradually entered an abandoned monastery in the area where leaf-eating people lived. The novice prepared the elder's dwelling place. The elder gave advice to the novice and entered his dwelling. The novice thought, 'There is no limit to the lives lost in unfortunate realms; I will attend upon the Buddhas,' and went to the cetiya courtyard to clear the weeds. Trembling from lack of food for about a week, he fell down and, while lying there, pulled up grass. Some people wandering in the forest found honey and, taking firewood and edible leaves, they approached the novice, thinking from the movement of the grass, 'Could this be a deer?' They asked, 'What are you doing, novice?' 'I am gathering a bundle of grass, O lay followers.' 'Is there anyone else, venerable sir?' 'Yes, O lay followers, my preceptor is inside the inner chamber.' 'Give this to the great elder and then you may eat, venerable sir.' They gave the honey to the novice, told him their own dwelling place, and said, 'We will go along breaking branches. With this as a sign, you should bring the elder, noble one,' and then they left.

Sāmaṇero madhuṃ gahetvā therassa santikaṃ gantvā bahi ṭhatvā “vandāmi, bhante”ti āha. Thero ‘sāmaṇero jighacchāya anuḍayhamāno āgato bhavissatī’ti tuṇhī ahosi. So punapi “vandāmi, bhante”ti āha. “Kasmā, sāmaṇera, dubbalabhikkhūnaṃ sukhena nipajjituṃ na desī”ti? “Dvāraṃ vivarituṃ sāruppaṃ, bhante”ti? Thero uṭṭhahitvā dvāraṃ vivaritvā “kiṃ te, sāmaṇera, laddhaṃ”ti āha. Manussehi madhu dinnaṃ, khādituṃ sāruppaṃ, bhante”ti? “Sāmaṇera, evameva khādituṃ kilamissāma, pānakaṃ katvā pivissāmā”ti. Sāmaṇero pānakaṃ katvā adāsi. Atha naṃ thero “manussānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pucchasi, sāmaṇerā”ti āha. Sayameva ācikkhiṃsu, bhante”ti. “Sāmaṇera, pātova gacchantā kilamissāma; ajjeva gamissāmā”ti [V 0.0425] pattacīvaraṃ [M 0.0432] gaṇhāpetvā nikkhami. Te gantvā manussānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānassa avidūre nipajjiṃsu.

The novice took the honey and went to the elder. Standing outside, he said, 'I pay homage, venerable sir.' The elder, thinking, 'The novice must have come tormented by hunger,' remained silent. He said again, 'I pay homage, venerable sir.' 'Why, novice, do you not allow a weak monk to lie down in comfort?' 'Is it suitable to open the door, venerable sir?' The elder got up, opened the door, and said, 'What have you obtained, novice?' 'People gave honey, venerable sir. Is it suitable to eat?' 'Novice, if we eat it just as it is, we will become weary; let us make a drink and drink it.' The novice prepared the drink and gave it to him. Then the elder said to him, 'Novice, did you ask the people their dwelling place?' 'They told me themselves, venerable sir.' 'Novice, going in the morning, we will become weary; let us go today.' Having had his bowl and robe taken, he set out. They went and lay down not far from the people's dwelling place.

Sāmaṇero rattibhāge cintesi – ‘mayā pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya gāmante aruṇaṃ nāma na uṭṭhāpitapubba’nti. So pattaṃ gahetvā aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetuṃ araññaṃ agamāsi. Mahāthero sāmaṇeraṃ nipannaṭṭhāne apassanto ‘manussakhādakehi gahito bhavissatī’ti cintesi. Sāmaṇero araññe aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā pattena udakañca dantakaṭṭhañca gahetvā āgami. “Sāmaṇera, kuhiṃ gatosi? Mahallakabhikkhūnaṃ te vitakko uppādito; daṇḍakammaṃ āharā”ti. “Āharissāmi, bhante”ti. Thero mukhaṃ dhovitvā cīvaraṃ pārupi. Ubhopi manussānaṃ [P 0.0451] vasanaṭṭhānaṃ agamaṃsu. Manussāpi attano paribhogaṃ kandamūlaphalapaṇṇaṃ adaṃsu. Theropi paribhuñjitvā vihāraṃ agamāsi. Sāmaṇero udakaṃ āharitvā “pāde dhovāmi, bhante”ti āha. “Sāmaṇera, tvaṃ rattiṃ kuhiṃ gato? Amhākaṃ vitakkaṃ uppādesī”ti. “Bhante, gāmante me aruṇaṃ na uṭṭhāpitapubbaṃ; aruṇuṭṭhāpanatthāya araññaṃ agamāsi”nti. “Sāmaṇera, na tuyhaṃ daṇḍakammaṃ anucchavikaṃ amhākameva anucchavika”nti vatvā thero tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne vasi; sāmaṇerassa ca saññaṃ adāsi “mayaṃ tāva mahallakā; ‘idaṃ nāma bhavissatī’ti na sakkā jānituṃ. Tuvaṃ attānaṃ rakkheyyāsī”ti. Thero kira anāgāmī. Taṃ aparabhāge manussakhādakā khādiṃsu. Sāmaṇero attānaṃ rakkhitvā bhaye vūpasante tathārūpe ṭhāne upajjhaṃ gāhāpetvā upasampanno buddhavacanaṃ uggahetvā tipiṭakadharo hutvā vattabbakanigrodhatthero nāma jāto.
