The novice thought during the night, 'Since the time I went forth, I have never before roused the dawn in the vicinity of a village.' Taking his bowl, he went into the forest to rouse the dawn. The great elder, not seeing the novice in his sleeping place, thought, 'He must have been seized by man-eaters.' The novice, having roused the dawn in the forest, returned carrying water and a tooth-stick in his bowl. 'Novice, where have you been? You have caused an elder monk to worry; bring the penalty.' 'I will bring it, venerable sir.' The elder washed his face and put on his robe. Both went to the people's dwelling place. The people gave them roots, tubers, fruits, and leaves for their consumption. The elder, having partaken, went to the monastery. The novice, bringing water, said, 'I will wash your feet, venerable sir.' 'Novice, where did you go at night? You caused us to worry.' 'Venerable sir, I had never before roused the dawn in the vicinity of a village; I went to the forest for the purpose of rousing the dawn.' 'Novice, the penalty is not appropriate for you, but it is appropriate for us,' said the elder, and he remained right there. And he gave the novice a warning: 'We are old; it is not possible to know what might happen. You should protect yourself.' The elder, it is said, was a non-returner. Later, man-eaters devoured him. The novice, having protected himself, and when the danger had subsided, took a preceptor in a suitable place and became fully ordained. Having learned the Buddha's word, he became a bearer of the Three Baskets and was known as Elder Nigrodha the Speaker.

Pitumahārājā rajjaṃ paṭipajji. Parasamuddā āgatāgatā bhikkhū “kahaṃ vattabbakanigrodhatthero, kahaṃ vattabbakanigrodhatthero”ti pucchitvā tassa santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Mahābhikkhusaṅgho theraṃ parivāresi. So mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivuto anupubbena mahāvihāraṃ patvā mahābodhiṃ mahācetiyaṃ thūpārāmañca vanditvā nagaraṃ pāyāsi. Yāva dakkhiṇadvārā gacchantasseva navasu ṭhānesu ticīvaraṃ upapajji; antonagaraṃ paviṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya mahāsakkāro uppajji. Iti kālavipattiyaṃ tālaphalakandamūlapaṇṇampi dullabhaṃ jātaṃ. Kālasampattiyaṃ evarūpo mahālābho uppannoti. Evaṃ kālavipattipaṭibāhitattā [M 0.0433] vipākaṃ dātuṃ asakkontāni kālasampattiṃ āgamma vipaccantīti pajānāti.

The grandfather king assumed the kingdom. Monks coming from across the ocean, repeatedly asking, 'Where is Elder Nigrodha the Speaker? Where is Elder Nigrodha the Speaker?' went to his presence. A great Saṅgha of monks surrounded the elder. Surrounded by the great Saṅgha of monks, he gradually reached the Mahāvihāra, paid homage to the Great Bodhi Tree, the Great Cetiya, and the Thūpārāma, and then proceeded to the city. As he went as far as the southern gate, sets of the three robes arose in nine places. From the time he entered the city, great honor arose. Thus, in a time of misfortune, even palm fruits, roots, tubers, and leaves became scarce. In a time of fortune, such great gain arose. Thus one understands that deeds, being hindered by unfavorable times and thus unable to give their result, ripen upon encountering favorable times.

Aparassāpi [V 0.0426] bahūni kalyāṇakammāni honti. Tāni payogavipattiyaṃ ṭhitassa na vipacceyyuṃ. So pana ekena kalyāṇakammena sammāpayoge patiṭṭhito tīṇi sucaritāni pūreti, pañcasīlaṃ dasasīlaṃ rakkhati. Kālasampattiyaṃ nibbattassa rājāno sabbālaṅkārapatimaṇḍitā rājakaññāyo ‘etassa anucchavikā’ti pesenti, yānavāhanamaṇisuvaṇṇarajatādibhedaṃ taṃ taṃ paṇṇākāraṃ ‘etassa anucchavika’nti pesenti[P 0.0452].

Moreover, a person may have many wholesome deeds. For one who abides in adverse application, they might not ripen. But that person, established in right application through a single wholesome deed, fulfills the three kinds of good conduct and observes the five precepts and the ten precepts. For one who has arisen in a time of fortune, kings send royal maidens adorned with all ornaments, thinking, 'She is fit for him.' They send various tributes such as vehicles, jewels, gold, and silver, thinking, 'This is fit for him.'

Pabbajjūpagatopi mahāyaso hoti mahānubhāvo. Tatridaṃ vatthu – kūṭakaṇṇarājā kira girigāmakaṇṇavāsikaṃ cūḷasudhammattheraṃ mamāyati. So uppalavāpiyaṃ vasamāno theraṃ pakkosāpesi. Thero āgantvā mālārāmavihāre vasati. Rājā therassa mātaraṃ pucchi – “kiṃ thero piyāyatī”ti? “Kandaṃ mahārājā”ti. Rājā kandaṃ gāhāpetvā vihāraṃ gantvā therassa dadamāno mukhaṃ ulloketuṃ nāsakkhi. So nikkhamitvā ca bahipariveṇe deviṃ pucchi – “kīdiso thero”ti? “Tvaṃ puriso hutvā ulloketuṃ na sakkosi; ahaṃ kathaṃ sakkhissāmi? Nāhaṃ jānāmi kīdiso”ti. Rājā ‘mama raṭṭhe balikāragahapatiputtaṃ ulloketuṃ na visahāmi. Mahantaṃ vata bho buddhasāsanaṃ nāmā’ti apphoṭesi. Tipiṭakacūḷanāgattherampi mamāyati. Tassa aṅguliyaṃ ekā piḷakā uṭṭhahi. Rājā ‘theraṃ passissāmī’ti vihāraṃ gantvā balavapemena aṅguliṃ mukhena gaṇhi. Antomukheyeva piḷakā bhinnā, pubbalohitaṃ anuṭṭhubhitvā there sinehena amataṃ viya ajjhohari. Soyeva thero aparabhāge maraṇamañce nipajji. Rājā gantvā asucikapallakaṃ sīse ṭhapetvā ‘dhammasakaṭassa akkho bhijjati akkho bhijjatī’ti paridevamāno vicari. Pathavissarassa asucikapallakaṃ sīsena ukkhipitvā vicaraṇaṃ nāma kassa gatamaggo? Sammāpayogassa gatamaggoti. Evaṃ payogavipattipaṭibāhitattā vipākaṃ dātuṃ asakkontāni payogasampattiṃ āgamma vipaccantīti pajānāti. Evaṃ catūhi vipattīhi paṭibāhitaṃ kalyāṇakammaṃ vipākaṃ adatvā catasso sampattiyo āgamma deti.

Even after going forth, one can be of great fame and great power. Here is a story: King Kūṭakaṇṇa, it is said, esteemed the Elder Cūḷasudhamma, a resident of Girigāmakaṇṇa. While residing at Uppalavāpī, he summoned the elder. The elder came and stayed at the Mālārāma Monastery. The king asked the elder’s mother, 'What does the elder like?' 'Tubers, great king,' she replied. The king had tubers procured and went to the monastery to offer them to the elder, but he was unable to look up at the elder’s face. Leaving, he asked the queen in the outer courtyard, 'What is the elder like?' 'You, a man, were unable to look up at him—how could I? I do not know what he is like.' The king exclaimed, 'In my own kingdom, I cannot bear to look at the son of a tax-paying householder. Truly, the Buddha’s dispensation is great!' and he clapped his hands. He also esteemed the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga. A boil arose on one of the elder’s fingers. The king, thinking, 'I will see the elder,' went to the monastery and, with great affection, took the finger in his mouth. Right inside his mouth, the boil burst, and without spitting, he swallowed the pus and blood with affection, as if it were nectar. That very elder later lay on his deathbed. The king went and placed a vessel of filth on his head, lamenting as he wandered about, 'The axle of the Dhamma cart is breaking, the axle is breaking!' For a lord of the earth to wander about carrying a vessel of filth on his head—whose path is that? It is the path of right application. Thus, one understands that deeds, unable to give their result because they are obstructed by a failure of application, ripen upon encountering a success of application. In this way, a wholesome deed, obstructed by four kinds of failure, does not give its result; but upon encountering four kinds of success, it does give its result.

Tatridaṃ bhūtamatthaṃ katvā opammaṃ – eko kira mahārājā ekassa amaccassa appamattena kujjhitvā taṃ bandhanāgāre bandhāpesi. Tassa ñātakā rañño [M 0.0434] kuddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā kiñci avatvā caṇḍakope vigate rājānaṃ tassa niraparādhabhāvaṃ jānāpesuṃ. Rājā muñcitvā tassa ṭhānantaraṃ paṭipākatikaṃ akāsi. Athassa tato tato āgacchantānaṃ paṇṇākārānaṃ pamāṇaṃ nāhosi. Manussā sampaṭicchituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Tattha [P 0.0453] rañño appamattakena kujjhitvā tassa bandhanāgāre [V 0.0427] bandhāpitakālo viya puthujjanassa niraye nibbattakālo. Athassa ñātakehi rājānaṃ saññāpetvā ṭhānantarassa paṭipākatikakaraṇakālo viya tassa sagge nibbattakālo. Paṇṇākāraṃ sampaṭicchituṃ asamatthakālo viya catasso sampattiyo āgamma kalyāṇakammānaṃ devalokato manussalokaṃ, manussalokato devalokanti evaṃ sukhaṭṭhānato sukhaṭṭhānameva netvā kappasatasahassampi sukhavipākaṃ datvā nibbānasampāpanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Here is a simile concerning a true event: Once, a great king, angered by a certain minister's slight fault, had him imprisoned. His relatives, knowing the king's anger, said nothing, and after his violent rage had subsided, they informed the king of his innocence. The king, releasing him, restored him to his former rank. Then, gifts coming to him from here and there were beyond measure, so that people were unable to receive them all. Here, the time when the king, angered by a slight fault, had him imprisoned is like the time when an ordinary person is reborn in hell. The time when his relatives informed the king and had him restored to his former rank is like the time when that person is reborn in heaven. The time of being unable to receive the gifts should be understood as being like when the four kinds of success, having come to one's wholesome deeds, lead one from the world of the gods to the world of humans, and from the world of humans to the world of the gods, thus from one happy state to another, giving a happy result for even a hundred thousand eons, until the attainment of Nibbāna.

Evaṃ tāva pāḷivaseneva dutiyaṃ balaṃ dīpetvā puna “ahosi kammaṃ ahosi kammavipāko”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.234) iminā paṭisambhidānayenāpi dīpetabbaṃ. Tattha ‘ahosi kamma’nti atīte āyūhitaṃ kammaṃ atīteyeva ahosi. Yena pana atīte vipāko dinno, taṃ sandhāya ‘ahosi kammavipāko’ti vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādīsu pana bahūsupi āyūhitesu ekaṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ vipākaṃ deti, sesāni avipākāni. Ekaṃ upapajjavedanīyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhati, sesāni avipākāni. Ekenānantariyena niraye upapajjati, sesāni avipākāni. Aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu ekāya brahmaloke nibbattati, sesā avipākā. Idaṃ sandhāya ‘nāhosi kammavipāko’ti vuttaṃ. Yo pana bahumpi kusalākusalaṃ kammaṃ katvā kalyāṇamittaṃ nissāya arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, etassa kammavipāko ‘nāhosi’ nāma. Yaṃ atīte āyūhitaṃ etarahi vipākaṃ deti taṃ ‘ahosi kammaṃ atthi kammavipāko’ nāma. Yaṃ purimanayeneva avipākataṃ āpajjati taṃ ‘ahosi kammaṃ natthi kammavipāko’ nāma. Yaṃ atīte āyūhitaṃ anāgate vipākaṃ dassati taṃ ‘ahosi kammaṃ bhavissati kammavipāko’ nāma. Yaṃ purimanayena avipākataṃ āpajjissati taṃ ‘ahosi kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipāko’ nāma.

Thus far, the second power has been expounded by way of the Pāḷi text itself. Now, it should also be expounded by way of the analytical knowledge, with the phrase, 'There was kamma, there was kamma-result' (Paṭis. I 234). Here, 'There was kamma' means that kamma accumulated in the past existed in the past itself. As for 'there was kamma-result,' this is said with reference to that which gave result in the past. However, among the many kammas accumulated, such as those to be experienced in this very life, only one gives a result in this very life, while the rest are without result. One kamma to be experienced in the next life draws forth rebirth-linking, while the rest are without result. By one kamma with immediate result, one is reborn in hell, while the rest are without result. Among the eight attainments, by one of them one is reborn in the Brahma world, while the rest are without result. It is with reference to this that it is said, 'There was no kamma-result.' But for one who, having performed much wholesome and unwholesome kamma, attains arahantship by relying on a spiritual friend, the kamma-result is said to be 'there was none.' That kamma accumulated in the past which now gives a result is called 'there was kamma, there is kamma-result.' That which, by the former method, becomes without result is called 'there was kamma, there is no kamma-result.' That kamma accumulated in the past which will give a result in the future is called 'there was kamma, there will be kamma-result.' That which, by the former method, will become without result is called 'there was kamma, there will be no kamma-result.'

Yaṃ [M 0.0435] etarahi āyūhitaṃ etarahiyeva vipākaṃ deti taṃ ‘atthi kammaṃ atthi kammavipāko’ nāma. Yaṃ purimanayeneva [P 0.0454] avipākataṃ āpajjati taṃ ‘atthi kammaṃ natthi kammavipāko’ nāma. Yaṃ etarahi āyūhitaṃ anāgate vipākaṃ dassati taṃ ‘atthi kammaṃ bhavissati kammavipāko’ nāma. Yaṃ purimanayeneva avipākataṃ āpajjissati taṃ ‘atthi kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipāko’ nāma.

That kamma accumulated now which gives a result now itself is called 'there is kamma, there is kamma-result.' That which, by the former method, becomes without result is called 'there is kamma, there is no kamma-result.' That kamma accumulated now which will give a result in the future is called 'there is kamma, there will be kamma-result.' That which, by the former method, will become without result is called 'there is kamma, there will be no kamma-result.'

Yaṃ sayampi anāgataṃ, vipākopissa anāgato taṃ ‘bhavissati kammaṃ bhavissati kammavipāko’ [V 0.0428] nāma. Yaṃ sayaṃ bhavissati, purimanayeneva avipākataṃ āpajjissati taṃ ‘bhavissati kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipāko’ nāma.

That kamma which is itself future, and its result is also future, is called 'there will be kamma, there will be kamma-result.' That which will itself be future, and by the former method will become without result, is called 'there will be kamma, there will be no kamma-result.'

Idaṃ tathāgatassāti idaṃ sabbehipi etehi ākārehi tathāgatassa kammantaravipākantarajānanañāṇaṃ akampiyaṭṭhena dutiyabalaṃ veditabbanti.

This is the Tathāgata's. This knowledge of the Tathāgata, the knowledge of the distinctions of kamma and kamma-result in all these aspects, should be understood as the second power by virtue of its unshakeability.

Dutiyabalaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Elucidation of the Exposition of the Second Power.

Tatiyabalaniddeso

The Exposition of the Third Power

811. Tatiyabalaniddese maggoti vā paṭipadāti vā kammassevetaṃ nāmaṃ. Nirayagāminītiādīsu nirassādaṭṭhena niratiatthena ca nirayo. Uddhaṃ anugantvā tiriyaṃ añcitāti tiracchānā; tiracchānāyeva tiracchānayoni. Petatāya petti; ito pecca gatabhāvenāti attho. Pettiyeva pettivisayo. Manassa ussannatāya manussā; manussāva manussaloko. Dibbanti pañcahi kāmaguṇehi adhimattāya vā ṭhānasampattiyāti devā; devāva devaloko. Vānaṃ vuccati taṇhā; taṃ tattha natthīti nibbānaṃ. Nirayaṃ gacchatīti nirayagāmī. Idaṃ maggaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Paṭipadā pana nirayagāminī nāma hoti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Idaṃ sabbampi paṭipadaṃ tathāgato pajānāti.

811. In the exposition of the third power, 'path' or 'practice' is a name for kamma. In the phrases 'leading to hell' and so on, 'hell' (niraya) is so called because it is devoid of enjoyment (nirassāda) and lacking in delight (nirati). Those who go horizontally, bending over, are 'animals' (tiracchānā); the animal realm (tiracchānayoni) is simply the animal womb. Petatā means 'ghost-state'; the meaning is, 'because of having gone from here after death.' The ghost realm (pettivisayo) is simply the ghost sphere. Humans (manussā) are so called because of the elevation of their minds; the human world (manussaloko) is simply the human state. Gods (devā) are so called because they delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure or because of the exceeding attainment of their station; the divine world (devaloko) is simply the god state. 'Vāna' is said to be craving; where that is not, that is Nibbāna. One who goes to hell is a hell-goer (nirayagāmī). This is said with reference to the path. But a practice is called 'hell-bound' (nirayagāminī). The same method applies to the remaining terms. The Tathāgata fully understands all this practice.

Kathaṃ[M 0.0436]? Sakalagāmavāsikesupi hi ekato ekaṃ sūkaraṃ vā migaṃ vā jīvitā voropentesu sabbesampi cetanā parassa jīvitindriyārammaṇāva hoti. Taṃ pana kammaṃ tesaṃ āyūhanakkhaṇeyeva nānā hoti. Tesu hi eko ādarena chandajāto karoti. Eko ‘ehi tvampi karohī’ti parehi nippīḷitattā karoti. Eko samānacchando viya hutvā appaṭibāhiyamāno vicarati. Tesu eko teneva kammena niraye nibbattati, eko tiracchānayoniyaṃ, eko pettivisaye. Taṃ tathāgato āyūhanakkhaṇeyeva ‘iminā nīhārena āyūhitattā esa niraye nibbattissati[P 0.0455], esa tiracchānayoniyaṃ, esa pettivisaye’ti pajānāti[V 0.0429]. Niraye nibbattamānampi ‘esa aṭṭhasu mahānirayesu nibbattissati, esa soḷasasu ussadanirayesu nibbattissatī’ti pajānāti. Tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattamānampi ‘esa apādako bhavissati, esa dvipādako, esa catuppādako, esa bahuppādako’ti pajānāti. Pettivisaye nibbattamānampi ‘esa nijjhāmataṇhiko bhavissati, esa khuppipāsiko, esa paradattūpajīvī’ti pajānāti. Tesu ca kammesu ‘idaṃ kammaṃ paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhituṃ na sakkhissati, dubbalaṃ dinnāya paṭisandhiyā upadhivepakkaṃ bhavissatīti pajānāti.

How? When all the villagers together deprive one pig or deer of life, the intention of all is indeed focused on the life faculty of another. However, that kamma becomes diverse for them at the very moment of its accumulation. Among them, one does it with eagerness, born of desire. Another does it because they are pressured by others, saying, 'Come, you too, do it.' Another wanders about as if sharing the same intention, not resisting. Of these, one is reborn in hell because of that very kamma, another in the animal realm, and another in the ghost realm. The Tathāgata knows at the very moment of the kamma's accumulation: 'Due to having accumulated kamma in this manner, this one will be reborn in hell, this one in the animal realm, this one in the ghost realm.' Even for one being reborn in hell, he knows: 'This one will be reborn in the eight great hells, this one in the sixteen subsidiary hells.' For one being reborn in the animal realm, he knows: 'This one will be legless, this one two-legged, this one four-legged, this one many-legged.' For one being reborn in the ghost realm, he knows: 'This one will be consumed by thirst, this one tormented by hunger and thirst, this one living on what is given by others.' And regarding these kammas, he knows: 'This kamma will not be able to draw forth rebirth-linking; being weak, it will ripen as a supportive kamma for the rebirth-linking that has been given.'

Tathā sakalagāmavāsikesu ekato piṇḍapātaṃ dadamānesu sabbesampi cetanā piṇḍapātārammaṇāva hoti. Taṃ pana kammaṃ tesaṃ āyūhanakkhaṇeyeva purimanayena nānā hoti. Tesu keci devaloke nibbattissanti, keci manussaloke. Taṃ tathāgato āyūhanakkhaṇeyeva ‘iminā nīhārena āyūhitattā esa manussaloke nibbattissati, esa devaloke’ti pajānāti. Devaloke nibbattamānānampi ‘esa paranimmitavasavattīsu nibbattissati, esa nimmānaratīsu, esa tusitesu, esa yāmesu, esa tāvatiṃsesu, esa cātumahārājikesu, esa bhummadevesu; esa pana jeṭṭhakadevarājā hutvā nibbattissati, esa etassa dutiyaṃ vā tatiyaṃ vā ṭhānantaraṃ karonto paricārako hutvā nibbattissatī’ti pajānāti. Manussesu nibbattamānānampi ‘esa khattiyakule nibbattissati, esa brāhmaṇakule, esa vessakule, esa suddakule; esa pana manussesu rājā hutvā nibbattissati, esa etassa dutiyaṃ vā tatiyaṃ vā ṭhānantaraṃ karonto paricārako hutvā nibbattissatī’ti pajānāti[M 0.0437]. Tesu ca kammesu ‘idaṃ kammaṃ paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhituṃ na sakkhissati, dubbalaṃ dinnāya paṭisandhiyā upadhivepakkaṃ bhavissatī’ti pajānāti.

Similarly, when all the villagers together offer almsfood, the intention of all is indeed focused on the almsfood as its object. Yet that kamma becomes diverse for them at the very moment of its accumulation, by the former method. Among them, some will be reborn in the deva world, some in the human world. The Tathāgata knows at the very moment of the kamma's accumulation: 'Due to having accumulated kamma in this manner, this one will be reborn in the human world, this one in the deva world.' Among those reborn in the deva world, he knows: 'This one will be reborn among the Paranimmitavasavattī devas, this one among the Nimmānaratī devas, this one among the Tusita devas, this one among the Yāma devas, this one among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, this one among the Cātumahārājika devas, this one among the Bhummadevas; and this one will be reborn as the chief deva-king, while this one will be reborn as his attendant, occupying the second or third position.' Among those reborn among humans, he knows: 'This one will be reborn in a khattiya family, this one in a brāhmaṇa family, this one in a vessa family, this one in a sudda family; and this one will be reborn as a king among humans, while this one will be reborn as his attendant, occupying the second or third position.' Regarding these kammas, he knows: 'This kamma will not be able to draw forth rebirth-linking; being weak, it will ripen as a supportive kamma for the rebirth-linking that has been given.'

Tathā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapentesuyeva yena nīhārena vipassanā āraddhā, ‘esa arahattaṃ pāpuṇissati, esa arahattaṃ pattuṃ na sakkhissati, esa anāgāmīyeva bhavissati, esa sakadāgāmīyeva, esa sotāpannoyeva; esa pana maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā sacchikātuṃ na sakkhissati, lakkhaṇārammaṇāya vipassanāyameva ṭhassati; esa paccayapariggaheyeva, esa [P 0.0456] nāmarūpapariggaheyeva, esa arūpapariggaheyeva, esa rūpapariggaheyeva ṭhassati, esa mahābhūtamattameva vavatthāpessati, esa kiñci sallakkhetuṃ na sakkhissatī’ti pajānāti.

Similarly, among those who establish insight, he knows by what means the insight was undertaken: 'This one will attain arahantship; this one will not be able to attain arahantship; this one will only become a non-returner; this one will only become a once-returner; this one will only become a stream-enterer; but this one will not be able to realize the path or the fruit; his insight will remain merely with the characteristics as its object; this one will remain only with the discernment of conditions; this one will remain only with the discernment of name-and-form; this one will remain only with the discernment of the formless; this one will remain only with the discernment of form; this one will only discern the mere great elements; this one will not be able to notice anything.'

Kasiṇaparikammaṃ karontesupi ‘etassa parikammamattameva bhavissati, nimittaṃ uppādetuṃ [V 0.0430] na sakkhissati; esa pana nimittaṃ uppādetuṃ sakkhissati, appanaṃ pāpetuṃ na sakkhissati; esa appanaṃ pāpetvā jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhissatī’ti pajānātīti.

Even among those doing the preliminary work on a kasiṇa, he knows: 'For this person it will only be preliminary work; he will not be able to produce the sign. But this person will be able to produce the sign, yet will not be able to attain absorption. This person, having attained absorption and made the jhāna a basis, will establish insight and attain arahantship.'

Tatiyabalaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Elucidation of the Exposition of the Third Power.

Catutthabalaniddeso

The Exposition of the Fourth Power

812. Catutthabalaniddese khandhanānattanti ‘ayaṃ rūpakkhandho nāma…pe… ayaṃ viññāṇakkhandho nāmā’ti evaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ pajānāti. Tesupi ‘ekavidhena rūpakkhandho…pe… ekādasavidhena rūpakkhandho. Ekavidhena vedanākkhandho…pe… bahuvidhena vedanākkhandho…pe… ekavidhena saññākkhandho…pe… ekavidhena saṅkhārakkhandho…pe… ekavidhena viññāṇakkhandho…pe… bahuvidhena viññāṇakkhandho’ti evaṃ ekekassa khandhassa nānattaṃ pajānāti. Āyatananānattanti ‘idaṃ cakkhāyatanaṃ nāma…pe… idaṃ dhammāyatanaṃ nāma. Tattha dasāyatanā kāmāvacarā, dve catubhūmakā’ti evaṃ āyatananānattaṃ pajānāti. Dhātunānattanti ‘ayaṃ cakkhudhātu nāma…pe… ayaṃ manoviññāṇadhātu nāma. Tattha soḷasa dhātuyo kāmāvacarā, dve catubhūmakā’ti evaṃ dhātunānattaṃ pajānāti.

812. In the exposition of the fourth strength, 'diversity of aggregates' means one understands the differentiation of the five aggregates thus: 'This is called the form aggregate … this is called the consciousness aggregate.' And in regard to these, one understands the diversity of each aggregate thus: 'The form aggregate in one way … the form aggregate in eleven ways. The feeling aggregate in one way … the feeling aggregate in many ways … the perception aggregate in one way … the formations aggregate in one way … the consciousness aggregate in one way … the consciousness aggregate in many ways.' 'Diversity of sense bases' means one understands the diversity of the sense bases thus: 'This is called the eye base … this is called the mind-object base. Herein, ten bases are of the sense sphere, two are of the four planes.' 'Diversity of elements' means one understands the diversity of the elements thus: 'This is called the eye element … this is called the mind-consciousness element. Herein, sixteen elements are of the sense sphere, two are of the four planes.'

Puna [M 0.0438] anekadhātunānādhātulokanānattanti idaṃ na kevalaṃ upādinnakasaṅkhāralokasseva nānattaṃ tathāgato pajānāti, anupādinnakasaṅkhāralokassāpi nānattaṃ tathāgato pajānātiyevāti dassetuṃ gahitaṃ. Paccekabuddhā hi dve ca aggasāvakā upādinnakasaṅkhāralokassāpi nānattaṃ ekadesatova jānanti no nippadesato, anupādinnakalokassa pana nānattaṃ na jānanti. Sabbaññubuddho pana ‘imāya nāma dhātuyā ussannāya imassa nāma rukkhassa khandho seto hoti, imassa kāḷako, imassa maṭṭo; imassa bahalattaco, imassa tanuttaco; imāya nāma dhātuyā ussannāya imassa rukkhassa pattaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivasena evarūpaṃ nāma hoti; imāya pana dhātuyā [P 0.0457] ussannāya imassa rukkhassa pupphaṃ nīlakaṃ hoti, pītakaṃ, lohitakaṃ, odātaṃ, sugandhaṃ[V 0.0431], duggandhaṃ hoti; imāya nāma dhātuyā ussannāya phalaṃ khuddakaṃ hoti, mahantaṃ, dīghaṃ, rassaṃ, vaṭṭaṃ, susaṇṭhānaṃ, dussaṇṭhānaṃ, maṭṭhaṃ, pharusaṃ, sugandhaṃ, duggandhaṃ, madhuraṃ, tittakaṃ, ambilaṃ, kaṭukaṃ, kasāvaṃ hoti; imāya nāma dhātuyā ussannāya imassa rukkhassa kaṇṭako tikhiṇo hoti, atikhiṇo, ujuko, kuṭilo, tambo, kāḷako, nīlo, odāto hotī’ti evaṃ anupādinnakasaṅkhāralokassa nānattaṃ pajānāti. Sabbaññubuddhānaṃyeva hi etaṃ balaṃ, na aññesanti.

Again, the phrase 'the diversity of the world with its manifold and diverse elements' is taken to show that the Tathāgata understands the diversity not only of the appropriated conditioned world, but also of the unappropriated conditioned world. For Paccekabuddhas and the two chief disciples understand the diversity of the appropriated conditioned world only partially, not exhaustively, and they do not understand the diversity of the unappropriated world. But the Omniscient Buddha understands the diversity of the unappropriated conditioned world as follows: 'When such and such an element is predominant, the trunk of such and such a tree is white, of another it is black, of another it is smooth; of one the bark is thick, of another it is thin. When such and such an element is predominant, the leaf of such and such a tree has such and such a form by way of color, shape, and so on. When such and such an element is predominant, the flower of such and such a tree is blue, yellow, red, white, fragrant, or foul-smelling. When such and such an element is predominant, the fruit is small, large, long, short, round, well-formed, ill-formed, smooth, rough, fragrant, foul-smelling, sweet, bitter, sour, pungent, or astringent. When such and such an element is predominant, the thorn of such and such a tree is sharp, very sharp, straight, crooked, copper-colored, black, blue, or white.' Indeed, this is the strength only of the Omniscient Buddhas, and not of others.

Catutthabalaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Fourth Strength.

Pañcamabalaniddeso

The Exposition of the Fifth Strength

813. Pañcamabalaniddese hīnādhimuttikāti hīnajjhāsayā. Paṇītādhimuttikāti kalyāṇajjhāsayā. Sevantīti nissayanti allīyanti. Bhajantīti upasaṅkamanti. Payirupāsantīti punappunaṃ upasaṅkamanti. Sace hi ācariyupajjhāyā na sīlavanto honti, saddhivihārikā sīlavanto honti, te attano ācariyupajjhāyepi na upasaṅkamanti, attanā sadise sāruppabhikkhūyeva upasaṅkamanti. Sace ācariyupajjhāyā sāruppabhikkhū, itare asāruppā, tepi na ācariyupajjhāye upasaṅkamanti, attanā sadise hīnādhimuttike eva upasaṅkamanti.

813. In the exposition of the fifth strength, 'those of inferior inclination' means those with base intention. 'Those of superior inclination' means those with wholesome intention. 'They associate' means they depend on or cling to. 'They frequent' means they approach. 'They attend upon' means they repeatedly approach. For if the teachers and preceptors are not virtuous, but the co-residents are virtuous, they do not approach even their own teachers and preceptors, but only approach monks suitable to themselves. If the teachers and preceptors are suitable monks, but the others are unsuitable, they too do not approach their teachers and preceptors, but only approach those of inferior inclination similar to themselves.

Evaṃ [M 0.0439] upasaṅkamanaṃ pana na kevalaṃ etaraheva, atītānāgatepīti dassetuṃ atītampi addhānantiādimāha. Taṃ uttānatthameva. Idaṃ pana dussīlānaṃ dussīlasevanameva, sīlavantānaṃ sīlavantasevanameva, duppaññānaṃ duppaññasevanameva, paññavantānaṃ paññavantasevanameva ko niyāmetīti? Ajjhāsayadhātu niyāmeti. Sambahulā kira bhikkhū ekaṃ gāmaṃ gaṇabhikkhācāraṃ caranti. Manussā bahubhattaṃ āharitvā pattāni pūretvā “tumhākaṃ yathāsabhāgena paribhuññathā”ti datvā uyyojesuṃ. Bhikkhūpi āhaṃsu “āvuso, manussā dhātusaṃyuttakamme payojentī”ti. Tipiṭakacūḷābhayattheropi nāgadīpe cetiyaṃ vandanāya pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ gacchanto ekasmiṃ gāme manussehi nimantito. Therena ca saddhiṃ eko asāruppabhikkhu atthi. Dhuravihārepi [V 0.0432] eko asāruppabhikkhu atthi. Dvīsu bhikkhusaṅghesu gāmaṃ [P 0.0458] osarantesu te ubhopi janā, kiñcāpi āgantukena nevāsiko nevāsikena vā āgantuko na diṭṭhapubbo, evaṃ santepi, ekato hutvā hasitvā hasitvā kathayamānā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Thero disvā “sammāsambuddhena jānitvā dhātusaṃyuttaṃ kathita”nti āha.

Approaching in this manner, however, is not only for the present; to show that it applies to the past and future as well, the text states 'past time' and so forth. Its meaning is evident. Now, what determines that the immoral associate with the immoral, the virtuous with the virtuous, the unwise with the unwise, and the wise with the wise? The element of inclination determines it. It is said that once, many monks went to a village for a group alms round. The people brought much food, filled their bowls, and having given it, sent them off, saying, 'Partake according to your respective shares.' The monks remarked, 'Friends, these people are acting in accordance with the connection of elements.' The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya, while traveling to Nāgadīpa with five hundred monks to pay homage to a shrine, was invited by the people in a certain village. With the Elder was one unsuitable monk. In Dhuravihāra, there was also one unsuitable monk. When the two groups of monks were entering the village, these two individuals—although the visitor had never seen the resident, nor the resident the visitor—even so, came together, and laughing and chatting, stood to one side. Seeing this, the Elder said, 'The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One spoke of this connection by elements, knowing it well.'

Evaṃ ‘ajjhāsayadhātu niyāmetī’ti vatvā dhātusaṃyuttena ayamevattho dīpetabbo. Gijjhakūṭapabbatasmiñhi gilānaseyyāya nipanno bhagavā ārakkhaṇatthāya parivāretvā vasantesu sāriputtamoggallānādīsu ekamekaṃ attano attano parisāya saddhiṃ caṅkamantaṃ oloketvā bhikkhū āmantesi “passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, sāriputtaṃ sambahulehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ caṅkamanta”nti? “Evaṃ, bhante”ti. “Sabbe kho ete, bhikkhave, bhikkhū mahāpaññā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.99) sabbaṃ vitthāretabbanti.

Having stated, 'Thus, the element of inclination determines,' this very meaning should be elucidated by means of the Connected Discourses on Elements. For while the Blessed One was lying on a sickbed at Vulture's Peak, with Sāriputta, Moggallāna, and others surrounding him and dwelling there for his protection, he observed each one walking back and forth with his own retinue. He then addressed the monks: 'Do you see, monks, Sāriputta walking back and forth with many monks?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'All these monks, monks, are of great wisdom' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.99). The entire passage should be elaborated.

Pañcamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Fifth Strength.

Chaṭṭhabalaniddeso

The Exposition of the Sixth Strength

814. Chaṭṭhabalaniddese āsayanti yattha sattā āsayanti nivasanti, taṃ tesaṃ nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ vā yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ vā. Anusayanti appahīnānusayitaṃ [M 0.0440] kilesaṃ. Caritanti kāyādīhi abhisaṅkhataṃ kusalākusalaṃ. Adhimuttanti ajjhāsayaṃ. Apparajakkhetiādīsu paññāmaye akkhimhi appaṃ parittaṃ rāgadosamoharajaṃ etesanti apparajakkhā. Tasseva mahantatāya mahārajakkhā. Ubhayenāpi mandakilese mahākilese ca satte dasseti. Yesaṃ saddhādīni indriyāni tikkhāni, te tikkhindriyā. Yesaṃ tāni mudūni, te mudindriyā. Yesaṃ āsayādayo koṭṭhāsā sundarā, te svākārā. Viparītā dvākārā. Ye kathitakāraṇaṃ sallakkhenti, sukhena sakkā honti viññāpetuṃ, te suviññāpayā. Viparītā duviññāpayā. Ye ariyamaggapaṭivedhassa anucchavikā upanissayasampannā, te bhabbā. Viparītā abhabbā.

814. In the exposition of the sixth power, "reside" (āsayanti) means where beings dwell and abide; that is their place of dwelling, be it a view or knowledge as it really is. "Latent tendencies" (anusayanti) refers to unabandoned underlying defilement. "Conduct" (caritanti) means wholesome or unwholesome volitional formations effected by body, etc. "Inclination" (adhimuttanti) means one's underlying disposition. In the case of "those with little dust in their eyes" (apparajakkhā), etc., in the eye of wisdom, "little dust" means they have little or limited dust of lust, hatred, and delusion. Due to the greatness of that, they are called "those with much dust" (mahārajakkhā). Both terms show beings with minor and major defilements. Those whose faculties—faith and so on—are sharp are called "sharp-facultied" (tikkhindriyā). Those whose faculties are dull are called "dull-facultied" (mudindriyā). Those whose aspects—such as their tendencies—are beautiful are called "well-formed" (svākārā). The opposite are "ill-formed" (dvākārā). Those who discern the stated reason and can easily be instructed are called "easy to instruct" (suviññāpayā). The opposite are "difficult to instruct" (duviññāpayā). Those who are fit and endowed with the supporting conditions for realizing the noble path are called "capable" (bhabbā). The opposite are "incapable" (abhabbā).

815. Evaṃ [V 0.0433] chaṭṭhabalassa mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā idāni yathāpaṭipāṭiyā bhājento katamo ca sattānaṃ āsayotiādimāha. Tattha [P 0.0459] sassato lokotiādīnaṃ attho heṭṭhā nikkhepakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1105) vuttoyeva. Iti bhavadiṭṭhisannissitā vāti evaṃ sassatadiṭṭhiṃ vā sannissitā. Sassatadiṭṭhi hi ettha bhavadiṭṭhīti vuttā; ucchedadiṭṭhi ca vibhavadiṭṭhīti. Sabbadiṭṭhīnañhi sassatucchedadiṭṭhī hi saṅgahitattā sabbepi diṭṭhigatikā sattā imāva dve diṭṭhiyo sannissitā honti. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “dvayasannissito kho panāyaṃ, kaccāna, loko yebhuyyena – atthitañceva natthitañcā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.15). Ettha hi atthitāti sassataṃ, natthitāti ucchedo. Ayaṃ tāva vaṭṭasannissitānaṃ puthujjanasattānaṃ āsayo.

815. Having thus established the framework for the sixth power, now, analyzing in due order, he says, beginning with: "And what is the abode of beings?" Herein, the meaning of "the world is eternal," and so on, has indeed been stated below in the commentary on the section on enumeration in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī commentary (DhsA. 1105). Thus, "or those dependent on views of existence" means those who rely on eternalist views. Here, eternalist view is called "view of existence," and annihilationist view is called "view of non-existence." For since all views are included under eternalism and annihilationism, all beings who hold views rely on these two views. This has also been stated: "This world, Kaccāna, for the most part depends on a duality—on existence and on non-existence" (SN 12.15). Here, "existence" is eternalism, and "non-existence" is annihilationism. This, then, is the abode of ordinary beings who are dependent on the round of existence.

Idāni vivaṭṭasannissitānaṃ suddhasattānaṃ āsayaṃ dassetuṃ ete vā pana ubho ante anupagammātiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ete vā panāti eteyeva. Ubho anteti sassatucchedasaṅkhāte dve ante. Anupagammāti anallīyitvā. Idappaccayatā paṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesūti idappaccayatāya ceva paṭiccasamuppannadhammesu ca. Anulomikā khantīti vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Yathābhūtaṃ vā ñāṇanti maggañāṇaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yā paṭiccasamuppāde ceva paṭiccasamuppannadhammesu ca ete ubho sassatucchedaante anupagantvā vipassanā paṭiladdhā, yañca tato uttarimaggañāṇaṃ – ayaṃ sattānaṃ āsayo, ayaṃ vaṭṭasannissitānañca vivaṭṭasannissitānañca sabbesampi sattānaṃ āsayo, idaṃ vasanaṭṭhānanti. Ayaṃ ācariyānaṃ samānatthakathā.

Now, to show the abode of pure beings who are dependent on liberation, it is said, "Or these, not approaching the two extremes," and so on. Herein, "or these" means just these. "The two extremes" refers to the two extremes known as eternalism and annihilationism. "Not approaching" means not clinging. "In conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena" means in both conditionality and in dependently arisen phenomena. "Conformity tolerance" is insight knowledge. "Or knowledge as it really is" is path knowledge. This is what is said: The insight that is attained regarding both dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena without approaching these two extremes of eternalism and annihilationism, and the subsequent path knowledge—this is the abode of beings. This is the abode of all beings, whether they are dependent on the round of existence or on liberation; this is their dwelling place. This is the teachers' common explanation of the meaning.

Vitaṇḍavādī [M 0.0441] panāha – ‘maggo nāma vāsaṃ viddhaṃsento gacchati, nanu tvaṃ maggo vāsoti vadesī’ti? So vattabbo ‘tvaṃ ariyavāsabhāṇako hosi na hosī’ti? Sace pana ‘na homī’ti vadati, ‘abhāṇakatāya na jānāsī’ti vattabbo. Sace ‘bhāṇakosmī’ti vadati, ‘suttaṃ āharā’ti vattabbo. Sace āharati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ; no ce āharati sayaṃ āharitabbaṃ – “dasayime, bhikkhave, ariyavāsā, ye ariyā āvasiṃsu vā āvasanti vā āvasissanti vā”ti (a. ni. 10.19). Etañhi suttaṃ maggassa vāsabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Tasmā [P 0.0460] sukathitamevetanti. Idaṃ pana bhagavā sattānaṃ āsayaṃ jānanto imesañca diṭṭhigatānaṃ vipassanāñāṇamaggañāṇānaṃ appavattikkhaṇepi jānāti eva. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

A sophist, however, says, 'The path, by its nature, proceeds by destroying a dwelling. Do you not say that the path is a dwelling?' He should be told, 'Are you a reciter of the Noble Dwellings or not?' If he says, 'I am not,' he should be told, 'You do not know because you are not a reciter.' If he says, 'I am a reciter,' he should be told, 'Bring forth the sutta.' If he brings it forth, that is good; if he does not, it should be brought forth by oneself: 'These, bhikkhus, are the ten noble dwellings in which the noble ones have dwelt, dwell, or will dwell' (AN 10.20). This sutta indeed reveals the nature of the path as a dwelling. Therefore, it is indeed well-spoken. Moreover, the Blessed One, knowing the abodes of beings, knows even at the moment of non-arising of insight-knowledge and path-knowledge in these holders of views. And this has been said:

“Kāmaṃ [V 0.0434] sevantaññeva jānāti ‘ayaṃ puggalo kāmagaruko kāmāsayo kāmādhimutto’ti. Nekkhammaṃ sevantaññeva jānāti ‘ayaṃ puggalo nekkhammagaruko nekkhammāsayo nekkhammādhimutto’ti. Byāpādaṃ…pe… abyāpādaṃ… thinamiddhaṃ…pe… ālokasaññaṃ nekkhammaṃ sevantaññeva jānāti sevantaññeva jānāti ‘ayaṃ puggalo ālokasaññāgaruko ālokasaññāsayo ālokasaññādhimutto”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.113).

"One knows a person who pursues sensual pleasures: 'This person is devoted to sensual pleasures, resorts to sensual pleasures, and is intent on sensual pleasures.' One knows a person who pursues renunciation: 'This person is devoted to renunciation, resorts to renunciation, and is intent on renunciation.' One knows a person who pursues ill will... One knows a person who pursues non-ill will... One knows a person who pursues sloth and torpor... One knows a person who pursues the perception of light: 'This person is devoted to the perception of light, resorts to the perception of light, and is intent on the perception of light.'" (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.113)

816. Anusayaniddese kāmarāgo ca so appahīnaṭṭhena anusayo cāti kāmarāgānusayo. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Yaṃ loke piyarūpanti yaṃ imasmiṃ loke piyajātikaṃ. Sātarūpanti sātajātikaṃ assādapadaṭṭhānaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ. Ettha sattānaṃ rāgānusayo anusetīti etasmiṃ iṭṭhārammaṇe sattānaṃ appahīnaṭṭhena rāgānusayo anuseti. Yathā nāma udake nimuggassa heṭṭhā ca upari ca samantabhāge ca udakameva hoti, evameva iṭṭhārammaṇe rāguppatti nāma sattānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇā. Tathā aniṭṭhārammaṇe paṭighuppatti. Iti imesu dvīsu dhammesūti evaṃ imesu dvīsu kāmarāgapaṭighavantesu iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇadhammesu. Avijjānupatitāti kāmarāgapaṭighasampayuttā hutvā ārammaṇakaraṇavasena avijjā anupatitā. Tadekaṭṭhoti tāya avijjāya [M 0.0442] sampayuttekaṭṭhavasena ekaṭṭho. Māno ca diṭṭhi ca vicikicchā cāti navavidho māno, dvāsaṭṭhividhā diṭṭhi, aṭṭhavatthukā ca vicikicchā. Bhavarāgānusayo panettha kāmarāgānusayeneva saṅgahitoti veditabbo.

816. In the exposition of latent tendencies, sensual desire, because it has not been abandoned, is a latent tendency, and thus is the latent tendency of sensual desire. The same method applies to the remaining terms. 'That which is pleasing in the world' means that which is of a pleasing nature in this world. 'Agreeable' means of an agreeable nature, a basis for pleasure, a desirable object. Herein, 'the latent tendency of lust lies dormant for beings' means that in this desirable object, the latent tendency of lust lies dormant for beings because it has not been abandoned. Just as for one submerged in water there is water below, above, and all around, so too for beings is the arising of lust in desirable objects a thing frequently and fully engaged in. Similarly, the arising of aversion occurs in undesirable objects. Thus, 'in these two phenomena' means in these two phenomena possessing sensual desire and aversion, namely, desirable and undesirable objects. 'Ignorance follows along' means that ignorance, being associated with sensual desire and aversion, follows along by way of taking them as its object. 'It has the same substance' means it has the same substance by way of association with that ignorance. Conceit, views, and doubt are nine kinds of conceit, sixty-two kinds of views, and doubt based on eight grounds. The latent tendency of craving for existence should be understood as included herein within the latent tendency of sensual desire.

817. Caritaniddese terasa cetanā puññābhisaṅkhāro, dvādasa apuññābhisaṅkhāro, catasso āneñjābhisaṅkhāro. Tattha kāmāvacaro parittabhūmako, itaro mahābhūmako. Tīsupi [P 0.0461] vā etesu yo koci appavipāko parittabhūmako, bahuvipāko mahābhūmakoti veditabbo.

817. In the exposition of conduct, thirteen volitions are the meritorious volitional formation, twelve are the demeritorious volitional formation, and four are the imperturbable volitional formation. Herein, that of the sense-sphere is of limited scope, while the others are of great scope. Or, among these three, whatever has little result should be understood as of limited scope, and whatever has much result is of great scope.

818. Adhimuttiniddeso heṭṭhā pakāsitova. Kasmā panāyaṃ adhimutti heṭṭhā vuttāpi puna gahitāti? Ayañhi heṭṭhā pāṭiyekkaṃ baladassanavasena gahitā, idha sattānaṃ tikkhindriyamudindriyabhāvadassanatthaṃ.

818. The exposition of inclination has already been explained below. But why is this inclination, though already stated below, taken up again here? For below, it was taken up individually to show its power; here, it is to show the sharp and dull faculties of beings.

819. Mahārajakkhaniddese [V 0.0435] ussadagatānīti vepullagatāni. Pahānakkamavasena cesa uppaṭipāṭiyā niddeso kato.

819. In the exposition of the great defilements, 'grown excessive' means become extensive. And this exposition is made in reverse order, according to the sequence of abandonment.

820. Anussadagatānīti avepullagatāniṃ. Tikkhindriyamudindriyaniddese upanissayaindriyāni nāma kathitāni. Uppaṭipāṭiyā niddese panettha payojanaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

820. 'Not grown excessive' means not become extensive. In the exposition of keen and dull faculties, the supporting faculties are mentioned. The purpose of the exposition in inverted order here should be understood in the manner stated previously.

823. Tathā dvākāraniddesādīsu pāpāsayāti akusalāsayā. Pāpacaritāti apuññābhisaṅkhāraparipūrakā. Pāpādhimuttikāti sakkāyābhiratā vaṭṭajjhāsayā.

823. Similarly, in the exposition of the ill-formed and so on, 'evil intention' refers to unwholesome intention. 'Evil conduct' refers to those who fulfill demeritorious volitional formations. 'Evil resolution' refers to those who delight in their own person and are inclined to the cycle of existence.

824. Svākāraniddese yasmā kalyāṇako nāma anusayo natthi, tasmā kalyāṇānusayāti na vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttavipariyāyena veditabbaṃ.

824. In the exposition of the well-formed, since there is no latent tendency called 'wholesome,' therefore 'wholesome latent tendency' is not stated. The rest should be understood by the opposite of what has been stated.

826. Bhabbābhabbaniddese kammāvaraṇenāti pañcavidhena ānantariyakammena. Kilesāvaraṇenāti niyatamicchādiṭṭhiyā. Vipākāvaraṇenāti ahetukapaṭisandhiyā. Yasmā pana duhetukānampi ariyamaggapaṭivedho natthi, tasmā duhetukapaṭisandhipi vipākāvaraṇamevāti veditabbā. Assaddhāti [M 0.0443] buddhādīsu saddhārahitā. Acchandikāti kattukamyatākusalacchandarahitā. Uttarakurukā manussā acchandikaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhā. Duppaññāti bhavaṅgapaññāya parihīnā. Bhavaṅgapaññāya pana paripuṇṇāyapi yassa bhavaṅgaṃ lokuttarassa pādakaṃ na hoti, so duppaññoyeva nāma. Abhabbā niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattanti kusalesu dhammesu sammattaniyāmasaṅkhātaṃ maggaṃ okkamituṃ abhabbā.

826. In the exposition of the capable and incapable, 'hindered by kamma' refers to the fivefold immediate kamma. 'Hindered by defilements' refers to fixed wrong view. 'Hindered by result' refers to rebirth without root causes. However, since even for those with two root causes there is no penetration of the noble path, rebirth with two root causes should also be understood as hindered by result. 'Lacking faith' means devoid of faith in the Buddha and so on. 'Lacking desire' means devoid of wholesome desire to act. The humans of Uttarakuru are said to have entered a state of lacking desire. 'Lacking wisdom' means deficient in the wisdom of the life-continuum. Even if one is fully endowed with the wisdom of the life-continuum, if their life-continuum does not serve as a foundation for the supramundane, they are still called 'lacking wisdom.' 'Incapable of entering the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states' means incapable of entering the path, which is designated as the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.

827. Na kammāvaraṇenātiādīni vuttavipariyāyena veditabbāni. Idaṃ dvinnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ bhājanīyaṃ – indriyaparopariyattiñāṇassa [P 0.0462] ca āsayānusayañāṇassa ca. Ettha hi āsayānusayañāṇena indriyaparopariyattiñāṇampi bhājitaṃ. Iti imāni dve ñāṇāni ekato hutvā ekaṃ balañāṇaṃ nāma jātanti.

827. 'Not hindered by kamma' and so on should be understood in the opposite way to what was stated. This is the subject matter for two knowledges: the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of others' faculties and the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies. Herein, the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of others' faculties is also analyzed by means of the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies. Thus, these two knowledges, having come together, become what is called a single power-knowledge.

Chaṭṭhabalaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixth Power.

Sattamabalaniddeso

Exposition of the Seventh Power

828. Sattamabalaniddese [V 0.0436] jhāyatīti jhāyī. Cattāro jhāyīti jhāyino cattāro janā vuccanti. Tattha paṭhamacatukke tāva paṭhamo samāpattilābhī samānoyeva ‘na lābhīmhī’ti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ samānaṃyeva ‘na kammaṭṭhāna’nti saññī hoti. Ayaṃ appaguṇajjhānalābhīti veditabbo. Dutiyo samāpattiyā alābhīyeva ‘lābhīmhī’ti, akammaṭṭhānaṃ samānaṃyeva ‘kammaṭṭhāna’nti saññī hoti. Ayaṃ niddājhāyī nāma. Niddāyitvā paṭibuddho evaṃ maññati. Tatiyo samāpattilābhī samāno ‘samāpattilābhīmhī’ti, kammaṭṭhānameva samānaṃ ‘kammaṭṭhāna’nti saññī hoti. Ayaṃ paguṇajjhānalābhīti veditabbo. Catuttho alābhīyeva ‘alābhīmhī’ti, akammaṭṭhānaṃyeva ‘akammaṭṭhāna’nti saññī hoti. Evamettha dve janā ajjhāyinova jhāyīnaṃ anto paviṭṭhattā jhāyīti vuttā.

828. In the exposition of the seventh power, 'one who meditates' (jhāyī) is one who practices jhāna (jhāyati). 'Four meditators' refers to four kinds of persons who are meditators. Among them, in the first set of four: The first, though actually attaining absorption, perceives, 'I do not attain,' and though the meditation subject is present, perceives, 'This is not a meditation subject.' This should be understood as one who attains jhāna with weak qualities. The second, though not attaining absorption, perceives, 'I attain,' and though there is no meditation subject, perceives, 'This is a meditation subject.' This is called a sleepy meditator. Having slept and awakened, he thinks thus. The third, actually attaining absorption, perceives, 'I attain absorption,' and with the meditation subject present, perceives, 'This is a meditation subject.' This should be understood as one who attains jhāna with strong qualities. The fourth, though not attaining, perceives, 'I do not attain,' and with no meditation subject, perceives, 'This is not a meditation subject.' Thus, herein, two persons, though not actually meditators, are called meditators because they have entered into the category of meditators.

Dutiyacatukke sasaṅkhārena sappayogena samādhipāribandhikadhamme vikkhambhento dandhaṃ samāpajjati nāma. Ekaṃ dve cittavāre ṭhatvā sahasā vuṭṭhahantā khippaṃ vuṭṭhahati nāma. Sukheneva pana samādhipāribandhikadhamme sodhento khippaṃ samāpajjati nāma. Yathāparicchedena avuṭṭhahitvā kālaṃ [M 0.0444] atināmetvā vuṭṭhahanto dandhaṃ vuṭṭhāti nāma. Itare dvepi imināva nayena veditabbā. Ime cattāropi janā samāpattilābhinova.

In the second set of four: one who, by suppressing the obstructive factors to concentration with effort and exertion, is said to attain absorption slowly. One who, having stayed for one or two thought-moments, emerges suddenly, is said to emerge quickly. One who, by easily purifying the obstructive factors to concentration, is said to attain absorption quickly. One who, not having emerged according to the predetermined time but emerging after letting time pass, is said to emerge slowly. The other two should also be understood in this same way. These four persons are all attainers of absorption.

Tatiyacatukke ‘idaṃ jhānaṃ pañcaṅgikaṃ, idaṃ caturaṅgika’nti evaṃ aṅgavavatthānaparicchede cheko samādhismiṃ samādhikusalo nāma. Nīvaraṇāni pana vikkhambhetvā cittamañjūsāya cittaṃ ṭhapetuṃ acheko no samādhismiṃ samāpattikusalo nāma. Itarepi tayo imināva nayena veditabbā. Imepi cattāro samāpattilābhinoyeva.

In the third set of four: one who is clever in discerning the constituent factors, thinking, 'This jhāna has five factors, this has four,' is called one skilled in concentration. But one who is unskillful in placing the mind in the mind-receptacle, having suppressed the hindrances, is not called one skilled in attainment. The other three should be understood in this same way. These four are indeed attainers of absorption.

Idāni yāni jhānāni nissāya ime puggalā ‘jhāyī’ nāma jātā, tāni dassetuṃ cattāri jhānānītiādimāha. Tattha cattāri jhānāni [P 0.0463] tayo ca vimokkhā atthato heṭṭhā dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāyameva (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 160, 248) pakāsitā. Sesānampi vimokkhaṭṭho tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Apicettha paṭipāṭiyā satta appitappitakkhaṇe paccanīkadhammehi vimuccanato ca ārammaṇe ca adhimuccanato vimokkho nāma. Aṭṭhamo pana sabbaso saññāvedayitehi [V 0.0437] vimuttattā apagatavimokkho nāma. Samādhīsu catukkanayapañcakanayesu paṭhamajjhānasamādhi savitakkasavicāro nāma. Pañcakanaye dutiyajjhānasamādhi avitakkavicāramattasamādhi nāma. Catukkanayepi pañcakanayepi upari tīsu jhānesu samādhi avitakka avicārasamādhi nāma. Samāpattīsu hi paṭipāṭiyā aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ ‘samādhī’tipi nāmaṃ ‘samāpattī’tipi. Kasmā? Cittekaggatāsabbhāvato. Nirodhasamāpattiyā tadabhāvato na samādhīti nāmaṃ.

Now, to explain the jhānas upon which these individuals rely and are called 'meditators,' he begins with 'the four jhānas.' Herein, the four jhānas and the three liberations have already been explained in meaning below in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī commentary (Dhs. Aṭṭha. 160, 248). The meaning of the remaining liberations should also be understood in the same way as explained there. Moreover, here, in sequence, the seven liberations are so called because of freedom from opposing states at the moment of absorption, and because of being intent upon the object. But the eighth is called the departed liberation because it is entirely free from perception and feeling. Among the concentrations, in the fourfold and fivefold methods, the first jhāna concentration is called 'with initial thought and sustained thought.' In the fivefold method, the second jhāna concentration is called 'concentration with only sustained thought.' In both the fourfold and fivefold methods, the concentration in the upper three jhānas is called 'concentration without initial thought and without sustained thought.' Regarding the attainments, in sequence, the eight attainments are called both 'concentration' and 'attainment.' Why? Because of the presence of one-pointedness of mind. The attainment of cessation is not called 'concentration' because of the absence of that.

Hānabhāgiyo dhammoti appaguṇehi paṭhamajjhānādīhi vuṭṭhitassa saññāmanasikārānaṃ kāmādianupakkhandanaṃ. Visesabhāgiyo dhammoti paguṇehi paṭhamajjhānādīhi vuṭṭhitassa saññāmanasikārānaṃ dutiyajjhānādianupakkhandanaṃ. Vodānampi vuṭṭhānanti iminā paguṇavodānaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ nāma kathitaṃ. Heṭṭhimaṃ heṭṭhimañhi paguṇajjhānaṃ uparimassa uparimassa padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Tasmā vodānampi vuṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ. Tamhā tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhānampi vuṭṭhānanti iminā bhavaṅgavuṭṭhānaṃ nāma kathitaṃ. Bhavaṅgena hi sabbajjhānehi vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Nirodhato pana phalasamāpattiyāva vuṭṭhahanti. Idaṃ pāḷimuttakavuṭṭhānaṃ nāmāti.

The dhammas that partake of decline are the inclining of perception and attention of one who has emerged from the first jhāna, etc., of inferior quality, toward sensual pleasures, etc. The dhammas that partake of distinction are the inclining of perception and attention of one who has emerged from the first jhāna, etc., of superior quality, toward the second jhāna, etc. 'Purification is also emergence': by this, emergence which is a well-mastered purification is spoken of as emergence. For each lower jhāna that is well-mastered is the basis for the higher one. Therefore, it is said, 'Purification is also emergence.' 'Emergence from that very concentration is also emergence': by this, emergence from the life-continuum is spoken of as emergence. For emergence from all the jhānas is through the life-continuum. However, from cessation, they emerge only by means of the attainment of fruition. This is called 'emergence not found in the Pāḷi.'

Sattamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Seventh Power.

Aṭṭhamabalādiniddeso

The Exposition of the Eighth Power and Others

829. Aṭṭhamabalaniddese [M 0.0445] anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsantiādi sabbampi visuddhimagge vitthāritameva. Navamabalaniddesepi [P 0.0464] dibbena cakkhunātiādi sabbaṃ tattheva vitthāritaṃ.

829. In the exposition of the eighth power, everything beginning with 'the manifold recollection of past lives' is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. In the exposition of the ninth power as well, everything beginning with 'with the divine eye' is explained in detail there.

Navamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Ninth Power.

Dasamabalaniddeso

The Exposition of the Tenth Power

831. Dasamabalaniddese [V 0.0438] cetovimuttinti phalasamādhiṃ. Paññāvimuttinti phalañāṇaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthameva. Ayaṃ tāvettha ācariyānaṃ samānatthakathā. Paravādī panāha – “dasabalañāṇaṃ nāma pāṭiyekkaṃ natthi, sabbaññutañāṇassevāyaṃ pabhedo”ti. Taṃ na tathā daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aññameva hi dasabalañāṇaṃ, aññaṃ sabbaññutañāṇaṃ. Dasabalañāṇañhi sakasakakiccameva jānāti. Sabbaññutañāṇaṃ pana tampi tato avasesampi jānāti. Dasabalañāṇesupi hi paṭhamaṃ kāraṇākāraṇameva jānāti, dutiyaṃ kammantaravipākantarameva, tatiyaṃ kammaparicchedameva, catutthaṃ dhātunānattakaraṇameva, pañcamaṃ sattānaṃ ajjhāsayādhimuttimeva, chaṭṭhaṃ indriyānaṃ tikkhamudubhāvameva, sattamaṃ jhānādīhi saddhiṃ tesaṃ saṃkilesādimeva, aṭṭhamaṃ pubbenivutthakhandhasantatimeva, navamaṃ sattānaṃ cutipaṭisandhimeva, dasamaṃ saccaparicchedameva. Sabbaññutañāṇaṃ pana etehi jānitabbañca tato uttaritarañca pajānāti. Etesaṃ pana kiccaṃ na sabbaṃ karoti. Tañhi jhānaṃ hutvā appetuṃ na sakkoti, iddhi hutvā vikubbituṃ na sakkoti, maggo hutvā kilese khepetuṃ na sakkoti.

831. In the Exposition of the Tenth Power, 'liberation of mind' means the concentration of fruition. 'Liberation by wisdom' means the knowledge of fruition. The rest is clear in meaning throughout. This, to begin with, is the teachers’ explanation of the common meaning. But an opponent says: “There is no distinct knowledge called the knowledge of the ten powers; this is merely a division of omniscient knowledge.” That should not be regarded as such. For the knowledge of the ten powers is one thing, and omniscient knowledge is another. The knowledge of the ten powers knows only its own respective functions. But omniscient knowledge knows that as well as what remains beyond it. For among the knowledges of the ten powers: the first knows only what is possible and impossible; the second knows only the various results of various actions; the third knows only the delimitation of karma; the fourth knows only the cause of the diversity of elements; the fifth knows only the dispositions and inclinations of beings; the sixth knows only the keenness or dullness of the faculties; the seventh knows only their defilements, etc., together with the jhānas, etc.; the eighth knows only the continuity of aggregates previously inhabited; the ninth knows only the passing away and rebirth of beings; the tenth knows only the delimitation of the truths. But omniscient knowledge understands what is to be known by these and what is even further than that. But it does not perform all of their functions. For it, having become a jhāna, is not able to enter absorption; having become a psychic power, is not able to perform transformations; having become the path, is not able to destroy the defilements.

Apica paravādī evaṃ pucchitabbo – “dasabalañāṇaṃ nāma etaṃ savitakkasavicāraṃ, avitakkavicāramattaṃ, avitakkāvicāraṃ, kāmāvacaraṃ, rūpāvacaraṃ, arūpāvacaraṃ, lokiyaṃ, lokuttara”nti? Jānanto “paṭipāṭiyā satta ñāṇāni savitakkasavicārānī”ti vakkhati; tato “parāni dve ñāṇāni avitakkāvicārānī”ti vakkhati; “āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ siyā savitakkasavicāraṃ, siyā avitakkavicāramattaṃ, siyā avitakkavicāra”nti vakkhati. Tathā “paṭipāṭiyā [M 0.0446] satta kāmāvacarāni, tato dve rūpāvacarāni, avasāne ekaṃ lokuttara”nti vakkhati; “sabbaññutañāṇaṃ pana savitakkasavicārameva, kāmāvacarameva, lokiyamevā”ti vakkhati. Iti aññadeva dasabalañāṇaṃ, aññaṃ sabbaññutañāṇanti.

Furthermore, the opponent should be asked: “Is this knowledge of the ten powers accompanied by initial and sustained thought; without initial thought but with only sustained thought; without initial thought and without sustained thought; pertaining to the sense sphere; pertaining to the form sphere; pertaining to the formless sphere; mundane; or supramundane?” One who knows would say: “In sequence, seven knowledges are accompanied by initial and sustained thought.” Then they would say: “The next two knowledges are without initial thought and without sustained thought.” They would say: “The knowledge of the destruction of the taints might be accompanied by initial and sustained thought, might be without initial thought but with only sustained thought, or might be without initial thought and without sustained thought.” Similarly, they would say: “In sequence, seven pertain to the sense sphere, then two pertain to the form sphere, and finally one is supramundane.” However, they would say: “The knowledge of omniscience is accompanied only by initial and sustained thought, pertains only to the sense sphere, and is only mundane.” Thus, the knowledge of the ten powers is one thing, and the knowledge of omniscience is another.

Sammohavinodaniyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya

In the Sammohavinodanī, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga,

Ñāṇavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of Knowledge is concluded.

17. Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅgo

17. The Analysis of Minor Matters

1. Ekakamātikādivaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Mātikā of Ones and Others

832. Idāni [P 0.0465][M 0.0447][V 0.0439] tadanantare khuddakavatthuvibhaṅgepi paṭhamaṃ mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā nikkhittapadānukkamena niddeso kato. Tatrāyaṃ nikkhepaparicchedo. Ādito tāva jātimadotiādayo tesattati ekakā nikkhittā, tato kodho ca upanāho cātiādayo aṭṭhārasa dukā, akusalamūlādayo pañcatiṃsa tikā, āsavacatukkādayo cuddasa catukkā, orambhāgiyasaṃyojanādayo pannarasa pañcakā, vivādamūlādayo cuddasa chakkā, anusayādayo satta sattakā, kilesavatthuādayo aṭṭha aṭṭhakā, āghātavatthuādayo nava navakā, kilesavatthuādayo satta dasakā, ajjhattikassa upādāya aṭṭhārasa taṇhāvicaritānītiādayo cha aṭṭhārasakāti sabbānipi etāni aṭṭha kilesasatāni nikkhittānīti veditabbāni. Ayaṃ tāva nikkhepaparicchedo.

832. Now, immediately following that, in the Khuddakavatthu Vibhaṅga, the first matrix is established, and the exposition is done according to the order of the terms laid down. Here is the section on the enumeration. First, from “jātimadoti” and so on, seventy-three single terms are laid down. Then, from “kodho ca upanāho ca” and so on, eighteen pairs. Next, from “akusalamūlādayo” and so on, thirty-five triplets. Then, from “āsavacatukkādayo” and so on, fourteen quadruplets. Following that, from “orambhāgiyasaṃyojanādayo” and so on, fifteen pentads. Then, from “vivādamūlādayo” and so on, fourteen hexads. Next, from “anusayādayo” and so on, seven heptads. After that, from “kilesavatthuādayo” and so on, eight octads. Then, from “āghātavatthuādayo” and so on, nine nonads. Following that, from “kilesavatthuādayo” and so on, seven decads. Finally, from “ajjhattikassa upādāya aṭṭhārasa taṇhāvicaritāni” and so on, six sets of eighteen rovings of craving. All these should be understood as eight hundred defilements laid down. This, then, is the section on the enumeration.

(1.) Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Exposition of Single Items

843-844. Idāni yathānikkhittāya mātikāya tattha katamo jātimadotiādinā nayena āraddhe niddesavāre jātiṃ paṭiccāti jātiṃ nissāya. Ettha ca atthipaṭiccaṃ nāma kathitaṃ, tasmā jātiyā satīti ayamettha attho. Gottaṃ paṭiccātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Madanavasena mado. Majjanākāro majjanā. Majjitabhāvo majjitattaṃ. Māno maññanātiādīni heṭṭhā dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1121) vuttatthāneva. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evaṃ jātiyā sati taṃ jātiṃ nissāya uppanno majjanākārappavatto māno jātimadoti vuccati. Svāyaṃ [V 0.0440] khattiyādīnaṃ catunnampi vaṇṇānaṃ uppajjati. Jātisampanno hi khattiyo ‘mādiso añño natthi. Avasesā antarā uṭṭhāya khattiyā jātā. Ahaṃ pana vaṃsāgatakhattiyo’ti mānaṃ karoti. Brāhmaṇādīsupi eseva nayo. Gottamadaniddesādīsupi imināvupāyena attho veditabbo. Khattiyopi [P 0.0466] hi ‘ahaṃ koṇḍaññagotto, ahaṃ ādiccagotto’ti mānaṃ karoti. Brāhmaṇopi ‘ahaṃ kassapagotto[M 0.0448], ahaṃ bhāradvājagotto’ti mānaṃ karoti. Vessopi suddopi attano attano kulagottaṃ nissāya mānaṃ karoti. Aṭṭhārasāpi seṇiyo ‘ekissā seṇiyā jātamhā’ti mānaṃ karontiyeva.

Now, according to the matrix laid out, in the section on exposition that begins with “What is the intoxication of birth?” and so on, it is said: “jātiṃ paṭicca” (dependent on birth), that is, “jātiṃ nissāya” (relying on birth). Here, the term ‘atthipaṭicca’ (dependent on existence) has been explained. Therefore, the meaning here is: “when birth exists.” The same method applies to “gottaṃ paṭicca” (dependent on lineage) and so on. Intoxication (mado) is in the sense of being intoxicated. The act of exalting is exaltation. The state of being exalted is exaltedness. “Conceit is the act of imagining,” and so on—these meanings have already been stated in the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī (DhsA. 1121). This is called: “When birth exists, this conceit that arises based on that birth, manifesting as the act of exalting, is called the intoxication of birth.” This arises among the four castes—khattiyas and so on. For a khattiya who is well-born thinks, “There is no one else like me. The rest are merely khattiyas born in between. But I am a khattiya of pure lineage,” and thus he becomes conceited. The same applies to brahmins and others. In the exposition of intoxication due to lineage and so on, the meaning should be understood in this same way. For even a khattiya thinks, “I am of the Koṇḍañña lineage, I am of the Ādicca lineage,” and becomes conceited. A brahmin thinks, “I am of the Kassapa lineage, I am of the Bhāradvāja lineage,” and becomes conceited. A vessa or a sudda likewise becomes conceited based on their own clan and lineage. Even the eighteen guilds think, “We are born of one guild,” and become conceited.

Ārogyamadādīsu ‘ahaṃ arogo, avasesā rogabahulā, gadduhanamattampi mayhaṃ byādhi nāma natthī’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno ārogyamado nāma.

Regarding the intoxication of health and so on, the conceit that arises due to intoxication, thinking, “I am healthy, while others are mostly sick; not even a trace of illness exists in me”—this is called the intoxication of health.

‘Ahaṃ taruṇo, avasesasattānaṃ attabhāvo papāte ṭhitarukkhasadiso, ahaṃ pana paṭhamavaye ṭhito’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno yobbanamado nāma.

“I am young, the bodies of other beings are like trees standing on a precipice, but I stand in the prime of youth”—the conceit that arises due to intoxication is called the intoxication of youth.

‘Ahaṃ ciraṃ jīviṃ, ciraṃ jīvāmi, ciraṃ jīvissāmi; sukhaṃ jīviṃ, sukhaṃ jīvāmi, sukhaṃ jīvissāmī’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno jīvitamado nāma.

“I have lived long, I live long, I will live long; I have lived happily, I live happily, I will live happily”—the conceit that arises due to intoxication is called the intoxication of life.

‘Ahaṃ lābhī, avasesā sattā appalābhā, mayhaṃ pana lābhassa pamāṇaṃ nāma natthī’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno lābhamado nāma.

“I am a gainer, while the remaining beings are of little gain, and there is no limit to my gains”—the conceit that arises due to intoxication is called the intoxication of gain.

‘Avasesā sattā yaṃ vā taṃ vā labhanti, ahaṃ pana sukataṃ paṇītaṃ cīvarādipaccayaṃ labhāmī’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno sakkāramado nāma.

“The remaining beings obtain whatever they can, but I obtain well-made and excellent requisites such as robes”—the conceit that arises due to intoxication is called the intoxication of honor.

‘Avasesabhikkhūnaṃ pādapiṭṭhiyaṃ akkamitvā gacchantā manussā ayaṃ samaṇotipi na vandanti, maṃ pana disvāva vandanti, pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya garuṃ katvā aggikkhandhaṃ viya ca durāsadaṃ katvā maññantī’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno garukāramado nāma.

“People walking by, even stepping on the footrests of other monks, do not even pay respects to those ascetics. But upon seeing me, they pay respects, honoring me like a stone parasol and regarding me as unapproachable like a blazing fire”—the conceit that arises due to intoxication is called the intoxication of respect.

‘Uppanno [V 0.0441] pañho mayhameva mukhena chijjati, bhikkhācāraṃ gacchantāpi mameva purato katvā parivāretvā gacchantī’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno purekkhāramado nāma.

“Any arisen question is resolved through my mouth alone. Even when going for alms, they go surrounding me and placing me in front”—the conceit that arises due to intoxication is called the intoxication of precedence.

Agārikassa tāva mahāparivārassa ‘purisasatampi purisasahassampi maṃ parivāreti,’ anagāriyassa pana ‘samaṇasatampi samaṇasahassampi maṃ parivāreti, sesā appaparivārā, ahaṃ mahāparivāro ceva suciparivāro cā’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno parivāramado nāma.

For a householder with a large retinue, the thought arises: “Even a hundred or a thousand men attend upon me.” For a homeless one, the thought arises: “Even a hundred or a thousand ascetics attend upon me. The rest have small retinues; I alone have a large and pure retinue.” The conceit that arises due to intoxication is called the intoxication of retinue.

Bhogo [M 0.0449] pana kiñcāpi lābhaggahaṇeneva gahito hoti, imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne nikkheparāsi nāma gahito; tasmā ‘avasesā sattā attano paribhogamattampi na labhanti, mayhaṃ pana nidhānagatasseva dhanassa pamāṇaṃ natthī’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno bhogamado nāma.

Although wealth (bhoga) is included under gain (lābha), in this context it is taken to mean a heap of stored treasure. Therefore, “Other beings do not obtain even enough for their own use, while for me there is no measure to the wealth stored away”—the conceit that arises due to intoxication is called the intoxication of wealth.

Vaṇṇaṃ [P 0.0467] paṭiccāti sarīravaṇṇampi guṇavaṇṇampi paṭicca. ‘Avasesā sattā dubbaṇṇā durūpā, ahaṃ pana abhirūpo pāsādiko; avasesā sattā nigguṇā patthaṭaakittino, mayhaṃ pana kittisaddo devamanussesu pākaṭo – itipi thero bahussuto, itipi sīlavā, itipi dhutaguṇayutto’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno vaṇṇamado nāma.

“Vaṇṇaṃ paṭicca” (dependent on appearance) means dependent on both physical appearance and the appearance of qualities. “Other beings are ugly and unattractive, but I am beautiful and pleasing; other beings are without virtue and of ill-repute, but my reputation is well-known among gods and humans—this elder is learned, virtuous, and endowed with ascetic qualities”—the conceit that arises due to intoxication is called the intoxication of appearance.

‘Avasesā sattā appassutā, ahaṃ pana bahussuto’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno sutamado nāma.

“The remaining beings are of little learning, but I am highly learned”—the conceit that arises due to intoxication is called the intoxication of learning.

‘Avasesā sattā appaṭibhānā, mayhaṃ pana paṭibhānassa pamāṇaṃ natthī’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno paṭibhānamado nāma.

“The remaining beings are witless; but there is no limit to my wit”—the conceit that arises due to intoxication is called the intoxication of eloquence.

‘Ahaṃ rattaññū asukaṃ buddhavaṃsaṃ, rājavaṃsaṃ, janapadavaṃsaṃ, gāmavaṃsaṃ, rattindivaparicchedaṃ, nakkhattamuhuttayogaṃ jānāmī’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno rattaññumado nāma.

“I am experienced; I know the lineage of the Buddhas, the royal lineage, the lineage of districts, the lineage of villages, the divisions of day and night, the conjunction of constellations and auspicious moments”—the conceit that arises due to intoxication is called the intoxication of experience.

‘Avasesā bhikkhū antarā piṇḍapātikā jātā, ahaṃ pana jātipiṇḍapātiko’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno piṇḍapātikamado nāma.

“‘The remaining monks became alms-goers in the interim, but I am an alms-goer by nature’—the conceit that arises by way of intoxication is called the intoxication of being an alms-goer.”

‘Avasesā [V 0.0442] sattā uññātā avaññātā, ahaṃ pana anuññāto anavaññāto’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno anavaññātamado nāma.

“‘The remaining beings are despised and disdained, but I am approved and not disdained’—the conceit that arises by way of intoxication is called the intoxication of not being disdained.”

‘Avasesānaṃ iriyāpatho apāsādiko, mayhaṃ pana pāsādiko’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno iriyāpathamado nāma.

“‘The posture of the remaining ones is ungraceful, but mine is graceful’—the conceit that arises by way of intoxication is called the intoxication with posture.”

‘Avasesā sattā chinnapakkhakākasadisā, ahaṃ pana mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo’ti vā ‘ahaṃ yaṃ yaṃ kammaṃ karomi, taṃ taṃ ijjhatī’ti vā majjanavasena uppanno māno iddhimado nāma.

“‘The remaining beings are like crows with broken wings, but I am one of great psychic power and great influence,’ or ‘Whatever action I do, that succeeds’—the conceit that arises by way of intoxication is called the intoxication with psychic power.”

Heṭṭhā parivāraggahaṇena yaso gahitova hoti. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne upaṭṭhākamado nāma gahito. So agārikenapi anagārikenapi dīpetabbo. Agāriko hi ekacco aṭṭhārasasu seṇīsu ekissā jeṭṭhako hoti, tassa ‘avasese purise ahaṃ paṭṭhapemi, ahaṃ vicāremī’ti[M 0.0450]; anagārikopi ekacco katthaci jeṭṭhako hoti, tassa ‘avasesā bhikkhū mayhaṃ ovāde vattanti, ahaṃ jeṭṭhako’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno yasamado nāma.

Below, by the inclusion of ‘retinue,’ fame is already covered. Here, however, the intoxication with attendants is what is taken. It should be explained by both householders and renunciants. For a householder, someone may be the chief among the eighteen guilds, thinking, ‘I establish the remaining men, I manage them.’ Similarly, a renunciant may be the chief somewhere, thinking, ‘The remaining monks conduct themselves according to my instruction, I am the chief.’ The conceit that arises by way of such intoxication is called the intoxication with fame.

‘Avasesā sattā dussīlā, ahaṃ pana sīlavā’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno sīlamado nāma. ‘Avasesasattānaṃ kukkuṭassa udakapānamattepi kāle cittekaggatā natthi, ahaṃ pana upacārappanānaṃ lābhī’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno jhānamado [P 0.0468] nāma.

“‘The remaining beings are immoral, but I am virtuous’—the conceit that arises by way of intoxication is called the intoxication with virtue. ‘The remaining beings do not have one-pointedness of mind even for the time it takes a chicken to drink water, but I am a gainer of access and absorption’—the conceit that arises by way of intoxication is called the intoxication with jhāna.”

‘Avasesā sattā nissippā, ahaṃ pana sippavā’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno sippamado nāma. ‘Avasesā sattā rassā, ahaṃ pana dīgho’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno ārohamado nāma. ‘Avasesā sattā rassā vā honti dīghā vā, ahaṃ nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno pariṇāhamado nāma. ‘Avasesasattānaṃ sarīrasaṇṭhānaṃ virūpaṃ bībhacchaṃ, mayhaṃ pana manāpaṃ pāsādika’nti majjanavasena uppanno māno saṇṭhānamado nāma. ‘Avasesānaṃ sattānaṃ sarīre bahū dosā, mayhaṃ pana sarīre kesaggamattampi vajjaṃ natthī’ti majjanavasena uppanno māno pāripūrimado nāma.

“‘The remaining beings are unskilled, but I am skilled’—the conceit that arises by way of intoxication is called the intoxication with skill. ‘The remaining beings are short, but I am tall’—the conceit that arises by way of intoxication is called the intoxication with height. ‘The remaining beings are either short or tall, but I am perfectly proportioned like a banyan tree’—the conceit that arises by way of intoxication is called the intoxication with proportion. ‘The bodily forms of the remaining beings are misshapen and repulsive, but mine is pleasing and inspiring’—the conceit that arises by way of intoxication is called the intoxication with form. ‘In the bodies of the remaining beings there are many faults, but in my body there is not even a hair-tip of a fault’—the conceit that arises by way of intoxication is called the intoxication with perfection.”

845. Iminā [V 0.0443] ettakena ṭhānena savatthukaṃ mānaṃ kathetvā idāni avatthukaṃ nibbattitamānameva dassento tattha katamo madotiādimāha. Taṃ uttānatthameva.

845. Having explained conceit with a basis in this way to this extent, now, showing conceit that arises without a basis, he says, beginning with, ‘Herein, what is intoxication?’. That meaning is clear.

846. Pamādaniddese cittassa vossaggoti imesu ettakesu ṭhānesu satiyā aniggaṇhitvā cittassa vossajjanaṃ; sativirahoti attho. Vossaggānuppadānanti vossaggassa anuppadānaṃ; punappunaṃ vissajjananti attho. Asakkaccakiriyatāti etesaṃ dānādīnaṃ kusaladhammānaṃ bhāvanāya puggalassa vā deyyadhammassa vā asakkaccakaraṇavasena asakkaccakiriyā. Satatabhāvo sātaccaṃ. Na satatabhāvo asātaccaṃ. Na sātaccakiriyatā asātaccakiriyatā. Anaṭṭhitakaraṇaṃ anaṭṭhitakiriyatā. Yathā nāma kakaṇṭako thokaṃ gantvā thokaṃ tiṭṭhati, na nirantaraṃ gacchati, evameva yo puggalo ekadivasaṃ dānaṃ vā datvā pūjaṃ vā katvā dhammaṃ vā sutvā samaṇadhammaṃ vā katvā puna cirassaṃ karoti, na nirantaraṃ pavatteti, tassa sā [M 0.0451] kiriyā anaṭṭhitakiriyatāti vuccati. Olīnavuttitāti nirantarakaraṇasaṅkhātassa vipphārasseva abhāvena līnavuttitā. Nikkhittachandatāti kusalakiriyāya vīriyachandassa nikkhittabhāvo. Nikkhittadhuratāti vīriyadhurassa oropanaṃ, osakkitamānasatāti attho. Anadhiṭṭhānanti [P 0.0469] kusalakaraṇe patiṭṭhābhāvo. Ananuyogoti ananuyuñjanaṃ. Pamādoti pamajjanaṃ. Yo evarūpo pamādoti idaṃ atthapariyāyassa byañjanapariyāyassa ca pariyantābhāvato ākāradassanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yvāyaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya dassito pamādo, yo aññopi evamākāro evaṃjātiko pamādo pamajjanākāravasena pamajjanā, pamajjitabhāvavasena pamajjitattanti saṅkhaṃ gato – ayaṃ vuccati pamādoti. Lakkhaṇato panesa pañcasu kāmaguṇesu sativossaggalakkhaṇo, tattheva satiyā vissaṭṭhākāro veditabbo.

846. In the exposition of heedlessness, ‘the relinquishment of the mind’ means the mind's abandonment without being restrained by mindfulness in these instances; the meaning is the absence of mindfulness. ‘Repeated relinquishment’ means the repeated application of relinquishment; the meaning is repeatedly letting go. ‘Careless action’ is the careless performance of wholesome qualities such as giving, due to lack of care for the person or for the object to be given. ‘Continuity’ is the state of being constant. ‘Non-continuity’ is the state of not being constant. Not acting with continuity is non-continuous action. Unsteady performance is unsteady action. Just as a chameleon walks a little and stops a little, not moving continuously, so too a person who gives gifts, makes offerings, listens to the Dhamma, or practices the ascetic duties for one day and then does so again only after a long time, not maintaining it continuously—his action is called unsteady action. ‘Sluggish behavior’ is sluggishness due to the absence of that very vigor which is known as uninterrupted effort. ‘Abandoned desire’ is the abandonment of zeal for wholesome action. ‘Abandoned burden’ is the laying down of the burden of effort; the meaning is a mind that has shirked. ‘Non-determination’ is the lack of a foundation in doing good. ‘Non-application’ is not applying oneself. ‘Heedlessness’ is negligence. ‘Whatever heedlessness is of such a kind’—this is a showing of its form, since there is no end to the expression of its meaning and wording. This is what is said: whatever heedlessness has been shown from the beginning, or any other heedlessness of such a kind, of such a nature—reckoned as negligence by way of the mode of negligence, by way of the state of having been negligent—this is called heedlessness. By way of characteristic, however, it has the characteristic of the relinquishment of mindfulness regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure; there, it should be understood as the mode of having forsaken mindfulness.

847. Thambhaniddese thaddhaṭṭhena thambho; khaliyā thaddhasāṭakassa viya cittassa thaddhatā ettha kathitā. Thambhanākāro thambhanā. Thambhitassa bhāvo thambhitattaṃ. Kakkhaḷassa puggalassa bhāvo kakkhaḷiyaṃ. Pharusassa puggalassa bhāvo phārusiyaṃ. Abhivādanādisāmīcirahānaṃ tassā sāmīciyā akaraṇavasena ujumeva ṭhapitacittabhāvo ujucittatā. Thaddhassa amuduno bhāvo amudutā.
