Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ thambho nāma vuccati, yena samannāgato puggalo gilitanaṅgalasīso viya ajagaro, vātabharitā viya bhastā cetiyaṃ vā vuḍḍhatare vā disvā onamituṃ [V 0.0444] na sakkoti, pariyanteneva carati. Svāyaṃ cittassa uddhumātabhāvalakkhaṇoti veditabbo.

847. In the explanation of obstinacy, ‘obstinacy’ means stiffness. Here, the stiffness of the mind is described as being like a cloth stiffened with paste. The mode of stiffening is ‘stiffening.’ The state of being stiffened is ‘stiffened-ness.’ The nature of a harsh person is ‘harshness,’ and the nature of a rough person is ‘roughness.’ The state of mind being kept rigid due to the non-performance of proper conduct such as salutation is ‘rigid-mindedness.’ The nature of one who is stiff and not gentle is ‘non-gentleness.’ This is called ‘obstinacy’—endowed with which, a person is like a python that has swallowed a ploughshare, or like a bellows filled with wind; upon seeing a shrine or an elder, they are unable to bow down and keep to the periphery. This should be understood as having the characteristic of a puffed-up state of mind.

848. Sārambhaniddese sārambhanavasena sārambho. Paṭippharitvā sārambho paṭisārambho. Sārambhanākāro sārambhanā. Paṭippharitvā sārambhanā paṭisārambhanā. Paṭisārambhitassa bhāvo paṭisārambhitattaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ sārambho nāma vuccati. Svāyaṃ lakkhaṇato karaṇuttariyalakkhaṇo nāma vuccati, yena samannāgato puggalo taddiguṇaṃ taddiguṇaṃ karoti. Agāriko samāno ekenekasmiṃ gharavatthusmiṃ sajjite aparo dve vatthūni sajjeti, aparo cattāri, aparo [M 0.0452] aṭṭha, aparo soḷasa. Anagāriko samāno ekenekasmiṃ nikāye gahite, ‘nāhaṃ etassa heṭṭhā bhavissāmī’ti aparo dve gaṇhāti, aparo tayo, aparo cattāro, aparo pañca. Sārambhavasena hi gaṇhituṃ na [P 0.0470] vaṭṭati. Akusalapakkho esa nirayagāmimaggo. Kusalapakkhavasena pana ekasmiṃ ekaṃ salākabhattaṃ dente dve dātuṃ, dve dente cattāri dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Bhikkhunāpi parena ekasmiṃ nikāye gahite, ‘dve nikāye gahetvā sajjhāyantassa me phāsu hotī’ti vivaṭṭapakkhe ṭhatvā taduttari gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati.

848. In the explanation of rivalry, `sārambha` is rivalry. Retaliatory rivalry is `paṭisārambha`. The mode of rivalry is `sārambhanā`. The mode of retaliatory rivalry is `paṭisārambhanā`. The state of one who has engaged in retaliatory rivalry is `paṭisārambhitattaṃ`. This is what is called rivalry. By its characteristic, this is called having the characteristic of outdoing, whereby a person endowed with it does things doubly and redoubly. When one householder prepares one household item, another prepares two items, another four, another eight, another sixteen. When one homeless one has taken up one Nikāya, another, thinking, 'I will not be inferior to this one,' takes up two, another three, another four, another five. For it is not proper to take them up out of rivalry. This is the unwholesome side, a path leading to hell. But on the wholesome side, when one gives one ticket-meal, it is proper to give two; when two are given, to give four. It is also proper for a bhikkhu, when another has taken up one Nikāya, to take up more while standing on the side of spiritual progress, thinking, 'It is convenient for me to recite having taken up two Nikāyas'.

849. Atricchatāniddese yathā ariyavaṃsasutte (a. ni. 4.28) ‘lāmakalāmakaṭṭho itarītaraṭṭho’ evaṃ aggahetvā cīvarādīsu yaṃ yaṃ laddhaṃ hoti, tena tena asantuṭṭhassa; gihino vā pana rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbesu yaṃ yaṃ laddhaṃ hoti, tena tena asantuṭṭhassa. Bhiyyokamyatāti visesakāmatā. Icchanakavasena icchā. Icchāva icchāgatā, icchanākāro vā. Attano lābhaṃ aticca icchanabhāvo aticchatā. Rāgotiādīni heṭṭhā vuttatthāneva. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ aticchatā nāma vuccati. Atricchatātipi etissā eva nāmaṃ. Lakkhaṇato pana sakalābhe asantuṭṭhi paralābhe ca patthanā – etaṃ atricchatālakkhaṇaṃ. Atricchapuggalassa hi attanā laddhaṃ paṇītampi lāmakaṃ viya khāyati, parena laddhaṃ lāmakampi paṇītaṃ viya khāyati; ekabhājane pakkayāgu vā bhattaṃ vā pūvo vā attano patte pakkhitto lāmako viya, parassa patte paṇīto viya khāyati. Ayaṃ pana atricchatā pabbajitānampi hoti gihīnampi tiracchānagatānampi.

849. In the explanation of excessive greed (`atricchatā`), as in the Ariyavaṃsa Sutta (A.N. 4.28), the phrase 'of inferior and more inferior quality, one worse than the other' illustrates the state of one who, not grasping contentment, remains dissatisfied with whatever robes or other requisites are obtained. Similarly, a householder remains dissatisfied with whatever forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or touches are obtained. The desire for more is `visesakāmatā`. Craving is `icchā`. Craving itself is `icchāgatā`, or the mode of craving, `icchanākāro`. The state of desiring beyond one’s own gain is `aticchatā`. Terms like 'lust' (`rāga`) have the same meaning as previously stated. This is called `aticchatā`. `Atricchatā` is also its name. Its characteristic, however, is dissatisfaction with one's own gains and longing for the gains of others—this is the mark of excessive greed. For a person with excessive greed, even excellent things obtained by oneself seem inferior, while inferior things obtained by others seem excellent. Porridge, cooked rice, or cakes prepared in one pot, when placed in one's own bowl, appear inferior, while the same in another’s bowl appears excellent. This excessive greed occurs among the ordained, among householders, and even among animals.

Tatrimāni vatthūni – eko kira kuṭumbiko tiṃsa bhikkhuniyo nimantetvā sapūvaṃ bhattaṃ adāsi[V 0.0445]. Saṅghattherī sabbabhikkhūnīnaṃ patte pūvaṃ parivattāpetvā pacchā attanā laddhameva khādi. Bārāṇasirājāpi ‘aṅgārapakkamaṃsaṃ khādissāmī’ti deviṃ ādāya araññaṃ paviṭṭho ekaṃ kinnariṃ disvā, deviṃ pahāya, tassānupadaṃ gato. Devī nivattitvā assamapadaṃ gantvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañca ca abhiññāyo patvā nisinnā [M 0.0453] rājānaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā ākāse uppatitvā agamāsi. Rukkhe adhivatthā devatā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Here are these stories: It is said that a certain householder invited thirty bhikkhunīs and offered them a meal with cakes. The senior nun, having had the cakes in all the bhikkhunīs' bowls exchanged, afterward ate only what she herself had received. The king of Bārāṇasī, thinking, "I will eat meat roasted on coals," took the queen and entered the forest. Seeing a kinnarī there, he abandoned the queen and followed after her. The queen turned back, went to a hermitage, practiced the kasiṇa meditation, attained the eight attainments and the five higher knowledges, and sat down. Seeing the king approaching, she rose into the sky and departed. A deity dwelling in a tree spoke this verse:

Atricchaṃ atilobhena, atilobhamadena ca;

Evaṃ hāyati atthamhā, ahaṃva asitābhuyāti. (jā. 1.2.168);

Through excessive craving and excessive greed, and through the intoxication of excessive greed, thus one falls from one's welfare, as I did from Asitābhū.

Yathā [P 0.0471] candakinnariṃ patthayanto asitābhuyā rājadhītāya hīno parihīno, evaṃ atricchaṃ atilobhena atthamha hāyati jīyatīti devatā raññā saddhiṃ keḷimakāsi.

Just as he who desired the Candakinnarī was deprived and bereft of the princess Asitābhū, so too, through excessive craving and excessive greed, one declines and wastes away from one's welfare—thus the deity jested with the king.

Kassapabuddhakālepi mittavindako nāma seṭṭhiputto assaddho appasanno mātarā ‘tāta, ajja uposathiko hutvā vihāre sabbarattiṃ dhammasavanaṃ suṇa, sahassaṃ te dassāmī’ti vutte dhanalobhena uposathaṅgāni samādāya vihāraṃ gantvā ‘idaṃ ṭhānaṃ akutobhaya’nti sallakkhetvā dhammāsanassa heṭṭhā nipanno sabbarattiṃ niddāyitvā gharaṃ agamāsi. Mātā pātova yāguṃ pacitvā upanāmesi. So sahassaṃ gahetvāva yāguṃ pivi. Athassa etadahosi – ‘dhanaṃ saṃharissāmī’ti. So nāvāya samuddaṃ pakkhanditukāmo ahosi. Atha naṃ mātā “tāta, imasmiṃ kule cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ atthi; alaṃ gamanenā”ti vāresi. So tassā vacanaṃ anādiyitvā gacchati eva. Sā purato aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ kujjhitvā ‘ayaṃ mayhaṃ purato tiṭṭhatī’ti pādena paharitvā patitaṃ mātaraṃ antaraṃ katvā agamāsi. Mātā uṭṭhahitvā “mādisāya mātari evarūpaṃ kammaṃ katvā gatassa me gataṭṭhāne sukhaṃ bhavissatī”ti evaṃsaññī nāma tvaṃ puttāti āha. Tassa nāvaṃ āruyha gacchato sattame divase nāvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha te manussā “addhā ettha pāpapuriso atthi; salākaṃ dethā”ti salākā dīyamānā tasseva tikkhattuṃ pāpuṇi. Te tassa uḷumpaṃ datvā taṃ samudde pakkhipiṃsu. So ekaṃ dīpaṃ gantvā vimānapetīhi saddhiṃ sampattiṃ anubhavanto tāhi “purato mā agamāsī”ti vuccamānopi taddiguṇaṃ sampattiṃ passanto anupubbena khuracakkadharaṃ ekaṃ purisaṃ addasa. Tassa taṃ cakkaṃ padumapupphaṃ viya upaṭṭhāti. So taṃ āha – “ambho, idaṃ tayā piḷandhapadumaṃ [M 0.0454] mayhaṃ dehī”ti. “Nayidaṃ, sāmi[V 0.0446], padumaṃ; khuracakkaṃ eta”nti. So “vañcesi maṃ tvaṃ. Kiṃ me padumaṃ na diṭṭhapubba”nti vatvā “tvañhi lohitacandanaṃ limpetvā piḷandhanaṃ padumapupphaṃ mayhaṃ na dātukāmosī”ti āha. So cintesi – ‘ayampi mayā katasadisaṃ kammaṃ katvā tassa phalaṃ anubhavitukāmo’ti. Atha naṃ “handa re”ti vatvā [P 0.0472] tassa matthake cakkaṃ pakkhipitvā palāyi. Etamatthaṃ viditvā satthā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the time of the Buddha Kassapa, there was a merchant’s son named Mittavindaka who was faithless and lacking in devotion. His mother said to him, "Dear son, observe the Uposatha today, stay in the monastery all night, and listen to the Dhamma. I will give you a thousand coins." Driven by greed for wealth, he undertook the Uposatha precepts, went to the monastery, and thinking, "This place is safe from all dangers," lay down beneath the Dhamma seat and slept all night before returning home. Early in the morning, his mother prepared rice-gruel and offered it to him. He took the thousand coins and then drank the gruel. Then he thought, "I will gather more wealth." He decided to set sail on a ship. His mother tried to dissuade him, saying, "Dear son, our family has forty crores of wealth; there is no need to go." But he ignored her words and went anyway. She stood in front of him. Angered, he thought, "She stands in my way," and kicked her, causing his mother to fall down. Stepping over his fallen mother, he left. She got up and said, "My son, having done such a deed to a mother like me, you are indeed one who thinks that there will be happiness in the place you are going!" As he sailed on the ship, on the seventh day, the ship stopped. The people aboard said, "Surely, there is an evil person here; let us draw lots." When the lots were cast, his name came up three times. They gave him a raft and cast him into the sea. He reached an island where he enjoyed pleasures with celestial nymphs. Though they warned him, "Do not go further ahead," seeing even greater delights, he gradually went on until he saw a man carrying a razor-wheel. To him, the wheel appeared like a lotus flower. He said to him, "Friend, give me that lotus you are wearing." The man replied, "This is not a lotus, sir, but a razor-wheel." He said, "You deceive me. Have I not seen a lotus before? You must have smeared red sandalwood paste on it and do not wish to give me the lotus you are wearing." The man thought, 'This one too, having done a deed similar to mine, has come to experience its fruit.' Then he said, "Here you go," placed the wheel on his head, and fled. Understanding this matter, the Teacher spoke this verse:

“Catubbhi aṭṭhajjhagamā, aṭṭhahi pica soḷasa;

Soḷasāhi ca bāttiṃsa, atricchaṃ cakkamāsado;

Icchāhatassa posassa, cakkaṃ bhamati matthake”ti. (jā. 1.1.104);

With four, he attained eight; with eight, likewise sixteen; with sixteen, thirty-two; through excessive craving, he came upon the wheel. For a person struck by craving, the wheel spins on his head.

Aññataropi atriccho amacco sakavisayaṃ atikkamitvā paravisayaṃ pāvisi. Tattha pothito palāyitvā ekassa tāpasassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pavisitvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya nipajji. So tāpasena ‘kiṃ te kata’nti pucchito imā gāthāyo abhāsi –

A certain greedy minister, having transgressed his own territory, entered another's territory. There, having been beaten, he fled and entered the dwelling place of an ascetic. Having undertaken the Uposatha precepts, he lay down. When the ascetic asked him, "What have you done?" he spoke these verses:

“Sakaṃ niketaṃ atihīḷayāno,

Atricchatā mallagāmaṃ agacchiṃ;

Tato janā nikkhamitvāna gāmā,

Kodaṇḍakena paripothayiṃsu maṃ.

Having scorned my own dwelling, driven by excessive greed, I went to the wrestlers' village. Then people, issuing forth from the village, struck me all around with clubs.

“So bhinnasīso ruhiramakkhitaṅgo,

Paccāgamāsiṃ sakaṃ niketaṃ;

Tasmā ahaṃ posathaṃ pālayāmi,

Atricchatā mā punarāgamāsī”ti. (jā. 1.14.138-139);

With a split head and limbs smeared with blood, I returned to my own abode; therefore I observe the Uposatha, lest excessive greed bring me back again.

850. Mahicchatāniddese mahantāni vatthūni icchati, mahatī vāssa icchāti mahiccho, tassa bhāvo mahicchatā. Lakkhaṇato pana asantaguṇasambhāvanatā paṭiggahaṇe ca paribhoge ca amattaññutā – etaṃ mahicchatālakkhaṇaṃ. Mahiccho hi puggalo yathā nāma kacchapuṭavāṇijo piḷandhanabhaṇḍakaṃ hatthena gahetvā ucchaṅgepi pakkhipitabbayuttakaṃ pakkhipitvā mahājanassa passantasseva [V 0.0447] “ammā, asukaṃ gaṇhatha, asukaṃ gaṇhathā”ti mukhena saṃvidahati. Evameva so appamattakampi attano sīlaṃ vā ganthaṃ vā dhutaguṇaṃ vā antamaso araññavāsamattakampi mahājanassa jānantasseva sambhāvetukāmo [M 0.0455] hoti, sambhāvetvā ca pana sakaṭehipi upanīte paccaye ‘ala’nti avatvā gaṇhāti. Tayo hi pūretuṃ na sakkā – aggi upādānena, samuddo udakena, mahiccho paccayehīti.

850. In the explanation of wanting much, one desires great things, or has a great desire—this is one who wants much; the state of such a person is wanting much. By characteristic, it is the proclaiming of qualities one does not have, and immoderation in receiving and using things—this is the characteristic of wanting much. For a person who wants much is just like a peddler with a basket of goods: having taken an ornament in his hand, he places another suitable item into his lap, and while the crowd watches, he calls out, "Here, take this, take this!" with his mouth. In the same way, even a trifling virtue of his—whether it be his precepts, his learning, his ascetic qualities, or even just dwelling in the forest—he wants the crowd to know about it. And having made it known, when requisites are brought even by cartloads, he does not say "enough" but keeps taking. For three things cannot be filled: fire with fuel, the ocean with water, and a person who wants much with requisites.

Aggikkhandho samuddo ca, mahiccho cāpi puggalo;

Bahuke paccaye dente, tayo pete na pūraye.

A mass of fire, the ocean, and a person who wants much—though given many requisites, these three can never be filled.

Mahicchapuggalo [P 0.0473] hi vijātamātuyāpi manaṃ gaṇhituṃ na sakkoti, pageva upaṭṭhākānaṃ.

A person who wants much cannot please even his own mother, let alone his attendants.

Tatrimāni vatthūni – eko kira daharabhikkhu piṭṭhapūve piyāyati. Athassa mātā paṭipattiṃ vīmaṃsamānā ‘sace me putto paṭiggahaṇe mattaṃ jānāti, sakalampi naṃ temāsaṃ pūveheva upaṭṭhahissāmī’ti vassūpanāyikadivase parivīmaṃsamānā paṭhamaṃ ekaṃ pūvaṃ adāsi, tasmiṃ niṭṭhite dutiyaṃ, tasmimpi niṭṭhite tatiyaṃ. Daharo ‘ala’nti avatvā khādiyeva. Mātā tassa amattaññubhāvaṃ ñatvā ‘ajjeva me puttena sakalatemāsassa pūvā khāditā’ti dutiyadivasato paṭṭhāya ekapūvampi na adāsi.

Here is a story on this matter: A certain young monk, it seems, was fond of flour cakes. His mother, wishing to examine his conduct, thought, "If my son knows moderation in receiving, I will provide him with flour cakes for the entire three months." On the day of entering the rains retreat, she examined him, first giving him one flour cake. When that was finished, she gave him a second, and when that too was finished, a third. The young monk, without saying "enough," kept eating. Knowing his lack of moderation, his mother thought, "Today my son has eaten the flour cakes for the entire three months." From the next day onwards, she did not give him even a single flour cake.

Tissamahārājāpi devasikaṃ cetiyapabbate bhikkhusaṅghassa dānaṃ dadamāno ‘mahārāja, kiṃ ekameva ṭhānaṃ bhajasi? Kiṃ aññattha dātuṃ na vaṭṭatī’ti jānapadehi vutto dutiyadivase anurādhapure mahādānaṃ dāpesi. Ekabhikkhupi paṭiggahaṇe mattaṃ na aññāsi. Ekamekena paṭiggahitaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ dve tayo janā ukkhipiṃsu. Rājā dutiyadivase cetiyapabbate bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantāpetvā rājantepuraṃ āgatakāle “pattaṃ dethā”ti āha. “Alaṃ, mahārāja, attano pamāṇena bhikkhaṃ gaṇhissatī”ti ekabhikkhupi pattaṃ na adāsi. Sabbe pamāṇayuttakameva paṭiggahesuṃ. Atha rājā āha – “passatha tumhākaṃ bhikkhūsu ekopi mattaṃ na jānāti. Hiyyo kiñci avasesaṃ nāhosi. Ajja gahitaṃ mandaṃ, avasesameva bahū”ti tesaṃ mattaññutāya attamano itaresañca amattaññutāya anattamano ahosi.

King Tissa, while daily offering alms to the Saṅgha of monks at Cetiyapabbata, was asked by the people of the country, 'Great king, why do you frequent only one place? Is it not fitting to give elsewhere?' The next day, he arranged a great almsgiving in Anuradhapura. Not a single monk knew the limit in receiving. The food and drink received by each monk had to be lifted by two or three people. The next day, the king invited the Saṅgha of monks from Cetiyapabbata. When they arrived at the royal palace, he said, 'Give me your bowls.' But not a single monk gave a bowl, saying, 'Enough, great king, each will take alms according to his own measure.' All received only what was appropriate for their measure. Then the king said, 'See, among your monks, not one knows moderation. Yesterday, nothing was left over. Today, what was taken is little, and much remains.' He was pleased with the moderation of the Cetiyapabbata monks but displeased with the immoderation of the others.

851. Pāpicchatāniddese [V 0.0448] assaddho samāno saddhoti maṃ jano jānātūtiādīsu evaṃ icchanto kiṃ karoti? Assaddho saddhākāraṃ dasseti; dussīlādayo sīlavantādīnaṃ ākāraṃ dassenti. Kathaṃ? Assaddho [M 0.0456] tāva mahāmahadivase manussānaṃ vihāraṃ āgamanavelāya sammajjaniṃ ādāya vihāraṃ sammajjati, kacavaraṃ chaḍḍeti, manussehi diṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ gacchati, tatthāpi sammajjitvā kacavaraṃ chaḍḍeti, vālikaṃ samaṃ karoti, āsanāni dhovati, bodhimhi udakaṃ siñcati. Manussā disvā ‘natthi maññe añño bhikkhu vihārajagganako, ayameva imaṃ vihāraṃ paṭijaggati, saddho thero’ti gamanakāle nimantetvā gacchanti. Dussīlopi [P 0.0474] upaṭṭhākānaṃ sammukhe vinayadharaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchati “bhante, mayi gacchante goṇo ubbiggo. Tena dhāvatā tiṇāni chinnāni. Sammajjantassa me tiṇāni chijjanti. Caṅkamantassa me pāṇakā mīyanti. Kheḷaṃ pātentassa asatiyā tiṇamatthake patati; tattha tattha kiṃ hotī”ti? “Anāpatti, āvuso, asañcicca asatiyā ajānantassā”ti ca vutte “bhante, mayhaṃ garukaṃ viya upaṭṭhāti; suṭṭhu vīmaṃsathā”ti bhaṇati. Taṃ sutvā manussā ‘amhākaṃ ayyo ettakepi kukkuccāyati! Aññasmiṃ oḷārike kiṃ nāma karissati; natthi iminā sadiso sīlavāti pasannā sakkāraṃ karonti. Appassutopi upaṭṭhākamajjhe nisinno “asuko tipiṭakadharo, asuko catunikāyiko mayhaṃ antevāsiko, mama santike tehi dhammo uggahito”ti vadati. Manussā ‘amhākaṃ ayyena sadiso bahussuto natthi, etassa kira santike asukena ca asukena ca dhammo uggahito’ti pasannā sakkāraṃ karonti.

851. In the exposition of evil desires, when an unfaithful person, being unfaithful, wishes to be known as faithful, what does he do? The unfaithful one displays the appearance of faith; the immoral and others display the appearance of the virtuous. How so? First, the unfaithful one, on a great festival day, when people are about to arrive at the monastery, takes a broom and sweeps the monastery. He removes the rubbish, and knowing he is being observed, he goes to the shrine courtyard. There too, he sweeps, removes rubbish, levels the sand, washes the seats, and sprinkles water on the Bodhi tree. Seeing this, people think, 'It seems there is no other monk who looks after the monastery; this one alone tends to it. The elder is faithful,' and they invite him when they depart. The immoral one, in the presence of his supporters, approaches a Vinaya master and asks, 'Venerable sir, while I was walking, an ox became startled. As it ran, it cut off some grass. As I swept, grass was cut. As I walked, some insects died. When I spat out phlegm unmindfully, it fell on the top of a blade of grass. What is the offense in each of these cases?' When told, 'There is no offense, friend, if one did not intend, was unmindful, and did not know,' he says, 'Venerable sir, this seems serious to me. Please investigate it thoroughly.' Hearing this, people think, 'Our elder is so scrupulous even about such a small matter! What would he do in a gross matter? There is no one as virtuous as him,' and, pleased, they make offerings. Even one who is unlearned, sitting among his supporters, declares, 'So-and-so is a Tipitaka-holder, so-and-so is a four-Nikāya master—they are my students. They learned the Dhamma from me.' People think, 'There is no one as learned as our elder. Indeed, so-and-so and so-and-so learned the Dhamma from him,' and, pleased, they make offerings.

Saṅgaṇikārāmopi mahāmahadivase dīghapīṭhañca apassayañca gāhāpetvā vihārapaccante rukkhamūle divāvihāraṃ nisīdati. Manussā āgantvā “thero kuhi”nti pucchanti. “Gaṇṭhikaputtā nāma gaṇṭhikā eva honti. Tena thero evarūpe kāle idha na nisīdati, vihārapaccante divāṭṭhāne dīghacaṅkame viharatī”ti vadanti. Sopi divasabhāgaṃ vītināmetvā nalāṭe makkaṭasuttaṃ alliyāpetvā pīṭhaṃ gāhāpetvā āgamma pariveṇadvāre nisīdati. Manussā “kahaṃ, bhante, gatattha? Āgantvā na addasamhā”ti vadanti. “Upāsakā, antovihāro ākiṇṇo; daharasāmaṇerānaṃ vicaraṇaṭṭhānametaṃ saṭṭhihatthacaṅkame divāṭṭhāne nisīdimhā”ti attano pavivittabhāvaṃ jānāpeti.

Even one fond of company, on a great festival day, having had a long bench and a reclining chair brought, sits for the midday rest at the root of a tree on the monastery boundary. People come and ask, 'Where is the elder?' They say, 'Those who are fond of company are indeed entangled. Therefore, the elder does not sit here at such a time; he dwells in a daytime resting place on a long walking path at the monastery boundary.' After spending part of the day, he has a cobweb stuck to his forehead, has a bench brought, returns, and sits at the door of his cell. People say, 'Venerable sir, where have you gone? We came but did not see you.' He replies, 'Lay devotees, the inner monastery is crowded; this is a place where young novices wander about. We sat in a daytime resting place on a sixty-cubit walking path,' thus making known his secluded state.

Kusītopi upaṭṭhākamajjhe nisinno “upāsakā, tumhehi ukkāpāto diṭṭho”ti vadati. “Na [V 0.0449] passāma, bhante; kāya velāya ahosī”ti [M 0.0457] ca puṭṭho “amhākaṃ caṅkamanavelāyā”ti vatvā “bhūmicālasaddaṃ assutthā”ti pucchati. “Na suṇāma, bhante; kāya velāyā”ti puṭṭho “majjhimayāme amhākaṃ ālambanaphalakaṃ apassāya ṭhitakāle”ti vatvā “mahāobhāso ahosi; so vo diṭṭho”ti pucchati. “Kāya velāya, bhante”ti ca vutte “mayhaṃ caṅkamamhā otaraṇakāle”ti vadati. Manussā [P 0.0475] ‘amhākaṃ thero tīsupi yāmesu caṅkameyeva hoti; natthi ayyena sadiso āraddhavīriyo’ti pasannā sakkāraṃ karonti.

Even a lazy one, sitting among his supporters, says, 'Lay devotees, did you see a shooting star?' When asked, 'We did not see it, venerable sir; at what time was it?' he replies, 'During our walking meditation,' and then asks, 'Did you hear the sound of an earthquake?' When they say, 'We did not hear it, venerable sir; at what time was it?' he answers, 'During the middle watch of the night, while standing leaning against the support plank,' and then asks, 'There was a great light; did you see it?' When they ask, 'At what time, venerable sir?' he says, 'When I was descending from my walking meditation.' Pleased, people think, 'Our elder is always on the walking path during all three watches of the night; there is no one as energetic as him,' and they make offerings.

Muṭṭhassatīpi upaṭṭhākamajjhe nisinno “mayā asukakāle nāma dīghanikāyo uggahito, asukakāle majjhimo, saṃyuttako, aṅguttariko; antarā olokanaṃ nāma natthi, icchiticchataṭṭhāne mukhāruḷhova tanti āgacchati; ime panaññe bhikkhū eḷakā viya mukhaṃ phandāpentā viharantī”ti vadati. Manussā ‘natthi ayyena sadiso upaṭṭhitasatī’ti pasannā sakkāraṃ karonti.

Even one of confused mindfulness, sitting among his supporters, says, 'At such and such a time, I learned the Dīgha Nikāya, at such a time the Majjhima, the Saṃyutta, the Aṅguttara; there is no need to look it up in between, the text comes to my mouth just as I wish, wherever I wish; but these other monks live twitching their faces like goats.' Pleased, people think, 'There is no one like the venerable one with established mindfulness,' and they make offerings.

Asamāhitopi upaṭṭhākānaṃ sammukhe aṭṭhakathācariye pañhaṃ pucchati – ‘kasiṇaṃ nāma kathaṃ bhāveti? Kittakena nimittaṃ uppannaṃ nāma hoti? Kittakena upacāro? Kittakena appanā? Paṭhamassa jhānassa kati aṅgāni? Dutiyassa tatiyassa catutthassa jhānassa kati aṅgāni”ti pucchati. Tehi attano uggahitānurūpena kathitakāle sitaṃ katvā ‘kiṃ, āvuso, evaṃ na hosī’ti vutte ‘vaṭṭati, bhante’ti attano samāpattilābhitaṃ sūceti. Manussā ‘samāpattilābhī ayyo’ti pasannā sakkāraṃ karonti.

Even one who is not concentrated asks the commentary teachers questions in the presence of his supporters: “How does one develop a kasiṇa? At what point is the sign said to have arisen? At what point is there access concentration? At what point is there absorption? How many factors does the first jhāna have? How many factors do the second, third, and fourth jhānas have?” When they answer according to what they have learned, he smiles. And when they say, “What, friend, is it not so?” he says, “It is fitting, venerable sir,” thereby indicating his own attainment of absorption. People, being pleased, think, “This venerable one has attained absorption,” and pay him homage.

Duppaññopi upaṭṭhākānaṃ majjhe nisinno ‘majjhimanikāye me pañcattayaṃ olokentassa sahiddhiyāva maggo āgato. Pariyatti nāma amhākaṃ na dukkarā. Pariyattivāvaṭo pana dukkhato na muccatīti pariyattiṃ vissajjayimhā’tiādīni vadanto attano mahāpaññataṃ dīpeti. Evaṃ vadanto panassa sāsane pahāraṃ deti. Iminā sadiso mahācoro nāma natthi. Na hi pariyattidharo dukkhato na muccatīti. Akhīṇāsavopi gāmadārake disvā ‘tumhākaṃ mātāpitaro amhe kiṃ vadantī”ti? “Arahāti [M 0.0458] vadanti, bhante”ti. ‘Yāva chekā gahapatikā, na sakkā vañcetu’nti attano khīṇāsavabhāvaṃ dīpeti.

Even one who is of little wisdom, sitting among his supporters, declares such things as: “While I was looking at the Pañcattaya Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya, the path came to me along with psychic power. The study of the scriptures is not difficult for us. But one devoted to study is not freed from suffering, so we have abandoned study,” thereby revealing his own great wisdom. By speaking thus, he strikes a blow at the Teaching. There is no greater thief than this one. For it is not so that one who upholds the scriptures is not freed from suffering. Even one whose taints are not destroyed, upon seeing village children, asks: “What do your parents say about us?” “They say you are an Arahant, venerable sir.” “How clever these householders are! They cannot be deceived,” he says, thereby indicating his own state as one whose taints are destroyed.

Aññepi [V 0.0450] cettha cāṭiarahantapārohaarahantādayo veditabbā – eko kira kuhako antogabbhe cāṭiṃ nikhaṇitvā manussānaṃ āgamanakāle pavisati. Manussā ‘kahaṃ thero’ti pucchanti. ‘Antogabbhe’ti ca vutte pavisitvā vicinantāpi adisvā [P 0.0476] nikkhamitvā ‘natthi thero’ti vadanti. ‘Antogabbheyeva thero’ti ca vutte puna pavisanti. Thero cāṭito nikkhamitvā pīṭhe nisinno hoti. Tato tehi ‘mayaṃ, bhante, pubbe adisvā nikkhantā, kahaṃ tumhe gatatthā”ti vutte ‘samaṇā nāma attano icchiticchitaṭṭhānaṃ gacchantī’ti vacanena attano khīṇāsavabhāvaṃ dīpeti.

Others here, such as the pot-arahant, the branch-arahant, and the like, should be understood. It is said that a certain deceiver buried a large pot in an inner chamber and would enter it when people came. People would ask, “Where is the elder?” When told, “In the inner chamber,” they would enter and search, but not seeing him, would come out and say, “The elder is not here.” When told again, “The elder is indeed in the inner chamber,” they would enter once more. The elder would then emerge from the pot and be sitting on a seat. When they asked, “Venerable sir, earlier we did not see you and left—where had you gone?” he would reply, “Ascetics go wherever they wish,” thereby indicating his own state as one whose taints are destroyed.

Aparopi kuhako ekasmiṃ pabbate paṇṇasālāyaṃ vasati. Paṇṇasālāya ca pacchato papātaṭṭhāne eko kacchakarukkho atthi. Tassa pāroho gantvā parabhāge bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhito. Manussā maggenāgantvā nimantenti. So pattacīvaramādāya pārohena otaritvā gāmadvāre attānaṃ dasseti. Tato manussehi pacchā āgantvā ‘katarena maggena āgatattha, bhante’ti puṭṭho ‘samaṇānaṃ āgatamaggo nāma pucchituṃ na vaṭṭati, attano icchiticchitaṭṭhāneneva āgacchantī’ti vacanena khīṇāsavabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Taṃ pana kuhakaṃ eko viddhakaṇṇo ñatvā ‘pariggahessāmi na’nti ekadivasaṃ pārohena otarantaṃ disvā pacchato chinditvā appamattakena ṭhapesi. So ‘pārohato otarissāmī’ti ‘ṭha’nti patito, mattikā patto bhijji. So ‘ñātomhī’ti nikkhamitvā palāyi. Pāpicchassa bhāvo pāpicchatā. Lakkhaṇato pana asantaguṇasambhāvanatā, paṭiggahaṇe ca amattaññutā; etaṃ pāpicchatālakkhaṇanti veditabbaṃ.

Another deceiver lived in a leaf-hut on a certain mountain. Behind the leaf-hut, at the edge of a precipice, there was a kacchaka tree. A branch of it extended and was rooted in the ground on the other side. People coming along the path would invite him for a meal. Taking his bowl and robe, he would descend by the branch and show himself at the village gate. Later, when people who had arrived after him asked, “By which path did you come, venerable sir?” he would reply, “It is not proper to ask ascetics about the path they came by; they come by whatever way they wish.” With these words, he indicated his own state as one whose taints are destroyed. However, a shrewd man, knowing him to be a fraud, thought, “I will catch him.” One day, seeing him descending by the branch, he cut it from behind, leaving only a little attached. He, thinking, “I will descend by the branch,” fell with a thud. His earthen bowl shattered. Realizing, “I am found out!” he departed and fled. The state of one with evil desires is evil desire. Its characteristic, however, is the affecting of non-existent virtues and immoderation in receiving; this should be understood as the characteristic of evil desire.

852. Siṅganiddese vijjhanaṭṭhena siṅgaṃ; nāgarikabhāvasaṅkhātassa kilesasiṅgassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Siṅgārabhāvo siṅgāratā, siṅgārakaraṇākāro vā. Caturabhāvo caturatā. Tathā cāturiyaṃ. Parikkhatabhāvo parikkhatatā; parikhaṇitvā ṭhapitasseva daḷhasiṅgārabhāvassetaṃ nāmaṃ[M 0.0459]. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Evaṃ sabbehipi padehi kilesasiṅgāratāva kathitā.

852. In the explanation of ‘siṅga’ (horn), it is a ‘horn’ in the sense of piercing; this is a name for the ‘horn of defilements,’ which is designated as sophistication. The state of being adorned is ‘siṅgāratā’ (adornment), or it is the manner of creating adornment. The state of being clever is ‘caturatā’ (cleverness). Likewise, ‘cāturiyaṃ’ (skillfulness). The state of being fortified is ‘parikkhatatā’ (fortification); this is a name for the state of firm adornment, as if established after digging a trench around it. The other term is a synonym for that. Thus, by all these terms, only the adornment of the defilements is described.

853. Tintiṇaniddese tintiṇanti khīyanaṃ. Tintiṇāyanākāro tintiṇāyanā. Tintiṇena ayitassa tintiṇasamaṅgino bhāvo tintiṇāyitattaṃ. Lolupabhāvo loluppaṃ. Itare dve [V 0.0451] ākārabhāvaniddesā. Pucchañjikatāti [P 0.0477] lābhalabhanakaṭṭhāne vedhanākampanā nīcavuttitā. Sādhukamyatāti paṇītapaṇītānaṃ patthanā. Evaṃ sabbehipi padehi suvānadoṇiyaṃ kañjiyaṃ pivanakasunakhassa aññaṃ sunakhaṃ disvā bhubhukkaraṇaṃ viya ‘tava santakaṃ, mama santaka’nti kilesavasena khīyanākāro kathito.

853. In the explanation of ‘tintiṇa,’ ‘tintiṇa’ means pining. The manner of pining is ‘tintiṇāyanā.’ The state of one who is endowed with pining, who has pined, is ‘tintiṇāyitattaṃ.’ The state of greed is ‘loluppaṃ.’ The other two terms are explanations of manner and state. ‘Pucchañjikatā’ is agitation and trembling in a place where gain is to be had, and it is base conduct. ‘Sādhukamyatā’ is the desire for the finest things. Thus, by all these terms is described the manner of pining that arises through the defilements, which is like a dog drinking sour gruel from a dog's trough that, on seeing another dog, barks possessively over what is ‘yours’ and ‘mine’.

854. Cāpalyaniddese ākoṭitapaccākoṭitabhāvādīhi cīvarassa maṇḍanā cīvaramaṇḍanā. Maṇivaṇṇacchavikaraṇādīhi pattassa maṇḍanā pattamaṇḍanā. Cittakammādīhi puggalikasenāsanassa maṇḍanā senāsanamaṇḍanā. Imassa vā pūtikāyassāti imassa manussasarīrassa. Yathā hi tadahujātopi siṅgālo jarasiṅgālotveva ūruppamāṇāpi ca gaḷocilatā pūtilatātveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati, evaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇopi manussakāyo pūtikāyotveva vuccati. Tassa antarantarā rattavaṇṇapaṇḍuvaṇṇādīhi nivāsanapārupanādīhi sajjanā maṇḍanā nāma. Bāhirānaṃ vā parikkhārānanti ṭhapetvā pattacīvaraṃ sesaparikkhārānaṃ; athavā yā esā cīvaramaṇḍanā pattamaṇḍanāti vuttā, sā tehi vā parikkhārehi kāyassa maṇḍanā tesaṃ vā bāhiraparikkhārānaṃ maṇḍetvā ṭhapanavasena maṇḍanāti evamettha attho veditabbo. Maṇḍanā vibhūsanāti ettha ūnaṭṭhānassa pūraṇavasena maṇḍanā, chavirāgādivasena vibhūsanāti veditabbā. Keḷanāti kīḷanā. Parikeḷanāti parikīḷanā. Giddhikatāti gedhayuttatā. Giddhikattanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Capalabhāvo capalatā. Tathā cāpalyaṃ. Idaṃ vuccatīti idaṃ cāpalyaṃ nāma vuccati, yena samannāgato puggalo vassasatikopi samāno tadahujātadārako viya hoti.

854. In the explanation of frivolity, the adornment of robes by such means as beating and re-beating them is 'robe adornment.' The adornment of the bowl by such means as giving it a jewel-like color and finish is 'bowl adornment.' The adornment of one's personal lodging with decorative work and so on is 'lodging adornment.' 'Of this foul body': this means of this human body. For just as a jackal, even one born that very day, is reckoned a decrepit jackal, and a guḷūcī creeper, even one as thick as a thigh, is reckoned a rotting creeper, so too a human body, even one with a golden complexion, is called a foul body. The adorning of it from time to to time with undergarments and outer robes of red, yellow, and other colors is what is called 'adornment.' 'Or of external requisites': this means of the remaining requisites apart from the bowl and robes. Alternatively, the 'robe adornment' and 'bowl adornment' already mentioned should be understood here as either the adornment of the body with those requisites, or as the adornment of those external requisites by way of decorating and arranging them. 'Adornment and embellishment': here, 'adornment' should be understood as filling a deficiency, and 'embellishment' as beautifying by means of cosmetics and so on. 'Play' (keḷanā) is amusement (kīḷanā). 'Diversion' (parikeḷanā) is dalliance (parikīḷanā). 'Greediness' (giddhikatā) is being possessed by greed. 'Greed' (giddhikatta) is a synonym for that. 'Frivolity' (capalatā) is the state of being frivolous. Likewise for 'frivolity' (cāpalya). 'This is called': this is what is called frivolity, endowed with which a person, even if a hundred years old, is like a newly born child.

855. Asabhāgavuttiniddese vippaṭikūlaggāhitāti ananulomaggāhitā. Vipaccanīkasātatāti [P 0.0478] vipaccanīkena paṭiviruddhakaraṇena sukhāyanā. Anādarabhāvo anādariyaṃ. Tathā anādariyatā. Agāravassa bhāvo agāravatā. Jeṭṭhakabhāvassa akaraṇaṃ appatissavatā. Ayaṃ [M 0.0460] vuccatīti ayaṃ asabhāgavutti nāma vuccati; visabhāgajīvikatāti attho; yāya samannāgato puggalo mātaraṃ pitaraṃ vā gilānaṃ paṭivattitvāpi na oloketi; pitusantakassa kāraṇā mātarā saddhiṃ, mātusantakassa kāraṇā pitarā saddhiṃ kalahaṃ karoti; visabhāgajīvitaṃ jīvati, mātāpitūnaṃ santakassa kāraṇā jeṭṭhena vā kaniṭṭhena vā bhātarā saddhiṃ kalahaṃ karoti, nillajjavacanaṃ vadati, ācariyassa vā upajjhāyassa vā vattapaṭivattaṃ na karoti, gilānaṃ na upaṭṭhāti, buddhassa bhagavato cetiyadassanaṭṭhāne uccāraṃ vā passāvaṃ vā karoti, kheḷampi [V 0.0452] siṅghāṇikampi chaḍḍeti, chattaṃ dhāreti, upāhanā āruyha gacchati, buddhasāvakesu na lajjati, saṅghe cittīkāraṃ na karoti, mātimattapitimattādīsu garuṭṭhānīyesu hirottappaṃ na paccupaṭṭhāpeti. Tassevaṃ pavattamānassa sabbā pesā kiriyā mātarītiādīsupi vatthūsu asabhāgavuttitā nāma hoti.

855. In the explanation of uncongenial conduct, 'taking a contrary course' means taking a course that is not compliant. 'Delighting in opposition' means taking pleasure in hostile and contrary action. 'Disrespect' (anādariyaṃ) is the state of being disrespectful. Likewise for 'disrespectfulness' (anādariyatā). 'Irreverence' (agāravatā) is the state of being irreverent. 'Lack of deference' (appatissavatā) is not paying respect to seniority. 'This is called': this is what is called uncongenial conduct; the meaning is living a discordant life. A person endowed with this does not even look back at his sick mother or father. He quarrels with his mother for the sake of his father's property, and with his father for the sake of his mother's property. He lives a discordant life. He quarrels with his elder or younger brother for the sake of his parents' property. He speaks shameless words. He does not perform his duties and services for his teacher or preceptor. He does not attend to the sick. At a place for viewing a shrine of the Blessed One, the Buddha, he defecates or urinates, or spits and blows his nose. He carries an umbrella and walks about wearing sandals. He is not ashamed before the Buddha's disciples. He shows no respect for the Sangha. He does not establish moral shame and moral dread toward those in a position of respect, such as his mother and father. For one who behaves in this way, all such actions in regard to his mother and others are called 'uncongenial conduct.'

856. Aratiniddese pantesūti dūresu vivittesu vā. Adhikusalesūti samathavipassanādhammesu. Aratīti ratipaṭikkhepo. Aratitāti aramaṇākāro. Anabhiratīti anabhiratabhāvo. Anabhiramaṇāti anabhiramaṇākāro. Ukkaṇṭhitāti ukkaṇṭhanākāro. Paritassitāti ukkaṇṭhanavaseneva paritassanā.

856. In the explanation of discontent: 'in remote places' means in distant or secluded places. 'In higher wholesome states' refers to the states of serenity and insight. 'Discontent' (arati) is the rejection of delight. 'Discontentedness' (aratitā) is the manner of not delighting. 'Not taking delight' (anabhirati) is the state of not taking delight. 'Not delighting' (anabhiramaṇā) is the manner of not delighting. 'Dissatisfaction' (ukkaṇṭhitā) is the manner of being dissatisfied. 'Anxiety' (paritassitā) is trembling on account of that dissatisfaction.

857. Tandīniddese tandīti jātiālasiyaṃ. Tandiyanāti tandiyanākāro. Tandimanakatāti tandiyā abhibhūtacittatā. Alasassa bhāvo ālasyaṃ. Ālasyāyanākāro ālasyāyanā. Alasyāyitassa bhāvo ālasyāyitattaṃ. Iti sabbehipi imehi padehi kilesavasena kāyālasiyaṃ kathitaṃ.

857. In the explanation of lethargy: 'lethargy' (tandī) is congenital laziness. 'Being lethargic' (tandiyanā) is the manner of being lethargic. 'Lethargic-mindedness' (tandimanakatā) is the mind being overwhelmed by lethargy. 'Laziness' (ālasya) is the state of being lazy. 'Being lazy' (ālasyāyanā) is the manner of being lazy. 'The state of having been lazy' (ālasyāyitatta) is the state of one who is lazy. Thus by all these terms bodily laziness due to the defilements is described.

858. Vijambhitāniddese jambhanāti phandanā. Punappunaṃ jambhanā vijambhanā. Ānamanāti [P 0.0479] purato namanā. Vinamanāti pacchato namanā. Sannamanāti samantato namanā. Paṇamanāti yathā hi tantato uṭṭhitapesakāro kismiñcideva gahetvā ujukaṃ kāyaṃ ussāpeti, evaṃ kāyassa uddhaṃ ṭhapanā. Byādhiyakanti uppannabyādhitā. Iti sabbehipi imehi padehi kilesavasena kāyaphandanameva kathitaṃ.

858. In the explanation of stretching: 'yawning' (jambhanā) is a tremor. 'Stretching' (vijambhanā) is repeated yawning. 'Bending forward' (ānamanā) is bending to the front. 'Bending back' (vinamanā) is bending to the back. 'Bending around' (sannamanā) is bending all around. 'Straightening up' (paṇamanā) is the raising of the body upright, just as a weaver who has risen from his loom takes hold of something and raises his body straight. 'Sickness' (byādhiyaka) is the state of having fallen ill. Thus by all these terms is described nothing but bodily movement due to the defilements.

859. Bhattasammadaniddese [M 0.0461] bhuttāvissāti bhuttavato. Bhattamucchāti bhattagelaññaṃ; balavabhattena hi mucchāpatto viya hoti. Bhattakilamathoti bhattena kilantabhāvo. Bhattapariḷāhoti bhattadaratho. Tasmiñhi samaye pariḷāhuppattiyā upahatindriyo hoti, kāyo jīrati. Kāyaduṭṭhullanti bhattaṃ nissāya kāyassa akammaññatā.

859. In the explanation of drowsiness after a meal: 'of one who has eaten' (bhuttāvissa) means of one who has eaten (bhuttavato). 'Stupor from food' (bhattamucchā) is sickness from food; for by a heavy meal one becomes as if fallen into a stupor. 'Fatigue from food' (bhattakilamatho) is the state of being fatigued by food. 'Burning from food' (bhattapariḷāho) is feverishness from food. For at that time, with the arising of a burning sensation, one's faculties are impaired and the body wastes away. 'Bodily grossness' (kāyaduṭṭhulla) is the body's unwieldiness on account of the meal.

860. Cetaso līnattaniddeso heṭṭhā dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttatthoyeva. Imehi pana sabbehipi padehi kilesavasena cittassa gilānākāro kathitoti veditabbo.

860. The explanation of the mind's sluggishness has the same meaning as was stated previously in the commentary to the Dhammasaṅganī. It should be understood, however, that by all these terms the sickly state of the mind due to the defilements is described.

861. Kuhanāniddese [V 0.0453] lābhasakkārasilokasannissitassāti lābhañca sakkārañca kittisaddañca nissitassa, patthayantassāti attho. Pāpicchassāti asantaguṇadīpanakāmassa. Icchāpakatassāti icchāya apakatassa, upaddutassāti attho.

861. In the explanation of scheming: 'of one who relies on gain, honor, and fame' means of one who relies on gain, honor, and the sound of fame; the meaning is 'of one who desires them.' 'Of one with evil desires' means of one who desires to display qualities he does not possess. 'Of one overcome by his wishes' means of one ruined by desire; the meaning is 'of one who is afflicted.'

Ito paraṃ yasmā paccayapaṭisevana sāmantajappanairiyāpathasannissitavasena mahāniddese tividhaṃ kuhanavatthu āgataṃ, tasmā tividhampi taṃ dassetuṃ paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātena vāti evamādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha cīvarādīhi nimantitassa tadatthikasseva sato pāpicchataṃ nissāya paṭikkhipanena, te ca gahapatike attani suppatiṭṭhitasaddhe ñatvā puna tesaṃ ‘aho ayyo appiccho, na kiñci paṭiggaṇhituṃ icchati, suladdhaṃ vata no assa sace appamattakaṃ kiñci paṭiggaṇheyyā’ti nānāvidhehi upāyehi paṇītāni cīvarādīni upanentānaṃ tadanuggahakāmataṃyeva āvikatvā paṭiggahaṇena ca tato pabhuti asītisakaṭabhārehi upanāmanahetubhūtaṃ vimhāpanaṃ paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthūti veditabbaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ mahāniddese (mahāni. 87) –

Hereafter, because in the Mahāniddesa the threefold basis of scheming is presented by way of reliance on the use of requisites, suggestive talk, and deportment, to show it in its threefold aspect, the passage beginning 'by what is reckoned as the use of requisites' is introduced. Herein, when one who has been invited with robes and other requisites, though he desires them, refuses them out of evil desire; and when, having known that those householders have well-established faith in him, they bring him fine robes and other things by various means, saying: 'Oh, the venerable sir has few wishes! He does not want to accept anything. It would be a great gain for us if he would accept just a little!'; then, by accepting them while making it appear that he is doing so only out of a desire to favor them, he causes an astonishment that from then on becomes the reason for their bringing him eighty cartloads of goods. This should be understood as the basis of scheming reckoned as 'the use of requisites.' This too is stated in the Mahāniddesa (MNid 87):

“Katamaṃ paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthu? Idha gahapatikā bhikkhuṃ nimantenti [P 0.0480] cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārehi. So pāpiccho icchāpakato atthiko cīvara [M 0.0462]…pe… parikkhārānaṃ bhiyyokamyataṃ upādāya cīvaraṃ paccakkhāti, piṇḍapātaṃ paccakkhāti, senāsanaṃ paccakkhāti, gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ paccakkhāti. So evamāha – “kiṃ samaṇassa mahagghena cīvarena? Etaṃ sāruppaṃ yaṃ samaṇo susānā vā saṅkārakūṭā vā pāpaṇikā vā nantakāni uccinitvā saṅghāṭiṃ katvā dhāreyya. Kiṃ samaṇassa mahagghena piṇḍapātena? Etaṃ sāruppaṃ yaṃ samaṇo uñchācariyāya piṇḍiyālopena jīvikaṃ kappeyya. Kiṃ samaṇassa mahagghena senāsanena? Etaṃ sāruppaṃ yaṃ samaṇo rukkhamūliko vā assa sosāniko vā abbhokāsiko vā. Kiṃ samaṇassa mahagghena gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārena? Etaṃ sāruppaṃ yaṃ samaṇo pūtimuttena vā harītakīkhaṇḍena vā osadhaṃ kareyyāti. Tadupādāya lūkhaṃ cīvaraṃ dhāreti, lūkhaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjati, lūkhaṃ senāsanaṃ paṭisevati, lūkhaṃ gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ paṭisevati. Tamenaṃ gahapatikā evaṃ jānanti – ‘ayaṃ samaṇo [V 0.0454] appiccho santuṭṭho pavivitto asaṃsaṭṭho āraddhavīriyo dhutavādo’ti bhiyyo bhiyyo nimantenti cīvara…pe… parikkhārehi. So evamāha – ‘tiṇṇaṃ sammukhībhāvā saddho kulaputto bahuṃ puññaṃ pasavati – saddhāya sammukhībhāvā saddho kulaputto bahuṃ puññaṃ pasavati, deyyadhammassa…pe… dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ sammukhībhāvā saddho kulaputto bahuṃ puññaṃ pasavati. Tumhākañcevāyaṃ saddhā atthi, deyyadhammo ca saṃvijjati, ahañca paṭiggāhako. Sacāhaṃ na paṭiggahessāmi, evaṃ tumhe puññena paribāhirā bhavissatha; na mayhaṃ iminā attho, apica tumhākaṃ eva anukampāya paṭiggaṇhāmī’ti. Tadupādāya bahumpi cīvaraṃ paṭiggaṇhāti, bahumpi piṇḍapātaṃ…pe… bhesajjaparikkhāraṃ paṭiggaṇhāti. Yā evarūpā bhākuṭikā bhākuṭiyaṃ kuhanā kuhāyanā kuhitattaṃ – idaṃ vuccati paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthū”ti.

“What is the basis for deceit reckoned as the use of requisites? Here, householders invite a bhikkhu, offering robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites. Being of evil desires, overcome by longing, and eager for more robes… and other requisites, he refuses the robes, refuses the almsfood, refuses the lodging, and refuses the medicinal requisites. He says: ‘What need has a recluse for a costly robe? It is fitting for a recluse to gather rags from a charnel ground, a rubbish heap, or a shop, make them into a patched-robe, and wear it. What need has a recluse for fine almsfood? It is fitting for a recluse to maintain himself by gleaning for scraps of almsfood. What need has a recluse for a fine lodging? It is fitting for a recluse to be a tree-root dweller, a charnel-ground dweller, or an open-air dweller. What need has a recluse for costly medicinal requisites? It is fitting for a recluse to make medicine from putrid urine or a piece of myrobalan.’ On that account, he wears coarse robes, consumes coarse almsfood, uses a coarse lodging, and uses coarse medicinal requisites. The householders come to know him thus: ‘This recluse is of few wishes, content, secluded, unsociable, energetic, and an exponent of the ascetic practices.’ They invite him again and again, offering robes… and other requisites. He then says: ‘When three things are present, a faithful clansman generates much merit. When faith is present, a faithful clansman generates much merit; when a gift is present… and when worthy recipients are present, a faithful clansman generates much merit. You have this faith, and the gift is available, and I am the recipient. If I do not accept, you will be deprived of merit. I have no need for this, but I accept it out of compassion for you.’ On that account, he accepts many robes, much almsfood… and medicinal requisites. Whatever such frowning, scowling, hypocrisy, scheming, and deceitfulness there is—this is called the basis for deceit reckoned as the use of requisites.”

Pāpicchasseva pana sato uttarimanussadhammādhigamaparidīpanavācāya [P 0.0481] tathā tathā vimhāpanaṃ sāmantajappanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthūti veditabbaṃ. Yathāha – “katamaṃ sāmantajappanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthu[M 0.0463]? Idhekacco pāpiccho icchāpakato sambhāvanādhippāyo ‘evaṃ maṃ jano sambhāvessatī’ti ariyadhammasannissitaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati – ‘yo evarūpaṃ cīvaraṃ dhāreti, so samaṇo mahesakkho’ti bhaṇati; ‘yo evarūpaṃ pattaṃ, lohathālakaṃ, dhamakaraṇaṃ, parisāvanaṃ, kuñcikaṃ, upāhanaṃ, kāyabandhanaṃ, āyogaṃ dhāreti, so samaṇo mahesakkho’ti bhaṇati; ‘yassa evarūpo upajjhāyo, ācariyo, samānupajjhāyo, samānācariyako, mitto sandiṭṭho, sambhatto, sahāyo; yo evarūpe vihāre vasati – aḍḍhayoge, pāsāde, hammiye, guhāyaṃ, leṇe, kuṭiyā, kūṭāgāre, aṭṭe, māḷe, udosite, uddaṇḍe, upaṭṭhānasālāyaṃ, maṇḍape, rukkhamūle vasati, so samaṇo mahesakkho’ti bhaṇati.

Further, for one of evil desires, bewildering others by speech that intimates the attainment of states superior to the human condition should be understood as the basis for deceit reckoned as allusive talk. As it is said: “What is the basis for deceit reckoned as allusive talk? Here, someone of evil desires, overcome by longing and intent on gaining esteem, thinking, ‘In this way people will esteem me,’ utters speech connected with the noble teaching, saying: ‘A recluse who wears such a robe is one of great power.’ He says: ‘A recluse who carries such a bowl, a bronze bowl, a water strainer, a water filter, a key, sandals, a waistband, or a shoulder strap is one of great power.’ He says: ‘A recluse who has such a preceptor, a teacher, a fellow preceptee, a fellow student, a friend, an intimate, a companion, or a comrade; or who dwells in such a dwelling—a half-gabled building, a long-house, a storied building, a cave, a rock shelter, a hut, a gabled house, a watchtower, a hall, a plastered house, a shed, a service hall, a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree—is one of great power.’”

“Atha vā korajikakorajiko bhākuṭikabhākuṭiko kuhakakuhako lapakalapako mukhasambhāvito ‘ayaṃ samaṇo imāsaṃ evarūpānaṃ santānaṃ vihārasamāpattīnaṃ lābhī’ti tādisaṃ gambhīraṃ gūḷhaṃ nipuṇaṃ paṭicchannaṃ lokuttaraṃ suññatāpaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kathaṃ katheti. Yā evarūpā bhākuṭikā bhākuṭiyaṃ kuhanā kuhāyanā kuhitattaṃ – idaṃ vuccati sāmantajappanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthū”ti.

“Or, being peevish and sullen, a hypocrite and a fraud, a talker and a chatterer, smooth-tongued, he gives a talk that is profound, deep, subtle, concealed, supramundane, and connected with emptiness, so that others will think: ‘This recluse is surely a gainer of such peaceful abidings and attainments.’ Whatever such frowning, scowling, hypocrisy, scheming, and deceitfulness there is—this is called the basis for deceit reckoned as allusive talk.”

Pāpicchasseva [V 0.0455] pana sato sambhāvanādhippāyakatena iriyāpathena vimhāpanaṃ iriyāpathasannissitaṃ kuhanavatthūti veditabbaṃ. Yathāha – “katamaṃ iriyāpathasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthu? Idhekacco pāpiccho icchāpakato sambhāvanādhippāyo ‘evaṃ maṃ jano sambhāvessatī’ti gamanaṃ saṇṭhapeti, sayanaṃ saṇṭhapeti, paṇidhāya gacchati, paṇidhāya tiṭṭhati, paṇidhāya nisīdati, paṇidhāya seyyaṃ kappeti, samāhito viya gacchati, samāhito viya tiṭṭhati, nisīdati, seyyaṃ kappeti, āpāthakajjhāyīva hoti. Yā evarūpā iriyāpathassa āṭhapanā ṭhapanā saṇṭhapanā bhākuṭikā bhākuṭiyaṃ kuhanā kuhāyanā kuhitattaṃ – idaṃ vuccati iriyāpathasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthū”ti.

Furthermore, for one of evil desires, bewildering others by means of posture with the aim of gaining esteem should be understood as the basis for deceit connected with posture. As it is said: “What is the basis for deceit reckoned as posture? Here, someone of evil desires, overcome by longing and intent on gaining esteem, thinking, ‘In this way people will esteem me,’ composes his walking, composes his lying down; he walks with deliberation, stands with deliberation, sits with deliberation, lies down with deliberation. He walks as if concentrated, stands as if concentrated, sits as if concentrated, lies down as if concentrated; he appears to be one absorbed in meditation. Whatever such posturing, posing, composing of posture, frowning, scowling, hypocrisy, scheming, and deceitfulness there is—this is called the basis for deceit reckoned as posture.”

Tattha [P 0.0482][M 0.0464] paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātenāti paccayapaṭisevananti evaṃ saṅkhātena paccayapaṭisevanena. Sāmantajappitenāti samīpe bhaṇitena. Iriyāpathassāti catuiriyāpathassa. Āṭhapanāti ādiṭhapanā, ādarena vā ṭhapanā. Ṭhapanāti ṭhapanākāro. Saṇṭhapanāti abhisaṅkharaṇā, pāsādikabhāvakaraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhākuṭikāti padhānapurimaṭṭhitabhāvadassanena bhākuṭikaraṇaṃ, mukhasaṅkocoti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhākuṭikaraṇaṃ sīlamassāti bhākuṭiko; bhākuṭikassa bhāvo bhākuṭiyaṃ. Kuhanāti vimhāpanaṃ, kuhassa āyanā kuhāyanā. Kuhitassa bhāvo kuhitattanti.

Herein, reckoned as the use of requisites means: by the use of requisites thus reckoned. By allusive talk means: by what is spoken nearby. Of posture means: of the four postures. Posturing (āṭhapanā) means initial placing, or placing with care. Posing (ṭhapanā) means the mode of placing. Composing (saṇṭhapanā) means constructing; that is, making oneself appear graceful. Frowning (bhākuṭikā) means making a frown by showing a state of being foremost in striving; that is, a contraction of the face. One whose habit is making a frown is a frowner (bhākuṭiko); the state of a frowner is scowling (bhākuṭiyaṃ). Hypocrisy (kuhanā) is bewildering. The source of hypocrisy is scheming (kuhāyanā). The state of being a hypocrite is deceitfulness (kuhitattaṃ).

862. Lapanāniddese ālapanāti vihāraṃ āgatamanusse disvā kimatthāya bhonto āgatā? Kiṃ bhikkhū nimantetuṃ? Yadi evaṃ gacchatha; ahaṃ pacchato bhikkhū gahetvā āgacchāmī’ti evaṃ āditova lapanā. Atha vā attānaṃ upanetvā ‘ahaṃ tisso, mayi rājā pasanno, mayi asuko ca asuko ca rājamahāmatto pasanno’ti evaṃ attupanāyikā lapanā ālapanā. Lapanāti puṭṭhassa sato vuttappakārameva lapanaṃ. Sallapanāti gahapatikānaṃ ukkaṇṭhane bhītassa okāsaṃ datvā suṭṭhu lapanā. Ullapanāti ‘mahākuṭumbiko, mahānāviko, mahādānapatī’ti evaṃ uddhaṃ katvā lapanā. Samullapanāti sabbatobhāgena uddhaṃ katvā lapanā. Unnahanāti ‘upāsakā, pubbe īdise kāle dānaṃ detha; idāni kiṃ na dethā’ti evaṃ yāva ‘dassāma, bhante, okāsaṃ na labhāmā’tiādīni vadanti tāva uddhaṃ nahanā, veṭhanāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā ucchuhatthaṃ disvā ‘kuto āgatā, upāsakā’ti pucchati. ‘Ucchukhettato, bhante’ti. ‘Kiṃ tattha ucchu madhura’nti? ‘Khāditvā, bhante, jānitabba’nti. ‘Na, upāsakā, bhikkhussa ‘ucchuṃ dethā’ti vattuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti yā evarūpā nibbeṭhentassāpi [P 0.0483] veṭhanakakathā, sā unnahanā[V 0.0456]. Sabbatobhāgena punappunaṃ unnahanā samunnahanā. Ukkācanāti ‘etaṃ kulaṃ maṃyeva jānāti, sace ettha deyyadhammo uppajjati, mayhameva detī’ti evaṃ ukkhipitvā kācanā ukkācanā; uddīpanāti vuttaṃ hoti.

862. In the exposition of talkativeness: Accosting (ālapanā) is when, on seeing people who have come to the monastery, one asks: ‘Sirs, for what purpose have you come? To invite the bhikkhus? If so, you may go; I will bring the bhikkhus and come along behind.’ This is accosting from the start. Or, it is self-promoting talk, presenting oneself by saying: ‘I am Tissa. The king has confidence in me; such and such royal ministers have confidence in me.’ This is also accosting. Talkativeness (lapanā) is the same kind of talk when one is asked a question. Chattering (sallapanā) is speaking well after giving an opening to householders who are discontented or afraid. Lauding (ullapanā) is extolling someone, saying: ‘He is a great family man, a great ship-owner, a great patron of the Sangha.’ Excessive lauding (samullapanā) is extolling someone in every way. Insinuation (unnahanā) is tying them up until they say things like: ‘Lay supporters, you used to give gifts at such a time in the past; why do you not give now?’—‘We will give, venerable sir, but we do not get the chance.’ This is called insinuation or wrapping up (veṭhanā). Or, on seeing someone with sugarcane in hand, one asks: ‘Where have you come from, lay supporter?’ ‘From the sugarcane field, venerable sir.’ ‘Is the sugarcane there sweet?’ ‘One must eat it to know, venerable sir.’ ‘No, lay supporter, it is not proper for a bhikkhu to say, “Give me sugarcane.”’ Such talk that wraps up even while extricating oneself is insinuation. Insinuating repeatedly in every way is excessive insinuation (samunnahanā). Boasting (ukkācanā) is extolling oneself, saying: ‘This family knows only me. If any gift arises there, they give it only to me.’ This is called boasting or making prominent (uddīpanā).

Telakandarikavatthu cettha vattabbaṃ. Dve kira bhikkhū ekaṃ gāmaṃ pavisitvā āsanasālāya nisīditvā ekaṃ kumārikaṃ disvā pakkosiṃsu. Tāya [M 0.0465] āgatāya tatreko ekaṃ pucchi – ‘ayaṃ, bhante, kassa kumārikā’ti? ‘Amhākaṃ upaṭṭhāyikāya telakandarikāya dhītā, āvuso. Imissā mātā mayi gehaṃ gate sappiṃ dadamānā ghaṭeneva deti, ayampi mātā viya ghaṭeneva detī’ti ukkāceti.

Here the story of Telakandarikā should be related. Two bhikkhus, it seems, entered a village and sat down in a rest hall. Seeing a young girl, they called her over. When she approached, one asked the other: “Venerable sir, whose daughter is this?” “Friend, she is the daughter of our supporter, Telakandarikā. When I go to the house, her mother gives me ghee by the potful; this one too, like her mother, gives by the potful,” he boasted.

Sabbatobhāgena punappunaṃ ukkācanā samukkācanā. Anuppiyabhāṇitāti saccānurūpaṃ vā dhammānurūpaṃ vā anapaloketvā punappunaṃ piyabhaṇanameva. Cāṭukamyatāti nīcavuttitā; attānaṃ heṭṭhato ṭhapetvā vattanaṃ. Muggasūpyatāti muggasūpasadisatā. Yathā muggesu paccamānesu kocideva na paccati, avasesā paccanti; evaṃ yassa puggalassa vacane kiñcideva saccaṃ hoti, sesaṃ alikaṃ – ayaṃ puggalo muggasūpyoti vuccati. Tassa bhāvo muggasūpyatā. Pāribhaṭayatāti pāribhaṭayabhāvo. Yo hi kuladārake dhātī viya aṅkena vā khandhena vā paribhaṭati, dhāretīti attho; tassa paribhaṭassa kammaṃ pāribhaṭayaṃ; pāribhaṭayassa bhāvo pāribhaṭayatāti.

Repeated extolling in every way is thorough extolling. Speaking what is pleasing means repeatedly speaking only what is pleasing, without considering what is true or in accordance with the Dhamma. Fawning is base behavior; it is behaving by placing oneself in a lowly position. Being like mung-bean soup means resembling mung-bean soup. For just as when mung beans are being cooked, some do not cook while the rest do, so too, when a certain person speaks, a little of it is true but the rest is false—this person is called 'like mung-bean soup.' The state of this is being like mung-bean soup. Being a toady is the state of being a toady. For one who carries a child of a good family on the hip or shoulder like a nurse—'supports' is the meaning—the action of that toady is toadyism; the state of being a toady is toadyism.

863. Nemittikatāniddese nimittanti yaṃkiñci paresaṃ paccayadānasaṃyojanakaṃ kāyavacīkammaṃ. Nimittakammanti nimittassa karaṇakosallaṃ.

863. In the explanation of making signs: a 'sign' is any bodily or verbal action connected with the giving of requisites by others. 'The act of making a sign' is skill in making a sign.

Tatridaṃ vatthu – eko kira piṇḍapātiko upaṭṭhākakammārassa gehadvāraṃ gantvā ‘kiṃ bhante’ti pucchito cīvarantarena hatthaṃ nīharitvā [P 0.0484] vāsipaharaṇākāraṃ akāsi. Kammāro ‘sallakkhitaṃ me, bhante’ti vāsiṃ katvā adāsi. Obhāsoti paccayapaṭisaṃyuttakathā. Obhāsakammanti vacchakapālake disvā ‘kiṃ ime vacchā khīragovacchā, takkagovacchā’ti pucchitvā ‘khīragovacchā, bhante’ti vutte ‘na khīragovacchā, yadi khīragovacchā siyuṃ bhikkhūpi khīraṃ labheyyu’nti evamādinā nayena tesaṃ dārakānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ nivedetvā khīradāpanādikaṃ obhāsakaraṇaṃ. Sāmantajappāti samīpaṃ katvā jappanaṃ.

Here is the story: It is said that a certain alms-goer went to the door of his supporter, a blacksmith, and when asked, 'What is it, venerable sir?' he stretched out his hand from under the edge of his robe and made a gesture as if striking with an adze. The blacksmith, thinking, 'I have understood, venerable sir,' made an adze and gave it to him. 'Insinuation' is talk connected with requisites. 'The act of insinuating' is, for example, seeing some calf-herds and asking: 'Are these calves milk-fed or buttermilk-fed?' When they reply, 'They are milk-fed, venerable sir,' one says: 'They are not milk-fed. If they were milk-fed, the bhikkhus would get milk.' By informing the parents of those children in this way, causing them to give milk and so on, this is the act of making an insinuation. 'Muttering nearby' is muttering after drawing near.

Jātakabhāṇakavatthu [V 0.0457] cettha kathetabbaṃ. Eko kira jātakabhāṇakatthero bhuñjitukāmo upaṭṭhāyikāya gehaṃ pavisitvā nisīdi. Sā adātukāmā ‘taṇḍulā natthī’ti bhaṇantī taṇḍule āharitukāmā viya paṭivissakagharaṃ gatā. Bhikkhu antogabbhaṃ pavisitvā olokento kavāṭakoṇe [M 0.0466] ucchuṃ, bhājane guḷaṃ, piṭake loṇamacchaphālaṃ, kumbhiyaṃ taṇḍule, ghaṭe ghataṃ disvā nikkhamitvā nisīdi. Gharaṇī ‘taṇḍulaṃ nālattha’nti āgatā. Thero ‘upāsike, ajja bhikkhā na sampajjissatī’ti paṭikacceva nimittaṃ addasa’nti āha. ‘Kiṃ, bhante’ti? ‘Kavāṭakoṇe nikkhittaṃ ucchuṃ viya sappaṃ addasaṃ; ‘taṃ paharissāmī’ti olokento bhājane ṭhapitaṃ guḷapiṇḍaṃ viya pāsāṇaṃ leḍḍukena; pahaṭena sappena kataṃ, piṭake nikkhittaloṇamacchaphālasadisaṃ, phaṇaṃ; tassa taṃ leḍḍuṃ ḍaṃsitukāmassa, kumbhiyā taṇḍulasadise dante; athassa kupitassa, ghaṭe pakkhittaghatasadisaṃ, mukhato nikkhamantaṃ visamissakaṃ kheḷa’nti. Sā ‘na sakkā muṇḍakaṃ vañcetu’nti ucchuṃ datvā odanaṃ pacitvā ghataguḷamacchehi saddhiṃ adāsīti. Evaṃ samīpaṃ katvā jappanaṃ sāmantajappāti veditabbaṃ. Parikathāti yathā taṃ labhati tathā parivattetvā parivattetvā kathanaṃ.

Here the story of the Jātaka reciter should be told. It is said that a certain elder who was a Jātaka reciter, wishing to eat, entered his female supporter's house and sat down. She, being unwilling to give, said, 'There is no rice,' and went to a neighbor's house as if to fetch some. The bhikkhu entered the inner chamber and, looking around, saw sugarcane in a corner by the door, jaggery in a bowl, a slice of salt-fish in a basket, rice in a pot, and ghee in a jar. Having seen this, he came out and sat down. The housewife returned, saying, 'I could not get any rice.' The elder said: 'Lay follower, today I will not get any almsfood; I saw an omen just now.' 'What was it, venerable sir?' 'I saw a snake like the sugarcane placed in the corner of the door. As I was looking, thinking, "I will strike it with a clod," I saw a stone like the lump of jaggery placed in the bowl; the hood made by the snake when struck, which resembled the slice of salt-fish placed in the basket; its teeth, as it wished to bite that clod, which resembled the rice in the pot; and then, as it became angry, the venom-mixed spittle coming from its mouth, which resembled the ghee put in the jar.' She, thinking, 'It is not possible to deceive this shaveling,' gave him the sugarcane, cooked the rice, and served it to him with ghee, jaggery, and fish. Thus, muttering after drawing near should be understood as 'muttering nearby.' 'Talking around' is to talk again and again in a roundabout way so that one obtains something.

864. Nippesikatāniddese akkosanāti dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosanā. Vambhanāti paribhavitvā kathanaṃ. Garahanāti [P 0.0485] ‘assaddho appasanno’tiādinā nayena dosāropanā. Ukkhepanāti ‘mā etaṃ ettha kathethā’ti vācāya ukkhipanaṃ. Sabbatobhāgena savatthukaṃ sahetukaṃ katvā ukkhepanā samukkhepanā. Athavā adentaṃ ‘aho dānapatī’ti evaṃ ukkhipanaṃ ukkhepanā. ‘Mahādānapatī’ti evaṃ suṭṭhu ukkhepanā samukkhepanā. Khipanāti ‘kiṃ imassa jīvitaṃ bījabhojino’ti evaṃ uppaṇḍanā. Saṅkhipanāti ‘kiṃ imaṃ adāyakoti bhaṇatha yo niccakālaṃ sabbesampi natthīti vacanaṃ detī’ti evaṃ suṭṭhutaraṃ uppaṇḍanā. Pāpanāti adāyakattassa avaṇṇassa vā pāpanaṃ. Sabbatobhāgena pāpanā sampāpanā. Avaṇṇahārikāti ‘evaṃ me avaṇṇabhayāpi dassatī’ti gehato gehaṃ, gāmato gāmaṃ, janapadato janapadaṃ avaṇṇaharaṇaṃ. Parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatāti purato madhuraṃ bhaṇitvā parammukhe avaṇṇabhāsitā. Esā hi abhimukhaṃ oloketuṃ asakkontassa parammukhānaṃ piṭṭhimaṃsakhādanaṃ viya hoti. Tasmā parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatāti vuttā. Ayaṃ vuccati nippesikatāti ayaṃ yasmā veḷupesikā viya abbhaṅgaṃ parassa guṇaṃ nippeseti nipuñchati, yasmā vā gandhajātaṃ nipisitvā gandhamagganā viya [V 0.0458] paraguṇe [M 0.0467] nipisitvā vicuṇṇetvā esā lābhamagganā hoti, tasmā nippesikatāti vuccatīti.

864. In the explanation of crushing: 'Abuse' is reviling by means of the ten grounds for reviling. 'Scorning' is speaking contemptuously. 'Reproach' is ascribing faults in such ways as, 'He is faithless, without confidence.' 'Uplifting' is verbally elevating someone, saying, 'Do not say that here.' 'Thorough uplifting' is uplifting someone in every way, with reason and cause. Alternatively, 'uplifting' is extolling one who does not give, saying, 'Oh, what a donor!' 'Thorough uplifting' is extolling someone well, saying, 'What a great donor!' 'Derision' is taunting, as in, 'What is the life of this seed-eater?' 'Thorough derision' is taunting even more, as in, 'Why do you call him a non-giver, who always gives the reply "I have nothing" to everyone?' 'Conveying' is conveying another's non-giving or disrepute. 'Thorough conveying' is conveying it in every way. 'Carrying disrepute' is carrying disrepute from house to house, from village to village, from country to country, thinking: 'In this way he will give to me even out of fear of disrepute.' 'Backbiting' is speaking sweetly to one's face but speaking ill behind one's back. For this is like eating the back-flesh of those one is unable to look in the face. Therefore it is called 'backbiting.' This is called 'crushing' because, like a bamboo sliver, it grinds and wipes away another's unblemished virtue; or because, like one who seeks perfume by grinding fragrant substances, this is a seeking of gain by grinding and crushing another's virtues. Therefore it is called 'crushing'.

865. Lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatāniddese nijigīsanatāti magganā. Ito laddhanti imamhā gehā laddhaṃ. Amutrāti amukamhi gehe. Eṭṭhīti icchanā. Gaveṭṭhīti magganā. Pariyeṭṭhīti punappunaṃ magganā. Ādito paṭṭhāya laddhaṃ laddhaṃ bhikkhaṃ tatra tatra kuladārakānaṃ datvā ante khīrayāguṃ labhitvā gatabhikkhuvatthu cettha kathetabbaṃ. Esanātiādīni eṭṭhītiādīnaṃ vevacanāni, tasmā eṭṭhīti esanā, gaveṭṭhīti gavesanā, pariyeṭṭhīti pariyesanā. Iccevamettha yojanā veditabbā.

865. In the explanation of desiring to obtain gain with gain: 'Desiring to obtain' means seeking. 'Gained from here' means gained from this house. 'There' means in such-and-such a house. 'Wishing' is desiring. 'Seeking' is searching. 'Searching for' is repeatedly searching. Here the story should be told of the bhikkhu who, starting from the beginning, gave whatever almsfood he received to the children of various families here and there, and in the end, having received milk-rice, he departed. 'Searching' and so on are synonyms for 'wishing' and so on. Therefore, 'wishing' is searching (esanā), 'seeking' is searching (gavesanā), and 'searching for' is thorough searching (pariyesanā). Thus the application should be understood here.

866. Seyyamānaniddese [P 0.0486] jātiyāti khattiyabhāvādijātisampattiyā. Gottenāti gotamagottādinā ukkaṭṭhagottena. Kolaputtiyenāti mahākulabhāvena. Vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti vaṇṇasampannasarīratāya. Sarīrañhi pokkharanti vuccati, tassa vaṇṇasampattiyā abhirūpabhāvenāti attho. Dhanenātiādīni uttānatthāneva. Mānaṃ jappetīti etesu yena kenaci vatthunā ‘seyyohamasmī’ti mānaṃ pavatteti karoti.

866. In the explanation of the conceit of superiority: 'By birth' means by the asset of birth, such as being a khattiya. 'By clan' means by a high clan, such as the Gotama clan. 'By family status' means by being of a great family. 'By beauty of complexion' means by having a body endowed with a good complexion. For the body is called a 'lotus' (pokkhara), so the meaning is by being handsome through the asset of its complexion. 'By wealth' and so on have an obvious meaning. 'He generates conceit' means that on the basis of any of these grounds, one produces and makes the conceit, 'I am superior.'

867. Sadisamānaniddese mānaṃ jappetīti etesu yena kenaci vatthunā ‘sadisohamasmī’ti mānaṃ pavatteti. Ayamettha atthato viseso. Pāḷiyaṃ pana nānākaraṇaṃ natthi.

867. In the explanation of the conceit of equality: 'He generates conceit' means that on the basis of any of these grounds, one produces the conceit, 'I am equal.' This is the difference in meaning here. In the Pāli text, however, no distinction is made.

868. Hīnamānaniddese omānaṃ jappetīti heṭṭhāmānaṃ pavatteti. Omānoti lāmako heṭṭhāmāno. Omaññanā omaññitattanti ākārabhāvaniddeso. Hīḷanāti jātiādīhi attajigucchanā. Ohīḷanāti atirekato hīḷanā. Ohīḷitattanti tasseva bhāvaniddeso. Attuññāti attānaṃ hīnaṃ katvā jānanā. Attāvaññāti attānaṃ avajānanā. Attaparibhavoti jātiādisampattināmameva jātāti attānaṃ paribhavitvā maññanā. Evamime tayo mānā puggalaṃ anissāya jātiādivatthuvaseneva kathitā. Tesu ekeko tiṇṇampi seyyasadisahīnānaṃ uppajjati. Tattha ‘seyyohamasmī’ti māno seyyasseva yāthāvamāno, sesānaṃ ayāthāvamāno. ‘Sadisohamasmī’ti [V 0.0459] māno [M 0.0468] sadisasseva yāthāvamāno, sesānaṃ ayāthāvamāno. ‘Hīnohamasmī’ti māno hīnasseva yāthāvamāno, sesānaṃ ayāthāvamāno.

868. In the explanation of inferior conceit: 'He generates inferior conceit' means he produces a low conceit. 'Inferior conceit' is a base, low conceit. 'Belittling' and 'the state of having belittled' is an explanation of its mode and nature. 'Contempt' is self-disgust on account of birth and so on. 'Excessive contempt' is contempt in excess. 'The state of excessive contempt' is an explanation of its nature. 'Self-disparagement' is knowing oneself by making oneself out to be inferior. 'Self-contempt' is despising oneself. 'Self-scorn' is thinking with scorn of oneself thus: 'I am born with only the name of the accomplishment of birth, and so on.' Thus these three kinds of conceit have been explained based on the grounds of birth and so on, without reference to a person. Each of them arises in the superior, the equal, and the inferior. Therein, the conceit 'I am superior' is a conceit in accordance with reality for one who is superior, but not in accordance with reality for the others. The conceit 'I am equal' is a conceit in accordance with reality for one who is equal, but not in accordance with reality for the others. The conceit 'I am inferior' is a conceit in accordance with reality for one who is inferior, but not in accordance with reality for the others.

869. Tattha katamo seyyassa seyyohamasmītiādayo pana nava mānā puggalaṃ nissāya kathitā. Tesu tayo tayo ekekassa uppajjanti. Tattha dahatīti ṭhapeti. Taṃ nissāyāti taṃ seyyato dahanaṃ nissāya. Ettha pana seyyassa seyyohamasmīti māno rājūnañceva pabbajitānañca uppajjati. Rājā hi ‘raṭṭhena vā dhanena vā vāhanehi vā ko mayā sadiso atthī’ti etaṃ mānaṃ karoti. Pabbajitopi ‘sīladhutaṅgādīhi [P 0.0487] ko mayā sadiso atthī’ti etaṃ mānaṃ karoti.

869. Now, the nine conceits, beginning with that of a superior person thinking 'I am superior,' are spoken of in dependence on a person. Of these, three arise for each one. Therein, dahati means 'establishes.' 'In dependence on that' means in dependence on that establishing of superiority. Here, the conceit of a superior person thinking 'I am superior' arises in kings and in the ordained. A king indeed makes this conceit: 'Who is there equal to me in kingdom, wealth, or vehicles?' An ordained person, too, makes this conceit: 'Who is there equal to me in virtue, ascetic practices, and so on?'

870. Seyyassa sadisohamasmīti mānopi etesaṃyeva uppajjati. Rājā hi ‘raṭṭhena vā dhanena vā vāhanehi vā aññarājūhi saddhiṃ mayhaṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇa’nti etaṃ mānaṃ karoti. Pabbajitopi ‘sīladhutaṅgādīhi aññena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ mayhaṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇa’nti etaṃ mānaṃ karoti.

870. The conceit of a superior person thinking 'I am equal' also arises in these same individuals. A king indeed makes this conceit: 'In respect to kingdom, wealth, or vehicles, what is the difference between me and other kings?' An ordained person, too, makes this conceit: 'In respect to virtue, ascetic practices, and so on, what is the difference between me and another bhikkhu?'

871. Seyyassa hīnohamasmīti mānopi etesaṃyeva uppajjati. Yassa hi rañño raṭṭhaṃ vā dhanaṃ vā vāhanāni vā sampannāni na honti, so ‘mayhaṃ rājāti vohārasukhamattameva; kiṃ rājā nāma aha’nti etaṃ mānaṃ karoti. Pabbajitopi ‘appalābhasakkāro ahaṃ. Dhammakathiko bahussuto mahātheroti kathāmattameva. Kiṃ dhammakathiko nāmāhaṃ, kiṃ bahussuto nāmāhaṃ, kiṃ mahāthero nāmāhaṃ yassa me lābhasakkāro natthī’ti etaṃ mānaṃ karoti.

871. The conceit of a superior person thinking 'I am inferior' also arises in these very individuals. For a king who is not endowed with a kingdom, wealth, or vehicles generates this conceit, thinking: 'My being called ‘king’ is a mere verbal convention; what kind of king am I?' A renunciant, too, generates this conceit, thinking: 'I have little gain and honor. It is mere talk that I am a Dhamma teacher, a learned one, or a great elder. What kind of Dhamma teacher am I? What kind of learned one am I? What kind of great elder am I, since I have no gain or honor?'

872. Sadisassa seyyohamasmīti mānādayo amaccādīnaṃ uppajjanti. Amacco hi raṭṭhiyo vā ‘bhogayānavāhanādīhi ko mayā sadiso añño rājapuriso atthī’ti vā ‘mayhaṃ aññehi saddhiṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇa’nti vā ‘amaccoti nāmamattameva mayhaṃ; ghāsacchādanamattampi me natthi. Kiṃ amacco nāmāha’nti ete māne karoti.

872. Conceits such as that of an equal person thinking 'I am superior' arise in ministers and others. For a minister or a provincial official generates these conceits, thinking: 'What other royal official is equal to me in possessions, mounts, vehicles, and so on?' or 'What distinction is there between me and others?' or 'The title ‘minister’ is just a name for me; I do not even have enough food and clothing. What kind of minister am I?'

875. Hīnassa seyyohamasmīti mānādayo dāsādīnaṃ uppajjanti. Dāso hi ‘mātito vā pitito vā ko mayā sadiso añño dāso [M 0.0469] nāma atthi’ aññe jīvituṃ asakkontā kucchihetu [V 0.0460] dāsā nāma jātā. Ahaṃ pana paveṇīāgatattā seyyo’ti vā ‘paveṇīāgatabhāvena ubhatosuddhikadāsattena asukadāsena nāma saddhiṃ kiṃ mayhaṃ nānākaraṇa’nti vā ‘kucchivasenāhaṃ dāsabyaṃ upagato. Mātāpitukoṭiyā pana me dāsaṭṭhānaṃ natthi. Kiṃ dāso nāma aha’nti vā ete māne karoti. Yathā ca dāso evaṃ pukkusacaṇḍālādayopi ete māne karontiyeva.

875. Conceits such as that of an inferior person thinking 'I am superior' arise in slaves and others. For a slave generates these conceits, thinking: 'By way of my mother or father, what other slave is there equal to me? Others, unable to make a living, have become slaves for the sake of their bellies. But I am superior because I come from a hereditary line,' or 'What distinction is there between me and so-and-so slave, given that I am a hereditary slave and a slave of pure descent on both sides?' or 'I have come to servitude for the sake of my belly, but on my mother’s and father’s side, there is no slave status for me. What kind of slave am I?' And just as a slave does, so too do Pukkusas, Caṇḍālas, and others generate these conceits.

Ettha ca ‘seyyassa seyyohamasmī’ti uppannamānova yāthāvamāno, itare dve ayāthāvamānā. Tathā ‘sadisassa sadisohamasmī’ti ‘hīnassa hīnohamasmī’ti uppannamānova yāthāvamāno, itare dve ayāthāvamānā. Tattha yāthāvamānā arahattamaggavajjhā, ayāthāvamānā sotāpattimaggavajjhā.

Here, the conceit that arises for a superior person as 'I am superior' is a factual conceit, while the other two are non-factual conceits. Similarly, the conceit that arises for an equal person as 'I am equal' and for an inferior person as 'I am inferior' are factual conceits, while the other two in each case are non-factual conceits. Among these, the factual conceits are abandoned by the path of arahantship, while the non-factual conceits are abandoned by the path of stream-entry.

878. Evaṃ savatthuke māne kathetvā idāni avatthukaṃ nibbattitamānameva [P 0.0488] dassetuṃ tattha katamo mānotiādi vuttaṃ.

878. Having thus explained conceit with a basis, now to show conceit that is produced without a basis, the passage beginning, 'Therein, what is conceit?' was stated.

879. Atimānaniddese seyyādivasena puggalaṃ anāmasitvā jātiādīnaṃ vatthuvaseneva niddiṭṭho. Tattha atimaññatīti ‘jātiādīhi mayā sadiso natthī’ti atikkamitvā maññati.

879. In the exposition of overweening conceit, it is explained without reference to a person in terms of superiority and so on, but solely on the basis of such grounds as birth. Therein, 'one has overweening conceit' means that one conceives having surpassed others, thinking: 'In birth and so on, there is no one equal to me.'

880. Mānātimānaniddese yo evarūpoti yo eso ‘ayaṃ pubbe mayā sadiso, idāni ahaṃ seṭṭho, ahaṃ hīnataro’ti uppanno māno. Ayaṃ bhārātibhāro viya purimaṃ sadisamānaṃ upādāya mānātimānoti dassetuṃ evamāha.

880. In the exposition of conceit and overweening conceit, 'that which is of such a nature' refers to the conceit that has arisen thus: 'This person was formerly my equal; now I am superior, now I am inferior.' This, like a burden upon a burden, is said thus to show that it is 'conceit and overweening conceit' by reference to the previous conceit of equality.

881. Omānaniddeso hīnamānaniddesasadisoyeva. Veneyyavasena pana so ‘hīnohamasmī’ti māno nāma vutto – ayaṃ omāno nāma. Apicettha ‘tvaṃ jātimā, kākajāti viya te jāti; tvaṃ gottavā, caṇḍālagottaṃ viya te gottaṃ; tuyhaṃ saro atthi, kākassaro viya te saro’ti evaṃ attānaṃ heṭṭhā katvā pavattanavasena ayaṃ omānoti veditabbo.

881. The exposition of inferiority conceit is just like the exposition of low conceit. However, for the sake of those to be trained, that conceit 'I am inferior' is spoken of as māna, while this is called omāna. Moreover, this should be understood as inferiority conceit in the sense that it proceeds by debasing oneself thus: 'I am of high birth, but my birth is like that of a crow; I am of high lineage, but my lineage is like that of a caṇḍāla; I have a voice, but my voice is like that of a crow.'

882. Adhimānaniddese [M 0.0470] appatte pattasaññitāti cattāri saccāni appatvā pattasaññitāya[V 0.0461]. Akateti catūhi maggehi kattabbakicce akateyeva. Anadhigateti catusaccadhamme anadhigate. Asacchikateti arahattena apaccakkhakate. Ayaṃ vuccati adhimānoti ayaṃ adhigatamāno nāma vuccati.

882. In the exposition of overestimation, 'perceiving the unattained as attained' means having the perception of having attained the four truths without having attained them. 'The undone' means when the task to be done by the four paths is still undone. 'The unrealized' means when the Dhamma of the four truths is unrealized. 'The not directly realized' means when it has not been directly realized through arahantship. This is called overestimation; this is called the conceit of attainment.

Ayaṃ pana kassa uppajjati, kassa nuppajjatīti? Ariyasāvakassa tāva nuppajjati. So hi maggaphalanibbānapahīnakilesāvasiṭṭhakilesapaccavekkhaṇena sañjātasomanasso ariyaguṇapaṭivedhe nikkaṅkho. Tasmā sotāpannādīnaṃ ‘ahaṃ sakadāgāmī’tiādivasena māno nuppajjati; dussīlassāpi nuppajjati; so hi ariyaguṇādhigame nirāsova. Sīlavatopi pariccattakammaṭṭhānassa niddārāmatādimanuyuttassa nuppajjati.
