Now, in whom does this arise, and in whom does it not arise? Firstly, it does not arise in a noble disciple. For he, joyful from reviewing the path, the fruition, Nibbāna, the abandoned defilements, and the remaining defilements, is without doubt about his penetration of the noble qualities. Therefore, in a stream-enterer and the other noble ones, the conceit “I am a once-returner,” and so on, does not arise. Nor does it arise in an immoral person, for he is without hope of attaining the noble qualities. It also does not arise in a virtuous person who has abandoned his meditation subject and is devoted to such things as fondness for sleep and company.

Parisuddhasīlassa pana kammaṭṭhāne appamattassa nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapetvā paccayapariggahena vitiṇṇakaṅkhassa tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā saṅkhāre sammasantassa āraddhavipassakassa uppajjati; uppanne ca suddhasamathalābhī vā suddhavipassanālābhī vā antarā ṭhapeti. So hi dasapi vīsampi tiṃsampi vassāni kilesasamudācāraṃ [P 0.0489] apassanto ‘ahaṃ sotāpanno’ti vā ‘sakadāgāmī’ti vā ‘anāgāmī’ti vā maññati. Samathavipassanālābhī pana arahatteyeva ṭhapeti. Tassa hi samādhibalena kilesā vikkhambhitā, vipassanābalena saṅkhārā supariggahitā. Tasmā saṭṭhipi vassāni asītipi vassāni vassasatampi kilesā na samudācaranti; khīṇāsavasseva cittacāro hoti. So evaṃ dīgharattaṃ kilesasamudācāraṃ apassanto antarā aṭṭhatvāva ‘arahā aha’nti maññati, uccamālaṅkavāsī mahānāgatthero viya, haṅkanakavāsī mahādattatthero viya, cittalapabbate niṅkapoṇṇapadhānagharavāsī cūḷasumatthero viya ca.

But it arises in a practitioner of purified virtue who is diligent in his meditation subject, one who has initiated insight, having defined mind-and-matter, overcome doubt by grasping conditions, applied the three characteristics, and commenced the contemplation of formations. And when it has arisen, one who is an obtainer of bare serenity or an obtainer of bare insight may posit an attainment midway. Not seeing an occurrence of the defilements for ten, twenty, or thirty years, he thinks: “I am a stream-enterer,” or “a once-returner,” or “a non-returner.” But one who is an obtainer of both serenity and insight posits an attainment only at arahantship. For him, the defilements are suppressed by the power of concentration, and the formations are well-grasped by the power of insight. Thus, for sixty, eighty, or even a hundred years, the defilements do not occur; his mental process is like that of one whose taints are destroyed. Not seeing an occurrence of the defilements for such a long time, he thinks, while not yet having reached the goal, “I am an arahant,” like the Elder Mahānāga, the resident of Uccamālaṅka; the Elder Mahādatta, the resident of Haṅkanaka; and the Elder Cūḷasumana, the resident of the Niṅkapoṇṇa meditation hall on Cittalapabbata.

Tatridaṃ ekavatthuparidīpanaṃ – talaṅgaravāsī dhammadinnatthero kira nāma eko pabhinnapaṭisambhido mahākhīṇāsavo mahato bhikkhusaṅghassa ovādadāyako ahosi. So ekadivasaṃ attano divāṭṭhāne nisīditvā ‘kinnu kho amhākaṃ ācariyassa uccataliṅkavāsīmahānāgattherassa samaṇakiccaṃ [M 0.0471] matthakaṃ patto, no’ti āvajjanto puthujjanabhāvamevassa disvā ‘mayi agacchante puthujjanakālakiriyameva karissatī’ti ca ñatvā iddhiyā vehāsaṃ uppatitvā divāṭṭhāne nisinnassa therassa samīpe orohitvā vanditvā vattaṃ dassetvā [V 0.0462] ekamantaṃ nisīdi. ‘Kiṃ, āvuso dhammadinna, akāle āgatosī’ti ca vutto ‘pañhaṃ, bhante, pucchituṃ āgatomhī’ti āha.

Here is an illustrative story. It is said that the Elder Dhammadinna of Talaṅgara was a great arahant who had attained the analytical knowledges and was an advisor to a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus. One day, while seated in his daytime quarters, he reflected: “I wonder whether our teacher, the Elder Mahānāga of Uccataliṅka, has reached the culmination of the ascetic’s task or not?” Seeing that he was still a worldling, and knowing, “If I do not go, he will pass away while still a worldling,” he rose into the air by psychic power, descended near the elder who was seated in his daytime quarters, paid homage, performed his duties, and sat down to one side. When asked, “Friend Dhammadinna, why have you come at an unseemly time?” he replied, “Venerable sir, I have come to ask a question.”

Tato ‘pucchāvuso, jānamāno kathayissāmī’ti vutto pañhāsahassaṃ pucchi. Thero pucchitapucchitaṃ pañhaṃ asajjamānova kathesi. Tato ‘atitikkhaṃ te, bhante, ñāṇaṃ. Kadā tumhehi ayaṃ dhammo adhigato’ti vutto ‘ito saṭṭhivassakāle, āvuso’ti āha. ‘Samādhimpi, bhante, vaḷañjethā’ti? ‘Na idaṃ, āvuso, bhāriya’nti. ‘Tena hi, bhante, ekaṃ hatthiṃ māpethā’ti. Thero sabbasetaṃ hatthiṃ māpesi. ‘Idāni, bhante, yathā ayaṃ hatthī añcitakaṇṇo pasāritanaṅguṭṭho soṇḍaṃ mukhe pakkhipitvā bheravaṃ koñcanādaṃ karonto tumhākaṃ abhimukho āgacchati tathā taṃ karothā’ti. Thero tathā katvā vegena āgacchato hatthissa bheravaṃ ākāraṃ disvā uṭṭhāya palāyituṃ āraddho. Tamenaṃ khīṇāsavatthero hatthaṃ [P 0.0490] pasāretvā cīvarakaṇṇe gahetvā ‘bhante, khīṇāsavassa sārajjaṃ nāma hotī’ti āha. So tasmiṃ kāle attano puthujjanabhāvaṃ ñatvā ‘avassayo me, āvuso dhammadinna, hohī’ti vatvā pādamūle ukkuṭikaṃ nisīdi. ‘Bhante, tumhākaṃ avassayo bhavissāmiccevāhaṃ āgato, mā cintayitthā’ti kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi. Thero kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā caṅkamaṃ āruyha tatiye padavāre aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Thero kira dosacarito ahosi.

When he was told, “Ask, friend; if I know, I will explain,” he asked a thousand questions. The elder answered every question that was asked without faltering. Then Dhammadinna said: “Venerable sir, your knowledge is exceedingly sharp. When did you realize this Dhamma?” He was told: “Sixty years ago, friend.” “Venerable sir, do you also practice concentration?” “That is not difficult, friend.” “In that case, venerable sir, please create an elephant.” The elder created an all-white elephant. “Now, venerable sir, make it so that this elephant comes towards you with its ears pricked up, its tail extended, and its trunk placed in its mouth, making a terrifying trumpeting sound.” The elder did so, but when he saw the terrifying appearance of the elephant rushing towards him, he got up and started to flee. The elder who was an arahant stretched out his hand, grabbed the corner of his robe, and said: “Venerable sir, can one whose taints are destroyed have fear?” At that moment, realizing he was still a worldling, he said, “Friend Dhammadinna, be my support!” and sat down on his haunches at his feet. Dhammadinna said: “Venerable sir, I came precisely to be your support, do not worry,” and he gave him a meditation subject. The elder took up the meditation subject, mounted the walking path, and at the third footstep he attained the highest fruit, arahantship. It is said that the elder was one of a hating temperament.

883. Asmimānaniddese rūpaṃ asmīti mānoti ‘ahaṃ rūpa’nti uppannamāno. Chandoti mānaṃ anugatacchandova. Tathā anusayo. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo.

883. In the exposition of the “I am” conceit, the conceit “I am form” is the conceit that arises as “I am form.” “Desire” here means the desire that accompanies that conceit. The same holds for the underlying tendency. This same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates.

884. Micchāmānaniddese pāpakena vā kammāyatanenāti ādīsu pāpakaṃ kammāyatanaṃ nāma kevaṭṭamacchabandhanesādādīnaṃ kammaṃ. Pāpakaṃ sippāyatanaṃ [M 0.0472] nāma macchajālakhipanakuminakaraṇesu ceva pāsaoḍḍanasūlāropanādīsu ca chekatā. Pāpakaṃ vijjāṭṭhānaṃ nāma yā kāci parūpaghātavijjā. Pāpakaṃ sutaṃ nāma bhāratayuddhasītāharaṇādipaṭisaṃyuttaṃ. Pāpakaṃ paṭibhānaṃ nāma dubbhāsitayuttaṃ kappanāṭakavilappanādipaṭibhānaṃ. Pāpakaṃ sīlaṃ nāma ajasīlaṃ gosīlaṃ. Vatampi ajavatagovatameva. Pāpikā diṭṭhi pana dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhigatesu yā kāci diṭṭhi.

884. In the exposition of wrong conceit, in the passage beginning 'by an evil sphere of action,' an evil sphere of action is the work of fishermen, fish-trappers, hunters, and so on. An evil sphere of craft is skill in casting fishing nets, making fish-traps, setting snares, setting up stakes, and so on. An evil branch of knowledge is any knowledge for the harm of others. Evil learning is lore connected with the Bhārata war, the abduction of Sītā, and so on. Evil ingenuity is the ingenuity connected with wrong speech, for composing plays, lamentations, and so on. Evil virtue is goat-virtue and cow-virtue. The observance, too, is just the goat-observance and the cow-observance. As for an evil view, it is any view among the sixty-two speculative views.

885. Ñātivitakkaniddesādīsu ‘mayhaṃ ñātayo sukhajīvino sampattiyuttā’ti evaṃ pañcakāmaguṇasannissitena [V 0.0463] gehasitapemena ñātake ārabbha uppannavitakkova ñātivitakko nāma. ‘Khayaṃ gatā vayaṃ gatā saddhā pasannā’ti evaṃ pavatto pana ñātivitakko nāma na hoti.

885. In the expositions of thoughts about relatives and so on, a thought that has arisen concerning one's relatives out of household-based affection connected with the five cords of sensual pleasure—such as, 'May my relatives live happily, endowed with wealth!'—is called a thought about relatives. But a thought that proceeds thus: 'They have gone to ruin, they have reached old age; they were faithful and confident,' is not called a thought about relatives.

886. ‘Amhākaṃ janapado subhikkho sampannasasso’ti tuṭṭhamānassa gehasitapemavaseneva uppannavitakko janapadavitakko nāma. ‘Amhākaṃ janapade manussā saddhā pasannā khayaṃ gatā vayaṃ gatā’ti evaṃ pavatto pana janapadavitakko nāma na hoti.

886. A thought that has arisen for one who is pleased, by way of household-based affection—such as, 'Our country is prosperous, with abundant crops!'—is called a thought about one's country. But a thought that proceeds thus, 'In our country the people are faithful and confident; they have gone to ruin, they have reached old age,' is not called a thought about one's country.

887. Amaratthāya vitakko, amaro vā vitakkoti amaravitakko. Tattha ‘ukkuṭikappadhānādīhi dukkhe nijjiṇṇe samparāye attā [P 0.0491] sukhī hoti amaro’ti dukkarakārikaṃ karontassa tāya dukkarakārikāya paṭisaṃyutto vitakko amaratthāya vitakko nāma. Diṭṭhigatiko pana ‘sassataṃ vadesī’tiādīni puṭṭho ‘evantipi me no, tathātipi me no’ aññathātipi me no, notipi me no, no notipi me no’ti (dī. ni. 1.62) vikkhepaṃ āpajjati, tassa so diṭṭhigatapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko. Yathā amaro nāma maccho udake gahetvā māretuṃ na sakkā, ito cito ca dhāvati, gāhaṃ na gacchati; evameva ekasmiṃ pakkhe asaṇṭhahanato na maratīti amaro nāma hoti. Taṃ duvidhampi ekato katvā ayaṃ vuccati amaravitakkoti vuttaṃ.

887. A thought for the sake of immortality, or an immortal thought, is a thought about immortality. Herein, for one undertaking a difficult practice with the thought, 'When suffering has been worn away by such practices as the squatting posture and exertion, in the future life the self will be happy and immortal,' the thought connected with that difficult practice is called 'a thought for the sake of immortality.' As for the one holding a speculative view, when asked such questions as, 'Do you say it is eternal?' he resorts to equivocation, saying: 'I do not say it is so, I do not say it is thus, I do not say it is otherwise, I do not say it is not, I do not say it is not not' (DN 1.62). That thought of his connected with his speculative view is the 'immortal thought.' Just as a fish called an 'eel' (literally, 'immortal') cannot be caught and killed in the water, as it darts here and there and evades capture, so too, because he does not commit himself to one position, he is not 'pinned down' (literally, 'does not die'); hence he is called an 'eel-wriggler' (literally, 'immortal'). It is said that by combining these two, this is called 'a thought about immortality.'

888. Parānuddayatāpaṭisaṃyuttoti anuddayatāpatirūpakena gehasitapemena paṭisaṃyutto. Sahanandītiādīsu upaṭṭhākesu nandantesu socantesu ca tehi saddhiṃ diguṇaṃ nandati, diguṇaṃ socati; tesu sukhitesu [M 0.0473] diguṇaṃ sukhito hoti, dukkhitesu diguṇaṃ dukkhito hoti. Uppannesu kiccakaraṇīyesūti tesu mahantesu vā khuddakesu vā kammesu uppannesu. Attanā vā yogaṃ āpajjatīti tāni tāni kiccāni sādhento paññattiṃ vītikkamati, sallekhaṃ kopeti. Yo tatthāti yo tasmiṃ saṃsaṭṭhavihāre, tasmiṃ vā yogāpajjane gehasito vitakko – ayaṃ parānuddayatāpaṭisaṃyutto vitakko nāma.

888. 'Connected with sympathy for others' means connected with household-based affection in the guise of sympathy. In the passage beginning 'rejoicing together,' when his attendants rejoice or grieve, he rejoices doubly and grieves doubly with them; when they are happy, he is doubly happy, and when they are afflicted, he is doubly afflicted. 'When duties and obligations arise' means when great or small tasks arise for them. 'He applies himself' means that in carrying out those various duties, he transgresses the monastic rules and damages the practice of effacement. 'Whatever thought there' means whatever household-based thought there is in that intimate association or in that application of himself—this is called a thought connected with sympathy for others.

889. Lābhasakkārasilokapaṭisaṃyuttoti cīvarādilābhena ceva sakkārena ca kittisaddena ca saddhiṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasena paṭisaṃyutto.

889. 'Connected with gain, honor, and fame' means connected with the gain of robes and so on, with honor, and with the sound of fame, by way of taking them as an object.

890. Anavaññattipaṭisaṃyuttoti [V 0.0464] ‘aho vata maṃ pare na avajāneyyuṃ, na pothetvā viheṭhetvā katheyyu’nti evaṃ anavaññātabhāvapatthanāya saddhiṃ uppajjanavitakko. Yo tattha gehasitoti yo tasmiṃ ‘mā maṃ pare avajāniṃsū’ti uppanne citte pañcakāmaguṇasaṅkhātagehanissito hutvā uppannavitakko. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭamevāti.

890. 'Connected with not being despised' is a thought that arises along with the aspiration for a state of not being despised, thus: 'Oh, that others might not despise me, that they might not speak to me in a crushing and harassing way!' 'Whatever household-based thought there' means: when the thought 'May others not despise me!' has arisen, it is the thought that arises based on the household sphere, which is reckoned as the five cords of sensual pleasure. The rest is clear in all respects.

Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Single Items.

(2.) Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā

(2) The Commentary on the Exposition of the Pairs.

891. Dukesu kodhaniddesādayo heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Heṭṭhā anāgatesu pana upanāhaniddesādīsu pubbakālaṃ kodhaṃ upanayhatīti aparakālakodho upanāho nāma. Upanayhanākāro [P 0.0492] upanayhanā. Upanayhitassa bhāvo upanayhitattaṃ. Aṭṭhapanāti paṭhamuppannassa anantaraṭṭhapanā mariyādaṭṭhapanā vā. Ṭhapanāti pakatiṭhapanā. Saṇṭhapanāti sabbatobhāgena punappunaṃ āghātaṭṭhapanā. Anusaṃsandanāti paṭhamuppannena kodhena saddhiṃ antaraṃ adassetvā ekībhāvakaraṇā. Anuppabandhanāti purimena saddhiṃ pacchimassa ghaṭanā. Daḷhīkammanti thirakaraṇaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ upanandhanalakkhaṇo veraṃ appaṭinissajjanaraso upanāhoti vuccati; yena samannāgato puggalo veraṃ nissajjituṃ na sakkoti; ‘evaṃ nāma maṃ esa vattuṃ ananucchaviko’ti aparāparaṃ anubandhati; ādittapūtialātaṃ viya jalateva[M 0.0474]; dhoviyamānaṃ acchacammaṃ viya, vasātelamakkhitapilotikā viya ca na parisujjhati.

891. In the pairs, the exposition of anger and so on should be understood in the way stated above. But among those not mentioned above, in the exposition of resentment and so on: because one bears a grudge (upanayhati) about a previous anger, resentment (upanāho) is anger at a later time. The mode of bearing a grudge is upanayhanā. The state of having borne a grudge is upanayhitattaṃ. Aṭṭhapanā (establishing) is the immediate establishing of what first arose, or the establishing of a boundary. Ṭhapanā (placing) is the natural placing. Saṇṭhapanā (firmly placing) is the repeated establishing of hatred from all sides. Anusaṃsandanā (connecting up) is the making of a unity with the initially arisen anger, showing no interval. Anuppabandhanā (binding on) is the joining of a later anger with a former one. Daḷhīkammaṃ (making firm) is strengthening. 'This is called' means this resentment, which has the characteristic of bearing a grudge and the function of not relinquishing enmity, is so called. A person endowed with it cannot relinquish enmity; he pursues it again and again, thinking: 'It was so unfitting for him to speak to me like that!' It keeps on burning like a blazing, stinking firebrand; like a bear's hide being washed, or like a rag smeared with fat and oil, it does not become clean.

892. Makkhanabhāvavasena makkho; paraguṇamakkhanāya pavattentopi attano kāraṇaṃ, gūthapaharaṇakaṃ gūtho viya, paṭhamataraṃ makkhetīti attho. Tato parā dve ākārabhāvaniddesā. Niṭṭhurabhāvo niṭṭhuriyaṃ; ‘taṃ nissāya ettakampi natthī’ti kheḷapātananti attho. Niṭṭhuriyakammanti niṭṭhuriyakaraṇaṃ. Gahaṭṭho vā hi gahaṭṭhaṃ, bhikkhu vā bhikkhuṃ nissāya vasanto appamattakeneva kujjhitvā ‘taṃ nissāya ettakampi natthī’ti kheḷaṃ pātetvā pādena maddanto viya niṭṭhuriyaṃ nāma karoti. Tassa taṃ kammaṃ niṭṭhuriyakammanti vuccati. Lakkhaṇādito panesa paraguṇamakkhanalakkhaṇo [V 0.0465] makkho, tesaṃ vināsanaraso, parena sukatānaṃ kiriyānaṃ avacchādanapaccupaṭṭhāno.

892. Contempt (makkho) is so called by way of its nature of smearing (makkhanabhāva); the meaning is that although it proceeds to smear the good qualities of another, it first smears one's own cause, just as dung does to one who is throwing it. After that are the expositions of two modes of being. Harshness (niṭṭhuriyaṃ) is the state of being harsh; the meaning is spitting with the thought, 'Relying on him, not even this much is gained.' An act of harshness (niṭṭhuriyakammaṃ) is the doing of a harsh act. For when a householder is living in dependence on a householder, or a monk on a monk, having become angry over some trifle, he spits with the thought, 'Relying on him, not even this much is gained,' and as if trampling him with his foot, he performs what is called harshness. That act of his is called an act of harshness. As to its characteristic, etc., this contempt has the characteristic of smearing the good qualities of others, its function is their destruction, and it is manifested as the concealing of good deeds done by others.

Paḷāsatīti paḷāso; parassa guṇe dassetvā attano guṇehi samaṃ karotīti attho. Paḷāsassa āyanā paḷāsāyanā. Paḷāso ca so attano jayāharaṇato āhāro cāti paḷāsāhāro. Vivādaṭṭhānanti vivādakāraṇaṃ. Yugaggāhoti samadhuraggahaṇaṃ. Appaṭinissaggoti attanā gahitassa appaṭinissajjanaṃ. Lakkhaṇādito [P 0.0493] panesa yugaggāhalakkhaṇo paḷāso, paraguṇehi attano guṇānaṃ samakaraṇaraso, paresaṃ guṇappamāṇena upaṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhāno. Paḷāsī hi puggalo dutiyassa dhuraṃ na deti, samaṃ pasāretvā tiṭṭhati, sākacchamaṇḍale aññena bhikkhunā bahūsu suttesu ca kāraṇesu ca ābhatesupi ‘tava ca mama ca vāde kiṃ nāma nānākaraṇaṃ? Nanu majjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇaṃ viya ekasadisameva amhākaṃ vacana’nti vadati. Issāmacchariyaniddesā vuttatthā eva.

One is domineering (paḷāsati), thus it is 'domineering' (paḷāso); the meaning is that one makes one's own qualities equal to the qualities of another that have been pointed out. The arising of domineering is paḷāsāyanā. And that domineering is a 'sustenance' (āhāro) because it brings (āharaṇato) one's own victory; thus it is paḷāsāhāro. 'A basis for dispute' (vivādaṭṭhānaṃ) is a cause for dispute. 'Grasping the yoke-end' (yugaggāho) is taking up an equal yoke. 'Non-relinquishing' (appaṭinissaggo) is not giving up what one has grasped. As to its characteristic, etc., this domineering has the characteristic of taking up an equal yoke, its function is to make one's own qualities equal to those of others, and it is manifested as presenting oneself according to the measure of others' qualities. For a domineering person does not yield the foremost position to another but stands stretching himself out equally. In a discussion circle, even when another bhikkhu has cited many suttas and reasons, he says: 'What difference is there in your statement and mine? Is not our speech exactly the same, like a piece of gold split down the middle?' The expositions of envy and stinginess have the meaning already stated.

894. Māyāniddese [V 0.0466] vācaṃ bhāsatīti jānaṃyeva ‘paṇṇattiṃ vītikkamantā bhikkhū bhāriyaṃ karonti, amhākaṃ pana vītikkamaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthī’ti upasanto viya bhāsati. Kāyena parakkamatīti ‘mayā kataṃ idaṃ pāpakammaṃ mā keci jāniṃsū’ti kāyena vattaṃ karoti. Vijjamānadosapaṭicchādanato cakkhumohanamāyā viyāti māyā. Māyāvino bhāvo māyāvitā. Katvā pāpaṃ puna paṭicchādanato aticca āsaranti etāya [M 0.0475] sattāti accāsarā. Kāyavācākiriyāhi aññathā dassanato vañcetīti vañcanā. Etāya sattā nikarontīti nikati; micchākarontīti attho. ‘Nāhaṃ evaṃ karomī’ti pāpānaṃ vikkhipanato vikiraṇā. ‘Nāhaṃ evaṃ karomī’ti parivajjanato pariharaṇā. Kāyādīhi saṃvaraṇato gūhanā. Sabbatobhāgena gūhanā parigūhanā. Tiṇapaṇṇehi viya gūthaṃ kāyavacīkammehi pāpaṃ chādetīti chādanā. Sabbatobhāgena chādanā paṭicchādanā. Na uttānaṃ katvā dassetīti anuttānīkammaṃ. Na pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetīti anāvikammaṃ. Suṭṭhu chādanā vocchādanā. Katapaṭicchādanavasena punapi pāpassa karaṇato pāpakiriyā. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ katapaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā māyā nāma vuccati; yāya samannāgato puggalo bhasmāpaṭicchanno viya aṅgāro, udakapaṭicchanno viya khāṇu, pilotikāpaliveṭhitaṃ viya ca satthaṃ hoti.

894. In the explanation of deceit, one speaks words, knowing full well, 'The bhikkhus who transgress a rule make it a heavy offense, but for us there is no occasion for transgression,' thus speaking as if peaceful. One strives with the body, thinking, 'Let no one know this evil deed done by me,' thus making an effort with the body. Because it conceals existing faults, it is deceit, like a magic trick that deludes the eye. The state of being deceitful is deceitfulness. Having done evil and then concealing it, beings thereby go to excess; this is 'going to excess.' Deceiving by showing something different through bodily and verbal actions is deception. Through this, beings act wrongly—this is trickery; the meaning is to act falsely. Scattering evil by saying, 'I do not do so,' is scattering. Avoiding by saying, 'I do not do so,' is avoidance. Hiding by means of the body and so on is hiding. Hiding in every way is thorough hiding. Covering up an evil deed with bodily and verbal actions, like covering dung with grass and leaves, is covering. Covering up in every way is concealment. Not making it open is non-disclosure. Not making it manifest is non-revelation. Thoroughly covering up is complete concealment. Doing evil again by way of concealing what has been done is evil-doing. This is called deceit, which is characterized by concealing what has been done. A person endowed with this is like an ember covered with ashes, a stump covered with water, or a sword wrapped in a rag.

Sāṭheyyaniddese [P 0.0494] saṭhoti asantaguṇaparidīpanato na sammā bhāsitā. Sabbatobhāgena saṭho parisaṭho. Yaṃ tatthāti yaṃ tasmiṃ puggale. Saṭhanti asantaguṇadīpanaṃ kerāṭiyaṃ. Saṭhatāti saṭhākāro. Kakkaratāti padumanālissa viya aparāmasanakkhamo kharapharusabhāvo. Kakkariyantipi tasseva vevacanaṃ. Parikkhattatā pārikkhattiyanti padadvayena nikhaṇitvā ṭhapitaṃ viya daḷhakerāṭiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Idaṃ vuccatīti idaṃ attano avijjamānaguṇappakāsanalakkhaṇaṃ sāṭheyyaṃ nāma vuccati; yena samannāgatassa puggalassa kucchiṃ vā piṭṭhiṃ vā jānituṃ na sakkā.

In the explanation of craftiness, 'crafty' means not speaking rightly because of displaying non-existent virtues. One who is crafty in every way is utterly crafty. 'That which is in that' refers to that which is in that person. 'Craftiness' is the displaying of non-existent virtues; it is fraudulence. 'Craftiness' is a crafty demeanor. 'Harshness' is a rough and coarse nature, incapable of being gently touched, like a lotus stalk. 'Harshness' is also a synonym for that same thing. By the two terms parikkhattatā and pārikkhattiyaṃ is meant a firm fraudulence, as if something were dug in and established. This is called craftiness, which is characterized by proclaiming virtues one does not possess; of a person endowed with this, it is not possible to know his belly or his back.

Vāmena sūkaro hoti, dakkhiṇena ajāmigo;

Sarena nelako hoti, visāṇena jaraggavoti.

On the left, a boar; on the right, a wild goat. By sound, a mongoose; by horns, an old ox.

Evaṃ vuttayakkhasūkarasadiso hoti. Avijjādiniddesā vuttatthā eva.

He is like the boar-like yakkha described above. The explanations of ignorance and so on are as already stated.

902. Anajjavaniddese anajjavoti anujutākāro. Anajjavabhāvo anajjavatā. Jimhatāti candavaṅkatā. Vaṅkatāti gomuttavaṅkatā. Kuṭilatāti naṅgalakoṭivaṅkatā. Sabbehipi imehi padehi kāyavacīcittavaṅkatāva kathitā.

902. In the explanation of dishonesty: 'dishonest' means having a non-upright demeanor. The state of being dishonest is dishonesty. 'Crookedness' is the crookedness of the moon. 'Bentness' is the crookedness of a cow's stream of urine. 'Twistedness' is the crookedness of a plowshare's tip. By all these terms the crookedness of body, speech, and mind is described.

Amaddavaniddese na mudubhāvo amudutā. Amaddavākāro amaddavatā. Kakkhaḷabhāvo kakkhaḷiyaṃ. Maddavakarassa sinehassa abhāvato pharusabhāvo phārusiyaṃ. Anīcavuttitāya ujukameva ṭhitacittabhāvo ujucittatā[M 0.0476]. Puna amudutāgahaṇaṃ tassā visesanatthaṃ ‘amudutāsaṅkhātā ujucittatā, na ajjavasaṅkhātā ujucittatā’ti.

In the explanation of harshness: not being soft is harshness. A harsh demeanor is harshness. The state of being hard is hardness. Because of the absence of affection that makes one gentle, the state of being rough is roughness. Because of unbending conduct, the state of a mind that stands straight is straightness of mind. The taking up again of 'harshness' is for the purpose of specifying it thus: 'straightness of mind designated as harshness, not straightness of mind designated as honesty.'

903. Akkhantiniddesādayo khantiniddesādipaṭipakkhato veditabbā.

903. The explanations of impatience and so on should be understood as being opposed to the explanations of patience and so on.

908. Saṃyojananiddese ajjhattanti kāmabhavo. Bahiddhāti rūpārūpabhavo. Kiñcāpi hi sattā kāmabhave appaṃ [P 0.0495] kālaṃ vasanti kappassa catutthameva koṭṭhāsaṃ, itaresu tīsu koṭṭhāsesu kāmabhavo suñño hoti tuccho, rūpārūpabhave bahuṃ kālaṃ vasanti, tathāpi nesaṃ yasmā kāmabhave cutipaṭisandhiyo bahukā honti, appā rūpārūpabhavesu, yattha ca cutipaṭisandhiyo bahukā tattha ālayopi patthanāpi abhilāsopi bahu hoti, yattha appā tattha appo, tasmā kāmabhavo [V 0.0467] ajjhattaṃ nāma jāto, rūpārūpabhavā bahiddhā nāma. Iti ajjhattasaṅkhāte kāmabhave bandhanaṃ ajjhattasaṃyojanaṃ nāma, bahiddhāsaṅkhātesu rūpārūpabhavesu bandhanaṃ bahiddhāsaṃyojanaṃ nāma. Tattha ekekaṃ pañcapañcavidhaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “pañcorambhāgiyāni pañcuddhambhāgiyānī”ti. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – oraṃ vuccati kāmadhātu, tattha upapattinipphādanato taṃ oraṃ bhajantīti orambhāgiyāni. Uddhaṃ vuccati rūpārūpadhātu, tattha upapattinipphādanato taṃ uddhaṃ bhajantīti uddhambhāgiyānīti.

908. In the explanation of the fetters, 'internal' means the plane of sensual existence; 'external' means the fine-material and immaterial planes of existence. For although beings dwell in the plane of sensual existence for a short time—only for the fourth part of an aeon, since in the other three parts the plane of sensual existence is empty and void—and they dwell in the fine-material and immaterial planes for a long time, still, because their deaths and rebirth-linkings are many in the plane of sensual existence and few in the fine-material and immaterial planes, and where deaths and rebirth-linkings are many, there is also much attachment, longing, and craving, while where they are few, there is little—therefore the plane of sensual existence has come to be called 'internal,' and the fine-material and immaterial planes 'external.' Thus, the fetter in the plane of sensual existence, designated 'internal,' is called the internal fetter; the fetter in the fine-material and immaterial planes, designated 'external,' is called the external fetter. Each of these is of five kinds. Hence it is said: 'the five lower fetters and the five higher fetters.' Herein, this is the word-meaning: 'the lower part' refers to the sense-sphere realm; because they pertain to the lower part by bringing about rebirth there, they are called the lower fetters. 'The higher part' refers to the fine-material and immaterial realms; because they pertain to the higher part by bringing about rebirth there, they are called the higher fetters.

Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Twos.

(3.) Tikaniddesavaṇṇanā

(3.) Commentary on the Exposition of the Triads

909. Tikaniddese tīhi akusalamūlehi vaṭṭamūlasamudācāro kathito. Akusalavitakkādīsu vitakkanavasena vitakko, sañjānanavasena saññā, sabhāvaṭṭhena dhātūti veditabbā. Duccaritaniddese paṭhamanayo kammapathavasena vibhatto, dutiyo sabbasaṅgāhikakammavasena, tatiyo nibbattitacetanāvaseneva.

909. In the Exposition of the Triads, the occurrence of the root of the round of existence through the three unwholesome roots is explained. In regard to unwholesome thoughts and so on, 'thought' should be understood as thinking in the sense of its function of thinking, 'perception' as perceiving in the sense of its function of perceiving, and 'element' as element in the sense of its intrinsic nature. In the Exposition of Misconduct, the first method is analyzed by way of the courses of action, the second by way of all-inclusive action, and the third simply by way of the volition that has arisen.

914. Āsavaniddese suttantapariyāyena tayova āsavā kathitā.

914. In the Exposition of the Taints, only three taints are explained in accordance with the Suttanta method.

919. Esanāniddese [M 0.0477] saṅkhepato tattha katamā kāmesanāti ādinā nayena vutto kāmagavesanarāgo kāmesanā. Yo bhavesu bhavacchandotiādinā nayena vutto bhavagavesanarāgo bhavesanā. Sassato lokotiādinā nayena vuttā diṭṭhigatikasammatassa brahmacariyassa gavesanā diṭṭhi brahmacariyesanāti veditabbā. Yasmā ca na kevalaṃ rāgadiṭṭhiyo eva esanā, tadekaṭṭhaṃ pana kammampi esanā eva, tasmā taṃ dassetuṃ dutiyanayo vibhatto. Tattha tadekaṭṭhanti sampayuttekaṭṭhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha [P 0.0496] kāmarāgekaṭṭhaṃ kāmāvacarasattānameva pavattati; bhavarāgekaṭṭhaṃ pana mahābrahmānaṃ. Samāpattito vuṭṭhāya caṅkamantānaṃ jhānaṅgānaṃ assādanakāle akusalakāyakammaṃ hoti, ‘aho sukhaṃ aho sukha’nti vācaṃ bhinditvā assādanakāle vacīkammaṃ, kāyaṅgavācaṅgāni [V 0.0468] acopetvā manasāva assādanakāle manokammaṃ. Antaggāhikadiṭṭhivasena sabbesampi diṭṭhigatikānaṃ caṅkamanādivasena tāni hontiyeva.

919. In the Exposition of Searches, in brief, by the method beginning, 'What is the search for sensual pleasures?,' the lust that is the seeking of sensual pleasures is called the search for sensual pleasures. By the method beginning, 'Whatever desire for existence in the various forms of existence...,' the lust that is the seeking of existence is called the search for existence. By the method beginning, 'The world is eternal...,' the seeking of a holy life approved by one holding a certain view is to be understood as the view-based search for a holy life. And since not only lust and views are searches, but action having the same object is also a search, the second method is analyzed to show this. Here, 'having the same object' should be understood as having the same object by way of association. In this case, that which has the same object as sensual lust pertains only to beings of the sense-sphere realm, while that which has the same object as lust for existence pertains to the Great Brahmās. For those who, having emerged from an attainment, are walking to and fro, unwholesome bodily action occurs at the time of savoring the jhāna factors; verbal action occurs at the time of breaking silence and savoring by exclaiming, 'Ah, what happiness! Ah, what happiness!'; and mental action occurs at the time of savoring with the mind alone, without moving the bodily or verbal faculties. For all who hold such views, these actions certainly occur through walking to and fro and so on, in accordance with their extremist views.

920. Vidhāniddese “kathaṃvidhaṃ sīlavantaṃ vadanti, kathaṃvidhaṃ paññavantaṃ vadantī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.95) ākārasaṇṭhānaṃ vidhā nāma. “Ekavidhena ñāṇavatthū”tiādīsu (vibha. 751) koṭṭhāso. “Vidhāsu na vikampatī”tiādīsu (theragā. 1079) māno. Idhāpi mānova vidhā nāma. So hi seyyādivasena vidahanato vidhāti vuccati. Ṭhapanaṭṭhena vā vidhā. Tasmā ‘seyyohamasmī’ti evaṃ uppannā mānavidhā mānaṭhapanā seyyohamasmīti vidhāti veditabbā. Sesapadadvayesupi eseva nayo.

920. In the Exposition of Discriminations, in passages such as 'Of what kind do they say one is virtuous? Of what kind do they say one is wise?' (SN 1.95), 'discrimination' (vidhā) means kind, manner, or form. In passages such as 'The basis of knowledge in one way' (Vibh 751), it means a part. In passages such as 'He is not shaken by discriminations' (Thag 1079), it means conceit. Here, too, 'discrimination' means conceit. For because it strikes based on notions of superiority and the like, it is called 'discrimination.' Or 'discrimination' is used in the sense of establishing. Therefore, the conceit-discrimination that arises as 'I am superior,' which is an establishing of conceit, is to be understood as the discrimination 'I am superior.' The same method applies to the remaining two terms.

921. Bhayaniddese jātiṃ paṭicca bhayanti jātipaccayā uppannabhayaṃ. Bhayānakanti ākāraniddeso. Chambhitattanti bhayavasena gattacalanaṃ. Lomahaṃsoti lomānaṃ haṃsanaṃ, uddhaggabhāvo. Iminā padadvayena kiccato bhayaṃ dassetvā puna cetaso utrāsoti sabhāvato dassitaṃ.

921. In the Exposition of Fear, 'they fear on account of birth' means the fear that arises with birth as its condition. 'Terrifying' is an indication of its appearance. 'Stiffness' is the trembling of the limbs due to fear. 'Horripilation' is the bristling of the bodily hairs, their standing on end. Having shown fear by way of its function with these two terms, it is then shown by way of its intrinsic nature as 'terror of the mind'.

922. Tamaniddese vicikicchāsīsena avijjā kathitā. “Tamandhakāro sammoho, avijjogho mahabbhayo”ti vacanato hi avijjā tamo [M 0.0478] nāma. Tiṇṇaṃ pana addhānaṃ vasena desanāsukhatāya vicikicchāsīsena desanā katā. Tattha ‘kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atīte khattiyo ahosiṃ udāhu brāhmaṇo vesso suddo kāḷo odāto rasso dīgho’ti kaṅkhanto atītaṃ addhānaṃ ārabbha kaṅkhati nāma. ‘Kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ anāgate khattiyo bhavissāmi udāhu brāhmaṇo vesso…pe… dīgho’ti kaṅkhanto anāgataṃ addhānaṃ ārabbha kaṅkhati nāma. ‘Kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ etarahi khattiyo udāhu brāhmaṇo vesso suddo; kiṃ vā ahaṃ rūpaṃ udāhu vedanā saññā saṅkhārā viññāṇa’nti kaṅkhanto paccuppannaṃ addhānaṃ ārabbha kaṅkhati nāma.

922. In the Exposition of Darkness, ignorance is explained with doubt as its head. For in accordance with the saying, 'Darkness, delusion, the flood of ignorance, a great fear,' ignorance is called 'darkness.' However, for the sake of facility in teaching, the exposition is made with doubt as its head in relation to the three periods of time. Here, one who doubts, wondering, 'Was I in the past a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa, or a sudda; dark or fair; short or tall?' is said to doubt concerning the past. One who doubts, wondering, 'Will I in the future be a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa ... or tall?' is said to doubt concerning the future. One who doubts, wondering, 'Am I now a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa, or a sudda; or am I form, or feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness?' is said to doubt concerning the present.

Tattha kiñcāpi khattiyo vā attano khattiyabhāvaṃ, brāhmaṇo vā brāhmaṇabhāvaṃ, vesso vā vessabhāvaṃ, suddo vā suddabhāvaṃ ajānanako nāma natthi, jīvaladdhiko [P 0.0497] pana satto khattiyajīvādīnaṃ vaṇṇādibhedaṃ sutvā ‘kīdiso nu kho amhākaṃ abbhantare jīvo – kiṃ nu kho [V 0.0469] nīlako udāhu pītako lohitako odāto caturaṃso chaḷaṃso aṭṭhaṃso’ti kaṅkhanto evaṃ kaṅkhati nāma.

Here, although there is no khattiya who does not know he is a khattiya, no brahmin who does not know he is a brahmin, no vessa who does not know he is a vessa, and no sudda who does not know he is a sudda, still a being who subscribes to a life-principle, having heard of the distinctions of color and so on among the life-principles of khattiyas and others, doubts thus: 'What kind of life-principle is inside us? Is it blue, or yellow, or red, or white; four-cornered, six-cornered, or eight-cornered?' Such a one is said to doubt in this way.

923. Titthāyatanānīti titthabhūtāni āyatanāni, titthiyānaṃ vā āyatanāni. Tattha titthaṃ nāma dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo. Titthiyā nāma yesaṃ tā diṭṭhiyo ruccanti khamanti. Āyatanaṭṭho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Tattha yasmā sabbepi diṭṭhigatikā sañjāyamānā imesuyeva tīsu ṭhānesu sañjāyanti, samosaramānāpi etesuyeva samosaranti sannipatanti, diṭṭhigatikabhāve ca nesaṃ etāniyeva kāraṇāni, tasmā titthāni ca tāni sañjātānītiādinā atthena āyatanāni cāti titthāyatanāni; tenevatthena titthiyānaṃ āyatanānītipi titthāyatanāni. Purisapuggaloti satto. Kāmañca purisotipi puggalotipi vutte sattoyeva vutto, ayaṃ pana sammutikathā nāma yo yathā jānāti tassa tathā vuccati. Paṭisaṃvedetīti attano santāne uppannaṃ jānāti, paṭisaṃviditaṃ karoti anubhavati vā. Pubbekatahetūti pubbe katakāraṇā, pubbe katakammapaccayeneva paṭisaṃvedetīti attho. Ayaṃ nigaṇṭhasamayo. Evaṃvādino pana te kammavedanañca kiriyavedanañca paṭikkhipitvā ekaṃ vipākavedanameva sampaṭicchanti. Pittasamuṭṭhānādīsu (mahāni. 5) ca aṭṭhasu ābādhesu [M 0.0479] satta paṭikkhipitvā aṭṭhamaṃyeva sampaṭicchanti, diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādīsu ca tīsu kammesu dve paṭikkhipitvā ekaṃ aparāpariyavedanīyameva sampaṭicchanti, kusalākusalavipākakiriyasaṅkhātāsu ca catūsu cetanāsu vipākacetanaṃyeva sampaṭicchanti.

923. 'Bases of sectarian resorts' (titthāyatanāni) means bases that are sectarian resorts, or the bases of the sectarians. Here, 'sectarian resort' (tittha) refers to the sixty-two views. 'Sectarians' (titthiyā) are those who favor and accept those views. The meaning of 'base' (āyatana) has been explained below. Since all who hold such views, when they arise, arise in these three grounds, and when they converge, they converge and assemble in them, and since these are the causes for their holding such views, they are 'bases of sectarian resorts' because they are sectarian resorts and because they are bases in the sense of being a cause of their arising, etc. For the same reason they are also 'bases of the sectarians.' 'Man or person' (purisapuggala) means a being. Although when 'man' or 'person' is said, a being is spoken of, this is conventional speech: one speaks to a person in the way he understands. 'He experiences' (paṭisaṃvedeti) means he knows what has arisen in his own continuity; he makes it felt, or he undergoes it. 'Because of what was done in the past' (pubbekatahetu) means for a reason made in the past; the meaning is that one experiences it solely with a past deed as condition. This is the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas. Those who hold this view, however, reject feeling that is kamma and functional feeling, and accept only resultant feeling. Among the eight kinds of ailments, such as those arising from bile (see Mnd 5), they reject seven and accept only the eighth. Among the three kinds of kamma—that to be experienced in this very life, etc.—they reject two and accept only the one to be experienced in a future life. And among the four kinds of volition—wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional—they accept only resultant volition.

Issaranimmānahetūti issaranimmānakāraṇā; brahmunā vā pajāpatinā vā issarena nimmitattā paṭisaṃvedetīti attho. Ayaṃ brāhmaṇasamayo. Ayañhi nesaṃ adhippāyo – imā tisso vedanā paccuppanne attanā katamūlakena vā āṇattimūlakena vā pubbe katena vā ahetuappaccayā vā paṭisaṃvedetuṃ nāma na sakkā; issaranimmānakāraṇā eva pana imā paṭisaṃvedetīti. Evaṃvādino panete heṭṭhā vuttesu aṭṭhasu ābādhesu ekampi asampaṭicchitvā sabbaṃ paṭibāhanti. Tathā diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādīsupi sabbakoṭṭhāsesu [P 0.0498] ekampi asampaṭicchitvā sabbaṃ paṭibāhanti.

'Because of creation by a lord' (issaranimmānahetu) means for the reason of creation by a lord; the meaning is that one experiences because of being created by a lord, that is, by Brahmā or Pajāpati. This is the doctrine of the brahmins. For this is their opinion: these three kinds of feelings cannot possibly be experienced because of a cause made by oneself in the present, or because of a command, or because of what was done in the past, or without cause and condition; rather, one experiences them only for the reason of creation by a lord. Those who hold this view, however, reject all of the eight ailments mentioned above, not accepting even one. Similarly, in regard to all the divisions such as kamma to be experienced in this very life, they reject them all, not accepting even one.

Ahetu appaccayāti hetuñca paccayañca vinā akāraṇeneva paṭisaṃvedetīti attho. Ayaṃ [V 0.0470] ājīvakasamayo. Evaṃ vādino etepi heṭṭhā vuttesu kāraṇesu ca byādhīsu ca ekampi asampaṭicchitvā sabbaṃ paṭikkhipanti.

'Without cause, without condition' means that one experiences without cause and without condition, for no reason at all. This is the doctrine of the Ājīvakas. These too, who hold this view, reject all of the causes and ailments mentioned above, not accepting even one.

924. Kiñcanāti palibodhā. Rāgo kiñcananti rāgo uppajjamāno satte bandhati palibundheti, tasmā kiñcananti vuccati. Dosamohesupi eseva nayo. Aṅgaṇānīti “udaṅgaṇe tattha papaṃ avindu”nti (jā. 1.1.2) āgataṭṭhāne bhūmippadeso aṅgaṇaṃ. “Tasseva rajassa vā aṅgaṇassa vā pahānāya vāyamatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.184; a. ni. 10.51) āgataṭṭhāne yaṃ kiñci malaṃ vā paṅko vā. “Sāṅgaṇova samāno”ti (ma. ni. 1.57) āgataṭṭhāne nānappakāro tibbakileso. Idhāpi tadeva kilesaṅgaṇaṃ adhippetaṃ. Teneva rāgo aṅgaṇantiādimāha.

924. 'Impediment' (kiñcana) means an obstruction. 'Lust is an impediment' means that when lust arises, it binds and obstructs beings; therefore it is called an impediment. The same method applies to hatred and delusion. 'Stain' (aṅgaṇa): in the passage, 'In the courtyard he found no evil' (Ja 1.1.2), aṅgaṇa is a plot of ground. In the passage, 'He strives for the abandoning of that dust or stain' (MN 1:184; AN 10:51), it is any kind of blemish or mud. In the passage, 'Being with a stain' (MN 1:57), it is various kinds of intense defilements. Here, too, that same defilement-stain is intended. For that reason it is said, 'Lust is a stain,' and so on.

Malānīti malinabhāvakaraṇāni. Rāgo malanti rāgo uppajjamāno cittaṃ malinaṃ karoti, malaṃ gāhāpeti, tasmā malanti vuccati. Itaresupi dvīsu eseva nayo.

'Stains' (malāni) are things that cause a state of being stained. 'Lust is a stain' means that when lust arises, it stains the mind and makes it acquire a stain; therefore it is called a stain. The same method applies to the other two.

Visamaniddese [M 0.0480] yasmā rāgādīsu ceva kāyaduccaritādīsu ca sattā pakkhalanti, pakkhalitā ca pana sāsanatopi sugatitopi patanti, tasmā pakkhalanapātahetuto rāgo visamantiādi vuttaṃ.

In the Exposition of Unevenness: because beings stumble in lust and so on and in bodily misconduct and so on, and having stumbled they fall away from the Teaching and from a good destination, therefore, because it is a cause of stumbling and falling, it is said, 'Lust is unevenness,' and so on.

Aggīti anudahanaṭṭhena aggi. Rāgaggīti rāgo uppajjamāno satte anudahati jhāpeti, tasmā aggīti vuccati. Dosamohesupi eseva nayo. Tattha vatthūni – ekā kira daharabhikkhunī cittalapabbatavihāre uposathāgāraṃ gantvā dvārapālakarūpaṃ olokayamānā ṭhitā. Athassā anto rāgo uppanno. Sā teneva jhāyitvā kālamakāsi. Bhikkhuniyo gacchamānā ‘ayaṃ daharā ṭhitā, pakkosatha na’nti āhaṃsu. Ekā gantvā ‘kasmā ṭhitāsī’ti hatthe gaṇhi. Gahitamattā parivattitvā patitā. Idaṃ tāva rāgassa anudahanatāya vatthu. Dosassa pana anudahanatāya manopadosikā devā daṭṭhabbā. Mohassa anudahanatāya khiḍḍāpadosikā devā daṭṭhabbā. Mohanavasena hi tesaṃ satisammoso hoti. Tasmā khiḍḍāvasena āhārakālaṃ ativattitvā kālaṃ karonti. Kasāvāti [P 0.0499] kasaṭā nirojā. Rāgādīsu ca kāyaduccaritādīsu ca ekampi paṇītaṃ ojavantaṃ natthi, tasmā rāgo kasāvotiādi vuttaṃ.

'Fire' (aggi) means 'fire' in the sense of burning. The fire of lust: when lust arises, it burns and consumes beings; therefore, it is called 'fire.' The same method applies to hatred and delusion. Here are the stories: It is said that a certain young nun, having gone to the Uposatha hall in Cittalapabbata Monastery, stood there gazing at the figure of the doorkeeper. Then lust arose within her. Consumed by it, she died. The nuns, passing by, said, 'This young one is standing; call her in.' One went and, taking her hand, asked, 'Why are you standing here?' The moment she was touched, she spun around and fell. This is indeed a story of lust's burning. For the burning of hatred, one should consider the Manopadosika devas, and for the burning of delusion, the Khiḍḍapadosika devas. For due to delusion, their mindfulness becomes confused. Thus, engrossed in play, they let their feeding time pass and die. 'Taints' (kasāvā) means foul and impure. Among lust and the other defilements, as well as bodily misconduct and the like, there is nothing refined or nourishing; therefore, it is said, 'lust is a taint,' and so forth.

925. Assādadiṭṭhīti [V 0.0471] assādasampayuttā diṭṭhi. Natthi kāmesu dosoti kilesakāmena vatthukāmapaṭisevanadoso natthīti vadati. Pātabyatanti pātabbabhāvaṃ paribhuñjanaṃ ajjhoharaṇaṃ. Evaṃvādī hi so vatthukāmesu kilesakāmaṃ pivanto viya ajjhoharanto viya paribhuñjati. Attānudiṭṭhīti attānaṃ anugatā diṭṭhi. Micchādiṭṭhīti lāmakā diṭṭhi. Idāni yasmā ettha paṭhamā sassatadiṭṭhi hoti, dutiyā sakkāyadiṭṭhi, tatiyā ucchedadiṭṭhi, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ sassatadiṭṭhi assādadiṭṭhītiādimāha.

925. 'The view of gratification' (assādadiṭṭhi) is a view associated with gratification. 'There is no harm in sensual pleasures' means one says there is no fault in indulging in sensual objects with sensual desire. 'Drinkability' (pātabyatā) refers to the state of being drinkable, consuming, and ingesting. One who speaks thus, indeed, enjoys sensual objects as if drinking and ingesting sensual desire. 'Self-view' (attānudiṭṭhi) is a view that follows the self. 'Wrong view' (micchādiṭṭhi) is a base view. Now, since here the first is the eternalist view, the second the personality view, and the third the annihilationist view, therefore, to show that meaning, he said, 'The gratification view is the eternalist view,' and so on.

926. Aratiniddeso ca vihesāniddeso ca vuttatthoyeva. Adhammassa cariyā adhammacariyā, adhammakaraṇanti attho. Visamā cariyā, visamassa vā kammassa cariyāti visamacariyā. Dovacassatāpāpamittatā niddesā vuttatthā eva. Puthunimittārammaṇesu pavattito nānattesu saññā nānattasaññā. Yasmā vā aññāva kāmasaññā, aññā byāpādādisaññā, tasmā [M 0.0481] nānattā saññātipi nānattasaññā. Kosajjapamādaniddesesu pañcasu kāmaguṇesu vissaṭṭhacittassa kusaladhammabhāvanāya ananuyogavasena līnavuttitā kosajjaṃ, pamajjanavasena pamattabhāvo pamādoti veditabbo. Asantuṭṭhitādiniddesā vuttatthā eva.

926. The expositions of 'discontent' (arati) and 'harming' (vihesā) are as previously stated. 'Unrighteous conduct' (adhammacariyā) is conduct contrary to the Dhamma, meaning unrighteous action. 'Uneven conduct' (visamacariyā) is conduct that is unfair, or the conduct of unfair deeds. The expositions of 'difficulty of admonition' (dovacassatā) and 'bad friendship' (pāpamittatā) are as previously stated. 'Diverse perceptions' (nānattasaññā) are perceptions arising in relation to various diverse signs and objects. Alternatively, because perceptions of sensual pleasure are one thing, and perceptions of ill-will and the like are another, therefore perceptions that are diverse are also 'diverse perceptions.' In the expositions of 'laziness' (kosajja) and 'negligence' (pamāda), laziness should be understood as the sluggishness of a mind given over to the five strands of sensual pleasure, due to non-application to the cultivation of wholesome qualities; negligence should be understood as the state of being heedless due to carelessness. The expositions of 'discontent' (asantuṭṭhitā) and so on are as previously stated.

931. Anādariyaniddese ovādassa anādiyanavasena anādarabhāvo anādariyaṃ. Anādariyanākāro anādaratā. Sagaruvāsaṃ avasanaṭṭhena agāravabhāvo agāravatā. Sajeṭṭhakavāsaṃ avasanaṭṭhena appatissavatā. Anaddāti anādiyanā. Anaddāyanāti anādiyanākāro. Anaddāya ayitassa bhāvo anaddāyitattaṃ. Asīlassa bhāvo asīlyaṃ. Acittīkāroti garucittīkārassa akaraṇaṃ.

931. In the exposition of 'disrespect' (anādariya), disrespect is the state of disrespectfulness which consists in not taking up advice. The manner of disrespect is 'disregard' (anādaratā). The state of not dwelling with a teacher is 'irreverence' (agāravatā). The state of not dwelling with elders is 'insubordination' (appatissavatā). 'Not taking up' (anaddā) means not heeding. 'The act of not taking up' (anaddāyanā) is the manner of not heeding. The state of one who has not taken up is 'the state of not having taken up' (anaddāyitattaṃ). The state of one without virtue is 'immorality' (asīlyaṃ). 'Not showing respect' (acittīkāro) means not showing reverence to those worthy of reverence.

932. Assaddhabhāvo assaddhiyaṃ. Asaddahanākāro asaddahanā. Okappetvā anupavisitvā aggahaṇaṃ anokappanā. Appasīdanaṭṭhena anabhippasādo.

932. The state of lacking faith is 'faithlessness' (assaddhiyaṃ). The manner of not believing is 'disbelief' (asaddahanā). 'Lack of conviction' (anokappanā) is not grasping after having placed confidence and entered into a matter. 'Lack of clear confidence' (anabhippasādo) is due to a lack of serenity.

Avadaññutāti thaddhamacchariyavasena ‘dehi, karohī’ti vacanassa ajānatā.

'Ungenerosity' (avadaññutā) is, due to stubbornness and miserliness, not knowing the words, 'Give, do this.'

934. Buddhā [P 0.0500] ca buddhasāvakā cāti ettha buddhaggahaṇena paccekabuddhāpi gahitāva. Asametukamyatāti [V 0.0472] tesaṃ samīpaṃ agantukāmatā. Saddhammaṃ asotukamyatāti sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhammā saddhammo nāma, taṃ asuṇitukāmatā. Anuggahetukamyatāti na uggahetukāmatā.

934. 'Buddhas and disciples of the Buddha'—here, by the term 'Buddha,' Paccekabuddhas are also included. 'Desiring not to meet' (asametukamyatā) means not wishing to approach them. 'Desiring not to hear the true Dhamma' (saddhammaṃ asotukamyatā)—the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are called the true Dhamma; this means not wishing to hear it. 'Desiring not to learn' (anuggahetukamyatā) means not wishing to take up instruction.

Upārambhacittatāti upārambhacittabhāvo. Yasmā pana so atthato upārambhova hoti, tasmā taṃ dassetuṃ tattha katamo upārambhotiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha upārambhanavasena upārambho. Punappunaṃ upārambho anupārambho upārambhanākāro upārambhanā. Punappunaṃ upārambhanā anupārambhanā. Anupārambhitassa bhāvo anupārambhitattaṃ. Uññāti heṭṭhā katvā jānanā. Avaññāti avajānanā. Paribhavanaṃ paribhavo. Randhassa gavesitā randhagavesitā. Randhaṃ vā gavesatīti randhagavesī, tassa bhāvo randhagavesitā. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ paravajjānupassanalakkhaṇo upārambho nāma vuccati, yena samannāgato puggalo, yathā nāma tunnakāro [M 0.0482] sāṭakaṃ pasāretvā chiddameva oloketi, evameva parassa sabbepi guṇe makkhetvā aguṇesuyeva patiṭṭhāti.

'The state of having a fault-finding mind' (upārambhacittatā) is the nature of having a fault-finding mind. Since this is essentially fault-finding, to illustrate this, it is said, 'Here, what is fault-finding?' and so on. In this context, 'fault-finding' (upārambho) is by way of finding fault. Repeated fault-finding is 'persistent fault-finding' (anupārambho). The manner of fault-finding is 'the act of finding fault' (upārambhanā). Repeatedly finding fault is 'the persistent act of finding fault' (anupārambhanā). The state of one who has persistently found fault is 'the state of persistent fault-finding' (anupārambhitattaṃ). 'Contempt' (uññā) means knowing by depreciating. 'Disdain' (avaññā) means despising. 'Humiliation' (paribhavanaṃ) is contempt (paribhavo). 'Seeking for defects' (randhagavesitā) is the seeking of defects. Or, one who seeks defects is a 'defect-seeker' (randhagavesī), and their nature is 'defect-seeking' (randhagavesitā). This is called 'fault-finding' (upārambho), which is characterized by seeing others' faults. A person endowed with this, just as a tailor spreads out a cloth and only looks for holes, so too do they, smearing over all the virtues of others, establish themselves only in their faults.

936. Ayoniso manasikāroti anupāyamanasikāro. Anicce niccanti anicceyeva vatthusmiṃ ‘idaṃ nicca’nti evaṃ pavatto. Dukkhe sukhantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Saccavippaṭikulena cāti catunnaṃ saccānaṃ ananulomavasena. Cittassa āvaṭṭanātiādīni sabbānipi āvajjanasseva vevacanāneva. Āvajjanañhi bhavaṅgacittaṃ āvaṭṭetīti cittassa āvaṭṭanā. Anuanu āvaṭṭetīti anāvaṭṭanā. Ābhujatīti ābhogo. Bhavaṅgārammaṇato aññaṃ ārammaṇaṃ samannāharatīti samannāhāro. Tadevārammaṇaṃ attānaṃ anubandhitvā uppajjamāne manasikarotīti manasikāro. Karotīti ṭhapeti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ anupāyamanasikāro uppathamanasikāralakkhaṇo ayonisomanasikāro nāma vuccati. Tassa vasena puggalo dukkhādīni saccāni yāthāvato āvajjituṃ na sakkoti.

936. 'Unwise attention' (ayonisomanasikāro) means attention by wrong means. 'The impermanent as permanent' means, in regard to an impermanent thing, proceeding thus: 'this is permanent.' The same method applies to cases such as 'suffering as happiness,' and so on. 'And opposed to the truth' means in a way that is not in accordance with the four truths. 'Turning of the mind' (cittassa āvaṭṭanā) and so on are all simply synonyms for 'adverting' (āvajjana). For adverting turns the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅgacitta); therefore it is called 'turning of the mind' (cittassa āvaṭṭanā). Turning again and again is 'repeated turning' (anāvaṭṭanā). 'It bends towards' means 'inclination' (ābhogo). Bringing to mind an object other than the object of the life-continuum is 'application' (samannāhāro). Giving attention to that very object as it arises in connection with oneself is 'attention' (manasikāro). 'He does' (karoti) means he places. This is called 'unwise attention' (ayonisomanasikāro), which is characterized by attention by wrong means, attention on the wrong path. Because of that, a person is not able to properly advert to the truths such as suffering.

Kummaggasevanāniddese yaṃ kummaggaṃ sevato sevanā kummaggasevanāti vuccati, taṃ dassetuṃ tattha katamo kummaggoti [P 0.0501] dutiyapucchā katā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

In the exposition of 'following wrong paths' (kummaggasevanā), it is said that the following of one who follows a wrong path is called 'following a wrong path.' To demonstrate this, the second question is asked: 'Here, what is the wrong path?' The rest is self-evident throughout.

Tikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of Triads is concluded.

(4.) Catukkaniddesavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Exposition of Tetrads

939. Catukkaniddese [V 0.0473] taṇhuppādesu cīvarahetūti ‘kattha manāpaṃ cīvaraṃ labhissāmī’ti cīvarakāraṇā uppajjati. Itibhavābhavahetūti ettha itīti nidassanatthe nipāto; yathā cīvarādihetu evaṃ bhavābhavahetūtipi attho. Bhavābhavoti cettha paṇītapaṇītatarāni telamadhuphāṇitādīni adhippetāni. Imesaṃ pana catunnaṃ taṇhuppādānaṃ pahānatthāya paṭipāṭiyāva cattāro ariyavaṃsā desitāti veditabbā.

939. In the Exposition of Tetrads, concerning the arisings of craving, the phrase 'due to robes' means that craving arises for the sake of robes with the thought, 'Where can I obtain a pleasant robe?' In the phrase 'due to existence and non-existence, and so on' (Itibhavābhavahetūti), the word 'iti' is a particle in the sense of an example; the meaning is that just as craving arises for the sake of robes and so on, so too it arises for the sake of existence and non-existence. Here, by 'existence and non-existence' are intended various refined and more refined things such as oil, honey, and molasses. It should be understood that the four noble heritages have been taught in sequence for the purpose of abandoning these four arisings of craving.

Agatigamanesu [M 0.0483] chandāgatiṃ gacchatīti chandena pemena agatiṃ gacchati, akattabbaṃ karoti. Parapadesupi eseva nayo. Tattha yo ‘ayaṃ me mitto vā sandiṭṭho vā sambhatto vā ñātako vā lañjaṃ vā pana me detī’ti chandavasena assāmikaṃ sāmikaṃ karoti – ayaṃ chandāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Yo ‘ayaṃ me verī’ti pakativeravasena vā taṅkhaṇuppannakodhavasena vā sāmikaṃ assāmikaṃ karoti – ayaṃ dosāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Yo pana mandattā momūhattā yaṃ vā taṃ vā vatvā assāmikaṃ sāmikaṃ karoti – ayaṃ mohāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Yo pana ‘ayaṃ rājavallabho vā visamanissito vā anatthampi me kareyyā’ti bhīto assāmikaṃ sāmikaṃ karoti – ayaṃ bhayāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Yo vā pana bhājiyaṭṭhāne kiñci bhājento ‘ayaṃ me mitto vā sandiṭṭho vā sambhatto vā’ti pemavasena atirekaṃ deti, ‘ayaṃ me verī’ti dosavasena ūnakaṃ deti, momūhattā dinnādinnaṃ ajānamāno kassaci ūnakaṃ kassaci adhikaṃ deti, ‘ayaṃ imasmiṃ adīyamāne mayhaṃ anatthampi kareyyā’ti bhīto kassaci atirekaṃ deti, so catubbidhopi yathānukkamena chandāgatiādīni gacchati nāma. Ariyā etāya na gacchantīti agati, anariyā iminā agatiṃ gacchantīti agatigamanaṃ. Imaṃ dvayaṃ catunnampi sādhāraṇavasena vuttaṃ. Chandena gamanaṃ chandagamanaṃ. Idaṃ dosādīnaṃ asādhāraṇavasena vuttaṃ. Sakapakkharāgañca parapakkhadosañca purakkhatvā asamaggabhāvena gamanaṃ vaggagamanaṃ. Idaṃ chandadosasādhāraṇavasena vuttaṃ. Vārino viya yathāninnaṃ gamananti vārigamanaṃ. Idaṃ catunnampi sādhāraṇavasena vuttaṃ.

Regarding going on wrong courses, 'one goes the course of desire' means that due to desire and affection, one takes a wrong course and does what should not be done. The same method applies in the other cases. Here, one who, out of desire, makes what is unowned owned—thinking, 'This is my friend, acquaintance, associate, relative, or one who gives me bribes'—is said to go the course of desire. One who, out of aversion—either due to established enmity or momentary anger—makes what is owned unowned, thinking, 'This is my enemy,' is said to go the course of aversion. One who, due to stupidity and utter delusion, says this or that and makes what is unowned owned is said to go the course of delusion. One who, out of fear, makes what is unowned owned—thinking, 'This person is a favorite of the king or a person of influence; they might harm me'—is said to go the course of fear. Or, when distributing something, one who gives more to a friend, acquaintance, or associate out of affection; gives less to an enemy out of aversion; gives less to some and more to others out of utter delusion, not knowing what has been given and what has not; or gives more to someone out of fear, thinking, 'If I do not give to this person, they might harm me'—such a person, in these four ways, is said to go by the course of desire, aversion, delusion, or fear, respectively. Because noble ones do not go by it, it is a 'wrong course' (agati); because ignoble ones go on a wrong course by this, it is 'going on a wrong course' (agatigamana). This pair is stated as common to all four. Going by desire is 'going-by-desire' (chandagamana). This is stated as not common to aversion and so on. 'Factional-going' (vaggagamana) is going with disharmony by promoting attachment to one's own side and aversion to the other side. This is stated as common to desire and aversion. 'Water-going' (vārigamana) is going according to the slope, like water. This is stated as common to all four.

Vipariyāsesu [P 0.0502] aniccādīni vatthūni niccantiādinā nayena viparītato esantīti vipariyāsā, saññāya vipariyāso saññāvipariyāso. Itaresupi dvīsu eseva nayo. Evamete catunnaṃ [V 0.0474] vatthūnaṃ vasena cattāro, yesu vatthūsu saññādīnaṃ vasena dvādasa honti. Tesu aṭṭha sotāpattimaggena pahīyanti. Asubhe subhanti saññācittavipallāsā sakadāgāmimaggena tanukā honti, anāgāmimaggena pahīyanti. Dukkhe sukhanti saññācittavipallāsā arahattamaggena pahīyantīti veditabbā.

Regarding the perversions: they are called 'perversions' (vipariyāsā) because things such as the impermanent are regarded perversely as permanent, and so on. The perversion of perception is the 'perversion-of-perception'. The same method applies to the other two. Thus, based on the four objects, there are four perversions; and based on perception, mind, and view, they become twelve in total. Of these, eight are abandoned by the path of stream-entry. The perversions of perception and mind that perceive the foul as beautiful become attenuated by the path of the once-returner and are abandoned by the path of the non-returner. The perversions of perception and mind that perceive suffering as pleasure, it should be understood, are abandoned by the path of arahantship.

Anariyavohāresu [M 0.0484] anariyavohārāti anariyānaṃ lāmakānaṃ vohārā. Diṭṭhavāditāti ‘diṭṭhaṃ mayā’ti evaṃ vāditā. Ettha ca taṃ taṃ samuṭṭhāpikacetanāvasena attho veditabbo. Saha saddena cetanā kathitātipi vuttameva. Dutiyacatukkepi eseva nayo. Ariyo hi adisvā vā ‘diṭṭhaṃ mayā’ti disvā vā ‘na diṭṭhaṃ mayā’ti vattā nāma natthi; anariyova evaṃ vadati. Tasmā evaṃ vadantassa etā saha saddena aṭṭha cetanā anariyavohārāti veditabbā.

Regarding ignoble speech: 'ignoble speech' refers to the speech of ignoble, base people. 'Speaking of what is seen' means saying, 'I have seen it.' Here, the meaning should be understood according to the intention that gives rise to each case. It has also been stated that intention is spoken of together with speech. The same method applies in the second tetrad as well. For a noble one does not say, 'I have seen it,' without having seen it, nor does one say, 'I have not seen it,' after having seen it. Only an ignoble person speaks in such a way. Therefore, for one who speaks thus, these eight intentions, together with speech, should be understood as ignoble speech.

Duccaritesu paṭhamacatukkaṃ veracetanāvasena vuttaṃ, dutiyaṃ vacīduccaritavasena.

Regarding misconduct, the first tetrad is stated in terms of volitions of enmity, and the second in terms of verbal misconduct.

Bhayesu paṭhamacatukke jātiṃ paṭicca uppannaṃ bhayaṃ jātibhayaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Dutiyacatukke rājato uppannaṃ bhayaṃ rājabhayaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

Regarding the fears: in the first tetrad, the fear that has arisen in dependence on birth is the fear of birth. The same method applies to the rest. In the second tetrad, the fear that has arisen from a king is the fear of kings. The same method applies to the rest.

Tatiyacatukke cattāri bhayānīti mahāsamudde udakaṃ orohantassa vuttabhayāni. Mahāsamudde kira mahindavīci nāma saṭṭhi yojanāni uggacchati. Gaṅgāvīci nāma paṇṇāsa. Rohaṇavīci nāma cattālīsa yojanāni uggacchati. Evarūpā ūmiyo paṭicca uppannaṃ bhayaṃ ūmibhayaṃ nāma. Kumbhīlato uppannaṃ bhayaṃ kumbhīlabhayaṃ. Udakāvaṭṭato bhayaṃ āvaṭṭabhayaṃ. Susukā vuccati caṇḍamaccho; tato bhayaṃ susukābhayaṃ.

In the third tetrad, the four fears are the fears spoken of for one descending into the water of the great ocean. It is said that in the great ocean a wave named Mahindavīci rises sixty yojanas, one named Gaṅgāvīci rises fifty, and one named Rohaṇavīci rises forty yojanas. The fear that has arisen in dependence on such waves is named the fear of waves (ūmibhaya). The fear that has arisen from a crocodile is the fear of crocodiles (kumbhīlabhaya). The fear from a whirlpool is the fear of whirlpools (āvaṭṭabhaya). A susukā is said to be a fierce fish; the fear from it is the fear of the susukā (susukābhaya).

Catutthacatukke attānuvādabhayanti pāpakammino attānaṃ anuvadantassa uppajjanakabhayaṃ. Parānuvādabhayanti parassa anuvādato uppajjanakabhayaṃ. Daṇḍabhayanti agārikassa raññā pavattitadaṇḍaṃ, anagārikassa vinayadaṇḍaṃ paṭicca uppajjanakabhayaṃ. Duggatibhayanti cattāro apāye paṭicca uppajjanakabhayaṃ. Iti [P 0.0503] imehi catūhi catukkehi soḷasa mahābhayāni nāma kathitāni.

In the fourth tetrad, the fear of self-reproach is the fear that arises for an evil-doer who reproaches himself. The fear of others' reproach is the fear that arises from the reproach of others. The fear of punishment is the fear that arises in dependence on the punishment imposed by a king for a householder, or the disciplinary punishment for a homeless one. The fear of a bad destination is the fear that arises in dependence on the four planes of misery. Thus, by means of these four tetrads, sixteen great fears have been taught.

Diṭṭhicatukke [V 0.0475] timbarukadiṭṭhi (saṃ. ni. 2.18) nāma kathitā. Tattha sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkhanti vedanaṃ attato samanupassato vedanāya eva vedanā katāti uppannā diṭṭhi. Evañca sati tassā vedanāya pubbepi atthitā āpajjatīti ayaṃ sassatadiṭṭhi nāma hoti. Saccato thetatoti saccato thirato. Paraṃkatanti [M 0.0485] paccuppannavedanato aññaṃ vedanākāraṇaṃ vedanattānaṃ samanupassato ‘aññāya vedanāya ayaṃ vedanā katā’ti uppannā diṭṭhi. Evaṃ sati purimāya kāraṇavedanāya ucchedo āpajjatīti ayaṃ ucchedadiṭṭhi nāma hoti. Sayaṃkatañca paraṃkatañcāti yathāvutteneva atthena ‘upaḍḍhaṃ sayaṃkataṃ, upaḍḍhaṃ parena kata’nti gaṇhato uppannā diṭṭhi – ayaṃ sassatucchedadiṭṭhi nāma. Catutthā akāraṇā eva sukhadukkhaṃ hotīti gaṇhato uppannā diṭṭhi. Evaṃ sati ayaṃ ahetukadiṭṭhi nāma. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthamevāti.

In the tetrad of views, the view from the Timbaruka Sutta (SN 12.18) is discussed. Therein, for one who regards pleasure and pain as self-made, seeing feeling as the agent, the view arises that 'feeling is made by feeling itself.' This being so, it follows that the feeling must have existed previously; this becomes the view of eternalism. 'Truly and firmly' (saccato thetato) means truly and steadfastly (saccato thirato). As to 'made by another': for one who sees a cause of feeling—a feeling-self—that is other than the present feeling, the view arises that 'this feeling is made by another feeling.' This being so, it follows that the prior, causal feeling is annihilated; this becomes the view of annihilationism. As to 'both self-made and other-made': this is the view that arises for one who holds, in the sense already stated, that 'half is self-made and half is made by another'; this is the view of partial eternalism and annihilationism. The fourth is the view that arises for one who holds that pleasure and pain occur without any cause. This being so, this is the view of non-causality. The rest here has a plain meaning, in accordance with the method stated previously.

Catukkaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Tetrads is finished.

(5.) Pañcakaniddesavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pentad

940. Pañcakaniddese yasmā yesaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhiādīni appahīnāni, te bhavaggepi nibbatte etāni ākaḍḍhitvā kāmabhaveyeva pātenti, tasmā orambhāgiyāni saṃyojanānīti vuttāni. Iti etāni pañca gacchantaṃ na vārenti, gataṃ pana ānenti. Rūparāgādīnipi pañca gacchantaṃ na vārenti, āgantuṃ pana na denti. Rāgādayo pañca lagganaṭṭhena saṅgā, anupaviṭṭhaṭṭhena pana sallāti vuttā.

940. In the exposition of the pentad, because those for whom identity view and so forth have not been abandoned, even if reborn in the highest realm of existence, drag these along and cause them to fall back into the sensual realm; therefore, they are called the lower fetters. Thus, these five do not prevent one from going, but they do bring back one who has gone. The five beginning with lust for form and so forth also do not prevent one from going, but they do not allow one to return. The five beginning with lust are called bonds because of their sticking nature, but they are called darts because of their piercing nature.

941. Cetokhilāti cittassa thaddhabhāvā kacavarabhāvā khāṇukabhāvā. Satthari kaṅkhatīti satthu sarīre vā guṇe vā kaṅkhati. Sarīre kaṅkhamāno ‘dvattiṃsavaralakkhaṇapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ nāma sarīraṃ atthi nu kho natthī’ti kaṅkhati. Guṇe kaṅkhamāno ‘atītānāgatapaccuppannajānanasamatthaṃ sabbaññutañāṇaṃ atthi nu kho natthī’ti kaṅkhati. Vicikicchatīti vicinanto kicchati, dukkhaṃ āpajjati, vinicchetuṃ na sakkoti. Nādhimuccatīti [P 0.0504] ‘evameta’nti adhimokkhaṃ na paṭilabhati[V 0.0476]. Na sampasīdatīti guṇesu otaritvā nibbicikicchabhāvena pasīdituṃ anāvilo bhavituṃ na sakkoti.

941. Mental barrenness refers to the rigidity, impurity, and thorniness of the mind. Doubting the Teacher means doubting the Teacher’s body or qualities. One who doubts the body doubts, “Is there really a body adorned with the thirty-two excellent marks or not?” One who doubts the qualities doubts, “Is there really the omniscient knowledge capable of knowing the past, future, and present or not?” To doubt means to struggle while investigating, to fall into suffering, to be unable to decide. Not being convinced means not obtaining the conviction that “it is so.” Not being serene means not being able to enter into the qualities and become clear, free from doubt.

Dhammeti pariyattidhamme ca paṭivedhadhamme ca. Pariyattidhamme kaṅkhamāno ‘tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ caturāsītidhammakkhandhasahassānīti vadanti, atthi nu kho etaṃ natthī’ti kaṅkhati. Paṭivedhadhamme kaṅkhamāno ‘vipassanānissando maggo nāma[M 0.0486], magganissando phalaṃ nāma, sabbasaṅkhārapaṭinissaggo nibbānaṃ nāmāti vadanti, taṃ atthi nu kho natthīti kaṅkhati’.

Regarding the Dhamma, it refers to both the textual Dhamma and the Dhamma of realization. One who doubts the textual Dhamma thinks, “They say the Buddha’s word is the three baskets, the eighty-four thousand aggregates of teachings—does this really exist or not?” One who doubts the Dhamma of realization thinks, “They say there is a path that is the fruit of insight, a fruition that is the fruit of the path, and the relinquishment of all formations called Nibbāna—does this really exist or not?”

Saṅghe kaṅkhatīti ‘ujuppaṭipannotiādīnaṃ padānaṃ vasena evarūpaṃ paṭipadaṃ paṭipannā cattāro maggaṭṭhā cattāro phalaṭṭhāti aṭṭhannaṃ puggalānaṃ samūhabhūto saṅgho nāma atthi nu kho natthī’ti kaṅkhati. Sikkhāya kaṅkhamāno ‘adhisīlasikkhā nāma adhicittasikkhā nāma adhipaññā sikkhā nāmāti vadanti, sā atthi nu kho natthī’ti kaṅkhati.

Doubting the Saṅgha means doubting, “Is there really a Saṅgha, the assembly of the eight individuals—the four standing on the paths and the four standing in the fruits—who have entered upon such practice, in terms of the words beginning with ‘practicing uprightly’—or is there not?” Doubting the training means doubting, “They speak of the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom—does this really exist or not?”

Cetasovinibandhāti cittaṃ bandhitvā muṭṭhiyaṃ katvā viya gaṇhantīti cetasovinibandhā. Kāmeti vatthukāmepi kilesakāmepi. Kāyeti attano kāye. Rūpeti bahiddhā rūpe. Yāvadatthanti yattakaṃ icchati tattakaṃ. Udarāvadehakanti udarapūraṃ. Tañhi udaraṃ avadehanato udarāvadehakanti vuccati. Seyyasukhanti mañcapīṭhasukhaṃ utusukhaṃ vā. Passasukhanti yathā samparivattakaṃ sayantassa dakkhiṇapassavāmapassānaṃ sukhaṃ hoti, evaṃ uppannasukhaṃ. Middhasukhanti niddāsukhaṃ. Anuyuttoti yuttapayutto viharati. Paṇidhāyāti patthayitvā. Sīlenātiādīsu sīlanti catupārisuddhisīlaṃ. Vatanti vatasamādānaṃ. Tapoti tapacaraṇaṃ. Brahmacariyanti methunavirati. Devo vā bhavissāmīti mahesakkhadevo vā bhavissāmi. Devaññataro vāti appesakkhadevesu vā aññataro. Kusaladhamme āvaranti nivārentīti nīvaraṇāni.

Mental bonds means seizing and clenching the mind, as if making a fist. Sensual pleasure means both object-based desire and defilement-based desire. The body means one’s own body. Forms mean external forms. “As much as one desires” means as much as one wishes. “Filling the belly” means filling the stomach, which is called “filling the belly” because it satisfies the stomach. The pleasure of lying down means the comfort of beds and chairs, or seasonal comfort. The pleasure of ease means the comfort experienced when turning from side to side while lying down. The pleasure of sleep means the comfort of slumber. “Being devoted” means living engaged and applied. “Aspiring” means wishing for. Regarding virtue, etc., virtue means the fourfold purification of virtue. Observance means undertaking a vow. Austerity means the practice of asceticism. The holy life means abstinence from sexual activity. “I will become a god” means I will become a deity of great power, or another lesser deity. They obstruct and prevent wholesome qualities; therefore, they are called hindrances.

Mātā jīvitā voropitā hotīti manusseneva sakajanikā manussamātā jīvitā voropitā hoti. Pitāpi [P 0.0505] manussapitāva. Arahāpi manussaarahāva. Duṭṭhena cittenāti vadhakacittena.

“The mother has been deprived of life”—this means one’s own human mother has been deprived of life by a human. The father too is a human father. The Arahant too is a human Arahant. “With a corrupt mind” means with a murderous mind.

Saññīti saññāsamaṅgī. Arogoti nicco. Ittheke abhivadantīti itthaṃ eke abhivadanti, evameke abhivadantīti attho. Ettāvatā soḷasa saññīvādā kathitā. Asaññīti [V 0.0477] saññāvirahito. Iminā padena aṭṭha asaññīvādā kathitā. Tatiyapadena aṭṭha nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā kathitā. Sato vā pana sattassāti athavā pana vijjamānasseva sattassa. Ucchedanti upacchedaṃ. Vināsanti adassanaṃ. Vibhavanti bhāvavigamaṃ. Sabbānetāni aññamaññavevacanāneva. Tattha dve janā ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhanti – lābhī [M 0.0487] ca alābhī ca. Tattha lābhī arahato dibbena cakkhunā cutiṃ disvā upapattiṃ apassanto, yo vā cutimattameva daṭṭhuṃ sakkoti na upapātaṃ, so ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. Alābhī ‘ko paralokaṃ jānātī’ti kāmasukhagiddhatāya vā ‘yathā rukkhato paṇṇāni patitāni na puna viruhanti, evaṃ sattā’tiādinā vitakkena vā ucchedaṃ gaṇhāti. Idha pana taṇhādiṭṭhīnaṃ vasena tathā ca aññathā ca vikappetvāva uppannā satta ucchedavādā kathitā. Tesañhi idaṃ saṅgahavacanaṃ. Diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ vā paneketi ettha diṭṭhadhammoti paccakkhadhammo vuccati. Tattha tattha paṭiladdhattabhāvassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Diṭṭhadhamme nibbānaṃ diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ; imasmiṃyeva attabhāve dukkhā vūpasammanti attho. Idaṃ pañcannaṃ diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādānaṃ saṅgahavacanaṃ.

‘Perceptive’ means endowed with perception. ‘Healthy’ means eternal. ‘Some assert thus’ means some assert in such a manner; this is the meaning. With this, the sixteen doctrines of perception are explained. ‘Non-perceptive’ means devoid of perception. By this phrase, the eight doctrines of non-perception are explained. By the third phrase, the eight doctrines of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are explained. ‘Or of an existing being’ means or rather, of an existing being. ‘Annihilation’ means cutting off. ‘Destruction’ means disappearance. ‘Non-existence’ means the departure of existence. All these are synonyms for one another. Here, two people hold the annihilation view—the one who has attainments and the one who does not. Among them, the one who has attainments, having seen the passing away of an Arahant with the divine eye but not seeing their rebirth, or one who can only see the moment of death but not the arising, holds the annihilation view. The one who does not have attainments, thinking, ‘Who knows the next world?’ due to greed for sensual pleasures, or through reasoning, ‘Just as fallen leaves fall from a tree and do not grow again, so too beings,’ holds the annihilation view. Here, however, seven doctrines of annihilation are explained, arising from craving and views, speculating thus and otherwise. This is a summary statement for them. ‘Or else, Nibbāna in the seen-and-now’—here, ‘in the seen-and-now’ refers to directly experienced phenomena. This is a designation of the state of having attained it in each case. Nibbāna in the seen-and-now is Nibbāna in the seen-and-now; meaning, in this very existence sufferings cease. This is a summary statement for the five doctrines of Nibbāna in the seen-and-now.

942. Verāti veracetanā. Byasanāti vināsā. Akkhantiyāti anadhivāsanāya. Appiyoti dassanasavanapaṭikūlatāya na piyāyitabbo. Cintetumpi paṭikūlattā mano etasmiṃ na appetīti amanāpo. Verabahuloti bahuvero. Vajjabahuloti bahudoso.

942. ‘Hostility’ means a hostile intention. ‘Disaster’ means destruction. ‘Intolerance’ means lack of forbearance. ‘Displeasing’ means unpleasant because of revulsion upon seeing or hearing; not to be loved. ‘Unpleasant’ means that even when thinking of it, the mind is not drawn to it because it is repulsive. ‘Full of enmity’ means having much hostility. ‘Full of faults’ means having many faults.

Ājīvakabhayanti ājīvaṃ jīvitavuttiṃ paṭicca uppannaṃ bhayaṃ[P 0.0506]. Taṃ agārikassapi hoti anagārikassapi. Tattha agārikena tāva ājīvahetu bahuṃ akusalaṃ kataṃ hoti. Athassa maraṇasamaye niraye upaṭṭhahante bhayaṃ uppajjati. Anagārikenāpi bahu anesanā katā hoti. Athassa maraṇakāle niraye upaṭṭhahante bhayaṃ uppajjati. Idaṃ ājīvakabhayaṃ nāma. Asilokabhayanti garahabhayaṃ parisasārajjabhayanti katapāpassa puggalassa sannipatitaṃ parisaṃ upasaṅkamantassa sārajjasaṅkhātaṃ bhayaṃ uppajjati. Idaṃ parisasārajjabhayaṃ nāma. Itaradvayaṃ pākaṭameva.

‘The fear concerning livelihood’ means fear arising dependent on one’s livelihood and means of living. This applies both to householders and renunciants. In the case of householders, much unwholesome action is done for the sake of livelihood. Then, at the time of death, fear arises as hell presents itself. For renunciants too, much improper seeking is done. Then, at the time of death, fear arises as hell presents itself. This is called the fear concerning livelihood. ‘The fear of ill-repute’ means the fear of blame. ‘The fear of embarrassment before an assembly’ means when a person who has done evil approaches a gathered assembly, fear arises, known as embarrassment. This is called the fear of embarrassment before an assembly. The other two are self-explanatory.

943. Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāresu pañcahi kāmaguṇehīti manāpiyarūpādīhi pañcahi kāmakoṭṭhāsehi bandhanehi vā. Samappitoti suṭṭhu appito allīno hutvā. Samaṅgībhūtoti samannāgato. Paricāretīti tesu kāmaguṇesu yathāsukhaṃ indriyāni cāreti sañcāreti ito cito [V 0.0478] ca upaneti; atha vā pana laḷati ramati kīḷatīti. Ettha ca duvidhā kāmaguṇā – mānussakā ceva dibbā ca. Mānussakā mandhātukāmaguṇasadisā daṭṭhabbā; dibbā paranimmitavasavattidevarājassa kāmaguṇasadisāti. Evarūpe kāme [M 0.0488] upagatañhi te paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto hotīti vadanti. Tattha paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānanti paramaṃ diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ, uttamanti attho.

943. In the section on Nibbāna visible here and now, ‘with the five strands of sensual pleasure’ means by the five portions of sensuality, such as agreeable forms, etc., or by bonds. ‘Well attached’ means being thoroughly attached and clinging. ‘Equipped’ means possessed of. ‘Indulges’ means one moves and directs the senses among those sensual pleasures as one pleases, leading them here and there; or else, one sports, delights, and plays. Here, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures: human and divine. Human sensual pleasures should be seen as similar to the sensual pleasures of King Mandhātu; divine sensual pleasures are like those of the King of the Paranimmitavasavatti gods. Indeed, they say that one who has entered into such sensual pleasures has attained the supreme Nibbāna visible here and now. Here, ‘the supreme Nibbāna visible here and now’ means the ultimate Nibbāna visible here and now; ‘the highest’ is the meaning.

Dutiyavāre hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā; paṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhā; pakatijahanaṭṭhena vipariṇāmadhammāti veditabbā. Tesaṃ vipariṇāmaññathābhāvāti tesaṃ kāmānaṃ vipariṇāmasaṅkhātā aññathābhāvā. ‘Yampi me ahosi tampi me natthī’ti vuttanayena uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Tattha antonijjhāyanalakkhaṇo soko; tannissitalālappalakkhaṇo paridevo; kāyapaṭipīḷanalakkhaṇaṃ dukkhaṃ; manovighātalakkhaṇaṃ domanassaṃ; vighātalakkhaṇo upāyāso.
