In the second instance, they should be understood as impermanent in the sense of having been and then not being; as suffering in the sense of oppression; and as subject to change in the sense of abandoning their nature. ‘Their change and otherness’ means the otherness of those sensual pleasures, reckoned as change. Sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair arise in the way described by ‘what was mine, that too is no more.’ Here, sorrow has the characteristic of internal brooding; lamentation has the characteristic of wailing based on that; pain has the characteristic of bodily oppression; distress has the characteristic of mental vexation; despair has the characteristic of torment.

Vitakkitanti abhiniropanavasena pavatto vitakko. Vicāritanti anumajjanavasena pavatto vicāro. Etena etanti etena vitakkena ca vicārena ca etaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ oḷārikaṃ sakaṇṭakaṃ viya khāyati.

‘Initial application’ means initial application that proceeds by way of directing the mind. ‘Sustained application’ means sustained application that proceeds by way of sustained examination. By this—that is, by this initial application and sustained application—this first jhāna appears coarse, like something with thorns.

Pītigatanti pītimeva. Cetaso uppilāvitanti cittassa uppilabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Cetaso ābhogoti jhānā vuṭṭhāya [P 0.0507] tasmiṃ sukhe punappunaṃ cittassa ābhogo manasikāroti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

‘Rapture’ means simply rapture. ‘Elation of mind’ means causing elation of the mind. ‘Mental application’ means the mind repeatedly applying itself, attending, to that bliss after rising from jhāna. The rest is self-explanatory everywhere.

Pañcakaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the fives is concluded.

(6.) Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixes

944. Chakkaniddese yasmā kuddho vā kodhavasena, sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī vā sandiṭṭhiparāmāsitāya [V 0.0479] kalahaṃ viggahaṃ vivādaṃ āpajjati, tasmā kodhādayo ‘vivādamūlānī’ti vuttā.

944. In the exposition of the sixes, because an angry person through anger, or one clinging to views through that clinging, engages in quarrels, disputes, and arguments, therefore anger and the like are called ‘roots of disputes.’

Chandarāganiddese kāmagehasitattā chandarāgā gehassitā dhammāti saṅgahato vatvā puna pabhedato dassetuṃ manāpiyesu rūpesūtiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha manāpiyesūti manavaḍḍhanakesu iṭṭhesu. Virodhā eva virodhavatthūni. Amanāpiyesūti aniṭṭhesu.

In the exposition of desire and lust, it is stated in summary that desire and lust are phenomena based on the household, because they are rooted in the household of sensual pleasures; then, intending to show the distinctions, ‘in agreeable forms,’ etc., is said. Here, ‘agreeable’ means delighting the mind and desirable. ‘Oppositions’ are indeed grounds for opposition. ‘Disagreeable’ means undesirable.

945. Agāravesu agāravoti gāravavirahito. Appatissoti appatissayo anīcavutti. Ettha pana yo bhikkhu satthari dharamāne tīsu kālesu upaṭṭhānaṃ na yāti, satthari anupāhane caṅkamante saupāhano caṅkamati[M 0.0489], nīce caṅkame caṅkamante ucce caṅkame caṅkamati, heṭṭhā vasante upari vasati, satthudassanaṭṭhāne ubho aṃse pārupati, chattaṃ dhāreti, upāhanaṃ dhāreti, nhāyati, uccāraṃ vā passāvaṃ vā karoti, parinibbute vā pana cetiyaṃ vandituṃ na gacchati, cetiyassa paññāyanaṭṭhāne satthudassanaṭṭhāne vuttaṃ sabbaṃ karoti – ayaṃ satthari agāravo nāma. Yo pana dhammasavane saṅghuṭṭhe sakkaccaṃ na gacchati, sakkaccaṃ dhammaṃ na suṇāti, samullapanto nisīdati, na sakkaccaṃ gaṇhāti, na sakkaccaṃ vāceti – ‘ayaṃ dhamme agāravo nāma. Yo pana therena bhikkhunā anajjhiṭṭho dhammaṃ deseti, pañhaṃ katheti, vuḍḍhe bhikkhū ghaṭṭento gacchati, tiṭṭhati, nisīdati, dussapallatthikaṃ vā hatthapallatthikaṃ vā karoti, saṅghamajjhe ubho aṃse pārupati, chattupāhanaṃ dhāreti – ayaṃ saṅghe agāravo nāma. Ekabhikkhusmimpi hi agārave kate saṅghe agāravo katova hoti. Tisso sikkhā pana apūrayamānova sikkhāya agāravo nāma. Appamādalakkhaṇaṃ ananubrūhayamāno appamāde agāravo nāma. Duvidhaṃ paṭisanthāraṃ akaronto paṭisanthāre agāravo nāma.

945. ‘Disrespectful’ (agāravo) means devoid of respect. ‘Unsubmissive’ (appatissa) means not submitting and behaving without humility. Here, a monk who, while the Teacher is living, does not attend upon him at the three times of day, walks with sandals when the Teacher is walking without, walks on a high walking-path when the Teacher walks on a low walking-path, dwells above when the Teacher dwells below, covers both shoulders in a place where the Teacher is to be seen, carries an umbrella, wears sandals, bathes, urinates or defecates, or after the Teacher’s final Nibbāna, does not go to pay respects at a shrine—or in a place where a shrine is visible, does all that is mentioned regarding a place for seeing the Teacher—this is called disrespect toward the Teacher. One who does not attentively go to hear the Dhamma when it is announced, does not listen to the Dhamma respectfully, sits chatting, does not receive it respectfully, and does not recite it respectfully—this is called disrespect toward the Dhamma. One who teaches the Dhamma or asks questions when uninvited by a senior monk, jostles elder monks while walking, standing, or sitting, makes a lap-robe or covers his hand with his robe, covers both shoulders in the midst of the Sangha, or carries an umbrella or sandals—this is called disrespect toward the Sangha. For if disrespect is shown even to a single monk, it is considered disrespect toward the Sangha. Not fulfilling the three trainings is called disrespect toward the training. Not developing the characteristic of diligence is called disrespect toward diligence. Not practicing the twofold cordiality is called disrespect toward cordiality.

Parihāniyā dhammāti parihānakarā dhammā. Kammārāmatāti [P 0.0508] navakamme vā cīvaravicāraṇādīsu vā kammesu abhirati yuttapayuttatā. Bhassārāmatāti tiracchānakathāvasena bhasse yuttapayuttatā. Niddārāmatāti niddāya yuttapayuttatā. Saṅgaṇikārāmatāti saṅgaṇikāya yuttapayuttatā. Saṃsaggārāmatāti savanasaṃsagge, dassanasaṃsagge, samullāpasaṃsagge, paribhogasaṃsagge, kāyasaṃsaggeti pañcavidhe saṃsagge yuttapayuttatā. Papañcārāmatāti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhipapañcesu yuttapayuttatā.

Qualities leading to decline are qualities that cause decline. Delight in work is being devoted and attached to work, whether new construction or tasks such as examining robes and so on. Delight in chatter is being devoted and attached to chatter in the manner of animal talk. Delight in sleep is being devoted and attached to sleep. Delight in association is being devoted and attached to association. Delight in intimacy is being devoted and attached to five kinds of intimacy: intimacy through hearing, intimacy through seeing, intimacy through conversation, intimacy through sharing, and intimacy through bodily contact. Delight in proliferation is being devoted and attached to proliferation consisting of craving, conceit, and views.

946. Somanassupavicārādīsu [V 0.0480] somanassena saddhiṃ upavicarantīti somanassupavicārā. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvāti cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ passitvā. Somanassaṭṭhāniyanti somanassassa ārammaṇavasena kāraṇabhūtaṃ. Upavicaratīti tattha vicārappavattanena upavicarati. Vitakko pana taṃsampayutto vāti iminā nayena tīsupi chakkesu attho veditabbo.

946. In the case of joyful reflections, etc., those that reflect together with joy are joyful reflections. Having seen a form with the eye—that is, having seen a form with eye-consciousness. The condition for joy—that which is the cause by way of being the object of joy. One reflects—that is, one reflects by the activity of sustained thought there. Or initial thought is associated with it—in this way, the meaning should be understood in all three sets of six.

947. Gehasitānīti kāmaguṇanissitāni. Somanassānīti cetasikasukhāni. Domanassānīti cetasikadukkhāni. Upekkhāti aññāṇasampayuttā [M 0.0490] upekkhā vedanā, aññāṇupekkhātipi etāsaṃyeva nāmaṃ.

947. ‘Gehasitāni’ means dependent on the strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Somanassāni’ refers to mental pleasures. ‘Domanassāni’ refers to mental pains. ‘Upekkhā’ is the feeling of equanimity associated with ignorance; ‘aññāṇupekkhā,’ or ‘ignorant equanimity,’ is also a name for this.

948. Atthi me attāti vāti sabbapadesu vā-saddo vikappattho; evaṃ vā diṭṭhi uppajjatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Atthi me attāti cettha sassatadiṭṭhi sabbakālesu attano atthitaṃ gaṇhāti. Saccato thetatoti bhūtato ca thirato ca; idaṃ saccanti suṭṭhu daḷhabhāvenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Natthi me attāti ayaṃ pana ucchedadiṭṭhi, sato sattassa tattha tattha vibhavaggahaṇato. Atha vā purimāpi tīsu kālesu atthīti gahaṇato sassatadiṭṭhi, paccuppannameva atthīti gaṇhantī ucchedadiṭṭhi. Pacchimāpi atītānāgatesu natthīti gahaṇato ‘bhasmantā āhutiyo’ti gahitadiṭṭhikānaṃ viya ucchedadiṭṭhi, atīteyeva natthīti gaṇhantī adhiccasamuppannikasseva sassatadiṭṭhi. Attanā vā attānaṃ sañjānāmīti saññākkhandhasīsena khandhe attāti gahetvā saññāya avasesakkhandhe sañjānanato ‘iminā attanā imaṃ attānaṃ sañjānāmī’ti evaṃ hoti. Attanā vā anattānanti saññākkhandhaṃyeva attāti gahetvā itare cattāro khandhe anattāti gahetvā saññāya tesaṃ jānanato evaṃ hoti. Anattanā vā attānanti saññākkhandhaṃ anattāti [P 0.0509] itare ca cattāro khandhe attāti gahetvā saññāya tesaṃ jānanato evaṃ hoti. Sabbāpi sassatucchedadiṭṭhiyova.

948. In ‘There is a self for me, or…,’ the word ‘or’ (vā) in all instances signifies an alternative; this means it is said, ‘or a view arises thus.’ ‘There is a self for me’—here, the eternalist view grasps the existence of a self in all times. ‘Truly and permanently’ means truly and firmly; this is called ‘truth’ due to its very firm nature. ‘There is no self for me’—this, however, is the annihilationist view, from grasping the annihilation of an existent being here and there. Alternatively, the former view, by grasping existence in the three times, is the eternalist view, while a view that grasps existence only in the present is the annihilationist view. The latter view also, by grasping non-existence in the past and future, is the annihilationist view, like that of those who hold the view that ‘offerings end in ashes.’ By grasping non-existence only in the past, it is the eternalist view of one who holds to fortuitous origination. ‘By self, I perceive self’—this comes about by taking the aggregates headed by the perception aggregate as self, and perceiving the remaining aggregates through perception; thus it is: ‘By this self, I perceive this self.’ ‘By self, I perceive non-self’—this comes about by taking the perception aggregate itself as self and the other four aggregates as non-self, and perceiving them through perception. ‘By non-self, I perceive self’—this comes about by taking the perception aggregate as non-self and the other four aggregates as self, and perceiving them through perception. All are merely eternalist and annihilationist views.

Vado vedeyyoti ādayo pana sassatadiṭṭhiyā eva abhinivesākārā. Tattha vadatīti vado; vacīkammassa kārakoti vuttaṃ hoti. Vedayatīti vedeyyo; jānāti anubhavati cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Idāni yaṃ so vedeti taṃ dassetuṃ tatra tatra dīgharattaṃ kalyāṇapāpakānantiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatra tatrāti tesu tesu yonigatiṭhitinivāsanikāyesu ārammaṇesu vā. Dīgharattanti cirarattaṃ. Paccanubhotīti paṭisaṃvedayati. Na so jāto nāhosīti so attā ajātidhammato [V 0.0481] na jāto nāma; sadā vijjamāno yevāti attho. Teneva atīte nāhosi, anāgatepi na bhavissati. Yo hi jāto so ahosi, yo ca jāyissati so bhavissatīti. Athavā ‘na so jāto nāhosī’ti so sadā vijjamānattā atītepi na jātu nāhosi[M 0.0491], anāgatepi na jātu na bhavissati. Niccoti uppādavayarahito. Dhuvoti thiro sārabhūto. Sassatoti sabbakāliko. Avipariṇāmadhammoti attano pakatibhāvaṃ avijahanadhammo kakaṇṭako viya nānappakārattaṃ nāpajjati. Evamayaṃ sabbāsavadiṭṭhi (ma. ni. 1.17 ādayo) nāma kathitā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

"Speaker, feeler" — these terms are, however, modes of adhering to the eternalist view. Here, "speaker" means one who speaks; it is said to refer to the agent of verbal action. "Feeler" means one who feels; it is said to refer to one who knows and experiences. Now, to show what that one feels, it is said, "For a long time, good and bad," etc. Here, "here and there" refers to those various destinations of rebirth, abodes, dwelling-places, communities, or objects of focus. "For a long time" means for a long period. "Experiences" means feels. "He is not born, nor was he" — this self, because it is by nature unborn, is not born; it always exists — this is the meaning. Therefore, in the past, it was not, and in the future, it will not be. For what is born was, and what will be born will be. Alternatively, "he is not born, nor was he" means that since it always exists, in the past it never was not, nor in the future will it ever not be. "Permanent" means without arising and passing away. "Enduring" means stable, essential. "Eternal" means existing at all times. "Not subject to change" means a nature that does not abandon its inherent condition, like a chameleon, not undergoing manifold changes. Thus, this is called the view of all cankers (as in Majjhima Nikāya 1.17, etc.). The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixes.

(7.) Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā

(7.) Commentary on the Sevenfold Exposition.

949. Sattakaniddese thāmagataṭṭhena appahīnaṭṭhena ca anusentīti anusayā. Vaṭṭasmiṃ satte saṃyojenti ghaṭentīti saṃyojanāni. Samudācāravasena pariyuṭṭhahantīti pariyuṭṭhānāni. Kāmarāgova pariyuṭṭhānaṃ kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhānaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

949. In the sevenfold exposition, they lie latent by reason of their strength and not having been abandoned, thus they are latent tendencies (anusayā). They bind and connect beings in the round of existence, thus they are fetters (saṃyojanāni). They obsess by way of their active manifestation, thus they are obsessions (pariyuṭṭhānāni). Sensual desire itself is an obsession, hence 'sensual desire obsession.' The same method applies to the rest.

950. Asataṃ dhammā, lāmakaṭṭhena vā asantā dhammāti asaddhammā. Rāgādīhi dosehi duṭṭhāni caritānīti duccaritāni. Tena tenākārena maññantīti mānā.

950. They are states of the ignoble, or they are states that are not good by reason of their inferiority, thus they are ignoble states (asaddhammā). Behaviors corrupted by defilements such as lust, thus they are misconducts (duccaritāni). They conceive in various ways, thus they are conceits (mānā).

951. Diṭṭhiniddese rūpīti rūpavā. Cātumahābhūtikoti catumahābhūtamayo. Mātāpitūnaṃ etanti mātāpettikaṃ. Kintaṃ? Sukkasoṇitaṃ. Mātāpettike sambhūto jātoti mātāpettikasambhavo. Idha rūpakāyasīsena manussattabhāvaṃ attāti vadati. Dutiyo taṃ paṭikkhipitvā dibbattabhāvaṃ vadati. Dibboti devaloke sambhūto. Kāmāvacaroti chakāmāvacaradevapariyāpanno[P 0.0510]. Kabaḷīkāraṃ bhakkhayatīti kabaḷīkārabhakkho. Manomayoti jhānamanena nibbatto. Sabbaṅgapaccaṅgīti sabbaṅgapaccaṅgayutto. Ahīnindriyoti paripuṇṇindriyo; yāni brahmaloke atthi tesaṃ vasena, itaresañca saṇṭhānavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Ākāsānañcāyatanūpagoti [V 0.0482] ākāsānañcāyatanabhāvaṃ upagato. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

951. In the exposition of views, 'possessing form' (rūpī) means having form (rūpavā). 'Composed of the four great elements' (cātumahābhūtiko) means made up of the four great elements (catumahābhūtamayo). 'From mother and father' (mātāpettikaṃ) means that which belongs to mother and father. What is that? Semen and blood. 'Born from mother and father' (mātāpettikasambhavo) means born and arisen from mother and father. Here, by 'a being with a physical body and head' (rūpakāyasīsena), one speaks of human existence as the self. The second, rejecting that, speaks of divine existence as the self. 'Divine' (dibbo) means born in the deva world. 'Belonging to the sense sphere' (kāmāvacaro) means included among the six sense-sphere devas. 'Consuming morsel food' (kabaḷīkārabhakkho) means one who eats morsel food. 'Mind-made' (manomayo) means produced by the mind of jhāna. 'Complete in all parts' (sabbaṅgapaccaṅgī) means endowed with all parts and minor parts. 'With faculties unimpaired' (ahīnindriyo) means with faculties fully developed; this is said in reference to those existing in the Brahma world, and also to others based on their physical configuration. 'Attained to the base of the infinity of space' (ākāsānañcāyatanūpago) means having reached the state of the base of the infinity of space. The same method applies to the others. The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.

Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Sevenfold Exposition.

(8.) Aṭṭhakaniddesavaṇṇanā

(8.) Commentary on the Exposition of the Eights.

952. Aṭṭhakaniddese [M 0.0492] kilesāyeva kilesavatthūni. Kusītavatthūnīti kusītassa alasassa vatthūni, patiṭṭhā, kosajjakāraṇānīti attho. Kammaṃ kātabbaṃ hotīti cīvaravicāraṇādikammaṃ kātabbaṃ hoti. Na vīriyaṃ ārabhatīti duvidhampi vīriyaṃ nārabhati. Appattassāti jhānavipassanāmaggaphaladhammassa appattassa pattiyā. Anadhigatassāti tasseva anadhigatassa adhigamatthāya. Asacchikatassāti tasseva asacchikatassa sacchikaraṇatthāya. Idaṃ paṭhamanti ‘idaṃ handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti evaṃ osīdanaṃ paṭhamaṃ kusītavatthu. Iminā nayena sabbattha attho veditabbo.

952. In the Exposition of the Eights, the defilements themselves are the bases of defilements (kilesavatthūni). 'Grounds for laziness' (kusītavatthūni) means the grounds, foundations, or causes of laziness for a lazy, indolent person—that is the meaning. 'Work to be done' (kammaṃ kātabbaṃ hoti) means work such as considering robes, etc., is to be done. 'Does not arouse energy' (na vīriyaṃ ārabhati) means he does not arouse either of the two kinds of energy. 'For the sake of attaining what has not been attained' (appattassa) means for the sake of the attainment of the qualities of jhāna, insight, path, and fruit that have not been attained. 'For the sake of realizing what has not been realized' (anadhigatassa) means for the sake of the realization of those same unachieved qualities. 'For the sake of experiencing what has not been experienced' (asacchikatassa) means for the sake of the direct experience of those same unrealized qualities. 'This first' (idaṃ paṭhamaṃ) means the initial sinking down, thinking, 'Well then, I will lie down,' is the first ground for laziness. In this way, the meaning should be understood throughout.

Māsācitaṃ maññeti ettha pana māsācitaṃ nāma tintamāso; yathā tintamāso garuko hoti, evaṃ garukoti adhippāyo. Gilānā vuṭṭhito hotīti gilāno hutvā pacchā vuṭṭhito hoti.

'He thinks it is heavy as a month's accumulation' (māsācitaṃ maññeti) – here, 'heavy as a month's accumulation' (māsācitaṃ) means a three-month period; just as a three-month period is weighty, so the intended meaning is weighty. 'Has recovered from illness' (gilānā vuṭṭhito hoti) means having been ill and then having recovered.

954. Aṭṭhasu lokadhammesūti ettha lokassa dhammāti lokadhammā. Etehi vimutto nāma natthi, buddhānampi honti eva. Tasmā ‘lokadhammā’ti vuccanti. Paṭighātoti paṭihaññanākāro. Lābhe sārāgoti ‘ahaṃ lābhaṃ labhāmī’ti evaṃ gehasitasomanassavasena uppanno sārāgo; so cittaṃ paṭihanati. Alābhe paṭivirodhoti ‘ahaṃ lābhaṃ na labhāmī’ti domanassavasena uppannavirodho; sopi cittaṃ paṭihanati. Tasmā ‘paṭighāto’ti vutto. Yasādīsupi ‘ahaṃ mahāparivāro, ahaṃ appaparivāro, ahaṃ pasaṃsappatto, ahaṃ garahappatto, ahaṃ sukhappatto, ahaṃ dukkhappato’ti evametesaṃ uppatti veditabbā. Anariyavohārāti anariyānaṃ vohārā.

954. 'In the eight worldly conditions' (aṭṭhasu lokadhammesu) – here, 'conditions of the world' are worldly conditions (lokadhammā). There is no one who is freed from these; even for the Buddhas they exist. Therefore, they are called 'worldly conditions.' 'Repulsion' (paṭighāto) means the manner of striking back. 'Attachment to gain' (lābhe sārāgo) means the attachment that arises based on the joy of a householder, thinking, 'I have gained'; this strikes the mind. 'Aversion to loss' (alābhe paṭivirodho) means the aversion that arises based on sorrow, thinking, 'I have not gained'; this too strikes the mind. Therefore, it is called 'repulsion.' Regarding fame and so on, their arising should be understood thus: 'I have a large retinue,' 'I have a small retinue,' 'I have attained praise,' 'I have attained blame,' 'I have attained happiness,' 'I have attained suffering.' 'Ignoble behavior' (anariyavohārā) means the behavior of the ignoble.

957. Purisadosāti [V 0.0483] purisānaṃ dosā. Na sarāmīti ‘mayā etassa kammassa kataṭṭhānaṃ na sarāmi na sallakkhemī’ti [P 0.0511] evaṃ assatibhāvena nibbeṭheti moceti. Codakaṃyeva paṭippharatīti paṭiviruddho hutvā pharati, paṭibhāṇitabhāvena tiṭṭhati. Kiṃ nu kho tuyhanti ‘tuyhaṃ bālassa abyattassa bhaṇitena nāma kiṃ’ yo tvaṃ neva vatthunā āpattiṃ, na codanaṃ jānāsī’ti dīpeti; ‘tvaṃ pi nāma evaṃ kiñci ajānanto bhaṇitabbaṃ maññissasī’ti [M 0.0493] ajjhottharati. Paccāropetīti ‘tvaṃ pi khosī’tiādīni vadanto paṭiāropeti. Paṭikarohīti desanāgāminiṃ desehi, vuṭṭhānagāminito vuṭṭhāhi tato suddhante patiṭṭhito aññaṃ codessasī’ti dīpeti.

957. 'Purisadosā' means the faults of men. 'I do not remember' (na sarāmīti) means 'I do not remember, I do not recognize the place where this deed was done by me'—thus, through lack of mindfulness, he evades and avoids. 'He strikes back at the accuser' (codakaṃyeva paṭippharatīti) means he opposes and strikes back, standing firm with a show of eloquence. 'What is it to you?' (kiṃ nu kho tuyhaṃ) means he declares, 'What use is there in the words of you, foolish and incompetent one, who knows neither the subject of the offense nor the accusation?' He overwhelms him, thinking, 'How can you, knowing nothing, presume to speak?' 'He throws back the blame' (paccāropeti) means he throws back the blame, saying, 'You too are like this,' and so on. 'Make amends!' (paṭikarohi) means he instructs him to declare what leads to confession, to rise from what leads to rehabilitation, and then, having been purified, to stand firm before accusing another.

Aññenāññaṃ paṭicaratīti aññena kāraṇena vacanena vā aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ vacanaṃ vā paṭicchādeti. ‘Āpattiṃ āpannosī’ti vutto ‘ko āpanno? Kiṃ āpanno? Kathaṃ āpanno? Kismiṃ āpanno? Kaṃ bhaṇatha? Kiṃ bhaṇathā’ti vadati. ‘Evarūpaṃ kiñci tayā diṭṭha’nti vutte ‘na suṇāmī’ti sotaṃ vā upaneti. Bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmetīti ‘itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ āpannosī’ti puṭṭho ‘pāṭaliputtaṃ gatomhī’ti vatvā puna ‘tava pāṭaliputtagamanaṃ na pucchāmā’ti vutte ‘tato rājagahaṃ gatomhī’ti ‘rājagahaṃ vā yāhi, brāhmaṇagehaṃ vā; āpattiṃ āpannosī’ti? ‘Tattha me sūkaramaṃsaṃ laddha’ntiādīni vadanto kathaṃ bahiddhā vikkhipati. Kopanti kupitabhāvaṃ. Dosanti duṭṭhabhāvaṃ. Ubhayampetaṃ kodhasseva nāmaṃ. Appaccayanti asantuṭṭhākāraṃ; domanassassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Pātukarotīti dasseti pakāseti. Bāhāvikkhepakaṃ bhaṇatīti bāhā vikkhipitvā alajjivacanaṃ vadati. Vihesetīti viheṭheti bādhati. Anādiyitvāti cittīkārena aggahetvā avajānitvā; anādaro hutvāti attho.

'One conceals one thing with another' (aññenāññaṃ paṭicarati) means he hides one action or statement with another action or statement. When told, 'You have committed an offense' (āpattiṃ āpannosi), he says, 'Who has committed it? What has been committed? How was it committed? In what was it committed? Whom are you speaking about? What are you saying?' When told, 'Have you seen anything like this?' (evarūpaṃ kiñci tayā diṭṭhaṃ), he holds out his ear, saying, 'I do not hear' (na suṇāmi). 'Diverting the talk externally' (bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmeti) means when asked, 'You have committed such-and-such an offense,' he says, 'I went to Pāṭaliputta,' and when told, 'We are not asking about your going to Pāṭaliputta,' he says, 'Then I went to Rājagaha.' When they say, 'Go to Rājagaha or to a brahmin’s house; have you committed an offense?' he says, 'There I got pork,' and so on—thus he scatters the talk externally. 'Anger' (kopaṃ) means the state of being angry. 'Hatred' (dosaṃ) means the state of being hostile. Both of these are names for anger. 'Discontent' (appaccayaṃ) means the state of being dissatisfied; this is a name for displeasure. 'He makes it known' (pātukaroti) means he shows it, displays it. 'Speaking with arm-waving' (bāhāvikkhepakaṃ bhaṇati) means speaking shameless words while waving his arms. 'Harasses' (vihesati) means he troubles, oppresses. 'Disregarding' (anādiyitvā) means not taking it to heart with attention, looking down on it; the meaning is being without respect.

Atibāḷhanti atidaḷhaṃ atippamāṇaṃ. Mayi byāvaṭāti mayi byāpāraṃ āpannā. Hīnāyāvattitvāti hīnassa gihibhāvassa atthāya āvattitvā; gihī hutvāti attho. Attamanā hothāti tuṭṭhacittā hotha, ‘mayā labhitabbaṃ labhatha, mayā vasitabbaṭṭhāne vasatha, phāsuvihāro vo mayā kato’ti adhippāyena vadati.

'Excessive' (atibāḷhaṃ) means overly strong, beyond measure. 'Engaged with me' (mayi byāvaṭā) means occupied with me. 'Turning back to the inferior' (hīnāyāvattitvā) means turning back for the sake of an inferior householder life; the meaning is, having become a householder. 'Be joyful' (attamanā hotha) means be contented in mind; he speaks with the intention, 'What should be gained by me, may you gain; where I should dwell, may you dwell; a comfortable dwelling has been provided for you by me.'

958. Asaññīti pavatto vādo asaññīvādo; so tesaṃ atthīti asaññīvādā. Rūpī attātiādīsu lābhino kasiṇarūpaṃ attāti gahetvā rūpīti diṭṭhi uppajjati; alābhino takkamatteneva[P 0.0512][V 0.0484], ājīvakānaṃ viya. Lābhinoyeva ca pana arūpasamāpattinimittaṃ attāti gahetvā arūpīti diṭṭhi uppajjati; alābhino takkamatteneva, nigaṇṭhānaṃ viya. Asaññībhāve panettha ekanteneva kāraṇaṃ na pariyesitabbaṃ. Diṭṭhigatiko [M 0.0494] hi ummattako viya yaṃ vā taṃ vā gaṇhāti. Rūpī ca arūpī cāti rūpārūpamissakagāhavasena vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ diṭṭhi rūpāvacarārūpāvacarasamāpattilābhinopi takkikassāpi uppajjati. Neva rūpī nārūpīti pana ekantato takkikadiṭṭhiyeva. Antavāti parittakasiṇaṃ attato gaṇhantassa diṭṭhi. Anantavāti appamāṇakasiṇaṃ. Antavā ca anantavā cāti uddhamadho sapariyantaṃ tiriyaṃ apariyantaṃ kasiṇaṃ attāti gahetvā uppannadiṭṭhi. Nevantavā nānantavāti takkikadiṭṭhiyeva. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

958. 'Non-percipient' (asaññī) means the view that has arisen is the view of non-perception; because this exists for them, they are holders of the view of non-perception (asaññīvādā). In doctrines like 'the self is material' (rūpī attā), for those who have attained, taking the kasiṇa form as the self, the view 'it is material' (rūpī) arises; for those who have not attained, it is merely speculative, like the Ājīvakas. However, for those who have attained, taking the object of the formless attainments as the self, the view 'it is immaterial' (arūpī) arises; for those who have not attained, it is merely speculative, like the Nigaṇṭhas. But in the case of the state of non-perception, no single definitive reason should be sought here. For one driven by wrong views is like a madman, grasping at anything whatsoever. 'Both material and immaterial' (rūpī ca arūpī ca) is stated based on grasping a mixture of material and immaterial. This view arises both for those who have attained the material and immaterial spheres of absorption and for mere speculators. 'Neither material nor immaterial' (neva rūpī nārūpī), however, is purely a speculative view. 'Finite' (antavā) is the view of one who takes a limited kasiṇa as the self. 'Infinite' (anantavā) is the view of one who takes an unlimited kasiṇa. 'Both finite and infinite' (antavā ca anantavā ca) is the view that arises from taking a kasiṇa as the self, bounded above and below, but unbounded horizontally. 'Neither finite nor infinite' (neva antavā nānantavā) is purely a speculative view. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.

Aṭṭhakaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Exposition of the Eights.

(9.) Navakaniddesavaṇṇanā

(9.) Commentary on the Exposition of the Nines.

960. Navakaniddese nava āghātavatthūnīti sattesu uppattivaseneva kathitāni. Purisānaṃ malānīti purisamalāni. Navavidhāti navakoṭṭhāsā navappabhedā vā.

960. In the Exposition of the Nines, the nine grounds for resentment are explained solely in terms of their arising in beings. ‘The stains of men’ (purisamalāni) are the impurities of men. ‘Ninefold’ (navavidhā) means nine divisions or nine kinds.

963. Taṇhaṃ paṭiccāti taṇhaṃ nissāya. Pariyesanāti rūpādiārammaṇapariyesanā. Sā hi taṇhāya sati hoti. Lābhoti rūpādiārammaṇapaṭilābho. So hi pariyesanāya sati hoti. Vinicchayo pana ñāṇataṇhādiṭṭhivitakkavasena catubbidho. Tattha “sukhavinicchayaṃ jaññā, sukhavinicchayaṃ ñatvā ajjhattaṃ sukhamanuyuñjeyyā”ti (ma. ni. 3.323) ayaṃ ñāṇavinicchayo. “Vinicchayoti dve vinicchayā – taṇhāvinicchayo ca diṭṭhivinicchayo cā”ti (mahāni. 102) evaṃ āgatāni aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritāni taṇhāvinicchayo. Dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo diṭṭhivinicchayo. “Chando kho, devānaminda, vitakkanidāno”ti (dī. ni. 2.358) imasmiṃ pana sutte idha vinicchayoti vutto vitakkoyeva āgato. Lābhaṃ labhitvā hi iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ sundarāsundarañca vitakkeneva vinicchināti – ‘ettakaṃ me rūpārammaṇatthāya bhavissati[V 0.0485], ettakaṃ saddādiārammaṇatthāya[M 0.0495], ettakaṃ mayhaṃ bhavissati, ettakaṃ parassa, ettakaṃ paribhuñjissāmi, ettakaṃ nidahissāmī’ti. Tena vuttaṃ “lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo”ti.

963. ‘Dependent on craving’ (taṇhaṃ paṭicca) means relying on craving. ‘Searching’ (pariyesanā) is the searching for objects such as forms. For this exists when there is craving. ‘Gain’ (lābha) is the acquisition of objects such as forms. For this exists when there is searching. Discernment (vinicchaya), however, is fourfold by way of knowledge, craving, views, and thought. Herein, ‘One should know the discernment of pleasure; having known the discernment of pleasure, one should pursue inner pleasure’ (MN 3.323)—this is discernment by knowledge. ‘Discernment is of two kinds: discernment by craving and discernment by views’ (Mahāniddesa 102)—thus, the one hundred and eight modes of craving-conduct that are presented are discernment by craving. The sixty-two views are discernment by views. ‘Desire, O lord of gods, is rooted in thought’ (DN 2.358)—in this sutta, what is called ‘discernment’ (vinicchaya) is precisely thought. For having gained an object, one discerns what is desirable and undesirable, beautiful and ugly, merely by thought: ‘This much will be for the sake of form-objects, this much for sound-objects, etc.; this much will be mine, this much another’s; this much I will enjoy, this much I will store away.’ Therefore, it is said, ‘discernment dependent on gain.’

Chandarāgoti evaṃ akusalavitakkena vitakkite vatthusmiṃ dubbalarāgo ca balavarāgo ca uppajjati. Idañhi idha chandoti dubbalarāgassādhivacanaṃ[P 0.0513]. Ajjhosānanti ahaṃ mamanti balavasanniṭṭhānaṃ. Pariggahoti taṇhādiṭṭhivasena pariggahakaraṇaṃ. Macchariyanti parehi sādhāraṇabhāvassa asahanatā. Tenevassa porāṇā evaṃ vacanatthaṃ vadanti – “idaṃ acchariyaṃ mayhameva hotu, mā aññassa acchariyaṃ hotūti pavattattā macchariyanti vuccatī”ti. Ārakkhoti dvārapidahanamañjusagopanādivasena suṭṭhu rakkhaṇaṃ. Adhikarotīti adhikaraṇaṃ; kāraṇassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Ārakkhādhikaraṇanti bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ; ārakkhahetūti attho. Daṇḍādānādīsu paranisedhanatthaṃ daṇḍassa ādānaṃ daṇḍādānaṃ. Ekatodhārādino satthassa ādānaṃ satthādānaṃ. Kalahoti kāyakalahopi vācākalahopi. Purimo purimo virodho viggaho, pacchimo pacchimo vivādo. Tuvaṃ tuvanti agāravavacanaṃ, tvaṃ tvanti attho.

‘Desire-lust’ (chandarāga) arises in an object that has been thought upon with unwholesome thought; both weak lust and strong lust arise. For here, ‘desire’ (chanda) is a designation for weak lust. ‘Clinging’ (ajjhosāna) is the strong conviction of ‘I’ and ‘mine.’ ‘Possessiveness’ (pariggaha) is the act of possessing through craving and views. ‘Stinginess’ (macchariya) is the inability to tolerate sharing with others. Therefore, the ancients explain the meaning of the term thus: ‘Because it arises with the thought, “Let this precious thing be mine alone, and not belong to another,” it is called stinginess.’ ‘Guarding’ (ārakkha) means thorough protection, such as barring doors, concealing valuables in chests, and the like. That which is made an issue is a ‘cause’ (adhikaraṇa); this is a name for a cause. ‘Guarding as a cause’ (ārakkhādhikaraṇa) is an abstract neuter noun; the meaning is ‘because of guarding.’ ‘Taking up the rod’ (daṇḍādāna) means taking up a stick for the purpose of restraining others. ‘Taking up a weapon’ (satthādāna) means taking up a single-edged blade or the like. ‘Quarreling’ (kalaha) refers to both physical conflict and verbal conflict. The former is opposition and strife; the latter is contention. ‘You, you’ (tuvaṃ tuvaṃ) is a disrespectful way of speaking; the meaning is ‘you, you.’

964. Iñjitānīti iñjanāni calanāni. Asmīti iñjitametantiādīhi sabbapadehi mānova kathito. Ahanti pavattopi hi māno iñjitameva, ayamahanti pavattopi, nevasaññīnāsaññī bhavissanti pavattopi. Sesanavakehipi mānova kathito. Māno hi iñjanato iñjitaṃ, maññanato maññitaṃ, phandanato phanditaṃ, papañcanato papañcitaṃ. Tehi tehi kāraṇehi saṅkhatattā saṅkhatanti ca vuccati. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

964. ‘Agitations’ (iñjitāni) means movements, stirrings. By all the terms, such as ‘“I am” is an agitation,’ conceit alone is spoken of. For conceit is indeed an agitation, whether it arises as ‘I am,’ as ‘I am this,’ or as ‘I will be neither percipient nor non-percipient.’ Conceit is spoken of even in the remaining ninefold division. For conceit is called ‘agitation’ (iñjita) because it agitates, ‘conceiving’ (maññita) because it conceives, ‘throbbing’ (phandita) because it throbs, and ‘proliferating’ (papañcita) because it proliferates. Because it is conditioned by these various causes, it is also called ‘conditioned’ (saṅkhata). The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Navakaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Exposition of the Nines.

(10.) Dasakaniddesavaṇṇanā

(10.) Commentary on the Exposition of the Tens.

966. Dasakaniddese kilesā eva kilesavatthūni. Āghātavatthūni panettha “anatthaṃ me acarī”tiādīnaṃ [V 0.0486] vasena avikopetabbe khāṇukaṇṭakādimhipi aṭṭhāne uppannāghātena saddhiṃ vuttāni.

966. In the Exposition of the Tens, the defilements themselves are the bases of defilement. Herein, the bases of hatred are stated together with hatred that has arisen in an inappropriate situation—even over things that should not provoke agitation, such as stumps and thorns—by way of such thoughts as, ‘He has done me harm.’

970. Micchattesu micchāñāṇanti pāpakiriyāsu upāyacintāvasena pāpaṃ katvā ‘sukataṃ mayā’ti paccavekkhaṇākārena uppanno moho. Micchāvimuttīti [M 0.0496] avimuttasseva sato vimuttasaññitā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

970. Among wrongnesses, ‘wrong knowledge’ (micchāñāṇa) is delusion (moha) arising in the form of reviewing and thinking, ‘I have done well,’ after performing evil deeds through scheming. ‘Wrong liberation’ (micchāvimutti) is the notion of being liberated when one is not liberated. The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Dasakaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Exposition of the Tens.

Taṇhāvicaritaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of Craving’s Conducts.

973. Taṇhāvicaritaniddese taṇhāvicaritānīti taṇhāsamudācārā taṇhāpavattiyo. Ajjhattikassa upādāyāti ajjhattikaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ upādāya. Idañhi upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Asmīti hotīti yadetaṃ ajjhattaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ upādāya taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena samūhagāhato ‘asmī’ti hoti, tasmiṃ satīti [P 0.0514] attho. Itthasmīti hotītiādīsu pana evaṃ samūhato ‘aha’nti gahaṇe sati tato anupanidhāya ca upanidhāya cāti dvidhā gahaṇaṃ hoti. Tattha anupanidhāyāti aññaṃ ākāraṃ anupagamma sakabhāvameva ārammaṇaṃ katvā ‘itthasmī’ti hoti; khattiyādīsu ‘idaṃpakāro aha’nti evaṃ taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena hotīti attho. Idaṃ tāva anupanidhāya gahaṇaṃ. Upanidhāya gahaṇaṃ pana duvidhaṃ hoti – samato ca asamato ca. Taṃ dassetuṃ evasmīti ca aññathāsmīti ca vuttaṃ. Tattha evasmīti idaṃ samato upanidhāya gahaṇaṃ; yathā ayaṃ khattiyo, yathā ayaṃ brāhmaṇo, evaṃ ahampīti attho. Aññathāsmīti idaṃ pana asamato gahaṇaṃ; yathāyaṃ khattiyo, yathāyaṃ brāhmaṇo, tato aññathā ahaṃ hīno vā adhiko vāti attho. Imāni tāva paccuppannavasena cattāri taṇhāvicaritāni. Bhavissantiādīni pana cattāri anāgatavasena vuttāni. Sesaṃ purimacatukke vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Asmīti sassato asmi. Sātasmīti asassato asmi. Asasmīti satasmīti vā pāṭho. Tattha atthīti asaṃ; niccassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sīdatīti sataṃ; aniccassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Iti imāni [V 0.0487] dve sassatucchedavasena vuttānīti veditabbāni. Ito parāni siyantiādīni cattāri saṃsayaparivitakkavasena vuttāni. Tāni purimacatukke vuttanayeneva atthato veditabbāni. Apāhaṃ siyantiādīni pana cattāri “api nāmāhaṃ bhaveyya”nti evaṃ patthanākappanavasena vuttāni. Tāni purimacatukke vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Evametesu –

973. In the Exposition of Craving’s Conducts, ‘craving’s conducts’ (taṇhāvicaritāni) refers to the occurrences and manifestations of craving. ‘Regarding the internal’ (ajjhattikassa upādāya) means in relation to the internal five aggregates. For this is a genitive case in the sense of usage. ‘There is “I am”’ (asmīti hoti) means that when, by grasping the internal five aggregates as a whole through craving, conceit, and views, there arises the notion ‘I am’; the meaning is ‘when that exists.’ In ‘there is “I am thus”’ (itthasmīti hoti) and so on, when there is such a grasping of ‘I’ as a whole, then grasping occurs in two ways: without comparison and with comparison. There, ‘without comparison’ (anupanidhāya) means not taking up another aspect but making one’s own nature the object, thus ‘I am thus’ arises; among the khattiyas and so on, it means ‘I am of such a kind’ through craving, conceit, and views. This, then, is grasping without comparison. Grasping with comparison, however, is of two kinds: equal and unequal. To show this, ‘I am thus’ (evasmīti) and ‘I am otherwise’ (aññathāsmīti) are stated. There, ‘I am thus’ refers to grasping with equal comparison; it means ‘just as this khattiya is, just as this brahmin is, so am I.’ ‘I am otherwise’ refers to grasping with unequal comparison; it means ‘just as this khattiya is, just as this brahmin is, I am different—either inferior or superior.’ These, then, are the four craving’s conducts in terms of the present. ‘I will be’ (bhavissaṃ) and so on are the four stated in terms of the future. The rest should be understood in the same way as explained in the first tetrad. ‘I am’ (asmi) means ‘I am eternal.’ ‘I am’ (sātaṃ asmi) means ‘I am non-eternal.’ Alternatively, the reading may be ‘I am not’ (asasmīti) or ‘I am’ (satasmīti). There, `asaṃ` means ‘that which exists’; this is a designation for the permanent. `Sataṃ` means ‘that which perishes’; this is a designation for the impermanent. Thus, these two should be understood as stated in terms of eternalism and annihilationism. After this, ‘might I be’ (siyaṃ) and so on are the four stated in terms of doubt and speculation. These should be understood in terms of their meaning in the same way as explained in the first tetrad. ‘Would that I might be’ (apāhaṃ siyaṃ) and so on are the four stated in terms of longing and aspiration, meaning ‘if only I could be’ (api nāmāhaṃ bhaveyya). These should be understood in the same way as explained in the first tetrad. Thus, among these—

Dve [M 0.0497] diṭṭhisīsā cattāro, suddhasīsā sīsamūlakā;

Tayo tayoti etāni, aṭṭhārasa vibhāvaye.

Two are the view-heads, four are the pure heads, twelve are the root-heads; thus these eighteen should be understood.

Etesu hi sassatucchedavasena vuttā dve diṭṭhisīsā nāma. Asmīti, bhavissanti, siyanti, apāhaṃ siyanti ete cattāro suddhasīsāeva. Itthasmīti ādayo tayo tayoti dvādasa sīsamūlakā nāmāti. Evamete dve diṭṭhisīsā, cattāro suddhasīsā, dvādasa sīsamūlakāti aṭṭhārasa taṇhāvicaritadhammā veditabbā.

Among these, the two stated in terms of eternalism and annihilationism are called view-heads (diṭṭhisīsā). ‘I am’ (asmi), ‘I will be’ (bhavissaṃ), ‘I might be’ (siyaṃ), and ‘would that I might be’ (apāhaṃ siyaṃ)—these four are the pure heads (suddhasīsā). The threefold beliefs beginning with ‘I am thus’ (itthasmīti) are the twelve root-heads (sīsamūlakā). Thus, these two view-heads, four pure heads, and twelve root-heads should be understood as the eighteen phenomena of craving’s conducts.

974. Idāni paṭipāṭiyāva te dhamme bhājetvā dassetuṃ kathañca asmīti hotītiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha kañci dhammaṃ anavakāriṃ karitvāti rūpavedanādīsu kañci ekadhammampi avinibbhogaṃ [P 0.0515] katvā, ekekato aggahetvā, samūhatova gahetvāti attho. Asmīti chandaṃ paṭilabhatīti pañcakkhandhe niravasesato gahetvā ‘aha’nti taṇhaṃ paṭilabhati. Mānadiṭṭhīsupi eseva nayo. Tattha kiñcāpi ayaṃ taṇhāvicaritaniddeso, mānadiṭṭhiyo pana na vinā taṇhāya, tasmā tadekaṭṭhavasena idha vuttā. Taṇhāsīsena vā papañcattayampi uddiṭṭhaṃ. Taṃ uddesānurūpeneva niddisitumpi mānadiṭṭhiyo gahitā. Taṇhāpapañcaṃ vā dassento teneva saddhiṃ sesapapañcepi dassetuṃ evamāha.

974. Now, to explain these states in sequence, the section beginning with ‘How does “I am” arise?’ has been commenced. Here, ‘without making any phenomenon inoperative’ means not separating any single phenomenon such as form or feeling, not grasping them individually, but taking them as a whole. ‘He obtains the desire “I am”’ means taking the five aggregates without remainder and obtaining the craving ‘I am.’ The same method applies to conceit and views. Although this is an exposition on the courses of craving, conceit and views do not exist without craving; therefore, they are mentioned here due to their unitary nature. Alternatively, the threefold proliferation is indicated with craving as its head. To explain it in accordance with that indication, conceit and views are also included. Or, while showing the proliferation of craving, he speaks thus to show the remaining proliferations along with it.

Tasmiṃ sati imāni papañcitānīti tasmiṃ “asmīti chandaṃ paṭilabhatī”tiādinā nayena vutte papañcattaye sati puna imāni “itthasmīti vā”tiādīni papañcitāni hontīti attho.

‘When that exists, these proliferations occur’ means that when the threefold proliferation—expressed in the manner beginning with ‘he obtains the desire “I am”’—is present, then these proliferations such as ‘I am thus’ arise.

Khattiyosmītiādīsu abhisekasenāmaccādinā ‘khattiyo ahaṃ’, mantajjhena porohiccādinā ‘brāhmaṇo ahaṃ’, kasigorakkhādinā ‘vesso ahaṃ’, asitabyābhaṅgitāya ‘suddo ahaṃ’[V 0.0488], gihibyañjanena ‘gahaṭṭho aha’nti iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Evaṃ itthasmīti hotīti evaṃ khattiyādīsu khattiyādippakāraṃ attani uppādayitvā ‘itthaṃpakāro aha’nti hoti.

In ‘I am a noble’ and so on, the meaning should be understood thus: ‘I am a noble’ because of consecration, army, ministers, and so on; ‘I am a brahmin’ because of studying mantras, priesthood, and so on; ‘I am a merchant’ because of agriculture, cattle-herding, and so on; ‘I am a servant’ because of service and obedience; ‘I am a householder’ because of the signs of a householder. In this way, ‘I am thus’ occurs by producing in oneself the characteristics of a noble and so on, and thinking, ‘I am of such a kind.’

Yathā so khattiyotiādīsu ‘yathā so abhisekasenāmaccādinā khattiyo, tathā ‘ahampi khattiyo’ti iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Dutiyanaye ‘yathā so abhisekasenāmaccādinā khattiyo, nāhaṃ tathā khattiyo; ahaṃ pana tato hīno vā seṭṭho vā’ti [M 0.0498] iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Bhavissantiādiniddesādīsupi eseva nayo.

In ‘Just as that noble is,’ and so on, the meaning should be understood in this way: ‘Just as that one is a noble by means of consecration, army, ministers, and so on, so too am I a noble.’ In the second way, the meaning should be understood in this way: ‘Just as that one is a noble by means of consecration, army, ministers, and so on, I am not such a noble; rather, I am either inferior or superior to him.’ The same method applies to the explanations beginning with ‘will be,’ and so on.

975. Evaṃ ajjhattikassa upādāya taṇhāvicaritāni bhājetvā idāni bāhirassa upādāya taṇhāvicaritāni bhājetuṃ tattha katamānītiādimāha. Tattha bāhirassa upādāyāti bāhiraṃ khandhapañcakaṃ upādāya. Idampi hi upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Imināti iminā rūpena vā…pe… viññāṇena vā. Avasesaṃ pana uddesavāre tāva vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

975. Having thus classified the courses of craving based on the internal, now, in order to classify the courses of craving based on the external, it is said, beginning with ‘What are these?’ Here, ‘based on the external’ means based on the external five aggregates. This, too, is a genitive case in the sense of application. ‘By this’ means by this form... or by this consciousness. The rest, however, should be understood in the same way as stated in the outline section.

976. Niddesavāre pana avakāriṃ karitvāti vinibbhogaṃ katvā. Iminā asmīti chandaṃ paṭilabhatītiādīsu iminā rūpena vā…pe… viññāṇena vāti evaṃ pañcakkhandhe ekadesato gahetvā iminā ‘aha’nti chandādīni paṭilabhatīti evamattho veditabbo.

976. In the exposition section, however, ‘making a distinction’ means having made a separation. In such phrases as ‘By this, one obtains the desire “I am,”’ the meaning should be understood thus: by taking one part of the five aggregates—that is, by this form... or by this consciousness—one obtains by this the desire and so on, ‘I am.’

Iminā khattiyosmītiādīsu ‘iminā chattena [P 0.0516] vā khaggena vā abhisekasenāmaccādinā vā khattiyo aha’nti evaṃ purimanayeneva attho veditabbo. Imināti padamattameva hettha viseso.

In such phrases as ‘By this, I am a noble,’ the meaning should be understood in the same way as before: ‘By this umbrella or sword, or by consecration, army, ministers, and so on, I am a noble.’ Here, only the word ‘by this’ is the distinguishing feature.

Yathā so khattiyotiādīsupi imināti vuttapadameva viseso. Tasmā tassa vasena yathā khattiyo, evaṃ ahampi iminā khaggena vā chattena vā abhisekasenāmaccādinā vā khattiyoti evaṃ yojetvā sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Iminā niccosmīti pañcakkhandhe anavakāriṃ katvā rūpādīsu ekameva dhammaṃ ‘aha’nti gahetvā ‘iminā khaggena vā chattena vā ahaṃ nicco dhuvo’ti maññati. Ucchedadiṭṭhiyampi eseva nayo. Sesaṃ sabbattha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Even in ‘Just as that noble is,’ and so on, the distinguishing feature is the word ‘by this’ itself. Therefore, based on that, the meaning should be understood in all instances by connecting it thus: ‘Just as one is a noble, so too am I a noble by this sword or umbrella, or by consecration, army, ministers, and so on.’ In ‘By this I am eternal,’ having treated the five aggregates as inseparable, one grasps a single phenomenon among form and so on as ‘I,’ and conceives, ‘By this sword or umbrella, I am eternal, permanent.’ The same method applies to the annihilationist view. The rest should be understood in the same way as explained everywhere.

Iti evarūpāni atītāni chattiṃsāti ekekassa puggalassa atīte chattiṃsa. Anāgatāni chattiṃsāti ekekasseva anāgate chattiṃsa. Paccuppannāni chattiṃsāti ekekassa vā puggalassa [V 0.0489] yathālābhavasena bahunaṃ vā paccuppanne chattiṃsa. Sabbasattānaṃ pana ekaṃseneva atīte chattiṃsa, anāgate chattiṃsa, paccuppanne chattiṃsāti veditabbāni. Anantā hi asadisataṇhāmānadiṭṭhibhedā sattā. Aṭṭhataṇhāvicaritasataṃ hotīti ettha pana aṭṭhasatasaṅkhātaṃ taṇhāvicaritaṃ hotīti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

Thus, there are thirty-six of such kind in the past for each individual. Thirty-six in the future for each individual. Thirty-six in the present for each individual according to what is obtained, or for many. However, for all beings, it should be definitively understood that there are thirty-six in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six in the present. For beings are infinite, with dissimilar kinds of craving, conceit, and views. Here, where it is said, ‘There are one hundred and eight courses of craving,’ the meaning should be understood as ‘there are courses of craving numbering one hundred and eight.’ The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Taṇhāvicaritaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Courses of Craving.

Diṭṭhigataniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of Views.

977. Diṭṭhigataniddese [M 0.0499] brahmajāle veyyākaraṇeti brahmajālanāmake veyyākaraṇe, dīghanikāyassa paṭhamasuttante. Vuttāni bhagavatāti satthārā sayaṃ āhacca bhāsitāni. Cattāro sassatavādātiādīsu “te ca bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kimāgamma kimārabbha sassatavādā sassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññāpenti catūhi vatthūhī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.29-30) brahmajāle vuttanayeneva pabhedo ca attho ca veditabboti.

977. In the Exposition of Views, ‘in the Brahmajāla, an explanation’ means in the explanation named the Brahmajāla, the first discourse of the Dīgha Nikāya. ‘Spoken by the Blessed One’ means spoken directly by the Teacher himself. Regarding ‘the four eternalist doctrines,’ and so on, the classifications and the meaning should be understood in the same way as stated in the Brahmajāla, in the passage beginning: ‘And those venerable ascetics and brahmins, relying on what, based on what, do they, as eternalists, declare the self and the world to be eternal on four grounds?’

Sammohavinodaniyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya

In the Sammohavinodanī, the Commentary to the Vibhaṅga

Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of Minor Topics is concluded.

18. Dhammahadayavibhaṅgo

18. The Analysis of the Heart of the Dhamma.

1. Sabbasaṅgāhikavāravaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the All-Embracing Section.

978. Idāni [P 0.0517][M 0.0500][V 0.0490] tadanantare dhammahadayavibhaṅge pāḷiparicchedo tāva evaṃ veditabbo – ettha hi āditova khandhādīnaṃ dvādasannaṃ koṭṭhāsānaṃ vasena sabbasaṅgāhikavāro nāma vutto. Dutiyo tesaṃyeva dhammānaṃ kāmadhātuādīsu uppattānuppattidassanavāro nāma. Tatiyo tattheva pariyāpannāpariyāpannadassanavāro nāma. Catuttho tīsu bhūmīsu uppattikkhaṇe vijjamānāvijjamānadhammadassanavāro nāma. Pañcamo tesaṃ dhammānaṃ bhūmantaravasena dassanavāro nāma. Chaṭṭho gatīsu uppādakakammaāyuppamāṇadassanavāro nāma. Sattamo abhiññeyyādivāro nāma. Aṭṭhamo sārammaṇānārammaṇavāro nāma. Navamo tesaṃ khandhādidhammānaṃ diṭṭhasutādivasena saṅgahetvā dassanavāro nāma. Dasamo kusalattikādivasena saṅgahetvā dassanavāro nāma.

978. Now, immediately following that, the division of the Pāli text in the Analysis of the Heart of the Dhamma should be understood as follows: Here, first, the section named the ‘Comprehensive Section’ is stated by means of the twelve portions of aggregates, etc. Second is the section named the ‘Section on Arising and Non-arising’ of those same phenomena in the sensual realm, etc. Third is the section named the ‘Section on What is Included and Not Included’ therein. Fourth is the section named the ‘Section on the Presence and Absence of Phenomena’ at the moment of arising in the three planes. Fifth is the section named the ‘Section on Other Planes’ for those phenomena. Sixth is the section named the ‘Section on Productive Kamma and the Measure of the Lifespan’ in the destinies. Seventh is the section named the ‘Section on What is to be Directly Known, etc.’. Eighth is the section named the ‘Section on What Has an Object and What is Objectless’. Ninth is the section showing the grouping of those phenomena of aggregates, etc., according to what is seen, heard, etc. Tenth is the section showing their grouping according to the wholesome triad, etc.

979. Evaṃ dasahi vārehi paricchinnāya pāḷiyā paṭhame tāva sabbasaṅgāhikavāre “avīcito yāva bhavaggaṃ etthantare kati khandhā”ti pucchite “ekoti vā…pe… cattāroti vā chāti vā avatvā pañcāti vattuṃ samattho añño natthī”ti attano ñāṇabalaṃ dīpento pañcakkhandhāti pucchānurūpaṃ vissajjanaṃ āha. Yathāpucchaṃ vissajjanañhi sabbaññubyākaraṇaṃ nāmāti vuccati. Dvādasāyatanānītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Rūpakkhandhādīnaṃ pabhedo khandhavibhaṅgādīsu vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

979. Thus, in the Pāli text delimited by ten sections, firstly in the Comprehensive Section, when the question is asked, 'From Avīci up to the highest existence, how many aggregates are there in between?', he gave the answer 'five aggregates,' which was appropriate to the question, thereby demonstrating his power of knowledge, for without saying 'one... or four, or six,' there is no one else capable of saying 'five.' For answering in accordance with the question is indeed called the declaration of the Omniscient One. This same method applies also to the twelve sense bases, etc. The distinctions of the aggregate of form, etc., should be understood in the way explained in the Analysis of Aggregates, etc.

2. Uppattānuppattivāravaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Section on Arising and Non-arising

991. Dutiyavāre [V 0.0491] ye dhammā kāmabhave kāmadhātusambhūtānañca sattānaṃ uppajjanti – kāmadhātuyaṃ pariyāpannā vā apariyāpannā vā – te sabbe saṅgahetvā kāmadhātuyā pañcakkhandhātiādi vuttaṃ. Rūpadhātuādīsupi eseva nayo. Yasmā pana rūpadhātupariyāpannānaṃ sattānaṃ ghānāyatanādīnaṃ abhāvena gandhāyatanādīni āyatanādikiccaṃ na karonti, tasmā rūpadhātuyā cha āyatanāni, nava dhātuyotiādi vuttaṃ[M 0.0501]. Yasmā ca okāsavasena vā sattuppattivasena [P 0.0518] vā apariyāpannadhātu nāma natthi, tasmā apariyāpannadhātuyāti avatvā yaṃ yaṃ apariyāpannaṃ taṃ tadeva dassetuṃ apariyāpanne kati khandhātiādi vuttaṃ.

991. In the second section, all phenomena that arise in sensual existence or for beings born in the sensual realm—whether included in the sensual realm or not—are gathered together, and it is said: 'In the sensual realm, there are five aggregates,' etc. The same method applies to the form realm, etc. However, because beings included in the form realm lack the nose sense-base, etc., the smell sense-base, etc., do not perform the function of a sense-base. Therefore, it is said that in the form realm, there are six sense-bases, nine elements, etc. Moreover, since there is no realm called ‘unincluded’ in terms of location or the arising of beings, it is not said, 'in the unincluded realm,' but rather, to show whatever is unincluded, it is said, 'in the unincluded, how many aggregates are there?' etc.

3. Pariyāpannāpariyāpannavāravaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Section on What is Included and Unincluded

999. Tatiyavāre kāmadhātupariyāpannāti kāmadhātubhajanaṭṭhena pariyāpannā; taṃnissitā tadantogadhā kāmadhātutveva saṅkhaṃ gatāti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Pariyāpannāti bhavavasena okāsavasena ca paricchinnā. Apariyāpannāti tathā aparicchinnā.

999. In the third section, 'included in the sensual realm' means included in the sense of partaking of the sensual realm; dependent on it, contained within it, and reckoned as the sensual realm itself. This is the meaning. The same method applies to the remaining terms. 'Included' means delimited by way of existence and by way of location. 'Unincluded' means not delimited in that way.

4. Dhammadassanavāravaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Section on Showing Phenomena

1007. Catutthavāre ekādasāyatanānīti saddāyatanavajjāni. Tañhi ekantena paṭisandhiyaṃ nuppajjati. Iminā nayena sabbattha attho veditabbo. Sattake “devānaṃ asurāna”nti gativasena avatvā avisesena gabbhaseyyakānanti vuttaṃ. Tasmā yattha yattha gabbhaseyyakā sambhavanti tattha tattha tesaṃ sattāyatanāni veditabbāni. Tathā dhātuyo. Sesamettha uttānatthameva. Pañcamavāre yaṃ vattabbaṃ taṃ dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttameva.

1007. In the fourth section, 'eleven sense bases' excludes the sound base, for that certainly does not arise at rebirth-linking. The meaning should be understood in this way throughout. In the set of seven, instead of saying 'of gods and asuras' by way of destiny, it is stated without distinction as 'of those lying in a womb.' Therefore, wherever those lying in a womb are possible, their seven sense bases should be understood there. Likewise the elements. The rest here is of plain meaning. In the fifth section, what is to be said has already been stated in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī commentary.

6. Uppādakakammaāyuppamāṇavāravaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Section on Productive Kamma and the Measure of the Lifespan

(1.) Uppādakakammaṃ

(1.) Productive Kamma

1021. Chaṭṭhavāre [V 0.0492] pañcahi kāmaguṇehi nānappakārehi vā iddhivisesehi dibbantīti devā. Sammutidevāti ‘devo, devī’ti evaṃ lokasammutiyā devā. Upapattidevāti devaloke uppannattā upapattiyā devā. Visuddhidevāti sabbesaṃ devānaṃ pūjārahā sabbakilesavisuddhiyā devā. Rājānoti muddhābhisittakhattiyā. Deviyoti tesaṃ mahesiyo. Kumārāti abhisittarājūnaṃ abhisittadeviyā kucchismiṃ uppannakumārā.

1021. In the sixth section, 'gods' (devā) are those who revel (dibbanti) in the five kinds of sensual pleasures or in various kinds of special powers. 'Conventional gods' are those called 'god' or 'goddess' by worldly convention. 'Gods by rebirth' are those who are gods by rebirth, having been born in a deva world. 'Gods by purification' are those worthy of veneration by all gods due to their complete purification from all defilements. 'Kings' are khattiyas consecrated by anointing on the head. 'Queens' are their chief consorts. 'Princes' are sons born from the womb of a consecrated queen of a consecrated king.

Uposathakammaṃ [M 0.0502] katvāti cātuddasādīsu aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ uposathaṃ upavasitvā. Idāni yasmā parittadānādipuññakammaṃ manussasobhagyatāya paccayo, mattaso kataṃ manussasobhagyatāya adhimattaṃ, adhimattabhāvepi nānappakārabhedato nānappakārassa khattiyamahāsālādibhāvassa paccayo, tasmā tassa vasena upapattibhedaṃ dassento appekacce gahapatimahāsālānantiādimāha. Tattha [P 0.0519] mahāsāro etesanti mahāsārā; ra-kārassa pana la-kāraṃ katvā mahāsālāti vuttaṃ. Gahapatiyova mahāsālā, gahapatīsu vā mahāsālāti gahapatimahāsālā. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Tattha yassa gehe pacchimantena cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ nidhānagataṃ hoti, kahāpaṇānañca pañca ambaṇāni divasavaḷañjo nikkhamati – ayaṃ gahapatimahāsālo nāma. Yassa pana gehe pacchimantena asītikoṭidhanaṃ nidhānagataṃ hoti, kahāpaṇānañca dasaambaṇāni divasavaḷañjo nikkhamati – ayaṃ brāhmaṇamahāsālo nāma. Yassa pana gehe pacchimantena koṭisatadhanaṃ nidhānagataṃ hoti, kahāpaṇānañca vīsati ambaṇāni divasavaḷañjo nikkhamati – ayaṃ khattiyamahāsālo nāma.

'Having performed the Uposatha observance' means having observed the Uposatha endowed with its eight factors on the fourteenth and other days. Now, because meritorious deeds such as small giving are a condition for human prosperity, and when done moderately are a condition for abundant human prosperity, and even when abundant, due to various distinctions, are a condition for various kinds of status such as being a wealthy khattiya, etc., therefore, showing the diversity of rebirths based on that, he said, 'some as wealthy householders...' and so on. Here, 'mahāsārā' means 'those who have great substance'; but by changing the 'r' to an 'l,' it is said 'mahāsālā.' They are either householders who are very wealthy, or the very wealthy among householders—thus, 'gahapatimahāsālā.' The same method applies to the rest. Here, one in whose house at least forty crores of wealth are stored, and whose daily expenditure amounts to five ambaṇas of coins—this one is called a 'wealthy householder'. One in whose house at least eighty crores of wealth are stored, and whose daily expenditure amounts to ten ambaṇas of coins—this one is called a 'wealthy brahmin'. One in whose house at least one hundred crores of wealth are stored, and whose daily expenditure amounts to twenty ambaṇas of coins—this one is called a 'wealthy khattiya'.

Sahabyatanti sahabhāvaṃ; sabhāgā hutvā nibbattantīti attho. Cātumahārājikānantiādīsu cātumahārājikā nāma sinerupabbatassa vemajjhe honti. Tesu pabbataṭṭhakāpi atthi, ākāsaṭṭhāpi; tesaṃ paramparā cakkavāḷapabbataṃ pattā. Khiḍḍāpadosikā, manopadosikā, sītavalāhakā, uṇhavalāhakā, candimā devaputto, sūriyo devaputtoti ete sabbepi cātumahārājikadevalokaṭṭhakā eva.

Companionship means co-existence; the meaning is that they are born as co-partakers. Among the Cātumahārājikas and others, the Cātumahārājika deities are located in the middle of Mount Sineru. Some of them dwell on the mountains, others in the sky; their succession extends to the Cakkavāḷa mountain. The Khiḍḍāpadosikā, Manopadosikā, Sītavalāhakā, Uṇhavalāhakā, Candimā the devaputta, and Sūriyo the devaputta—all these are located in the Cātumahārājika heaven.

Tettiṃsa [V 0.0493] janā tattha upapannāti tāvatiṃsā. Apica tāvatiṃsāti tesaṃ devānaṃ nāmamevāti vuttaṃ. Tepi atthi pabbataṭṭhakā, atthi ākāsaṭṭhakā. Tesaṃ paramparā cakkavāḷapabbataṃ pattā. Tathā yāmādīnaṃ. Ekadevalokepi hi devānaṃ paramparā cakkavāḷapabbataṃ appattā nāma natthi. Tattha dibbaṃ sukhaṃ yātā payātā sampattāti yāmā. Tuṭṭhā pahaṭṭhāti tusitā. Pakatipaṭiyattārammaṇato atirekena ramitukāmakāle yathārucite bhoge nimminitvā ramantīti nimmānaratī. Cittācāraṃ ñatvā parehi nimmitesu bhogesu vasaṃ vattentīti paranimmitavasavattī.

Thirty-three beings were reborn there; therefore, they are Tāvatiṃsa. Moreover, it is said that 'Tāvatiṃsā' is simply the name of those deities. Among them, some reside on mountains, and some in the sky. Their succession reaches the Cakkavāḷa mountain, and likewise for the Yāma deities and others. Indeed, in any world of deities, there are none whose succession does not reach the Cakkavāḷa mountain. There, divine happiness is attained, reached, and experienced; therefore, they are Yāma. Pleased and delighted; therefore, they are Tusita. Desiring to enjoy pleasures beyond those ordinarily prepared, they create enjoyable objects according to their liking and delight in them; therefore, they are Nimmānaratī. Knowing the inclinations of others' minds, they wield control over pleasures created by others; therefore, they are Paranimmitavasavattī.

(2.) Āyuppamāṇaṃ

(2.) Measure of Lifespan

1022. Appaṃ [M 0.0503] vā bhiyyoti dutiyaṃ vassasataṃ appatvā vīsāya vā tiṃsāya vā cattālīsāya vā paññāsāya vā saṭṭhiyā vā vassehi adhikampi vassasatanti attho. Sabbampi hetaṃ dutiyaṃ vassasataṃ appattattā appanti vuttaṃ.

1022. The phrase 'a little or more' means exceeding one hundred years by twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty years, without reaching a second century. All this is called 'less' because it does not reach a second century.

1024. Brahmapārisajjādīsu mahābrahmānaṃ pārisajjā paricārikāti brahmapārisajjā. Tesaṃ purohitabhāve ṭhitāti brahmapurohitā. Vaṇṇavantatāya [P 0.0520] ceva dīghāyukatāya ca mahanto brahmāti mahābrahmā, tesaṃ mahābrahmānaṃ. Ime tayopi janā paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyaṃ ekatale vasanti; āyuantaraṃ pana nesaṃ nānā.

1024. Among the Brahmapārisajjā and so on, the attendants of the Great Brahmās are called Brahmapārisajjā. Those who hold the position of chaplain to them are called Brahmapurohitā. Because of their beauty and long lifespan, they are great Brahmās, thus Mahābrahmās. These three kinds of beings dwell on the same level in the plane of the first jhāna, but their lifespans differ.

1025. Parittā ābhā etesanti parittābhā. Appamāṇā ābhā etesanti appamāṇābhā. Daṇḍadīpikāya acci viya etesaṃ sarīrato ābhā chijjitvā chijjitvā patantī viya sarati visaratīti ābhassarā. Imepi tayo janā dutiyajjhānabhūmiyaṃ ekatale vasanti; āyuantaraṃ pana nesaṃ nānā.

1025. Their light is limited; therefore, they are the Limited-Radiance deities. Their light is immeasurable; therefore, they are the Immeasurable-Radiance deities. Like the flame of a torch, radiance from their bodies seems to break off and scatter, spreading and radiating forth; therefore, they are the Radiant deities. These three kinds of beings dwell together on the plane of the second jhāna, but their lifespans differ.

1026. Parittā subhā etesanti parittasubhā. Appamāṇā subhā etesanti appamāṇasubhā. Subhena okiṇṇā vikiṇṇā, subhena sarīrappabhāvaṇṇena ekagghanā, suvaṇṇamañjusāya ṭhapitasampajjalitakañcanapiṇḍasassirīkāti subhakiṇhā. Imepi tayo janā tatiyajjhānabhūmiyaṃ ekatale vasanti; āyuantaraṃ pana nesaṃ nānā.

1026. Their beauty is limited, thus they are called the Limited-Beauty deities. Their beauty is immeasurable, thus they are called the Immeasurable-Beauty deities. They are filled and pervaded with beauty; their body's aura is of a single, solid mass of beauty, possessing the splendor of a lump of shining, burning gold placed in a golden casket—thus they are called the All-Beautiful deities. These three kinds of beings dwell together on the plane of the third jhāna, but their lifespans differ.

1027. Ārammaṇanānattatāti [V 0.0494] ārammaṇassa nānattabhāvo. Manasikāranānattatādīsupi eseva nayo. Ettha ekassa pathavīkasiṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti…pe… ekassa odātakasiṇanti idaṃ ārammaṇanānattaṃ. Eko pathavīkasiṇaṃ manasi karoti…pe… eko odātakasiṇanti idaṃ manasikāranānattaṃ. Ekassa pathavīkasiṇe chando hoti…pe… ekassa odātakasiṇeti idaṃ chandanānattaṃ. Eko pathavīkasiṇe patthanaṃ karoti…pe… eko odātakasiṇeti idaṃ paṇidhinānattaṃ. Eko pathavīkasiṇavasena adhimuccati…pe… eko odātakasiṇavasenāti idaṃ adhimokkhanānattaṃ. Eko pathavīkasiṇavasena cittaṃ abhinīharati…pe… eko [M 0.0504] odātakasiṇavasenāti idaṃ abhinīhāranānattaṃ. Ekassa pathavīkasiṇaparicchindanakapaññā hoti…pe… ekassa odātakasiṇaparicchindanakapaññāti idaṃ paññānānattaṃ. Tattha ārammaṇamanasikārā pubbabhāgena kathitā. Chandapaṇidhiadhimokkhābhinīhārā appanāyapi vattanti upacārepi. Paññā pana lokiyalokuttaramissakā kathitā.

1027. The diversity of objects means the variety of objects. The same principle applies to the diversity of attention and so on. Here, one takes the earth kasiṇa as an object…pe… another takes the white kasiṇa—this is the diversity of objects. One attends to the earth kasiṇa…pe… another attends to the white kasiṇa—this is the diversity of attention. One has desire for the earth kasiṇa…pe… another for the white kasiṇa—this is the diversity of desire. One aspires toward the earth kasiṇa…pe… another toward the white kasiṇa—this is the diversity of aspiration. One resolves upon the earth kasiṇa…pe… another upon the white kasiṇa—this is the diversity of resolution. One directs the mind toward the earth kasiṇa…pe… another toward the white kasiṇa—this is the diversity of application. One has wisdom that discerns the earth kasiṇa…pe… another that discerns the white kasiṇa—this is the diversity of wisdom. Here, object and attention are discussed in terms of the preliminary stage. Desire, aspiration, resolution, and application occur both in absorption and access concentration. Wisdom, however, is discussed as a mixture of mundane and supramundane.

Asaññasattānanti saññāvirahitānaṃ sattānaṃ. Ekacce hi titthāyatane pabbajitvā ‘cittaṃ nissāya rajjanadussanamuyhanāni nāma hontī’ti citte dosaṃ disvā ‘acittakabhāvo nāma sobhano, diṭṭhadhammanibbānameta’nti [P 0.0521] saññāvirāgaṃ janetvā tatrūpagaṃ pañcamaṃ samāpattiṃ bhāvetvā tattha nibbattanti. Tesaṃ upapattikkhaṇe eko rūpakkhandhoyeva nibbattati. Ṭhatvā nibbatto ṭhitako eva hoti, nisīditvā nibbatto nisinnakova nipajjitvā nibbatto nipannova. Cittakammarūpakasadisā hutvā pañca kappasatāni tiṭṭhanti. Tesaṃ pariyosāne so rūpakāyo antaradhāyati, kāmāvacarasaññā uppajjati; tena idha saññuppādena te devā tamhā kāyā cutāti paññāyanti.

'Non-percipient beings' means beings devoid of perception. Some, having gone forth in the abodes of other sectarians and seeing fault in the mind, think, 'Because of the mind, there arise attachment, aversion, and confusion.' Thinking, 'The state of non-mind is excellent; this is Nibbāna in this very life,' they generate disenchantment with perception, develop the fifth attainment that leads to that state, and are reborn there. At the moment of rebirth, only the aggregate of form arises for them. Having been born standing, they remain standing; having been born sitting, they remain sitting; having been born lying down, they remain lying down. Having become like painted figures, they persist for five hundred eons. At the end of that time, that form-body disappears, and perception pertaining to the sense-sphere arises. Thus, through the arising of perception here, those deities are known to pass away from that body.

Vipulā phalā etesanti vehapphalā. Attano sampattiyā na hāyanti na vihāyantīti avihā. Na kañci sattaṃ tappantīti atappā. Sundarā dassanā abhirūpā pāsādikāti sudassā. Suṭṭha passanti, sundarametesaṃ vā dassananti sudassī. Sabbehi eva guṇehi ca bhavasampattiyā ca jeṭṭhā, natthettha kaniṭṭhāti akaniṭṭhā.

Their fruits are abundant, thus they are called the Greatly Fruitful deities. They do not decline or diminish in their attainments, thus they are called the Non-Declining deities. They do not afflict any being, thus they are called the Untroubled deities. They are lovely to behold, beautiful, and inspiring confidence, thus they are called the Beautiful deities. They see excellently, or their appearance is beautiful, thus they are called the Clear-Seeing deities. They are foremost in all qualities and in prosperity of existence, with none inferior—thus they are called the Peerless deities.

1028. Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upagatāti ākāsānañcāyatanūpagā. Itaresupi eseva nayo[V 0.0495]. Iti cha kāmāvacarā, nava brahmalokā, pañca suddhāvāsā, cattāro arūpā asaññasattavehapphalehi saddhiṃ chabbīsati devalokā; manussalokena saddhiṃ sattavīsati.

1028. `Ākāsānañcāyatanūpagā` means those who have attained the base of infinite space. The same principle applies to the others. Thus, there are six sense-sphere realms, nine Brahmā realms, five pure abodes, and four formless realms—which, together with the realm of non-percipient beings and the Greatly Fruitful realm, make twenty-six celestial realms; with the human world, there are twenty-seven in total.

Tattha sammāsambuddhena manussānaṃ devānañca āyuṃ paricchindamānena catūsu apāyesu bhummadevesu ca āyu paricchinnaṃ taṃ kasmāti? Niraye tāva kammameva pamāṇaṃ. Yāva kammaṃ na khīyati, na tāva cavanti. Tathā sesaapāyesu. Bhummadevānampi kammameva pamāṇaṃ. Tattha nibbattā hi keci [M 0.0505] sattāhamattaṃ tiṭṭhanti, keci addhamāsaṃ, keci māsaṃ, kappaṃ tiṭṭhamānāpi atthiyeva.

There, while the Fully Enlightened One was defining the lifespan for humans and devas, for what reason was the lifespan not defined in the four states of deprivation and for the terrestrial devas? In hell, in the first place, kamma alone is the measure. As long as the kamma is not exhausted, they do not pass away. The same applies to the other states of deprivation. For the terrestrial devas as well, kamma alone is the measure. Among those reborn there, some beings remain for only a week, some for half a month, some for a month, and there are even those who remain for an entire aeon.

Tattha manussesu gihibhāve ṭhitāyeva sotāpannāpi honti, sakadāgāmiphalampi anāgāmiphalampi arahattaphalampi pāpuṇanti. Tesu sotāpannādayo yāvajīvaṃ tiṭṭhanti. Khīṇāsavā pana parinibbāyanti vā pabbajanti vā. Kasmā? Arahattaṃ nāma seṭṭhaguṇo, gihiliṅgaṃ hīnaṃ, taṃ hīnatāya uttamaṃ guṇaṃ dhāretuṃ na sakkoti. Tasmā te parinibbātukāmā vā pabbajitukāmā vā honti.

Among humans, even while living as householders, there are those who are stream-enterers, who attain the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arahantship. Among them, stream-enterers and the others remain so for life. However, those whose taints are destroyed either attain final Nibbāna or go forth. Why? Arahantship is the highest quality, while the householder state is inferior. That inferior state cannot sustain the supreme quality. Therefore, they wish either to attain final Nibbāna or to go forth.

Bhummadevā pana arahattaṃ patvāpi yāvajīvaṃ tiṭṭhanti. Chasu kāmāvacaradevesu sotāpannasakadāgāmino yāvajīvaṃ tiṭṭhanti; anāgāminā rūpabhavaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭati, khīṇāsavena parinibbātuṃ. Kasmā[P 0.0522]? Nilīyanokāsassa abhāvā. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacaresu sabbepi yāvajīvaṃ tiṭṭhanti. Tattha rūpāvacare nibbattā sotāpannasakadāgāmino na puna idhāgacchanti, tattheva parinibbāyanti. Ete hi jhānaanāgāmino nāma.

However, terrestrial devas, even after attaining arahantship, remain for life. Among the six sense-sphere devas, stream-enterers and once-returners remain for life; it is fitting for a non-returner to go to the form realm, and for an arahant to attain final Nibbāna. Why? Because there is no opportunity for seclusion. In the form and formless realms, all remain for life. There, stream-enterers and once-returners reborn in the form realm do not return here again; they attain final Nibbāna right there. These, indeed, are called jhāna-non-returners.

Aṭṭhasamāpattilābhīnaṃ pana kiṃ niyameti? Paguṇajjhānaṃ. Yadevassa paguṇaṃ hoti, tena uppajjati. Sabbesu pana paguṇesu kiṃ niyameti? Patthanā. Yattha upapattiṃ pattheti tattheva upapajjati. Patthanāya asati kiṃ niyameti? Maraṇasamaye samāpannā samāpatti. Maraṇasamaye samāpannā natthi, kiṃ niyameti? Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpatti. Ekaṃsena hi so nevasaññānāsaññāyatane upapajjati. Navasu brahmalokesu nibbattaariyasāvakānaṃ tatrūpapattipi hoti uparūpapattipi na heṭṭhūpapatti. Puthujjanānaṃ pana tatrūpapattipi hoti uparūpapattipi [V 0.0496] heṭṭhūpapattipi. Pañcasu suddhāvāsesu catūsu ca arūpesu ariyasāvakānaṃ tatrūpapattipi hoti uparūpapattipi. Paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyaṃ nibbatto anāgāmī nava brahmaloke sodhetvā matthake ṭhito parinibbāti. Vehapphalā, akaniṭṭhā, nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti ime tayo devalokā seṭṭhabhavā nāma. Imesu tīsu ṭhānesu nibbattaanāgāmino neva uddhaṃ gacchanti, na adho, tattha tattheva parinibbāyantīti. Idamettha pakiṇṇakaṃ.

But for those who have attained the eight meditative attainments, what determines it? Their proficient absorption. In whatever absorption is proficient for them, in that they arise. But when all absorptions are proficient, what determines it? Their aspiration. Wherever they aspire to be reborn, they are reborn precisely there. If there is no aspiration, what determines it? The attainment into which they are entered at the time of death. If there is no attainment into which they are entered at the time of death, what determines it? The attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. For they are invariably reborn in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. For noble disciples reborn in the nine Brahmā realms, there is rebirth in that same realm or a higher one, but not a lower one. But for worldlings, there may be rebirth in the same realm, a higher one, or a lower one. In the five Pure Abodes and the four formless realms, for noble disciples there is rebirth in that same realm or a higher one. A non-returner reborn in the first jhāna realm, having purified the nine Brahmā realms and standing at the summit, attains final Nibbāna. Vehapphala, Akaniṭṭha, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these three deva worlds are called the supreme existences. Non-returners reborn in these three places go neither higher nor lower; they attain final Nibbāna right there. This here is the miscellaneous section.

7. Abhiññeyyādivāravaṇṇanā

7. Exposition of the Section on What is to be Directly Known, etc.

1030. Sattamavāre [M 0.0506] salakkhaṇapariggāhikāya abhiññāya vasena abhiññeyyatā veditabbā. Ñātatīraṇapahānapariññānaṃ vasena pariññeyyatā. Sā ca rūpakkhandho abhiññeyyo pariññeyyo na pahātabbotiādīsu ñātatīraṇapariññāvaseneva veditabbā. Samudayasaccaṃ abhiññeyyaṃ pariññeyyaṃ pahātabbantiādīsu pahānapariññāvasena.

1030. In the seventh section, the state of being directly knowable should be understood by means of direct knowledge that grasps characteristics. The state of being fully comprehensible should be understood by means of the full understanding of knowing, investigating, and abandoning. And this full comprehensibility, in cases such as 'the form aggregate is to be directly known, to be fully understood, not to be abandoned,' should be understood only by means of the full understanding of knowing and investigating. In cases such as 'the truth of origination is to be directly known, to be fully understood, and to be abandoned,' it should be understood by means of the full understanding of abandoning.

Aṭṭhamavāre rūpādiārammaṇānaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ vasena sārammaṇānārammaṇatā veditabbā. Navamavāro uttānatthoyeva. Dasamavārepi yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā taṃ sabbaṃ tattha tattha pañhāpucchakavāre vuttamevāti.

In the eighth section, the state of having an object and not having an object should be understood in terms of objects such as form, etc., and eye-consciousness, etc. The ninth section has an obvious meaning. As for the tenth section, whatever might need to be said has all been stated in the respective question-and-answer sections.

Sammohavinodaniyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Sammohavinodanī, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga

Dhammahadayavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Dhammahadaya Vibhaṅga is completed.

Nigamanakathā

Concluding Words

Ettāvatā [P 0.0523][M 0.0507] ca –

And thus far—

Abhidhammaṃ desento, dhammagaru dhammagāravayuttānaṃ;

Devānaṃ devapure, devagaṇasahassaparivāro.

Teaching the Abhidhamma, himself revering the Dhamma, to the devas endowed with reverence for the Dhamma; in the city of the devas, surrounded by a thousandfold host of devas.

Dutiyaṃ [V 0.0497] adutiyapuriso, yaṃ āha vibhaṅgapakaraṇaṃ nātho;

Aṭṭhārasahi vibhaṅgehi, maṇḍitamaṇḍapeyyaguṇo.

That which the incomparable person, the Lord, declared as the second treatise, the Vibhaṅga; adorned with eighteen divisions, its qualities like a decorated pavilion.

Atthappakāsanatthaṃ, tassāhaṃ yācito ṭhitaguṇena;

Yatinā adandhagatinā, subuddhinā buddhaghosena.

For the purpose of clarifying its meaning, I was requested by the one of established virtue, by the monk of unhurried pace, of excellent wisdom, by Buddhaghosa.

Yaṃ ārabhiṃ racayituṃ, aṭṭhakathaṃ sunipuṇesu atthesu;

Sammohavinodanato, sammohavinodaniṃ nāma.

Which I began to compose, a commentary on very subtle meanings; because it dispels delusion, it is called 'The Dispeller of Delusion'.

Porāṇaṭṭhakathānaṃ, sāraṃ ādāya sā ayaṃ niṭṭhaṃ;

Pattā anantarāyena, pāḷiyā bhāṇavārehi.

Having taken the essence of the ancient commentaries, this very work has reached completion without obstacle, in accordance with the recitation sections of the Pāli text.

Cattālīsāya yathā, ekena ca evameva sabbepi;

Niṭṭhaṃ vajantu vimalā, manorathā sabbasattānaṃ.

Just as this work of forty-one sections has reached completion, even so may all the stainless aspirations of all beings be fulfilled.

Saddhammassa ṭhitatthaṃ, yañca imaṃ racayatā mayā puññaṃ;

Pattaṃ tena samattaṃ, pāpuṇatu sadevako loko.

For the stability of the True Dhamma, and whatever merit has been gained by me in composing this, by that merit, may the entire world, together with the devas, attain completeness.

Suciraṃ tiṭṭhatu dhammo, dhammābhirato sadā bhavatu loko;

Niccaṃ khemasubhikkhādi-sampadā janapadā hontūti.

May the Dhamma long endure; may the world always delight in the Dhamma; may the lands always be endowed with safety, prosperity, and abundance.

Paramavisuddhasaddhābuddhivīriyapaṭimaṇḍitena sīlācārajjavamaddavādiguṇasamudayasamuditena sakasamayasamayantaragahanajjhogāhaṇasamatthena paññāveyyattiyasamannāgatena tipiṭakapariyattippabhede sāṭṭhakathe satthusāsane appaṭihatañāṇappabhāvena mahāveyyākaraṇena [P 0.0524] karaṇasampattijanitasukhaviniggatamadhurodāravacanalāvaṇṇayuttena yuttamuttavādinā vādīvarena mahākavinā pabhinnapaṭisambhidāparivāre chaḷabhiññāpaṭisambhidādippabhedaguṇapaṭimaṇḍite uttarimanussadhamme suppatiṭṭhitabuddhīnaṃ theravaṃsappadīpānaṃ therānaṃ [M 0.0508] mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ vaṃsālaṅkārabhūtena vipulavisuddhabuddhinā [V 0.0498] buddhaghosoti garūhi gahitanāmadheyyena therena katā ayaṃ sammohavinodanī nāma vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathā.

This Vibhaṅga Commentary, called 'The Dispelling of Delusion,' was composed by the Elder whose name, Buddhaghosa, was accepted with reverence by the teachers, who was adorned with supremely pure faith, wisdom, and energy, endowed with a multitude of virtues such as moral conduct, propriety, honesty, and gentleness, capable of deeply penetrating his own and other schools of thought, possessed of intellectual acumen, by the power of his unobstructed knowledge in the Teacher’s Dispensation, which is divided into the three Piṭakas and their commentaries, a great grammarian whose sweet and elevated speech, issuing from the accomplishment of skillful composition, is endowed with charm, speaking what is reasoned and well-expressed, foremost among disputants, a great poet, the ornament of the lineage of elders dwelling in the Great Monastery—who are a lamp to their lineage, their minds well-established in superhuman states adorned with qualities such as the six higher knowledges and the varieties of analytical knowledges, and attended by the differentiated analytical knowledges—and who possessed a vast and purified intellect.

Tāva tiṭṭhatu lokasmiṃ, lokanittharaṇesinaṃ;

Dassentī kulaputtānaṃ, nayaṃ paññāvisuddhiyā.

May it remain in the world so long, for those seeking to cross over the world, showing the path to the purification of wisdom to those of good family.

Yāva buddhoti nāmampi, suddhacittassa tādino;

Lokamhi lokajeṭṭhassa, pavattati mahesinoti.

So long as even the name 'Buddha' of the pure-minded Such One, the foremost of the world, the great sage, prevails in the world.

Sammohavinodanī nāma vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Vibhaṅga Commentary named 'The Dispeller of Delusion' is completed.
